<header>DEDICATION.</header>
<meta>bleed-through from previous page visible</meta>

It was, after all, chiefly through your effort and kindness that several years ago—though I had no such expectation, let alone merit—I was received into the ranks of those men, most excellent in dignity, **scholarship**, and nobility, who adorn the **Royal Prussian Society of Sciences**. <note>The *Societas Regia Scientiarum Borussica* was the precursor to the Prussian Academy of Sciences, founded by Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz in 1700.</note> By this very act, you have more than sufficiently demonstrated your singular affection toward me. For although I may perhaps not be the sort of person worthy of being joined to such a splendid circle of most learned and excellent men, you have nonetheless testified by your judgment and kindness that you wish the best for me and that you judge with favor my pursuit of **scholarship**, <note>original: "de Litteris"; literally "of letters," referring to the broader field of humanist learning and academic study.</note> such as it may be. It is, therefore, most fitting that I acknowledge and praise that inclined goodwill of yours toward me with a public testimony of my gratitude. You, moreover, most learned men, were the ones who urged

that I should collect and publish these **minor works** <note>original: "opuscula"; referring to the collection of shorter essays and treatises contained in this volume.</note> of mine, whatever their quality, which were previously scattered here and there. This kind judgment of yours carried such weight with me that, setting aside the various reasons that might have held me back, I added my **white pebble** <note>original: "album adjecerim calculum"; an ancient Roman metaphor for a vote of approval or a favorable judgment.</note> to your opinion. For although it is sometimes the case that friends, moved by a singular affection, might flatter us and make us overly confident and bold, I could not persuade myself—given your kindness toward me and your well-known **scholarship** <term>Eruditio: a term denoting the vast, multi-disciplinary knowledge expected of an Enlightenment intellectual.</term>—that you would have wished to give me this advice to publish these works unless it had been known and evident to you that they could contribute something to both public and private utility. Relying on this hope, I thought that something ought to be attempted, regardless of the outcome. Finally, you are accustomed to adorning and increasing my **modest library** <note>original: "reculam meam librariam"; a humble diminutive suggesting the author's personal book collection.</note> with your own most learned volumes, and so [you show] your inclined goodwill

It is not my intention, Kind Reader, to delay your time with a long preface. I shall therefore encompass in just a few words those things I believe must be said. Into your sight come these **dissertations** <note>original: "dissertationes"; formal academic essays or treatises intended for scholarly debate or publication.</note> on various subjects, written and published by me at different times. I wished to collect these scattered pieces and publish them together: partly because I have been informed by reliable evidence that they have pleased those who study **Theology**; and partly because I have very often been invited to attempt this task by the encouragement of certain learned men, whose opinions I hold in high regard. I submit to your judgment. But if I have committed an error here or there, being mindful of human nature, interpret it kindly, and show me its source with gentle words. # MEDITATIONS
### CONCERNING THE
### CAUSES OF THE INCREASINGLY PREVAILING
# UNBELIEF,
### AND THE REMEDY TO BE APPLIED TO THIS EVIL.

->PART I.<-

->Section I.<-

<margin>Diverse judgments concerning the present state of the Republic of Letters and the Church.</margin>
THOSE who are accustomed to turn the eyes of the mind toward the present state of the **Republic of Letters** <note>original: "Respublica Literaria"; the international community of scholars, scientists, and intellectuals during the Enlightenment.</note> and the Church, and who carefully weigh each thing that occurs among the Learned, bring forth diverse judgments about its condition. There are some among the Learned who can scarcely find words enough to extol the happiness of our age. All sciences, especially the **Sacred Sciences** <note>original: "Scientiæ Sacræ"; specifically referring to theology, biblical exegesis, and ecclesiastical history.</note>, if you listen to them, have reached their peak in our time; this they attempt to prove through learned discourse by examining each field in turn. The disciplines (namely, they say) <term>propaedeutic</term> <note>original: "προπαιδευτικαὶ"; referring to introductory studies such as logic, grammar, and linguistics that prepare students for higher fields like theology or law.</note>, which pave the way to a solid knowledge of things divine and human, are taught in Academies and Schools by the most learned men with incredible diligence and no less skill. We possess Greek and Latin authors, presented not only with great elegance but also correct-

<summary>The author concludes his preface by asking for constructive criticism and apologizing for printing errors before beginning a formal investigation into why skepticism and unbelief are rising despite the apparent progress of 18th-century scholarship.</summary>
<keywords>Unbelief, Republic of Letters, Enlightenment scholarship, sacred sciences, propaedeutic studies, skepticism, ecclesiastical state</keywords>

--- Page 9 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's survey of the flourishing state of 18th-century scholarship and theology, before introducing a more skeptical counter-argument. The catchword "tissime" from the previous page completes the word "eruditissime" (most learnedly).</meta>

### MEDITATION I.

...most [finely] printed, but also furnished with the most learned commentaries and useful notes. There is no lack of men skilled in the knowledge of Oriental languages who devote all their effort and diligence to elucidating the Holy Scriptures. **Critical Art** <note>original: "Ars Critica"; here referring to textual criticism, the scholarly method of determining the original wording of historical texts.</note> has not only been reduced to certain rules, but those skilled in this art use them successfully to explain and correct all the best writers. The writings of the Fathers <note>The "Church Fathers," early influential Christian theologians.</note> have never been examined with such precision <note>original: "ἀκρίβεια" (akribeia); Greek for "exactness" or "meticulous accuracy."</note> as has been done in our age. Learned men everywhere are beginning to judge more correctly the value of these writings, and are not so easily led astray by the authority of the Fathers. In England, France, Italy, and indeed in our own Germany, the most ancient monuments and fragments of these same ecclesiastical writers—which bring much light to the understanding of the discipline and customs of the Early Church—are being rescued from neglect and decay. Philosophy, that most noble science (so these learned men continue), is cultivated with emulation, especially by our Germans. Moreover, where this flourishes, it is impossible for the remaining disciplines, especially the sacred ones, not to maintain their own honor. And to come closer to the more sacred disciplines, there is a great and immense abundance of interpreters of Holy Scripture, especially those who, having gathered the resources of philology and antiquity from all sides, pour an unusual light upon the difficult passages of both Covenants. **Theology** itself, or the systematic method of handing down religion, is not only bound to more accurate laws of method, but also shines forth more pure and chaste, after it has been freed and purged here and there from so many scholastic terms and petty questions of little profit. The **Christian Religion**, through the care of most learned, sharpest, and most pious men, has been demonstrated by so many weighty reasons, and the arguments and objections of unbelievers have been shaken by such sharpness of wit, that (unless a perverse mind stands in the way) no one can fail to perceive the admirable power and excellence of this most chaste and holy discipline. Controversies are handled with greater modesty than in the age of our fathers, and their importance is carefully considered. Everywhere, those rigid and fretful theologians are despised who extol all minute opinions as being of great importance, and who either cannot or will not make a distinction between the trivial and the momentous. **Christian Ethics**, once neglected or entangled in scholastic intricacies, is more skillfully taught in academies and schools; and the admirable beauty of virtue and piety itself is delineated and inculcated with great zeal by learned and pious men. To this fact, so many **books** published on this subject in our Germany can bear witness, to say nothing of the English and French. To the **Religion** of the Protestants (they continue), through the unusual conversions of the Salzburgers and Bohemians, <note>Refers to the 1731 expulsion of Protestants from Salzburg and subsequent migrations of "Exulanten."</note>

<column-break/>

<page-num>3</page-num>
# ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

not only has a great addition been made, but the rays of divine light have penetrated even to the most remote nations, to the Garamantes <note>A term often used classically for North African peoples.</note> and the Indians, and to the coldest regions of the North; which pious minds can understand from publicly published reports, not without remarkable joy and delight. (*) Finally, they say, if we turn the eyes of the mind to the uprightness of morals and the observance of the right worship of God and piety, it must be confessed that there is no lack of pious hearts here and there, kindled with a burning zeal for the love of GOD and our Savior, who contribute whatever they can to promote the salvation of others. Hence so many Societies, especially in England, for promoting Religion among barbarous and uncultivated nations; hence so many seminaries of Piety established; and finally, so many workshops of good arts and disciplines founded everywhere. And thus indeed, certain learned men are accustomed to judge the state of our times.

<margin>Although this speech is most honorable and not everything can be denied, there are nonetheless those who think the happiness of our times is extolled beyond measure.</margin>

II. Others, however, distinguished by no less praise for wisdom and learning, think that the happiness of our times in this matter is extolled beyond measure. I gladly confess that I am also among their number. Indeed, we would be unjust toward the singular benevolence of the Great and Good God <note>original: "O. M. Numinis"; referring to *Optimi Maximi*, "The Best and Greatest."</note> toward the human race—especially the Christian Church and the assembly devoted to purer sacred rites—if we did not acknowledge with a most grateful mind the benefits conferred upon us, and publicly confess that it is not without His help that so many men distinguished by piety and learning flourish here and there in academies and schools. For since, according to *Socrates*, good and wise men are born only by a divine gift <note>original: "θεία μοίρα" (theia moira); a "divine portion" or "divine lot."</note>; or to speak more correctly with the Apostle James, since every good work and gift granted to mortals is from the Father of Lights [James 1:17]: it is manifest that the most ample causes and occasions for celebrating God are supplied to us (**), if we turn the eyes of our soul to the progress of the disciplines, especially the more sacred ones, and to the labors of so many men outstanding in wit and learning. Nor indeed...

---

> (*) The celebrated *Fabricius* <note>Johann Albert Fabricius (1668–1736), a famous classical scholar and bibliographer.</note> of blessed memory <note>original: "Μακαρίτης" (makaritēs); Greek for "one who has died/is blessed."</note> diligently and learnedly collected the things that pertain to this in the book titled: *The Saving Light of the Gospel Rising over the Whole World through Divine Grace: or a historico-chronological, literary, and geographical account of the propagation of Christian rites throughout the whole world.* Also deserving of mention here is the most praiseworthy plan of the celebrated *Callenberg* <note>Johann Heinrich Callenberg (1694–1760), known for his mission to Jews and Muslims.</note>, namely of calling back the Jews and Muslims from their errors—to say nothing of the efforts of the Count von Zinzendorf <note>Nikolaus Ludwig von Zinzendorf (1700–1760), leader of the Moravian Brethren.</note>, concerning which there are diverse judgments. What I once said here concerning the efforts of Count Zinzendorf, with the modesty that befits a theologian, must be judged with a grain of salt; since it was afterwards discovered through many signs that the discipline of this assembly, of which that illustrious man is the Leader, deviates from the simplicity of Christian doctrine and inclines strongly toward enthusiasm and mysticism.
> (**) Since I mention this famous passage of the Apostle James, I cannot restrain myself from bringing forward here the excellent words of *Socrates* about to proclaim the virtues of God. They are found in *Xenophon*.

<summary>This page discusses the 18th-century "Republic of Letters," praising the era's advancements in theology, missions, and textual criticism, while introducing the author's argument that these successes may be over-celebrated. It highlights scholarly efforts to reach distant nations and the internal theological shift away from rigid scholasticism toward a more refined, critical piety.</summary>
<keywords>Enlightenment theology, textual criticism, Church Fathers, missions, Fabricius, Callenberg, Zinzendorf, Socrates, Apostle James, Republic of Letters</keywords>

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's critique of contemporary intellectual overconfidence. While the previous page listed the many scholarly achievements of the 18th century, this page begins to pivot, arguing that academic learning is useless if it does not lead to moral and spiritual improvement.</meta>

->### MEDITATION I. ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.<-

->A 3<-

...we are even such unfair critics that we think, in order to obtain that happiness, nothing is required but Platonic Republics and Churches—that is, the kind in which all citizens are perfectly measured against the exact standard of wisdom, erudition, and virtue. We well remember that prudent saying of Antoninus the Philosopher <note>The Roman Emperor Marcus Aurelius, often called "The Philosopher."</note>, an Emperor renowned for his singular praise of wisdom, which goes: **do not hope for Plato's Republic, but be satisfied if even the smallest thing goes forward.** <note>original Greek: "τὴν πλάτωνος πολιτείαν μὴ ἔλπιζε, ἀλλὰ ἀρκέσϑω βραχύτατον πρόεισι"</note> If we look at the nature of the disciplines—especially the more sublime ones—there are nearly infinite things which can be rightly understood by no sharpness of wit, no study, and finally no labor; nor will we ever arrive at a knowledge of them while we dwell on this earth and in this "fog of things." He who looks on one hand at the nature and character of things divine and human, and on the other at the limits of human wit and our faculties, will admit this of his own accord even if I remain silent. Indeed, I am not so arrogant as to believe that I can clearly prove, regarding all the disciplines with which the care of most learned men is occupied, how much each lacks the praise of perfection. The lifespan and study of even a man of great talent hardly permits him to rightly know and see into any one discipline and its individual parts, let alone be able to deliver an accurate judgment on every single one. If it has been given to others to know this, let them applaud themselves; I, a man of meager wit and a **novice theologian**, <note>original: "hesternus Theologus"; literally "a theologian of yesterday," implying he is junior or newly arrived to the field.</note> do not take so much upon myself. Perhaps I could bring forward some things that are not useless regarding the more sacred disciplines, and show how many things are still required for them to be more fully known and handed down, and what obstacles prevent us from attaining an accurate knowledge of these matters; but I prefer these things to be said and repeated by others rather than by someone as insignificant as myself. Nevertheless, this notwithstanding (and saving the better judgment of others), I believe it can be said without the mark of pride that the present state of the **Republic of Letters** <term>The "Republic of Letters" (Respublica Literaria) was the long-distance intellectual community of scholars and writers in the 17th and 18th centuries.</term> and the Church is being extolled beyond measure. To prove this, there is no need for one to have seen into every individual part of all disciplines...

<margin>
Xenophon, *Memorabilia of Socrates*, page 505, Basel edition. They sound like this: **And he who coordinates and holds together the whole world, in which all things are honorable and good, and who—while we always use them—nevertheless gives them to us always fresh, healthy, and ageless more quickly than a man can think, and administers them to us without fail; he is seen performing the greatest deeds, but while governing this whole, he is invisible to us.** <note>original Greek: "Καὶ ὁ τὸν ὅλον κόσμον συντάττων τε καὶ συνέχων, ἐν ᾧ πάντα καλὰ καὶ ἀγαϑά ἐσι, καὶ ἀεὶ μὲν χρωμένοις ἀτριβῆ τε καὶ ὑγιῆ καὶ ἀγήρατα παρέχων, ϑᾶττον δὲ νοήματος ἀναμαρτήτως ὑπηρεϑοῦντα, οὗτος τὰ μέγισα μὲν πράττων ὁρᾶται, τάδε δὲ οἰκονομῶν, ἀόρατος ἡμῖν ἐσίν"</note> That is: He also who orders and contains the whole orb, in which all things are honest and good, and who, though we always use them, nonetheless gives them to us always fresh, healthy, and immortal faster than a man can think, and administers them to us without defect, he indeed is understood to be working the greatest things, but while governing this whole he is invisible to us.
</margin>

<column-break/>

...but rather that he turns his mind to the end, the goal, and the use of erudition, the arts, and the disciplines—especially the sacred ones. The chief end of Literature, unless I am mistaken, is this: that as many as devote themselves to it with care should receive a notable utility from it; that all—the greatest, the middling, and the least—through the cultivation of the disciplines (by whatever name they go) should become wiser, more modest, and more loving of virtue; so that it may be clear from the whole way of life of the learned what great and incredible power the disciplines and arts have for perfecting the mind, for moderating and taming wicked passions, for governing the State and Church wisely, piously, and happily; and finally for bringing forward and enlarging the Kingdom of our most holy **Savior** <note>original: "Soter"; the Greek word for Savior, used here in a Latin context.</note> Jesus Christ. If the disciplines do not obtain this end—if it is manifest that the men of our age are no more pious, modest, peaceful, and wise than others who lived in previous centuries—then most learned men will forgive me if I say, or if that is not allowed, at least if I think silently to myself, that we are far from the happiness of those times which they so greatly praise. For suppose there are many who are remarkably refined in the more humane and elegant letters, but that these same men are at the same time no more prepared to perform the duties of humanity and of a good man than anyone from the common crowd; certainly the knowledge of those disciplines will be of little benefit. Suppose you have crawled through every corner of philosophy, have embraced its whole face in your mind, and can prove all the propositions of your system through a linked series of demonstrations; but at the same time you are a philosopher **only in word, without action**; <note>original Greek: "μέχρι τοῦ λέγειν, ἄνευ τοῦ πράττειν"</note> that you do not love and care for what is true and right in every kind of life any more than one of the many; that you do not think more magnificently of GOD, do not love, worship, or trust Him more, and are no more solicitous for promoting His glory—in a word, that you are no more pious, chaste, peaceful, and loving of equity than the rest; what, I ask, will that much-celebrated knowledge of philosophical disciplines, acquired with so many cares, vigils, and meditations, finally contribute to your salvation or that of others? Suppose you are a Theologian who has every part of your system seen and known: who can not only count on your fingers all present, past, and almost future controversies, but can also weigh the importance of each, detect the sources of all errors, and stop the mouths of all who disagree with you; but at the same time you lack true piety; that you have not reported even one victory over the vices to which you are devoted; that you are empty of [practical] theology...

<summary>The author argues that the "golden age" of 18th-century scholarship is hollow if it does not produce better people. He asserts that true learning should lead to virtue and piety, rather than just academic mastery or the ability to win theological arguments.</summary>

->### MEDITATION I.<-

...that wisdom of James, which is <note>James 3:17</note> *first pure, then peaceable, gentle, easy to be entreated, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy*? <note>original Greek: "πρῶτον μὲν ἁγνή ἐστιν, ἔπειτα εἰρηνική, ἐπιεικής, εὐπειθής, μεστὴ ἐλέους καὶ καρπῶν ἀγαθῶν, ἀδιάκριτος, καὶ ἀνυπόκριτος"</note> If you, on the contrary, are morose, proud, greedy, or held captive and bound by other wicked desires, what use will all that <term>theological equipment</term> <note>apparatus Theologicus: the collection of books and linguistic skills used by scholars</note> finally be? Suppose you are beautifully equipped with all those protections required of a learned Interpreter of the Sacred Volumes, contributing much to unearthing the hidden meanings of the Holy Scriptures, and far surpassing others; yet at the same time you stumble against the most common commands of God and our Savior, which any rustic understands no less than yourself—what benefit will you finally perceive from that laborious and learned interpretation and knowledge of the Sacred Scriptures?

The same can be said of the other parts of Theological Erudition. For if you were to judge their excellence based on the utility and goals of the disciplines, I do not know if much would be lost from the so greatly praised "happiness of our times." To know and prove that very few perceive true utility from the cultivation of <term>Letters</term> <note>Literarum: referring here to academic and classical learning</note>, we do not need to call upon the amplifications of rhetoricians for help, but we simply bid anyone to look into human life as if into a mirror, and to gaze upon the morals of men in this corner of the world in which we live, in a <note>original Greek: "ἀθερὶ παθῶν" — likely referring to a "haze of passions"</note> haze of passions, and I believe the matter will be manifest. For who does not know that the number of those adorned with true piety, candor, equity, sincerity, etc., is exceedingly small? Who does not see that faith in friendship is rare even among the most learned? Who is ignorant that the common duties of humanity and piety are trampled underfoot by all? Among those who ought to be mutually bound by the most holy bonds of love, suspicions, angers, and enmities are nourished; most serve their own interests, speak splendidly of Religion, but live most wickedly. 

What shall I say of the controversies and lawsuits that have been stirred up with the greatest fervor among the <term>Ministers of the Word of God</term> for some years, and are still stirred up? Read, whoever you are that so greatly praises the happiness of our times, what the continuator of the *Church History* begun by the famous *Heinsius* has collected from only the year 1731 to 1745, and you will be stunned when you see that *such great anger dwells in heavenly minds.* <note>A famous quote from Virgil’s Aeneid: "tantaene animis caelestibus irae," used here to mock the bitterness of religious scholars.</note> How many are there still among the Protestant Theologians themselves who fight with tooth and nail <note>original: "pedibus manibusque obluctantur," literally "struggle with feet and hands"</note> against sacred peace—which is pleasing to God and most useful to the State and the Church? Certainly, if the excellence of our century consisted in the fact that many of the learned of our age are more ingenious and crafty than our ancestors in circumventing and deceiving others, or in covering and crusting over frauds and illicit arts with a greater appearance of righteousness, there would be no reason for anyone to move a controversy against it...

# DE CAUSIS INCREDULITATIS.
### ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

...we should fear. But no one of sound mind, let alone a pious person, will contend that the happiness of our century is placed in that. It is not my intention to exaggerate the state of degenerate Christianity. Meanwhile, we cannot, in good conscience and faith—which ought to be in every upright person—deny those things which strike the eyes and senses. As long as the number of the truly pious, the wise-hearted, and those who love God and their neighbor is not greater than it is now; as long as most of those called "Learned" are immersed in the same vices as those who are tainted by no learning; as long as this so greatly praised Erudition does not spread a greater utility into the Church, the State, and all conditions and statuses of life, there is no reason why we should extol the happiness of the <term>Republic of Letters</term> <note>The international community of scholars and intellectuals</note> and the Church in such wondrous ways. (*)

<margin>
The most manifest, but at the same time the saddest, indication of degenerate Christianity and the unhappiness of our times is the daily increasing vice of Unbelief.
</margin>

III. If by chance these things brought forward so far to show that the happiness of our century is not as great as many would wish seem trivial or not weighty enough to anyone, here is an argument greater than any exception by which it may be proved! It is sought, namely, from the vice of unbelief increasing more and more daily, by which the primary heads of Natural and Revealed Religion are attacked in speech and writing. That this vice spreads widely and has gained strength by moving, no one can deny unless they are ignorant of what goes on in the scholarly world and the daily commerce of men. It is known that in England, France, Italy, Belgium, and even in our own Germany, there is a numerous army of men who think very poorly of Religion. I would easily concede that there are fewer from that number who call the very existence of the Divine into doubt; for to do this, open war must be declared against reason. Meanwhile, from the pamphlet of *Count Boulainvilliers*, published in Belgium last year, in which he wished to place the obscure principles of *Spinoza* in a clearer light and accommodate them to the grasp of all, it is clear that men of this kind are not lacking, to whom the most foolish opinion of this Atheist is pleasing. I also do not know into which class I should refer a certain famous society of men whom the French call the *Freemasons* <note>original: "des Franc Maçons"</note>. For if the fundamental and chief article of these men's religion is that which the author of the *Swiss Mercury* <note>original: "Mercurii Helvetici"</note> asserts, it does not differ from the opinion of *Spinoza*...

...under how great a night our days in these lands have lain, and how sinister are the opinions of mortals living on earth concerning Religion, they discourse in a grave oration. Soon these same men learnedly and at length discourse on how much damage **superstition**, and especially **priests**, have brought to the human race: but they twist everything so that all who have a nose <note>A Latin idiom meaning "all who have any discernment or common sense"</note> may smell out that they wish to utterly overturn all Religion along with superstition. (\*) 

Again, others, putting on a most honorable persona, complain about the multitude of controversies which all but overwhelm the Christian world, and learnedly show how frequently and bitterly men have disputed over things of no importance: how great were the rages in "heavenly minds" <note>An allusion to Virgil’s *Aeneid*: "tantaene animis caelestibus irae?"</note>: how many innumerable evils have been born from this untimely itch for disputing about things regarding Religion. Yet at the end of the speech—the minds of the readers being, as they think, sufficiently prepared against any Theologians and their contests by these attractive words—they discuss all the controversies of Religion in such a way that it is clear they wished to prove that all are of the same, that is, clearly of no, importance or value. 

Some, touched as if by mercy and love for the human race, repeat that everything must be attempted anew to improve mankind; they say the precepts of the Christian Religion must therefore be more correctly cultivated, and must be delivered and instilled with a greater weight of arguments; that once these are properly instilled, men become better, rather than by the profession of I-know-not-what obscure propositions. By this reasoning, they naturally intend to strip all credit from what the Christian Religion teaches concerning **Mysteries** and **Miracles**. 

Again, others, in order to alienate the minds of men from the Christian Religion, describe the customs, habits, and precepts of a certain nation (for example, the **Spartans**) with much anxiety and care, but against all laws of history and truth. They most foolishly and impudently wish to persuade mortals that the most divine Author of the Christian Religion, Jesus Christ, cannot be compared with the Legislators of that nation (such as *Lycurgus*), nor the precepts of the Christian Religion and the virtues of Christians with the Laws and virtues of the *Spartans*. ...they would have it that these men <note>Referencing the authors of religious texts</note> are to be considered most fit for engineering a fraud and ingeniously devising a fable. Others, however, go in the opposite direction, yet tending toward the same end; they think so meanly of them and wish to persuade others that they were so dull-witted and foolishly credulous that they leave them with scarcely any common sense. Finally, there are those from this crowd—among whom **Collins** <note>Anthony Collins (1676–1729), a prominent English deist and author of "A Discourse of Free-Thinking"</note> has raised his head—who use heavy arguments to argue for freedom of conscience. They elegantly show how much weight this liberty carries for the advancement of divine and human literature, and conversely, how much detriment it brings to superstition and tyranny. However, while they wish to prove this liberty by introducing men who think most meanly and foolishly about religion, they show more than enough that "thinking freely" and "holding divine and human things as the same" are one and the same thing in the mouths of such men. And who could recount all the cunning methods <note>original: μεθοδείας</note> of these men? (\*) If these men fought only with arguments, and with that modesty which ought to hold a place among the learned, they could still be endured; for it can easily be conceived how men, through various reasons, might fall into such opinions and errors. Nor should it be considered a crime if someone, led by a love of searching for the truth, communicates his doubts to the learned. Modesty, at least, is to be praised in all things, especially where the most sacred matters are concerned. But alas, many of the **Unbelievers**, carried away by a certain insane blindness of mind, bark with an impure mouth against everything most sacred with bitter jests and great impudence. They perhaps think that laughter and mocking cackles will add great and incredible weight to their audacity; in this, however, they are most greatly deceived. They often deceive unrefined men, who are prone to snatch up every impious and frequently foolish opinion; but to the learned, who are moved only by the weight of reasons to either embrace or reject something, they are an object of ridicule. Yet it is not only the learned and disciplined **Unbelievers** who are accustomed to labor under this disease; this plague has seized every age and sex, and all conditions and statuses of life. Young men, often untouched by literature, fortified by no safeguards for reasoning correctly, and even ignorant of the principles of their own religion, take a singular pleasure in grazing against the most sacred things—things which, in the judgment of all wise men, are most worthy of attention. These men, made "to the nail" <note>An idiom meaning "perfected" or "highly polished," though used here sarcastically</note>, have surely read certain fresh little books in which religion is attacked not with arguments, but with bitter insults—

But I proceed to others. It is a long-standing and widespread rumor that there is a great number of such men among those who frequent the Courts of Princes. For since they wish to advance to dignities and riches by any art, and since this cannot always be done while keeping piety intact, religion must often be trampled underfoot, or it must be held merely as a tool or a political art so that they may reach the end they intend. Others, seeing this everywhere and inflamed by the same desires, conclude that a wise man ought to believe in the matter of religion only what he perceives to be to his own advantage. And not only these, but even worthless men <note>term: "triobolares homines," literally "three-obol men," referring to people of very low status or value</note> who profess a manual trade, very often attack religion—if not with arguments (which they cannot do because of their slow wit and shameful ignorance of divine things), then at least with insults. This is not because they know what religion is, but because they foolishly think that an unbridled audacity in speaking about sacred things is a sign of wisdom. The matter has certainly been reduced to such a point among some that they think that saying of **Juvenal** <note>A Roman satirical poet</note> was meant for them:

# MEDITATION I.

<meta>catchword: resisting-</meta>

Speaking generally about this disease, a foolish opinion has certainly gained ground in this unhappy age of ours: that those men alone are brilliant and learned, and truly set a price on things and Literature, who think it makes no difference what opinion you hold concerning Religion. They believe the very sinews and joints of wisdom consist in disputing both sides of matters pertaining to Religion. Any cold joke, often devoid of wit and sense, is considered a prudent saying provided it stabs at Religion. Sometimes a most unlearned man—in whom no good person ever praised anything except his physical form and noble face—is seen by many mockers of Religion as a man of elegant and sharp intellect, so long as he babbles with a foul mouth <note>original: "illoto ore," literally "with an unwashed mouth," a common idiom for coarse or disrespectful speech</note> about the most sacred things. He who is ignorant of this "art," and who anxiously repeats that truth must be discerned from falsehood and thinks that moderation must be kept in all things, is dismissed as merely a "good man" or as foolishly credulous.

<margin>This evil is harmful to the happiness of the human race and greatly hinders the progress of true religion.</margin>

IV. Indeed, no one who has integrity at heart will doubt that this epidemic vice of our century hinders not only the progress of the most chaste Religion, but also the happiness of the human race. For since true Religion commands and enjoins nothing else than that we compose our lives according to the will of the Holy Divinity <note>original: "S. Numinis," referring to God as the governing power of the universe</note>; since it throws a bridle upon the wicked desires of the soul; since it brings the weightiest arguments and incentives for practicing every kind of virtue; and since, finally, it is by its very nature suited to promote our internal and external happiness: it is easy to judge that men destitute of these protections will be less fit and prepared to promote their own happiness and that of others. I know that not all errors indiscriminately harm good morals and the State; I disapprove of those who, because of any sort of disagreement in the business of Religion, fill everything with tragic outcries. I am not ignorant of the fact that vices hinder the safety of the State more than errors do. But that is not the issue here: the question is simply whether men who are persuaded of the divine origin of <term>Natural and Revealed Religion</term> <note>Natural Religion refers to truths about God discoverable by reason alone; Revealed Religion refers to truths made known through scripture.</note> are not more fit for practicing virtue and piety, and for performing the duties of a good man and noble citizen, than others who call these fundamental heads of Religion into doubt. And this, I believe, will be affirmed by all who properly attend to the actions of men and their principles and incentives for acting. Since Unbelievers are fashioned from the same clay as other men, and since they are equally exposed to all those circumstances by which men can be pulled away from what is true and right, it is clear that those who are touched by reverence for the Divine, and who are equipped with so many safeguards and incentives for acting rightly, will—all else being equal—be far more fit for resisting—

<column-break/>

<page-num>13</page-num>
## ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

**B 3**
<meta>catchword: satisfying</meta>

—resisting the wicked desires of the soul. This is because, in addition to the fear of punishments, the praise of a good reputation, the desire to promote our own happiness, and whatever else besides Religion can keep men in their duty, there is added that most certain and deeply fixed persuasion: that God will deal with mortals after this life according to the manner of their past life; that the pious will enjoy the singular Favor of God through an unending eternity, while the wicked will be subjected to the most grievous punishments. 

I know what the Unbelievers will say. They will contend that men do not always act in accordance with their principles, and therefore it does not follow that those who attack the principal heads of Religion, or doubt their truth, will rush into every wickedness. Nor would I claim that Unbelievers will always let loose the reins of their desires. I know there are many things, as I have already said, that can keep them in their duty. Yet these same men, if they wish to speak the truth, will concede that it is very difficult to subdue nature and tame the seething affections of the soul; that long exercise is needed to restrain the wicked desires of the heart; and that, finally, very few mortals reach this degree of wisdom and self-control. 

They will concede, moreover, if truth is a care and concern to them, that when a firm persuasion concerning the Divine will, Reward, and the punishments to be expected after this life is added to all those external things which keep men in their duty, men will be driven by greater stings <note>original: "stimulis," meaning spurs or incentives</note> to act rightly. And this is the one thing we wish to show. For I cannot be led to believe that these very people with whom we are now dealing would argue that reasons sought from Religion and fixed deeply in the soul can contribute nothing at all to directing and moderating the inclinations of the mind; for by the Unbelievers' own confession, even <term>superstition</term> <note>In this context, "superstition" refers to a distorted or excessive religious fear, which the author argues still has the power to influence behavior.</note> has great power over the minds and morals of men. 

But if Religion, as we contend, is built upon certain foundations; if a man ought daily to weigh these principles recalled deeply to the mind; if, finally, the incentives of Religion can incline the will of man: it is manifest that Religion has more power for moderating the affections of the soul and restraining the wicked desires of minds than mere temperament, or fear of punishment, or other external things by which the morals of men are bent. Let us suppose two Unbelievers devoted to the same affections of the soul—for example, pleasures. Suppose these same men are led by a love of health, a concern for reputation, and the preservation of tranquility to resist the powerless desires of the soul, to hold a limit in pleasures, and are so far hindered by these and other reasons and aids from yielding to the passions, for the satisfying of which—

He counters the "free-thinking" trend of his time, which treats religious skepticism as a mark of intelligence.</summary>

# MEDITATION I.

...satisfy those [desires] which nature stimulates. Although I believe very few people would exercise such self-restraint, I will grant it for the sake of argument. Let us suppose, however, that one of these individuals, having conducted a careful examination of Religion, discovers not only that there is a Supreme Divinity <note>original: "Numen supremum"</note>—the wisest, best, and most powerful Governor of the entire Universe—but also that He has given the human race most equitable laws rooted in human nature, the observance of which makes men happy. This individual realizes that God affects the human race with innumerable benefits and will make those minds—touched by love for Him and mindful of His most holy precepts—partakers of eternal happiness after death, while subjecting the wicked to the most severe punishments according to the gravity of their crimes. Suppose he learns that this same Best and Most Holy God, driven by love for the human race, has revealed the decrees of His will to men through trustworthy witnesses and confirmed the same with stupendous miracles to provide credibility to His most worthy Ambassadors; and indeed, that He sent a *Savior* <note>original: "Soterem," from the Greek Sōtēr, meaning 'Deliverer' or 'Preserver'</note> to earth to recall men from errors and sins and to make them happy. I shall pass over the remaining Decrees of the Christian Religion in silence, as they are well enough known. Suppose, I say, that this man not only understands these individual principles and precepts of Religion, trusts them, and considers them as sublime truths worthy of attention, but also sinks them deep into his soul and firmly believes them. Finally, by the force of this persuasion, he is compelled to confess that this Religion is not only most true and consistent with reason, but that it is necessary for him to compose all his future actions according to the will of the Best Divinity. Given this, I appeal to the conscience of all who are accustomed to valuing things at their true worth: would this man not be better suited to perform every kind of duty than he was before, when he was deterred from evil only by certain external incentives? Nor does it help the *Unbelievers* <note>original: "Incredulos"</note> to say that very few of those who have given their name to the Christian Religion compose their lives and morals according to the decrees of that Religion. We admit, certainly, that the number of such [truly devout] men is not large; we admit that many, throughout their entire lives, have never examined the foundations of the Religion to which they profess to be addicted; we admit that many cling to the sect into which they were tossed—as if by a storm—like a barnacle to a rock; we admit many think the height of Religion is placed in this: if they can fight bravely and fiercely for its individual opinions and decrees (even those of minor importance), discourse learnedly about it, attack dissenters with fervor, and perform external worship with singular zeal.

# ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

All these things we willingly admit and lament. But what do the *Unbelievers* gain from this? Does it therefore follow, by the legitimate laws of consequence, that the Christian Religion has no power or efficacy to recall men from evil? Are all the arguments and incentives by which it commends virtue therefore vain? Truly, this would be the same as if someone, because of calculations poorly performed by a Mathematician, were to conclude that the precepts of Arithmetic are built upon no certain foundations; or as if someone were to infer from the loose morals of certain Citizens that the laws of the Republic in which those men live are plainly absurd and impious, or at least entirely unsuited to promoting the welfare of the citizens. When we attack the principles of action by which they are moved and assert that—once the primary heads of Natural and Revealed Religion are denied—scarcely any barrier remains against the force of the soul's depraved desires, and that it cannot happen otherwise than that they very frequently rush into every kind of crime and sin, the *Unbelievers* themselves are accustomed to respond: "Men do not always act consistently with their principles." Let them apply this to the profession of Christian doctrine, and they will give themselves the answer to this objection: namely, that the chief cause why Christians lead a life so foreign to the precepts of their Religion is primarily to be sought in the fact that they do not daily recall these principles to mind and follow them. (*) But if, on one hand, by the confession of the *Unbelievers* themselves, men very frequently deflect from the principles of their actions, and on the other hand, those very people who are imbued with the precepts of a most holy Religion and are persuaded of their truth and divine origin daily feel how much anxiety, circumspection, mental alacrity, and finally prayer are needed to repress depraved impulses and habits confirmed by long custom—then they will forgive us if we think that men stripped of so many protections, and destitute of so many weight arguments and incentives for loving virtue and piety, will very frequently satisfy the depraved desires of the soul. Nor should the *Unbelievers* oppose us with I know not what *Theology* of the *Chinese* <note>original: "Sinensium." During the 18th century, European philosophers often debated whether the Chinese were "virtuous atheists" who lived morally without Christian revelation.</note>—a nation they consider most wise—which they claim is supported by no ideas or principles of divine attributes or the Will of a Divinity, but only by a persuasion of order and the intrinsic morality of actions. For besides the fact that all those things which are said concerning these principles of Theology or Philosophy—

<margin>This evil must be countered, yet in such a way that we use only lawful means, and those suited to diminishing and removing this evil.</margin>

V. Since it is clear from what has been said that this evil <note>the spread of unbelief</note> is not only creeping far and wide but also significantly hindering the progress of true Piety and the salvation of the human race, it is the duty of all who love truth and Piety—especially those equipped with solid Erudition and higher disciplines—to discern by what means that evil might be repelled, or at least diminished by reduction, if it cannot be entirely removed (which can hardly be hoped for with any appearance of truth). However, although all good and learned men easily agree that all powers of the intellect must be spent on suppressing this evil, they diverge as soon as they come to the matter itself or the method of confronting the evil. There are, for instance, those who think that books of this kind which attack Religion should be suppressed at their very birth, or, if they are published to the light of day, should be delivered to **Vulcan** <note>original: "Vulcano"; an allusion to the Roman god of fire, meaning the books should be burned</note> without delay; and that the authors themselves should immediately be either thrust into perpetual prisons or led to the stake. They argue that one must simultaneously abstain from the reading and refutation of such writings: for since the general points of Natural and Revealed Religion are admitted by the common consent of Christians, there is no need for learned men to exhaust themselves without necessity in confirming and defending these articles. And (1.) indeed it would be greatly desired that those who apply their minds to writing and publishing books would bring forth nothing but what is full of good fruit—that is, things that serve to promote Virtue, piety, and the salvation of all. It is to be wished that not only those books which declare war on the chief heads of Religion, but also those which harm good morals and corrupt the young (whose minds are soft like wax and most inclined to fulfilling the perverse desires of the soul), would be suffocated at their very birth. But since this can never be hoped for given the great number of luxuriating wits with which the Literary World is filled, and since there are very few who, when they set their mind to writing, are anxious for the glory of GOD and the promotion of true human virtue, we must see by what skill that which cannot be entirely prevented may be corrected. It is certainly argued in vain how the publication of such books might be hindered, and much more so how their reading can be prohibited once they are published. Among us, indeed, it is sufficiently provided for by public laws that such books are not published; but since we have no jurisdiction over other Nations, we cannot prevent them from being brought to us. It is well known that in *England*, the *Netherlands* <note>original: "Belgio"</note>, and elsewhere, notwithstanding the decrees and censures of those in power, writings of this kind are committed to the presses, and the greed for profit with which many printers burn eludes all the cares of the Censors. Not even the leaders and defenders of that sacred Tribunal which goes by the name of the **Inquisition** can prevent the books of *Unbelievers* and *Protestants* from being bought and read everywhere: I do not see, therefore, how such pamphlets can be entirely kept away from Protestant gatherings, where greater liberty flourishes.

# MEDITATION I.

...than men who are sick in spirit; but a physician does not beat the sick with lashes, but brings medicine that can pull the evil out by its roots. Nor do I know whether they serve the Christian Religion well who advise that everyone who attacks the principles of the Christian Religion should be subjected to the heaviest punishments. I speak, however—*and this should be noted well*—of those who merely inquire into truths otherwise accepted by common consent through reasons and arguments alone, and who communicate their doubts to the Learned with the modesty that is proper. In place of arguments, I will set before those who think otherwise the words of one who, writing against the *Manichaeans* <note>A major dualistic religious movement of the late Roman Empire that taught a struggle between light and darkness.</note> regarding what they call the *Foundation* (Chapter II, Tome VIII, and Benedictine Edition, Column 151), speaks thus: <margin>Augustine, a man most pleasing to that class of people with whom we are dealing.</margin> *“Let those be harsh toward you who do not know with what labor truth is found, and how difficult it is to avoid errors. Let those be harsh toward you who do not know how rare and arduous it is to overcome carnal phantasms by the serenity of a pious mind. Let those be harsh toward you who do not know with what difficulty the eye of the inner man is healed so that it may gaze upon its Sun. Let those be harsh toward you who do not know with what sighs and groans it is achieved that God may be understood even in the smallest part. Finally, let those be harsh toward you who have never been deceived by such an error as they see has deceived you.”*

(3.) When it is said that such books ought neither to be read nor refuted, because the principles of the Christian Religion are commonly accepted and built upon the firmest foundations, one must respond to this with a distinction. The question is not whether the reading of such books is to be recommended to everyone indiscriminately. No one is so foolish as to suggest this. For we admit that the reading of such books has cast many—who are not sufficiently trained in the higher disciplines and the art of thinking—into the gravest errors; indeed, as we shall prove in what follows, we count such reading among the causes of growing *Unbelief* <note>original: "Incredulitatis"</note>. But the question is this: whether such books should not even be read or publicly refuted by those who are sufficiently trained in Philosophical and Theological disciplines, and who, in everyone's judgment, are able to weigh the importance of objections. And we assert that this not only can be done, but that it is the duty of public Teachers to attack and tear down pestilential errors that would harm the salvation of men with heavy arguments. “But these articles,” (you say) “which the *Unbelievers* attack, are accepted by all consent and rest upon firm foundations.” I do not deny it; but does it follow from this that the truth itself should not be defended? Truly, I seem to hear a man devoted to the rites of the *Romanists* <note>The author's term for Roman Catholics.</note> thundering against the reading of books published by the Reformed, even on the grounds

on the grounds that the One, Holy, and Catholic Church has already made manifest through public decrees what is false and true, what is to be believed and what is not to be believed; and that they are therefore rash, proud, and even wicked men who, after so many infallible decrees of the most holy Mother Church, wish to submit the most evident and certain articles to examination, and to that end even wish to unroll the books of the Reformers. What, I ask, would men devoted to our sacred rites <note>Meaning the Protestant/Reformed readers of this text.</note> say to such a speech? Would they not cry out that such a Romanist man sins against the rule of Logicians which forbids <term>begging the question <note>original: "το ἐν ἀρχῃ λαμβανειν" (to en archē lambanein)</note></term>? Would they not repeat that men devoted to the Religion of the Romanists who spend time reading our books would be out of danger of error, if the Catholic faith were built upon such evident, solid, and unshakable reasons? I know there is a very great difference between the decrees of the Christian Religion itself and the opinions held by the Roman Church; but that is not the point. The question is merely whether, in the argument of those who proscribe the examination of the books of *Unbelievers* because the truth of the Christian Religion has been sufficiently proven, there is not the same <term>lack of logical reasoning <note>original: "ἀσυλλογισία" (asyllogisia)</note></term> that exists in the reasoning of the Catholic Teacher who proscribes the reading of Protestant books on the grounds that the Catholic Religion has been sufficiently proven? Certainly, in the method of reasoning, there is no difference. And what, I ask, prevents learned men from publicly defending the cause of our most holy Religion against the objections of *Unbelievers*? Shall it be permitted for *Unbelievers* to attack all the most holy things with impunity, but not for those who love truth and right to defend the same?

The Christian Religion is true, I confess, and built upon certain foundations. But are all who are called Christians persuaded and convinced of it? Oh, how we wish this were true! How we wish that most Christians, indeed all, were not just able to repeat the sounds of their Teachers, but rather to give the reasons for their faith with the weightiest arguments! How I wish they could dispel the objections of *Unbelievers* without effort! But since this is not the case, and on the contrary it is clear that many have admitted the Articles of Religion without examination, it must be the work of public Teachers to prove the divine Origin of the Christian Religion—without which persuasion no one can rightly be called a Christian—with the most evident and weightiest arguments on every given occasion, and to tear down the errors of *Unbelievers* which lay snares for truth and piety. In a word: either it must be said that the decrees of the Christian Religion are contrary to the principles of right reason, destitute of all foundation, and unable to withstand the objections of *Unbelievers*...

# MEDITATION I.

...objections will clearly not suffice; or on the other side it must be asserted, that these religious truths are resting upon certain Principles, and against all insults of the *Unbelievers*, if they are rightly defended, are sufficiently fortified, and finally of such a nature that they can draw into assent anyone not captured by sinister opinions and depraved desires. The *former* no one of sound mind would say. For this would be to hand over the palm of victory <note>original: "herbam porrigere" — a Latin idiom meaning to admit defeat or surrender</note> to the *Unbelievers*, and to confess that Religion and the most foolish superstition differ in nothing but name. The *latter* must therefore be asserted, namely that it is not only permitted for the Learned to read, weigh, and refute pamphlets of this kind; but it is also the duty of public Teachers, that they not only seriously plead the cause of Holy Religion and prove its admirable excellence with the most evident arguments, but also show their disciples the way by which the minds of the pious are to be fortified against the difficulties of the *Unbelievers*. And to say it as it is, this is the one and best method and way of repressing the insults of the *Unbelievers* and placing Religion in safety. Namely, arguments must be opposed by the arguments of the *Unbelievers*, and every nerve of the intellect must be strained so that we might not only solidly prove the truth of divine and heavenly discipline, but also vindicate the same against their various objections. Indeed, it is so far from the case that we should blame those Learned Men who have demonstrated the truth of the Christian Religion and examined the individual difficulties of the *Unbelievers*, that we should rather count it among the *Happiness* of the century in which we live, that Men most Eminent in Learning and piety, especially the *English*, have most learnedly and solidly confirmed the truth of the Christian Religion. From which the most excellent *Burnet, the most worthy son of the Great and Illustrious Parent G. Burnet, formerly Bishop of Salisbury*, has deserved well of the Learned, indeed the whole Christian World, because he has reduced to a compendium <note>A shortened summary of a larger work</note> those things which were said most learnedly and accurately by the most excellent Scholars of *England* according to the institution of the illustrious and pious *Boyle* <note>Robert Boyle, the famous chemist, established a lecture series (the Boyle Lectures) specifically to defend Christianity against "infidels."</note>, worthy of eternal praise, for Natural and Revealed Religion, and recently shared them with the Learned World. Truly, this book is most worthy of being held in the hands of all who care for truth and piety day and night as a *Handbook* <note>original: "Enchiridii"</note>. In the meantime, we owe to the *Unbelievers* themselves so many writings of exquisite Learning; certainly the capital truths would never have been placed in such light, unless the Learned among the *Unbelievers* had imposed the necessity upon wise and learned Men, by their plausible objections, of examining and defending the individual heads of Religion with the greatest skill. # MEDITATION I.

...to **Man**, distinguished from that which is only the ***Accessory***, <note>original: "à l'Homme, distinguée de ce qui n'en est que l'Accessoire"</note> intending to smooth the way for convincing the **Unbelievers**, he asserts that nothing more right could be done than if we should concede for a time to the **Unbelievers** that, for the sake of holding faith in the Christian Religion, there is no need to admit Mysteries and miracles. (*) However, how little suited these methods are, I shall show in a separate dissertation by way of a digression, with God's help.

<margin>To perceive the force of arguments fighting for the truth of the Christian Religion, there is need not only of attention, but also of a mind free from all prejudiced opinions and depraved desires.</margin>VI. Among other things that hinder the growing vice of **Unbelief** from being repressed, this stands out most of all: that the minds of very few are rightly disposed to weigh the arguments fighting for the Truth of the Christian Religion. This is because **Unbelievers** are imbued with many prejudiced opinions against Christian discipline; many of them do not know how to reason correctly; and most do not consult reason, but rather their own depraved passions. I shall pass over in silence for now the other points which I am about to bring forward in the progress of these meditations, if God grants further life. Certainly, to undertake an Examination of Religion—specifically the Christian one—which is a matter of the gravest importance, there is required a sincere heart, most loving of truth, and one that is led to either side only by the force of arguments. When a man is empty of these virtues, yet intends to examine Religion, it cannot happen by the nature of things that arguments exert their power. <term>Lactantius</term> <note>Lactantius (c. 250–325 AD) was an early Christian advisor to Constantine I; he is known as the "Christian Cicero" for his elegant Latin style.</note> speaks rightly and elegantly on this subject when he is about to prove the immortality of the human soul and explain the nature of the final judgment. In *Book VII, Chapter 1*, among other things, he says: *In the meantime, I think it necessary to warn my Readers that these things which we hand down, wicked and corrupt minds will either not understand at all (for their sharp edge is blunted by earthly desires, which weigh down all the senses and render them weak), or even if they do understand, they will nonetheless ignore them and be unwilling for these things to be true. This is because they are dragged away by vices, and knowingly they favor their own evils, by whose sweetness they are captured; thus they desert the way of virtue, by whose bitterness they are offended. For those who burn with avarice and a certain insatiable thirst for wealth—because they cannot live a life of meager means after selling or giving away the things they love—doubtless prefer that to be a fiction which forces them to renounce their desires. Likewise, those incited by the stings of lust who (as the Poet says) rush into furies and fire, assuredly*

*assuredly say that we bring forward incredible things; because the precepts of self-control wound their ears, prohibiting them from those pleasures to which they have sentenced their soul along with their body.* Truly, those who are puffed up with ambition or inflamed by the love of power, and have applied all their study to acquiring honors, will not grant faith—not even if we should carry the sun itself in our hands—to that doctrine which commands them to live humbly, despising all power and honor, and to be so humble that they can both receive an injury and be unwilling to return it if they have received one. Such are the men who bark against the Truth with closed eyes in every way. But those who shall be healed—that is, those not so immersed in vices that they are incurable—they will both believe and freely approach these things. Whatever we say will seem open, plain, simple, and (what is most necessary) irreproachable to them. No one favors virtue except he who can follow it; but to follow is not easy for everyone.

But I seem to hear the **Unbeliever** responding, not without indignation, that this demand of ours is inept and worthy of laughter; namely, that we demand of **Unbelievers** that they have a mind ready to receive our opinions—that is, a credulous mind. He might say this is the same as if someone, intending to reason with another and lead him to his own opinion, demanded that he first admit the conclusion of the argument, and only then examine the premises.

But the **Unbelievers** misunderstand our sentiment, or they deliberately twist it into a foreign sense. For we do not demand from **Unbelievers** that, before the examination of the reasons which we are accustomed to bring forward to prove the truth of the Christian Religion, they should have faith in us and think magnificently of Religion. We would without doubt be foolish if we wished this to be granted to us. We demand nothing else than what all the wise men of all ages require from those who wish to know the truth when the gravest questions are to be weighed: namely, this one thing, that they bring to the examination of the question an attentive mind, free from the zeal of parties, and uniquely intent on perceiving and pondering the force of reasons. The greater the importance of inquiring after the truth—the more the solution of the question is joined with the salvation or detriment of the human race—the more necessary it is that those about to examine those questions be attentive and free from bias. A corrupt judge examines the truth poorly. We demand nothing here but what the **Unbelievers** themselves are accustomed to demand of us when they bring forward their doubts and objections against Religion: they cry out, forsooth, that for a time we must set aside opinions drunk in almost with our mother’s milk, inculcated by our teachers, and firmly fixed in the mind by long habit as if they were axioms.

# MEDITATION I.

...impressed by eternal truth, repeating that those things which are brought forward, even if they are perhaps unpleasant, must be weighed <note>original: "ἀθερ παθῶν" (ater pathōn), a Greek phrase meaning 'without passions' or 'dispassionately'</note> and with a serene mind. Why should they not grant us the same right? We are so persuaded of the goodness of our cause that we believe our reasons—if set out in due order and weighed and considered with an attentive mind—will either draw the **Unbelievers** into agreement or at least ensure that hereafter they think more rightly and better concerning the nature and character of the Christian Religion. We contend, moreover, that the question debated between us and the **Unbelievers** is both most grave and of such a kind that, to solve it rightly, there is need not only of judgment and attention, and a certain sincere desire for knowing the truth, but also of a mind prepared to arrange all its actions, desires, and endeavors according to the <term>norm of truth and rightness</term>. For the right unfolding of this Question is hindered not only by a dull wit and prejudiced opinions, but most of all by the wicked interests of the soul and perverse desires. The reason for this is readily apparent. For here we are not dealing merely with directing the Ideas of the intellect, but primarily with moderating our actions according to a certain rule. Furthermore, it is not a matter—to use the terms of the <term>Schools</term> <note>Referring to 'Scholasticism,' the traditional method of university teaching in the Middle Ages and Early Modern period</note>—that is merely abstract; for example, a geometric problem or even a critical or historical question. Rather, it concerns the most grave and momentous question of all that could ever be raised among mortals, upon which depends the entire way of conducting our lives. For it is *asked* whether the best and wisest Ruler of the world is to be adored, and to be worshipped and venerated with the mind, with words, and with the entire conduct of life; whether, in all the conditions of this fleeting and perishing life, He is to be clung to, and whether all things which He disposes for us according to His infinite wisdom are to be received and borne with a pious and constant mind. It is *asked* whether our souls lack death <note>i.e., whether they are immortal</note> or not, and thus whether God, who is most desirous for the human race, will affect the pious with rewards and the impious with punishments after this falling life. It is *asked* whether the Christian Religion is of divine and heavenly origin, or truly a fable recklessly invented by idle men. It is *asked* not only whether the decrees of this Religion are true and <note>original: "πασης ἀποδοχης ἀξια", a Greek phrase meaning 'worthy of all acceptance'</note>, but also whether we are bound by the force of the divine will to arrange all our thoughts, desires, and actions according to the norm of the divine precepts prescribed in Revelation, and to remain in this constant confession of truth and course of piety even to the very end of life, amidst all adversities, afflictions, and even the most exquisite tortures. This is the sum of the Question

<column-break/>

# ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

debated between us and the **Unbelievers**. Either we have lost the true names of things and do not know what is light or what is momentous, or this question is difficult enough and most grave. If the **Unbelievers** wish hereafter to deny that the unfolding of this question requires not only sharp judgment and attention but also a mind free from prejudiced opinions, wicked interests, and affections, they must necessarily say one of two things: either that the question proposed thus far is not of such great moment as is commonly said, or that **Unbelievers** are men entirely free from all prejudiced opinions and foreign to every appearance of corruption. If they assert the former, they will not only have the learned and wise men of every age and time opposing them, but they themselves must see by what reasoning they can reconcile this judgment of theirs with their own actions and institutions. For if this question is so light and of no value, why do they strain every nerve and power of their wit to attack Religion? Why do they cry out that Religion is the cause of all evils in the world? Why do they so greatly insult the defenders of Religion? Certainly, there is no need for so many meditations, so much labor, and so many writings if that question concerning the truth of Natural and Revealed Religion is of no moment at all. As for the latter point, I truly do not believe the **Unbelievers** themselves would ever say it publicly. For they are men of more elegant and acute wit—at least the Learned among this flock—than to be accustomed to proclaim such things about themselves. But if indeed some from this number should openly assert that only the **Unbelievers** are wise and free from all wicked affections, I know well enough that the rest would disapprove of such inept boasting and more-than-Stoic impudence, and reject it with indignation. However, whatever may be the case regarding this confession of the **Unbelievers**, we shall certainly prove in the following pages, by the induction of most manifest examples, that very often the most learned of the **Unbelievers** have allowed themselves to be carried away from the laws and decrees of right reason. From this, it is gathered more than enough that we establish nothing at all absurd or abhorrent to the decrees of reason when we contend that, to institute an accurate Examination of Religion, it is necessary that minds be foreign to prejudiced opinions and partisan zeal.

# MEDITATION I.

<margin>...one should take care for oneself; the general causes and occasions by which men are accustomed to rush into this precipice must be recognized.</margin>...and gradually, for various reasons, one can fall into those errors, and what generally stands in the way of those in error so that they do not offer an open ear to the truth. Indeed, it will be clear from what is to be said—and anyone who has ever seriously meditated on these things will easily perceive—that not only can men easily fall into such pestilential errors, but there are also certain general arguments, or to speak more correctly, **sophisms** <note>sophisms: clever but false arguments intended to deceive</note> and false opinions, by which men are frequently hindered from approaching a careful **Examination** of all the reasons upon which Religion rests. It is therefore the duty of public teachers, and indeed of all lovers of the truth, to diligently turn their minds to these things and to take care that men are fortified early against those various and manifold causes of erring.

And this also moved me to wish to treat this material a little more fully, according to the measure of my talent (which I well know to be weak), and to diligently lay open the causes which can cast many mortals into those errors—enemies to piety and Religion—and confirm them in those errors; and finally, by removing or at least diminishing this evil, to bring the best remedies into the open. Other factors also occurred which led me to put my hand to elaborating this argument. Among them, the primary place is held by the *Magnitude* and the *Most Immediate Danger* of the evil itself, of which we have spoken thus far and shall deal with more diligently hereafter. Learned and pious men cry out and groan, even in our own lands, that this vice of **Unbelief** <note>original: "Incredulitas"</note> is growing and gaining strength, and that despite the light in which we live, many—to speak with *John* <note>A reference to the Gospel of John 3:19: "And this is the condemnation, that light is come into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light..."</note>—*love the darkness more than the light*.

It is therefore the duty of all who serve in sacred offices to see to it that the holy city suffers no harm, and to weigh diligently at the same time by what means this evil may be met, and how its proper honor may be kept safe and unharmed for truth and piety. To obtain this, however, as much as can be done in this "fog of affairs," one must not use vague cries and lamentations, much less persecutions; rather, means must be brought forward that are suited to removing or diminishing this disease. Before all else, one must inquire solicitously into the causes of the disease in the manner of **Physicians**, and only when this is done, with all modesty and prudence applied, should the most excellent means be brought forward by which minds—whether doubtful and wavering regarding Religion, or already deluded and captured by false opinions—may be led back to the path and confirmed in the most holy profession of Religion. If all <term>Ministers of the Divine Word</term> <note>original: "V. D. Ministri," an abbreviation for Verbi Divini Ministri</note> are bound to do this, it nevertheless falls upon the **Professors of Theology** in a singular way to see that their students, who are especially dedicated and consecrated to the sacred Ministry, are early...

# ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

...early not only taught how easily men can rush into these precipices, what the causes of this evil are, and what they ought to say and do publicly and privately to guard against them; but also to clearly and early show them by what reasons and arguments those captured by perverse opinions are to be led back, and how errors harmful to piety are to be removed from them. And this ought to be performed all the more by the Professors of the holier disciplines because it is more than sufficiently clear—as will be plain in due time, God willing, from the progress of our meditations—that the ignorance of many who serve in sacred offices regarding the recognition of this evil and how to meet it is no small cause of its growth. 

The more grave this evil is, and the more harmful to the salvation of men; the more widely it creeps daily; the more, finally, it commends itself with a certain appearance of erudition or wisdom and insinuates itself into the minds of the unwary; so much more ought the men of our Order to strain every nerve of their talent, sparing no labor, vigils, and meditations to uproot pestiferous opinions from the minds of men, and to demonstrate the admirable power and excellence of Truth and Piety. In other times, other things were more frequently to be repeated and drummed in; now such is the unhappiness of our age that everywhere the first and principal heads of <term>Natural Religion</term> <note>Natural Religion: Truths about God and morality that can be discovered through human reason and nature</note> and <term>Revealed Religion</term> <note>Revealed Religion: Truths that can only be known through God's specific revelation, such as the Bible</note> must be explained, inculcated, and defended.

For besides the fact that no one knows in what places, by the dispensation of divine Providence, he will scatter the seeds of heavenly wisdom—and it is the duty of all who apply their minds to knowing and passing on the holier disciplines and who wish to discharge their most grave office with fruit, that they ought to know how to detect the sources of errors early enough and by what means they can be met—it must also be known that such people are found everywhere, even among the country folk, who, if they do not attack Religion with sharp reasons, nevertheless doubt the most momentous truths. It is true that among the country folk and the common people, there are more who are foolishly **Credulous** than **Unbelievers**. But besides the fact that the vice of **Unbelief** easily creeps into the minds of all, though from different causes, and minds not sufficiently fortified against the difficulties of the **Unbelievers** can easily be circumvented, an accurate knowledge of the evil will be joined with the greatest success and fruit. For thus they will learn early what the principal causes of **Unbelief** are, how minds are to be fortified against these vices, and by what reasons...
