<margin>Different Classes of Unbelievers are established.</margin>
VIII. Before we approach the causes of *Incredulity* itself, which is increasingly gaining strength, different Classes of Unbelievers must be established. For since Unbelievers rely partly on different principles and wander more or less from the truth—and since the constitution of the mind by which they are moved to attack Religion is also different—it is necessary that we not only distinguish them into various Classes, but also that we take account of this diversity of characters and errors when bringing forward means to diminish these evils. For just as it would be foolish if a Physician wanted to prescribe the same regimen <note>original: *δίαιτα* (diaita)</note> to all patients and use the same medicines to restore them, so likewise it would be contrary to reason to hold all those in error in the same place and use the same arguments to recall them from their errors and lead them back to the path of truth. We bring this up to the end that it may be clear why, in the following parts of our meditation, we use different methods of arguing to recall Unbelievers. If, therefore, the cohort of Unbelievers is to be distributed into certain Classes, there are first those who merely *doubt* concerning the principal chapters of Natural and Revealed Religion. There are, on the other hand, those who attack Religion in words or writings. In both...

<column-break/>

<page-num>29</page-num>

...classes, different degrees of those doubting or denying can be distinguished. Some, finally, begin to doubt for various reasons (which we shall bring forward in due time), yet because the love of Religion holds their souls firmly enough, they are ignorant of what should or should not be done. Others go further and think that there is a certain equilibrium between the reasons for doubting and not doubting; these either think this examination should be postponed to another time, or, deterred by difficulties, think the matter should be left undecided throughout their whole life. Some, having weighed individual chapters of Religion on both sides, agree only with those which they can fully grasp in every respect; they think that all the rest can rightly be doubted. Others, finally, doubt because they *want* to doubt, and they pursue some kind of reputation for erudition and sharp wit from the scruples and objections which they can bring forward on any given occasion. These, for the most part, use no certain principles to attack Religion, but having seized any occasion which seems to add weight to doubt, they are carried hither and thither in uncertainty. Nor is it possible to define in words to which precise degrees the force of doubt reaches, since the degrees of doubting are as diverse as the diversity of reasons, characters, and affections. Those who *attack* religion itself, by mouth or by writings, either hold all the principles of Natural and Revealed Theology as suspected of falsehood, or they repudiate only a part of each. And with respect to Natural Theology, there are those who attack the very existence of the Divine Power. And these indeed, along with *Spinoza*, most foolishly imagine only one infinite and eternal substance, consisting of two attributes—namely, extension and thought—of which all parts of the universe, minds and bodies, are nothing but modes. <note>Spinoza's Pantheism: The philosopher Baruch Spinoza argued that God and Nature are one and the same substance, and that everything in the universe is just a "mode" or manifestation of God.</note> *Those* others, however, contend that everything that is or can be, whether intelligible <note>original: *νοητα* (noēta)</note> or sensible, <note>original: *αἰσθητα* (aisthēta)</note> arose from a chance collision of infinite particles, which they call atoms. I know that by learned men—for example, *Buddeus* in his *Theses on Superstition and Atheism*, and *Cudworth* in his *Intellectual System*—other and more species of Atheism are established. But in my opinion, all things can and should be recalled to those two heads: for either it must be said that this whole universe, and its individual parts, derive their origin from a certain cause that is not only eternal and infinite, but also most powerful, most wise, most good, and entirely distinct from this visible world; or it must be asserted that the universe itself, and the individual parts of which it consists, [exist] by a certain intrinsic and absolute necessity of nature without an external and free cause...

...to have existed; or finally, everything must be attributed to some unknown chance. If anyone denies the first of those three theses <note>The three theses: 1. The world is eternal, 2. God created it, 3. It happened by chance.</note>, they must necessarily establish either the second or the third. It must be admitted, however—though this is not the place to discuss the systems of the ancient philosophers—that as far as I can tell from the records of literary history, very few of the *Unbelievers* rise to such a level of audacity that they call the very existence of the Divinity <note>original: *Numen*. A Latin term for divine power or a deity.</note> into doubt. For no one can judge those thoughts which some perhaps revolve silently in their own minds without being reckless. Nor should those be placed in this class who err regarding one or another attribute of God, especially physical ones, or those who, through long and winding paths of reasoning, are accused of a very serious error which they themselves cannot see.

Others, and indeed most *Unbelievers*, admit the existence of a most good and wise Divinity, but they call into doubt God's providential care for all things. They imagine that this machine <note>A common Enlightenment-era metaphor for the universe as a complex clockwork mechanism.</note> of the world, once produced, can subsist without further care from God, and that God leads a carefree life, far removed from the affairs of this world, living in the deepest peace. 

Some indeed affirm that this universe is preserved by the care and power of God, but they deny that this same care extends to the free actions of human minds. These people have come to such thoughts either because they are entangled in the more subtle disputes of the learned concerning the origin of evil, or because they have been affected by various adversities. All of these, if they wish to reason correctly and consistently with their own principles, cannot properly admit the laws of nature, insofar as those laws rest upon the attributes and perfections of the Divinity.

Again, others do not doubt the existence and providence of the Divinity at all, but they nevertheless deny that human minds lack death <note>i.e., they deny the immortality of the soul.</note>; they instead determine that everything is confined within the boundaries of this life. By this very act, they remove the strongest incentive for living piously and rightly. For if you take away the rewards and punishments that are to follow after this life, the love of piety and virtue must necessarily perish.

There are also many—and of these there is indeed a great number—who admit the principal heads of <term>Natural Theology</term> <note>The study of God based on reason and the observation of nature, rather than on divine revelation.</note>, but they utterly deny the need for any divine <term>Revelation</term> <note>The communication of truth from God to humanity, such as through scripture.</note>. They assert that the decrees of right reason concerning God are sufficient to establish a worship pleasing to Him. 

Finally, there are those who admit both Revelation and Natural Religion, at least regarding the precepts of Christ and the Apostles; however, they explode the miracles and mysteries, contending that these were invented by malicious men—the ones who first spread the books containing the dogmas of the Christian Religion among the common people—in order to win greater authority for these writings. All of these men, according to the diversity of their judgment,

Once the students of this more sacred discipline have read these with an attentive mind more than once and recalled them to heart, the path will be easy for examining greater and more difficult matters. <margin>The first cause of Unbelief is a certain shameful ignorance of divine things.</margin>

IX. We shall finally approach the causes of *Unbelief* themselves, after we have given a brief warning regarding the definition of Unbelief and the method of treating this argument. Although an attentive reader may easily notice from what has been said so far what we understand by the names *Unbelief* and *Cause*, lest we sin against the rules of the schools, the notions of *Unbelief* and *Cause* must be defined. By the name of *Unbelief*, therefore, we understand that affection of the mind according to which someone—for whatever causes it may finally happen—either calls into doubt or denies either all the chapters of Natural and Revealed Religion, or only a part of them. By the name of *Cause*, however, we understand everything that moves the mind toward Religion...

->### MEDITATION I.<-

...can lead one to consider [the truth] of little value, to despise it, or clearly to oppose it. I know that others distinguish the *Causes* of unbelief from the *Occasions*, but we wish all things to be included under the name of a general *Cause* or "fountainhead"—namely, those things which can move a person to deny Religion. By "Religion," we mean those principal heads of Natural and Revealed Religion (for we are not dealing here with this or that error defended by specific patrons of various sects). We shall proceed with this argument in such a way that, first, we uncover the principal *causes of unbelief*. Second, we will weigh the general reasons that lead *unbelievers* to carry a mind alienated from Religion; *and third*, finally bringing a remedy to this disease, we will bring forward various means and arguments for leading men away from this evil, or for calling back those already bound by errors.

All causes of *unbelief* can be conveniently reduced to two main headings. Specifically, those causes arise either from the *disposition and state* of the soul itself, or they approach from the outside and incline minds toward such thinking. In a word, those causes are either *Internal* or *External*. Beginning with the former, we assert that the *First Cause of Unbelief*, which arises from the very disposition of the soul, is *a certain shameful ignorance of divine things*. To be sure, the human mind in its first constitution is ignorant of all things, as is sufficiently clear from infants recently brought into the light. Certainly, we detect nothing in them besides certain confused sensations. If you wish to climb higher and know the state of human minds in their very first origin, when they are joined to the body, you will learn by experience after long meditations and windings that you can bring forth nothing into the open but conjectures. The state of the body corresponds to the weakness of the mind. Even the heathens were not ignorant of that miserable state of the human race from its first origin. Hence *Cicero* said in *Book III of the Republic*: *man was brought forth into life by nature not as if by a mother, but as if by a stepmother; with a body naked, fragile, and weak; with a mind anxious toward troubles, humble toward fears, soft toward labors, and prone to lusts; in which, however, there remained a certain buried divine fire of the mind.* <note>original: "non ut a matre, sed ut a noverca natura editum esse hominem..." Cicero was a Roman statesman and philosopher; here he reflects on the inherent flaws and potential of human nature.</note> From this arose the innumerable complaints of the heathens regarding the unhappiness of the human race, which *Bayle* <note>Pierre Bayle (1647–1706), a philosopher famous for his "Historical and Critical Dictionary," which often highlighted the paradoxes and miseries of human existence.</note> brings forward in public, citing testimonies from all sides but for a very bad end, under the entry *Xenophanes*. Yet they were unable to uncover the source of the evil. We, to whom Revelation has been granted, know full well from where that disaster was brought upon the human race. Nor is it necessary now, since our business is with the *Unbeliever*, to prove this with passages of Scripture; it is enough that experience teaches anyone that men, in respect to both mind...

->### ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.<-

...and body, are exceedingly weak when they are brought into the light. But we are now concerned not so much with the body as with the mind. Besides the ignorance in which all the minds of infants dwell, it is established by experience that all men perceive with difficulty those things that are abstract and do not strike the senses. Hence, it is not without great labor that children attain some knowledge of spiritual, abstract, and moral things. Indeed, how few there are, even among adults, who have a more accurate knowledge of these things! When one must think about GOD himself, the most excellent Being of all, imagination hinders most mortals from being able to meditate on so great an object with a pure sharpness of mind. *Lactantius* <note>An early Christian author (c. 250 – c. 325) often called the "Christian Cicero" for his eloquent Latin.</note> beautifully and truly says in *Book V, Section 7*: *When the intention, sharpness, and memory of the human mind reaches that point, it stops, clings, and fails, as if all paths were withdrawn and exhausted; nor is there anything further to which it can proceed.* <note>original: "Cum ad illum mentis humanæ intentio... subsistit, hæret, deficit..."</note> Furthermore, it is difficult to acquire for oneself a somewhat fuller knowledge of the divine attributes. For since, to attain a knowledge of the divine attributes, it is necessary that we first descend into ourselves and rightly know the dispositions of our own minds—and only when those are known can it be inferred that such things exist in God, but without the mixture of defects, and indeed in the most eminent degree (which we nevertheless cannot conceive)—it is clear enough that there is a need for no small amount of attention, which you would seek in vain in most mortals. I would say the same regarding the knowledge of the existence, character, and nature of the Natural Laws, and the duties that must be performed by mortals toward GOD and others. This (2.) natural weakness notwithstanding, daily experience—and indeed the experience of all ages—teaches that men, by applying whatever diligence they can, are able to arrive at a knowledge of the arts and sciences which are very useful to the human race, and likewise to a sufficient knowledge of divine things and the duties by which the worship of the Deity is fulfilled. For in a wonderful way, the Greatest and Best and Most Benignant God meets our need and ignorance: for he did not give us eyes and a mind for the purpose of knowing the intimate essence <term>of intelligible things and of sensible things</term> <note>original: "των νοητων &amp; των αισθητων" (tōn noētōn kai tōn aisthētōn). These are Greek philosophical terms for things perceived by the mind/intellect versus things perceived by the physical senses.</note>, but rather so that, having looked into the attributes of both kinds, we might contemplate objects only insofar as they contribute to our happiness. (3.) Moreover, a person rightly notices that to attain a knowledge of things divine and human, there is a need for a certain cultivation of talent, attention, meditation, and labor. For life has given nothing to mortals without great labor. (4.) Furthermore, once even a moderate knowledge of divine things has been acquired, a person no less perceives those objects...

<summary>This section identifies the primary cause of unbelief as "shameful ignorance," rooted in the natural weakness of the human mind and its difficulty in grasping abstract or divine concepts. The author cites classical authors like Cicero and Lactantius to illustrate the inherent limitations of human reason while asserting that God provides enough clarity for humans to understand their moral duties through effort.</summary>

<page-num>34</page-num>
<header>->MEDITATION I.<-</header>
<meta>catchword: negli- / neglecting</meta>

...neglected, the matters with which Religion is concerned are things most worthy of human knowledge and love, and they contribute greatly to promoting the happiness of oneself and others. Furthermore, the more one is captured by the contemplation of these things, and the more one gazes upon God's care and benevolence toward the human race, the more one will feel obligated to perform duties toward God. Truly, from the observance of these duties—which are most agreeable to reason—there will arise a sweet sensation and delight in the soul; for a person learns by experience that the powers of the mind are thus gradually perfected and one's own happiness is increased.

However, although no one can deny that mortals, by employing these aids, can arrive at a knowledge of Religion and their duties, it must be confessed—alas!—that many people exist who live in extreme ignorance of divine things. It is no wonder, then, if many doubt the chief articles of Religion. Since these truths must be investigated with some degree of study, and yet most people are held by no desire to know or unearth the truth, what wonder is it if those people not only fall into foolish opinions unworthy of God, but are also far too easy and inclined to snatch up any ideas from Unbelievers?

And I would not wish this to be understood only regarding the "barbarous" <note>The author reflects the common 18th-century European view of non-Western cultures as intellectually "uncivilized" or "barbaric."</note> peoples of *Africa* and *America*, who, having cast aside almost all study of divine things, obey only their bellies, and whom Christians can scarcely bring to even a mediocre knowledge of divine matters; rather, we speak especially of those who live in the most flourishing regions of *Europe*. How many, I ask, live their entire lives in the deepest ignorance of the most sacred things? How many are there who believe "what is believed," <note>original: "credunt, quod creditur" — meaning they follow blind tradition without personal understanding.</note> even though they do not know what it is that others believe? How many cannot distinguish superstition from Religion? How many are there to whom it is all the same what they believe? How many are there who think nothing is less worthy of a man's care than the Examination of Religion?

Is it any wonder that such men easily fall into foolish opinions unworthy of God? Is it any wonder that they cannot withstand any attack from Unbelievers, but immediately "stretch out the grass" <note>original: "herbam porrigere" — an ancient Roman idiom meaning to acknowledge defeat or surrender.</note> in surrender? Is it any wonder that, according to the diversity of times and occasions, they change the principles of their Religion, are cast from one doubt into another, and—as wicked desires of the soul rush in—declare war on Religion? What happened to the Gentiles who neglected the knowledge of divine things is elegantly taught by *Paul in his Epistle to the Romans, chapter 1.* Such men not only give their "white stone" <note>original: "album adjiciunt calculum" — an ancient Greek and Roman custom of using a white stone to signify a vote of approval or acquittal.</note> of approval to any foolish opinions and are easily led away from what is true and right, but also, as long as they remain as they are—that is, as long as they voluntarily neglect the examination of the most worthy things—it is difficult...

...for them to be led back to the right path. For a solid persuasion regarding the weightiest and most important articles of faith, insofar as it can be obtained by human help, at least two things are required. *First*, that a person not only understands the propositions that must be admitted, but can also draw out the consequences that flow immediately from them. *Second*, that to obtain this, he institutes some kind of examination and, with a serious and attentive mind, weighs the matters subject to examination <term>without passions</term> <note>original Greek: "ἄθερ παθῶν" (ater pathon) — the author emphasizes that objective study requires setting aside emotional biases.</note> on both sides. Where these things are not done, where all care for Religion is postponed, where insane men utterly hate the examination of such matters, it is no wonder if they admit the most foolish opinions, rush into every wickedness, and rest comfortably even in ruinous ideas.

From this, it is clear enough that a shameful ignorance of divine things not only prevents men from knowing those first and principal Heads of Religion, but also causes them to lend their ears to the most absurd opinions—those most harmful to Religion—and to be very easily captured by the objections of Unbelievers. This ignorance in matters regarding Religion not only makes men prone to seizing upon any portentous and foolish opinions, but Unbelievers themselves, having noticed such great ignorance among Christians, are confirmed in the opinion they have once embraced. For when they see that most Christians have given their name to Religion without a sufficient Examination, and that they merely defend those opinions which are commonly accepted in the province where they were born, they conclude—though most foolishly—that Religion itself is built upon no certain foundations.

How little these points actually do to support the cause of Unbelievers, we shall say shortly. Meanwhile, if we wish to descend to the sources of this evil, we shall find two primary causes. The *first* is a certain inertia and torpor that occupies the minds of most mortals when it comes to things that do not strike the senses, but must be investigated by reasoning. The examination of things divine and human demands an attentive mind, inflamed by a zeal and love for seeking the truth. To approach this with any hope of success, a certain amount of labor is required. But most mortals flee from this labor—where the powers of the soul must be strained—as if it were a plague; they prefer to rest in those things that are already fixed in their minds. Linked with this torpor is a certain foolish complacency and sweetness. For indeed, as *Tacitus says in the Life of Agricola*: "The sweetness of inactivity itself steals over us, and the sloth that was at first hated is eventually loved." Hence, there is nothing so absurd or foreign to reason that certain minds cannot stomach it. This shameful torpor increases when...

### MEDITATION I.

...when they see that men inflamed with true love very often bring troubles upon themselves and provoke the anger of others against them. Hence we see *Muslims*, *Jews*, and among *Christians* many who, through their whole life, despising every new examination, cling to the opinions to which they were carried as if by a storm, just as if to a rock. At that time when our Holy *Savior* <note>original Latin: S. Soter</note> Jesus Christ lived among mortals and confirmed his most holy teaching with proofs and miracles, there were very few who were willing to weigh his words and deeds according to the norm of reason and the Decrees of the Old Testament Oracles; instead, carried away by inertia and a love for preconceived opinions, they remained settled in the views once fixed in their minds. In this they were confirmed, since the public Teachers themselves were little concerned with pure and chaste Religion, and preferred that men be captured by blind faith rather than submit matters of the greatest importance to examination. Hence the *Holy Savior* called them, in Matthew 15, "blind leaders of the blind." (*) A later cause of evil is that most mortals everywhere have little care for the truth. They are driven mostly toward those things that are pleasing to the senses and the passions, and they strive with all the contention of their strength to obtain these. Hence, those things which relate to <term>unexamined matters <note>original Greek: pros ta akrita</note></term> are desired first; indeed, with respect to most men, it can be said that these alone are the ends of all desires and actions. Even the most noble disciplines would lie miserably neglected unless their cultivation satisfied the greed for possession or the pleasures of many. Many are confirmed in this opinion of theirs when they see everywhere not the zeal for inquiring into the truth, but far other things that win over friends and patrons. They observe, moreover, that most people believe those things which can serve their own advantages, honors, and desires. Some are of such light character that they would change their opinions every single day, provided they were persuaded it would be to their benefit. X. However, although it is certain and indubitable that all those who so shamefully neglect their intellect—than which no greater or more excellent thing has been given to human nature—and who proscribe and cast away every Examination of the most healthy and holy things, lie easily open to the insults of *Unbelievers* and can easily be led to seize upon foolish opinions hostile to Religion; nevertheless, there is no reason why *Unbelievers* should applaud themselves and firmly defend the opinions they have once seized. For if they were to meditate on the causes of this ignorance without prejudiced opinions, they would easily discover that it does not prevent many men, outstanding in judgment, genius, and exquisite Erudition, from not only understanding Religion beautifully but also proving it with the sharpest and weightiest reasons. I do not think so meanly of the Erudition and fairness of *Unbelievers* as to believe that they indiscriminately regard all defenders of Religion as having the most stupid minds, as if they had a <term>pumpkin for a brain</term> <note>original: pepo pro cerebro</note>. Even if *Unbelievers* did not confess this by voice and writings, that very same incredible diligence in weighing and picking at every single one of our arguments would teach this more than sufficiently. This having been established, however, let us see what the argumentation of the *Unbelievers* is like. To be sure: countless Christians, having neglected the cultivation of reason and cast aside the examination of Religion, cling indiscriminately to any opinion and are easy to admit anything; Therefore, the Christian Religion itself is built upon no solid arguments; therefore, all Christians, captured only by prejudiced opinions, give their name to Religion; Therefore, we may rest securely in our Unbelief. What "sharpness"! Do they not daily observe that the followers of other disciplines sin in a similar way, and yet nothing of the excellence of the disciplines is lost because of it? # MEDITATION I.

...enlisted in this faction from the dregs of the common people, they blaspheme what they do not know; they rashly and foolishly insult Religion, which they have never examined throughout their lives. Are we to say, then, that all Unbelievers are equipped with no talent? That they are ignorant of all the laws of reasoning? That all the objections and doubts they bring forward are clearly foolish and tasteless? I know well that they would cry out at the top of their voices that an injustice was being done to them if we were to treat them this way. Hence they even complain about the *Leipzig Lover of Freedom* <note>original Latin: Phileleutherus Lipsiensis</note>, that is, the most learned *Bentley*, because in almost every page of his defense he charged them with the most shameful ignorance. Therefore, what they wish to be done for themselves (for I believe they admit this principle even if it is drawn from Holy Scripture, since *Radicati, Count of Passeran*, a name not unknown to Unbelievers, in his *History of the Ancient and Modern Priestly Profession, p. 242*, is so candid and liberal as to say: <insert>It must be noted that the Freethinkers <note>original French: Esprits forts</note> admit all the passages of Scripture that seem to favor their opinions</insert>), they must necessarily grant to others. Or are all Unbelievers at last Geometers, Philosophers, Historians, or Critics? Are they all at last endowed with excellent talent and judgment? Has no one at last given their name to this faction unless they have subjected the foundations of both Natural and Revealed Religion to the most rigid examination, and scrutinized every argument of the most learned men among us? And indeed, with such care and such rigor that, having weighed and compared everything, they finally correctly concluded that the principles of the Unbelievers rest on the firmest foundations, and thus war must necessarily be declared against Religion? These clever men will forgive us if we say that the history of *Deists* and *Atheists* is not entirely unknown to us, and the merits and monuments of talent by which they have attained their fame are well perceived by us. We are not ignorant—though we grieve to know it—that certain men of outstanding talent, who would have given great examples had they chosen to be wiser, wished to be counted among the Unbelievers; but at the same time, we also well know that most of this tribe, in order to indulge the base passions of the mind, subscribe to the decrees of the Unbelievers without conducting any examination. Certainly, to obtain the name and title of an "Unbeliever," there is no need for exquisite erudition, sharp wit, or long experience in affairs. # MEDITATION I.

...to dwell in ignorance of divine things, and never to have examined or skillfully weighed the principles of Religion! Certainly, it does not follow that the opinions by which they have hitherto defended their *Unbelief* <note>original Latin: *Incredulitatem*</note> are built upon unshakable and mathematical arguments. And this must be called to the memory of the *Unbelievers* <note>original Latin: *Incredulis*</note> all the more because neither our Holy *Savior* <note>original Greek/Latin: *Soter*</note> Christ, nor his disciples, commended a blind and foolish Credulity, but rather invited and exhorted everyone to examine the Religion handed down by them. No one who has ever unrolled these writings with care and attention would doubt this assertion of ours. Christ, when about to lead men to accept his heavenly doctrine, appeals to the excellence of the doctrine itself, and does not wish them to have faith in his miracles without Examination. Thus in John 5:31 he says: "If I testify about myself, my testimony is not true" <note>original Greek: Ἐὰν ἐγὼ μαρτυρῶ περὶ ἐμαυτοῦ, ἡ μαρτυρία μου οὐκ ἔστιν ἀληθής</note>. The Apostles did the same: Paul says in so many words in 1 Thessalonians 5:21: "Test all things; hold fast to what is good" <note>original Greek: Πάντα, αυδι πάντα δοκιμάζετε, τὸ καλὸν κατέχετε</note>. In 1 John 4:1, the Apostle exhorts Christians thus: "Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test whether they are from God, because many false prophets have gone out into the world" <note>original Greek: Ἀγαπητοί, μὴ παντὶ πνεύματι πιστεύετε, ἀλλὰ δοκιμάζετε, εἰ ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐστιν, ὅτι πολλοὶ ψευδοπροφῆται ἐξεληλύθασιν εἰς τὸν Κόσμον</note>. 

But this cannot be done without examination. The Jews of Berea are praised in Acts 17:11 because they diligently examined the scriptures of the Old Testament and compared them with the Apostolic doctrine. I pass over many other passages that our theologians are accustomed to bring forward against the Catholics <note>original Latin: *Pontificios*, referring to the Roman Catholic Church</note>, who proscribe the general examination of Religion. Furthermore, the Apostles everywhere exhort everyone to be more and more confirmed in the knowledge of piety as much as truth, which undoubtedly demands some Examination and study. From this it is also clear that *Unbelievers* act foolishly when they cry out that Christians themselves do not know what they mean by the name of *faith*. Has it not at last been sufficiently explored and explained by learned men among Christians what the *faith* of Christians is? Should a certain perverse interpretation of the common people, embracing a hodgepodge of uncertain opinions under the name of *faith*, be the reason why it can be publicly said and written that Christians generally do not know what power they attribute to the word *faith*? It is a wonder that those men insult us for that reason, when they themselves, though asked a hundred times, have not even been able to explain or define until now what they mean by the name of *Nature* sustaining all things, or *Chance* effecting the whole order of the world. But if this or that public teacher has spoken somewhat obscurely about faith either in general, or about *justifying* faith in particular, should this therefore be attributed to all Christians in general? Where do the laws of equity and reasoning...

## ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

...reasoning remain? But there is no need for us to be more wordy here; let Chapter 1 of Part II of the treatise by *Jean Le Clerc on Unbelief* <note>original Latin: *Joh. Clerici de Incredulité*. Le Clerc was a famous 17th-century Swiss theologian and scholar.</note> be consulted.

<margin>The question is asked whether there exists an invincible ignorance of natural religion, or of the principles of Natural Law.</margin>

Since we have shown in the preceding sections in what shameful ignorance of the most holy things many men dwell, someone will perhaps ask whether we therefore think there exists, as Theologians and Jurists <note>original Latin: *Jcti*, abbreviation for *Jurisconsulti*</note> say, a certain *Invincible Ignorance* <term>Invincible Ignorance: A theological and legal term for a lack of knowledge that a person cannot overcome despite reasonable effort; such ignorance usually excuses a person from moral or legal blame.</term> of the principles of Natural Law. Before we pronounce anything on either side regarding this question, some things must necessarily be put forward for the explanation of this argument. 

And (1.) indeed we say that the diversity of human minds seems to be infinite, both with respect to the original nature they received from the Great and Good Divinity <note>original Latin: *O. M. Numine*, likely *Optimo Maximo Numine*</note>, and with respect to culture and reason. As for the *former*, it is known from experience that men are distinct from one another by infinite degrees with respect to the faculty of perceiving, imagination, and memory. And this diversity of minds seems to take place before all instruction and meditation. For since God has fashioned an infinite variety of corporeal things, so that in the opinion of more recent philosophers <note>Likely referring to Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz and his theory that no two things in the universe are identical.</note>, no body exists that is similar to another in all respects, I do not know why it should finally be said that human minds are similar in all respects regarding their origin. We certainly see twins, brought into the light under the same sky, born of the same parents, raised and nourished by the same food and drink, differ from one another by a surprising amount if we look at the powers of the mind; whence that diversity of talent exerts itself early in infants. The reason for this, in our opinion, is better sought from the original constitution of the mind than from the structure of the body and the operations of the animal spirits <note>In early modern science, "animal spirits" were thought to be very fine fluids that traveled through the nerves to move the muscles and convey sensations.</note>. Whatever the case may be, it is certain that the variety of human talent is infinite. 

(2.) It is certain that all men can contribute much to polishing and perfecting the faculties of the soul. (3.) We contend, as is clear to everyone by itself, that some attention and meditation are needed to know those principles of Natural Law and the first chapters of Natural Religion. (4.) When we say that men can know these principles of Natural Law, we do not understand by the name of Natural Theology a philosophical science of these principles consisting of definitions, axioms, and propositions evidently connected to one another. Very few mortals are equipped with such knowledge, even if they in no way doubt the truth of these principles. But by the name of knowledge, we understand a persuasion of the truth of these principles, even if they cannot accurately show by what reason they have their origin and are connected to one another.

# MEDITATION I.

So, for example, by experience all mortals know that an effect implies a cause, and that whatever is created in an orderly fashion requires a cause equipped with intelligence. All men who are endowed with common sense <note>original Latin: *sensu communi*</note> admit these propositions; they can therefore apply these same principles to the questions at hand: namely, that the World has a cause, and that this cause is most wise, most powerful, and Best. They can see that this Cause presides over the world, and that just as there is an intrinsic difference between a Triangle and a Cube, so too is there a difference between sobriety and drunkenness, between mercy and cruelty; and finally, that the observance of duties makes men happy, and so on. (5.) When we assert that all men are able to know these general principles, we do not wish this to be understood as if there were absolutely no man, in whatever state he might be placed, who does not actually know these principles; for there are men who, from birth or by the defect of disease or from other causes, are unable to use their reason, as far as is known. Furthermore, there are those who are so brutalized by a kind of wildness that they differ little from beasts. But we mean that universality to be understood in this way: that all men endowed with common sense, by applying some effort of the mind and moderate attention, are able to arrive at the knowledge of these principles. Having noted these things in advance, we assert that there is no <term>Invincible Ignorance</term> <note>original Latin: *Ignorantiam invincibilem* - a theological term for ignorance that cannot be overcome by reasonable effort, and thus might excuse a person from sin</note> of these principles. We are led to this opinion by the following reasons. And (1.) it is established by experience that all men endowed with common sense are able to arrive at the knowledge of many arts and sciences. For although there is a great diversity of human talents in this regard—so much so that some make the greatest progress, while others understand slightly more difficult things only with effort—it is nevertheless certain that all can achieve much through labor and diligence. Yet we contend that the knowledge, at least the popular knowledge, of the principles of Natural Religion is no more difficult for the grasp and Understanding than this very skill in arts and disciplines. Hence even the Theology of the nations <note>meaning the pagans or non-Christians</note>, although encrusted with the most foolish superstition, nevertheless everywhere admitted those general principles. Nor is it an obstacle that the common people among the Gentiles followed the delusions of priests and Poets rather than the Decrees of Philosophers. For this objection proves only this one thing: namely, that men who took no care of their intellect, who admitted every foolish thing without examination, and who did not think about their own origin and the origin of all things throughout their lives, believed these foolish opinions. But we had said before that some attention is necessary to know those principles; and it does not prove,

it does not prove that Religion is a thing whose nature and character cannot be known even when all diligence and attention are applied. It should be observed, moreover, that the Gentiles foully mixed the principles of Natural Theology with the opinions commonly received about the Gods; hence sometimes, for example, they speak so magnificently of Jupiter that it is easily apparent that those ideas were not drawn from the teaching of priests and Poets, but are merely the remains of a knowledge of GOD, received either through reasoning or through Tradition. The same happens to the Common People among Christians who are devoted to the Papal Religion. The worship of God and of the saints is everywhere foully mixed. Yet no one would safely conclude from this that the Romanist commoners who frequent the sacred rites utterly do away with all the decrees of Natural and Revealed Religion. (2.) Since it is established from the very Creation of man, as well as from the faculties given to him by GOD and from other reasons, that men were made for worshipping the Deity and for their own legitimate preservation, it would follow that God obliges most men to the impossible, unless those principles could be known by applying some diligence and attention. No one fails to see how impious it is to think such a thing of God. <margin>Concerning Caligula, *Suetonius* testifies in chapter 41.</margin> Regarding *Caligula*, *Suetonius* testifies in chapter 41 of the life of this Emperor that he ordered the tablets of the laws to be written in such small characters and hung them so high that they could not be read, yet he nonetheless subjected transgressors to punishments. These things could only be done by a cruel Tyrant. What, therefore, would be more unworthy of the Goodness of God than to create minds and send them into this tiny little body, to equip them with the noblest faculties, to obligate them to perform worship to the Deity, and yet at the same time to fashion them so that they are utterly destitute of the strength to understand the prescribed laws? Or to grant them some power of reasoning, but at the same time to prescribe such duties as not even one in a thousand could know, even if they applied all diligence and labor? (3.) The *Apostle Paul* in Romans Chapters 1 and 2 not only asserts that what can be known about God naturally was manifest to the gentiles; but also that the natural law is written in their hearts. Although interpreters do not wish these two testimonies to be understood in the same sense in every detail, all nevertheless agree on this: that it is the nature of those laws that they can be rightly understood if any diligence whatsoever is applied. Otherwise, how could the Gentiles, who foully neglected the knowledge of the Deity, be called <term>without excuse</term> <note>original Greek: *ἀναπολόγητοι* (anapologētoi)</note>? On what foundation could the same Apostle assert that God would judge the gentiles—who certainly did not have the revealed law—according to the natural law? Why would God have burned with such anger against the Gentiles, as the Apostle says, if He had known...

# MEDITATION I.

...that no one among them, even with whatever care and solicitude applied, could ever have reached the knowledge of those principles and duties? Nor do the testimonies of travel writers—to which *Locke*, *Bayle*, and others appeal—overturn this thesis. They cite these writers to prove that there are nations so wild with savagery that they have no sense of the Deity, or at least show no manifest signs of being instructed in any knowledge of the principles of Religion and Natural laws. *First*, however, testimonies contrary to those can be offered, as has been done by very learned men such as Fabricius (\*), la Croze (\*\*), Fenelon (\*\*\*), Grapius (\*\*\*\*), and others. *Second*, very few people rightly understand the languages of Barbarian Nations; hence, after so much labor and meditation, for example, scholars still do not agree whether the *Chinese*, by the names TIEN and THANG-TI, understood heaven itself or the Lord of heaven. *Third*, most of these writers did not live among those people long enough to have gained an exact perspective on their customs and opinions. Thus, it has often happened that learned men discovered through their own work that they had been deceived; they had previously thought certain people were destitute of all knowledge of the Deity, but upon looking closer at the matter and correctly understanding their customs and languages, they found otherwise. # ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

Whatever the case may be regarding those Barbarian nations, the solution to this question helps the *Unbelievers* <note>original: *Incredulos*</note> very little. For they themselves live in the most flourishing regions of Europe, where sciences and arts are cultivated. And although a noble part of Europe has stained a chaste and pure Religion with foul superstition, nevertheless these general principles are everywhere admitted among all. Therefore, the *Unbelievers* would have to prove either that those general principles of Natural Religion are merely contradictory propositions, or so false that their vanity appears immediately as soon as they are understood. No one of sound mind, as far as I know, has ever asserted the former; but if our *Unbelievers* defend the *latter*, they foolishly demand that we grant them what we deny. And if (as we said above) those principles rest on such a weak support, and if they can be torn down by any man of mediocre talent, why do they spend all the talent and sharp wit they have to subvert what they please to call "straw" propositions? And where on earth are those <term>phortika</term> <note>original Greek: φορτικα - meaning vulgar, burdensome, or "heavy-handed" arguments.</note> arguments by which sharp men have proved all religion to be a falsehood? Truly, if weightier arguments than those brought forward by Spinoza, Collins, and Toland—the *Champions* <note>original: *Hyperaspistis* (shield-bearers or defenders)</note> of the Unbelievers—are not produced, there is no reason why the Learned should hereafter greatly fear the objections of the *Unbelievers*. # THEOLOGICAL
### AND PHILOSOPHICAL THESES (*)

I. *The resurrection of Christ from the dead most clearly proves the truth of the Christian Religion.*
II. *It is the most consistent doctrine of the Holy Scriptures that Jesus Christ offered himself as an atoning sacrifice for our sins.*
III. *If anyone should doubt whether they are <term>reborn</term> <note>The process of spiritual renewal or "regeneration" in Christian theology.</note> or not, it is safest for them to believe they are not yet reborn.*
IV. *The fairness of the <term>Apostolic precept</term> <note>Referring to Romans 14:23: "Everything that does not come from faith is sin."</note>—namely, that whatever does not arise from faith is sin—was recognized even by the Pagans. According to Cicero in Book I of "On Duties," they taught that nothing should be done if you doubt whether it is right or wrong.*
V. *Since God, who is the Author of Revelation, is also the Author of reason, it is impossible for Revelation to teach anything that is contrary to the most manifest principles of reason.*
VI. *Logical conclusions drawn from clear passages of Scripture are, for us, a more certain word of God than the immediate sense of difficult and ambiguous passages.*
VII. *The fact that the Roman Church holds a gross contradiction as a most serious dogma of faith is enough to prove that it is fallible.* <note>Likely referring to the doctrine of Transubstantiation, which critics during the Enlightenment often called a "contradiction" of the senses and reason.</note>
VIII. *There is no system of Theology or Philosophy that perfectly satisfies all the difficulties encountered regarding the origin of moral and physical evil.*
IX. *Knowledge of <term>Oriental languages</term> <note>In this period, this primarily meant Hebrew, Aramaic, and Syriac.</note>, ancient histories, customs, rites, and opinions cannot be acquired today in such a great measure as to suffice for understanding all passages of scripture, solving all difficulties and doubts, and reconciling all apparent contradictions.*
X. *Only He who is the Lord of salvation and destruction can decide what must necessarily be believed to achieve salvation, or what error excludes one from it.*

XI. *It is entirely false, as the Atheists contend, that the proposition "the world was made out of nothing" involves a contradiction.*
XII. *The weightiest argument for the immortality of human minds that reason provides must be sought from the moral virtues of God.*
XIII. *The definition of God provided by the illustrious <term>Wolff</term> <note>Christian Wolff (1679–1754), an influential Enlightenment philosopher who sought to prove religious truths through reason.</note>—namely, that He is a Being in whom is found a sufficient reason for the existence of all things—is quite harmless, and is as different as the whole sky from the delusions of <term>Spinoza</term>.* <note>Baruch Spinoza was often accused of "Atheism" or "Pantheism" (identifying God with nature), which the author here rejects.</note>

XVIII. *Since we have adequate knowledge of neither the mind nor the body, it follows that no system can be constructed to explain the union that exists between body and mind based on demonstrable principles.*
XIX. *Although all hypotheses about the "commerce" <note>Interaction or communication.</note> between body and mind are subject to various difficulties, the system of <term>occasional causes</term> <note>Occasionalism: the theory that created substances cannot be efficient causes of events, but rather God causes every movement on the "occasion" of a mental or physical change.</note> seems to us the most dangerous of all and hostile to Religion.*

#### *Section I.*

<margin>A transition is made to listing the following causes of Unbelief.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring floral motifs and a central figure within a square frame.</image-desc> We now approach the other causes that can cast the minds of men into the vice of *Unbelief*. And here, above all, if we wished to follow the natural order of discourse, we should speak of the false and foolish opinions with which men are everywhere imbued—opinions that clash with the most holy tenets of Religion. For it is established by sad experience—alas!—that many false, trivial, and indeed pestilential opinions, unworthy of the Majesty of the Divinity, have been accepted among men and are most deeply fixed in their minds, especially among the common people. These not only stand in the way of pure and chaste Religion and the rational <note>original: "$\lambda o \gamma \iota \kappa o \varsigma$" (logikos)</note> worship of the Divinity taking root in the soul, but they also lead others to think meanly of Religion, causing the Unbeliever to cling to these seized-upon opinions as if to a rock. Furthermore, such is the nature of preconceived opinions that they are not easily removed from the mind: the deeper the roots they have struck, the more difficult they are to pull out. Not wrongly did the illustrious Verulam <note>Referring to Francis Bacon, Lord Verulam (1561–1626), an influential philosopher of the scientific revolution.</note> call such commonly accepted opinions the *Idols of the Human Race*. For just as a man captured by foul superstition and bound by a vain fear of Gods or Saints not only thinks of them with magnificence and reverence and accepts all the fables handed down about them, but attempts and does nothing without first consulting these

<meta>catchword: so</meta>

<column-break/>

<page-num>49</page-num>
<header>ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.</header>

so dear Protectors, and even wishes ill upon all who seem to detract from their merits, Power, and Majesty; so too are men usually affected when imbued and deluded by foolish opinions. They highly prize the views on Religion they received from childhood, kissing them as if they were axioms subject to no exceptions, and ultimately measuring their reasonings and actions against them as if against a touchstone. But if we turn our minds to contemplating these opinions, it will be clear that they are not so much born with the mind itself, nor drawn from its nature and character, but are rather due to poor Instruction, Education, Reading, or the examples of others. Therefore, they should be referred to *external causes* that can invite the mind toward *Unbelief*, rather than to *internal* ones that spring, so to speak, from the bottom of the heart. It is necessary, therefore, before we deal with those opinions hostile to Religion that draw their origin from elsewhere, that we first concern ourselves with the *internal* causes leading the soul away from pure Religion.

<margin>Corrupt inclinations and passions of the soul are the primary causes of Unbelief.</margin> II. And here, if we rightly contemplate the nature and constitution of the human mind, we first encounter those small inclinations and affections of men which Philosophers usually call *Passions* <term>Affects</term> <note>The Latin "Affectus" refers to emotional states or impulses that move the soul, often contrasted with calm reason.</note>. Regarding these Passions viewed in themselves—their origin, nature, and power—we shall not say much, since these are treated at great length by Philosophers and students of moral disciplines, and are outside our current purpose. We shall only mention a few things about them that seem relevant to our goal. By passions (to reveal our mind in a few words), we understand corrupt inclinations and more violent disturbances of the soul by which, having neglected the laws of reason and despised divine and human commands, men meditate upon, strive for, and desire with all their heart only those things which are pleasing, delightful, and acceptable to themselves. Inclinations of the mind, viewed in themselves, are not evil; indeed, they were wisely implanted in our minds by the supreme Moderator of all things and are entirely necessary for exercising every kind of virtue. However, they become evil not only when they are too violent and harm the powers of the mind and body, but especially when they are not subjected to the Decrees of right reason and the norm of the divine will. Reason was given to us by the Best Divinity for this purpose: to hold command over our inclinations and the affections of the soul like a Ruler. The precepts of reason and Revelation are the norms according to which we are bound to arrange our actions. When these are neglected, men live a beast-like rather than human life

<header>MEDITATION II.</header>

...men live. But these things are better known than to need a prolonged explanation. It is established, however—as no one is ignorant—that most mortals, captured by sinister opinions and driven by perverse affections of the soul, measure their judgments and actions not so much by the standard of truth and right, nor by the rules of the most soul-strengthening precepts, but rather by the wicked desires of the heart. Moreover, such is the nature of these passions that the deeper they have driven their roots into the soul, the more men obey them, dragging the other faculties into agreement, or rather, binding them as if with chains. The intellect, which is the light of the mind, is darkened; or to speak more clearly, the vehemence of the will and the passions causes men to wish to conceive and judge things in such a way that pleases a mind captured by perverse opinions and baited by the love of forbidden things. Hence, everywhere that moral matters are discussed, you may hear men—otherwise not unlearned and well-cultivated in various disciplines—arguing most perversely because they are captured by wicked pursuits. Indeed, you could often scarcely persuade yourself that such a different way of judging and feeling could exist within the same man. Just as those more violent impulses bring harm to all faculties of the mind, so they especially obstruct the light of the intellect, which is the eye of the mind. **Boethius** <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher and author of *The Consolation of Philosophy*.</note> rightly said:
> The mind is clouded
> And bound with bridles
> Where these [passions] rule.

Hence our Holy Savior <note>original: "Soter"</note> says in Matthew 6:23: *But if your eye is bad, your whole body will be full of darkness; if then the light that is in you is darkness, how great is that darkness!* <note>original Greek: "Ἐὰν δὲ ὁ ὀφθαλμός σου πονηρὸς ᾖ..."</note> With these warnings of the Savior agree those things which are cited everywhere by **Hierocles** <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> in his Commentary on the *Golden Verses of Pythagoras*. Thus, immediately after the beginning on page 4 of the Curterius edition, he says: *Just as it is impossible for a bleary and unpurified eye to see very bright things, so it is impossible for a soul that does not possess virtue to mirror the beauty of truth.* (*) <note>original Greek: "ὥσπερ γὰρ ὀφθαλμῷ λημῶντι..."</note> that is: *For as an eye laboring under inflammation and not cleansed cannot see things that are very bright, so the beauty of truth is not discerned by a soul lacking virtue.* And on page 282: *Since in showing something, he indicates that the actions of two persons must run together into one (for how could you show what you wish to a blind man, even if you presented it a thousand times? Or how could you show it to one who sees if you presented nothing?), it is necessary for both to be present...*

*...it is necessary for both to be present: both the good presented by the one who shows, and the discerning eye of the one to whom it is shown, so that the object seen may meet with the vision itself to complete the demonstration.* <note>original Greek: "παρεῖναι δεῖ..."</note> That is: *Since indeed, for the purpose of showing any thing to anyone, it is established that the actions of two persons must concur into one (for how could you show what you desire to a blind man, even if you brought it forth a thousand times? Or how would you demonstrate to one who sees that which you do not bring forth?), it is certainly fitting that both be present: the good proposed by him who shows, and the eye capable of seeing it belonging to him to whom the thing is shown; so that on one hand the object of sight, and on the other the vision itself, may concur to the effect of the demonstration.*

That these passions are the cause preventing men from judging rightly about the most serious matters—especially those pertaining to Religion—will be noticed by all who attend for a moment to the nature of **Truth**. For while in the inquiry of truth, consideration should only be given to the connection of propositions from which the knowledge of error or truth arises, men instead are carried away by powerless passions and look only to those things which are pleasing and acceptable. It is no wonder, then, that they most willingly acquiesce in those conclusions and opinions that conspiratorially agree with the wicked desires of the soul. If the mind is once breathed upon by this plague, there is nothing so inept and ridiculous, nothing so monstrous and detestable, that those men will not approve and defend with their assent.

This holds true most especially, as I have said, in matters regarding Religion and the duties of piety. The goal of the true—that is, the Christian—Religion is not primarily to make us sharper, more learned, or more eloquent, but to make us better, or as I may speak with the **Apostle Paul** in 2 Timothy 3:17, so that we may be *equipped for every good work.* <note>original Greek: "πρὸς πᾶν ἔργον ἀγαθὸν... ἐξηρτισμένους"</note> This Religion, as the same **Apostle** warns in Romans 12:2, wants us *to be transformed by the renewal of the mind.* <note>original Greek: "μεταμορφοῦσθαι τῇ ἀνακαινώσει τοῦ νοὸς"</note> *This divine Philosophy,* to use the words of **Erasmus**, *teaches us to do, not just to say. This is situated in pious affections rather than in Syllogisms; it is life more than dispute, inspiration rather than Erudition, and finally transformation more than mere reason.* He who weighs these things will easily perceive that men captured by wicked passions and devoted to vices cannot judge rightly and sincerely about such holy and divine matters. It is one thing to judge historical or critical matters, or philosophical questions that do little or nothing to form one’s character; it is quite another to weigh dogmas which, by their nature and the most evident laws of consequence, bind minds to live piously and to say farewell to all wicked desires, and indeed under the penalty of eternal destruction. For it cannot happen otherwise than that...

...that such men, having heard such unpleasant <note>original: "ingratis"</note> precepts, become indignant, and either wish to interpret them in a completely different way or deny that they are worthy of any attention at all. Lest some should cry out that I say these things in vain, I shall bring forward, as a means of confirmation, the words of two <term>theologians</term> <note>A theologian is a scholar who studies the nature of the divine, religious truth, and practice.</note> most eminent in learning, piety, and genius—namely, Samuel *Werenfels* and *Jean-Frédéric Osterwald*—who were occupied with this same argument. The former, in his examination of the question: *Why the Incentives of Scripture are often Ineffective*, on page 149 of the earlier edition, speaks thus: *Men immersed in the world lose all taste for spiritual goods: so much so that, in the end, they are no more fit for knowing and perceiving them than a "pig from the herd of Epicurus" <note>This is a famous quote from the Roman poet Horace, used to mock those who seek only physical pleasure and ignore the soul.</note>, who spends his life fattening his belly, is able to conceive of the kind of pleasure a Philosopher takes in the contemplation of truth. For it is certain that most greedy, ambitious, and pleasure-seeking men have a taste so depraved that nothing is savory to them except their gold and silver; to those [the ambitious], nothing is sweet except when they feel themselves pulled from the crowd and pointed out with a finger; these [the pleasure-seekers], finally, can conceive of no idea of pleasure in their minds except that which strikes the coarse organs of the senses. Propose to these people goods of another kind, however excellent, and it is just as if you were commending the beauty of form to a blind man, or praising the sweetness of music to the deaf.* 

The latter [Osterwald], however, in his most useful and fruitful little book titled *The Source of Corruption* <note>original: "Source de la corruption"</note>, on page 249, according to the Latin version of the celebrated *Werenfels* himself, explains his mind in this way: *It is impossible for religion and virtue to be loved by one who has surrendered his heart to the world. "No one," says Christ (Matthew 6:24), "can serve two masters," and John (1 John 2:15) denies that the love of God is in him who loves the world. Spiritual things are so distant from corporeal things that all those who are deeply occupied with the latter become unfit for the former. Indeed, by those earthly cares, men are gradually made so carnal—and, if one may say so, they become so "fattened up" and brutish—that, like beasts, they perceive nothing except what affects the senses. What else? That the soul is thus gradually nourished by ignorance and sloth, and all its inclinations are fixed to the earth. When things reach this point, spiritual goods become vile, and man is rendered incapable of valuing them according to their merit or seeking them with sincere zeal. And who, I ask, will believe that those who think of nothing else than how they might scrape together wealth, court the favor of the powerful, or scramble toward dignities and honors—who, I say, will believe that these people can be touched by any care for salvation? No one fails to see that such diverse cares cannot exist at the same time.* So says that pious and distinguished <term>theologian</term>.

<margin>Ambition is especially harmful to religion.</margin>
III. Among all the passions hostile to religion, and which can easily drive men headlong into the vice of *Unbelief*, you may rightly include *Ambition*. Those who labor under this vice not only think magnificently of themselves and their own virtues, but they also burn with an incredible desire for praise and honor. The pursuit of these things impels them to look about anxiously for ways to achieve a reputation for genius and learning. It is not so much the unlearned, the dull, or those uncultivated in any discipline who tend to fall into this vice, but rather the half-learned, or even those adorned with a more outstanding intellect. Most of this number do not cultivate letters <note>In this context, "letters" refers to literature, philosophy, and academic study.</note> so that they might turn out wiser and better, but rather so that they might acquire, by any means, the reputation of being learned and sharp-witted men. 

Hence, they are entirely devoted to imbuing the mind with the knowledge of various—especially abstruse—matters, so that they might hold forth on everything, dispute against anyone, tear down what is unshakable, and devise new opinions and sentiments (even if they will be of no use to the human race), and thus "fly through the mouths" <note>A Latin idiom meaning to become famous or a common topic of conversation.</note> of celebrated men. Whatever, therefore, can contribute anything toward achieving that praise, they seize most greedily. It is not the intention here to show how shamefully many of those vexed by that empty glory and reputation for learning have often made themselves a laughingstock. This would lead us too far from our purpose. It must only be proven by us that those burning with *Ambition* and an immense desire for praise are often swept away into *Unbelief*. 

Doubtless, these men know that those things which pertain to religion and the worship of the Divine are held by most mortals to be most sacred and of the greatest importance; they are, moreover, not ignorant that many Articles of Religion are given which are admitted by all—or at least most, and even the most learned and sharp-witted men—as the most certain and evident truths. Therefore, they think it is to their advantage to tear down those things which seem most certain, weighty, and unshakable, and to bring forward new and paradoxical opinions about religion into the public eye. They hope, if possible, to shake the arguments of the most learned men, with which they have hitherto defended religion, so that everyone, having heard such rare and unheard-of propositions and objections, will be swept into the greatest astonishment, and will admire such sharpness of genius and rare gifts of mind, extolling them to the heavens with public praise. Fired by this zeal, they not only defend the most monstrous opinions in conversations and writings, and laugh at and explode <note>In the older sense of "hissing off the stage" or rejecting with contempt.</note> the most serious heads of religion, but they also apply every care and anxiety so that these rare...

Their <note>original: "Ευρηματα" (Heurēmata)</note> "discoveries" must be made known to the learned world. Below, by introducing the most obvious examples, we shall prove how greatly that foul plague—I mean *Ambition*—has corrupted the finest minds. Here it is helpful to bring forward only two examples. The first is that of John Toland, that famous <term>Atheist</term> <note>A term often used broadly in this period for anyone challenging orthodox Christian dogma.</note> or <term>Deist</term> <note>A Deist believes in a creator who does not intervene in the universe; Toland was a controversial Irish-born philosopher.</note>. For he defended the most foolish opinions, to the detriment of his fortune and reputation, right until the end of his life. When he was still a young man devoting himself to literature at Leiden...

(*) Even *Epicurus* himself, whom *Lucretius* extols with such great praise, was seized by a most vain desire for glory, if we believe *Plutarch*. For he was so insanely obsessed with glory from his very swaddling clothes, and so agitated for it, that he not only denied having used any teachers, but also quarreled with Democritus over syllables and accents (even though he had stolen Democritus's doctrines word-for-word). For just as bodies deprived of food are forced by hunger to seek nourishment from themselves against nature, so ambition produces this evil in souls: that being greedy for praise, when it is not bestowed by others, they praise themselves."

...in the Netherlands, and was especially applying himself to the study of Church Antiquity under the guidance of the celebrated *Spanheim*, and making no small progress in learning, he boasted that as soon as he arrived in England, he would become the head of a new sect. Certainly, *Locke*, *Le Clerc*, and *Molyneux*—most learned men and skillful judges of character—perceived early on that Toland suffered gravely from this "disease" of ambition. See the celebrated *Mosheim* discussing these matters at greater length in his *Commentary on the Life, Fate, and Writings of Toland*, page 23 and following.

A second example is provided by a certain *Anonymous* writer who, in a letter sent to the famous *Le Clerc* and inserted into the *Ancient and Modern Library*, contended that the "fable" about Christ and his Apostles' writings only arose in the fifth century. He claimed that during the great <term>Migration of Nations</term> <note>This refers to the period between AD 300–500 when various tribes moved across Europe, leading to the fall of the Western Roman Empire.</note> in that century, certain fraudulent impostors came from the remotest regions of the North and forged the New Testament and all those other monuments of the Christian religion (as we other "little men" consider them). When the famous *Le Clerc* wished to teach this man better and urged him to look into himself and discern, <note>original: "αθερ παθων" (ater pathōn) — without passion</note> without passion, whether he had been led to defend such a monstrous and stupid opinion by foul ambition—recommending he read his booklet *On the Causes of Unbelief* for that purpose—the man replied that after a diligent reading of the book and searching all the corners of his mind, he found nothing that could induce him to change his opinion, much less could he admit that he had been carried away by pride, ambition, or any other foul affection.

And yet, who does not see that the opinion invented by this man is plainly stupid? Surely that ridiculous pride with which such men swell often blunts the edge of the intellect so much that they prefer to stubbornly defend the most absurd opinions rather than admit they were driven to bring forth paradoxical views by an insatiable desire for ambition. This affection receives a great boost from the praise of others. Indeed, there is never a shortage of men—either of a similar madness (that is, stung by the gadfly of ambition) or flatterers and parasites—who raise to the heavens with praise the inventors of new, paradoxical, and even the most foolish opinions. To be sure, it is a fine thing to be praised and for it to be said: "This is that incomparable man, who was the first and only one to look into the vanity of all sciences; who showed to the eye that the principles of mathematical disciplines rest on no foundation at all; who declared war on all religion and tramples it under his feet; who has thoroughly embarrassed all the ministers of holy things and exposed their frauds..."

# MEDITATION II.

...he uncovered frauds with a fearless spirit, and so on. Is it any wonder that a man swollen with pride and the love of praise—by those flattering and most pleasant words and acclamations—should raise his crest, knit his brows, and nearly burst with vanity? But let such men be mindful of the saying of **Aristotle**, or whoever the author of the *Great Ethics* may be (Book I, chapter 5), who declared: <note>original: "Ἐάν τινα ποιήσῃς ἄφοβον ὡς τε μήτε Θεὸς φοβεῖσθαι ἐκ ἀνδρίος, ἀλλὰ μαινόμενος"</note> *If you make someone so fearless that they do not even fear the Gods, they are no longer brave, but insane.* (*) Hence, it is also difficult for these men to be brought back to a sounder mind. The distinguished philosopher **Epictetus** saw this in his own time; for after he had recounted and exploded the perverse opinions of the Academics and Epicureans <note>The Academics were skeptics, while the Epicureans were often accused of atheism for claiming gods do not intervene in human affairs.</note>, he adds these words at the end of Chapter XX, Book II, as recorded by **Arrian**: <note>original: "πολὺ νὴ Δία μᾶλλον τες κιναίδες ἐλπίσει τις ἂν μεταπείσειν, ἢ τες ἐπὶ τοσῦτον ἀποκεκωφωμένες καὶ ἀποτετυφλωμένες τῶν περὶ αὑτὲς κακῶν"</note> *By Zeus, one might sooner hope to change the mind of a profligate than those who have become so deaf and blind to the evils surrounding them.*

<margin>Many other evils are often joined with this wicked affection.</margin>
**IV.** From this wicked disposition of the mind, other evils often follow. For such people not only defend all kinds of paradoxes that are hostile to Religion and abhorrent to any appearance of truth, but, puffed up and blinded by vain pride, they wish everything to be referred back to themselves. They bear adverse fate with a most unjust spirit and dispute the causes of their own and others' misfortunes with "unwashed mouths" <note>A Latin idiom meaning to speak irreverently or without proper preparation.</note> and a lack of that reverence owed to the best Divinity. When everything does not succeed according to their heart’s desire, they begin to doubt whether there is a Ruler of the world. They themselves wish to walk only through lilies and roses, and they believe that God, in favor of men endowed with such great talent, judgment,

and erudition, ought to ensure that they are esteemed by all, that they live in an abundance of all things, and that everyone—as if in a formed column—should rush to praise and heap honors and benefits upon men adorned with such great virtues and endowed with such excellent talent. (*) Unless I am greatly mistaken, we must also attribute to this passion, among other things, that excessive zeal for investigating all the ways of God, and the causes of why He permitted both moral and physical evil, or why He did not create this world differently. The question is not whether the **Providence** of God ought to be defended against Unbelievers or not; nor whether true solaces should be offered to mortals struggling with various adversities—for no one of sound mind doubts this. Rather, the question is chiefly this: after it is more than sufficiently known and demonstrated that it is impossible for us to know all the causes and ends of divine counsels, or to unravel all the doubts that occur regarding the administration of the world in the realms of Nature and Grace (especially when one comes down to this or that individual case), is it not consistent with reason if, having dismissed curious disquisitions and <term>hypotheses</term>—which for the most part do not remove difficulties but increase them, and provide material for the unbelieving to triumph—we stand firm in those things that serve to celebrate the divine virtues, and in the rest, admit our ignorance? Certainly, he takes much upon himself—and has never, or rarely, thought about the weakness of human minds and the very narrow boundaries of human knowledge—who thinks he can perceive with total accuracy the causes of all divine counsels and events occurring in the administration of the human race.

---

(*) Lest anyone think there are hardly any examples of men so dull and seized by such inept Pride, I will provide one, which was communicated to me by letter by the most celebrated and kindly man, **C. A. Heumannus**, a very famous theologian in the University of Göttingen. He wrote thus in a letter dated July 24, 1728: *Before I finish writing, I want you to know that I once encountered a truly atheistic man, who said, or rather feigned, that his name was Willenberg. He was skilled beyond the common sort in Medicine and Mathematics and wished to be called by the title of Doctor. When asked by me to produce a demonstration of his "non-existence of God," he reasoned thus: "If God exists, it follows that there is a providence. But the latter is false, therefore the former is also false." "Prove," I said, "that there is no Providence." Behold the proof of this fool-philosopher: "I am," he said, "a man endowed with the highest wisdom and erudition, and so excellent in virtues that I lack every vice; and yet I must live miserably, and I wander perpetually. Therefore, there is no God. For if there were a God, He could not bear for a man so learned and so good to be miserable."* After he had narrated this, that most learned man added: *I know you will be in doubt, best of men, whether to follow this man's madness with laughter or with pity; I do not know where he was carried off to afterwards.*
