# MEDITATION II.
## ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

III.) These same unsound men, either to win a semblance of truth for the intricate opinions they cherished, or to cover their own ignorance, used certain barbaric words under which they nevertheless asserted sublime mysteries were hidden; by this very act, they deservedly earned a reputation for foolish, arrogant character. For he who seriously loves the truth, and desires to commend it to others whom he believes to be mistaken, acts with every ounce of effort to use clear and transparent words to introduce it; above all, he is concerned with this if the things he brings forward are new, or if the subject is known but new vocabulary must be used to explain it. But who is unaware of how many intricate and perplexed words *Valentinus* <note>Valentinus (c. 100–160 AD) was the most influential Gnostic Christian theologian, known for his complex cosmology of 'Aeons.'</note> used? It is true indeed that the words *pleroma* <term>Pleroma (Fullness)</term>, *bythos* <term>Bythos (the Deep or the Abyss)</term>, and so on, are employed in the New Testament; but all learned men know that this was done in a sense plainly different from what that teller of monstrosities <note>original Greek: τερατολογος (teratologos) - a speaker of marvels or tall tales, often used as a derogatory term for someone making up myths.</note> intended. Meanwhile, he never clearly explained his own mind, nor exhibited accurate definitions, nor was he even able to give them. Hence, not only do modern scholars get stuck in explaining those words, but even the most ancient Fathers—*Irenaeus* <note>Irenaeus of Lyons, a 2nd-century bishop who wrote 'Against Heresies' to debunk Gnostic systems.</note> for example, who was the first to present the Valentinian system—did not always have a clear view of the true meaning of his vocabulary. The illustrious *Le Clerc* <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), a famous Swiss theologian and critic.</note> judged *Valentinus* quite to the point and according to my own thinking in his *Ecclesiastical History, page 586*, speaking thus: *Furthermore, if Valentinus had only wished to say things that were already agreed upon among Christians, he was a mere charlatan who veiled his ignorance with new words; and if he withdrew from other Christians only for the sake of these words, he must have been an impostor and a turbulent spirit. But if he thought he was bringing to light something new and previously unknown, as it seems he did, he ought to have spoken more clearly, or at least not used words to which only an absurd meaning could be attributed, and because of which his opinion would be rejected as ridiculous by all men of sound brain. It is not a fault that anyone can forgive if the truth is expressed in such a way that it can be brought into disrepute because of it; nor could I easily persuade myself that there was anyone who, having exceptional things to say, would want to clothe them in obscure and absurd speech.* Similarly, *Basilides* <note>Basilides was an early Gnostic religious teacher in Alexandria who taught during the 2nd century.</note>, besides those things he had babbled about the orders of Aeons, spirits, and heavens, used certain barbaric words in explaining which scholars sweat in vain. Thus, what that *cau-lacau* <note>A mystical term used by Basilides, likely a corruption of a Hebrew phrase from Isaiah 28:10 meaning 'line upon line.'</note> of *Basilides* signifies, even the most learned interpreters of *Irenaeus*, *Grabe* and *Massuet*, confess they do not know. In explaining the words *Abraxas* and *Abracadabra*, *Chifflet*, *Basnage*, *Beausobre*, and others twist themselves marvelously. Yet this impostor contended not only that there was a miraculous power in this word *Abraxas* inscribed on gems, but also that those who were capable of his discipline

<column-break/>

could strive straight for heaven and not be seen by the Angels, just as was also done by *Cau-Lacau*. See *Irenaeus, Book I, page 81, Massuet edition.* <margin>(*)</margin> Many similar things occur in the system of *Mani* <note>Mani (c. 216–274 AD), the founder of Manichaeism, which taught a dualistic struggle between light and darkness.</note>, just as the most learned *Beausobre* has shown at length, to say nothing of others. Are these not clear enough traces of imposture, ridiculous pride, and impudence?

IV.) These same men do not hesitate to deny the most evident points of the Christian religion and to twist them into a ridiculous sense, so that they might seek protection for their own inept hypotheses and the ravings of their brains. To be sure, there have always been, and still are, among scholars those who strive to reconcile preconceived opinions with the decrees of the Christian religion; but this is usually done (at least by the more modest) only where either the text of the Holy Scriptures itself is somewhat obscure, or where phrases and words here and there seem to be able to endure new explanations of that kind built upon non-negligible hypotheses. But these men interpreted the most evident points of religion, upon which the whole system of the Christian religion rested, against the clearest sense of the words. Thus, for example, among the most ancient heretics were those called *Docetae* <term>Docetists (from the Greek word for 'to seem'; they believed Jesus' physical body was an illusion)</term>. These seem to have arisen while the Apostles were still living; hence certain scholars have thought that *John the Evangelist, chapter 1, verse 14*, where he says the *Word* <note>original Greek: τον λογον (ton logon).</note> was made flesh, was looking toward these men. Certainly *Cotelerius* <note>Jean-Baptiste Cotelier (1629–1686), a French scholar of the early Church Fathers.</note>, a man most well-versed in Ecclesiastical antiquity, says in his notes to the *Epistle of Ignatius to the Romans, page 24*: *He would deny that the sun shines at midday, who would deny that the Docetae and phantom-believing heretics had broken out in the time of the Apostles.* The no less illustrious *Pearson* <note>John Pearson (1613–1686), Bishop of Chester and a noted theologian.</note> agrees in his *Vindication of Ignatius, Part II, chapter 1, page 344*. But whatever the case may be, this is more than clear enough from the monuments of the ancients: that those heretics, called Docetists, denied that Jesus Christ had a true body and truly suffered, but was clothed in a shadow instead of a body. Others distinguished Jesus from Christ; all the rest, to pass over other things, asserted that the world was created by evil angels. But the reason why they descended into these paradoxical and pestilential opinions was that they firmly believed matter was the cause of evil. But what, I appeal to everyone’s conscience, is more open and clear from a reading of the New Testament?

than that Jesus had a true body, that he ate, drank, spoke with others, walked, and so on? Can these things be said of a man destitute of a body? Who does not recall the equally unsound opinion of *Epicurus* <note>Epicurus (341–270 BC) was a Greek philosopher who taught that the gods existed in a state of perfect detachment and did not possess solid physical bodies.</note>, who asserted that the gods do not have a body, *but a quasi-body*; that they do not have blood, *but quasi-blood*—an idea mocked by *Cicero*? <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero was a Roman statesman and philosopher who criticized Epicurus's vague definitions in his work *On the Nature of the Gods*.</note> Who could believe that those men did not clearly see that once such a foolish thesis was posited, it would follow that Christ did not truly suffer, was not truly recalled to life from the dead, and did not truly ascend into the heavens? Could they not, moreover, easily conclude—since they spoke with such confidence and expressed their opinion in such clear words—that they were either destitute of common sense or were the most impudent of impostors? To put it in a word, did they not see that in this way the Christian religion is changed into a mere fable? Yet despite these facts, these terrible actors and impostors, in order to keep their highly uncertain hypothesis safe, do not hesitate to corrupt the clearest testimonies of Christ’s most faithful followers. The same may be said regarding the creation of the world. Who, unless he is of a deranged mind, could deny that Moses and all the writers of the Old and New Testaments asserted in the clearest words that this world was created by God? Nevertheless, even this dogma, which is clearer than light, had to be denied, lest a rashly adopted opinion might waver.

V.) Finally, those heretics, *having despised the dogmas of the Christian religion that were joined with some difficulty, devised hypotheses that were not only liable to far greater doubts, but were of such a kind that they required innumerable fictions to establish them with any appearance of truth.* It is permitted to all—indeed, all are bound—to profess and defend those dogmas which are weighed down by the fewest difficulties. He who would admit no religion except one that is everywhere plain, very easy to grasp, and liable to no doubts at all—or one consisting of continuous demonstrations equaling mathematical evidence—that man would have to believe either nothing at all or very few things indeed. The Christian religion hands down clearly and transparently all those things which can lead to the worship of God and the attainment of true happiness. But who can deny that many things are also handed down in it which we either do not know at all, or know only obscurely and imperfectly? To this category, setting aside many other things, belong the questions regarding the origin of moral and physical evil <note>The "problem of evil" asks how an all-powerful, all-good God can allow suffering (physical evil) and sin (moral evil) to exist.</note>. The question is asked, namely, by what reasoning can the permission of evil (to say nothing of more subtle hypotheses) be reconciled with the divine virtues? Revelation hands down many things to clarify that question—

<column-break/>

<page-num>87</page-num>
<header>ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.</header>

and the decrees of right reason add no small weight to them. But no prudent person would say that all difficulties can be solved, that the causes for the permission of evil can be given, or that sufficient reasons for the Divine Counsels can be provided to completely untie the knot. Meanwhile, everyone, to whatever sect they may be addicted, ought to strain all the powers of their intellect to vindicate the divine virtues and to devise a system that is liable to the fewest or no difficulties. Although, regarding this last point, I doubt whether it can ever be obtained in this current "fog of things." (*) But if we weigh the systems of the *Gnostics* <note>Gnostics were early religious groups who believed that the material world was created by an inferior or evil deity rather than the supreme God.</note>, of *Valentinus*, of the *Manichaeans* <note>Followers of Mani, who taught a dualistic struggle between a good realm of light and an evil realm of darkness.</note>, and of others—whether ancient *Philosophers* or *Heretics*—it will be established that those men, having dismissed Revelation, wished to devise systems that would be free from all difficulties regarding the origin of moral and physical evil. The goal itself is good and laudable, if they intended only this. But was Revelation itself and its most evident decrees to be attacked for that reason, twisted into the worst sense, or rendered suspect of being spurious <note>original Greek: νοθείας (notheias) - illegitimacy or tampering.</note>? Could those men persuade themselves that Christians—who had some reverence for God and the Holy Scriptures, and whom these unhealthy men wished to draw into their own opinion—could they, I say, persuade themselves that those Christians would immediately walk over to their side? Could it be, finally, that those men were unable to see that by seizing upon opinions built on no foundations, the difficulties occurring around this matter were clearly not

> (*) The illustrious *Leibniz* <note>Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646–1716) was a polymath who famously coined the term "Theodicy" to defend God's goodness in the face of evil.</note> himself, who entered upon a new way to solve the difficulties moved by Bayle <note>Pierre Bayle (1647–1706) was a skeptical philosopher who argued that the problem of evil could not be solved by human reason.</note> regarding this argument, indicated clearly enough that it cannot be done by the powers of the human intellect in this world that all difficulties occurring here be completely removed. For in the Preface of the book titled *Essays on Theodicy, etc.*, page 66, he brings forward these words of Bayle: <note>original: "M. Bayle a pu esperer, que son travail piqueroit d'honneur quelques un de ces grands genies qui forment de nouveaux systêmes & qu'ils pourroient inventer un denouëment inconnu jusqu'ici."</note> *“Mr. Bayle was able to hope that his work would prick the honor of some of those great geniuses who form new systems, and that they might be able to invent a solution [unraveling] unknown until now.”* To which, having been cited, he adds these things: <note>original: "Il semble que pour ce denouëment il entend une explication du Mystere, qui iroit jusqu'au comment, mais cela n'est point necessaire pour repondre aux objections."</note> *“It seems that by this 'solution' he means an explanation of the Mystery that would go as far as the 'how,' but that is not at all necessary to answer the objections.”* Truly, in the Dissertation annexed to this book, theses 143 and 144, he speaks thus: “But the Abyss <note>original: βυθὸς (bythos) - the Deep or the Void, a term Leibniz adopts from Gnostic vocabulary to describe the unsearchable depths of God.</note> itself lies hidden in the treasures of divine Wisdom, or in the ‘hidden God’ (which comes to the same thing) in the universal harmony of things; which made it so that this series of the universe—encompassing events which we marvel at and judgments which we adore—was judged by God to be the best and preferable to all others. But the most excellent part of things, the City of God, is a spectacle to whose beauty we shall finally be admitted more closely to know, once we are illuminated by the light of divine glory. For now, it can be reached only by the eyes of faith, that is, by the most certain trust in divine perfection; where, the more we understand that not only power and wisdom but also the goodness of the supreme mind is exercised, the more we are warmed by the love of God, and inflamed toward a certain imitation of divine goodness and justice.”

<summary>This page critiques early heretics for denying the physical reality of Christ and the biblical creation to avoid intellectual difficulties, arguing instead that faith must accept certain divine mysteries. It cites the philosopher Leibniz to show that while human reason has limits in explaining the origin of evil, divine goodness remains trustworthy.</summary>

# MEDITATION II.
## ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

<page-num>88</page-num>
<header>MEDITATION II.</header>

...not removed, but rather multiplied? For example, could they explain by what reasoning matter could be the cause of moral evil? From where did those "evil spirits" <note>original: "mali genii"</note> they imagined arise—were they from God, or truly from matter? Could they give sufficient reasons for how pure minds, once thrust into bodies, immediately become evil? Can they, according to those systems, explain to us the cause of why God permitted pure minds to be subject to so many miseries? Or why He gave those same evil spirits the power to build a world in which such great evils would take place? I pass over countless other things that could be objected to, for it is not my intention to show just how many difficulties those systems are liable to. There is no one, even moderately well-versed in these matters, who will not discover this upon reading those systems.

Added to this is the fact that, besides many insoluble difficulties, they had need of various supports to fashion their hypotheses—that is, highly precarious opinions which can be drawn with no appearance of truth either from the decrees of reason or of Revelation. These opinions, nevertheless, should have been proven by those "new theologians" before the entire system was properly joined together. Thus, they tell many stories about the *constitution of the intellectual world before all ages*; about the *pleroma* <note>A Gnostic term meaning "fullness," referring to the totality of divine powers.</note>; about *aeons* <note>Divine beings or emanations that mediate between God and the universe.</note> emanating from God or the intellectual world; about the *manner of this emanation*; about *various spirits and their orders*; about the *state of human minds before they were thrust into bodies*, and so forth. All of these are mere soothsaying and the dreams of idle men. 

It is not my intention to offer the entire series of such "profound" meditations to the reader's eyes. Let those who care for such things read the thoughts of the most learned men among the moderns—namely *Buddeus, Massuet, Basnage, Brucker, Beausobre*, and others—concerning the systems of *Valentinus* and the *Manicheans*. It will be manifest how clearly uncertain and flimsy the hypotheses were upon which their entire theology, or rather <term>vain talk <note>original: ματαιολογία (mataiologia)</note></term>, was built. Nevertheless, so that our students may have some taste of the "admirable" theological erudition of these men, I will set down here the principal propositions sought from the system of *Manes* <note>Also known as Mani (c. 216–274 AD), the Persian founder of Manichaeism.</note>. I do this all the more willingly because that man patched together most things from the principles of the *Gnostics* and *Valentinians* and enriched them, as was necessary, with his own excellent fabrications. He who wishes to know everything explained and illustrated more at length may consult the most learned work of the praised *Beausobre*.

->The following are the principal points:<-

1.) God is a living and immaterial Substance, residing in heaven from all eternity.

<column-break/>

<page-num>89</page-num>
<header>ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.</header>

2.) From all ages, aeons or spirits emanated from the Essence of God, because nothing can be made from nothing.
3.) The supreme heaven, and the celestial intelligences that dwell there, make up the *intelligible world*.
4.) The supreme heaven exists no less by itself than God does.
5.) The Son and the Holy Spirit emanated from the Essence of the Father. The *former* has fixed seats in the Sun and Moon; the *latter* resides in the air; here they execute the commands of the Father until the end of the world.
6.) In a certain corner of immense space, a certain malignant Substance has resided from all eternity; whether you call it matter, or a demon, or darkness, it is all the same.
7.) The empire of this malignant Substance was divided into five regions. In each region there were certain elements and living creatures, arisen from these elements.
8.) The commanders of the Kingdom of Darkness wanted to make an incursion into the Kingdom of Light; but God opportunely met the light through a certain being named the *first man*, with a company of five elements and a certain vivifying Spirit; yet it happened so that from that conflict a certain mixture of light and darkness arose thereafter.
9.) That vivifying Spirit distributed the subjugated demons into various regions of the air, in which they are accustomed to stir up storms, thunder, rain, and pestilence.
10.) Minds consist of a certain celestial light: but when thrust into bodies, they drink a certain poison, which once taken, causes them to forget all things.
11.) To counter this evil, God sent holy and wise men into the world, among whom was also Christ.
12.) Since flesh consists of matter, and all matter is evil, it could not be that Christ was clothed in flesh; and so he had only a shadow of a body, and therefore, properly speaking, he could not eat, drink, or suffer.
13) The crucifixion of Christ and His resurrection were at least mystical <note>In this context, meaning symbolic or allegorical rather than physical.</note>, from which, however, miserable minds bound by the chains of the body ought to learn how depraved affections are to be subdued.
14.) Purified minds will migrate to the Moon, to be delivered afterward to the Sun, from which they are to be carried to a place titled: *The Column of Glory*.
15.) The Holy Spirit is present as a help to all souls existing in the air; the Sun, truly, gradually wears away the dross still adhering to them, so that they can more easily ascend to the higher places.
16.) After all minds have been purged, God will command fire to come forth from I know not what caverns, and a certain angel called *Omophore* <note>The "world-bearer" in Manichean mythology who holds up the earth.</note> will cast the earth, which he has supported until now, into the fire, and will finally thrust the entire mass into a place outside the world which the Holy Scriptures call the *outer darkness*.

# MEDITATION II.

<page-num>90</page-num>

And these are the main components of the system of the *Manicheans* <note>Followers of Mani (3rd century AD) who believed the universe was a struggle between two equal powers: Good (Light/God) and Evil (Darkness/Matter).</note>. From these, any prudent person will be able to judge whether—given these groundless propositions—it is easier to solve the difficulties regarding the origin of evil than by using the answers provided by reason and Revelation. On the contrary, is it not clearer than the midday sun that these unbelievers have rejected the clear truths of Revelation because of certain difficulties, yet at the same time, moved by empty pride, have devised systems consisting mostly of mere inventions of the brain which do not remove the difficulties at all? But enough about those heretics.

We could deservedly add to this crowd the *most cunning impostor, Muhammad*, who used a variety of fraud and malice to establish his opinions (to say nothing of violence). However, everything that could be said on this subject has been collected with great industry, judgment, and integrity from Oriental writings and explained by the most learned *Gagnier in the life of this famous Impostor*, published in two octavo volumes. (*) We are indeed aware that before him, the *Count of Boulainvilliers* <note>Henri de Boulainvilliers (1658–1722), a French historian whose "Life of Mahomet" was seen by contemporaries as a veiled attack on Christianity.</note> set forth the life and teachings of *Muhammad*; but it was done in such a way that our thesis is wonderfully confirmed by his example. Specifically, it shows that unbelievers do not hesitate to pervert all the laws of history and utter the densest lies, if only they can detract from the Christian Religion. But it is no wonder these things were done by that nobleman, since it is known from other sources that he was a follower of the monstrous opinions of *Spinoza* <note>Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677), a philosopher whose radical rationalism and perceived pantheism were often equated with atheism by 18th-century theologians.</note>. See the preface of the most learned *Gagnier* to the work just mentioned.

(*) In the following dissertation, however, we shall bring forward from his work and from the writings of other learned men those points which seem to serve our purpose.

->A PAIR<-

# OF THEOLOGICAL THESES.

I. *Natural Religion is indeed sufficient to convict a person of their duty, but not to restore a sinner to God’s grace; for it belongs to the divine will alone both to receive a sinner into grace and to prescribe the condition through which they should be received.*

II. *The definition of faith provided by the author of the "Letters on Essential Religion" <note>Referring to the 1738 work "Lettres sur la religion essentielle" by Marie Huber, which argued for a simplified, non-dogmatic faith.</note>—namely, that it is the "evident perception of the Deity and His essential attributes"—is not only diametrically opposed to Revelation but also shakes the very foundations of Natural Religion.*

->PART III.<-

->Section I.<-

<margin>The connection with the preceding text and the author's purpose is shown.</margin>

In our second dissertation on the causes of the ever-increasing power of Unbelief, we showed through examples that many unbelievers reject the most serious points of both Natural and Revealed Religion, and sometimes even bitterly attack them. At the same time, however, they very frequently subscribe to the most uncertain propositions—indeed, sometimes to foolish and plainly absurd ones. From this, we conclude that such men, having despised the laws of right reason, defend only that which is pleasing and acceptable to their base desires. Indeed, we can hardly be led to believe that a person of sound mind—especially one who is learned and weighs everything by the standard of right reason—could reject a well-founded system or opinion as absurd and contrary to reason after thoroughly weighing all its parts, yet simultaneously and with equal attention give their approval in all seriousness to opinions which are not only more uncertain than those they rejected, but which in the judgment of the most learned men are plainly foolish and built on no foundation. The more these people see clearly and are educated in various disciplines, the less we believe that a lack of talent or judgment prevented them from subscribing to more evident...

decrees and opinions they have written. We know, of course, that it is not uncommon for many among Christians to defend inept and foolish opinions, while paying little attention to the most significant teachings that are most consistent with reason and the discipline of Jesus Christ. But these people, shrouded in a shameful ignorance and having never applied a serious examination to Religion, adhere to opinions they have swallowed as if with their mother's milk. It is no wonder that such people find rest in even the most foolish opinions; for they have no better understanding of their own religious views than they do of others. 

But those with whom we are now concerned have a thorough understanding of the character and nature of the Christian Religion; they well know the reasons upon which its truth is built and are generally men of great talent. Despite this, they uphold and defend opinions that are clearly weak and trivial, and they look down with high-minded disdain upon those who value the Christian Religion most highly. From this, we believe it is manifest that they were led to defend such monstrous opinions by ambition and a desire for fame, or by other no less shameful passions. We proved this in the second part of our dissertation by the example of the ancient and modern *Jews*, as well as certain *Heretics* of the Apostolic age. Since examples have a great influence on the minds of men and bring much light to the position we are defending, the Blessed Reader will not be surprised if, in this very dissertation, we confirm our thesis with more examples, both ancient and recent. To that end, I shall bring onto the stage from more remote centuries the Pythagorean-Platonic philosophers who vehemently attacked Religion, as well as the impostor *Muhammad*; and from the unbelievers of the more recent age, *Spinoza, Toland, Woolston*, and others.

II. Among those Platonic-Pythagorean philosophers <note>Commonly known today as Neoplatonists, these thinkers combined Plato's philosophy with mystical elements from Pythagoras to create a rival system to Christianity in the 3rd–5th centuries AD.</note>, the most eminent are *Plotinus, Porphyry, Iamblichus, Proclus, Hierocles, Amelius, Eunapius, Marinus, Julian* <note>Known as Julian the Apostate, the last pagan Roman Emperor.</note> and others. It is not my intention to explain the lives, fates, manners, and doctrines of these men, for that does not serve our purpose; most learned men have already done this abundantly. Two among them stand out: the first is the celebrated *Mosheim* <note>Johann Lorenz von Mosheim (1693–1755), a famous Lutheran church historian.</note>, both in his learned notes on *Cudworth’s Intellectual System* and in his unique dissertation *On the Church Disturbed by the Recent Platonists*. The second is that most learned and dear friend, *Johann Jakob Brucker*, in his *History of Philosophy, Volume III*. Here, he has not only accurately represented the lives and doctrines of these men but has also collected with great care and diligence everything that can serve to uncover their manners and deceptions.

He illustrated this matter with even greater diligence and an apparatus of learning in his *Critical History of Philosophy*, a work received with the applause of the learned. Those who wish to acquire a more accurate knowledge of the lives and doctrines of these philosophers should consult these works. 

Our sole intention is to prove, by the example of these philosophers, that on one hand they were moved by ambition and sectarian zeal to despise the most weighty principles of the Christian religion and often attacked them more bitterly than was right; while on the other hand, they gave their approval to the most uncertain and inept opinions—indeed, mostly mere delusions of a corrupted imagination. In doing this, we wish to take nothing away from the learning of these men, in which many flourished; on the contrary, we grieve that men endowed with no small talent and cultivated in the disciplines—living in times when the nature of the Christian religion could be sufficiently known and understood to captivate the minds of truth-lovers—should have allowed themselves to be so shamefully deceived by their passions. 

I here adopt the words of the most learned *Holstenius* <note>Lucas Holstenius (1596–1661), a German humanist and geographer who converted to Catholicism and worked in the Vatican Library.</note>, which on page six of his *Life of Porphyry (Cambridge Edition)* read as follows: *"I cannot help,"* he says, *"but pity the lot of the most excellent geniuses who lived at the time when the Christian Religion was raising a new and unaccustomed light for the minds of mortals—I mean Numenius, Plotinus, Porphyry, Amelius, and their like. These men, having perceived a taste of divine truth from the Holy Scriptures and the teachers of the nascent Church or from the mouths of Christian instructors, diverted the purest streams of truth into the muddy pools of Pythagoras and Plato, and obscured the sparks of divine light with the smoke and darkness of lies. For what would they not have achieved in the solid defense of truth, they who cultivated a few thin scraps of it with such admirable happiness of genius and rich elegance of speech that they drew the most learned leaders of the Christian Religion into admiration of them?"* So says *Holstenius*. 

Certain members of this crowd, such as *Porphyry, Hierocles, and Julian*, attacked the discipline of Christ with deliberate effort; yet they all simultaneously fashioned a theological system that was diametrically opposed to the life of our Savior, his miracles, and his decrees. Regarding *Porphyry*, it is well known that he was most hostile to the sacred rites of the Christians. By *Cyril (Book I against Julian, page 28)* he is called "the godless Porphyry who is against us" <note>original Greek: "ἄθεος καὶ ἡμᾶς πορφύριος"</note>. He was well-versed in the reading of the Old and New Testaments, and he strained every nerve of his intellect to find fault with them, according to the testimony of *Eusebius (Preparation for the Gospel, Book X, Chapter IX)*, *Theodoret (Healing of Greek Affections, Sermon VII)*, *Jerome (Letter 101 to Pammachius)* and others whom *Holstenius* cites in the *Life of Porphyry, Chapter X*. *Hierocles* wrote a book distinguished by the title: *The Lover of Truth* <note>original Greek: "λόγον φιλαλήθη"</note>, in which institutions between Christ...

It is well known from the writings of **Eusebius** and **Lactantius** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea and Lactantius were 4th-century Christian authors who wrote extensively against pagan philosophers.</note> that some have tried to prove, by way of comparison, that **Apollonius of Tyana** <note>A 1st-century Greek philosopher often portrayed by pagans as a wonder-working rival to Jesus.</note> was far superior to our **Christ**. **Philostratus**, a follower of this sect, intended the same in his *Life of Apollonius*. Finally, it is known to everyone that **Julian** <note>Emperor Julian "the Apostate" (reigned 361–363 AD), who attempted to revive Roman paganism.</note> frequently attacked **Christ** and his decrees.

<margin>It is shown first through the example of Porphyry that he attacked the Christian religion because of certain slight difficulties, while at the same time he fiercely defended the most absurd ideas.</margin>
III. To prove that these philosophers, though captivated by foolish opinions, wished to disparage the decrees and excellence of the Christian religion while simultaneously subscribing to the most absurd views, we shall reduce our observations to certain propositions (albeit briefly). First (1), these men dismiss the Apostles as "idiots" and simpletons, claiming they cannot be trusted; yet at the same time, they slander them by claiming they were shrewd and fraudulent. **Lactantius** testifies to this in *Divine Institutes*, Book III, chapter II, when discussing **Porphyry** <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD), a Neoplatonist and fierce critic of Christianity.</note> or **Hierocles**. *Especially,* he says, *he tore into Paul and Peter and the other disciples as sowers of deceit, yet he also testified that these same men were unrefined and unlearned, for he noted that some of them made their living by the craft of fishing—as if he were offended that some Aristophanes or Aristarchus had not composed the story instead.* <note>Aristophanes and Aristarchus were famous Greek literary figures; the critic is mocking the "low-class" origins of the New Testament writers.</note> Here you see the character of a shameless man who shifts into every possible shape just to disparage the truth: the Apostles and Disciples of Jesus Christ are "idiots" <note>original: "Idiotæ"; in this context, it refers to common, uneducated people rather than a modern slur.</note> barely endowed with common sense; yet, if it pleases the gods and those like **Porphyry**, they are also the most cunning men the earth has ever produced. **Porphyry** accuses the Apostles of cunning and deceit here, yet in his *Life of Pythagoras* and his *Life of Plotinus*, he casts aside all shame and relates such obvious lies and stinking fables that only a person with a disturbed mind could listen to them. If you were to compare the books of **Porphyry** and **Plotinus** regarding "the intelligible realms" <note>original: "τοις νοητοις" (tois noētois); a Platonic term for the world of pure ideas.</note> and the "Cave of the Nymphs," everyone who examines these things impartially <note>original: "ἀμεροληπτως" (amerolēptōs)</note> will admit that the writings of those "idiots" are pure light when compared to the difficult nonsense of these miracle-mongers. I have said that **Porphyry** poured out many stinking lies in the lives of **Pythagoras** and **Plotinus**. This is so obvious that to have read him is to have proven it. For instance, he reports (as does **Iamblichus**, a man of the same sort) in the *Life of Pythagoras*, page 112 of **Küster’s** edition, that **Pythagoras** was present on one and the same day in **Metapontum** in Italy and **Tauromenium** in Sicily, and spoke with the disciples in both places, despite the vast distances of land and sea between them, which no one could cross in many days. **Philostratus** tells similar things about his own fanatic, **Apollonius**, in Book 10, chapter X. And yet these men regard Christ's disciples and Apostles as deceptive triflers, unworthy of our trust

trust when they narrate the things done by Christ in a simple style. But these men of such "sublime genius" are not content with this; they openly assert that it is permissible to lie if it seems to benefit religion—that is, if it benefits the foolish opinions they were defending. It is true, of course, that among all sects and orders of men there have always been those who had little regard for the truth; especially, there are many who, when telling the history of religious matters, explain in great and accurate detail those things that are dishonorable to their opponents, but when they come to narrating the fate of their own sect, they tend to cover up the vices of their own people, interpret misdeeds kindly, change the circumstances, or pass over them in total silence. And while they do this, they still wish to be seen and held as good men and honest narrators of events. But in these men we are now discussing, every bit of shame has vanished from their brow. They assert it is *permissible* to act this way: you could call these men **"Jesuits before the Jesuits."** <note>The author is comparing the pagan philosophers to his contemporary theological enemies, the Jesuits, whom he accuses of intellectual dishonesty.</note> For although there have been those since the beginning of the world who used "mental reservations"—having one thing closed in their heart and another ready on their tongue—and although honest and truthful men are, alas, very rare birds on earth, very few (if you set aside certain companions of **Loyola** <note>Ignatius of Loyola, the founder of the Jesuit order.</note>) have progressed to such a degree of impudence that they dared to publicly defend these most shameless, pestilential errors, devised for the destruction of civil society. The former does so in his *Dissertation on the Church disturbed by the New Platonists*, Section XXIV and following; the latter in his *History of Philosophy*, Volume II, page 1019. Indeed, a mere reading of the biography of **Pythagoras** written by **Iamblichus** and **Porphyry** will convince anyone of the truth of our assertion.

...incited by zeal for public affairs to act in such a way: we must therefore be content with the small objections of **Porphyry** <note>A Phoenician Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 AD) and one of the most formidable intellectual opponents of early Christianity.</note> that survive here and there. **Jerome** <note>Saint Jerome (c. 342–420 AD), the scholar responsible for the Vulgate Latin Bible, who frequently quoted his opponents to refute them.</note> mentions the objection just cited in the *Preface to his Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians*, saying: <note>original: "Quod nequaquam intelligens Bataneotes & sceleratus ille Porphyrius..."</note> "That scoundrel Porphyry from Batanea, not understanding this at all, objected in the first book of his work against us that Peter was rebuked by Paul because he 'did not walk uprightly' in preaching the Gospel. He intended to stain the one with the mark of error and the other with the mark of impudence, and to accuse them both of lying about a fabricated doctrine, since the leaders of the Churches were in disagreement." He testifies to the same in *Letter 89 to Augustine* and elsewhere. The same **Jerome** (or whoever the author of the *Commentaries on Psalm 77* may be) testifies that **Matthew** was accused of ignorance because, in Chapter 13, verse 35, he supposedly wrote "**Isaiah**" instead of "**Asaph**" the Prophet. Indeed, **Christ** our Savior was accused of inconstancy and changeability because in **John**, Chapter 7, verse 8, he said: "You go up to this feast; I am not going up," and yet he later went up. From these examples, it is easily seen what **Porphyry** took it upon himself to prove: namely, that there are places in the writings of the Apostles that clash with one another, and that the first followers were inconsistent in the articles of Religion, and finally, driven by the corrupt passions of pride, they rebuked one another. But certainly, the points brought forward here are not so great that the faith of the Apostles should waver because of them. It is not my intention here to labor over proving and vindicating the honesty and truthfulness of the Evangelists and Apostles, but at least to offer a few reminders on the occasion of **Porphyry’s** objections. First, even if it were granted that there are such places in the Old and New Testaments that can only be reconciled with difficulty, it by no means follows that the entire history is false, or that the authors did not agree on the core of the matter; for the former can easily happen for many reasons. One would have to prove that the Apostles and Evangelists did not agree on the history of the life and death of the Holy Savior, and on the Articles of Religion that constitute the essence of Christian discipline—which is utterly false. The **Great Grotius** <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch jurist and theologian whose "On the Truth of the Christian Religion" was a standard work of defense for the faith.</note> summarized the points to be opposed to this objection in his golden little book *On the Truth of the Christian Religion*, Book III, whose words are worth setting down here: "It is often objected by some," he says, "that there is sometimes a certain discrepancy of meaning in these books; but on the contrary, anyone who wishes to judge this matter with a fair mind will find that this too can be added to the arguments for the authority of these books: that in matters which have some weight for doctrine or history, there is everywhere a most manifest agreement. Such a consensus is found nowhere else among writers of the same sect—whether you take the Jews, the Greek Philosophers, the Physicians, or the Roman..."

<page-num>97</page-num>
<header>ON THE CAUSES OF INCREDULITY.</header>
<sig>N</sig>
<meta>catchword: autem (however)</meta>

**Legal Experts**, among all of whom you will very often find not only those of the same sect fighting each other (such as **Plato** and **Xenophon**), but even the same writer asserting now this and now that, as if he had forgotten himself or was uncertain of what to conclude. But these writers of whom we speak instill the same things to be believed, give the same precepts, and tell the same story about Christ’s life, death, and return to life: the core is everywhere the same. As for some tiny circumstances and matters of no consequence, it could easily be that a convenient reconciliation is not lacking, but rather lies hidden from us because of similar things happening at different times, the ambiguity of names, or a person or place having several names, and other similar things. Indeed, this very fact ought to free those writers from all suspicion of fraud; for those who testify to falsehoods are usually accustomed to narrate everything by agreement so that not even a hint of anything different appears. If, because of some slight discrepancy—even one that could not be reconciled—the credibility of entire books were to vanish, then no book, especially of history, could be believed; yet our authority remains firm regarding the core of the matter in **Polybius**, **Dionysius of Halicarnassus**, **Livy**, and **Plutarch**, even though such discrepancies are found in them. How much more reasonable is it that nothing of the sort should destroy the faith of those whom we see, from their own writings, to have always been most studious of piety and truth?" Thus says the illustrious **Grotius**. However, something must be added about the two passages that **Porphyry** attacked. The first is found in **Matthew** 13:35. In our Greek manuscripts today, it reads: <note>original: ὅπως πληρωθῇ τὸ ῥηθὲν διὰ τοῦ προφήτου</note> "so that it might be fulfilled what was spoken through the prophet"; the name of the prophet itself is not added. **Jerome**, in his commentary on this place, has this to say: "I read in some manuscripts (and a studious reader might perhaps find it), in that place where we have placed it and where the common edition has it, 'it was said through the prophet saying'; there it was written 'through the prophet **Isaiah** saying.' Because this was not found in Isaiah at all, I think it was removed by prudent men; but it seems to me it was originally published as: 'Through **ASAPH** the Prophet.' For the seventy-seventh Psalm, from which this testimony is taken, is inscribed with the title of **Asaph** the Prophet; and the first scribe did not understand who Asaph was and, thinking it was a scribe's error, 'corrected' it to the name of **Isaiah**, whose name was more familiar." From these words it is clear enough that **Jerome** believed the name of **Asaph** was originally placed in the text, which was later wrongly changed into the name of **Isaiah** by the ignorance of some copyist. In this regard, he is followed by **Critobulus Hierapolitanus**—that is, **Jean Le Clerc** <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736) was a famous theologian and critic; he used "Critobulus" as a pseudonym in his debates.</note> (not **Richard Simon**, as the celebrated **Wolf** wrote on this passage)—in a letter given to **Origen Adamantius** (that is, **Richard Simon** <note>Richard Simon (1638–1712) was a French priest and a pioneer of biblical criticism; "Origen Adamantius" was used here as a code for him.</note>), which was added to the book titled: *Defense of the Sentiments of Some Dutch Theologians on the Critical History of the Old Testament, page 439.* **Jerome’s**...

However, this conjecture rests on no foundation, for the name of *Asaph* was found in none of the Manuscripts. If this had been the case, there is no doubt that the Church Fathers would have added the name of *Asaph* in place of *Isaiah*. Furthermore, **Jerome** <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the primary translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible.</note> himself admits that the name of *Asaph* did not exist in the most ancient Italian version <note>The *Vetus Latina*, the "Old Latin" translations that preceded Jerome's Vulgate.</note>. The question is simply this: since the name of *Isaiah* did not exist before the age of **Porphyry**, and no Manuscript has been found by **Mill** <note>John Mill (1645–1707), an English theologian famous for his critical edition of the Greek New Testament.</note> in which the name of *Isaiah* appears today, by what means did the name of *Isaiah* creep into certain manuscripts? We are convinced by the opinion of <term>the late</term> <note>original Greek: "tou makaritou," a respectful term for a deceased scholar.</note> **Olearius** in his commentary on this passage. He believes that the name of *Asaph* never existed in the text, but that some scholarly scribe, reading simply "the Prophet," thought it should be interpreted <term>pre-eminently</term> <note>original Greek: "kat’ exochēn," meaning by way of excellence or as the primary example.</note> as *Isaiah*, and decided it should be written in the margin, from where it was subsequently introduced into the text itself. Even suppose for a moment that the name of *Isaiah* did exist in some manuscripts at that time; was **Matthew** to be accused of ignorance on that account? Could not far more copies be shown to him from which that name was plainly absent? Was it not enough that **Matthew** applied the title of "Prophet," a title which is attributed to *Asaph* in 2 Chronicles 29:30? And what is the logic of this consequence: that because the word *Isaiah* was thrust into this passage of Matthew by the fault of some scribe, therefore Matthew himself—a man most worthy of trust in all other matters and an <term>eyewitness</term> <note>original Greek: "autoptēs."</note> of the things done by Christ—is an ignorant writer, and therefore must not be heard in other matters as well?

The other passage which, according to **Jerome**, Porphyry had thrown in the teeth of the Christians, is found in John 7:8, where Christ says: <term>"You go up to this feast; I am not going up."</term> <note>original Greek: "hymeis anabēte eis tēn heortēn tautēn. egō ouk anabainō."</note> Indeed, this is how it is read today. However, the **Cambridge Manuscript** <note>Also known as Codex Bezae (5th century), famous for its unique variations from other biblical manuscripts.</note> reads "not" <note>original Greek: "ouk."</note> instead of "not yet" <note>original Greek: "oupō."</note>. Aside from certain versions, some Fathers follow this reading, though they are few in number. Among the moderns, however, **Grotius**, **Mill**, **Richard Simon**, **Pfaff**, and others have been moved to think this way, primarily by the testimony of Jerome and the accusation of **Porphyry**. Hence **Grotius** says: *If "not yet" had been there in Porphyry's time, he would never have slandered Christ here regarding a lie; for in the word "not yet" would have been the solution to the knot.* However, although not much weight can be given to the Cambridge Manuscript (which often departs from others) in a disputed cause, it still cannot be denied that in the time of **Porphyry**, "not" was read in certain manuscripts. What those who weighed Porphyry’s censures might have responded is not entirely certain; yet if we admit the explanation of **Chrysostom** <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), Archbishop of Constantinople known for his eloquence.</note>—who undoubtedly studied the writings of those men who entered the arena against **Porphyry**—they could have stopped Porphyry's mouth even if the reading "not" were true. They could say that an elliptical way of speaking occurs here, and after the words

<column-break/>

<page-num>99</page-num>

<sig>N 2</sig>

words <term>"I am not going up,"</term> the little word <term>"just now"</term> <note>original Greek: "arti."</note> is to be understood. And so **Chrysostom**, adding: <term>"I am not going up once and for all, but [not] now; that is, with you,"</term> commends this interpretation from verses 6 and 8; see the "Cares" of the celebrated **Wolf** <note>Johann Christoph Wolf (1683–1739), a German Hebraist and theologian.</note> on this passage. Whatever the truth of it, it is clear that **Porphyry** read the New Testament with the intention not of learning from it what might contribute to proving the truth, but so that he might have a pretext for find fault and carping. It could easily have been established for him from the reading of the Evangelists that our Savior not only had insight into the most secret thoughts and endeavors of men, but that he also clearly foresaw the fates he was to experience on earth. It is strange, however, that **Porphyry** should think ill of the Christian religion and its followers because he seemed to detect some <term>apparent contradictions</term> <note>original Greek: "enantiophaneias."</note> in their writings, when he himself—in order to extol the doctrine of **Pythagoras**—was able not only to invent the crudest lies, but also to defend them by asserting that Pythagoras was in two places simultaneously at one and the same moment in time.

But a zeal for glory, says **Porphyry**, was present in those disciples; yet from where is this proved? Certainly, that passage in **Galatians** proves this least of all. To be sure, Paul addresses Peter (who had fallen through weakness and timidity) with gentle words, and warns him lest by his example he invite others to err. Therefore, says Porphyry, Paul did this led by ambition; therefore, good men allowed themselves to be carried away by a shameful impulse of the passions. One must certainly be "all eyes" to see the force of this logic. For that the phrases <term>"I withstood him to his face,"</term> <term>"because he was to be blamed,"</term> and <term>"you compel the Gentiles to live as Jews"</term> <note>Key phrases from Galatians 2:11-14 regarding the conflict between Paul and Peter at Antioch.</note> are to be interpreted more leniently was taught long ago on this passage by the **Illustrious Grotius**, whom you may consult. **Toland** <note>John Toland (1670–1722), a controversial Irish rationalist philosopher.</note>, a man of similar character, follows **Porphyry** here, and attacks Paul, but from another source; regarding this argument, see the "Vindication of the Ancient Christian Discipline" by the celebrated **Mosheim**, page 319 and following. Here again, however, it is clear how proud, malignant, and hostile to the Christian religion **Porphyry** was. He attributes an innocent disagreement to the ambition of the Apostles; yet he himself and the other Platonists, especially **Plotinus**, were mere "creatures of glory." They boasted of nothing but perpetual conversations and commerce with Demons and Gods; they babble that they were sometimes raised on high, and even—fools that they are—boast that they have seen God himself. On the occasion of this friendly dispute between Paul and Peter, a question has arisen among theologians: namely, whether the Apostles enjoyed the gift of inspiration perpetually or not. We do not examine that here, as it is foreign to our purpose. See *The Sentiments of some Theologians of Holland on the Critical History of the Old Testament* composed by **Father Simon**, page 250.

See the defense of that same book, and the celebrated **Witsius’** *Sacred Miscellany, Volume I, Chapter XXII* <note>Herman Witsius (1636–1708) was a Dutch theologian known for his attempts to reconcile different theological factions.</note>. But we must proceed. This same **Porphyry** <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher and a famous critic of early Christianity.</note> had attacked the Prophet Daniel, as **Jerome** <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the biblical scholar and translator of the Vulgate.</note> testifies in his *Commentary on this Prophet*. His words sound as follows: *Porphyry wrote his twelfth book against the Prophet Daniel, being unwilling to believe that it was composed by the man whose name it bears, but rather by someone in Judea during the time of Antiochus, who was called Epiphanes. He claimed that Daniel did not so much predict future events as recount past ones; finally, he argued that whatever Daniel said up to the time of Antiochus contains true history, but if he envisioned anything beyond that, he was lying because he did not know the future.* <note>original Latin: "contra Prophetam Danielem duodecimum librum scribit Porphyrius... non tam Danielem futura prædixisse, quam illum narrasse præterita..."</note> It is not my intention to show how false this opinion of Porphyry’s is, nor how it is built upon no arguments; for this has been abundantly demonstrated by learned men, such as **Pierre Daniel Huet** <note>A French bishop and scholar (1630–1721) who defended the authenticity of the Bible.</note> and others. I would wish only one thing to be observed: namely, that Porphyry accuses Daniel of lying because he attributed to himself the faculty of predicting the future, and likewise because he predicted as future things what were, in his own opinion, already long past. Yet Porphyry himself ascribes the power of predicting the future to his own **Pythagoras** <note>The ancient Greek philosopher; Porphyry wrote a biography of him portraying him as a semi-divine figure.</note>; and **Philostratus** <note>Flavius Philostratus (c. 170–250 AD), who wrote a highly sensationalized life of the philosopher Apollonius of Tyana.</note> imagines his **Apollonius** to be not only adorned with the same gift, but even contends that he understood the songs of birds. Moreover, this same Porphyry, with his whole crowd of most deceitful Sophists, dared to forge various books—for example, those of **Orpheus**, **Zoroaster**, etc. They sold these as genuine, and thus wished to add a veneer of truth to their most foolish opinions. Who does not see that these men have cast all shame from their brows? They accused the innocent, while at the same time binding themselves to the gravest crimes, not being embarrassed to offer the coarsest lies. Many testimonies of books forged by this crowd of "Sages" were brought forward by the famous **Brucker** <note>Johann Jakob Brucker (1696–1770), a German historian of philosophy.</note> in his *History of Philosophy, Vol. III, p. 544*, and the famous **Mosheim** <note>Johann Lorenz von Mosheim (1693–1755), an influential German Lutheran church historian.</note> in his *Dissertation on the Causes of Supposititious Books*. This same Porphyry, as **Eusebius** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), the "Father of Church History."</note> testifies in his *Ecclesiastical History, Book VI, Chapter 19*, had bitterly mocked the method of interpreting the Scriptures used by certain interpreters—especially **Origen**—and vehemently attacked his allegorical interpretations. Let us hear Eusebius himself: *Porphyry himself (he says), who lived in Sicily almost within our own memory, wrote books against our faith in which he attempted to calumniate the divine Scriptures. Mentioning those who interpreted them, since he could in no way criticize the dogmas and assertions themselves for lack of reasons, he turned to insults and accused the interpreters themselves. Among these, he especially strives to calumniate Origen; yet in reality, he unintentionally commends the man, partly by speaking the truth where he could not do otherwise, and partly by lying whenever he hoped he could remain hidden. And at times he accuses him as a follower of Christ; at other times...*

<column-break/>

<page-num>101</page-num>

<sig>N 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: Nimi-</meta>

*...at other times he admires and proclaims his extraordinary learning in philosophical matters.* But let us bring forward Porphyry’s own words: *Some, eager to find a solution for the wickedness of the Jewish writings rather than abandoning them, turned to certain interpretations that were inconsistent and ill-fitting to the texts. These did not provide a defense of that foreign sect, but rather brought approval and praise for their own doctrines. For after boasting that the things clearly spoken by Moses were riddles, and treating them with divine reverence as oracles full of hidden mysteries, they fascinated the critical faculty of the soul with such vanity and then brought forward their own interpretations.* <note>original Greek: "Της δη μοχθηριας των Ιουδαϊκων γραφων... επαγωσιν εξηγησεις." Translated here into English via the author's Latin version by Henri Valois (Valesius).</note> It is clear from these words that Porphyry was pointing his finger at certain allegorical interpretations of **Origen** <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253 AD), an early Christian scholar known for interpreting the Bible on literal, moral, and allegorical levels.</note>. And it is indeed true that this otherwise most learned man was too devoted to this pursuit; his commentaries, which are still extant, can serve as witnesses. Indeed, the matter is too well known to be proven with more words. We do not wish to excuse Origen here; rather, we regret that by this distorted explanation of Holy Writ, he gave occasion for attacking the Christian religion. For through these allegorical interpretations, in the judgment of **Calvin** <note>John Calvin (1509–1564), the Protestant Reformer.</note> on *Genesis 11:10*, not only was the simplicity of Scripture corrupted, but faith was nearly undermined, and a door opened to many delusions. Nevertheless, despite this, Porphyry shows his impudence in this judgment. For even though Origen often abused allegorical interpretations, it is certain that where dogmas were concerned, he very clearly opened his meaning; let his book written *Against Celsus* be a witness, which is indeed filled with great learning. Furthermore, should the entire Scripture be rejected because of the errors of one or more writers, especially since Porphyry was hardly ignorant of which dogmas the Christians subscribed to? But what shows his detestable malice is this: that he himself, along with his fellow **Platonists**, wanted everything that the poets imagined about their gods to be interpreted allegorically, so that he might cover up shameful nonsense with artificial interpretations if possible. See Porphyry’s little book *On the Cave of the Nymphs*, which is added to the Oxford edition of the treatise *On Abstinence from Animal Food* <note>original Greek: "περι αποχης Εμψυχων" (Peri apoches empsychon), a work advocating for vegetarianism based on Neoplatonic philosophy.</note>.

Clearly, he contends that **Homer's** narrative about this Cave <note>A reference to Porphyry's famous work *On the Cave of the Nymphs*, where he provides a philosophical allegory for a scene in Homer’s *Odyssey*.</note> is not a fable, nor is it a literal and certain description of a place, *but that the Poet is allegorizing something through these things, having mystically placed an olive tree nearby* <note>original Greek: "ἀλληγορειν δε τι δι' ἀυτὰ τον ποιητην, προσθεντα μυσικως κὴ ἐλαιας φυτον πλησιον"</note>. That is, something is signified through his hidden meanings by the Poet, who places an olive tree near the cave for a mystical reason (page 251). Moreover, it is sufficiently clear to an attentive reader that **Homer** intended nothing less than to reveal the "Phenomena" of this world and the nature of intellectual and sensible things <note>original Greek: "ἀνοητων & νοητων" — referring to things perceived by the senses versus those understood by the mind.</note> through a certain philosophical and metaphysical method. Furthermore, **Porphyry** himself, in his *Life of Plotinus*, confesses that **Origen** <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253 AD), an early Christian scholar who frequently used allegorical interpretation to explain the Bible.</note> delighted in the writings of the **Pythagoreans**. From these, he obtained that allegorical discipline so highly commended to this class of men. Yet, when Origen applies this method to explain many passages of the Old Testament, he is "flogged" by **Porphyry**. However, when **Porphyry** himself and his companions use it to practice games of the imagination and wit—forging anything they please out of anything else, even when dealing with matters of religion—then, if it please the gods, they are considered Great Philosophers. (*)

V. But we must proceed to other examples from which it can be most clearly established that those Philosophers, so hostile to the Christian religion, were devoted to opinions that cannot be compared in any way to the evidence and truth of Christian dogmas. We shall show this briefly. Reason teaches anyone that God is an Infinite, eternal,

---

<note>The following note is in French in the original text.</note>

(*) The author of the book titled *Alciphron, or the Minute Philosopher* <note>George Berkeley (1685–1753), an Anglo-Irish philosopher. *Alciphron* is a defense of Christianity against "free-thinkers."</note> seems to me to have elegantly painted the character of **Porphyry's** mind. For in Volume II, page 97, the Author speaks in the name of **Crito**: *"I confess that* **PORPHYRY** *was truly an infidel, although he does not seem at all to have been an unbeliever. He seems to have believed in diviners and sorcerers and to have admitted the Mysteries, Miracles, and Predictions of the Egyptian Priests. He affected to express himself in an obscure manner and claimed to have Ecstasies. In a word, this 'Great Man' was as unintelligible as a Scholastic, as superstitious as a Monk, as fanatical as a Quietist: and to complete his Portrait as a 'minute philosopher,' he was more than once tempted to kill himself. To form a just notion of this Patriarch of the 'strong-minded,' one only has to pay attention to his way of thinking on points other than the Christian Religion. Such was his penetration that he had discovered that the souls of insects, when separated from their bodies, became rational souls; that one can compose filters and charms with the help of Demons, whose spiritual bodies are nourished and fattened by the vapors of libations and sacrifices; that the spirits of those who die a violent death are accustomed to prowl around their graves. The same Philosopher advises a wise man not to eat meat, for fear that the impure soul of the animal might enter his body with its flesh. He adds, as a fact confirmed by several experiments, that those who wish to possess the souls of animals that have the gift of foretelling the future need only eat some noble part—the heart, for example—of a deer or a mole; and that by this means they will receive the soul of the animal, which will prophesy in them like a God. Do you find it strange that men credible enough to admit such 'pretty' things should have an aversion to the Gospel?"*

<column-break/>

<page-num>103</page-num>
<header>ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.</header>

and purely intellectual substance, most far removed from every object that meets the eyes. Revelation confirms this and testifies that "God is a Spirit" (John 4:24), that "no one has ever seen Him" (John 1:18), and that He "dwells in unapproachable light" (1 Timothy 6:16). But these things do not please our Philosophers, who consider themselves highly refined men. They impudently assert that they have seen God Himself with their own eyes without an image. Thus the words of **Porphyry** stand in the *Life of Plotinus*, page 137 of Fabricius's edition. Furthermore, these men could not stomach what is said in the Holy Scriptures regarding the Origin of all things—namely, that God produced all things out of nothing <note>The doctrine of *creatio ex nihilo*.</note>—but they contended instead that all substances, intellectual and material alike, emanated from the divine essence. It is indeed true that we are ignorant of the *manner* in which all things were produced; that is, we cannot show the link that exists between the will of the Infinite Mind and the existence of matter and intellectual substances. Meanwhile, it can be most evidently demonstrated *a posteriori* <note>A philosophical term meaning reasoning from observed effects back to causes.</note> that there exists an eternal Cause, distinct from the world, which gave existence to all things. However, we conceive of that other proposition—namely, that all things flowed out of the nature of God—with far more difficulty. If we turn our minds to the nature of all substances, it will be clear that they are finite, fleeting, changeable, and subject to various imperfections. Now, this being established, one must either assert that they belong to the eternal nature of God, or say that they existed in God as a fish, for example, exists in water. If the former is asserted, God would be both most perfect and most imperfect at the same time, which is absurd <note>original Greek: "ἄτοπον"</note>. If the *latter*, then it must be said either that they were created by God, or that they existed by the necessity of their own nature no less than God did. They refuse to admit the former; therefore, they must necessarily concede the latter. But how will they prove that which is fleeting, changeable, and not equally eternal as God Himself—nay, which does not even belong to the nature of God—nevertheless exists by necessity? Yet it is this very principle, most uncertain and indeed false, that those Philosophers used to defend innumerable silly opinions, as has been abundantly shown by very learned men, especially **Brucker** <note>Jacob Brucker (1696–1770), a German historian of philosophy whose *Historia Critica Philosophiae* was a standard text.</note>. Whether, therefore, it should be asserted that these Philosophers professed the same opinion that **Spinoza** <note>Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677), whose pantheism was often equated by later critics with Neoplatonic emanation or ancient paganism.</note> defended in the age of our fathers, we shall discuss at length elsewhere. But these things may seem trivial compared to those that follow. It is well known that Christ our Holy Savior was illustrious for His miracles, and this is sufficiently confirmed by the consensus of all the Evangelists who described the life and fate of Christ. To these miracles the students of the most holy discipline <note>Referring to the early Christians and their teachers.</note> appealed. To strip these of their credibility, those Philosophers spent every effort. Hence **Hierocles** and **Philostratus**... <note>Hierocles and Philostratus were authors who promoted Apollonius of Tyana as a pagan rival to Jesus, often by attributing similar miracles to him.</note>

<header>MEDITATION III.</header>
<meta>catchword: whether</meta>

...not only did they set up their own *Apollonius* <note>Apollonius of Tyana, a 1st-century philosopher whose life was often framed by pagans as a parallel to Jesus.</note> against Christ, but *Plotinus*, *Porphyry*, and the rest were also—if you believe their **biographers** <note>original Greek: "βιογράφοις"</note>—illustrious for their miracles. They were said to have conversed most familiarly with Gods and Demons; they exercised power over malignant spirits; they were often raised many feet from the ground; they delighted in visions; and, as we said previously, they claimed to have beheld the very substance of God without any bodily image. It is not necessary for me to prove each point with testimony, since these things have long been accepted and approved by the consensus of all learned men. See *Brucker*, *Olearius*, *Mosheim*, and others.

However, I have no doubt that by doing so, they wished to attack the most holy discipline of Christ and to show that nothing in the Christian religion is so excellent or outstanding that it is not far surpassed by the precepts, deeds, and gifts of the philosophers devoted to their own sect. Although, I say, there is no doubt about that, it is nevertheless not far from the truth that the boasted visions of certain *Pseudo-Christians* or the credulous of that age, the casting out of Devils from the sick, and other such **monstrosities** <note>original Greek: "τερατωδη"</note> gave those philosophers the occasion for inventing and spreading among the common people more extraordinary acts of that kind. 

We have shown elsewhere that many uncertain, indeed false, visions were boasted of everywhere in that age in which most of those philosophers flourished; and it would be easy to show that not everything narrated here and there concerning the casting out of Demons, especially in the third or fourth century, should be rashly admitted. At the very least, one will have difficulty believing *Tertullian*, who in his *Apology, Chapter XXIII*, attributes the faculty of expelling Demons to all Christians indiscriminately, saying: *Let someone be produced here before your Tribunals who is known to be possessed by a Demon; if commanded to speak by any Christian whatever, that Spirit will as truly confess itself to be a Demon as it elsewhere falsely claimed to be a God.* And *Origen*, in *Against Celsus, Book VII, page 334*, says **"for the most part it is private individuals who do such things."** <note>original Greek: "επιπαν γαρ ὡς ιδιωται το τοιουτον πραττουσι"</note> I omit other testimonies. I do not know on what basis the illustrious *Bingham* (*Volume II, page 21*) wished to prove that this gift was conferred upon Bishops and Presbyters in a more special way. 

Whatever the case may be, it is manifest that these most wicked men preferred to devise the most uncertain and vain things imaginable to overturn the most Holy discipline of Jesus Christ, raising their own trifles and fanatic opinions to the heavens with praise, rather than cross over into the camp of the Christians. For do they prove with historical arguments that Jesus Christ never existed on earth, or that he performed no miracles? Not at all. *Porphyry* himself, as witnessed by *Eusebius* in *Demonstration of the Gospel, Book III, chapter 9*, not only mentions Jesus Christ but does not deny that he flourished in innocence of life. Julian—

<meta>catchword: Julian</meta>

—who was devoted to this same faction, did not deny that Jesus performed miracles, as is well known to everyone; See *Cyril against Julian, Book VI, Edition III of Spanheim*. Regarding the truth of the actual events, they were therefore persuaded, as it seems. However, lest they appear to lack arguments with which to attack the conclusions that could be drawn from the truth of Jesus Christ's miracles, they fled to the vainest figments of the brain, inventing a certain secret science called <term>Theurgy: A high form of magic or "god-working" where the practitioner claims to influence or summon divine agencies.</term>. By the power of this science, they claimed Demons could be forced to perform whatever was commanded, and even to work miracles. See the letter of *Porphyry* to *Anebo the Egyptian*, prefixed to the work of *Iamblichus*. Thus they contended that by the same means, Christ and his disciples were able to perform wonderful portents. 

While they might occasionally speak highly of Christ and not deny that he performed miracles, it is clear enough that these most impudent men merely wished to give the Christians empty words. This is because, even while granting Christ and his disciples the power to perform miracles, they nevertheless celebrated only their own men as divine and fallen from heaven, shouting that their own discipline alone was worthy of veneration. Furthermore, they made a distinction between **Theurgy** and <term>Goetia: Derived from the Greek word for wailing or moaning, this refers to "low" magic, sorcery, or the conjuring of malevolent spirits.</term>, asserting that the former could only be performed by purified minds and consisted of familiar commerce with good spirits, while the latter was granted only to the impure and wicked, who held power over evil spirits and those hostile to the human race. 

From this, one can sufficiently gather what those imposters thought of our **Savior** <note>original Latin: "Sotere"</note> and his disciples when they heard that he had freed those possessed by Demons. However, how futile and vain that art of conversing with spirits and employing them at will for every kind of service actually is, is too well known for us to teach at length. Indeed, by what reasoning could they show to men of sound mind that they were using spirits familiarly? And how did they know that spirits of any kind could change the laws fixed by God? Could not Christians similarly attribute to themselves such a faculty of speaking with spirits? And if those spirits had the power to perform miracles by the will of the Deity, is it credible that good Demons would do such things to confirm the foulest superstition? 

But there is no need to fall into such arguments, since everything narrated about the portents of those philosophers rests only on the authority of most lying men. Indeed, the biography of *Pythagoras* alone, written by *Iamblichus* and *Porphyry*, suffices to convict those men of imposture: for they tell such foul fables about him, supported by no firm witnesses, that it is believable they published these booklets for the sake of children, not men.

**Porphyry** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 AD) and student of Plotinus who was a major opponent of early Christianity.</note> himself wrote the biography of **Plotinus** <note>The founder of Neoplatonism.</note> at last thirty years after the death of **Plotinus**, as is clear from a comparison of the second, ninth, and twenty-third chapters. I say nothing of the narrative itself, which is so constructed that it could only persuade the most foolish that the things he tells about **Plotinus** could be true. Thus, among other things in chapter 22, he appeals to the **Oracle of Apollo**, by which it was supposedly proven that **Plotinus**, along with **Pythagoras** and **Plato**, enjoys the highest happiness in some fields or other—even though, in the judgment of the more prudent pagans themselves, these oracles should be attributed to the deceptions of priests. See **Cicero**, Book II *On Divination*. Among more recent writers, the illustrious **Van Dale** <note>Antonius van Dale (1638–1708), a Dutch scholar who argued that ancient oracles were human frauds rather than demonic interventions.</note> has placed this matter in a clear light in his work *On the Oracles of the Gentiles*. 

We heard above that those traveling charlatans assert that only impure men use the service of evil demons and practice magical arts through them; yet here our **Porphyry**, in chapter 10, relates that a certain **Olympius** of Alexandria attacked **Plotinus** with a mind so intent on malice <note>original Greek: "ὡς καὶ ἀστροβολῆσαι αὐτον μαγευσας ἐπεχείρησεν"</note> that he attempted to "strike him with the stars" <note>An ancient belief in "sidereal" or star-based magic meant to paralyze or wither an opponent.</note> by means of certain magical incantations. But our "pious" **Plotinus** eluded the art with his own art, and caused **Olympius’s** body to shrivel up like a pouch, with all his limbs crushed against one another. From this it follows that **Plotinus** understood magical arts no less than he did theurgy <note>High ritual magic intended to invoke the presence of gods, which Neoplatonists distinguished from "low" sorcery.</note>; and thus, based on **Porphyry’s** own principles, one must conclude that **Plotinus** was at once a divine man and a most wicked scoundrel. That **Julian** <note>Roman Emperor Julian "the Apostate" (r. 361–363 AD), who attempted to revive paganism.</note> was also skilled in these magical arts is testified by **Sozomen**, Book V, chapter <note>A specific chapter number appears to be omitted in the original print.</note>, **Theodoret**, Book III, chapter III, and **Ammianus Marcellinus**, Book XXI, chapter I. Similar things could be brought forward regarding **Iamblichus**, **Apollonius**, **Proclus**, and the rest of that crowd of fanatics, if that were our current task.

Furthermore, I do not doubt that **Porphyry**, in order to weaken or at least cast suspicion upon <note>original Greek: "τὴν τοῦ λόγου ἐνσάρκωσιν"</note> the **Incarnation of the Word**, wrote in chapter 10 of the *Life of Plotinus* that a certain Egyptian saw a demon summoned by **Plotinus**—indeed, a God—so that upon seeing this he exclaimed: <note>original Greek: "Μακάριος εἶ Θεὸν ἔχων τὸν Δαίμονα καὶ ὁ τῷ ὑφειμένῳ γένει τὸν συνόντα."</note> *“Blessed are you, O Plotinus, who have a God for a guardian spirit, and have not been allotted a familiar guide from an inferior race.”* That **Julian** felt despicably toward Christ our most Holy Savior and His discipline is too well known to require much proof. With this philosophy, which had the appearance of the greatest wisdom, they said that an external worship must be joined, concocted from the rites of all nations, while despising at least the sacred rites prescribed by Christian discipline.
