This being the case, what I ask can anyone find worthy of admiration in these last words of **Plotinus**? His mind was a part of God while living, and it is a part of the same after death; it necessarily had to be joined with this essence, just as his body was joined with the remaining bodies: a wonder indeed, and a comfort worthy of a **fanatic** <note>In this period, "fanatic" usually referred to someone claiming direct, irrational divine inspiration.</note>, not a man of sound brain! VI. But we proceed to another, and indeed a famous Impostor, namely **Muhammad**, who, by the work of certain crafty men skilled in the Jewish and Christian Religions, intending to introduce a new Religion, rejected those things which are most excellent in the Christian Religion, keeping only those which were to his taste, while adding other clearly inept and tasteless opinions. It is my intention to deal with him in few words, not only so that it may be clear that men moved by ambition and other passions follow the worse after rejecting the better, but also because, in such light of Letters and Religion, there are those who admire the discipline of **Muhammad**, and praise and extol his deeds—though they are contrary to divine and human laws alike—not without detriment to the Christian Religion.

Before we approach the matter itself, we confess that we are indeed lacking in the Arabic language; yet at the same time, we have sought all the things we shall bring forward from those writers who, in the judgment of all the learned, were most skilled in the Oriental languages, such as **Hottinger, Pococke, Reland, Maracci, Gagnier, and others.** <note>These were prominent 17th and 18th-century scholars of Oriental languages and Islam.</note> However, it is very difficult to know accurately what is to be attributed to **Muhammad** himself and what to his associates, on account of the disagreement among the writers of the life and fates of **Muhammad**. For just as those who wrote the *Lives of the Saints*, even where they seem to speak the truth, lose credibility because they have mixed innumerable manifestly false and ridiculous things with the probable; so the same thing usually happens in this business. It has been some time since the celebrated **Reland**, in his *Elucidations of Muhammadan Theology*, showed that many things were rashly attributed to **Muhammad**, either out of ignorance of the Arabic language or out of excessive hatred by Christians. The learned man **Jacob Ehrhart** of Memmingen showed the same in his dissertation *On the Principal Errors of Illustrious and Obscure Writers in the History of Muhammad and their Causes*, published at Ulm in 1731. And that men otherwise most learned and most skilled in the Arabic language, like **Maracci** and **Prideaux**, are not immune to this vice was shown by the celebrated **Gagnier** in the preface to the *Life of Muhammad*, written by **Abul-feda** <note>Abu al-Fida (1273–1331), a Kurdish historian and geographer whose work was a primary source for early modern European scholars.</note>. But other factors arise which prevent us from easily distinguishing truth from falsehood in this matter. For not only does the **Sunnah** <note>The body of traditional social and legal custom and practice of the Islamic community.</note> itself—that is, the Collection of Traditions which the Muhammadans believe to be no less sacrosanct than the **Quran**—disagree within itself, but it often conflicts with the writers of the life and deeds of **Muhammad**. These writers themselves patched everything together from the most uncertain traditions, a fact which the famous **Gagnier** diligently noted in his French biography of this Impostor. Furthermore, the most celebrated writers of the life of **Muhammad** among the Arabs belong to an age too recent for us to safely trust them. **Abul-Feda**, to whom the famous **Gagnier** frequently appeals, lived in the 14th century; **al-Jannabi** in the 16th; **Bar Hebraeus** <note>referred to as Abulpharajus</note> in the 11th. 

Even if we go back to the first collectors of the Traditions, the same obscurity occurs. The famous **Gagnier** (Volume I, page 349), drawing from the *Life of Abu Bakr* written by **Abul-Feda**, teaches that the copy of the **Quran** which was in the hands of **Muhammad's** wife, named **Hafsa**, was collected by **Abu Bakr**, the first Caliph (that is, the successor of Muhammad). He notes that **Uthman** <note>The third Caliph.</note> then saw to it that many copies were transcribed according to this first version and distributed through all the provinces of the Empire, while suppressing all other collections that were at hand. 

Moreover, the famous **Gagnier** records (page 105) that on the night of *Al-Qadr* <note>Laylat al-Qadr</note>—that is, the Night of the Divine Decree—in the 40th year of **Muhammad’s** age, the entire **Quran** descended from heaven, and was afterwards sent down from heaven only in parts over a span of 23 years. Yet **Muhammad** died, according to the calculation of the famous **Gagnier**, in the 63rd year of his age; from which it follows that parts of the **Quran** were continuously falling from heaven right up until the end of his life. Hence, at the time of his death, two versions of the **Quran** must have existed. By what right, then, was one preferred to the other—one suppressed and the other preserved? Furthermore, it is manifest that the first impostors patched the **Quran** together at their own whim; for **Muhammad** died in the eleventh year of the **Hijra** <note>The migration to Medina; the start of the Islamic calendar.</note>, but **Hafsa** only died in the forty-fifth year. Within that span of time, there was ample room for innumerable frauds. Certainly, the first collector, **Abu Bakr**, was a shameless impostor—if this were not clear from any other argument than that which is found on page 251 of the *Life of Muhammad* by the famous

famous **Gagnier**, it would suffice. It is reported there that this man was a witness—and a faithful one at that—to that nocturnal journey from *Mecca* to *Jerusalem* and then through the seven heavens, which **Muhammad** is said to have completed in a single night. This would be more than enough to demonstrate the stupidity and impudence of this man. For besides the fact that nothing more foolish, ridiculous, false, and unworthy of God could be devised than this narrative, that **Abu Bakr** testified that this journey truly happened before **Muhammad** himself, or anyone else, had told him any such thing! 

When asked by certain members of the **Quraysh** tribe (page 256 of the cited work) who were calling this nocturnal journey into doubt, whether he knew what **Muhammad** was saying about this matter, he responded as if ignorant of everything: *"Has Muhammad then asserted these things?"* Indeed they said he had; then he replied: *"I bear witness and profess that if Muhammad narrated these things, they are true."* When they pressed him, asking whether these things seemed to merit belief, he responded again: *"I contend that everything Muhammad said is true, even though you accuse him of lying."* Only after giving this response did he go to **Muhammad** himself and ask whether he had ever affirmed that he made such a journey by night. Behold, a wondrous witness! 

And yet this man, if you believe **Muhammad** (page 258 of the cited work), is not only the great witness of truth, but also the first Editor of the **Quran**. Truly, those who first set their minds to writing the life and fates of **Muhammad** were equipped with a greater capacity of imagination for inventing incredible <term>monstrous fables <note>original Greek: τερατολογιας</term></note> than with the skill to weigh a fictional tale against the laws of probability. 

But there are other things that sufficiently show that certain insane impostors aided **Muhammad’s** desire and zeal for rising to power and dominance through frauds and the appearance of religion. The famous **Pococke** <note>Edward Pococke (1604–1691), a renowned English Orientalist.</note> in his *Specimen of Arab History* (page 156) narrates that **Muhammad** could neither read nor write, according to the testimony of the Muhammadans themselves. This is confirmed by the famous **Gagnier** and other writers of his life and deeds, who assert that he was called the "unlettered and illiterate Prophet" by his followers. To this unlettered man (according to **Gagnier**, Volume I, page 105), who had hidden for some time in a certain cave on Mount *Hira*—driven, naturally, by a love of solitude—there appeared in the 40th year of his age (which was the first year of his prophetic mission according to the Muhammadans) the Angel **Gabriel**. He brought the entire written **Quran** with him and, addressing **Muhammad**, said: *"Read."* *"I cannot read,"* he replied. The Angel retorted: *"Read in the name of the Lord who created all things; who formed man from a small mass of congealed blood; He taught man to use the pen, and by it He taught those things which he did not know."* Lest anyone doubt these words, they are found in the **Quran, Surah 96, verse 1 and following.**

<header>MEDITATION III.</header>

What does our candidate for the office of Apostle, **Muhammad**, have to say to this? **Abul-Feda** <note>Ismail Abul-Feda (1273–1331), a Syrian historian and geographer whose biography of Muhammad was a primary source for European scholars.</note> reports on page 16 of his *Life*, that Muhammad recited the same words of the Angel and at the same time heard a voice sent down from heaven sounding as follows:

> ->*O Muhammad, you are the Apostle of God, and I am the Angel Gabriel.*<-

Upon returning to Mecca, **Muhammad** recounted these things that had happened to him to his wife **Khadija**. She, leaping for joy, not only swore by God that he would be the Prophet of his nation, but immediately went to a certain man named **Waraka**. He was a man described as learned and well-versed in the teachings of the Jews no less than those of the Christians. She explained to him what her husband had related. This man not only declared that the opinion of **Muhammad’s** wife was true, but even contended that his arrival had long ago been predicted in the Law of Moses. **Gianabi**, a biographer <note>original: "βιογραφος" (biographer)</note> of **Muhammad**, adds that on the same day, **Gabriel**, digging deep into the earth with his foot, caused water to spring forth. He then taught **Muhammad** the ritual of sacred washing <term>ablution; the ritual washing before prayer known as Wudu</term>—which is counted among the five fundamental practical articles <note>The Five Pillars of Islam.</note>—and likewise the manner of praying, to be performed with two inclinations of the body <term>Rak'ah; a unit of Islamic prayer involving standing, bowing, and prostration</term>. After this, **Muhammad** returned to his wife, stayed with her, and led her to the miraculous spring. By his own example, he showed her how one must wash and pray according to the Angel's command. She diligently imitated him and was the first to give her name to **Islamism**, that is, the religion of **Muhammad**. She was followed by **Ali**, who had been raised in **Muhammad’s** house; he was followed by **Zaid**, **Muhammad’s** servant. Then followed **Abu Bakr**, who persuaded others to do the same. Behold the first beginnings of the Muhammadan religion!—if these writers are to be believed. Before we proceed further, it is helpful to pause here a moment, since it can be shown clearly from what has been said how **Muhammad** obtained the name of Prophet.

And 1) indeed, **Muhammad** seems to have sought out this cavern or cave in the manner of certain impostors. Historians of a similar grain, such as **Iamblichus** and **Porphyry**, relate that **Pythagoras** <note>The famous Greek philosopher, often depicted in later antiquity as a mystical or miraculous figure.</note> often did the same. It is not probable that **Muhammad** did this out of a love for solitude; for besides the fact that he possessed a lively and noble disposition, was affable, and had a deep understanding of human nature—prepared as he was by various travels to skillfully carry out mercantile business—he kept his servants with him in this cave, staying there with them for a month. Surely, if a love of solitude and the contemplation of divine or abstruse matters had invited him to do this, he would have entered the cave alone in the manner of the hermits <note>original: "Anachoretarum" (anchorites/hermits)</note>. Therefore, there is no doubt that those servants were intended to be witnesses to the "voice sent from heaven."

2) It shrinks from every appearance of probability that an **Angel** would bring down from heaven, in the name of God, a writing of the greatest importance to a man who could neither read nor write. Indeed, I can scarcely believe that a man could have conducted trade so prudently and successfully, as the Arabian writers relate, without the skill of reading and writing; but, if he could not, as they claim, why does the Angel command him to read?

3) I do not know whether to wonder at or rather laugh at the stupidity of the **Angel Gabriel**, or **Muhammad**, or finally the impudence of the historian. **The Angel Gabriel** teaches **Muhammad** that God created all things. Was the future Prophet so brutish and stupid as to have been ignorant of this? And what do the Angel's words mean, *that God taught men to use the pen*? Do they mean that God furnished men with faculties so that they could, among other things, also learn how a pen is to be used for writing? Was a man practiced in the art of trade ignorant of this as well? Furthermore, that Angel lies when he asserts that God made men from a congealed *mass of blood* <note>A reference to Surah 96 of the Quran, which describes man being created from a "clot" (Alaq).</note>. To be sure, the illustrious **Gagnier** reminds us in his notes that, according to **al-Raich**, a famous commentator on the **Quran**, **Adam**, **Eva**, and **Jesus** must be excepted from this. But even if you except these, it still cannot be said of the rest of mankind.

4) How did he know the voice of the Angel was sent from heaven? Perhaps the servants were able to send this voice without any miracle.

5) **Khadija** was a wealthy wife, inflamed with a singular love for **Muhammad**, as is taught in Chapter VI of Book I. Who then should wonder that a woman became the leader of the deed and of the clever plan? Hence, she not only immediately offers a willing ear to her husband, but pronounces him the future Prophet without delay. It was undoubtedly by her arts and money that **Waraka**, that man cultivated in literature, was made to persuade others that the arrival of such a Prophet had long ago been predicted in the Holy Scriptures. (*)

6) All the others were perfectly equipped to manufacture the fraud. **Maisar**, a servant of **Khadija’s**, tells of the wonders that happened on the journey just before the arrival of Gabriel; the other servant **Zaid** was **Muhammad’s** slave. **Ali** was raised in his own house, and was later among his first legates and ministers. What kind of disposition he had is clear from those things extant on page 116 of the *Life of Muhammad*: for when those present were asked by **Muhammad** who would take up the heavy office of Legate to propagate Islam—

VII. But we return to those witnesses, to prove further that they are not such that we may safely trust them. It is certain, and more than sufficiently proven by learned men, that there were many Christians and Jews in Arabia during the time of **Muhammad**. See **Pococke**, *Specimen of Arabic History*, page 136; **Hottinger**, *Oriental History*, Book II, chapter II; **Mill**, *Dissertation on Muhammadanism before Muhammad*, page 340; and the famous **Veissière la Croze**, *Historical Dissertations*, page 12. I have no doubt that by this fable these liars wanted to show that **Muhammad** was indeed infected with the stain of original sin <term>original sin; the Christian doctrine of a corrupted human nature inherited from Adam</term>, but that it was already deleted in the third year of his age, so that they might show him to be little inferior in dignity to Christ. From which it is clear, as I note in passing, that the story related by John from verses 1 to 11 was found in the ancient codices of the New Testament...

...to be held as unfaithful men. It is not my intention to describe this ridiculous narrative <note>The author refers to the *Isra and Mi'raj*, Muhammad's night journey from Mecca to Jerusalem and his ascent through the seven heavens.</note>: this much is certain, that one could hardly devise a fable more strange and more ridiculous than those which nurses are accustomed to tell their little children. Hence the **Muslims** <note>original: "Mahomedani"</note> disagree among themselves whether **Muhammad** made this journey *in the body* or whether it occurred to him merely through a dream. It is clear from many accounts that he wished the former to be believed; see Volume II, page 36, and also page 367, in the works of the Illustrious **Gagnier** <note>Jean Gagnier (c. 1670–1740), an Orientalist scholar at Oxford.</note>: many others support him. Others, on the contrary, contend that the journey from **Mecca** to **Jerusalem** was made in the body, but that the journey through the seven heavens occurred only during sleep. Those who contend that both journeys were made by **Muhammad** in the body dispute whether he saw God with his mind alone or with his body; **al-Jannabi** <note>original: "Giannabi," referring to the 16th-century historian Abu al-Abbas Ahmad ibn Yusuf al-Jannabi.</note> testifies that the latter opinion is approved by most.

However, whether these writers assert the former or the latter, it is plain that they are lying most impudently. For if they say this was done in the body, God would have to be said not only to have performed innumerable miracles, but also to have provided them to confirm most foul lies—things contrary to common sense, impossible, and most unworthy of God; for innumerable such things are related in this journey. The same must be said if they contend such a vision occurred from the Deity during sleep; for then again it would have to be asserted that God intervened with His extraordinary power to persuade **Muhammad** of things openly false and absurd. But who, in whom there is any sense of piety, can admit these things? From this, any sensible person may gather how trustworthy these merchants of nonsense <note>original: "nugivenduli," literally "trifle-sellers."</note> who write these histories are, and what value is to be attributed to the **Sunnah** <note>original: "Sonne"</note>, that is, the collection of most absurd and uncertain traditions. 

I have no doubt that **Muhammad** told his friends, who were conscious of the fraud and imposture, that some dream had occurred to him; they then, adding lies to lies to keep the story from leaking <note>original: "ne perpluant," literally "lest they rain through," a metaphor for a leaky roof or a story that doesn't hold water.</note>, spread little tales among the common people, which were eventually increased by the compilers of the Traditions with more significant additions, as is usually done, and finally gave birth to that marvelous fable. That **Muhammad** himself was a bold, warlike, unjust, and lustful man is clear from the entire narrative of his life and deeds. That this impostor was warlike and unjust is sufficiently shown by so many wars undertaken against innocent people: thus, in Volume II, page 385, he himself asserts that he killed those who wished to prove him a liar, following the "manner of the Prophets." In Volume I, page 406, he not only relates that the Angel **Gabriel** was the author of his persecution of most innocent **Jews** and the putting of many of them to death, but also confirms that this cruel deed was sanctioned from heaven. In Volume II, page 47, he prays to God that He might grant him the spoils of the **Jews** whom he wished to attack without cause...

<page-num>119</page-num>
<header>ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.</header>

...in a word: he was a notorious robber who, neglecting all shame and law, attacked the most innocent under the appearance of a Religion which he himself did not understand. A certain masked Arab Physician, in a letter given to the Celebrated Professor at **Halle** <note>Halle was a major center for Pietism and Oriental studies in Germany.</note> as the title declares, wished to free **Muhammad** from this crime. He wants to accomplish this with three arguments: the first is this: namely, that **Muhammad** only wished to recover by arms the **Sherifate** <note>original: "Chérifiatum," the office of the Sharif, the traditional governor of Mecca.</note> of the city of **Mecca** and the dignity of the High Priest in the temple of this city, with which offices his ancestors had been honored. The *second* is: that **Alexander**, **Caesar**, and others have been praised to the heavens, although they were usurpers. The *third*: that among Christians there are many who assert that it is permitted to use arms to propagate Religion. 

I respond to the first: no evidence is brought forward by that masked Physician by which he might prove his opinion. All writers testify that **Muhammad** was born from the noble tribe of the **Quraysh** <note>original: "Koreischitarum"</note> but was poor: but I do not remember having read that his ancestors held these offices. But suppose it were so: the question is whether they were justly removed from this rank of dignity or not; for if they had lost these offices by law, he could not have used arms to recover that which depended on the judgment of others. But let us assume what he says is true; why was he indiscriminately cruel toward all his neighbors? Why did he oppress the **Jews** who deserved no such thing? Why did he always repeat that he was sent by God to root out idolatry and to tear down the false dogmas of Christians and Jews alike? Why do all the Arab writers give a completely different reason for his mission and the wars he undertook? 

As for the second argument, it is true that **Alexander**, **Caesar**, and others, who nevertheless brought wars upon others with no right, are praised by both ancients and moderns. But if they are praised for that reason alone, no lover of truth and right will approve of it. It is well known that **Alexander** was called a "great robber" by **Seneca**. And such also was **Muhammad**. Finally, neither does what is brought forward in the third place prove anything. The opinion that Religion is to be propagated by force and arms is horrible and foreign to humanity. Those who defend this must undoubtedly also absolve the unjust wars of **Muhammad**. But in the meantime, men who love the truth will not cease to detest such violence, by whomsoever it is either inflicted or praised. Indeed, we assert that Christians, though surrounded by the greater light of truth, who yet use those violent arts, are worthy of heavier punishments than **Muhammad** himself. That **Muhammad** was a most impure goat <note>original: "hædum," literally a young goat or kid, used here as a pejorative for a lustful person.</note> is proven not only by the fact that he had 15 or 17 wives, to say nothing of concubines, but also that he acted against the decrees of the **Quran**...

...decrees, he had relations with the maidservant **Zaynab** <note>original: "Zaida"; the author refers to Zaynab bint Jahsh, whose marriage to Muhammad was a frequent point of contention in Western polemics.</note>, and feigned that this fornication was approved by God. Hence also, in Volume II, page 323 of the *Life* by the Illustrious **Gagnier** <note>Jean Gagnier, an Oxford scholar who wrote a significant biography of Muhammad in 1723.</note>, he affirms that he was wonderfully incited to prayer by the company of women; and on page 326, among the virtues with which he was supposedly more adorned than others, he records that he was most ardent in **Venus** <note>A classical reference to sexual passion or lust.</note>. I pass over other matters. And yet here is that famous Prophet, supposedly raised by God to found a new Religion, for whose sake—as claimed on page 365—all creatures were created. But as the tree is, so is its fruit; as he and his fellow soldiers were, such also is the **Quran**. It is surely a most wretched writing, full of many ridiculous absurdities and contradictions; when they cannot resolve these latter, they flee to the coldest and most trivial distinctions, as many Learned Men have shown.

The most celebrated **Mill** <note>original: "Millius," likely David Mill (1692–1756), a German orientalist and theologian.</note>, who was most skilled in Oriental Literature, after recounting in his *Dissertation on Muhammadanism before Muhammad* (page 306) the praises with which **Muhammad** himself and his companions adorn the **Quran**, responds thus: *“But however splendid the boasts Muhammad makes regarding divine Revelations, they are entirely false and fashioned in the manner of crafty men—such as **Numa Pompilius** <note>The legendary second king of Rome who claimed his laws were inspired by the nymph Egeria.</note> boasting of his dealings with the Nymph Egeria, or **Lycurgus**, **Zamolxis**, and others like them, who boasted that they enjoyed the help and inspiration of the Gods so that they might win greater authority for their institutions. It is manifest that the Quran itself is the offspring of a human mind, and one not even particularly sharp; for its contents are so useless, vain, and repeated a hundred times over—so poorly stitched together—that they seem scarcely worthy of a man of sane mind. Finally, he so plundered the chests of the Pagans, Jews, and Christians, that if everything were restored to its rightful owners, he would be left almost naked, like the **jackdaw of Aesop**.”* <note>Referring to the fable of the bird who dressed himself in the feathers of others to appear beautiful, only to be stripped bare when the other birds reclaimed their plumage.</note> So says the Illustrious **Mill**, as the reading of the text itself teaches anyone. Nor do I think it necessary that I should appeal to the **Quran** itself or confirm the sayings of **Mill** and others by a long list of examples. Since versions of the **Quran** are available everywhere, this "noble" writing can be read by anyone.

<margin>
The miracles of Muhammad rely on the most uncertain traditions and are suspected of fraud.
</margin>

VIII. It remains for me to say something about the miracles attributed to him. In the **Quran** itself, I have nowhere found clear passages in which the Impostor boasts of having performed miracles. Indeed, in **Quran Sura III, verse 29**, he says he has no need of miracles, because God allows a man, if He wills, to be devoted to errors; but in **Sura XVII, verse 60**, he ascribes to himself the power of performing miracles. Other **Muslim** writers, however, attribute innumerable portents to him, as is abundantly clear. But what kind of witnesses those were, we have shown above more than enough. Yet besides the futility of the witnesses, there are many things that persuade us to believe the Impostor was famous for no miracles at all. We shall show this in a few words for the sake of our listeners (for to the Learned

<column-break/>

<page-num>121</page-num>
<header>ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.</header>

these things are very well known). And first, if we turn our mind’s eye to the character and disposition of this man, no one could persuade himself that the most holy God, who is most loving of the truth, would instruct a man who was plainly unlearned, lustful, a liar, rapacious, and not sufficiently knowledgeable in either the Christian or Jewish Religion, with the power of performing miracles to confirm a new doctrine that is plainly abhorrent to Christianity. The Christian religion had been confirmed by so many arguments and miracles that there was no need for new ones, even if he had been sent to confirm it. In **Sura XXXII, verse 38**, to pass over other places, he boasts that he was called by God to prove the **unity of the Godhead** <note>original: "unitatem Numinis"</note>, to overturn Idolatry, and to demonstrate and vindicate the sense of the **Law and the Gospel** <note>The Torah and the New Testament.</note> which had been corrupted by Christians and Jews. But another defender, if indeed one were necessary, would be needed to prove this.

To draw out the true sense of the Gospel, it would have been necessary without doubt for him to have looked into the Gospels themselves, so that he might show in what ways the Jews and Christians had finally wandered from the true meaning; but this man was so far from being able to provide this that he could not even read or write, if you listen to the **Muslims** themselves. Both the Arabs and the Christians and Jews admitted the Unity of the Godhead; thus there was no need for **Muhammad** to teach them this truth, let alone confirm it with miracles. **Pococke** <note>original: "Pokokius"; Edward Pococke (1604–1691), a famous English Orientalist and professor at Oxford.</note>, a man most skilled in these matters, teaches at length in his *Historical Specimens of the Arabs* (page 108) and **Mill** in the place cited, that before **Muhammad**, the Arabs worshiped one God and held the other gods merely as ministers. But if the Arabs had been ignorant of this, they should have been persuaded by arguments and reasons—which **Muhammad** never provided—instead he used weapons to harass the wretched. It is true that the Arabs also defiled themselves with foul Idolatry; but the laws of the Christians and Jews had forbidden it, so that there was no need for such a great Teacher. If he truly wished to proscribe all Idolatry, why then did he tolerate the **Sabeans** <note>original: "Zabios"; an ancient religious group mentioned in the Quran, often associated with star worship in early modern scholarship.</note>, who worship spirits and stars? Why did he finally attack with arms the Jews, who abhorred Idolatry and confessed the Unity of the Godhead, and why did he rage against them so greatly? Christians, as is well known, admitted the Unity of the Godhead. It is true that there was a dispute among Christians concerning the **Trinity** and the three persons; but if he had wished to attack that dogma, it would have been necessary above all for him to understand the mind of the Christians correctly. But the most learned men **Marracci**, **La Croze**, and others show that he speaks most ignorantly of this dogma, and in the **Quran** always brought forward only this one argument: namely, that God **does not beget; that He has no wife, and hence has neither son nor companion.** <note>The author argues that Muhammad misunderstood the Trinity as a biological family unit.</note>

But if indeed that warlike Apostle <note>A common polemical reference to Muhammad, acknowledging his title of "Apostle" but emphasizing his military conquests.</note> had wished to defend the opinion of **Arius** <note>Arianism: a 4th-century theological position that held that Jesus was a created being, subordinate to God the Father; many early modern scholars viewed Islam as a survival or offshoot of this "heresy."</note>, he ought to have proved it with passages from Scripture and with reason. But he learned to use the sword rather than syllogisms. Thirdly, finally, it is well known that most of those wonders which the Arabs commonly report him to have performed were fabricated not to prove the unity of the Divine Power, but to justify many absurdities and rituals. Therefore, I shall add nothing regarding the quality of the witnesses. However, it is not my intention to defend the discipline of the Christians at length against the nonsense of this man and his followers; this has been done abundantly by Learned Men. Certainly, if anyone were to compare the foundations upon which the Christian Religion is built—dogma with dogma, precept with precept, and finally the worship which the Christian Religion demands—with the rites and worship of **Muhammad** and his followers, it will be clear that **Muhammad** and his first partners in fraud, whether they were **Jews** or **Christians** (for the **Quran** and **Islam** should be attributed to these as the inventors rather than to **Muhammad**, whom they used as a figurehead to gain a semblance of Religion), were impostors. They either attacked and corrupted or utterly denied the most serious principles of Religion, though these principles were supported by no small defenses. They sought many things from the Jews and Christians to adorn their own Religion, yet they contaminated them with foolish opinions and superstitious rites; and while preserving only a few truths, they turned the primary worship of the Deity into a <term>bodily worship</term> <note>original: "σωματικην λατρειαν" (somatiken latreian). This refers to a religion focused on physical rituals and outward ceremonies rather than spiritual transformation.</note>, and a vain one at that. From this, our thesis is once again more than sufficiently confirmed. Indeed, **Muhammad** could not have won a semblance of Religion unless there had been among both Christians and Jews men of no faith, prepared for every wickedness, who—having renounced their most holy Religion—had aided the plans and efforts of this crafty man with innumerable invented fictions. Furthermore, the Illustrious **Grotius** <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a famous Dutch legal scholar and theologian.</note> shows in summary, among many others, what the causes were for such stupendous progress made by the Muhammadans, why they seized so many noble provinces, and what contributed most to the propagation of the Muhammadan Religion, in his golden little book *On the Truth of the Christian Religion*.

...the founder of the *English Library* <note>original: "Bibliothecæ Anglicanæ Conditor," referring to Michel de la Roche, a Huguenot refugee and journalist.</note>. While he was in Volume I, part II of this Library, exhibiting a compendium of those things contained in Volume II of the various short works of Duke **Blackmore**, he mentioned, among other things, **Mahomed Effendi**. According to the testimony of **Rycaut** <note>Sir Paul Rycaut (1629–1700), an English diplomat and historian who wrote extensively on the Ottoman Empire.</note>, this Effendi is said to have been put to death in Constantinople for Atheism. Upon this, the famous **de la Roche** broke out into these words: *“I do not know whether that author (meaning Rycaut) was rightly informed about the true cause of the punishment inflicted upon Mahomet Effendi. For since the Mohammedan Religion (he appeals here to the notes on Reland <note>Adrian Reland (1676–1718), a Dutch scholar whose work "De religione Mohammedica" was a pioneering, more objective study of Islam.</note>) is the most simple, it seems that far fewer Atheists can exist among the followers of Muhammad than among Christians. This judgment of mine rests on the foundation that, clearly, the great number of dogmas and superstitious rites with which the Christian Religion is burdened do much to promote Atheism.”*

So says the celebrated **de la Roche**. It is no wonder that this judgment by a learned man has offended some, who believe he was speaking about the Christian Religion in general. However, since he joins "superstitious rites" to "dogmas," it is more credible that he intended to attack the Religion of the Romanists <note>A common 18th-century term for Roman Catholics.</note>. And indeed, it is true that the Religion of the Papists is burdened with so many silly rites, so many fables are imposed on men to be believed, and so many miracles are boasted of here and there to confirm the most vain opinions—for example, **Transubstantiation** <note>The doctrine that the bread and wine in the Eucharist become the actual body and blood of Christ.</note>, to say nothing of the prohibition against examining one's Religion—that many who see and hear all these things, yet are not better instructed, cannot help but fall into the vice of Unbelief. We shall deal with this more extensively in the progress of these Exercises at the proper time. We admit that, in this sense, the Christian Religion cannot be called "most simple."

But if this learned man had wished to speak either of the Christian Religion as viewed in itself, or of the Religion of Protestants specifically—though this does not seem likely to me—we deny that the Mohammedan religion, compared with the Christian in this sense, is simpler. However, lest we fall into a dispute over words <term>logomachiam</term>, we must know what the learned man understands by the name of "simplicity." As far as can be gathered from the words cited, he calls a "simple" Religion one that consists of few articles. But in that case, neither the Christian nor the Mohammedan, but only the Religion of the **Deists** <note>Deism: a belief in a creator God based on reason rather than revelation, popular in the Enlightenment.</note> would be called the "most simple." For they, as is well known, subscribe to only a few articles. Therefore, one must look not only at the number of articles to be believed, but primarily at their truth, utility, and ease of understanding. For once the truth of the Christian Religion is established, it is not within our power to restrict the number of articles contained in it at our whim, although we readily concede that some articles are more or less

<column-break/>

<page-num>125</page-num>
<header>ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.</header>

easy to grasp, some are more frequently emphasized, and others less so. Some are presented in such a way that it is manifest they cannot be denied without detriment to one's salvation; others, however, can be ignored without danger to salvation. From this, the distinction made by theologians between "fundamental" and "non-fundamental" articles arose. 

Moreover, the learned man knows that for the unrefined and the common folk, only clear, transparent, and easy-to-learn articles of faith are proposed in the **Catechisms** <note>Instructional manuals used to teach the core principles of the Christian faith.</note>. Nevertheless, all are encouraged indiscriminately to apply their minds, as far as their talents allow, to rightly perceiving all the articles of the Christian Religion, and to spend the strength received from God toward that end. And in this sense, if the truth of the Christian Religion is admitted, those articles delivered in the Catechisms as absolutely necessary to be believed for salvation are not only few in number, but are also true, useful, easy to grasp, and thus *simple*.

But let us set these things aside and ask the learned man whether, by the name of "Religion," he understands Revelation itself in its pure form—that is, as it is presented in the books of the Old and New Testaments—or rather those various systems which Christians have fashioned, either according to the different nature of their talent and capacity, or from certain hypotheses. Whether the learned man asserts the *former* or the *latter*, we contend that the Christian Religion is simpler than **Islam** <note>original: "Islamismo"</note>. Come, let us show this here in a few words. 

Above all, we must repeat what we said before: namely, that the simplicity of any Religion is placed not only in the ease of its articles, but most especially in their truth, utility, and ease of understanding. For if two propositions were proposed to someone to be believed, but they were either manifestly contradictory or at least false, such a confession of faith would indeed be "short" if you look at the number—that is, "simple"—but in reality, it would be most confused and absurd—that is, most "complex"—because their truth would either be plainly undemonstrable, or it would need countless equally false propositions to give it a semblance of color. Why these things are said will soon be clear. 

Let us therefore compare the theoretical and practical principles of the Mohammedans with the theoretical and practical articles of the Christians that are necessary to be known or believed. **Maracci** <note>Ludovico Maracci (1612–1700), an Italian priest who published an influential Latin translation and refutation of the Quran.</note>, in his *Introduction* <note>original: "Prodromo"</note>, Part IV, reduces the sum of **Islam** to five heads. Two of these are theoretical, the rest are practical. Among the theoretical ones, the *first* is this: that there is only one God. The *second* is that Muhammad was a prophet raised up by God, whose sayings contained in the **Quran** <note>original: "Alcorano"</note> are to be held as divine Oracles. Regarding the first article, there is nothing for us to remark upon. This article is easy to grasp and suited to the talents of all, if you set aside curious questions about the nature of certain attributes of God. But as for...

# MEDITATION III.

...on the other hand, as it pertains to that second article <note>The "second article" refers to the Islamic declaration that Muhammad is the messenger of God.</note>, it is not only far from simple and extremely complex, but it shrinks so far from any appearance of truth that whatever "Mystery" exists in the Christian Religion is easy and plain when compared with this article. For this proposition—*Muhammad is a Prophet sent by God*—to hold its truth, it would have to be proven that he provided such evidence of his divine mission that it could not be called into doubt by anyone who loves the truth. But this latter point cannot be demonstrated. For one must say he is a Prophet either because *Muhammad* himself asserted it, or because his followers asserted it, or because he both did and taught things that necessarily prove he was sent to earth by God's will to promote the salvation of mankind. The first is foolish to assert, because then every dull-witted person would have to be considered a Prophet; the second is no less weak, unless his followers provide such arguments that necessarily compel our assent—and we have already heard above what kind of witnesses these are. Therefore, the whole question returns to the third proposition, which consists of two parts. Specifically, it must be demonstrated, first, that the Decrees and precepts of *Muhammad* are so composed that they could have no other than a divine origin; second, it must be proven that God demonstrated this man was sent by God through distinguished miracles. To prove the first proposition, one must look into both the theoretical and practical Decrees of *Muhammad*, seeing not only whether they are consistent with divine virtues and fit for perfecting the human race, but also whether they were previously unknown and thus necessary to be learned. But many things stand in the way of a Muslim being able to prove those propositions. First, regarding that fundamental article of *Muhammad*, namely that there is one God: certainly the confession of this article does not prove he was a Prophet; for if so, almost all Pagans, Jews, and Christians would have to be called Prophets. We showed above that many among the Pagans admitted this article; therefore, it was not necessary for such a Prophet to be sent down from heaven to prove this. God certainly does not perform extraordinary acts where easy means are at hand. This is the first theoretical article, which is followed by the other—namely, that *Muhammad* is a Prophet—about which more must be said shortly. The practical articles include the following chapters: *namely, that Alms are to be paid to the poor, that one must devote oneself to Prayer and Fasting, and that a Pilgrimage to the shrine at Mecca must be undertaken*; to which *Abulpharagius* <note>Gregory Bar Hebraeus (1226–1286), a high-ranking official in the Syriac Orthodox Church and a prolific historian.</note> in *Pococke's* <note>Edward Pococke (1604–1691), a renowned English Orientalist and professor of Arabic at Oxford.</note> *Historical Specimens of the Arabs, page 30*, adds: *that cleanliness must be maintained in the extremities of the human body*. But who does not see that even if *Muhammad* had highly comm-

<column-break/>

# ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

-ended these things to his followers, it would not therefore follow that he was a future Prophet, or that these decrees came to him through Revelation? The laws of humanity alone demand that alms be paid to the poor; and anyone, by turning their mind to the state of wretched men and weighing what they would want done for themselves if they were needy, will easily perceive the necessity of this duty without Revelation—to say nothing of how frequently this duty was enjoined by Christ and the Apostles. Moreover, *Maracci* <note>Ludovico Maracci (1612–1700), an Italian priest and translator of the Quran into Latin.</note> observed in his *Introduction, page 31*, that most Alms are to be collected by Muslims for the purpose of using this money whenever they must fight against infidels, that is, Christians. Regarding *prayers*, the followers of *Muhammad* are bound to pour out certain formulas of prayer five times a day (*); but even if these were exactly as they ought to be, this does not prove that man was divinely raised up. For the fact that prayers should be offered was not unknown even to the Pagans themselves, to say nothing of Jews and Christians. Nor were Christians or Jews unaware that one should occasionally devote time to *Fastings*. However, the Fast of which *Muhammad* makes mention in the *Quran, Surah II, verse 179* <note>Modern numbering: Surah 2, verse 187.</note> is strange; for he speaks there as follows: *It is permitted to you on the night of the Fast to have sexual access to your wives; for they are a covering for you, and you are a covering for them. God knows that (in the beginning of Islam) you deceived your own souls, and so He has had mercy on you and indulged you. Now therefore go in unto them and desire what God has prescribed for you; and eat and drink (namely, throughout the whole night) until the white thread can be distinctly recognized from the black thread at dawn.* Finally, regarding that pilgrimage to the Shrine at Mecca and the cleanliness of the body, it is plain how little this worship is worthy of God, much less that it could contribute anything toward proving the divine mission of *Muhammad*. If Muslims wish to prove that theoretical article—namely, that *Muhammad was a Prophet raised up by God*—they must have recourse to the *Quran* itself; in this patchwork <note>original: "centone," a term implying a literary work made up of scraps from other sources.</note> you find innumerable inept, ridiculous, and God-insulting things that openly conflict with one another, which have long since been collected by learned men. Is this, then, a simple Religion?

...can it be called simple? We will indeed gladly grant to the famous <term>Reland<note>Hadrian Reland (1676–1718) was a pioneering Dutch orientalist who argued that many European ideas about Islam were based on misconceptions.</note></term>, to whom the Learned Man appeals, that many things were falsely attributed to *Muhammad*. Yet, beyond the fact that the Arabs scattered many more and most shameless lies about *Muhammad* and his words and deeds among the common people—as the biography of *Muhammad* written by the most erudite <term>Gagnier<note>Jean Gagnier (c. 1670–1740) was a French scholar who wrote an influential life of Muhammad based on Arabic sources.</note></term> teaches—it is clearer than the midday sun that the *Quran is a patchwork* <note>original: "Alcoranum Centonem"; a 'cento' refers to a poem or work made up of various scraps and fragments from other sources.</note> of the most foolish sentiments, rather than a true divine Revelation. If you look at the Ethics or the moral precepts of the *Quran*, you will find that the transgression of the holiest precepts is often counted among indifferent or lawful matters. See, for example, what is said throughout the *Quran* about exercising vengeance against enemies; about dissimulation in the cause of Religion; about the ease of eluding Oaths, etc., not to mention more of this kind, which the famous <term>Michaelis<note>Johann David Michaelis (1717–1791), a German biblical scholar and orientalist.</note></term> exhibits in his summary in the *Dissertation on the Moral Laxity of the Quran*. But do these things prove that *Muhammad is a Prophet for the correction of the human race?* Did he perhaps perform miracles? But we have heard above that he did not dare to openly confess this himself. It is true that his shameless, trifle-peddling followers attributed countless miracles to him after his death; but it is very clear what sort they are, or for what purpose they are said to have been produced—namely, only to win authority for a crafty and warlike man. The witnesses themselves, if you consider the age in which they lived (to say nothing of other characteristics), are not worthy of belief. *In vain do you seek ancient writers of the life of Muhammad who were either his contemporaries <note>original Greek: ὁμηλίκας</note> or close to his age.* The most ancient book of the highest authority among the greater part of the Muhammadans is the <term>Sunnah<note>The body of traditional social and legal custom and practice of the Islamic community, often based on the words and deeds of Muhammad.</note></term>, in which, among other oral traditions, many things are found written down regarding the *sayings, deeds, and utterances of Muhammad*, and likewise miracles and prophecies. This was not cobbled together from various narrations of various people, sought and collected from everywhere, until the end of the second century after Muhammad’s death, or after it had already passed, by Abu-Abdollah, commonly called <term>Al-Bukhari<note>Muhammad ibn Ismail al-Bukhari (810–870 AD), compiler of one of the most authoritative Sahih (authentic) Hadith collections in Sunni Islam.</note></term> from his homeland of Bukhara, and his associates. For this reason, the *Persians* <note>Referring to the Shia Muslims, who generally reject the Sunni Hadith collections like Al-Bukhari.</note> also reject the credibility of this book of legends. So says the famous and most friendly *Grynæus*, a most erudite Professor of Theology, in letters sent to me on this subject. Regarding his character, we have said enough above: he was certainly a man fond of women, eager for revenge, and a most unjust oppressor of the innocent. Far from being able to be regarded as a Prophet sent from heaven, he does not even deserve the title of a good man. From these things, to be brief, it is sufficiently established that the fundamental proposition of the Muhammadans—namely, that *Muhammad is a prophet divinely raised up*—can be proved by no reason, and thus their dogmas can be called neither true, nor probable, and consequently not even *simple*. But if most...

The whole ethical compendium of the Christian Religion is comprised in the love of God and neighbor; indeed, where the love of God alone is present and has taken root in the mind, there also a perpetual zeal for pleasing God—that is, virtues of every kind—will have a place. If you join all these things together, it will be clear in our opinion that the Christian Religion, viewed in itself, is far simpler than the *Muhammadan* Religion. Secondly, all Protestants can, in matters of doubt, return to the Sacred Scripture, which everyone is bound to read. # MEDITATION III.

But even if Muhammad cannot be entirely excluded from the rank of religious fanatics, he deserves even more to be classified among shrewd and clever impostors. Whether he was truly "greedy for glory" in the sense that certain Church Fathers called the ancient pagan philosophers "animals of glory" <note>A phrase used by early Christian writers like Tertullian to describe philosophers who sought worldly fame rather than divine truth.</note>—striving to acquire or devise a reputation for himself that was, if not good, then certainly great—I am somewhat doubtful. I judge that such a desire for propagating one's name to posterity belongs more to the genius of more refined nations, like the Greeks and Romans, than to the ferocious Arabs of that time or to the "illiterate prophet" himself <note>original: **נביא אמי** (Navi Ummi), a term from the Quran usually translated as the "Unlettered Prophet."</note>.

However, I do not hesitate to affirm that he was greedy for rule and dominion over his countrymen, always seeking to further extend the empire he desired and eventually achieved. Furthermore, he was excessively devoted to women and lust. To satisfy these depraved desires as his primary goal, he directed all his thoughts. He falsely claimed to have received his laws from God, craftily adapting both his character and his manner of dealing with those he sought to win over to achieve that same end.

Just how devoted he was to lust is clear enough from the fact that he was by no means content with two, three, or four wives—the number he permitted his followers to marry—but joined many more to himself in marriage. Those who claim the highest number *assign seventeen to him*, says Abulpharaius (e); those who claim the fewest say thirteen. Abulfeda (f) records that he married fifteen and had relations with eleven of them. To show that this was permitted to him, this impure man introduces God in Sura 33, verse 47 (g), granting him—as a "holy man" and a Prophet, of course—a singular privilege above the rest of the faithful: the power to marry as many wives as he wished, and furthermore to take concubines. Indeed, with truly incredible impudence, he even feigns that he was rebuked by God for abstaining from intercourse with his Egyptian maidservant Maria, and that he was released from the religious obligation of the oath he had made to his wife Hafsa, promising that he would leave that Maria alone in the future, as seen in Sura 66, verses 1 and following. That this is the meaning of the passage we have just explained—

—is openly taught by the Arabic commentators Jalal ad-Din, Yahya, and al-Zamakhshari in the works of Maracci. But enough, or even more than enough, on this subject.

It follows that we should show how this lustful Prophet also greatly sacrificed to ambition, and was greedy for seizing power over his countrymen and extending his empire further. We read in Abulpharaius (h) and Abulfeda (Chapter 51) that at the time when Muhammad approached to capture Mecca, accompanied by ten thousand soldiers, one of the citizens of Mecca, Abu Sufyan the Qurayshite, seeing this extraordinary and well-equipped army, turned to Al-Abbas, Muhammad's uncle, and exclaimed: *“Truly the kingdom of your brother’s son has now turned into a great kingdom!”* <note>original: **מלך אבן אחיך מלוך עטמא לקד אצבת**</note>. But in truth, there can be no doubt that Muhammad imposed upon the ignorant under the guise of prophecy or a prophetic office, and aimed for a kingdom—and an earthly one at that, which he indeed attained—if only we weigh what and how much he demanded from all his followers, and what he understood by those words when he wanted to be recognized by them as the *Messenger of God* <note>original: **רסול אללה** (Rasul Allah)</note>. In his first *pledge of allegiance* <note>original: **ביעה** (Bay'ah), a formal oath of fealty to a leader.</note>, when he did not yet think himself sufficiently protected by wealth and power (i), he was content with an oath of obedience and loyalty offered by a few of the Ansar <note>The "Helpers," residents of Medina who accepted Islam.</note>, fearing to impose on them the necessity of waging war on his behalf. But when he had later gained a few more followers, in the second pledge he required of them (k) that they should swear in these words: *“that they would defend him from every insult, just as they were accustomed to defend their own wives and children”*—that is, even by force and arms. Ebn Isaac observes that at that time the power to wage war and to repel force with force was first given to him, and verse 41 of Sura 22 was then sent down from heaven. Finally, having become more secure as the number of his followers increased, and conceiving a greater hope in his heart every day for the happy success of his imposture, he began not only to defend against force but to inflict it on others. To cloak this purpose with a respectable appearance—or rather, to cover crime with crime—he took up the cause of propagating his religion by arms: that is, of enlarging his kingdom through war, and pursuing with war all those who rejected his rule until, broken by calamities, they submitted themselves to him—

# MEDITATION III.

...to cast them down, or to destroy them in a massacre, he dared to fabricate a command enjoined upon him by God. This is sufficiently clear—not to pile up further testimonies—from Sura 66, verse 9, and Sura 8, verse 39 alone. All of these things certainly do not suit a Prophet eager to promote divine glory and human salvation, but rather a cunning Impostor solely intent on establishing his kingdom and increasing his power under the pretext of religion.

To achieve this goal more easily and to draw as many men of every kind as possible to his side, he fashioned his new Law in such a way that he did not entirely alienate the minds of Jews and Christians from embracing it, while also greatly enticing all his fellow Arabs, of whatever religion they might be, even idolaters.

Hence, he did not reject the religions of the Jews and Christians as false. Instead, he professed (l) that both Moses and Christ were prophets sent by God—the former to bring the Book of the Law and the latter the Gospel to mankind in God’s name. He demanded to be recognized as a third prophet, either similar to those earlier ones or perhaps superior, and even foretold by them, the "Seal of the Prophets" (m). He required that his Quran be joined and added to the Law and the Gospel as their completion. He hoped to obtain this more easily from Jews and Christians than if he simply ordered them to defect from Moses and Christ by condemning the religions in which they had been nurtured as impostures.

Especially, however, to better entice all his fellow Arabs to receive and embrace his new Law, he accommodated the nature of that Law to their character, customs, prejudices, and finally their desires as much as he could.

From this, firstly, arose and was born that strange and perverse method of propagating religion by arms and thrusting it upon all by using military force, which is taught in many places in the Quran (n). This could not fail to greatly please the Arabs, a fierce and warlike people accustomed to living by plunder, since they saw that power was thus given to them to invade all their neighbors whenever they pleased, to pursue them in war, to slaughter those resisting and defending themselves and their property, to plunder their resources, occupy their goods, and finally to subdue them and subject them to their rule—

—subjection. Everyone knows how eagerly the Muslims have used this religious—or should I say irreligious—license until now, especially to the great detriment of the Christian cause.

II. Since Muhammad judged others by himself and was not ignorant of how devoted his countrymen were to lust, he thought that the license for divorce and repudiation should be recalled and expanded from the Law of Moses (o). He also decided that, with the severity of the Christian Law mitigated, polygamy should again be permitted, so that it is right and lawful for any faithful Muslim to join four legitimate wives to himself in marriage according to Sura 4, verse 3. To ensure they might enjoy a solid and perpetual happiness, he also gave them hope for a future life after this one to be spent in all the pleasures of the flesh, and especially in the constant embrace of the most beautiful virgins (p). Some Muhammadans who are ashamed of this Paradise wish to claim these were said in figurative speech, but the most excellent interpreters of the Quran (q) and the Book of the Sunna (r) show they were understood literally by Muhammad himself and are thus to be understood. And why should the Prophet not place the happiness of the future life in those things in which he himself confesses he takes such great delight in this life, God willing, as recorded in the work of Abulfeda <note>A 14th-century Kurdish historian and geographer</note> in these words: <note>original Arabic in Hebrew script: **אללה געל לדתי פי אלנסא ו אלטיב**</note> *“God placed my delight in women and sweet scents”* (s).

To provide a reason for this change, he claimed that the house was built by Abraham and was therefore older and more excellent than the one in Jerusalem. (b)

Regarding other matters, such as the miracles we read that Moses and Christ performed—undoubted wonders published openly in the light of day before many onlookers—Muhammad was so far from being able to appeal to such things in the Quran that, on the contrary, whenever either the Jews or the Arabs required such signs as the most certain <term>criteria <note>original Greek: κριτήρια; standards of judgment</note></term> of the divine mission he claimed, he clearly confessed as many times that he had not been equipped by God with the power to perform signs (l). For what the Muslims <note>original: Mohammedani</note> say—that certain indications (m) of miracles performed by their Prophet are found in the Quran itself—is of no weight at all. For why would Muhammad have wished to allude to these wonderful works obscurely, rather than appealing to them openly in the manner of true Prophets? Why would he, who observed no restraint in preaching his Quran and cried out that the excellence of that Book alone was sufficient to gain him faith, not have also extolled his other miraculous works with the highest praise, had he performed any, and beaten the ears of all with frequent mention of them? What is said of miracles may also be affirmed regarding the gift of prophecy: that Muhammad nowhere arrogated or claimed it for himself in the Quran; indeed, when asked by his Companions about secret or future matters, he professed that knowledge of them was by no means granted to him, and that he was ignorant of what would happen to himself or to them (o). What I think of this, I shall set forth in a few points: I. Indeed, I will not deny that Muhammad—besides the fact that he denied Christ was crucified by the Jews—hardly rejected other dogmas of the Christian Religion in express words, except those in which even Christians do not deny some difficulty exists: namely, the dogma of the Holy Trinity, eternal generation, and the Incarnation of the Son of God.

II. I observe that Muhammad either never understood or was able to comprehend the mind of Christians regarding those dogmas (due to his lack of skill and gross ignorance of the Gospel), or (due to his wickedness) he knowingly and willingly attributed to them an opinion foreign to them and plainly absurd, so that he might have something to attack. For who among Christians ever established that *God is the third of three*—that is, that besides God there are yet two others, and thus three Gods? Or who affirmed that God, with the Virgin Mary, the Mother of God, as His wife, and Christ the son of both, are those three Gods and constitute the Trinity of the Christians? Yet the Impostor <note>The author uses "Impostor" as a polemical label for Muhammad, common in 17th and 18th-century European scholarship.</note> falsely attributes this opinion to Christians and then rejects it in the Quran, Surah 4, verse 169, and Surah 5, verses 82 and 125.

III. The dogma of Christians regarding the Holy Trinity, the generation, and the Incarnation of the Son of God—if indeed it is explained correctly and according to their mind—is rightly judged by you to be "most worthy of belief." This is because it is read as revealed in express words in the <term>divinely inspired <note>original Greek: θεοπνεύσοις (theopneustois); literally "God-breathed" scriptures</note></term> Scriptures which do not know how to lie. Furthermore, it in no way contradicts sound reason and its evident dictates, even though we cannot precisely define the nature of that distinction of the three (as we call them) Persons in one and infinite Divine nature or essence, how the Son emanated from the Father or was begotten from eternity, or in what manner the divine nature assumed the human into the unity of the person.

But if, IV., there remains some mystery in this Christian dogma which we do not fully grasp—and perhaps will never plainly perceive until we comprehend the infinite nature of God with our finite minds—by contrast, in Muhammad's Quran, many things are discovered that are not mysteries, but are decrees openly clashing with the primary principles of <term>Natural Religion <note>A 17th-18th century concept of religion based on reason and morality common to all humans, independent of specific revelation.</note></term> and sound moral doctrine. madmen even after the death of that wretched man. Indeed, we are not unaware that there have been learned men who thought, and still think, that many among the ancient philosophers of the East and Greece defended this very same System. Thus <term>the late</term> <term>Buddeus</term> <note>Johannes Franz Buddeus (1667–1729), a prominent German Lutheran theologian and philosopher.</note> wrote a dissertation on "Spinozism before Spinoza." <term>Bayle</term> <note>Pierre Bayle (1647–1706), author of the influential "Historical and Critical Dictionary."</note> attempted the same under the entry for <term>Xenophanes</term>. This much is certain: no one among the Ancients—if one wishes to argue that any were addicted to this error—ever reduced this monstrous opinion into the form of a System. But Spinoza finally attempted this with an ill-fated daring, going so far as to approach the treatment of this argument with a mathematical method <note>Spinoza's "Ethics" was written in a "geometrical order," using definitions, axioms, and proofs like a math textbook.</note>. Whatever the case may be, this is certain: no system could be devised that is more inept, monstrous, and hostile to Religion—none that so overflows with such gross and absurd ideas as this one. It is a wonder that a man who was not unlearned and was more than moderately versed in philosophical disciplines could have given his vote of approval to such a portentous opinion. It is even more wonderful that after him, even though all the foundations of this system had been shattered by sharp-witted men, many were still able to defend it. Among them was also Count <term>Boullainvilliers</term> <note>Henri de Boulainvilliers (1658–1722), a French nobleman who wrote a famous but controversial summary of Spinoza’s philosophy.</note>, and among the most recent, <term>Edelmann</term> <note>Johann Christian Edelmann (1698–1767), a radical German pietist turned freethinker.</note>, about whom I shall have occasion to speak elsewhere. However, it is not my intention to refute the System of Spinoza at length, or to weigh every single point part by part—which would be the work of an entire volume, and because this has already been performed by many learned men. Instead, I will only briefly, and according to the understanding of my audience, show how many contradictions it overflows with, and how one must renounce a sound mind if they wish to protect this System. I do this solely for the purpose of making it clear that Unbelievers often defend the most absurd things while rejecting things that are more certain and far more evident. ...whether intellectual or extended, he concludes that there is only that one substance. Third: *This one Substance, or what is the same thing, this Universe, is God, or that Being whom we are accustomed to call God.*

<margin>According to Spinoza’s System, no Substance exists, which is diametrically opposed to his own system.</margin>

II. However, so that it may be clear how monstrous this System is, and how many contradictions it abounds with, we shall arrange our thoughts into certain articles.

Come, let us prove this in a few words: Spinoza admits two eternal attributes of things, namely infinite thought and infinite extension. To infinite thought belong all thinking Beings, which are nothing but modes <note>In Spinoza’s philosophy, a "mode" is a specific manifestation or "version" of an attribute, like a single thought being a mode of Thought.</note> of that thinking attribute. To infinite extension belong all individual bodies, of whatever nature they may be, which are nevertheless merely modes of the attribute of extension. Now, if these things are true, not only are multiple substances not granted, but not even One is granted. To be sure, all thinking substances together make up the attribute of thought; but as is the nature of the modes, such is also the nature of the attributes. Yet all modes are merely individual—for example, of this angelic or human thinking Being; whether these modes are called infinite or finite, they remain modes. However, no substance can be fashioned from modes taken together. Therefore, in the System of *Spinoza*, there are only infinite intellectual or thinking modes, but no thinking Substance, which is absurd.

The same can be said of the attribute of extension: all individual bodies—for example, air, fire, water, earth, etc.—are infinite modes of that attribute of extension. Those modes making up the attribute of extension always remain modes according to *Spinoza*; the attribute of extension has no extended substance in which it might "inhere" <note>To "inhere" means to exist within or belong to a subject, like the color red inheres in an apple.</note>, because it is nothing but a collection of modes considered under the concept of an infinite extended attribute. From which it follows that no extended substance is granted either, and consequently, according to *Spinoza’s* System, neither an intellectual nor an extended substance is granted. This is not only absurd but is diametrically opposed to his own fundamental proposition, in which he established that only one substance is granted. We can indeed, through a certain precision of the mind, contemplate all intellectual and extended substances as a kind of "one," or as some single substance; but it is well known that such abstractions do not exist outside the mind. Since, however, in *Spinoza’s* System all substances are nothing but modes, and su—

---

<page-num>145</page-num>
<header>ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.</header>

—ch modes indeed, which do not inhabit certain individual substances (for he does not admit more than one), it follows that nothing is given but infinite modes considered under the idea of THE ONE, but properly *no Substance is given*, which overthrows the System of *Spinoza* itself.

<margin>Modes can subsist without a subject according to Spinoza, which is most absurd.</margin>

III. From this first Article follows the *Second*, no less foolish than the first: namely, *that modes can subsist without a subject*. It is a metaphysical axiom, as everyone knows, that modes cannot exist without a subject. For example, roundness cannot exist without a round body. But if we listen to Spinoza, this Axiom is false. For individual extended substances, according to Spinoza, are nothing but a heap of extended modes; individual intelligent substances are nothing but modes; nothing outside those modes can be given or conceived; nor do extended modes inhabit extended substances, nor do thinking modes inhabit thinking substances. From this it necessarily follows, according to *Spinoza's* hypothesis, that modes can exist without a subject, which is contrary to the most evident Axiom, and therefore absurd.

<margin>According to Spinoza, the same thing can simultaneously be that which it is not.</margin>

IV. The Third Article follows: It is a metaphysical and logical Axiom that *the same thing cannot simultaneously exist and not exist, or be and not be.* Upon this Axiom all our reasoning and the foundations of the art of thinking rest. This, however, is removed by the System of Spinoza; whence it is established that it is necessarily false. To be sure, this axiom is true not only with respect to the existence and essence of things, but also to all the "affections" <note>In this context, "affections" refers to qualities, states, or feelings.</note> belonging to both the mind and the body. Thus the proverb goes: *No one can blow and swallow at the same time.* <note>original: "Nemo potest simul flare & sorbere."</note> But if the truth of this System is granted, all contrary things must be said. That one substance is at rest and in motion at the same time; it feels and does not feel; it affirms and denies; it grieves and rejoices at the same moment; it is round and square at once; it detests and praises; it sleeps and does not sleep; it is ignorant of Mathematics and at the same time most subtly geometrizes <note>original: "γεωμετρεῖ" (geometrizes), referring to performing complex mathematical proofs.</note>, etc., etc.

What mortal could, I will not say assert this with some appearance of truth, but even merely conceive of it? Bodies can indeed admit a thousand shapes successively; but that plainly opposite shapes—for example, round and square—should be in one and the same body at the same moment of time, cannot happen by the nature of things. Likewise, our mind admits many ideas or thoughts; but that it should simultaneously think and not think, doubt and not doubt, affirm and deny, is impossible. Since, however, that God of *Spinoza*, or that one substance, is properly nothing besides the collection of infinite substances which we call modes—and since modes in the whole Universe are at every moment diametrically—

<summary>The author critiques Spinoza’s Monism by arguing that if everything is just a "mode" of one substance, then Spinoza has effectively deleted the concept of substance entirely. Furthermore, the author argues that Spinoza's system violates the Law of Non-Contradiction, as the "One Substance" (God) would have to possess contradictory qualities simultaneously across different parts of the universe.</summary>

# MEDITATION III.

...posited as opposites, it is necessary that Spinoza’s <note>Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677), a philosopher who argued that everything in the universe is part of one single substance, which he called "God or Nature."</note> single substance must simultaneously be and not be, move and not move, sleep and not sleep, etc., which is absurd and foolish.

<margin>According to Spinoza’s system, nothing could have originated; and thus, if it were valid, nothing would exist, which is absurd.</margin>

V. **Fourth Article:** *If Spinoza’s opinion is true, then it follows that nothing can arise; or what is the same thing, that things—whether intellectual or extended—must owe their existence to Nothing, which is absurd.* In the preceding sections, we heard that all creatures, whether intellectual <note>Minds or souls.</note> or extended <note>Physical matter or bodies.</note>, are nothing but "modes" <term>mode: in Spinoza's thought, a specific "version" or "state" of a substance, like a ripple is a mode of water.</term> in Spinoza's system. Yet, according to Spinoza’s system, no modes can give existence to themselves. From this, it follows that all intellectual and extended modes, taken together, cannot give existence to themselves. Since, however, nothing exists besides those individual substances <note>The author uses "substances" here to refer to individual things Spinoza calls modes.</note> which are nothing but modes in Spinoza's system, it follows that there is absolutely no cause for existing things—or, what is the same, that things currently existing arose from Nothing, which is most absurd. And let no one say that Spinoza’s substance is eternal; for it must be firmly held that this substance of Spinoza is not distinct from all those things that make up the world. Therefore, whatever the logic is for all individual things, such is also the logic for the whole. Since the individual things are nothing but modes, it follows that all of them, taken together, are modes. And because no mode can give existence to itself, it follows that they all lack this power; and thus, no cause for existing things is provided, which is an absurdity <note>original Greek: ατοπον (atophon), meaning "out of place" or "absurd."</note>. The same can be proved by another line of reasoning, namely: Whatever exists has the cause of its existence either in itself or in another; there is no third option. All bodies, according to Spinoza’s mind, are nothing but modes, and thus they do not have the cause of existence in themselves. I would say the same for all minds. Modes joined together do not constitute a substance existing by itself; therefore, they must necessarily have the cause of their existence from another substance. But in Spinoza’s system, no cause is provided that is distinct from those individual substances he calls modes. Therefore, there is absolutely nothing that can give the principle of existence to those substances. But since such substances do exist, one would have to say they existed without any cause, which is a contradiction. But if someone should say that, according to Spinoza’s mind, all things flow in infinite modes from the infinite nature of God, and so absolutely everything is eternal and necessary, I would ask him what he understands by the words *all things, infinite nature,* and *God.* (*) In Spinoza's system, these three words

VI. **Fifth Article:** *If we consider the matter of the origin of motion, it will again be clear with how many difficulties Spinoza's system teems.* For he must either assert that *no motion is granted*, or if there is any in the nature of things, that *it arises from Nothing*, both of which are senseless to say. We prove this as follows: According to Spinoza and all the Atheists I know (*), motion does not necessarily belong to the essence of bodies, because there are also bodies at rest. If motion does not necessarily belong to the essence of a body, and yet there are bodies that move (as Spinoza does not deny), some cause for this effect or motion must be rendered. The attribute of extension <note>Matter/Physicality.</note> consists of nothing but a complex of infinite individual substances. Whatever the logic is for the whole, such is also the logic for the individuals. But since motion does not belong to the essence of this or that body, and yet some things move and have been moved, and there are no substances other than those individual extended ones, it follows necessarily that according to Spinoza, motion either cannot be granted in any way, or if it is granted, it draws its origin from nothing—both of which are foolish to say.
