He wraps himself in the remainder of his discourse in the obscurity of ambiguous expressions with the intention of eluding the arguments by which he foresaw his system would be attacked. For after having advanced without detour that every substance exists necessarily, one would say he is afraid of having said too much, and that under the pretext of explaining himself, he retracts; for he adds that the reason why each thing exists necessarily, and could not be in any respect other than it is now, is because each thing flows necessarily from the Divine Nature. The reader who is not on his guard might perhaps imagine that he means by this that if things are necessarily, as we see them today, it is because an infinite wisdom and goodness could only make them in the most suitable and wise order. ...of motion, which he posits **Spinoza**, gave the beginning of motion to bodies. Yet this can have no place in the System of **Spinoza**. This man's opinion is well known, debated by himself and his disciples with no small appearance of truth, which goes as follows: things that have nothing in common with each other cannot act upon each other; but thinking substances <note>The "soul" or "mind."</note> have nothing in common with the body. Therefore [they cannot move the body]. For if motion does not belong to the essence of bodies, and intellectual substances have absolutely no connection with matter—and thus also cannot move matter—it necessarily follows, once again, that either motion is not given, or if it is given (which **Spinoza** concedes), it must be attributed to "Nothing," which is plainly absurd.

<margin>Countless absurdities, and plainly ridiculous, indeed detestable things, necessarily arise from Spinoza's hypothesis through evident laws of consequence, especially if we consider the worship of the Divine.</margin>

VII. Sixth Article: Finally, to pass over many other things in silence, how monstrous and foolish this System is becomes most evident if we turn our minds to the worship of the Divine and to Religion. **Spinoza** contends here and there in his *Ethics* that worship is due to his God. But since it is clearer than the midday sun that the whole Universe, with all its individual substances and accidents <term>accident: a non-essential quality of a thing, like its color or shape, as opposed to its "essence."</term>, constitutes that God of **Spinoza**, anyone could easily gather—even if I remained silent—what the nature of such worship would be. To be sure, Air, Fire, Earth, Plants, Animals, Insects, etc., belong no less to the essence of that God than the Sun, Moon, and other vast bodies floating in the heavens. This God moves here, rests elsewhere, sleeps and wakes, eats and drinks, but is also eaten and drunk; in a word, he is a Proteus <note>A shape-shifting sea god from Greek mythology; the author uses this to show how Spinoza's God is constantly changing form.</note>, taking on various forms. If the truth of this System were granted, there is no reason why we should worship the Sun and Moon more than Cats and Dogs. Furthermore, the most wicked and foolish man is no less a part of God than the wisest and best. Here that God acts as a scholarly teacher; elsewhere he understands more correctly. He believes all things have arisen simultaneously by chance and by necessity. If we admit this System, not only do Divinities <term>Numina: a Latin term for divine powers or local gods.</term> grow in every garden, but whatever you see, whatever you hear, whatever you taste, whatever you touch, is God; nor is there more reason why I should consider the stars as Gods than this paper on which I smear these characters, or the desk that supports the paper. Indeed, since everyone is nearest to himself and we are all drawn by a certain love for ourselves, nothing prevents me from counting myself among the principal parts of this Divinity. The difficulty grows and becomes more monstrous if we set before our eyes the countless successes and changes to which creatures are subject—both those endowed with life and sense, and those lacking such faculties. Here that God is harmed, beaten, lies deathly ill, is extinguished by flames; elsewhere he dances, triumphs, sings. Here he plays

odd or even <note>original: "par impar" — a common ancient game of chance.</note>, rides on a long reed <note>A "hobby-horse" or child's toy.</note> and moves mice to the post; there he geometrizes <note>original: "γεωμετρεῖ" (geometrei). A reference to the ancient saying "God always geometrizes," here mocked because Spinoza's God is also doing trivial things.</note>, acts as an orator, and bites his nails, etc. etc.—for I am weary of these follies. What man of sound mind, however, would contend that such a multiform and imperfect God ought to be worshiped? Who could think of such a blasphemous opinion without horror, let alone be able to subscribe to it with any appearance of truth? Hence it is a marvel that not only **Spinoza**, but others after him, were able to defend such a monstrous opinion. Alberto Radicati, Count of Passerano, who had been imbued with that most foolish opinion, confessed in his final illness to which he succumbed that it was impossible for a thing subject to such great imperfections, changes, and successions to be a part of God. We have provided the testimony in the first Dissertation on the *Inappropriate Methods of Disputing against Unbelievers by Certain Recent Scholars*. By right and merit, we apply to this System the words of Cicero from *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book I, Section XVI, which he used when about to attack the hypothesis of Zeno <note>The founder of Stoicism.</note>, saying:

> *I have truly set forth,* he says, *not the judgments of philosophers, but the dreams of madmen; nor indeed are those things much more absurd which, poured out in the voices of poets, have done harm by their very sweetness; for they introduced Gods inflamed by anger and raging with lust, and they brought it about that we saw their wars, fights, battles, and funerals; furthermore their hatreds, disagreements, discords, births, deaths, complaints, lamentations, and lusts poured out in every intemperance, adulteries, chains, intercourse with the human race, and mortals procreated from the Immortal.*

Nor is there any reason for someone to say that we dispute against **Spinoza** through circuitous consequences and with empty talk <note>original: "ματαιολογικῶς" (mataio-logikos).</note>; for all these consequences follow necessarily from the very character and nature of the System, which those who have properly examined this System will easily notice. We are indeed not ignorant that it is necessary for those who apply their minds to overturning the entire System of **Spinoza** to pay proper attention to his individual definitions, and especially to that which he had given regarding the nature of Substance. However, to show how absurd and monstrous the System is when viewed in itself, it is enough if those fundamental propositions on which it rests are clearly explained and handed down, and that it be shown not only how little they cohere with each other, but also how manifestly they fight against other truths—and those most certain and evident. If **Spinoza** had set forth his opinion openly and candidly in clear words, setting aside all ambiguities and verbal tricks, and had wished to prove it with arguments, I am persuaded that no one of sound mind, and even moderately skilled in the art of reasoning, [would have given] their vote to this monstrous opinion...

<header>MEDITATION IV.</header>

...it was proven by testimony. Yet, because this cunning man played with words and dressed up an offspring worthy of eternal darkness in mathematical clothing, many—swept away by blind admiration—believed there was something solid in this labor. But besides the fact that even mathematicians, when they treat other disciplines, can err no less than anyone else, it is well known that the certainty and evidence of any proposition or opinion does not depend on terms—that is, definitions, axioms, and so on—but on the very nature of things themselves. However that may be, it is clear enough that this System, viewed on its own, teems with innumerable follies and contradictions, and can in no way be compared with the clarity of the System professed by Christians and all others touched by a certain love for Religion. 

For once we posit the existence of a Divine Being <note>original: "Numinis"</note> who is most good, most wise, most powerful, and entirely distinct from this universe, the cause of the existence and essence of all things becomes clear. It is manifest that all things were made for a certain and most noble end; it is clear from where extended and intellectual substances <note>Extended substances refer to physical matter; intellectual substances refer to minds or souls.</note> drew their origin, and why that same Being equipped these noble substances with these specific faculties rather than others. At the same time, all who refuse to close their eyes can see upon what foundation all Religion, the worship of Him, and reverence for the laws rests, once the existence of the Divine is established. There is no one who, setting a fair value on each thing, will not admire the virtues of so great a God, seek His protection in narrow straits, compose his life and character according to His will, and most firmly believe that a Nature so excellent, wise, and kind would direct all His decrees for the use of the human race. I pass over many other things in silence which can easily be drawn out through the laws of logical consequence from the general propositions of Natural and Revealed Theology <note>Natural Theology is the study of God based on reason and nature; Revealed Theology is based on scripture.</note>. 

If, however, we turn the eyes of the mind toward the System of Spinoza, everything is filled with darkness. We can give no reason why creatures exist, or why they are endowed with these faculties rather than others; we can detect no beginning of things. Therefore, one must say that such Beings exist because they exist; that the causes of their existence can be sought and found neither in the nature of these Beings nor in another eternal cause distinct from them. One must say such things exist because all these things have been in infinite ways from eternity, and arose through some kind of blind **Fate** <note>original Greek: "Ειμαρμενην" (Heimarmene) - the Stoic concept of inescapable destiny.</note>. Hence Spinoza says in Proposition XVI:

> From the necessity of the divine nature, infinite things in infinite ways (that is, all things which can fall under a divine intellect) must follow. <note>original: "Ex necessitate divinæ Naturæ..."</note>

All "ends" or purposes must be banished from the Universe, which Spinoza also affirmed in just as many words; thus in Proposition XXIX:

> All things are determined by the necessity of the divine...

...divine nature, not only to exist, but also to exist and operate in a certain way, and no "contingent" thing <note>A "contingent" thing is something that could have been otherwise; Spinoza argues everything is strictly necessary.</note> is granted. In the Corollary to Proposition XXXII:

> God does not operate from freedom of the will. <note>original: "Deus non operatur ex libertate voluntatis."</note>

In the demonstration of Proposition XXXIII, he says:

> If things could have been of another nature, or determined to operate in another way, so that the order of nature were different, then God’s nature could also be different than it now is.

In the appendix to Proposition XXXVI, he says:

> Nature has no end set before itself, and all final causes <note>A "final cause" is the purpose or goal for which something exists.</note> are nothing but human fictions.

Hence, in the same place, he denies that eyes were made for seeing, teeth for chewing, plants and animals for food, the sun for illuminating, or the sea for nourishing fish. Whatever others say about the wise connection of things and the elegant symmetry of parts are "mere words," if you listen to Spinoza and his followers. In man-made objects, a craftsman deserves praise for his ingenuity in making a machine for the most beneficial uses, since everyone who is not completely dull—and certainly those skilled in art—can see the structure of all the parts, their purpose, their connection, and the utility resulting from the whole work and the functions of the individual parts. 

Yet all these things, skillfully made and arranged by human art and industry, are mere child’s toys compared with the structure of a plant, an animal, or even the smallest insect. No anatomist or botanist ever satisfies himself, nor will he ever satisfy himself in his whole life, in investigating and celebrating these things. But if you listen to Spinoza, no order is granted in the nature of things, no connection, nothing contingent or free. It was no less necessary for Spinoza to die at The Hague <note>original: "Hage-Comitum"</note> than it is necessary for a triangle to have three angles and three sides. I remain silent on many other absurd and impious things which necessarily follow from the nature of this System. Things being so, it is most manifest that all Religion and virtue are banished. For where there is no Divine Being distinct from the visible university of things, not even a shadow of Religion can have a place.

<margin>Spinoza seems to have clearly perceived the futility of this system.</margin>

VII. Anyone who rightly considers what we have said briefly so far about the System of Spinoza—and if I am not mistaken, according to the grasp of our audience—will wonder how a man of sound mind, and moreover cultured in philosophical disciplines, could have given his approval <note>original: "album calculum adjicere," literally "to add a white stone," an ancient way of voting 'yes' or for acquittal.</note> to such a monstrous opinion. The question is whether Spinoza himself perceived the vanity of his own System, and—carried away by a singular desire for fame—undertook its defense against the dictates of his conscience. We answer that it is often very difficult to judge whether someone is addicted to this or that hypothesis seriously and from the heart's true opinion; for human dispositions are varied, and the human mind has strange folds. # MEDITATION IV.

...is evident from the various Philosophical & Theological Hypotheses which hold a place everywhere among the Learned, and are often sharply defended with mutual accusations and apologies. This much is certain, and confirmed by experience: it often happens, such is the weakness of the human mind, that men who are not unlearned, deluded by an erring conscience, can retain and defend gross errors either for a long time or even until the end of their lives. This, however, is most likely to happen if the System itself possesses no small appearance of truth and is confirmed by the authority of many powerful and Famous men of talent; or if it is so subtle that even men of sharp wit can easily be deceived. Just as it is told of *Bredenburg* <note>Johannes Bredenburg (1643–1691) was a Dutch merchant and theologian who set out to refute Spinoza's *Ethics* but found himself so entangled in its logic that he was accused of becoming a Spinozist himself.</note>, namely, that when he set out to examine and refute the *Ethics* of *Spinoza*, he was cast into such difficulties that he hardly saw how to steady his mind against so many obstacles rushing upon him like a formed battle line. Thus we know, for example, of Men of the most outstanding and sharpest talent who held the argument of *Descartes* for the existence of God—drawn from the idea of God and *a priori* <note>An "a priori" argument is one based on theoretical deduction rather than observation or experience.</note>, as they say—to be a *perfect Demonstration*, and though they were warned, they were simply unable to feel the force of the reasons brought against it. From this it is clear that those who, having detected no other signs of vanity or a wicked mind, immediately cry out that this or that person subscribes to this or that opinion for the sake of appearances, and that having been persuaded of better things, they refuse to send away their erroneous opinions for this or that reason, act wrongly. 

Nevertheless, many signs are present which seem to prove that *Spinoza* had thoroughly perceived all the peaks and depths of the consequences of his system. For first, it is well known among all the Learned that he was unwilling to hand over his *Ethics* to the press while alive, but that here and there in Letters given to Friends, he brought forward certain sketches of his opinion, fearing no doubt that if his pestilential opinion were detected and brought into the open, it would stir up harmful dangers for him. For this reason also, he refused to accept the post of Professor of Philosophy offered on most honorable conditions by the most Famous Theologian of Heidelberg, *Johannes Ludovico Fabricius*, alleging among other things that he did not know how far that liberally offered freedom of philosophizing might extend. Added to this is the fact, proved by no contemptible evidence, that in the *Manuscript of his Ethics*, at the persuasion of his friend *Lodewijk Meyer*, the name of God was substituted in place of the word *Nature*, doubtless for the purpose of preventing the fraud from being detected too quickly. For there is no doubt that the *Opinion of Spinoza* was thoroughly perceived and known by *Meyer* himself. The same is suggested by the fact that in a Letter given to *Oldenburg* <note>Henry Oldenburg was the first secretary of the Royal Society in London and a frequent correspondent with Spinoza.</note>, he openly asserted that he held an

<column-break/>

# ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

opinion which was plainly abhorrent to the opinion of other Christians. For when *Oldenburg* had said these things, among others, in Letter XX: *I cannot but approve your purpose, by which you signify that you wish to illustrate and soften those things which, in the Theological-Political Treatise, caused the Readers to stumble. I should think those things are primarily what seem to be handed down ambiguously there concerning God and Nature; which two things very many people judge to be confounded by you*; *Spinoza* responded thus: *To open my mind to You, I say that I cherish an opinion concerning God and Nature far different from that which Modern Christians are accustomed to defend. For I establish God as the immanent cause <note>An "immanent" cause is one that acts from within, meaning Spinoza believed God is the world itself, rather than a separate creator acting upon it.</note>, as they say, of all things, but not truly the transient cause. All things, I say, are in God and move in God, affirming this with Paul <note>A reference to Acts 17:28 in the New Testament.</note> and perhaps also with all ancient Philosophers, though in another way; and I would even dare to say with all the ancient Hebrews, although one may only conjecture this, as their traditions have been corrupted in many ways.* From these things it is sufficiently clear that *Spinoza* had thoroughly perceived the consequences to which his opinion was subject. Hence, in his *Theological-Political Treatise*, he asserted that by the word Jehovah <note>original Hebrew: יהוה</note> only a "necessary Being" is to be understood. In this part, he was followed by *Toland* <note>John Toland (1670–1722), an Irish rationalist who is credited with coining the term "pantheist."</note>, of whom we shall say more below; namely, he asserts that the Pantheists (that is, those following *Spinoza’s* opinion concerning a single Substance) contend that *Moses* was addicted to this opinion. Hence he speaks thus in *The Origins of the Jews* <note>original: "Orig. Jud."</note> page 157: *Hence they would have it that the Sacred and ineffable name Jehovah supports them, since it emphatically signifies only necessary existence, or that (whatever it may be) which exists through itself, in clearly the same sense in which "The Being" <note>original Greek: τὸ Ὄν</note> of the Greeks most often signifies the incorruptible, eternal, and interminable world.* 

Doubtless, men addicted to the most pestilential and absurd opinions are accustomed to seek protection for them in the Holy Scriptures; hence *Spinoza* wished not only to draw *Moses* into his party, but also the Apostle *Paul* himself, who in the Acts of the Apostles Chapter XVII verse 28 had said: *In him we live and move and are* <note>original Greek: Ἐν αὐτῷ ζῶμεν καὶ κινούμεθα καὶ ἐσμέν</note>; as if, to remain silent about many other things, it were not a common Hebraism to interpret that *in him* as *through him*, or *by his benefit*. The same is clear enough from those things which he had babbled concerning the principal Articles of Religion in his *Theological-Political Treatise* before the *Ethics* was published. Concerning miracles, he felt that they are surely necessary events of nature; but that we, being ignorant of their causes, sell them to ourselves as the extraordinary operations of God—that is, as miracles. Thus at the very beginning of Chapter VI of the cited treatise, he opens his mind, saying: *Just as men have been accustomed to call that knowledge which surpasses human understanding "divine," so they call a work whose cause is commonly unknown "divine," or the work of God; for the common people then see the power and providence of God most clearly...*

<header>MEDITATION IV.</header>

...he [Spinoza] thinks it is established when something unusual occurs in nature, contrary to the opinion he holds from custom regarding nature; especially if it results in his own gain or convenience. He believes that the existence of God can be proven from nothing more clearly than from the fact that nature, as they think, does not maintain its order. Therefore, they think that all those who explain or seek to understand things and miracles through natural causes are doing away with God, or at least with Divine Providence. And a little further down: "The common people therefore call unusual works of nature 'miracles' or the 'works of God,' and partly out of devotion, partly out of a desire to oppose those who cultivate natural sciences, they wish to remain ignorant of the natural causes of things, and they only long to hear those things which they are most ignorant of, and which they therefore admire."

When Henry Oldenburg <note>Henry Oldenburg (c. 1619–1677) was a diplomat and the first secretary of the Royal Society in London, who maintained a famous correspondence with Spinoza.</note>, in Letter XXII, had asked him in what sense he considers "miracles" and "ignorance" to be synonymous and equivalent, since the raising of Lazarus from the dead and the resurrection of Jesus Christ from death surpass all the power of nature and belong solely to divine power, he replied in the following letter thus: *I have taken miracles and ignorance as equivalent because those who attempt to establish the existence of God and Religion through miracles wish to demonstrate an obscure thing through another even more obscure thing, which they are most ignorant of; thus they introduce a new kind of arguing, reducing the matter not to an impossibility, as they say, but to ignorance.* It is not my intention to show the vastness of this System in this place, since it has been abundantly demonstrated by learned men. I will note only one or two points which show that the man played around on purpose in a most serious matter and preferred a most foolish opinion over a most certain judgment. Thus, he ridiculously asserts that knowledge which surpasses human capacity is called "divine" by Christians; for if every knowledge of things whose nature humans cannot perfectly know must be called divine, then almost all our science and Learning would have to be called divine. The intolerable pride of this man also shines through, as he thinks he alone knows what is divine. And how, finally, can there be a knowledge of divine things if, besides the world—that is, a certain infinite series of contingent substances—nothing at all exists? 2.) Those things which he says about the nature of miracles rely on a mere *begging of the question* <note>original: "petitione principii"</note>; that is, he places as his foundation that only one substance is given in the nature of things, from which all things necessarily arise. Would it not have been better to deny that any miracles were ever performed at all, rather than to concede that such things did indeed happen, but to contend that they are nothing but the necessary effects of nature? Could he himself finally gather from the nature of a Being acting so necessarily what can and cannot happen? And

how, finally, could Christ and the Apostles have known that at this or that moment of time, necessary nature would evolve itself in such a way that they could persuade the present spectators that at this point in time something wonderful and unusual would happen? I pass over many other things that could be said, and I proceed to the other monstrous opinions of this crafty man. In Letter XX, Oldenburg requested that he clearly open his mind concerning Jesus Christ, the Redeemer of the World, and His satisfaction <note>In theology, "satisfaction" refers to Christ's atonement for human sin.</note>. He did so in the following letter, and indeed in this way: *I say that for salvation it is not at all necessary to know Christ according to the flesh; but concerning that eternal Son of God, that is, the eternal wisdom of God, which has manifested itself in all things and especially in the human mind and most of all in Christ Jesus, one must think far otherwise. For no one can arrive at a state of blessedness without this, since it alone teaches what is true and false, good and evil.* And because, as I said, this wisdom was most manifested through Jesus Christ, therefore his disciples preached the same, insofar as it was revealed to them by him, and they showed that they could boast of that Spirit of Christ above others. As for what some Churches add to these things—that God assumed human nature—I have expressly warned that I do not know what they are saying; indeed, to tell the truth, they seem to me to speak no less absurdly than if someone were to tell me that a circle had taken on the nature of a square.

What, finally, could be more twisted and foolish (to say nothing of the nonsense he prattles about regarding the conjunction of two natures) than what he trifles here concerning Christ? He says it is not necessary that we acknowledge Christ according to the flesh, but insofar as he is eternal wisdom, **Note Well** <note>original: "NB." for "nota bene"</note>, manifesting itself in all things—that is, a part of the world, or an attribute of the infinite thinking [substance]. Apparently, it interests us most to know that through the inevitable necessity of things, two particles of one substance—namely, body and mind, making up Christ—existed. These things, forsooth, contribute wonderfully to the study of piety! Who does not recall that saying of the Apostle concerning the ancient Philosophers in the Epistle to the Romans: *claiming to be wise, they became fools*? <note>original Greek: "φασκοντες ειναι σοφοι εμωρανθησαν" (Romans 1:22)</note> He thinks no less foolishly regarding the death of Christ, his resurrection, and ascension. In Letter XXIII, he speaks of the resurrection in this way: *The resurrection of Christ from death was in truth spiritual and was revealed to the faithful alone according to their capacity; namely, that Christ was endowed with eternity, and rose from the dead (I understand "the dead" here in the sense in which Christ said, "let the dead bury their dead") as soon as he gave an example of singular holiness by his life and death; and he raises his disciples from the dead to the extent that they [follow] this example of his life and death...*

## MEDITATION IV.

...follow. Nor would it be difficult to explain the whole doctrine of the Gospel according to this hypothesis. Indeed, Chapter XV of 1 Corinthians can be explained from this hypothesis alone, and Paul’s arguments understood, whereas otherwise, following the common hypothesis, they appear weak and can be easily refuted; not to mention that Christians have interpreted spiritually everything that the Jews interpreted carnally. However, when Oldenburg <note>Henry Oldenburg (1619–1677), Secretary of the Royal Society, who corresponded extensively with Spinoza.</note> pressed him and, in the subsequent Letter XXIV, urged the simplicity of the narration of the Evangelists and Apostles regarding the truth of the passion, resurrection, and ascension of Jesus Christ, Spinoza replied thus: *The passion, death, and burial of Christ,* he said, *I accept literally with you, but his resurrection I take allegorically.* I confess indeed that this is narrated by the Evangelists with such circumstances that we cannot deny that the Evangelists themselves believed that Christ’s body rose again and ascended to heaven to sit at the right hand of God, and that it could even have been seen by unbelievers if they had been present in those places where Christ himself appeared to the disciples; in which, however, without harm to the doctrine of the Gospel, they could have been deceived, as happened also to other prophets. 

A truly remarkable response, and one worthy of such a philosopher! He admits and concedes that the Apostles and Evangelists simply narrate what they had seen, and that nothing is contained in the words they use that forces us to depart from the literal sense; yet he maintains this resurrection must be understood allegorically. That is, he admits the premises but denies the conclusion: the disciples had seen Jesus Christ restored to life, and for that reason, they firmly believe it; but they could nonetheless have been deceived. Christ "rose" because he gave an example of singular piety in life and death, and the disciples "rise" when they follow the example of his life and death. This resurrection, being metaphorical, was revealed only to the faithful, and yet the unbelievers themselves, had they been present in those places, could have been persuaded of the truth of the matter—that is, no less than the faithful, they would "grasp at a shadow instead of Juno" <note>original: "umbram pro Junone captare." A classical idiom meaning to be deceived by an illusion or a phantom, based on the myth of Ixion.</note>, and all could have been deceived even with eyes wide open. 

Who would not marvel at the man’s sharpness and the loftiness of his genius? Indeed, who would not detest the man’s impudence, who was accustomed to babble out whatever came into his mouth? Hence even those who are accustomed to think more freely about religion than the reverence we owe to Holy Scripture permits, confess that atheists and despisers of religion not only abundantly betray their own impudence, but also fall into opinions that are plainly foolish and devoid of any appearance of truth. Among them is Pierre Bayle <note>A French philosopher known for his *Historical and Critical Dictionary*; though often labeled a skeptic, he frequently critiqued the internal logic of atheism.</note>, who in his book on Comets, p. 237, flatly confessed this. a prodigious ignorance of the nature of things, a spirit that overturns all the laws of common sense, and which creates for itself a manner of reasoning that is false and more disordered than can be said."

-noza said that there is no Natural Right <note>original: "jus Naturae." Historically, this refers to universal moral laws; Spinoza redefined it as the natural power of an entity.</note>, but that everything consists in the more powerful exercising their power over those below them by whatever means it can be done; just as small fish are swallowed and eaten by larger ones. He opens his mind on this subject flatly and without ambiguity in the *Theological-Political Treatise*, Chapter XVI. *By Natural Right and Institute,* (he says,) *I understand nothing other than the rules of the nature of each individual, according to which we conceive each thing to be naturally determined to exist and operate in a certain way. For example: Fish are determined by nature to swim, the large ones to eat the smaller; and so fish possess the water by the highest natural right, and the large eat the small. For it is certain that nature, considered absolutely, has the highest right to all that it can do—that is, natural right extends as far as its power extends; for the power of nature <note>original: "NB" (Nota Bene/Note Well)</note> is the very power of God, who has the supreme right to all things; but because the universal power of the whole of nature is nothing besides the power of all individuals together, it follows from this that each individual has the supreme right to all that it can do, or that the right of each individual extends as far as its determined power extends.* 

Therefore among men, as long as they are considered to live under the rule of nature alone, both he who does not yet know reason, or who does not yet have the habit of virtue, lives by the highest right from the laws of appetite alone, just as he who directs his life from the laws of reason. That is, just as the wise man has the supreme right to all that reason dictates, or to living by the laws of reason; so too the ignorant and those powerless of mind have the supreme right to all that appetite persuades, or to living by the laws of appetite. Natural right, therefore, of each man is determined not by sound reason, but by desire and power. 

In a word; everything cries out that this man intended to declare war on all religion by his work, and, in order to seem wise, "attacked heaven itself with his folly" <note>A metaphor likening Spinoza to the mythical Giants who attempted to storm Olympus.</note>. What the Unbelievers are accustomed to boast about his life—that it was composed with modesty and a mind perhaps content with its lot—I shall weigh further below, where we shall bring forward certain objections of the Unbelievers.

It is not necessary for us to spend time subverting this system, since it collapses under its own futility. Indeed, to claim that humans, plants, and animals—to say nothing of the vast bodies floating in the heavens and running their orbits in a most beautiful order—arose by a fortuitous concourse of atoms is not to *philosophize* but to *rave in delirium*. For this reason, even the most learned of the Ancients, such as *Cicero*, *Plutarch*, and others, laughed at the *Epicureans* <note>Followers of the philosopher Epicurus, who taught that the world was formed by the random collision of indivisible particles called atoms.</note> with what they deservedly called "white teeth" [wide grins]. I shall cite only the words of *Cicero* that appear in *On the Nature of the Gods, Book II, chapter 37*: "At this point, should I not marvel at anyone who persuades himself that certain solid and individual bodies are carried along by their own force and weight, and that a world so adorned and beautiful is created from the fortuitous collision of those bodies? If anyone thinks this could happen, I do not understand why he would not also think that if countless sets of the twenty-one letters of the alphabet—whether made of gold or any other material—were thrown together, the *Annals of Ennius* <note>original: "Annalis Ennii." Quintus Ennius (c. 239–169 BC) was the father of Roman epic poetry; his *Annals* was a massive history of Rome.</note> could be produced from them when shaken out onto the ground so that they could then be read; yet I doubt whether chance could succeed in producing even a single verse." The same is found in chapters 34 and 35: "But if all parts of the world are so constituted that they could neither be better for use nor more beautiful in appearance, let us see whether these things are accidental, or whether they are in a state where they could in no way hold together except by a moderating sense and divine providence. If, therefore, the things perfected by Nature are better than those perfected by art, and art performs nothing without reason, then nature itself must not be considered devoid of reason. How is it consistent, then, that when you look at a painted tablet, you know that art was applied; and when you see from afar the course of a ship, you do not doubt that it is moved by reason and logic; or when you see a *Sun-dial* <note>original: "Solarium." This refers to ancient timekeeping devices or astronomical models.</note> etc.? But if someone were to carry into *Scythia* or *Britain* this Sphere which our friend *Posidonius* <note>A Stoic philosopher and polymath (c. 135–51 BC) who built an orrery—a mechanical model of the solar system.</note> recently constructed, each revolution of which performs the same movement for the *Sun*, the *Moon*, and the five wandering stars [planets] that is performed in the Heavens every day and night: who in those barbarian lands would doubt that this Sphere was perfected by reason? Yet these people doubt whether the world itself, from which all things arise and are made, was itself the effect of chance or of reason and a divine mind! And they think *Archimedes* <note>A famous Greek mathematician (c. 287–212 BC) who also designed mechanical spheres representing the movements of the heavens.</note> had more power in imitating the revolutions of the sphere than Nature had in creating them, especially since the real things are more perfect in many ways than these clever imitations," etc. Among more recent scholars, men eminent in dignity and learning such as *Tillotson* <note>John Tillotson (1630–1694), Archbishop of Canterbury.</note> and *Fénelon* <note>François Fénelon (1651–1715), a French Catholic archbishop and writer.</note> have shown the vanity of this opinion through various arguments and systematic comparisons. The former in his *Sacred Sermons, Volume I*, and the latter in an entire treatise on the divine existence. And indeed, it is scarcely credible that a man of sound mind, having seriously and sincerely weighed the nature and faculties of created things, could subscribe to such an inept opinion

as being able. We know, of course, that the opinions of other ancient philosophers regarding the origin of things were also built upon ruinous foundations. But if that "old man of Gargettus" <note>A reference to Epicurus, who was born in the Athenian district (deme) of Gargettus.</note> had wished to come to the aid of a failing cause, he ought to have corrected what was hollow or plainly inept in the systems of others, rather than adding errors to errors. But we know it has very frequently happened that Unbelievers, while they have attacked and condemned opinions that were either plainly certain and firm or at least highly probable, have brought forward hypotheses subject to far greater difficulties; and it is established that the same happened in the example of *Epicurus* and his followers. For this system is supported by no foundations at all, but can be simply denied with the same right by which it was put forward. For example: 1.) He established that "nothing is made from nothing," and yet he gave motion to atoms, though he nowhere proves that they have or can admit such motion. 2.) He attributed to atoms the power of "swerving" <note>The "clinamen," a random unpredictable motion Epicurus used to explain how atoms collide and to allow for free will.</note> themselves, but he could give no cause for this inclination. 3.) He attributed a certain power of feeling and understanding to our souls, yet he could not derive these faculties from the nature of atoms or their collision with any appearance of truth. Yet this is that distinguished philosopher, worthy to be raised to the heavens with praises by his panegyrist *Lucretius* <note>Titus Lucretius Carus (c. 99–55 BC), the Roman poet whose work *On the Nature of Things* is the main source for Epicurean philosophy.</note>. This is he who, forsooth:

> "First found the plan of life, that which
> is now called wisdom, and who through his art
> rescued life from such great waves and such great darkness,
> and placed it in such tranquility and such clear light." <note>A translation of Lucretius, *De Rerum Natura*, Book V, lines 9-12.</note>

Something could indeed be granted to *Epicurus* if we consider the times in which he lived. For then Religion was so hedged in and oppressed by so many inept superstitions and "old wives' tales" that it was no wonder a man wished to rush into any other direction. Furthermore, the philosophical disciplines—*Astronomy*, *Physics*, *Botany*, and *Anatomy*—were poorly developed. But those among the Unbelievers who patronize such a system in our own age "close their eyes to the sun." For it is well known that men most excellent in genius and learning have most clearly demonstrated—from the structure of animals, humans, and plants, and from experiments most accurately performed for that purpose—that all bodies in the world are constructed with divine and wonderful art, and all are fashioned according to certain and most wise ends. Certainly, whoever dares to assert hereafter, in such great light, that the most beautiful order of things is to be attributed only to a fortuitous concourse of matter, is playing games with a most sacred subject and clearly demonstrates that he is captivated by a plainly ridiculous and inept ambition.

X. But let us set aside the followers of *Epicurus* and come to other Unbelievers who have defended opinions that are plainly foolish and paradoxical. Among these, we rightly include the *study of Judicial Astrology* <note>Judicial Astrology is the practice of predicting human affairs and character based on the positions of celestial bodies, which theologians often condemned as superstitious or deterministic.</note>. Certainly, if this futile guesswork is worthy of the name "art," it is built upon no foundations, and we cannot see how a person of sound mind could be devoted to it. Nevertheless, it is clear from experience that many among the Unbelievers have been captivated by a love for it. It is well known of *Vanini* <note>Lucilio Vanini (1585–1619), an Italian philosopher executed for atheism and magical practices.</note> that he greatly loved this art, as is evident from his biography, which several learned men have written. Regarding the Illustrious *Shaftesbury* <note>Anthony Ashley-Cooper, 3rd Earl of Shaftesbury (1671–1713), a famous moral philosopher.</note>, the grandson of that most celebrated *Anthony Ashley*, Earl of *Shaftesbury*, whose life *Locke* wrote, the Reverend Father in Christ *Burnet* affirms the same in his *Commentaries on the events of his own time* <note>original: "Commentariis rerum suo tempore gestarum," referring to Bishop Gilbert Burnet's "History of His Own Time."</note>. Most learned men have placed him in the rank of the Unbelievers. The celebrated *Mosheim* in his *Prolegomena to July* <note>original: "primit. Jul."</note>, page 57, pronounces this regarding him: *Furthermore, I do not doubt that this most sagacious man was among those who, either hindered by a love of vices or by perverse opinions, refuse to see the truth of the Religion handed down by Christ.* And in his *Recent Ecclesiastical History*, page 380, speaking of the same man, he says: *This most ingenious man laughs, even when he seems to speak most holily of sacred things; and by his arguments he strips away all virtue from the pious and honest life that is handed down and insisted upon in the divine books; indeed, while he commends some sublime virtue, placed above the opinions of the common folk and content with itself, he actually dissuades one from all pursuit of virtue.* A similar judgment is rendered of him by the Reverend *Berkeley* on page 201 of the book titled *The Minute Philosopher* <note>original: "Le petit Philosophe," referring to Bishop George Berkeley’s "Alciphron, or The Minute Philosopher," a critique of "free-thinkers."</note>.

> For as much (he says) as concerns certain points of Religion, such as for example the belief in a future state of rewards and punishments, this great man openly declares that people of high fashion <note>original: "gens du Bel-Air."</note> could only regard such things as tales fit to amuse children and terrify the common people. Thus, to render a signal service to the most choice part of humankind, he has had the goodness and wisdom to invent another motive—namely, a certain taste or pleasure—which, he assures us, cannot fail to produce its effect. Since, according to him, as soon as one has the true taste of politeness, one has at the same time a certain disposition to be transported by the mere contemplation of everything that is truly beautiful.

The celebrated *Pfaff*, in his *Tübingen Memoirs*, page 44, judges him thus: *No one has attacked the doctrine of spiritual taste with a sharper pen than the Illustrious Shaftesbury—a man of sharp wit indeed, but one who seems to me to have been little convinced of the Christian Religion.* The words of the Illustrious *Burnet* are these:

> As for his Religion, to speak of it favorably is to say that he was a Deist. He was nevertheless as mad for Astrology as one can be:

<note>original: "pro anu vatidica"</note> mocked the idea of a prophetic old woman along with the Epicureans, yet he asserted that the entire universe and all things within it are ruled by the influence of the stars. Regarding **Isaac Vossius**, **Saint-Evremond** records that he held the customs and manners of almost every nation in his ready memory, yet remained ignorant of his own century. In daily gatherings of the most honorable men, he spoke so filthily that you would have thought you were listening to a book of commentaries on **Juvenal** or **Petronius**. At the same time that he wished to prove the Septuagint <note>original: "LXX. Versionem" — the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> was of divine origin, he openly showed that he had no faith in Revelation itself, a fact that the end of his life more than sufficiently proved. For he could be moved by no arguments to subscribe even to the primary articles of the Christian religion; meanwhile, he most willingly accepted everything unusual, fabulous, and abhorrent to any appearance of truth. These things I narrate were reported by **Saint-Evremond**, who was an intimate friend of **Vossius**. After the biographer of **Saint-Evremond**, the most learned **des Maizeaux**, set these things forth, he broke out into these words:
> *Let certain know-it-alls go then and cry out in the future that Unbelievers are free from all prejudiced opinions, and that only those **endowed with the sharpest intellect** and **moved by nothing but the most evident reasons** are accustomed to being led to believe or reject anything.*

The Count **BOULAINVILLIERS** (these are the words of the celebrated Mosheim in his *Recent Ecclesiastical History*, page 388) was so inconsistent with himself that he granted almost equal room in his ill-composed mind to superstition and Atheism. For although he thought there was no other God than the nature of things, he nevertheless did not doubt that Muhammad was a Legate of God to the human race, and he judged that the fates of both individual men and of republics could be predicted from the stars.
**Collins** <note>Anthony Collins (1676–1729), a prominent English deist and author of "A Discourse of Free-Thinking."</note>, who is rightly numbered among the leaders of the Unbelievers known through public writings, showed more than once that he allowed himself to be carried away by this zeal:

that is, he subscribed to the most trivial opinions as long as they were hostile to Religion, while rejecting those which are most firmly established in the Christian Religion. To this you may refer, among other things, the fact that in order to render the authenticity of the New Testament suspect, he appealed to **Victor of Tunnuna**, who is said to have claimed:
> *During the consulship of the illustrious Messala at Constantinople, the most Holy Gospels were corrupted and corrected by order of the Emperor Anastasius.* <note>Victor of Tunnuna was a 6th-century chronicler; this specific claim of universal Gospel corruption was a common talking point for 18th-century skeptics like Collins.</note>

Many, however, have refuted this most trivial objection, and quite learnedly too, among whom the celebrated **Pfaff** should be rightly mentioned, whose singular dissertation on this matter is found in the *Tubingen First-Fruits*. **Phileleutherus Lipsiensis** (that is, the most learned **Bentley** <note>Richard Bentley (1662–1742), a famous English classical scholar who wrote under this pseudonym to debunk Anthony Collins.</note>) showed through clear examples that Collins often intentionally truncated the passages of ancient authors—especially in the first edition of his little book on the freedom of thinking—whenever he judged it would serve his purpose. See the book titled: *The Lay Roguery of the Pretended Freethinkers of England, 1738 Edition.* I shall say nothing of his perpetual zeal for insulting the overseers of Religion without any distinction, since others who wish to be regarded as Unbelievers are usually afflicted by this same disease. To these we can add the famous Jesuit **Hardouin**, a Frenchman. For although he is not commonly listed among the Unbelievers, he nevertheless brought forward such paradoxes as to pave the way for the undermining of Revelation. No one would deny that **Hardouin** was a learned man, well-versed in philology, chronology, and the art of coinage. Yet no one who is touched by any love of truth can deny that he simultaneously defended monstrous opinions that shrink from any appearance of probability. For instance, it is well known that he asserted:
> *Cicero, Pliny, Virgil’s Georgics, and the Satires and Epistles of Horace—aside from a very few inscriptions and some calendars—are the only sincere remains of antiquity; the rest of the harvest of false doctrines was poured out from an execrable and detestable workshop nearly five hundred years ago,*

whose prince and primary **Architect** of the work was jokingly called *Severus Archontius* by his associates. Everyone sees that this ridiculous opinion—that this "execrable workshop" existed in the 13th century after the birth of Christ—is opposed to the truth of the Christian Religion. At first, some thought the learned man was joking, because it did not seem credible that a man otherwise learned and of excellent talent could seriously defend such an inept opinion. But others, among whom the most learned **Veyssière de La Croze** (who is now **among the saints** <note>original: "ἐν ἁγίοις" — a Greek formula used to indicate someone has passed away in the faith.</note>) was prominent, judged that the Jesuit’s goal was this: that by shaking the Sacred Volumes and the most ancient writings of the Fathers—those great defenses of the Christian cause—out of the hands of Christians, he might in this way protect and promote the authority of the Roman Pontiff.

# MEDITATION IV.

To that end, that learned man published the *Vindication of Ancient Writers* <note>original: "Vindicias Veterum Scriptorum"</note>, a work full of good fruit, to which was added a learned dissertation by the celebrated **des Vignoles**. In this piece, using the principles of chronology, he attacked the Jesuit’s <note>Jean Hardouin (1646–1729), a Jesuit famous for his theory that most ancient Greek and Roman texts were forgeries.</note> opinion and utterly subverted it. Whether **Hardouin** alone devised this opinion, or whether it was rather a coordinated effort—which was the view of the most learned **la Croze**—I do not wish to inquire. This much is certain: Hardouin, equipped as he was with a sharp mind, *easily perceived* that this sentiment would render suspect not only the Holy books of the New Testament, but also the monuments of the most ancient Fathers, to which not only Protestants, but especially the Papists themselves, are accustomed to appeal. 

The same man, in a posthumous work, regarded **Jansenius**, **Quesnel**, and all those who defended what they call "efficacious grace" as atheists, using the flimsiest arguments to prove it—arguments which are available everywhere in the *Journals of the Learned* <note>original: "Diariis Eruditorum"</note> and can be read there. I shall say nothing now of his unusual and forced explanation of certain inscriptions. Finally, in his *Commentary on the New Testament*, published a year before these words were written, one may find many paradoxical interpretations scattered throughout. Specimens of these have been shown by, among others, the very learned authors of the French literary journal titled *The Reasoned Library* <note>original: "Bibliotheque raisonnée"</note>, final volume. These things have led learned men to think that Hardouin was perhaps not of sound mind when he wrote such things. Certainly, the epitaph placed for him by the Reverend and most learned **Vernet**, a Professor at Geneva and our most honored friend, is worthy of the man. XI. Before I put an end to this argument and thesis, I shall bring forward only three specific examples, from which it will be clear with what impudence certain **Unbelievers** are accustomed to disparage Christian teaching and defend the most foolish and paradoxical opinions. The first is **John Toland**, the second is **Woolston**, and the third is the author of that most impudent pamphlet, worthy of the underworld <note>original: "orco digni"</note>, titled *The Malabar Princesses* <note>original: "les Princesses Malabares"</note>. ...and slanderous, to which he prefixed the title ***The Tribe of Levi*** <note>original: "Tribus Levi"</note>, in which, right at the beginning, he asserts that the order of Priests is the most calamitous of all calamities, and that nothing more heavy or troublesome has ever existed for any Republic. I cannot say more about this book, as the celebrated **Mosheim** <note>Johann Lorenz von Mosheim (1693–1755), a highly influential German Lutheran church historian known for his objective approach.</note> did not bring more into public view concerning the treatment of the whole argument. From what has been presented, however, it is clear enough that the man, puffed up with youthful arrogance, sufficiently betrayed his impiety and impudence by so bitterly criticizing all ministers of the Sacred Rites indiscriminately, without making any distinction. Afterward, he turned his mind to writing a book titled ***Christianity Not Mysterious*** <note>original: "Religio Christiana Mysterii expers"; this 1696 work was Toland's most famous, arguing that nothing in the Gospel is contrary to reason.</note>. The celebrated **Mosheim** explains in the place cited what fate this little book suffered in England. The judgments of learned men regarding it were, of course, varied. There were those who said its author was an enemy of all religions; others called him a Deist or a disciple of **Socinus** <note>Followers of Socinianism rejected the Trinity and the divinity of Christ, emphasizing rational interpretation.</note>. Others disapproved of only certain things, contending that the rest could be tolerated, especially after **Toland** exerted all the strength of his talent to show that his words could carry a much milder sense if a genuine explanation were applied. But the outcome, and those things which he later brought to light, sufficiently showed that the man only intended to deceive others with words. For soon another unfortunate offspring of his intellect followed, from which it was clear enough that **Toland** burned with an incredible desire to defend new and paradoxical opinions. Specifically, in the year **1704**, he published ***Letters to Serena***, by which name he meant the most Illustrious **Queen of Prussia** <note>Sophia Charlotte of Hanover (1668–1705), a friend of Leibniz and a patron of the arts and sciences.</note>, who was living at that time. There were five letters in total, the arguments of which are displayed in the place cited. We take account only of those things which serve our purpose. In the second *Letter*, he presents a history of the doctrine of the immortality of the soul among the Nations. I shall set forth his opinion on this matter in the words of the celebrated **Mosheim**, since the book is not at hand:

> He thinks this dogma took its rise from the Egyptians; that the Greeks received it from them and, having sent their colonies into Asia and Europe, passed it on. Nor is it so surprising that the ROMANS also approved it, since it is well known that they borrowed both their Laws and Religion from the Greeks. He considers that these same Egyptians shared this doctrine of the permanence of minds with the Sages of the Indians and Chaldeans, who in turn were the authors of its adoption by the Scythians, Germans, Gauls, and Britons.

But from where did this wisdom come to the Egyptians? Nothing is easier for our author to explain.

> This entire persuasion flowed from the funeral rites customary among the Egyptians, according to his own judgment. It was their custom to smear corpses with ointments of various kinds so they would not rot, and thus hide them in a certain peculiar place, which they called the Elysian fields, outside

outside the city of **Memphis**. From this, before any suspicion of the immortality of minds arose, those expressions about the dead had already become prevalent: that they had "crossed the river Acheron" and were "translated to the Elysian fields." *These modes of speaking subsequently generated the opinion that the minds of those whose bodies were preserved inviolate also remained.* In the fourth Letter, he wished to recall a certain learned man who was burning with great zeal for **Spinoza** <note>Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677), a philosopher often accused of atheism or pantheism.</note> and his philosophy; yet in it, he posited among other things that a "striving for motion" <note>original: "conatum ad motum"</note> exists in all matter. But whoever weighs the method of reasoning of this most learned man will easily perceive that he *uses a continuous irony*, and wished to mock **Toland** in a witty way. > *...contrary to what Moses hands down, he affirms that the land of Palestine is horrid and sterile, and he proposes several other paradoxes of this kind. Let the more prudent judge whether this is indeed anything other than waging open war against Religion.*

Nor was this unhappy man content with these things, but he proceeded on the same foot he began—that is, he further strived to satisfy his incredible desire for spreading new and unusual opinions so that he might achieve the reputation of a man of singular Erudition. I. From the miracles which Christ demonstrated in the cure of various diseases, and for which he rightly obtained singular praise and fame, it cannot be gathered that he is the Messiah, nor can an argument be sought from them for the divine authority he claimed for himself to bring forth a new Religion.

II. That the literal narrative of many miracles, which are said to have been done by Christ according to the witness of the Evangelists, is absurd, far from probability, and indeed incredible; and that therefore it should not be believed that these miracles took place, whether we look at all of them or only some; but all these are to be understood *prophetically* and *parabolically*, that is, they signify only what Jesus was to perform in the future in a certain *mystical* and plainly wonderful way.

III. That where Christ appeals to his miracles as to an authentic testimony of his heavenly authority, he did not properly refer to those miracles which he had done while living on earth, but to those which he would one day perform in the Spirit, of which the former were nothing but *types* and *figures*.

There is no one who possesses even a grain of good sense, and who is knowledgeable of the Christian Religion, who does not feel and almost touch with their hands how inept, monstrous, and impudent these propositions are. The heart of the matter turns on whether Christ actually performed miracles while he lived on earth. The Evangelists narrate in the clearest words that Christ performed various miracles; they recount various kinds of diseases healed by Christ; they set forth the circumstances of places and persons. Yet all these, according to him, are only to be understood *improperly* and *mystically*. Men freed from these or those diseases, and indeed in the sight of many people, were not actually healed, but were supposed to believe that a merely metaphorical medicine had been brought to them. Christ appeals to the miracles themselves in expressive words as the most certain argument of his divine mission;

# MEDITATION IV.

...but Christ is to be understood in such a way, as if he were speaking of things not actually performed, and was appealing to some kind of mystical healing to be carried out in following ages. Does not anyone see that this man is playing games with a most holy matter, and is worthy to be sent to **Anticyra** <note>A Greek city famous in antiquity for its hellebore, a plant used to treat madness; to be sent there was a common idiom for being insane.</note>, or to use a phrase from **Plautus**, to the "islands of whip-bearing and iron-clanking," where "dead oxen attack living men" <note>original: "sustitudineas & ferricrepidineas insulas, ubi vivos homines mortui incursant boves"; a comic reference to slavery or punishment where leather whips (dead oxen) are used on people.</note>. Does this wretched man not show us by his own example how true it is what we have warned several times: namely, that many Unbelievers, having cast aside all shame and rejected the clearest and most sacred truths, bring forth the most foolish and monstrous opinions, and spout and defend them with ridiculous boasting? This is all the more manifest because this man, though reduced to a stalemate <note>original: "ad incitas redactus"; a metaphor from a board game meaning backed into a corner or checkmated.</note> by the arguments of so many most learned men, nevertheless defended his most absurd opinion **with fist and heel** <note>original: "πυξ και λαξ" (pyx kai lax); a Greek idiom meaning "tooth and nail" or with total stubbornness.</note> until the very end of his life.

It is not my intention, as I said above, to run through the individual theses of this unhappy man and tear them down, or to weigh the arguments by which he wished to give a clever appearance to his impious opinion; for this has been done abundantly by most learned men. I shall merely bring forward those points which the Reverend Father in Christ, **Edmund [Gibson]**, Bishop of London <note>Edmund Gibson (1669–1748), a prominent English bishop who published "Pastoral Letters" defending Christianity against deism.</note>, presented in summary to demonstrate the futility of the system in his *Pastoral Letters*, translated from English into French by the most learned **le Moine**. 

After the Reverend Bishop had warned on page 49 in general how foolish it is to maintain that the miracles performed by Jesus Christ, which the sacred writers mention, are to be interpreted not literally but allegorically, and that such an interpretation could only be defended by a man destitute of common sense or an open enemy of religion, he showed by a list of examples what a **train** <note>original: "συρμα" (syrma); Greek for a long trailing robe or a sequence of things.</note> of most absurd consequences that monstrous opinion drags behind it. 

"If the opinion of **Woolston** were valid," says the Reverend Bishop, "it would have to be said that when Christ appealed to his miracles—as he often did—to prove his divine mission, he meant not **real** but **allegorical** miracles. That when the crowd asked one another whether the Messiah, if he came, would do greater miracles than those they already saw performed by Christ, they were not speaking of **real** miracles, but merely **imaginary** ones. That when Jesus Christ had ordered the disciples of **John the Baptist** to tell their Master the miracles they had seen, to convince them that he was the Messiah because he was performing the same miracles which, according to the Oracles of the Prophets, were to be performed by the Messiah, neither the Prophets nor Jesus Christ, by the name of miracles—

---

# ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

—meant miracles **in the true sense of the name**. It would mean that all those Jews who had given their name to the most holy discipline <note>That is, those who became followers of Christianity.</note>, after they had seen Christ heal the sick and recall the dead to life by a word alone, did not see in the work itself men who were **first sick and dead, and afterwards healthy and living**; and that consequently, they did not have sufficiently solid reasons for believing the Christian religion to be of divine origin. It would mean that the huge multitude of people who flocked to Christ to be freed from various diseases they suffered from, after seeing with their own eyes that this benefit had happened to many, nevertheless saw nothing in the act itself that could induce them to return to Christ. 

It would mean that the **Leper**, who had given thanks to Christ for bringing a healing hand to the grave disease from which he suffered, was not **really** healed, and that therefore he thanked Christ for no reason at all. It would mean that when the people, seeing so many miracles, were seized with admiration, this admiration was **plainly vain and backwards**, because they saw nothing that could strike the eyes. It would mean that when the Jews, having seen so many miracles, feared lest other men should believe Jesus to be the true Messiah for that reason, and on that account wished to place an obstacle to this persuasion elicited by miracles, they feared **shadows and ghosts**, and took counsel to restrain a **thing that did not exist**. 

It would mean that when they wanted to kill him because he had healed a lame man on the Sabbath day, he had nevertheless performed nothing in the act itself. It would mean that those men who wanted to proclaim him King after they had seen so many wonders performed by him, nevertheless **noticed** that nothing had been done by him other than what **anyone from the common crowd** could perform. It would mean that the Pharisees, who slandered him as performing miracles through **Beelzebub**, were not at all persuaded that he had done miracles, but were induced to think and speak this way moved by entirely different reasons. 

It would mean that the people, seized with the greatest admiration when they saw a sick man healed in the name of Jesus by Peter—a man who had previously been carried to the temple doors to beg for alms—did not however see him **truly walking** afterward; and that although the **Leaders of the Sanhedrin** could not deny that this miracle had truly happened, the **Assessors and judges** were no less deceived than the **people** themselves. It would mean that **Simon Magus**, wishing to buy the gift of miracles for a price, wished to acquire for himself no other faculty than that with which he was already equipped—that is, **none at all**. It would mean that the **people of Lystra**, who took Paul and Barnabas for Gods, nevertheless detected nothing in them that was worthy of such great admiration. It would mean that the Jews from every nation gathered in Jerusalem for the feast of Pentecost, and in the highest...

...great admiration for the use of various languages through which the Apostles had expressed the feelings of their souls, they nevertheless saw nothing that was worthy of any attention. XIII. About to finally bring an end to this dissertation, we will briefly mention an anonymous Frenchman who commanded a child of his mind—one worthy of eternal darkness—to come into the light under the title: **The Malabarian Princesses, or Philosophical Celibacy; an interesting and curious work, with historical and critical notes.** <note>original: "Les Princesses Malabares, ou le Celibat philosophique..." published anonymously in 1734, often attributed to Adrien-Claude-Marie-Benoît de Maillet</note>. This man certainly yields to none of the Unbelievers in impudence, scurrilous wit, and the zeal for profaning the most sacred things. It is not my intention to individually review, weigh, and tear down all those things which he has insolently brought forward against our most holy discipline and its gravest articles. This would be the work of an entire volume. Nor is the impudent author worthy of being refuted at length; for he presents the most foolish opinions everywhere as if they were **oracles pronounced from the tripod** <note>A reference to the Delphic Oracle; meaning he speaks as if he were divinely inspired despite having no proof.</note>, yet he strengthens them with no reasons at all. Hence, the celebrated **Mosheim** <note>Johann Lorenz von Mosheim (1693–1755), a famous Lutheran church historian.</note> proved the futility of this little book in a summary in the dissertation titled: **The Frenchman, a detractor of the glory of Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit, exposed to public dispute.** <note>original: "Gallus gloriae Jesu Christi, Spiritusque Sancti obtrectator..."</note> We shall prove the man's impudent audacity and his unbridled license to babble anything at all by inducing just a few examples. In the preface itself, on page 2, he confesses in naked words that he will bring forward such things as the force of an excited imagination would supply, nor does he promise the reader that everything he is about to narrate will be consistent with the dictates of **right reason**. What else does this mean than that he wishes to loosen the reins of a luxuriant wit and say **whatever comes into his mouth**? <note>original: "quicquid in buccam venerit"; a Latin idiom for speaking without thinking or filter.</note> If he were dealing with a playful matter, and the author wished to tickle the ears of the people with festive little stories, this kind of writing could be tolerated. You would believe such men were equipped with very rare manuscripts that no one had seen until now, so confidently do they appeal to I-know-not-what books.

In Chapters VIII and IX, among other things, he asserts that reason suffered such great damage after the Fall that it very often does not know whether it is being deceived or not; and he claims this is the reason why one cannot safely give one's name to the Christian religion. **How wise!** <term>wisely</term> <note>original: "σοφως" (sophōs). > This comedian—or rather, Malabarian tragedian—so often makes a mockery of the most holy discipline which we have received from the Son of God, and in such unworthy ways (even though he shows a pretended goodwill toward it), that it is difficult to say and intolerable for ears that are not entirely profane. First, he asserts that all religions are entirely similar to each other and of the same kind and nature, differing in nothing except the magnitude of their goals and the dissimilarity and abundance of their rituals—that is, he claims they are all inept and futile. He says they all entice and deceive their worshippers with vain promises; they all trample and overturn the law of nature; they are all examined with fear if they should happen to catch sight of sound reason, and therefore, with joined resources and arms (even though they may be set in a great variety of opinions), they rush against reason as if against a common enemy, etc.

If babbling whatever comes into one's mouth is the same as proving a thesis with solid reasons, then everyone is bound to subscribe to the words of this man of "subtle wit." In Chapters VI and VII, he treats the progress of **paganism** and the different kinds of Deists. Among other things, he says that after a most foul superstition had, as it were, flooded the world, certain men arose who were not lacking in wit, who drummed in the worship of a single Divine Power. He calls these men Deists. Among their number, he claims, were **Melchizedek** and **Abraham**—pious men indeed, but very simple. He claims the latter (with respect to Abraham) is evident from the fact that he enjoined circumcision upon his friends. # MEDITATION IV.

...narrates things published with the help of alchemy, he did not devise them from his own brain <note>original: "ex cerebro proprio," meaning his own imagination</note>, but followed companions of the same "faith." For I remember reading such things in the *Travels* of James *Massey*—whose true author is the physician *Tyssot* <note>Simon Tyssot de Patot (1655–1738), a French-Dutch author known for his skeptical and utopian writings</note>—and in the *History of the Sevarambians* <note>A famous 17th-century utopian novel by Denis Veiras that often critiqued European religion</note>. In Book III, page 97 and following, there exists a narrative no less foolish and impious at once concerning the faith of Christians in Jesus the crucified. This most impudent man asserts that Christ, having stirred up discord between the Jews and the Gentiles, provoked the wrath of both parties against Himself, to such an extent that it was spread among the common people that He had been handed over to death. However, since others—among whom Paul stood out—knew perfectly well that He was alive and had fought for His authority; and when Jerusalem was finally destroyed, many were led to believe that He had truly died and been recalled to life. But he claims they were deceived because, according to the testimony of *Basilides* <note>An early Gnostic teacher who claimed Jesus did not actually die on the cross</note> and his followers, another died in Christ's place. Therefore, he says, Christians are merely playing a game when they say He is both alive and yet dead, present and yet absent. Who would deny that these things are utterly *paradoxical* <note>original Greek: παραδοξα</note>, and for that reason, highly "sublime"? I see that I have guessed, not without cause, that these most learned men are equipped with the rarest manuscripts, inspected until now by no one except men of the inner circle. It is therefore finally to be hoped that these things might be dragged into the public light. For there are even among us certain Unbelievers whose doubts and impudence must be addressed. I pass over many other impious and silly inventions of the same kind, by which he wished to detract from the dignity of the Christian Religion.

From these examples, in my opinion, our Thesis stated in the preceding pages is more than sufficiently confirmed: namely, that most Unbelievers are accustomed to reject the Christian religion because of certain dogmas that are difficult to grasp; yet at the same time, they subscribe to opinions which not only cannot be compared in certainty with those views they loathe, but which are clearly foolish, futile, and abhorrent to every appearance of truth. From which, by a legitimate logical consequence, it follows: such men were induced, and are still induced, to bring forth and defend such monstrous opinions not by a love of truth, but moved and carried away by a zeal for perverse passions—ambition and pride above all. As a finishing touch, we add an Epigram of the celebrated *Werenfels* <note>Samuel Werenfels (1657–1740), a Swiss theologian known for his defense of Christianity against skepticism</note>, which he placed at the end of his dissertation against worldly security and the profane, and it goes like this:

> Now lift your crests and pride yourself in your impiety:
> And consider all others to be stupid compared to you.
> If you wish hereafter, Unbeliever, to rightly mock the pious,
> First prove to yourself that your own brain is sound.

### Section I.

We have reviewed so far in our dissertations on the causes of increasingly prevalent Unbelief the most powerful causes, which are accustomed to arise from the state of the corrupted mind itself, and especially from perverse passions. We have proven and expanded upon our thesis by the introduction of examples of both ancient and more recent Unbelievers. However, we thought it necessary that it be shown through more examples how even the best and greatest talents—which would have provided great examples if they had been more rightly wise—were corrupted chiefly by ambition and a burning desire to become famous. This is necessary because Unbelievers peddle what is usually said by learned men, and especially by theologians, on this subject as mere exaggerations and arguments fetched from envy. To that end, it had to be demonstrated—both from the character and nature of the sentiments and opinions which certain Unbelievers (having attained a reputation for learning and talent among their own) hold, and from the method of championing and defending them—that no more probable cause can be given for such a burning zeal for defending monstrous and unusual opinions, harmful to both natural and revealed Religion, and finally to civil society, than the perverse passions of their minds, to which they are vehemently devoted.
