# MEDITATION V.

They cry out that an injury is being done to them when we contend that they were led to bring to light and defend these or those opinions—not out of a zeal for truth, but either to show off their learning, to pursue fame, or even out of a love for vice. Instead, they argue that the reasons for their undertaking should be sought in the very articles of religion (whether natural or revealed) which they attack. It would therefore be necessary for me, in part, to examine the manner in which they wish to defend themselves; and in part to bring forward those general **prejudices** <note>original: "praejudicia," meaning preconceived notions or biases that prevent objective judgment</note>, as they are usually called, which prevent them from being able to agree with the rest of mortals on the most weighty points of religion, and to weigh them against the standard of right reason and truth. However, since the order of our treatment requires that, having brought forward the *internal* causes of unbelief, we should add the *external* ones—that is, education, a corrupt upbringing, etc.—and since it is clear that external causes marvelously reinforce internal ones, we preferred first to bring forward everything else that can cast men into unbelief. Only after this is done will we look a little more closely at the arguments by which the unbelievers try to prove that they have the most just reasons for attacking the chief points of religion and for dissenting from all other Christians.

<margin>An infant, coming forth into the divine breezes of light, is occupied by the greatest ignorance—as in other matters, so especially in those which pertain to religion.</margin>

### II. Before we deal with corrupt education—which, as will be clear from what follows, is not the least among other causes that tend to cast men headlong into the vice of unbelief—we must see what state men are in when they are born, both in respect to the body, and especially the mind. Now, all who pay attention to the birth of men know that infants come into the light with a naked and weak body, plainly destitute of the strength to help themselves, so much so that without the care and providence of others, they would soon perish. I cannot express their state in more significant words than those used by the *Illustrious Pufendorf* <note>Samuel von Pufendorf (1632–1694), a highly influential German jurist and philosopher</note> in his *Book on the Duty of Man and Citizen, Book I, chapter III.* He says:

> *Man seems to be in a worse condition than the beasts, because hardly any other animal is accompanied by such great weakness from birth; so much so, that it would be like a miracle if anyone reached a mature age unless the help of other men were added. Since now, among so many inventions for human necessity, many years of careful instruction are required so that one can provide food and clothing for oneself by one's own effort: let us imagine a man grown to a robust age without any care or culture coming from other men, who has no knowledge except what sprouted forth, as it were, of its own accord from his own natural talent; and suppose the same man were destitute in solitude of all help and society of other men—surely a more miserable animal would hardly be found; speechless indeed and*

> *naked, to whom nothing else is left but to pluck herbs or roots, or to gather fruits born of their own accord, to quench thirst at a chance spring, river, or pool, to enter caves to repel the injuries of the air, or to cover the body somehow with moss or grass, to spend a most tedious time in idleness, to tremble at every noise or the encounter of another living creature, and finally to perish by hunger, cold, or a wild beast.*

Thus says *Pufendorf*. Nor do the fictional examples of <term>self-taught</term> <note>original Greek: "αὐτοδιδάκτων" (autodidakton), referring to those who learn without a teacher</note> men delay us here (such as, for example, was that Arab whose life and deeds the *Celebrated Pococke* <note>Edward Pococke (1604–1691), an English orientalist who translated the Arabic philosophical novel "Hayy ibn Yaqdhan" by Ibn Tufail, which depicts a child growing up alone on a desert island and discovering philosophical truths</note> presented in Latin and Arabic) who, equipped with a natural goodness of talent, are said to have devised and learned by their own effort, without the help of any others, all those things which can lead to spending this life well and happily: for such men exist nowhere except in the brains of certain learned men. This is certain, and confirmed by continuous experience: that newly born infants, except for certain confused perceptions and sensations, are destitute of all knowledge. No clear traces of knowledge of things pertaining to religion are noticed in them; rather, the principles of religion must be instilled, fixed, and drummed into them. Everyone who has ever spent time in their life forming youth knows that this itself is not done without great trouble, industry, and skill.

I know indeed that there are many theologians and philosophers who think there are certain <term>innate</term> <note>original Latin: "innatas," ideas present from birth</note> ideas, which they call <term>common notions</term> <note>original Greek: "κοινὰς ἐννοίας" (koinas ennoias), a Stoic term for universal concepts shared by all humans</note>, or implanted notions of things, as if signed into our minds at our very origin; likewise theoretical and practical principles concerning the first elements of natural religion. I would not wish to dispute this argument here on purpose, both because this <term>treatment</term> <note>original Greek: "διασκευῆς" (diaskeues), referring to the systematic arrangement or preparation of a subject</note> belongs rather to another discipline, and because—with respect to the necessity of good education and instruction, which is the argument we chiefly wish to deal with in this dissertation—it is all the same whether you establish such innate ideas about divine things or not.

The author is currently examining the writings of the Apostle Paul to prove that the "knowledge of God" mentioned in the Bible refers to the reasoned observation of the world by adults, rather than a mystical knowledge held by infants in the womb.</meta>

# MEDITATION V.

Theology—both theoretical and practical—is continually present. The reasons taken from the cited texts themselves are as follows. First, no one would deny that Paul, in those two chapters, is dealing primarily with adults among the gentiles, and not with infants themselves. This is most clearly evident from his list of the most serious and foul crimes in which the Apostle shows they were immersed. From this, it can also be easily gathered that when he sternly rebukes them for sinning shamefully against the dictate of conscience and the knowledge of the natural law with which they had been imbued, he understands this as a knowledge of the entire natural law. He does not mean a few very obscure ideas which they might perhaps have had before any reflection or instruction. Hence, there are also learned men who wish to understand <term>that which is known of God</term> <note>original Greek: "to gnoston tou Theou"</note> as not only that which *can* be known about God, but also that which *ought* to be known about Him, as far as the powers of reason alone permit. Among Reformed theologians, the Blessed Bullinger (*) interpreted these words in this way in his commentary on this passage, as did the celebrated Berlin Interpreters. This interpretation is also urged again by <term>the late</term> <note>original Greek: "ho makaritēs," a respectful term for the deceased</note> the distinguished Beausobre in his *New Critical-Historical Observations added to various places of the New Testament*. Now, if this interpretation stands, who will say that all infants, while still enclosed in the mother's womb, had clearly perceived all those things which can be known about the natural law by the help of meditation and instruction? Secondly, the Apostle himself in verse 20 shows clearly enough where the Gentiles, who were destitute of the light of revelation, drew their knowledge of the Divine. For he says that the invisible virtues and perfections of God are perceived <term>by the things that are made</term> <note>original Greek: "tois poiēmasi"</note>, that is, by the help of created things. For the words <term>to make</term> <note>Greek: "poiein"</note> and <term>a thing made</term> <note>Greek: "poiēma"</note>, as the celebrated Wolfius rightly notes on this passage, are generally used by sacred and secular writers to refer to the divine works produced through creation. Therefore, the Apostle here argues most wisely—as we are accustomed to say in the schools—<term>a posteriori</term> <note>a logical term meaning "from the latter," or arguing from effects (the world) back to their cause (God)</note>. That is, he argues from the contemplation of created things, their beauty, their ends, and their use. This method of arguing is suited to the intellects of all people and has greater force in the minds of most men than the most subtle metaphysical reasoning. An argument from innate ideas of God would have been subject to many objections.

---

(*) The words of the Blessed Man sound thus: "To the Apostle, truth is God himself and true religion, just as injustice is superstition. Therefore, the Gentiles corrupted true religion with their superstition. And lest anything doubtful or obscure should lie beneath the words, he adds by way of interpretation: 'Because that which is knowable of God is manifest to them,' that is, when I say truth was corrupted by the Gentiles, I say it because <term>the knowable</term> <note>Greek: "to gnoston"</note>, namely that which can be known and understood about God—as far, finally, as is lawful for man (note this!)—is manifest to them."

...sought from innate [ideas]. For the Gentiles could have responded that they were plainly ignorant of those things which were present to their minds before they were born, to say nothing of other points. But here he appeals to those things which cannot be called into doubt by anyone who has not become completely brutish. Add to this that the most excellent among the Gentiles themselves confessed that from the contemplation of the universe, they knew God, who is otherwise invisible. By this very fact, the Apostle’s argument is sufficiently confirmed. It is helpful to cite one or two passages. Socrates, in Xenophon’s <term>Memorabilia</term> <note>Greek: "Apomnēmoneumata," memoirs of Socrates</note> page 505, according to the version by Bessarion, speaks thus on this argument: *“That the Gods exist, therefore, and have a care for men, you too, Euthydemus, will recognize, if you do not wait until you see the forms of the Gods. For it will be enough to worship and honor them by considering their works. Reflect, moreover, that the Gods themselves show themselves to us in this way. For the other Gods, while they provide all good things to us, grant none of these by appearing openly. He too, who orders and contains the whole world, in which all things are good and honorable, and who—since we always use them—nevertheless gives them to us always fresh, healthy, and immortal faster than a man can think, and administers them to us without fail: He is understood as performing the greatest things, but while governing this whole, He is invisible.”* The soul of man also, if anything else human does, participates in the divine nature. For it is manifest that it rules within us, yet it is seen not at all. *“When someone considers these things, he ought not to neglect the invisible things, but <term>recognizing their power from the things that come to pass</term> <note>Greek: "ek tōn ginomenōn tēn dynamin autōn katamanthanonta"</note>, he should proceed to honor the Gods.”* Thus spoke Socrates. Epictetus, in Arrian, pronounces in a plainly similar way in many places; let one stand in place of all, found in Book I, Chapter VI: “From every single thing,” says the Philosopher (according to the version by H. Wolf), “that happens in the world, Providence can easily be praised, if someone possesses these two things: first, the faculty of perceiving the nature of each thing; and second, a grateful mind. For otherwise, he will either not understand the manifold uses of created things, or he will not be grateful for them. If God had made colors, but had not made the power of sight, what use would they be? None at all. Again, if He had made that power, but the nature of things was not such as to fall under the power of sight, what use would it be then? None at all. But what if He had made both? Not even then would there be any use. Who is it, then, who fitted this with that, and that with this? Who is it who fitted the scabbard to the sword, and the sword to the scabbard? No one? And yet from the very structure of finished things, we are accustomed to declare that they are entirely the work of some craftsman. Do these individual things then [require] a craftsman...?”

# MEDITATION V.

...demonstrate their own origin, but do respectable things, and sight, and light, not demonstrate it? Is it so that male and female, and the eagerness of both for mating, and the ability to use the parts destined for that purpose: do not even these things demonstrate a Craftsman? Certainly, these things do demonstrate him. Moreover, the nature of our thought is such that the forms of sensory things are not simply impressed upon us, but are endowed with such power that we may even gather and abstract something from them, so that we may add something to the things perceived by the senses, and compose certain ideas through them, and thus pass from some things to others closely related to them. Can these things not move some people and drive them to such a sense of shame that they do not abandon the Craftsman? Let them explain to us, then, what it is that performs each of these tasks? Or how it could be possible that things so wonderful and skillfully made came into existence by chance or accident?

**AND WITH A FEW WORDS INTERPOSED:** What, then, is the purpose and, as it were, the construction of every living creature? One is destined for food, another to be useful for farming, and another for some similar utility. For these purposes, what need is there to understand visions and to discern them?

God, however, **NB.** <note>Latin "nota bene," meaning "mark well" or "take notice."</note> introduced man into life to be a spectator both of Himself and of His works—and not merely a spectator of them, but also an explainer. Therefore, it is shameful for a man to begin and end in the same place as the irrational animals. Rather, one ought to begin there, but end where nature itself has ended within us. Now, nature has ended in contemplation and understanding, and in a way of life consistent with the whole of nature. Therefore, take care that you do not die without sharing in this spectacle. You travel to the Olympic Games to see some work of Phidias, <note>Phidias was a famous ancient Greek sculptor, known for the Statue of Zeus at Olympia.</note> and each of you counts it among his misfortunes if he dies without having seen those things. But will you not run eagerly to see and understand those works for which no travel is required, which are already present, and which are right at hand? Will you not finally understand who you are, or why you were born, or even what that thing is which you have been given the opportunity to behold? Cicero argues by the same reasoning in *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book II, chapter 5, saying:

> If someone enters a house, a gymnasium, or a marketplace, and sees the logic, order, and discipline of all things, he could not judge that these things happen without a cause; rather, he would understand that there is someone in charge whom others obey. Much more so in such great motions and such vast successions of so many and such great things—orders in which immense and infinite antiquity has never played false—must he conclude that such great motions of Nature are governed by some Mind.

And in Book I of *On the Laws*, chapter 23, he says:

> When the same soul has surveyed the heavens, the lands, the seas, and the nature of all things, and has **NB.** almost grasped the one who moderates and rules them,

which final words clearly agree with the word <term>grope after</term> <note>original Greek: "psēlaphēseian," meaning to touch, handle, or feel for in the dark.</note> which Paul uses in Acts 17:27 when occupied with a similar argument. See the inter-

-preters on this passage. I omit many other similar testimonies of the Gentiles <note>In this context, "Gentiles" refers to the non-Christian, classical Greek and Roman philosophers.</note> which I could easily bring forward. From these cited passages of the most excellent men that the Gentile world produced, it is clear that they were accustomed to prove the existence of the most good and excellent Divine Power, His perfections, and His providential care in the very same way as was done by the Apostle. Therefore, no necessity compels us to interpret the Apostle's words according to the mind of those who establish certain innate ideas about God and divine things.

3) The same is proved by the fact that Holy Scripture in various places, such as Deuteronomy 1:39, Isaiah 7:14-16, and Jonah 4:11, testifies that infants cannot distinguish good from evil. By this phrase, it is signified that they either dwell in total ignorance of all things, or at least are equipped with no knowledge of moral good and evil.

Louis Cappel <note>Ludovicus Cappellus (1585–1658) was a famous French Protestant huguenot and Hebrew scholar.</note> defends the former interpretation of the words in his *Critical Notes* on Genesis. In Genesis 3:5, the words sound like this: *You shall be as Angels, knowing good and evil*; that is, all things. For by that phrase **GOOD** and **EVIL**, all things are understood, for there is nothing at all that is not either good or evil; all things entirely are contained under the embrace of good and evil. This, therefore, is what the Devil means: that by eating from this tree, man will obtain a knowledge of all things far greater than he had then—so great, indeed, that it would equal the Angels themselves, to whom nothing seems to be unknown, but all things are known and open.

This explanation seems to be confirmed by the words of the woman of Tekoa to David in 2 Samuel 14:17: *My Lord is like an Angel of God* <term>to discern good and evil</term> <note>original Hebrew: "lishmoa ha-tov ve-ha-ra," literally "to hear the good and the bad."</note> *to hear*, that is, one who understands good and evil. For this is what that woman means: "You are most wise and prudent, and almost equal to the Angels themselves; nothing is unknown to you, you know all things, you easily catch what I mean by this speech; there is no need for me to explain my mind to you more openly, you understand it well enough on your own." A little further down in verse 20, she expresses the same thing in other words, by which it is manifest that by that phrase "good and evil," the same thing as **ALL THINGS** is signified. For she says: *My lord is wise, according to the wisdom of an Angel of God,* <term>to know everything that is on the earth</term> <note>original Hebrew: "lada'at et kol asher ba-aretz."</note>. It is clear that by these words, the same thing is signified as she had signified above by those others, "to discern good and evil."

Furthermore, that same phrase "good and evil" joined with a negation signifies the same as **Nothing**: as when it is said in the preceding chapter that Absalom did not speak to his brother Amnon <term>anything, good or bad</term> <note>original Hebrew: "li-mera ve-ad tov," literally "from bad even unto good."</note>; that is, not at all. And in Genesis 31:29, God, speaking to Laban, says: *Take heed that you speak not to Jacob* <term>either good or bad</term> <note>original Hebrew: "mi-tov ad ra."</note>; that is, that you object nothing at all harsh or troublesome to him.

Thus far the celebrated Cappel.

Vitringa <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722) was a prominent Dutch theologian and Hebraist.</note> inclines toward almost the same opinion in his *Commentary on Isaiah*, chapter 7.

# MEDITATION V.

VII. [In Isaiah] chapter 7, verse 15, he who takes the phrase "to know to refuse the evil and choose the good" as referring to the "age of discretion" (as it is commonly called), appeals to Grotius's <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645) was a Dutch legal scholar and theologian whose works were foundational for international law and biblical interpretation.</note> notes on Deuteronomy 1:39. ->I know each thing,<-
->The good and the bad. Formerly, I was a child.<-
<note>original Greek: οἶδα ἕκαστα / Ἔσθλα τε καὶ τὰ χέρεια. πάρος δέ τε νήπιος ἦα</note>

An adult age is said to be that which knows how to reject evil and choose good, as in Isaiah 7:14, 15, 16. Vitringa <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722) was a famous Dutch theologian and Hebraist.</note>, already cited, explains his opinion on this phrase even more clearly in his *Sacred Observations* [Book 4, chapter 12, page 1046], saying: *To know, or to recognize good and evil in the biblical style means to have the nature of good and evil, right and wrong, known and explored, and to arrange one's judgment according to that knowledge so that one chooses the good, avoids the evil, clings to the good, and separates oneself as far as possible from the evil. He admits this interpretation and no other for Chapter 3 [of Genesis], in the Devil’s speech to the woman: "For God knows that on the day you eat of it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil."* And a few words later: *Behold the clearest passage, Deuteronomy 1:39, which is the only one he knows containing this phrase besides those already mentioned: "And as for your little ones, of whom you said they would be a prey, and your children who today do not know good and evil"—surely to know the nature of good and evil means to direct one's judgment according to that knowledge, so that you choose the good and reject the evil. In Isaiah, this is elegantly expressed as "knowing how to refuse the evil and choose the good." God, in Jonah, uses a similar phrase regarding infants, saying they do not know the difference between their right and left; that is, they do not know how to distinguish and discern with a right and free judgment.* 

But if, according to the style and testimony of the Holy Scriptures themselves, infants brought into the light are in such ignorance of all things, who will easily be persuaded to believe that these same children—before they were born and while still hidden in the mother's womb—had knowledge of the first and principal chapters of Theology and Natural Law? Who would trust those who claim to remember everything they pondered while shut up in that dark prison [the womb]?

III. Finally, to this argument, we add another taken from the very passage of the Apostle Paul to the Romans, to which those who disagree appeal. For in verse 15 of chapter 2, he testifies that it is clear that the Gentiles have the precepts of natural law well-perceived, since they are able to conform their actions to the law and judge whether they have acted rightly or badly—

<column-break/>

# ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

—acted. Without a doubt, he intended this to be understood regarding adults, or at least those who have sufficient knowledge of the law and their duties and actions, and thus can give an account of their actions—not regarding infants enclosed in the mother's womb. Certainly, for someone to rightly perform that duty mentioned by the Apostle, it is necessary that they have the character and nature of the law and their duties well-perceived; that they be well-conscious of their actions with respect to their purpose and circumstances; and finally, that they render a fair and sincere judgment. Who would defend the idea that such things are done by those not yet born? Indeed, whenever pagan writers treat duties and the law, they always speak in such a way that it is perfectly clear they mean only adult men are bound by them, or at least those who, by their age, can be properly taught about them. 

Learned men cite many such passages from the ancient Gentiles regarding the testimony and judgment of conscience—Grotius on the cited passage of the Apostle, Gataker <note>Thomas Gataker (1574–1654) was an English scholar and cleric known for his commentary on the meditations of Marcus Aurelius.</note> in his excellent observations on Marcus Antoninus, Huetius <note>Pierre Daniel Huet (1630–1721) was a French bishop and polymath.</note> in his *Alnetan Questions*, and many others whom those eager for the truth may consult. 

But let us hear briefly what is brought against our interpretation by those who disagree. First, they strongly urge the words of the Apostle saying: *What may be known of God is manifest in them* <note>original Greek: τὸ γνωστὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ φανερὸν ἐστὶν ἐν αὐτοῖς</note>, as if that phrase *in them* <note>original: ἐν αὐτοῖς</note> necessarily proves that notions of God are innate. But besides the fact that the particle *in* <note>original: ἐν</note>, as elsewhere (for example, Matthew 16:7, Luke 8:5), can denote *among*, I respond that whether you refer that "in them" to the Gentiles themselves or to their minds, it denotes nothing other than this: it is manifest to them; they have perceived this well. For *what may be known of God* signifies nothing else, as J. Cappel <note>Jacques Cappel (1570–1624) was a French Protestant theologian and professor of Hebrew.</note> rightly notes on this passage, than *what is naturally known concerning God* <note>original Greek: τὸ φύσει γνωστὸν περὶ τοῦ Θεοῦ</note>. 

The question, however, is where that knowledge originates. If you say it is innate, you are assuming the very point in question. But you say, *God has shown it* <note>original Greek: Θεὸς ἐφανέρωσε</note> is added. As if God could not present himself to be known in any other way than through certain inborn ideas impressed on the mind from conception itself? And if the words were to be taken in this sense, why does the Apostle appeal to *the things that are made* <note>original Greek: τὰ ποιήματα</note> below? On the contrary, our interpretation flows naturally. For the Apostle first lays down as a foundation that what can be known about God through reason was perceived by the Gentiles, God himself helping them; then he reveals the method of that revelation when he immediately adds: *being understood through the things that are made, they are clearly seen* <note>original Greek: τοῖς ποιήμασι νοούμενα καθορᾶται</note>. He explains this further when he says that from those things that meet the eyes, *His eternal power and Godhead* <note>original Greek: ἀΐδιον αὐτοῦ δύναμιν καὶ Θειότητα</note> are grasped. They object that the heaven, the earth, and other created things meeting the senses...

# MEDITATION V.

...[they argue] that nothing has a likeness to the idea we ought to have of God, and therefore that natural knowledge of the Divine cannot arise from the contemplation of created things. I respond: First, why then does the Apostle appeal to <term>the things that are made</term> <note>original Greek: ποιήματα (poiēmata). Referring to Romans 1:20.</note> to prove that some natural knowledge of God is given? Second, if this argument of my opponents is solid, all the arguments sought by theologians and philosophers from the order and ends of created things will hereafter be worthless; no atheist could be convicted of the existence of the Divine unless he admits an innate idea of God—that is, unless he takes as true the very thing he demands be proved. And why, I ask, is it not permitted to conclude from the effect to the cause, from the building to the builder, from a thing that is indeed contingent but rightly arranged, to an intelligent cause? And what, finally, should be said of the prophets, the apostles, and Christ himself, who send men to the contemplation of creatures for the purpose of learning, from the order, greatness, and use of created things, to recognize and proclaim the virtues of the best, wisest, and most powerful God? This would be useless if this contemplation of created things could contribute nothing to the knowledge of the Divine attributes. See at least *Psalm 19:1ff, Job 12:7–9, Isaiah 1:3, Psalm 104, Jeremiah 8:7, Proverbs 6:6ff, Matthew 6:26, etc.*

III. This argument of the opponents proves more than what ought to be proved, and thus it proves nothing. For if this were true (to omit other arguments sought from philosophical principles), it would follow that the ideas of all things are innate to us, which is not only false but also contrary to the distinction the adversaries themselves make between *innate* and *acquired* ideas. But they continue, and especially urge the words of the Apostle in chapter 2, verse 15 [of Romans], where he says: <term>the work of the law written in their hearts</term> <note>original Greek: το έργον του νόμου γραπτον εν ταις καρδίαις</note>: here they dwell upon the words <term>being written in their hearts</term>. But how it can be firmly gathered from this phrase that the main points of the natural law are innate to the mind before any reasoning, reflection, or instruction, I cannot yet perceive. Everyone confesses that this phrase cannot be taken in its literal sense. If it is understood metaphorically, it can denote nothing other than something we know well and turn over in our mind; something that is properly preserved in the memory. Very learned men have illustrated this phrase: Grotius on this chapter and on 2 Corinthians 3:3; Le Clerc in his *Ars Critica* (part 2, section 1, chapter 4); Fabricius in his notes on the *Apocryphal Code of the New Testament*; the commentators on Diogenes Laërtius; Pufendorf in his *Apology*, and others. I shall bring forward only a few examples, as a sample, collected by those learned men, so that it may be clear that the phrase cannot admit any other meaning. The celebrated Wolf, on this chapter of Paul’s letter to the Romans, brings forward a passage from Julian <note>Julian the Apostate (r. 361–363 AD), the last non-Christian Roman emperor.</note>, cited from his seventh Oration by the famous Bos in his *Exercitations*, from which that blessed man thinks it clear that the phrase "inscribed on the soul" signifies more than merely holding in the memory, but having it thoroughly perceived. The passage from Julian sounds like this: <term>But also the laws as if inscribed by the Gods in our souls, by which we are all persuaded without a teacher that there is something Divine</term>. But I would wish it to be noted here that Julian uses the word *as if* inscribed, and thus "to write in" the soul is not explained directly so; but from the following phrases it is clear that a knowledge is denoted which can be achieved with reason alone as a guide, without laborious instruction. But this does not conflict with the opinion of those who say that all men, having applied a moderate amount of attention and contemplation of created things, can easily be persuaded of the existence of a most wise Deity. When, therefore, Julian says that there is a God is "as if inscribed" on the soul, he wants nothing other than this: that such is the nature of this truth that it can be easily known. The Hebrews themselves use this phrase in this sense: thus in *Proverbs 3, verse 3*, Solomon says: "Let not mercy and truth forsake you; bind them around your neck; <term>write them upon the table of your heart</term> <note>original Hebrew: כתבם על לוח לבך (katveim al luach libecha)</note>," that is, fix them most deeply in your soul, and be always mindful of those precepts. Likewise, when in *Jeremiah chapter 31:33* God promises the faithful of the New Testament that he will give a copious knowledge of the mysteries of the Gospel, he says among other things that he will write the law on their hearts, that is, he will bring it about by his grace

<header>MEDITATION V.</header>

...so that they will not only know the discipline of Christ far more *clearly* than the believers of the Old Testament, but will also perceive a singular pleasure from serious meditation upon it and apply themselves most ardently to the pursuit of holiness. However, although this phrase can have a broader power in this context if we consider the matter signified, that primary notion of the *inscription of the law in the heart* does not lose its customary and accepted meaning. For when God is said to inscribe the law on the heart, it signifies above all else, without doubt, that He will bring it about that the faithful have a more excellent knowledge of the *doctrine of grace*; <note>original: "doctrinæ gratiæ"</note> for if this were lacking, the pursuit of sanctity could not produce healthy fruits. From this it is clear that the phrase always preserves its meaning, namely *to bring it about that something is properly known*.

Hence our theologians, when they treat the benefits of the New Testament specifically, include among them a broader knowledge of the Mysteries of the Gospel, and they appeal to this passage, following the lead of the Apostle Paul in *Hebrews chapter 8, verse 10.* The celebrated *Cocceius* <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian known for federal theology.</note> briefly paraphrases <note>original Greek: παραφράζει</note> the words of *Jeremiah* thus: *I will make it so that they receive my law, delight in it, and do not forget it.* Regarding the passage in *Romans 2*, he says: Moreover, *to be written in the hearts* <note>original: "inscriptum esse in cordibus"</note> here signifies only knowledge. See also our celebrated *Heidegger* <note>Johann Heinrich Heidegger (1633–1698), a Swiss Reformed theologian.</note> in his *Body of Theology, Topic 20, Thesis 47*; and *Gürtler* in his *Institutes of Theology, chapter 33, Thesis 35*, to pass over others. 

From the passages cited, it seems to me to be more than sufficiently clear what the true meaning of the phrase *to inscribe on the heart*, or *to be inscribed on the heart*, actually is. If, therefore, we apply this phrase to the passage of Paul, it will be manifest that Paul's intention is that God adorned the human race with such faculties that, without great trouble or abstruse and difficult reasoning, men are able to know that there exists a most wise, good, and powerful Divinity, whom all are bound to worship and to conform their actions to His will. Or, if anyone prefers to admit the interpretation of this passage by *Pufendorf* <note>Samuel von Pufendorf (1632–1694), a highly influential German jurist and philosopher of natural law.</note> which appears on page 35 of his *Apology*, the sense is: *The knowledge of natural law, drawn from the dictate of reason, is so firmly impressed on the minds of the Gentiles, and they were so evidently convinced of its certainty, that they could never shake it off, even if they tried with all their might to cast those things from their minds to soothe the stings of conscience.*

Certain theologians—for example, the late <note>original Greek: ὁ μακαρίτης (ho makaritēs), a respectful term for the deceased.</note> celebrated *Buddeus* <note>Johann Franz Buddeus (1667–1729), a Lutheran theologian.</note>, following *Musaeus* and others in his *Moral Theology, Part 2, page 399*—are unwilling to admit innate ideas of God in the sense of Descartes, yet they are not ready to join the opinion of those who contend that knowledge of the natural law is acquired with the help of sensation, reflection, and instruction. Instead, they flee to some sort of "propensity," or as the celebrated
<meta>catchword: Bud-</meta>

<header>ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.</header>

Buddeus is accustomed to say, they flee to a certain *potential knowledge*, by which a human being who has reached the use of reason can, by means of inspecting his own nature and aided by the powers of the intellect, acquire a knowledge of <term>Natural Law</term> <note>original: "juris Naturæ." The universal moral principles believed to be discoverable by human reason.</note> with the easiest effort, through a "proximate power." 

But I, in the first place, deny that any third option exists between *innate and acquired knowledge*. Second, that "potential knowledge" would be nothing other than a propensity to assent to all those things whose clear knowledge is observed by the mind; this brings absolutely no light to the question at hand, since not even our opponents—that is, those who deny that such "congenital" ideas of natural law are given—deny that men can arrive at a knowledge of Natural Law with the help of sensation and meditation as soon as they begin to weigh things. 

Hence the most learned *Barbeyrac* <note>Jean Barbeyrac (1674–1744), a famous legal scholar known for translating Pufendorf.</note>, in the *preface prefixed to the work of Pufendorf, Section 4*, making mention of this opinion of *Buddeus*, rightly says: *It is to surrender one's weapons at the same time as one makes a show of attacking an opinion.* From this it can also be judged what should be thought of those who say that people who deny those innate ideas of natural law are championing the cause of Atheists. Certainly, they should not be dismissed without censure. Who, for example, would say that men of exquisite learning—who have applied singular diligence in explaining, elucidating, and proving the precepts of Natural Law, such as *Pufendorf, Barbeyrac, and Cumberland* <note>Richard Cumberland (1631–1718), an English philosopher who argued against Hobbes using natural law.</note>, to say nothing of many most learned and excellent theologians—wished to favor Atheists who proscribe all natural law? For this reason, the already praised *Barbeyrac* sharply, and in my opinion justly, criticized *Sherlock* <note>William Sherlock (1641–1707), an English divine.</note>—a man otherwise most excellent and renowned for many published writings—for repeating that same old song. <meta>This page continues the debate over "innate ideas"—the theory that humans are born with a basic knowledge of God and morality. The author is specifically refuting the interpretations of Faustus Socinus, a 16th-century Italian theologian whose followers (Socinians) argued that man has no natural knowledge of God and requires direct revelation for even the simplest religious truths.</meta>

# MEDITATION V.

From what has been said, it can also be gathered that learned men do not favor *Socinus* <note>Faustus Socinus (1539–1604), a controversial figure who founded a movement that denied the Trinity and stressed human reason, yet paradoxically argued that natural man had no inherent knowledge of God.</note>, even those who contend that it cannot be proved from the cited passages of the Apostle Paul that innate ideas of God and natural law are given. For they grant—and indeed prove with the strongest arguments—that certain general headings of Natural Theology are given; they allow that these can be easily grasped by anyone through the help of attention and meditation. They argue that the Apostle, in the two cited passages <note>Referring to Romans 1 and 2</note>, does this to show that the Gentiles sinned most gravely because they did not attend to that light. 

*Socinus*, however, goes off in an entirely different direction. By a distorted interpretation, he twists those things which Paul had warned concerning the natural knowledge of God to refer instead to the knowledge of the Gospel. The words of *Socinus* interpreting the passage of the Apostle in Chapter 1, verse 20, sound like this: 

> *It must be known that the words "from the creation of the world" ought to be joined with the word "invisible." Therefore, in that place, the Apostle says that the eternal divinity of God—that is, what God perpetually wants us to do (for divinity is also expressed in this sense elsewhere in his writings, as in Colossians 2:9)—and his eternal power, or promises that will never fail (in which sense he had said a little earlier that the Gospel is the power of God); these things, I say, which had never been used by men since the world was created, and had not been known to them, were perceived through works—that is, through the miraculous operations of God Himself and of divine men, especially indeed of Christ and His Apostles.*

Who does not see that Socinus plainly recedes from the opinion of those who contend that the natural knowledge of the law is being discussed here? See also what theologians have warned against this interpretation of *Socinus*; for example, *Pearson* <note>John Pearson (1613–1686), Bishop of Chester, famous for his "Exposition of the Creed."</note> in his work on the *Apostles' Creed*, page 31; and against the author of the *Racovian Catechism* <note>The formal statement of Socinian belief.</note> who subscribes to the same interpretation, the esteemed *Oeder* <note>Georg Ludwig Oeder (1694–1760), a German theologian.</note> in his refutation of this Catechism, page 65. It must be confessed, however, that *Crellius* and *Schlichtingius* <note>Johannes Crellius and Jonas Schlichting, major Socinian theologians who moderated some of Socinus's more extreme views.</note> departed from the opinion of Socinus on this.

<margin>Bad Education is not the least cause of Unbelief</margin>
IV. However you may feel about this argument—whether you say the first rudiments of Religion are engraved and innate in our minds, or you contend that they are acquired by meditation and instruction—it is certain and confirmed by 

> to form right ideas on this, they <note>Referring to humans</note> can also remain in ignorance, or even fall into error on this subject, if they do not make good use of their lights; and this response is entirely solid. God having endowed man with the faculties of knowing which he possesses, was no more obliged by His Goodness to engrave innate notions of Religion and Morality in his soul than to build him bridges or houses, after having given him reason, hands, and materials. To allege, therefore, the abuse that men make of natural lights in matters of Morality as a proof that there is nothing certain there, is to reason as pitifully as the Epicureans, who, to overturn Religion, display all the evils, all the crimes, and all the extravagances birthed by false zeal, or superstition, or even hypocrisy hidden under the specious veil of piety.

# ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

experience that infants recently brought into the light dwell in supreme foolishness, ignorant of all things as well as of Religion; and thus, for the nature and character of Religion to be rightly known, there is a need for right education and instruction. Certainly, all those who have more diligently investigated the causes of Unbelief, as well as Impiety—evils which are spreading everywhere among Christians—

<margin>Alas! they have fallen, and still fall, into the same.</margin>
have discovered that bad education, preposterous instruction, and evil examples are to be counted among those things which usually corrupt tender minds and harden them against the love of Religion. See what the Venerable Old Man (now enrolled in the heavenly choir) *J. F. Ostervald* <note>Jean-Frédéric Ostervald (1663–1747), a Swiss Protestant pastor known for his work on the decay of Christian piety.</note>, a most excellent theologian, discusses piously and prudently on this argument in a book full of good fruit, titled: *The Source of Corruption, which reigns today among Christians*. Part I, chapters 1, 2, 7; part II, chapter 5; and elsewhere throughout. The most learned man, the now-sainted <note>original Greek: ὁ νυν ἐν ἁγίοις</note> *M. V. la Croze* <note>Maturin Veyssière de La Croze (1661–1739), a scholar and librarian.</note>, agreed with him in his *Conversations on Various Subjects*, page 271:

> *The frightful disorders of men* (he is speaking of Atheism) *have established it on all sides, and it seems that it is now more than ever on the verge of increasing from day to day, and from generation to generation. Parents teach their children by their examples, which means that no age and no sex is exempt. One is most often raised by people in whom one sees not a shadow of virtue: one hears them lie for interest and by habit, and unfortunately one receives the first principles of Religion from the mouths of people who make no scruple of telling a thousand impertinent fables, and of disguising their sentiments every time they believe they will draw some utility from it. As one advances in age, one learns to know these people, and as one distrusts these tellers of fables, the truths of the Gospel, which have passed through their mouths, begin to become suspect. This is usually the first step toward Unbelief.*

In so clear a matter, it is not necessary to bring forward more testimonies. Come, let us also show briefly the same thing that has been examined more at length by others. To detect the sources of corruption, we must see above all to whose care and custody recently born infants are entrusted. Who does not know that humans most unfit for rightly shaping the tender minds of infants—namely, wet-nurses—bear the first care of infants? In many places, the infants of the wealthy, as if unworthy of the sight and love of their parents, are carried outside the father's house and handed over to others, so that—to say nothing of other inconveniences—they must lack that sweet food, namely their mother's milk; which, without doubt, goes against the end and goal of the Creator.

# MEDITATION V.

There is no doubt that this is a failing of nature. On that account, the late John Tillotson <note>original: "Tillotsonius"</note>, the most worthy Archbishop of Canterbury, once vehemently reproached mothers in his *Sacred Sermons*, Volume 6, page 243. Infants are thus handed over into the hands of nurses <term>Nutricularum; women hired to breastfeed and care for infants</term>, who are talkative women but for the most part lacking in true wisdom; the children hear many ridiculous, absurd, and false things. For in order to soothe them, these women use various kinds of stories and little songs, which are often tasteless and scarcely have any meaning. To these they often mix in monstrous tales about specters and ghosts <note>original: "spectris & lemuribus"</note>, poured out with groans, wonder, and great strain of voice. In his own time, Plato—as Plutarch testifies in *On the Education of Children* <note>original: "περι παιδων ἀγωγης" (peri paidon agoges)</note>—proscribed such things and did not want them told in the presence of infants. "And it seems to me," he says in the cited passage, page 282 of the Zurich edition, "that the divine Plato rightly exhorts nurses not to tell just any stories to children, lest it happens that their souls are filled from the beginning with foolishness and corruption." <note>original Greek: "καὶ μοὶ... δοκει πλατων ὁ δαιμονιος ἐμμελως ταις τιτθαις μη τας τυχοντας μυθας τοις παιδιοις λεγειν, ἵνα μη τας τωτων ψυχας ἐξ ἀρχης ἀνοιας και διαφθορας ἀναπιμπλασθαι συμβαινη"</note> What Plato, a pagan <note>original: "homo gentilis"</note>, forbade to be done, no one is ignorant is nevertheless frequently committed today among Christians.

In the meantime, the infant hears truth mixed with falsehood and fixes it in his mind; if infants are left to their mothers, those women for the most part walk the same path as the nurses. Most parents—to speak generally on this subject—have neither a knowledge of right education, nor do they think themselves bound by natural law and revelation to establish it properly. This is so much the case that, unless a singular care of divine Providence were to intervene, infants would often rush headlong into every wickedness and perish miserably. Some are not entirely ignorant of the necessity of this duty, but they either do not know, or only obscurely understand, wherein the true happiness of man is to be placed, and what must be provided for children in this life so that they may become participants in it. Truly, that happiness is acquired only through the cultivation of the mind and the love of virtue. Since parents either do not know this, or at least believe that true happiness can be obtained without these things, it cannot happen otherwise than that children—destitute thus far of better safeguards and incentives—should hanker after all those things and seek with all their prayers and desires what is pleasing and acceptable to the depraved cravings of the soul. Once this zeal and desire is deeply lowered into the minds of infants, they will only with difficulty admit the precepts of religion later. We see daily, alas! that most parents place all their zeal and all their care in this: that when they provide for their children, they look especially to those things which are necessary to sustain this life, and then that they may abound, if possible, in those goods

<column-break/>

# ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

which are considered primary among mortals, namely riches, honors, and so forth. If the children have obtained these goods, or do not have a vain hope that they will attain them, the parents proclaim themselves blessed and most happy. From this source, another evil is accustomed to flow—usually joined with the former—namely, the perpetual praise of those things in which many parents falsely believe true happiness to be placed. Depending on whether the parents are enticed by the love of riches, or pleasures, or honors, they will likewise commend those goods in the presence of their children. Those whom the greed for possession torments frequently mingle conversations about the happiness of those who abound in riches; they tell of how much care and anxiety is needed to acquire them, keep them, and transmit them to their descendants. They extol these goods with praises; indeed, sometimes they discuss them as if it were permitted to snatch them for oneself by any art, through right or wrong <note>original: "per fas et nefas"</note>. In a word, they speak like that man in the Poet: *O Citizens, citizens, money must be sought first. Virtue after coins.* <note>A famous quote from Horace, *Epistles* 1.1.53-54, satirizing the Roman obsession with wealth.</note> Those who are addicted to pleasures consume much time in praising delicate foods and sumptuous banquets. Children often hear a parent over lunch, not without a cheerfulness of voice and brow, recounting how pleasantly he spent the previous day drinking, playing, and laughing; with how many jokes the company was seasoned; how much fun this or that person provided; in what precious clothes, perfectly fitted to the taste of the present age, this or that woman was dressed, and so on. Others, finally, mingle nothing but talk about the noble lineage from which they sprang; they point with their fingers to how many images of illustrious ancestors they can show off; what dignities their grandfathers, parents, and most of those joined by blood have held and still hold; how much nobility contributes to obtaining offices of various kinds, etc. etc. When children hear these things repeated everywhere daily, it cannot be but that they are inflamed with a vehement love of these things. For while on the one hand they do not yet know wherein the true happiness of man is to be placed, and what is the price of virtue and wisdom; on the other hand, a desire has been deeply injected into their minds for possessing all those things which can sweetly soothe the senses and bring pleasure to the soul. It cannot happen otherwise than that they should value highly those things which they had heard extolled with praise by their parents so many times, and afterwards strive with all the contention of their strength so that they might enjoy such precious goods through life. Nor does the evil often stay within these bounds, but proceeds further. For there are, alas! parents who not only speak magnificently of those goods and praise and commend them, but who also, as it were, lead their children by the hand to the perpetration of various kinds of vice.

# MEDITATION V.

For there are those who tell the grossest lies in the presence of their children, and strive to give these lies a sense of truth by any means. There are some who, without any shame, describe the sins they committed in their youth, adding not even the slightest testimony of a soul pained by them or touched by grief. There are those who tear apart and slander their neighbor while a child is listening; they expound at length upon all sorts of rumors—even if they are false and fictional—as if they were the absolute truth, and they do so with a certain joy in their hearts. I will say nothing of other sins of this kind, such as the brawls, contentions, and cursings of the spouses themselves. Oh, how rare are the parents of whom you could rightly say what God testifies about Abraham in Genesis chapter XVIII, verse 19, saying: *I know that he will command his children and his household after him to keep the way of the Lord by doing righteousness and justice.* <note>original: "Scio suis Eum liberis & porro suæ in posterum stirpi præcepturum esse, ut ad Jehovæ normam vitam dirigentes justitiam colant atque jus."</note> Who then would wonder if the seeds of impiety and unbelief <term>Incredulitas; a lack of religious faith or a state of skepticism</term> are sown early in the minds of infants?

Surely shame should be cast upon those parents who boast that they have given their name to Christ, by the lessons that Horace <note>Quintus Horatius Flaccus, a Roman poet</note> says were ingrained in him by his own father in his *Satires* <note>original: "Serm. IV. Lib. I."</note>. Listen to him:

> *My excellent father accustomed me to this:*
> *that I should flee from vices by noting examples of them,*
> *when he exhorted me to live sparingly and frugally,*
> *and to be content with what he himself had provided for me.*
> *“Do you not see,” he would say, “how poorly Albius’s son lives? And how*
> *Barrus is in want? A great lesson, lest anyone should wish*
> *to waste his paternal estate.” When he would deter me*
> *from the shameful love of a harlot: “Do not be like Sectanus.”*
> *Lest I should follow adulteresses when I could enjoy*
> *permitted love: “The reputation of Trebonius, when caught, is not good,”*
> *he would say.*

Moreover, this evil is increased when children very rarely or never hear their parents mention the excellence of virtue, the fleeting nature of life, or the vanity of earthly things. They hear nothing of the rewards and punishments to come after this life, the nobility and immortality of the mind, or the divine origin and dignity of the Christian religion. They are not told of the true characteristics and duties of Christians, of self-denial, or of the doctrine, merits, precepts, and innocence of the life of Christ our Savior—nor of any other virtues which alone can make us truly happy and blessed. What else, I ask, will an infant gather from this—having as yet no taste for true religion and virtue—except that earthly goods, which are 

<column-break/>

# ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

praised so highly by their parents, are to be numbered among those things which must be sought and desired first, and that religion does not carry much weight in making a human being happy?

<margin>Most parents lack an accurate knowledge of religion, and thus cannot properly pass on the precepts of religion to their children, though it is necessary.</margin>

V. Not only are infants corrupted early enough by the talk and examples of their parents, but most parents are generally unfit for properly teaching the precepts of religion, which ought to be instilled early into tender minds. Many parents are found who are equipped with very little and obscure knowledge of religion, though it is their duty to pass it on to their children at home. Who does not know that not only among the peasants, but even among citizens educated in the largest cities, many are found who cannot even explain the first catechetical precepts <term>Catechismus; a summary of religious doctrine used for instruction, often through questions and answers</term> to their children? 

Most boys or young men born of citizens, after they have committed the precepts of the Catechism to memory in whatever way and have been admitted to the Holy Supper <note>Holy Communion</note>, are handed over to a craftsman or master to learn some trade by which they may later sustain their life and family. Whether these young people, if any leisure is given, take up books containing the dogmas and precepts of religion, or attend sacred services at the proper time, parents and masters for the most part care very little, considering it enough if they apply diligent effort to learning their trade. 

Thus, little by little, it happens that while they are entirely intent on these things, they unlearn what they had once perceived and committed to memory. After the time of apprenticeship has passed, the young man travels to foreign lands to gain a fuller knowledge of his trade. Here, however, our man—left entirely to himself—is clearly careless of things pertaining to religion, for he thinks himself in no way bound to know it more correctly. He holds it as a law for himself that the Lord’s Day is to be spent in drinking bouts, and the rest of the time (if money does not fail) in physical exercise and service. Often, he spends several years in places where he cannot hear the precepts of pure religion publicly taught—a fact that does not trouble him at all. But in whatever place he lives, he leads a life as loose as possible, with all guardians who could teach and warn him of better things mostly removed. If he stays in places where a religion flourishes that is different from the one in which he was raised, he often hears religion disputed on both sides, and the dogmas of his own sect attacked. But since he is far from knowing what those who differ from his religion think—since he does not even rightly understand for himself the Decrees defended by the Church to which he has given his name—he often begins [to doubt] the truth of the articles which [he holds] obscurely...

It contrasts the behavior of modern parents with the virtuous upbringing described by the Roman poet Horace and the biblical example of Abraham.</summary>

-># MEDITATION V.<-

...perceived thus far, to either doubt or at least to think that those things which pertain to Religion do not belong to him, but rather to those who have been consecrated to the Holy Ministry from their very youth. And when he sees everywhere men who, though following the decrees of different Religions, are nevertheless for the most part addicted to the same vices, he concludes that Religion can be changed according to the diversity of places and the will of Rulers without any harm. And would that such men did not so often take part in the conversations of people who laugh at all Religion "with white teeth" <note>original: "albis dentibus ridentium"—a Latin idiom meaning to laugh mockingly or to sneer openly</note>, asserting either that everything said about the state of a future life is false, or at least that it should be numbered among those things which are doubtful and uncertain.

Returning to his homeland from abroad, he is now anxious above all else for the means by which he might endure the labor of his hands for a living, and be able to nourish himself and his own. To that end, he takes a wife, procreates children, and devotes diligent effort to his domestic affairs. The care of this matter occupies him entirely from then on, so much so that he cannot be concerned with other business—much less with knowing Religion more rightly or passing it on to his children. Meanwhile, so that he may nevertheless appear to be a religious man, he finds time for external worship according to the laws of the city, and for the most part abstains from those vices which are usually branded with public infamy. No one would deny that many citizens are educated and lead their lives in this way. Who, then, would believe that such men will either think rightly about the excellence of Religion and its genuine nature, or that they will apply themselves with singular care to instill and commend the precepts of religion to their children early on with all zeal and care?

Yet it should not be thought that only those who must be primarily anxious throughout life about earning their bread sin in this matter; alas, this vice dominates more widely! It has also seized those who are supplied with resources, abound in greater leisure, and have for the most part been imbued from childhood with the precepts of both divine and human disciplines. These men think they would not be properly looking after their own dignity if they were accustomed to hand down the first Elements of Religion to their infants, and to converse with them about the gravest of all matters—namely, divine ones. They leave this business to others. The cares of this age occupy them entirely, so much so that they themselves are concerned with increasing the splendor of the family, scraping together wealth, or tasting delights of every kind, rather than with the right education of their children—especially in instilling Religion, without the knowledge and love of which men can never be happy. To these people, surely, that saying of *Crates* found in *Plutarch* should be repeated: *O men, where are you being carried? You who indeed apply all care to possessing wealth, but take* <note>original Greek: "Ω ανθρωποι ποι φερεσθε; οιτινες χρηματων μεν κτησεως περι πασαν ποιεισθε σπουδην, των δ' υιεων, οις ταυτα καταλειψετε, μηδεν φροντιζετε"</note>

-># ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.<-

*who indeed apply all care to possessing wealth, but take no care for your sons, to whom you leave these things.* Nor do these same people only believe this duty to be placed beneath their dignity, but they are also often accustomed to commend vices themselves under the appearance of virtue. Thus, when they see their boys or girls falsely mocking others, devising a lie with ingenuity, or being able to exercise some sort of "authority" over others in a gathering, they not only rejoice in their hearts, but they applaud with words in the presence of the children. Whence it cannot happen otherwise than that children are early on imbued with backward opinions concerning virtues and vices, and the seeds of Religion are all but suffocated. And when they see and notice everywhere that those with whom they are more familiar in youth are imbued with the same opinions and addicted to similar pursuits, they scarcely—if at all—offer open ears to others later advising better things; instead, they think those people are too peevish who wish to bind them to the laws of a stricter discipline, and who want to commend the precepts or worship of Religion so frequently and diligently.

<margin>Many Parents, though not lacking in the knowledge of religion, do not know the art of skillfully passing it on and explaining it.</margin>

VI. Meanwhile, it must not be denied that there are also Parents so kindled by the love of Religion that they themselves apply no small care to instilling and commending the precepts of Religion to their children. In which matter no sane person would easily doubt that they are to be praised. Nevertheless, there are many things which prevent them from performing this duty skillfully and obtaining the end which they intend.

*First*, for they are accustomed to hand down the dogmas and precepts of Religion in the same manner in which they themselves had once been taught about them; meanwhile, no care is applied during that time to acquire a more accurate knowledge of the things they once heard. Hence, for the most part, they enjoin their infants to learn by heart passages of Holy Scripture <note>original: "Loca S. Literarum"</note> usually brought forward to prove this or that dogma, even though these passages often prove nothing less than that which they were brought forward to confirm. This very thing can disturb their minds not a little at a more mature age. Whence it would be desirable that in all catechetical <term>Catechetica; the practice of religious instruction through questions and answers</term> instructions, only a few passages of Holy Scripture were used—but the clearest ones, and the most effective for proving the point. For in this way, they would feel, as they unroll the Holy Scriptures and weigh Religion with increasing age, that the articles of religion—which as youths they had fixed deeply in their memory and mind—are built upon firm safeguards.

II. Most Parents are not supplied with those faculties of mind, nor endowed with that judgment, such that they can clearly instill those things which pertain to religion into the souls of others, and hand them down in such a way that the children cannot fail to grasp them: it is an art to perform this duty, which can only be done by those...

<header>MEDITATION V.</header>

...can be exercised, who not only have an accurate knowledge of things pertaining to religion, but also know how to instill the precepts of religion by an easy and plain method. Hence, for the most part, parents are content if their children can repeat in almost the same words those things which they have received by ear or committed to memory, caring little whether they understand the sense and force of the matters proposed or not. Parents ought to imitate Socrates, who said he performed the office of a midwife <note>original: "obstetricis officio"—referring to the Socratic method of "birthing" ideas from a student through questioning</note>, while he himself did not so much teach his disciples with many words, but rather compelled them—even against their will—to express their own opinions on the matters turning in their minds. 

III. Most parents sin in this: that they are more concerned with exercising the memory than with rightly instilling the simplest heads of religion. Whence it commonly happens that they declare their infants "blessed" if they hear them quickly commit to memory and recite very long prayer formulas (even if not understood) or psalms. Indeed, this "blessed memory" is very often the sole reason that parents decide early on that a boy—who might be far better suited for other duties—should be consecrated to the Sacred Ministry <note>The professional clergy</note>. It is true, of course, that it is necessary for children in their tender age to learn the precepts of religion, prayers, and moral maxims; but these ought to be few in number and clear. Respecting the rest, one must wait until the capacity of the mind is greater for rightly grasping more numerous and difficult things, and fixing them equally in the soul and the heart. If anywhere, certainly in the right delivery of the principles of Religion, there is need for the greatest circumspection. For the worship of the Deity, if built upon a false or confused knowledge, can never produce solid piety. 

IV. To rightly deliver the Elements of Religion, it is necessary that parents, intending to hand down an accurate knowledge of the articles of religion to their children, use words and speech that are clear and removed from all ambiguity. For besides the fact that many people, either through weakness of intellect or through laziness, are intent on words rather than things, it cannot happen otherwise than that, if this is neglected, they will only obscurely understand matters most worthy of attention. But alas, how few parents attend to this! How few there are who have learned to propose matters looking toward religion in such a way that infants cannot help but grasp their meaning! The common crowd of men cares for nothing less than clarity of speech, and often thinks that some unknown power lies beneath the most obscure words and phrases. Indeed, there are parents who vehemently applaud themselves when they can hand down to their infants certain phrases that seem sublime and breathe an affection of piety—drawn from ascetic or mystical books—when nevertheless neither the parents...

...themselves, much less the infants, sufficiently understand the thing itself expressed by the words. The illustrious *Saurin* <note>Jacques Saurin (1677–1730), a famous French Protestant preacher</note> laments in the preface to his *Catechetical Instructions* that many Catechisms are filled with phrases of this sort. 

V. Furthermore, parents sin in that they deliver the precepts of religion with too much rigor in the first stage of life, and are often too severe and peevish regarding the time in which they are to be instructed, the task which is demanded, and the lapses which the children might have committed. For thus it happens, bit by bit, that children begin to feel an aversion toward all those things which pertain to the business of Religion. Well known are the things which Philosophers deliver concerning the *Association of Ideas* <note>original: "Idearum Consociatione"—a reference to the psychological theories of John Locke</note>, which experience confirms more than enough. To be sure, human nature is so constituted that as often as things which once excited a vehement pain are presented again to the mind, people are not only mindful of almost all the circumstances which were joined with that trouble and weariness, but they especially attend to the cause of the excited pain, and want it removed far from them for their entire life. Thus it often happens that as young people progress in age, they perform the duties of piety with reluctance and apply themselves to the meditation of divine things only with struggle, because they were only joined to learning the first Elements of Religion by force in their tender age. (*) 

Thus it is known that many infants and boys are so bound to a schedule that they are driven at the sound of the hour to pour forth prayers or recite religious precepts, even though it may be manifest that their minds are still fixed entirely on their toys and youthful exercises, from which they have been dragged away not without trouble and weariness. The same must be said of the task which they are held to complete: some parents think they have done their duty well if every day their children...

---

(*) The Most Reverend Father in Christ *Tillotson* <note>John Tillotson (1630–1694), Archbishop of Canterbury</note> taxes this same evil custom in his *Sacred Sermons, Vol. VI, p. 309*. "A great severity," he says, "often produces an effect quite contrary to that which is intended. How often does it happen that those who have been raised by harsh masters hate study all their lives because of the cruel treatments used toward them to constrain them to it? Likewise, when one wants to lead children to Piety and virtue by unreasonable rigor and an excessive exactness, one often inspires in them a long-term disgust for Religion and violent prejudices against it. One teaches them, as *Erasmus* used to say, *to hate and know virtue at the same time* <note>original: "virtutem simul odisse & nosse"</note>. For one thus paints virtue for them under a hideous form; one makes them feel good and evil too close to one another. So that when the ideas of Religion and virtue present themselves to their mind, they immediately recall also the memory of the severity with which one was accustomed to accompany the lessons given to them thereupon; and the natural repugnance that men have for punishment then spreads onto Religion itself. Ultimately, can one hope that children will love their duty when they have never heard it spoken of without seeing the rod all ready to fall upon them?" Compare the most acute Locke's <note>John Locke (1632–1704)</note> third chapter of his treatise *On the Education of Children*.

<header>MEDITATION V.</header>
<meta>catchword: De-</meta>

...to recite everything concerning all parts of Religion that they have committed to memory. However, since at this fleeting age children are impatient with long delays, they hurry vehemently to reach the end of their prescribed task. For this reason, it cannot happen otherwise than that they handle Sacred matters with boredom, and pay little or no attention to what they have recited. The same can be repeated if we look at the *places* where they are meant to devote time to Religion at home. They are required to recite psalms and pour out prayers, often in the presence of the entire family, with servants coming and going, while the mother often talks or quarrels with a maid about various business matters. On one hand, the child’s mind is distracted; on the other, he believes he has fulfilled his duty well, provided that the *number* of things to be recited is finished and brought to an end. Furthermore, he believes that matters regarding Religion are to be counted among those things that can be handled amidst a thousand cares and distractions. No sane person would easily doubt that all these things, in the course of time, obstruct a pure love and worship of Religion and bear crooked fruit.

On the contrary, there is a need for gravity and the highest circumspection when Parents wish to hand down the first Elements of Religion to their Infants. It must be ensured, as much as possible, that children feel early on that Religion is a most momentous matter and most worthy of human attention. VI. Finally, Parents hinder their Children from thinking magnificently and reverently about Religion when—while handing down its first Elements according to their capacity or enjoining them to find time for prayers—they do not first, and indeed very frequently, repeat what use Religion has in this and the future life; what kind of and how much tranquility of mind a good conscience brings with it in every state of life; how great the rewards are laid up for the pious; how Venerable and worthy of love is the Deity <note>original: "Numen"—a term for divine power or a godhead</note> whom we worship, etc. Since the child’s mind shrinks from everything that requires some attention, yet is usually moved most effectively by arguments drawn from *utility* <note>The author suggests children respond best to practical benefits rather than abstract theology</note>, it must be shown early on that reverence for the Deity, devoted prayers, and a correct and solid knowledge of the Lord’s precepts are joined with singular utility, and that those are the happiest of all mortals who begin to keep God's precepts from their very Youth, etc. Sad experience, alas, teaches that these things are neglected everywhere by Parents. They speak much of the necessity of external worship; but they rarely speak with their children about the internal purity of the soul, or the reverence and love for the Deity. They occasionally discourse at length on the power of God upon the occasion of a gathering storm; but regarding His goodness and singular care for mortals, they mostly maintain a deep silence.

Children perceive, moreover, that on feast days, for instance, their Parents put on some kind of austerity, use food and drink more sparingly, and open books which they rarely touch on other occasions; but once those days have passed, they are more cheerful, indulge their inclinations, and put on their former habits. From this, children conclude that the Deity can be easily appeased, that Religion is completed by the observation of certain rituals, and that duties of piety can be performed without any singular change of mind.

<margin>These evils are increased, partly because most Parents have little care for the cultivation of reason in educating children, and partly because they do not early on accustom them to subject sensory appetites to the precepts of reason and Revelation.</margin>

VII. These, and many other things (for we wish to bring forward only the more significant impediments to a correct Education), cause Children to have an incorrect perspective on the nature and character of religion, and to be imbued with many distorted opinions about the true Worship of the Deity. There are, however, two things in particular that have great power in promoting a preposterous Education and in confirming the neglect of religion. *The first is*; that most Parents have either no care or very little care for the *cultivation of reason*; *The second*; that they do not instill in Children early enough that, just as it is required for spending one's whole life happily, so it is especially required for performing duties to the Deity, that men must early on subdue appetites that are hostile to our tranquility and crooked affections, and submit them to the will of the Deity. As for the *first* point, no one who can make a correct judgment of things would deny that it contributes greatly to performing the business of this life rightly, and to offering true worship to God, if Parents bring all care and diligence to ensure that Children early and rightly cultivate *reason*—than which nothing more excellent has been given to mortals in this life. If this is neglected, they move as if in darkness through their whole life, they handle matters of the greatest importance poorly, and they go where others go, not where they ought to go. But above all, the neglect of the cultivation of reason harms Religion, which Parents ought to be most solicitous to instill into tender minds. The more the mind is persuaded of the truth, excellence, and utility of the Christian religion, the more fit it is to offer right worship to God. But how, pray, will the mind of a child be persuaded of this truth, unless it is shown that the *use of reason* was given to us for this chief end: that we might know and worship God; that we might apply ourselves to virtue and promote our own happiness and that of others? By what means will Parents obtain this end, unless they clearly show them that religion is consistent with the principles of reason; that piety is most closely joined with our true happiness; and that true piety consists in a right sense of the Deity, His worship, and a perpetual desire to please Him, etc. But so that these things might have their force in minds...
