# MEDITATION V.

...their [faculties] are to be exercised, they must be taught above all things that nothing should be done rashly—as in the whole of life, so most especially in the matter of Religion. They must learn that worship is not pleasing to God if the mind of the worshiper is absent; that it is not a matter of indifference what we think of God or by what method we worship Him, and so forth. But when most parents neglect to instill these things, it is no wonder that children later either fall into superstition, or rashly subscribe to almost everything handed down by others, or never think of Religion with any magnificence. This parental neglect is surely to blame for the fact that most people, without any examination, rest throughout their entire lives in those opinions which they had swallowed, as it were, with their mother's milk. 

And if only there were no parents—themselves once seduced by unsound teachers—who would instill in their children early enough that *it is to be believed, not examined* <note>original: "credendum, non examinandum"</note>, and thus prepare for them a path toward either foolish credulity or the vice of unbelief! But alas, there are those who think that while reason should indeed be used in other affairs, it is extremely dangerous to call it into counsel when dealing with Religion. They claim that reason is like a double-edged sword, which you cannot touch without injury; hence they babble much about "corrupted reason" <note>original: "corrupta ratione"</note> and what evils have been brought into Churches, Schools, and Republics through it. Thus, it cannot happen otherwise than that they embrace with blind assent whatever is handed down by parents and later by teachers, without examination, and can scarcely ever be drawn toward a serious examination of the things to be believed. The celebrated *Crousaz* <note>Jean-Pierre de Crousaz (1663–1750) was a Swiss philosopher and theologian who advocated for the role of logic and reason in education.</note> brilliantly and pointedly criticized this vice of parents and teachers in his excellent treatise on the *Education of Children*. 

Furthermore, just as parents make their children unhappy when they neglect those things which necessarily pertain to the cultivation of reason, and are the cause of them not thinking rightly and piously about Religion; so too they shamefully fail in their duty when they do not, as much as they are able, accustom their children early on to subject the wicked affections and cravings of the heart to the command of reason and Revelation. No one is ignorant of the fact that, to spend life well and happily, it is necessary for the mind to be pulled away little by little from the love of earthly things, and for the more violent affections—harmful alike to the mind and body—to be tamed. True worship of God does not consist primarily in this: that we rightly understand certain dogmas and precepts of Religion; but rather that we obey the will of the most holy Divinity, that we are daily conformed more and more to the divine image, that we resist the wicked affections of the mind, and that we bend our corrupted nature by the help of divine grace. He who neglects this, though he may have the widest knowledge of divine things, does so in vain, because he is destitute of that without...

---

# ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

...which true Religion and piety cannot exist. But since, alas, many parents everywhere are unmindful of this duty and contribute nothing or very little to restraining the impulses of wicked desires—the signs and traces of which they detect early enough in their children—and since they do not early and frequently repeat that we are, through our whole life, entirely devoted to God, and that we ought to meditate on this one thing and act with every contention of our strength so that, aided by the help of divine grace, we may compose our actions according to the will of the best Divinity; it cannot happen otherwise than that, with the passage of time, the mind—captured and constricted by wicked pursuits—breaks out into innumerable evils. 

For from this it usually happens that children bear adverse fortune with a most unfair mind and often foster sinister opinions regarding the divine administration of human affairs. Hence they measure all things by utility, even those pertaining to Religion; and according as a precept of Religion either agrees or conflicts with the desires of the mind, they think it should either be observed or neglected. It is all the same to them what they believe, provided that Religion does not cast a bridle upon those affections and desires of the mind which they value highly and for which they burn with great longing. To this evil must be attributed the fact that they later often firmly believe that the things said about the innocence of the life of the godly and true Christianity in general are to be counted among "sweet dreams," similar to those which *Plato* once feigned concerning the inhabitants of the world he represented in his mind. 

Alas, parents have often learned through experience that what is said here is true. Holy Scripture exhibits a sad example of this matter in *1 Samuel chapter 2*, regarding the *sons of Eli* the Priest <note>Hophni and Phinehas, who ignored their father's rebukes and acted wickedly in the Tabernacle.</note>. See also chapter 30 of *Sirach* <note>Also known as Ecclesiasticus, a book of the Apocrypha/Deuterocanon containing practical ethical advice.</note>, in which are contained excellent precepts about restraining the wicked character of children early on. Add to what has been said the fact that many parents neglect to continually implore divine grace and to intercede with God for the salvation and true happiness of their children, which is placed chiefly in the pursuit of virtue! Since they themselves are entirely captured by the love of earthly things, they desire above all else that their children abound in all those things which can serve to spend this life with joy; yet at the same time, alas, completely unmindful of that golden precept of the Apostle *James* which stands in *chapter 1, verse 17*, teaching that *every good gift and every perfect boon is from above, coming down from the Father of lights*, they place all their care and solicitude only in looking for the means by which they may make their children partakers of those goods—which, however, they can never rightly enjoy without the love of piety and true wisdom.

to the early ruin of the souls of children; so no one would deny that it often happens through faulty instruction that these same children are imbued with sinister opinions regarding divine matters, which as they grow older sometimes exert such force upon their minds that they fall into the abyss of either Unbelief or Impiety. It must therefore be shown in a few words how, little by little, minds can be corrupted by faulty instruction. All sensible people agree that it matters greatly from whom children hear their first precepts—as in all disciplines, so especially in Religion. Hence every most prudent person has always taken the greatest care that children be handed over for instruction to those who know the true value of Literature and excel in the integrity of their character. The most learned <note>original: πολυμαθεστατος (*polymathéstatos*), meaning "very learned" or "well-read"</note> *Plutarch* strongly commends this duty to parents in his *On the Education of Children*. *Quintilian, in his Institutes of Oratory, Book 1, Chapter 2, says that the primary concern for the prudent should be to choose the most upright teachers.* It is evident throughout the published letters of that most literate and prudent man, *Pliny the Younger*, that he looked out for the children of his friends by seeking learned and well-mannered teachers with no small care; see among others Letter 3, Book 4, to *Cornelia Hispulla*, in which he closes the letter with these words: *Therefore, with the gods favoring you, hand him over to a teacher from whom he may learn character first, and soon eloquence, which is poorly learned without character.* If, therefore, the skill of the teacher contributes so much to learning humane letters and philosophical disciplines, all who have a more accurate knowledge of Religion will easily conclude that it matters greatly in what way the elements of the most holy discipline are handed down and fixed in the minds of youth. Truly, those are to be called happy who happened upon teachers skilled in divine matters, who handed down and proved the dogmas and precepts of the Christian Religion no less solidly than clearly; happier still are those who, besides the ability to rightly transmit the articles of Religion, obtained masters who can say along with Paul speaking to his Timothy: *But you have followed my doctrine, manner of life, purpose, faith, longsuffering, charity, patience, persecutions, afflictions, etc.* <note>original: συ δε παρηκολουθηκας...; the OCR garbles the Greek of 2 Timothy 3:10–11</note> (*) Come, let us see in what way, by faulty or pre-

posterous instruction, children are often corrupted early in matters pertaining to Religion. And **I.** indeed, many teachers often sin in this, that they are more concerned that students commit many chapters of religion to memory and can recite them successfully, than that they truly understand and grasp those things which are proposed. There are many who think they have performed their duty excellently, and that all sorts of distinguished things can be expected from their students hereafter, if their minds are early equipped with a promiscuous knowledge of many things—in which, however, they are vehemently mistaken. For although they are to be praised in that they want their students early imbued with knowledge of divine matters, they nevertheless act preposterously in that they take more account of the number of things committed to memory than of accurate knowledge. For it often happens this way: not only do they learn and hear matters regarding Religion with a certain weariness, because they were forced without small trouble and labor to build up greater tasks, but they also rest in those things they have learned, though not understood, as if they were for the most part most certain. Nothing, however, is more harmful to youth than if they have learned to repeat in the "manner of parrots" <term>manner of parrots: rote repetition of words without understanding their meaning</term> those things which were indeed committed to memory, but by no means rightly understood. For on one hand, it is impossible for them to rightly know the value and importance of Religion and be captured by love for it; on the other hand, they are very easily defeated by others who instill things contrary to what was committed to memory, or at least they begin to doubt vehemently the truth of those things which were handed down. It follows that as they grow older, they contract a certain habit of admitting anything without discrimination; from which it is easy to guess that if they come across books in which the first foundations of Religion are made suspect or attacked, they will either yield to the arguments of adversaries or at least vehemently doubt the truth of those things which they learned as youths (but did not understand). **II.** Often the formers of youth, having made no selection of the articles of faith, propose weighty and difficult...

# MEDITATION V.
## ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

...they deliver things difficult to grasp as well as easier things indiscriminately, and they do not dwell long enough on those matters which ought to be placed at the beginning; nor do they instill them in such a way that the youth cannot help but understand them properly. No one will deny that not only in teaching any discipline, but especially in explaining and proving the rudiments of Religion, one must take into account the intelligence, capacity, and age [of the student], as well as the nature of the subjects themselves that are to be instilled. It is established, moreover, that in the matter of Religion, some things must be placed as a foundation, while others are to be built upon it; some are of greater importance, others of less; some are absolutely necessary to know, while others are not. 

If the teacher makes no distinction in these matters; if he indiscriminately mixes arduous things with less necessary ones; if he begins with things more difficult to grasp, [the students] will not be able throughout their whole life to distinguish the trivial from the momentous—which greatly hinders a more accurate knowledge of Religion and often draws countless evils in its wake. The same happens if those things which ought to be placed as a foundation are not frequently repeated and fixed in their minds so that they have a clear knowledge of them. Tender youth indeed easily drinks in the precepts of wisdom and fixes them in memory; but since it is fluid at this age and very easily distracted by various things, they must be frequently recalled to memory. 

Finally, it is well known that those things which are explained clearly are understood far more easily and remain fixed in the mind than those which are delivered obscurely and perplexely. But here too, many formers of youth very often sin. Many wish to teach others who yet themselves do not know how to distinguish the arduous and grave from the less momentous. How many are there who themselves acquiesce in an obscure knowledge of divine things and merely repeat the sounds of their own Masters! How many are there who, having set aside a clear explanation of things, command their disciples to commit everything indiscriminately to memory! How many are there who pour into the hearts of youth everything whatever that they once admitted themselves without their own examination! Truly, what <term>James the Apostle</term> <note>original: Jacobus Apostolus</note> instilled in the Christians of his time in his epistle, chapter 3, verse 1, saying: *Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers* <gloss>original: Μη πολλοι διδασκαλοι γινεσθε αδελφοι</gloss> ought to be sung as a warning to many of those who apply their minds to instituting youth, especially in our age, in which many are eager to perform this duty. We ourselves, who publicly deliver, prove, and defend the most holy dogmas of Religion to studious youth, know by experience that some wish to explain the precepts of Religion to others who yet have not themselves duly weighed the same through an established examination, let alone being able to duly and solidly convince others of their truth. 

III. Many of those teaching either do not at all, or only strictly and while doing something else, deliver the first and fundamental heads of Natural Religion <note>Natural Religion refers to truths about God and morality that can be discovered through human reason and observation of the world, such as the existence of a Creator, rather than through divine revelation (Scripture) alone.</note>

<column-break/>

heads to tender youth, but they proceed immediately at the threshold of instruction to instill various articles of revealed Religion; yet all who have accurately looked into the nature of Religion and know what is necessarily required to demonstrate the truth of the Christian Religion know that this cannot be done quite successfully without knowledge of the principal heads of Natural Religion. 

Lest I seem to be the only one to feel this way, I will bring forward the judgments of at least two most excellent theologians of the Reformed Church who agree with me from a great abundance. The first is <term>Jenkin Thomas</term> <note>original: Jenkin Thomasius. An English author known for his "History of Atheism" (1713).</note>, an Englishman, who wrote a brief History of Atheism and dedicated it to the most magnificent leaders of the Republic of Zurich <note>original: Tigurinæ</note>, and whose booklet on the ecclesiastical government of the first three centuries of the Christian Church was adorned with worthy praise by the late <gloss>the late / of blessed memory (original: ὁ μακαρίτης)</gloss> and distinguished man, <term>Johann Jakob Hottinger</term> <note>original: J. Jac. Hottingerus (1652–1735), a Swiss theologian and church historian.</note>. He, on page 8, inquiring into the causes of Atheism, pronounces in the following manner:

> *Add to this (he says) the extreme negligence of parents and teachers, by which the chief article of Religion is neglected in cultivation and in being instilled in youth, so that you may find everywhere men grave in age, supremely knowledgeable of the articles regarding the Mysteries of the Christian faith, and wonderfully skilled in every civil and religious duty, yet if you should ask them to deign to propose some arguments by which the existence of God or the immortality of the soul is proved (the same could be said of the remaining heads of Natural Theology), they would be utterly stunned, as if suddenly struck and shaken by a lightning bolt, so that they have nothing (unless perhaps curses) to put forward in return. Whence, I ask, comes such great stupidity and ignorance, if not from the fact that we wish to be considered no common Christians, while meanwhile the duties of a human being are hidden from us. The Aristotelians indeed favored this stupidity, asserting that those who deny principles must be disputed with not with words but with whips. Far better do those eminent men of our time deserve of the Christian cause, who have industriously applied no useless labor to cultivating Natural Theology; no effort could be more effective than this for stopping the course of Atheism.*

Would that all who undertake catechetical instructions for the use of Christian youth would seriously consider this with themselves; for if they did this, they would not hasten with such a light touch, or as is usually done, with the foundations of Natural Religion untouched, to other more difficult questions. 

The second is the most learned <term>Pierre Roques</term> <note>original: P. Roques (1685–1748), a French Protestant pastor in Basel.</note>, a most worthy Pastor of the French Church which is gathered for Christ at Basel <note>original: Basileæ</note>, who in his excellent treatise on the excellence of the Evangelical Ministry, chapter 8, among the chief causes which hinder the works of the Evangelical Ministry from leading more people to the study of virtue and piety, also reports this: namely, that many Christians in their youth [neglect] the fundamental heads of Natural Religion...

# MEDITATION V.
## ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

...they have not properly perceived the principles of Natural and Revealed Religion. Hear the very words of a most excellent man: 
> <note>original: "Comment precautionner la jeuneſſe..." This quote is originally in French.</note> *How can we protect youth against the corruption of the age, against Deism and Libertinism <note>Libertinism here refers to a lack of moral or intellectual restraint, often associated with a rejection of religious authority.</note>, if not by giving them early on an exact knowledge of the truths of Religion and the proofs upon which they are supported? It is not surprising that young people, whose passions are lively, allow themselves to be seduced by the intemperate and by the "freethinker" <note>original: "l'esprit fort"—literally "the strong spirit," a term used for those who claimed to rely only on reason rather than faith.</note> when they have no solid knowledge of Religion. They find nothing within themselves that can counterbalance the force of seduction. But if we had made them understand and feel the truth, the importance, and the holiness of the maxims of the Christian Religion, they would find in this enlightened faith a shield impenetrable to the sharpest arrows of the worldly and the profane.*

Because of this, men eminent in piety and learning have wished that certain systems of <term>Natural Theology</term> <note>The study of God based on reason and the observation of nature, rather than on sacred texts.</note> might be written, tailored to the method of a <term>catechism</term> <note>A summary of religious doctrine often used for teaching through questions and answers.</note> and adapted to the capacity of youth; (*) for they clearly perceived that in this way, not only could the true principles upon which <term>Revelation</term> <note>Knowledge of God given directly through scripture or divine communication.</note> must be built be provided, but the minds of the young could also be best fortified early enough against the vice of unbelief and formed toward piety. However, many of those who shape our youth either have little knowledge of these chapters of study, or they do not know the method by which those principles should be solidly explained and proved according to the capacity of the young; or finally, even if they are not ignorant of the facts, they think these things should be instilled lightly, as if doing something else. In this way, however, it is impossible for these matters—which are most worthy of being known—to take firm root in the minds of the youth. I confess that it is an art to adapt these topics to the understanding of tender youth, to explain them clearly, to illustrate them with examples, and to confirm them with few but solid reasons. But he who does not know how to provide this performs the duty of a Teacher recklessly. Where these things are delivered skillfully and instilled early and frequently into tender minds, it cannot happen otherwise than that they will hereafter think magnificently of God and divine things, and they will become better suited to admit, rightly understand, and worthily value Revelation.

(*) The Reverend *Bartholomæus* collected the pious wishes of certain learned Protestant theologians regarding this subject in his *Continued Useful Remarks on Various Matters of Theology, Church, and Literary History*, see pages 73, 144, and 867. # ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

...value it. But so that it may be clear how much the neglect of this matter hinders the progress of true Religion and piety, we appeal to the principal chapters of Natural Religion themselves. These can (we are speaking here only of the theoretical aspects) be conveniently reduced to five chapters. The *first* treats the existence of God; the *second*, the divine attributes; the *third*, Providence; the *fourth*, natural laws; and finally, the *fifth*, the immortality of the soul. That all Religion is built upon a certain and infallible persuasion of the existence of a Deity is too well known for us to need to prove it. But if the truth of the existence of a Deity—who is plainly distinct from all created things—is not proved clearly and solidly by one or two arguments; if youth are not rightly persuaded of this truth, or if they have only a confused notion of some "first being," who could believe that they will always think and speak of Him as magnificently as they ought throughout their whole lives? What kind of worship will they give this Deity if they have only a shadowy knowledge of the divine attributes? There are three virtues of God in particular—namely His wisdom, goodness, and omnipotence—whose nature, character, and excellence the teacher of youth ought to rightly explain and commend. These shine forth most clearly from an attentive contemplation of the universe, its order, and its purposes. That these virtues reside in God can be, so to speak, felt with one's very hands. But if the excellence and truth of those virtues are not fixed very deeply in the minds of the youth, their knowledge and admiration of God’s virtues will be very weak, and their worship of such a great Deity will be very lukewarm. They will look up at the sky, they will contemplate trees and crops, they will enjoy the light of the sun, they will taste their food daily, and enjoy other benefits on this earth; but they will rarely and hardly ever seriously think thereafter that these great goods can only arise from a most good, most wise, and most powerful Deity. The same will happen if the mind is not properly persuaded regarding <term>Providence</term> <note>The protective care and guidance of God over the world and its inhabitants.</note> as it administers, cares for, and distributes everything for the use of the human race. For, in order that men may frequently celebrate the praises of the Deity, pour out most ardent prayers to God, seek His help in narrow circumstances, and bear unfortunate fates with an even mind, it is necessary that they believe that God not only created this universe (and man especially) for the wisest ends, but that He also takes care of all things at every moment. I know indeed that the doctrine of God's Providence is exposed to various doubts, and that "knots" occur here that are not easily untied even by the learned; but those things which occur regarding this argument that are more difficult to grasp should be pushed back to another time. Nor should the things necessary to be known about this matter be neglected for that reason, but rather they should be more [carefully instilled] into tender...

# MEDITATION V.

...[these principles] must be instilled in their minds and fortified against one or two objections that can easily creep into the soul. It is necessary for young people to have some knowledge of <term>Natural Laws</term> <note>The moral principles believed to be inherent in human nature and discoverable by reason, independent of specific religious revelation.</note>. Above all, that general precept, **"What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to another,"** <note>The "Golden Rule," cited here in its negative Latin form: *tibi fieri non vis alteri ne feceris*.</note> must be fixed most deeply in the minds of the youth. For if they are not fully imbued with these principles, they will gradually learn to measure everything by its utility; they will refer everything to themselves and will come to believe that we are bound to fulfill our mutual duties out of necessity rather than by divine laws—to say nothing for now of the other evils that usually arise from ignorance of this point. These things must be instilled all the more because, alas, we see every day—even among those who boast of being followers of the most holy discipline—the common duties of humanity being trampled underfoot. Finally, unless young people are properly taught and persuaded that religion is not confined within the boundaries of this life, but that the most certain, excellent, and everlasting rewards are set before the worshippers of God after this life, everything said about divine worship and laws will have little power over their minds. From this it follows that they must be taught early enough what the mind is, what its excellence and dignity are, for what purpose we were created, how religion is a serious but also a joyful thing, and how kind the Deity is toward the pious. They must learn how all other things are to be held as worthless <note>original: *flocci habenda*—literally "to be held as a tuft of wool," an idiom for something of no value.</note> compared to the pursuit of piety and virtue, and so on. From these few points, it is manifest not only that no one can be persuaded of the truth and divine origin of <term>Revelation</term> <note>Truths communicated by God to humanity, such as those found in the Bible.</note> without a knowledge of these articles, but also that it is impossible for religion to take deep root in the soul and lead men to offer a rational worship to God unless they are clearly convinced and persuaded of these principles. (*)

IV. Just as many who apply their minds to instructing youth either teach the main points of Natural Religion lazily <note>original: *oscitanter*—literally "with a yawn."</note> and pass over them lightly, or do not prove them with arguments suited to the capacity of the student's intellect and age; so likewise, they either do not know how to properly prove the truth of the Christian Religion, or if they are not poorly versed in this subject, they do not dwell upon it long enough or sufficiently. Yet without this foundation, all other things cannot stand firmly. Because of this, it cannot happen otherwise than that young people rest in an obscure knowledge of Religion. No one who has ever seriously weighed Religion will deny that a solid and true persuasion of certain articles of the Christian Religion is impossible unless the mind is properly persuaded of the truth and divine origin of the Christian Religion. Notwithstanding this, many shamefully neglect this most difficult matter. Some of those teaching are not themselves properly persuaded of this most grave point. Others treat this argument lazily enough; again, others approach the task not unskillfully, but move too quickly to instilling specific articles of faith. Finally, many—before they have proven with historical arguments suited to the grasp of their listeners that the first followers of the Christian Religion both *could* and *wished to* <note>original: *potuisse & voluisse*—meaning the witnesses were both competent to know the truth and morally honest enough to tell it.</note> speak the truth—appeal to certain passages of Scripture, and thus reason quite backwardly. 

From this, unless a better light shines upon their minds hereafter, they may rest for their whole lives in a confused knowledge of this most grave subject. If they happen upon a book or men who attack the truth of the Christian Religion with even lightweight arguments, they begin to doubt what was taught to them in the past; indeed, sometimes when the worst judges—namely, depraved affections of the soul—are added to the mix, they fall into the vice of Unbelief itself. And I consider this to be the chief cause of the daily increasing Unbelief and Impiety. Unless this is countered more correctly than is commonly done; unless this argument is taught to youth with the greatest diligence, zeal, and effort, repeated and so fixed in the mind that the mind can be persuaded of it, it is impossible to conceive how true piety can take root in the souls of the young, and how barriers can be placed against both credulity and Unbelief. And from where, I ask...

# MEDITATION V.

...is it the case that so many sacred sermons, which are held everywhere, nevertheless exert such a small power over the minds of men? I know that several causes are given, which I will not bring forward here. Among the most prominent, however, I count this: that very few of the listeners were properly imbued with those capital truths <note>Fundamental or essential principles of faith and reason.</note> in their youth. **V.** But many of those who teach not only deliver the main chapters of <term>Natural and Revealed Religion</term> <note>Natural religion refers to truths known through reason; Revealed religion refers to truths known through scripture.</note> to the youth with enough negligence or lack of accuracy, but they also explain the precepts of Ethics in a meager way, or do not sufficiently prove them with the dignity the matter deserves, nor do they show the origins and use of our duties. 

Certain teachers, either shamefully captured by perverse opinions or led by ignorance, think that great care need not be taken with moral precepts. They believe it is enough if young people hold firmly to certain articles of Religion and subscribe without hesitation to all of them—the weightiest and the less necessary to know alike. Thus, however, it cannot happen otherwise than that they attain only a shadowy knowledge of true piety. In this way, they do not know for what purpose the most holy Religion was given to mortals; thus they sometimes persuade themselves that true Religion can be separated from piety, and they imagine that the true worship of the Divine is fulfilled by a knowledge of certain articles of Religion. 

Moreover, imbued with these perverse opinions, they will not only lack a great zeal for piety, but they will also be unable to feel correctly about the Christian Religion, which is the knowledge of truth according to piety. Some of those teaching do indeed hand down the precepts of Ethics to the youth, but they neglect to bring forward the *reasons*—which in the schools we call *motives* or *incentives* for acting—by which alone the minds of men are usually moved to perform the duties of piety. Indeed, no one can easily conceive by what logic men might be led to duties of every kind, unless the reasons why they are bound to perform them are constantly placed before their eyes. For from the reasons brought forward, not only does the obligation itself become clear, but also the necessity and utility of Religion and its individual articles. And this must be held all the more in the instruction of youth, because young people are prone to perform only those things which they either think or truly judge to be connected with utility. 

Furthermore, some formers of youth err in this: that while they do not neglect to hand down the precepts of Ethics, they stop at more general precepts. They do not show, by one or another specific example or case, how widely the duties of a Christian man extend, how strictly they must be observed, how easily men deceive themselves regarding this or that duty, and how nothing should ever be performed or omitted while the conscience is reluctant, and so on. Hence, it is no...

# ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

...wonder that everywhere, not only the youth and the common crowd, but even men cultured and learned in various disciplines—and I add, even often the <term>Ministers of the Word of God</term> <note>original Latin: "V. D. Ministros," short for "Verbi Divini Ministros."</note>—possess a very small and obscure knowledge of the doctrine of morals. Whence it is likewise no wonder that many daily trample the most holy duties underfoot, regarding grave sins as mere errors which human nature poorly avoids; indeed, they even everywhere neglect those precepts which are enjoined upon us by the laws of humanity and the strict precepts of Natural Law. 

Take, for example, the single subject of *Restitution* <note>The moral obligation to return stolen goods or repair damages caused to others.</note>. Examine anyone from the middle of the crowd about the individual parts of this duty, and it will be clear how thin and very lacking their knowledge of this argument is. Others, when they are about to commend the study of virtue and piety, describe the exercise of true piety as if it were a most troublesome thing, joined with innumerable pains—a gloomy thing which cannot be carried out without a love of solitude, a flight from even the lawful pleasures which the Most Kind Deity nevertheless granted to mortals, and a certain perpetual sadness. By this very act, they harden the minds of the youth against Religion—since the young flee everything that usually excites pain and trouble—rather than leading them to love and cherish it. Or if they gain anything, they make men who are gloomy and superstitious, not truly pious. 

It is true indeed that for adults, or those who have contracted a habit of vice and are not yet reborn, and who defer the work of conversion from day to day, it must be shown how poorly they provide for themselves in this way: how much strength vices will acquire in the course of time, how difficult they make the work for themselves by the procrastination of conversion, and that true <term>repentance</term> <note>original Greek: "μετανοια" (metanoia), meaning a transformative change of heart and mind.</note> is not performed without a most profound sense of sin, pain, and a great struggle. But our talk here is of the instruction of children, who have not yet contracted habits in these or those vices, and who are placed as if on the border between virtue and impiety. 

To these, I say, Religion must be proposed as a thing not only worthy of attention, but also greatly lovable and desirable. To these it must be shown that virtue is a thing so noble and excellent that no one who is wise could or should fail to desire it. To these it must be frequently instilled that the chief happiness of man is situated in a good conscience; that it is prepared by virtue; that if they are equipped with this, true tranquility will not be lacking in every case and state of life. Those who devote themselves early to the study of true piety always have the most just reasons for rejoicing; only vices and the ignorance of the most holy things make men wretched, etc. etc. However, when the contrary to these things is sometimes instilled, and religion is depicted as a very burdensome and gloomy thing, it is no wonder that often, at an early age...

# MEDITATION V.

### That the minds of the young are drawn away from the love of virtue.

Nor do I doubt that this has also contributed much: the fact that they are often driven to perform the duties of external worship early enough by threats and beatings alike, while nevertheless, it has not yet been sufficiently shown to them what the end and goal of such worship is. Others fall plainly into the opposite vice, namely, when they hand down precepts for living rightly that are too vague and principles that are too loose—that is, such as are able to produce a "good citizen" (if indeed they can even manage that) rather than a true Christian and a follower of the most holy precepts. Even the Heathens <note>Non-Christian philosophers of antiquity, such as the Stoics.</note> recognized that far more must be provided by a man who is wise and a lover of virtue than what is prescribed by civil laws.

<margin>Book II of *On Anger*, chapter XXVII.</margin>

*How narrow a thing is innocence,* says Seneca, *to be "good" only according to the law? How much wider is the Rule of duties than the rule of legal right? How many things do piety, humanity, justice, and faith require, all of which are outside the public records?* <note>original: "Quam angusta... innocentia est ad legem bonum esse? quanto latius patet officiorum quam juris Regula? quam multa pietas, humanitas, justitia, fides exigunt, quæ omnia extra publicas tabulas sunt?"</note> No one, indeed, denies that virtue contributes much to promoting the welfare of society as a whole and of individuals, and that it makes for good Rulers, citizens, fathers of families, and so on. But at the same time, care must be taken lest the young think that true piety is placed solely in these things. If it happens otherwise, there is no way that the precepts of Christian discipline can be sincerely observed. Or from where, I ask, does it come that so many men—not lacking in talent and seeing quite sharply in other matters—firmly persuade themselves that they are "fine Christians" when they discharge the duties that must be performed by a citizen, which can easily be kept without an internal change of mind? They attend public worship, yet they have a very meager knowledge of the precepts of Christian Ethics, or they have been imbued only with the general headings of the duties of a Christian man.

Nor are there lacking, at times, certain mad instructors of Youth, who often commend even vices under the appearance of virtue. Such are those who, occupied only with <term>catechetical instructions</term> <note>Formal, question-and-answer religious teaching.</note>, wish to instill a hatred against any dissenters in boys who are ignorant of all controversies. They think they have performed their duty excellently if they perceive that the boys think it is lawful to hate men who differ from their own opinions, and that they will one day turn out to be the best evaluators and defenders of Religion. Yet nothing is further from the truth and the right than this. For in this way, they not only judge perversely when they eventually come to examine the opinions that others hold about Religion—being deluded by false opinions and a blinded mind—but they also acquire a habit of "exchanging the saw of disputations" <note>A Latin idiom for endless, back-and-forth arguing.</note> with anyone about anything, and of

---

<page-num>215</page-num>
<header>ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.</header>

insulting others, magnifying the smallest errors, and often trampling underfoot the most holy duties of love for one's neighbor because of a slight disagreement. Nothing can be more harmful to public tranquility than this. Lest anyone think that I alone feel this way, I will cite below the testimonies of most excellent and learned men. (*) 

Again, others—with good intentions, I suppose—prevent the precepts of Christian Ethics from exerting their power upon the minds of men early on. These are they who exhibit an image of virtue in general, or Christian virtue in particular, that is so beautiful, so accurate, and so perfect in every detail that not even a shadow of any defect is present in it. They do not consider that this is merely an abstract idea of virtue, and that it is necessary to teach at the same time that even the best men, and those most loving of virtue, who keep the image of true virtue constantly before their eyes, are nevertheless subject to various infirmities in this world. Against these, one must fight with the strength given by God through all of life—indeed, even to the last breath of life. Unless the instructors of Youth emphasize these things, so far from the image of such perfect virtue leading them to live rightly, it will instead call their minds away from the love of it as they grow older. For they discover, wherever they cast their eyes, and...

> (*) The Most Reverend Archbishop of Canterbury, **Tillotson**, in Sermon S. Vol. VI page 305, speaks thus of this depraved custom: *“Children who are raised with strong prejudices for or against certain practices or opinions usually become, with age, people of a narrow genius, peevish, ill-humored, uncharitable, and often great Bigots, Zealots either of superstition or of a party, according as the principles that have been inspired in them carry them to one or the other. It rarely happens that they strip themselves enough of their prejudices to become wise, peaceful Christians, attached to what is solid.”* <note>original: "Les Enfans qui sont elevés dans des forts préjugés... attachés au solide."</note> In a word, if one takes good care, one will find that when Children have been raised in such an injudicious manner, there is as much difference between their piety and that of a moderate Christian of good sense, as there is in the commerce of the world between the manners of people who have had ignorant and headstrong Masters, and those of persons who have had a fine education. 

> The most learned **Lauffer**, who is now among the Saints <note>original: "ὁ νῦν ἐν Ἁγίοις" — a Greek formula indicating the person is deceased.</note> and was formerly an illustrious Professor of the Gymnasium of Bern, speaks thus of this argument in his dissertation on the *Right Education of Children*: "Let those to whom the care of boys is entrusted take especial care that they do not imbue their minds with the principles of persecution in the business of Religion. For these principles directly rise up against reason and Religion itself—which, initiated by the absolutely perfect example of the patience of the Savior and then corroborated by the death of the Apostles and so many Martyrs, breathes nothing but gentleness, humanity, and patience—and they produce disastrous effects. For since, for example, this false principle was persuaded to the <term>Papists</term> <note>A term used by Protestants to refer to Roman Catholics.</note> to the shame of the Christian name—that all who dissent from them can be rightly forced by power, sword, and flames to feel the same as they do—the peace and tranquility of human society has been disturbed; faith and what men hold most holy have been violated; any inhuman and detestable crimes, slaughters, robberies, and parricides have been perpetrated with impunity under the plausible pretext of religion; and charity, humanity, and gentleness, along with the rest of the virtues, have been ordered to go into exile from the Christian world." 

> Compare the celebrated **Crousaz**, *New Maxims on the Education of Children*, Chapter II, to pass over others in silence.

# MEDITATION V.

...and with those with whom they finally associate, [they find] some flaws even in upright men and those who are, by the judgment of all, lovers of virtue. From this, they conclude that a beautiful image of virtue was once indeed presented to them, but that it exists only in the brains of the Learned and has no place elsewhere; nor, therefore, is it necessary to apply themselves to virtue and piety with such great striving of strength. In a word: they will think that the dictates of their teachers are similar to those which the Stoics <note>A school of ancient Greek philosophy that held the "Sage" or perfectly wise person as an ideal of unattainable moral perfection.</note> once fashioned about their "wise man," than which nothing more hinders the pursuit of true piety. Nor should those be acquitted who, in order to demonstrate the power of human corruption and the weight of our misery, and having made no distinction at all, ascribe most human actions—even those contaminated by no stain of vice if you look at the outward appearance—to depraved causes and motives of the soul. In this, the ingenious *Frenchman* <note>Jacques Esprit (1611–1677), a French writer and moralist.</note> seems to have sinned in the book he wrote titled: *On the Falsity of Human Virtues*. This displeased the Illustrious Leibniz, who in his *Essays on Theodicy, page 79,* judges it thus:

> I approve even less of books such as that of Abbé Esprit, *On the Falsity of Human Virtues*, of which an abridgment has recently been given to us: such a book serves to turn everything to the bad side, and to make men such as it represents them. <note>original French: "J'approuve encore moins les Livres tels, que celui de l'Abbé Esprit de la fausseté des vertus humaines... un tel livre servant à tourner tout du mauvais coté, & à rendre les hommes tels, qu'il les représente."</note>

Finally, to pass over many other things in silence, Teachers also often sin in this: that when they are about to explain the dogmas and precepts of the Christian Religion to youth, they often use obscure, mystical, and too metaphorical words. I could easily believe that this is not done with a bad intention; I am persuaded that men of this sort have contracted a habit of using no other style from their frequent reading of ascetic books. Although I also believe there are some among them who think that no small part of piety is placed in a certain choice of words, which those whom they think excel others in piety are accustomed to use. But sensible men should have reflected that a teacher cannot use words that are clear enough; and that it is not voices, phrases, and I know not what noise of words, but arguments and the sense hiding beneath the speech that alone have power over minds. They should reflect that the young, being hindered by a certain natural sluggishness, are not usually so concerned about the meanings of words, but easily acquiesce to the words heard from a Teacher; and that a Speech filled with flowery phrases of this sort might indeed cast the mind for a time into admiration and a kind of stupor, but it cannot, unless it is rightly understood, impel one to think or act in one way or another. Who, indeed, will rightly demand of a youth that he convert a figurative Speech into a simple one, if he has either no knowledge or a plainly weak one of the things themselves which lie hidden under the figures? I know indeed that the shapers of such Youth—
<meta>catchword: —shape</meta>

***

<page-num>217</page-num>

—shapers [of youth] say that in Holy Scripture many such metaphorical expressions are found where the internal state of the mind is discussed, which no one denies. But it is the duty of the teacher to accommodate words and phrases to the capacity of the young, and first to strive with all his might that the young have a distinct knowledge of moral precepts; only after this is done will it be permitted, as they grow in age, to show which words the sacred writers of the Old and New Testament were accustomed to use to describe this or that state of the mind.

IX. But before I proceed to other things, I see that I must address certain objections which are usually brought forward by some against what I have said regarding the necessity of instilling the dogmas of <term>Natural Theology</term> <note>The study of God based on reason and the observation of nature, rather than on divine revelation.</note>, the truth of Religion, and Christian Ethics. For there are those who say: **I.** That it cannot happen, or at least only with difficulty, that the young understand the arguments by which the heads of Natural Theology and the truth of the Christian Religion are proved. **II.** That we live among Christians, and therefore it is not so necessary that the truths of Natural and Revealed Religion, about which either no one or very few doubt, be instilled into youth with such great zeal. **III.** That experience testifies that many, only after reading those things which were said about the certainty of those first truths and the general objections against them, began to doubt them. **IV.** Finally, that it is not so necessary for the precepts of Christian ethics to be instilled into youth, since the duties of piety can easily be gathered from the individual articles of the Christian Religion. We will respond briefly to each of these: And **(1)** indeed we note that when we contend that the first heads of Natural and Revealed Religion must be instilled early and properly in youth, we by no means demand that subtle Metaphysical arguments be employed to prove these heads, or that objections be brought forward which can only be solved by the Learned. It would be plainly tasteless if anyone wished to enter this path, since such a method of instruction is not at all tempered to the capacity of youth. But we want this one thing: namely, that the teacher propose these dogmas as clearly as the nature of the thing and the capacity of the youth allow, prove them with one or two arguments that are solid and easy to grasp, and solve one or two objections which could easily disturb the mind of the learner. What we advise here regarding the method of proving the heads of Natural Theology, we also want to be understood regarding the manner of demonstrating the truth of the Christian Religion. But those who object to such things to us seem to go further, and to think that it is not so necessary that the principles of Natural Theology be instilled into youth, since they themselves either touch those arguments only with a finger <note>A Latin idiom meaning to treat a subject superficially or briefly.</note>, or do not explain them enough.

# MEDITATION V.

They explain and prove: But perhaps these very men have never properly examined and weighed these core topics throughout their lives; perhaps they do not know the method of instilling them into tender minds; perhaps they have never actually attempted an experiment to see what might be valued in this approach. If this were the case, as it seems to some, they have no reason to complain about the weakness of the youth's intellect. Whatever the truth of that may be, this much is certain: the truth of the Christian Religion is built upon **Natural Religion**, <note>Natural Religion refers to truths about God—such as His existence and goodness—that can be discovered through human reason and observing nature, without needing the Bible.</note> and without the latter, the former cannot be properly demonstrated. Therefore, one must either say that these chapters of Natural Theology are so difficult to grasp, so intricate and obscure, that they can only be understood and proven by the most learned, and even then with difficulty; or that they are so composed that anyone, with a moderate amount of attention, can understand and learn them. If they assert the former, they not only contradict experience but are also unjust toward the Author of human nature Himself. For what would be more repugnant to the goodness, wisdom, and equity of the Divine Power than this: namely, that He would equip humans with the faculty of reasoning as a primary instrument for the purpose of being imbued with a true knowledge of Himself, yet at the same time oblige those same people to admit principles that could scarcely be grasped by men of the most subtle intellect? Would God not thus be binding the majority of mortals to the impossible? Would not those who were ignorant of these principles be <gloss>without excuse</gloss> <note>original: ἀπολογητοὶ</note>? Would this not contradict Paul, who asserts that <gloss>that which is known of God</gloss> <note>original: τὸ γνωστὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ; a reference to Romans 1:19</note> is manifest to everyone without distinction? Certainly, if the speech of those men were true, one would have to say the same about the first and principal chapters of Religion that the first teachers of the Christian Church rightly complained about regarding the inventions of the Philosophers and their decrees on divine matters: namely, that they were so constructed that they could not be understood by the common people, and therefore could not benefit the vast majority of the human race. For thus Lactantius <note>Lactantius (c. 250–325 AD) was an early Christian advisor to Emperor Constantine, often called the "Christian Cicero" for his eloquent style.</note> in his *Divine Institutes, Book III, Chapter XXV* attacks the decrees of the Philosophers concerning divine matters: "That greatest," he says, "*imitator of ours, Plato,* <note>Lactantius is referring to Cicero here, who followed Plato's philosophy.</note> *thought that Philosophy was not for the common people, because only learned men could attain it: Philosophy, he said, is content with few judges, the multitude deliberately avoids it. It is not, therefore, Wisdom, if it shrinks from the assembly of men; since wisdom was given to man without any distinction; it was given to all, so that there is no one so lowly that they cannot grasp it. But if they embrace a virtue given to the human race in such a way that they seem to want to enjoy the good alone, they are as envious as if they did not want the sun to be seen or the true light to be increased or unearthed for others. For what else is it to deny wisdom to men than to take away the true and divine light from their minds? But if the nature of man is capable of wisdom,*

it was necessary for artisans, and peasants, and women, and finally all who bear human form, to be taught so that they might be wise, and for the people to consist of every language, condition, sex, and age. It is therefore the greatest argument that Philosophy neither tends toward wisdom nor is wisdom itself, because its mysteries are celebrated only by the beard and the cloak." <note>A reference to the traditional attire of Greek philosophers; Lactantius is arguing that true wisdom shouldn't require a professional philosopher's "uniform."</note> Since, therefore, it is clearly repugnant to the divine virtues to think such things about Religion, we must say that the principles upon which the Christian Religion rests are clear enough and suited to the intellects of all. If this is true, why could they not be explained and proven to the capacity of the Youth? Indeed, why should they not be instilled with every bit of diligence used? I confess the same must be said about the truth of **Revealed Religion**. <note>Revealed Religion refers to truths that can only be known through God's specific communication, such as the Bible or the life of Jesus.</note> Just as the truth of the Christian Religion cannot be properly proven without the principles of Natural Religion, so no one will be able to subscribe to the particular articles of Revelation with a firm assent of the mind unless they are properly persuaded of the divine origin of the Christian Religion in general. He, therefore, who asserts that young people cannot grasp the arguments by which the truth of the Christian religion is usually proven, must necessarily hold that it is necessary for young people to subscribe to Articles of Religion which they have not yet been able to know for certain are divine; nothing more foreign to reason than this can be defended. But those who have ever devoted effort to instructing youth know that this argument can be handled easily and within the grasp of the young. It is known, for example, that the truth of the Christian religion can be proven in a summary way by demonstrating that Jesus Christ was called back to life; let the instructors of Youth, therefore, take into their hands, for instance, the first of the *Sacred Sermons* composed by the celebrated *Werenfels*, <note>Samuel Werenfels (1657–1740) was a prominent Swiss theologian known for his defense of the core tenets of Christianity through clear, logical reasoning.</note> in which he proved the truth of the resurrection of Christ with arguments suited to everyone’s capacity with wonderful simplicity and clarity: let him weigh each proposition one by one, and having done this, explain them to the youth, and it will be clear—provided our teacher is not entirely ignorant of the art of reasoning—that these arguments do not exceed the capacity of the Young. The second objection is no more 2) weighty. Let us suppose that most of the Christians among whom we live do not doubt the truth of Religion, much less attack it; can it therefore be concluded with any appearance of truth that the capital heads of natural and Revealed Religion are not to be instilled into tender youth? Is not everyone bound to know both what Religion is and upon what foundations it is built? Just because others are persuaded, should we be careless about divine matters? <meta>This page continues the author’s argument that religious skepticism is more prevalent than many realize. # MEDITATION V.

...principles upon which Religion rests, but rather to cling without hesitation to those things which were handed down in youth? You say that **Unbelievers** <note>original: "Increduli"</note> who attack Religion are rare among Christians. Would that this were as certain as you so confidently assert! Perhaps you, who reason thus, do not yet sufficiently understand who should be included in the catalog of Unbelievers. 

Certainly, for someone to earn the name of an Unbeliever, it is not necessary that he be equipped with a subtle genius or refined by many disciplines; nor that he have all the objections usually leveled against Religion ready at hand; nor that he be able to gloss over his errors learnedly and with some appearance of truth, or attack the fundamental dogmas of Religion in publicly edited writings. It is enough if that man, on any given occasion, speaks doubtfully about religion in general; if he believes it can be safely disputed from either side; if, in the manner of a jester, he mocks the most holy dogmas or precepts of Religion; if he confidently maintains that it does not matter what one believes; if he thinks Religion was merely invented to keep men in their place; if he shows by any means that he is touched by little or no concern for Religion; if he contends that Religion can be changed according to the diversity of times and places or the will of Rulers, and so on. 

If he is imbued with these and other opinions and sentiments, and openly defends them, he must be counted among the Unbelievers. Daily experience teaches that, alas, many such people are found among men and women, nobles and commoners, citizens and peasants, the learned and the unlearned. Therefore, lest the youth be corrupted by the words and examples of these men, the main points of **Natural and Revealed Religion** <term>Natural Religion refers to truths about God reached through reason; Revealed Religion refers to truths known through the Bible.</term> must be instilled in them early and handed down correctly. 

3.) It is true that some people, by reading books in which fundamental truths are attacked, have fallen not only into various doubts but often even into **Deism** or **Atheism**. <note>Deism is the belief in a God who created the world but does not interfere with it; Atheism is the denial of God's existence.</note> But we by no means assert that such books should be recommended to Youth; on the contrary, we assert that the reading of books of that kind is very harmful to Youth, about which we will give further warning in what follows regarding books written by Unbelievers. This, therefore, is all we want: namely, that the first foundations of Religion be properly explained and proven to Young People, and that one or two objections which could easily creep into their minds be brought forward and solidly resolved. So far is it from the truth that Young People, upon hearing or reading one or two objections opposed to Religion, would immediately throw up their hands in defeat; rather, they will use the principles with which they were imbued to refute those objections, or at least to conduct a more accurate examination of the things they once accepted. Or where does it come from, I ask, that many men are so easily confused by—

<meta>catchword: the most trivial—</meta>

<column-break/>

## ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

—even the most trivial objections of Unbelievers, if not because in their youth they did not properly perceive the fundamental heads of Religion, but having only lightly tasted them, merely committed these or those articles to memory? How does it happen that even men who are not unlearned shudder at the very name of an Unbeliever and think that Religion is all but finished if its objections are made public? It is only because they are destitute of a solid knowledge of the Christian religion and have not exercised their intellect in examining primary truths. 

Certainly, in my opinion, these evils—which increase daily—cannot be more rightly countered than if youths and adolescents alike properly know, weigh, and deeply fix in their minds the primary heads of Religion. Finally, 4.) we admit that the Christian Religion, commending itself by its native simplicity, is a doctrine of truth "which is according to godliness"; and from its individual articles, when properly and skillfully proposed, many consequences for living piously can be drawn. But it does not yet follow from this that the precepts for living rightly should not be handed down individually to the youth, or that they should not be recalled to various circumstances of life. 

Everyone knows it is necessary that one have an accurate knowledge not only of virtue in general, but of all virtues specifically. This cannot happen unless mature and, as far as possible, exact definitions of them are provided. However, the **Holy Scriptures** <note>original: "S. Literæ"</note> do not provide these everywhere. Furthermore, the Scriptures sometimes hand down general principles of this or that virtue, the parts and consequences of which we only know by the help of genuine instruction. Who does not know, moreover, how easily men—especially young men—wish to measure the duties prescribed by our **Savior** <note>original: "Sotere"</note> by the measuring rod <note>original: "decempeda"</note> of a corrupt mind, and to interpret them in such a way that the evil affections to which they are devoted suffer no loss? 

Finally, it is necessary that we have a thorough perspective on the reasons by which we are impelled to perform our duties; for the more we are persuaded of them all, the greater force they will have upon our souls. From these things we conclude that it is necessary for the youth to properly know the precepts of living piously at an early age. I omit other things that could clearly show the vanity of this objection, and I here bring an end to this meditation.

MEDITATION V.

# SUPPLEMENT <note>original: "ἘΠΙΜΕΤΡΟΝ" (Epimetron)</note>
# OF THEOLOGICAL THESES.

I. Since God, who is the Author of Revelation, is also the Author of reason, it is impossible that God would enjoin through revelation such things to be believed by men which are contrary to the most manifest principles of reason.

II. Although the precise number of "fundamental articles" <note>Essential core beliefs of the Christian faith.</note> cannot be defined, the distinction made by theologians between fundamental and non-fundamental articles remains true; it does much to distinguish those matters in theological controversies which are more or less momentous.

III. Protestants admit no rule of faith other than Scripture. Therefore, they believe that the writings of the Church Fathers, the Acts of the Councils, and all other books—whether public or private, written by whomever—must be weighed according to the norm of Scripture alone.

IV. Since it is manifest from the Holy Scriptures that our Holy Savior Jesus Christ, the **God-Man** <term>original: "Θεανθρωπον" (Theanthropon), a term expressing that Christ is both fully God and fully human</term>, suffered death for us sinners, they labor in vain who anxiously inquire whether God could have provided for the human race in any other way than this.

<margin>John Calvin, *Antidote to the Acts of the Council of Trent*, regarding Session VI, chapter 6.</margin>
V. Although Protestants distinguish Justification from Sanctification, and contend that men are justified by faith and not by works, it should not be concluded from this that they assert anyone can obtain the remission of sins and be certain of their salvation without a perpetual pursuit of holiness. The illustrious doctors of the Protestant Churches confessed this at the beginning of our separation from the Roman Church. <note>The "secession" refers to the Protestant Reformation.</note> On this subject, Calvin speaks thus:
> It cannot be denied that these two things, sanctification and justification, are perpetually joined and cohere: but it is incorrectly inferred from this that they are one and the same. We confess that as soon as anyone is justified, a renewal necessarily follows. Nor is it doubted whether Christ sanctifies those whom he justifies. For this would be to tear the Gospel apart, and even to pluck Christ himself into pieces, if anyone wished to separate the righteousness which we obtain by faith from repentance.

VI. Those who would wish the "Way of Examination" <note>The practice of critically examining religious claims using reason.</note> in matters regarding religion to be outlawed, and who rail against reason, do not defend the cause of religion and piety, but rather the cause of fanaticism and skepticism.

---

DE CAUSIS INCREDULITATIS. <note>On the Causes of Unbelief.</note>

VII. Free will, by its native powers and human instruction, is worth something regarding the affairs of temporal life:
> The wicked hate to sin for fear of punishment. <note>A quote from the Roman poet Horace, *Epistles* 1.16.52.</note>
But that kind of innocence has no promises for the heavenly life:
> "I have not committed theft, nor have I run away," if a 
> Slave says this to me, I say, "You have your reward, you do not feel the whip." 
> "I have not killed a man." "Then you shall not feed the crows on the cross." <note>Also from Horace, *Epistles* 1.16.73-75. The poet argues that doing right just to avoid punishment is not true virtue.</note>
But to live a life worthy of a Christian man, and to perform truly good works, there is need of a new birth, which happens through the word of the Gospel and the internal help of the Holy Spirit.

VIII. Even if some miracle were performed in favor of **Transubstantiation** <note>The doctrine that the bread and wine in the Eucharist become the actual body and blood of Christ.</note>, we still could not admit it. For in order for me to have faith in a miracle, I have need of my senses; but if I have faith in my senses, then Transubstantiation is disproven <note>This is a classic rationalist argument: if your eyes tell you a miracle happened, you trust your eyes. But your eyes tell you the bread is still bread, so you cannot use your eyes to prove it changed into something else.</note>.

IX. Those who say that it matters not which religion we uphold have never seriously weighed either Natural or Revealed religion throughout their lives.

X. Whatever good is in us is owed to God, however much it may be. For He is the Author of the beginning, the progress, and the completion of our salvation. But whatever evil is in us must be attributed to us alone.

XI. When it concerns ourselves, it is safer to avoid even the smallest errors as if they were pestilential. But when others are to be judged, it is safer and more worthy of a Christian man to lean toward the more lenient side. **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Younger, a Roman statesman.</note>, a Gentile man, recognized the fairness of this judgment when he pronounced in his Letters (Book VIII, letter XXII) in this manner:
> I consider him best and most faultless who forgives others as if he himself sins daily; yet abstains from sins as if he forgives no one. Therefore, let us hold to this at home, abroad, and in every walk of life: that we be implacable toward ourselves, but exorable even to those who know not how to grant pardon to anyone but themselves.

### PART VI.
#### Section I.

<margin>The connection of this Dissertation with the preceding ones.</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter 'I' set within a square border featuring scrolling foliage and floral motifs.</image-desc>In the dissertation immediately preceding, we began to describe the external causes that can gradually cast men into the vice of Unbelief. Among the primary causes, we rightly listed the corrupt *Education and Instruction of Children.* For it often happens through this that young people are touched by little or no concern for religion; instead, being carried away by youthful passions and the wicked examples that—alas—present themselves everywhere, they shake off all reverence for the Divine Power. We have dealt sufficiently with these matters in the appropriate place, according to the plan of our undertaking. We must now proceed and see how older adults—especially those who wish to be called practitioners of divine and human disciplines—very often depart from the true and right through their own fault and patronize Unbelief. Then, indeed, they are hardened against the worship and love of pure Religion by the vices and examples of those who ought to imbue them with a solid knowledge of divine matters and recommend a most burning zeal for piety. However, as I must touch upon these wounds after many other most celebrated and excellent men before me have poured out complaints about certain abuses, I easily see and feel that I must speak circumspectly and prudently,

<meta>catchword: loquen- (speaking-)</meta>

<page-num>225</page-num>
<header>ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.</header>
---

speaking, lest I seem either to disparage that which is good and laudable, or to have brought forward anything for the sake of insulting men who have served the Churches and Schools well out of some perverse zeal. To that end, in the following sections, I shall use not so much my own words as those of the most excellent theologians; for I have been taught by experience that those things which I brought forward myself after others, with the best of intentions, were often not received with an even temper.

<margin>Academies are indeed useful for advancing the study of letters, but they also often contribute much to fostering and promoting Unbelief.</margin>
II. While I am intent on showing that not only those who are at leisure for Letters, but also the Professors of arts and disciplines, are part of the cause why religion and piety cannot take deep root in the minds of men, I easily perceive that something must be said in advance about Academies <note>In this context, "Academies" refers to universities or institutions of higher learning.</note> and the way of life of those who are accustomed to frequent them. And here we confess, above all, that the leading men who founded such workshops of the best arts and disciplines, and established within them most learned men equipped with a diverse apparatus of Erudition, are to be extolled with the greatest praise. For since most of those who wish to devote effort to more serious Letters lack the opportunity to learn them at home, they undoubtedly deserve well of Erudition and Religion who show others the way by which a most wholesome knowledge of things can easily be reached.

We confess that many benefits for both public and private utility redound from the Academies, as the celebrated Christopher Iselin—who is now among the saints <note>original: "ὁ νυν ἐν Ἁγιοις" (ho nyn en Hagiois), a Greek formula for the deceased, implying he is in heaven.</note> and was once a great ornament of the Academy of Basel—showed in a singular Oration inserted in *Helvetic Temples, Vol. I, Section III.* We refer the reader to that. From this, it is clear that we by no means subscribe to the opinion of those who, because of certain inconveniences—which usually arise not so much from the design of these Societies as from certain circumstances of places and persons—would wish them all to be abolished. This is sometimes done by those who, though driven by a certain pious desire and wishing to look out for a degenerate Christianity, bring forward remedies for that purpose that are not sufficiently tempered to the rules of reason and prudence. There is an abuse of all even the most excellent things; if the use of a thing had to be removed because of its abuse, one would have to say goodbye to the common Fatherland of all—that is, the earth. Nor should this be attributed indiscriminately to the Teachers of the best arts, even if certain evils are accustomed to flow from those Societies. For although they strive with all their might to render their listeners not only learned but also, as far as lies within them, pious and lovers of virtue, they are hindered...

nevertheless, in this fragility of human affairs, they could not prevent themselves from being frequently abandoned by their most praiseworthy vows and falling away. Even here the words of the Poet find a place: *a few swimmers in the vast abyss* <note>original: *rari nantes in gurgite vasto*; a quote from Virgil’s *Aeneid* describing survivors of a shipwreck, here used to describe the few virtuous students in a sea of vice</note>. There are few students whose hearts have been touched by a certain burning zeal for virtue; true piety can only take root in noble souls illuminated by divine grace, the number of whom, however, is small.

Although what has been said so far sufficiently proves that I place a true value on Universities, no one whose heart cares for piety and the study of truth can deny that many things occur in Universities—especially those where there is a great influx of students—which can contribute greatly to nourishing and promoting the *vice of Unbelief*. This will become clear if we turn our attention not only to the lives of the many who devote their leisure to Letters therein, but also to the citizens and inhabitants themselves, before whose eyes the way of life of these men is daily displayed. 

Regarding the students of Letters, it is well known that many are sent off to Universities at an age when they are not yet equipped with a solid knowledge of divine matters, nor fortified by those safeguards which are so effective in restraining the unruly impulses of the mind. Such young men easily rush into every kind of wickedness. There are not a few who frequent Universities for the very purpose of giving free rein to the depraved passions by which they are already driven, so that, having left the paternal threshold and removed all guardians, they may establish a life according to their own pleasure and squander their resources—often collected by their parents with great shame—upon their whims. These men easily find companions in such places. Thus, it cannot happen otherwise than that minds already seized and constricted by the love of vice are drawn further and further away from the love of virtue and the worship of the Divine Power. 

Once the will has been captured by depraved desires, it easily drags the intellect into agreement, persuading itself that what is pleasing and acceptable is actually true and laudable—or at least not so destructive. Added to this is the fact that these men, seeking a pretext for their vices, appeal to some sort of *Academic Liberty* <term>original: *Libertatem Academicam*; historically, this referred to the legal privileges and exemptions from city law granted to students, which were often abused to avoid punishment for misconduct</term>, by which name they seem to understand nothing other than an unbridled license to think and do whatever they wish; as if the workshops of the finest arts and disciplines had been established primarily for the purpose of learning how virtue and reverence for the laws might be abolished.
