# MEDITATION VI.

...we should be mindful of the most useful labors which teachers are accustomed to expend in commending the cultivation of religion and piety to their listeners. Not only do we wish to detract nothing from their virtues and learning, but we rather publicly profess that they are to be magnified and praised. This notwithstanding, it is permissible—and indeed without seeking to offend anyone—to show the reasons why the souls of many are drawn away from the love of religion and piety, and are very often plunged into the very abyss of <term>unbelief</term> <note>original: "incredulitatis barathrum"; an "abyss" or "pit" of doubt.</note> through the carelessness, negligence, backwards instruction, and life examples of those who serve as public Professors of Theology and <term>Ministers of the Word of God</term> <note>original: "V. D. M." (Verbi Divini Minister), the standard title for a Protestant clergyman.</note>. It is helpful to demonstrate this point by point:

And (1) indeed, there are many teachers in Universities and <term>Gymnasiums</term> <note>In this period, a Gymnasium was a high-level secondary school preparing students for university.</note> who believe their only assigned task is to make their listeners *learned*, instructed in a variety of useful things—and often things of very little use at all. Meanwhile, those things which pertain to the *practice* of virtues, and especially those duties most necessary for a future Minister of the Word to know, they either completely neglect or are accustomed to deliver quite carelessly. From this very thing, innumerable evils overflow into the Church, among which <term>Unbelief</term> and contempt for religion must undoubtedly be numbered. No one is ignorant of how necessary a more accurate knowledge of Christian Ethics is for a student and future Minister, so that he may conform his own life to the precepts of Jesus Christ, conquer the vices spreading everywhere in the congregations, detect the causes and sources of degenerate Christianity, and provide the most wholesome counsel for meeting such great evils. Furthermore, it is well known that it is impossible for a Pastor to perform his duty rightly unless he himself not only burns with an ardent zeal for piety, but also possesses a clear understanding of all those things required to properly fulfill the pastoral office. Thus, he ought to know the right method for teaching the precepts of true religion and piety to children; what should be most emphasized publicly and privately; and how to handle those who are self-assured, hypocrites, those weighed down by hardships, the weak in faith, or those anxious about their salvation. Since all these and more must be directed and moderated according to the circumstances and the people involved, everyone sees that it is necessary for a future Minister to have the most accurate knowledge of all parts of his duty. However, that there are many public teachers who either neglect all these things entirely or treat them superficially is, alas, known by experience. There are those who think it beneath the dignity of a Doctor of Theology to teach those "easy" precepts (as they think them) of Christian Ethics; they imagine that their disciples will notice the things pertaining to the duties of Ministers on their own, led by experience in due time. They believe they must now urge

indeed urge studies in dogmatics, <term>exegesis</term> <note>The critical explanation or interpretation of scripture.</note>, prophecy, <term>typology</term> <note>A method of biblical interpretation where people or events in the Old Testament are seen as "types" or symbols foreshadowing Christ.</note>, and so on, and that they must arm their disciples against every kind of heretic—even those of whom their listeners have never heard a single word. Such men, for the most part, perform the tasks required of their office with boredom or treat them carelessly; they are positively nauseated by *practical studies*, thinking these things should be left to lesser minds. It is as if some new explanation of this or that scripture passage, the invention of these or those new hypotheses, or a true or imaginary victory over this or that adversary (whose foolish and stupid opinions often not even one in a hundred understands, let alone is in danger of supporting), would bring greater utility to the Church of God than an accurate instruction in those things which can promote true piety in Christian gatherings.

How many evils arise from this negligence can scarcely be expressed in words. For many students, fired by the desire for learning and for becoming famous, and compelled by the example of their teachers, devote themselves only to those studies which can help them achieve a reputation for erudition. But as for being pious themselves, or urging the pursuit of virtue in their own time, they expend very little care. Hence, when they are called to lead this or that congregation, they seem to themselves to have been transported to another world. They realize that from all that vast apparatus of various learning, very little can be drawn that fits the state of their listeners, or that can contribute most to rightly conquering all kinds of vice and promoting true piety. Thus, it cannot happen otherwise than that impiety and unbelief lift their heads everywhere, because those means which ought to be applied to uproot these evils are either totally neglected, or are instilled with little wisdom and less frequency. And these evils are all the more to be deplored because the public teachers are not ignorant of the fact that most of their listeners will, in their own time, serve as Ministers of the Word in village parishes. Surely it is not only impious, but also ridiculous and foolish, to treat carelessly or neglect entirely those things without which future Ministers cannot rightly perform their duties, while focusing on all other things which do not carry such weight toward reaching this goal.

# MEDITATION VI.

...they cannot <note>This sentence continues from the previous page, referring to the duties of teachers.</note> do otherwise than urge these things with incredible zeal and diligence. However, I would not wish for anyone to interpret what I have said as if I wanted this one thing alone to be provided by public Doctors: namely, that they should be occupied only in explaining moral truths and the duties of Ministers, while neglecting those disciplines and arts which are required as necessary for a more accurate knowledge of Theology. I am very far from such an opinion, knowing full well that the cultivation of the most noble disciplines not only does nothing to hinder the pursuit of piety, but that when they are rightly cultivated and applied in their proper places and times, they bring many excellent aids and protections for promoting true piety. This one thing, therefore, is what we desire: that the <term>practice of piety</term> <note>original: "praxis pietatis"; a central concept in Pietism focusing on lived faith rather than just doctrinal knowledge.</note> in Universities and Gymnasiums, and those things which pertain to the duties of Ministers, should be handed down and urged no less than those things which are required to obtain an accurate knowledge of theological studies.

And indeed, whoever turns the eyes of his mind to the present state of the Churches—to the vices everywhere rampant, to degenerate Christianity, and to <term>Unbelief</term> <note>original: "Incredulitatem"; refers here to a lack of living faith or a drift toward atheism.</note> which is always increasing day by day and creeping like a plague—will easily perceive that the neglect of those duties we have just mentioned is not the least cause of such great evils. This has been acknowledged by the most excellent among the Protestant Theologians, whose testimonies and most justified complaints necessity demands I bring forward here.

And already in his own time (to begin with those things which arise from the neglect and ignorance of the duties required of Ministers), *Erasmus* complained about how badly those people act who set over Christian assemblies such Doctors who are ignorant of the things necessarily demanded to perform this office rightly. In his work *On the Method of Preaching* <note>original: "De ratione concionandi," a famous 1535 treatise by Erasmus on homiletics.</note>, p. 66, he pronounces in the following manner:

> *Is it not (he says) backward to examine the faith and skill of one to whom you intend to commit your oxen or horses, and yet to have no concern for the one to whom you commit the souls of men, for whom Christ died? You remove a tenant farmer who is negligent or unskillfully cultivating your fields, and do you not remove a Pastor who casts bad seed into the Lord's good grain? Is it not backward, in navigation, not to commit the oars to just anyone, nor to move just anyone to the helm, but only him who is skilled in steering; and yet to commit the care of the Church to anyone at all without selection? If someone should say to you, "Let this man sit at the helm, for he is well-born, he is very rich and has much to give (and gives liberally), he is favored by the Prince, and finally, he is your near kinsman and friend"—would you not immediately cry out: "What does it matter to me what he is like in other things? This storm requires a skilled and vigorous pilot; otherwise, everyone is in danger"*

<meta>catchword: danger-</meta>

***

# ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

> *...of being ruined. And do these things come to no one's mind when the danger is far more serious? In a shipwreck, goods are endangered, bodies are endangered, although many swim out unharmed when the ship is broken, and the sea itself casts much merchandise onto the shore. In this [spiritual] shipwreck, souls come into extreme danger—the most dear merchandise of Christ.*

*William Ames* <note>original: "G. Amesius" (1576–1633), a highly influential English Puritan theologian whose works were standard textbooks in Northern Europe.</note>, a most excellent Theologian of the previous century, also vigorously touches upon this wound in his *Exhortation to Students*, saying:

> *In the preceding year, seeing that a necessary matter was being omitted, I attempted to see if I could call Theology away, in some part, from certain thorny, perplexed, and less necessary questions and controversies, and lead it toward life and practice, so that students might begin to think seriously about the conscience and its care. I know that my counsel is approved by every good man. For this is what all pious people in our Universities have desired for a long time now—and certainly too long. This very thing, which is the weightiest of all, the pitiable Church of God demands from all Universities as if by its own right; the Church cries out that it is being betrayed and plainly destroyed while the task of caring for the consciences of men is mandated to those who have learned no part of the art of this thing. They seem not to know whether such doctrine is necessary, or if it even exists at all; they have hardly ever chosen even one precept (not already known to everyone) that looks directly to this end for their own diligent meditation, nor have they heard it diligently instilled by others. The first and most capital error, to which almost all others owe their origin, consists in this: that those who enroll their names among its pupils think rarely and too little about the proper goal of Theology. For what wonder is it if they never reach the mark, when they have never aimed at it with intent eyes? But what ought to be the goal of the Theologian? The Apostle teaches in a few words in 1 Timothy 4:16: namely, that he should save himself and those who hear him; that is, living unto God himself, he should also bring others to God; or, that he should assign and devote himself entirely to the glory of God and the building up of the Church.*

And a few lines later:

> *But those who neglect the principles and almost all practical matters as if they were commonplace, easy, and exposed to everyone—and who meanwhile languish over certain more subtle questions and tangled controversies—when they later come to preaching, they are indeed too pleasing to themselves, but they are accustomed to move all more prudent people sometimes to laughter and sometimes to pity. To laughter, when having seized upon even the smallest handle, they bring forth more about some unnecessary controversy than a merchant ship could contain. To pity, when being forced to speak of practical matters, they seem translated into another world, and are more cold than many of the common people would be if placed in their position. Truly, if practice is absent along with skill in these things, shame [remains]...*

# MEDITATION VI.

It is a shameful thing to contemplate what kind of spectacle a "Master of Controversies" of this sort provides. He contends most fiercely that the Saints and Angels are not to be invoked; yet in the meantime, he either does not know how or neglects to invoke God, the Best and Greatest. He sharply defends the position that the body of Christ is present neither in the sacramental bread nor under its outward appearance; yet he treats communion with Christ as if it were a mere phantom or some indignity. He solicitously proves that all sins are mortal; yet he lives as if no crime stood in need of pardon. He demonstrates with many testimonies and arguments that a man is not justified by works; yet he never shows his own faith to be living and true through any works. Will he not surely "build up" the people with his controversies? Concerning these evils, <term>the late</term> <note>original: "ὁ Μακαρίτης" (ho Makarites); a Greek term of respect for a deceased person, similar to "of blessed memory."</note> the celebrated Werenfels <note>Samuel Werenfels (1657–1740) was a Swiss theologian known for his moderate views and critique of scholastic hair-splitting.</note> also complained here and there throughout his theological works. He deals with this most excellently and solidly, as he always does, in the *Dissertation on the Aim of the Theologian*, which ought to be read and weighed most frequently by all Professors of Theology and students of Holy Scripture. We shall select only certain passages from it which especially serve our present purpose. **On page 395 of the first edition**, <term>the late</term> author declares as follows:

> "Those Doctors omit the things necessary for instructing a Pastor who teach their disciples only what is to be believed and not what is to be done; they spend all their time handing down dogmas which consist in speculation, while neglecting the branch of practical Theology. Truly, they omit the part most necessary for the Ministers of the Church. How will those be able to correct the morals of others who have never touched upon the doctrine of morals? How will they be able to exhort any of their listeners to their Duty, when they do not know in what each person’s duty consists? How will they be able to direct the consciences of others, when they do not know how to define what conscience demands in any given case? How will they be able to heal the diseases of the soul when they are ignorant of the origin, nature, and symptoms of these diseases—to whom the hearts of men, which are to be cured, are utterly unknown? It is no wonder that time and again not only private individuals, but even Synods, have earnestly demanded that specific Professors of Practical Theology be established in the reformed Universities, just as is the case in the Universities of the Roman Church. I truly do not know whether the Popish Doctors might not with some right reproach us for this defect, and from there conclude—not without some appearance of truth—that it is true what they so often object against us: that good works are made of little account by us, or at least not of such great account as they are in their own Church, where they are taught with such care and solicitude. Those Doctors also neglect the things necessary for instructing a Pastor who, while they do indeed hand down the dogmas of Religion—theoretical and practical—and simultaneously keep watch over the students' morals, nevertheless do not instruct them for the office they must perform, or at least do not..."

"...instruct them as much as is necessary. This is indeed just as if a Shoemaker were to teach his apprentice many things that are not useless to a Shoemaker, but did not teach him how to make shoes. Such are the Doctors who hand down to their disciples many things that are not to be despised, but do not in the least instruct them in those things which they must do daily when they eventually perform their Sacred Ministry. They do not instruct them in how to rightly perform the functions of a Minister: how to direct and moderate public worship; how to pour forth prayers of every kind; how to deliver sacred sermons for the edification of the audience; how to adapt catechetical exercises to a child’s understanding; how to govern the Church which they will one day lead, how to moderate Consistories, or how to exercise the <term>use of the keys</term> <note>The "power of the keys" refers to the authority of the church to exercise discipline, based on Matthew 16:19.</note>; how to convert sinners of every kind; how to lift up the tempted, comfort the sick, and strengthen the dying—and six hundred other things which occur to a Pastor of souls to be performed every single day and hour. Of the Orators who come out of the Schools of Rhetoric into the forum, the <term>Satirist</term> <note>likely referring to Petronius in the *Satyricon*, who critiqued the disconnect between school declamations and real-life legal battles.</note> once said: 'These men seem to themselves to have been transported into another world.' This can be said with even greater justice of University Students when they are called to feed a particular Church. They seem to themselves to have been transported into a new world. In the Schools, they heard their Doctors disputing subtly about various matters. Now, in the Church over which they have been placed, it is not at all a matter of disputing: now sermons must be held, now prayers must be poured out, soon they must devote themselves to catechetical exercises; now sinners must be rebuked, now the afflicted comforted, now the sick visited, and other things of this kind performed—none of which they ever learned in the Schools. In the Schools, they heard how Heretics are to be refuted and the Heterodox disproven. Here, they encounter no Heretics or Heterodox people to refute; but they repeatedly encounter obstinate sinners whom they must rebuke and restrain with the severity of discipline. In the Schools, they heard nothing else praised but those who argue well about various things, judge well, and reason well. Here, it is of little account to argue well, judge well, or reason well: action must be taken daily, and for acting well, there is need now of wisdom and prudence, now of gentleness and moderation, now of patience, fortitude, and constancy—virtues which they had no opportunity to exercise in the Schools. I know it is said that many things are learned by the Pastor through use itself when he performs his office, and that 'a craftsman,' as the proverb goes, 'is made by crafting'; that a Pastor, by performing pastoral functions daily, is rendered more fit for performing them and becomes more perfected in them day by day. But to commit the care of souls to a man who does not even distinctly know what the functions of a Pastor are, or what is required to exercise them rightly—indeed, who has heard scarcely anything about these things in the Schools—I know not whether this is a matter of rashness, not to say impiety. ### MEDITATION VI.

...when novices approach the practice of medicine, it is commonly said that *a new cemetery must be built for them*. But what shall we say of such a novice Pastor? *Must a new hell be built for him*, in which those people may be tortured, along with whose eternal destruction he lays down the first crude attempts of his craft? A new one would surely have to be built, if that place which God destined for the punishments of the damned were not already spacious enough to hold these men as well. Thus far that eminent Theologian <note>Referring back to Samuel Werenfels.</note>. Compare his *Examination of the question, whether the habit of Theology required in a Minister of the Church or that required in an Academic Doctor requires more*, inserted into the new edition of his works, page 298, Volume II.

Others raise the same complaints. Among them is also the Excellent *Pfaff* <note>Christoph Matthäus Pfaff (1686–1760), a prominent Lutheran theologian and chancellor at the University of Tübingen.</note>, who speaks everywhere in his writings about the neglect of these studies. In the previously cited *Oration on the vices of those who perform sacred duties*, page 15, he says: *In the Universities, Moral Theology <term>Moral Theology: the study of Christian ethics and how a believer should live</term> is either completely neglected, or it is treated for the most part in a theoretical way and in the form of a rigid System. And just as in the teaching of Moral Philosophy, the goal is not to instill in the listeners the precepts of right conversation and the proper direction of the emotions, nor to fill and amend the minds of the students with a hatred of vice and a love of virtue—which is nonetheless the most important thing—so too one sees the same in the academic treatment of Moral Theology. There you see too much indulgence in theory, while the ascetic <note>In this context, "ascetic" refers to practical spiritual exercises and the inner life of the soul.</note> development of matters is wrongly neglected. You see effort spent on curious and scholarly little questions that are beside the point, when instead the crooked recesses of vice ought to be investigated above all else. The fountain and abundance of evils, and the poison within, should be uncovered to bring conviction to every person; the true character and supreme excellence of virtue should be shown; and the interior ways by which we are led to a deeper union with God and bring sin entirely under the yoke should be demonstrated here.* And after a few words: *It is a matter of grief that those things which pertain to Pastoral Theology are commonly neglected.* I shall not bring forward more: let one read in addition what men most experienced in Moral Theology have written about the evils reviewed so far—namely, the Venerable *Ostervald* <note>Jean-Frédéric Ostervald (1663–1747), a Swiss Protestant pastor known for his work on church reform and the "Source of Corruption."</note> in the whole of Chapter III of *The Source of Corruption*; the Distinguished *Roques* in his treatise *On the Dignity of the Ecclesiastical Ministry*, Chapter VIII; and the Celebrated *Hottinger*, a theologian of Heidelberg, in the Preface to his *Model of the Christian Life*, and elsewhere in other practical works.

### ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

<margin>but they are too laborious in handing down particular truths or hypotheses.</margin>
singular care and diligence. It is well known that in the Universities, "colleges" (as they are called) are held for preaching, interpretation, prophecy, polemics <term>Polemics: the art of theological argument and the refutation of errors</term>, and so on. No one denies that these can be of remarkable use. But it is a grief that those things which are the most excellent of all, and the most necessary to know, are often neglected, or at least treated with less dignity than the matters deserve. In my opinion, before "Dogmatic Systems" (as they are called) are explained to students, it would be necessary for the individual chapters of Natural and Revealed Religion to be handed down with great care, for the objections of Unbelievers to be sincerely represented and solidly demolished. Only after this is done should one proceed to the "Systems." Why I think this way is not obscure. For first, it is clear to all who are even moderately versed in the sacred disciplines that particular truths cannot be clearly demonstrated unless the essential points of Religion upon which they rest are solidly proven and placed beyond the risk of doubt. It is necessary, therefore, that these arguments be treated with singular industry. But if the students of Holy Scripture are not truly persuaded of these things, in what way—once moved into the Sacred Ministry for their whole life—will they seriously and eagerly defend the cause of Religion? What Zeal will there be for the Glory of God? With what heat will they finally apply themselves, publicly and privately, to promoting the study of piety? With what spirit will they receive all the adversities occurring in this office? By what means will they be able to convince those who think poorly or doubt the first truths of Religion of their errors, and teach them better things? I call to witness the conscience of anyone: will not a lack of this conviction often hinder them, and those who hear them, from satisfying their duties? Add to this that today there is a great number of books in which the most holy points of Religion are attacked. These are worn thin in the hands of many who do not have the nature and character of Religion clearly understood. The public Teachers are not ignorant of these things; indeed, they know them, and for that reason, they complain loudly. Therefore, instead of the complaints which they pour out on every given occasion, they would do best if they fortified the Students of Holy Scripture against the public enemies of Religion, and supplied them with weapons with which they could solidly demolish those errors and place the truths of the greatest importance in safety. Most of those who frequent the Universities and schools are at an age where they can properly feel the force of arguments. Yet the Teachers very often neglect to do this, as those who have attended the Universities know. These teachers surely not only fail to perform their duty properly, but they are also the cause that many of their listeners, once admitted to public office, [neglect] the cause of religion—

### MEDITATION VI.

...they unhappily defend religion. <note>The word "ligionis" is the end of "Religionis" (Religion) from the previous page.</note> (*) It is a cause for grief that these same men, who fail in this regard, often attack or defend particular truths and new hypotheses with such fervor that you would think the very core of Religion was placed in these specific articles; from this, many evils once again overflow into the Church. As soon as some Professor defends a new opinion or hypothesis, it usually happens that others concede to his view, and—seeking to please this Teacher—strenuously defend his cause. Others, however, rush to the opposite side, choosing to follow a Teacher who sharply attacks the new hypothesis. From this, not only do the most bitter disputes often arise among brothers, but students, while they ought to be applying themselves to all other things and rather learning and weighing matters of greater importance, spend the greatest part of their Academic life in correctly learning, defending, or attacking these new hypotheses.

Not content with this, upon returning home to their own country, they firmly retain these same views, are diligent enough in recommending them, and desire to demonstrate their skill in theological study to everyone chiefly by that name. They cling sharply to these new opinions for most of their lives, and whenever they must speak publicly, they do not choose those texts which contain the primary heads of religion necessary for everyone to know, or the virtues to be instilled in all Christians; rather, they choose those which provide material for lecturing on the weight of their new hypotheses. If they find supporters of these new opinions in their homeland, they join themselves to them and extol them to the heavens with praise; they believe these men alone understand what is serious and momentous in Theology, while the rest flit about like shadows, ignorant, forsooth, of such precious truths. They further join these opinions and hypotheses with the articles accepted in the Church, and persuade themselves that true **Orthodoxy** <term>Orthodoxy: literally "right belief"; the adherence to accepted norms or creeds</term> is placed in their strenuous defense. From this, new seeds of strife and contention are often sown in the Church. No one who has a clear view of the fates of things done among Theologians will deny those things which I have brought forward here sincerely and for the best purpose.

---

(*) The Very Reverend and most Learned Man, Johann Friedrich Stapfer <note>Johann Friedrich Stapfer (1708–1775), a Swiss Reformed theologian known for his work on "Polemics" or the defense of the faith.</note>, Minister of the Word of God at Bern, candidly and wisely taxes this negligence of certain Theologians regarding this argument in his distinguished work, full of the best fruit, namely in *Institutes of Polemical Theology*, Volume II, Chapter X, page 906. This Learned Man speaks thus: *There are Theologians who possess great erudition in divine matters, who hold particular truths of Religion to the fingernail <note>Latin: "ad unguem"; an idiom meaning "perfectly" or "to a T"</note>, for which they are not to be despised but esteemed; yet if they were led back to the first principles of Religion, if they were led to those general truths, if they were required to hand over distinct notions of them to others, if they were obliged to defend the Most Holy Religion against the tricks of the Deists, Epicureans, and Naturalists <note>Deists believed in a creator who does not intervene; Epicureans were associated with materialism; Naturalists believed only natural laws operate in the world</note>, if they had to dispute against the objections of the Socinians <note>Socinians denied the Trinity and the divinity of Christ</note> from first principles and universal notions, they would perhaps be struck dumb for the greatest part of that controversy.*

### ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

It will be helpful, however, to confirm our opinion by the authority of Theologians, and those most excellent ones (as I promised I would do at the beginning of the dissertation). The most Excellent **Pfaff**, who is deservedly numbered among the Princes of Protestant Theologians, when about to rebuke that singular care of certain Theologians for defending newly received opinions, speaks thus in his *Oration on the Vices of those who perform Sacred Duties*, page 10: *We deplore that there are those who occasionally bestow the distinguished and most excellent name of Orthodoxy upon the private opinions of Teachers, eventually received everywhere by use, for the purpose of stirring up the opinions of others and sending their minds under a yoke; opinions which are often at least merely fabricated and consist in naked scholastic subtleties and an academic style of instruction <note>original: "τροπο παιδειας" (tropos paideias)</note> that is exceptionally suited for sowing disputes.* Now, *since diverse "Orthodoxies" flourish in almost every Academy, where each school thinks itself to have reached the summit of dogmatic purity, and takes it poorly if anyone calls this into doubt—instilling the same opinion of itself into its "sons"—the zeal of a Sect (which the Apostle Paul, by a certain right of his own, numbers among the works of the flesh in Galatians 5:20) cannot but play a leading role <note>original: "utramque paginam facere"; literally "to do both pages," an idiom meaning to be the whole story or play the main part</note>, and prescribe what is to be held in place of truth. By this reasoning, when the order of things is broken, and truth is measured by the authority and judgment of men—rather than the judgment of men being weighed against the norm of truth, which loves to be investigated without the zeal of parties—anyone can see what great evils flow from this into the Church, and what great dissensions, what great disputes, joined with theological hatred <note>original: "odio theologico"</note> (than which none is more deadly), arise from this.*

The same most excellent man, in his *Oration on the spiritual signs of the present times*, pronounces in the following manner: *Orthodoxy of faith ought to prepare the way for that practice which we so greatly commend; she is the mother of true piety, of true and masculine virtue, and she alone produces such distinguished fruits. It is utterly dry and tasteless what certain meddlesome and incredulous men do in plucking at Orthodoxy, which is nothing other than divine truth. Who indeed would not kiss divine truth, who would not hold the principles of true faith in place of half his soul—that most noble chain of the articles of Christian doctrine, which is brought forth clearly and perspicuously enough in Holy Scripture? And indeed, we reached that opinion long ago, so that we have said: true piety cannot exist without orthodoxy, and certainly it never flows from perverse principles and superstition.* This one thing must be noted: true Orthodoxy must be rightly distinguished and separated from the "putative" <note>imagined or supposed</note> kind, lest we embrace **a cloud instead of Juno** <note>original: "nubem pro Junone"; a classical reference to Ixion being deceived by a phantom, meaning to mistake a fantasy for the reality</note>, or a specter of Orthodoxy instead of Orthodoxy itself. To be sure, things are occasionally so compared...

### MEDITATION VI.

...human temperaments are such that they peddle the perverse offspring of their own intellect—those deep and subtle opinions on divine matters, the prejudices they drank in with their mother's milk, and common concepts of sacred things—as **Orthodoxy** simply because they are common. To me, however, Orthodoxy is of far greater value, something we ought to embrace and make our own. It consists of a few articles, most clearly and evidently revealed in the Holy Scriptures; it is joined with a great simplicity of faith, great humility, modesty, and the sincerity of one who rejoices in it, and especially with divine light. No one who is "Orthodox" in my view "thinks too highly of himself" <note>original: "altum sapit," a reference to Romans 11:20 warning against intellectual pride</note> or creates a fundamental dispute out of those dry scholastic questions—those which eventually descend into quarrels over mere words—nor does he use philosophical reasoning to determine matters not defined in Holy Scripture, condemning those who refuse to walk the same path. Thus far the celebrated Pfaff <note>Christoph Matthäus Pfaff (1686–1760), a Lutheran theologian known for proposing "ecclesial collegialism" and a more moderate approach to dogma.</note>. 

Let him be followed again by the late <note>original: "Μακαρίτης" - a Greek term of respect for the deceased, similar to "of blessed memory"</note>, celebrated Werenfels <note>Samuel Werenfels (1657–1740), a Swiss theologian famous for his work on the "struggles of the preachers" and his opposition to rigid dogmatism.</note>, whose words, though lengthy, are most worthy of being seriously weighed by all public Teachers and students of Holy Scripture. In the same dissertation, he discusses the Goal of the Theological Teacher as follows: "All those polemical and Eristic <term>Eristic: from the Greek word for "strife," referring to the practice of arguing for the sake of conflict or victory rather than truth</term> theologians poorly spend the time intended for training a pastor. Their hands are armed against everyone, and in turn, everyone’s hands are seen armed against them. They spend their entire lives in perpetual bickering and fighting, thinking of nothing else but harassing, depressing, overthrowing, and anathematizing the adversaries they have—and often have stirred up for themselves. They fiercely defend every word they have spoken, and strive to vindicate and secure their reputation (however slightly damaged by an opponent) or their authority (however lightly diminished)."

"Those Teachers also poorly spend the time intended for training a pastor who spend a great part of it arming disciples against those heretics and unorthodox people whom they will never see in the towns, villages, and countryside where they are called to preach the Gospel. These Teachers behave exactly like those who, in regions where there are no lions, leopards, or crocodiles, would teach sheep-herders with great effort how to drive those terrible animals away from the flocks and folds. For indeed, we must consider that the time spent in Academies <note>meaning universities or seminaries</note> for training pastors is far too short, while the "art" they must learn from us is very long. Once we have cut away not only the frivolous things but also those which have only slight utility, the things that remain for performing this duty properly—which are necessary in every respect—are themselves numerous and great enough. Therefore, those who keep their disciples held back in—"

### ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

"—held back in things they must eventually forget and unlearn when they wish to properly fulfill the care of souls. 'If much time were left,' I use the words of Seneca <note>Roman Stoic philosopher; this is a paraphrase of his sentiments in 'On the Shortness of Life'</note>, 'it would still have to be spent sparingly to suffice for so many necessary things; now, what madness it is to teach superfluous things in such a great shortage of time!'"

We must consider that most students do not have such diligence or such a lucky intellect that they can suffice for learning many superfluous things along with the necessary ones. We have done much if we correctly teach students—such as we usually have, with such talent and such diligence, in so short a time—those things without which an Evangelical Minister cannot fulfill his duty for the building up of the Church. But if, on top of this, we wish to overwhelm them with a jumble of useless things, we achieve only this: that while wishing to learn anything at all, they learn nothing. Or at least they carry away from our schools no other knowledge but one so vague and confused that it is worse than the densest ignorance, or certainly not much better. 

I know that those **Systems** <note>referring to "Systematic Theology," the organized categorization of all Christian doctrines</note> are commonly held to be the most perfect which embrace the most things in a short space, leaving no little question debated among theologians untouched. In my judgement, however, those Systems would be the best and most useful to students which contained nothing except what is necessary in every respect for future pastors—but with these matters treated somewhat more fully and solidly than is usually done. For it is better to know a few necessary things correctly and solidly than to have a slight, confused, and superficial knowledge of many things, most of which are of little use. Finally, we must consider that the judgements of the youths we instruct are not yet firm or mature. At this age, they usually do not know how to weigh the importance of things or judge

-> *"What distinguishes bronze from lupins."* <- <note>A quote from the Roman poet Horace; "lupins" (bitter beans) were used as play-money on stage. The phrase means knowing the difference between what is truly valuable and what is worthless junk.</note>

When they notice that we, their Masters, consume much time and effort on things of little use—especially if we handle them with a wrinkled brow, a stern gaze, and a magisterial face—they become accustomed to considering those things as matters of great importance, and as dogmas upon which the whole of Christianity turns. This opinion, drunk in at the schools, they later retain for the rest of their lives. From this (Note!) single source flow those innumerable fights over trivial matters and scandalous contests, than which there is scarcely a greater evil in the Church—unless perhaps it is this other evil flowing from the same source: that those who have heard so many useless things in the Academies, later called to Churches, feed their sheep on these minutiae—not to say trifles and follies—at every opportunity. Having passed over the things that are healthy and saving, they give this in their sermons to their listeners...

...and they press them home again and again. And why should we wonder? Indeed, these are the very things that were once held in great esteem in the Schools; these are nearly the only things they have retained from that time. Now, however, they do not wish to have heard all these things in vain, and:

->What the young have learned, the old must confess should be discarded.<-
<note>original: "Quæ Juvenes didicere, senes perdenda fateri." This is a play on a classical sentiment regarding the difficulty of unlearning youthful errors in old age.</note>

Those Doctors <note>In this context, "Doctors" refers to university professors or high-ranking theologians.</note> neglect what is necessary in the education of young men consecrated to the Holy Ministry. They labor only so that their disciples know how to distinguish—in whatever way—orthodox dogmas from heterodox ones, and that they can recite from memory those dogmas along with the scriptural sayings and arguments brought forward in the "Systems" <note>The "Systems" refers to Systematic Theology textbooks, which organized Christian doctrine into logical, often rigid, frameworks.</note> to prove them, and defend themselves in disputations with certain frivolous little distinctions. But they labor very little—at least not seriously enough—to ensure that their disciples are fully convicted in their hearts and deeply persuaded of the truth of the dogmas of salvation. 

Or, if they are concerned with persuading them, they only strive to persuade them of the truth of the dogmas that are currently under controversy, which distinguish the Reformed <note>The "Reformed" refers to the Calvinist tradition of Protestantism.</note> from other sects. They do not focus on the truth of the Christian Religion in general, or the dogmas in which all Christians agree: concerning God as the Creator of this vast Universe; His Providence extending to all things; the Supreme Judge who sees all the deeds, words, and thoughts of men, rewarding the good and punishing the evil; the immortality of the soul; the eternal happiness of the godly after this life and the eternal torments of the Wicked; the great benefit of Redemption provided by the Son of God Himself; the nature of faith in Him and of repentance, and their necessity for obtaining salvation; the necessity of divine help in all our actions, especially those regarding our eternal salvation; the necessity of holy prayers, and so on. 

Concerning these and other dogmas of this kind: he who is not deeply persuaded in his heart is not a Christian; how then could he be a Minister of Christ, or a Pastor of the Christian Church? Without this firm persuasion, whoever performs the Holy Ministry must necessarily fulfill all his duties negligently, coldly, and merely for the sake of appearance. Indeed, without this persuasion, a so-called Pastor is in reality a godless hypocrite, a mime, and a hired actor—nothing but a pure charlatan <note>original: "Agyrta," a Greek-derived term for a traveling quack or religious fraud.</note>. When he preaches, when he pours out prayers to God, when he administers the Sacraments, when he exercises discipline in the name of Christ, when he consoles the sick, or when he seems to prepare the dying for a better life—in all these things (it is a horrible thing to say) he does nothing seriously, nothing from the heart; he is practicing stage-craft and acting out a role assigned to him in a play. Thus far the most excellent Werenfels.

...that it is enough, to be a good Minister, to know how to preach—that is to say, to know how to collect upon a text everything that has the slightest connection to it, and to speak for an hour without hesitating and without coming to a standstill. <note>original: "qu'il suffit, pour être un bon Ministre de savoir prêcher..." This opening section is in French, continuing the critique of superficial academic standards.</note> From all of this, one would conclude that the Ministry is an occupation where one burdens oneself with a greater number of useless things than with important and solid truths, and that it is made more for show than for edification. This is a conclusion which, not being at all false when one stops to consider what happens in this regard in many Academies, tends to inspire a distance from the Ministry and a contempt for those who are invested in it.

There are, moreover, many in the Academies who (having spurned more serious disciplines and neglected the examination of the weightiest heads of Natural and Revealed Religion) devote themselves solely to the study of Literary History. <term>Literary History (Historia Literaria)</term> <note>In the 18th century, this referred to the history of scholars, books, and bibliography rather than the study of fiction.</note> By this means, it happens not only that they neglect those things which are necessary to be known throughout life, and judge wrongly those things which they read due to a lack of accurate knowledge of the subjects themselves, but they also often begin to doubt the primary heads of Religion by this method. 

Indeed, while they turn over the various *Journals of the Learned* and books pertaining to Literary History, they notice how great the disagreement among men has always been regarding various points of Religion. They read, furthermore, what Unbelievers have brought forward against the most momentous truths, along with the responses of Learned Men; yet, due to a lack of solid Erudition, they are unable to judge the dispute. From this it happens—with <term>self-love</term> <note>original Greek: φιλαυτία (philautia)</note> especially approaching—that they not only frequently doubt the weightiest heads of religion throughout their whole lives, but sometimes even seek glory in attacking them in whatever way they can. 

Many Students of Theology certainly have a thorough perspective on the "Antediluvian" Literary History, <note>A sarcastic reference to scholars obsessed with trivial, ancient, or legendary history from before the Biblical Flood.</note> yet they are ignorant of the characteristics of sincere repentance and saving faith. Because of that superficial knowledge of various things, they applaud themselves marvelously, and (to use the words of the Illustrious Menckenius) <note>Johann Burkhard Mencke (1674–1732), author of "On the Charlatanry of the Learned," a famous satire of academic vanity.</note> they think they have reached the very summit of Letters if they know how many wives Calovius <note>Abraham Calovius (1612–1686), a prominent and combative Lutheran theologian.</note> married, or how many cups Baudius <note>Dominique Baudius (1561–1613), a scholar known for his poetry and his struggles with alcoholism.</note> drained, or if they have learned to a tee how many strokes of the rod Scioppius <note>Caspar Schoppe (1576–1649), a controversialist who was physically attacked in Madrid at the instigation of the English ambassador.</note> was mangled with by order of the English Ambassador, how many years Leo Allatius <note>Leo Allatius (1586–1669), a scholar and Vatican librarian who allegedly used the same pen for forty years.</note> used the same pen, or how many hairs Francesco Philelphus <note>Francesco Filelfo (1398–1481), a Renaissance humanist famous for his bitter intellectual feuds.</note>—victorious in a grammatical dispute—plucked from the beard of his adversary Timothy.

V. Nor is there any doubt that those Theologians and Ministers of the Word of God <note>V.D.M. stands for Verbi Divini Minister.</note> who, when about to prove the principal heads of the Christian Religion or defend them against the objections of Unbelievers, use weak arguments to perform this, promote the cause of Unbelief in a marvelous way—especially if those same men cry out (as many are accustomed to do) that it is all over...

<page-num>247</page-num>

<meta>catchword: for</meta>

<margin>...for the points to be proved; they patronize the cause of Unbelief beyond their own intention.</margin>

...with those truths and with the whole of Religion, if the arguments brought forward are not admitted. Everyone sees that these things are not to be taken as if those Theologians intended to use weak arguments on purpose; for no one in whom there is a grain of good sense, and in whom there is any reverence for the Deity, would ever do this. Therefore, they sin against their own intention while they believe that there is solid strength in those arguments they use to prove those truths. 

Anyone can see how easily this can happen. Namely, it usually happens either by a certain weakness of judgment, a lack of examination, a love for their Teachers, or from other causes, that we admit these or those arguments as if they were firm enough. We stand and fight for their truth, even though, after a new examination is undertaken, we later discover that there is in reality no power of proof in them, and that we have been deceived by a certain appearance of truth. No one who has ever devoted himself with care to the more serious disciplines will fail to testify that this has happened to himself. 

But if a man who loves the truth discovers that he has been deceived, he lets these arguments go for the future and is anxious to bring better and stronger ones into the open. There are, however, many who admit and bravely defend all the arguments heard and received in their youth; indeed, they contend with no small Zeal that if these are not admitted, it is all over with the most holy heads of Religion. These men, by acting in this way, do not attack errors, but often render them invincible; they do not root them out, but spread them widely; they do not remove them, but propagate them in a marvelous way. 

For if others, seeing more sharply, clearly perceive that there is no solid strength in those arguments, and yet they cannot bring forward stronger ones either by their own wit or by the help of others, they begin to doubt the truth of the most excellent things themselves. The greater the Zeal with which certain people defend these weak arguments, the more those people who are inclined toward Unbelief—or who have long been seized by this vice—are confirmed in their opinions. They assert that if these truths rested upon such immovable foundations, the Theologians who have spent a lifetime in such studies would use those arguments which no one could reasonably contradict. The question is not whether Unbelievers reason correctly in this way or not. Rather, the question is only whether, by acting thus, it can easily happen that many fall into the vice of Unbelief—which perhaps no one familiar with these matters will call into doubt. It is not my intention to prove this thesis by an induction of many Examples. These things are well enough known to those who are versed in the Literary History of Theology and Philosophy. <page-num>248</page-num>
<header>MEDITATION VI.</header>

...reasoning, with *Descartes* <note>original: "Cartesii"</note> attributing incredible force to certain arguments for demonstrating the existence of God, and the *Illustrious Wolff* <note>original: "Wolfii," referring to Christian Wolff (1679–1754), a major Enlightenment philosopher</note> repudiating certain commonly used arguments and showing another way of demonstrating the truth. I do not wish to bring forward other examples, because many people, despite the great light of literature available, insist on those arguments they learned as beardless youths; they are not so inflamed by a love of the truth that they are willing to lend an empty ear to those asserting better things.

This evil is increased because, in Theological Systems, arguments drawn from less-than-certain hypotheses are often employed to prove, illustrate, and defend various essential articles of faith—hypotheses which are nevertheless sold as certain truths. It is well known, and confirmed by daily experience, that the principles of Philosophy (both certain and uncertain alike) have been used for many centuries in Theological Systems to confirm Religion. From this, many inconveniences have arisen, to say nothing of bitter disputes and innumerable contests. Many have begun to doubt the weight of this or that article of religion when they perceived that this or that hypothesis or philosophical argumentation had been convicted of being false by others. I am not one who would wish to see Philosophy and the cultivation of right reason entirely separated from Religion; on the contrary, I believe that whatever can be sought from those most noble disciplines to prove and establish Religion ought to be asserted. I would wish, however, that learned men would properly distinguish those things which are certain and evident from those which are built upon mere hypotheses. I would wish that, once the truth of the Christian Religion and the necessary articles of Natural Religion have been duly proven, they would be drawn out from Holy Scripture, explained, and placed in a clear light through the principles of correct Philology <note>The study of language in historical sources</note> and the application of genuine rules of Interpretation, rather than being proven through certain uncertain hypotheses or arguments sought from reason that have not yet been raised to a solid degree of evidence. But who will bring a remedy to this disease? Certainly not I, for I clearly foresee that most will always use the same method of teaching that has been employed until now. What can be said of Theologians can also be applied—and perhaps with greater justice, as they are more numerous than Academic Doctors—to **Ministers of the Word of God.** <term>V. D. M. (Verbi Divini Minister)</term> It is the duty of public speakers <note>preachers</note> as much as Professors to explain and prove the heads of theoretical and practical Religion necessary to be known or believed. To perform this, they ought to use clear arguments suited to the temperaments of all. And this must be observed by them all the more because most listeners acquiesce in those arguments they have heard publicly; but if it happens otherwise,

<meta>catchword: happens,</meta>

happens, and light and weak reasons are brought forward to prove truths of the greatest importance, not only can no solid persuasion be born in the minds of the listeners, but even those who see more sharply and detect the weakness of the arguments will often call the truths themselves into doubt, or plainly deny that they are certain. It must not be denied—and for this reason I proclaim the happiness of our century—that today a great number of sacred orations <note>sermons</note> are published, elaborated with such precision <note>original: $\alpha\kappa\rho\iota\beta\epsilon\iota\alpha$ (akribeia)</note> that they are worthy of being read even by the most learned men. There are available the sacred discourses of the most learned *Englishmen*, *Frenchmen*, *Germans*, and *Swiss*, in which the principal heads of Natural and Christian Religion are not only explained in a plain and clear style, but are also proven by firm and most solid reasons. Indeed, there is no doubt that such sacred orations are not only heard with great fruit where they are held publicly, but are also read privately at home. And would that more people took delight in the reading of such books! For in this way, Religion would take deeper roots in the minds of men than we—alas!—see happening. This notwithstanding, no one perhaps will deny that there are many Ministers in the Protestant congregations who use very little care in proving the articles of heavenly doctrine. I shall say nothing of those who use "meteors of speech," <note>Flashy or ostentatious rhetoric</note> similes, and allegories in place of arguments, and marvelously applaud themselves for it. That this method of preaching pleased many Englishmen in the last century was shown by the learned English theologian *Eachard* <note>John Eachard (c. 1636–1697), author of "The Grounds and Occasions of the Contempt of the Clergy"</note> in his booklet *On the Causes of the Contempt of the Ministry and Religion*, where he brought forward many plainly ridiculous examples; and *Burnet* <note>Likely Gilbert Burnet (1643–1715), a prominent historian and Bishop</note> also complained in the History of his times about the same perverse way of delivering sacred orations. Of these, I say, I shall say nothing. But there are **Ministers of the Word** to whom it is all the same what they say; whatever arguments they find seem weighty enough to them to prove what they intend. They think that for the sake of the common people they need not devote time to sharp meditation; they have no or little regard for order, no selection of arguments, and they often bring forward the weakest reasons to prove the most serious articles of religion. Where this evil originates is not difficult to say. (*) Many are destitute of a more accurate knowledge of Religion,

In this case, however, the Catholic <note>original: "Pontificiis," referring to the Roman Catholic Church</note> Teachers sin far more gravely than the Protestants. Hence the great crowd of Unbelievers in such places. For on one hand, many are either refined by philosophical disciplines or so equipped by a certain natural goodness of talent that they can easily discern the true from the false; yet at the same time, they have so little taste for the true Religion handed down by Christ and the Apostles that they cannot rightly distinguish it from superstition. Hence, for the most part, they fall into the vice of Unbelief...

VI. There are, moreover, Theologians and Ministers of the Divine Word <note>original: "V. D. M." for Verbi Divini Minister</note> who often, having no regard for it, think so despicably of reason that they claim it is blind, foolish, and deceitful when dealing with matters pertaining to Religion. They believe that the more they depress reason, the more ready men will be to receive the most serious chapters of Religion; in this, however, they are vehemently deceived. For nothing can make Religion more suspicious to a wise man than if it is said that it cannot be admitted or held as true if you wish to subject it to the decrees of right reason. Indeed, this is the very thing that unbelievers intend and strive for with all their might <note>original: "pedibusque et manibus," literally "with feet and hands"</note>; for they say that, things being so, they cannot subscribe to the Christian Religion. Thus it is well known that *Pierre Bayle* <note>A hugely influential skeptical philosopher (1647–1706) known for his "Historical and Critical Dictionary"</note>, thinking more freely than is proper about many chapters of Religion, wished among other things to prove that there is a perpetual conflict between reason and Religion. He thought that once this thesis was admitted, the truth of Revelation would be finished, or at least few who care for the cultivation of reason would think highly of Religion. All those who have applied themselves to opposing him have noted this: *Leibniz*, *Pfaff*, *Crousaz*, *Jaquelot*, *Le Clerc*, and many others. And certainly, whoever seriously attends to the business at hand will easily perceive that it cannot be otherwise than that such vague and ridiculous declamations made against reason turn the minds of wise men away from the love of religion and wonderfully confirm Unbelievers in their opinions. (**)

(**) I shall bring forward only one testimony to confirm my opinion, namely that of a most grave man, *Tillotson*, formerly the most worthy Archbishop of Canterbury. *The Illustrious Beausobre* the son, in the preface to the 7th volume of Sacred Sermons, presents his words translated from the English language into the French idiom; hear them: "Before" (he says) "coming to the proofs that I propose to allege to convince the Unbelievers, I believe it is appropriate to dispel, if possible, a prejudice that has been conceived against all those who work to make Religion reasonable. One would say that Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a Cardinal and influential defender of Catholic doctrine</note> was right when he said that it would be better to define faith as ignorance rather than knowledge; which means in plain French <note>original: "en bon François"</note> that if men believe the Gospel, it is for lack of good sense, and that if they were more enlightened, one would see no Christians at all. I do not know where this prejudice can come from, whether it is a trick of the Popish party, which hates the light because it fears it will be condemned and made known, or if it has its source in the ignorance of a great number of well-intentioned Protestants; I do not know, I say, where this prejudice comes from, but unfortunately it exists, and as soon as one undertakes to give a reason for his faith and to establish Religion on solid foundations, immediately one brands a man with the odious title of Socinian <note>A term of abuse for rationalist Christians who were often accused of denying the Trinity</note>. We have a sad example of this in the incomparable Chil-..."

<header>MEDITATION VI.</header>
<meta>catchword: word-</meta>

...If one asks what Theologians and Philosophers mean by the name of reason, let them be heard. Specifically, by reason *firstly* they understand that faculty of the mind by whose help we perceive the connection of any proposition. We use this faculty in the examination of things both divine and human. Without it, we can prove or deny no proposition. Therefore, he who asserts that this faculty is plainly blind and unfit for conducting an examination of Religion must, by this very fact, concede not only that true religion cannot be discerned from false, but also that all the safeguards by which the truth of Religion can be proved have been taken away from us. What could be more foolish—indeed, what is more impious—than to maintain this? Why then, if such is the case, do these men dispute and rail against Heretics and Unbelievers, if reason, taken in this sense, is so deceptive and uncertain? Secondly, by reason they understand Metaphysical axioms and the first principles of Natural Theology <note>Natural Theology refers to knowledge of God obtained through observed facts and experience apart from divine revelation.</note>, by whose help we prove the Christian religion; that is, the complex of certain truths which we can acquire for ourselves concerning God and divine matters without Revelation. But who, if we take reason in this sense, could again prove with any appearance of truth that it is deceptive and plainly blind? For if it were so, not only would all principles of correct reasoning be removed, but it would also be impossible to demonstrate the truth of the Christian Religion. But if these men mean by the name of reason the false opinions received from infancy and perverse reasonings, then indeed it is true that reason taken in this sense is blind and deceptive; but beyond the fact that perceptive Theologians and Philosophers, when they speak of the use of reason in matters regarding Religion, never take the word "reason" in that sense; they ought to have defined in clear and transparent words what they understood by reason before they declaimed against it with such Zeal and mental strain. If anywhere, certainly here one must proceed cautiously, and all...

---

> Chillingworth <note>William Chillingworth (1602–1644), an English theologian known for his argument that the Bible is the sole source of authority, famously stating "The Bible, the Bible only, is the religion of Protestants."</note>, the glory of our Century and our Nation: for no other reason than having undertaken to make Religion reasonable, and to discover its solid foundations (a design he executed with as much dignity as success), he was paid with the stinging title I spoke of, that of Socinian <note>Socinians were followers of a 16th-century rationalist theology that denied the Trinity and the divinity of Christ; the term was often used as a slur for anyone over-emphasizing reason in faith.</note>. But there is no middle ground: if being a Socinian means deepening the foundations of Religion, and trying to discover reasons that can convince us of the obligation we have to believe it, then all sensible people, accustomed to reflecting, and who are above what is called Fanaticism and Enthusiasm, must be either Socinians or Atheists. I do not see how one can do a worse service to the Christian Religion than to destroy the solid foundations on which it is supported, by spreading through the world the idea that one must believe without reason. Is this not converting Faith into Credulity, and putting Religion on a level with the most despicable dreams, and those most destitute of common sense?

<page-num>253</page-num>
<header>ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.</header>
<sig>Ii 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: na-</meta>

...obscurity and ambiguity of words must be avoided. Wise Theologians and Philosophers grant that there are many things both in nature and in Revelation which the power of reason cannot reach; they grant that there are very many things which, after they have been revealed, are nevertheless known imperfectly: they confess, finally, that the accepted distinction between those things which are *above* and those which are *against* reason is built upon a solid foundation, even if Mr. Bayle <note>Pierre Bayle (1647–1706), a philosopher famous for his "Historical and Critical Dictionary" and his skeptical views on the compatibility of reason and faith.</note> denies it. But with these points established and conceded, nothing is taken away from the authority of reason; rather, its power and utility are placed in full light in this way. Would that all, as many as are consecrated to the Holy Ministry, would diligently devote themselves to the cultivation of reason, which is obtained by the help of philosophical disciplines, and would direct all the powers of reason toward proving, explaining, and commending Religion to others. For it could not happen otherwise than that, being simultaneously animated by piety and assisted by divine help, they would not only perceive a singular utility for themselves from this study, but would also lead more people to the love of religion and the pursuit of piety.

However, those who think so meanly of reason are accustomed to appeal to certain passages of Scripture to seek protection for their opinions. Among these, the passage of Paul the Apostle in 2 Corinthians 10:5 stands out, where among other gifts with which he and his colleagues were equipped, he mentions that they are able to "take every thought captive to the obedience of Christ" <note>original Greek: αἰχμαλωτίζειν πᾶν νόημα εἰς τὴν ὑπακοὴν τοῦ Χριστοῦ</note>. But the late Stephen Vitus <note>original: "ὁ Μακαρίτης Steph. Vitus," likely referring to the scholar Stephen White</note>, a most learned man, has established in a singular dissertation on this passage—which is inserted in the *Library of Bremen, Class II, book III*—that nothing is found in these words that could lead to the contempt of reason. He contends that the version of Blessed Luther and others who follow him, by which they translate those words, "every thought" <note>original Greek: πᾶν νόημα (pan noēma)</note>, as "all reason" <note>original German: "alle Vernunft"</note>, is not genuine, relying both on the meaning of the word "thought" and indeed on the definition of reason itself. He understands by reason the same thing we do: namely, both the faculty of intuiting the connection of some proposition, and the complex of truths which we can acquire for ourselves concerning God and divine matters by the help of reason; in a word, the theoretical and practical principles of Natural Theology. This Dissertation, as I have understood from the philological works of the celebrated Wolfius <note>Johann Christoph Wolf (1683–1739), a German Hebraist and philologist.</note> on this passage, was attacked by the Reverend Boernerus <note>Christian Friedrich Börner (1683–1753), a professor of theology at Leipzig.</note>; with what success I cannot say, as I have not seen or weighed it. I am firmly persuaded, however, that neither the most learned Boernerus nor anyone else will prove from Holy Letters that reason—in the sense in which we have defined it—is to be cast aside or neglected by a person desiring salvation and seriously occupied in the examination of religion, either in general or in certain articles in particular. To do so would be to discard all the safeguards on which the Christian Religion rests.

<header>MEDITATION VI.</header>

...divine truth, they would be subverted. Speaking generally about this argument, we say that all controversies concerning the use of reason in Theology for the most part turn into a **war of words** <note>original: "logomachian"</note>, because scholars make the definition of the word "reason" sometimes broader and sometimes stricter. Yet all agree among themselves on this: that humans have the faculty of comparing ideas with one another; that certain axioms of eternal truth are given; that the mind can, by the help of reasoning, gather several propositions concerning God and divine matters; and that contradictions and things contrary to divine virtues neither can nor ought to be believed. Regarding these points, there is no dispute or contention among most Christians. However, when it comes down to this or that specific dogma, they begin to move in different directions—not because of a disagreement about these principles, but because of the application of those same principles to certain specific articles of faith. For one person asserts that this or that dogma is contradictory, while another denies it; then indeed, when the blame ought to rather be laid on the zeal of parties and sects, one side or the other must bear the fault.

Hence, I am surprised that the celebrated **Wolff** <note>Christian Wolff (1679–1754), a major German Enlightenment philosopher</note> attributes to the Reformed, as if it were **something peculiar to them** <note>original: "privum quid"</note>, the contention that by the name of **every thought** <note>original: "pantos noematos," referring to 2 Corinthians 10:5</note> one cannot understand "reason" in every sense. For I am persuaded that this most learned man, if he had wished to explain his own mind and attend to the definition of reason used by **Vitus**, would have agreed with us. I gather this from the warnings he gave against the celebrated **Elsner**. When the latter had spoken at this passage, among other things, as follows: *The sense is not, as people commonly think, that it is a sin for believers to use considered and evident reason in matters of faith; rather, it is that once reason is suppressed, whatever it may teach to the contrary, one might admit monsters of interpretation with mind and eyes closed and believe them piously.* The Reverend **Wolff** objects, saying: *If by these words he wished to prick the opinion of our own theologians—which I suspect not without reason—he either is ignorant of their mind or interprets it poorly.* From these words, it seems to be gathered that he did not want reason to be proscribed in the sense in which we take this word, and thus he agrees with the famous **Elsner** and other Reformed thinkers.

However, so that we may rightly understand his mind, he appeals to **Zeltner** and **Boerner**, and likewise to **Fecht’s** examination of the theology of the Indifferentists <note>Indifferentists were those who held that religious differences were of no importance or that all religions were equally valid</note>. I have consulted them all, but from those things they discuss, I could not conclude that they think Paul understood "reason" by the name of **thought** <note>original: "noematos"</note> according to the definition given above. The Reverend **Boerner** understands by **the thought** <note>original: "to noema"</note> carnal desires or plans which exalt themselves against the knowledge of God: *but we do not wish such desires to be understood by the name of reason, although we do not call the matter itself into question.* **Ruarus**, in a letter given to **Calovius** (page 179 of his *Letters*), expresses his mind thus: *A "noema" is not reason, but a thought; which, since sometimes they are rightly*

agreeable to **reason**, yet sometimes proceed from the sense of the flesh; the Apostle wants the latter, not the former, to be led captive, as appears from the preceding context. Since this is the case, reason is not thrust into a prison, but rather asserted into liberty. What does **the late** <note>original: "ho Makaritēs," a Greek term of respect for the deceased</note> famous **Zeltner** say to this? *It is so,* (he says) *but what that sense of the flesh is—namely, that which is rebellious to the faith of Christ—is what is being investigated here.* For no one rejects reason **Note Well: as it is sound and right**, and when it modestly stays within its just limits. In our judgment, however, reason is always sound if we follow the given definition; for it stays within its limits as long as it does this one thing: to weigh the connection of propositions. On page 168, the same **Zeltner**, treating the same argument, says: *Whichever way you turn, or in whatever way you render the word* **thought** <note>original: "noematos"</note>, *it must certainly be confessed that nothing else is denoted than the judgments of reason—sound in itself, Note Well, but corrupted regarding matters of faith.* Therefore, **the late scholar** confesses that reason is sound in itself (that is, the faculty of judging is sound); he distinguishes that from corrupt judgments about matters of faith; therefore Zeltner agrees with us.

It is also necessary, therefore, that the celebrated **Wolff**, who appealed to **Zeltner** as being **of the same opinion** <note>original: "homopsēphon"</note>, subscribe to our sentiment. In **Fecht**, I find nothing that can bring greater light to this argument; he introduces an Indifferentist who understands reason to mean "disputations about sacred matters." He rejects this interpretation, saying: *reason is said to exalt itself against the knowledge of God; and thus the knowledge of the intellect from Holy Scripture is presupposed.* Disputation about sacred matters cannot be opposed to this knowledge, since it does not exalt itself above knowledge, but defends and vindicates the same. If I see anything clearly, this is what **Fecht** means: that the faculty of the mind weighing arguments about divine things is good in itself and not contrary to religion. And certainly **Cicero**, even in his own time, saw that the definition of reason should be taken in this way, when in Book I of *On Duties* <note>original: "de Officiis"</note>, Chapter IV, opening his mind thus, he says: *Man, because he is a participant in reason, through which he discerns consequences, sees the causes of things and is not ignorant of their progress and, as it were, their antecedents, compares similarities, and joins and annexes future things to present things.*

But so that it may be even more clearly established that there is no discrepancy between our Lutheran Brothers and our own [Reformed] regarding the use of reason, I appeal to the famous **Buddeus**, a name no less pleasing to them than to us. He explains his mind on this argument in his *Institutes of Theology* (page 157) as follows: *It must be observed,* (he says) *that the meaning of this word* (namely, reason) *is twofold. For either the human intellect itself is denoted by this name with its faculties and operations; or certain axioms or universal propositions so evident...*
