<header>MEDITATION VI.</header>

...so that none of them can be doubted for their truth; these are usually called principles. This is the same thing others say: that reason can be viewed either **subjectively** or **objectively**. If this term is taken in the former way—and considered as it actually exists in human beings after the Fall <note>original: "post lapsum," referring to the theological concept of human nature becoming corrupted after the sin of Adam</note>—we freely admit that in natural things (a category in which we include both moral and civil matters), although reason suffers from various weaknesses and infirmities and easily wanders from the right path, it is not entirely stripped of all power to know the truth. For daily experience teaches us all this. 

In divine matters, however, which must be spiritually <note>original: "πνευματικῶς" (pneumatikos)</note> discerned, reason left to itself is blind (2 Corinthians 4:4), obscured and wrapped in darkness (Ephesians 4:18, 5:8), so much so that the natural man <note>original: "ψυχικὸς" (psychikos), referring to a person not guided by the Holy Spirit</note> is unable to perceive any of the things that are of the Spirit of God (1 Corinthians 2:14). Indeed, since the intellect of such people is subject to the dominion of depraved desires, it cannot help but reject, condemn, and repudiate what the Holy Spirit teaches concerning God's Plan for leading humans to salvation, so much so that it seems like mere foolishness to him (1 Corinthians 2:14). Reason accepted in this way is so far from being a "principle of knowing" in Theology that the Holy Scriptures themselves teach it must rather be restrained and taken captive (Compare chapter 8:6-7; 2 Corinthians 10:5; compared with Romans 16:26; Colossians 2:8). 

Meanwhile, no one of sound mind would reject the instrumental <note>original: "organicum," meaning a functional tool or organ of the mind</note> use of reason even when accepted in this way; for reason, however blind and corrupt, still remains reason, by which a human knows, judges, and argues. Its use is required in all things that can and should be known, and thus also in Theology; for without reason—or the intellect and its faculties—nothing at all can be understood or known. If, therefore, reason is corrected, amended, and bathed in divine light, it correctly knows and discerns even the things of the Spirit of God; this is the very beginning of faith and thus of salvation itself. 

Furthermore, if by "reason" one means the "principles of reason," we must first look closely at whether they truly deserve this name. For it often happens, especially in matters pertaining to the practice of life, that people form certain rules of living that correspond to their depraved desires, which they then wrongly hawk as "principles of reason." Truly such principles are either formal, as they are accustomed to say in the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to Scholasticism, the traditional medieval and early modern method of academic logic and philosophy</note>, or material. The former, since they regard the form and manner of proper arguing, must be used daily in Theology just as in other sciences. For without them, no proof or demonstration could proceed correctly. But since the object upon which these principles exercise their power must come from elsewhere, it is manifest that these principles do not count when one is searching for a "principle of knowing"—that is, a source in which all conclusions are contained. Material principles are varied, according to the variety of the parts that constitute philosophy; some pertain to

<meta>catchword: Theo-</meta>

<column-break/>

<page-num>257</page-num>
<header>ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.</header>

Natural Theology <note>The study of God based on reason and nature rather than divine revelation</note>, others to Physics, and finally others to practical Philosophy. While the first of these find the most place here, it must be observed of all of them that they are confined within their own limits, which they cannot exceed. For these principles are formed from clear and distinct ideas which the consideration of things provides us. Thus far spoke the blessed **Buddeus** <note>Johann Franz Buddeus (1667–1729), a prominent Lutheran theologian known for his moderate views</note>. 

From what has been cited, it is most clear that Buddeus concedes two things to us: namely, that even after the Fall, there remains in every human the faculty of judging divine as well as human matters, and this cannot be taken away by any means; and further, that certain principles of Natural Theology are given, which humans must use in the demonstration of theological truths. And this is what we encompass under the name of "reason." What he adds regarding reason being captured by depraved opinions and the limits of Natural Theology, we do not deny, but rather concede. From all this we conclude that between our Lutheran brothers and our own theologians, there is no true disagreement regarding the use of reason, but a mere **war of words** <note>original: "logomachiam"</note>. 

It also follows, if these learned men are to be consistent with themselves, that Paul could not have meant "reason" itself by the term "thoughts" <note>original: "νοήματα" (noemata)</note>, according to the definition of reason given by us and conceded by them—to say nothing of those brothers who follow the illustrious **Wolff's** <note>Christian Wolff (1679–1754), a leading Enlightenment philosopher whose logical method was controversial in theology</note> way of philosophizing and who agree with us in the definition of reason. (Compare Chapter 12 of the *Examination of the Theology of P. Bayle*, written by the celebrated **Jaquelot** <note>Isaac Jaquelot (1647–1708), a French Protestant who defended religion against the skepticism of Pierre Bayle</note>, in which he explains the opinions of Reformed theologians regarding the use of reason in Theology). What we have said should be applied to all those passages from Holy Scripture that are typically cited by some against reason.

<margin>The extremely bitter contests and brawls of theologians over matters of lesser importance contribute much to this.</margin>

### VII

Moreover, there is no doubt that those innumerable brawls and contentions—often regarding matters of no or very little importance, conducted with great heat of spirit—have led many to a contempt for all religion. Anyone who reads only what has been disputed within the Protestant groups themselves since the time of the Reformation regarding various arguments (which you can find narrated at great length in the works of writers of Theological Literary History, such as **Pfaff**, **Buddeus**, **Walch**, and others) will discover with astonishment that men have often disputed with the greatest heat and intolerable bitterness of words, setting aside all laws of gentleness and prudence. They fought either over things that ended in mere wars of words, or over arguments of minor weight and less fundamental importance—matters upon which it should have been permissible to disagree while preserving the friendship that ought to flourish among brothers. Since no educated person today is ignorant of what we are saying, there is no need for a lengthy list of examples. What little weight exists in most of the controversies that—

### MEDITATION VI.
### ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

It is now well known to everyone that in the previous century, various opinions were debated among Reformed theologians, especially those in the Netherlands <note>original: "Belgas," referring to the Low Countries/Netherlands</note>. However, at that time, when theologians were occupied in the heat of disputes and fervor, those questions were debated with such mental strain and such passion that you would have thought the very essence of the entire Religion was at stake. *What disputes* (these are the words of <term>the late</term> <note>original: "του Μακαρίτου" (tou Makaritou), a Greek honorific for the deceased</note> most celebrated Werenfels, from his work *On the Word-Wars of the Learned*, page 483) *with the stubborn Jewish nation, with the impure followers of Muhammad, with blasphemers, with Libertines, with Atheists, and mockers of all religion, were ever as combative as those recent word-wars—whether pure or mixed—which we mentioned above in Chapters II and III, occurring both in other Academies and Schools, and especially in the Netherlands? Envy laughed; malice exulted; rivals mocked us, not without great joy, regarding the "double kappa"* <note>original: "διπλᾶν κάππα" (diplan kappa). This likely refers to the "Cocceians" and "Krabbe" or "Kortholt," or a similar academic pun on rival factions starting with 'K' or 'C' in Dutch theology</note> *infesting the Netherlands; there were those who plucked "choice blossoms"—that is, formulas for insults—from the books written about these controversies. Truly, just as quarrels between brothers and neighbors, whenever they are ignited, are usually the most burning: so you might most truly say that between those who are closest in their opinions, and even those who differ sometimes only in words, the most heated altercations usually occur.* What <term>the late</term> <note>original: "ὁ Μακαρίτης" (ho Makarites)</note> lamented as happening among Dutch theologians could also be said of many contentions and controversies stirred up in Germany. The *Spenerian* controversies <note>refers to the disputes over Pietism involving Philipp Jakob Spener</note> alone, to say nothing of many others, can provide sad examples of this matter. Alas, with what great emotional disturbance were those debated! With how many slanders was that learned and pious man attacked, along with those who stood on his side? And who does not know—indeed, who does not deplore with hot tears—that those who agree on fundamental matters necessary to be known for salvation (I mean, of course, the Lutheran and Reformed brothers), have very frequently and shamefully torn each other apart with mutual insults? And that in refuting opinions they consider erroneous, some have set no limit? Truly, it cannot be expressed in words how much evil has overflowed into Republics, Churches, and the civil life of men from insane brawls of this kind. For in fighting this way, the love of neighbor is wounded, which nonetheless, by the testimony of the Infallible Teacher Jesus Christ, is the banner and most important character of Christianity. In John Chapter XIII:35, He says: *By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another* <note>original Greek: "Εν τούτω γνώσονται πάντες ότι εμοί μαθηταί εστε, εάν αγάπην έχητε έν αλλήλοις"</note>. Between the closest friends and brothers, the bond of brotherhood is broken by factions arising from disagreements—

<column-break/>

—and everything is disturbed by foul quarrels, and the most healthy counsels, which tend solely toward the benefit of Churches and Schools, are thus rejected. After others, the wise theologian J. F. Buddeus frankly confessed this very thing while he was alive in his *Introduction to Theological History*, Volume II, page 1424. *The history itself* (he says) *of theological battles through all the centuries from the birth of Christ down to our own age, could easily throw someone into a stupor. Now, if someone should further consider with what great emotional disturbance people have fought—not rarely over matters of no or little importance—or how many sharp contentions vanished into mere word-wars* <note>original: "λογομαχίας" (logomachias)</note>; *if he weighs that even those who stood for the truth have occasionally defended it with inept and frivolous reasons, or used slanders, insults, and outrages instead of reasons, or used wretched sophistries; if he reflects that very often one side attributed an opinion to the other that was entirely foreign to it, or that both sides, having not correctly established the state of the question, "beat the air," and other things of the same kind; he will find that he has the most just causes for deploring the wretched lot of mortals—who achieve nothing with such great effort, but rather bind themselves with the gravest sins, and hinder the fruits of the truth for which they boast themselves to be champions—and for deploring at the same time the foul and dirty face of the Church, involved in this way in perpetual disturbances and wars. For truly, since men ought to be moved through the knowledge of truth revealed by God toward faith, and from there toward the study of a holy life and the cultivation of peace and concord with all people, everything is instead filled with anger, hatred, and malice by these wars and perpetual battles. The minds of many are carried away so that they think of anything rather than what the serious pursuit of obtaining salvation requires.* And since those who are the authors of such unnecessary battles wish to seem to be watching over salvation, it usually happens that they themselves not only lose salvation along with the truth, but also drag others with them into destruction. And so, what ought to have been a remedy for repelling errors and preserving truth is, in the view of many, turned into a poison by which they must perish. See his own commentary *On the Study of Polemical Theology to be Conducted Solidly and Soberly*, which is found in his *Collection of Theological Dissertations*. (*)

---

(*) What the illustrious *Tillotson*—a theologian, if ever there was one, learned and perceptive—thought about those disputes and the unnecessary battles of the brothers, the Reverend *Burnet* explains in the *Funeral Oration* held for this great man, page 76, volume 1 of Tillotson's Sermons. *He estimated* (he says) *that the great goal of Christianity is to reform and rectify human nature, to direct our actions, to repress our desires and our passions, to soften our inclinations and our temperaments, to regulate our affections, to detach our spirits from the interests and follies of this present age, and to raise them to the hope and pursuit of eternal happiness. The body of Christian doctrine appeared to him...* <note>original: French quote from Gilbert Burnet's funeral oration for John Tillotson</note>

The author cites prominent scholars like Werenfels, Buddeus, and Tillotson to argue that such disputes prioritize ego and terminology over the true goal of faith: the reformation of human nature.</summary>

### MEDITATION VI.

And as for the controversies agitated—alas!—with such great heat of spirit among the Protestants themselves, learned men have shown that these have been a stumbling block not only to Roman Catholics <note>original: "Pontificiis"</note> and the Greeks <note>Eastern Orthodox Christians</note>, but even to the Jews and Muslims <note>original: "Mahumedanis"</note>. A shining witness to this fact is Johann Heinrich Hottinger, the most celebrated theologian of Zurich <note>original: "Tigurinus"</note>. In his *Assertion of the Reasons Recommending Ecclesiastical Peace*, published at Heidelberg in 1656, on page 13, he declares the following: "The ministers of the Church are called 'Evangelists of Peace' <note>original: "Ἐυαγγελιζόμενοι εἰρήνην" (Euangelizomenoi eirēnēn); see Romans 10:15 and Isaiah 52:7</note>. But if they themselves now stir up lawsuits, how great an 'Iliad of evils' <note>A classical metaphor for a long series of disasters</note> follows? Who does not know that by the schism of the Protestants, not only the West but also the Entire East has been offended and shaken? For nothing deters men from the Gospel as much as our discord," writes Philip Melanchthon, the common teacher of Germany <note>original: "Germaniæ Præceptor"</note>, to Bucer in the year 1535. I have a letter from the Illustrious Philip, Landgrave of Hesse, written at Speyer in the year 1529 to Zwingli and signed by Philip's own hand, in which he says among other things: <note>original German: "Dann auf diesem Reichstag die N. N. zu Erhaltung ihres verkehrlichen Lebens sich nicht zu behelffen vvis-sen, dann dafs vvir, die dem reinen lautern Wort Gottes anhangen, unter einandern selbst nicht eines Verstands feyen: sonst vväre denen Dingen leichtlich zu rahten."</note> "For at this Diet, the [opponents] do not know how to help themselves in maintaining their perverse way of life, except by pointing out that we, who cling to the pure and clear Word of God, are not of one mind among ourselves; otherwise, these matters would be easily settled." The persistence of this evil has even reached the Greeks, Jews, and Muslims. Regarding the Greeks, one may consult the *Acts of Jeremiah, Patriarch of Constantinople*, page 377. Concerning the Jews, the author of *Response to the Problems concerning the Plans for Ecclesiastical Peace to be Undertaken* speaks on page 6: "I testify by our hope in Jesus Christ, that this very thing was thrown in my face and used as a reproach by the enemies of the faith, the Jews, as an argument that Christ has not yet come." That our dissensions are not unknown to the Arabs or Muslims is clear from this: when the most famous Pococke <note>Edward Pococke (1604–1691), an English Orientalist</note> once spent effort on a translation of Hugo Grotius’s book *On the Truth of the Christian Religion* <note>Grotius's famous work of apologetics</note>, nothing interfered with his efforts more strikingly than our domestic evils and internal contentions,

---

[The author] showed a system of principles which all clearly tend toward that end. He regarded disputes over matters of little consequence, or over subtleties related to matters of the highest importance, as one of the greatest artifices used by the power of darkness to ruin the true ends of the Son of God’s coming into the world. He saw clearly that disputes lead into very dry discussions accompanied by great animosity: so that, while people heat themselves up to form factions and make their opinions prevail, they relax more and more in the practice of the great Duties, which are the principal goal of the Christian Religion. Thus says the celebrated Burnet <note>Gilbert Burnet (1643–1715), Bishop of Salisbury</note>. Henry Wotton <note>An English diplomat and author</note>, likewise a learned Englishman, ordered this epitaph to be placed for himself in his will: *Here lies the first author of this sentence: THE ITCH FOR DISPUTING IS THE SCAB OF THE CHURCHES.* Search elsewhere for the name; see the *Leipzig Acts, Supplement Vol. 1*, page 84.

### ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.
<sig>Kk 3</sig>

concerning which the Muslims, warned by apostates <note>Converts from Christianity to Islam</note>, tell us to stay at home with our own kind. And this was once related to me in Paris by Hugo Grotius himself. He who is well-versed in the histories of the Arabs cannot be ignorant of the fact that the greatest growth of Muhammadanism came from the dissensions of Christians, a matter we noted in *Oriental History*, Book III, chapters 1 and 2. Let us therefore beware, as much as possible, lest that "Woe" denounced by the Savior against the man through whom scandal comes (Matthew 18:7) should fall upon our own heads. Thus says Hottinger. The words of the Blessed Zwingli to Luther in his *Exegesis of the Eucharist* are also notable: "I pray," he says, "that there has been enough dissent, enough tumult, enough ferocity. Rise up now, most welcome Morning Star; let the Sun of Justice shine forth. For when there is contention, that holiness which You alone require of us is neglected. You see that we never return better from a dispute. For it is a work of the flesh, from which no one can retreat without a stain. On the contrary, those who are strangers to it have always been the best of men." 

But it is not my intention here to deal specifically with the Unhappy Schism which—alas!—stands between us and our Lutheran brothers, nor with the many evils that have arisen from mutual battles. Rather, let us show from those innumerable contentions stirred up over matters of either no moment or minor importance—and the singular fervor with which they were agitated—that Unbelief is promoted to the highest degree. To be sure, men who are neither sufficiently skilled in the art of reasoning nor knowledgeable enough in religion conclude from such a vast number of disputes that it is impossible for Religion to be rested upon certain foundations; otherwise, the Learned, who have spent a lifetime examining those truths and are endowed with singular sharp-wittedness, would easily agree. And when those who are a little more perceptive see that these men cry out and make as much of a "tragic scene" <note>original: "paratragædiari," a term for over-acting or exaggerated drama</note> over matters of minor significance as they do when the Sum of Religion is at stake, they conclude that all articles of Religion are equal—that is, uncertain—because theologians differ so vehemently about every single one. Therefore, they think it suffices if one is content with certain general articles of Natural Religion and lets everything else go. This is certainly how the author of *Essential Religion*, Tyndall <note>Matthew Tindal (1657–1733), author of 'Christianity as Old as the Creation,' a key Deist text</note>, and many others who go by the name of Deists, reason. Furthermore, if they see that those very people who wish to be called defenders of the Christian religion tear each other apart over a difference in minor opinions, and trample all laws of humanity and love under their feet, they judge it impossible that those men could be persuaded of the divine origin of the precepts of Christ, since it is well known how often and with what great arguments the love of neighbor is insisted upon in Holy Scripture. ### MEDITATION VI.

Indeed, all the Dogmatists <note>Those who assert certain truths as settled</note> vehemently disagree among themselves, while the Sceptics rest in that one <term>incomprehensibility</term> <note>original: ἀκαταληψίᾳ (akatalēpsia) — the philosophical position that nothing can be known with certainty</note> of theirs. The question is not whether these men reason correctly, or whether it can be concluded from those disagreements in matters of lesser importance that the fundamental articles of Religion are also uncertain; but rather this: whether that immoderate desire and ardor for disputing over matters of lesser importance, and for anathematizing others, can easily plunge men into the vice of Unbelief, or confirm them in it—a point which I believe no one will easily doubt. At least, the most learned Protestant theologians have judged so before me. Let us hear one or two. *Jenkin Thomasius, a most excellent English theologian, in his History of Atheism, page 13, treating its causes, speaks thus among other things: To this are added the sword-clashes of theologians and the bitterness of spirits, even regarding articles that often concern neither good morals nor eternal life; yet if anyone recedes even a fingernail’s breadth from the received systems, woe to the man! All hope of friendship is finished, and in the Papacy he is to be held as a heretic and punished by being burned alive <note>original: "vivicomburio"</note> unless he sings a retraction <note>original: "palinodiam"</note> as quickly as possible. This way of proceeding undoubtedly imbues the minds of onlookers with a certain coldness, or rather hatred, toward all Religion. Nor are the Protestants to be excused entirely in this part, who by some evil fate—even if they agree well among themselves on all things necessary for salvation—nevertheless attack each other so bitterly with every exertion and dissension of spirit over manufactured articles of faith unknown to the primitive Christians, over things regarding external worship, over the tips of words and syllables, or finally over things far exceeding our grasp. One could easily guess that these infinite quarrels were derived from hatred of an adversary rather than love of the truth. From this, men who feel little kindness toward Religion advise Princes to neglect all religion, asserting that a prince can only obtain perpetual peace and concord in his empire if he strictly prohibits all the quarrels and hateful questions which theologians are accustomed to stir up. For they say from these disputes arise diverse sects which different people join, and thus, stimulated by mutual fights against each other, diverse judgments, hatreds, insults, and slanders are born, which sometimes provide no small occasion for internal war.* I would warn you not to fear that I disapprove of all disputes concerning divine matters; not at all: for often the necessity of the Church and our duties demand this. But there is a limit in things; I would not want Christian men to cut and tear each other apart, lest the profane dance for joy and shout out in insult to Religion, "Where is your God?"

VIII. But this evil—that is, Unbelief—is promoted not only by the multitude of controversies over matters of minor importance, but also by the shameful zeal of those who exaggerate the smallest errors and compare even those who err slightly to loathed Heretics. They imagine that by acting in this way, they will not only be regarded as excellent pillars of orthodoxy, but will also easily triumph over their enemies—that is, those who disagree with them. The question is not whether men who err even less seriously should be warned and freed from their errors; for no one who cares for the truth would doubt this. The question is chiefly by what method it ought to be done. Now, there is no more suitable way of convincing one who errs than if you deal with him calmly and modestly; if you prove by clear arguments not only that he errs, but also at the same time uncover the source and causes of the error; if you suggest that he did not fall into that error out of a bad heart, and so on. In this way it will happen that if the man is able to reason and is possessed by a love of the truth, he will see the error and bid it farewell; or if he does not do so because of the power of preconceived opinions, <term>blindness</term> <note>original: ἀβλεψίαν (ablepsian)</note>, or ambition, he may at least feel kindly toward you and praise your noble and honest sincerity, which is worthy of a Christian man. But alas! sad experience has taught and still teaches that many have neglected and still neglect this most fair way of convincing those who err. There are and have been many theologians and Ministers of the Word of God <note>original: "V. D. M." (Verbi Divini Minister)</note> who have exaggerated very slight errors and turned <term>flies into Elephants</term> <note>A proverbial expression similar to "making a mountain out of a molehill"</note>, and to that end have often compared most innocent men to loathed people, that is, heretics. This method of treating those who err not only drags infinite evils in its wake, but also greatly increases Unbelief. For first, those who purposefully strive to amplify the seriousness of errors through a maze of consequences do a grave injury to the one who errs; they expose him to the fury of the common people and of zealots, and often cast him into the greatest calamities. By this very act, they sin most gravely against the love of neighbor, and thus err far more seriously than the one who subscribed to the erroneous opinion. Secondly, this very way of acting confirms the erring person in his error rather than correcting him, because he clearly sees that these arguments are sought only from envy. Moreover, comparisons of the erring with loathed heretics not only do not recall the erring from their mistakes, but also expose such handlers of controversies to the mockery of the learned. Suppose you call a man who errs slightly in the matter of the "aids of grace" <note>A complex theological debate regarding how God's grace assists human will</note> a Pelagian...

### MEDITATION VI.

...or call him a Semi-Pelagian <note>Followers of a 5th-century doctrine that sought a middle ground between Pelagius (who denied original sin) and Augustine; often used as a theological insult for those emphasizing human free will.</note>, have you therefore convicted him of error? Not at all: for he will reply, "What Pelagius or the Semi-Pelagians believed matters little to me; rather, you should show by clear arguments that I myself have erred." This vice is especially to be blamed when, in sacred sermons, such comparisons are brought before the common people, who shudder at the name of a "Heretic" as if it were some horrendous and giant monster. Certainly, the most learned men among the Protestants have always disapproved of these parallels drawn with ancient heretics.

I will bring forward the judgment of only one man, but one who is most celebrated and learned—namely, the Venerable *Mosheim* <note>Johann Lorenz von Mosheim (1693–1755), a famous German Lutheran church historian known for his objective approach.</note>—regarding this practice of comparing those who wander in thought with hated heretics. In his *Modest Inquiry into the new explanation of the doctrine of the Holy Trinity*, which the distinguished *Paul Maty* recently proposed (page 79), he pronounces the following:

*“With the permission of these most learned men, whose erudition and merits we otherwise venerate, we—though we do not deny that the comparison of old and new sects and errors sometimes brings some utility to disputes—nevertheless believe that for the most part, when the goal is simply to illustrate and defend the truth, it brings more disadvantage than benefit. First, disputes that could have been settled with easier effort are prolonged and amplified by this method. For if the matter is handled this way, the question is no longer merely about the truth or falsehood of a dogma, but other historical controversies are born at the same time, which are extremely entangled and laborious: namely, the history of ancient sects must be explored—which is deeply obscure and hedged in by various difficulties—and one must carefully judge what new errors have in common with those ancient ones, which is not done without long labor. Furthermore, if anyone should successfully finish this labor and show that new sects are entirely similar to ancient ones, he will gain little or no fruit from it toward healing the mind of the one in error or fortifying others against the force of that error. For since the ancients could have erred in assessing the opinions of others (and indeed erred more than once), the fact that the same thing which a man holds as true seemed false to certain ancient councils cannot yet convict him of error. Rather, if he has the talent, he will argue that injustice and envy prevented his ancestors from seeing the truth, and that those whom the councils branded with the mark of heresy were actually healthy and wise. What a wealth of new turmoil is here, which cannot help but disturb the minds of men and lead them away from what was alone necessary toward things of little use!”*

To this is added the fact that the names of ancient Heretics are used today as insults and reproaches, so that, for example, he who is called a *Tritheite* <note>One accused of believing the Trinity consists of three separate gods.</note>, or a *Pelagian*, or a *Sabellian* <note>Followers of Sabellius, who taught that God is one person who appears in three "modes."</note>, is afflicted with almost the same injury
<meta>catchword: as</meta>

---

### ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

as one who is called a monster, a freak of a man, a blockhead, a stump, or a rascal. But our Savior wants all desire for mockery to be absent from Christian disputes, and he forbids men—unhappy enough because of their errors—from being received with new evils of ignominy and injury. *Compare Galatians 6:1, 1 Corinthians 11:16, 2 Timothy 2:24.*

Thus far that learned man. Indeed, the gravest evil that can arise from this type of exaggeration of errors and comparison with hated men (that is, Heretics) is this: men of a somewhat sharper wit, but who care little for truth or piety, see that an injury has been done to these people. They then conclude that all controversies are of the same weight—which is to say, of no weight at all; that they are <term>disputing about goat’s wool</term> <note>original: "de lana caprina" — a classical idiom for arguing over something completely trivial or non-existent.</note> and that all those battles are to be attributed to nothing but <term>theological hatred</term> <note>original: "odio theologico"</note>, etc. In this way, the most holy religion is often exposed to laughter, and the weightiest matters within it—which are necessary to be known or believed by all lovers of truth—are confused with minute opinions. Everything said about ancient Heresies is then regarded as mere "priestly fraud."

And truly, this can easily happen when even orthodox and learned men, having weighed the errors that were thrust upon most innocent men in the age they lived, begin to doubt whether everything said about the Ancient Heretics by the Church Fathers is true or not. The Blessed *Spener* <note>Philipp Jakob Spener (1635–1705), the founder of Pietism, who emphasized personal piety over rigid dogma.</note> testifies that this happened to himself in his *Latin Theological Counsels, Part III, page 187*: *"As often as I weigh,"* he says, *"what is happening and has happened in our time, and recall various slanders to mind, so often do the things which antiquity reports about many heretics become very doubtful to me."*

And many fall into this opinion all the more easily because very few monuments <note>In this context, written records or original works.</note> of the Ancient Heretics have reached our hands, and more often we must judge the minds of these men only from the writings of their enemies. Suppose, for example, that *Spener*, of whom we speak, had lived in the 2nd or 3rd Century after the birth of Christ; suppose all his own writings had perished by the injury of time, or by fraud, etc., and only the accusations of his adversaries remained—who, I ask, would not today consider *Spener* a notorious Heretic, especially if you heard that he had been compared by some glowing zealot to Spinoza? <note>Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677), whose pantheistic philosophy was considered equivalent to atheism by his contemporaries.</note> Indeed, most excellent men who are suspected of no heterodoxy <note>Holding non-standard or unorthodox beliefs.</note> have shown that many errors were very often falsely pinned on ancient Heretics. (*) The celebrated *Mosheim* proved this regarding the ancient *Simonians* <note>Followers of Simon Magus, often cited as the first heretics.</note> (a);

### MEDITATION VI.

...on the *Montanists* <note>A 2nd-century prophetic Christian movement.</note> by *Ittigius* and *Daillé*; (b) on the *Manicheans* by *Beausobre* (c); on *Nestorius* by *Veissiere La Croze*, *Jablonsky*, and *Saligius* (d); and recently on the *Bogomils* <note>A medieval Bulgarian sect.</note> by *Ludwig Oeder*, a most learned young man (e)—not to bring forward more examples. Indeed, how easy certain ancient writers were—even extravagant—in swelling the number of heretics is clear from *Augustine’s* short book *On Heresies*. Mention is made here of the *Artotyrites* <note>original: "Artotyritarum"; from the Greek words for bread (artos) and cheese (tyros).</note> to whom (to use *Augustine’s* words) their offering gave this name; *for they offer bread and cheese, saying that offerings from the fruits of the earth and sheep were celebrated by the first humans.* There are heretics called the *Quartodecimans* <note>original: "Tessaresdecatitæ"; those who observe the "fourteenth" day.</note>, named from the fact that they celebrate Easter only on the fourteenth moon of the month of March, no matter what day of the seven-day week it falls on; and if it falls on a Sunday, they fast and keep watch on that very day. Worthy of the name of heretics are the *Melchizedekians*, who *judge that Melchizedek, the Priest of the most high God, was not a man, but is a power of God.* They are heretics, if you listen to *Augustine*, the *Valezianism*, *who castrate themselves and their guests, thinking in this way they ought to serve God.* In the number of heretics are to be held the *Ascitae*, so called from a wineskin, for <term>askos</term> <note>original: "ἀσκος"</note> is said in Greek, and *uter* in Latin; *whom they describe as going around like revelers with an inflated and covered skin, as if they themselves were the new Evangelical skins, filled with new wine.* Finally, to omit others, the *Pattalorhynchites* <note>original: "Pattalorinchitæ"; from the Greek for "peg" and "snout."</note> are to be referred to the class of heretics if you listen to *Augustine*, *who study silence to such an extent that they place a finger to their noses and lips, lest they even break that very silence with a voice when they judge they must be silent.* Thus says *Augustine*; it is a wonder he did not include among the heretics those who are accustomed to eat cheese without bread. It is commonly known how little credit the learned grant to *Epiphanius* <note>4th-century bishop known for his "Panarion," a massive catalog of heresies often criticized for its inaccuracies.</note> and *Philastrius* in this business. But if the most excellent men among theologians are forced to admit that false errors have been fastened upon many ancients and moderns alike, and that slight opinions have often been peddled as the gravest errors, what wonder is it if men who have a meager knowledge of divine things—or who cannot discern a grave and momentous truth from an erroneous opinion—and who at the same time (as not infrequently happens) burn with a hatred of the clergy; what wonder, I say, if such men finally assert that all controversies are of no importance, and contend that one can dispute on either side of any issue, and that it matters not at last which religion we protect?

<margin>An inquiry is made into the causes of this evil, which we treated in the two preceding sections.</margin>
IX. It helps, however, to inquire a little more diligently into the causes of the evils about which we spoke in the two sections immediately preceding. For once the causes of a disease are detected, the cure will be easier. And I. indeed, it is well known that many who are accustomed to handle controversies and judge the opinions of those who disagree, did not cultivate their minds in youth with those disciplines required for a solid examination of somewhat more abstract views; whence it cannot be otherwise than that they bring forward preposterous judgments about the true opinions of these people, and attribute many things to them from which they often vehemently recoil. Hence the multitude of lawsuits and contentions. To be sure, for a precise examination of a new system or hypothesis to be undertaken, more things are required than is commonly thought. It is necessary above all that we attend closely to the individual definitions of those who disagree, because often more or less is included in them than we, using the same terms, might think; unless this is observed, word-battles <note>original: "logomachiæ"</note> and false conjectures arise. Then all parts of the system must be compared with one another; one must see whether those opinions detract anything from fundamental truths or not, and for what purpose these or those propositions were brought into the open. Where the author has explained his mind more obscurely, judgment must either be suspended, or light must be kindled from his clearer statements, and so on. A distinguished example of this prudence and candor was given to us by the most excellent French theologian Louis *le Blanc* in his *Theological Theses, published in folio at London, 1683.* See what is advised by him in the preface on handling controversies, and compare also Johann Fabricius’s introduction to the consideration of controversies. Those who are tasked with examining these arguments know that those who are equipped with the gifts of intellect required here are truly rare. Hence it cannot be otherwise than that contentions are increased, especially if the stings of reputation and ambition are added. These men often "see" what even the most clear-sighted cannot discern. And so, from one controversy, ten or more often arise.

II. Much is contributed to this by prejudiced opinions about dissenters accepted from teachers. There are few who read the writings of the adversaries they wish to attack; fewer still who unroll them without bias <term>without passions</term> <note>original: "ἄνευ παθῶν"</note>; most rest content in the judgments that their own teachers have delivered concerning them. But if those teachers either misunderstood the opinions of the dissenters or exaggerated the disagreement with a haughty air, it cannot be otherwise than that the students feel the same way and walk the same path in battling new opinions, if any are spread. Hence the seeds of new lawsuits,

<header>MEDITATION VI.</header>

...seeds, and innumerable contentions arise in Schools and Churches. From this, any prudent person can easily judge that those Churches and Schools should be called happy in which men flourish who are not only learned, insightful, and wise, but above all moderate, gentle, and peaceable. For in this way, students turn out not only more learned, but also more modest, and better suited to weighing the opinions over which controversies are stirred in the Christian Church. This evil is increased if young people prematurely stumble upon books in which the opinions of dissenters are not properly represented, but their principal arguments are either shrouded in silence or handed down in a sinister way, and finally, only those things which might cause offense are placed before the reader's eyes—to say nothing of the other tricks that certain practitioners of controversy are accustomed to using. For theological arguments derived from envy <note>original: "ab invidia petita"; referring to the practice of attacking an opponent's character or motives rather than their logic.</note> are already well known to the common people. Those who have stumbled upon such books, and who do not weigh matters carefully—either due to weakness of mind or laziness—see monsters and specters of opinions everywhere, where others, who love the truth at least as much, cannot detect even a shadow of any danger.

III. The third cause of this evil is that certain public Teachers do not sufficiently distinguish what is excellent and primary in the Christian religion from accessory views and opinions of lesser importance. In handling controversies and judging the opinions of others regarding Religion, we must proceed in such a way that we first discern whether the opinions of our adversaries take anything away from the fundamental truths, or not. If we see that they do not touch even with a finger those truths in which the essence of Religion is placed, then if it becomes necessary to refute them, we should do so with such modesty and circumspection that the dissenters have no cause at all to complain about us. He who neglects this will necessarily multiply controversies without reason. But who does not know that there have always been such people in the Churches, and there are still some today, who do not sufficiently recognize what is excellent and momentous in the Christian religion above all else? Indeed, it cannot happen otherwise than that they fight no less spiritedly for tiny opinions than for fundamental truths, and that they think a necessity is imposed upon them, given any opportunity, to attack anyone and to trade blows in debate with everyone. Many have spent no diligence in learning and properly demonstrating those truths without which true Religion and piety cannot exist; yet they have wasted the best part of their lives in refuting tiny opinions that exclude no one from heaven.
<meta>catchword: exclude</meta>

---

<page-num>269</page-num>
<header>ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.</header>

(*) Finally, there have been found at all times those who think all theological questions, tossed to and fro in their Systems, are so connected with saving faith that they cry out that Religion itself has been brought into danger if others have either doubted their value or asserted that they are less momentous. Is it any wonder, then, that such men put singular industry into multiplying controversies and prolonging lawsuits?

IV. They also sin who, when they have discovered certain new hypotheses concerning these or those parts of Religion, not only immediately thrust them into public view—even though they bring no or very little utility to piety and religion—but also extol their value and look down with a haughty brow on others who will not immediately admit these new ideas <term>enthymemata</term> <note>original: "ἐνθυμήματα"; refers here to clever rhetorical arguments or newly conceived ideas.</note>. A wise man and a lover of truth is convinced that there are more than enough controversies among Christians, and that more study should be placed on knowing, proving, and defending useful truths, and taming evil passions, than on fashioning new opinions. He knows that many things exist which can be unknown without harming piety and religion; furthermore, he clearly perceives how uncertain the end of our life is, and how it is circumscribed by very narrow limits; hence he thinks his time should be spent as much as possible in the most useful exercises. Finally, he is not ignorant of the habits of most learned men: few are able to bear disagreement with a calm mind.
<meta>catchword: are</note>

> (*) Prudent and wise Theologians have grieved that, with so many new controversies having arisen, time—which could and should be spent much better—must be wasted in either investigating or refuting new opinions. The famous *Witsius* <note>Herman Witsius (1636–1708), a Dutch theologian known for attempting to reconcile theological factions.</note>, among others, in his Prologue to the British Theologians, thus opens the feelings of his mind: *I think it was never better for the Christian people than when, wrapping itself in its integrity of believing the Gospel and living holily, it was far from the commanded subtleties of curious questions and delighted in the chaste love of God and Christ and the certain expectation of eternal life. Thus the ancient race of the faithful had learned Christ from the Apostles; they were taught in simple and unpolished speech, but were moved by the incredible holiness of the orators sent to them by God. They were set on fire with Zeal, persuaded by miraculous works, and—with the internal illumination of the divine spirit approaching—were effectively convinced of the truth. Fleeing to Jesus Christ the Son of God as the sole author of salvation, they gave themselves over to be led and ruled by his will: as ignorant of subtle disputes as they were studious of piety. That was when the Christian faith exercised its full power in the souls of mortals, and encouraged them more toward bravely seeking death for Christ than toward bitterness in contention over the more obscure articles of Religion. And it is from this that I have often thought to myself that things go most happily, perhaps, for those men who, knowing nothing except Jesus Christ and him crucified, and living temperately, justly, and piously according to the prescription of the Gospel, have not even heard of the brawls of Theologians. And I judge this to be—Note Well—not the least of our calamities, or certainly the most troublesome part of our duty, that we who profess Christian things are forced to expend frequent and lengthy labor in untying the difficulties of thorny controversies. Such is the age: everything resounds with lawsuits. Not even that temple is excepted, which God consecrated for peace and concord.*

### MEDITATION VI; ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

...they are hard to bear; they do not wish to be taught by others, because they believe that in this way something is being taken away from their own reputation. And this is the reason why prudent men weigh long within themselves whether they should bring to public light this or that opinion which they think they have discovered. The question is not whether it is permitted to bring forward some new hypothesis concerning these or those parts of even theological learning. No one would easily deny that. It would go poorly indeed <note>original: "male profecto"; an expression of strong concern.</note> (*to use the words of the celebrated Witsius in his Oration on the Modest Theologian*) for liberal minds, if the ability to strive further were forbidden to them, and if nothing could be brought into public for which they could not praise another author before them; and it would have been a very bad thing for the theological enterprise if our ancestors had lived by that same law. Oh, how many and how excellent observations we would lack, which we now look up to as if they were little gems of sacred learning. The gold mines of divine things are not yet so exhausted that new treasures do not remain to be found by those who search diligently, as a reward worthy of their industry. To despise the praise of a new discovery, which is open to all, is a mark not of a modest mind, but of a lazy one. Moreover, to envy that praise in others is proof of a malevolent spirit. Nor would I wish to attribute it to modesty that you think you must follow the guide you once happened upon in your studies—whether by chance or by judgment—so closely in all things that you do not depart a hair's breadth from those decrees. It is a beautiful thing which I remember Galen recorded about Posidonius: <note>Galen was a famous Greek physician; Posidonius was a Stoic philosopher. The author is praising the intellectual honesty of choosing truth over loyalty to a specific "school" or "sect."</note>

->HE PREFERRED TO DESERT HIS SECT RATHER THAN THE TRUTH.<-

But today we see not a few people so disposed that they swear by all the dictates of their Master without any prior examination or any admission of better information. They stubbornly defend opinions snatched up at random, fighting for them as if for "altars and hearths" <note>original: "pro aris & focis"; a classical idiom meaning to fight for one's home and most sacred values.</note>. And because they cannot prevail with decisive weapons, they often childishly take a stand with clumsy and crude blows; they place the "prow and stern" <note>original: "proram & puppim"; an idiom meaning the beginning and end, or the sum total of a matter.</note> of all wisdom in these things alone. Those who do not rise up in agreement with them, they hang from a "hooked nose" <note>original: "adunco suspendant naso"; a Roman expression for mocking or sneering at someone.</note> as if they were ignorant little men <note>original: "homunciones"</note>; or, what is certainly no better, they slanderously traduce them as suspects of wicked novelty. These points brought forward by the celebrated Theologian do not prevent it from being true that many who offer new opinions—which will often profit religion little or not at all—do so with a haughty contempt for others, and are the cause of contentions and lawsuits.

V. Nor would I doubt that a less accurate and insufficiently diligent cultivation of Ecclesiastical History—especially that part which deals with ancient Heresies—also contributes much to increasing these evils. Most learned men complain that this part of history is not yet sufficiently refined. Those who have treated this subject most diligently confess 
<meta>catchword: often [sæpe]</meta>

<column-break/>

often, where the opinions of the Ancients are concerned, that one must resort to <term>epoché</term> <note>original: ἐποχὴν; a Greek philosophical term referring to the "suspension of judgment" when evidence is unclear.</note>. But on the contrary, most who write systems of Ecclesiastical History follow their predecessors without a new examination. They say that certain people were imbued with Heretical or Schismatic opinions simply because they find them commonly recorded by those who previously wrote on this subject. Hence, not only are the guilty mixed with the innocent, and monstrous opinions often attributed to those who are most distant from them, but by an improperly established parallelism with ancient Heretics, the multitude of erroneous opinions is not only increased, but material is supplied for new lawsuits and contentions.

VI. Among all the causes of such great evils, I might rightly include a certain perverted desire for renown, and a zeal for the glory of God that is falsely named. There are among those who devote themselves to Holy Letters (to say nothing of others) not a few who burn with a singular desire for becoming famous. Since they are not always equipped with such stores of learning that they can attain fame among the more learned, they wish nevertheless to become famous among their own fellow citizens. They think they will easily obtain this if they attack any minute opinions of dissenters, if they seek occasions for quarreling with anyone at all, and if they rave strenuously against the "Heterodox" in front of the common people and those who are ignorant of the weight of the controversies. When they hear themselves praised by some for that fervor, they imagine themselves to be Lights of the Church, Pillars of Orthodoxy, and "Hammers of Heretics" <note>original: "Hæreticorum malleos"; a title often given to fierce defenders of the faith.</note>. By this method they deceive the ignorant, while they are a laughingstock to those who know better. However, there is never a lack of people who celebrate such men with praise. "They alone are holy," (*I use again the words of the celebrated Werenfels from his work On the Word-Wars of the Learned, chapter 4*), "they alone are religious, they are the Zealots, they are the pillars of Orthodoxy, who concede nothing at all to their adversaries; who know how to transform all their words into heresies, and how to monstrously exaggerate every slightest disagreement; who execrate all tolerance, all gentleness, and all concord as if it were the fellowship of Christ with Belial; who repeatedly from the chair and the pulpit repeat the swan-song of Virgil's Dido:" <note>Belial is a term for the devil or personified wickedness. The quote that follows is from the Aeneid, where Dido curses Aeneas's future descendants (the Romans).</note>

<header>MEDITATION VI.</header>

...has he attacked those who wished to be our brothers? With what passion did he cast them down to hell? <note>original: "in orcum deturbavit"</note> This is the man, this is he! This man knows how to conquer his adversaries! By this, Orthodoxy stands! But these men do not only applaud themselves; what is most wretched is that they call this zeal of theirs—for defending every minute opinion and for attacking any others—a "Zeal for the glory of God." They measure their own piety by the magnitude of this Zeal, and they think they will be more pleasing to God the more violent it becomes. These men (to use the words of *Werenfels* <note>Samuel Werenfels (1657–1740), a Swiss theologian known for his moderate views and critique of religious fanaticism.</note> again) are so pleased with themselves in this Zeal that they believe they can redeem and atone for whatever other vices they may have: they think all their stains are washed away by it, and their defects abundantly compensated, even to the point that God himself is somehow obligated to forgive his so-called devoted and fervent worshippers for many things that he could not tolerate in others. (*Opuscula*, page 153).

Let no one interpret this as if we were denying that it is necessary for the Ministers of God's Word and Theologians to be armed with Zeal. On the contrary, we count Zeal of the true name among the heroic virtues of theologians. But Zeal of the true name is that which is measured against reason and the Gospel of Jesus Christ; it is calm and tempered; it is suited to the gravity of the matter at hand; it is no less opposed to serious errors—serious, I say—than it is to vices, and so on. No one fails to praise this kind of Zeal. However, it is clear that this is not what we are talking about now. Is it any wonder that the number of controversies, lawsuits, and contentions in the Churches increases where such Teachers dominate or are held in high esteem?

VII. Finally, to omit other things, the singular desire of some to determine every single thing in the business of Religion contributes greatly to this problem. Even those who are equipped with only a modest knowledge of divine things feel that this often cannot be done without rashness. It is impossible for all parts of theological learning to be brought to the highest degree of evidence. In many things, a prudent man has need of <term>suspension of judgment</term> <note>original: ἐποχὴ (epoche); a Greek term used by skeptics and later moderate theologians to describe the practice of withholding a final verdict when evidence is unclear.</note>. All people are indeed bound to diligently cultivate the most holy disciplines and, as far as the capacity of their talent allows, to make happy progress in them. In the meantime, however, if they are not lacking in judgment and talent, they see clearly that sometimes one must find rest in a more obscure knowledge; they see that the thing itself has truly been revealed to us, but the *manner* of the thing is hidden from us.

But these men of whom we speak embrace all the definitions and explanations of the schools—whether received from their elders and teachers or invented by their own wit—as if they were their own sweethearts. To these men, nothing is obscure, nothing is uncertain; everything has already been sufficiently explained and determined by this or 그 person whom they hold in high regard, and

---

<page-num>273</page-num>
<header>ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.</header>

whom they think alone are wise in these arguments. Those men could be tolerated, and could enjoy this theological omniscience of theirs, if only they would grant others the liberty of feeling differently—that is, of judging according to their own degrees of knowledge. But since they are unwilling to do this, and accuse others who lack such a "happy talent" and such accurate and exquisite learning of either shameful ignorance or heterodoxy <note>Holding "different" or unorthodox beliefs.</note>, they expose themselves to the ridicule of the truly learned, while simultaneously increasing the number of disputes and contentions. Meanwhile, by this reasoning, those things which could serve to heal the wounds of the Church, to reform a degenerate Christianity, and to foster and bind more tightly the fraternal union of minds, are shamefully neglected. One may compare what the Excellent *Pfaffius* <note>Christoph Matthäus Pfaff (1686–1760), a Lutheran theologian who advocated for church unity.</note> warned regarding this argument in his dissertation on *Theological Prejudices*, Section XVII and following. ...is none, or at least slight enough. This much is certain: neither side can entirely resolve all the doubts that arise here.

II. Our Holy Savior himself reveals the primary cause of Unbelief <note>original: "Incredulitatis"</note> to us in John Chapter 7:17, saying: "If anyone wills to obey God’s will, he shall know of the doctrine, whether it be of God, or whether I speak of myself."

III. The most certain and evident character of a sincere love for God is the observance of the commandments of Jesus Christ; for to this end, the other signs of divine love recorded here and there in the Holy Scriptures are directed. See the passages in John 14:15, 21, 23, 24; 1 John 2:4-6; 1 John 5:3; Matthew 6:24, etc. <note>The original text cites John 16:15, though the context suggests the author intended John 14:15: "If ye love me, keep my commandments."</note>

IV. The principal requirement for students of Holy Scripture and Ministers of the Divine Word <term>V.D.M.</term> <note>Abbreviation for *Verbi Divini Minister*, a formal title for a clergyman.</note> is Piety. This alone grants true value and honor to all the duties they must fulfill throughout their lives. *“If you love Christ”* (thus the late <note>original Greek: ὁ Μακαρίτης (ho Makarites), a respectful term for the deceased.</note> celebrated Werenfels <note>Samuel Werenfels (1657–1740), a Swiss theologian who advocated for moderation and criticized the "prejudices" of theologians.</note> addresses his disciples in his *Dissertation on the Goal of a Theological Teacher*), “this will do much to ensure great progress in your studies: for Christ manifests his secrets to his friends above all others. *If you love Christ*, you will also sincerely love his sheep, and you will direct all your labors solely to promoting their salvation. *If you love Christ*, you will seek the things that belong to Christ in all matters, rather than the things that are your own. *If you love Christ*, you will also imitate Christ and strive to be like Him, so that one day each of you can say to your sheep with Paul: ‘Be imitators of me, just as I am of Christ.’ *If you love Christ*, all the labors you endure for his sake will seem easy to you. For love makes all things not only tolerable, but even pleasant. *If you love Christ*, you will not refuse to suffer something for your Christ; you will not fear any dangers too much; finally, you will desire death itself rather than fear it, as that which will join you with Christ; and as soon as it pleases God, you will desire to be dissolved and to be forever with your Christ.”

V. Among the other gifts that a learned interpreter of Holy Scripture ought to possess, we rightly include a prudent and circumspect suspension of judgment <term>epoche</term> <note>original Greek: ἐποχή (epoche); the practice of withholding one's consent or judgment when evidence is unclear.</note>. Worthy of attention here are the words of the most learned Isaac Casaubon <note>A renowned classical scholar and philologist (1559–1614).</note>—a man most skilled, if anyone ever was, in languages and the critical arts—which appear in his *Exercises against Baronius*, page 71: *“That there are certain difficulties <note>original Greek: ἄπορα (apora), meaning 'impasses' or 'unsolvable problems.'</note> in the Divine Scripture, as in all disciplines, will be confessed, I believe, by all men who are mindful of human weakness. Therefore, the proverb of the Rabbis must necessarily be employed in some cases: 'Wait for Elijah' <note>original: 'expectandus Elias'; a Hebrew traditional phrase used when a legal or scriptural problem was so difficult it could only be solved by the prophet Elijah upon his return.</note> to loosen the hard and currently inextricable knots of scripture. This is better than pronouncing rashly on everything, as is the custom of those who think it a disgrace to admit they are ignorant of something—even in those matters where human industry can today bring nothing to the search except naked conjectures.”*

# MEDITATION
## ON THE

### PART VII.

->Sect. I.<-

<image-desc>A decorative rectangular woodcut frame containing the initial letter "P". The frame is ornamented with architectural elements, scrollwork, and a small heraldic shield at the base.</image-desc>

<margin>The Author's aim in this Dissertation.</margin>
Proceeding now, by God's grace, we move to uncover the remaining causes of the Unbelief that is, alas, spreading so widely among Christians. And here, among others, the greatest cause of all presents itself to us: the *corruption of morals* among mortals, especially those who are accustomed to taking the name of Christian discipline. There is no doubt that this has plunged many into the abyss of Unbelief, or confirmed those already leaning toward vice. But before we show how men, by contemplating such great evils, easily fall headlong into error, some things must be noted concerning the corruption itself, which provides the occasion for this most serious mistake. The judgments of men, both learned and unlearned, vary on this subject. Some exaggerate the evil beyond measure; others, however, wish to diminish it more than the laws of truth permit. The former, though unintentionally, cautiously detract from the divine virtues, promises, and God's providential care for His Church; the latter, while wishing to minimize or deny the evils staring them in the face, seem to patronize impiety itself. Therefore, this subject is worthy of being properly weighed.

Here, the author specifically addresses how certain thinkers and groups exaggerate the moral failings of humanity—and Christians in particular—to serve their own philosophical or religious agendas.</meta>

<header>MEDITATION VII.</header>

<margin>There are those who, in order to prove certain hypotheses, are accustomed to exaggerate the corruption of the human race, and of Christians especially.</margin>

II. Those who are accustomed to lament the magnitude of the great corruption spreading everywhere do not all have the same goal, nor do they proceed by a single path to prove what they intend. There are some who describe the most corrupt morals of men—especially of those who are accustomed to take the name of the Christian Religion—in vivid colors, in order to confirm certain hypotheses. Among these, Pierre Bayle <note>Pierre Bayle (1647–1706) was a French philosopher famous for his *Historical and Critical Dictionary*. He was known for his skepticism and for highlighting the difficulties in reconciling faith with reason.</note> is deservedly counted, a man of excellent talent and vast erudition, though he more than once misused these most outstanding gifts of the mind. Here, among other opinions which he defended most fiercely against very learned adversaries, he also defended this one: namely, that no sect exists among men, nor can any hypotheses be devised by the human mind, which can satisfy the doubts occurring regarding the origin of moral and physical evil. 

It can indeed easily be proved—if we argue *a priori* <term>a priori</term> <note>From first principles or theoretical deduction rather than observation.</note>, as we are accustomed to speak in the schools—that the system of the Manichaeans <note>The Manichaeans were a dualistic sect that believed in two equal powers of Good and Evil, often used as a philosophical foil for discussing the "Problem of Evil."</note> is inept and monstrous. However, when we turn our eyes to the many evils to which the human race is subject, and especially the sins of those to whom the most holy religion (namely, the Christian one) has been granted, it is necessary that we yield to the Manichaeans and either cross over into their camp or confess that the doubts occurring here cannot be solved. This is to say, as he interprets it, that the objections of the Manichaeans are far stronger than the responses of the Christians. 

To prove this thesis of his, he appealed partly to daily experience and partly to the complaints of ancient as well as recent writers regarding the magnitude of the corruption spreading among mortals. In his *Dictionary* and in other small books written on this subject, he represented these complaints with a great display of erudition and exaggerated them in a marvelous way. But for what purpose the learned man did this, other scholars disagree. There are those who think Bayle was persuaded that those arguments were indeed impossible to solve, but at least in this life. This is how the illustrious Leibniz <note>Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646–1716), a German philosopher who wrote the *Theodicy* to counter Bayle's skepticism.</note> interprets his mind in the *Discourse on the Conformity of Faith with Reason*, page 24: 

<note>original: "Il semble, qu'il ne prend les objections pour invincibles que par rapport à nos lumiéres presentes, & il ne deśpere pas même dans cette Reponse p. 35. que quelqu'un ne puiśse un jour trouver un denouëment peu connu juśqu'ici. Et pag. 67. Il eśt a esperer que M. Bayle ſe trouve maintenant environné de ces lumieres qui nous manquent ici-bas: puisqu'il y a lieu de śuppoſer, qu'il n'a point manqué de bonne volonté."</note>

*It seems that he takes the objections to be invincible only in relation to our present light, and he does not even despair in that Response (p. 35) that someone might one day find a solution little known until now. And on page 67: It is to be hoped that Mr. Bayle now finds himself surrounded by those lights which we lack here below: since there is reason to suppose that he did not lack good will.*

Others believe that he wished to show the power of his talent by attacking those things which were held as most certain by others. Finally, there are those who affirm that Bayle deliberately wished to attack Divine Providence. As for me, I leave these things to be judged by Him who has accurate knowledge and insight into all the recesses of human minds. Nor do I agree with the opinion of those who think that no one can communicate their doubts about the weightier articles of Religion to the learned for a good purpose. It is not my intention here to deal with the subject of the controversy itself that is debated among scholars. The writings of the most learned men—Jean Le Clerc, Jaquelot, Clarke, Leibniz, and others—are well known. We only say this: that Bayle exaggerated beyond measure the corruption that takes place among mortals.

<margin>There are those who, not with bad intent, but deceived by a false image of piety, are accustomed to increase the corruption of the human race.</margin>

III. Among those who lament the atrocity of the corruption spreading among Christians, there are some who do so without bad intent. First, there are those who are deceived by a certain false appearance of piety. These, led by a kind of slavish fear, represent to themselves an image of Christianity that is plainly false and abhorrent to both reason and Christian discipline. These people think, for instance, that only those deserve the name of "lovers of virtue" who, entirely immersed in certain mystical contemplations, lead a life either completely removed from the society of other men, or at least consisting only in the familiar interaction of those touched by the same affection of piety. 

They think they were born for no other purpose than to exercise the body with various mortifications <note>original: "macerationibus," referring to ascetic practices like fasting or self-flagellation.</note> and to restrain themselves from all those things that can bring joy to the mind, believing themselves to be closer to heaven the more they moisten their cheeks with perpetual tears. They curse the life of other men as if it were dross, and they consider the rules of prudence to be little more than suggestions of the Devil; they often mistake hypochondriacal attacks and the unusual images of a disturbed imagination for divine responses. Hence, they always imagine God as angry with them, and ready to most severely punish every error that human nature fails to avoid. While they look upon the life and morals of other men, they fill everything with tragic outcries, and [describe] a most foul image...

...they represent [this corruption] to the minds of other mortals. Hence, with the ancient poet, they break out into these words:

> No longer is any immortal God revered,
> and the race of pious men has perished;
> they no longer know the laws, nor even piety.

<margin>that is:</margin>
> *Neither does anyone revere the immortal Gods;*
> *the race of religious men has perished, and they no longer*
> *know the laws, nor piety.*
<note>original Latin: "Neque Deos quisquam reveretur immortales / religiosorum virorum genus periit, neque jura / amplius norunt neque pietatem."</note>

In this way, many feel—to say nothing of others—who follow the discipline of the Jansenist School. <note>The Jansenists were a reform movement within the Catholic Church, named after Cornelius Jansen, known for their strict moral rigor and belief in the total depravity of human nature.</note> I cannot more correctly explain their mind than in the words of the **Celebrated Mosheim**. <note>Johann Lorenz von Mosheim (1693–1755) was a renowned German Lutheran historian known as the "Father of Modern Church History."</note> In his *Inquiry into the Truth of the Miracles of François de Pâris, the Wonder-worker of Our Century*, Section XVI, he speaks thus: "For as the Jansenists are accustomed to extend the limits of all Christian duties much further than the divine law requires, so also they prescribe a difficult, severe, and inhuman penance for their followers. They think, for instance, that by the word 'Penance' is meant not an internal change of mind, but the punishments with which we afflict ourselves because of our sins, or voluntary tortures; and that one ought to spontaneously undertake as much more misery and labor as the more offenses he has contaminated himself with. If they merely wished it to be understood that everyone who knows they have committed something vicious should, in a way, discipline themselves and chastise their senses in proportion to the sin, they would only slightly depart from the common opinion of the Roman Church. But they not only dictate great and exquisite punishments for even small faults, but they also pronounce everyone to be holier and more blessed the less they spare themselves and their bodies, and more pleasing to the Supreme Deity the more industrious they are in agonizing and afflicting themselves. What is most significant is that they want not only vicious acts to be expiated in this way, but they also command that our innate corruption and propensity toward sinning be paid for daily by voluntary miseries. From this it follows that, since no mortal casts off this inherent flaw of nature while he lives, the life of a Christian man ought to be a perpetual penance—that is, a perpetual calamity and misery. And they believe those are closest to God who, having left all business behind, desert the company of men and, far from the crowd and the provocations of lust, gradually kill the body through thirst, hunger, sleeplessness, and labor. Nor do they reject this as a mere conjecture, but rather they defend it fiercely. In this matter, they so exceed all measure and reason that those who impose such a mass of troubles upon themselves that they faint and hasten death—</margin>

—themselves, knowingly and willingly accelerating it before their time by the magnitude of their punishments, they place in the number of the friends of God and the saints, and call them by the magnificent title **VICTIMS OF PENANCE**, or say they were **CONSUMED BY THE HEAT OF LOVE.**" These people, however, are so far from contributing anything to the amendment of men devoted to vice, or from persuading others of the magnitude of those evils in which many mortals are immersed, that they instead provide others with an occasion to often think basely of the most holy discipline of Christ itself. For who (they will say) will love virtue, if it is not even permitted to do those things without which the social life of mortals cannot exist? Who will fulfill the duties of a good citizen and a father of a family, if the true piety of a Christian man consists in a certain perpetual silence, in abstruse meditations, perpetual sighs, and abstinence from those things which the Best Deity has willingly granted to the human race?

Again, there are others who have clearly perceived the character of true piety and, as far as can be seen, driven by a genuine **Zeal**, apply their minds to routing out all kinds of vices. Yet often, in order to obtain what they intend, they reason incorrectly. Namely, when they rail against the corrupt morals of the Age, they find barely enough words and hyperboles to depict the magnitude of the universal corruption of all mortals—so much so that if you wished to cut the force of the words they use to the quick, not even one mortal would exist to whom you could justly ascribe the name of a pious man. These people, in our opinion, defend a good cause with too little circumspection; indeed, often against their own will, they confirm men captured by wicked pursuits and pleasures rather than calling them back from vice. For wicked men are accustomed to seek a defense for their bad cause in the very multitude and, so to speak, **Universality** of those who err and sin, saying that wherever they turn their eyes, they find men devoted to similar vices; that we are all sinners, though in different ways, and that no one can bring a remedy to a desperate disease. Hence, they applaud themselves on that account and are accustomed to relegate what is said about true Christianity to the realm of "sweet dreams." Finally, there are men who, to demonstrate the foulness of the corrupt human race, imprudently appeal to the **Incentives** by which all men are usually driven to act. Namely, they judge the internal actions of men without any restriction, such that you would think they believe everyone is driven to act well only by ambition, utility, or the force of temperament, but not by any love of God; these same people think themselves excessively clever and pious if they can show that this or that person...
