# MEDITATION VII.

...that those men have obtained praise for piety without reason, and were moved to perform this or that righteous deed not so much by the love of virtue as by the love of a certain depraved inclination. For these people, it is not only always on their lips, that saying of **Augustine**: namely, that the virtues of the Pagans are nothing but splendid sins; <note>original Latin: "virtutes nempe Gentilium nonnisi esse splendida peccata." This is a famous maxim often attributed to St. Augustine, suggesting that without Christian faith, even the most seemingly "virtuous" acts are fundamentally flawed by pride or lack of proper intent.</note> but they express their opinion in such general terms that you might rightly conclude from them that it is doubtful whether even a single one of those who flourished with the praise of virtue among Christians was truly pious. By reasoning in this way, they not only frequently do an injustice to the best and most excellent men, but they also turn out to be masters of iniquity. While they say that those whom all good people praise for their outstanding virtues were adorned with nothing but a vain splendor of virtue, they make the examples of the best men—which the teachers of morals and even the Holy Scriptures themselves urge us to follow—suspect and hateful as much as they can. Thus, they teach people to follow the principles not so much of Jesus Christ as of **Machiavelli** in their actions. <note>Niccolò Machiavelli (1469–1527) was an Italian political philosopher often associated with cynicism and the idea that "the end justifies the means."</note> This error was certainly held by the author of the book *The Falsity of Human Virtues*, <note>original French: "la fausseté des vertus humaines." This work, published in 1678 by Jacques Esprit, argues that what we call "virtues" are often just hidden vices like vanity or self-love.</note> who was devoted to the Jansenist family, as I have already warned in the previous sections regarding the factions of Unbelief, and confirmed by the testimony of the Illustrious **Leibniz**. <note>Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646–1716) was a German polymath who famously argued against the extreme moral pessimism of the Jansenists.</note>

<margin>What should be thought concerning the piety of the Christians of the first centuries, compared with the morals of the Christians of our own age.</margin>
IV. There are many among the theologians who, in order to depict the foul face of the degenerate Christianity in this age we live in, appeal to the morals of those who gave their name to the Christian Religion in the first three centuries. If you listen to them, the men of our century are scarcely worthy of the name of Christians when compared to those first pupils of Christian discipline. For they depict these—either all or most of them—as if they had dropped down from heaven, perfected in every virtue, and entirely immune to every stain of crime. But those who reason this way not only often cross the boundaries of truth and are more unfair to many who shine with true piety in our time, but at the same time, they also needlessly extol the magnitude of the corruption spreading among Christians. It is helpful, therefore, to examine this opinion a little more carefully, because it is worthy of examination for several reasons. I will deal with this argument in such a way—saving the opinions of others—that on one hand, I detract nothing from the true virtues of the early Christians, but on the other hand, I in no way defend the vices to which, alas! the people of our century are devoted. We say, therefore: 1) in general, it is very difficult to establish a fair comparison between men who are extremely distinct from one another in education, instruction, morals, laws, etc. For from those different relations and states, various inclinations and studies arise among men, as well as various incitements to this or that type of vice.

<column-break/>

## ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

Men born and educated among the most savage persecutions, who have experienced the harsh misery of fate throughout life, and who expect an imminent death almost every single day and hour—and those who were born and educated during a flourishing state of the Republic and have led a tranquil life; among such people, I say, a fair comparison is difficult to establish. Nor is it easily decided how much the virtue of both groups prevailed or did not prevail in such different conditions of life. But let us set aside these generalities and come closer to the proposed question. We say, therefore: 2) It is established from the indubitable records of the Apostolic writers that there is scarcely any kind of vice which the Apostles did not publicly rebuke; from which it is most manifest that in those gatherings of the first pupils of Christian discipline, there were many who were contaminated by various vices. To prove this, one need only read the letters given by the Apostles to the various gatherings of Christians. The **Late** <note>original Greek: "ὁ Μακαρίτης" (ho Makaritēs) - a respectful way to refer to a deceased person, similar to "of blessed memory."</note> and Celebrated **Sontagius** <note>Christopher Sontag (1654–1717) was a German Lutheran theologian at Altdorf.</note> proved this with great effort in his dissertation *On the Corruptions of the Apostolic Churches*, published at Nuremberg in the year 1717. 3) All theologians, to whatever opinions they may be devoted regarding the helps of grace, confess that the true and salvific change of minds is not completed in a single moment, but that it takes on increases step by step. Who then would believe that men born among Pagans or Jews, and not only imbued with pestilential opinions but also devoted to various vices, were entirely changed immediately upon hearing the holier discipline, and that no traces of the "old fraud" <note>original Latin: "veteris fraudis." This refers to the habitual sins or deceptive lifestyles of their former non-Christian lives.</note> were left in them? 4) There is a small supply of trustworthy records from which a certain judgment can be made about the piety of Christians in the first century after the death of Christ. Men most well-versed in Ecclesiastical History have deplored the scarcity of these records. I will bring forward just one testimony, which can stand in the place of many: namely, that of the Celebrated **Daillé** <note>Jean Daillé (1594–1670) was a French Protestant scholar famous for his critical approach to the writings of the Early Church Fathers.</note> which appears in Chapter 1 of his excellent little book *On the Use of the Fathers*: the words of that most excellent man sound thus: *“it seems that most of the faithful of those times considered it enough to write their faith into the hearts of men by the splendor of a blameless life and by the blood which they most constantly shed for Christ, but labored little in writing books: whether that pleased them which **Origen** <note>Origen (c. 185–253) was a major early Christian scholar from Alexandria.</note> elegantly teaches, that Christianity ought to be propagated and retained by innocence of life and honesty of morals rather than by oratorical flourishes; or whether they were not permitted to apply their minds to it through the continuous calamities by which they were afflicted; or whether they were deterred or called away from writing by some other cause. However it may be, it is certain that, except for the sacred volumes of the Apostles, very few in those first times devoted their effort to composing books: hence that [history of] **Eusebius**...”* <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339), the "Father of Church History," whose records are the primary source for the early centuries of the Church.</note>

The author argues that historical context—such as persecution versus peace—makes comparisons difficult and notes that even the Apostles recorded many vices among their early converts.</summary>

# MEDITATION VII.

...of **Eusebius** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), often called the "Father of Church History."</note> at the beginning of his history, there was a sense of anxiety because little, or rather no light, shone from any other source for him to follow; no tracks appeared for him to tread upon, since the path he was taking had been worn by none of his predecessors. Furthermore, not even all those works which the Christians produced at that time have reached us, few though they were. The greater part has perished, either through the injury of time, which consumes all things, or by the fraudulent audacity of men in destroying things that did not suit their taste.

*For example, the five books of **Papias**, Bishop of Hierapolis; the Apologies of **Quadratus of Athens** and **Aristides**; the work of **Castor Agrippa** against the twenty-four books of the heretic **Basilides**; the five books of **Hegesippus**; the works of **Melito**, Bishop of Sardis, **Dionysius of Corinth**, and **Apollinaris of Hierapolis**; likewise the letter of **Pinytus of Crete**; the monuments of **Philip**, **Musanus**, **Modestus**, **Bardesanes**, **Pantaenus**, **Rhadon**, **Miltiades**, **Apollonius**, **Serapion**, **Bacchylus**, **Polycrates** (Bishop of Ephesus), **Heraclius**, **Maximus**, **Hammonius**, **Trypho**, **Hippolytus**, **Julius Africanus**, **Dionysius of Alexandria**, and others, of whom only bare names and titles remain to us in the writings of **Eusebius**, **Jerome**, and others. So says **Daillé**.* <note>Jean Daillé (1594–1670) was a prominent French Protestant theologian known for his work on the use of the Church Fathers.</note>

5) It is established from Ecclesiastical History that soon enough after the death of Christ and the Apostles, the Church began to be contaminated not only by profane opinions but also by various vices. **Eusebius**, in his *Ecclesiastical History, Book III, Chapter 32*, proves this by the testimony of **Hegesippus**, a most weighty writer. After this, says **Eusebius**, quoting the same writer (i.e., **Hegesippus**) according to the version by **Valesius** <note>Henri Valois (Valesius), a 17th-century scholar famous for his editions of Greek ecclesiastical historians.</note>, while commemorating the events of that age, he adds:

> *The Church remained a pure and uncorrupted virgin until these times (that is, until the time of the Emperor **Trajan**); for those who endeavored to corrupt the right rule of evangelical preaching still lurked in obscure hiding places. But after the sacred company of the Apostles had been extinguished by various kinds of death, and the generation of those men who had earned the right to hear that divine wisdom with their own ears had passed away, then finally the conspiracy of impious error arose through the fraud and malice of false teachers. Since none of the Apostles were left alive, these men henceforth, with "bare heads" as they say <note>original: "nudo, quod ajunt, capite" — an idiom meaning "openly" or "shamelessly."</note>, attempted to thrust their adulterated doctrine against the preaching of the truth.*

Thus far **Eusebius**. The most learned **Valesius**, in his notes on this passage, wants the things **Hegesippus** says about the Church in general to be understood only regarding the congregation at Jerusalem. Truly, however, if anyone rightly weighs the passage of the same **Hegesippus** which **Eusebius** cites in *Book IV, Chapter 22*, he will see that his words should not be taken as referring to this congregation alone; for so many heretics, whom **Hegesippus** mentions here, did not come forth from the Church of Jerusalem alone. What the same learned man discusses regarding the purity of the Catholic Church savors of sectarian zeal; for the **Romanists** <note>A term used by Protestant writers to refer to Roman Catholics.</note> are accustomed to fashion for themselves some sort of Platonic idea of the Catholic Church...

<page-num>283</page-num>
# ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

...regarding which, however, this is not the place to speak. But if Christians, once such great Teachers were removed from their midst, could be imbued with false and perverse opinions and be corrupted by "Heretics" (as they are called), why could it not have happened that some of them began to loosen the reins of vice? It is known by the experience of all ages that men are not so much prone and inclined toward inventing and defending new and unusual opinions as they are toward various vices that flatter their depraved affections. I am not one who would easily subscribe to the testimonies regarding the most wicked vices of the *Heretics*; yet, if the good faith of the ancients does not entirely waver, it can hardly be denied that some were stained with quite serious crimes.

<margin>The same argument is continued.</margin>
V. 6) I am not unaware that those who think more magnificently than is proper about the piety and virtues of the Christians of the first three centuries appeal to certain testimonies of the *Fathers*; yet these do not prove the very point that is chiefly in question. Thus, the first Teachers of the Christian Church were accustomed, in their *Apologies* <note>Formal defenses of Christianity written to Roman authorities.</note>, to strenuously defend their innocence and prove that they were entirely foreign both to the crime of Atheism and to the various and most foul crimes of which they were accused. But anyone can easily perceive that this is not enough to prove that all Christians, with very few exceptions, were inclined toward the pursuit of virtue and were entirely immune from every stain of sin. Modern Christians—at least those who are devoted to a purer form of worship—can publicly profess that the discipline they follow patronizes neither errors nor vices, even though, alas, there are many among them who live a life utterly abhorrent to the precepts of the Christian religion. But let us look, as an example, at one or two testimonies upon which those people rely who claim that the primitive Christians were, without distinction, adorned with all virtues. Thus, for example, they appeal to the words of **Lactantius** <note>Lactantius (c. 250–325 AD), an early Christian author and advisor to Constantine I.</note> which appear in the *Divine Institutes, Book III, Chapter 26*, where he speaks as follows among other things:

> *Give me a man who is hot-tempered, abusive, and unrestrained; with only a few words of God, I will return him as calm as a sheep. Give me one who is greedy, avaricious, and stingy; I will soon give him back to you liberal and shedding his money with full hands. Give me one who is afraid of pain and death; he will soon despise crosses, fires, and the bull of Phalaris. <note>A notorious ancient Greek instrument of torture.</note> Give me one who is lustful, an adulterer, and a glutton; you will soon see him sober, chaste, and continent. Give me one who is cruel and bloodthirsty; that fury will soon be changed into true clemency. Give me one who is unjust, foolish, and a sinner; immediately he will be just, prudent, and innocent.* Such is the power of divine wisdom that, when infused into the breast of a man, it [becomes] the mother...

The author critiques idealized views of early Christian virtue while acknowledging the transformative power of the faith as described by Lactantius.</summary>

# MEDITATION VII.

*...might expel the folly of sins with one single impulse. Thus far Lactantius.* <note>original: "delictorum stultitiam uno semel impetu expellat. Hactenus Lactantius." Lactantius (c. 250–325 AD) was an advisor to Constantine and a famous rhetorician often called the "Christian Cicero."</note>

Indeed, if it were not already clear from other sources that this Father was accustomed to speaking rhetorically, it would be abundantly clear from this testimony. For what mortal could claim such power for himself that, by his own arguments, encouragements, or rebukes, he could—in a tiny moment of time—inflame men totally immersed in vice with a fierce zeal for virtue, and utterly transform minds captured by sinister opinions and estranged from all love of piety? If **Lactantius** merely meant that the excellence of the Christian religion and the power of its precepts are such that they *can* turn the souls of men toward the good—provided those men have set aside their wicked passions and are burning with a love for truth—then this is true. Indeed, our Holy Savior long ago advised this in **John 7:17**: <note>"If anyone chooses to do God’s will, he will find out whether my teaching comes from God or whether I speak on my own."</note> but this does not prove that all, or even most, Christians were actually so inclined. 

Others, following the same line of thought, point to that most celebrated *Letter of Pliny the Younger* <note>Pliny the Younger (61–113 AD) was a Roman lawyer and magistrate. His letter to Emperor Trajan is one of our earliest non-Christian accounts of the movement.</note> sent to **Trajan**. Because it is so well known, I will not transcribe it here. In it, he explains the nature of the confession of faith and religion to which the Christians swore, and their manner of worshiping God. Yet it does not follow from this that all those Christians were perfectly trained <term>examussitatos</term> <note>a technical term derived from a carpenter's rule (amussis), meaning "perfectly aligned" or "exact."</note> in the pursuit of virtue, nor that they never strayed from the laws of their most holy discipline. 

Arguments proving the contrary can be drawn from this very letter. For many from this crowd, when summoned by **Pliny**, denied that they were or ever had been in the number of Christians; and, so that **Pliny** would have less doubt, they made supplications to the statues of the Gods and the image of the Emperor. There were others who said they were Christians, but soon denied it. Still others confessed they had been Christians but had long ago returned to the public rites of the Pagans. All of these venerated the image of **Caesar** and the statues of the Gods, and simultaneously cursed Christ. No one would assert that these were "Christians" in the true sense of the name. Their crime was all the more serious because it occurred so close to the age of the Apostles. 

To these points, setting others aside, I add the testimony of **Tertullian** <note>Tertullian (c. 155–220 AD) was a prolific early Christian author from Carthage.</note>, which is frequently cited by those who tend to extol the virtues of the first Christians beyond measure. He writes thus in his *Apology, chapter 44*:

> *We call to witness your own actions, you who preside daily over the judging of prisoners. So many guilty men are reviewed by you under various criminal charges: Which assassin among them, which pickpocket, which sacrilegious man, or corrupter, or thief of the bath-houses, is also listed as a Christian? Or when Christians are brought forward under their own name, who among them is like these many criminals? Your prisons always boil with your own—* <note>original: "De vestris semper æstuat car-"</note>

<column-break/>

<page-num>285</page-num>
# ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

> *—people; your mines always groan with your own people; the wild beasts are always fattened on your own people; the managers of the games always feed their herds of criminals with your own people. No Christian is there, unless for that name alone; or if he is there for something else, he is no longer a Christian.*

This testimony, however, proves nothing other than this: namely, that the number of extremely wicked men among the Pagans was very large, while very few among the Christians were found guilty of such great crimes. Let it be so; but does it follow from this that all, or most, Christians were therefore uncontaminated by any crimes? Or that, because they restrained themselves from the more serious offenses, they were infected by no others? Indeed, the very last words of this Father add strength to our opinion.

7) Some, however, in order to prove their opinion, point to the number and constancy of the Martyrs. From this, they believe it follows that all or most Christians of the first centuries were instructed with an accurate knowledge of religion and incensed with a vehement love of piety, showing themselves most ready to undergo every kind of torture. 

Far be it from me to wish to detract anything from the praises of the true Martyrs, or to cast doubt on the piety through which many shone brightly. I do not deny that many, inflamed by a love of truth and helped by the singular aid of God, set their minds to undergo martyrdom with a constant spirit. However, I would like the following points to be noted regarding this argument:

**a.** The persecutions were not as universal or continuous, nor was the number of Martyrs as large, as is commonly thought. Although I do not entirely agree with **Henry Dodwell** <note>Henry Dodwell (1641–1711) was a scholar who argued in "De Paucitate Martyrum" that the number of early martyrs had been greatly exaggerated.</note>, who greatly reduced the number of Martyrs and the duration of the persecutions, it is nevertheless certain that they have been increased beyond measure by many writers. Consequently, the most learned men today walk a middle path between **Dodwell** and **Ruinart** <note>Thierry Ruinart (1657–1709), a Benedictine scholar who defended the traditional accounts of the martyrs against Dodwell’s skepticism.</note>, who engaged in a sharp back-and-forth debate <term>ferram Disputationis... reciprocarunt</term> <note>literally "moved the saw of dispute back and forth."</note> on this subject.

**b.** There exist so many Edicts of the ancient Emperors in favor of the Christians that it is clearly not likely that everyone was granted the power to act cruelly against them. Even today, in the works of **Eusebius** and others, one can find the Edicts of **Trajan**, **Hadrian**, **Antoninus the Philosopher** <note>Marcus Aurelius.</note>, **Gallienus**, **Maximus**, and **Constantine Licinianus**. I say nothing of those which no longer exist but which were mentioned by trustworthy ancient authors, such as those of **Tiberius**, **Antoninus Pius**, **Hadrian**, **Domitian**, **Nerva**, **Aurelian**, and **Alexander Severus**. From these, it is clear that the heat of persecution was often tempered; or, once the innocence of the people was recognized, care was taken so that they would not be raged against indiscriminately. Add to this that not only Princes, but also Provincial Governors and Philosophers, often gave clear examples of their favor toward the Christians, which the most learned man has collected...

c. It must furthermore be observed that many things said concerning the "Sayings and Deeds" of the first Martyrs are highly doubtful. This is because, as **Ruinart** <note>Thierry Ruinart (1657–1709) was a Benedictine scholar known for his "Acts of the Martyrs," though even he admitted to the late date of many sources.</note> himself admits in the preface to his *Sincere Acts of the Martyrs*, it was only in the seventh century—when superstition and barbarism began to reign—that such collections of the martyrs' words and actions were published. It is entirely to be lamented, as the Most Reverend Bishop **Fell** <note>John Fell (1625–1686) was the Bishop of Oxford and a significant editor of the works of Cyprian.</note> says in a note to **Cyprian’s** twelfth Epistle: *The Acts of the Martyrs (a genre of writing than which Christian piety knows nothing more ancient or useful) have been so contaminated and swollen by the interpolations of later times, monstrous miracles, and old wives' tales, that almost nothing remains genuine or untouched.* Indeed, **Jacques Basnage** <note>Jacques Basnage (1653–1723) was a celebrated French Huguenot historian.</note> in his *History of the Church, Book XIX*, shows clearly to the eye that there was a massive number of fictional martyrs. Furthermore, groups like the **Marcionites, Montanists, Novatians, and Donatists** <note>These were various groups deemed "heretical" by the early orthodox Church, yet they also claimed their own histories of martyrdom.</note> also had their own martyrs.

d. One must also consider that there were many among the Christians who, when persecutions broke out, shamefully abandoned the Christian religion. From this group came those who spoke evil of Christ. Some, when asked if they were Christians, denied it; for this reason, they were called <term>Negatores</term> <note>Deniers: those who publicly renounced their faith.</note>. There were also various types of <term>Libellatici</term> <note>From "libellus" (document): those who did not sacrifice but purchased official certificates stating they had complied with Roman law.</note>. There were the <term>Sacrificati</term> <note>Sacrificers: those who actually offered sacrifices to pagan idols.</note> who offered libations to idols; and there were the <term>Thurificati</term> <note>Incensers: those who offered incense at the statues of the gods.</note> who petitioned the images of the deities with incense. Such people were found not only among the common folk but even among the Bishops. If you listen to **Philostorgius** <note>A 4th-century church historian.</note>, men such as *Eusebius of Nicomedia, Maris of Chalcedon, Theognis of Nicaea, Leontius of Antioch, Antonius of Tarsus, Menophantus of Ephesus, Numenius, Eudoxius, Alexander, and Asterius the Cappadocian* all sacrificed to the gods of the Gentiles during the time of the Diocletian persecution. Even **Origen** <note>One of the most influential early Christian theologians, though his reputation for orthodoxy was often debated.</note> is stained by this mark, a view not opposed by the most learned men such as **Petavius, Huet, and Antoine Pagi**, though **Dupin and Cave** disagree. There were also <term>Traditores</term> <note>Traitors (literally "handers-over"): those who gave up the holy scriptures and other religious books to the enemies to be burned.</note>. Furthermore, there were those among the Christians who, moved by an imprudent zeal, provoked the anger of Princes and idol-worshippers against themselves for various reasons without any urgent necessity; many documents of this matter exist in the works of **Eusebius** and others. e. Even if it were granted that the number of Martyrs was enormous in those early times, and that many suffered various evils for well-reasoned causes (which I do not deny), it is nevertheless certain that the actions of men must be judged by the eternal rules of virtue and piety, not by unusual sayings and deeds. Many suffer many things, but against their will. These same people, if fortune favored them, would indulge their own inclinations. When human affairs flourish and men enjoy peaceful times, they are usually more insolent and less ardent in the study of piety. Since it is well known that in those first centuries the Christians had their "Halcyon days" <note>A period of peace or calm.</note>, there is no doubt that many also indulged in vices. Certainly, by the second and third centuries, ambition and the lust for power had seized many Bishops, as is clear from the examples of the Roman Popes **Victor and Stephen**, to say nothing of others. # MEDITATION VII.

->MEDITATION VII.<-

...[not] helping the needy, desiring to possess silver in abundance, seizing estates with treacherous frauds, and increasing gain through multiplying usury. Do we not deserve to suffer such things for sins of this kind? For divine judgment long ago forewarned and said: 
> If they forsake my law and do not walk in my judgments, if they profane my justifications and do not observe my precepts, I will visit their crimes with a rod and their sins with scourges. <note>original: "Si dereliquerint legem meam... visitabo in virga facinora eorum." This is a quote from Psalm 89:30-32.</note>

These things were announced to us and predicted beforehand: but we, unmindful of the law and the observance given to us, acted through our sins in such a way that, while we despised the Lord's mandates, we came to more severe remedies for the correction of our offense and the testing of our faith. Nor did we at last, even late, turn to the fear of the Lord, so that we might patiently and bravely undergo this correction of ours and this divine testing. At the very first words of the threatening enemy, a very great number of brothers betrayed their faith; they were not even prostrated by the force of the persecution, but prostrated themselves by a voluntary lapse. <note>The "lapsi" (the lapsed) were Christians who renounced their faith or performed pagan sacrifices under threat of Roman persecution.</note> *Thus far Cyprian.* <note>St. Cyprian of Carthage (c. 210–258 AD), a bishop who wrote extensively on Church discipline during the Decian persecution.</note> *Dionysius of Alexandria* <note>Bishop of Alexandria (d. 264 AD), whose letters are preserved in Eusebius’s history.</note> describes a similar slaughter of the Lapsed in Egypt at this same time at length in *Eusebius, Book VI.* *Justin Martyr, a writer of the 2nd Century*, speaks thus in his *Second Apology, page 64*, concerning the Christians of his age to *Antoninus Pius*: <note>Roman Emperor from 138 to 161 AD.</note> *But indeed, those who are found not living as he (namely, Christ) taught, that is a certain proof that they are not Christians, even though they profess the doctrine of Christ with their tongue. For he says that not those merely professing, but those confirming their profession by their works at the same time, shall be saved.* Furthermore, we ask that those who lead a life less consistent with his precepts and are only called Christians should also be punished by you. Surely that distinguished man would not have spoken so if all the Christians of his time had been perfectly aligned <term>perfectly aligned: the Latin 'examussitati' refers to being measured accurately by a mason's rule (amussis)</term> with virtue. Nor does it help those who take too much upon themselves in excessively extolling the virtues of the ancient Christians, claiming that in those centuries closest to the age of the Apostles, many were equipped with extraordinary gifts <note>Specifically referring to miraculous powers like healing or prophecy.</note> which men of the present century lack; for besides the fact that men should not be blamed for those things which are not placed in their own power, it is certain by the authority of the Infallible Teacher *Jesus Christ* himself in *Matthew 7:22, 23*, that such people can exist who nevertheless do not keep the most holy precepts of God. Erudition of any kind does not prevent men from indulging in their vices. 8) Finally, there are others who, in order to praise that singular virtue of the first Christians and the happiness of those centuries, while simultaneously proving the magnitude of the corruption raging today, appeal on one hand to the *Lives of the Fathers* of the primitive Church, and on the other hand to the scarcity of Atheists and Deists <note>Deists believe in a creator god based on reason but reject organized religion and divine revelation.</note>, whose number is becoming huge today among Christians. # ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

->ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.<-

it is easy to show that these things have little to do with the matter. Let us examine these points in a few words. We desire to detract nothing from the true virtues of the Fathers of the primitive Church. We praise the good things which the Supreme Deity granted to them. We profess that the blemishes to which they were liable should by no means be exaggerated. But if the same is done in the examination of the lives of those who lived among Christians in this age and the age of our fathers, we contend that many could be brought forward who shone no less in piety, sincerity, and other virtues which can fall upon Christian men and Overseers of Religion <note>Referring to bishops and clergy.</note> than the Fathers did. We can demonstrate this more evidently because far more certain records of the lives and deeds of the more recent Teachers are in our hands than those which have been handed down by ancient writings. Many have indeed described the lives of the Fathers in such a way that it is easily apparent they crossed the boundaries of truth. These things are today acknowledged among the learned. Therefore, just as those who sharply criticize every blemish of the Fathers and extol their errors into something greater act poorly; so likewise do those sin gravely who are accustomed to judge the vices, morals, and blemishes of the more recent Overseers of Religion more harshly than is fair. And indeed, it is a wonder that some see so keenly into the vices of the Moderns, and are at the same time so dim-sighted—nay, even blind—in perceiving the vices of the Teachers of the ancient Church. In a word, that comparison is of little value for extolling the virtue of the ancients while depressing the distinguished deeds of the moderns. As for what concerns the Deists, we confess their number is great in the most flourishing parts of Europe; but we deny that such a crowd of Atheists, properly so-called, can be found as some claim, or can be proven by certain testimonies. Whatever the case may be, it is equally certain that in the apostolic age there were men imbued with the most foul opinions. If anyone were to weigh the systems of these men called Heretics according to their "godless passions," <note>original: "ἀθέῳ παθῶν" (atheo pathon)</note> he will clearly perceive that they are not a bit better than those things brought forward by the more recent Deists. Certainly, if the things reported about the unspeakable crimes of certain Gnostics <note>An early group of diverse religious movements that claimed secret knowledge (gnosis) and were often accused of moral depravity by mainstream Christian writers.</note> are true—about which I will dispute with no one here—there is no doubt that they were far worse than the Deists themselves. We truly wonder by what means it could have happened that, while the Apostles and Apostolic Men equipped with extraordinary gifts were still breathing, such portentous opinions could nevertheless arise so early among Christians. We shall at some time, with God's help, treat this argument more fully. This is certain: the men who were called Heretics shamefully mixed those things which they had learned as youths concerning philosophy, rituals, and traditions, after they had given their name to the Christian religion.

# MEDITATION VII.

->MEDITATION VII.<-

From this it can easily be gathered that many from the common people formerly devoted to the sacred rites of either the Gentiles <note>The "Gentiles" here refers to pagans or non-Christians in the Roman world.</note> or the Jews did not immediately part ways with the unfortunate opinions they had seized upon when they came to the Christian religion. To this is added, finally, that the more recent Doctors <note>In this context, "Doctors" refers to learned theologians or teachers of the faith.</note> of the Holier discipline are far more successful than the Church Fathers in attacking erroneous opinions and proving fundamental truths. For example, let the disputation of *Justin Martyr* against the Jew <note>Referring to Justin Martyr's *Dialogue with Trypho*, written in the 2nd century.</note> be compared with those things which in our age *Limborch*, *Kidder*, and others have brought against the "circumcised nation," <note>original: "recutitam gentem" — a term used to refer to the Jewish people, often with a focus on the rite of circumcision.</note> and it will be most manifest that what we assert is true. *Jerome*, in Letter 13 to Paulinus, judging the writings of *Lactantius*, speaks thus among other things: *Would that he had been able to confirm our own things as easily as he destroyed those of others.* <note>original: "Utinam tam nostra confirmare potuisset, quam facile aliena destruxit." Jerome is noting that Lactantius was better at arguing against paganism than explaining Christian doctrine.</note> This same saying could be applied to most of the writings of the Fathers. From all these things brought forward by us so far, I think it is sufficiently clear that those do not act rightly who extol the corruption of our own century so much, and, having dismissed better arguments and safeguards, are accustomed to send people away without discrimination to imitate the customs of the Ancient Christians.

VI. > *Those are well known who have set forth by design the life and customs of the first Christians, the most learned men Jean Fronton, William Cave, Gottfried Arnold, and others; who, although they are by no means to be despised and have said and advised many things both true and useful, have nevertheless long seemed to eminent men to have exceeded the limit.*
> 
> *In my judgment, these following points were chiefly admitted [as errors] by them. (1) They act no differently than if their entire assembly of those who professed Christ in the first centuries had been free of vicious men and those ignorant of sinning. In which they are clearly mistaken. For the letters and writings of Paul and the other Apostles, of Clement, Ignatius, and others, clearly show that the Church of Christ was always like a field in which the wheat was mixed with unhappy weeds [tares], and that a crowd of greedy, lustful, ambitious, and contentious men also polluted the golden age of religion. What else do the very frequent and vehement exhortations and rebukes of those holy men signify? Many took care to have themselves inscribed in the Christian—*

(*) He now indeed performs the duty of Chancellor, as is known, in the University of Göttingen.

> *—number, whose sole purpose was to enjoy the liberality and love of the brothers, and to lead a lazy and soft life among vices. Others joined them, so captured by the love of the perverse opinions and institutions to which they had been accustomed from their infancy <note>original: "a teneris" — literally "from tender [years]."</note> that they could be drawn away from them in almost no way; yet prudence did not allow everyone affected in that way to be deprived of sacred communion. These things will not be unknown to those by whom the old books of the Christians and the writings of the Apostles themselves have been read with care. (2) They do not distinguish the eras accurately: which nevertheless must be done, and under the name of the "ancient Christians" they designate all those who lived up to CONSTANTINE, or rather even after CONSTANTINE, which is manifest from the testimonies they apply. But those not ignorant of ancient affairs know how great a harvest of evil men already besieged the Church in the second century, which took on greater increases with time, and in the fourth century so clearly infected the whole flock that few traces of the ancient faith and integrity remained. (3) From those things which Tertullian, Clement, Irenaeus, or even Jerome and Augustine, prescribe, hand down, and teach about arranging life rightly and instituting it according to the rule of Christ, they estimate the life of Christians: but who, I ask, does not see how preposterously this is done? For what kind of reasoning is this? The Teachers of the Christians prescribe many things excellently and outstandingly concerning piety, sanctity, reverence toward God, and love: Therefore the ancient Christians, at least the greatest part of them, were pious, holy, full of love, and most studious of God. One or another of the ancient Teachers also proclaims and aptly declares his own holiness and piety: Therefore all Christians were similar to this one. For it is established among all that the words and deeds of men very often differ wonderfully among themselves. (4) Whatever was said, done, and written by one or a few certain people, they regard no differently than if it were the voice and action of the whole Church. Most of those who handle the affairs of the Ancient Christians labor under this vice, or at least some part of it. For what they see narrated or sanctioned by this or that person, they very frequently refer to as among the common rites, opinions, and institutions of the ancient Christians: by what right this is done is manifest. (5) Nor would I think this even to be approved: that they persuade themselves that the Christian assembly was such in every part as it is described in the Apologies <note>The "Apologies" were formal legal defenses of Christianity written to Roman officials, such as those by Justin Martyr or Tertullian.</note> which Christians offered to Magistrates and Emperors. For who is ignorant that those who undertake the defense of some Society are accustomed to commemorate only those things which lead to its praise and commendation, but to omit the stains and diseases by which it is pressed? Nor is this done basely or shamefully, but honestly and prudently, provided the intent of deceiving and harming is absent. Besides, all [reprehensions]...*

->MEDITATION VII.<-

...praises and commendations are usually sought from him, as is typical for one who is most prominent and distinguished in a certain matter or family. That the ancient Christians were not unmindful of this custom will be easily understood by anyone who compares what Tertullian <note>Tertullian (c. 155 – c. 220 AD) was a prolific early Christian author from Carthage, known as the "Father of Latin Theology."</note> relates in his *Apologetic* books regarding the morals of Christians with those things which he reports and laments elsewhere throughout his other writings. (6) It is certain that there were dissensions of no small importance among the ancient Christians concerning moral matters and the duties of Christians, and that one person stood out as more lenient or more severe than another. For this reason, the life of Christians was not one and the same in all places; rather, it must have been varied and diverse according to the differing opinions of those who were in charge of the assemblies. Those who delight in the knowledge of these matters know that Christians have felt differently since the most ancient times regarding the necessity and utility of human learning <note>original: "Eruditionis humanae" — secular or classical education.</note>, the harmony between the Christian Religion and the State, the duties of spouses, war, commerce, and infinite other things. 

Those individuals whose cause is being discussed here collect the precepts given by a single sect of Christians on these matters and want us to believe that they represent the common opinion of the entire Christian community—and not just their opinion, but their actual life and conduct as well. After a few intervening words, a Most Learned Man <note>This likely refers to a contemporary critic of the idealized view of church history.</note> finally concludes his argument thus: *Indeed (he says), I feel that if anyone thinks they should walk the path that Gottfried Arnold* <note>Gottfried Arnold (1666–1714) was a German historian whose work "Unbiased History of the Church and Heretics" was controversial for its sympathetic view of "heretics" and its critique of the institutional church.</note> *held in his "Delineation of the Ancient Christians," written in German, it would not be difficult for them—provided they are well-versed in ancient monuments—to compose from those same records a volume of equal size regarding the vicious and perverse life of the Christians.* Without controversy, the older assemblies of Christians, especially those that flourished in the first and second centuries, were better than those of today, and for that reason, they can be set forth as an example to that degenerate people who today call themselves Christ’s. But those who decree that they were perfect in every respect are mistaken and arm the scoffers of all religion against us. Thus says that celebrated theologian. 

Let the most famous theologian of Jena, J. G. Walch <note>Johann Georg Walch (1693–1775) was a prominent Lutheran theologian and historian.</note>, follow him. In his *Ecclesiastical History*, page 394 and following, he opens his mind on this argument as follows: *Although (he says) the ancient Christians in the Apostolic Church abounded in the praise of piety and holiness, it is by no means to be thought that this assembly was entirely free from blemishes, or that it excluded all vices and sins; for besides the fact that hypocrites could occasionally be in that society, even the true and faithful worshippers of Christ were subject to weaknesses and gave clear evidence of them. Contentions and schisms arose; there were other things to be amended and corrected, from which anyone can understand that the Apostolic Church was not perfect or finished in every part.* Having proved these things in the observations subject to the text, he proceeds in Section VIII.

# ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

->ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.<-

Which things being so, in describing and judging the holiness of the Apostolic Church, such caution must be applied so that what is excessive may be avoided. The illustrious examples of virtues that Christian men gave in the first century are by no means to be neglected, but are to be praised and studiously commended to others for imitation; yet in such a way that no more than is fitting is attributed to them, nor should it be thought that all vices were removed from their Christian society. 

And a little later: *Those who have commented on the life and morals of the first Christians sometimes seem to have exceeded the limit. First, they sometimes speak of their assembly as if no vicious men or men devoid of divine grace had any place in it—neither those who openly followed their depraved desires, nor those who put on a show of holiness—in which they are greatly mistaken. For just as, in the opinion of Christ himself, the Church is like a field in which wheat is found together with tares* <note>A reference to the Parable of the Weeds in Matthew 13:24-30.</note>, *so the writings of the Apostles and Apostolic men clearly show that the Church which flourished in their age was not without evil men.* Those things which a few said and did are attributed to everyone or to the whole assembly by an unjust method of reasoning. Furthermore, they allow too much in this cause when they ascribe more than is proper to those who were truly devoted to Christ and, being estranged from the things of the world, sought nothing but the heavenly and eternal. They adorn their remarkable virtues with praises—rightly and by all law, indeed—but they are entirely silent about their weaknesses, as if they had been completely free from them. Added to this is the fact that they think the praise of holiness, which is proper to the Apostolic age, pertains to three or four centuries, not considering that the Christians of following times fell away significantly from the holiness of their ancestors, and that already in the second century a multitude of evil men polluted the Church. 

To these two, I subjoin the judgment of my sweetest friend, N. Nonnen <note>Nicolaus Nonnen (1701–1772) was a theologian from Bremen.</note>, a most famous theologian of Bremen, who in his *Oration on the signs of the times* <note>original: "Oratione de signis temporum"</note>—especially those preceding the present more fortunate century—reasons thus on this question: *The judgments of men (he says) are pulled apart concerning the face of morals and virtue to be established in the present century, if it is measured against an older age, as to whether the palm of victory should be granted to this age or to ours. This deserves to be weighed in the balance by those most skilled in ancient history. It is certain that many are led by opinions and that common sentiments, which are believed without proper examination, are the causes and occasions of complaints that morals are daily rushing into worse states and that every kind of vice is increasing. That common refrain is far too often shaken out. Shall religion, the preaching of the word, the wise laws of the state, and the care spent on educating youth be thus deprived of all fruit? Every century has its own vices, which reign widely, and every century has remedies which are opposed to them.* I was moved toward the opinion I defend by a book of the second...

VII. Furthermore, there are among learned men those who do not deny that great corruption under which the human race labors—indeed, they confess and deplore it—but they think much of this deformity is removed if it is asserted that there are an infinite number of people living on other planets who are far more excellent and happy than the inhabitants of our globe. This opinion was championed by the illustrious **Leibniz** <note>Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646–1716), a German polymath and philosopher who famously argued that we live in the "best of all possible worlds."</note> and many others after him. It is helpful to quote some of his words; in his *The Cause of God Pleaded*, section 58, he says: *Our Earth is nothing but a satellite of a single Sun ☉; there are as many Suns as there are fixed stars; ✶ and it is credible that there is a vast space beyond all the fixed stars. Therefore, nothing prevents either the suns, or especially the region beyond the suns, from being inhabited by happy creatures. Although planets could also be, or become, happy in the likeness of Paradise. Regarding the many mansions in our Father's house, Christ spoke specifically of the heaven of the Blessed, which some theologians call the Empyrean <note>term: Empyrean (from the Greek "pyr" meaning fire). In ancient and medieval cosmology, the highest part of heaven, believed to be the dwelling place of God and the angels, composed of pure light or fire.</note> and place beyond the stars or suns, even if nothing certain can be affirmed about the location of the blessed. Meanwhile, it can be judged likely that in the visible world there are many habitations of rational creatures, some happier than others.* In his *Theodicy* <note>original: "Theodicea," Leibniz's 1710 work defending God's justice in the face of evil.</note> on page 84 of the Amsterdam 1720 edition, he speaks thus: *Today, whatever limits one gives, or does not give, to the universe, it must be recognized that there are an innumerable number of globes as large as and larger than ours, which have as much right as it does to have rational inhabitants, though it does not follow that they are men. It is possible that all the Suns are inhabited only by happy creatures, and nothing obliges us to believe that there are many damned, for a few examples or a few samples suffice for the utility that good derives from evil. Moreover, as there is no reason to believe that there are stars everywhere, is it not possible that there is a vast space beyond the region of the stars? Whether it be the Empyrean Heaven or not, this immense space which surrounds all this region could always be filled with happiness and glory. It could be conceived as the Ocean, where the rivers of all blessed creatures flow when they have reached their perfection in the system of the stars. What will become of the consideration of our Globe and* <note>The previous two paragraphs translate Leibniz's original Latin and French text into English.</note>

The existence of such inhabitants cannot be demonstrated by certain arguments; nor is anything known to us about the state of these beings. Even if you assume there is a vast number of humans (if we may at least call them that) who are most happy, this will not have much strength in the minds of those people who are submerged in waves of doubt regarding the **Providence of God**. Certainly, this contemplation will have little power in the minds of those who struggle with many evils on this earth and are oppressed by the insolence of the wicked. Suppose you encounter a great crowd of people who have been cast into a most miserable state by the savage War which, alas! rages violently today in the most flourishing parts of Europe, and they explain their misfortunes to you with hot tears. If you were to tell them, among other things, to be of good heart for the reason that in other orbits in the heavens there is an infinite number of most happy people who have never experienced any evils, plagues, or wars—do you think they would receive this speech with a serene brow? Is it not more likely that they would grieve for this very reason: that they did not occupy those places from which such great evils were so far removed, but instead live in places where perpetual wars and other innumerable evils are to be feared? Again, if such inhabitants exist, it is asked whether they are equipped with a mind and some kind of small body <note>original: "corpusculo"</note> or not. If you say yes, it must be proven that these small bodies are subject to no diseases or pains, and that their minds cannot deviate from the true and the right. If both can happen, the magnitude of corruption is not removed, but increased. If

VIII. But it is time that we also explain our own opinion on this argument. And first, indeed, we think that two extremes must be avoided; we must certainly be careful on one hand that we do not exaggerate evils beyond measure and make all men indiscriminately worse than they are. For those who judge in this way perceive the divine promises and the Christian Church with too little foresight and caution, and they strengthen the arguments of the Unbelievers <note>original: "Incredulorum"</note> against divine Providence—though against their own intention. Nor should a **Platonic Republic** <note>original: "Respublica platonica." A reference to Plato's *Republic*, describing an ideal, perfect state that does not exist in reality.</note> be set before the mind when a judgment is to be made about the life and morals of men. Whoever considers the nature of men, their education, and their status, will easily discover that it cannot happen otherwise than that many wander far from the true and the right. (*) At the same time, however, we must not commit the error on the other side of wanting to diminish the number of sinners and the gravity of the evil—which strikes everyone's eyes—by denial, or of selling atrocious crimes as mere "infirmities of nature," or finally, of measuring the purity of the lives of Christians by the truth of public religious confessions. For in this way, evils would rather be increased, since most mortals are by nature prone and very inclined to dissolve the bonds of the most holy duties, and to seek a way by which they might somehow indulge their false and depraved desires under the cover of religious zeal. # MEDITATION VII.

->MEDITATION VII.<-

Among Christians, a sign of corruption is that Oaths, which are held as a most sacred thing among all nations, are nevertheless kept with little reverence by many Christians; indeed, they are neglected everywhere. (*) (c) There is a meager knowledge among Christians of pure and chaste Religion, and of the duties prescribed in the Gospel of Jesus Christ—a point we have remarked upon several times in the preceding dissertations of this work. Since a more accurate knowledge of Religion supplies the most effective motives for pursuing piety and virtues of every kind, one can easily judge how little power those motives will have over the minds of men who are equipped only with a confused and weak understanding of divine matters. (d) Very few Christians have a clear perspective on what the true nature and character of internal divine worship consists of; hence, most are content with the observance of external Worship, and they persuade themselves that the greater part of piety is situated in this. Others—which amounts to the same thing—think they are fine Christians if they not only adhere firmly to certain articles of Religion learned in childhood, but also stand up for them and defend them most fiercely. (**) (e) There is a massive crowd of hypocrites of every kind and rank among Christians. Many "imitate Curius while living like Bacchanals." <note>original: "Multi Curios simulant, & Bacchanalia vivunt." <meta>This page continues the author's argument that while individual Christians are flawed, the current age provides more resources for piety and truth than ever before, eventually transitioning into a discussion on how the poor behavior of believers fuels atheism and skepticism.</meta>

<page-num>302</page-num>
<header>MEDITATION VII.</header>

->MEDITATION VII.<-

There are those whose weaknesses are more or less obvious to the eye: there are those who return to a productive life <note>original: "ad frugem redeant," an idiom for returning to virtue or sobriety</note> later, and those who do so sooner. In everyone, no matter what level of piety they have reached, some measure of weakness remains which cannot easily be removed from the eye's view. And this imperfection, by which even the best men are burdened, results in their value not always being properly recognized. Furthermore, because mortal eyes more willingly feast upon the contemplation of the flaws with which even godly men are usually afflicted, many people can hardly be induced to honestly and frankly praise and proclaim the virtues present in others. 

But if we furthermore turn our attention to the safeguards by which both truth and piety are usually promoted among mortals, there are many things which prove that our current age is not so barren of virtues. Never has the truth, excellence, and divine origin of the Christian Religion been proven by so many arguments as in our own time. Never have the divine virtues shining forth from the work of Creation been placed in such a clear light as in this age in which we live. We rejoice that never before have so many books been painstakingly produced for the conversion of the Gentiles <note>In this context, meaning non-Christians or "heathens"</note> and for convincing Unbelievers of their error as has been done in this our age. Never before has the excellence of Christian Ethics been demonstrated with such force of reasoning as we now see being done through the work of men of most excellent talent and judgment. Never have the sources of superstition been so skillfully uncovered, nor the detestable arts of heretics so clearly exposed as in our time; never has liberty of conscience been asserted and defended by such clear arguments as in this passing century. Indeed, it should be counted among the blessings of our age that men eminent in piety and learning have shown in many volumes how much slaughter has been brought not only upon the Holy City, but also upon Empires and Republics, by the violent persecutions undertaken in the name of Religion; and how much, by contrast, a moderate spirit and a tolerance for dissenters within their proper limits contribute to public peace. 

I will say nothing for now of the many nurseries of piety and virtue—the schools and societies for the propagation of the Christian Religion—established everywhere. I know quite well that it can hardly be concluded from this that all Christians, or even most of them, make use of these excellent means and become better people. But sensible men will grant me this: that these safeguards, by their very nature, contribute much to the cultivation of piety and virtue; and it is impossible that no Christians at all have been led to a better way of living by the help of those safeguards. For if those things which the Gentiles themselves warned about regarding the scarcity of men who love virtue—for example, *Cebes* in his "Tablet" <note>An allegorical Greek work describing the path to virtue</note> and *Xenophon*—are compared with what our *Holy Savior* <note>original: "S. Soter," from the Greek "Soter" meaning Savior</note>

<meta>catchword: concerning</meta>

<page-num>303</page-num>
<header>ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.</header>

spoke concerning the narrow and the wide paths, it will not be surprising that in such great light there are still many Christians who are either blind or dim-sighted. If we weigh everything that has been said so far, it will be established that the face of Christianity in our times is indeed very foul; but it is not actually worse if it is compared with the morals and lives of Christians of preceding centuries.

<margin>This great corruption of Christians is a primary cause of Unbelief.</margin>

IX. Whatever the case may be, this much is certain: the degenerate life of the majority of Christians is a primary cause of the Unbelief that is spreading everywhere. Although all who consult their reason understand why this happens, it must nevertheless be demonstrated in a few words. 

1) First, it is established by the experience of all ages that most mortals do not model their lives so much on the decrees of right reason and the nature of duties prescribed by the Law of Nature and Revelation, but rather on the examples and customs of others. Hence, they look into the lives of other men as if into a mirror, not so much for the purpose of rightly discerning what should be followed or avoided, but rather to remove the troublesome examination of themselves and to cover their own errors with the examples of others, or to diminish the foulness of those errors. 

2) Since these same people only act with pleasure upon, and follow, those things which favor their own wicked passions, and since such people are found everywhere among Christians who, having despised Religion, are immersed in every kind of vice, they seek a defense for their own bad cause in this very multitude of sinners. 

3) This being established—that is, having seen such a crowd of vicious men among people of every rank and dignity—they conclude that Religion is not built upon such certain principles as is commonly believed, nor that God will punish the vicious so severely. Furthermore, they conclude that vices are so connected with the constitution of human nature that they cannot be avoided by any means. They believe those who urge the study of virtue so strongly are merely following Platonic ideals <note>meaning "Platonic ideas" or "Utopian dreams"—theories that are perfect in thought but impossible to practice</note>, that is, they are drumming in things that are plainly impossible to achieve. 

It is added that such men, lacking a taste for pure religion, often notice that men who are not unlearned—those who are held by others' judgment to be pious and lovers of virtue—are actually regarded as hypocrites in whom no faith should be placed. Since the number of the godly is small, while the crowd of those who have adapted themselves to the morals of a corrupt age is huge, they think they can easily excuse their way of life, however shameful it has been thus far. The error is increased if they see that those very people who devote themselves to the pursuit of virtue with all their might are often subject to the contempt and persecution of others,

If they have obtained this, they think they have provided more than enough for their own security. X. But if truly the immense corruption which, alas, spreads and dominates everywhere among Christians, casts many into the vice of Unbelief, it is manifest that the depraved morals of men of the Sacred Order <note>The clergy or ministry.</note> contribute much to greatly increasing this evil. Honesty and piety prevent us from not touching this ulcer. However, we shall deal with this argument in such a way that none of those who are held by the study of piety and truth will have cause to complain about us: we wish to insult no one, but will show at least candidly and modestly how those who are accustomed to go by the name of Teachers, Pastors, and Leaders of Religion, by the worst example of a corrupt life, can be not only a grave scandal to others but also increase the prevailing Unbelief. That there are many among Christians who criticize, exaggerate, and blow out of proportion every single blemish of the Ministers of the Word of God <note>original: "V. D. Ministrorum", abbreviation for *Verbi Divini Ministri*.</note> is established by sad experience. But who would deny that these critics sin gravely? No one has ever said that Ministers of Religion are immune to all blemishes and errors. Certainly, those who look upon them as if they were men dropped from heaven, and desire almost nothing less than angelic purity in them, demanding all their actions meet this image, are vehemently mistaken. It is true that the nature of the office they perform requires that they excel in the pursuit of piety and be an example to their flocks: but this does not prevent them from having their own blemishes, provided they are few in number and they take serious pains so that, urged by the stings of conscience, they daily improve their nature more and more with divine help. <page-num>308</page-num>

# MEDITATION VII.

It must be admitted that injury has been done to the men of the [Sacred] Order <note>The clergy or ministry.</note> when they have been harassed without cause; yet, at the same time, it cannot be denied that there have always been—and alas, still are!—men of this order who, unmindful of the most holy office they are tasked to perform, live a life contaminated by various vices. There have always been, and still are among them, those who are quarrelsome, greedy, lustful, eager for revenge, proud, burning with a lust for power, and animated by a false—indeed, a tyrannical—spirit against those who disagree with them, as well as those devoted to other vices. Among these brothers, even grace is rare. Sincere love is rare, which nevertheless Christ commended so many times to his disciples. And from this have arisen the most justified complaints of men eminent in piety and learning concerning the perpetual brawls and contentions among the teachers of the most holy discipline. From these, it is alas most manifest that many Teachers are led by public depraved passions rather than by the rules of Christian discipline, though they ought to present a face to others characterized by a zeal for moderation, peace, and fraternal love. Let us hear the most grave and observant **Samuel Werenfels** <note>A Swiss theologian (1657–1740) known for his moderate views and critique of scholarly arrogance.</note>, a theologian by the consensus of all the learned, complaining of this evil. In his excellent little book *On the Word-Battles of the Learned* <note>Original title: *De Logomachiis Eruditorum*.</note>, Chapter VII, he opens his mind on this subject, saying:

> Nor should anyone ask me whether even those who are called learned, who are called Philosophers (we add: Theologians and Ministers of the Word of God), and who are called wise, are subject to this disease (he is speaking of the passions). For who does not know the hatreds that exist between different sects and religions, the hatreds between Academies, the hatreds between men of different studies, the hatreds and rivalries of colleagues and fellow students: the hatreds between those who prefer the old things and those who prefer the more recent: the hatreds toward all whom we think diminish or obscure our own learning: the hatreds of those who do not embrace our opinions or venerate them; who dare to disagree with us, or seem to disagree? And who could ever enumerate them all? When truly these hatreds borrow the holy name of Zeal for God, for religion, and for truth: then indeed it is utterly lost: then nothing more is seen nor understood: then, to not see horrendous heresies in others—even if they are nowhere to be found—is considered impiety; to not condemn the innocent and hand them over to hell is considered lukewarmness in religion; to not twist everything into the worst possible sense is considered treason; to not cry out, not clamor, and not throw heaven and earth into confusion is held to be **atheism** <note>Original Greek: ἀθεώτης (*atheotēs*).</note>.

Thus far that distinguished theologian. Now, since the times of **Constantine the Great** <note>The first Roman Emperor to convert to Christianity (reigned 306–337 AD), often blamed by later writers for the Church's loss of spiritual focus as it gained political power.</note> (to say nothing of what happened before), many Bishops and Sacred Ministers of lower rank were driven headlong by ambition, the lust for power, and greed. These evils increased so much over the course of time, as Church history bears witness,

that you read hardly anything else in the histories of those times than the vices of the Clergy. The illustrious **Grotius** <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a Dutch jurist and theologian; he argues here that the rise of Islam was a divine judgment on a corrupt Christian Church.</note>, explaining the causes of God’s judgments upon the Church on the occasion of the rise of Muhammadanism <note>Islam.</note>, says:

> That true and simple piety (he says) which had flourished among the most severely harassed and oppressed Christians began gradually to cool from the time when, through Constantine and the following Emperors, it was brought about that this profession was not only safe but also honored—the world being, as it were, thrust into the Church. Bishops fought most bitterly among themselves for the highest seats; and just as once the tree of knowledge, preferred over the tree of life, had produced the greatest evils, so then also curious Learning was preferred to piety, and religion was made into an art. It followed from this that, after the example of those who built the tower of Babel, the rash affectation of sublime things produced discordant speech and discord. Seeing this, the common people, often not knowing where to turn, cast the blame on the Holy Scriptures and began to flee them as if they were poisoned. Religion, moreover, began everywhere to be placed not in purity of mind, but (as if Judaism were brought back) in rituals and in those things which consist more of exercise of the body than amendment of the soul, and likewise in a burning zeal for the factions once chosen. At last, it happened that everywhere there were Christians in name, but in reality very few. (*On the Truth of the Christian Religion*, Book VI, Section I).

Long before Muhammad, many leaders of the Church complained of the prevailing corruption of Christians. See the testimonies collected by **Rittersbusius** <note>Conrad Rittershuis (1560–1613), a German jurist and scholar.</note> in his notes on **Salvian** <note>A 5th-century Christian writer who famously argued that the fall of Rome was a punishment for the moral decay of Christians.</note>, and the notes of learned men on this very passage of Grotius. Prætextatus (he says), who died as Consul-designate, used to say jokingly to the Blessed Pope Damasus: "Make me Bishop of the city of Rome, and I will be a Christian immediately." <note>This anecdote highlights how wealthy and powerful the Roman Bishopric had become by the 4th century.</note> After those times, everything rushed toward the worse, so much so that the many scandalous actions of Bishops and Monks can hardly be read without horror. The corruption of the Clergy certainly reached such a height that entire nations, just before the **Amendment of the sacred things** <note>The Reformation.</note> was undertaken, deposited their complaints in the lap of the Emperors. After the times of the Reformation, some of this order have conducted themselves more cautiously, and as they have cultivated various disciplines with greater zeal and effort, so likewise many have been found here and there who amended their morals; although it is to be wished that they would compose their way of life according to the discipline of Christ rather than the rules of certain monks. But why do we speak so much of the corruption of the Roman clergy? Let us rather frankly confess that here and there in the gatherings of Protestants are found not a few Leaders of the Sacred Rites who lead a life entirely foreign to the most holy Religion they profess. <header>MEDITATION VII.</header>

Moreover, the public confessions of these men are pure, and their rules for living are excellent; therefore, it offends all lovers of piety and honesty all the more to see the lives of certain individuals so abhorrent to the precepts of Jesus Christ. Nor is it a wonder that many, having seen and caught so many vices in men of this order, are plunged into the very **Abyss of Unbelief**. For these men are usually better instructed in the knowledge of divine matters than others; they are accustomed—indeed, they are bound—to rail against the wicked ways of the world, to set a strong heart against a corrupt and degenerate Christianity, to proclaim the excellence of the Christian Religion, to urge a diligent observance of Christ's commands, and, as much as possible, to uproot the very seeds of vice, and so on. But if they truly act contrary to all these things and are immersed in various kinds of vices, touched by little care for their conscience, it cannot happen otherwise than that those who are not sufficiently persuaded of the truth of Religion, or those who have minds prone to vice, begin to doubt the chief heads of Religion. For they can hardly bring themselves to believe that men so well-instructed in the knowledge of divine things, and who "thunder" so loudly against vice while being simultaneously contaminated by shameful vices, are seriously persuaded of the truth of those matters which they are accustomed to instill and commend publicly with such a show of piety and zeal. And indeed, alas! sad experience proves that examples of this sort carry much weight in confirming Unbelief. Certainly, they do more harm than the most subtle books published by Unbelievers against Religion, because most mortals are not endowed with the intellect to weigh the force of subtle objections, but such vices can almost be felt with the hands by any common person. There exist the confessions of men who have publicly joined the ranks of unbelief, in which they freely and roundly admit that the corrupt morals of men of the Holy Order contributed most to their repudiation of the Christian Religion. Well known is the testimony of the *Earl of Rochester* <note>John Wilmot, 2nd Earl of Rochester (1647–1680), a famous poet and "libertine" known for his rakish lifestyle before a deathbed conversion.</note> cited by Bishop *Burnet* <note>Gilbert Burnet (1643–1715), Bishop of Salisbury and author of "Some Passages of the Life and Death of John Earl of Rochester."</note> in the biography of this noble man. Because this serves our Purpose, I shall provide it here. It appears on page 83 of the French edition published in Zurich. *The Count (says the Illustrious Bishop) told me frankly, that nothing had more incited him, along with many others, to Libertinism* <note>original: "Libertinage." In this context, it refers to both moral profligacy and the intellectual rejection of religious authority.</note>, *than seeing the loose life, full of hypocrisy, of those who made profession of following Piety. He confessed that, if Religion were not a pure artifice, it was undoubtedly the most important thing it was possible to imagine: and that if he could once believe it to be true, he would apply himself with much ardor and zeal to living conformably to the faith. But on one hand, the passion for advancement, which he had found in some ecclesiastics—*

<meta>catchword: tics</meta>

<page-num>311</page-num>
<header>ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.</header>

*—at the Court, joined to the low and servile manner in which they went about it; and on the other hand, the animosities that reign among them over trifles, had often obliged him to conclude that they themselves doubted everything they preached to others. He alleged a great number of examples, of which I knew several were nothing but pure calumnies or false interpretations of certain actions quite innocent in themselves; but unfortunately there were some that were only too true. I publish it with all the more boldness as I would like to remind those who claim to have Religion, and above all those who are its Ministers, of the engagement they are under to live in a manner suitable to their profession, if they do not wish to be responsible for a great part of the Atheism and Impiety that exists in the world. Profligates are delighted when they find something to bite into regarding the conduct of Good People, and above all those who must serve as an example to others, such as the Preachers of the Gospel. They do not fail to conclude from this, not only that some so-called Devout people are Hypocrites, but that Religion itself is nothing but charlatanry.* <note>original: "charlatanerie."</note> Thus says Burnet. Alphonse Rosset, the most celebrated Professor at Lausanne, grants the same opinion in his *General Reflections on Deism*, page 219. *I cannot (he says) help but remark here, that the bad conduct of Christians, and in particular the vices of the Clergy, can provide a secondary occasion for Deism to appear. When one sees Christians, but above all the Ministers of Religion, conducting themselves in a fashion entirely opposite to their Principles: being the Slaves of passions that they condemn in others, and of vices they make profession of fighting; one is violently led to presume that they do not believe at all what they profess to believe, and that if they show so much zeal for Religion, it is rather in view of advancing their worldly interests and dominating over consciences, than out of respect or esteem for it. Now, once one has come to that point: one does not delay in looking at the Religion itself that they profess as a political ruse, or as a fraud of the Clergy. One is wrong to reason thus; (Who doubts it?) but the thing is no less sad.*

<margin>Another cause of Unbelief is the reading of books favoring Atheism and impiety.</margin>
XI. But let us finally leave these matters and proceed to uncover another fountain of impiety. No one would doubt that the frequent reading of those books in which, by deliberate effort, the heads of natural and revealed religion are attacked, or in which all kinds of vices are commended under various pretexts and different colors, contributes much to [corrupting] minds either imbued with a meager knowledge of divine things or strongly prone to vice,
