...greatly, they are to be imbued with pestilential opinions, and torn away from the love of piety. But before we prove this, the reasoning of our plan requires us to advise something in advance concerning the publication and reading of those books. And **firstly**, it is indeed admitted that not only do all men enjoy the right of investigating the truth, but they are also bound by the Supreme Power to examine all truths which can lead to achieving internal and external happiness. The greater the importance of those truths, the more effort everyone must exert to seek a solid understanding of them, according to their individual capacity. The more accurate knowledge of the principal heads of Natural <note>Religion based on reason and the observation of nature.</note> and Revealed Religion <note>Religion based on divine communication, such as the Bible.</note> contributes most to obtaining that happiness, as agreed by all who have not become dull-witted. From which **II.** it clearly follows that everyone is bound to conduct that examination. Since experience bears witness that many have attacked Religion in public writings, and still attack it with various arguments, it is necessary that those who are not only held by a love of religion but are also officially bound to imbue others with solid knowledge of divine things, should seriously and carefully weigh the reasons by which those most weighty truths are attacked, without any party bias and <term>dispassionately</term> <note>original Greek: ἀμερπαθῶν (amerpathon), meaning without being swayed by emotion or prejudice.</note>. This cannot be done otherwise than if those books are diligently unfolded, and the weakness of the reasons brought against them is demonstrated by solid arguments; certainly, there is no safer way to lead the wandering back to the path, and to recall from errors those who are held by a love of truth or who have been deceived by reading such books. **III.** Just as everyone has the right to examine Religion and weigh the arguments of opponents, it is likewise permitted for those who doubt these or those heads of Religion to bring forward their doubts modestly with supporting reasons in public, and to communicate them with the Learned, especially if they are persuaded that they have not been satisfied in private conversations. In this way, it often happens that not only are the wandering recalled to the path and the sources of error detected, but the truth itself, which was previously attacked, is placed in a clearer light. Thus it is known that England is most fertile in books in which Religion is attacked either harshly or modestly; but it is also found at the same time that there is a distinguished abundance of most learned and excellent men in this most flourishing Island, who, with great sharpness of mind and a distinguished apparatus of Learning, have not only most solidly vindicated Religion but have also supplied many new safeguards for defending it more correctly on this occasion. I know by some...

...by some it is said that Unbelievers are moved to publish those doubts not by a love of knowing the truth, but by a desire to disseminate grave errors; but this does not prevent these books from being read and examined by learned men, even if it were mostly true. It cannot be so easily shown that this or that person, who publicly brings forth doubts that have arisen in their mind against certain articles of Religion, does so for an evil end; nor is it necessary that we should always be attentive to the end which the writer perhaps intends, but rather the matter itself is to be weighed, and it must be seen how the error can be met and the truth vindicated by solid reasons. If this is accomplished, the matter is on safe ground, and it is all the same whether the writer communicated his doubts to the Learned World for an evil or a good end. There are even those among the defenders of truth who defend many heads of religion not out of love for the truth and solid persuasion, but ignited by a desire for glory or advantage, which nevertheless does not prevent those books from being worn out in the hands of readers. From what we have said so far, it is clear what, in my opinion, learned men and those concerned with Religion should attempt against the books that have been and are still being published by <term>Unbelievers</term> <note>original: Incredulis</note> among the common people. There are indeed some who think that all those books should be proscribed and handed over to the <term>Fire</term> <note>original: Vulcano (Vulcan, the Roman god of fire)</note>, because the minds of many are surely corrupted by such reading. Others do not think those books should be eliminated, but rather that they should only be read by those who are skilled in the art of reasoning and well-versed in the more severe disciplines; these men not only defend the freedom of publishing such books but also wish that the writings of the most ancient Heretics and enemies of the Christian religion had been transmitted down to our age. Lest I seem to have said these things for no reason, I will bring forward some testimonies: among those who have most learnedly and sharply defended the Christian Religion against the insults of Unbelievers, it is known to all the Learned that the Most Reverend Bishop <term>Chandler</term> <note>Edward Chandler (1668–1750), an English bishop known for his defenses of Christianity against deism.</note> is to be numbered. In his defense of Christianity, according to the German version of the preface to <term>Tindal</term> <note>Matthew Tindal (1657–1733), an influential English deist whose work "Christianity as Old as the Creation" challenged traditional revelation.</note> written by a most learned author, he opens his mind, saying: *“The cause of God and of Truth can never suffer from a well-ordered discussion and from the sharpest and an entirely impartial investigation. I would be heartily pleased to see all objections against Christianity in their greatest light, so that I might know all the better whether my confession and my hope as a Christian are built upon a firm and rational ground or not. If our present-day unbelievers clearly show...”*

### MEDITATION VII.

...be able to prove that Christianity is a fraud, I will let it go immediately; but if they cannot do so, then all their objections against it will only confirm its divine authority all the more. <note>original German: "gen können, daß das Christenthum ein Betrug sey..."</note> Thus far that distinguished Prelate. The most learned **Foster** <note>James Foster (1697–1753), a popular English Baptist preacher known for defending the reasonableness of Christianity.</note> delivers the same judgment at the beginning of his refutation of **Tyndal's** book <note>Matthew Tyndal (1657–1733), an English deist whose book *Christianity as Old as the Creation* argued that revelation was unnecessary. This sparked a massive literary debate across Europe.</note>. The words sound thus:

> Since religion is a matter of the highest importance to the human race, everyone should be allowed the freedom to bring forward their objections against it. This is the only way to determine its true nature and set it on a firm foundation; otherwise, truth and falsehood, superstition and irrational piety might rise up together under this venerable name without distinction. When religion is supported by coercion and force, it not only violates the most sacred natural rights of humans but also brings shame upon religion itself. A good cause becomes immediately suspicious, and its opponents already gain a small advantage with third parties if, instead of presenting solid evidence, one only puts on a show of probability. Since every upright person looks for nothing but the truth and never allows their inclinations, prejudices, or worldly gain to influence their investigations of religion, they must necessarily desire nothing so much as that the reasons on both sides be presented with proper clarity and given all the strength they can have.

Finally, the famous theologian of Halle, **Baumgarten** <note>Siegmund Jakob Baumgarten (1706–1757), a transitional figure in German theology between traditional Lutheranism and the Enlightenment.</note>, says in his *Ecclesiastical History* recently published: *We rightly lament the loss of many writings, even of the heretics and most hostile adversaries of Christendom.* As to why these sensible men feel this way, they bring forward several reasons; I will mention only one or two: they say religion itself is made suspect if the arguments that can be opposed to it are not allowed to be brought into the open and weighed and read by others. For it could easily happen that some people convince themselves that religion is not built on reasons that can withstand a rigid examination. Indeed, the most ample opportunity for triumphing is given to the Unbelievers, since by acting in this way, people of sharp insight will judge that those who profess religion cannot withstand the force of the reasoning used by this class of men. 2) By the banning and burning of such books, those in error are not led back to the path, which is the one thing that the leaders of religion <note>original: "Religionis Antistiti-bus"</note>—

---

<page-num>315</page-num>
### ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

—should care for. 3) In this way, only the greed and desire for profit of the **printers** <note>original: "Typographorum"</note> are served: it is well known that as soon as such books are banned, many burn with the desire to read them, which the printers turn to their own advantage, increasing the price as much as they can. Moreover, it is clear that through various tricks and ways, if only money is not lacking, such books can easily be obtained. 4) Finally, these learned men add that those among the Protestant theologians who want all those books of Unbelievers proscribed and knocked out of everyone's hands are inconsistent with themselves, while they vehemently criticize and lash out at Catholic <note>original: "Pontificios"</note> doctors and Inquisitors for raging against books written by Protestants—when, in the judgment of the Catholics, these books harm religion no less than the writings of Unbelievers. (*) I leave these and other points brought forward by learned men to be judged by those sharper than myself. But just as there is a use and an abuse of all things, so it must be admitted at the same time that by the indiscriminate reading of such books, many have been cast into the vice of **Unbelief**, and alas, many still fall into it. This often happens to those who are either imbued with no discipline or only lightly so, and have never devoted diligent effort to more serious literature. No one is unaware that the objections of Unbelievers are mostly of such a nature that to blunt them, one needs keen judgment and sophisticated <note>original: "non proletaria," literally "not of the common sort."</note> erudition. But since many delight in reading such books who can indeed feel the force of the objections but are destitute of those defenses required to solve those difficulties, it cannot happen otherwise than that they begin to doubt truths of the gravest importance. If wicked passions are added to this, it can hardly turn out otherwise than that they **give their approval** <note>original: "albos calculos adjiciant"—literally "add white stones," a reference to the ancient Roman practice of voting for acquittal or agreement with white stones.</note> to those things which seem pleasing and acceptable to those worst of advisors. I do not think it necessary to prove this truth with many examples; for anyone who has insight into the customs of men and what is accustomed to happen here and there...

---

(*) Among the more sensible and learned Catholic doctors themselves are those who grieve that Censors and Inquisitors remark upon writings of theological or philosophical argument more harshly than is fair. Among these should be counted the celebrated **Muratori** <note>Ludovico Antonio Muratori (1672–1750), a renowned Italian historian and priest who advocated for moderate reform within the Catholic Church.</note>, Librarian to the Illustrious Duke of Modena, who speaks thus in a booklet published under the name *Lamindus Britannius*, *On the Moderation of Wits in the Business of Religion, Chapter V, p. 266:*

> We know of those who—lest they should have to struggle with the ignorance and powerlessness of certain Censors—have abandoned theological and philosophical studies and thrown themselves entirely into secular scholarship <note>original: "Eruditionem profanam"</note>, from which, if not equal praise, certainly less danger and more peace was to be expected. Therefore, not only are private studies hindered by these censors, but also the public utility and the Church, which needs Theological writers who are not flatterers while they write, nor burning with immoderate zeal while they judge, but filled with solid Erudition and free from all superstition and emotion.

...notices, no one will doubt that many have been driven headlong into ruin by the frequent reading of these books. It is helpful to bring forward one example among a thousand: namely, **Charles II**, *the most illustrious King of England*, who had been corrupted by reading the books of *Hobbes* <note>Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679), whose political and philosophical works like *Leviathan* were often accused of promoting atheism and materialism.</note>. The Reverend Bishop of Salisbury, *Burnet*, recounts the matter in his *Memoirs to serve as a History of Great Britain* <note>original title in French: "Mémoires pour servir à l'Histoire de la Grande Bretagne," referring to Gilbert Burnet's famous historical accounts.</note>. After he had described the character of the Duke of *Buckingham*, he continues thus:

> Upon returning (speaking of this Duke) from his travels to Paris, he found there the Prince of Wales, whom Charles I, his father, had sent there during the collapse of his affairs. Perceiving that this Prince had a penchant for receiving bad impressions, he made it a study to corrupt him. Involved himself in all the impieties and all the libertinism of the age, and supported in this design by Lord Percy, he succeeded only too easily. To complete his ruin and under the pretext of teaching him mathematics, these two lords presented him to Hobbes, who explained his systems to him regarding both religion and politics. Lessons which were deeply imprinted in his mind and which were never erased from it.

So says that famous Bishop. What happened to the most celebrated theologian *F. Junius* <note>Franciscus Junius (1589–1677), a pioneering philologist and theologian.</note>, who too much admired the writings of *Epicurus* in his youth, is well known from his own autobiography, which he himself prepared. These evils are increased in our century, in which the study of Literary History flourishes greatly. There are many who, before they have enriched their hearts with the necessary knowledge of the most excellent things, unroll almost all the *Journals of the Learned* <note>A reference to the "Diaria Eruditorum," the academic and literary periodicals that became popular in the 17th and 18th centuries.</note>. There, as if in a small picture, they discover the unusual opinions of certain scholars; they see that no opinion is so certain or momentous that it has not been attacked by this or that scholar. Hence, carried away by lack of skill in the art of reasoning and ignorance of more rigorous disciplines, they conclude that both sides can be argued concerning all things, especially religion. 

Equally harmful to piety are those books which deal with obscene matters, and which—alas!—have for a long time now been regarded as classic books, commonly called "Romances" <note>The author uses "fabulas Romanenses" to refer to early novels or chivalric romances, which were often viewed by moralists as scandalous and unrealistic.</note>. For besides the fact that they set sail with the most shameful passions, they often make religion itself suspect; it is true that in writings of this sort the dogmas of religion are not directly attacked, but such things are handed down in them from which sinister opinions about religion easily arise. Thus it is often shown by what frauds, lies, and perjuries—scorning all religion and faith—men inflamed with the fires of the most shameful love reached the ends they intended. From which the mind,

<meta>catchword: corrupted</meta>

<page-num>317</page-num>
<header>ON THE CAUSES OF INCREDULITY.</header>

corrupted by this madness, concludes that where the calming of passions is concerned, not much account should be taken of religion. Often also, so that the propriety <note>original Greek: πρεπον (prepon) - the literary concept of "decorum" or what is fitting for a story's characters and plot.</note> of the story may be maintained, and the reins loosened for depraved desires, and the minds of the readers softly soothed, it is shown how the delights of Venus, through some truly wondrous paths amid a thousand obstacles, attained their goal. From this, men clearly maddened by impure love can easily fall into the opinion that all these things happened not without the singular care of Divine Providence. 

Finally, to these we add the reading of the most eloquent masters of wickedness, such as *Catullus*, *Tibullus*, *Petronius*, etc., as well as the authors of Fescennine verses <note>term: Fescennine (fescenninorum) - a type of ancient Roman poetry known for being bawdy, ribald, and often scurrilous.</note>. More regard should always be given to piety than to speech. See on this matter the last chapter of the pious and venerable old man (now, while I write this, received into heaven), *J. Fr. Ostervald*, in his *On the Sources of Corruption Creeping Among Christians Today*. But let these things suffice.

<page-num>318</page-num>
<header>MEDITATION VIII.</header>

# MEDITATION
## ON THE
### CAUSES OF THE EVER-INCREASING GROWTH OF
# UNBELIEF,
## AND THE
## REMEDY TO BE BROUGHT TO THIS EVIL.
### PART VIII.

->Section I.<-

<margin>The remaining causes of Unbelief are reviewed, among which Superstition is the first to be recorded. A definition of it is given.</margin>

<image-desc>A decorative square woodcut initial letter 'A'. The interior of the letter contains a landscape scene with a flowing river or waterfall, rocky outcrops, and foliage.</image-desc>
At last, with God’s blessing, we come to recounting the remaining causes of Unbelief. Among the chief causes, we rightly include *Superstition*, a most foul evil and one deeply opposed to a chaste and pure Religion. Among the Latins as well as the Greeks, this word "Superstition"—and <note>original: "δεισιδαιμονία" (*deisidaimonia*)</note>—is a "middle" term <note>A "middle term" (meson) refers to a word that can be used in either a positive or negative sense depending on the context.</note>, and is taken in both a good and a bad sense, as learned men have proven with many examples. One may look to what has been brought forward regarding the Book of Acts, chapter 17, verse 22, by *Cornelius Adami*, *Wolf* in his *Curae Philologicae*, *Hammond*, and others. The ancients generally understood the name of Superstition to mean any delirious or "old wives'" tale in which there is an empty fear of the Gods, just as *Cicero* speaks in *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book I, Section 42; it refers, moreover, to every troublesome and foolish religion. *Theophrastus*, in his *Characters*, defined Superstition thus: <note>original Greek: "’Αμέλει ἡ δεισιδαιμονία δόξειεν εἶναι δειλαία πρὸς τὸ δαιμόνιον"</note> which means: *We can surely define Superstition as a cowardly disposition toward the Divine*. *Isaac Casaubon* <note>A famous French classical scholar (1559–1614).</note> notes on this passage that others defined Superstition so: that <note>original Greek: "δεισιδαιμονία"</note> is a *fear of gods and demons*; where that learned man adds the following: *Theophrastus*, he says, by the word *demons*, has em-
<meta>catchword: braced</meta>

<column-break/>

<page-num>319</page-num>
<header>ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.</header>

braced both the *Gods* and *Demons*, and whatever part of Divinity the unhealthy mind of antiquity thought existed. We take Superstition in a broader sense, and by it we mean every preposterous worship of the Divine—whether of one or of many—which is clearly contrary to reason and Revelation. It is not our intention here to deal with the various parts of Superstition and Idolatry; those learned men who have examined this subject with dedicated effort should be consulted.

<margin>Nevertheless, the ancient Gentiles distinguished religion from Superstition.</margin>
II. Although the religion of the Gentiles <note>Non-Christians, specifically the ancient Greeks and Romans.</note>, being destitute of the light of Revelation, was greatly superstitious, the learned men among them nevertheless wished it to be distinguished from Religion. To prove this, the small book by *Plutarch* titled *On Superstition* would be sufficient on its own. But certain other testimonies should be brought forward. Thus *Cicero* speaks in *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book II, Section 28: *The worship of the Gods is best, and likewise the most chaste, holy, and full of piety, so that we always venerate them with a pure, integral, and uncorrupted mind and voice; for not only Philosophers, but also our ancestors, separated Superstition from Religion. For those who prayed and sacrificed all day long so that their children might survive them [superstites], were called superstitious—a name which later took on a wider meaning. Those, however, who diligently reconsidered [retractarent] and, as it were, "reread" [relegere] everything pertaining to the worship of the Gods, were called religious from "re-reading" [relegendo], just as "elegant" comes from "selecting" [eligendo], "diligent" from "valuing" [diligendo], and "intelligent" from "understanding" [intelligendo]. For in all these words, there is the same force of "reading" [legendi] as in the word "Religious." Thus it happened that between "Superstitious" and "Religious," the former became a name for a vice, and the latter a name for praise.* *Lactantius* <note>An early Christian author (c. 250 – c. 325) often called the "Christian Cicero."</note> cites this origin of the word superstition in his *Divine Institutes*, Book IV, Section 38, and disapproves of it: *They are called superstitious (he says) not because they hoped their sons would survive them (for we all hope for that), but either those who worship the surviving memory of the deceased, or those who, surviving their parents, worshipped their images at home as Household Gods [Penates]. For those who took up new rituals for themselves, so as to honor the dead in place of Gods—whom they thought were received into heaven from among men—these they called superstitious. But those who worshipped the public and ancient Gods, they named religious; whence Virgil says: "Vain superstition, ignorant of the ancient Gods."* Whatever the truth may be regarding the origin of this word, the more learned among the Gentiles confessed that a great difference lies between Religion and Superstition. The same *Cicero* said in Book II of *On Divination*: *Just as Religion—which is joined with the knowledge of Nature—is to be propagated, so the roots of superstition are to be cast out.* *Casaubon*, in the place cited, says: *Varro* <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC), a Roman scholar.</note> wisely said, as quoted in *Augustine*, *that God is revered by the religious man, but feared by the superstitious one.* *Seneca* states it even more clearly in *Epistle 47*: *It is enough for God that He is worshipped.*

<summary>This page begins an analysis of Superstition as a primary cause of Unbelief, distinguishing it from true Religion through the definitions of classical authors like Cicero, Theophrastus, and Lactantius. The author argues that while the terms were sometimes used interchangeably, the ancients recognized superstition as a "fear-based" or "preposterous" corruption of genuine piety.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of superstition from page 319, moving from definitions to historical and philosophical distinctions. It specifically examines how the confusion between true religion and superstition is used by "Free-thinkers" and "Deists" to undermine faith entirely.</meta>

<page-num>320</page-num>
<header>MEDITATION VIII.</header>

[God] is worshipped and loved: love cannot be mixed with fear. The same author says better elsewhere: Religion worships the Gods; Superstition violates them. Maximus Tyrius, in his fourth Discourse, distinguishes piety from Superstition in this way: <note>original Greek: "εἰ δὲ ἔσι καὶ ἀνθρωποις προς Θεὸς ἐπιμιξία; ὁ μὲν εὐσεβὴς Φίλος Θεῷ, ὁ δὲ δεισιδαίμων κολαξ"</note> "If there is indeed any interaction between men and Gods, the pious man is a friend to God, while the superstitious man is a flatterer." Indeed, it is very clear from the booklets of Plutarch *On Isis and Osiris*, and likewise *On Superstition*, that the Ancients distinguished Religion from Superstition. In the booklet *On Isis and Osiris*, page 378, he speaks thus: <note>original Greek: "Ἐνιοι ἀποσφαλεντες πανταπασιν εἰς δεισιδαιμονίαν ἔλισθον, οἱ δὲ φεύγοντες ὥσπερ ἕλως την δεισιδαιμονίαν, ἔλαθον αὖθις ὥσπερ εἰς κρημνον ἐμπεσοντες την ἀθεοτητα"</note> "Some, slipping away entirely, fall into superstition; while others, fleeing superstition as if from a marsh, find themselves unexpectedly falling as if into a pit of atheism." And in the same place, making mention of the Superstition of the Egyptians, he says: <note>original Greek: "Ἀιγυπτιων δε οἱ πολλοι θεραπευοντες αὐτα τα ζωα... [to] θηριωδεις λογισμος"</note> that is: *But most of the Egyptians, by worshipping the animals themselves and treating them as Gods, have not only exposed the whole system of their sacred rites to laughter and mockery (for this is the smallest evil to come from such foolishness), but a powerful opinion is bred in the minds, which leads the weak and simple into pure Superstition; while it drives the more vigorous and bold into atheism and beast-like reasoning.* He repeats this same point frequently in his booklet *On Superstition*.

These things should be observed against more recent Deists, who, when they discuss religion and cry out that it is the cause of all evils that burden the human race, confuse superstition with Religion. They are wonderfully pleased with themselves when they stumble upon the verses of *Lucretius*, where he says: *So much evil could Religion persuade!* likewise *Religion gave birth to wicked and impious deeds.* Similarly, they applaud themselves when they discuss the frauds of the ancient Gentile priests, thinking that they have thus struck at the throats of all who are called <term>V. D. M.</term> <note>Latin: *Verbi Divini Minister*, or Minister of the Word of God.</note> and Theologians. This could easily be shown through the examples of *Toland*, *Collins*, *Passerat*, and others, if it were a matter that learned men doubted. However, for the sake of those who do not have such writings at hand, it is helpful to provide one or two testimonies. That *Spinoza* was an Atheist and devoid of all Religion is well known to the public. Yet he held Religion and Superstition in the same regard. This is abundantly clear both from the system he followed and from the preface to his *Theologico-Political Treatise*. For that preface begins thus: *If men could manage all their affairs by a certain plan, or if fortune were always prosperous for them, they would be held by no su-*

<meta>catchword: per-</meta>

<header>ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.</header>

perstition. But since they are often reduced to such straits that they can offer no plan, and because they waver miserably between hope and fear due to the uncertain goods of fortune which they desire without limit, they generally have a mind most prone to believe anything. While the mind is in doubt, it is easily driven here and there; and it hesitates much more easily while it is agitated by hope and fear, being otherwise arrogant, boastful, and timid. And I think no one is ignorant of these things, though I believe most people are ignorant of themselves. And a few lines later: *If they see anything unusual with great wonder, they believe it to be a prodigy indicating the wrath of the Gods or the supreme Divinity, and thus men liable to superstition and opposed to Religion think it a sin not to appease it with sacrifices and vows; and in this manner they imagine infinite things and interpret nature in strange ways, as if all of nature were insane along with them.* *Spinoza* follows, though from another source, the opinion of *Epicurus*, who attributed to fear and ignorance of causes what others attribute to the persuasion of conscience regarding the Divine. For *Lucretius* speaks thus in *Book VI*:

> The rest of the things which mortals see happening in the lands 
> and the sky, when they often hang with trembling minds, 
> make their souls humble with fear of the Gods 
> and press them down to the earth: because 
> ignorance of causes forces them to attribute things 
> to the empire of the Gods and to grant them the kingdom. 
> Of which works they can see the causes by no reason, 
> and they think they happen by divine power.

*Collins* also seems to have placed Superstition and Religion into the same class in his very well-known treatise on "Free-thinking." At least, the celebrated *Bentley* interprets his mind thus in the book titled *The Layman’s Roguery of the so-called Free-thinkers*. On page 85, that most learned man speaks thus: <note>original French: "Ce mal si terrible... qu'en se defaisant de l'autre."</note> "This evil so terrible (speaking of superstition), this so capital a defect, cannot be avoided according to him except by joining the party that thinks freely: that is to say, in the true sense of his wordiness, by renouncing all Religion. A strange thing! For two thousand years already, Religion has been distinguished and separated from superstition. However, this author still confuses them, and insists so much that they are the same thing that, in his opinion, one cannot be cured of the one without getting rid of the other."

### III. Those captured by perverse Superstition can easily fall into Deism or Atheism, as proved by both the nature of the matter and the confession of the Gentiles themselves.

<margin>It is shown by what means seduced men can fall into Atheism.</margin>
The passage of Plutarch just now cited is clear. But if you rightly attend to the nature of superstition, it is manifest that this can happen in two ways.

# MEDITATION VIII.

...it will be manifest. He who fosters foolish opinions about the <term>Deity</term><note>Latin: *Numine*. This refers to the divine power or essence of God.</note>, or about the Gods; he who religiously worships fictitious Gods or created things; he who is moved not by love, but by a servile fear of the Divine; he who admires any foolish rites and admits the most trifling opinions handed down by Priests: he who sells every portent—no matter how foolish or incredible—as a divine event, and then finally believes he is pleasing the Deity if he retreats as far as possible from those things which <term>right reason</term><note>Latin: *recta ratio*. A philosophical concept referring to the innate human ability to discern truth and moral law through logic.</note> and Revelation teach concerning God and His worship; such a person is to be judged exactly as if he were entirely destitute of any knowledge of the Deity.

For just as one who denies that God takes any care for human affairs removes, as far as he is able, all the protections and incentives for worshipping God—even though it is one thing to assert that God does not exist, and another to say that He exists but takes no care for the human race—so likewise, if someone fosters plainly ridiculous and foolish opinions about the Deity, or strives to appease God with foolish rites, and believes that the whole of religious worship (or at least its most important part) is fulfilled by these things, he acts exactly as if he lacked rational worship and knowledge of the Deity. 

If one considers the opinions of the modern as well as the ancient barbarian nations regarding the Gods, and their rites for worshipping them; if he reflects on how much power opinions "drunk in with a mother's milk" (so to speak) have over the minds of men, however ridiculous and foolish they may be; if he considers within himself how difficult it is for men to withdraw from those things which have been handed down and hammered in by Priests devoted to a depraved superstition: he will easily discover that it cannot happen otherwise than that minds hedged in by such darkness, and equipped with a plainly weak knowledge of Religion, should follow a mere shadow of Religion instead of the worship of the Deity, and that the remaining ideas of the Deity should be all but entirely suppressed. 

Hence, whenever we read the opinions of ancient and modern nations concerning the Gods, we wonder and grieve—not without amazement—at how much and what incredible power superstition has over the minds of men. On this account, certain learned men wish to "move every stone"<note>A Latin idiom meaning "to leave no stone unturned" or to make every possible effort.</note> to free certain nations, both ancient and modern, from the suspicion of ignorance of the Deity or <term>Atheism</term>. 

Truly, the way in which men—born and raised as if in the very schools of superstition—gradually and slowly withdraw from the worship of the Deity and instead rest in the most foolish rites and opinions, will be manifest if we turn our minds partly to the power of superstition and partly to the weak knowledge of the Deity which is naturally inherent in mortals. It is true that human minds are naturally equipped with faculties for worshipping and knowing God; but at the same time, it is also confessed that a more accurate knowledge of the Deity is not reached without meditation, study, and sharp attention of the mind.

***

# ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

This is known to all who have devoted their labor to the instruction of youth. Religion is chiefly concerned with things that do not strike the eyes, but with celestial things—that is, things to be perceived by the mind alone. Yet most mortals are led by the senses alone and are carried away to contemplate and pursue those things which are pleasing and acceptable to their bodies. 

Certainly, unless a noble education and diligent, prudent instruction were to intervene early, most people would almost turn into beasts. Cicero well recognized this weakness of nature, saying: 

> *Nature has given us small sparks [of virtue], which we quickly extinguish through bad habits and depraved opinions, so that the light of nature appears nowhere. For there are seeds of virtues innate in our characters, which, if they were allowed to grow to maturity, nature herself would lead us to a happy life. But now, as soon as we are brought forth into the light and taken up, we are continually engaged in every depravity and in the greatest perversity of opinions; so that we seem to have sucked in error almost with our nurse’s milk.* 

> *When, however, we are returned to our parents—that is, handed over to teachers—we are then imbued with such various errors that truth yields to vanity, and nature itself yields to confirmed opinion.* <note>Quoted from Cicero's *Tusculan Disputations*, Book III, section 11.</note>

Hence we also see that young people look not so much to those things prescribed by divine and human laws, but rather to those things that are pleasing to them. If to that weakness of character, natural perversity, and corruption, there is added a foolish and foul superstition—so much so that from their very youth children hear and see almost nothing else than what can imbue their minds with ridiculous opinions—it can easily be gathered what the religion of those men will be in the future. 

Furthermore, since there are very few who cultivate Religion, and the "common people"<note>Latin: *plebs*. Referring to the general populace or lower social orders.</note> (who make up the largest part of any nation) take care for the body and the cattle rather than for reason, it cannot happen otherwise than that men born and raised in such places—and among men so devoted to superstition—should be imbued with the most foolish and perverse sentiments concerning Religion. 

Sad experience teaches (alas!) that this has indeed happened in practice. It is true that not only the "Barbarians" but also the Greeks and Romans had their workshops of science and their schools. But in these, they did not so much hand down those things which could lead to the true worship of the Deity, but rather those things which could contribute most to civil life and the arts useful to men—for example, to Eloquence and the skill of debating. See the learned booklet of *Wowerus on the Polymathy of the Ancients*<note>Original: *Wovveri de Polymathia Veterum*. Refers to Johann von Wowern (1574–1612), whose work discussed the broad, "universal" learning of ancient scholars.</note>. 

Even suppose that in these Gymnasiums care was also taken for Religion; it could not be any other religion than that which was publicly received and approved by the Priests. Now, however, it is well known that the Gen... <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely "Gentiles" or "Gentes" (nations).</note>

# MEDITATION VIII.

...that all nations, destitute of the light of Revelation, were as if immersed in detestable superstition; hence the precepts of religion scarcely extended beyond certain dictates of the law of nature, and even those were highly corrupted. But if you look to those who were bound to promote the cultivation of religion and reason, it will be manifest that they handed down many things which served more to obscure and pervert pure notions of the <term>Deity</term><note>Latin: *Numine*. Referring to the divine power or essence of God.</note> than to elucidate and commend them. Who does not know that the Poets handed down such stories about Gods and Goddesses that could not help but vehemently offend chaste minds? *Cicero* himself admits this in the passage already praised: *“The Poets also join in,”* he says, *“who, having presented a great appearance of learning and wisdom, are heard, read, learned by heart, and sink deep into minds.”* <note>original: "Accedunt etiam Poëtæ..." from Cicero's *De Natura Deorum*.</note> This was so well known that the wise among the Gentiles, especially the Platonists and Stoics, wished to explain physically those things handed down by the Poets concerning the Gods, thereby adorning a shameful matter with an honorable title. And if certain things regarding virtue and honesty were sprinkled here and there in these writings, they were nonetheless tempered to public opinions and depraved by absurd fables about the Gods. The Philosophers were more concerned with explaining the origin of all things through innumerable sophisticated questions than with handing down a true and chaste Religion and uprooting superstition from the minds of men. Public worship was to be conducted according to the laws not of Philosophers, but of <term>Sacrificers</term><note>Latin: *Sacrificulorum*. A diminishing term for petty priests or those who performed sacrifices.</note>—men who were most vain and astute impostors. He who performed these rites correctly—that is, according to the minds of these men—was held to be religious. These matters, briefly set forth here, are copiously and learnedly examined by the celebrated *Barbeyrac* <note>Jean Barbeyrac (1674–1744), a famous jurist known for his translations and commentaries on legal and moral philosophy.</note> in his most learned preface to the version of *Pufendorf's* work, which lovers of truth may read with profit. But many other things were added which could pervert men, especially those of sharper wit, and provide a convenient occasion for exploding all religion; these I wish to set forth briefly, as the matter is well known to the learned. To this belong, above all, the *Oracles*, which were said to reveal the will of the Deity to Priests; yet there, impostures could easily be detected by those whose minds were not dull, and they were detected more than once. It is accepted today among almost all the learned that those responses given everywhere were certainly not due to the arts of the Devil, but to the frauds of the Priests. Furthermore, the most wicked men were often recorded among the number of the Gods, though their foul and detestable lives were clearly known to most. In certain festivals, for example those of *Bacchus*, such crimes were committed that shame prevents their telling: but if anyone attempted to expose those shameful

This was especially true since the doctrine concerning the immortality of the soul was built upon a clearly weak foundation, and there was great disagreement among the Philosophers regarding this argument.

<margin>Superstition rampant among Christians contributes greatly to promoting Unbelief.</margin>

IV. Hitherto we have seen in what way superstition can easily cast men, who are deprived of the light of Revelation, into Unbelief: but now a few things must still be said about the Superstition rampant among Christians, and the danger that threatens Religion therefrom. It is known that in the most flourishing parts of Europe (to say nothing now of the Superstition brought into the <term>New World</term><note>Referring to the Americas.</note>), a shameful superstition, unworthy of Christians, still greatly prevails. It is not my intention to exaggerate the matter, nor to place trust indiscriminately in all writers and fabricators of travelogues. Nor would I wish to rely solely on the faith of Protestants and their testimonies, if I were to undertake to prove, with deliberate effort, how much Superstition still reigns in the assemblies devoted to the religion of the <term>Pontiff</term><note>The Pope; the author is referring to the Roman Catholic Church.</note>, or how the Priests, the authors and promoters of Superstition, have exceeded all bounds in increasing absurd rites—for example, concerning relics, the worship of saints (whether unknown or known), concerning the worship of Mary, the Canonization of Saints, etc. Learned men of the Roman Church, such as *Mabillon, Thiers, and Launoy*, have admitted that everywhere false miracles are peddled as true, and that Saints who clearly never existed in the nature of things have nevertheless been religiously worshiped. *The knowledge of the fledgling Church is to know only Jesus Christ, and Jesus Christ crucified: the rest, being only accessory, ought to be reserved for a more suitable time.* <note>original: "La Science des Eglises naissante est, de ne connoitre que Jesus Christ, & Jesus Christ crucifié..."</note> This pure and most true judgment of a most learned man greatly displeases Laubrusselius the Jesuit, in his little book *On the Abuse of the Critical Art*.

*The most beautiful and largest Monastery is that of the Cordelier Fathers <note>French: "Pères Cordeliers," a name for Franciscans referring to the knotted cord they wear as a belt.</note>, which occupies a considerable plot of land. I was assured that the Ornaments of the Church that day amounted to more than ten million Piastres <note>A Spanish silver coin widely used in colonial trade.</note>: indeed, one could see nothing more magnificent.*

Both pages of the missionary commentaries (to use the words of the celebrated Weismann in the previously cited oration, page 289) are filled with: *the Hail Mary, Rosaries, Agnus Dei <note>Small wax disks impressed with the figure of a lamb, blessed by the Pope and used as devotional objects.</note>, holy water, fraternities, processions, and auricular confession* (regarding how constantly the missionaries hammer this into the poor people, and what kind of things are contained in the catechisms handed down on this subject, see the celebrated La Croze’s *History of Christianity in the Indies*, page 679 of the German edition). They also teach *weekly fasts, the invocation of Saints, self-flagellation*, and many other well-known practices of that kind. These poor people are taught to have the Spanish formula constantly on their lips: *Praise to the immaculate virgin and the most holy Sacrament of the Altar, namely that placed in the tabernacle and displayed in the churches for perpetual worship.* <note>original: "laudes immaculate virgini & sanctissimo Altaris Sacramento sc. in cibario reposito atque in templis prostanti, ad cultum perpetuum."</note> However, wise and sensible men among the Catholics are so far from thinking such things should be instilled into the Gentiles <note>Non-Christians</note> that they rather assert such opinions and rituals ought to be absent from the Catholic Religion. The illustrious author of the *Sketch of the Truly Catholic Church* <note>original: "Delineationis Ecclesiæ vere Catholicæ"</note>, who is certainly esteemed by learned Germans, reveals his mind on this subject in the cited work on page 252:

*“Furthermore, all special devotions and secondary cults are not to be considered Roman Catholic, much less universally Catholic, such as: the Rosary; the Scapular; the Belt of St. Augustine; the Cord of St. Francis; or devotion to this or that specific image. Likewise the brotherhoods of this or that Saint; as well as the devotions and services to certain Saints set for several weeks, days, or hours, and the like. Page 254: Further, the excessively great and almost exclusive veneration and invocation of the Saints is not to be considered Roman Catholic, nor even less universally Catholic: whereby the dear God is almost entirely forgotten (except perhaps during the Mass, at which most people still direct their devotion to the Mother of the Lord or other Saints by reciting the Rosary and secretly reading all sorts of prayers). He is prayed to little and only superficially, and trust is not placed in Him alone, but in fact far more in the Saints. Page 264: Still further, the imagination that has mostly taken hold of Western Christians is not to be considered Roman Catholic, much less universally Catholic: namely, that a certain divine power resides in the so-called ‘Miraculous Images’ <note>original: "Gnaden-Bildern," literally "Grace-Pictures."</note> of the Holy Virgin and Mother of the Lord to grant graces, heal diseases, and perform miracles. Therefore, people go on pilgrimages there and not to another place. People are also of the constant opinion that help from heaven and the power of the Saints are so firmly tied to this consecrated image that if it were to fall apart or be taken away, then the Saint would also cease to be in this place and to perform miracles.”*

> Sometimes the Demon is forced to bear witness to the truth of our holy Religion. What happened to Father Bernard de Sá deserves to be reported to you. I add nothing to what he told me. The Gentiles <note>The author's term for non-Christians, specifically Hindus</note> brought to him an Indian man whom the Demon was tormenting in a cruel manner. The Father interrogated him in the presence of a great number of idolaters, and his answers greatly surprised those present. He first asked him where the Gods were that the Indians worshipped; the answer was that they were in Hell, where they suffered horrible torments. "But what becomes," the Father continued, "of those who worship the false Divinities?" "They go to Hell," he replied, "to burn there with the false Gods they have worshipped." Finally, the Father asked him which was the true Religion, and the Demon replied through the mouth of the possessed man that there was no true religion except that which was taught by the Missionary, and that it was the only one that led to heaven. With these things—

I omit many other examples that are reported in these Jesuit Letters. What Protestants might think of these things, the Doctors of the Roman Church will easily judge: namely, they can hardly be brought to believe that the most holy God would perform miracles to promote the worship of Mary and the saints—and furthermore of relics and things of this kind—yet perform none at all in those places where the writings of Christ and the Apostles are worn thin in the hands of Christians, and where all superstition is plainly exiled. We wonder indeed that such things are appealed to in such an enlightened age, after wise men of the Roman Church have long lamented that so many forged miracles have been sold as true by monks and petty priests everywhere. It is helpful to have cited one or two testimonies. Étienne Baluze, a most learned man, in his notes on the *Life of Saint Maximinus*, speaks thus on page 487 of the works of Servatus Lupus: "Therefore it was already clear even then that the *Acts of the Saints* were defiled by many prodigious fables, and it has always been thus in this world..."

Richard Simon, in the third volume of his *Critical Library*, chapter 22, deals entirely with the frauds of fabricated miracles, which is a profitable read. He inquires into the causes of the great revenues and riches that accrued to monasteries. Among other things, he speaks thus:

->*The clergymen, and primarily the monks, abused the simplicity of the people, especially in the eleventh and twelfth centuries, by certain pious frauds, if I may be permitted to speak in such a manner. They created "Lives of the Saints" according to their own ideas; they fabricated relics, most of which, according to them, came from the lands of the Levant <note>The Eastern Mediterranean</note>; and to give them more authority, they drew up legal records of them as they pleased. They spread word everywhere of the frequent miracles these relics performed. The credulous people, who added faith to these fictions, flocked from all sides to the churches of the monks to make their offerings there. The histories—not to call them fables—that one still finds today in the archives of monasteries and in their sacristies regarding the origin of these relics are evident proofs of what has just been stated. And what is most surprising is that even the richest monasteries made use of this pious artifice.*<-

The celebrated Muratori, in Book III, chapter 6 of *On Regulating the Imagination in Religious Matters*, wisely warns that superstition in the Church must be confronted. The same author, in Book III, page 487, reveals what he thinks of most modern miracles, saying: *The faithful should not seek miracles; for the true faith and the Church no longer need them to demonstrate their truth. That coercion in matters of religion is contrary to religion, humanity, and conscience is a fact proven by the most evident arguments. <header>MEDITATION VIII.</header>

For they act to prove, in the judgment of most Pontificians <note>A term used by Protestant authors to refer to Roman Catholics</note>, that it is *necessary* for those minute opinions and superstitious rites to be instilled even in those who ought to be imbued with true knowledge of the Christian religion. (*) Now, indeed, how much strength *Incredulity* <note>Unbelief or skepticism</note> can draw from this, no one can be ignorant who cares for pure religion from the heart and who understands human nature. *First*, if one observes on one hand the stupor of those nations, their thickest ignorance of divine matters, and their plainly barbarian and ridiculous superstition; and on the other hand the cult of the Saints, of Mary, and the other parts of the Pontifician worship, it is manifest that a system of religion arises from this so absurd and ridiculous that you might doubt whether it would not be just the same if those nations were plainly destitute of the Christian religion. Certainly, we have either lost the true meanings of words, or these plainly inept and ridiculous opinions and these frivolous and superstitious rites are unworthy of the name of religion. Thus, superstitions are added to superstitions, and while these miserable people are deprived of the saving light of the Gospel, which is found in the Holy Scriptures alone, nothing is left but a thin shadow and the name of religion. The difficulty is increased by the testimony of the Missionaries, that those blind nations snatch up everything that is handed down without any examination. The celebrated *Weismann* cited two testimonies from that Stöklin collection <note>Likely the *Neuer Welt-Bott*, a collection of Jesuit missionary letters edited by Joseph Stöcklein</note> on page 288; one is from the Jesuit *Bonani*, the other from *Richter*, a man of the same Society. The former speaks thus of the inhabitants of Northern California: *I found Indians in no other place so eager for the true faith and so capable of attaining the Christian Mysteries. For they believe everything (NB. <note>Note Well</note>) without delay, and whatever they hear from our mouths is a settled matter to them.* The latter, speaking of the Indians in general, says: *If the oppressions of the civil governors (of the Christian name, that is) were absent, there is no doubt that the whole of India would embrace the Gospel of Christ; for nothing more is required for this than a certain freedom from the tribes and Missionaries equipped with small gifts.* When I give an axe to a certain primary man among them, the whole continuous flock follows the leader into the sheepfold of Christ. Incredulity can be promoted in the second place if what is told by the Missionaries about the astounding progress of the Catholic religion is taken as true.

<page-num>341</page-num>
<header>ON THE CAUSES OF INCREDULITY.</header>
<sig>V v 3</sig>

Christian theologians are accustomed, among other arguments by which they prove the divine origin of the Christian Religion, to appeal also to that wonderful and plainly astounding progress of the Christian Religion which took hold immediately after the death of Christ our Savior. Now, what will men say who are not sufficiently familiar with pure Religion, and who are inclined toward Incredulity, or already suffering from this disease, if they hear that a vain superstition has such power over the minds of mortals that many thousands of men willingly offer empty ears to it and embrace it? Will they not rather contend that such success of the Christian Religion should be attributed to the stupor of men? Will they not repeatedly claim that arguments sought from miracles to confirm the Christian religion are destitute of all strength? It is true, indeed, that they reason poorly and that many things can be opposed to this argument. But notwithstanding this, it will be very true that those who attribute such great power to foul superstition weaken the principal argument for the truth of the Christian religion and patronize Incredulity. *Thirdly* and finally, Superstition vehemently promotes Incredulity because it is contrary to all principles of right reason: no one who has a sound mind and who understands the nature of true Religion can approve of superstition with his vote. But he who is not properly knowledgeable of the Christian Religion, and is at the same time given over to depraved affections, easily falls into Incredulity itself. For what will men imbued with various disciplines, especially philosophical ones—of which it is known there is a great number in *Italy*, for example—but who are destitute of a solid knowledge of the Christian Religion, think if they hear: that a true religion is indeed given, but it is not to be examined; that the certain way of salvation is shown in the Holy Scriptures, but they cannot be safely read by anyone; that the Legends, as they call them, can be unrolled without danger; that portents are produced by the power of I-know-not-what relics or Saints; that Transubstantiation is to be numbered among the most excellent Mysteries of religion; that Saints must be diligently worshiped, either imaginary ones, or those whose brains black bile <note>original: "atra bilis"; a reference to the four humors, suggesting Saint Francis suffered from clinical melancholy or madness</note> seems to have weakened (as was Saint *Francis*, if the things which the authors of his biography tell of him are true); or those who were promoters of superstition and violent persecutions, such as *Dominic* was, etc. etc. Upon hearing these things, will he not reject all religion as being plainly contrary to reason (we speak of a man of sharp wit indeed, but who has no taste for the true Religion handed down in the Sacred Scriptures)?

<header>ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.</header>
<meta>catchword: most excellent.</meta>

<margin>...greatly promote incredulity.</margin>
And this is the force inflicted upon consciences, and the violent persecutions which are usually applied against those who err, or against those who are thought to err. Alas! the sad experience of all ages teaches that men have used mutual oppressions and the most violent persecutions because of disagreement in religion. The monuments of history testify, not without horror and detestation, that Pagans raged against Christians; Christians against Pagans and Jews; and Christians against Christians. As often as I read of the oppressions undertaken not only against the first Christians, but especially those of the "Pontificians" <note>Roman Catholics</note> against the *Waldensians*, *Hussites*, and *Protestants* in *Germany*, *France*, the *Low Countries*, *Piedmont*, etc., my soul shudders and recoils in grief. I am more and more confirmed in that opinion, which has long been fixed deep in my mind: namely, that perhaps no error is more deadly than that by which men persuade themselves that it is lawful to use violence of every kind against those whom we think to be in error in the matter of religion. Certainly, unless it were proven by so many manifest monuments and documents, I would scarcely believe the accounts of so many accursed and more-than-bestial oppressions which Christians (if indeed those men are worthy of this name who seem to have cast off their humanity) have exercised against Christians. Nothing more horrendous can be imagined, nor anything more contrary to both divine and human laws, than to subject to violent and exquisite punishments those who feel differently about divine matters than we do—especially when those who seem to us to be in error believe they would be sinning most gravely against God if they felt otherwise or attempted to worship the Deity in any other way. For this reason, I think none should be less tolerated in society than those who contend that dissenters in religion ought to be subjected to any punishments whatsoever, because in doing so, the primary rights of divine and human law are violated. Hence also the celebrated *Barbeyrac* <note>Jean Barbeyrac (1674–1744), a famous jurist</note>, in his notes on *Pufendorf's Law of Nature and Nations*, on the occasion of the Spanish Inquisition and the Tribunal of the Inquisition, maintains that Christians would be doing right if they entered into a plan to exterminate those horrendous tribunals. And indeed, if we recall to mind the innumerable evils which have been brought upon the most flourishing kingdoms by such inquisitors of "heretical depravity," it will be manifest that they have harmed the human race more than the worst of heresies. For this reason, the most learned men among the Protestants, suspected of no heterodoxy, hold the opinion of those who contend that such oppressions for religious disagreement are lawful to be the most pestilential of heresies. Among a thousand, I bring forward only one witness: namely, the most excellent, Reverend and Learned *Roque*, Pastor of the French Church of Basel.

"...origin from God <note>The catchword "O." from the previous page likely began the phrase "Optimus Maximus" (The Best and Greatest) or continued the word "Originem."</note> which commands all the precepts of natural law to be trampled underfoot." In this, surely, all theologians and philosophers of sound mind agree: that a religion cannot be divine unless it admits, approves, and confirms the precepts of Natural Theology and Natural Law. Now, however, such barbarous and execrable violence—to which so many thousands of men have been subjected at different times—can be reconciled neither with the love of God and neighbor, nor with justice and equity.

There will perhaps be those who object to us using the example of the Israelites, who by the command of God gave the Canaanites and other peoples devoted to idolatry over to slaughter. But this objection was answered long ago and at length by the most learned men. For our part, striving for brevity, we note only this:
1) Those peoples had contaminated themselves with the gravest crimes and were worthy of punishment, not so much because of errors of the intellect as for a life contaminated by every vice and crime.
2) There was present here a most manifest and express command of the Deity; the Spaniards, however, could show no such thing, unless they wished to hold the will of the Roman Pontiff, devoid of reason, as an Oracle. If this right alone were granted to them—namely, that they might deliver peoples devoted to idolatry to death—then Protestants, who consider those devoted to the Pontifical religion to be idolaters, could use the same right and pretext, not only against the Spaniards but against all who approve the worship of saints, etc., and thus a perpetual war would be fostered among Christians.
3) God has the right over the lives of men: whether, therefore, He removes the wicked from our midst by various types of diseases or by the labor of men, it is all the same, provided that there is an express command—the likes of which we do not find in the New Testament against those who err.

Grotius puts it briefly but forcefully: "The Canaanite people were condemned by divine sentence, and the Israelites were the delegated executors of that sentence." Whence these wars in the Holy Scriptures are properly named the *Wars of God*. When the celebrated <term>Heumannus</term> <note>Christoph August Heumann (1681–1764), a German theologian and scholar of the Enlightenment</note> had cited these words of Grotius in his *Dissertation on Zeal*, he broke out into these words: "How horrific a sin, therefore, did Abbot Bernard <note>Bernard of Clairvaux, who was instrumental in promoting the Second Crusade</note> once commit when, with an argument drawn from this expedition of the Israelites against the Canaanites, he set the minds of Kings on fire to amplify the Christian Religion by the force of arms, and stood forth as the author and persuader of a truly 'holy' war!" And in a note subject to the text: "Most poorly, therefore, did <term>Bongarsius</term> <note>Jacques Bongars (1554–1612), a French scholar and diplomat</note> title that volume in which he collected the historians of those wars: *The Deeds of God through the Franks* <note>original Latin: "Gesta Dei per Francos"</note>, when it ought to have been titled *The Deeds of the Popes through the Franks*."

<page-num>346</page-num>
# MEDITATION VIII.
<meta>catchword: publicly</meta>

...they admit [new forms of worship], even if their conscience resists; little by little, however, lured and led astray by the examples of others, they begin to suppress the stings of conscience as much as they can. Thus, step by step, they grow accustomed to accommodating themselves to the new form of worship, persuading themselves that it makes no difference what opinions we hold about God and divine matters. In this way, they are led into the thickest **Indifferentism** <term>Indifferentism: the belief that all religious beliefs are equally valid or that religious differences are unimportant</term>, prepared hereafter—should persecutions arise—to go over to either the Jews or the Muslims. If a person finally reaches the point where it is all the same to them what they think of God and divine things, they are not far from **Atheism** <term>Atheism: here meaning a total disregard for divine authority or the existence of a moral judge</term> itself. 

The words of our celebrated Heidegger <note>Johann Heinrich Heidegger (1633–1698), a prominent Swiss Reformed theologian</note> in his *Dissertation on the Violent Conversion of the Erring*, Thesis 53, are weightily set against this argument. He says: "So far is it from being the case that external violence makes men religious—when they are not yet convinced by the power of truth—that it is clearly born and suited to make them hypocrites and turbulent Atheists; and thus, in this way, piety perishes by means of [enforced] piety." Experience, a rich witness, confirms this. For when you believe you have most successfully imposed the necessity of believing upon others, what else have you introduced but hypocrisy and simulation—a thing which, if anything else is, is most powerfully opposed to piety? Perhaps through hatred <note>original Greek: ἀπεχθίᾳ</note>, while pretending to serve God <note>original Greek: θεὸν θεραπεύοντας</note>, you have made them worshippers of your royal purple <note>referring to the power of the State or the Emperor</note>, not of God (as Themistius speaks in Socrates’ *Ecclesiastical History* <note>A 5th-century history of the early Church by Socrates Scholasticus</note>)—whether you urge a true religion or an idol. 

In those people in whom there is not as much integrity and power of conscience as there ought to be, when they are harassed for the sake of religion, their conscience is overwhelmed. From this arises hypocrisy and the simulation of the religion to which they are driven; this is most harmful both to the hypocrites themselves, who by this means secure their own eternal destruction, and to the Church, which they hate most burnsly within and attack with curses. Or even the power of conscience is utterly extinguished, and thus Atheism and profanity are born, holding nothing truly sacred. So says the distinguished Heidegger. 

All those who attend to the customs and conditions of the majority of men will easily perceive that this can be achieved through persecutions. Many adhere to a specific sacred Society, not because they have examined the dogmas that this or that Church teaches and have seen them rightly, but because they were born, raised, and educated in it. These people follow the opinions of their parents, relatives, and fellow citizens. But when persecutions rush in, especially if sophisticated frauds and plausible reasons are added, they are easily led to change their religion. Furthermore, most are captivated by a love of earthly things; since they do not want to be defrauded of these goods, and cannot sustain the force of their passion, they frequent the public worship which they detest in their hearts. These people, while they wish to deceive God and men, and shrink from that which they

# ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.
<meta>catchword: complain</meta>

publicly adore and worship, how little do they differ from those who mock Religion? In the eyes of God, they will certainly be regarded as such. It is true, indeed, that the Rulers and Inquisitors, who must rightly be considered the primary cause of these persecutions, sin gravely because they plunge men into such serious offenses; nor do we doubt that, if the appointed day of punishment comes, they will experience the heaviest penalties for that reason. In the meantime, however, even those who act against the dictates of conscience, being captivated by the love of earthly things when they ought to obey God rather than the desires of their passions, are certainly not free from guilt.

->III.<-

Finally, by the force of persecutions, men can fall into **Unbelief** because on this occasion they often begin to doubt the most wise governance of God and His provident care for the pious, and to complain against it. It is known by experience that men in whose hearts true piety has not taken deep root—when struggling with various diseases or pressed by adversities—often pass unfair judgments on the goodness and wisdom of God, and sometimes call the very **Providence** <term>Providence: the protective care of God as a spiritual power</term> of God into question. This can even happen to the godly sometimes, but only for a time, in such a way that those anxious doubts are tempered by various comforts which, like a gentle wind, can refresh their souls. 

If men are accustomed to falling into these evils because of diseases (which for the most part they bring upon themselves), much more will this happen when violent persecutions rush in on account of religion. As the poet says, "it is difficult to contain a spirit which, conscious of its sincere integrity, is pressed by the insolence of the harmful." Certainly, those men who are pressed by such violent persecutions believe that they think rightly about God and divine things, and that they would sin gravely if they thought or worshipped God otherwise. They know that no right over the conscience belongs to men; and they are simultaneously persuaded that God wishes well for those who worship Him rightly, and thus He cannot fail to protect the cause of the innocent. But since they cannot reconcile this with the most violent oppressions to which God allows them to be exposed, they begin first to doubt the certainty of Providence, or even sometimes they deny it altogether. The question is not whether this reasoning is logically sound, but only what power it can have in the minds of these men. Certainly, those whose hearts are not fortified by true piety and the love of God, and who are not prepared to suffer anything for the sake of the true worship of God or to undergo the harshest fates (of whom, alas, there is a great number in all gatherings of Christians!), have often been unable to restrain themselves from believing that it is all the same whichever [religion] we uphold...

<meta>This page continues from the previous page's discussion on how religious persecution damages faith. The text begins mid-word, continuing from "veneramur" (we revere).</meta>

...revere Religion, when God—who is most loving of truth—seems to take no greater care for the most faithful than for those who err gravely and are contaminated by vices. On one hand, the more violent the persecutions are and the longer they last; and on the other hand, the more those oppressed by such persecutions feel a magnificent sense of their own virtues, yet find themselves unable to bear their adverse fate, the more easily they tend to fall into this gravest of errors. Yet these are the "distinguished fruits" of violent persecutions undertaken in the name of defending religion. Hence, it is to be hoped that at last all men might be better taught on this subject and might think more rightly. But we can hope rather than believe that men will ever fully admit the doctrine of **liberty of conscience** <term>liberty of conscience: the principle that an individual should be free to follow their own religious convictions without state or ecclesiastical coercion</term> to be granted to all. No better idea could be devised for the benefit of civil society in general and for all individual men in particular. Yet we see even in the assemblies of Protestants—whose principles should shrink from all violence—that there are those who detest all violence in words, while simultaneously urging that such means be used against those in error that are more intolerable than death itself. I say nothing of most of the Roman Catholic <note>original: "pontificiis"</note> teachers, who cannot draw those who follow the clearer <note>original: "defaecatiora," literally "more purified" or "filtered"</note> precepts of reason and Revelation toward their own opinion without violence or political arts—those who are captured and set on fire by the love of pure and chaste divine worship. Certainly, from the very books written by the missionaries of the Roman Church (as we saw above), it is clear that some confess it is impossible for the Gentiles to sincerely subscribe to the opinions and worship received in the Roman Church without violence. We, however, along with the wisest and most learned Teachers devoted to the Protestant Confessions, contend that the opinion that persecutions and violence of every kind should be inflicted on those in error is to be numbered among the most **pestilential Heresies**.

<margin>The various abuses of the doctrine of Providence promote Unbelief.</margin>
IV. But let us proceed to explain another very grave cause of Unbelief. This one is drawn from the *various abuses of the doctrine of divine Providence*. All who have ever seriously turned their minds to the various systems of theologians and philosophers; to the objections regarding God’s providential care over moral and physical actions; and finally to those things that happen daily among mortals, will admit that the argument concerning Providence is like a ship tossed by winds, where you may easily fall into either **Scylla or Charybdis** <note>A classical metaphor for being caught between two equally dangerous options; here, it refers to either diminishing God's power or making Him responsible for human sin</note>. That is, you may either take away something from the divine administration, or attribute such things to it that would either wound the divine virtues or destroy the obligations of men.

<column-break/>

<page-num>349</page-num>

The manner in which this happens must now be explained. And *first*, it is well known that certain learned men have constructed such systems of Providence in which much seems to be taken away from human liberty and the obligation to align one's actions with the standard of the law. For if you listen to them, God alone is established as the immediate Author of both natural and moral effects. These men usually use a specious pretext, contending that they do this to extol the virtues of God—namely, the independence and omnipotence of the Deity. But while they try to reconcile this opinion with that natural faculty called **liberty**, it is no wonder if men given over to vices gladly seize upon these opinions and wish to transfer the blame for their crimes onto God. This error is undoubtedly grave and shakes the very foundations of Religion. I will not mention here the systems of **Epicurus** or **Spinoza**, which are opposite to each other but are such that all providence is removed by them. But I will mention only the system of **occasional causes** <term>Occasionalism: the philosophical theory that created substances cannot be efficient causes of events, but that God is the sole true cause who acts on the "occasion" of natural triggers</term>, which was first adorned by **Malebranche** but was adopted and approved by others with less caution. According to this system, all moral and physical actions of men are nothing but the immediate effects of Almighty God; a creature cannot properly be called the cause of any actions. Thus, while men think they have done this or that freely, they are vehemently deceived. Therefore, if this hypothesis stands, neither the free worship of God can be established, nor can bad and good actions be attributed to rational creatures. The matter is so evident that anyone even slightly practiced in reasoning will easily perceive it. However, I do not say these things because I think these learned men approved this system so that they might more successfully attack divine Providence; far be such a thought from me. For from the other articles of Religion to which they subscribe, it is manifest that they either did not sufficiently direct their minds to the consequences that flow from this system, or, if they saw them, they shrank from them and did not want them attributed to themselves. By what right, I shall not now ask.

Certainly, from this system and the less-cautious speech of certain authors, it has come to pass that not only the common people but also others who ought to be wiser think less honorably of God’s providence. You may hear some speak in such a way that you would think they believe God brings about all the good and evil actions of men. We often find the most wicked men, when they have fallen into grave crimes not by deliberate intent but by anger, heat, and depraved lust, shifting those crimes away from themselves and [blaming God]...
