### MEDITATION VIII.

...unwilling to attribute it to some hidden direction of God. But whoever feels this way about God declares war on Religion and is not far removed from the highest degree of Impiety. 

II. Among learned men, there are those who speak of the **physical powerlessness** <term>physical powerlessness: the philosophical idea that created beings lack the inherent power to act on their own without direct divine intervention</term> of intelligent creatures in such a way that you would think they believe people cannot accomplish anything—not even in natural, household, or civil affairs—but that everything is driven by some kind of mechanism and special direction. But whatever their reasons for thinking this, it is clear that they hold views contrary to the universal rules prescribed by the best Divinity through the laws of **Natural Law** <term>Natural Law: a system of right or justice held to be common to all humans and derived from nature rather than the rules of society</term>; for these laws assume that all people, even those without divine revelation, are capable of both reward and punishment, and they bind all rational creatures to perform the duties imposed by Nature. 

Therefore, those who speak in such a way that you would think they take away all power of acting from a rational creature, even in natural things, either use harsher and more obscure words than they intend, or they are addicted to the **System of Occasional Causes** <term>System of Occasional Causes: or Occasionalism; the theory that created substances cannot be efficient causes of events, but instead God is the only true cause who acts on the "occasion" of a natural event</term>, which, as we have heard, is subject to very dangerous consequences. 

But if they actually shrink from this system, it is necessary for them to express their minds more clearly, lest simpler people be offended and seek a pretext for their negligence and sins elsewhere—not without a appearance of truth—attributing them to some kind of necessity. And this is all the more necessary because all Christians agree on certain principles when this subject is discussed. For they all agree: 

1. That God is not, and cannot be, the cause of sins. Hence, even though they may disagree on many articles of religion, they all believe (to say nothing of arguments sought from reason) that those passages of Scripture which seem to prove God is the author of certain sins must be explained more correctly and rescued from malicious interpretations. 

2. They agree that God permits evils and does not hinder the occasions of sinning through a miracle; yet He moderates all things in a way that is consistent with His virtues. 

3. Finally, all confess that in things pertaining to the maintenance of this life and necessary for conducting the business of this life, humans are so capable by their native powers that they can perform certain duties and abstain from certain actions. Hence, all interpreters of Natural Law prove that all humans are naturally bound to perform what is fair and just, and that no one is drawn to transgress moral duties by either internal or external necessity. 

In these things, I say, all Christians agree. But if you pay attention to what is said daily among people—especially the simpler folk—you would surely think they had all been educated in the schools of either **Thomas Aquinas** <note>Thomas Aquinas: the 13th-century theologian who emphasized divine "concurrence," or God acting in every action of a creature</note>

### ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

or **Malebranche** <note>Nicolas Malebranche: a 17th-century philosopher famous for Occasionalism, the idea that God is the only true cause of movement or thought</note>; for they speak as if they thought humans were unfit for all civil business, and as if there were no power in the natural faculties with which the most kind God has equipped humanity. 

Thus, when a wicked boy, though equipped with sufficient gifts of body and mind, is sent to learn some craft but neglects what he ought to perform, you may often hear his parents say: *“That boy is destitute of divine help”* <note>original: "Puer ille destituitur auxilio divino"</note>; as if God were bound to be present for him in some singular and unusual way. Likewise, when men gripped by foul vices commit sins, you may often hear these words repeated: *“God allowed them to fall”* <note>original: "Deus ipsos labi passus est"</note>. By these words, they do not mean that God did not prevent the fall—which is very true—but they mean to suggest that God, by some secret force, had plunged the person into this evil. 

To say such a thing about God is impious. Truly, those who feel this way are not far from **Unbelief**; indeed, they sin just as much as those who withdraw most or all things from the governance of divine providence. This much is certain: these opinions are all the worse because they exert their force on the behavior of men, calling them away from the duties they owe to God, to other men, and to ourselves. This is especially true because all humans are so inclined that they wish all their faults to be removed from themselves and transferred to others. And even if such people have heard nothing of the opinions of Malebranche or the Thomists throughout their lives, it is just the same if they think and act as if they had a thorough understanding of those men's systems.

<margin>An inquiry into the causes of this abuse regarding the providence of God.</margin>

V. If we inquire into the causes that have led many of the learned and unlearned to fall into these unfortunate opinions, several present themselves, some of which I will represent here. 

1. Indeed, just as in other chapters of Religion, so too in this one, there has been a widespread departure from the simplicity that should have a place in explaining and handing down divine matters. Everywhere, most loving men complain that Religion has been made too artificial; many things are publicly disputed which could have been ignored without harm to piety and religion. Many articles of religion have been discussed with such subtlety that they cannot be understood by the common people by any skill, even though God willed that their salvation be most greatly provided for in things necessary for salvation. Many complaints from very excellent men exist regarding this matter. Now, anyone who understands what has been disputed among theologians and philosophers regarding the preservation and "concurrence" <note>concurrence: the theological concept of how God's power "runs alongside" or cooperates with human action</note> of the divine will admit that many have progressed further in this matter than is proper. 

2. The learned, moved by an insatiable desire to know everything, have without necessity sought the manner of divine administration...

<meta>This page continues the author's critique of philosophers and theologians who attempt to define the precise mechanisms of divine providence. It follows a discussion on how extreme views of human powerlessness can lead to impiety by undermining the basis of moral responsibility.</meta>

...they have attempted to determine the workings of divine providence in every individual case and action. Because of this, they are often cast into such difficulties that they can only escape with great effort, or not at all—to say nothing of the harm that has spread from these ideas to the common people. It would have been enough to establish the following: that all things—the greatest, the smallest, and everything in between—are produced by God; that these same things are preserved and governed by Him; that God exercises His power daily upon both body and mind; that He preserves and directs the faculties of our minds; and that whatever good is in us should be attributed to God, while whatever is evil should be attributed to ourselves. These points, and others like them, would have sufficed for what can and ought to be known about Divine Providence. 

But these were not enough for learned and curious minds. Instead, they felt a need to investigate the exact nature of God's cooperation in every single human action. They wanted to define precisely how much the creature acts and how much God acts; to determine the cause of how ideas are triggered in the mind; to explain the method of divine operation on the senses and the appetite; and the manner of divine motion within the body, and so on. 

From this, various **Philosophical Systems** arose, often intertwined with the Christian religion. The learned have since clashed over these systems, and as far as one can judge from the current state of affairs, they will never stop "drawing the saw of dispute" <note>original: "serram disputationum... reciprocare"; a Latin idiom for an endless, back-and-forth argument</note> back and forth. While they wish to define everything so authoritatively and explain the inner workings of such obscure subjects, they often establish principles that are vulnerable to very dangerous consequences—consequences they themselves cannot resolve. 

Read for yourself—whoever you are, if what I say is not yet clear—the responses of **Malebranche** <note>Nicolas Malebranche (1638–1715) was a French philosopher known for "Occasionalism," the idea that created things have no power of their own and that God is the only true cause of all events.</note> given to those who attacked his **System of Occasional Causes**. You will see which way this sharp-witted man turns; how much he sweats, and how subtle the answers he provides are—answers that are, for the most part, more obscure than the very principles on which his system rests. For alas, many learned men are so constituted that they would rather defend their cause with foolish little arguments than yield and admit they have gone further than they should have. 

When some people deal with this subject and find they cannot resolve the doubts of their opponents, they appeal both to the difficulty of the matter and to the weakness of the human mind. But they ought to have remembered this advice *before* they attempted to define everything without necessity—not only at the end, after they have poured a darkness over the mind that they were later unable to dispel. 

To this is added 3) a certain sinister opinion regarding the way to promote **Divine Glory**. If someone wishes to rightly value the glory of the divine virtues, they must not turn their mind to only one or two of them, but to all of them equally, comparing them with one another, 

<column-break/>

->DE CAUSIS INCREDULITATIS.<-
->(ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF)<-

bringing them together, and taking diligent care that they do not clash or that one does not oppose the other. Furthermore, one must also look toward man, who is capable of obligation, religion, and even punishment and reward. These things must be reconciled in such a way that—whether you look at man in a state of nature or a state of grace—nothing is established that contradicts all the divine virtues compared together, and nothing that is clearly repugnant to the obligations of man and his essential faculties. 

If anyone now looks closely into the **System of Occasional Causes**, it will be clear that the authors of this system act only to extol the power and independence of God. They do not take the account they should of God’s other virtues; they are so little concerned with man—indeed, they think so poorly of his natural powers—that you would think he is being judged as a piece of wood, moved by another’s strings <note>original: "pro ligno, alienis nervis mobili"; a metaphor for a puppet.</note>. 

I, however, would hardly believe that God’s glory is greatly exalted by those subtle opinions drawn from metaphysics which exceed the grasp of simpler people. Rather, in my view, the person who truly acknowledges and celebrates the glory of God is the one who loves God as He is presented to us in the **Holy Scriptures**, places their trust in Him, burns with an incredible zeal to rightly keep the divine commands, guards themselves from vice as much as is possible in this imperfect state of things, bears all life's adversities with a patient mind, and spends every effort so that they may have God's favor through Jesus Christ. 

Unless, perhaps, the people devoted to that other opinion think that only someone who clearly understands the views of Malebranche and the **Thomists** <note>Thomists: followers of the theological system of Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), who held specific views on how God's "concurrence" or cooperation works with human will.</note> regarding God’s cooperation—and can count their arguments on their fingers and solve every difficulty arising here—truly worships God. 

4) As for the fact that opinions contrary to divine providence and freedom are found everywhere among the common people, I can attribute this to no other cause than the less-than-careful speech on this subject by certain theologians, and especially by **Preachers** <note>original: "Oratorum Sacrorum"; literally "Sacred Orators."</note>. The common people certainly pay more attention to the words of their Pastors than to the systems of philosophers. Now, it is known from experience that many, while wishing to demonstrate the moral powerlessness of man or to proclaim the power and efficacy of the will of God’s grace, use such hyperbolic words and exaggerations that, if you wanted to take their words literally and "cut to the quick" <note>original: "ad vivum... resecare"; to examine something with extreme, painful precision.</note>, it would have to be concluded that humans are entirely deprived of all freedom, even in natural things and actions pertaining to this animal life. To be sure, theologians and public speakers act rightly if, according to the guidance of the Holy Scriptures, they preach the necessity, power, and efficacy of divine aid for attaining eternal salvation...

# MEDITATION VIII.

...they show [truth], as there is a measure in things, and matters which are confined within certain limits of truth must not be exaggerated. Certainly, while we must speak of the **moral impotence** of man, the greatest care must be taken lest the reader or listener—not without a show of truth—should think that man is endowed with no more freedom for acting or not acting than **a stone or a log**. For two evils arise from those careless expressions. 

The first is that men use them either to diminish the gravity of their sins or to excuse them entirely. It is well known that impious men (whose number, alas, is very large among Christians!) seek protection from this very "impotence," when misunderstood, to cover their malice. They vehemently applaud themselves when they hear public Teachers <note>Referring to professors or officially sanctioned preachers</note> "pleading their case" (as they think). For they interpret the teachers' minds as if they taught that men cannot restrain themselves, even by nature, from those things which are prescribed for all mortals by natural law. And from this, it cannot happen otherwise than that they "loosen the reins" on their depraved affections and perform their duties with a soul that follows only with reluctance. 

The second evil is that, by this reasoning, many begin to feel less reverence for the **goodness of God** and His wisdom, which stands as no small obstacle to the pursuit of true piety. For among the virtues of God, none attracts man more than His **Goodness**. If men judge this incorrectly, the primary strength of their incentives toward the pursuit of virtue is lost. It is to be lamented, therefore, that this evil has infected many men like a poison! It is certainly clear from the common talk of men—and especially from the excuses they use to minimize their sins—that many think in such a perverted and impious way about the providence of God. 

Therefore, Theologians and public Orators are to be exhorted to always speak cautiously and circumspectly regarding this argument. Meanwhile, it must be admitted that although Theologians are imbued with different opinions regarding the extension of providence to evil, they all agree amicably when they come to that clear passage of Holy Scripture in which God is absolved of all evil, and is said neither to tempt nor invite anyone to evil. See the Interpreters on the passage in **James, Chapter I, verse 13.** Among the most recent Interpreters of this Epistle, one must include **Heisenius**, a most learned Reformed Theologian from Bremen. Indeed, after listing certain "cruder" expressions of the older Reformers on page 516, he speaks thus: 

"Whatever the case may be, it is better to abstain from phrases of that kind, and so to defend the providence of God (which extends to all things, even sins themselves) and the dependence of man upon God, so that no injury is done to the most pure holiness of that same God, and the free-

-dom of the human will, and so that the sinner does not seem to be pronounced immune from guilt. Those ill-advised and unformed voices lie open to the accusations of opponents, and they seem to fight 'face to face' against the style of the New Testament. For, I ask you, dear Reader, what else is 'God impels toward evil works' than 'God tempts to evil'—which **James** expressly forbids us both to believe and to say? The diction of Moses and the Prophets is more sublime, and must more frequently be explained soberly through figures of speech <note>original: "per tropum"; referring to metaphorical or non-literal interpretation</note>. I shall never be led, and I hope no other prudent and God-revering person will ever be led, to think that the words of **Ezekiel 14:9**—*If the (false) prophet is enticed to speak a word, I, Jehovah, have enticed that prophet*—are to be understood properly and according to the Letter."

The first Theologians of the Reformers, **Theodore Beza**, **Peter Martyr**, and others, often used expressions harsher than was right; but even **Luther** himself did not sufficiently guard himself against them, as is commonly known. But the more recent ones, which I praise, have moved to soften them. After the most celebrated Theologian of Tübingen, **Weissmann**, had cited these words of **Heisenius**—as well as those of **Vitringa** on Isaiah 6:10 and **Witsius** in his *Miscellanies*, Volume II, Exercise I, who are "playing the same flute" <note>original: "eandem tibiam inflantium"; an idiom meaning they are in total agreement</note>—he broke out into these words: 

"We think such declarations are entirely worthy of attention, and we sincerely praise Heisenius's candor most highly. If, henceforth, the Theologians of the Reformed party abstain from renewing those cruder principles, and our own side employs fairness here against all [hostility], that hateful controversy about God being the author and cause of sin will finally cease, in my opinion. Would that Protestants might feel as one, not only on this argument, but also on the remaining controversies that linger; or, where that cannot be done in all things, that they might finally coalesce into one body notwithstanding a slight disagreement!"

<margin>The prosperity of the Wicked excites sinister opinions about God’s providence.</margin>
**VIII.** But there are also other causes which result in men often fostering sinister opinions about the Providence of God—indeed, sometimes reaching such a point of impiety that they deny there is a Ruler of the world at all. Among these, not the least is the **prosperity of the Wicked**, and, conversely, the oppressions and afflictions of the pious. There are, to be sure, noble and ignoble men who are touched by very little reverence for the Divine; who laugh at things human and divine, and trample Religion under their feet. There are those who circumvent their neighbor with various tricks and frauds, who despoil widows and the poor of their goods; in a word, there are men who are contaminated and covered with every crime. Yet these men often flourish and abound in those things which mortals think are primary—namely, riches, honors, and delights of every kind in this life. On the contrary, you may often see the best men and those most loving of piety either struggling with the most stubborn diseases, or [suffering] from the [hatred] of the harmful...

# MEDITATION VIII.

...to be pressed by insolence, or to labor under heavy poverty, or to feel the evils of most unjust wars, or to be subject to other miseries and afflictions. Now, indeed, it cannot happen otherwise than that diverse judgments are formed about these states of men. Those who are not sufficiently persuaded of the excellence and truth of the Christian Religion, and who at the same time have little skill in <term>Natural Theology</term> <note>The study of God and religious beliefs based on reason and experience rather than on revealed scripture</note>; those who are inflamed by the love of earthly things; those who were previously accustomed to a more delicate way of life and are afterwards reduced to desperation; those who are of a more agitated mind and a <term>choleric temperament</term> <note>In the ancient theory of the "four humors," a choleric person was thought to be easily angered or highly emotional</note>; those who have a false idea of true happiness deeply fixed in their minds; those who think that the pursuit of true piety must necessarily and always bring back its rewards in these lands; those who think more magnificently of themselves and their virtues than is right—all these, I say, will easily either fall into perpetual doubts about the providence of the <term>Numen</term> <note>A Latin term for divine power or the will of God</note>, or will altogether deny that God has any care for human affairs. 

Moreover, the greater the evils by which such men are pressed; the more flourishing the state they were in before they fell into various calamities; and the more they are persuaded of their own innocence, the deeper are the sorrows and complaints stirred up in their souls. Now, indeed, those affections are often so vehement that the reasons brought forward to calm them do not have enough weight, as much as would be necessary, to recall the mind to tranquility. The Examples—sought both from Holy Scripture and the experience of all ages, which have been collected here and there by learned men—bear witness that it has happened even to the pious and the best of men to have doubted, at intervals, the care of God toward them, and therefore to have filled all things with complaints. 

It is helpful to bring forward only one or two passages. Thus <term>Lactantius</term> <note>An early Christian author (c. 250 – c. 325) often called the "Christian Cicero"</note> testifies in his *Divine Institutes, Book III, chapter 17*, that among other arguments used by **Epicurus** to attack <term>Providence</term> <note>The belief that God actively intervenes in and governs the world</note> was also this one of which we speak. *Epicurus saw (he says) that adversities always happened to the good—poverty, labors, exiles, and the loss of loved ones; while the wicked, on the contrary, were blessed, increased in power, and affected with honors. He saw that innocence was less safe, and crimes were committed with impunity; he saw that death raged without choice of character, without order or distinction of years; but that some reached old age, others were snatched away as infants, others died while already robust, and others were extinguished by untimely funerals in the first flower of youth; and that in wars, the better men were more likely to be both conquered and to perish.* But it moved him most of all that men who were especially religious were affected by the heavier evils, while those who either neglected the Gods entirely or did not worship them piously felt either smaller inconveniences or none at all. The verses of **Claudian** in *Book I, Against Rufinus*, speaking thus, are very well known:

<meta>catchword: Often</meta>

<column-break/>

# ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

> Often has the thought drawn my mind into wavering,
> Whether the Powers Above care for the lands, or if there were no
> Ruler, and mortal affairs flowed by uncertain chance.

And having brought forward certain arguments fighting for divine providence, he breaks out again in these words:

> But when I saw the affairs of men rolled in such thick darkness,
> and the guilty flourishing happily for a long time
> while the pious were harassed: again my Religion collapsed
> and fell, etc.

More examples and testimonies have been brought forward by **Pfannerus** in *Theology of the Pagans, chapter VIII*, and **Hadrian a Cattenburg** in *Theological Gleanings, pages 284, 285*. From the Sacred Writings, the book of **Job**, **Psalm 73:2**, and **Jeremiah 12:1** can serve as examples. What, indeed, should be responded to this plausible objection, we shall see elsewhere. Let the meditations and responses of the most learned men who have clashed with **P. Bayle** <note>Pierre Bayle (1647–1706), a philosopher famous for his *Historical and Critical Dictionary*, who famously grappled with the problem of how a good God could allow evil</note> be read. 

Meanwhile, I do not doubt that the more subtle controversies about the origin of **moral and physical evil**, when translated into the <term>vernacular languages</term> <note>Common spoken languages like German or French, as opposed to the scholarly Latin</note>, have thrown many into doubts rather than freed them; for those objections are easily understood, but for someone to understand the strength of the responses, he must be equipped with a more accurate knowledge of Theology and Philosophy. 

Finally, I think this also contributes not a little to why certain men feel doubtfully about God's providential care: namely, that in the common speech of men, individual Elections and the distributions of offices and dignities—conferred equally upon the worthy and the unworthy—are attributed to some singular direction of providence, even when it is clearer than the midday sun by what "arts" <note>Tricks, maneuvers, or political schemes</note> men were raised to adorn this or that post. No one doubts that these things happen by the permission of the Numen; nor do we deny that sometimes, from a comparison of all circumstances, it is clear that the minds of certain men were disposed to help others not without the direction of the Divine. 

But in other daily Elections and the dispensations of offices made by votes, it is not credible that something singular intervenes, or that minds are inspired in some unusual way so that *this* man rather than *another* is chosen and carries the majority of the points. Nevertheless, in the meantime, everyone who has been admitted even to the most lowly office speaks in common conversation as if this had been done by a singular dispensation of the Numen. By this reasoning, however, it happens that many—once they have detected the real reasons for this or that promotion (which for the most part can be felt with the hands), yet which is still attributed to the singular direction of the Divine—begin to doubt the divine Government itself of human affairs. Certainly, just as nothing [diminishes] the divine...

# MEDITATION VIII.

...ought to be withdrawn from <term>providence</term> <note>The protective care of God or nature as a spiritual power</note>, since it extends itself to the greatest, the middling, and the smallest things; so, on the other hand, it is agreed among all that God does not impede certain things, but permits them, and does not truly intervene in every individual matter—certainly not in civil affairs—as if always by a miracle.

<margin>
The abuse of oaths causes many to either foster sinister opinions about divine providence or to flatly deny it.
</margin>

IX. Among those things which ought to excite reverence for the <term>Numen</term> <note>Latin for divine power or the presence of a deity</note> in the minds of men, oaths must rightly be included. These have certainly been held as a most sacred thing among all peoples, so much so that even the Gentiles <note>In this context, non-Christian ancient Greeks and Romans</note> not only counted perjurers among the most abandoned of the human race, but also asserted that such people would be afflicted with the heaviest punishments in Tartarus <note>The deep abyss in Greek mythology used as a dungeon of torment for the wicked</note>, as learned men who have laboriously examined this argument have shown at length. It is helpful to bring forward a single passage, namely from Plato. In his *Laws*, Book II, he speaks thus: <note>original Greek: Ψεῦδος μηδεὶς... translated below</note> *“Let no one admit anything false, deceitful, or corrupted, whether in words or in deed, by invoking the race of the Gods, unless he wishes to be most hateful to the Gods. For God pursues him with hatred who, having neglected the most sacred authority of the divine Power, speaks a false oath.”* And truly, whoever seriously directs his mind to the nature of an oath will easily be persuaded of the gravity of the matter. For in an oath, we not only profess that God is an infallible witness of the heart, words, and deeds; but we also voluntarily provoke divine wrath upon ourselves if we are guilty. Notwithstanding this, it is most true that many perjurers are found among Christians; many who, for the lightest reasons, would be most ready to perform oaths; and finally, many who count perjuries among "little sins." When these men, although they have provoked divine indignation against themselves, are seen to be only rarely subjected to punishment, others—whose religion is either wavering or whose mind is greatly corrupted—begin to doubt whether God has any care for human affairs. They think that God, to terrify the rest, ought to subject such heavy sinners to the gravest punishments immediately, as if God were obliged to perform this in an instant, or as if there would be no place for punishments after this life. If we inquire into the causes of so many false oaths which take place everywhere among Christians, various reasons offer themselves, which we will represent here briefly, since we are not dealing with this argument exhaustively. And 1) it is certainly true that among those who live in Christian assemblies, many wicked people exist, touched by no care, or very little, for religion. These care little for whatever is sacred and venerable, concerned only with those things which can lead to a pleasant life. 

<column-break/>

# ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

It is not strange, however, that such people transgress the most holy laws and duties. 2) There are those among Christians who labor under a gross ignorance of divine and moral matters. These do not have a sufficient knowledge of the nature of oaths, their force, obligation, and gravity; they also more rarely hear this subject discussed. However, the less men are persuaded of their duties, the more prone they are to neglecting and transgressing them. Many among the Gentiles thought more reverently about oaths in this regard than Christians do; thus that character in Terence’s *The Mother-in-Law* (Act V, Scene 1) says: *“If I knew anything else more sacred than an oath, by which I could strengthen my faith with you, I would promise that to you, Laches.”* 3) The very custom of performing oaths frequently causes men to discharge this most holy duty less religiously. In certain Kingdoms and Republics, oaths are imposed on many where matters of no great importance are concerned. Yet it is the nature of human minds that whatever must be performed most frequently becomes cheap. Thus we know that the frequent custom of attending church so often causes many to be less attentive to the business of religion, nor do they take from the sacred prayers they hear that utility which ought to be perceived from a matter of such great importance. In the same way, since in many places no one is admitted to the administration of any office, often a minor one, without an intervening oath, it cannot happen otherwise than that men, moved by the habit of swearing, treat oaths more negligently. Certainly, if they were rarer, and imposed only in the gravest business and cases, a place for so many perjuries would not be left. Truly the Gentiles themselves recognized that oaths are to be performed *more rarely*, which learned men prove by citing various passages of the Ancients. It is helpful to bring forward at least one or two. Quintilian in his *Institutes of Oratory* (Book IX, Chapter 11) says: *“To swear at all, unless where it is necessary, is little becoming of a grave man.”* Epictetus in his *Enchiridion* (Chapter 44) says: <note>original Greek: ὅρκον παραιτήσαι... translated below</note> *“Refuse an oath, if it be possible, altogether; but if not, as much as you can.”* Hierocles, in his commentary on the *Golden Verses of Pythagoras* at verse 2, says: *“The best method and care for preserving its cult (i.e., the Oath) would be if you use it neither frequently, nor rashly, nor in just any matters; neither for the amplification of speech, nor for the confirmation and faith of a narration.”* And on page 34: <note>original Greek: Τὸ δὴ σεβα ὅρκον... translated below</note> *“To ‘revere an oath’ signifies not only to swear truly, but also to abstain from swearing: for thus we might maintain the habit of always swearing truly, if we do not abuse oaths. For in the frequency of swearing, one might easily fall into perjury...”*

...perjury. Restraint follows upon keeping [the law]. For she who does not swear at all will, when she does swear, swear truly. And this is true whether the tongue runs ahead through habit, or the mind slips through a lack of control over the passions. <note>original Greek: ἐπιορκίαν. Φειδὼ δὲ τηρήσεως ἕπεται... This is a continuation of the quote from Plato’s Laws begun on the previous page.</note> That is to say: Because he commands that an oath be honored, he teaches not only that one must not commit perjury, but that one should even abstain from swearing. For in this way we will always be free from perjury, if we never abuse an oath. Indeed, through the habit of swearing, we easily fall into perjury. It will happen that restraint follows the practice of abstinence. For either one does not swear at all; or when one does swear, it is done in a holy and just manner. Furthermore, the tongue does not run ahead through habit, nor does the mind slip due to the intemperance of one's desires. Compare the illustrious Grotius <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a towering figure in Dutch law and theology</note> on *Matthew 5:33-34.* 

Added to this is the fact that people everywhere hear that solemn pacts and treaties, even those confirmed by oaths, are poorly observed by leading men—indeed, they are dissolved just as they think it fits their own interests. Since what the people hear is more than once found to be perfectly true, those to whom piety is not so dear conclude that oaths were perhaps devised only for the purpose of keeping subjects in their duty. They believe princes impose a yoke upon them under the appearance of sanctity, a yoke which those leaders themselves are unwilling to bear. 

4) Oaths are often imposed on people for whom there is clear evidence that they care little for religion or the laws of conscience. Such people, especially if they suffer from the <term>accursed hunger for gold</term> <note>original: "sacra auri fame," a reference to Virgil's Aeneid</note>, will not hesitate to treat the most sacred thing of all with contempt whenever they think it will benefit them. 

5) The impunity of this crime attracts even more people. For success is accustomed to calling many toward their own destruction. Often, those who could be proven guilty by significant evidence and testimony are let go without punishment; when others see this, they use the same tricks. 

6) Finally, I believe that certain word formulas by which oaths are composed contribute no small amount to this. These are often arranged in such a way that, if you wanted to interpret the words literally, you would have to conclude that the oath binds us to the impossible. From this very fact, people of a shallow mind conclude that the strict observance of oaths need not be insisted upon, since no one could keep them if they followed the literal force of the words. I have no doubt that the authors of such formulas sometimes used such effective, or rather <term>hyperbolic</term> <note>Exaggerated for emphasis</note>, expressions with good intentions. For they thought the force of the obligation was strengthened this way. But if caution is needed in any business, it is certainly here, for those who are accustomed to creating oath formulas; not only should the words of oaths be clear, transparent, defined, and free from all metaphors, but the oath itself which is to be performed must be suited to human strength. Unless that happens, men begin to use various exceptions and restrictions,

<header>ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.</header>

to use, and indeed often such that the force of the obligation is either greatly diminished or entirely removed.

Finally, to these causes of <term>unbelief</term> <note>original: "Incredulitatis"; a lack of faith or skepticism toward religious truth</note> already reviewed, there are added (lest I bring forward too many) various injuries and frauds decorated with the title of sanctity and piety, devised by men of the ecclesiastical and political orders to deceive others or defraud them of their resources. These often cause men, who are not sufficiently wise or lovers of religion, to begin doubting religion as a whole. The most learned legal consultant Samuel Treverus, a Professor at Helmstedt, explained those deceptions and frauds in detail and confirmed them with a huge number of examples in three published dissertations on this subject, which are most worthy of reading. But let these things said about the causes of unbelief suffice.

-> ADDITION <-
<note>original: Ἐ Π Ι Μ Ε Τ Ρ Ο Ν (Epimetron); an afterword or supplemental measurement</note>

## THEOLOGICAL THESES.

I. Arguments for the existence of God, <term>a posteriori</term> <note>Reasoning from observed effects back to their cause</note> as they are called—or those sought from the most beautiful effects we perceive in this world—are suited to the intelligence of all people. For that reason, they are especially to be urged by public preachers. However, we believe those arguments which are too subtle should be omitted, since they are not understood by the general crowd.

II. No one is assigned to eternal destruction except on account of perseverance in sin.

III. Just as it is certain that God’s <term>Providence</term> <note>God's divine guidance and care over the world</note> extends itself to the greatest, the <term>middling</term> <note>original: "medioxuma"; the intermediate or average things</note>, and the smallest matters—and thus all those who wish to withdraw anything from divine Providence act wrongly—so, on the other hand, we must beware lest we establish anything that could take away the obligation of man as a rational and free creature. For if liberty is taken away, all religion perishes.

IV. Those who deny that <term>hyperbolic</term> expressions are given in Holy Scripture either do not know what hyperbole is, or they are playing with words.

V. A minister of the Word of God who is adorned with no talents of the mind (or only meager ones), and who is equipped only with a superficial knowledge of theological matters, will not only contribute little to confirming true religion, but will also bring the sacred ministry and religion itself into contempt.

From what follows, it is clear that those who are tasked with appointing ministers must take into account not only piety—though that is the primary virtue of a Pastor—but also the Erudition with which a <term>Candidate of Theology</term> <note>A student or applicant for the ministry.</note> ought to be equipped. Regarding this matter, the words of the most insightful theologian, 
<margin>Stephen Gaussen.</margin> <note>Stephen Gaussen (c. 1638–1675) was a French Protestant theologian known for his works on logic and homiletics (the art of preaching).</note> are grave. They sound as follows:
> We are of the opinion that an adulterer or a murderer has never harmed Society as much as a Preacher <note>original: "Ecclesiastes," here referring to a church orator or preacher.</note> who, "against the grain" <note>original Latin: "invita Minerva," a classical idiom meaning acting without natural talent or inspiration.</note> as they say, and equipped with no clear gifts for the task, preaches <note>original Greek: ἐκκλησιάζει (ekklesiazei)</note> for thirty whole years to the same people without the help of a better Colleague. For first, that situation breeds contempt and hatred for the Cleric himself; contempt and hatred make the Listeners more negligent in hearing sacred sermons; and you can easily understand how small the gap is between contempt for sacred sermons and a total loathing of sacred things themselves. Furthermore, what else will a loathing of sacred things produce but impiety? And impiety will bring about the ruin of both the soul and the Commonwealth. *On the Art of Preaching, page 147, Kassel edition.*

VI. It no more follows from the words of Christ to Peter in *John 21:17*, **feed my sheep**, that the Roman Bishop is the Monarch of the whole Church, than it follows from that line of Virgil: *Tityrus, while I return (the way is short), feed the goats,* <note>From Virgil’s Eclogues, IX.23.</note> that Tityrus and all his successors would be infallible; or that they are the Kings of the earth because Kings are called "shepherds" <note>original Greek: ποιμένες (poimenes)</note> in Homer.

VII. Although, alas, it cannot be denied that many Protestants abuse the doctrine of justification by faith to their own destruction, it is nevertheless certain that the dogma itself is true and harmless. For they establish, on one hand, that no price of such a kind is to be placed upon good works—or even upon our faith itself—that its efficacy would merit justification before God; but on the other hand, they hold that a dead faith is not true faith, but only a mask of faith, and that it is considered dead if it is without works (*James 2:26*); that is, a faith which does not have good works joined to it, unless perhaps the faculty for working or the opportunity is entirely lacking.

VIII. How much absurd dogmas can contribute to the promotion of Unbelief is clear, among other things, by the example of Averroes, <note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd, 1126–1198), a medieval Andalusian philosopher who commented extensively on Aristotle.</note> the famous Philosopher among the Arabs, who is reported to have spoken thus: *Since Christians eat what they worship, let my soul die the death of the Philosophers.* <note>Averroes was famously repulsed by the doctrine of Transubstantiation, where the bread and wine are believed to become the actual body and blood of Christ.</note>

IX. Since it is certain that no one, in life or death, can take true comfort from being addicted to the system of the <term>Universalists</term> or the <term>Particularists</term>, <note>These terms refer to the 17th- and 18th-century debates over the extent of God's grace: "Universalists" believed God intends to save everyone; "Particularists" (often strict Calvinists) believed God's saving grace is intended only for the elect.</note> but rather from the fact that he perceives within himself the fruit of singular and individual grace

<column-break/>

<page-num>363</page-num>
<header>ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.</header>

and the testimony of a good conscience, it is manifest that Theologians and Ministers of the Word of God <note>original: "V. D. Ministris," abbreviation for "Verbi Divini Ministris."</note> should not labor so much to dispute at length before the common people about the order and manner of operating grace, but rather should seriously and gravely exhort Christians to strive to possess the characteristics of the truly Elect and Justified. The truth of this sentiment is evident even from the fact that the Reformed and Lutherans alike assert that no one can be certain of their election and justification except the one in whom a saving faith exists, along with repentance and a zeal for good works.

X. Lest this thesis of ours seem unusual to anyone, I shall bring forward the testimonies of two Theologians flourishing in the praise of Erudition and piety. The first is that of the Blessed <note>original Greek: Μακαρίτου (Makaritou), a term used for the deceased.</note> Johann Jakob Grynaeus, <note>Johann Jakob Grynaeus (1540–1617), a prominent Swiss Protestant theologian.</note> a theologian most worthy of a longer life, a man renowned not only for his singular Erudition but also for his piety. In his *Remains* <note>original Greek: λειψάνοις (leipsanois), referring to posthumous literary works.</note> recently published by the celebrated Frey (to whom all who have a taste for true Erudition will give thanks on that account), on page 171, he pronounces thus:
> I wish it were permitted for us to wrap in eternal silence the controversies that come between us and our brothers of the Augsburg Confession, <note>The primary confession of faith of the Lutheran Church.</note> the harsh handling of which, while giving rise to unhappy discord, has inflicted an incurable wound on the Church of God and brought irreparable loss to the Protestant public interest. Indeed, I am not far from saying that many—nay, most—of the things about which we disagree are debated with more curiosity than utility.

Saint Peter indeed exhorts the faithful—as many as desire an entrance into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ to be provided for them (*2 Peter 1:10-11*)—that they should strive to make their calling and election firm; but he does not command them to inquire into the secret causes of this calling and election, much less does he require of them that they should have the order, manner, and every reason of the divine decrees as ready at hand as if they had been present at God's councils. The second testimony is from a man likewise most distinguished and a lover of peace, namely J. C. Klemm, <note>Johann Christian Klemm (1688–1754), a professor of theology and philosophy at Tübingen.</note> a most excellent theologian of Tübingen. In the year 1742, he published an *Exegetical-Dogmatic Dissertation* on *Luke 13:23-24*. The words of the Evangelist sound like this: *And someone said to him, "Lord, are there few who are saved?" And he said to them, "Strive to enter through the narrow gate," etc.* <note>The original text provides the quote in Greek: 'Είπε δε τις αυτω, κυριε, ει ολιγοι οι σωζομενοι: ο δε είπε προς αυτες, αγωνιζεσθε εισελθειν δια της σενης πυλης.</note> After he had briefly explained these words, he proves that the response of Jesus Christ is most wise, and better than all the responses that could be given by Theologians from their own systems. He proves his opinion by the following general syllogism:
> Whatever possesses every degree of perfection in its kind is the best. That which is safest, wisest, holiest, infallible, and adequate...

and decisive; that which is plain and clear, not perplexed, not thorny, which is most peaceful, etc. That [response] possesses all perfections in its kind. That which turns away all danger of erring and suffering harm is the safest. That which attains its end by the most apt means, with obstacles removed, is the wisest. That which serves the holiness of Christians—or their duties toward God, themselves, and their neighbor—to the greatest extent, is the holiest. That which is incapable of being deceived or deceiving is infallible. That which removes all difficulties and fully satisfies is decisive. That which delivers a judgment without hidden meanings, evasions, or "thorns" is plain and clear. That which cuts off all disputes and promotes peace is peaceful: finally, the reasoning for opposites is opposite, etc. Now, the Renowned Man <note>Latin: *Vir. Cl.* (Vir Clarissimus), a traditional title of respect for scholars.</note> proves point by point that such is the response of Christ, to which all those attributes belong.

XI. The consciousness of committed outrages often strikes terror into the worst of men and consumes them with anguish. This power of conscience perhaps does not *directly* prove that God exists (the one whom the impious fear as the avenger of crimes). But it does prove this: that in the other arguments which demonstrate the existence of God and press themselves upon our minds from every side, there is such force and efficacy that they extort agreement even from the unwilling. This is the 18th Thesis of the <note>original Greek: μακαρίτου (makaritou), meaning "of blessed memory."</note> Renowned Grynaeus <note>Johann Jakob Grynaeus (1540–1617) or perhaps a later member of the prominent Swiss Protestant family of theologians.</note> in the work cited, page 125 and following. The same can be said about the argument for the existence of God drawn from the common consensus of Nations. That consensus of all or most Nations does not directly prove the existence of a Deity; but this can still be gathered from it: that the truth about the existence of a Deity is so clear and plain that it can be known by anyone who is not completely stupid, provided they apply a modest amount of effort.

XII. Those who reject the mysteries of the Christian Religion and contend that miracles have no power to prove anything, yet at the same time wish to be regarded as members of the Christian Church, foolishly persuade themselves that the true Followers of Christ lack the art of reasoning, while they alone are wise.

XIII. The method of preaching used by the modern English <note>likely referring to the late 17th-century "Latitudinarian" style of preaching, which favored plain English and rational argument over complex metaphors.</note> seems to me to be the most perfectly suited to the minds of everyone, the learned and the unlearned alike.

XIV. It is the duty of a learned and prudent <term>Theologian</term> and <term>Minister of the Word of God</term> <note>Latin: V. D. M. (*Verbi Dei Minister*), a common post-nominal title for Protestant clergy.</note> not to increase the number of controversies, but to decrease them as much as truth and the nature of things allow; to reduce true controversies to the smallest possible terms, to cut off clearly useless ones, and to make mention of them only <note>original Greek: ἱστορίας ἕνεκα (historias eneka), "for the sake of history."</note>. The same was felt by my highly praised and dearest friend, while the fates allowed, Grynaeus, in the cited work on page 158. *Miserable* (he says) *is the face of the Church in this age of ours, distracted by so many sects, <note>original Greek: σχίσμασι (schismasi), "schisms."</note> discords, and dissensions: foully...*

...in such a manner is that seamless tunic of Christ <note>A biblical reference to the robe of Jesus (John 19:23), traditionally used as a metaphor for the unity of the Christian Church.</note> torn apart. It can scarcely be hoped, indeed, that those <note>original Greek: γνήσιοι (gnesioi), meaning "genuine" or "sincere."</note> peaceful disciples of the Savior, who are concerned with healing and binding up these wounds of the Church, will achieve anything by their efforts, unless they show that the number of truly theological controversies is not as large as is commonly thought. They must show that many disputes, which have fathered great divisions of souls, are not worthy of being debated with such intensity; indeed, very often, if you carefully pay attention, no real matter for disagreement lies beneath them, and it is a mere lust for quarreling that keeps the controversy alive.

<margin>The Author's goal in this dissertation is shown.</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative square woodcut block containing the letter I, featuring ornate foliage and scrollwork.</image-desc>In the previous Dissertations published on this subject, I have diligently investigated the causes of Unbelief, and I have brought to light many of the factors that can alienate men from religion. It would now be time for me to show—as the title of these meditations also promises—what are the best means of meeting this evil, and in what manner one must deal with those who suffer from this disease <note>The author uses the metaphor of "disease" to describe skepticism, a common trope in 18th-century theological writing.</note>. I feel, however, that I cannot properly perform this unless I first weigh certain general arguments, or rather prejudices, which those who shrink from all religion, or at least from the Christian religion, are accustomed to use. This will not only provide us an opportunity to discuss matters of great importance, but also to prepare the minds of the Unbelievers—at least those who are kindled by some love of the truth—to accept their fates; that is, to weigh with a serene countenance the reasons put forward for the truth of the Christian religion. While we do this, the Reader should not expect from us a formal demonstration of either Natural Religion <term>Natural Religion: A system of belief based on reason and the observation of the natural world, rather than on divine revelation.</term> or Revealed Religion <term>Revealed Religion: Religion based on truths revealed by God through scripture or prophets, such as Christianity.</term>, much less a laborious examination of the objections with which Unbelievers are accustomed to attack the most serious points of Religion. For this has been performed by men most eminent in piety, erudition, and sharpness of intellect—the very "Happiness of our Century" <note>original: "Seculi nostri Felicitas"</note>—in such a way that, as far as the heart of the matter is concerned, nothing seems able to be added.

most eminent, such that nothing further can be added. We will only endeavor to sincerely present and weigh before the eyes of the Reader certain general objections of these men, which they are accustomed to call "legitimate prejudices." We truly pray to God from our heart that He might lead back one or two of this tribe, freed from errors and vices, into the way of truth, which is according to piety.

<margin>A certain general objection of the Deists is presented.</margin>II. Before I bring forward those general reasons of the Deists <note>Deists were thinkers who believed in a creator God based on reason but rejected the supernatural elements of Christianity.</note>, a certain objection must first be introduced which is opposed to those things I discussed at the beginning of our meditations regarding the causes of Unbelief. Namely, among the chief causes of Unbelief we listed ambition, the desire for fame, and the love of depraved pleasures. Here, however, some of the Unbelievers will complain and cry out that they are being treated unjustly; they contend that they were led to embrace their dogmas moved by a love of seeking truth and a desire for knowing religion. They claim that our previous objection—blaming their character—is too trivial and could easily be turned back against us: for many are devoted to the Christian religion and defend it for various worldly advantages, even if they are not truly persuaded of its divine origin. They argue that when dealing with various religious opinions, one should not judge based on the hidden motives that lead people to think one way or another. Instead, the thing itself must be considered as it is in itself; other matters should not be laboriously investigated, but should be left to God, the searcher of hearts (for our business is chiefly with those who admit the main points of natural Theology). They argue that experience testifies that many Deists live an honest life and do not allow themselves to be carried away by the impulse of passions. Furthermore, they note that most mortals do not always act consistently with their opinions. This is clear from the very confession of many Doctors of the Christian Church; for the Doctors themselves teach that while the Christian religion possesses an outstanding power over the minds of men, they cannot deny that the far greatest part of Christians—even those who should be leaders of others—are contaminated by various vices. From this, the Deists argue, it is clear that it is not so much one's opinions about religion, but rather the depraved inclinations of the mind that are the true causes of vice.

...and other passions <note>The Latin *affectus* refers to emotions or psychological states that influence judgment.</note> can lead a Philosopher to defend ridiculous opinions, or a Theologian to invent paradoxical dogmas, why could these same vices not lead someone to attack truths held most sacred by others, out of a desire for fame? I see no reason why unbelievers, if they consider this with a serene mind, would wish to deny it; unless, perhaps, they think themselves alone to be immune from every stain of vice.

(II.) It can easily be conceived how some may fall into Unbelief without malicious motives, however. There are, for instance, men who burn with such an incredible desire for accurate knowledge that they believe no proposition should be firmly held unless they think everything has been demonstrated with the utmost evidence—even if the very nature of the subject does not allow for it. There are those who, from their youth, have associated with people accustomed to attacking Religion with sharp arguments. There are those who, at an early age, came across those books in which the most excellent chapters of Religion are debated from both sides. There are those to whom the responses of certain Defenders of the Christian Religion seem too slight to knock them from the position of their previously held opinions. Certain minds seem as if they were made by nature for doubting; whatever arguments they examine, they find them hedged in by difficulties that are not easily resolved—so much so, indeed, that they often remain in doubt throughout their whole lives regarding what they should think of religion. 

If to these factors are added the disagreements of Theologians over various points of Religion, the forbidden examination of religion, persecutions on account of religion, and other things mentioned by us in previous Dissertations, it can easily happen that the mind of such a man might rest in unbelief without any evil motives. Therefore, a proper distinction must be made between purely speculative opinions and those dogmas which seem to impose a difficult yoke upon the will. Many can adhere to the former without the help of their passions, but not so with the latter. The things written on this subject by the most illustrious Monsieur de Beausobre the younger <note>Isaac de Beausobre (1659–1738) was a famous French Protestant theologian; his "son" here likely refers to Charles-Louis de Beausobre.</note> are pleasing, where he discusses the Unbelief of Thomas <note>Referring to "Doubting Thomas" the Apostle from the Gospel of John.</note> in Volume I of his *Historical Discourses, etc.*, pages 10 and 11. 

"One must," he says <note>Original text is in French.</note>, "properly distinguish between the sources of Unbelief. It has its source either in the mind or in the heart. In the mind, when it concerns truths incomprehensible to reason. In the heart, when it concerns adopting maxims that are restrictive and demand great sacrifices. For failing to make this distinction, people have placed, and continue to place every day, all Unbelievers into the same class. However, there is a very great difference between the one and the other. For after all, if the mind cannot acquiesce to the truths presented to it for belief, for lack—"

"—of evidence either in the object itself or in the proofs, can it be condemned? I would just as soon see a man condemned because he cannot bring himself to say that he sees when he does not see. Jesus Christ himself decided the question: *If you were blind,* he said, *you would have no sin.* <note>John 9:41.</note> But when the mind embraces certain truths, and the heart cannot resolve itself to the sacrifices they demand, it is then properly that Unbelief is criminal. It is a pure misfortune in the first case. It is a completely voluntary fault in the second. By this distinction, those people in the world who declaim against Unbelievers are often infinitely more guilty than they are; they believe, or pretend to believe, a Doctrine that obliges them to lead a pure and innocent life, yet they abandon themselves to shameful vices that reason condemns no less than faith—while the speculative unbeliever, faithful to his reason, listens to it, follows it, and lives as a man of good character. Thomas is of this character. His fault does not spring from his heart. It springs solely from his mind, and if he does not believe in the Resurrection of his Master, it is only because he could not persuade himself that his Master could rise again. Just as he could not get it into his mind that his Master should die—and much less die by a punishment as shameful as that of the cross—he could not get it into his mind that he should rise again. Seeing him dead, all his hopes vanished. My God! What obstacles prejudices place before Faith, and how difficult they are to root out. If we have even a little equity <note>Fairness or justice.</note>, what support ought we not have for the prejudices of others, we who so often need support for our own prejudices!"

Thus says that learned Man. Let us grant, therefore, that not all who are called Deists <note>Deists generally believed in a creator God based on reason but rejected supernatural revelation or church authority.</note> are driven by evil passions to defend the opinions they foster; yet it cannot be denied on that account that many more join this crowd and attack the Christian Religion in which they were born, driven by corrupt causes. He who not only turns the pages of these men's writings, but also pays diligent attention to those things which occur even among learned men, will clearly see that only a few of those who join this camp have been moved to embrace it by a careful examination and the weight of evidence. Some followers of this family boast that Collins <note>Anthony Collins (1676–1729), a prominent English Deist and author of *A Discourse of Free-Thinking*.</note>, for example, fought solely out of a love for truth; but he who reads what the author of *The Lay Roguery of the So-called Freethinkers* <note>Original: *de la Friponerie Laique des prétendus Esprits forts*. This was a polemic against Anthony Collins.</note> has brought forward will begin to doubt this. # MEDITATION IX.

...held this view, he turned his pen against him on page 15: *In his eyes, all the clergy were either Knaves or Fools; and by focusing on the former, who always lead the others, he concluded—with as little reason as he had confidence—that Religion itself was nothing in its entirety but a web of impostures. One cannot deny that such a principle, coming from the mouth of a "man of honor," was capable of dealing a blow. But was Mr. Collins himself an honest man? Was he truthful? Was he upright? Did no bad faith, prevarication, or knavery enter into his actions and his views? I know that the Deists will find these questions shocking coming from me. If they are to be believed, honor, uprightness, and good faith exist only among them. That is where they entrench themselves; it is primarily by this that they claim their value. They! To suspect them of underhanded trickery, of cowardly detours, or the sentiments and morals of the Rabble! For whom does one take them? It is to not know them. Ah, Gentlemen, we know you better than you think, and we are only doing you justice! A man who mocks God at every hazard can well mock men without consequence: and Mr. Collins, your Orator and your Hero, has pushed his contempt and his games with the Public so far, that your character and his will no longer deceive anyone but fools.* <note>The original text is in French, likely quoted from Isaac de Beausobre’s critique of Anthony Collins, a prominent English Deist known for his "Discourse of Free-Thinking" (1713).</note> Read the rest of this Preface. Whatever may be the case regarding him, it can sometimes be concluded with a fair amount of probability—and without fear of error—whether someone has subscribed to an error because they were led by ambition or other passions. 

Elsewhere we have established this rule: If someone of strong intellect and learning rejects truths that are most certain (according to the consensus of the wisest and most observant men, or at least fortified by the strongest appearance of probability) yet simultaneously and stubbornly clings to opinions that are either clearly foolish and ridiculous, or which in the view of the most sagacious men cannot in any way be compared—in terms of their degree of evidence—to the truths he denies, then it will be admitted by all wise people <note>original: *Gordatos* - a term for prudent or sensible people</note> that he is led by ambition or other corrupt pursuits rather than a love of seeking the truth. 

I will immediately add an example to this rule. A certain anonymous author, in a letter to the famous [Jean] Le Clerc <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736) was a famous Swiss theologian and scholar who edited the *Bibliothèque ancienne et moderne*.</note> (inserted, if I am not mistaken, in the *Ancient and Modern Library*), attempted to prove that the Christian Religion owed its origin to some unknown men living in the 5th Century who burst forth from the freezing regions of the North. Now, if anyone weighs even slightly the historical arguments by which the truth of the Christian Religion is usually proved and compares them with this ridiculous opinion, he cannot judge otherwise than that—

—this man, in his zeal for defending a new and unusual opinion, was carried away to such madness.

<margin>A further response to objections.</margin>
IV. In disputes with others (which I would like noted in the fourth place), we ourselves acknowledge that one must attend to the matter itself under discussion, and not inquire too curiously into the incentives <note>The psychological motives or "hidden agendas" behind an argument.</note> that might lead someone to feel one way or another. Indeed, we confess that in theological contests, sins are frequently committed in this regard. There are those who, to make an erring person appear truly hateful, invent innumerable causes for why he was led to think as he does. They also see dangerous consequences everywhere. "A scorpion sleeps under every stone" <note>A Latin proverb meaning hidden danger or malice lurks in every word.</note>: Thus, for example, if someone extols the power and excellence of reason in examining matters relating to religion, there are those who say he does this so that he can diminish the mysteries of the Christian religion. Those who refuse to admit the antiquity of the Hebrew points <note>The vowel marks added to the Hebrew Bible; in the 17th and 18th centuries, scholars debated whether these were original or added later, a debate tied to the absolute authority of the biblical text.</note> are often judged to do so for the purpose of rendering the authority of Holy Scripture doubtful and uncertain. 

I pass over a thousand other examples in silence. But such attacks are so far from gaining anything against the erring person that they instead confirm him in his own opinion and prevent him from weighing, with a serene mind, the reasons by which his error is being challenged. Meanwhile, this again does not prevent it from being said that ambition and other corrupt passions often lead men to defend monstrous opinions and hinder them from being able to see the light of truth. And since daily experience confirms that many even among those who call themselves Christians suffer from this disease, we see no reason why it cannot be asserted with equal right that the causes of Unbelief—and of other opinions built on no foundation yet brought forth with singular confidence—are the corrupt pursuits of the mind. 

Nor do we (V.) contend that everyone without distinction who does not admit revealed religion is ruled only by corrupt passions and lets loose the "reins of vice." For if someone admits natural and moral laws that are truly such—that is, laws which rest on the will and authority of the Divine Power—we see no reason why such people cannot follow them, if they wish, as much as the nature of human frailty allows. Men are not to be imagined worse than they are, nor are all those who are either entirely ignorant of the Christian Religion or reject it for various reasons to be represented as villains. Meanwhile, I believe lovers of truth will also grant me this: the more loosely men are bound by the chains of religion, the more frequently they will deflect from the true path of virtue. It is well known that temperaments and passions have great efficacy over minds...

# MEDITATION IX.

...especially upon the intellect of men. Even the best of people, those most deeply persuaded of the divine origin of the Christian Religion and whose hearts are touched by a sincere reverence for the <term>Divine Power</term><note>original: Numinis</note>, often cannot prevent the force and impulse of their hidden passions from breaking out into action. What, then, should be expected of a man who feels himself equipped with only the meager incentives of <term>Natural Religion</term><note>A belief system based on reason and the observation of the natural world, rather than on divine revelation or scripture.</note> for living a pious life, when he is stirred by the heat of his passions? Just as we have said above that men should not be depicted as worse than they are, so too, on the contrary, men should not be judged as better than the constant practice of all ages truly teaches us. (VI.) It is certain that men do not always follow their own principles. If they did, all Christians would be pious; for although they are pulled apart by a divergence of opinions, they all recommend piety—some a version that is purer and more solid, others a version contaminated with some superstition. In the same way, we concede that not all <term>Unbelievers</term><note>original: Incredulos; referring here to those who reject organized Christian revelation, such as Deists or Atheists.</note> always act in accordance with their principles. This very point has been used as an argument by those who have urged for liberty of conscience and political tolerance for those in error, asserting that many of those in error do not act according to their principles and thus do not harm the interests of civil society—though this is not the place to discuss that. However, this principle must not be extended so far as to suggest there is no distinction between errors, or as if it were a matter of indifference what opinion one holds about the Divine in one's mind. This is certain: most mortals gladly follow those opinions that flatter their depraved affections. Thus, most will provide a more receptive ear to a teacher who makes the gate to heaven wider than to one who represents the genuine idea of a Christian man’s duties without disguise. Therefore, although Unbelievers do not always follow their own principles, it remains certain on one hand that the Christian religion, properly understood, supplies far more certain and powerful incentives to piety than Natural Religion does—an point we will have a richer opportunity to discuss below. On the other hand, it cannot be denied that those who foster dangerous opinions about religion are very prone to vice.

<margin>The first general argument of certain Unbelievers is presented.</margin>

V. Having brought forward these points in advance regarding the objection raised, we proceed to certain general arguments of the Unbelievers which they are accustomed to use to show that they do not shrink from the Christian religion without cause. And 1) indeed they say: Those who wish to give their name to the Christian Religion must say goodbye to the freedom of reasoning about religion, which is unworthy of a free-born man. Nor, after one has entered into <term>Sects</term><note>Denominations or specific religious groups.</note>, is it permitted to choose that which seems best; one must subscribe to all—

—all those articles which this or that Sect has once embraced. Unless this is done, they say they will be regarded by Theologians as men of no religion and will be exposed to hatred and persecution. It is better, therefore, while preserving the freedom of philosophizing and the license to inquire into everything, to rest in those things which reason alone delivers concerning divine matters. There are many things that can be opposed to these claims, but we will represent them briefly. And 1) indeed, they do an injustice to the teachers of the Christian Church when they pronounce without distinction that once the Christian Religion is admitted, one must say goodbye to the cultivation of reason. On the contrary, the wisest among them contend that in the examination of religion, all the powers of reason must be exerted; they assert that one can only arrive at a certain, immovable, and saving knowledge of Religion by reasoning. Christians are not accustomed to proceed in any other way in proving the truth of the Christian religion than the laws of wisdom and truth require. Once the Christian religion has been admitted and built upon arguments, the Christian ought to properly obey the precepts of reason—unless perhaps the Unbelievers think it is "saying goodbye to reason" if someone, having admitted <term>Revelation</term><note>Truths communicated by God to humanity, which may not be discoverable by reason alone (e.g., the Bible).</note>, is willing and ought to rest in certain more obscure propositions, and that for the gravest of reasons. But if this were so, then the <term>Deists</term><note>Those who believe in God based on reason but reject supernatural revelation.</note> themselves would have to cast aside Natural Religion, because it is impossible for them to have an accurate knowledge of the nature and attributes of God, to say nothing of the administration of divine providence. Furthermore, the Unbelievers are hardly ignorant of the fact that there are very sharp Philosophers among the Christians, for whom even a love of the Christian religion does not prevent them from philosophizing most keenly. Certainly, just as there are those among Christians who properly exert the powers of reason and beautifully show what power it has in the examination of divine and human affairs, so too we do not deny that there are Christians here and there who follow the crowd of their predecessors without examination. So also, among Deists, there are those who properly weigh the principles of natural religion; but there are others who give their name to this family by a blind impulse—unless they would perhaps assert that all the peasants, soldiers, courtiers, and men of other ranks enrolled in the tribe of Deists have proscribed the Christian Religion after conducting a most rigid examination, and have decided to adhere to Natural Religion alone after weighing all the reasons usually brought forward by both sides. Nor should it be ascribed to all teachers in general that certain Christian Theologians rail against reason and its cultivation without enough circumspection. We know and grieve that not a few have existed and still exist who only then think they are rigid guardians of the truth...
