# MEDITATION IX.

...they think themselves to be, and to have fulfilled the duty of orthodox theologians, if they can amplify with tragic cries the danger which—if you listen to them—comes to religion from the cultivation of reason and philosophy. By this very act, they are so far from leading <term>Deists</term><note>Followers of a 17th- and 18th-century movement that accepted the existence of a creator based on reason but rejected supernatural revelation.</note> into the way of truth that they instead render their minds utterly alienated from the Christian Religion. But the learned and wise theologians among Christians are not accustomed to act in this way. Hence, to say nothing of others, the celebrated <term>Pfaff</term><note>Christoph Matthäus Pfaff (1686–1760), a prominent German Lutheran theologian known for his work on church law and his moderate stance.</note> rightly rebuked <term>Collins</term><note>Anthony Collins (1676–1729), an English philosopher and controversial Deist who advocated for "free-thinking."</note> for insulting Christian theologians by claiming that they all, without exception, condemn the use of reason and the examination of religion in matters pertaining to faith. See his *dissertations on prejudices*, page 85 of my copy. The famous <term>Crousaz</term><note>Jean-Pierre de Crousaz (1663–1750), a Swiss theologian and mathematician who defended the bridge between faith and reason.</note> had raised the same objection against Collins. So far is it from being the case that this [condemnation of reason] can be proved by the Deists, that we instead ask them to undertake a most accurate examination of the Christian Religion with all diligence, and to weigh it against the eternal laws of truth.

2) We assert nothing that is foreign to reason when we profess that, once the truth of Religion has been duly proven, one must duly inquire into the meaning of Revelation. For otherwise, it could not be properly understood. We urge that it be carefully seen to that all lovers of truth follow the rules of correct reasoning and interpretation, and weigh what is most essentially urged. All Christian teachers who admit revelation nevertheless confess that certain articles are so necessary to be known that without their profession, no one can be considered a Christian in the true sense of the name; these same articles are enjoined either in the most explicit words by Christ and the Apostles, or are drawn from them by the most evident consequence. We contend, moreover, that a lover of truth, having diligently read the writings of the Evangelists and Apostles, will easily discover such articles. Suppose now that a Deist, having undertaken a serious examination of religion, is persuaded that Jesus was called back from the dead to life; it will therefore be true that He is the Messiah sent from heaven; it will be true that His miracles are of divine origin; the doctrine delivered by Him will be true; it will be true that His death is not only an example of constancy which His genuine disciples ought to follow, but it will also be manifest, from the entire body of the Christian religion and the most explicit testimonies, that His bloody death is the unique cause of our reconciliation with God; it will be true that there is a resurrection of the dead; it will be true that minds are to endure eternally, etc. etc. Hence the illustrious <term>Locke</term><note>John Locke (1632–1704), the English philosopher whose work "The Reasonableness of Christianity" argued that the only essential belief for a Christian was that Jesus is the Messiah.</note> himself, who contends that all those who acknowledge Jesus as the Messiah sent from heaven are to be considered Christians, nevertheless clearly asserted that Christians persuaded of this article must afterward admit everything which they find clearly

inculcated in the Sacred Scriptures. <note>original: "On est obligé de recevoir toutes les parties de la Revelation divine avec docilité, & avec un esprit disposé à embrasser, & à croire toutes les verités, qui viennent de Dieu, & à consentir avec soumission à tout ce qui lui paroîtra porter ce charactere."</note> One is obliged (he says) to receive all parts of divine Revelation with docility, and with a spirit disposed to embrace and believe all the truths that come from God, and to consent with submission to all that appears to him to bear this character. *The Reasonableness of Christianity. Book I. chap. XV. and Book II. response to the first objection. page 87.*

3) Just as the Deists, who admit natural religion in theory and practice, do not wish to be confused with the disciples of <term>Spinoza</term><note>Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677), whose pantheist philosophy was often equated with atheism by his contemporaries.</note>, who admit no Divinity beyond this visible world; so they should not take it poorly that Christians, using a shared discipline, publicly profess that they agree in the confession of the most weighty articles of the Christian religion; it is enough that they grant <term>civil tolerance</term><note>The legal right to exist within a state without persecution, even if one's religious views differ from the established church.</note> to those in more serious error, and do not exclude anyone from their assemblies for minor errors, if they duly persist in their principles.

4) Wise and sensible theologians—of whom there is no small number in the assemblies of Christians, whatever the Deists may say—will not deal harshly with men who, at the beginning of an investigation, do not yet know all the dogmas of lesser importance, but who burn with a desire for knowledge and a love of truth, and strive to reach further according to the capacity of their intellect. Instead, they will calmly wait for the time when they can be imbued with better light: provided that those men do not scurrilously attack the weightier articles of the publicly accepted religion.

5) A Deist ought not to desist from the examination of the Christian Religion because of certain inconveniences that might perhaps happen to him. The question is certainly not about nothing—namely, whether the Christian Religion is of divine origin or not. If he believes this, he ought to seriously gird himself for the examination of this question: if, after the examination is made, he finds it agreeable to reason to embrace the Christian religion, he ought not to be anxious about the outcome of his affairs. God and time will happily untangle everything. If indeed he is duly persuaded of the primary points, even if he perhaps does not agree in all things with the founders of this or that system, yet has the genius of the Christian religion rightly in view, he will bear with an even mind certain inconveniences that may occur. But if he does not wish to undertake a serious examination of religion, or if, having done so, he cannot bring himself to subscribe to this Religion, what does it profit at last to speak of the inconveniences that might perhaps happen if he were to profess the Christian religion?

# MEDITATION IX.

<meta>catchword: or</meta>

<margin>The second objection of the Unbelievers is presented.</margin>

VI. In the second place, the Unbelievers object that *Christians are split into factions, yet everyone is simultaneously required to subscribe to such dogmas (for example, the Trinity, Transubstantiation, etc.) as can in no way be brought into harmony with the decrees of right reason; and since it is not within a man's power to believe what he wishes, anyone who listens to the Oracle of reason should rather reject revelation.*

We respond, (I.) that it is very true that Christians are distracted among themselves by a diversity of opinions. *We know and we grieve* that many trivial and unnecessary little questions have been sewn onto our simple and pure religion; *we know and we grieve* that many teachers, moved by pride and a zeal for knowing and determining everything, contend with others about any matter whatsoever; *we know and we grieve* that there has been fierce disputation over many questions which could have been ignored without harming piety, and not without the loss of brotherly love. *We know and we grieve* that many Christians are not so much concerned with promoting the study of piety as they are with protecting and defending minute opinions. All these things we know and we grieve. Meanwhile, Christian religion itself is not to be rejected because of this dissent. Not only do theologians disagree among themselves, but also philosophers, physicians, lawyers, and the teachers of all other disciplines. Yet no one, on that account, will pronounce the disciplines with which these teachers occupy themselves to be utterly useless. And indeed, if every one of the Unbelievers were to open up their own thoughts regarding the articles of religion, we believe it would be most manifest that they disagree vehemently among themselves. And what need is there for words, when experience and the reading of the books written by them teaches this—indeed, they themselves occasionally admit it. The authors of the *French Library, Volume XXVII, Part II* <note>original: "Bibliotheque Françoise Tom. XXVII. Part. II." A 18th-century literary journal.</note> relate the following concerning the Count of Passeran: <note>Alberto Radicati, Count of Passeran (1698–1737), an Italian freethinker and historian who lived in exile.</note> *He had reflected much on the difficulties of his own system, which were greater than those that had shocked him in Revelation: and on the prodigious diversity of sentiments which reign among the Unbelievers, to the point that he had not found two who held the same principles.* <note>original French: "Il avoit beaucoup refléchi sur les difficultés de son systéme plus grandes que celles, qui l'avoient choqué dans la Revelation: Sur la prodigieuse diversité des sentiments, qui regnent parmi les Incredules, jusques-là, qu'il n'en avoit pas trouvé deux, qui eussent les mêmes principes."</note> The Count had related these things when he was soon to pass away. However, that there is such great dissent in the business of Religion must be ascribed mostly to corrupt affections. Most of the public teachers and other Christians are unmindful of the human weakness that surrounds us while we are on this earth. Each one wishes to be more learned and more insightful than the next. Hence, the branches of the theological discipline have been increased and dilated immensely; new questions are always brought forward (often with no ill intent), but later, when they have been challenged, they were attached to necessary truths because of

the authority of this or that Master. And for these accessory little questions, men have often fought as if the most momentous matters were at stake. And what is worst in this case is that scarcely any room is left for a remedy. For if anyone, with the best intentions, tries to cut away these minute controversies—retaining only those things most necessary and useful to know, as inculcated by Christ and the Apostles—he is viewed with suspicion, hateful names are imposed upon him, and people cry out that such a man is nurturing some kind of monster. Hence, there is a lack of people to advise better things, since it is dangerous to have given such advice.

(II.) If, for a moment, the scholastic opinions and questions are set aside and we attend to those things which are of the greatest importance in religion, it will be manifest that the disagreement of opinions among Christians is not as great as is claimed. Since I have dealt with this argument more extensively elsewhere, I will not add another word here.

(III.) The <term>Deists</term><note>Those who believe in God based on reason but reject organized religion and supernatural revelation.</note>, who admit the theoretical and practical principles of Natural Theology, not only fail to agree among themselves in the choice of arguments by which they attempt to prove individual truths, but they are also—whether they like it or not—bound to admit something of mystery. For they do not perfectly know the most perfect nature of God, inasmuch as it is infinite; they do not know the nature of the ideas of intelligible and sensible things that have been present to the most perfect intellect of God from all eternity; they are ignorant of how God gazes upon every individual thing in the past, future, and contingent. When it comes to contemplating the divine attributes, it is most clearly apparent that the finite is not capable of containing the infinite. For all attributes exist in God in an infinite manner. It is confessed on both sides that God possesses all attributes in the most perfect degree; but who can explain that degree? The Deists admit as much as we do that God preserves all things and provides for them; I confess God is most powerful, but who can explain how an act of the divine will—an intellectual thing—exerts its force upon physical bodies? I shall say nothing of the origin of moral and physical evil, a question which the greatest and most acute philosophers admit mortals cannot *entirely* solve in this life; yet many Deists admit <term>Providence</term><note>The protective care of God or of nature as a spiritual power.</note>, and are no less bound to assert and defend it than Christians. And why is it a wonder that we are blind regarding these things, when philosophers themselves do not agree about the nature of ideas, sensation, imagination, memory, or the conjunction of the mind with the body, even after so many meditations and disputes? Even the nature of the smallest <term>atom</term> or <term>monad</term><note>In 18th-century philosophy, particularly that of Leibniz, a "monad" is an indivisible, simple spatial point or "soul-atom" that makes up the universe.</note> is most imperfectly known. Today, through the work of learned men and through experiments performed, many things are brought to light,

# MEDITATION IX.

...are seen, whose truth is sufficiently established from experience <note>original: "a posteriore"</note>, as we are accustomed to say, but it is often not granted to us to look into their causes and nature. I do not wish to defend the Mystery of the Trinity here with a dedicated work (to say nothing of the other dogmas) which they attack. I say only this: Christians, subscribing to Revelation, admit only one most perfect Divine Being. Yet, as that same divine Revelation testifies, there is a certain distinction in that unique and ineffable Being, which we cannot express sufficiently with words while we lack a clear notion of it; they do not think there is sufficient cause, once the character of this truly divine Revelation has been properly detected, to repudiate the entire religion on account of the more obscure knowledge of certain dogmas.

(IV.) The question will always remain whether the Deists believe a revelation is possible or not: or to speak more clearly, it is asked whether they affirm that God can reveal such truths to men which they themselves could not draw out from the depths of the mind and the principles of human knowledge by reasoning. I would scarcely believe that Deists, understanding their own principles, would dare to deny this. For to admit an omnipotent and all-wise God and to deny that He can perform this is a contradiction. But if they wished to prove this, it would have to be shown that something impossible <note>original Greek: "ἀδύνατον τι" (adynaton ti)</note> occurs here. This would have to be sought either in God, or in man, or in both. We do not see a cause why God, whose intellect is infinite and whose knowledge is most perfect, could not reveal new truths. Man himself is capable of greater levels of knowledge. We see children, with increasing age and helped by diligence and meditation, are able to learn the most subtle sciences: what, therefore, would prevent the mind from learning more truths hitherto unknown? But if revelation is possible, it does not yet follow from that fact that God therefore either willed or ought to have granted one to the human race; yet you may probably gather this: that if God willed to grant this benefit to mortals, He would communicate such things to them which could not be known by the help of reasoning alone, even with all care and anxiety applied. After so many centuries, Philosophers have reduced those things which pertain to religion to certain general heads, from which innumerable consequences can be drawn. And if our descendants should perhaps be more fortunate than we are in the method of demonstrating and applying the dogmas of natural Theology to other truths, yet everything must always be sought only from certain principles of reason. Now, since God, the wisest Being, does nothing without the weightiest reasons, and men, with all diligence and sharpness of wit applied, can detect nothing other than

what rests upon certain principles of reason, it is most highly agreeable to the truth that God, if he wished to deign to give them some revelation, would open something that would surpass the grasp of reason; yet in such a way that it would not destroy already known principles but would agree with them in a friendly manner. Now, if it can be proved by historical arguments that there existed men worthy of belief who, furnished with sufficient protections, could not only testify that they were sent by God to detect new truths, but also brought into the light such dogmas which, by the consensus of all wise men, cannot be drawn from the storehouse of reason, yet show the safest way to promote the happiness of men, then a reason would finally have to be given why those truths which we call mysteries should not be received with an obedient mind. Indeed, Christians think it can be shown by sufficiently weighty arguments that God has given such a revelation to mortals. However, men ask less prudently why He revealed these dogmas and not others to mortals; for if others had been given in place of these, a similar question would return. Any sane person will easily concede that those things which have been granted are such as are most tempered to the state of the human race and necessary to be known.

(V.) The Unbelievers retort that they would easily admit these things, if only those new dogmas which we call mysteries were agreeable to reason; but they contend that they are contradictory. I will not repeat what has been warned a hundred times by learned men regarding this objection. This one thing I say now: if anyone wishes to prove that this or that proposition is contradictory, it is necessary that he has the terms of the proposition clearly known. But now Christians confess that they do not distinctly know what, for example <note>original: "v. gr." - verbi gratia</note>, the nature of those persons in the Trinity is; it is therefore not possible for it to be shown that this dogma involves a manifest contradiction. The contrary can be shown where the talk is about <term>Transubstantiation</term> <note>Transubstantiation: The Catholic doctrine that the bread and wine in the Eucharist literally become the body and blood of Christ.</note>. For we know well enough what a body is; what it is to exist and not exist at the same time; what is one, and what is many. From these known terms, one can easily judge regarding Transubstantiation.

This is clear both from the nature of religion, whether natural or revealed, and from the weakness of our knowledge. # MEDITATION IX.

...they are accustomed to dispute about these things in such a great light of Learning: yet even a single atom can reduce a Philosopher to a suspension of judgment <note>original Greek: "ἐποχὴν" (epochē), a Skeptic term for withholding belief</note>. In our age and that of our fathers, Philosophers wanted to persuade us, against all likelihood, that animals <note>original: "bruta"</note> are mere machines. But now, a certain soul is attributed to every living thing, or creature; indeed, all the more recent thinkers contend that there is a "ladder of intelligent Beings." But who, since the number of such Beings is infinite, will reveal their nature, their grades of knowledge, and their capacity? If those living creatures could, for a few years, express the inner thoughts of their souls in words that could be understood by all—oh, how much they would demonstrate that we have lived in ignorance regarding these matters until now! How many Philosophers they would put to the blush! The more men inquire into the nature of divine and human things, the more they will also detect the traces of human frailty. If we look back at Religion in general, it will again be manifest that it is full of things which we know very imperfectly; Religion deals with God: but in God, all things are infinite. Infinite is the nature of God, infinite are His perfections; infinite is the knowledge of God, His power and wisdom; infinite are the counsels of God. Who then would wonder that we are ignorant of many things in these matters! Who would wonder that even when revelation is granted, many things remain unknown to us now and will be in the future? Oh, how happy mortals would be if, content with a manageable knowledge of divine things, they did not strive so much to subtly pry into everything, to know all, and to dispute about whatever they pleased, but rather, resting in this imperfect knowledge, they applied themselves with all their strength to organizing their lives according to the divine knowledge they can attain, and to growing perpetually in the love of God and the exercise of virtue. Certainly, just as the eye was not given to us for the purpose of looking through the nature of the body and the connection of its smallest particles, but for the end that we might promote our happiness by the help of sight: so likewise religion was not given to perfectly know the nature of the most divine things, but to amend and perfect the will. With an elegant comparison, the late <note>original Greek: "ὁ Μακαρίτης" (ho Makaritēs), an epithet for the blessed deceased</note> the Illustrious Turrettin <note>Francis Turretin (1623–1687), a prominent Reformed scholastic theologian</note> depicted the madness of most men regarding this argument in his *Reflections on Controversies*, in the third Thesis: *A Physician (he says) enters a Hospital, and having examined the state of the sick, he offers them suitable remedies: presently he departs, promising that he will return the next day. But as soon as he has left, those sick men engage in various conversations among themselves: for instance, about that Physician’s beard, about his hair, about his cloak; likewise about his stature, his fatherland, his Ancestors; then about the vials in which he enclosed...*

*...his medicines, whether they were of glass, or crystal, or made of some unknown material? etc. About these and other things they dispute among themselves, not calmly and as friends, as the matter required, but most bitterly; and from arguments they come to insults, and from insults to blows. Neither fists nor slaps are spared. And now torches and rocks fly; rage supplies arms <note>A quote from Virgil's Aeneid: "furor arma ministrat"</note>. Then someone, perhaps arriving, cries out: "What are you doing, you wretches? What madness, what heat of fever agitates you? Just take the remedies brought to you, and when you have been healed, then you will more conveniently dispute about those fine questions." But they neither listen to his words, nor would they have spared the advisor, unless he had snatched himself from their claws in headlong flight.* Suppose, however, that the knowledge of divine things is far wider than many indeed think; what would that more excellent knowledge help, if the mind were not incited to a greater reverence and love of God? God has a well-perceived grasp of the capacity of human minds; He knows how much each person, according to their status, can know of divine things. Everyone, therefore, ought to act only so that, according to the measure of their knowledge, they may call those things which they can know through reason and revelation to a salutary use. I shall close this response with the words of the Celebrated Werenfels <note>Samuel Werenfels (1657–1740), a Swiss theologian known for his moderate views</note>. After he had shown in many ways that we do not know what an atom is, he finally concludes thus: *You see here how small an atom even our mind is, if it be compared with that Mind which knows not only all and singular bodies, but also all and singular things in singular bodies; and not only in the bodies that are, but those which can be; and not only in bodies, but in all other things intimately and most perfectly, and that by a single thought: which at the same time most perfectly knows, not one, not a thousand, not as many as there are drops in the sea, but myriads of things; not—what is twice as great—the indefinite; not the indefinitely indefinite, etc. But (that which is infinitely greater than everything that men, by continuing in this way, could ever reach) the absolutely infinite—that is, all things. What is our mind compared to this Mind, to which the thousandth part of the smallest speck of dust is an unsearchable abyss? Learn modesty here, O man; you, to whom your mind seems the measure of things, and who boldly say that what you do not comprehend—or even more foolishly, what you do not imagine—does not even exist. Whatever God himself, the infinite, says of himself, of the infinite self, you do not believe: why, finally? "I do not grasp it," you say. O insane voice! Exercise your industry, exercise your insight—you who grant it so much—upon this little speck of dust; you will see how far your sharpness can penetrate. Then at last, weary with meditating, inquiring, and searching, when you have seen how little you have progressed, approach and reflect thus with yourself: If I know so little of the smallest things; if I know there are innumerable things which I do not perceive—what they are, of what sort they are, how they are—how great a...*

# MEDITATION IX.

...I am far from a full knowledge of the infinite! In this darkness, what other path is safer than to submit the mind to the Infinite Mind; to believe and hold fast to those things which are revealed by Him, and never to wander outside of them. Compare the work of the illustrious Christian Philosopher *Wolff*, titled *A Specimen of Physics Applied to Natural Theology*, which presents the notion of the divine intellect as illustrated through the works of nature.

<margin>A third general argument of the Unbelievers is brought forward.</margin>
VII. In the mouths of many Unbelievers, a certain response is frequently heard—one they admire greatly as a seemingly brilliant argument against the necessity of Divine Revelation. This was the reply of the King of Siam <note>This refers to King Narai of Siam (modern Thailand), who reigned 1656–1688.</note>, given to the Ambassadors of King Louis XIV of France, who wished to persuade him to embrace the Christian Religion. The words of this King, which we have produced elsewhere, sound like this, according to the testimony of Tachard <note>Guy Tachard (1651–1712), a Jesuit missionary and mathematician who wrote accounts of his voyages to Siam.</note>:

> <note>The following was originally written in French</note> *I am astonished that the King of France, my good Friend, takes such a strong interest in a matter that concerns God; a matter in which it seems God Himself takes no interest, and which He has left entirely to our discretion. For could not this true God, who created the heaven and the earth and all the creatures seen therein, and who gave them such different natures and inclinations—could He not, had He wished, have inspired them with the same sentiments for Religion and the path they must follow, and for the worship most pleasing to Him, and caused all Nations to be born under a single law? Since this order among men and this unity of Religion depends absolutely upon Divine Providence, which could as easily have introduced it into the world as the diversity of Sects that have been established at all times, must we not believe that this true God takes as much pleasure in being honored by different forms of worship and ceremonies as in being glorified by a prodigious quantity of creatures, each of whom praises Him in its own manner? Would this beauty and variety, which we admire in the natural order, be any less admirable in the supernatural order, or less worthy of the Wisdom of God?*

I will not inquire here whether this narrative is true, since it is well known that Tachard’s reliability is quite shaky; nor will I say that the argument of the King of Siam is tailored too closely to the tastes of the <term>Deists</term> living in Europe; finally, I will not even examine whether it is probable that a man educated in such superstition and so devoted to the religion of his homeland would speak so freely. I shall assume all these things are true, and I will weigh the matter itself. First, therefore, I say that this argument proves more than it ought to, and thus proves nothing at all. For if it were a matter of indifference to God which religion men held, the same would have to be said regarding the way men live—namely, concerning vices and virtues. For just as ideas about religion are formed...

---

# ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

...so too do men commonly tend to act. And although men do not always follow their own principles, their actions must nevertheless be judged according to the certain rules they admit. Now, if it were entirely indifferent to God which religious opinions men held, no reason could be given why He should be more attentive to virtue than to vice. From this it would follow that it is also a matter of indifference to Him whether men follow vice or virtue—a position which not even those called <term>Indifferentists</term> <note>Those who believe all religions are equally valid or that religious differences do not matter.</note> usually defend. For in that way, every notion of religion would be utterly destroyed.

2) This opinion does not even agree with the system of the <term>Deists</term> <note>Thinkers who believe in a creator God based on reason but reject supernatural revelation.</note>. For they admit and defend certain specific points of Natural Theology; by that very fact, they assert that one must insist upon certain principles of Religion. Hence, they not only disapprove of the views of the <term>Spinozists</term> <note>Followers of Baruch Spinoza, often accused of atheism or pantheism.</note> and others who depart further from the precepts of natural religion, but they even attack the Christian Religion on the grounds that they think those certain principles of Natural Religion cannot be reconciled with the primary Decrees of Revelation. Yet they would not admit this if they believed it was all the same to God what religious opinions men were imbued with.

3) This opinion foully confuses the *permission* of God with His most holy *will*. It could not even be said of a secular Prince—provided he is not entirely lacking in common sense and possesses some religious feeling—that it is indifferent to him what his subjects think about the obligation of divine and human laws; much less can this be asserted with any appearance of truth regarding the most holy God. It is true that various opinions about religion exist among men; it is also true that God permits men to be devoted to perverse opinions about religion. But to claim that He *approves* of foolish opinions that are contrary to His most holy virtues and will can only be asserted by a man devoid of all religion. Yet the King of Siam did not wish to be regarded as such. God could, by some secret means, draw all men to the same and correct sense of God. But since He wills that men embrace religion voluntarily, through the correct use of reason, He does not do this. Therefore, He will judge everyone in His own time according to His equity, which looks not only to the obligation of following Religion, but also to the strength of one's intellect and the innumerable circumstances in which men were placed in this life.

4) From what we have said so far, it can simultaneously be judged what should be thought of that "delight" of God which He is said to perceive from the variety of creatures...

# MEDITATION IX.

...what is said, it must be understood, namely with respect to virtue as well as to vice, to error as well as to truth. It is true that God wished His infinite wisdom and power to be manifested, among other things, by the fact that He willed to produce so many creatures adorned with such diverse properties. Indeed, this sentiment can even be applied to moral matters, insofar as the faculties, perfections, and the capacity of human minds are most diverse and admit infinite degrees, so much so that men, before any education or instruction, seem to be equipped with diverse gifts of mind by a certain *good Fate* <note>original: "Moira" (Greek: Μοῖρα), referring to one’s allotted portion or destiny.</note>. But these 
<margin>virtues</margin> should not be dragged toward ~~truths~~ and vices, or toward errors and truths. None but a madman, devoid of all Religion, can assert that God is equally delighted by the most holy things and the most foolish things—delighted, for example, by the slaughter of the innocent just as much as by beneficence. By the very nature of things, it is impossible for men to take equal pleasure from the most diverse things, such as painful things and pleasant things alike. Similarly, the most holy will of God could not approve of things that are both consistent and inconsistent with His nature and perfections, unless you wish to change God into a stump <note>original: "truncum," meaning a block of wood or a senseless object.</note>, plainly destitute of all ideas of things.

5) This opinion destroys the immutable notions of truth and error, as well as those of vice and virtue. It is true that not all the consequences which can be drawn from the general duties of the laws of nature are equally known to everyone; it is also true that through the gross ignorance of many nations and the foulest superstition, it has—alas!—come to pass that the most shameful vices were held by some either as minor sins or as plainly lawful things; however, the situation never reached the point where all notions of virtues and vices were plainly obliterated among the nations, as is more than sufficiently established from various testimonies that learned men have collected. Among the principal causes of this fact, we include the point that the notions of virtues and vices do not depend on human whim, but are immutable. Just as the idea of a triangle cannot be changed into the idea of a square, so neither can the idea of drunkenness be exchanged with the idea of sobriety. But if those notions of truth and virtue take the place of a standard <note>original: "normae," a rule or measuring tool.</note> according to which a rational creature ought to act, it will not be a matter of indifference to God whether men follow vice or virtue—which would nevertheless have to be said if the opinion proposed in their midst were valid.

<margin>A fourth objection of the Unbelievers is brought forward.</margin>
VIII. The Unbelievers <note>original: "Increduli," referring to skeptics or those who reject revealed religion.</note> go on and assert that it is scarcely credible that God, if He had willed to grant a Revelation to men, would have given one such as the Revelation which Christians accept. For besides the fact

Therefore, the Deists <note>Thinkers who believe in a creator God based on reason but reject supernatural revelation.</note> would do better to bring forward the most serious reasons by which they are moved to be unable to give their name to Revelation, rather than explaining in many words what kind of Revelation they demand. ### MEDITATION IX.

...everyone would be required to resolve [these doubts] before they could prove to others that this compendium had descended from heaven. This compendium, moreover, would have to be committed to paper so that it could reach all people. But no matter what language you imagine this compendium was written in, it would in turn have to be translated into various dialects; and those who wanted to be certain that the mind of the original writer agreed sincerely with the versions would need skill in many languages. And so, those same objections that the unbelievers are accustomed to throw at us would occur all over again.

(III.) Humans being what they are—given the perversity and mutability of human minds—they would not have been satisfied with that compendium, but over the course of time would have undoubtedly added innumerable glosses <note>original: "glossas," referring to brief marginal or interlinear explanations of a text.</note> and interpretations. Daily experience teaches us that this happens most frequently in every kind of discipline. This or that person makes a brief compendium of philosophy or Theology; soon another comes along who promises he will bring a "remarkable light" to it, and so from a compendium a thick volume is born; after some time has passed, another approaches who promises he will contract that larger work for the benefit of readers. This was even more certain to happen because this compendium would deal with matters concerning religion, a business in which men are most accustomed to indulge their own creative whims. Thus we know that the Lord's Prayer, the so-called Apostles' Creed, and catechetical instructions have been explained in laborious volumes. The Muslims boast that their religion is very brief and summarized; but who does not know how many different interpretations the Quran <note>original: "Alcoranus"</note> is subject to?

(IV.) This compendium would either have been composed with a scientific method, or it would have had to consist of various maxims and precepts joined by no natural connection to one another. If the *former* were the case, there would be no lack of people who would reject it, claiming that such a System was simply not suited to the minds of all men; to that end, they would appeal to the sluggishness and weakness of human intellects. If, however, it consisted of nothing but short precepts and maxims, it would not have pleased "proud" intellects, who would deem it unworthy of the Supreme Reason to hand down the decrees of religion to the human race without any necessary logical links. Hence there is no doubt that they would have been most anxious to reduce it to the form of an art, employing various principles taken from here and there; whence that system would not only have been wonderfully expanded over time, but also subjected to different and innumerable interpretations. From the present state of things, what would have happened in the future can be judged not ineptly.

### ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

Natural Theology <term>Theologia Naturalis: The study of God based on reason and the observation of nature rather than on supernatural revelation.</term> and Natural Law <term>Juris Naturae: A system of right or justice held to be common to all humans and derived from nature rather than from the rules of society.</term> can be handed down in a compendium. But who does not know by how many prolix commentaries both disciplines have been illustrated? How many different opinions there have been about the arguments themselves and the modes of proving them? How many innumerable particular questions—which most people contend belong to the core of the matter—have been brought forth and thrashed out?

(V.) It was not certain that God, even if He had granted such a compendium from heaven, would have achieved His goal. For who is unaware of the torpor of mortals in the business of religion and the power of depraved affections? Who is ignorant that among those to whom Revelation has been given, many—indeed, the majority—are found who daily trample the primary precepts of Natural Law and humanity under their feet?

(VI.) To these moral precepts and maxims contained in that compendium of Theology, either promises made to the keepers of the laws and punishments for transgressors would have been added, or not. If none had been made, the chief incentives for living rightly would have been removed. It is well known what power the certain hope of obtaining a reward has on the minds of men. If they *had* been added, men would have remained in the greatest doubt as to how far the limits of divine mercy would extend in such great corruption of the human race and such a lack of internal aids.

(VII.) Finally, it is known by experience and confirmed by innumerable testimonies of the Ancients that humans could have known the general dogmas of Natural Theology and Natural Law without any Revelation, if only they had applied the force of their intellect. All Theologians and Philosophers affirm that the law of nature can be known by the Gentiles <note>The "Gentiles" here refers to the non-Jewish nations of antiquity who did not have the Mosaic law.</note>, with Paul leading the way in *Romans 1 and 2*; but who at the same time is ignorant of how miserably this law was obscured by the fraud of Priests, the fictions of Poets, and the interminable brawls, contentions, and sophistries of Philosophers? Who does not know that they fell into the most foul idolatry and superstition—to say nothing of detestable crimes of every kind? From this it appears clearly enough that such a compendium would not have sufficed to engender true and salutary knowledge in minds or to repress the impulses of depraved affections; rather, there was a need for other and more salutary aids, which we Christians believe were uncovered in Revelation.

(VIII.) Since a small compendium of natural theology of this sort could have been found by the aid of reason alone, there is no doubt that in different parts of the earth—as we know has indeed happened—there would have arisen

### MEDITATION IX.

...men of outstanding genius who might have composed such summaries; but since these would have been different according to the diversity of minds and opinions, not only would there have been doubt as to which of those various versions should be accepted, but violent controversies would have arisen concerning the divine origin of that summary which we imagined was given from heaven. For since such things could be known by the power of reason, the other Founders of Systems would have cried out that the man who claimed to have received that collection of truths by some divine and extraordinary help was an impostor, and thus the minds of men would have wavered miserably among so many summaries. Furthermore, not enough protection would have been placed in the authors of those Systems: the authority of one would have been no greater than another; no one could have marketed himself as an infallible Legislator. The rights of all would have been equal, however much they disagreed in opinion. The most excellent philosopher <term>Locke</term> <note>original: "Lokius," referring to John Locke (1632–1704), an English philosopher central to the Enlightenment.</note> brilliantly illustrated this argument in chapter 14 of the booklet titled: *The Reasonableness of Christianity* <note>original: "Que la Religion chrétienne est très raisonnable," the French title of Locke's 1695 work.</note>. Let us bring forward some points relevant to this:

"Suppose," he says, "that one could gather all these precepts (he is speaking of the precepts of <term>Natural Law</term> <note>A system of ethics discoverable by human reason rather than through divine revelation alone.</note> and natural religion) from different places: That one takes some from Solon and Bias <note>Solon and Bias of Priene were two of the "Seven Sages" of ancient Greece.</note> in Greece, others from Cicero in Italy; and to make the work complete, let us go as far as China to consult Confucius, and borrow from Scythia the insights of the wise Anacharsis. How can all these gathered pieces make a complete System of Morality, which would be received by all the men of the world as the authentic rule of their lives and their morals? I will not speak here of the impossibility there would have been in collecting all these precepts from the writings of people so distant from one another by the time and places where they lived, as well as by their language. I suppose that there was then a Stobaeus <note>Joannes Stobaeus, a 5th-century compiler of Greek literary and philosophical extracts.</note> who was dedicated to gathering the moral sentences of all the wise men of the world. How could such a collection have become a fixed rule, and a true copy of the Law under which we live? Would it be from Aristippus or Confucius that it would have drawn its authority? Did Zeno <note>Zeno of Citium, the founder of Stoicism.</note> have the right to impose laws on the human race? If he did not, all that he or any other Philosopher could say was only counted as the opinion of a single man. So that other men could receive it or reject it as they found appropriate: or according as this opinion agreed with their interests, their passions, their principles and their particular inclinations. They were under no obligation in this regard. The opinion of whatever Philosopher it might be had no authority by itself. For if one

wants to look at any one in particular under this idea, one must grant the same right to everything said by the Philosopher who is its Author. All his maxims must pass for certain and indubitable laws: or else none of them must be received under that quality. For example, if you take as precepts of the Natural Law some of the moral sentences of Epicurus—of which there are several that Seneca <note>A Stoic philosopher who often quoted Epicurus despite their opposing schools of thought.</note> cites with marks of esteem and approval—you must receive all the rest of his doctrine on the same footing: or else all his authority disappears. From which it follows, that regarding everything that comes from Epicurus, or from some ancient Philosopher, one should receive nothing as part of the Law of nature, and under the idea of an indispensable Duty, except what they prove to be such effectively." And after a few words: "These detached sentences, which Philosophers and wise persons issued from time to time, however excellent they were in themselves, and for whatever good purpose they were proposed, could never make a Morality of the truth of which the World could be convinced so far as to submit to its maxims with an entire confidence. It is necessary that everything that must serve as a model upon which all men must regulate their morals be authorized by reason or by <term>Revelation</term> <note>Truths communicated directly by God to humanity.</note>. From this, if a person writes on Morality, or compiles what others have written on it, he does not by that very fact acquire the power of a Legislator over the human race: as if the rules he wished to prescribe to men became inviolable because he had inserted them into his Books, under the authority of such or such a Philosopher. Whoever pretends to set himself on that footing, and to pass off the rules he gives as authentic laws that one cannot dispense with observing, must prove one of these two things: either that he bases all his doctrine on principles of reason evident in themselves, so that he makes all the parts that compose it flow from a clear and sensible demonstration: or else, he must show that he is sent from heaven, and that he is authorized by God, to announce His will and His commandments to men. Now, no one that I know of has made or undertaken to make, before the coming of Jesus Christ, a Morality according to the first of these methods. There is, I confess, a Natural Law. But where is the one who had given it to us, or who had taken it upon himself to show it to us in its entirety as Law, without adding anything to it, and without taking away any of the duties it contained, and which were binding by themselves? Who has ever made known all the parts of this Law joined into a single Body? Who is it that has shown men the obligation they were under to observe them exactly? And where has one ever seen a...

IX. Regarding the remaining part of these objections, we can be briefer, because we remember that we have already dealt with them elsewhere. We therefore briefly note the following. *First*, we assert that Revelation—in which useful histories, most healthy examples of virtue, parables, very serious maxims, precepts and doctrines most worthy of attention are delivered in a simple style, along with representations of divine judgments and benefits, and every kind of incentive to love virtue and flee vice—is more attuned to the temperaments of all men than a compendium of the truths of <term>Natural Theology</term> <note>Theology based on reason and ordinary experience rather than divine revelation.</note> and <term>Natural Law</term> woven together by a most technical method. For the dispositions of men are clearly varied; one is moved more by a singular example than by the most evident reasons; the severity of divine judgments deters this person from vice; the representation of divine benefits gently draws another to virtue, and so on. But if, moreover, it is certain that the witnesses of this revelation are men worthy of trust, simple, and most loving of the truth, and that this revelation is confirmed by various miracles, we see no reason why men should complain about such a Revelation, especially if they consider that God wished to disclose the origin of all things in this revelation, and at the same time to explain and represent the different stages of His grace and revelation leading up to the times of Christ and the Apostles.

II. Those who are inflamed with a love for the sciences do not usually complain about the multitude of books and the size of volumes; even profane men find delight in the constant reading of various books that often corrupt the mind and morals. If men were burning with as great a desire for knowing divine things as they are for knowing things that are not profitable—or indeed harmful—there would be no place for that complaint.

III. No <term>Theologian</term> has ever asserted that everything delivered in the books containing revelation is of the same weight and equally necessary to be known for salvation. They always urge only this: that the things which are clearly necessary to be known are proposed so plainly and repeated so often that no lover of truth, having applied serious attention, can claim that he cannot grasp the doctrine of Jesus Christ.

IV. Christian Teachers are accustomed to include the doctrine of salvation in shorter summaries for the sake of the simpler people, which sufficiently provides for the weakness of those who cannot examine everything individually. And since the truths of the Christian faith in such booklets are usually fortified by clear and eloquent passages of Holy Scripture, readers have no reason to doubt the truth of the doctrine handed down, since they themselves can look up the passages taken from Holy Scripture to confirm any given dogma. If here or there they are perhaps troubled by doubts, they can consult those whom they believe to be furnished with an ample knowledge of divine things. Since those desirous of knowing the truth must do this in other disciplines, I do not see why such questioning should be bothersome to those who have the knowledge of heavenly doctrine at heart.

V. We assert that all versions of Holy Scripture are so prepared that from them all those things can be known which pertain to the core of the matter. Without doubt, many of the <term>Deists</term> <note>Followers of a rationalistic religion that believes in a creator who does not intervene in the universe.</note> read the excellent writings of the Greeks and Romans in their own native languages, and they do not doubt for that reason that they grasp the sense of the authors in most places, and learn from them those things which are most necessary to be known.

VI. Not only the common people, but even the most learned Interpreters and those most skilled in languages, are forced to confess their ignorance in certain places. No one will wonder at this who considers that many words, rituals, and circumstances of persons and places are not sufficiently known to us. Men most learned in Greek often admit that they do not understand <term>Plato</term>, <term>Aristotle</term>, and others everywhere; yet no one concludes from this that everything is entirely obscure, or that for that reason the most excellent Authors should not be studied... <note>The text cuts off here, continuing the thought on the next page.</note>

A fifth objection of the Deists is presented.

X. The Unbelievers <note>The author uses "Increduli" to refer to skeptics or those who reject the necessity of Christian revelation.</note> continue and say they wonder greatly why Christians work so hard to bring people into the fold of the Christian religion, since in the end, Christians and [the Deists] themselves agree on the core of the matter: namely, that Christians assert all articles of the Christian religion tend toward piety—that is, the love of God, our neighbor, and ourselves. Now, indeed, the Deists—at least those who accept all the theoretical and practical principles of **Natural Theology** <note>Natural Theology is the study of God based on reason and observation of the natural world, rather than on revealed scripture.</note>—urge the necessity of all these same duties with equal weight.

We respond: (I) It is true that all Christians confess that the articles of the Christian religion—indeed, all its mysteries, as far as they are known to us—contain within themselves the most serious **Incentives to piety**, from which we also prove the excellence of this religion. Indeed, they assert that the more the articles of religion inflame human minds toward the pursuit of piety, the greater their weight; but the fewer stimuli they have for loving piety, the less significant they are. From this also depends the weight of controversial opinions.

(II) The question is whether, once a Revelation is established that is added onto the principles of reason, men would not find greater aids for pursuing the study of true piety. I believe the Deists would hardly deny this. For since a wise person does nothing without the weightiest reasons, and God, in granting revelation to mortals, could seek nothing else than that they be equipped with greater aids for worshipping God and for more correctly knowing and performing all the duties of religion; it follows that, once a Revelation is established, there are simultaneously present weightier arguments and incentives for the love of true piety.

And it is the part of a wise man to choose that which is better, or best.

(III) For if the Unbelievers concede that Revelation (if God were to grant any to the human race) would be most illustrious and worthy of attention for this reason: that it would provide far more excellent **Incentives** for living piously, it must also be conceded that the same would encompass a greater and more exact knowledge of divine things. For incentives to perform moral actions cannot be drawn from a completely unknown thing. Therefore, whether you call those truths that cannot be unearthed through the principles of reason "mysteries," or by another name, it is the same. It is enough that those truths detected through Revelation—beyond those reasons recommending the study of piety that are gathered through the right use and application of reason—must include other necessary and far weightier truths, which provide broader and more excellent principles and aids for virtue.

(IV) Revelation, therefore, encompassing truths impassable to reason but having incredible power for promoting true divine worship, will be far more suitable than natural knowledge alone concerning God and the duties to be performed toward Him. And this will be clear if we properly weigh those incentives of piety—of the <term>ὧδε παθῶν</term> <note>original: "hode pathon," likely referring to the "internal passions" or "dispositions" of the soul.</note>—which are sought from the contemplation of Natural Theology, and see how little power they have had over the minds of men at all times. To do this properly, one should not so much consult the writers of modern Systems of Natural Theology, but rather turn one's mind to the teachings of Barbaric and more refined Nations who lacked revelation. Once these are properly examined, it will be clear how little power these incentives have had over the minds of men at all times. # MEDITATION IX.

...currently traveling on the main roads, applauds himself for the strength of his legs, which have carried him so far in such a small space of time. He attributes the entire cause of his speed to the strength of his temperament, hardly considering how much he is indebted to the labor of those who cleared the forests, drained the marshes, built the bridges, and made the roads passable—without which he would have become extremely tired and advanced very little. There are many things whose belief has been instilled in us from the cradle; so that since these ideas have become familiar and, so to speak, natural to us under the Gospel, we regard them as incontestable truths which are easy to see and to prove with the ultimate evidence, without considering that we might have doubted them or been ignorant of them for a long time if Revelation had said nothing about them. Thus, many are indebted to Revelation without realizing it.

In a similar manner, <term>the late</term> <note>original Greek: ó Μακαρίτης (ho makarités), a respectful term for a deceased person of high standing</note> the illustrious Werenfels <note>Samuel Werenfels (1657–1740) was a Swiss theologian known for his moderate views and critique of religious dogmatism.</note> declares in his *Dissertation on the Excellence of Revealed Religion*, page 275: "Our Rationalists," he says, "should see to it that they do not attribute too much to their own reason. They say that by the guidance of reason alone, that entire religion which is handed down in the Sacred Scriptures, or at least its most important part, can be found. Nothing is easier to say for those who already know that religion. This could only be claimed if they had heard nothing from anyone about this religion throughout their entire lives. But now they seem to me like those who, after they have learned everything they know from teachers, nevertheless wish to appear <term>self-taught</term> <note>original Greek: αὐτοδίδακτοι (autodidaktoi)</note>; or when they hear of excellent inventions, they think they would have invented all these things themselves if they had not already been discovered. If we wish to know what human reason can do in discovering religion, we ought not to consult our own reason—we whom the Word of God has led onto the path, whom it directs on that same path, and whom it warns, confirms, corrects, and orders to retrace our steps when we stumble or err in our reasoning—but rather the reason of those to whom this Word is unknown."

And indeed, if we attend to the knowledge of that **Natural Law**, it will be clear that it does not supply such strong incentives for loving God as Revelation provides, because of the many secondary factors by which natural knowledge is obscured. A person can know that he was created by a Most High Power and adorned with exceptional faculties: that God governs this universe and provides immense benefits to the human race. It is even highly probable that the mind will survive after this life, and that lovers of virtue will be happier than those who have lived in every kind of wickedness. It is therefore right that we give thanks to God for these things and live in accordance with reason. Let us suppose that these things are admitted by everyone who is destitute of the light of revelation; yet you will find that there are many things which prevent

And first of all, it is well enough known to scholars that among those who formerly handed down the precepts of the **Natural Law**, the followers of the **Stoic Philosophy** must be counted. Many excellent things on this subject are read in the writings of Arrian and Marcus Aurelius. <note>Arrian was a historian and philosopher who recorded the teachings of Epictetus; Antoninus refers to the Emperor Marcus Aurelius.</note> But it is well known that in their Ethics, they placed as a foundation the idea that some things are in our power, and others are not. Now, truly (*) if you once assume that God contributes absolutely nothing to the exercise of virtue, but that all good actions are owed only to human zeal, practice, and prudence, then much of the weight is lost from the arguments urging a person to love God above all things. Very few people are accustomed to being led to a true zeal for virtue by the mere contemplation of the Divine Nature. He who ascribes that which is most excellent in man—namely, piety—solely to his own strength, will think magnificently of himself throughout his life; nor, mindful of his own weakness, will he seek protection from Him who is the author of all true happiness. > (*) Cotta the Academic, in Cicero's third book *On the Nature of the Gods*, speaks on this subject as if this were the commonly accepted opinion of all the Gentiles <note>The non-Christian Greco-Roman world.</note>. Divine goodness is the primary incentive for loving God. But if God were to grant mortals only that which is shared in common, as it were, with the beasts, the stimulants of divine love would be greatly diminished or altogether removed. To this is added the fact that the incentives to love God cannot help but be very weak where there is a doubtful persuasion regarding the reward of virtue in this life and the next—not to mention how great the force of wicked affections is against a sincere zeal for virtue, given such great weakness in our nature. These things certainly hinder the pursuit of the love of God.

But if, on the other hand, one rightly weighs all those incentives which Sacred Revelation provides—especially those derived from the love of our <term>Savior</term> <note>original Latin: "Soteris," from the Greek "Soter" meaning Savior or Deliverer.</note> toward sinners—it will be most manifest that these are far stronger and more excellent than those which usually flow from the character of natural law. Since, however, it is not my intention here to demonstrate the excellence of the Christian Religion through a dedicated work, I do not bring forward those incentives individually and part by part.

**Secondly:** It is clear from constant experience that natural law has always had very little power to draw Gentile men away from vices. Added to this is the fact that throughout the entire world where the Christian and Jewish religions had not taken root, the opinion concerning two eternal principles—opposed to each other—was spread and accepted, which the famous <term>Wolff</term> <note>Christian Wolff (1679–1754), a central Enlightenment philosopher who wrote on "Manichaeism before the Manichaeans."</note> proved at length in his booklet on Manichaeism. Since men try as much as possible to repel those things which can bring pain and adversity, they were more concerned with reconciling themselves to the *evil* principle than to the *good* one. To this evil principle they attributed the origin of moral and physical evil. When they looked around wherever they went and discovered an immense jumble of evils, it could not have happened otherwise than that the sincere love of the Most High Deity was greatly diminished, if not extinguished, in the minds of most.

I say nothing now of the opinions concerning the deeds of the Gods and Goddesses; of the perceived value of Sacrifices and external worship, etc., which could not help but call men away from a pure love of God. I say nothing of **Aristotle**, who, in the judgment of most learned men, maintained that divine providence reached only as far as the moon. <note>This refers to the Aristotelian idea that the "sublunary" world—our world below the moon—is subject to change and chance, while only the "celestial" spheres are governed by divine order.</note> I shall say nothing of the Cynics, Sceptics, and the remaining opinions and manners of the Philosophers. This much is certain: they were all not so much occupied in promoting the pure worship of God and instilling it into the minds of mortals, as they were in showing off their talent and defending opinions once seized upon with a certain display of erudition.

It is not to be doubted that the Gentiles had some thin knowledge concerning the different state of men after death; but it was very obscure and so hedged about with many myths that it could have led men toward unbelief rather than toward a certain confidence in a future reward. Certainly, the most celebrated men of antiquity, the Greeks and Romans—who had spent their entire lives cultivating philosophical disciplines and were not lacking in the genius to perceive the truth—were nevertheless unable to abandon superstition and vain opinions. ### AFTER-WORD

## THEOLOGICAL THESES.

I. If the right to examine religion must be taken away for fear of heresies, it should be taken away from no one more than from the Teachers; for almost all heresies have taken their origin from the Teachers.

II. Between the Atheists and us, it is agreed that something has been eternal. The questions are: 1) what was that eternal thing? and 2) how did all the things that came after, and exist today, arise from that eternal thing? Whoever pays attention will easily perceive by how great a distance their hypothesis is surpassed by ours in both respects.

III. Nothing is more contrary to reason than the assertion of the <term>Romanists</term> <note>original: "Pontificiorum" — referring to the Roman Catholic Church.</note> who affirm that God indeed gave revelation to men for the purpose of learning the way to reach heavenly glory, but who simultaneously contend that this revelation is not to be read and examined indiscriminately by all to whom it has become known.

IV. Theologians who fight tooth and nail against establishing ecclesiastical peace among Protestants on fair conditions sin gravely.

V. The system of <term>Socinian</term> <note>Followers of a 16th-century movement that denied the Trinity and the full divinity of Christ, emphasizing rationalism.</note> theology contributes most by its very nature to undermining the divine origin of the Christian religion.

# MEDITATION
## ON THE
# CAUSES OF THE INCREASINGLY PREVAILING
# UNBELIEF,
## AND
# THE REMEDY TO BE BROUGHT TO THIS EVIL.

### PART X.

### Section I.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'I' within an ornate square frame featuring floral and scroll motifs.</image-desc>

<margin>
The sixth objection of the Unbelievers is presented.
</margin>

In the previous dissertation, we began to bring forward certain general prejudices by which those who hold minds alienated from religion are imbued; these prejudices stand in the way of weighing, with an attentive mind, the arguments which are usually brought forward to prove the divine origin of the Christian Religion. It remains for us to bring the rest, and indeed the most important ones, into the open and submit them to a calm examination. Namely, the <term>Unbelievers</term> <note>original: "Increduli" — refers to the skeptics and deists of the Enlightenment era who challenged traditional church doctrines.</note> say that *Christians contend that Mysteries must be counted among the primary objects of Religion. From these, all particular articles of the Christian Religion depend: therefore, they must be held with the firmest faith; without these, the entire Christian Religion rests on a ruinous foundation. Yet they simultaneously and roundly confess that these mysteries can be understood by no one. These assertions are, however, partly inconsistent* <note>original: "ἀσύστατα" (asystata) — a Greek term meaning logically incompatible or falling apart upon inspection.</note> *and partly obligate men to that which is impossible to perform.*

We respond (I.) It is true, Christians admit mysteries, and they judge it necessary to do so if they wish to defend the fact that <term>Revelation</term> has been granted to them by God. For by the name of Revelation, they understand a complex of such propositions which, by the help of reason alone, no mortal

<column-break/>

<page-num>403</page-num>
<header>ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.</header>

could have discovered. Those, therefore, who admit Revelation must by that very fact concede that mysteries are given in Christian teaching. For although the Christian Religion also hands down such dogmas as can be drawn from the storehouse of reason without revelation, God nevertheless wished, in His infinite goodness and wisdom, to communicate to mortals those things especially which He judged necessary to know for attaining salvation. We have proved in the preceding sections that God, whose knowledge is infinite, can provide to humans a greater light of knowledge than that which is elicited merely by reasoning; and Christians are persuaded by certain arguments that such light was brought through Revelation.

(II.) It is also true that those mysteries of the Christian Religion are considered by the students of Christian teaching as the first and principal foundations upon which the other dogmas and precepts are built. Nor do I detect anything here that shrinks from reason. The Philosophers of all sects have their <term>fundamental principles</term> <note>original: "κυρίας δόξας" (kyrias doxas) — a term borrowed from Greek philosophy, particularly Epicureanism, meaning the "sovereign maxims" or core tenets of a system.</note> upon which particular opinions depend. Since God, intending to provide for the human race, wished to give new principles of knowledge to mortals, it is fitting that these be counted among the primary truths. From this it is also clear that the <term>Socinians</term> <note>original: "Sociniani" — a rationalist Christian movement that rejected the Trinity and other mysteries, arguing that anything contrary to reason could not be part of divine revelation.</note>, who admit Revelation and confess it to be of divine origin, act wrongly while they repudiate all mysteries contained in the Holy Scriptures. For they act just as if someone wished to be held as a disciple of <term>Plato</term> or <term>Zeno</term> <note>Zeno of Citium, the founder of Stoicism.</note> and yet at the same time proscribed the very principles upon which the Decrees of these men are supported.

(III) But, the Unbelievers say, these mysteries cannot be known, and therefore cannot be believed. To remove this difficulty as much as is necessary, one must attend to what is understood by the word <term>mystery</term> <note>original: "mysterium" / "μυστήριον" — in a theological sense, a truth that remains partly hidden even after it is revealed.</note>, and in what way we either understand them or do not know them. We have already said above that by the name of mysteries, we understand a complex of truths which, by the aid of reason alone, no mortal could have found. In the Holy Scriptures, the word "mystery" is not taken in only one sense. Thus the calling of the Gentiles and the rejection of the Jews is called a Mystery by Paul in *Romans* 16:25, because men had a clearly weak knowledge of this matter before the coming of Jesus Christ: but after Christ’s ascension into heaven, the matter itself became clear by the event, and thus far this mystery can be known. So the entire doctrine of the Gospel is everywhere referred to by the name of "mystery." *Matthew* 13:11, *1 Corinthians* 2:6-7, *1 Corinthians* 4:1. Especially <term>the incarnation of the Word</term> <note>original: "ἡ ἐνσάρκωσις τȣ λογȣ" (hē ensarkōsis tou logou) — the central Christian doctrine of God becoming flesh in Jesus.</note> is called a mystery in *1 Timothy* 3:16 and *Colossians* Chapter 2, verse 2. Paul testifies that in the mystery of God and of the Father and of Christ all [the treasures of] wisdom...

<meta>This page continues the defense of Christian "mysteries" against the charge of irrationality. It builds on the previous discussion by distinguishing between what is "unintelligible" (logically impossible) and what is "incomprehensible" (beyond full human understanding), focusing on the limits of human reason when faced with the nature of God.</meta>

<page-num>404</page-num>
<header>MEDITATION X.</header>

the treasures of wisdom are hidden: hence the dogma of the Holy Trinity itself is rightly called a "mystery" by theologians. Therefore, when Christians say they do not sufficiently know those mysteries, they mean that the human mind cannot look into the internal nature and connection of these truths. For "to know" and "to understand" is to have a clear perspective on the nature, properties, and causes of things. Such knowledge primarily takes place in the mathematical disciplines. From this it follows that we *believe* these mysteries rather than truly *know* them. We are said to believe in this matter when we subscribe to certain propositions contained in the Holy Scriptures, not because of the self-evidence of the thing or object itself, but because of the authority of the God who reveals them, designated in clear words. Thus, we believe that Jesus Christ is God, blessed forever, because divine names, divine attributes, divine works, and finally divine worship are attributed to Him in the Holy Scriptures; however, *how* the same Holy Savior is distinct from the Father and from the Holy Spirit, which the Holy Scriptures clearly testify, we do not know: yet we believe it, because God reveals those things. From what has been said, it is at the same time manifest that Christians do not admit <term>senseless things</term> <note>original: "ἀνόητα" (anoēta) — irrational or logically absurd concepts.</note> when they say that mysteries must be believed as primary heads of religion, and yet those same things cannot be sufficiently known. For there is nothing absurd in subscribing to a thing or a proposition expressed by God in clear words, even if the nature of the thing is very imperfectly known. Thus we believe that the whole universe <note>original: "τῷ ῥήματι τοῦ Θεοῦ" (tō rhēmati tou Theou) — by the word of God.</note>, as Paul speaks in *Hebrews 11:3*, <note>original: "Κατηρτίσθαι τοὺς αἰῶνας" (Katērtisthai tous aiōnas) — that the worlds/ages were framed.</note> was prepared, although no mortal will be able to demonstrate a clear connection between the will of an intellectual substance (even a most perfect one) and the production and preservation of the entire universe. (*)

(IV.) The <term>Unbelievers</term> <note>original: "Increduli"</note> always confuse that which is plainly unintelligible and contradictory with that which cannot be sufficiently comprehended. Learned men, who have sharpened their pens against the Unbelievers, noted this long ago. This proposition is unintelligible, indeed contradictory: *a square circle is given*. But this: *the Son of God was manifested in the flesh*, that is, was made a partaker of human nature, is not a proposition that is unintelligible in every part, although the manner of that sonship and of that conjunction with human nature is not sufficiently established. Nor does God himself demand that we know the *mode* of these things.

First, the very condition of human nature does not allow us to know all things that pertain to establishing religion clearly and distinctly—that is, adequately. If you except those things which are either most evident by their own nature or can be proven through certain demonstration, men (even regarding divine matters) must remain in various degrees of probability. Where there is the greatest convergence of these probabilities, the mind ought to rest, even if the truth cannot be elevated to a geometric demonstration. See *Ditton on the truth of the Resurrection of Jesus Christ.* <note>Humphrey Ditton (1675–1715) was an English mathematician and theologian whose work was popular in the 18th century for defending Christian miracles using quasi-mathematical logic.</note> Second: The character and nature of the dogmas of religion themselves do not permit us to know clearly and distinctly all things that must be believed. God is the primary object of Religion. But who is so self-assured that he would dare to contend that he can clearly and distinctly know the divine nature? And this must be said with respect to the dogmas of <term>Natural and Revealed Theology</term> <note>Natural Theology refers to truths about God found through reason and nature; Revealed Theology refers to truths known only through Scripture.</note>; however, since I have dealt with this argument at greater length elsewhere, I will not add more here. Indeed, as must be noted in the third place, this obligation to believe only what can be clearly and distinctly known would conflict with the most wise will of God. For God, on the one hand, is mindful of the weakness of human minds; He knows that there are infinite degrees of their capacity; He perceives that some men spend their lives in such places and are placed in such circumstances that they cannot devote time to the cultivation of reason for long. Therefore, the equity of God and His justice, which is directed by wisdom, does not allow Him to obligate all men to believe that for which they are by nature unfit. It is enough, therefore, if we know as much about God and divine things as is sufficient to worship Him. Let us take, for example, this proposition from Natural Theology: *God preserves the universe and all its parts at every single moment.* This is sufficient for me to adore, worship, and give thanks to God, even if I am ignorant of the method of that preservation. Let us take this—

> For, when we deal with divine things, and strive to 
> imagine in our minds Him who lacked a beginning 
> and shall lack an end, and who was prior to Chaos 
> and created the world, the power of human genius 
> is small, and its narrowness is great for such a task. 
> Since nature is lesser, even if it tries to exert itself 
> more sharply and penetrate the secrets of the 
> supreme God, who would doubt that the fragile 
> strength of the exhausted mind is disturbed in 
> the small breast by a false vision, and sinks 
> dull under powerless cares?

This point is to be held all the more firmly because the Apostles themselves, though instructed with an extraordinary knowledge of divine things, assert that our knowledge of divine matters in this life *is very imperfect*. The seventh objection of the Unbelievers is brought forward.
