II. There are those among the number of Unbelievers who argue in this way: *If*, they say, men are obligated to embrace revealed Religion wherever the Christian Religion has taken root, it is manifest that they are simultaneously bound to embrace often grave errors and to profess the most foul superstition. For it is well known that in many of the most flourishing regions of Europe, religion is shamefully stained with errors and foolish opinions and rites. Yet, as soon as anyone gives their name to the Christian Religion, they say all people are indiscriminately forced to embrace such things. Since this is the case, they argue the safest path must be taken: that is, the Christian Religion should be repudiated along with the superstition, and only the Oracles of Reason should be listened to. Regarding this objection, we note the following: First, we do not deny that here and there among the Romanists <note>original: "Romanenses" — a term used by Protestant authors to refer to members of the Roman Catholic Church.</note>, religion is so covered with many minute and erroneous opinions, and so many silly rites, that people from the dregs of the common folk can hardly distinguish the precious from the worthless. That this is the case is shown by public writings, testified by travelogues, and by <term>eyewitness account</term> <note>original: "αὐτοψία" (autopsia) — the act of seeing something for oneself.</note>. We have dealt with this argument at greater length elsewhere, and we have shown that the superstition spreading not only among the Heathens but also especially among Christians is a primary cause of Unbelief.

( II ) Furthermore, we grieve from our very heart for the condition of men in those places where foul superstition dominates. For since we know how great is the weakness of intellect in many men; how many are the obstacles to seeking the truth; and how great is the force and efficacy of superstition when drunk in as if with one's mother's milk, we easily see it cannot happen otherwise than that most people acquiesce in the opinions they have once seized upon and follow the religion of their fathers. We see that even among those to whom a purer religion has fallen, and for whom the examination of religion is not only permitted but commanded, there are very few who actually inquire into the truth of the publicly received dogmas and compare them with the Holy Scriptures. From this, it is easy to guess what the religion of those men will be who live in those regions where the examination of religion is utterly proscribed, and where chaste religion...

<page-num>407</page-num>
<header>ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.</header>

...religion is corrupted by foul superstition. For these men, we repeat, we grieve for their miserable lot.

(III.) Notwithstanding this, I see no reason why the Unbelievers should triumph on that account, and draw poisoned arrows against the Christian religion from their quivers. For they know perfectly well, if they are willing to speak sincerely and candidly, that the Christian religion is the most hostile enemy to superstition, and that it commends a worship which is entirely consistent with reason. Hence the Apostle Paul explains this clearly in *Romans, chapter 12, verses 1 and 2*—to say nothing now of other passages to be brought forward below—in which <term>reasonable service</term> <note>original: "λογικη λατρεια" (logikē latreia) — often translated as "rational worship" or "spiritual service."</note> is established. These things, I say, the Unbelievers know—at least those who have ever seriously weighed the Christian Religion; therefore I see no reason why, knowing these things, they should be so anxious about those who have been so unhappy as to live among people whose religion is imbued with depraved superstition, while they themselves neglect the examination of the Christian religion.

(IV.) As for those men who live in assemblies where chaste religion is defiled by silly rites and errors, they are not all to be placed in the same category. There are those who are endowed with such weak intellects that they are poorly suited for the examination of religion and for distinguishing error from truth. There are others who could, if they wished, undertake an examination of religion and distinguish superstition from pure religion. These, again, are clearly different with respect to their degrees of knowledge or their diligence and skill in seeking the truth. However, according as each is endowed with mental faculties, and more or less exerts the powers of his intellect, and more or less uses his opportunities to avoid superstition and follow the truth, so much more or less is the state of such a man either happy or miserable and deplorable. There is also greater or lesser hope that God, who has seen into all the corners of human minds, will deal with him more mildly or more strictly when the appointed day of punishment arrives. This at least is certain: there are many errors or rites which can be detected without great mental sharpness or acute judgment, if only some attention of the mind and a zeal for the truth are applied. Thus, one does not need great mental acumen to believe that God, who is Almighty and Omniscient, is alone to be worshipped; that bread which is eaten is not a man, whether living or dead; and that no power resides in stone, wood, or marble to heal men sick in mind or body—to say nothing of other opinions of the same sort. This is manifest from the fact that among the Heathens, many laughed openly <note>original: "albis dentibus riserint" — literally "laughed with white teeth," an idiom for mocking or laughing scornfully.</note> at the spreading superstition, distinguished it from religion, and followed only the guidance of reason.

There is no doubt that in *Italy*, *France*, and other places where there is a great abundance of learned men, and where books written by *Protestants* are frequently handled by *learned doctors*, many—each according to their own level of understanding—would clearly wish to see superstition removed.

(V.) While I would not wish to deny that the foulest superstition reigns everywhere in the Roman Church, and that many ridiculous errors are admitted on all sides, it must simultaneously be affirmed that the fundamental tenets of Religion—concerning God, His attributes, Providence, the divine origin of the Holy Scriptures, and Christ's birth, teaching, miracles, death, and resurrection, etc.—are not entirely shrouded in silence. They have their Catechisms, in which these general principles are presented, albeit not without a mixture of such opinions that are far removed from pure religion. Those who have traveled here and there through places where the Roman religion dominates have been able to show, by citing many examples, that one frequently encounters people who, despite superstition and the fear of the Inquisition, judge religion well enough and rightly see through the errors of the common people.

(VI.) This argument of the Unbelievers proves more than was intended, and therefore it proves nothing at all <note>original: "plus probat, quam probandum erat, atque adeo nihil probat." A logical principle stating that if an argument's premises lead to an absurdly broad conclusion, the argument itself is invalid.</note>. For if the Christian Religion were to be bid farewell entirely for the reason that errors and foul superstition are mixed in everywhere among Christians alongside the true articles of religion, then rational religion itself <note>Natural religion based on reason alone.</note> would also have to be rejected; for it has never been spread through the world on its own without errors and superstition. What the state of affairs was among the Romans and Greeks regarding Religion—to say nothing of other peoples—is well enough known. Therefore, if you listen to our Unbelievers, the most excellent men of Antiquity would have done rightly if they had utterly eradicated all religion from their own minds and the minds of others along with superstition. Yet this does not agree with the opinions of those who labor so hard to defend natural religion. 

Meanwhile, the Unbelievers have something to consider. Many of them live in places where all superstition is exposed to laughter and contempt, while on the contrary, Religion and the cultivation of reason flourish. Why then do they reject the Christian religion entirely, making no distinction between the Religion brought forth by Christ and the Apostles and these rash opinions and superstitions? And while they ought to look to their own interests, why are they so worried about those who refuse to discern the true from the false? If, however, they live in places where, constrained by fear of the Inquisition, they are held to celebrate silly and superstitious rites with others against the dictates of their conscience, why

<margin>The eighth objection is presented.</margin> VIII. The eighth objection of the Unbelievers follows, derived from miracles. Namely, the Unbelievers say: 
> Christians take their primary argument for proving the divine Origin of the Christian Religion from miracles. Yet they are not consistent with themselves in this matter, seeing as some ascribe the power of performing miracles to God alone, while others grant the same power to good and evil spirits <note>original: "geniis"</note> alike. By this reasoning, the argument derived from miracles is rendered useless, or at least greatly weakened.

To these things, we reply as follows. And (I.) indeed we confess that Theologians do not agree among themselves regarding the origin of miracles. There are those who attribute this power to evil and good spirits alike, among whom in our age the most eminent were *Locke* <note>John Locke (1632–1704), likely referring to his posthumous "A Discourse of Miracles."</note> in his posthumous works, and *Jean Le Clerc* <note>A Genevan theologian (1657–1736) famous for his biblical commentaries.</note> in his *Pneumatics* and in his *Commentary on Exodus*. The Venerable *Mosheim* <note>Johann Lorenz von Mosheim (1693–1755), a major Lutheran church historian.</note> cites several others defending the same opinion in his observations on *Cudworth* <note>Ralph Cudworth (1617–1688), an English philosopher; Mosheim translated his work into Latin with extensive notes.</note>, page 866. Others, however, such as *Werenfels*, *Turrettini*, *Sercius*, *Noltenius*, and several others, assert that God alone can perform miracles in the true sense of the word; they argue that Demons can do certain unusual things in this universe, but these are such that they do not surpass the laws of nature.

(II.) We will also not deny that those who establish that certain substances—greater than human power and either friendly or hostile to the human race—can perform miracles in the true sense, do expose the argument derived from miracles to certain difficulties, since they seem to reduce everything to the doctrine itself which the miracles are meant to defend—to say nothing of other points which these praised men have brought forward, and which can be read in their proper places.

(III.) However, the opinion of those learned men is not to be interpreted as if they intended to make the doctrine of miracles suspect. Let this wicked suspicion be far removed! For we know that those most learned men worked specifically to prove the truth of the Christian Religion, and thus sufficiently showed that they were persuaded of the divine Origin of the Christian Religion. Hence they also believe that their own opinion on the origin of miracles in no way undermines the argument usually brought forward to prove the divine Origin of the Christian Religion—namely, that derived from miracles. For they lay down (a) as a foundation that God, who has the power of performing miracles, will only use them to prove and confirm a salutary doctrine; whereas the Devil will employ them to defend lies and frauds. For my part, I do not deny that these matters are so arranged that, even if the opinion of these learned men is not entirely free from all difficulties, I readily grant that it was undertaken and defended for a good purpose. If you depart from the authority of the Holy Scriptures, everything told regarding the power of evil spirits is uncertain. The example of the Magicians in Egypt is of such a kind that it can be attributed to fraud rather than to the power of the Devil, as the celebrated **Heumann** <note>Christoph August Heumann (1681–1764), a notable German theologian and scholar of the Enlightenment.</note> recently showed with great skill, following others, in his dissertation *On the Wonder-Workers of Egypt*. The Devil is said to perform <term>lying wonders</term> <note>original Greek: "τερατα ψευδες" (*terata pseudes*)</note>, that is, fraudulent arts; he is called the Prince of the Air; but one who can stir up the various celestial bodies and, in a certain marvelous way, either condense or expand the air, is not immediately a "Wonder-Worker" <note>original: "Thaumaturgus"</note>; he works in the Children of Darkness, but it is not necessary to say that this happens immediately through a miracle. More on this can be read in the works of the praised authors.

(V.) Unbelievers, if they are kindled with a love for the truth, are bound in this case to do what prudent men are accustomed to do in other affairs; namely, between two opinions that differ from each other in some part, they ought to choose that which is most like the truth—unless, along with *Spinoza* and his followers, they wish to count miracles among <term>the impossible things</term> <note>original Greek: "τα ἀδυνατα" (*ta adynata*)</note>. Either of the cited opinions regarding the origin of miracles tends not toward destroying the truth of miracles, but toward vindicating it. If, therefore, Unbelievers believe that God can perform miracles; if they do not doubt that Christ performed such things and that the witnesses of this matter are worthy of belief; if they at least hold Christ to be a great and Holy Prophet; if they cannot persuade themselves that a God who is Most Holy and most loving of the human race would abuse His power to protect lies, nor that the Devil would ever be concerned with confirming the truth; then it will be certain that the miracles performed by Christ are of divine origin. Thus the matter will be safe, whatever distinction they may establish between the two systems regarding the origin of miracles mentioned above. (*)

Yet from the general way of life of Christians, the opposite is clear. There are good and bad among Christians; indeed, the crowd of the wicked is greater than that of the upright. The same holds true among all nations and among the Deists themselves.*

deny, but rather vehemently grieve, that Christians are rare who compose their lives according to the rule of this most holy discipline. One would have to be blind, and forced to deny those things placed before one's eyes, to wish to call this into doubt. Men eminent in learning and piety have deplored this sad fate in entire volumes, and have brought forward to the best of their ability those means which might recall men from this insanity, if they were wise and sought true happiness. Read only what has been meditated on this subject (to say nothing of many other things) by those most excellent men, <term>who are now among the Saints</term> <note>original Greek: "οἱ νυν ἐν Ἁγιοις" (*hoi nyn en Hagiois*)</note>: *Jean-Frédéric Osterwald* in his book full of the best fruit, entitled *The Source of Corruption, etc.*, and *Samuel Werenfels* in his examination of the question: *Why the incentives of Holy Scripture do not have more efficacy among Christians.*

(II.) When we seek an argument from the efficacy of the Christian Religion to prove its heavenly origin, we do not mean that all men indiscriminately who give their name to the Christian Religion and profess it publicly will immediately experience its force and efficacy in their minds. Rather, we mean only this: such is the character and nature of this Religion, so many safeguards and incentives for stirring up the study of piety are within it, that all those who know how to value all things at their proper price, and are accustomed to judge matters of Religion without passions, cannot fail to recognize the excellence of that Religion—and indeed in such a way that, by that serious contemplation, they feel the stings of virtue stirred up in their minds. From this it follows that what is required in this business is a teachable mind, greedy for the truth, touched by a love of religion, and finally a mind prepared to lead one’s life according to the measure of knowledge this religion demands. Without this, the most excellent religion and precepts most worthy of attention have no power. Hence our Holy Savior himself warns everywhere that only those will perceive the power and efficacy of his doctrine who are seriously concerned about their salvation. Thus in *John* chapter III, verse 19, he says: <term>The Light has come into the world and men loved darkness rather than the light, for their works were evil.</term> <note>original Greek: "Το Φῶς εληλυθεν εις τον κοσμον και ἠγαπησαν οἱ ἀνθρωποι μαλλον το σκοτος ἢ το φῶς, ἦν γαρ πονηρὰ ἀυτων τα ἐργα."</note> And in chapter VII, verse 17: <term>If anyone wills to do His will, he will know concerning the teaching, whether it is from God, or I speak from myself.</term> <note>original Greek: "Ἐάν τις θέλῃ το θέλημα ἀυτᾶ ποιεῖν γνώσεται περι της διδαχῆς, ποτερον ἐκ τε Θεε ἐσιν, ἢ ἐγὼ ἀπ᾿ ἐμαυτᾶ lαλῶ."</note> For this reason, not only the most excellent Theologians but also the most distinguished Philosophers have affirmed that men captured and bound by wicked pursuits cannot admit the force of truth and the excellence of the most serious duties.

(III.) Therefore, the Christian religion remains pure and untouched despite degenerate Christianity; those firm incentives to piety remain.

...honor is established and remains due to this Religion. (IV.) We do not deny that among the Heathens and Deists there are men who, to a greater or lesser degree, regulate their actions according to the natural law, because that law can impel men to perform the duties of the law insofar as it is more or less known. But the question is always whether stronger and more excellent protections and incentives are not found in the Christian Religion than in the natural law alone. Either there is no Revelation at all, or if there is one—as we Christians contend—it must embrace greater principles for living piously than those learned by reason alone, because this ought to be the primary purpose of any Revelation. If this is the case, as Christians prove with arguments not to be despised, the Christian Religion retains its own glory.

(V.) Finally, when we speak of "degenerate Christianity," we argue—as we are accustomed to say in the Schools—**based on the more significant part** <note>original Latin: "a potiore." A logical term meaning to judge a group by its best or most characteristic members rather than its exceptions.</note>, nor do we believe that every single Christian has strayed from piety. In all times, especially in the first centuries after the death of Christ (though we do not believe the Christians of the earliest times were accustomed to the pursuit of virtue in every single thing), the excellence of Religion manifested its power in the minds of very many. Nor should we focus here on the errors which human nature does not easily avoid. Perhaps even many are counted among the wicked who are not actually so. Often you may find a common man from the dregs of the populace or a peasant who uniquely reveres God according to the measure of his knowledge, and worships Him more than many of the Learned are accustomed to do. Christians worthy of the name often lie hidden in secret, and their piety is not joined with any outward splendor that catches the eye. By saying this, however, we in no way wish to diminish the magnitude of the evil that creeps so widely.

Oh, how miserably the Learned sometimes torment themselves regarding certain questions which they are under no law to decide! How much more rightly they would act if, having implored divine aid, they strained every nerve so that they themselves might have a certain and unshaken hope of obtaining salvation, rather than anxiously deliberating what kind of fate others are to experience after the end of this life.

(III.) <meta>This page continues the author’s response to the "Increduli" (Unbelievers or Deists). <page-num>420</page-num>
<header>MEDITATION 10.</header>

...it is not surprising if they themselves begin to doubt the truth of the miracles related in the Old and New Testaments, especially since in every age rumors have been spread here and there concerning certain miracles which are nevertheless called into doubt by Christians themselves. Furthermore, they add that because of the great length of time since the miracles of Moses and Christ are said to have occurred, much of the strength of such persuasion is lost.

Regarding this objection, we advise the following. And (**I.**) indeed, it must be asked of those who raise such objections whether they believe the miracles attributed to Christ and the Apostles in the New Testament were truly performed or not. If they deny that they happened, it is either because they deny such things *can* happen, or because they consider the witnesses of these miracles to be impostors in whom no faith can be placed. Whether they affirm the former or the latter, the truth of Christ's miracles is finished, and it is useless to seek to confirm a doctrine built upon mere deceptions. But if they believe they were truly performed, arguments must be brought forward to prove why the faith in miracles performed by Christ and the Apostles should be weakened simply because the same things are not repeated today.

(**II.**) Even if we could not provide sufficient reasons why God performs no miracles today to prove or confirm religion, the authority of those already performed would not be removed for that reason. Many things were done in the past that are not accustomed to happening today. Many things happen in this universe whose causes are hidden from us. Our adversaries admit the existence of **Divine Providence** <note>The belief that God intervenes in the world and sustains his creation.</note> and assert that God is most equitable, just, and holy; yet, in the meantime, they cannot give sufficient reasons in every respect for why God permits so many evils, plagues, the oppression of orphans and the best men, and so many disastrous wars in which the guilty are punished along with the innocent, nor why He does not prevent them in some unusual way through miracles. Yet this does not prevent these very men from believing that God takes care of human affairs. The same must be said of miracles: God could, if He willed, perform such things today; perhaps also in respect to many people they would have their use. It is necessary, therefore, that God has His own most wise reasons why He does not do them.

(**III.**) If we look closely at for whose sake these miracles should be performed, it will be partially manifest that they are not as necessary today as these men think. They say, first, that these miracles ought to be performed for the sake of the **Gentiles** <note>Here referring to non-Christian peoples globally.</note>. But how nearly innumerable would the number of Christ’s legates have to be who would announce the Gospel of Christ in Asia, Africa, and America? Then, before it could be con-

What power, then, would miracles ultimately have on the minds of men so disposed? Can a Deist be confirmed by a miracle when he rejects the very doctrine for which the miracle is applied as proof? <page-num>422</page-num>
<header>MEDITATION X.</header>

In that case, one could say that God would be, in some sense, obliged by His goodness to assist the Unbelief in which one found oneself. Thus, those who had made good use of the revelation of the Old Testament, and who might have doubted the Mission of Jesus Christ and His Apostles—not out of stubbornness, but because the proofs were unknown to them, having not yet been able to learn them—were favored by heaven with many miracles in the time of our Lord. But let us suppose there are people in a completely opposite disposition: that they fulfill poorly the duties which the light of reason alone teaches us; that they have no love for the truth; that they are stubborn with a thousand ill-founded prejudices and blinded by their unregulated passions; that they have examined nothing, and that by a voluntary disorder of the mind and heart, they doubt everything. Can such people complain that God does not perform miracles in their favor? Would they dare say that the abuse they have made of all the graces they have received makes them worthy of new benefits? If the Unbelievers of today take the trouble to examine themselves against this portrait, they will easily find the answer we could give them.

**(IV.)** From Gospel History and the writings of the Apostles, it is manifest that even when stupendous miracles were placed before their eyes, and those most frequent, **Unbelief** was not always conquered. The Jews, notwithstanding the miracles of Christ—to which He Himself appealed as the most certain sign of His divine mission—rejected Christian doctrine; indeed, some of the Pharisees reached such a point of malice that they blasphemously asserted the miracles were performed by the work of evil spirits. If we inquire into the causes of this, it will be manifest that it did not happen because they persuaded themselves that miracles could not occur, or because they thought they could be attributed to natural causes; rather, preconceived opinions stood in the way, as did novel interpretations of Holy Scripture, traditions, the authority of their Teachers, intolerable pride, and other things that hindered them from rightly weighing the doctrine of Christ itself. Many recent Unbelievers not only reject the Mysteries and the precepts of the Gospel built upon them, but even say that miracles have no weight in moving a wise man. See the *Author of Essential Religion* <note>The author likely refers to a Deist tract popular in the 18th century</note> arguing thus throughout his work. What, therefore, would those new miracles achieve? They might perhaps strike the minds of some; but they would have little power over the minds of those who find the Christian doctrine itself displeasing.

**(V.)** The nature of the times in which Christ and the Apostles lived was one thing;

<meta>catchword: lived</meta>

<column-break/>

<page-num>423</page-num>

ours is another. For whether we look to the state of the Jews or the condition of the Gentiles <note>non-Jewish nations, specifically the Greeks and Romans</note>, it will be clear why miracles were then necessary and highly profitable. To be sure, it had been promised to the Jews by God in *Deuteronomy chapter XVIII* that a great Prophet similar to Moses would come. But Moses was not only a Prophet and Lawgiver, but also a <term>Wonder-worker</term> <note>original: Θαυματουργος (Thaumatourgos), one who performs miracles</note>. It was necessary, therefore, that Christ demonstrate by miracles—and indeed by more excellent and frequent ones than those Moses had performed—that He Himself was that promised Messiah. For that principal article of faith had to be placed in safety against the clever excuses of the Jews. The time had arrived when, little by little, ceremonies were to be abolished, and God was to be worshiped in spirit. Opinions concerning the true Messiah were greatly corrupted among this nation; therefore, the mere warnings and precepts of Christ would have profited little. Something greater had to be brought forward, which even the Jews themselves, following their own principles, could not deny: namely, Miracles. For if our Jesus had not performed such things, the Jews would not have turned their minds to hearing the doctrine of Christ, but would have always cried out that *Moses, Moses* had been illustrious for miracles, but Christ was not. From this it is clear that it was necessary for Him to confirm His doctrine with miracles. The Gentiles, being plainly destitute of all revelation, would not have been led to embrace Christian doctrine by its excellence alone, but would have regarded Christ merely as some new Philosopher. However, upon seeing so many miracles, their minds were moved to attention, such that in the first centuries, a great many passed over into the camps of the Christians.

**(IV.)** <note>The author or printer repeats number IV, likely meaning VI</note> Unbelievers are by no means ignorant that there are among Christians **Men** eminent for their learning and sharpness of wit; **Men** skilled in those sciences that require an exquisite mental edge; **Men** most foreign to every appearance of superstition; **Men** who are accustomed to admit nothing without the most rigid examination; **Men** most loving of the truth; and finally, **Men** who, without fear of persecution, could follow the principles of the Deists if they wished. Yet these are no less persuaded of the truth of the Christian Religion and the divine origin of the miracles performed by Christ than they are of other most certain truths not regarding religion. To these, the miracles performed long ago are sufficient, nor do they require new ones. Therefore, before they call for new miracles, Unbelievers must show either that this persuasion is feigned and impossible, or they are bound to open up the causes of this (as they think) "credulity," or finally confess that this persuasion is true. How they might prove this persuasion to be feigned, I know not; I know not

# MEDITATION X.

<page-num>424</page-num>
->**MEDITATION X.**<-

I do not know whether it is not contrary to all humanity and equity to want to deny all credit to learned and honest men who publicly profess some truth. If any were to say that **Deists**—if they claim to sincerely subscribe to all the heads of Natural Theology <note>Natural Theology refers to knowledge of God obtained through reason and the observation of nature, rather than through supernatural revelation.</note>—are in fact "pure and simple" <note>original: "puros putos"</note> **Atheists**, and hold all religion to be a fable, I know well enough that they would signal with bitter words that an injustice was being done to them. But perhaps it is impossible for this persuasion to be true; yet how will they prove this? They must either show that no historical faith <note>The term "historical faith" refers to the intellectual acceptance of facts recorded in history, as opposed to "saving faith" or personal religious conviction.</note> can be granted, or that God cannot perform a miracle. However, no matter how much they sharpen the edge of their wit, they will be able to prove neither. 

Therefore, they must resort to other causes. Perhaps they will say that this persuasion is owed to education and upbringing; but how, again, will they prove this? We grant that many of the common people, and indeed very often even learned men, follow the crowd of those who came before them and cling to what they learned as youths as if to a rock. But can it be concluded from this that absolutely no one can undertake an examination of religion and subscribe to certain articles with the full assent of the mind? Is it credible that men who spare no labor in examining these or those parts of the sciences would embrace Religion without any examination? 

Suppose, for example, that **Ditton** <note>Humphry Ditton (1675–1715), an English mathematician and theologian known for his work defending the Resurrection of Christ using logical and mathematical principles.</note> as a youth had learned, among other things, that the doctrine of Christ was confirmed by miracles; can it be said with any appearance of truth that he learned this method of demonstrating the truth without the most accurate examination and meditation? Great, it is true, is the force and efficacy of education and early upbringing. But daily experience teaches us that opinions drawn in, as it were, with one’s mother's milk can be overcome. I see no reason, therefore, why the **Unbelievers** should assert that men who love the truth cannot be truly persuaded and convinced of the truth of the miracles performed by Christ in the past. But if indeed, by applying accurate examination and meditation, lovers of truth can properly understand and admit this truth, what need is there, finally, for perpetual miracles?

**(VII)** Those who call for new miracles, or demand that God should perform miracles either every day or at least every year through messengers sent by God—or at least within the span of a hundred years, and specifically now in these, now in those parts of the world where the Christian Religion is known—should consider this: if the former were to happen, men would pay little attention to them. For men care little for what is accustomed to happen daily, but pass over it lightly. Those who contemplate the heavens, and the earth teeming with innumerable fruits most skillfully woven together, and living creatures of every kind, etc., can almost grasp the omnipotence, wisdom, and goodness of God with their hands. 

<column-break/>

<page-num>425</page-num>
->**ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.**<-

But how few there are who pay attention to these things! Indeed, there is no doubt that the same would happen if miracles occurred daily. But if they were to occur at intervals of time—for example, only recurring every century—the same question would return; for the men who died within the span of that time would ask why miracles had not been performed in their own age? 

We said above that God would not perform miracles for the sake of the **Unbelievers**. For the sake of Christians, however, who have faith in the miracles of Jesus Christ, it is not necessary that new ones be performed. In many places where the Christian religion indeed flourishes, but is obscured by many fables and foul superstition, new miracles would be of little value. This is partly because miracles are said to be performed almost every year to confirm the authority of this or that saint, and partly because the credulous common people—and all those who do not follow the pure and chaste doctrine of Christ and the Apostles—would not wish the rampant superstition to be rebuked. They would not offer open ears to miracles, thinking that their authors' only aim was to send a final farewell <note>original: "nuntium mittant," an idiom meaning to renounce or break off from something.</note> to their ancestral religion.

**(VIII.)** Finally, it is frivolous for some to say that the credit of those miracles which are said to have been performed by Christ and the Apostles is diminishing due to the antiquity of the times. I know indeed that a certain **English scholar** (*) wished to prove through calculations at what time all persuasion concerning the truth of the Christian Religion would cease. But experience itself confounds him. For the most learned and celebrated men have proven—and still prove—things done in the most ancient times by no less trustworthy testimonies than things done a hundred years ago. No one doubts these things, unless perhaps some **Hardouin**. <note>Jean Hardouin (1646–1729) was a French Jesuit scholar who famously claimed that most ancient Greek and Roman texts were forgeries by monks in the 13th century.</note> 

**Socrates** lived 500 years before Christ, and yet no one doubts his tragic death. In this controversy, however, it must be warned that we are not speaking here of every individual circumstance of the event, but of the substance of the matter. Thus, although perhaps those who wrote the deeds of **Alexander the Great** added many things and exaggerated the deeds done by so great a King, no one will doubt for that reason that **Alexander** defeated **Darius, King of the Persians**, and brought the entire Persian Monarchy under his power. The reasoning for similar things is the same. Finally, since the history of a fact cannot be proven through algebraic calculations, but through the concurrence of many probabilities, it is manifest that it cannot be decided even by mathematical reasons how long a firm [persuasion will remain] in the minds... <note>The sentence cuts off here as per the catchword "animis".</note>

Chriſti Lib. II. propoſit. XVI."</note>

# MEDITATION X.

<page-num>426</page-num>
->**MEDITATION X.**<-

persuasion about the truth of past events exists in the minds of men. Everything returns (after the events themselves which are narrated are held to be possible) to the quality and quantity of the witnesses; if their authority is placed beyond the risk of doubt, everything that can lead to eliciting assent is present. Thus, men who are true lovers of truth no more doubt whether **Socrates** perished by poison or **Caesar** by the sword, than they doubt whether **Zwingli** was slaughtered in the disaster at Kappel <note>Huldrych Zwingli (1484–1531) was a leader of the Reformation in Switzerland; he died during the Second War of Kappel.</note>. Therefore, it is not the length of time or its recentness, but rather the number and quality of witnesses that cause the truth of past events to take deep roots in the minds of men. Where these witnesses are lacking, even if it is said to have happened in our own age, faith wavers. It is true that the mind is moved more toward believing something when the thing itself is presented to be seen with one's own eyes; but since History is a narration of things not seen by us that is worthy of attention, all historical faith would vanish if direct sight were required for it. When, however, we speak of the firmness of this persuasion, we simultaneously demand that the mind attend to all the circumstances of the historical account, and that it moderate its assent according to the smaller or larger degrees of probability, just as if different weights were placed on a scale. We believe, moreover, that the historical faith regarding the resurrection of **Jesus Christ** and his miracles is provided with as many degrees of likelihood as are necessary to grant it assent. These arguments having been brought forward, it can be said by way of confirmation that an Atheist—intending to deny the creation of all things and the origin of the human race specifically—could use the same argument used by Unbelievers to attack the faith of miracles performed long ago. That argument was brought forward by the most learned and dear friend **Vernet** <note>Jacob Vernet (1698–1789), a prominent Genevan theologian and author of "Treatise on the Truth of the Christian Religion."</note> in his treatise *On the Truth of the Christian Religion, Section VII, chapter XXV.*

> "What would the Deists say," (he says), "who profess with us to adore a God who is the Creator of the world and the Author of the human race, if someone more skeptical than they, such as an Atheist or a Pyrrhonist <note>A follower of Pyrrho, representing extreme skepticism that doubts the possibility of any certain knowledge.</note>, said: 'I cannot believe that the Universe was created, nor that there was a first man, the stem of all others, who came immediately from the hands of God, because we see nothing similar happening today. All animals are born through generation, and all bodies are formed from pre-existing matter and with mechanical skill. Why does the Divine Power no longer create anything new? Why do men no longer emerge from the mud, and why do we no longer see new Stars appear, nor new species of beasts, so that we might believe what is told to us about the origin of the world?' If someone reasoned thus, a true Deist (by which I—"

The necessity of creating is no longer the same. A miracle was needed to form the Universe and to set up the machine as we see it. To demand more would be a rashness and an indiscretion, since the nature of the thing does not require it.' This response, which would be very just in the mouth of the Deist, will also be ours. VII. Others from this tribe are accustomed to reason in this way: Namely, they say that Christian Theologians, after they have extolled the excellence of **Christian Ethics** with enough praise, must nevertheless confess that no one can properly observe the precepts of **Jesus Christ**, and for that reason they contend that one must take refuge in the most perfect merit of Christ. They argue that **Deists** likewise confess that no one can exactly keep the precepts of the Law of Nature, and thus they themselves recur to divine mercy as if to a certain sacred asylum; nor is it doubtful that God, being most fond of the human race and well aware of the weakness of human nature, will kindly remit those sins which human nature struggles to avoid. From this it appears that the **Deists** agree with the **Christians** in the sum of the matter, and thus it is not necessary for them to give their name to the Christian Religion.

We respond: (I.) Christians do not praise and extol **Christian Ethics** without cause, since it contains precepts far more excellent than those which reason and philosophy alone supply. Since learned men have demonstrated this extensively and with dedicated effort, I will not discuss it further.

(II.) We do not assert that the divine precepts are entirely impossible to perform; (*) for in that way we would utterly remove their power to bind us; but—

we say that these things can be observed with the addition of divine help. According to the conviction of Christians, this help is given to all those who sincerely implore the grace of God. However, those who admit only the precepts of **Natural Law** <note>Natural Law refers to a system of ethics supposedly inherent in human nature and discoverable by reason, without the need for divine revelation.</note>, with incentives sought from the storehouse of reason, cannot certainly expect such help, because those prayers are not supported by any certain promises of being heard.

(III.) Although we assert that the precepts of Christ can be kept with the addition of divine grace, we nevertheless freely confess that such is the weakness of human minds that no mortal can keep them without any mixture of error or sin. Notwithstanding this, Christians in name and truth have a most ready defense against this evil—namely, the most powerful intercession of Jesus Christ, obtained through his bloody death. Thus says the Apostle John (to remain silent on many other passages) in his first Epistle, Chapter 2, verses 1 and 2: *“My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. And if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous. And he is the propitiation for our sins.”* <note>original Greek: "Τεκνία με, ταῦτα γράφω ὑμῖν ἵνα μὴ ἁμάρτητε. Καὶ αὐτὸς ἱλασμός ἐστι περὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν."</note> By the power of this death and intercession, true Christians are most certainly persuaded that God will forgive their sins and, despite various infirmities, will nevertheless deal with them mercifully. But **Deists** <note>Deists believe in a God who created the world but does not intervene in it or provide specific revelations.</note> cannot flee to that safe **Asylum** <note>Here used in the classical sense of a "place of refuge" or "sanctuary."</note>, because the precepts of reason are supported by no certain promises, nor do they show that condition by which divine mercy is obtained. And who among the Deists, finally, will assert that he has sinned throughout his whole life only through carelessness; that he has never let loose the reins of evil desires; that he has never struck against the clearest dictates of conscience? Now, those same precepts of Natural Law teach (which even the Gentiles acknowledged) that God indeed wishes well to the good, but that He also hates the wicked. But to what extent God will be gracious to sinners is known only somewhat obscurely from reason alone.

Now, if this proposition is true, as Christians rightly believe, the Deists are vehemently deceived when they certainly promise themselves the forgiveness of sins—

<margin>XIII. Objection of the Unbelievers follows.</margin>

VIII. Furthermore, the Unbelievers persist and cry out that the Christian religion is the primary cause of superstition. **Tindal** <note>Matthew Tindal (1657–1733), an English Deist famous for his work "Christianity as Old as the Creation."</note> urged this objection in his most well-known work. (**) Having dismissed those points which may have been brought forward by others, we respond with the following. And (I.) indeed we say that this argument proves more than was intended to be proved. For if any force were in it, it would follow that no religion at all should be admitted: both because the human mind, imbued with whatever religion it may be, is most fertile in feigning various things about God and divine matters; and because it is established by the experience of all ages that those who had been instructed by natural law alone fell into the crudest superstition. Because if this reasoning is valid—"on the occasion of revealed religion, certain men have lapsed into superstition, therefore Revelation is to be rejected"—this [counter-argument] will also maintain its strength: "Men using the natural law alone, as witnessed by the experience of all ages, were devoted to idolatry and crude superstition; therefore natural religion is to be outlawed." -># MEDITATION X.<-

<page-num>430</page-num>
<header>MEDITATION X.</header>
<meta>catchword: cos</meta>

Atheism would triumph, which would nonetheless be contrary to the opinions of those with whom we are now dealing <note>The author refers to the Deists, who believed in a God but rejected organized revelation; they would not want atheism to win, yet the author argues their logic leads there.</note>.

(II.) It is manifest that in those places where pure Religion and its simple worship flourish, men are most alienated from superstition; on the contrary, it is well known that superstition raises its head among those who have not hesitated to add perverse opinions and foolish worship to the Christian Religion. This could not happen if the Christian Religion, viewed in itself, threw men into superstition. Therefore, it is not so much revelation, but rather the inventions of the human mind that cause men to be imbued with superstition.

(III.) We do not deny that a shameful superstition spreads here and there in the most flourishing kingdoms and provinces of Europe; indeed, we grieve that even among the most remote Nations, which ought to be led to the public profession of the Christian Religion, opinions contrary to pure religion and superstitious rites are being sown by men who least ought to do so, rather than the pure doctrine of the Gospel. Furthermore, we do not deny that many Christian Doctors, after the departure of Christ and the Apostles, often turned away from that native and simple doctrine of the *Savior* <note>original: "Soteris" (Greek: Σωτήρ), meaning Savior.</note>. Nor can it happen otherwise when men, having set aside the cultivation of reason and cast away an accurate examination of things to be believed, begin to cling to those things which they have sucked in almost with their mother’s milk—following the examples of others in religion, admiring the opinions of the religious leaders as if they were Oracles, being struck with wonder by external rituals, making a profit out of religion, and feigning false miracles to deceive the simpler folk, among other things by which the minds of men are led away from pure religion. Is it any wonder that such men confuse superstition itself with religion? Moreover, there is an abuse of all things, even the most sacred; yet no man of sound mind will condemn the use of the best and most useful things because of that abuse.

(IV.) The Apologies of the Ancient Christians <note>The "Apologies" were formal defenses of the faith written by early church fathers like Justin Martyr and Tertullian to explain Christianity to the Roman authorities.</note> do much to refute the objection of *Tyndal* <note>Matthew Tindal (1657–1733), an influential English Deist who argued that "Christianity is as old as the Creation" and that positive religion was a superstitious corruption of natural reason.</note>. For it is clear from them that most Christians, after they had given their name to the Christian Religion, sent a message of divorce to the idolatry raging among the Gentiles; they mocked it with "white teeth" <note>An idiom meaning to laugh openly or mock heartily; original: "albis dentibus riserint."</note>, and indeed, often could not be induced to embrace it even by torments. This is a manifest sign that superstition does not have its origin from the Christian Religion. At the same time, I will not deny that many fell away shamefully in the heat of the most cruel persecutions; nor will I deny that many remnants of pagan superstition were retained by the simpler people, which pure religion nonetheless proscribed. On the contrary, it must be observed

### MEDITATION X.

Will a greater reputation for that era actually win us over to it? What if that very man <note>Referring to Cyprian of Carthage (c. 210–258 AD), a highly influential bishop and martyr.</note>, beyond all measure, laid the foundations of Church domination? What if his authority was by no means universal, since the same *Cyprian* bitterly complained about the loosening of its bonds? What if he primarily attacked the more atrocious crimes—specifically apostasy—while neglecting many others? What if the very laws introduced concerning the levels of penance had no small amount of "self-imposed worship" <note>original: ἐθελοθρησκείας (*ethelothrēskeias*); a term from Colossians 2:23 meaning a religion of one's own making or "will-worship."</note> and superstition mixed in? What if the unwise zeal of the Bishops in excommunicating people was already apparent then? If these points are supported by reliable evidence, should we not judge those who write panegyrics <note>A speech or text in high praise of someone.</note> rather than history? They are the ones who, disregarding more recent examples, pretend that nothing more sublime in the exercise of holiness can be found than that which breathes the air of this antiquity. Thus says **the late, renowned Lampe**. 

These things are not brought up with the intent of magnifying the errors of these men, nor to detract from their piety. For opinions and customs that are deeply rooted in the mind are not cast off in one blow or in a few moments, but only gradually. Rather, they are brought up so that certain good people may learn that not everything commonly said in historical handbooks on this subject is certain and beyond doubt. Even the books of the New Testament alone teach us that Christians did not immediately bid farewell to all erroneous opinions and vices as soon as they gave their name to the Christian Religion.

(V.) Even if in certain places Religion is handed down not without a mixture of superstition, this should not prevent Unbelievers from accepting Revelation, unless they have their minds turned away from Religion for entirely other reasons. In our dissertations on this subject, we have proved that even the wiser among the Heathen were well able to distinguish superstition from religion. Why, then, could Unbelievers not separate Religion from depraved opinions and introduced superstitions? Indeed, it is a mere pretext for those men when they assert they reject the Christian Religion because in many places it has been contaminated by various superstitions.

(VI.) Finally, the most manifest argument proving that Revelation is not the cause of Superstition is that, on the one hand, it condemns Idolatry and all kinds of superstitions; and on the other hand, it commends the internal worship of God as the primary thing. I would exceed the limits set for public disputes if I wished to collect all the passages that pertain to this; therefore, it will suffice to bring forward one or two. At the very beginning of Revelation, God is said to have created heaven and earth; this was undoubtedly said to oppose the foolish and superstitious

<column-break/>

<page-num>435</page-num>
# ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

fictions about the origin of all things that were accepted by the Egyptians and other Eastern peoples. In Joshua 24, verses 2 and 3, it is recounted that God called Abraham out of Ur of the Chaldeans, where idolatry was rampant. The many afflictions of the Jewish people, recounted throughout the sacred texts, are said to have occurred primarily because that nation had contaminated itself with various kinds of superstitions and Idolatry. And what would you hear more frequently in the writings of the Prophets than lamentations over the Jews' minds being inclined toward superstition? In the New Testament, not only is it commanded that God alone be adored (*Matthew 4:10*), and indeed in spirit and in truth (*John 4:23–24*), but it is also declared in plain words in *Romans chapter 12, verse 1* in what "reasonable service" <note>original: ἡ λογικὴ λατρεία (*hē logikē latreia*); often translated as "spiritual worship" or "rational service."</note> consists. Indeed, the entire Christian Religion sometimes goes by the name of love for God and neighbor, which has been explained and proved more extensively by learned men who have demonstrated the excellence of the Christian Religion. Is it possible, then, that God, the Author of Revelation, would prohibit and condemn superstition while at the same time prescribing a religion that necessarily excites a love of superstition in the minds of men?

(VIII.) Finally, *Tindal* <note>Matthew Tindal (1657–1733), an English Deist famous for arguing that Christianity is merely a "republication" of the religion of nature.</note> and those who follow him, if they wish their thesis to be upheld, must show that superstition follows necessarily from the very nature and character of the doctrines and precepts of the Christian Religion. For it does not follow that because this or that person misunderstood the sense of Holy Scripture here and there, or because others added much from their own prolific imagination, or because many Christians accepted certain superstitious rites along with religion, therefore religion itself is the cause of this mixture and these fictions. In the same way, it does not follow that because fictions of various kinds, superstitions, and trivial opinions have been added by men to the principles of Natural Theology, therefore Natural Theology is the mother of superstition. The warnings *Tindal* gives regarding the two sacred rites, Baptism and the Lord's Supper, have been properly refuted by the **Renowned Foster** <note>James Foster (1697–1753), a Baptist preacher who wrote a famous rebuttal to Tindal's Deism.</note>.

From this definition, it is sufficiently clear that Revelation must encompass certain things that are not found within the embrace of natural religion. ### MEDITATION X.

...collection of truths that exceed the boundaries of reason cannot be maintained. To establish this thesis, however, they are required to show by certain arguments that the revelation of such truths is either *impossible*, or that it is *contrary to divine virtues and the laws of nature*; or finally, that it is a *condition of Revelation*—which Christians hold to be divine—*that all propositions handed down in it can be drawn from the storehouse of Natural Religion*. 

Regarding the *first* argument, we assert that everything is held by us to be possible which involves no manifest contradiction. We see no such contradiction in this case, whether we look to God or to the truths that are said to be Revealed. So great is the **Abyss of the divine intellect**, so infinite the abundance of Ideas appearing before the divine mind, that nothing prevents Him from being able to communicate certain new and hitherto unknown truths with men, if He so wills. Nothing stands in the way regarding the truths that can be revealed. For by these, we do not mean a "cento" <note>original: *centonem*; a patchwork garment or a poem made of recycled verses. Here, it refers to a jumbled collection of nonsense.</note> of unintelligible propositions or things fighting against each other with opposing fronts, but rather a complex of salutary truths which **God, the Best and Greatest**, wished to disclose according to His most free and wise will to sharpen, extol, and perfect the chapters of **Natural Theology**, even if we cannot know them in their fullness in this life.

But neither can it be shown in the *second* place that Revelation is contrary either to divine virtues or to Natural Law. It cannot be said to be less fitting to divine attributes when it tends solely toward promoting happiness. But a new light, kindled in the minds of men, promotes human happiness; therefore, it must beautifully harmonize with divine virtues. God, who gave men reason and the faculty of knowing natural laws, foreknew before the event that most mortals would not follow the light kindled through reason, but would rather obscure it by rashly seizing upon various opinions. What, then, is contrary to divine goodness, equity, and wisdom, if truths are shared with the human race—or at least with a great part of it—which can not only add weight to **Natural Religion** <term>Natural Religion: The belief in God and morality based on reason and nature alone, without the need for supernatural revelation.</term> but also surpass it in many ways? Nor does it hinder anything that He did not grant that revelation to absolutely everyone always and all at once. For God was bound by no law to provide that, but according to His most wise will—all the causes of which we do not have clearly perceived—He was able to distribute His goods either among a greater or a smaller number. It is pious and just to rest in this will of the best Deity. For just as a Father of a family can pursue all his children with the most tender love,

<column-break/>

## ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.
<page-num>437</page-num>

while at the same time acting more confidently with one of them for reasons perceived by himself, but not equally by all; so in like manner God can act. This is manifest not only from the diverse dispensation of divine revelation but also from the daily distribution of His Goods. 

It likewise cannot be shown that revelation is contrary to divine natural laws. Certainly, the systems of the Learned, in which they have explained the precepts of **Natural Law** at length, would not be so clear, nor supported by such great weight, unless the light of Christian doctrine had been added. I know, indeed, it can hardly happen that one who has sincerely embraced the Christian religion would fail to observe the rules of Natural and Civil Law. But he who weighs the cited passages according to the genuine rules of Interpretation will see that they are only difficult to perform with respect to certain times and persons. The **Holy Savior** <note>original: *S. Soter*; from the Greek *Sōtēr*, meaning Savior, referring to Jesus Christ.</note> himself testifies that he came into the world not to abolish but to confirm natural law. Since Natural Law required some light and a certain protection with respect to the source of moral actions, their end, and their incentives, thanks must undoubtedly be given to our **Savior**, because he not only placed them in a clearer light but also showed another, and indeed stronger, bond of obligation.

Finally, I am not permitted to be so sharp-witted as to be able to affirm that in Revelation only those things are contained which comprise the natural law. The **Deists** <term>Deists: Enlightenment thinkers who believed in a creator based on reason but rejected supernatural revelation and miracles.</term> themselves cry out that, among other reasons, they are hindered from giving their name to the Christian Religion because various dogmas are found in it which seem unable to stand with the decrees of Natural Law and the precepts of reason; by which very fact they confess that these things cannot be drawn from the principles of natural theology. I know that some from this tribe approve of the **Socinians'** <term>Socinians: A rationalist sect that denied the Trinity and the divinity of Christ, emphasizing a moralistic and reason-based interpretation of Scripture.</term> method of interpreting the Holy Scriptures, and think that in this way those things which are called mysteries can be easily understood; but whether that is done according to the rules of legitimate Interpretation is what is being asked. But why should you fight with those who do not admit the truth of the things narrated by the Evangelists and Apostles—who take the liberty, even if the truth of the deeds is granted, to fashion interpretations at their whim, and to hold those things which are designated in revelation in clear words, and indeed as principal matters, as less necessary, keeping only those which are to their palate and which can be easily understood without any revelation?

### MEDITATION X.

<margin>
The 15th objection of the Unbelievers is presented.
</margin>

XV. The Unbelievers, and among them *Tindal* <note>Matthew Tindal (1657–1733) was a leading English Deist whose work "Christianity as Old as the Creation" argued that Revelation was merely a republication of the Law of Nature.</note> in particular, say: *Those who labor to diminish the force of Natural Religion in order to exalt Revelation are declaring war on all religion; and there cannot exist a double rule of equal weight according to which men might govern their actions.* To this objection, we respond as follows. First, at a glance, the words of these men do not seem to contain anything false. Since Natural Religion <note>Natural Religion refers to truths about God and morality that can be discovered through human reason alone, without the help of the Bible.</note> was given by God and binds all people, it would be impious for anyone to wish to diminish its force and obligation. The Law of Nature is not opposed to the moral law handed down by Christ. Indeed, it is certain that without Natural Theology, the divine origin of the Christian Religion could hardly be proven. 

However, we must address the second point: the claim that it is an accepted dogma of all Christian theologians that the principles of Natural Theology must be suppressed so that the Christian Religion may be exalted. We do not deny that here and there among Christians there are such writers who seem to think themselves wise—and to have fulfilled the duties of pious theologians—only if they can thunder against reason and its cultivation at every opportunity. They shout that reason is so corrupt that one might think it was either given to us by God in vain, or granted like a double-edged knife into the hands of an infant. There are those who cannot bear to hear people praise the excellence of Natural Theology or recommend it to young men of good character. But these are generally people who have never properly examined these themes in their own lives, or whose brains are so filled with the opinions of the Schools <note>A reference to "Scholasticism," the traditional, often rigid academic method of the medieval and early modern universities.</note> that they cannot rightly weigh and value things of the highest excellence. Yet, this error should not be imputed to all Christian theologians in general. A distinction must be made between true Theologians and "Theologasters" <note>A derogatory term for shallow or pretentious theologians.</note>. *Tindal* in particular was well aware that in his own homeland of England, there were excellent men who demonstrated the use and excellence of Natural Theology with the most powerful arguments; indeed, he himself is very industrious in citing passages where they explained these arguments.

(III.) The Unbelievers stumble in the very way they cry out that others have sinned. For in order to exalt Natural Religion and its dignity (however much they may have otherwise despised its name), they do everything they think can diminish the excellence of Revelation and its precepts. They frequently and laboriously try to show how little efficacy the Christian religion has on the minds of men; how much Christian Ethics rests on fanatical opinions; how many people who

<column-break/>

### ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

sincerely wished to follow the precepts of the Christian religion were cast into melancholy and foolish opinions; how many strange things are explained in Revelation regarding certain internal sensations and actions of the pious; and how those "heavenly joys" built upon unintelligible mysteries are vain, and so on. 

But here, the Unbelievers should not wonder if sensible men among Christians not only defend their cause vigorously, but also show in turn how little power this "greatly celebrated" Natural Religion has had on the minds of men throughout history. They point out how great the disagreement was among the most ancient and learned philosophers and legal scholars regarding the explanation of the Natural Law; that this Natural Law was never the actual "norm" for what people believed, but rather the local state religion, however superstitious and foolish it might be. No such pure system of Natural Theology, free from all error, can be found among those who once followed the natural law alone. Instead, modern writers have gathered together scattered sentences from the ancient philosophers—without regard for the religion or the underlying hypotheses they followed—simply to make the face of that natural law look more attractive and to deceive the unlearned. Nevertheless, it should be noted that when learned men argue against the Unbelievers <term>by necessity of the case</term> <note>original: κατα βιαιον (kata biaion). This Greek phrase suggests an argument forced by the opponent's pressure or the necessity of the debate.</note>, they do not so much intend to attack the foundations of Natural Law or diminish its excellence, but rather to show that the modern "arrangers" of Natural Theology, if they were willing to tell the truth, actually owe a great deal to the Christian religion.

(IV.) I do not know why it should be seen as a fault in theologians that they exalt Christian Ethics above natural law. They cannot help but do this, partly because they are persuaded that Revelation is of divine origin, and partly because the very comparison of this natural law with Revelation makes the excellence of the latter beautifully manifest; which is why Christian Ethics has often been praised even by Unbelievers. Truly, one who rightly exalts something does not strip away the just value of the thing over which it is exalted.

(V.) Finally, the arguments regarding a "double rule" seem to carry little weight in this matter. For although a truth known by the light of Nature may differ from a revealed truth, they are not, properly speaking, two different rules of action, but rather one rule, applied to two different objects...

### MEDITATION IX.

...refined. Truly, the general rule of a wise and Christian man is this: whatever is consistent with reason, grave, momentous, and worthy of God—whether it becomes known through the natural light of reason alone or through some certain Revelation—that is to be followed, and life is to be established according to that light, from wherever it arose. And yet, in both natural and revealed religion, such precepts for thinking rightly about divine matters and for living piously are found which are consistent with reason and divine virtues. Therefore, it is consistent with reason that a wise man should admit and approve of them. Indeed, if the objects of belief themselves are considered, they can be said to be of two kinds—not in respect to their origin, for both have God as their author, but in the manner of their delivery. But since we should not argue over words, let us suppose that there is one rule which Revelation prescribes and another which Natural Theology <note>Natural Theology refers to truths about God and morality that can be discovered through human reason and the observation of nature, without the aid of scripture.</note> prescribes; I see no reason why both cannot stand together: one can deliver more sublime truths, while the other delivers truths more easily grasped. Even so, the rules themselves do not contradict one another.

<margin>The remaining objections of the Unbelievers are presented.</margin>

XVI. To bring this argument to a close, I shall group the remaining prejudices of these men against the Christian religion into a single bundle, as it were. They say, therefore, that most Christians take the name of the Christian religion without performing any examination, and would feel differently if they had been born and educated among other peoples; that there is no end to the controversies among Christians, and that new ones sprout daily alongside the old; that most public teachers of the Christian religion and leaders of sacred rites are seized by a foolish Zeal <note>In this historical context, "Zeal" (*zelus*) often refers to a harsh, narrow-minded religious passion or fanaticism.</note> against those who disagree; that a "sawing back and forth" of disputation occurs over the smallest trivialities, and these are often so exaggerated that very few among simpler folk eventually know what is necessary to know and believe for salvation; that the best and most outstanding men among Christians, who try to bring a remedy to this disease, are suspected by the others, and while they do not attack minor errors with an equally burning Zeal, they are often openly insulted; that everyone ought to judge according to the small measure of their own knowledge, and not extend their judgment beyond it; that God, who clearly sees the narrow limits of human knowledge, knows well that most mortals are in such a state that they cannot be concerned with seeking out the truth; and that the Deists <note>Deists were thinkers who believed in a creator God based on reason but rejected supernatural revelation and organized church dogma.</note>, being content with a few articles of religion, are free from those inconveniences listed above, and if any disagreement arises among them, they bear it with a most composed mind, etc., etc.

It is helpful now to respond to these point by point, but briefly, as we have touched upon one or another of these objections here and there in the previous sections. And first, it is indeed true what the Unbelievers say, that in all sects of Christians there are many who defend throughout their lives what they learned as youths

<column-break/>

### ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

without any examination: and we do not deny that their number is huge. Furthermore, we do not deny that among the <term>Ministers of the Divine Word</term> <note>original: "V. D. Ministri" (Verbi Divini Ministri). These are ordained clergy or preachers.</note> themselves, there are those who <gloss>are unable</gloss> to prove the truth of the Christian religion with clear and solid arguments, let alone blunt the more subtle objections of the Unbelievers. A lack of judgment and talent hinders some; others were not sufficiently taught about this subject in the Academies and Gymnasiums <note>A Gymnasium was a high-level secondary school preparing students for university study.</note>; many public teachers are accustomed to exhaustively dissecting controversies of minor importance, but often treat fundamental truths more negligently, thinking that these should be held as true by everyone as if they were unshakeable, and need not be anxiously examined. Hence it often happens that even they, when the primary truths ought to be clearly delivered and explained for the understanding of the unrefined, discourse obscurely on this subject. But how does this help the Unbelievers? Does it follow that because many among Christians adhere to religion by a blind impulse without conducting any examination, the Christian religion is built upon no certain foundations? Does it follow from this that all teachers of the Christian Church indiscriminately follow the crowd that went before? Do the Unbelievers alone weigh everything by the standard of reason, and can they demonstrate through an examination that what is said about the origin and excellence of the Christian religion is a mere fable? When it comes to the business of religion and the duties surrounding it, it will be clear that "sins are committed both inside and outside the walls of Troy" <note>This is a quote from the Roman poet Horace (*Iliacos intra muros peccatur et extra*), meaning that there are faults on both sides of a conflict.</note>. Nor will the sluggishness of certain doctors of the Christian Church serve as a defense for the audacity of the Deists.

(II.) It is admitted that the number of controversies stirred up among Christians is great, and that they increase daily. But about what things, I ask, do the learned not dispute—and have they not disputed at all times? Were there not formerly battles between the most famous philosophers of Greece and Rome? Have not many disputes and contentions arisen among legal experts, doctors, cultivators of elegant literature, philosophers, and historians concerning various topics? Is there not a great divorce of opinions among those very men who go by the name of "Free-thinkers"? Since the causes of these disagreements are obvious enough (and the Unbelievers clearly perceive them), it is unjust for the Christian religion itself to be despised on that account.

(III.) Nor do we deny, but rather sadly confess, that many theologians often show too much fervor in defending their own opinions, and sell their pride and stubbornness of mind under the name of "Zeal for the glory of God." But what is this against Religion? There are and always have been wise and peaceful theologians who, in examining theological questions, are circum-
