### MEDITATION X.

...circumspect men, though they are outnumbered by those who think the height of Theological learning consists in fiercely defending minor opinions. Nor are there lacking most excellent theologians who oppose these vices and depict the nature of genuine Zeal for the glory of God in vivid colors. It is true that some people exalt the smallest trivial questions <note>original: "minimas quæstiunculas"</note> beyond their importance. But what good, pious, and wise Christian theologian approves of this? Who does not grieve? Who will put a bridle on these wild, extravagant wits? Who can prevent men—who possess an arrogant spirit and are ignorant of what the excellence of Religion actually consists in—from stubbornly defending their petty opinions? The self-love <note>original: "φιλαυτία" (philautia), meaning an excessive or misplaced love of oneself</note> of many stands in the way, preventing men who truly love the truth from being able to counter these evils. But how does this help the Unbelievers? Why do they for this reason loathe the Christian religion, which nevertheless commends itself by its own simplicity and is entirely foreign to so many trivial questions with which the wits of the Learned miserably torment themselves? And indeed, he who unfolds the volumes of the New Testament without prejudice <note>original: "ἄτερ παθῶν" (ater pathōn), meaning without passions or bias</note>, and with the sole intent of finding what is true and salutary, will not be moved by the many trivial questions of these more recent "Wise ones."

(IV.) Nor is it far from the truth that those who skillfully discern momentous matters in religion from less necessary articles, and who commend simplicity in Theological matters, are often subject to the hatred and attacks of others. Nor is this surprising; for the temperaments and judgments of men are various: men who do not have their minds cultivated by weightier disciplines and have spent their entire lives amidst the noise of empty trivial questions cannot help but hate those who wish those questions were cut away. These things must be endured by the wise and those who love the truth. However, none of the sinister judgments of these "petty masters" <note>original: "Magistellorum," a diminutive, mocking term for teachers or scholars</note> against prudent theologians help the cause of the Unbelievers. Since these things are clear to them, why do they not follow those who commend themselves by their love of peace and who emphasize the weightiest matters? Why, because of the unjust judgments of others, do they neglect and despise that which is most holy in religion? Meanwhile, this also must be observed: by the name of "Scholastic controversies" we do not mean the momentous truths contained in the Holy Scriptures. For prudent theologians ought to defend these diligently. I note this for the reason that Deists would wish that theologians would not urge as necessary those things which are primary in Religion—for example, Mysteries, miracles, etc.—which the Author of *Essential Religion* <note>This likely refers to a specific contemporary text arguing that religion should only consist of universal moral truths accessible to reason alone.</note> especially thought should be done. For a theologian who admits Revelation cannot hold as trivial those things which are repeatedly emphasized by Christ and the Apostles as necessary to be believed,

<column-break/>

**PAGE 443**

### ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

neither ought he to imitate that farmer mentioned in Gellius <note>Aulus Gellius, a 2nd-century Roman author known for his "Attic Nights," a collection of notes on various subjects.</note> who rooted out the good herbs along with the noxious weeds.

(V.) It is admitted by all that everyone is bound to temper their judgment concerning religious matters to the measure of their own knowledge. But I do not see what this contributes to defending Unbelief, unless the Unbelievers say that after a most rigid examination of the Christian Religion, they have clearly discovered it to be plainly absurd and contrary to all laws of probability. But if this is what they intend, let them see to it that they do not extend their judgments over that which is true and certain. Let them see lest by judging in such a way, they offend not just one or two Christians, but a vast crowd of most excellent men who, throughout their entire lives, have duly and diligently examined Religion. No sane person demands of an Unbeliever that he subscribe to the Christian Religion without examination. We only want this: that everyone must labor according to their strength to duly weigh a matter most worthy of everyone's attention, and that they are not hindered by hatred, anger, and contempt from doing so. For he who judges in that manner acts not according to the measure of his knowledge, but according to the whim of his corrupt will. And what, finally, would the Deists respond to a man professing Atheism and saying that he must judge according to the measure of his own knowledge? Would they not contend that he had not applied the strength of his intellect in examining a most momentous question, and that he ought not to have denied the thing itself simply because of certain difficulties occurring in the argument?

(VI.) We also acknowledge that God will judge according to the diversity of faculties, talents, and the labor which each has expended in the examination of religion. But it does not follow from this that anyone can safely remain in the public profession of the religion in which he was born, or that any meager attempt at knowing the truth suffices. The Deists themselves confess that knowledge of Natural Theology is plainly necessary to be known. Therefore, it will not only be possible for men to be able to know the principles of this religion; but all will also sin, as many as do not apply the full strength of their talents to knowing all parts of this religion. The whole question therefore comes back to this: whether the nature of the Christian Religion is such that its truth can be tempered to the capacity of those who are not plainly devoid of common sense, and whether, this being granted, all Christians to whom this Revelation has been given can learn from it those things which are necessary to be known and believed. This is indeed what we Christians contend. Therefore, Unbelievers ought to look deep into themselves <note>original: "in se descendere"</note> and properly weigh whether they are equipped with those faculties of mind which are necessary for the examination of religion...

He asserts that while God judges based on one's capacity, individuals are still obligated to use their full intellectual powers to examine the truth of Revelation.</summary>

# MEDITATION X.

...are required for establishing [this examination]. I have no doubt that many will confess themselves to be adorned with sufficient intellectual gifts to perform this. But if, notwithstanding this, before they even begin this examination, they are occupied by prejudiced opinions against it, or do not weigh it carefully, let them judge for themselves whether it will be all the same to God, the Author of the Christian religion, whether they have seriously applied their minds to conducting this examination properly or not. They would certainly consider a man worthy of blame who has not worked to examine and understand the individual parts of Natural Religion <term>Natural Religion: a system of belief based on reason and the observation of the world rather than divine revelation</term>. Why then should God have no regard for that man who, although he both could and should have weighed the Christian religion, nevertheless neglected it, moved by I know not what pretext of "weakness"? In a word: either it must be said that God does not care for human affairs nor pay attention to the moral actions of men, or it will be true that the neglect of such a great business is a most serious sin, worthy of no light punishment. It is for everyone to look deeply into the spirit with which they have conducted their examination, and whether they have seriously wished to align their actions with the will of the Deity according to the powers of their mind’s faculties.

(VII.) Finally, we know that the Deists <term>Deists: 17th and 18th-century thinkers who believed God created the universe but does not interfere in it, rejecting miracles and revelation</term> admit only a few principles of religion; however, by what right this is done is rightly questioned. Whatever the case may be, we also assert that the Christian religion—insofar as it binds all Christians equally, without regard for the Learned or the common people—is not burdened with a multitude of articles of faith, as is clear from the catechetical instructions <note>original: "catecheticis institutionibus," the basic teaching manuals used to instruct people in the faith</note> prepared for the benefit of the common folk. But if, because of certain inconveniences that arise from different ways of conceiving the Christian religion, it were to be entirely rejected, then the same would happen to Natural Religion itself. The History of Philosophy and Literature can serve as abundant witnesses to what kind of consensus of minds existed in the past and exists now among those who have rejoiced only in the light of nature. Nor does that friendly "conspiracy of minds" <note>original: "animorum conspiratio," meaning a general agreement or shared outlook</note> which the Unbelievers boast of prove anything, since even the most shameful Idolaters and those in grave error can play the same tune <note>literally: "blow the same pipe" (inflare tibiam), a Latin idiom for being in agreement</note>.

### THEOLOGICAL THESES.

I. Paul’s saying in Romans Chapter 14, verse 23—"Whatever is not from faith is sin"—is wrongly applied to saving faith <note>The author suggests this verse refers to acting against one's conscience rather than the specific doctrine of faith in Christ</note>.

II. The Catholic <note>original: "pontificii" (the Pope's) doctors</note> serve their cause poorly when they appeal to the Mystery of the Holy Trinity in an attempt to defend the doctrine of Transubstantiation <term>Transubstantiation: the Catholic belief that the bread and wine of the Eucharist become the actual body and blood of Christ</term>.

III. Since a Christian cannot know whether they have shared in the benefit of justification <term>justification: being declared righteous or "right with God"</term> except through a zeal for holiness, it is clear that no one can be certain of attaining salvation without a sincere pursuit of piety.

IV. Those who outlaw the free Examination of Religion strongly promote the vice of Unbelief.

V. Reason’s cultivation is so far from hindering religion that, rather, the more one exerts the powers of reason, the more clearly they perceive the excellence of the Christian religion.

VI. Those citizens and subjects who are permitted to follow the dictates of conscience in matters regarding religion are the most faithful to their Rulers.

VII. The truly demonstrative method—whether synthetic or analytic—which Mathematicians use, is wrongly applied in teaching the more sacred disciplines and in the interpretation of Holy Scripture <note>The author is likely critiquing the "Geometric" style of philosophy and theology popular in the early 18th century</note>.

## PART XI.

->Section I.<-

<margin>The connection with the preceding sections is shown.</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'I' housed within an architectural portal or gateway, featuring columns and topped with a cluster of fruit and leaves.</image-desc> In the preceding Dissertations written on this subject, we have, on the one hand, diligently investigated the causes of Unbelief, and, unless I am mistaken, we have uncovered the principal ones. On the other hand, we have presented the general arguments that Unbelievers use to plead their case, and we have shown what, in our opinion, can and should be answered in response to them. The time has now come—as the title of these Meditations promises—for us to discern what remedy should finally be applied to this serious disease, which is prevailing more and more every day. This will be provided both in this and in the following 12th Dissertation, if I live so long; once that is completed, we shall bring these Meditations to a close. Since the material for discussion is fertile, yet we wish to include everything that must be said within just two Dissertations, we will follow the main outlines of the matter and present the primary aids against Unbelief without a more long-winded explanation of every point. In my opinion, all things that must be observed in this argument can be conveniently reduced to three heads: First, certain <term>preventative <note>original: προφυλακτικὰ (prophylaktika)</note></term> means must be brought forward, as they

<column-break/>

<page-num>447</page-num>
<header>ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.</header>

are called, by which care is taken so that no one falls into this serious disease. Second, it must be considered how to treat those who seem to be leaning toward this vice; and Third, we must finally see how those who have crossed over into the camp of the Unbelievers, and have been seized by this serious illness, are to be led back to the right path.

<margin>The duty of parents regarding this business is directed.</margin> II. We must see, therefore, before all else, what must be provided so that men may be fortified against the serious and fatal disease of Unbelief. Everyone sees that it must be met early. Therefore, from youth itself, all those things must be sedulously avoided which could, little by little, engender a contempt for Religion in the mind. On the other hand, everything must be provided with all care and solicitude that can instill a love of piety and virtue into tender infants. And this care falls upon *Parents, Teachers, High Schools* <note>original: Gymnasiis</note> and *University Administrators*, *Sacred Orators* <note>meaning: preachers or clergy</note>, and finally the *Rulers* themselves. Let us begin with *Parents* and their duties regarding the Education of their children. It is well known that newborn infants are destitute of all the protections by which they might look out for themselves; it is necessary, therefore, that others take care of those things pertaining to the sustenance of life. Now indeed, this first care falls upon the Parents, whose offspring they are, and into whose souls the best Deity has implanted a certain and indeed most tender love—so much so, that unless they are plainly <term>devoid of natural affection <note>original: ἄστοργοι (astorgoi)</note></term> and of cast-off audacity, they can hardly pluck these stings from their souls. Moreover, the duties of Parents toward their Children can be referred to three heads. Namely, Parents ought to look to the mind, to the body, and finally to the Fortune <note>meaning: the financial future or social standing</note> of their children. I do not wish to speak at length here about the latter two, although they can give children ample occasion for having little care for Religion. For if from youth itself parents feed them only with delicate foods and render the body effeminate, it can easily happen that in the future they are delighted only by those things which can sweetly tickle the senses. But since religion emphasizes such duties that are very unpleasant to crooked desires, it is manifest that an education of this sort renders minds alienated from religion. As for what pertains to the Fortune and external happiness of Children, Parents can often be the cause of virtue and religion failing to take root in the souls of their Children, and this can happen for various reasons: for example, when Parents squander their goods early enough, it often happens that the Children are either driven to despair, or are held to choose such a way of life in which they must be solely concerned with winning their daily bread. However, they ought to have the greatest regard for the culture of the mind.

<header>MEDITATION XI.</header>

**Parents:** It is well known that infants, newly brought into the light of day, live in ignorance of all things, especially divine matters. Certainly, once they have learned to express the feelings of their minds, we find no trace of any innate ideas concerning God and divine things, even though some—supported by no actual experience—assert this to be the case. <note>The author is siding with the "tabula rasa" (blank slate) theory of John Locke, arguing that children aren't born with the concept of God already in their heads.</note> It is equally manifest that they are driven to act or to refrain from acting by pain and pleasure. It is necessary, therefore, that help be brought from elsewhere to properly perfect the faculties of the mind. Parents must, above all else, be persuaded that the chief part of their duties toward their children consists in caring for the cultivation of their reason. This is achieved through the knowledge of the most excellent things and a love of virtue. Therefore, there are certain things parents must avoid, and certain things they must provide. Parents must take care lest, through their own neglect or bad example, such sentiments and opinions are instilled into tender infants that might, as they reach a more mature age, alienate their minds from the love of religion and virtue. On the other hand, they must strive with all zeal and mental effort to ensure that, as much as lies within them, a reverence for the Divine Power is fixed deeply in their souls, so that as they grow in age, it may produce joyful sprouts. We shall offer some advice on both points, though we refer the reader who is eager for more on these matters to those celebrated authors who have written dedicated works on the Education of Children. (*)

<margin>A detailed explanation of what parents must avoid.</margin> III. Above all, parents must be persuaded that infants are committed primarily to their own care, and not to the care of others—that is, to servants and maids. For God, who granted them these "pledges of love" <note>original: "pignora," a common Latin term for children as tokens of affection</note>, wills by that very act that parents be as solicitous as possible for their salvation. The primary happiness of children, as we said before, is placed in this: that they be adorned with distinguished qualities of mind and virtues, among which true piety stands preeminent. However, it is well known that most servants and maids are equipped with very little knowledge of pure and chaste Religion, and thus cannot hand down the first elements of piety to tender minds. Therefore, first (I), care must be taken that infants are not imbued early on with silly, fabulous, and superstitious opinions. It is common knowledge that maids and nurses—either to get them to sleep or to stop them from crying—tell children many stories that are ridiculous and absurd, for example, about specters and "lemurs" <note>original: "lemuribus." In Roman mythology, these were restless or malevolent spirits of the dead. Here, it refers to ghost stories or "bogeymen."</note>. Although these things may not be told with evil intent, they nonetheless leave deep and bitter roots in the minds of infants. Often these ridiculous fables even harm their health, as they not infrequently excite fear in their minds when night falls. When, therefore, parents notice that old women are handing down such silly fables to the little ones...

(*) Such authors include Fénelon, Crousaz, Locke, Tillotson, Sulzer, and many others. <note>These were prominent Enlightenment-era thinkers on education and philosophy.</note>

...they must be severely rebuked and ordered instead to explain to the infants those little stories which can both delight and be of use.

II. Nor should parents permit servants or maids to prescribe formulas of prayer and impress them upon the memory of infants according to their own whim or habit; for often these prayers either convey no meaning at all or are not suited to that age. Instead, the parents themselves should hand down to the boys and girls short and meaningful little prayers, and recite them in such a way that it is clear from their voice and gestures that the things being recited are worthy of the greatest possible attention.

III. Parents must take care lest they themselves, in the sight of their children (though this should always be avoided), provide the occasion through words or deeds for them to drink in distorted opinions about religion and virtue. This latter thing usually happens (a) if they speak of religious matters without due reverence, or if they shamelessly pour out their own conceived doubts about religion. Boys and girls tend to be more observant of these things than is commonly thought. The worst part of this business is that, once they have seized upon these opinions, they not infrequently grow accustomed to defending them by the authority of their own parents. (b) This also happens through the reckless habit of swearing. For children come to think that such a frequent habit of swearing either brings grace and ornament to speech, or is at least permissible. When they later learn the Ten Commandments and hear that "the name of the Lord must not be taken in vain," they do not believe they must adhere to this very strictly. When, later on, as they grow older, they hear that false oaths are extremely frequent among Christians, they are confirmed in their opinion. (c) Nor should parents speak much in the presence of their children about the excellence of riches, the beauty of form, the splendor of houses and villas, or the variety of food and drink and various types of delicacies. Otherwise, as sad experience alas! teaches, they easily believe that all true happiness is placed in the possession of these goods, and that money and other goods praised so highly must be sought first, and "virtue after money." <note>original: "virtutem post numos," a reference to the Roman poet Horace, who satirized those who prioritized wealth over character.</note> For since boys and girls gape most at those things which are pleasing and acceptable to the senses, they are carried toward such goods with incredible desire, and are often thereafter captivated by these delights throughout their whole lives. They declare those who lack these goods to be most unhappy; yet it is hardly possible for such people to seek any remarkable pleasure in the study of virtue and the exercises of piety.

(d) Parents must restrain themselves from quarrels, contentions, and brawls, but especially from coarse imprecations against themselves. For when infants notice such things, not only does their reverence toward their parents—whom they ought to love and honor—diminish...

...[the piety] is gradually diminished and often extinguished; but they are also invited, as it were, to commit similar acts against others, whereby the love of piety toward others is not a little undermined. (e) Above all, the ignorance of parents in matters pertaining to the true knowledge of religion and the worship of the Divine Power <term>Numen</term> <note>The author uses 'Numen' to refer to the Divine Will or Power, a common term in Enlightenment-era Latin for God’s active presence in the world.</note> greatly promotes impiety in children. For what they themselves do not value highly, they will not carefully commend to their children as they are bound to do. Hence such parents very rarely speak of God, of divine matters, of the excellence of virtue and its remarkable fruits, or of the foulness of vices; from which children conclude that these things do little to promote human happiness. Likewise, parents who frequently blurt out obscene and foul things in the presence of their children, or who gladly and frequently recite and amplify foul slanders spread against others without foundation, violently suppress the study of piety in the minds of children.

<margin>It is shown what must be performed by parents.</margin>
IV. After having briefly warned what parents ought to beware of and avoid, we shall show in a few words what they must perform. These consist of the following points: I. From a tender age, as much as the stage of life allows, reverence for the Divine Power must be implanted in children. To that end, one must very frequently discuss with them the wisdom, power, and goodness of the Divine Power, and the excellence and utility of virtue. II. Religion—that is, the sincere love and worship of God—must be represented as something that can promote our true happiness. One should not use fictions or hyperboles, but the clearest and simplest reasons. These must be repeatedly told, inculcated, and fixed in this fluid age. III. Religion is not to be depicted as something very gloomy and troublesome, but as something lovely and pleasant; and it must be shown that all duties of piety are not only consistent with reason, but also so arranged that if we perform them rightly, we most certainly promote our own happiness. Specifically, such duties are the following: that the best, wisest, and most beneficent God is to be loved and worshiped above all things; that all our trust is to be placed in Him; that prayers are to be poured out to Him; that we must comply with His will, which is always holy and beneficial to us; that we must provide to our neighbor what we would rightly wish to be provided to us; and finally, that our internal and external happiness is promoted by virtue, etc. IV. When boys or girls are entirely fixed upon youthful joys and games, they should not be dragged away immediately for prayers or other duties of piety to be performed at set hours; for they do this with resisting minds and, little by little, not

only become accustomed to pouring out prayers without attention, but they also view religion itself as something very burdensome and troublesome; by which fact they are drawn away from the love of it rather than led toward it. V. Nothing concerning the articles of religion is to be inculcated in children without a clear explanation. If this is not observed early, they settle for obscure ideas and are not later incited to a saving knowledge and love of religion. VI. Too many points concerning the articles of religion should not be fixed in the memory of tender infants at the same time. Even children of more fortunate talent are confused and fatigued by a multitude of things to be learned. <note>The author is criticizing "rote learning," where children memorize long passages without understanding the meaning.</note> Many parents sin in this regard, measuring the knowledge of religion with which their children are imbued by the multitude of prayers, maxims, and testimonies of Holy Scripture committed to memory. VII. Since depraved affections and inclinations toward evil manifest themselves early enough in infants, parents ought to oppose these with prudence, always adding a reason why this or that should be omitted. For although parents have enough authority to restrain the depraved impulses of children, it is better if reasons suited to the children's capacity are always added to the rebukes; for thus, as they grow in age, they feel that these things were disapproved or commended not because of the parents' authority, but because of the force of the reasons. (VIII.) It is incumbent upon the parents themselves to pour out frequent and ardent prayers to God for the salvation of their infants. For the more fluid and changeable this age is, the less they attend to what is saving and useful; the more it is known how subject improvident youth is to various accidents; and finally, the greater the love with which they follow their children, the more frequently they ought to pour out prayers to God for them and implore His help.

<margin>It is shown what must be performed in this matter by teachers.</margin>
V. We come now in the second place to the teachers of public schools, to see what they must perform in this matter. And here, first of all, since there are various classes of students according to the diversity of age and progress, we take it as certain that teachers will take account of those levels in the business of religion; although other disciplines should also be taught in such a way that when higher levels are reached, they serve the cultivation of reason and the study of virtue.

First, therefore, it is required of teachers that they briefly deliver and explain the principal heads of religion to the juniors, proving them by one or two arguments suited to their capacity. These must be frequently repeated and inculcated, and it must be ensured, as much as the nature of things and the capacity of their talents permit, that they have an accurate [understanding] of those articles.

# MEDITATION XI.
<meta>catchword: jorem</meta>

...should have knowledge. Summaries <term>Compendia</term> <note>These were short textbooks or handbooks used in the 18th century to provide students with a simplified overview of complex subjects.</note> of this kind exist everywhere, and their number increases daily, which is a blessing of our age. Meanwhile, however briefly and simply they are written, they are of little use unless the skill and wisdom of the teacher is added. Truly, in passing on the simplest truths, there is need for the greatest dexterity and a sharp edge of judgment. Nor is it as easy as some persuade themselves to rightly lay the first foundations of disciplines and religion.

(II.) These first and principal chapters of religion must be proposed in a style that is most clear and simple. For if teachers hand down the articles of religion to children using highly figurative words, the children will cling to them stubbornly and rest in them even if they are not sufficiently understood; then, if you later change the phrases or use clearer words, they are stunned and think the things themselves are being changed. I would not give this warning unless I had discovered that this disease—that is, the habit of expressing matters pertaining to religion in figurative words—had penetrated the schools themselves. Hence some children cannot even pour out prayers without using metaphorical expressions.

(III.) Whatever is handed down and instilled in students concerning religion must be explained in such a way that, as far as the nature of the subject allows, they cannot help but understand it. It can hardly be expressed in words how much utility this advice has as they grow older: for thus, little by little, there arises in their minds a clear and solid knowledge of truths. When they recall these truths to their conscience, they cannot help but feel their power, nor will they allow themselves to be carried away from a true and right sense of religion by a mixture of confused phrases.

(IV.) To achieve this, frequent catechetical exercises <note>A method of teaching using a question-and-answer format to test a student's comprehension rather than just their memory.</note> must be established, held for the specific purpose of making it clear how they understand the truths proposed. And here, the backwards custom of some is not to be followed, who—once a student has brought forward a sentence or testimony—discourse at length on the argument as if they were performing the office of a preacher. The main goal, however, is to know how the children understand the truths handed down, not how great the teacher's skill in divine matters might be. And here also there is need for greater art than is commonly thought. For the thoughts lying hidden in the minds of the children must be drawn out by questions and inquiries, and these must be corrected or approved: in this way, they become accustomed to meditating rightly on divine as well as human affairs.

(V.) In general, however, teachers must strive toward this: that they always have a greater...

...greater regard for judgment than for memory; for unless this is done, children will never arrive at a solid knowledge of human and divine matters. From this it is also manifest that it is necessary for teachers themselves, whatever part of the disciplines they are about to hand down, to be imbued with the precepts of the art of thinking <term>ars cogitandi</term> <note>The "Art of Thinking" usually refers to Logic, specifically influenced by the "Port-Royal Logic" which emphasized clear reasoning over formal syllogisms.</note>. In this way, the reason for their instruction will always be clear. From this also, this fruit will be born: that the more the children grow in age, the more they will learn the disciplines with joy and mental effort, for thus they perceive their use. But when things are committed to memory which they either do not understand at all, or at least not sufficiently, they apply their minds unwillingly to the prescribed tasks, and they begin to hate letters <note>meaning "literature" or "learning" in general</note> before they have acquired a more accurate knowledge of them. 

(VI.) Religion itself, and the precepts of God, must not only be represented to children as most agreeable to reason and most useful in all of life, but it must also be instilled in them that these things will later be very easy to perform if they obey them early. For young people are, as is known, so constituted by nature that they flee from everything that is troublesome and pursue only those things which seem pleasant to them. Therefore, the precepts of religion and virtue are to be handed down with a serene face, not a gloomy or "masterly" <note>haughty or overly authoritative</note> one. When religion is hammered in with a rod and a switch, the soul, struck by fear, ceases to love the thing itself, and values religion no more than the rules of grammar. 

(VII.) The chapters on natural theology <note>The study of God based on reason and the observation of nature, rather than solely on revelation or scripture.</note> and the truth of the Christian religion are to be diligently instilled according to the capacity of the child's age, and one must never stop fixing this doctrine in their minds. It must not be thought that children are incapable of understanding these truths! Experience has often taught me the contrary. But the teacher ought to hand down these truths by an easy method, and cut away all those things which belong to a more subtle demonstration of these truths, deferring them to another time. How this business ought to be established was shown by his own example by the Blessed <note>original: "ὁ Μακαρίτης" (ho Makaritēs)</note> and Venerable *Ostervald* in his *Catechism*. <note>Jean-Frédéric Ostervald (1663–1747) was a Swiss Protestant pastor known for his influential and practical approach to religious instruction.</note> Truly, what I am instilling here is of greater importance than is commonly thought. There are teachers who think they have performed their duty excellently if the children hold the entire Catechism in their memory, even though they do not rightly understand the principal articles contained in it. Often they also urge truths of lesser weight no less than the gravest ones, about which more will be said below. 

(VIII.) On every given occasion, the minds of children must be fortified against common, false, and superstitious opinions, which they either hear at home or have received from their classmates: for those opinions are for the most part enemies to pure religion...

...and take deep roots in our souls. I well remember that time when, in spring and summer, I sat upon the grass with my fellow students; with singular delight, we shared marvelous little tales of ghosts and spirits <term>lemures</term> <note>In Roman mythology, 'lemures' were the restless spirits of the dead who returned to haunt the living. The author uses this to describe the "boogeymen" of childhood.</note> and ominous stories about the immense power of witches. These ideas were so deeply ingrained in our minds that, even as grown men, we have scarcely been able to cast them aside. Teachers have many opportunities to speak of these matters and to debunk those <term>monstrous tales</term> <note>original: *τερατολογίας* (teratologias). This refers to the telling of tall tales, myths, or accounts of wonders that defy reason.</note>. It is a very bad thing that many people—imbued with such opinions but not cultivated by more rigorous disciplines, nor sufficiently knowledgeable in religion—begin to doubt religion itself when they live among foreigners and hear such stories debunked and <term>mocked openly</term> <note>original: *albis dentibus rideri* (literally "laughed at with white teeth"). This idiom suggests being held up to public ridicule or scorn.</note>. (IX.) As boys grow older and learn excellent sentiments drawn from Greek and Latin writers, it must be shown to them that the most distinguished men of every age took delight in these writings, not only for the purity and elegance of the style, but primarily for the purpose of drawing from them excellent precepts for living rightly. In this regard, teachers of the upper classes would do well to study the treatise by the most learned **Rollin**, *On the Method of Teaching Humanities* <note>Charles Rollin (1661–1741) was a famous French historian and educator whose works on education were highly influential in the 18th century.</note>. For it must be constantly repeated to boys that what they learn ought to be useful, and that languages are learned primarily so that we may apply to our own lives the noble words and deeds found in the writings of the most excellent men. (X.) As they age, they must progress deeper into the matter of religion, yet in such a way that the primary and most important principles are not only instilled and repeated time and again, but are also placed, little by little, in a clearer light according to their age and intellect. This should be understood to apply not only to theoretical articles of faith, but also to practical ones; indeed, nothing should be taught that is not serious, momentous, and useful, bringing with it its own advantages and true incentives toward piety. Mere hypotheses and minor controversies should be omitted at this age. (XI.) Students should be shown early on how much bad passions harm both the mind and the body, and, conversely, how much benefit the study of virtue brings. Finally, through examples—such as those of **Joseph** and the **Prodigal Son**—it should be demonstrated how completely different the outcomes of virtue and vice truly are. For these examples penetrate deeper into the souls of the young than bare precepts alone. (*) (XII.)

(XII.) —whenever teachers notice a student becoming arrogant—or <term>lifting his crest</term> <note>An idiom meaning to become conceited or stuck-up.</note>—because of some bit of scientific knowledge, this vice must be resisted early. It must be shown that this is not only a major obstacle to knowing the truth, but that such people are exposed to the laughter of all wise men. (XIII.) Indeed, even wicked men have often been touched, whether they wished it or not, by a sense of veneration for men who excel in piety and virtue.

<margin>On the duties of those who handle the more serious disciplines.</margin>
VI. We come now to those Doctors who teach the more serious disciplines in Universities and Gymnasiums <note>In this context, a Gymnasium refers to an advanced secondary school that prepared students for university.</note>, to see what they must provide when they wish to fortify their listeners against the danger of Unbelief and impiety. Most public teachers, even if they do not teach Theology, can contribute much to this task. Professors of the Humanities should certainly strive to ensure that students of the best literature rightly learn the elegance of Latin and Greek speech; however, they too can contribute much that can commend religion and wisdom, and this in two ways: the *first* is when they show their listeners how much reason is corrupted and weakened by depraved superstition, and how shamefully the most excellent men of Antiquity neglected the cultivation of reason. Because of this, they fell into many vices; contrast this with the happy condition of those who, from early youth, have been cultivated in the noblest disciplines far from all superstition, and were born in those places where pure and chaste religion flourishes. This must be shown through clear examples when the opportunity arises. The *second* way is if they show the students of the elegant arts that the most excellent and learned men of Antiquity not only clearly distinguished religion from superstition, but also always considered virtue as the principal pillar of public and private happiness. They viewed those men who declared war on all religion as a plague upon Empires and Nations...

...concerns of the states. To this end, students of the <term>humanities</term> <note>original: *humaniorum Litterarum*; the study of classical Greek and Roman literature, grammar, and rhetoric.</note> must be advised that they should attend not only to the style, but also to the subject matter itself. They should not merely smear excellent precepts for the pursuit of virtue onto paper, but should fix them deeply in their minds. For this is the chief fruit of reading the ancient writers and the masters of wisdom. To this end, teachers should read various *Chrestomathies* <note>Collections of choice passages from literature used for learning a language.</note> written by several learned men, in which excellent moral precepts are contained. Recently, through the work of the celebrated *Altmann*, there were published in Zurich excellent moral maxims sought from the books of *Cicero* and collected by the most learned Abbot *d'Olivet*, to which the editor added notes full of good fruit, written in the German language. Regarding the method by which the reading of the Greeks and Latins should be established so that it also aids morals, the previously praised *Rollin* has taught best in the third volume of his commended book, *On the Manner of Teaching and Studying the Humanities*. To these should be added what the most learned *Le Clerc* advised in the first chapter of his *Philological Miscellanies* added to the dialogues of *Aeschines the Socratic*. For the same purpose, our most celebrated and close colleague *Breitinger* recently collected excerpts <term>Eclogues</term> from the best Greek writers for the benefit of students and illustrated them with notes; these were published this very year in Zurich by the press of *Conrad Orell*.

But some testimonies of the ancients regarding this argument must be brought forward for the sake of our listeners, by which what I have said may be confirmed. *Quintilian*, in Book I, Chapter [8], declares: <note>original: *Tenere mentes, non modo quae diserta, sed vel magis quae honesta sunt discant.*</note> *"Let them hold their minds so that they learn not only what is eloquent, but even more what is honorable."* Therefore, you should choose not only the authors, but even specific parts of their works. For the Greeks wrote many things licentiously, and I would not wish to interpret *Horace* in certain passages. *Valerius Maximus*, in Book VI, Chapter 3, tells this of the lustful poet *Archilochus*: *"The Spartans ordered the books of Archilochus to be carried out of their city, because they considered the reading of them to be insufficiently modest and chaste. For they did not want the minds of their children to be imbued with things that might harm their morals more than they might benefit their wits."* Thus, they punished with exile the songs of a very great poet—or certainly one next to the greatest—because he had scarred a house hateful to him with obscene words.

Regarding divine worship and its necessity, *Cicero* spoke this way among others in *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book II, Section 28: <note>original: *Deos & venerari & colere debemus...*</note> *"We ought both to revere and worship the gods: moreover, the best worship of the gods, as well as the most chaste, most holy, and most full of piety, is that we always revere them with a pure, upright, and incorrupt mind and voice; for not only philosophers, but also our ancestors, separated superstition from religion."* In *On the Laws*, Book II, Section 7, he speaks thus: *"Let this, therefore, be persuaded to our citizens from the beginning: that the gods are the masters and regulators of all things, and that those things which are done are done by their authority*

and power; and that they deserve best of the human race; and that they observe what sort of person everyone is, what he does, what he admits into himself, with what mind and with what piety he observes religious rites; and that they take account of the pious and the impious. Who would deny that these opinions are useful, when he understands how many things are strengthened by an oath; how great is the safety in the religious sanctity of treaties; how many the fear of divine punishment has recalled from crime; and how holy is the society of citizens among themselves, when the immortal gods are interposed both as judges and witnesses?"

I will add only one testimony to these, namely that of *Arrian*, the most celebrated Stoic, who, disputing against the Epicureans and Academics, declares thus in Book II, Chapter 20, according to the version of *H. Wolf*: "What do you say, Philosopher? What indeed do you think about piety and sanctity? If you wish, shall I show that they are good things? By all means, show it, so that our citizens may be converted to the worship of the Divine Power and cast aside their neglect of the greatest matters. Do you have proofs? I have them. And I am grateful to you. Since, therefore, those things please you greatly, take the contrary: that the gods neither exist, nor if they exist, do they care for men; nor does any society exist between us and them; but that this piety and sanctity celebrated by the common run of men is a fiction of arrogant men and sophists and even of lawmakers for the purpose of terrifying and restraining wrongdoers. Well done, Philosopher! You have helped our citizens; you have already recalled the entire youth to a contempt for divine laws. What then? Accept now that justice is nothing. That shame is folly. That a father is nothing, a son nothing. Bravo, Philosopher! Go on, persuade the youth of these things, so that we may have more who both feel and say the same. Well-constituted Republics have been increased for us by these speeches! Sparta was formed by this kind of oratory! Lycurgus introduced these persuasions by his laws and institutions: that to be a slave is not more shameful than honorable, nor is liberty more honorable than shameful. Those who fell at Thermopylae fell because of these decrees! And the Athenians—for what other reasons did they abandon their city? And yet those who say such things take wives, procreate children, take part in the Republic, and appoint priests and prophets for themselves. Of whom? Of those who do not exist! And they themselves consult the <term>Pythia</term> <note>The priestess of the Oracle of Apollo at Delphi.</note> so that they may hear falsehoods, and they interpret oracles for others. O singular impudence and imposture!"

<margin>More is presented concerning the same duty.</margin>
VII. Furthermore, Professors of the philosophical disciplines can contribute much to the love and defense of religion. I shall briefly set forth what they ought to provide. And (I) indeed, it must be shown in a general way to those cultivating the best Literature how great and how precious a benefit of God it is that He has granted us the faculty of knowing both divine and human matters, as much as is necessary to promote our happiness. By the help of this faculty, not only are various arts and disciplines profitable to the human race learned, but also the virtues and will of the highest Divinity are known. From this, it is to be concluded that all the nerves of our talent must be strained toward cultivating this faculty granted to us from heaven. (II) Students are to be fortified against those Teachers who are accustomed to speak less circumspectly about the *use of reason* in Theology. For there are, alas! many who think they will greatly strengthen religion if, on any given occasion, they rave against reason and the study of Philosophy. They cannot, however, help but lead cautious men and those less skilled in the art of reasoning into the opinion that revealed religion delivers things that could in no way be brought into harmony with the decrees of right reason, which is a most pestilential error. *Pierre Bayle* <note>original: *P. Baylius*; a French philosopher (1647–1706) known for his influential *Historical and Critical Dictionary* which often used skeptical reasoning.</note> used, or rather abused, this worst of arts, not to defend religion and fix it most deeply in minds, but to render it suspect, or at least to demonstrate the sharpness of his own talent and his readiness and capacity for disputing on either side of any matter. Finally, it must be shown that it is only "shadowy" teachers <note>original: *Doctores umbraticos*; referring to those who live in the shadows of libraries or cloisters, lacking practical or enlightened perspective.</note>, ignorant of Philosophy, who thunder without distinction against those who diligently apply themselves to the cultivation of reason. On the contrary, it must be frequently repeated that the more one exerts the powers of reason, the more one will perceive the celestial origin of the Christian religion. Moreover, it must be proven by the induction of examples that many have fallen into Atheism or Deism because they did not sufficiently cultivate reason and neglected the study of Philosophy. The most celebrated *Le Clerc* <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), a Genevan theologian and scholar.</note> proved this in an entire chapter in his excellent little book *On the Causes of Unbelief* <note>original: *de causis incredulitatis*</note>. Let us assert one or two points from chapter IV.

> *There are people (he says) <note>original: *inquit*; Le Clerc's original text here is in French.</note> who have been occupied from their childhood in a trade, or in a demanding business, or in some other more significant occupation, without anyone having taken any care to form their minds, nor even to instruct them in Religion; and who, moreover, having found themselves of a natural disposition little suited to conceiving*

<meta>catchword: rele-</meta>

---

<page-num>459</page-num>
<header>ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.</header>

> *lofty things, yet nonetheless proud and presumptuous, have come to a mature age without further instruction and without correcting their Pride. These people are rarely well-persuaded of the truth of the Christian Religion; they even often reject it entirely, or at least in part; not only because they are ignorant of the proofs, but also because they do not understand them when they hear them spoken by those who know them. These gross and blind spirits imagine that there is nothing true except what the senses make them perceive, or what they have recognized by their own experience to be possible, or finally, what is found to be in conformity with their passions. It is not only among people occupied with a trade or a business that this kind of unbeliever is found; there are perhaps even more among those who aspire to great Offices, among men of the sword <note>original: *Gens d’épée*; the military nobility.</note>, and in general among persons of Quality. One might say that these kinds of persons have received more education than others regarding the manners of the world or the positions for which they were destined. But at heart, it is as common to hear this sort of person reasoning pitifully on Religion as the crudest among the populace. When they have grown old in thoughts little conforming to Christianity, their natural vanity, increased by age, renders them more stubborn and sometimes altogether inaccessible to the truth. It is in vain that one proposes to them the most convincing arguments; they look upon them as pure sophisms, although they do not know in what a Sophism differs from solid reasoning.*

Compare Chapter V, Part I of the same book. (III) The doctrine concerning <term>prejudices</term> <note>original: *præjudiciis*; here meaning pre-judgments or biases that cloud the mind before investigation.</note> leading men away from the knowledge of truth must be thoroughly instilled and illustrated with various examples; especially, it must be shown how much these harm religion, how easily they cast it into grave errors, or confirm those rashly admitted. Especially in this "slippery age," the prejudices of antiquity and novelty must be countered. Young men of more eager talent wish to rush toward the glory of Erudition sooner than is right, and they think they will easily obtain it if they bring forth new and paradoxical opinions; others, to whom a servile talent has fallen, prefer to follow the crowd of Predecessors and Elders. Both are to be exhorted to a serious love of the truth. Public Teachers must take special care lest they hold a Young man of more upright talent in hatred because he clings to new opinions; for by acting in this way, they easily bring not only themselves into contempt, but also those things which are being taught—though they be most excellent—are afterwards despised. (IV) Likewise, the doctrine of demonstration, and of the various degrees of <term>probability</term> <note>original: *verisimilitudinis*; literally "truth-likeness," a key concept in 18th-century logic regarding things that cannot be proven with absolute mathematical certainty.</note>, must be thoroughly...

must be emphasized; for in this way they learn how assent must be moderated, and how many things are required for a demonstration in the true sense of the word: it must be taught that a true demonstration concerns abstract and adequate ideas, such as those we find in numbers and figures; in other disciplines, we must for the most part be content with certain degrees of probability; therefore, those act foolishly who refuse to assent to certain truths because they have not been raised to the highest degree of evidence, and so on. These principles are then easily transferred to the holier disciplines <note>In this context, "holier disciplines" refers to Theology and the study of Scripture</note>. Nor will it be useless—since *Professors of Philosophy* ought to treat of speech and its legitimate use—to recommend to their listeners that excellent little book by *the late celebrated Werenfels, On the Word-Wars of the Learned* <note>original Latin: *τῷ Μακαρίτῃ Celeb. Werenfelsii de Logomachiis Eruditorum*; Samuel Werenfels (1657–1740) was a Swiss theologian famous for critiqued scholars who argued over terminology rather than substance</note>; for thus they learn early on what the sources of this evil are: how great the dissensions that have very often arisen because of them, even among brothers; how shamefully those have behaved who have stirred up the bitterest contentions either over words or over things of no importance, and how these must be countered.

Those who teach *Physics* <term>Physics: In the 18th century, "Physics" referred to "Natural Philosophy"—the study of the natural world, biology, and the laws of the universe</term> to students of the Liberal Arts should, for our purpose, primarily provide two things. The first is that, through the introduction of many examples, they should prove how imperfect our knowledge is concerning the essence of even the smallest bodies; how difficult it is for us, even through experiments, to penetrate into the causes of the innumerable effects occurring in nature: for thus they are taught little by little that it is no wonder if certain things more difficult to know are found in revelation itself. The already praised *late celebrated Werenfels* <note>original Greek: *ὁ Μακαρίτης* (the late/blessed one)</note> showed this use of physics through the example of the atom, whose *Epigram* on the infinity of parts in any body is also worth reading. The second consists in this: that he who explains physics to young men—who in their own time will perform the office of *Pastors* (of whom there is always a larger number than of others)—should show the ends and purposes of the *Creator*, and lead them to the *Veneration of the Divinity*, in such a way that, according to the measure of their age and capacity of their minds, they may feel that nothing was done by the *Best Divinity* <note>original: *Optimo Numine*</note> rashly or without cause, but that all things have been directed toward the wisest ends; consequently, it is impious and foolish to wish to find fault with the Author of nature because we cannot count on our fingers the uses and ends of every single body surrounding us. But since there is need for skill in the art of reasoning and an accurate use of judgment for demonstrating and understanding religion, and the *Mathematical* disciplines are very powerful for sharpening the mind, even the cultivators of the holier disciplines do not act badly if they devote themselves to these disciplines, as far as other studies permit,

<meta>catchword: at least</meta>

at least to the end that they may be very strong in reasoning. *The celebrated Werenfels*, after advising in Chapter 10 *On the Word-Wars of the Learned* that students at a tender age should not be too accustomed to the habit of contradicting, suggests that to avoid this evil, they should be thoroughly practiced in the mathematical disciplines. I, however, think they should be employed for sharpening the mind and for judging those things which are to be discerned in divine and human affairs. *Let them be exercised (he says on page 572) in those things where there is no room for disputes, such as arithmetic and geometric disputes, against which, if anyone wished to argue, he would be deservedly laughed at by everyone: which disciplines are also most useful for our purpose because no others lead us more from words to the things themselves. These alone have been thoroughly purged of all terms that signify nothing: In these alone, no one is deceived by the fact that, while remembering certain words to which no distinct notion in the mind corresponds, he seems to himself to understand the thing itself. I know that not everyone is permitted to grow old in these arts, but as a preliminary education* <note>original Greek: *προπαιδείας* (propaideias)</note> *to make a trial of them—at least for the end that we may learn early on to discern what it is to know and what it is to not know, and therefore, what we ourselves know and what we do not know, where we hold mere words and where we hold the things themselves—is permitted to everyone and useful to everyone, if not necessary.* Those who publicly teach *Ethics, whether Philosophical or Evangelical*, have a very wide opportunity to fortify their listeners against grave errors that are enemies to piety. Since all things emphasized by them tend toward the study of piety, there is no need for me to show in more detail in what way they can encounter this evil. (*) One

> (*) *Socrates*, easily the leader among the philosophers of the ancient age, bestowed the first praise upon *Moral Philosophy* <note>Ethics</note> among the other disciplines, as showing the way to true happiness: but he thought the others should be cultivated only insofar as they served this principal end, and he prudently advised that a limit must be kept in the study of wisdom. A famous passage on this matter exists in *Xenophon's Memorabilia, Book 4*, where he discusses it as follows, according to the version <note>the Latin translation of Xenophon being cited</note>: *He used to say that Geometry should be learned only so far as one could, if the need arose, either receive land by a correct method of measuring, or hand it over, or distribute it, or design a work. And this was so easy to learn that he who turned his mind to dimension could both know how large the earth itself was and depart with a known method of measuring; but he disapproved of progress in learning Geometry as far as descriptions difficult to understand. For he said he did not see what use that matter had, although he was not at all unacquainted with them: but he said they could consume a man's whole life and call him away from many other useful disciplines. He also encouraged them to exercise themselves in the doctrine of the stars <note>Astronomy</note> only so far as they could know the times of the night, the month, and the year, both for the sake of travel and navigation, and for the watch, and other things—whatever is done either through the night, or in the month, or in the year—so that they might use certain signs for these things, by which they might distinguish their times. And these things could easily be learned by those who hunt wild beasts by night, and by pilots of ships, and many others whose care it is to know these things. But to progress so far in learning Astronomy until even those things...*

...it will not be superfluous to have advised only one or two more things. And first, indeed, I would not want the minds of the Students to be held by various scholastic quibbles <note>original Latin: *scholaſticis quæſtiunculis*; these are the overly technical, often hair-splitting debates typical of medieval university philosophy</note> and distinctions; rather, I believe that those things which pertain to the pursuit of piety ought to be introduced with clear words and solid arguments. (**II.**) The duties of piety must not be urged in such a way that the performance of such duties could in no way be achieved even by a person of the best character and most reverent toward God. For such exaggerations, expressed in hyperbolic words, are so far from' inflaming the minds of men toward the pursuit of true piety that they instead call them away from the love of it. For by this very fact—because they perceive those things to be plainly impossible to perform—they are seized by a certain listlessness and lukewarmness. I will say nothing now of the many mystic booklets, and those which differ little from them, coming from I know not what "workshops of practical piety," in which things that should be proven and introduced with the clearest words and solid reasons are instead delivered in obscure and bombastic language—an evil about which I remember complaining elsewhere.

But especially (**III.**), the **doctrine of the affects** <term>Affects: In 18th-century philosophy, "affects" or "passions" referred to emotions like anger, lust, or pride that were thought to cloud rational judgment</term> must be diligently instilled in Students of Literature, and it must be demonstrated part by part how much those depraved commotions of the mind hinder not only the cultivation of letters and human happiness, but even talent and judgment itself; and how easily they pull men away from the love of religion (*) and, by the introduction of many examples, it must be shown how many men, not lacking in talent and learning, have been driven headlong by the allurements of the passions, and how many have fallen into the vice of unbelief—not for grave and momentous reasons, but...

---

> <note>This section is a paraphrased reference to the teachings of Socrates, likely drawn from Xenophon’s *Memorabilia*</note> ...they should recognize things that are not within the same reach; and he strongly discouraged them from tormenting themselves for a long time by inquiring into the wandering and straying stars <note>planets</note>, their intervals from the earth, their circuits, and their causes. Indeed, he said he saw no utility even in these things, although he was not ignorant of them; and he even added that a man’s life could be consumed by these studies, keeping him from many useful things. Finally, he discouraged anyone from expending study and effort on celestial matters in general—namely, by what craftsmanship God brings all things to pass. For he did not think these things could be discovered by men, nor did he believe he was doing a favor to the Gods by inquiring into those things which they did not wish to be manifest. He also encouraged them to learn the principles of numbers <note>arithmetic</note>, and in this, as in other things, he advised them to beware of vain occupation; he himself investigated this only so far as it was useful, and searched into it alongside his close friends. He also strongly encouraged his friends to take care of their health, partly by learning what they could from experts, and partly by observing themselves throughout their lives—what food, what drink, and what labor suited them, and how by using these they could enjoy the best possible health. For if someone took such account of himself, he said, it would be difficult for that person to find a physician who could judge what leads to health better than himself. If anyone wished to attain things greater than human wisdom allows, he gave this advice: that he should apply himself to divination <note>seeking divine revelation or prophecy</note>.

<page-num>463</page-num>
<header>ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.</header>

...but because of the judgments of these worst of counselors <note>referring back to the "passions" mentioned on the previous page</note>, they have fallen into the vice of **incredulity** and have thus stirred up the most harmful dangers for themselves. Furthermore, (**IV.**) the public Teacher of this most noble discipline will persuade his listeners to examine all the affairs of life—especially those which contribute to our religion and happiness—**without passion** <note>original Greek: *ἄνευ πάθους*</note>, and not to inquire whether these or those precepts are pleasing and acceptable to our emotions; but rather whether they are useful, consistent with the nature of things, and fitting for religion. If the minds of the Listeners are rightly imbued with these precepts, there is hope that they will weigh the more sublime headings of religion with a serene countenance.

Truly, so that wise young men may properly and accurately know that nothing should be done or established rashly—as in the other affairs of human life, so especially in those matters where the religion and worship of the Deity are concerned—it is the duty of the Professors of **Natural Law** and **Christian Ethics** to rightly and solidly deliver the doctrine concerning the character, nature, and obligation of **conscience** and its various parts. They are, moreover, bound to diligently instill that, in order to keep and guard it purely, it is necessary for men to be imbued with an accurate knowledge of religion, and to measure all their thoughts and articles of faith against it as the most holy standard.

In particular, it must be shown that no one among mortals has authority over consciences, and that neither Rulers nor Ministers of religion have any power to thrust articles of religion upon others at their whim; but rather that religion is a business whose examination belongs to all men, whether they are destitute of revelation or not. In this way, cultivators of the best literature, when they become public Teachers, learn that they must not act in these matters according to their own command or the lack of self-control in their minds, nor must they insult those who disagree with them; but rather that it is lawful for others to appeal to the most sacred rights of conscience. It must be taught that error can easily creep into the mind of even the best and most learned person, and that it can only be removed by arguments. Religion is a **free matter**, and the faith of Christians rests not on fear or the authority of others, but on the certainty and excellence of revealed things. Thus the Listeners see that they are being dealt with honestly, and they are not commanded to blindly follow the crowd of those who came before them in the business of religion.

Finally, to add nothing of other disciplines, those who professedly teach **Church History** ought to advise this among other things: that pride, superstition, the desire to insult others, ignorance, and the craving for fame have been—and still are—the causes of the principal heresies, contentions, and lawsuits that have arisen in the Churches. These vices have often stirred up so many violent persecutions, and very frequently by the Ortho- <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "Ortho-," likely leading into "Orthodox"</note>

## MEDITATION XI.

Both the Orthodox and Heterodox have sinned gravely in this business <note>meaning the "business" of theological education and religious debate</note>. Indeed, by the introduction of historical examples, students should be led toward maintaining modesty in religious matters. Furthermore, on the occasion of disputes over matters of minor importance—which are found in both ancient and recent history—it must be impressed upon them that minute opinions are not to be rashly attacked, nor should "horns" <note>original: *cornua*; a Latin metaphor for aggressive, bull-like attacks</note> be immediately raised against any who disagree. At the same time, however, it must be shown how poorly those have always looked out for their own interests who have not only attacked the most sacred pillars of religion—whether natural or revealed—with various objections, but also, casting aside all shame, have often criticized them with bitter words. In this way, students can be led to preserve prudence in the most serious business of religion.

<margin>The duties of Professors of Theology are presented.</margin>

**VII.** Since it is primarily the duty of Professors of Theology to timely enjoin upon their students everything that can draw their minds away from the vice of Unbelief and impiety, and instead impress and recommend reverence for religion and piety, we must see individually what they are to perform in this case. 

**I.** First, students must be timely taught what the nature of Christian Theology is, and for what primary purpose it was communicated to mankind: namely, not to burden the brain with a mass of infinite questions, nor for disputing and quarreling, but for knowing the most health-giving truths <note>original: *saluberrimas*; truths that promote the health of the soul</note>, for practicing virtue, and for stirring others to perform their duties to the Deity. From this they can easily conclude that this discipline is most serious and useful, and it is not to be blamed that in many places it has been clouded by "shaggy" little questions <note>original: *hirsutis quæstiunculis*; meaning overly complex, tangled, or trivial academic debates</note>, but this must be attributed to vain, proud, and scholastic minds. 

**II.** Since, despite this, many students imbued with perverted opinions often frequent even public Universities, these opinions must be uprooted from their minds as much as possible. Now it is clear to public Teachers that many students are imbued with a most pestilential opinion: namely, that the study of true piety is nothing but an "accessory," while the "pinnacle" of this science is placed in the knowledge of learned, necessary, and unnecessary questions. Whence also—alas!—many are accustomed to wander through the side-paths of so many useful and useless little questions; teachers must exert every nerve of their talent to tear this deadly error out from their hearts by the roots. 

**III.** Since experience has proven that pride <note>original: *fastus*</note> prematurely corrupts even the best talents and leads them to contempt for religion, the public Teacher must strive with all his strength to uproot this harmful weed from the minds

<meta>catchword: minds</meta>

---

<page-num>465</page-num>
## ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

of his students, as far as he is able. For this evil ensures that, before they have properly examined and weighed the weightier articles of religion and the nobler parts pertaining to theological studies, they think magnificently of themselves on account of I know not what disorganized erudition. They not only embrace "paradoxical" <note>meaning contrary to received wisdom or fringe opinions</note> opinions scraped together from here and there, but also recommend them to others as if they were very precious merchandise. In this case, Teachers must use the **Socratic method**, and those who suspect no such thing must be led to self-knowledge; once slightly more difficult questions are brought forward, they must be so constrained and driven into a corner that they are affected by a healthy shame. 

**IV.** In all parts of this most sacred discipline, such books should be recommended to students of Holy Literature <note>original: *S. L. studiosis*, likely *Sacrarum Literarum*; students of the Bible and Theology</note> which are held to be most excellent by the judgment of the most learned men. This advice is as necessary as possible for various reasons. It is well known that, in Universities and preparatory schools alike, "Systems" <note>theological textbooks that attempt to categorize all Christian doctrine into one logical system</note> are often handed to students that are somewhat obscure, and are suited to the students' progress neither in their method nor in their choice of articles and arguments—to say nothing of other defects. Hence it often happens that young men of more excellent talent, having acquired some knowledge of theological and literary history, when they hear better things recommended to them, not only begin to feel nauseated by the publicly received booklets, but also, with perverted judgment, they unselectively devour all the booklets that fall into their hands and are praised here and there. Thus it often happens that they not only greedily read things of little profit, but also those things which can cast minds not yet fortified by "masculine" erudition <note>meaning robust, mature, and disciplined scholarship</note> into dangerous and doubtful opinions. 

A prudent Teacher can timely counter this evil—though such a teacher is not one who recommends only those things that please him, but one who, aided by the meditation and reading of the most excellent authors, beautifully understands theological disciplines and their weight, and is equipped with excellent talent. I would not add this if it were not sufficiently clear that most theologians recommend those writings which were once recommended to them by their own teachers, whence such disciples usually turn out to be "shadow-teachers" <note>original: *Doctores umbratici*; academic teachers who dwell in the "shadows" of the classroom without practical experience or fresh thought</note>, and they "go where the crowd goes, not where they ought to go." It is to be deplored—these are the words of the **Celebrated Pfaff** <note>**Christoph Matthäus Pfaff** (1686–1760), a influential Lutheran theologian known for his work on church law and education</note> in his dissertation on the vices of those who perform sacred duties:

> *...those who handle Sacred Letters, when they happen upon a Teacher who himself follows a false method of Theology, and they are captivated by love for him (for so it usually happens, that the intellect of students, which is a **blank slate** <note>original: *tabula rasa*</note>, yields to the first occupant, who fills it with his own lines and his own ideas), they also drink in and taste the same principles and the same heap of false prejudices.*

### MEDITATION XL.

->so that at last, when the matter has turned into a scrupulous conscience, it becomes a point of religion for them either to shrink even a hair’s breadth <note>original: "latum saltem unguem," a Roman idiom for the smallest possible distance</note> from this path, or to call into doubt, even for a moment, those things which are already inscribed on their minds. Hence, when they see someone depart even slightly from the common path, they immediately tremble and are distressed, as if "Hannibal were at the gates," <note>original: "Hannibal ante portas," a Latin proverb used to describe a state of extreme urgency or imminent danger</note> and as if the entire faith, shaken by a new storm, were tottering. Therefore, when a learned and perceptive Theologian recommends excellent books to his students, he never does so as if he believes all theological knowledge is contained in these alone, or as if he despises the writings of others. For by his authority, he would bring it about that they would not so much weigh the importance of things, but rather, carried away by blind admiration, would follow the sayings of an Author without examination. To that end, it must be taught that theological wisdom is diffused among all Christian sects; and that even among those whom we rightly believe to be in error, there are found excellent men who are well-versed and highly sharp-sighted in certain parts of Theology. Meanwhile, in this current age <note>referring to the student's time in university</note>, it is better to have thoroughly studied one or two of the best authors and to have maintained a sense of order, lest minds be overwhelmed by a multitude of diverse things rather than being imbued with a solid knowledge of divine matters. Once the Academic course is finished, any lover of truth can roam into the widest field of theological learning; but in this current age, those things which are principal and most solid in this branch of literature must be built up and firmly held. Other things, which pertain to ornament and a more accurate knowledge of individual parts, should be deferred to another time. One must frequently and for a long time dwell upon those first and momentous chapters of Theology, so that the arguments by which those capital truths are proved may be fixed most deeply in the mind. Without this, the knowledge of the Christian religion is very weak, and not such as can weaken the objections of Atheists and Deists. **(V.)** Students are especially to be warned that a pure and saving knowledge of religion is to be drawn from the Holy Scriptures alone, and especially from the writings of Christ and the Apostles. All Systems <note>referring to "Systematic Theology" textbooks</note> must be measured against this standard, and early enough—not only after we have spent many years wearing ourselves out in unrolling these systems. Scripture, along with philological commentaries, must be read very frequently. All systems have something foreign mixed in that tastes of the "school" <note>referring to "Scholasticism," a method of learning that emphasized dialectical reasoning and often became overly technical</note>; so many different theological opinions and hypotheses have arisen from the fact that many teachers followed not so much the Holy Writers, but rather the inventions of their own brains or the authority of their own Masters. In these sacred Books are contained all things necessary to be known and done...

...without the mixture of human inventions, provided we read them for a good purpose, which is not only to learn the saving chapters of religion from them, but also to find the way to true happiness.
