The *Reverend Osterwald* <note>Jean-Frédéric Osterwald (1663–1747), a prominent Swiss Protestant pastor and theologian known for his Bible translations and efforts to modernize Reformed theology</note> judged rightly concerning this business in his theses on *Orthodoxy* inserted in Part VIII of the *Swiss Museum*. ---

(*) Since it is customary (he says) for everyone to think his own opinion is "Orthodox," it is necessary that we recur to a certain and constant rule and standard, from which one can determine who truly claims this title for himself and his opinion. This standard is none other than Holy Scripture, which alone is the certain and infallible word of God. For no other standard of Orthodoxy—that is, of right opinion concerning the dogmas pertaining to the Christian faith—is to be sought than that of the faith itself. This one thing must be drummed into the Reformed: that in their judgments of Orthodoxy they always be mindful of this principle, lest after they have rejected the traditions of the Papists, they substitute other human writings in their place, equate them with the Word of God, and attribute such authority to them that from them, as if they were writings "worthy of belief in themselves," <note>original Greek: *autopistois*</note> no return to Holy Scripture is allowed. The most excellent *Pfaff* <note>Christoph Matthäus Pfaff (1686–1760), a German Lutheran theologian known for his work on church law and "irenic" (peace-seeking) theology</note> whom I just cited, manfully insists upon the same truth. For these are his words in the passage cited: "Since different versions of Orthodoxy flourish in almost every Academy, each school thinks it has reached the pinnacle of theological purity, and takes it badly if anyone calls this into doubt. It instills this same opinion of itself into its 'sons.' One cannot help but know that the 'striving' which the Apostle Paul, by a certain right of his own, refers to among the works of the flesh in Galatians 5:20, plays every part here <note>original: "utramque heic paginam facere," to be the whole story</note> and prescribes what should be held in place of truth. By this method, since the order of things is broken, and truth is measured by the authority and judgment of men—rather than the judgment of men being measured by the standard of truth, which loves to be investigated without party zeal—anyone can see what great evils flow into the Church from here. How many disagreements, how many disputes joined with 'theological hatred' <term>odium theologicum: a famous term for the bitter animosity often found in religious debates</term>, than which none is more foul, arise from this! But indeed, I believe a man will deal with his affairs far more solidly and better if, leaving the place of even the most learned, sharpest, most eloquent, and most famous men, he gives himself over to be taught by his only Teacher and Prophet, Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit, whose anointing can teach us all things. Let him follow this light alone which he obtains, most pure, from these fountains. (But far be it from us here to pour cold water on those absurd men who are commonly called fanatics, and who, while laboring under a corrupt imagination, embrace a cloud instead of Juno <note>a mythological metaphor for chasing an illusion</note> and a wandering light instead of the true one). Let him, I say, follow this light uniquely, and let him not venerate his own Teachers and Theologians whose instruction he uses, except insofar as they show themselves to be 'taught by God' <note>original Greek: *theodidaktes*</note> by being drenched in this heavenly light, and lead their disciples by the hand, as it were, to these divine fountains. Whoever does this will indeed always follow the truth itself—that simple and pure truth, covered with no makeup of scholastic trifles, and also that holy truth joined in the closest bond with the pursuit of piety. This is that true Orthodoxy, which no one but the impious would despise."

### MEDITATION XI.

->...and to fortify them with sufficient arguments; meanwhile, it must always be cautioned that the **Authors of Systems** were human beings who could err and have erred more than once. Therefore, the waters of salvation are to be drawn more purely from the fountain itself <note>referring to the Holy Scriptures</note> than from the rivulets <note>referring to human theological commentaries or frameworks</note>. On this occasion, two dissertations by the celebrated men <term>J. A. Turrettini</term> <note>Jean-Alphonse Turrettini (1671–1737), a Swiss theologian known for "moderate orthodoxy"</note> and <term>L. Mosheim</term> <note>Johann Lorenz von Mosheim (1693–1755), a Lutheran church historian</note> on "listening to Christ" should be recommended to the students. 

(VI.) When students of Theology encounter those authors who depart further from the received Systems, they should not be hated for that reason, nor should what is laudable in those books be entirely condemned. There are certain teachers who, as soon as they hear that this or that student of Sacred Literature does not adhere solely to the received Systems, but is led by a certain curiosity to examine the books of those who dissent, they flare up in anger. They hold the student in suspicion, interpret innocent statements in the worst possible way, and betray through manifest signs that they wish that man ill. 

This way of acting is truly less than prudent or circumspect; for not only is it unhelpful for a student eager for new things, but his mind is made alienated from the teacher, and the received doctrine itself is made suspect—especially if he hears that far more kind judgments are passed on these authors by other learned men. Therefore, a Professor of Theology does better if he addresses the man gently and indicates to him that it is indeed free, and even sometimes necessary in the examination of religion, to study the systems of those who dissent. However, he should suggest that before the mind is cultivated by more solid sciences and persuaded of the most serious chapters of religion, it is better to insist on the well-trodden path, and to transfer those things which pertain to more subtle questions and controversies to another time. 

Undoubtedly, the principal chapters of religion must be solidly understood above all else before we commit ourselves to the high seas—that is, before we listen to the founders of plainly diverse Systems. But if the author of a book which the student is examining errs gravely, it must be shown to him courteously and with clear arguments how dangerous that error is, and what constitutes the man's <note>original: "πρῶτον ψευδος" (proton pseudos)</note> **fundamental error**. Furthermore, since many excellent things are very often found in the books of those who err, he must be cautioned that those things are not to be rejected. It should be shown at the same time which men, and of what sort, have solidly struck down these errors, and who have treated this or that argument more fully. In this way, we win over the minds of young men of superior talent to ourselves, and we ensure that on other occasions they listen to our advice with open ears. Those who do otherwise cause students either to subscribe slavishly to everything taught and recommended, or to fall into **Indifferentism** <note>the belief that all religions or doctrines are equally valid or unimportant</note> and other grave errors.<-

***

<page-num>469</page-num>
### ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

<margin>Other duties to be performed by Theologians are mentioned.</margin>

VIII. Especially (which is to be observed in the seventh place), books harmful to piety and good morals are to be vehemently discouraged for students of Sacred Literature. Among other things, these reasons should be used: that such is the corruption of the human heart, such the power of the passions, and finally such the levity of minds at this age, that they very easily withdraw the mind from the love of virtue and not infrequently cast it into grave and dangerous sins. Once they have arrived there, they cannot sincerely weigh religion, which is a doctrine not only of truth but also of piety. 

Furthermore, it should be warned that it is not the part of a prudent man to be intent on such studies by which they might easily suffer the shipwreck not only of piety but also of a good reputation. This should be proven by the introduction of examples. It must be shown in the second place how short and fleeting our life is; therefore, time must not be wasted in the reading of useless, let alone harmful, books. Life was given to us by the **Best Divinity** <note>a common Latin phrasing for God</note> for no other end than that we might promote our own happiness and that of other men; yet by the reading of these little books, minds are corrupted and rendered unfit for inquiring into the truth. 

A third argument can be sought from the multitude and gravity of the theological disciplines, which must be properly understood by a practitioner of Theology if he wishes to satisfy his duty and conscience. Who does not know how much labor and meditation is needed to study the Commentaries of the Ancient Doctors on Sacred Literature, to read the monuments of the earliest Christians, to learn the principal controversies which are debated among Christians? And this is to say nothing of the duties of **Pastors** and various cases of conscience, etc. Does the craftsman lack work? Should not the things that are healthy be pursued with all zeal, and the frivolous things cast away? 

But perhaps some student of the Best Literature will say that the mind must be relaxed after more severe cares and labors. Who would deny it? But are such things lacking which can honorably recreate the mind, so that one must fly toward reading futile and pestilential booklets, which were worthy of being smothered at their first birth? Let such a person take into his hands the most excellent writers of **Latin and Greece**; let him read those things in the Literary and Philosophical History of Theology which are most worthy of attention. Let him study the letters and biographies of the most excellent men; let him meet with friends who are lovers of piety and truth, with whom he can spend time pleasantly and usefully. Let him frequently meditate on his own progress or defect in piety and the study of erudition; let him often reflect with a pious mind how grave and momentous are the future duties of a **Minister of the Divine Word**; how many impediments occur here; how...

<summary>This page advises theology professors to guide students away from dogmatism and harmful literature through gentle persuasion rather than harshness. It emphasizes focusing on core scriptural truths and the practical duties of a minister over distracting controversies or immoral books.</summary>

### MEDITATION XI.

...let him think <note>The Latin text begins mid-word with 'gitet', likely 'cogitet'</note> about the means which are to be opposed to a degenerate Christianity; let him examine and look into the innermost recesses of his heart, to see what temptations of temperament and passions he is still prone to. Let him write some small dissertation to see what his powers are worth and what they refuse to carry; it will soon be clear that even if he reached his two hundredth year of life, there would still be no lack of honorable labor in which he could exercise the powers of his mind and body. If our student does not listen to such things, there is little hope that he will return to a better state or become someone who can truly value religion or rightly defend it against dissenters. On the contrary, those **Books** should be recommended to students which contain true and vigorous <note>original: "masculaque," literally 'masculine' or 'robust'</note> erudition, and in which the way to true wisdom is shown. The worst thing, however, is that the public teachers themselves often have no taste for true erudition, about which I would have more to say if this were the proper place.

Indeed, those students of Theology (to say nothing of those who cultivate other disciplines) are to be called happy who early on encounter such **Books** in which every part of theological study is treated rightly and solidly. Miserable, however, are those who—led either by the authority of "teachers of the shadows" <note>original: "Doctorum umbraticorum," referring to those who stay in the ivory tower of academic theory rather than practical reality</note> or by the advice of their fellow students—diligently read whatever books the common crowd of students values, without consulting better advisors. I have learned by experience that young men of no small talent, to whom obscure authors were early recommended or who chose them themselves, have achieved nothing despite much labor; and the more diligent they were in those obscure and grime-covered writings, the further they strayed from the path of true wisdom and erudition—indeed, they often exulted in a strange way in the very knowledge of obscure matters. 

When I say that the most excellent **Books** showing the way not only to solid erudition but also to wisdom and piety should be recommended to students of Sacred Literature, a teacher must carefully consider whether he himself has an accurate knowledge of such books. I will say in a few words what I think those books (I am speaking of books regarding Theology) ought to be: specifically, the simple doctrine of Christ and the Apostles concerning the duties and articles of faith of Christians should be represented in them with clear words and solid arguments, setting aside all mystical and metaphorical phrases. 

**Books** in which the Author exerts the full force of his talent so that what he brings forward is suited to the minds of all who are not entirely foolish. **Books** in which the study of virtue is made lovable, as something that tends uniquely toward promoting our happiness. (*)

---

### ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

...tend toward. (*) **Books** in which it is shown that the duties prescribed by the Christian religion agree amicably with the purest decrees of reason. **Books** in which not only the character and nature of Christian virtues are defined and explained skillfully and truly, rather than with exaggeration, but also in which the most effective incentives for practicing them are applied, the obstacles to them are clearly represented, and the defenses by which those obstacles can be removed (as much as can be done in this current darkness) are supplied. **Books**, finally, in which everything is grave, momentous, truly useful, and entirely free from "school-room trifles" <term>tricis scholarium</term> <note>refers to the overly complex, pedantic quibbling of the Scholastic tradition</note>. (**) Such books are useful to all men of every rank and dignity, and especially useful to those who either wish to write books tending toward piety themselves, or are compelled by their life’s work to deliver sermons to the people. There is no need for me to call by name those whom I most approve. I leave this to the prudent and erudite Teacher. Nor is there any doubt that a student, fired with the love of truth and virtue, will not only perceive a singular use from the reading of such books, but will also become most fit for rightly instilling the duties of Christian doctrine into his listeners, and for defending true piety against the insults of the unbelieving and the impious.

---

(*) Many Teachers err in this: that while they do indeed enjoin the duties of piety with the weightiest reasons, they do not simultaneously show that all these things tend toward our happiness. The celebrated **Bernard** <note>Likely Jean-Frédéric Bernard (1683–1744), a French writer and publisher</note> noted this error among others in his treatise *On the Excellence of the Christian Religion*, Volume I, page 33. Among other things, he speaks thus:

> We almost always look at the Religion that God has given us as a Duty; it is rare that we think to consider it as an advantage. From this it follows that we take as little of it as we can, if one may speak so, and if we still have our salvation a bit at heart, we observe precisely as much of religion as we believe necessary to obtain salvation, and no more. We very nearly look upon God as a peevish and severe Master who, being an enemy to the rest of his servants, demands of them a thousand useless labors rather than leave them with nothing to do, and who could have easily given them the reward without involving them in such a great number of annoying chores. Let us be disabused of this idea. Religion is entirely directed toward our good. It has the promises of the present life and the life to come. The more exactly one observes its precepts, the more happy one is, even on this earth. To exhort men to be religious is to exhort them to work actually for their present happiness. One can say that Preachers never climb into the pulpit without salvation and happiness climbing up with them. The result of all their sermons can be contained in this single word: *Be Happy.* <note>original: "Soyés Heureux"</note>

(**) **Acontius** <term>Giacomo Aconcio</term> <note>An Italian jurist, theologian, and philosopher (1492–1566) known for his work on religious tolerance and the "stratagems of Satan"</note> long ago emphasized this in his *On the Stratagems of Satan*, a man of sharp talent and prudence. On page 49 of that very well-known book, he says:

> The true method <note>original: "Vera ratio"</note> of leading men away from empty questions is this: if those whose duty it is either to instruct the people or to treat divine matters in the Schools, and those who apply themselves to writing, would cast aside curious questions and the vain display of talent, and insist only on those things—and urge those things—which pertain to strengthening faith, extirpating vices, instilling the fear of God, nourishing piety, comforting the afflicted and raising them to a better hope, and keeping those who wish to be called brothers in brotherly charity with a sweet consensus of minds among themselves.

It cites thinkers like Bernard and Acontius to argue that religion should be presented as a benefit to human joy rather than a burdensome chore.</summary>

### MEDITATION XI.

(VIII.) It contributes much to this end if the **public Teacher** (I am speaking here of professors of Theology) deems those students of **Holy Scripture** who are captivated by the love of Learning worthy of his familiar company and conversations. In this way, he has the most ample opportunity to propose various excellent warnings regarding education, piety, and wisdom, and to discuss the best **Books**. Indeed, all young men of a more excellent character are so disposed that they willingly pour out their inner thoughts on divine and human matters into the hearts of the Professors they love, and they especially explain which books they delight in.

Here, the public Teacher can often come to know the innermost recesses of the heart. He can warn one who is wandering or gasping after vain and little-profitable things; he can review the defects or show the value of this or that book (which he himself has thoroughly examined); and he can show what order must be observed in handling the individual parts of Theology. He can urge on the one who is already running, but especially enjoin him to primarily read and unroll those works which will be most useful for his future state <note>Refers to the student's future career as a pastor or scholar.</note>. It must not be kept silent that many things—as in other disciplines, so too in Theology—are superfluous and will benefit few; these must be cut away in a timely manner, and so forth.

Through this learned conversation, the wise Teacher will ensure that he confirms his student more and more in the study of truth and piety. All those means should be employed which can pull him back from the vice of **unbelief** as well as from **impiety**. Anyone can understand, even if I remain silent, what great advantages can flow from this to young men of good character.

However, before a student of Holy Scripture uses a public Teacher so familiarly and hands himself over to be molded by him, that Master must be thoroughly known. This can be established either from the monuments of his own genius that he has published, or from the judgment of the most learned and excellent men by common consent. This warning is not to be despised. For there are Teachers who value only the writings of their own sect; there are those who know little of how to distinguish heavy matters from light ones; there are those who magnify all slight errors into something greater; and there are those who think so magnificently of certain "new hypotheses" (which either they themselves invented or were devised by others) that you would think the **true core** <note>original: "verum nucleum"</note> of theological erudition was enclosed within them. These teachers, when they do not immediately gain your assent, are full of suspicions and lash out most harshly against those who dissent. If students of Holy Scripture fall into the hands of such men, it easily happens (as daily experience also testifies) that they sweat over superfluous and unnecessary things for the rest of their lives, and turn out to be litigious, biting, proud, and heretical men. But whether the stu-

(IX.) A **Theologian** who wishes to take care that none of his auditors fall into the vice of **unbelief** is bound above all to ensure that the student of Holy Scripture thoroughly understands the most weighty heads <note>main topics or chapters</note> of Theology. Specifically: the truth and divine origin of the Christian Religion; the **authenticity** <note>original: "αὐθεντίᾳ" (authentia)</note> of the Books of the Old and New Testament; the fundamental articles of faith; and the person, state, and offices of Jesus Christ. Without a solid knowledge of these, all that theological science would be built upon ruinous foundations, and they could never satisfy a **Deist** or an **Atheist**.

Hence it often happens that when such unskilled students, or even Ministers of the Word of God, encounter men who—either for the sake of exercise or seriously and from their true opinion—bring forward certain subtler arguments against religion, they get stuck. They provide material for clever men to triumph over them. And it cannot be denied that public Teachers not infrequently sin in this regard. For often, less principal topics are treated with equal length—for example, the divine decrees and their order, or the ceremonial and forensic laws of the Hebrews—as that most weighty topic of the truth and divine origin of the Christian Religion. Yet everyone who has a true image of religion fixed in their minds will concede that this is foolish.

These same teachers often neglect the proper order in demonstrating and defending the most serious points of religion, which greatly hinders the excitation of true persuasion in the mind; for the adversaries might deny one or two things that ought to have been established beforehand. Finally, they mix weak reasons with heavy and solid arguments. It can hardly be expressed in words what great evils this drags behind it. For the adversaries then make an attack on the light arguments that prove nothing; they expose them to laughter and sing their triumphs before the victory, even though they have often not even touched the solid and primary arguments with a finger. Only when this is done can he hope that the minds of his listeners will be flooded with true light. If, in public lectures, these themes cannot be sufficiently investigated due to the dignity and breadth of the subject, this must be provided in private colleges, or the most excellent books written on the subject should be recommended. Our current times demand this singular devotion to proving fundamental truths—times in which **unbelief** <note>original: *incredulitas*; refers to the rising skepticism and secularism of the Enlightenment era.</note> is raising its head among people of every sex and age. Here, and here most of all, the **Theologian** can demonstrate the sharpness of his own intellect, his learning, and his zeal for the glory of God. Men most eminent in doctrine and piety have recognized this; hence, as if marching in a single column <note>original: *agmine facto*</note>, they have directed the powers of their intellect toward placing this matter in full light, proving it, and defending it.

(X.) While the Theologian is engaged in this, he must not keep silent about the primary objections of **Deists** and **Atheists** (to say nothing of others who depart from pure and chaste religion). Instead, he should represent these objections sincerely and candidly, alongside a solid response full of light. Unless he does this, his listeners will never be sufficiently armed against the objections of adversaries; indeed, they usually grow to distrust the learning and capacity of the one teaching them. However, only the primary objections should be brought forward; the reading and meditation of the best books will supply the rest. In responding to objections, one must insist not on intricate and vain distinctions, but on solid arguments that go for the "throat of the cause" <note>original: *jugulum causae*; an idiom meaning to strike at the heart of the matter.</note>. This should be done in such a way—whether in private or public instruction—that it is clear our listeners have rightly perceived the force of the arguments. While we are doing this, we must abstain from hateful titles and insults. For although many of the unbelievers lash out more uncontrollably against other Christians in their writings, their example is not to be followed. Yet, where they keep no moderation in their accusations and stinging remarks, and mock the most holy things with "flashing white teeth" <note>original: *albis rident dentibus*; implies a sneering or mocking laugh.</note>, they may justly be drenched in **Italian vinegar** <note>original: *aceto perfundi Italico*; a classical metaphor for sharp, biting wit or satire.</note>. But even so, the weight of the arguments must be placed above all else.

Since it is not possible to satisfy all the doubts that can be opposed to **natural** and **revealed religion** <note>Natural religion refers to truths about God reachable by reason; revealed religion refers to truths known only through Scripture.</note>, nor to dissolve everything so that not a single scrap of doubt remains, our listeners must be taught that every discipline abounds in its own difficulties, and that this cannot be said only of reli-

The languages in which the Sacred Scriptures were composed present much of an obstacle to a more accurate knowledge of the Christian Religion; yet, the truths necessary to be known are scattered everywhere through the Sacred Scriptures—especially the New Testament—and are tempered to the intellects of all. The Apostles themselves, who were without controversy the most excellent Theologians, confessed that in this life **we know in part** <note>original Greek: *ἐκ μέρους γινώσκειν* (ek merous ginōskein); citing 1 Corinthians 13:9.</note>, and that only after this life will we attain a deeper knowledge of divine things. Furthermore, students of theological institutions who wish to examine those minute and controversial articles one by one not only spend their time poorly—time that should have been dedicated to better things—but are also generally rendered quarrelsome and argumentative. They think themselves to be fine fellows if they have at their fingertips all present and past controversies, however inept and useless they may be to anyone, or if they can even forge new ones or expand upon the old. In the course of time, these things only serve to stir up word-wars <note>original: *logomachias*; disputes over words rather than the underlying truth.</note> and nourish dissensions among brothers. This is also, among others, a primary reason why in Universities and Academies you will scarcely find two or three Theologians and **Ministers of the Divine Word** <note>original: *V. D. Ministros*, abbreviation for *Verbi Divini Ministros*.</note> between whom sincere and brotherly friendship has a place, even though our Holy Savior enjoined nothing more strictly upon his disciples and Apostles. Hear what he says in John, chapter 13, verse 35: *By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.* <note>original Greek: *ἐν τούτῳ γνώσονται πάντες ὅτι ἐμοὶ μαθηται έστε, ἐὰν ἀγάπην ἔχητε ἐν ἀλλήλοις.*</note>

Those minute opinions and controversies are even more harmful if their value is exaggerated, which sad experience teaches has happened very frequently and still, alas, happens today! There are certain Ministers of the sacred things who either suffer from a shameful ignorance of the most excellent matters, or are so corrupted by pride and false zeal that everything seems more serious to them than it actually is. If you listen to them, everything is full of danger; "a scorpion sleeps under every stone." Others, incited by a desire for fame and wishing to obtain the name of "Truly Orthodox," can scarcely express in words how much those opinions are subject to a **schism** <note>original Greek: *σχίσματι*.</note> of the most dangerous consequences. Yet a man who loves the truth and judges individual matters **without passion** <note>original Greek: *ἄτερ παθῶν*.</note>, even if he is most sharp-sighted, cannot see these dangers. Is it any wonder, then, if many students (while there is always a smaller supply of those who are truly wise), having been infected by this plague, as it were, not only transmit these minute controversies to a fierce posterity, but even often carry those raw and useless opinions into the sacred pulpits themselves?

Therefore, controversies of minor importance should be treated **for the sake of history** <note>original Greek: *ἱστορίας ἕνεκα*.</note> and as if doing something else. If students of **Sacred Scripture** <note>original: *S. L. studiosi*, likely *Sacrarum Literarum*.</note> wish to have some knowledge of them, they should be referred to the Literary History of Theology. It is the duty of Theologians, however, to repeat on every given occasion that the number of controversies of any real importance is not as great as is commonly thought. This has been the judgment of the most learned and excellent men of our order everywhere. I bring forward the testimony of only one, namely **of the late** <note>original Greek: *τοῦ Μακαρίτου*.</note> celebrated Grynaeus <note>Johann Jakob Grynaeus (1540–1617), a Swiss Reformed theologian from Basel known for his moderate views.</note>, a Theologian of Basel, who in his short works published at Basel on page 185, speaks thus: *That*

*videtur esse...* <note>The catchword "mine" from the previous page begins the word "videtur" here, continuing the Latin quote.</note> *seems to me to be the condition of the times in which we live, that he who wishes to consult the welfare of the Church of God and its salvation, and to accommodate his method of teaching to the capacity of our students, ought to be intent, first and foremost, on reducing the infinite number of theological controversies and inquiries, and then on reducing the perceived importance of the same. For the face of the Church in this age of ours is truly wretched, distracted by so many sects,* **schisms** <note>original Greek: *σχίσμασι*.</note>, *discords, and dissensions; that seamless tunic of Christ is torn in a foul manner. It can scarcely be expected that those who are concerned with healing and binding up these wounds of the Church as* **genuine** <note>original Greek: *γνήσιοι*.</note>, *peaceful disciples of the Savior, will profit anything by their efforts, unless they show that the number of truly theological controversies is not as great as is commonly estimated. They must show that many disputes, which have produced great divisions of minds, are not worthy of being agitated with such great contention. Indeed, very often, if you turn your mind to it diligently, there is no underlying matter of disagreement; it is mere lust for bickering that perpetuates the controversy.*

Furthermore, the condition of many, indeed most, of the students of the holier discipline among us is such that—whether you look at their talent, which is not granted to everyone to be capable of many things, or at the brevity of the time allotted to the course of theological studies, or at the multitude of things necessary to be known by a future Minister of the divine word—you may easily understand why we ought not to vex them with the heavy labor of examining curious or useless questions and difficult controversies, rather than those which greatly pertain to the doctrine of piety. We should not lead them by the hand to word-battles and contests that will hold no triumphs. It can be enough for the greatest number of students if they have learned to rightly judge theological questions that are of some importance, and to solidly confute from the word of God the primary errors that either overturn saving truth, or weaken our piety toward God, or diminish the pursuit of holiness, **and to refute those who contradict** <note>original Greek: *& τοὺς ἀντιλέγοντας ἐλέγχειν*.</note>. Thus far that pious Theologian.

(XIII.) When dealing with the theoretical articles of religion, it must always be demonstrated to the listeners what use we may perceive in life—especially in the pursuit of a Christian life—from the knowledge of them. For unless what we learn and teach is useful, our glorying is foolish. Indeed, a sentiment that is equipped with no incentives for living piously is unworthy of the title of an "article of the Christian religion." Those who, forced by necessity, have measured the entire field of polemical Theology know that there is no small number of such useless sentiments. Therefore, public Teachers must diligently strive (provided it can be done without forced application) to prove with solid arguments that this or that doctrine in the name of religion...

<summary>The author argues that theology students waste too much time on trivial, divisive controversies that fuel pride and conflict rather than piety. Citing the theologian Grynaeus, he advocates for focusing on essential truths that encourage a holy life and brotherly love.</summary>

...entrusted to me, that it is so arranged as to draw us toward the pursuit of virtue. For in this way, the mind of a student of Sacred Letters will burn with a love for knowing that doctrine, and on this basis, it can also be recommended to the Christian people. Indeed, if all the controversies stirred up among Christians had been tested—and were still tested—against this <term>Lydian stone</term> <note>original: *Lydium lapidem*; a touchstone used to test the purity of gold. Here it refers to using "the pursuit of virtue" as the standard for evaluating theological truth.</note>, it would be obvious that we could easily have done without the knowledge of many of them. To perform and designate this rightly, however, there is need for a Teacher of sharp intellect, sufficiently knowledgeable of the importance of religious doctrines, and at once prudent and circumspect. Otherwise, a student of Sacred Letters who has any sense of discernment will regard his Professor as a mere cloistered academic and a theatrical actor—one who, with a great noise of words, recommends a matter that will be of no use, yet extols it with a furrowed brow and high praise. Indeed, in the future, the student will listen to him not without suspicion and weariness, even when he speaks on weighty matters.

(XIV.) A Theologian ought to abstain, on the one hand, from arguments born of envy and insults; on the other hand, he ought to represent the errors of his adversaries candidly. In every age, eminent men have complained about many of those who usually handle theological controversies, because they are not so much concerned with rightly uncovering the sources and gravity of errors, or showing how the truth is built upon solid foundations, as they are with making their adversaries as hated as possible. The <term>celebrated Le Clerc</term> <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), a famous Genevan theologian and pioneer of biblical criticism.</note> showed this by the example of **Jerome** in a singular dissertation published on this subject. Oh, how many men not unlike **Jerome** could we point out in all the families of Christians who disagree with one another! But those who act this way neither seek the truth nor gain anything. Suppose someone feels a certain way about the freedom of the human will, such that in the exercise of virtue he attributes more to it than you think right, and because of this you call this man either a **Pelagian** or a **Semipelagian** <note>These terms refer to early Christian heresies that emphasized human effort over divine grace. In the author's time, they were often used as harsh insults to shut down debate.</note>—has his error been removed because of this, or has your own opinion been rightly established? Far from it; rather, you do nothing but stir up the hatred of your adversary against you. Such men, who use these arts—that is, insults instead of arguments—were called by a certain learned Frenchman *the Rabble of Theologians* <note>original: *La Canaille des Theologiens*</note>; and not inappropriately. For just as men from the dregs of the common people flee to accusations, or even often to stones, when they are destitute of reasons, many of those who handle controversies are accustomed to act in the same way: where they have little strength in reasoning, they wish to conquer with tragic shouting and insults. But the worst part of this business is that such a method of arguing
<meta>catchword: methodus (method)</meta>

<column-break/>

<page-num>479</page-num>
<header>ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.</header>
used in public writings makes men alienated from religion and the love of it. Afterward, many consider religion as a wide-open field in which public Teachers and those who handle controversies can give free rein to their passions. They therefore shrink from the examination of divine things and even from more serious controversies, thinking that time is wasted on these matters; they believe it is better if one simply follows the national religion, whatever it may finally be. What kind of laughter and triumphs such methods of disputing can excite among unbelievers is shown well enough by daily experience. Therefore, Theologians and those who handle controversies must abstain from such evil arts; rather, those who err are to be called back to the path of truth with gentleness, courtesy, and a friendly comparison of arguments. Their opinions should be represented sincerely, and the gravity of an error should not be judged by strings of consequences gathered here and there, but the adversary's system itself must be sincerely submitted to the judgment of the reader or listener.

(XV.) Especially, however, it must be shown to students of Sacred Letters how much damage bad passions <note>original: *affectus*; often translated as 'affections' or 'emotions,' referring here to biased or uncontrolled impulses.</note> bring not only to our will and true happiness, but also how much power they have to corrupt the human intellect and pull it away from pure and chaste religion. There is no need for me to establish this opinion of mine with many words; the nature of the matter and daily experience prove this enough. It is manifest that, with the passing of time and the impulse of the passions, the will is subjected to the command of the body: from this, the will cannot help but be carried toward that which is pleasing and acceptable to it. The will, excited by vivid sensations, very easily draws the intellect to its side. Therefore, he who gives free rein to these passions can hardly bring himself to avoid giving them some false justification. Hence, the true names of things are changed, and in the business of religion, those doctrines please which sail with the wind of the passions. Therefore, having brought forward arguments drawn from Philosophy and Theology, it must be shown that these things must be resisted early. Especially, that insane and pestilential opinion concerning **Freedom**, which they call **Academic**, must be driven out <note>Academic Freedom here refers to a specific skeptical tradition (the "New Academy") that argued one can never know the truth for certain, leading to moral and religious indifference.</note>. The dissertation of the <term>late celebrated Werenfels</term> <note>Samuel Werenfels (1657–1740), a Swiss theologian known for seeking common ground between different Protestant groups.</note>, which is inserted in the new edition of his works, should be recommended to students of Sacred Letters. Nor should these things be instilled as an afterthought, but they are to be urged and repeated with all zeal, both privately and publicly. And indeed, if Theologians instilled these things into students of Sacred Letters with as much zeal, labor, and mental effort as they often use to urge light and little-profiting questions, the appearance of the Churches and Academies would undoubtedly be far better than it is now. But since this does not happen in many places, piety—

# MEDITATION XI; ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.
<sig>Ppp</sig>

...frivolous minds consider piety to be a kind of secondary accessory, to be left to men of average judgment. Truly, so that this pestilent opinion may be uprooted from the minds of students of <term>Sacred Letters</term> <note>original: *S. Litterarum*; referring to the study of the Bible and theology.</note>—and indeed from all who cultivate other disciplines—the <term>Public Teacher</term> <note>original: *Doctor publicus*; a professor or official lecturer in a university or church setting.</note> ought to show that a student of Sacred Letters who is equipped with a smaller apparatus of erudition, but is set on fire with the pursuit of true piety, contributes more to promoting his own and others’ happiness and to commending religion than a most learned man contaminated by many vices. Indeed, such a man often hinders the progress of religion more than a heretic.

Now, when I speak of the piety of a Public Teacher, it is necessary to define what I understand by the name "piety," since certain teachers are often accustomed to recommend a distorted image of true piety to their listeners. Therefore, by the name *piety*, I do not understand some fanatical, superstitious, and monkish cult of religion that renders men gloomy, morose, and unfit for the business of civil life; nor a *piety* that consists in the observation of certain rituals, the strenuous defense of minute articles of faith, a kind of "sacred silence," or in filthy clothing and a furrowed brow. I do not mean a *piety* that declares war on all errors (which human nature can scarcely avoid) and wishes for all pleasures which mortals can use honorably to be severely outlawed. Rather, by the name of piety, we understand a tireless *study* of composing one’s actions, as far as is possible for a human being, to the will of the <term>Divine Power</term> <note>original: *Numen*; a classical Latin term for the divine will or presence.</note>: a *study* of promoting one’s own happiness and that of others.

This piety is tempered by courtesy, prudence, charity, and gravity; it shines forth no less in the gatherings of nobles and the learned than in those of citizens and rustics. Anyone who has ever weighed the true value of things throughout their life will sense that such a pursuit of piety does more to imbue others with true religion—and to fortify them against both fanaticism and unbelief—than any amount of erudition that is robbed of these virtues. I would not have added these things unless I had clearly seen that certain Public Teachers, though not with bad intentions, yet nonetheless imprudently demand such a pursuit of piety from students of Sacred Letters that it exceeds the strength of even those with the best natural disposition. This makes the more timid students appear ridiculous and fanatical, while it alienates the minds of others—who seem to themselves to be wiser and who reason more acutely—from religion, since they clearly see that everything is being exaggerated by their teachers and that things are being demanded which should be classified among <note>original: *τὰ ἀδύνατα* (ta adunata)</note> "the impossible." This error of certain teachers arises, among other reasons that could be brought forward, from the fact that when they are about to describe the true state of Christian piety,

<column-break/>

they use words and phrases taken from the Sacred Letters, but whose meanings are not clearly enough defined. Hence, we see mystics and fanatics everywhere, intending to prove their own wonderful opinions, clinging closely to the words of the sacred text while rejecting a plain explanation that is consistent with both religion and reason.

Meanwhile, it is most true, as we warned at the beginning of this section, that men adorned with any degree of erudition who are pious contribute more to inciting others to a love of religion than the learned who are contaminated by various vices. In the larger cities—to say nothing of the villages—there are very few who can form a fair judgment of the value of the erudition that ought to be present in a Public Teacher or a <term>Minister of the Word of God</term> <note>original: *V. D. Ministro* (Verbi Divini Ministro).</note>. People from the <note>original: *e faece plebis*; literally "from the dregs of the common people," reflecting the era's sharp social distinctions.</note> lowest classes, and those who (if you look at the cultivation of their reason and religion) are no better, care little whether he who delivers the precepts of religion is considered learned or not. But when they attend more diligently to his way of living, they are very quick to reason poorly about religion and the duties of piety.

Other Public Teachers make it their primary aim to render their listeners and disciples not so much pious as <term>Orthodox</term> <note>meaning "correct-thinking" or adhering strictly to established doctrines.</note>. If by this name they mean that it is necessary for students to have the chief heads of the Christian religion properly understood, to be able to commend them to others with the weightiest arguments, and to live a life worthy of such a holy religion, then I praise the institution. But if, under the name of "orthodoxy," they want all the minute opinions and private controversies of the sect they follow to be understood, and believe that the chief virtues of a future Public Teacher or Minister lie in that, they are in my opinion vehemently deceived; they will satisfy neither the learned nor the simpler folk.

Certainly those who, though not skilled in controversies of minor importance, have nonetheless cultivated their reason—whether they live in the country or the city—will attend most to what pertains to the nature and character of the assigned office. They will ask whether such a man is diligently devoted to his duty; whether he is pious, sincere, generous, peaceful, and a lover of truth; whether he loves and consults the interests of the rich and the needy alike. When men who are not entirely dull-witted see these virtues and others, they are swept into admiration and love for that Public Teacher, even if he is perhaps less learned or less addicted to all the opinions of his sect. Therefore, students of the <term>Best Letters</term> <note>original: *Optimarum Litterarum*; referring to the Humanities and classical/biblical studies.</note> must be taught to join true piety most closely with <note>original: *mascula eruditione*</note> "vigorous learning," for in this way they will best be able to resist both vice and unbelief in everyone.

(XVI) A stubborn desire for disputing about any opinions whatsoever, even the slightest, must be [removed] early from the minds of students of the Best Letters...

must be rooted out, and to that end, all <term>Public Teachers</term> <note>original: *publici Doctores*; official university professors or authorized church lecturers.</note> ought to pass over in silence those petty opinions <note>original: *proletarias*; literally "proletarian," meaning common, low-level, or trivial academic debates.</note> that are difficult to grasp and benefit no one. Instead, they should exhort their listeners to be so well-equipped with solid erudition that they can shut the mouths of enemies—those who either greet the most serious heads of the Christian religion with laughter or openly attack them—with solid arguments. For only then will it be manifest what kind of judgment they possess and how fit they are for blunting the arrows of the unbelieving.

When I speak of that stubborn zeal for disputing about anything at all, I do not warn without reason. Experience shows that those who delight in battling over every matter with everyone not only make themselves ridiculous throughout their lives and become troublesome and hated by all, but they also expose religion itself to contempt. They are often the authors of innumerable evils in both Churches and Republics. Furthermore, none are generally more alienated from true modesty (which is the varnish of all virtues) than these people; none have less taste for true erudition. While they run about through infinite little questions—more curious than useful—and applaud themselves vehemently on that account, they neglect matters of the greatest importance. They fall away not only from true theological learning but also from true piety. Hence, it is no wonder that not only the common people but even men of sharper intellect sometimes think that a more accurate knowledge of religion makes men morose, argumentative, and unfit for properly conducting the business of this life.

If we wish to inquire into the causes of this evil, it will be clear that they do not have to be sought from far away. Truly, it is manifest that this evil must be attributed to many Public Teachers. For they themselves are often destitute of a robust knowledge of the most excellent things; not content with accessible learning, they attempt to dispute about anything. They wish to know and demonstrate not only **the fact** <note>original Greek: <term>το ότι</term> (*to hoti*); a logical term referring to the knowledge that something exists or is true.</note> but also **the reason why** <note>original Greek: <term>το διοτι</term> (*to dioti*); a logical term referring to the underlying cause or explanation.</note> (as we say in the schools) regarding the most difficult questions that surpass the capacity of the human mind. In doing so, they frequently seize upon hypotheses that are not only dangerous but even more obscure than the question being debated. Thus, many anxiously weigh what the state of the human race would have been if the first parents of the human race had not sinned—as if this anxious care and debate could contribute anything to changing the present state of things! Indeed, such men seem to me like a man who knows by experience that his ancestors several centuries ago were very wealthy, but who, not knowing how to use what they had gathered, squandered their goods. Thus, they cast not only themselves but also their posterity and heirs into such a condition that

<meta>catchword: that</meta>

---

<page-num>483</page-num>

<page-type>text</page-type>

that they must seek their livelihood for themselves not without great trouble. At the same time, having been cast into this state, he would very frequently think to himself what the nature of his fortune would have been if his ancestors had preserved those gathered treasures for the use of his family up to his own age and had transferred them to him by legitimate right of inheritance. What comfort, pray, would such a man take from this debate? We know that God permitted the fall of our first parents; we know that once it was done, men come forth into the divine breezes of light contaminated by many physical and moral evils. We are not ignorant, moreover, of the way in which God later willed to return to favor with the human race. Let these things suffice for us.

Of the same nature are the questions of how God acts upon human minds at every single moment, or what the logic and order of the divine counsels taken from all eternity might be—to say nothing now of many questions of the same weight. Many of the Doctors are vehemently occupied in ventilating such little questions, and this is not done without pride. When their listeners—who have thus far been destitute of more solid knowledge—notice this, they are carried away into admiration of such supposedly "great" matters. They begin to babble about anything and everything, surpassing even the common women sitting in the marketplace in their talkativeness. When learned and prudent Professors ought to restrain these foolish impulses, or when the <term>Minister of the Word of God</term> <note>original: *V. D. M.* (*Verbi Divini Minister*); a title for a clergyman.</note> ought to do so, they instead often praise such sellers of trifles and vow they will be the future pillars of the <term>Orthodox Church</term>.

Hence, these students applaud themselves and carry high spirits, but they are a laughingstock to the learned. The more prudent people deplore the miserable fate of religion; those inclined toward unbelief laugh in their sleeves and explode these useless little questions, often to the detriment of the most serious articles of religion. Would that these things were only to be repeated about the times of the <term>Scholastic age</term>! <note>The medieval period of theology characterized by rigid logic and minute hair-splitting.</note> But that there is room for these complaints even now is known by everyone who is not a complete stranger to **Literary History** and who attends to those things that are done daily.

(XVII) Finally (to pass over many other things), it must be frequently impressed upon those who cultivate **Sacred Letters** that, no matter how much skill is applied in handing down the more sacred disciplines, it is impossible to prevent some disagreement of minds from arising regarding this or that head of religion, even among the most loving of truth. Anyone who rightly attends to the diversity of human intellects and the nature of theological disciplines will feel that this is an inevitable evil. Yet these things ought not to prevent the highest harmony of minds from taking place among the learned, nor should everything be turned into tragic

# APPENDIX,
## Of Certain Theological Theses.

I. Although the distinction between fundamental and non-fundamental articles of faith is necessary and useful, it is nevertheless extremely difficult to define, with respect to individual men, whether ignorance of this or that article excludes a man from the hope of salvation or not.

II. The disagreement that exists between Protestants regarding certain articles of religion is not fundamental, but could easily be settled without the authority of Rulers, or the labor of any Council or Synod.

III. The words of the Holy Spirit signify whatever they ought to signify. <note>This is a defense of the "perspicuity" or clarity of Scripture—the idea that the Bible's meaning is sufficient and intended as written, rather than requiring layers of scholastic speculation.</note>

IV. He has made much progress in Theology who says he is ignorant of certain things.

V. Emphatic is the description of divine wisdom and true Theology provided by the *Apostle James* in chapter 3, verse 17, speaking thus: "But the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial and sincere." <note>original Greek: ἡ δὲ ἄνωθεν σοφία, πρῶτον μὲν ἁγνή ἐστιν, ἔπειτα εἰρηνική, ἐπιεικής, εὐπειθής, μεστὴ ἐλέους καὶ καρπῶν ἀγαθῶν, ἀδιάκριτος καὶ ἀνυπόκριτος.</note>

VI. Although the opinion of the Reformed regarding the Holy Supper <note>The Eucharist or Communion.</note> is most consistent with reason and revelation, many nevertheless err gravely in the use of this sacrament; to which contribute many obscure phrases and rhetorical flourishes which Theologians and <term>Ministers of the Word of God</term> <note>original: *V. D. Ministri* or *Verbi Divini Ministri*.</note> often use when dealing with this subject.

VII. Any particular Church can err in non-fundamental rites and ceremonies. If Protestant Theologians frequently called this to mind, they would be more inclined toward peace and the study of a moderate mind than we—alas!—see happening.

VIII. Zeal for parties and sects is the greatest hindrance to Interpreters of Holy Scripture performing their duties rightly.

<meta>catchword: IX. Skill</meta>

<page-num>485</page-num>
<header>ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.</header>

IX. Skill in the critical art and in Languages contributes more to understanding the Holy Scriptures rightly than the cultivation of Philosophy, whether ancient or modern.

X. Learned ignorance in Theology is the best medicine against pride and the "itch for disputing." <note>original: *disputandi pruritum*; a common 18th-century metaphor for an unhealthy obsession with academic or sectarian argument.</note>

XI. This should be the motto of all Theologians: *In essentials unity, in non-essentials liberty, in all things, however, charity.* <note>The author quotes the famous irenic maxim "In necessariis unitas, in non-essensis libertas, in omnibus vero charitas," often used to promote Christian ecumenism.</note>

<header>MEDITATION XII.</header>

# MEDITATION
## ON THE CAUSES OF THE EVER-INCREASING
# UNBELIEF,
## AND
# THE REMEDY TO BE BROUGHT TO THIS EVIL.

### PART XII. & Final.

---

->Section I.<-

<margin>
What must be avoided and performed by the Ministers of the Word of God and Sacred Orators who seek to draw men back from the vice of Unbelief.
</margin>

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'I' featuring a landscape with a river and a stone archway.</image-desc>
IN the dissertation immediately preceding, we reached the final part of our Instruction, namely, by showing the means by which one can prevent men from falling into the vice of Unbelief. To that end, we have represented what *Parents, Teachers, Professors of the higher Sciences, and Theologians* especially ought to avoid and perform; it remains, before we proceed further, that we look at what should be performed in this grave business by *sacred Orators* <note>The author uses the term "sacred orators" to refer to preachers and ministers who deliver sermons.</note>, and by the Rulers of Empires and Republics themselves. Everything that can be impressed upon Sacred Orators can be conveniently reduced to two main headings: namely, certain things they must *avoid*, and certain things they must *perform*. Among the things to be *avoided*, this is the first warning: care must be taken that public Orators do not bring forward in their speeches and writings things that are *inept and superstitious*; for a man of sharp wit <note>original: "acutæ naris," literally "of a sharp nose," a Latin idiom for someone with keen discernment or a skeptical nature.</note> easily detects such things, and he not only laughs with bared teeth, but also begins to doubt the rest of the dogmas of Religion, even the true and certain ones. From this, it cannot happen otherwise than that in those places where gross superstition flourishes, there are many who reject religion itself along with the superstition. Thus Prea-

<meta>catchword: Prea-</meta>

<page-num>487</page-num>
<header>ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.</header>

Preachers among the Romanists <note>original: "Romanenses," referring to the Roman Catholic Church.</note>, if they wish to defend all the Decrees of their Religion, are very frequently bound to bring forward such things as cannot help but provide an occasion for laughter to those of sharper minds. According to their opinion, the Holy Scripture—being obscure and plainly not suited to the nature of the common people—should not be read; on the other hand, the cult of the Saints and of Mary is urged to the greatest degree; the power and efficacy of relics is preached, and innumerable miracles performed by the power of relics and the intercession of this or that Saint are related against every appearance of probability. In many places, they shamelessly affirm that the same body, or part of a body, is found in different locations, and a thousand other ineptitudes and fables are publicly narrated in Sermons. The effect of these is that the common people fall into the foulest superstition, while the more learned and wise fall into *Deism* <note>The belief in a creator who does not intervene in the universe.</note> or *Indifferentism* <note>The view that all religions are equally valid or that religious differences do not matter.</note>. I remember, however, that I have already dealt with this argument in the earlier parts concerning the causes of Unbelief. See the letters of *Emiliani*, in which there is one *concerning the manner of preaching used in Italy*.

II. *Orators must beware* lest, when they attempt to impress and prove the most weighty matters, they use either plainly weak arguments, or at least fail to make a prudent choice of them. If anywhere, certainly here the Ministers of the Word of God ought to be cautious. An argument that proves nothing not only has no force on the minds of men, but also renders the very articles of faith which are to be proved highly suspicious. When several weak points are mixed with one or two solid arguments, the simpler listeners will not be able to distinguish the force of the solid argument from the weak one, while those who see more sharply will not only think lowly of the Orator’s learning, but will also begin to doubt the truth of the articles themselves. Indeed, sacred Orators ought not here to follow *Cicero*, who says in the second book of *On the Orator*: *Every action of the orator is contained in opinions, not in knowledge* <note>original: "Scientia"</note>: *For we speak both among those who do not know, and we say things that we ourselves do not know.* From this (which we mention in passing), it is clear that he who wishes to discharge the duty of a sacred orator with fruit and praise ought to be equipped with solid learning. Nor should it be said that the Apostles were the best Orators although they were not cultured in various disciplines; for they were *carried by the Holy Spirit* <note>original: "φερομενοι ὑπὸ πνεύματος ἁγίου"</note> and were illustrious with miracles, so that there was no need for a long series of subtle arguments to prove this or that truth. Today, however, there is a need for judgment, meditation, and various disciplines to prove and vindicate the truths contained in the Holy Scriptures.

III. *The Sacred Orator must beware of the "Meteors of Speech,"* <note>The author uses this term to describe flashy, unstable, or overly dramatic rhetorical flourishes that lack substance.</note> bombastic and hyperbolic expressions, and allegorical and mystical phrases. For these do not—

The author emphasizes that modern ministers require solid education and sound reasoning rather than relying on the miraculous inspiration granted to the Apostles.</summary>

<header>MEDITATION XII.</header>

...not only bear no fruit, but they even provide the more learned with material for laughter and for the contempt of religion. A small book was written by a learned Englishman named *Eshchar* <note>original: "Eshchar"—likely a reference to John Eachard (c. 1636–1697), author of "The Grounds and Occasions of the Contempt of the Clergy and Religion Enquired into."</note>, under the title *On the Contempt of Religion Arising from Public Sermons*. This was translated into the German language with a learned preface by the late <note>original: "τοῦ μακαρίτου," a Greek expression of respect for the deceased.</note> and celebrated *Reinbeck* <note>Johann Gustav Reinbeck (1683–1741), a prominent Lutheran theologian.</note>. In this little book, such examples of inept, senseless, and ridiculous allegories, comparisons, and rhetorical flourishes are presented that I could scarcely have believed such ridiculous speakers existed among Protestants—especially the English—had not the *Illustrious Burnet* <note>Gilbert Burnet (1643–1715), Bishop of Salisbury and author of "History of His Own Time."</note> in the *History of his own Time* outlined the wretched state of sacred eloquence in that age, and explained through whom the true skill of speaking received its new splendor. Today, such is the happiness of our century that not only the *English*, but also the most excellent men of *Germany*, brilliantly represent the native character of masculine Eloquence through both rules and examples. Yet you will repeat this in vain to those who, lacking a sharp and refined judgment, are unskilled in the art of thinking. From this it is also clear how faulty and impious is the opinion of certain people who think that any arguments whatsoever, and any method of speaking and presenting divine matters, are sufficient for the common people.

IV. In Sacred Sermons, one must abstain from the treatment of subtle and less necessary controversies; for these exceed the capacity of most listeners, nor can the Speakers satisfy doubters if any happen to be in the assembly. Furthermore, the duty and office they perform does not require it. We expect from a sacred Speaker a clear and solid exposition of the saving truths contained in the Holy Scriptures, along with the weightiest incentives for pursuing virtue, and nothing more. But if that Pastor is so skilled in Controversies, he has a very wide and distinct field in which to demonstrate the sagacity <note>original: "ἀγχίνοιαν," Greek for quick-wittedness or mental sharpness.</note> of his genius and his Erudition with which he considers himself equipped; and there will be no lack of those who might oppose arguments with arguments and subject them to the sharpest examination (which is forbidden in the very assemblies where sermons are held).

V. In social conversation with wise men, they ought to prove by manifest signs that they are far from the "itch of disputing" about anything and everything. They should not strive for the zeal and reputation of some sort of rigid Orthodoxy in handling every controversy, but should commend themselves to everyone through their modesty and the pursuit of a moderate mind. Especially to be avoided are "inquisitorial arts," by which I mean a certain insane desire to attack anyone who disagrees with them, to detract from their repu-

<column-break/>

reputation, to make them hated by the leading men in the State, and finally to exaggerate their errors. For such men are not only regarded by the more Wise as "shadow-teachers" <note>term: "shadow-teachers" (doctoribus umbraticis), referring to scholars who live in isolation or deal with abstract theories rather than practical reality.</note>, but they also provide the Unbelievers with fertile material for criticism and bring religion itself into contempt, as the experience of all times has sufficiently taught, and as the books of the Deists prove.

The things that must be provided by the Sacred Orator and Minister of the Word of God can be reduced to the following: I. They must strive with all their strength to show that they are most knowledgeable in the Christian religion, that they have recognized and understood whatever in it is sublime, excellent, and beautiful, and that they are cultured in all those disciplines which can go into the making of an outstanding Speaker. Even the Unbelievers admire such men, and they lend an ear only to such men, and not at all to unskilled declaimers.

II. The principal dogmas of Religion must be proposed to the listeners solidly and clearly, and to that end, a clear and very simple style must be used. It is indeed well known that in certain Churches (as is the case among us) it is the accepted custom to explain either some Gospel or an apostolic epistle according to the series of chapters; but notwithstanding this, occasions must be sought and seized to present to the Christian people the principal heads of Natural and Revealed Theology, both Theoretical and Practical. The lazy ignorance of many people regarding these arguments is well known; it is known that the faith of these men wavers violently whenever certain doubts occupy their minds; and what kind of persuasion is it, after all, that lacks a more accurate knowledge of these articles? Hence, the institution of the most noble and learned Boyle <note>Referring to the Boyle Lectures, established by Robert Boyle to defend Christianity against infidelity.</note> was plainly laudable—namely, appointing such Speakers who would each year properly explain Natural and Christian religion and defend them in a masculine and learned way against Atheists and Deists.

III. Sacred Orators should always represent Religion as a thing greatly to be loved, consistent with reason, and given by the Best Deity for no other reason than to promote our happiness. For by this means alone are minds set on fire with the love of it. From this it is also clear that all those things which do nothing toward obtaining that end ought to be omitted by Speakers.

IV. The dogmas of Religion necessary to be known and understood must be frequently explained, proved, and commended clearly and solidly, setting aside the trifles of the Schools <note>term: "trifles of the Schools" (Scholarum tricis), referring to overly technical scholastic theological debates that the author finds useless for the general public.</note> and more obscure phrases. And in this, no labor...

<header>MEDITATION XII.</header>

...the Sacred Orator <note>original: "Orator Sacer," referring to a preacher or public speaker on religious themes.</note> must spare no labor; for he deals with matters of the highest gravity and greatest importance. One must not look to the number of arguments, but rather to their weight: for weak arguments not only have no power over the mind, but even bring religion itself into contempt. To achieve this, however, more things are required than is commonly thought.

V. From the pulpit <note>original: "Pro Cathedra," referring to the official seat or pulpit of authority.</note>, only those errors which are grave and harmful to piety should be refuted, and even then only when necessity demands it. Yet this must be done with such precision <note>original: "$\dot{\alpha}\kappa\rho\acute{\iota}\beta\epsilon\iota\alpha$," a Greek term for exactness or meticulous accuracy.</note> of judgment, such weight of argument, and such purity and simplicity of style, that even Unbelievers, should any be present, are forced to admit that the Preacher is skilled in the art of reasoning and is equipped with all the defenses necessary to prove and protect his opinion. From this it follows that those act foolishly who publicly attack trivial errors and hypotheses that contribute nothing to the pursuit of piety, and of which most of the audience are entirely ignorant.

VI. Since the wicked disturbances of the mind lay snares for religion and piety, Sacred Orators ought to be as skilled as possible in both Philosophical and Christian Ethics. With the help of these disciplines, they should uncover the attractive but false causes of prejudices and emotions. Regarding this subject, many Ministers of the Word <note>original: "V. D. Ministri," an abbreviation for *Verbi Divini Ministri*.</note> are in grave error. Many have not only failed to cultivate philosophical Ethics throughout their lives, but even consider it dangerous. Yet how, in the end, will these men be able to demonstrate the excellence and equity of the Christian religion and its precepts, and its agreement with reason? What could they answer an Unbeliever who attacks the precepts of the Christian religion and claims they were written for the sake of fanatical men and are contrary to all the decrees of right reason? And what, finally, is the reason why many Christians are so forgetful of the duties that belong to man, and fall into superstition and fanaticism, other than the fact that the Ministers of the Sacred Rites are themselves often ignorant of these disciplines? Indeed, many Orators cannot even tolerate those who value Christian Ethics highly and frequently use and urge them in sacred sermons; instead, they suspect them of some kind of Heterodoxy <note>Holding non-standard or unorthodox beliefs.</note>, shouting that "systematic truths," both the grave and the trivial, must be constantly hammered home. Hence it usually happens that these Orators either rest content with general precepts of Christian Ethics, or offer the people certain "mystical phrases," or exaggerate individual types of duties so much that a man of sound mind

<page-num>491</page-num>

can be led to the love of virtue by no rational means at all. Truly, a Minister of the Word must be blind in the business of religion if he does not see, and almost feel by touch, that it is no less necessary to frequently instill the precepts and incentives of Christian Ethics and its defenses for living piously, than it is to teach the dogmas <note>Established doctrines or core beliefs.</note> necessary to be known. Hear what the late <note>original: "$\dot{o}$ Μακαρίτης," a Greek term of respect for the deceased.</note> Samuel Werenfels <note>Samuel Werenfels (1657–1740), a Swiss theologian known for his moderate views and work on hermeneutics.</note>, a most excellent theologian, says on this subject in his dissertation *Why the Incentives of Scripture are Often Ineffective, page 150 and following*: 

*“I am not unaware,”* he says, *“of the complaints of certain Doctors who cry out that it is intolerable that religion today is being turned by many into pure and simple Ethics. These complaints are certainly most just, if they mean they do not want it turned into pagan Ethics, which proposes no more excellent virtue to us than the Gentile philosophers did, nor stirs us toward it with weightier incentives. But if someone, being properly persuaded of those great Mysteries of the Christian Religion which were unknown to the Philosophers of the Gentiles, thinks that he should not stop at the mere contemplation of them; but instead considers them all, as many as there are, as 'Mysteries of Piety'—that is, as so many incentives to piety and the virtues connected with it—if he thinks that God revealed them to him chiefly for this end; then either I am greatly mistaken, or he has finally conceived the true idea of the Christian Religion in his mind. Certainly, the affairs of the Church would be in a better state if all Christians turned their religion into Ethics in this way, rather than those who turn it into pure and simple Metaphysics and a barren contemplation of divine properties and works.”*

Regarding those who think the opinions of their own Sect should be frequently commended in sacred assemblies, the same Distinguished Man pronounces: *“He who thinks,”* he says, *“that the hinge of religion turns on this one thing: that the dogmas he professes are better and sounder than the dogmas of others who are called Christians, and that he should cling to that Church which distinguishes itself from the rest by the profession of such dogmas—that man will be moved by the gravest incentives we have mentioned to nothing else but to cling more firmly to his own Church and its opinions, to fight more fiercely for them, to turn away more from those who think differently, to inveigh more bitterly against them, and, where he is powerful enough, to pursue them more mercilessly, treat them more hideously, torture them more cruelly, and afflict them with more dire punishments.”* 

The Reverend Bowles <note>Oliver Bowles (c. 1577–1644), author of *De Pastore Evangelico* (The Evangelical Pastor), a manual on the duties of a minister.</note> complains of the same neglect of Practical or Christian Ethics in his book *On the Evangelical Pastor*. *“Those,”* he says, *“who neglect practical matters as if they were vulgar, common, and open to all, and who languish meanwhile over certain more subtle questions and tangled controversies—when they later come to preaching, they please themselves far too much, but are accustomed to move all prudent men now to laughter, now to pity. To laughter, when having seized upon the smallest opportunity, they speak about some controversy not...”*
