...necessary, they pour out more than is right; regarding mercy, when they are about to speak of practical matters, they grow entirely cold, as if they had been transported into another world.

VII. General prejudices, which are very harmful to religion and piety, must frequently be challenged regarding the true nature of piety, and the sources of these misguided opinions must be uncovered. These actually harm religion more than formal heresies. For instance, many among the learned believe that the height of piety consists in the pursuit of Orthodoxy—that is, in the most fierce defense of every opinion and hypothesis that our teachers have instilled in us. Others think that the greatest and most excellent part of divine worship is found in the constant attendance of churches and the diligent observation of accepted rituals. Others still claim that the hope of salvation is to be placed in a refuge in the mercy of Christ, yet without any change of mind <note>original: "sine ulla tamen mentis mutatione," referring to a lack of genuine repentance or inner transformation.</note>, and so on. Sacred Orators <note>A term for preachers or public religious speakers.</note> ought to challenge these destructive opinions with the most serious and clear arguments. The late <note>original: "ὁ Μακαρίτης," a Greek term of respect for the deceased.</note> and famous Werenfelsius <note>Samuel Werenfels (1657–1740), a Swiss theologian known for his moderate views and critique of religious hypocrisy.</note> showed an example to follow in his dissertation *On Carnal Security* <note>original: "De Securitate carnali."</note>.

VIII. In the performance of their duties, Ministers of the Word of God <note>original: "V. D. M." for Verbi Divini Minister.</note> ought to show that they care chiefly for those things which pertain to the progress of religion and piety. On the other hand, they should exert every effort to carry out those tasks that lead to the decrease and extinction of ignorance, superstition, and impiety. For in this way, others who see these things will firmly believe that the ministers are truly persuaded of the excellence of the Christian religion, and that it is not likely that such men are merely acting as stage-performers in matters concerning religion. Conversely, when people see that ministers perform their duties most negligently, are seekers of profit, and are more concerned with earning their bread than with truth and piety, many begin to doubt not only the ministers' own piety, but often even the truth of the Religion itself.

IX. Sacred Orators should not neglect the study of Philosophy. Besides the fact that it brings true grace and ornament to the study of other literature, it also ensures that the Orator proposes his topics in a solid and orderly way, distinguishes heavy and solid matters from the trivial, knows how to show the force and weight of arguments, and prudently avoids "meteor-like" oratory and the empty noise of words. This study is necessary because of those very people who either lean toward Unbelief or have already fallen into this disease. When such men know that a Sacred Orator is plainly unrefined in these disciplines, they hear him with nothing but disgust, and judge the things he brings forward as unworthy of being heard with attention. It is certain that Orators destitute of these defenses talk with Unbelievers in vain, nor can they rightly blunt their object-

-ions. Indeed, they rather provide the Unbelievers with various opportunities to despise religion itself and to mock the Ministers of the Word as authors of superstition and fanaticism.

X. When Sacred Orators are present at the gatherings of men of the political order <note>referring to statesmen, politicians, or civil authorities.</note>, as often happens, and these men speak more freely about matters concerning the business of Religion, the ministers ought to behave prudently and circumspectly. For often, by acting this way, these men seek nothing other than to learn through experience the extent of that Pastor’s skill in divine matters, and by what reasoning he might meet this or that difficulty. Here, it is surely necessary that the minister shows he has diligently searched into the causes of Unbelief, and is able to "hit the throat of the case" <note>original: "jugulum causæ petere," a Latin idiom meaning to get to the heart of the matter or the most vital point of an argument.</note>—that is, to skillfully remove the primary foundations of the difficulties brought forward. In this way, he not only gains some authority for himself, but also prevents these men from speaking more carelessly about religion on other occasions. However, a prudent Minister will be careful not to hate such men for this reason, nor to detract from their reputation and standing, much less to attack them from the pulpit <note>original: "de rostris," referring to the speaker's platform or pulpit.</note> with bitter words. For not only would he achieve nothing by this method, and by no means lead the erring back to the path, but he would also often stir up dangers harmful to himself.

XI. Ministers of holy things act prudently if they maintain a deep silence regarding their "vocations"—whether internal or external—unless some necessity demands it. I advise this because I have been taught by experience that those who consider Ministers of the Word to be authors and promoters of superstition seek food and defense for their Unbelief from these things. A Minister who stands out in learning and piety, and is intent on his duty as far as the weakness of human nature allows, has no need to speak words about his "internal calling." As for the nature of that calling which is termed "external" <note>the formal appointment or ordination by a church body, as opposed to a personal spiritual conviction.</note>, everyone knows it well; and if the other ornaments of the office are absent, it wins no true honor for the Teacher.

XII. Although Ministers of the Word, like other mortals, are not entirely immune to all errors and vices, they must nevertheless take the greatest care not to let themselves be carried away by the "torrent" of this or 그 (that) group. For even if it cannot be concluded from these faults that Religion itself is built upon no argument or a weak one, it can nevertheless provide an opportunity for the more unrefined people, who are not sufficiently knowledgeable in religion, to doubt the truth of religion. We remember, however, that we have already dealt with these matters in previous dissertations.

XIII. Hypotheses that are partly uncertain and partly of no use in the pursuit of piety should not be employed from the pulpit <note>original: "pro rostris," referring to the speaker's platform or pulpit.</note>. For the most part, more learned listeners do not accept them, and the rest, who make up the greatest number, do not understand them. In this category, we must also include an excessive eagerness for dreaming up new allegories and types <note>In this context, "types" refers to "typology," a method of biblical interpretation where Old Testament events are seen as foreshadowing New Testament ones.</note>, and for binding the obscure oracles of the ancient prophets to specific, fixed dates of the end times.

XIV. Finally (to pass over other matters in silence), if Ministers of the Word of God <note>original: "V. D. M." or "Verbi Divini Ministri."</note> ever know that there are some in their congregations who think a little too freely about religious matters, they should not for that reason be hated, or persecuted, or utterly neglected as if they were stubborn; rather, they should be led back to the right path with courtesy, modesty, and sound arguments. It must be shown that Ministers of the Word are not "heresy-hunters" <note>original: "Haeretifices," a derogatory term for those who are eager to find heresy in others.</note>, but lovers of religion. Often, through modesty and prudence, you obtain what you could in no way achieve through excessive severity. But more will be said on these matters in the progress of this dissertation. I have no doubt that if the Ministers of the Word and sacred public speakers lend an open ear to these words, they will perceive a most abundant fruit from them, and will thus be empowered to prevent the vice of Unbelief <note>original: "Incredulitas," referring here to a lack of faith or active skepticism regarding religious truths.</note> from creeping further and taking deep roots in the minds of men, so far as it lies within their power.

<margin>What must be performed by Rulers and Moderators of Republics in this matter is shown.</margin>

II. Thus far we have weighed what must be performed by Ministers of the Word if they wish to confront that most heavy evil, namely Unbelief, and to strengthen souls. It is now time for us to look into what Rulers and Moderators of Republics <note>The "Moderators of Republics" refers to civil magistrates or governing officials.</note> can contribute to hindering and suppressing this epidemic disease. We know, of course, that the chief care of Rulers is placed in promoting the advantages of civil society, and especially in caring for those things which can keep Republics safe and sound <note>original: "sartas tectasque," a legal idiom meaning "in good repair" or "well-maintained."</note>. We know too that they have no rights over the consciences of men, nor can they impose articles of belief upon their subjects at their own whim. But truly, when they are considered as Princes bound by the common bonds of religion and as members of Christian churches raised to the highest dignities, they can contribute much—not only regarding the external government of the Churches to avoid disorder <note>original: "$\dot\alpha\tau\alpha\xi\iota\alpha\nu$" (ataxian), meaning confusion or a lack of order.</note>, but also by supplying the most healthy counsels by which a true and saving knowledge of divine things can be handed down and instilled in their subjects. Thus, errors hostile to religion and civil society can be avoided. We therefore state as a principle that it is not only permitted, but it is their duty to recommend Religion to their subjects by *legitimate*—I say *legitimate*—means, and to perform everything they judge can contribute anything toward obtaining a saving knowledge of the Christian

<column-break/>

<page-num>495</page-num>
<header>ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.</header>

religion. I have said, however, that this ought to be done by *legitimate* means: by which very word we forbid all violence and all persecutions. For besides the fact that this way of acting is granted to them by neither divine nor human law, through violent means they only create hypocrites. They tear out the reverence due to themselves even from the minds of the best subjects; and as for those leaning toward Unbelief, they confirm them in the opinion they cherish: namely, that Religion depends on the nod and will of Princes, and therefore that those who follow the dogmas of whatever religion is accepted wherever and among whomever they live are doing exactly what is right.

Those legitimate means, however, can be referred chiefly to the following points. *First*, Rulers—or those to whom the care of appointing such offices has been entrusted—must take care that in public schools, gymnasiums, and academies, such teachers are appointed (especially theologians) who are not only equipped with a great store of solid learning, but who are also wise, circumspect, and peaceful. How much such teachers can do to diminish the vice of Unbelief does not require a laborious demonstration. On the contrary, these same Moderators and Curators of public schools ought to keep away from those places consecrated only to virtue and wisdom any spirits that are proud, argumentative, and made by nature, as it were, for stirring up and nourishing lawsuits and contentions. From this it is clear that learning alone, with which public teachers ought to be equipped, is not sufficient to suppress this evil; there must also be added a true insight of mind, prudence, a love for the most weighty truths, and the pursuit of a moderate character. For where men dominate who were "born when the gods were angry" <note>original: "Diis iratis nati," an idiom meaning people who are ill-fated or naturally prone to causing trouble.</note>, and who busy themselves with and seek nothing else than to "pull the saw of dispute back and forth" <note>original: "serram disputationum reciprocent," an idiom for engaging in endless, tedious bickering.</note> with anyone at all about any tiny little questions, not only are perpetual lawsuits and contentions stirred up between brothers and citizens, but Religion itself is brought into contempt, as if it were a thing designed only for nourishing quarrels. Indeed, for those who are sharper-witted but touched by little love for religion, this provides the most ample material for mockery.

II. Rulers ought to show, given every opportunity, that they not only wish well toward men who are learned, wise, and peaceful, but they are also bound to protect the reputation and esteem of these same men against the whispers and outcries of brawlers, heresy-hunters, and slanderers. For in this way, these men are more and more encouraged to perform their duties with a joyful mind, and they strive to penetrate into the inner shrines of truths with greater diligence. In this way, finally, it becomes clear to all that honor is given not to lineage or a desire for brawling, but to manly...

### MEDITATION XII.

#### XII.
That rewards are laid up for learning and true wisdom. However, when the Nobles and Governors of Republics show by clear signs that they favor and protect men inflamed by a foolish zeal—the "heresy-hunters" <note>original: "Hæretifices," those who manufacture accusations of heresy</note>—and easily allow them to insult the best and most excellent men, many are deterred from seeking the truth. They begin to act as hypocrites, publicly proclaiming their "Orthodoxy" while laughing at it in their hearts; thus they sin against the most holy voice of conscience. In the course of time, they reach a point where they become indifferent to what they actually believe regarding religion.

III. In order for those in power to avoid this evil, they should not easily lend an open ear to brawlers and secret accusers. Among the tricks of such men is this: they frequently visit princely men whom they know not only to be powerful in the State, but also to highly value and defend ancestral opinions and customs, even if they are trivial or of little use. Into the ears of these leaders, they pour the opinions of others, representing them as highly dangerous and comparing these views to names that are widely hated. As a result, it often happens that the Nobles harbor sinister opinions of the best and most innocent men, hating them without cause. To avoid this evil, leaders should either keep such "hornets" <note>original: "crabrones," a metaphor for stinging instigators</note> away from their sight, or, if they must admit them due to their persistence, they should calmly hear the accused before agreeing with the accusers. The points of accusation and the responses must be opened. When it later becomes clear either that the things these senseless men babbled were mere lies, or that a view was misrepresented, or finally that the dispute was about "goat's wool" <note>original: "lana caprina," a common Latin idiom for a trivial or worthless matter</note>—that is, a question of no importance—the leaders should not only quickly shut the "back door" on such mockers, but also receive them in such a way that they cast aside their desire for slandering and carping at others in the future.

IV. In matters that do not pertain to the **Essence of Religion**—such as critical, historical, or philosophical questions, and others of the same nature—those in power ought to grant a prudent and modest freedom of opinion. For where all dissent is proscribed, even in matters of minor importance, true and vigorous learning cannot raise its head, nor can the study of true wisdom flourish. Instead, ignorance, superstition, and hypocrisy will reign, which certainly do not promote religion but depress it, and indeed pave the way to **Indifferentism**. For what can a learned and sharp-witted man do, living in the bosom of, for example, the Roman Church, where he hears a thousand fables and ridiculous opinions that reason rejects,

---

DE CAUSIS INCREDULITATIS.
<meta>catchword: ditis (part of 'addictis' on the following page)</meta>

and yet which he is bound to admit and "kiss" <note>original: "deosculari," meaning to embrace or revere as a matter of faith</note> as articles of faith? He must either act the hypocrite and laugh in his heart at what he is bound to worship, or be handed over to the Inquisitors, or finally leave the sweet soil of his Fatherland. However, if some modest liberty were granted to him, he could deserve well of both Learning and the Republic. This advice must be repeated to Princes all the more because it is certain, by the very nature of things, that it is impossible for men who are devoted to the same religion in its essential chapters to agree in every particular hypothesis, or in critical, exegetical, and philosophical questions. Hence, either a most foul ignorance and superstition must be fostered (which is the mother of all impiety), or some freedom of opinion must be granted in such matters.

V. A Prince should not suppress the **loftier minds** <note>original: "Erectiora ingenia"</note> under the pretext that such people might excite new and unnecessary disputes in the Churches and Republics. By a man of a "lofty mind," I mean one who is led by an incredible zeal for seeking the truth; who weighs all things divine and human with all diligence; who is accustomed to distinguish the trivial from the momentous; who does not easily allow anything to be thrust upon him without sufficient reason; and who finally investigates diligently into publicly received opinions. We believe such minds should be fostered rather than hated. For it is by the work of these men alone that truth has been brought into the light in every age, and darkness dissipated. Our **Blessed Ancestors** <note>original: "B. Majores nostri," likely referring to the Reformers</note> can serve as an example; they strenuously attacked a religion defiled by foul superstition, even though it was publicly accepted, and restored it to its former luster. It is true that some of this number, either from a desire to know everything or from ambition, often wish to wander outside the proper orbit. This disposition of the mind shows itself early in such men. Where this is established by clear signs, such people should be handed over to Teachers eminent in learning and sharpness of mind, who may skillfully temper that heat implanted in their souls and lead them into a level path. This is done by offering them subjects and recommending disciplines through which they can learn how narrow the barriers are that circumscribe our knowledge—whatever it may be—and how many doubts occur in various disciplines, not so much because of the weakness of our minds, but because of the obscurity of the things themselves. In this way, that heat is restrained, and they begin to restrict their greed for knowledge to certain rules. Thus it has often happened that such men later deserved very well of Literature, the Church, and the Republic.

VI. I said above that Princes [should grant] a modest freedom of opinion to their subjects...

### MEDITATION XII.

### ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

...decided, it is right to yield to these men, especially in matters of minor importance. However, where they publicly attack one another with mutual insults, or wish to either defend or attack trivial opinions from the pulpit <note>original: "pro rostris," referring to the speaker's platform or the church pulpit</note>, this license must be restrained by public authority. For these contentions are joined by scandal and stir up strange ferments in the minds of the people. But where they set a limit on their disputing and exchange arguments in a friendly manner, those in power can view those imaginary wars with calm eyes.

**VII.** When dissensions arise concerning the more serious articles of religion—at least those that seem so to truly learned men (not to zealots, shadowy teachers <note>original: "doctoribus umbraticis," meaning scholars who live in the shadows of libraries rather than the real world</note>, or those equipped with little to no actual learning)—the accused should not immediately be treated as guilty, nor should they be condemned without being heard. Instead, the matter should be referred to the most learned men, those who are free from partisan bias and devoted to the same Sacred Rites; their advice must be heard. This is necessary because any side in a disagreement tends to minimize its own errors or exaggerate the danger of the other side. There are countless examples of this in both ancient and recent Church history. Once the judgments of these most excellent men have been heard, the accused must be granted a span of time to re-examine their own thoughts with a tranquil mind, to compare them with the judgments of others, and finally, after weighing everything, to present their opinion. Once everything has been considered and brought back to the rules of equity, the question arises as to how far ecclesiastical tolerance should be extended. For regarding political tolerance, there will be no need for a long discussion among legal experts—at least those who understand both Natural Law and the Laws of Conscience. In this business, one must be all the less hasty because experience shows that many who were charged with the gravest errors were, after a short time, acquitted and considered innocent, while the accusers were exposed to the hatred and detestation of all. What happened in the previous century in the case of <term>Descartes</term> <note>René Descartes (1596–1650), the philosopher whose work was often accused of leading to atheism</note>, and in our own age in the matter of <term>J. Wittich</term> <note>Jacob Wittich (1677–1739), a Dutch philosopher and theologian</note> and the illustrious <term>Wolff</term> <note>Christian Wolff (1679–1754), a major Enlightenment philosopher who was famously expelled from Prussia for his rationalist views</note>, is known to all the learned.

**VIII.** From what I have just said, it follows: those who wish to take charge of the State act best and most prudently if they strive to acquire for themselves a more accurate knowledge of the Christian religion, and especially of those articles which are held as fundamental by the most prominent theologians. For although it is not the role of Rulers to decide the weight of religious matters or to prescribe articles of religion according to their own whim, it is nevertheless extremely useful if they are not ignorant in these arguments. In this way, they do not easily allow themselves to be deceived by senseless zealots, and at the same time, they can better weigh the judgments of learned men concerning this or that controversial article.

<column-break/>

<header>ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.</header>

Truly, the leaders of Republics are to be praised if, when some leisure is granted from public cares, they study the writings of the most learned men regarding the principal articles of Natural and Revealed Religion. Blessed indeed is the State where *philosophers rule, or where those who rule philosophize.* <note>A famous reference to Plato's *Republic*</note>

**IX.** To prevent "Incredulity" <note>unbelief or skepticism</note> (as much as it lies within the power of Rulers) and to promote and confirm religion and piety, it does much good if, in the cities and countryside alike, such <term>Ministers of the Word of God</term> <note>original: "V. D. M." for Verbi Divini Minister</note> are appointed who stand out for their learning, prudence, a spirit of moderation, and diligence in performing their duties. It is especially necessary that this be done in the larger cities. For many of the listeners are skilled in the art of thinking and in both philosophical and theological disciplines; if the speakers use foolish reasons to prove the most holy things, religion itself cannot help but be brought into contempt.

**X.** The moderators of Republics must take primary care that schools are properly established in the countryside, that a prudent and pious selection of rural teachers is made, and that catechetical instructions are held most diligently. Without these, all sermons are in vain, and superstition, ignorance, and contempt for religion will triumph together.

**XI.** Great men should not allow speakers to mount the sacred pulpits without careful meditation and the writing down of those things that are to be proposed. Surely, if anyone is allowed to babble whatever comes to their mouth <note>original: "quicquid in buccam venit," a Latin idiom for speaking without thinking</note> and sell it as religion, religion cannot help but be exposed to laughter.

**XII.** Similarly, the moderators of Republics should not allow profane men and jokers to publicly mock the most holy heads of Natural and Revealed Religion with "white teeth" <note>original: "albis dentibus," a phrase meaning to laugh derisively or sneer openly</note> and thus, as much as they can, bring them into contempt. I will teach below that one must act differently with those who, moved by scruples of conscience, bring forth their arguments modestly.

**XIII.** Princes must make every effort so that subjects and citizens do not subscribe to the publicly accepted religion out of fear of persecution or through hypocrisy, but are persuaded of it as much as is necessary. Truly, there are no better citizens than those who are convinced of the primary arguments of religion, even if they perhaps err in matters of minor importance. But none are more harmful to States than hypocrites. For if a person is not seriously devoted to the worship of the Divine, how can he hold the Rulers and their decrees in high regard?

It highlights that true religious conviction, rather than forced hypocrisy, produces the best citizens.</summary>

### MEDITATION XII.

**XIV.** Much also contributes to this goal if the Rulers and Princes themselves love Religion and the worship of the Deity. On the contrary, where that well-worn saying holds true—*Let him who wishes to be pious depart from the court* <note>original: "Exeat aula, qui vult esse pius"</note>—many subjects will care very little for Religion. These are the things that Rulers can and should do to hinder Unbelief. Besides the advice I have given to Rulers so far, two points remain which were brought forward by <term>the late</term> <note>original Greek: "ὁ Μακαριτης"</note> the celebrated Werenfels <note>Samuel Werenfels (1657–1740), a Swiss Reformed theologian known for his moderate views and critique of religious fanaticism.</note> in his work *On the Right of the Magistrate over Consciences*:

*First, he says, that to refute grave errors, only men fit for this task should be employed. How much a pious Magistrate can contribute to this, if he ensures that no one is employed to refute errors, whether by voice or in writing, unless he is uniquely fit for the task; a man who has a thorough understanding of the nature of the evil he wishes to heal, its origin, and the most effective remedies. He should not only be capable of clearly showing the falsehood of a particular opinion, but also of removing the prejudices of the one in error and restraining those passions that hinder the acknowledgment of truth. Finally, he should be—as Quintilian <note>referred to here as "Fabius," the Roman rhetorician Fabius Maximus Quintilianus</note> requires of an Orator—a good man (and I add, a good Christian: pious, gentle, humble, etc.) skilled in speaking—that is, fit for persuading others of the truth. I say persuading, not commanding or threateningly thrusting it upon them. For nothing has greater power over most people than gentleness and mildness, supported by solid reasons. Gregory of Nazianzus <note>A 4th-century Church Father known as "The Theologian."</note> boasts that he brought back many separated people to the Catholic Church by this method, undoubtedly following that divine warning of Paul: The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but be gentle toward all, apt to teach, patient with the wicked, instructing with mildness those who are of a contrary mind, to see if God might at some time give them repentance to acknowledge the truth.* <note>Reference to 2 Timothy 2:24-25.</note>

---

A Magistrate can also contribute much here if he takes care that the cultivation of judgment and the pursuit of a sound mind flourish. For where this reigns, no applause is found for those empty opinions and dreams which so greatly recommend themselves to <term>visionary</term> <note>original Greek: "φαντασιατικοις," referring to people with overactive or delusional imaginations</note> men of weak judgment. These things corrupt their imagination more and more and sweep them away into I-know-not-what trackless wastes. From there, one proceeds by degrees to Fanaticism, an evil than which none in the Church is more contagious or less curable. This is especially true if ill-timed declamations against the use of reason in religion are added; these cause men to be all the more pleased with themselves and to applaud themselves the more they see themselves hissed at by Wise men. 

Above all, a pious Magistrate can contribute much to both avoiding and healing pestilential errors if he removes the scandals that exist in the Orthodox Church. These scandals make its doctrine so suspicious that those who are outside think it false because it bears such fruit;

### ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.

and many who are within the Church begin to doubt it, considering it as a fable that is believed by almost no one. Here the Magistrate has a wide field to demonstrate his zeal. Here he can compel, here he can punish; here laws have great efficacy. Here also the Magistrate can ensure that the authority of the Church and its discipline is maintained, and that this discipline is exercised with due severity and moderation. By this one remedy, the efforts of most seducers are rendered vain—those who mock others under the appearance of piety and, what is most deplorable, mock especially those who groan most deeply at the vices and sins running rampant. In this way, the strength of Anabaptism and fanaticism is cut off—but also that of Deism and Atheism. *For as long as so few live a life truly consistent with religion, Fanatics will not cease to thrust themselves upon the common people as Reformers of Christianity, nor will profane men cease to secretly suggest to people that the talk about religion is empty and is least of all believed by those very people who profess it.* So says that wisest of Theologians.

<margin>What must be done with those who lean toward the vice of Unbelief.</margin>

**III.** But it is time that we finally come to those who seem to lean toward the vice of Unbelief. Since, however, men can easily be deceived in their judgments, we will first show <term>by way of elimination</term> <note>original Greek: "κατ' ἄρσιν," a logical term meaning to define something by stating what it is not.</note> who should *not* be recorded in this catalog. 

**1.** Indeed, first, those should by no means be considered as such who do not admit all the decrees of the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to academic or scholastic theology, which could often be rigid and dogmatic.</note>, but often depart from them—even blaming and rejecting shameful errors that have become ingrained and confirmed by long use. Nor do they make much of that boasted "Orthodoxy" which every sect claims for itself; and in discussing matters both divine and human, they use a freedom of speech worthy of a free-born man. Such people are certainly not to be counted among the Unbelievers; for this often happens to the most excellent men, who are clearly far removed from any appearance of impiety. Indeed, an injustice is done to such men if they are weighed down by malicious suspicions. Men of more vehement temperament, having heard such calumnies, often become bolder; they regard their accusers as witless, unlearned, and "shadowy" teachers, and consequently begin to place higher value on those who have obtained some name among the Unbelievers.

**2.** Those are not to be included in this assessment who admit nothing without the weightiest reasons, but subject everything to the most accurate examination, and only after weighing the arguments on both sides do they either assent or not assent. Since such men are "rarer than white crows," while most people embrace ancestral decrees without delay, it is no wonder if such men are considered Unbelievers by the common crowd of the Learned. That an injustice is being done to them, however, is clear as day.

**3.** Nor should this hateful name be given to those who, in meet-

### MEDITATION XII.

...private steps for the sake of exercise, they challenge those things which others consider primary and immovable, for the purpose of training others or seeing what arguments they might use to establish this or that dogma. For often on these occasions, many unwillingly discover their own ignorance and are invited to undertake a new examination of the arguments they have used until now.

(4) Nor should those be referred to this category who publicly state that the arguments brought forward thus far to prove a fundamental truth are weak, and who offer reasons why they feel this way. It is well known within the memory of our fathers that among the arguments brought forward, for example, for the existence of God, there was the "consensus of the Nations," <note>original: "consensum Gentium"; the idea that because all cultures believe in a god, one must exist.</note> the "stings of conscience," the "notion of a most perfect Being," and the "idea of the Deity" implanted in all minds. Yet who does not know that the most learned men of our age have proved with solid arguments that these points are too weak to be used fruitfully against an Atheist, and have substituted far weightier arguments in their place? So far are such men from being considered unbelievers that thanks should rather be given to them for shedding new light on the truth. *There will certainly be those who will give advice, if giving advice were without danger, says Darius in the works of Curtius.* <note>Referencing Quintus Curtius Rufus, a Roman historian who wrote a biography of Alexander the Great. The quote suggests that critics often stay silent to avoid being labeled as heretics or troublemakers.</note>

(5) Furthermore, those who defend liberty of conscience should not be accused of this vice. They defend this truth with the weightiest arguments and show that this principle is built upon the most certain foundations. There are many among the <term>theologasters</term> <note>A derogatory term for petty, superficial, or incompetent theologians.</note> who, being ignorant of the decrees of the law of nature and conscience, cry out as soon as they hear this or that person defending the freedom of thought most sharply, claiming that this man is an "Indifferentist"—as if he actually favored all foolish and erroneous opinions simply because he asserts that those who dissent from us should at least be tolerated and not subjected to persecution.

(6) Finally, those who find "Eclectic Theology" <note>A method of theology that does not adhere strictly to one school (like Lutheranism or Calvinism) but chooses what it deems best from various systems based on reason and scripture.</note> pleasing should not be said to patronize unbelief. These are people who, while preserving the principal heads of Natural and Revealed Religion, do not follow either **Luther** or **Calvin** in everything else. Instead, they attentively follow the Holy Scriptures as the sole rule of faith, using all the aids of genuine interpretation, and admit what they judge to be revealed clearly enough in them. Such people are undeservedly counted among the number of **Indifferentists**. For to the Indifferentist, it is all the same whatever opinion they hold about religion. But those of whom I speak profess the fundamental heads of religion and recur to the unique norm of things to be believed—namely, the Holy Scriptures—while for the other, less fundamental articles which are defended in the

schools, they subscribe or do not subscribe according to the measure of their own understanding. And indeed (if only Protestants rightly recognized their own principles), such people cannot be regarded as Indifferentists or as favoring Unbelief.

<margin>By what characteristics it can be judged whether someone truly inclines toward Unbelief.</margin>
IV. We must now inquire <gloss>according to God</gloss> <note>original Greek: "κατὰ θεόν"; meaning according to God's standard or in a godly manner.</note> by what certain signs it may be proved that this or that person strongly inclines toward the vice of Unbelief. It is necessary above all else that he who wishes to pronounce a judgment on another in this matter should have a clear perspective of the person's character, morals, and entire way of life, either from familiar conversations or from their writings. Unless this is done, his judgment will often be doubtful and uncertain. For most men are not always consistent with themselves, but bring forth different judgments concerning human and divine matters according to their temperament, circumstances, and disposition of mind. In general, we represent here such characteristics as can be applied to most who are gripped by this disease.

*The first is:* If someone, under no pressing necessity and on every given occasion, brings forward nothing but paradoxes hostile to pure religion and which can offend every good person; yet at the same time, it is clear to all who know him intimately that he lacks all the tools to judge rightly concerning weightier arguments; we can say of him that he inclines toward Unbelief.

*Second:* He who sees doubts everywhere in the cause of Religion, yet does not deign to unroll and examine the writings of the most learned men who have attempted to remove those doubts, is suspected of this vice.

*Third:* He who exerts every nerve and every sharpness of his wit to attack the principal heads of Natural and Revealed Religion, yet at the same time wants to induce others to believe that this is only done so that the weakness of the human mind might be exposed. It is quite likely that such a man suffers from this disease, and he tries in vain to deceive the learned with this way of acting. It was primarily on this account that most excellent men judged the most learned **Bayle** <note>Pierre Bayle (1647–1706), a philosopher whose "Historical and Critical Dictionary" was famous for its skeptical rigor.</note> to have leaned toward Unbelief. However, one must feel differently about the Illustrious **P. D. Huet**, <note>Pierre-Daniel Huet (1630–1721), Bishop of Avranches, who argued for the limitations of human reason to promote faith.</note> who indeed patronized Scepticism in his booklet *On the Weakness of the Human Mind*, yet did so in such a way that he thought some defense for the Roman Church could be gained from it.

*The fourth is:* Those who, without respect for persons, represent all Theologians and Ministers of the Word of God as inept and foolish ranters and as promoters of superstition and tyranny, [are] justly [suspected] of this vice...

*The fifth sign is:* Those who extol all the writings of the Profane and Unbelieving to the heavens with praise, and kiss them as if they were Oracles given from heaven; yet they think lowly of the writings of all the most observant men—by the consensus of the learned—and are offended by a few blemishes and vehemently criticize the smallest errors they might happen to commit. They act as patrons for Unbelief.

*The sixth:* Those who marvelously rejoice when they hear that this or that argument—which until now were used by learned men as the strongest for either Natural or Revealed Religion—is being attacked. Even though they very often have not even weighed the force and weight of the objections (indeed, due to a lack of Erudition <term>Erudition: deep, scholarly learning</term>, they cannot weigh them), they are not undeservedly referred to this same class. In those whom these characters and others are detected, it can be said without fear of error that they are very prone to Unbelief. I have brought forward other signs of this disease, especially where the evil arises from ambition, in my previous dissertations written on this subject. The late <note>original: ὁ *Μακαρίτης* (ho Makaritēs); a Greek term used to respectfully refer to the deceased as "the blessed" or "of happy memory."</note> celebrated Barbeyrac represented these traits of a man inclining toward Unbelief in a single bundle, as it were, in the Preface to Volume IV of the *Sacred Sermons* of the illustrious Tillotson <note>John Tillotson (1630–1694), Archbishop of Canterbury, known for his influential sermons.</note>. The words on page 31 and following sound like this:

> *Regarding those who, after exaggerating difficulties to the extreme and ruining, as much as in them lies, the certainty of the purest lights of reason, declare that they believe despite the apparent absurdity of the principles of Religion; those people, I say, reveal themselves enough to authorize us not to place much stock in protestations that appear belied by their conduct. A perpetual affectation of not letting any difficulty pass, however small it may be, without raising it and pushing it to the uttermost; a pitiless obsession with criticizing all the works that appear in defense of Religion, and sometimes giving a disadvantageous opinion of them in advance, without waiting to have seen and examined them as they ought; an air of triumph, which marks clearly enough the secret joy one has in seeing the Defender of the common cause in embarrassments from which one implies he cannot extricate himself; all this, in my opinion, strongly smells of a man who betrays himself, and who betrays his party. I know that good faith requires one not to hide difficulties: but it in no way demands that one should display them oneself and press them without any necessity. It is enough to admit them on occasion; is it necessary to carefully warn—*

> *—the Enemy of weak spots, as if he did not know how to find them himself? These obscurities that God has found good to leave in our most necessary knowledge are a mortifying object for any person who loves the truth: Is it fitting to rejoice in them, and is that an act of that humiliation which it is said God intended to inspire in us by putting a perpetual contrariety between the lights of Faith and those of reason? Why not rather work to represent Religion as it is, both supremely advantageous and supremely reasonable, though one cannot always give a reason for the conduct of God, who is an infinite Being? Why not rather take as a task the dissipating of so many foreign obscurities that human ignorance or malice have spread over the clearest and most certain principles, to disentangle the Truths and Maxims of Religion from so many false glosses, so many forced explanations, so many misunderstood applications, so many unjust consequences, which, by disfiguring it, contribute perhaps more than anything else to prevent its effect? There would be a vast enough field there to exercise oneself, if one were as well-intentioned in favor of Religion as one wishes to persuade others.* So says that most learned man.

But before we show individually how to deal with the different types of men inclining toward Unbelief, some things in general must be advised regarding the manner of conversing with these men. Speaking generally on this subject, one must converse with them modestly, circumspectly, and with a testimony of sincere love. One must abstain from harsher words, which could alienate their minds from us, and from comparisons to those who have been counted among the Heretics. They are to be treated in the manner accepted by Physicians, that is, by not becoming angry with them, but by providing gentle remedies. To that end, we must ensure that we gain their favor and testify to our sincerity on every occasion. They should be asked to freely pour out the doubts sticking in their minds into our bosom, solemnly professing that not only will this be pleasing and acceptable to us, but that we embrace with favor those who, setting aside all hypocrisy, candidly set forth that which they think is true. It has often happened to the best, most excellent, and most truth-loving men that, either through more abstruse meditation or through the reading of the Ancients and Moderns, they began to doubt those things which they learned as youths; often a matter of small moment prevents us from feeling the force of the arguments brought forward for these or those articles of religion. It is not the mark of a wise and candid man to subscribe to the religion of his country without examination, but all things are to be examined impartially <note>original: *ἀδεκάστως* (adekastōs); Greek for "without being bribed" or "without bias."</note>. <header>MEDITATION XII.</header>

...moved <note>original: *commot-* (continuing the word *commoti* from the previous page's catchword)</note>, and we must ensure that they firmly believe we are moved solely by the love of truth when we wish to share our counsel with them.

<margin>
One must see for what reasons men incline toward Unbelief.
</margin>

V. Whoever wishes to draw back those men who are leaning toward Unbelief must carefully weigh whether this inclination is to be attributed only to *passions* <note>original: *affectibus*; in this context, it refers to emotional drives or irrational desires</note>, or indeed to *reasons* and *doubts* occupying the mind. If it is established by clear evidence—manifest, I say—that this or that person is moved by depraved inclinations to patronize Unbelief, one must discern which passion especially exerts its force upon his mind. For the most part, however, these men are hindered either by *ambition* or by the *love of pleasures* from subscribing to the most serious articles of the Christian religion. If it is apparent that a man is captured by a depraved ambition, 1) such a person must be told to look within himself and seriously weigh whether he is moved to approve or reject this or that opinion by a pure love of seeking the truth, or instead by a desire for novelty and for achieving praise in the learned world. 2) It must be shown how harmful this passion is to the pursuit of seeking the truth, and how unworthy it is of a Man who boasts that he is moved to assent or dissent by nothing but reason. 3) Since those who suffer from this vice are greatly different among themselves—one being destitute of the protections of true learning, while another is well-versed in the art of reasoning and cultivated in various disciplines—everyone sees that one must act with each in a different manner. He whom an ambitious desire to defend new and unusual things merely plagues, though he may be unfit to bring any color of truth to his opinion, can more easily be convicted of his own folly than he who is equipped with some apparatus of learning. This must be done, however, as modestly and foresightedly as possible. The article of faith which he attacks must be explained correctly, and that in sufficiently clear words; solid arguments, yet tempered to his own intellect, must be brought forward; and only after this is done should one hear what hinders him from offering open ears to the truth, and the sources of his errors must be uncovered. But if he is equipped with some learning, it must be shown (1) how unworthy it is of a sensible man <note>original: *viro cordato*</note> to wish to stubbornly defend paradoxes and things hostile to Religion for the sake of a fleeting and uncertain reputation; that the truth itself is not changed thereby; and that arguments alone add weight to the truth, for whatever reasons it may be attacked. 2) It must be shown that all passions indeed greatly hinder the love of knowing the truth, because they sweep us toward that side which most satisfies our desires; yet ambition has the most power in the minds of men, because it commends itself under some appearance of praise and the pursuit of seeking the truth;

---

<page-num>507</page-num>
<header>ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.</header>
<sig>Sss 2</sig>

3) It must be shown, by bringing forward various arguments sought from various disciplines, how narrowly our knowledge is enclosed within barriers. On this occasion, the *most noble Locke's book on human understanding* <note>original: *Nobilissimi Lokii de intellectu humano liber*—referring to John Locke’s *An Essay Concerning Human Understanding* (1689)</note> is to be commended, which can lead a man who loves truth, but who feels more magnificently about his own knowledge than is right, into a knowledge of himself. Certainly, on that account, this excellent book has always pleased me. 4) It must be shown by examples into how many dangers they have cast themselves, and how troublesome and bitter a life those suffering from this disease have made for themselves. 5) Especially, however, those doubts which he raises must be weighed and balanced with a most calm mind, so much so that whatever can be conceded to him is conceded; nor should one linger on trifles that do little or nothing for the matter itself, but the heart of the matter <note>original: *jugulum causæ*; literally "the throat of the case"</note> must be sought, setting aside hateful consequences, unless the absurdity of the very system he defends necessarily requires this. 6) He must be warned that we are dealing with a matter of the greatest importance; and that it is not all the same—provided we admit a Deity <note>original: *Numen*</note> who is not only the source of all things, but also holds all the hidden thoughts of human minds clearly in view—what we think about God, his virtues, and his will. It is necessary, therefore, that before we harden our minds against those things said about religion by the most learned men among Christians, we weigh everything seriously, and do not rush with too headlong an impulse toward the glory of praise, etc. But if it is manifest that a man inclining toward Unbelief is captured by the *love of depraved pleasures*, then before all else one must see that we seek opportune occasions for speaking with him. Such occasions are those where he hears reasons with a serene brow and his mind is not disturbed by the heat of passions; at that time it must be shown to him how shameful it is, and plainly unworthy of a wise man, to wish to admit only that in the business of religion which is pleasing and acceptable to the passions. No one will easily believe that such a person is led by the force of conscience and the love of truth, who betrays by open signs that he does one thing by attacking religion: namely, to loosen the reins of his passions. The more he obeys the counsels of these passions, the less fit he will be to examine the truth rightly; indeed, with the passage of time, he will come to the point where he cannot render a sound judgment on religion. Truths of any kind do not depend on our desires and will, but on the intrinsic constitution of things and the strength of arguments, etc. Meanwhile, his doubts must be heard with a tranquil mind, and one must deal with him placidly. Those things should be consulted which the illustrious Burnet advised in this case when he was about to lead the Earl of Rochester back to the path <note>original: *Ill. Burnetus Comitem Rocestriensem*—referring to Bishop Gilbert Burnet’s 1680 book on the deathbed conversion of the libertine John Wilmot, 2nd Earl of Rochester</note>.

<page-num>508</page-num>
<header>MEDITATION XII.</header>

Finally, there are those who incline toward **Unbelief** <term>Unbelief: original *Incredulitatem*, referring here to a lack of religious faith or skepticism toward church doctrine</term> though moved by no depraved passions. The mental constitution of some people is such that they feel the force of arguments very little, yet conversely see doubts everywhere. Some fell into the writings of **Skeptics** or **Deists** <note>Deists believe in a creator God based on reason but reject supernatural revelation or divine intervention</note> at an early age, while their minds were not yet sufficiently cultivated by more rigorous disciplines. Others have read authors who attempted to prove the most serious points of religion using weak arguments; finally, there are those who, despite their merits, are weighed down by countless evils at the hands of insolent men. These people begin to doubt divine **Providence**, and being cast from one doubt into another, they begin to *withhold their judgment* <note>original: *ἐπέχειν* (epechein), a Greek philosophical term for suspending one's assent to a proposition</note> regarding the truth of both Natural and Revealed religion.

With these individuals (1) one must deal circumspectly; whenever there is an occasion to address them, or if they are well known to us, they should be praised for the fact that they weigh religious matters *without passions* <note>original: *ἄνευ παθῶν* (aneu pathon), meaning objectively or unemotionally</note>, and do not immediately cast their vote for publicly accepted opinions without sufficient reasons. It should be shown (2) that it has happened even to the best and most excellent men that they doubted truths of the greatest importance for a time, but in the course of time, having weighed the matter better, they happily struggled out of this labyrinth. God, who sees into the innermost recesses of humans and clearly knows the reasons by which each person is led to either embrace or reject religion, will hardly interpret the scruples arising in the mind against this or that point of religion in a bad light—provided they act in such a way that they omit nothing which might stir a greater light of salutary truths in their souls.

To that end (third), it should be shown that in all disciplines, even those that promote the benefits of civil society, many uncertainties and doubts are nonetheless found; yet no one who is wise doubts the utility of those disciplines for that reason. God does not demand more concerning the knowledge of divine things than what each person can achieve by meditating, reading, or consulting others. One should primarily read those writers who have applied singular care and skill in examining and resolving the doubts by which the mind is currently being distressed. Great care must be taken (4) lest we attack the scruples occupying the minds of such people with "light weapons"—that is, with weak arguments or technical scholastic distinctions. Indeed, none are less fit for calling such men back to the path than those who have spent their lives reading minute controversies. On the contrary, it is necessary that such people associate familiarly with those who have imbued their minds with the most excellent disciplines, and who—just as in other

---

<page-num>509</page-num>
<header>ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.</header>

disciplines—have a known and clear perspective on what is solid and what is empty, especially in controversies. Such experts have studied the writings of the **Deists**, as well as those of the most excellent men among the Christians, with the greatest attention. Those who lack these resources and cling only to the decrees of the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to traditional academic or scholastic theology, often criticized here for being too rigid or out of touch</note> are so far from gaining anything that they rather confirm these individuals in the errors they cherish.

<margin>
An inquiry into how to handle those who have fallen into Atheism or Deism itself.
</margin>

VI. Finally, we must come to those who have fallen into the very Abyss of *Atheism* or *Deism*, and believe they can rest securely in this state. These people, as I say, profess either *Atheism* or *Deism*. As for the **Atheists**, some are deceived merely by false but subtle reasoning; others, however, are corrupted by depraved pursuits. They mock things divine and human, and from the talk of profane men, they draw arrows dipped in poison against those things which, in the judgment of all wise men, are most worthy of attention. They have never seriously heard the reasons fighting for religion, and having rejected the examination of matters of the weightiest importance, they cling to certain commonplaces which scoundrels are accustomed to use. These seem less worthy of a learned man's conversation. For what can you do with one who neither can nor will reason about a dogma of the greatest importance?

Meanwhile, however, these people are not to be entirely abandoned. It must be shown to them how contrary it is to reason to wish to use jokes and profanations—unworthy of any wise man—in place of arguments in a most serious matter. Any scoundrel or madman can laugh at the most holy things with "bared teeth" <note>original: *albis dentibus*; a metaphor for mocking or sneering</note>; but no one who is not utterly shameless would lend an ear to such a person, but would rather reject him with indignation and loathing. Since countless men—and those the most learned, sharp-sighted, and erudite—have proved the existence of God after conducting the most rigorous examination, it is not the part of a wise man to refuse to weigh the reasons upon which this truth is built in such a grave argument. If you find him teachable and he looks within himself, yet still does not perceive the subtler arguments of the Metaphysicians, it will be best if you use arguments drawn from the purpose, order, and use of created things—especially of animals and humans. Such booklets should be recommended to him as have purposefully proved the wisdom, power, and goodness of God shining forth from His creatures. In the meantime, one must wait to see what fruit these conversations and counsels have borne, and the advice must be moderated according to the circumstances.

But with those who have acquired some skill in reasoning and are equipped with some apparatus of learning, and have [developed] some system...

<header>MEDITATION XII.</header>
<meta>catchword: ...however</meta>

...however they are connected among themselves, any prudent person skilled in these matters will easily judge that one must act somewhat differently. Those who profess Atheism today mostly subscribe to the hypotheses of either **Spinoza** <note>Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677), a philosopher who argued that God and Nature are one and the same substance</note> or **Epicurus** <note>An ancient Greek philosopher who taught that the world is made of atoms and that gods have no concern for human affairs</note>. I am well aware of what learned men point out regarding *Aristotelian*, *Stratonic*, or *Kabbalistic* Atheism, and so on; however, those who suffer from this "disease" today do not usually fall into such opinions, but rather defend the views of either *Spinoza* or *Epicurus*. 

The disciples of *Spinoza* admit only one eternal substance, which is simultaneously "thinking" and "extended" <note>In Spinoza’s system, "thought" and "physical extension" are two ways of perceiving the same single reality</note>, acting by necessity from all eternity. All creatures that exist are merely parts of this one and eternal substance. If you listen to them, there is no distinct principle separate from this visible world; there is no <term>efficient cause</term> <gloss>the agent that brings something into being</gloss> or <term>final cause</term> <gloss>the ultimate purpose or goal for which something exists</gloss> of this universe. Instead, everything we can grasp through thought—whether they are <term>intelligible things</term> <note>original Greek: *νοητα* (noeta)</note> or <term>sensible things</term> <note>original Greek: *ἀισθητα* (aistheta), things perceived by the senses</note> that are seen and touched—make up only a single substance, of which not only humans, but also trees, cattle, metals, etc., are parts. In a word, the name "God" signifies nothing beyond the whole of the world. Among more recent writers, *Count Passerati* <note>Alberto Radicati, Count of Passerano, a radical philosopher</note> and *Edelmann* <note>Johann Christian Edelmann, a controversial German freethinker</note> were adherents to this view, to say nothing of others. 

The other system is that of *Epicurus*. Those who follow it, having rejected both final and efficient causes, attribute the whole universe and its individual parts to some sort of accidental collision of atoms—even though these parts are constructed with the greatest possible skill according to the judgment of everyone who has not abandoned common sense. Very few among recent unbelievers are actually devoted to this system; indeed, it is so dull and so far removed from any appearance of truth that anyone who wished to seriously defend it would rightly be exposed to the mockery of all wise men.

But regardless of which system such a person follows, first and foremost, the "sad condition" in which they find themselves must be shown to them through heavy arguments. However, one must deal with them in such a way that they feel we are driven by a love of truth, rather than merely trying to terrify them into deploring their lot. To that end—unless the matter is already publicly known—care should be taken to keep this business within private walls. At the very least, it should not be through our doing that a person in grave error is immediately brought to public shame by the authority of the Magistrate <note>A reference to the legal consequences, including imprisonment or exile, that "Atheists" could face from the government in the 18th century</note>. Before all else, one must think of their correction, which is only obtained through modesty, patience, and the weight of the arguments presented. To this end, men who are highly educated and well-versed in philosophy should meet frequently with such a person. And because time is needed to properly recognize and renounce an error, they should not be dismissed immediately just because they do not perceive the 

---

<page-num>511</page-num>
<header>ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.</header>
<meta>catchword: disciples</meta>

force of our arguments; nor should all care for them be cast aside. They should be warned, in the meantime, not to spread their error among the common people, lest they stir up dangerous perils for themselves.

In general, a person so gravely in error should be exhorted to look within themselves, and seriously examine and look down into all the recesses of their heart, to see if something other than logic has cast them into this error. It is easy for people to deceive themselves. Since almost all other mortals—not only the unrefined and uneducated, but also the most learned and sharp-witted, who are entirely free from any suspicion of gullibility or superstition—consider Atheism to be the greatest insanity and the crudest error, it is necessary that the person does not stubbornly cling to a view they have seized upon without further examination. Instead, they should act with the greatest foresight in a matter of such supreme importance. 

Therefore, system must be compared with system; reason with reason, doubt with doubt. The matter must be weighed anew as if it had never been considered before, and this must be done <term>without passion</term> <note>original Greek: *ἀϐερ παθον* (aber pathon), meaning without prejudice or emotional bias</note> for the sake of seeking the truth alone; for this is the duty of all wise men and lovers of truth. They should be asked to look again at the writings of the sharpest and most learned men, and especially to pay attention to those responses with which they attacked their specific difficulties. They should be warned above all not to regard the matter itself as suspect or plainly false just because of the weak arguments of certain people; for this can easily happen in other disciplines as well. It is not enough to bring forward certain doubts against the existence of God or His nature; rather, they must demonstrate that the reasons used by those who argue that a Divine Power is distinct from the visible world are entirely weak, and that the arguments by which Atheism (in whatever form) is recommended are not only solid, but stronger than those usually brought forward for the existence of God.

If the person follows the system of *Spinoza*, they must first of all be led back to the first principles of Metaphysics concerning the contingent and the necessary, the possible and the impossible, the notion of substance, etc. These must be explained in such a way that the person cannot fail to understand them. Once the first principles and definitions are properly established, the system itself must be attacked. Then, it should be shown what a <term>mass</term> <note>original Greek: *συγμα* (sygma), here meaning a heap or collection</note> of the most absurd and abominable consequences follows from this system through the most legitimate and clearest laws of reasoning. *Pierre Bayle* <note>A French philosopher known for his influential "Historical and Critical Dictionary"</note> took this path against *Spinoza*, and more recently, the most illustrious and learned *Meier* <note>Georg Friedrich Meier (1718–1777), a philosopher at the University of Halle</note>, Professor of Philosophy at Halle, did so against *Edelmann*. I know indeed that this method of arguing is not approved by some; but since from the very definition of God which *Spinoza* and his disciples...

[...which the] disciples use, it necessarily follows that the whole universe, all creatures, and its *parts* are God; I do not see why these consequences cannot be pressed <note>Meaning: the logical outcome of Spinoza's pantheism—that God is simply the sum of all material things—should be used to show the absurdity of the position.</note>. If, however, he follows the system of *Epicurus* <note>Epicurus (341–270 BC) taught that the world formed through the random collision of atoms without divine intervention</note>, then, having established the first principles regarding <term>final causes</term> <gloss>the purpose or "why" behind a thing's existence</gloss>, the nature of order, and the connection between a wise distinction and fatal necessity, one must appeal to the most skillfully crafted structure of animals and plants; to the harmony of the planetary system, to the first origin of humans, and so on. It must be shown through various reasons and examples how foolish it is to wish to ascribe a most masterfully crafted work to random chance. For private reading, one should recommend the writings of *Derham*, *Ray*, *Wolff*, and other learned men <note>William Derham, John Ray, and Christian Wolff were famous "physico-theologians" who wrote popular books arguing that the complexity of nature (like the human eye or the stars) proves the existence of a Creator</note>, in which they have industriously demonstrated the wisdom, power, and goodness of God shining forth from a careful contemplation of the universe.

However, the greatest care must be taken never to use arguments that either prove nothing or are subject to countless exceptions, such as—alas!—are found everywhere in the writings of certain people; for in this way, they are confirmed in their error rather than being drawn back from it. Certainly, nowhere is it more dangerous to wander than in this case. Finally, the brevity of human life must be placed before the eyes of such men, as well as the maximum danger into which they may fall if there is indeed some Divine Power that cares for human affairs. One must therefore proceed by searching, examining, and conferring with the most learned men; for although men of this sort might laugh with "white teeth" <note>An ancient idiom meaning to laugh mockingly or derisively</note> at what is said about the state of the ungodly after death, it must nevertheless be shown to them that it is plainly impossible for them to prove with invincible arguments that everything said about these matters is a mere fiction. And so, by reasoning, advising, and persuading, we ought to continue and not despair entirely of the happy success of our labor. Meanwhile, God must be prayed to at home, that He may dissipate the darkness of the deceived mind and kindle light within it.

Although we are dealing only with the moral means by which men ought to be called back from errors, it will not be out of place here to discuss how one should treat a person who is bound by this grave error and yet refuses to give a listening ear to salutary warnings and advice. Both theologians and legal consultants deal with this matter. I will bring forward the arguments of both those who affirm and those who deny this, as far as I have examined them, and I will allow the reader the freedom of judging the entire dispute, although I will not deny that I have always...

<meta>The catchword at the bottom of the previous page was "always," which connects to "always lean" at the top of this page.</meta>

...always lean toward that opinion which best agrees with natural equity and the right of conscience. In this section, we will represent the arguments of those who think that an Atheist can and should be affected by public and most severe punishments. Here, however, we warn in advance that we are not dealing with a man merely suspected of this vice, from whose system—against his own will—most dangerous consequences are woven; nor with one who either doubts the existence of God for a time or opens the secret of his mind to certain friends; but with one who not only confesses himself to be such, but also freely opens the thoughts of his mind in the presence of others and defends them in public writings. Secondly, it should be observed that this question, viewed in itself, is very grave and momentous; but if we consider that very few people would labor under such insanity as to publicly profess this error, this question seems unworthy of such solicitous and accurate examination, or at least less momentous. In regions where no lions or leopards occur, it does not seem so necessary to prescribe laws to hunters regarding the method by which they can cause those carnivorous animals to be put to flight. But let us come to the reasons themselves used by those who contend that a man professing Atheism should be subjected to heavy punishments, even the death penalty.

*The first argument* they bring forward is this: through the public profession of Atheism, it cannot happen otherwise than that many are induced to seize upon this pestilential opinion. Truly, those who are bound by depraved affections and vices will provide a ready ear to these men. It is the duty of rulers to strive with all their might so that the persuasion of religion remains firm; first, arguments should be used; but when they refuse to yield to them, they should be punished with public penalties, even death itself, not so much for the error as for their obstinacy in defending it.

*The second*: Faith, piety, and friendships—which are the strongest pillars of civil society—are so undermined by it; it is the duty of rulers to provide everything that can make those bonds tighter; conversely, they must cut away those things that can provide an occasion for dissension and distrust among citizens. To this end, they cite a passage from *Cicero's On the Nature of the Gods, Book II*, where among other things he says: 
> *If religion is taken away, trust and the society of the human race and that one most excellent virtue, Justice, are also removed from human affairs.* <note>original Latin: "Religione sublata, fidem etiam & Societatem humani generis & unam excellentissimam Virtutem Justitiam e rebus humanis tolli." Cicero argued that without a divine witness, no oath or contract could be trusted.</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the societal response to atheism. While the previous pages defined the philosophical systems of Spinoza and Epicurus, this section weighs the legal and moral arguments for and against the state-sponsored punishment of those who profess atheism.</meta>

<page-num>514</page-num>
<header>MEDITATION XII.</header>

...moreover, atheism must be considered the most atrocious of things; a man imbued with such a pestilential opinion will not only rush headlong into every kind of impiety himself, but will also invite others to do the same.

*Fourth*: Oaths are highly necessary in all republics <note>The author uses "republic" in the classical sense of any organized state or Commonwealth</note> for the preservation of public security and the maintenance of obedience; however, an oath cannot be prescribed to a man who admits no laws, whether natural or revealed. Therefore, such a person must either be outlawed and banished into exile with infamy, or, unless he repents, be subjected to the heaviest penalties.

*Fifth*: This can be done all the more rightly, and without injury, because an <term>atheist</term> <note>original Greek: ἄθεος (atheos), meaning "one without God"</note> can offer no reasons why he would wish to make his opinion public and recommend it to others. Other men, who are devoted to some sect among Christians, can at least defend themselves with this argument: that moved by the force of conscience, they cannot help but teach better things to others—whom they believe to be bound by grave errors—and draw them toward their own view. An atheist, however, can be induced by no stings of conscience to want to recommend his own opinion to others; it is, therefore, mere petulance and intolerable pride that stimulates him to bring such things forward in public.

*Sixth*: The more civilized nations, for example, the Greeks, subjected men who attacked the public religion to heavy penalties. It is well known from the writings of jurists that in judging natural laws, one must look not only to their standard and nature, but also to the most excellent men of antiquity—especially the philosophers and lawgivers—and to their judgments and decrees.

*Seventh*: The atheist is not punished because of an error of the intellect, but because of a vice of a corrupt will. For it is the will that causes him not only to make his opinion public imprudently and against the decrees of those in power, but also to remove the distinction between vice and virtue, making him like a man who sells poison as if it were a healthy medicine.

*Eighth*: In the Old Testament, false prophets and blasphemers were subjected to the punishment of death by divine command; from which it necessarily follows that this can be carried out much more so against a man professing atheism.

*Ninth*: Finally, those who hold this view add: unless serious measures are taken against those who scatter such profane opinions and defend the gravest errors, many more will be found—given such corruption of the human race—who are inclined to fall into this insanity, which flatters their wicked desires.

...inclined. Moreover, it is the duty of those in power to place a barrier against these evils in a timely manner.

VIII. We have brought forward the principal arguments of those who think that atheists should be subjected to civil penalties, even the most severe; it remains for us to hear those who think otherwise. They use the following arguments: <margin>The arguments of those who think otherwise are presented.</margin> *The first* is: It cannot be denied that atheism is a very grave error, but it is nonetheless an error of the intellect, from wherever it may have arisen. In this case, one should not employ coercive means, but only those consistent with the nature of the error—that is, the weightiest arguments. Errors are not removed from the one erring by punishments, but by showing them better things.

*Second*: An atheist bringing his opinion into the public sphere does not disturb the State or the citizens; for he merely reasons, and he cannot draw anyone toward assent against their will. For it lies in the power of the listeners either to dismiss his arguments or to weigh them seriously, and thus either to reject them or not. Furthermore, the truth of a Divine Power distinct from the visible world has struck such deep roots in the minds of most mortals that it is hardly credible that an atheist will draw many over to his opinion. If some, who were already previously inclined toward unbelief, are perhaps stirred by this reasoning to give their "white stone" <note>The "white stone" (album calculum) is a classical reference to a vote of approval or acquittal</note> to the atheist's reasons, this is to be attributed not so much to the atheist's arguments, but to the wicked inclination of those men. In general, those who think this way believe that this argument sought from "disturbances and contentions" proves more than it ought to prove, and thus proves nothing at all. For if this were valid, they say, not only heretics, but even the most innocent men who happen to disagree with the rest of the crowd would have to be subjected to civil penalties, which is nonetheless contrary to equity and justice. Let us suppose, they say, that a certain man devoted to the Protestant side were to openly defend the truth of his system in *Spain* or *Italy* and wish to draw men living in those places away from foul superstition using heavy arguments; without delay, the petty priests and Inquisitors <note>Members of the Inquisition, the ecclesiastical court of the Catholic Church tasked with suppressing heresy</note> will say that the man is not to be tolerated, but must be subjected to heavy penalties without delay. However vehement those penalties might be, if you listen to such barbaric men, even the most innocent people would be subjected to them; but this way of dealing with those who, in our opinion, are in error, is most unjust. It is always necessary, therefore, that those who say that the erring should be punished with heavy penalties must prove with the clearest arguments that a most manifest link exists between the defense of an error and the obligation and power to inflict such civil penalties.
