<header>MEDITATION XII.</header>
<page-num>516</page-num>

*Third:* It cannot be denied that the conviction regarding the Existence and Providence of the Divine is the strongest bond of civil society; yet it does not immediately follow from this that he who denies that dogma must be most severely punished. Other means exist that are more consistent with reason, such as teaching the man better things and leading him back to the path of truth. Furthermore, the bonds of Society are not necessarily broken by the opinion of the **Atheist**. <note>The author is navigating a middle path here: acknowledging religion's social utility while arguing against the death penalty for unbelievers.</note>

*Fourth:* Faith and piety, as well as mutual love—virtues rooted in religion—contribute much to the observation of the duties of civil society. It must be confessed, however, and it is simultaneously well known, that most Christians perform these mutual duties not because of the dictates of conscience, but because of the help they expect from others, necessity, and the fear of punishment. An **Atheist**, if he wishes to live quietly in Society, both can and ought to observe the civil laws; if he acts otherwise, he can be punished not as an **Atheist**, but as a rebellious person.

*Fifth:* It is true that **Oaths**, used to keep men to their duties, can contribute a great deal; however, they are not so necessary that no Republic can stand without them. It is very well known that in those places where oaths are more frequently insisted upon, men also generally neglect and transgress them. In *England*, the *Netherlands*, and other places, **Anabaptists** <note>A radical Protestant sect that famously refused to swear oaths based on their interpretation of the Sermon on the Mount.</note> are tolerated, and indeed safely so, even though they refuse to take oaths. An **Atheist** is either a citizen of some Empire and Republic, or a foreigner wandering here and there: If he is a citizen, he can be deprived of certain benefits and privileges enjoyed by other citizens who have bound themselves by oaths; and if he sins against the laws of Society, he may be punished. It is not necessary, however, that where he leads a quiet life and does not harm others, he should be punished either with heavy penalties or a violent death. We are not dealing with the case of the foreigner here.

*Sixth:* An **Atheist**, though he does not admit divine laws, will not for that reason immediately rush into every crime. Men do not always act consistently with their own principles, which is evident daily from the fact that Christians themselves trample the precepts of the most holy divine law under their feet. An **Atheist** can be hindered from giving free rein to this or that vice by the force of temperament, a love of peace, fear of punishment, etc. But if he should harm his neighbor, or perform such acts as are contrary to civil law, he can be punished just as other citizens, according to the gravity of the offenses.

*Seventh:* It is true that if there is no divine law, an **Atheist** is not bound to recommend his opinion to others; but it is one thing

to be merely reasoning and putting forward one's own opinion, and another to recommend and anxiously insinuate it. There are countless *grammatical, critical, historical, and philosophical* questions which the Learned bring to light and recommend as their "merchandise"; yet they are bound by no bonds of religion or conscience to do so. An **Atheist** might think that religion is the cause of superstition and many evils, and therefore believe that love of neighbor demands that men be taught better things. Furthermore, he might at least believe his arguments to be stronger than those brought forward for the existence of God. Besides, it is always permitted for those who hear such things to agree or not; and if they add their "white stone" <note>A classical reference to a vote of approval or acquittal in ancient Greece.</note> of support to pestilential opinions without examination, they must attribute it to their own folly.

*Eighth:* What is said regarding the custom of more civilized Nations—that men who are estranged from the ancestral religion (that is, the publicly accepted superstition) ought to be afflicted with public penalties—should move us very little. For besides the fact that it is highly doubtful whether such people utterly rejected all Divinity, the custom of the ancients does not obligate us. It must always be shown that the custom and Decrees of others harmonize with the nature of <term>Natural Law</term> <note>Lex Naturalis: The moral principles believed to be inherent in human nature and discoverable by reason, independent of revelation.</note>; unless this is manifest, the Decrees of others do not have the force of law. The **Catholics** <note>original: "Pontificios" (followers of the Pope).</note> could use the same argument against those who laugh at the little stories of so many male and female saints and explode their worship; such people, forsooth, would have to be punished with fire as Heretics. It has already been sufficiently proved by most learned men how many things contrary to Natural Law and equity those praised, more civilized Greeks and Romans introduced. It is true that the Athenians, for example, often took severe notice of those who despised the ancestral religion, that is, the worship of the Gods; but it ought to be asked by what right that was done. **Socrates** had to drink **hemlock**; yet how headlong this Decree of the Athenian Judges was is manifest from the fact that immediately after the death of so great a man, the same Athenian Judges condemned his accuser **Meletus** to death, and on that very day cast out **Anytus** into exile from the city. They also punished his other enemies with exile, lamented his death, placed a bronze statue in his honor, and built a temple in his memory called the *Socraterion* <note>A shrine dedicated to Socrates.</note>, all of which **Diogenes Laertius** recounts. Moreover, it is most dangerous to follow the examples of others in this matter. For if once a decree for killing an **Atheist** should have the force of law, most innocent men—accused of this error by certain people unskilled in difficult controversies but who possess great power—will easily be brought into the greatest danger of their lives. And in-

...surely if in our own age, men accused of **Atheism**—and indeed in public writings—had been immediately handed over to death, men would have been removed from our midst who were most distant from this crime and who had served the world of learning most excellently <note>The author likely refers to scientists and philosophers whose new ideas were initially branded as godless by traditionalists.</note>; therefore, one must proceed cautiously and with the greatest circumspection in this business.

*Ninth*: Concerning the **Atheist**, it cannot be said that he sins merely by a **vice of the will**, unless you argue that this very crime—the desire to share one’s thoughts with another—ought to be punished with a heavy penalty. Men devoted to vices often lead others to do the same by their example and reasoning; yet, unless those who allow themselves to be led into vice are completely infantile and senseless, they are not punished by death. One must especially notice those who, though they were taught better and perceived the foulness of vice, nonetheless lent their ears to the wicked advice of others—although those who lead others to commit evil through persuasion and reasoning are certainly not immune from punishment. Furthermore, this argument proves nothing, because it proves more than it ought: for by the same logic, it could be proved that a man devoted to the **Protestant** religion who shares his feelings on religion with others in, for example, **Spain**, sins by a vice of the will and could thus be subjected to the most atrocious punishments on that account. This, however, would be contrary to the very opinions of those who think one must deal so severely with **Atheists**. <note>The author is using a "consistency" argument: if Protestants want to be safe from the Inquisition in Catholic Spain, they shouldn't use the same "sharing thoughts is a crime" logic against atheists in their own lands.</note>

*Tenth*: Those who believe the **Atheist** should be treated more mildly continue, saying that an **Atheist** can in no way be called a **blasphemer**. For only he can be accused of this crime who admits to a most perfect and holy Divinity distinct from this visible world, but who simultaneously, against the decrees of his own conscience, pours out such words against God that are diametrically opposed to His most holy nature. Nor should a **Heretic**, who attacks the fundamental points of religion and thinks meanly of some of them, be called a blasphemer for that reason; for a man must be judged according to the decrees of his own opinion, not the opinions of others who think differently. It is true that a **false prophet**, according to the divine command enjoined upon the **Jews** in the Old Testament, was to be subjected to severe punishments; but such a person, who commended **Idolatry** and called the **Israelites** away from the God of **Israel**, was considered to have committed the crime of **High Treason** <term>Perduellionis: In a theocracy where God is the King, religious rebellion is legally equivalent to political treason</term>, according to the **Theocracy** of the Jewish people, as has been shown at length by learned men.

*Eleventh*: It can be observed that no one denies that **Atheists** who disturb society—that is, those who commit such crimes as are everywhere punished with heavy penalties—should be dealt with; however, **error** must always be properly distinguished from **crime**.

**Spinoza** lived peacefully in the **Netherlands** and did not disturb Society; all civil punishments ought to rest on equity; but it must be demonstrated that a heavy penalty imposed merely on one who errs is equitable. Furthermore, superstitious people very frequently disturb Kingdoms and Republics in civil society, yet they are not punished by death for it. Everyone detests the **Barbarity of the Spaniards** used against the **Americans**. <note>original: "Americanos." In the 18th century, this refers to the Indigenous peoples of the Americas and the perceived cruelty of the Spanish Conquest and Inquisition.</note>

*Twelfth*: If an **Atheist** (they further insist) is subjected to a heavy penalty—that is, death—after he has professed his error for some interval of time, he is thus necessarily cast into eternal misery. If, however, time were granted to him to weigh everything properly and freely, to study the most excellent books, and to confer with the most learned men, it could easily happen that he might finally return to a better state of mind and acknowledge his error. The history of all times teaches that men bound by the gravest errors, once their causes were weighed and they were taught better things, finally yielded to the truth.

*Thirteenth and last*: Finally, those who hold this view say that no one is infallible in judging, and even the most learned have often been deceived in their judgment of **Atheism**. It is well known what happened in the previous century to **Descartes**, and in our own age to **J. Wittich** and the **Illustrious Wolff**. <note>René Descartes, Jacob Wittich, and Christian Wolff were all famous philosophers who faced accusations of atheism or heresy by religious authorities despite considering themselves believers.</note> If it were once established by public laws that a man accused of **Atheism** must be punished with heavy penalties and a violent death, many inconveniences would necessarily arise in the Republic by establishing such things, and the guilty and the innocent alike would often be wrapped up in the same punishments. It is known how doubtful the judgments of learned men often are when a judgment must be made on the gravity of errors. One man claims that atrocious errors follow from a certain dogma, while another claims he can see no such thing. All things considered, nothing better can be provided than to use such means as can call back even the most gravely erring person to the right path. Such means, however, do not exist if you depart from solid arguments. And these are the principal reasons used by those who think the **Atheist** should be treated more mildly. By way of a conclusion, I will add two testimonies from recent scholars who favor this latter opinion. One is from a Legal Consultant, the other from a Theologian. **Johann L. <header>MEDITATION XII.</header>

That punishment can be imposed <note>original: *belegen*</note> is considered a settled matter; however, if one examines the matter itself, this **atheism** cannot possibly be viewed as a crime in the eyes of human society. For an atheist does not disturb the outward peace of the Republic, nor does he live any worse than a superstitious and godless hypocrite. And although one cannot deny that it is a very great crime in the sight of God, it does not follow that it must therefore be punished by men, or that such a person can be improved through human punishments. Not to mention that often people can fall into this through no fault of their own. Since one could instead pull them out of their folly with gentleness and patience, I do not see how one wants to clear this proceeding of great cruelty when such people are executed without the knowledge of God.

Another testimony is supplied to us by the very Reverend **A. F. W. Sack** <note>August Friedrich Wilhelm Sack (1703–1786), an influential German Reformed theologian and court preacher in Berlin</note>, Chaplain to the most powerful and wise King of Prussia, a man most excellent in erudition, piety, prudence, modesty, and the pursuit of a moderate mind. > **It is true that a certain freedom to think must take place among rational men, and nothing is more contrary to the spirit of true Christianity than persecution and coercion of conscience: And perhaps nothing has brought more harm to the faith of Christians than precisely the lack of proper gentleness toward those in error. Not only the laws of well-ordered states, but also the laws of the Gospel itself require that one tolerate them, and show them—even if they were actual atheists—all duties of humanity and love: so long as they keep themselves quiet and think for themselves alone, which they may always do quite unhindered, at their own risk. But as soon as they become so bold that they disturb the peace of human society, publicly mock the established religion of a country, go about in houses seeking followers, maliciously drag revelation through their speeches and writings, and thus, as it were, spit in the faces of Christians: then it seems to me that it is at least allowed to an honest man, and is indeed his duty, to publicly rescue his faith and that of many thousands of upright people against such insolent attacks of blasphemers who have become too bold: and to all reflective and impartial minds—**

### § IX.
<margin>How Deists can be called back to the path.</margin>
After we have shown more than enough in the preceding sections how **Atheists** are to be treated, it remains at last for us to consider what must be provided to win over the **Deists**. Before all else, however, it must be seen to which faction or sect they are attached. It is well known that although they all agree in this—that they do not admit <term>Revelation</term><note>The belief that God reveals truths directly to humanity, such as through the Bible, rather than just through nature or reason.</note>—they differ greatly among themselves, as the most learned men, **Clarke** in his *Demonstration of the Existence of God, etc., Volume II, Chapter II*, and recently the most illustrious and dear friend **Vernet** in *On the Truth of the Christian Religion, Volume I of the new edition, Chapter I*, have rightly observed. There are those among them who admit only the existence of God, but either call into doubt or utterly deny the other heads of **Natural Religion**; there are those who believe that **Providence** exists insofar as God preserves the universe, yet they contend that He does not care for human affairs individually, whence they also relegate everything said about the state of the pious and the impious after this life to the realm of fables; finally, there are those who come closer to the truth: these seriously profess all the heads of **Natural Theology** and **Natural Law**, but nevertheless deny the divine origin of the Christian religion for various reasons. Some appeal to that great disagreement among Christians and contend that this is a sign that the Christian religion is not resting upon certain principles. Some have stumbled upon theological books where everything is full of "bristly" <note>original: *hirsutis*, meaning rough, unpolished, or overly complex</note> and trivial opinions; hence they began to despise the Christian religion in general. Others have been driven off course by—

---

(*) To these must be added the learned, pious, and wise theologian **Johann Heinrich Hottinger**, the most illustrious Professor in the Academy of Heidelberg. Here, in a short book written against **Edelmann** <note>Johann Christian Edelmann (1698–1767), a famous radical pietist and early German advocate for Deism who was often persecuted for his views.</note>, after he had deplored the man's impudence, he breaks out into these words on page 5 of the booklet: *What is to be done? Should one fight against him with fleshly weapons? Should one excite the Emperor and Christian authorities against him to stop his mouth and have him drawn to a proper civil punishment? Far be it! Fleshly, worldly weapons are a shame to all sciences, especially to Christian truths. When executioners and dragoons must protect truths and religions, it is a miserable state of affairs. Where does the conviction in the conscience remain? How dangerous is such help? What if the Emperor himself joins in looking at the truth? If he himself through his ministers fights for errors and worldly maxims. It is much more to be praised in authorities who only care for justice and outward matters in the common wealth: who do not mix themselves with fleshly weapons in religious strife and questions of the Law and the Gospel.* You may read similar things in the *Life of F. Junius*, edited by Gerdes, pages 227 and 228, and in the work of the Reverend and most learned **Wagner** in his *Apology against Edelmann*, that most impudent despiser of religion, Volume I, page 205.

...firm arguments, which public Teachers <note>Referring to official university professors or state-sanctioned theologians</note>, when about to prove the fundamental truths of religion, have used. Regarding these causes, I will bring forward nothing here, since I believe that has been performed abundantly by us in what preceded. Truly, it is manifest that just as **Deists** <note>Those who believe in a God based on reason but reject supernatural revelation</note> concede more or fewer points of **Natural Theology**, one must reason with them in a like manner. Where it is certain that they are being carried away by depraved passions, all those things must be suggested to them which we brought forward above when we dealt with **Atheism**.

But let us suppose we are dealing with a man who candidly and sincerely admits all the points of Religion and Natural Law; then I think the following things ought to be observed and emphasized: (I.) It must be warned that in the business of religion, one should not expect mathematical demonstrations, but only such as can lead a man who loves the truth to a true knowledge of a saving persuasion. It is true that the existence of the Deity—that is, a Being plainly distinct from the world, who gave existence to all other beings—can be proved clearly enough; but when it comes to explaining the nature of such a great and excellent substance properly, we hesitate greatly, and we have a plainly imperfect knowledge of it, yet sufficient for knowing and worshiping it: I say the same regarding all His attributes, whether moral or physical. It is confessed by all that the <term>finite is not capable of the infinite <note>A common theological axiom: *finitum non est capax infiniti*</note></term>. Who does not know what great difficulties occur regarding the origin of moral and physical evil, even when admitting **Divine Providence** extending itself to all things—great, medium, and small? To remove these difficulties, as much as can be done in this darkness of things, not only Christians are bound, but also the Deists themselves, who seriously profess that God provides for human affairs, and that He is most holy, most equitable, and most just. The immortality of the mind can indeed be proved by sufficient reasons, both from the moral attributes of God and from the nature of a thinking being; but it cannot be said that mathematical evidence has a place here, whatever certain recent scholars may say, which I refrain from proving at length here. This will be the first step to arriving at the knowledge of historical truth: by comparing all four **Evangelists**, and attributing as much to them as is believed of any other truthful narrator of deeds. It will be manifest that they all agree in this: that Christ not only delivered an admirable doctrine and was illustrious for miracles, but also, being innocent, was handed over to a violent death, and was called back from the dead into life. # MEDITATION XII.

<meta>catchword: frequently</meta>

...which the first witnesses of this resurrection report, they cause him to hesitate, seeing whether, on account of some diverse narration of these circumstances, the most memorable event, that is, the resurrection of Christ, is to be called into doubt. Therefore, let our **Deist** <note>A person who accepts the existence of a God on the evidence of reason and nature, but rejects supernatural revelation</note> read once more the most learned defenders of this truth, especially the most noble **West** <note>Gilbert West (1703–1756), whose 1747 work "Observations on the History and Evidences of the Resurrection of Jesus Christ" was a famous defense against skepticism</note>, who accurately examines all those circumstances which might cause a truth-loving reader to hesitate. And since the resurrection of the dead is such an event that could not happen without a miracle—whether you attribute the matter to God or to Christ—one must proceed in the reading of the Gospels and see what kind of deeds are attributed to this Christ. 

Here, indeed, it will be plainly manifest that all four Evangelists agree on this: that Christ performed innumerable miracles of the most diverse kinds, in the presence of both enemies and friends; so much so, indeed, that some, whether they liked it or not, were forced to confess that these things were performed by the help of God. Others, however, since they could not deny that the events truly took place, ascribed them to the hidden operations of evil spirits. 

Here, indeed, our **Deist**, whom we now assume to be led by a love of truth, must either:
1. Deny that anything in this universe can happen outside the laws of nature; 
2. Or maintain that the narrative of the Evangelists is suspected of fraud; 
3. Or assert that these men were too credulous and simple to rightly judge what was natural and what was supernatural; 
4. Or, finally, he must confess that what is narrated truly took place. 

As for the first point, it can hardly be believed that a **Deist**, who confesses that God created all things great and small—that is, the entire universe—and indeed according to the wisest laws, would wish to deny that the same God, for the weightiest of reasons, could occasionally change those laws for a time. He will be bound to confess, therefore, if he rightly examines the system he defends, that miracles are not impossible. But perhaps the **Deist** will say: "It is not probable that the most wise God would change the laws He Himself established." We respond that it is true that miracles occur rarely, and indeed for many centuries none have occurred; it is enough, however, that He is able to perform such things if He wishes. And since God does nothing without <term>sufficient reasons <note>A reference to the "Principle of Sufficient Reason" championed by philosophers like Leibniz, suggesting everything has a logical cause</note></term> and adapts all things to the wisest ends, using means that contribute most to obtaining that end, it remains for the **Deist** to inquire whether certain miracles were performed, and once this is granted, to inquire for what end they were presented. 

For if he seriously reads and re-reads <note>original Greek: *αὐτὸν* — referring to the text itself or the person of Christ</note> the narratives of the Evangelists, he will hardly be able to restrain himself from believing that miracles were truly performed by Christ. For they explain everything in such clear words, narrate the circumstances of persons and places, and do so so...

...frequently, they repeat, that either their entire narrative is to be called into doubt and the authority of these witnesses plainly rejected, or it must finally be confessed that it is true that miracles were performed. Once this is granted, it will soon be clear for what purpose these were finally performed: partly because Christ himself, by testifying in express words, asserted that they were done to confirm his Gospel; and partly because the nature of the matter itself, and the state of the men living at that time, could designate the end for which they were done.

When God performs miracles among men, and those who perform them confess for what cause it is done, nothing else can be gathered from it than that they were done so that men might be taught about some grave and momentous truth. Men, indeed, can touch the **Omnipotence of God** from miracles, as if with a finger; but this truth can be known even without revelation and miracles. And what need is there for more words? No one who reads the Gospels—to say nothing of the Acts and Epistles of the Apostles—can be ignorant that Christ primarily acted to prove that he was that **Messiah** promised from heaven. This was, at that time among the Jews, the most famous question. The Jews did not deny that the Messiah was coming; but they waited for such a one as they desired according to their preconceived opinions. 

Christ performed miracles among this people because without them they could bring forward innumerable doubts against him and the doctrine he professed. But having seen so many miracles, and with the appeal to the miracles of the Old Testament, they could not bring forward <term>foundational causes <note>original: *causas fonticas* — primary or original reasons</note></term> why they should admit the miracles of Moses as divine, but not those of Christ, which they could see very frequently with their own eyes. 

But here already the most wise purpose of God was evident: namely, to exhibit the true characteristics of the Messiah and to move men to embrace his saving doctrine. Perhaps the **Deist** will say that God nevertheless did not obtain His end and goal among the Jews and their leaders, the Pharisees, who were nonetheless instructed with a greater apparatus of learning than the common folk. But these things will seem of little consequence to a wise man. God granted **reason** to mortals chiefly for this purpose: that from the contemplation of the universe they might perceive His majesty, wisdom, and power, and be induced to worship Him. Notwithstanding this, many—nay, most—are careless of the most beautiful things occurring in the universe, and are blind to such great perfections of <note>original: *O. N.* — likely *Optimi Nostri* (Our Best [God]) or *Omnipotentis Numinis* (of the Almighty Deity)</note> God. Has God, therefore, failed in what He intended? Are the stupendous and most skillfully constructed works of His hands in vain? I should not think so. If the **Deist** reads through the evangelical history as is fitting...

# MEDITATION XII.

->### ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF.###<-

If he <note>the Deist reader</note> reads and attends to the characters of the *Pharisees* and other leaders of this people, he will find without great effort the reasons why very many among the *Jews*, even after seeing so many miracles, nevertheless did not give their name to the Christian religion. To be sure, pride, dullness, ingrained opinions about the holiness and prerogatives of the Jewish *Nation*, admiration for the traditions received from the *Fathers*, a mind alienated from the internal worship of religion and clearly fixed upon the external, and other things hindered these wretched men from turning their minds attentively to those miracles and to the excellent doctrine. For although *God* performs miracles to persuade men of heavenly doctrine, He does not wish to drag the unwilling to assent through a miracle. Therefore, in our opinion, *God* was able to perform miracles for the sake of heavenly doctrine for plainly most wise reasons, even if many men closed their eyes to such great light. The same must be said of the *Gentiles* <note>non-Jewish peoples, particularly the Romans and Greeks of the period</note>, all of which would have to be demonstrated more at length if we were to set about proving the truth of the miracles with deliberate effort—a task which has already been abundantly performed by most learned men. From what has been said, at least this much is manifest: that our *Deist* argues poorly when he concludes from the narration of the *Evangelists* regarding such a great abundance of miracles performed by *Christ* that the *Evangelists* are suspected of fraud. For it would have to be proved above all that miracles are to be numbered among those things which are *impossible* <note>original Greek: ἀδύνατα</note>, which surely he cannot profess who admits a *God* distinct from this visible world. Nor, finally, does it follow in the third place that those men were too credulous and immediately recorded in the number of miracles those things which seemed wonderful to them. For they relate what they themselves had seen, and they do not anxiously inquire into what the nature of these deeds might be; they rather leave it to those who were *eyewitnesses* <note>original Greek: αὐτόπται</note> to judge what should be thought of these actions. Moreover, from the very judgments which were brought by the *Jews*, it was manifest that they had been seized with the greatest admiration, nor did they dare to ascribe those stupendous actions to I know not what concurrence of natural causes. If, according to the custom received in our learned age, they had begun to defend their cause with metaphysical arguments sought from the contingent and the necessary, the possible or impossible, etc., they would have rightly rendered themselves suspect; because in the very history which they narrate, they confess that they were born in a humble place, and spent a great part of their lives fishing rather than cultivating Letters <note>studying literature or formal academic subjects</note>. It rather falls upon the *Deists* themselves to prove that everything told by them concerning miracles can easily be explained by physical causes. After our *Deist* has seriously weighed all things and detected no frauds in the narration of the *Evangelists*, and

cannot deny that miracles were performed by *Christ*, he must again have recourse to the resurrection of *Jesus Christ* as a miracle plainly unusual and stupendous. For after he reads that *Christ* performed so many miracles in his life and was aided by the most present help of *God*, it is not to be wondered at if, by the same power, he was called back from the dead into life. Since the *Evangelists* set forth the miracles he performed in words just as eloquent as they do his resurrection, no less faith is to be had in the former testimony than in the latter. This being granted, the *Deist* himself will easily be able to draw the consequences that follow spontaneously from this revival of *Christ*. We shall give some; but we assume that our *Deist*, having read the *Gospels*, will proceed to the *Acts of the Apostles* and the epistles given to various nations, and will read through those things which are narrated to have happened after the resurrection with similar care and attention.

*Let the first be:* *Christ*, as we said above, performed miracles to establish the doctrine which he brought forward. Now, one must either say that *God* performed such miracles for the sake of an Impostor, or that He provided them to prove and confirm the doctrine announced by *Christ*. The *Deist* cannot maintain the former, because he admits the headings of *Natural Theology* and *Natural Law*, for this assertion would be contrary to all the virtues of *God*. Therefore, the latter must be said. This being established, not only the miracles of *Christ* will be of divine origin, but also his doctrine.

*Second:* All the *Evangelists* not only testify that *Christ* was called back into life and exhibited himself to be seen by a huge crowd, but also that he departed sublime into the heavens, while his disciples were watching; indeed, that he himself had predicted this would certainly happen. From which it follows that he was exalted by the power of *God*, and that *God* thus proved the doctrine which *Christ* announced to the *Jews* as true.

*Third:* *Christ* had promised the disciples, according to the testimony of the *Evangelists*, that after a brief interval of time, once he had been received into heaven, he would bestow upon them the gift of miracles and teach them all things which they could do to rightly understand the truth of the *Gospel* and announce it to others. No sooner said than done: after 50 days had elapsed, these *unlearned* <note>original Greek: ἀπαίδευτοι</note> men began to speak in various tongues and to preach *the mighty works of God* <note>original Greek: τα μεγαλεῖα τοῦ Θεοῦ</note>, which was the most certain sign of the exalted *Christ*. Whence it follows at the same time that they were not deceived by fantasy, but were taught by sense itself and experience, and that this benefit was to be attributed not to their own diligence or labor, but to *Christ*.

...had been called forth, and had ascended into heaven, traveling through Judea from here to there, they set forth these events everywhere with courage and fearlessness, and they allowed themselves to be led away from the confession of this truth by no threats; from which it can easily be gathered that they were intimately persuaded of the certainty of the events, for no more likely reason can be given for that constancy in asserting these truths.

**Fifth:** The disciples of Christ themselves, after he was received into heaven, were equipped not only with the gift of tongues but also with the power of performing miracles, as is most clearly evident from the *Acts of the Apostles*. Nor could they be deceived here, since all men together saw by the work itself those suffering from various diseases being healed, and the dead being recalled to life; let a fanatical man try to provide the same, and he will soon feel how plainly foolish and vain that effort is. Indeed, they said they performed all these things in the name of Jesus, who was recalled to life and exalted. Therefore, no other cause can be given for this remarkable power. Most of all, in this inquiry, it must be noted that the *Acts of the Apostles* was written by Luke immediately after he had composed his Gospel. In them, he not only sets forth that the Apostles themselves were famous for miracles, but he also narrates in which places this or that event took place; he brings onto the stage persons to whom the Gospel was announced, and with what success, and reveals so many circumstances that it is manifest to all that he was persuaded of the certainty of the events: surely a most malicious, yet not entirely stupid impostor, would not have dared to bring such things into the open at that time, when everything was fresh in memory, and if they had been false, he could have been convicted of open fraud. The most learned man *A. Youngs* <note>Likely Arthur Young (1693–1759), an English clergyman who wrote on the history of idolatry</note> urges this argument at greater length in his inquiry into *Idolatry, German edition, page 428 and following.*

Christ, his miracles, death, resurrection, ascension into heaven, and the outpouring of the Holy Spirit upon the Apostles; the fates of Christian doctrine; they agree in all things that pertain to the essence of the events. Here and there they intersperse the doctrine of Jesus Christ—delivered sometimes in open words and sometimes through parables—with their memory confirmed by that Spirit who had previously promised that he would teach them all truth. The sum of the truth was: that Jesus of Nazareth is the true Messiah, promised to the Fathers, and announced by many Prophets many centuries before. **Seventh:** Wherever we turn our eyes, looking back at the testimonies of the first disciples, their consensus in setting forth the events, and their clearly admirable constancy in adversity, we can find no other causes for this matter than the deepest persuasion regarding the certainty of the events. For the most part, ambition does not affect unrefined men, but learned men of more excellent talent are often accustomed to suffer from this "disease." And in what, finally, should the ambition of these men have consisted? They excelled neither in abundance of learning, nor in eloquence, nor in skill in philosophical disciplines. But suppose finally that even the most unrefined men were seized by ambition; I ask how those men could have properly invented so artful a fable so that the lie could not have been seen through? 

These men were born in Judea, but especially in Galilee; they invent—if you listen to the Unbelievers—that some Christ lived in Judea, famous for miracles, brought forth dogmas plainly foreign to the views of the Gentiles and Jews, that he lived a plainly austere and hard life, that he himself very frequently chastised the leaders of the people, the scribes and pharisees <note>Jewish legal and religious authorities</note>, for their hypocrisy and corrupted ancient religion, and finally, having been circumvented by the snares of these men, was delivered to death, but (what seems wonderful and incredible to most men) was recalled to life from the dead, and ascended into heaven, and reigns there, etc. 

Now if all these things had been invented, I do not know how those good men, seized by ambition forsooth, could have hoped with any appearance of probability that men not entirely destitute of common sense, and knowledgeable of the events in Judea, would have offered them an empty ear. Truly, this would have been such a kind of ambition that usually only torments the most stupid men. It is not the part of a crude fisherman, seeking a living by the labor of his hands, to devise some ingenious fable, crafted according to the laws of probability. More things are required here. # MEDITATION XII.

<page-num>530</page-num>

->### ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF ###<-

<meta>catchword: Eighth-</meta>

...if they had been [highly trained], they might have been able to persuade, and men of sound mind would have given them their assent. Finally, they do not use the artificial rules of Rhetoric to introduce these facts they narrate, nor do they intend to prove them with far-fetched arguments, but they speak as if the matter narrated were plainly known to everyone at that time. I will say no more about this objection, as it has little likelihood. I say the same regarding the *love of pleasures*, by which they might perhaps have been led to spread that little story among the common people. Lowborn and poor people do indeed long for pleasures, but usually only those that can abundantly satisfy their hunger and thirst. They do not seek sumptuous feasts; simple and common food, if sufficient, satisfies their desire. No one is less suited than such people for exhausting their brains by devising new and elaborate stories; they rather look after their own comfort <note>literally: "their own little skin"</note> and believe what the common people believe, without extending their concerns any further.

Finally, it is no more likely that the most wretched disease of *greed* <note>original: *avaritia*</note> occupied these first followers of Christian discipline. Those held by this insatiable desire not only wish to provide for themselves, but they extend their care to their family and to enriching their descendants; they greedily scrape together, by right or wrong, whatever can increase their already heaped-up piles. But first, a hunger for gold and silver rarely troubles the poor; second, these men could easily see that if they brought forward and spread a new doctrine, they would have to leave behind their home and country, and there would be no place left to scrape together money, neither among the Gentiles nor among the Jews. Among the Gentiles, there was already a sufficient number of petty priests whom the Rulers had to support, and the Christians—hated by everyone in those early times—could not promise themselves such things. 

You might say that experience proves that lowly and poor monks, while babbling beautifully about vows of poverty, eventually achieved immense riches, so much so that in many parts of Europe and America they can compete with Kings in wealth. This is true. But we must ask by whose protection and by what arts they reached that state. It is well known, of course, that superstitious Emperors and Popes <note>original: *Pontifices*</note> were the cause of this, believing they would do a thing most pleasing to God if they heaped unique benefits upon idle and fanatical men. The monks themselves, through fees, fake miracles, and relics, milked money from men captured by vain superstition. But the Apostles and the first followers of Christian discipline could by no means promise themselves such things, whether you look at the Jews or the Gentiles; it was enough for them to have received from the generosity of certain Christians only as much as was sufficient for food and clothing.

*Eighth*: The conversion of Paul, which was plainly miraculous, provides an irrefragable <note>undeniable or indisputable</note> argument for the truthfulness of the Apostles regarding the reality of the resurrection of Jesus Christ and his exaltation. For he, placed in the very heat of persecution, was so moved by a voice sent down from heaven, *Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?* that he was soon entirely changed and gave his name to the Christian discipline. With what incredible diligence he announced the Gospel of Jesus Christ everywhere, what labors and troubles he endured, and how he underwent death with a most constant mind, is clear from his own letters and the records <note>original: *monumentis*</note> of earliest antiquity. That this conversion of Paul was real and not imaginary is most manifest from the very things he taught and suffered after that vision. That he was certainly neither a fanatic nor an impostor was recently proven by the most noble and learned Englishman, Lyttelton <note>George Lyttelton, 1st Baron Lyttelton (1709–1773), who wrote a famous 1747 treatise on St. Paul's conversion as proof of Christianity</note>, in a singular book in which he draws an argument for the truth of the Christian religion from the conversion of Paul, his doctrine, and his deeds.

*Ninth and last*: The wonderful effects produced by that public profession—that Jesus Christ died for sinners, was called back from the dead to life, and ascended high into the heavens—sufficiently testify that the first Christians were persuaded of these truths. As is clear from the *Acts of the Apostles*, many from among the Jews and Gentiles gave their names to the Christian religion upon hearing this doctrine and seeing the miracles; indeed, many were even showered with extraordinary gifts. *Tacitus* <note>a Roman historian</note> is a serious author who confirms that there were already many Christians by the time of Nero. That many among the Gentiles, having cast away superstition and idol-worship, professed that simple doctrine of Christ (which does not flatter the passions), is testified not only by the *Acts of the Apostles* and the Epistles sent to various assemblies, but also by the records of the earliest church history. 

However, it must be carefully noted that we do not seek an argument for proving the divine origin of the Christian religion from the mere multitude of believers; for we know well that the impostor *Mohammed* had many followers, and still has them today, to say nothing of the many herds of monks among Christians. Our argument is drawn from the *manner of propagation*: from the *simplicity* of the first teachers; from the *prejudices* that had to be cast off; from the *obstacles* opposed to this doctrine; and finally, from the *constancy* shown in defending the most holy discipline. These are the principal conclusions that can be drawn from the truth of the resurrection of Jesus Christ without subtle meditation or force. I have suggested these things only briefly, because the most celebrated and learned men of the Christian religion...

# MEDITATION XII.

<page-num>532</page-num>

...those who have set out to prove the truth have examined all these matters quite fully with great effort, and they have responded at length to all the objections of the Deists.

So far, we have asked nothing else from our Deist than that he seriously weigh those things said by the disciples of Christ concerning the resurrection; let him properly examine the quantity and quality of the witnesses, and having performed the examination, let him judge what he ultimately thinks should be concluded about this testimony of the Apostles according to the laws of right reasoning. However, since even the greatest miracles—if indeed such things occurred—could contribute nothing toward drawing men into agreement if they were used to prove a nonsensical doctrine, full of mere contradictions and clearly contrary to divine virtues, it is necessary that we add something concerning the dogmas of the Christian religion and its moral precepts. A Deist who has properly weighed the truth of the resurrection of Jesus Christ as narrated by the unanimous consent of the Apostles will scarcely be able to restrain himself from feeling his mind inclined toward granting some assent to this narration; for this reason, I believe it has happened that the most learned among them, so far as I know, have left *Ditton’s* book <note>Humphrey Ditton (1675–1715) was an English mathematician and theologian whose 1712 work "A Discourse Concerning the Resurrection of Jesus Christ" was a famous defense of the faith using mathematical logic.</note> on the truth of Christ’s resurrection untouched until now. But when they come to the doctrine itself and the dogmas of the Christian religion, they think they find sufficient reasons for holding that entire history as suspect. They argue that the same Evangelists who set forth the clearly wonderful matter of the rising Christ simultaneously admit that he, and the so-called Apostles after him, handed down certain monstrous dogmas as necessary to believe—dogmas which, in their opinion, can by no skill be brought into harmony with the decrees of right reason. Into this category they specifically place the doctrine of the Holy Trinity. We must see, therefore, in a few words, whether the Deists have just cause for triumphing and rejecting the Christian religion on this account. To that end, we give them the following points to be properly weighed.

*The first is:* We think it is not only permissible but also necessary that all dogmas of the Christian religion, especially those called "Mysteries," be examined according to the most exact laws of reasoning. We do not want Deists to grant assent to the propositions discovered in the New Testament without the most accurate examination. But if, having properly weighed everything in that balance, they have scrutinized the dogmas of the Christian religion and yet cannot satisfy themselves so far, they ought to flee for a time to a <term>suspension of judgment</term> <note>original Greek: ἐποχή (epoche); a skeptical practice of withholding one's opinion until the truth is clear</note> before they flatly reject them, and put the matter off to another time for a new examination. For what seems difficult for me to conceive on the first occasion, at another time and with a different state of mind—

---

<page-num>533</page-num>

->### ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF ###<-

—disposition, can seem likely. We advise this before all else because certain theologians, when dealing with mysteries, wish that a more accurate examination of them be forbidden, and thus they provide the Deists with material for mocking them.

*Second:* We concede and admit that those things which involve a manifest contradiction cannot be believed. Thus, even if we wished, we cannot believe that a "squared circle" exists, or that the same body can be in several places at the same time. This proposition is the first rule of all right reasoning; if it is rejected, there is nothing so monstrous and absurd that it could not be introduced. As long, therefore, as Deists think that such dogmas are found here or there in the Christian religion, there is no reason for us to be angry with them. Let them follow the law of conscience; no one has cause to rebuke them while they are in this state. Not even God himself can force men to believe in <term>impossibilities</term> <note>original Greek: ἀδύνατα (adynata)</note>; for in contradictory things, one finds nothing but words devoid of sense.

*Third:* The dogmas of the Christian religion are not to be judged according to this or that system of Theology, but according to the very words which the sacred writers use, employing the rules of correct interpretation and the aids of sacred philology. If these things had been observed in ancient centuries by the Fathers of the primitive Church, room would not have been left for such innumerable contentions and lawsuits. According to the opinion of Protestants (would that they were always consistent with themselves in this and mindful of their principles!), no dogma of religion ought to be believed which is not either expressed <term>in the exact words</term> <note>original Greek: αὐτολεξεὶ (autolexei)</note> of the most clear passages in the Holy Scriptures, or drawn from them by the most evident consequence. Furthermore, we do not thrust upon Deists who are about to cross into the Christian camp this or that system, or these or those particular opinions of this or that sect, but we desire this one thing: that they weigh the New Testament <term>without bias</term> <note>original Greek: ἀβρε παλων (likely a corruption of a phrase meaning "with unbiased hands")</note>, persuaded that they will easily find the primary heads of the Christian religion therein.

*Fourth:* From which it follows by legitimate consequence that the Deist unfolding the New Testament must follow the sense latent under the words of the Evangelists and Apostles, and not seek only that which would be acceptable and pleasing to his own hypotheses or the perverse affections of his mind. If someone were to read *Plato* or a *Stoic* writer with the goal of finding the decrees of *Epicurus* everywhere, and thus twisted the meaning of these writers toward his <term>Principal Doctrines</term> <note>original Greek: Κυρίαι δόξαι (Kyriai doxai); the forty authorized ethical summaries of Epicureanism</note>, he would be considered a fool in the judgment of all who are wise. For although the Deist does not yet admit the divine origin of the Christian religion, he is nevertheless bound, unless he considers the writers of the New Testament to be...

...to treat them as foolish and fanatical people, to gather from them those things which are contained within them through legitimate rules of interpretation common to all interpreters. But if one gets stuck here or there, and cannot rest content with the explanations of the most learned interpreters who correctly understand the Greek style, he has a remedy he can use, namely *suspension of judgment* <note>original Greek: *epochē*</note>, which is something that not infrequently happens even to the most learned men.

*Fifth:* Since the Mysteries <term>Mysteries: In 18th-century theology, these are truths revealed by God that human reason is capable of understanding once revealed, but could never have discovered on its own.</term> found in Holy Scripture are "filth" in the eyes of the Deists <term>Deists: Thinkers who believed in a creator God based on reason and nature but rejected supernatural revelation, miracles, and organized religion.</term>, before we deal with those found in the New Testament, this must be noted: either the Deist admits that a revelation can be given, or he denies it. He cannot do the latter unless, before even admitting the possibility of revelation, he already assumes for certain that every Revelation contains "Mysteries"—that is, as he explains it, contradictory propositions. This, however, no Christian will grant him if the discussion is about true mysteries. For by Mysteries we mean such truths that can be found by no skill through the help of reason alone. A man deprived of revelation, however sharp his intellect may be, will not be able to prove the necessity of any revelation, nor even desire it, since he can have no idea of these truths. For whatever is placed outside the connection of truths to be found by the aid of reason, a man can neither conceive nor even seek after as necessary. For here that well-worn saying holds true: *There is no desire for what is unknown* <note>original Latin: "Ignoti nulla cupido"</note>. It is one thing to say that we, having admitted the truth and divine origin of the Christian religion, can prove the necessity of this revelation *after the fact* <note>original Latin: "a posteriori"</note>; it is quite another to say that a man deprived of all light of revelation can nevertheless know the necessity of a revelation—that is, of propositions not knowable by the workings of reason. He who is persuaded of the divine origin of the revelation granted to us can easily argue as follows: It pleased the most wise God to grant us a revelation containing truths that surpass the grasp of reason but are necessary to know; therefore, it was necessary that it be given to mortals. If a certain anonymous author—who recently criticized the distinguished Vernet <note>Jacob Vernet (1698–1789) was a prominent Genevan theologian who defended Christianity against Enlightenment skeptics.</note> in the *Swiss Mercury* <note>original Latin: "Mercurio Helvetico", a leading literary and scientific journal of the time.</note> because he had omitted the chapter on the *necessity* of revelation in the first volume of the new edition of his *Demonstration of the Truth of the Christian Religion*—had observed this distinction, perhaps he would have refrained from this censure. But if our Deist confesses that God can give a revelation to men, he must by that very fact also grant that mysteries can exist—that is, truths which can be deduced from no principles of reason, and which we would have been ignorant of through all eternity even if we had strained every nerve of our intellect. That He would suffer a violent death for the sins of men? That this death is the unique cause of our reconciliation with God? That He would be raised after death and depart sublime into the heavens? We have examined elsewhere the passage of *Socrates* which certain learned men bring forward to prove that the Gentiles recognized the necessity of revelation. The Gentiles could only know this one thing: that it would be useful if a new light were added to natural theology <term>Natural Theology: The study of God based on reason and the observation of nature rather than on supernatural revelation.</term> and men could know divine matters more accurately. And indeed, the desire of *Socrates* and of all the wise among the Gentiles would have been satisfied if a system of natural theology—such as the moderns among the learned have prepared, for example, those of *Clarke* or the illustrious *Wolff* <note>Samuel Clarke and Christian Wolff were famous philosophers who tried to prove the existence and nature of God using pure logic.</note>—had been placed in their hands.

*Sixth:* Since Deists attack the mysteries found chiefly in the New Testament, a few things must be noted, as we have spoken of this argument elsewhere in these dissertations.

1) Namely, they primarily attack the doctrine of the *incarnation of the Word* <note>original Greek: *ensarkōsei tou logou*</note>, the dogma of the Trinity, and the work of Redemption. Here we first confess indeed that those things narrated about these matters surpass our grasp, and they are known by us clearly in an obscure way; nor can it be otherwise, once we grant that those truths which we call mysteries are not a discovery of reason brought to light by the work of subtle minds.

2) The Sacred Writers themselves do not demand of us that we know the nature and character of these mysteries exactly, but that we at least hold them to be divine truths because we are persuaded by certain documents that they were revealed by God—especially because they cohere in an indissoluble bond with other truths occurring everywhere in the New Testament.

3) And we can do this all the more because the divine nature is infinite and ineffable, and many things can be in it that surpass our capacity.

4) All Christians, or at least most, even though they admit the mystery of the Trinity, nevertheless cry out and confess that they believe in a single, most perfect Deity, and they do not allow themselves to be torn away from this confession by any sophistries; and unless they were compelled by the most open passages of Scripture, they would not admit the Mysteries.

5) The word "Mystery" is taken in a double sense in the Holy Scriptures: for it either denotes the revelation of a truth that was previously unknown; having been manifested

# MEDITATION XII.

...indeed it can be clearly understood, just as the calling of the Gentiles <note>The "calling of the Gentiles" refers to the New Testament idea that God's salvation was extended to non-Jewish people, which was considered a "mystery" once hidden but now revealed.</note> is called a mystery. Or, a dogma is called a mystery when its character and true nature remain unknown even after revelation has been given, and it cannot be accurately grasped by human genius. It is this latter meaning that is being discussed here, and it is these Mysteries that the Deists reject.

6) Therefore, the Deist must prove only this one thing: that what is said regarding the Mystery of the Trinity involves a manifest contradiction. So far, I have not been able to persuade myself that this can be done. In order to prove that a manifest contradiction is contained in this or that proposition, I must accurately know both the subject and the predicate. For example, when I know what a "round body" is and what a "triangular" one is, I see a manifest contradiction if someone says a "triangular circle" exists, for the terms themselves cancel each other out. But when I say that in the infinite and inexpressible nature of God there is some distinction which goes by the name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit as three distinct persons, I am asserting something that I partly understand—namely, that there exists one Being, infinite, most perfect, etc.—and which is partly obscure—namely, when I say there are three persons in God. This is because I do not understand the word "person" in the sense it is commonly used; for these are not three individuals distinct from the Deity, since each one is a partaker of the Divinity in the Scriptures. Since I frankly confess that I cannot sufficiently define the word "person," no one can show me a true contradiction; for something being **incomprehensible** is one thing, and being **contradictory** is another. In explaining this question to some extent, one should not attend to the obscure phrases, distinctions, and comparisons of this or that theologian, but should simply stand by those things handed down in the Holy Scriptures. I ask the Deist, therefore, whether he thinks he is thinking and acting rightly if, on account of some rather obscure dogma concerning the infinite nature of God, he rejects the entire Christian Religion. In the New Testament, we read very frequently that Christ performed countless miracles, was called back from the dead to life, and (according to witnesses worthy of belief) ascended into the heavens; that he gave the Apostles the power to perform miracles and the gift of tongues; and that he set forth an admirable doctrine which far surpasses all the decrees of the philosophers living at that time. We read that he excelled in holiness of life, and that in his doctrine are found such excellent incentives to piety, etc. I ask, I say, whether such a man does not deserve belief when he says that there is one God, but that He is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

If someone, inflamed by a love of Platonic philosophy, had collected many beautiful things consistent with reason from the works of this Philosopher, but then happened upon his *Philebus* and *Timaeus* <note>Two of Plato's more difficult and metaphysical dialogues.</note> and encountered many things there which he could not understand due to their obscurity, should those dogmas found designated in clear words in *Plato's* other writings be rejected for that reason? Or should it be asserted that *Plato* was an incompetent Philosopher? Surely he would act more in accordance with reason if he followed Socrates, who, when he had read the writings of *Heraclitus* and was asked what he thought of their value, is reported to have said: *“What I understand seems beautiful and excellent to me; from which I conclude that the rest, which I do not sufficiently understand, will also be excellent.”* The application is easy: I truly do not know what the Deists think of Jesus Christ—who not only lived most piously, was famous for miracles, was recalled to life from the dead by the power of God, and was received into heaven, exercising his singular power over men—if they believe that he, as a fundamental article of his doctrine, would propose a "manifest contradiction" for his followers to believe.

Seventh: But the Unbelievers will say nonetheless that from an obscure and insufficiently understood proposition, no consequences can be deduced for thinking or living in one way or another. I respond that this is true if no knowledge at all is given of the article of faith which is commanded to be believed; but we deny that consequences for living piously cannot be deduced from a less known and more obscure knowledge of it, insofar as is required. This can be demonstrated even from the principles of the Deists themselves. They assert that God exists as an infinite, eternal Being, clearly distinct from the visible world; yet when they arrive at His Essence, the eyes of the mind grow dim, and they only acquire a sort of shadowy knowledge of the divine properties through a certain analogy with the spiritual properties inherent in our own minds. And yet, from this knowledge, they derive all the theoretical and practical duties which Natural Theology <term>Natural Theology: The study of God based on observed facts and experience apart from divine revelation.</term> and the Law of Nature <term>Law of Nature: A system of ethics or law supposedly determined by nature and thus universal.</term> prescribe. The logic is similar regarding our doctrine of the Most Holy Trinity. We confess that the dogma of the Trinity itself, and of the divine persons, is very obscure, and that our persuasion of the truth of this dogma rests not so much on an accurate knowledge of the nature of this dogma as on the explicit testimonies of Scripture. Meanwhile, the same Sacred Writers who command us to believe this dogma reveal such things about it as can serve to stir up a zeal for piety. Thus, in the business of salvation, clearly singular operations are ascribed to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, which can wonderfully excite attentive people to pursue various kinds of virtues. All those who assert that the creation of the universe was performed by God can gather from this, by a consequence that is not obscure, that we mortals all depend on God: that our life and all our faculties are suspended by the will of this Divine Power; that all are bound to the laws of such a great Power—insofar as those laws can be known—to harmonize their own will with His, and other consequences of the same nature. Yet at the same time, it is manifest that this creation of all things is known to us only *a posteriori* <note>original: "a posteriore" — a philosophical term meaning reasoning from observed effects back to their causes, rather than from first principles.</note>, as we are accustomed to say in the Schools. For when we attend only to the nature of an intelligent Being, we cannot conceive how, at His mere nod, both bodies and spirits were founded, nor what the connection is between the will of even the most perfect Spirit and the existence and preservation of such a vast mass of matter. Nevertheless, the Deists themselves, who do not wish to be numbered among the Atheists, admit and defend the dogma of the creation of all things by God as most certain.

Even if the doctrine of the Holy Trinity seems equally obscure to them and to us, they ought not on that account to "throw down their arms"—that is, to consider the Christian religion as plainly false—but should judge it worthy of more diligent inquiry. They know that in the age of the Church Fathers and in our own, many things previously unknown in the mathematical disciplines, astronomy, physics, the medical arts, and others have been brought to light. The same has happened in the more sacred disciplines, especially in the Interpretation of Holy Scripture: to this I also add that many useless, obscure, and "scholastic" <note>Referring to the complex, often pedantic style of medieval academic theology.</note> things that occurred here and there in the systems have been cut away by wise men and reduced to greater simplicity and use. We confess that we owe it to the Deists themselves that various kinds of doubts have been resolved by the most learned men, and a greater light has been kindled in all parts of theological learning. Therefore, one must not be headlong in this business; "day teaches day" <note>A Latin proverb (dies diem docet) meaning that we learn more as time passes.</note>; what we are ignorant of today, we learn in the following age. It is the part of a wise man, especially one who has abundant leisure, to spend the chief part of his life in inquiring after the truth. Meanwhile, we must always be mindful of "learned ignorance" <note>original: "docta ignorantia" — a philosophical concept suggesting that the highest point of human knowledge is recognizing the limits of what one can know.</note> and the very narrow limits by which our knowledge of both human and divine things is circumscribed. X. It remains that, before we put an end to our dissertations on the causes of Unbelief etc., we should briefly warn against those things which are objected to by the Deists regarding Christian Ethics. I say briefly, both because this matter has been most copiously treated by the most learned men who have dealt with the truth of the Christian religion, and because we are only inquiring here into what should especially be observed when a Deist attacks the moral precepts of Christian Ethics.

We shall reduce everything to certain rules, the fuller demonstration of which the Deists, as well as all lovers of truth, will seek from those who have intentionally demonstrated the excellence of Christian Ethics.

Now, the Deists use two kinds of arguments to attack the excellence of moral theology. The *former* is taken from the claim that it prescribes laws that are too harsh, impossible to perform, and which surpass the efforts of even the most virtuous man; such as those about loving enemies; about a perfection equaling the very perfection of God; about deserting one’s Fatherland, the sweet soil of one's birth, parents, wife, and the sweetest pledges of love; about the unlawfulness of self-defense; and other things which there is no need to recount at length here. The *latter* defense they seek in certain obscure and mystical expressions of Christ and the Apostles, which, if you listen to the Deists, either ground no meaning at all, or are at least so composed that not even one in a thousand mortals, even if he be most desirous of the truth, understands what such abstruse phrases finally signify. Such are, in their judgment, for example: the indwelling of the Holy Spirit in the truly pious; the participation in the divine nature; regeneration; that Christians are called Priests and Kings; being "in Christ"; being buried with him—to say nothing of many other phrases occurring especially in the Epistles of the Apostles.

As for the first part of the objection, we advise the following. 1) Christian Ethics ought to be neither too loose nor too strict. We call it "loose" when it is satisfied with such precepts as can be observed even by the most powerless and wicked man, and does not penetrate to the roots of vices. It is well known what men—even from the Roman Catholic fold itself—think about <term>Jesuit Ethics</term> <note>A reference to the "laxism" sometimes attributed to Jesuit casuistry, which critics argued made it too easy to justify sinful behavior.</note>. It is too strict when it requires such things

# MEDITATION XII

<page-num>540</page-num>

In this <note>practical theology</note>, requirements are made that no one—not even the most pious or the greatest lover of rectitude—could ever fulfill. Many public teachers among the Protestants who deal with practical theology err in this regard. They exaggerate individual arguments and often use such harsh amplifications that more prudent people easily notice that such Christians have never existed in the nature of things, nor will they ever be found in the future. Consequently, even those who are inclined toward the pursuit of virtue (though not without a struggle) are pulled back from a true and proper pursuit of Christian piety after hearing these overly rigid rhetorical flourishes and precepts that are plainly impossible to perform.

Christian ethics does not abolish the precepts of moral philosophy but assumes them. Its excellence, however, consists in this: that it sheds a more abundant light upon them; that it supplies arguments drawn from the very "marrow," so to speak, of Christian doctrine; that it brings and provides greater incentives for living piously than philosophical ethics does; and finally, that it promises greater assistance for performing these duties. These duties of Christian ethics should be proposed in a simple style and commended only insofar as they can actually apply to a person who is a student of virtue. For a Christian does not cease to be a human being. Those who act otherwise do the same as someone who would try to induce another to fly using many arguments, even though he knows just as well as everyone else that we are not equipped with that faculty. (*) <margin>II. Con-</margin>

(*) The Reverend and most learned man J. F. Jacobi <note>Johann Friedrich Jacobi (1712–1791), a German theologian</note> recognized this error of certain Doctors. In his *Reflections on the Wise Intentions of God in the Things we Encounter in Human Society and Revelation*, Volume III of that most useful book, pages 199 and following, he discusses this argument as follows: "That virtue," (he says) "which the *Fable of the Bees* <note>A reference to Bernard Mandeville's 1714 work which argued that "private vices" lead to "public benefits," a highly controversial text in the 18th century</note> describes is not the one which Christ and his first messengers taught, but rather that which some Oriental Sages, as well as the Stoics and Cynics, burdened upon men, and which many Christians later adopted from them. For just as the doctrines of faith were soon corrupted, now by the tenets of a Plato, now by the wisdom of an Aristotle; so too the very wise and pleasant moral teaching of Jesus Christ has been burdened with the intolerable and impossible laws of the aforementioned sects. The above-mentioned sects rejected sensory delights and almost all care for the body. They rather tortured the body in many ways and sought to bring such an insensitivity into their soul which is partly powerless, partly very harmful, and makes people into resentful and useless 'sour-pots' <note>original: "Saurtöpfe" — a German idiom for grumpy or morose people</note>. The teaching of Christ, however, is entirely contrary to this inhuman moral teaching. The Lord himself did not torture his disciples with many fasts. He let them go along as guests, and eat and drink what was there. And Paul reminds us more than once that the body too must have its maintenance and care. He warns that spouses should not put themselves into temptation through a forced abstinence. He attaches little use to such body-chastising exercises. Therefore, the moral teaching of Christ is very different from the moral teaching of various Christians. I note here how those who have just begun to harbor an enmity against true religion and the fear of God tend to act. They take

II. We grant to the Deists <note>Deists believed in a creator God based on reason but rejected supernatural revelation and church dogma</note> that moral precepts must be measured against the law of nature, and that nothing should be added that is plainly contrary to them. For since these laws have God as their Author and are always binding, it is impossible for the moral precepts of Christian ethics to contradict them. Far be it from us Christians to think despicably of the excellence of those natural laws; rather, we would wish that they were frequently commended to the Christian people from the pulpits. For we see—alas!—that they are daily trampled underfoot and neglected. Therefore, public teachers must first ensure that they instill in men those duties without which human society and the rational worship of the Divine Being cannot stand, before they invite them to observe the more internal and difficult precepts of Christian ethics.

III. One must not always cling strictly to the words, nor must every phrase that occurs here and there in the New Testament be cut to the quick <note>i.e., interpreted with absolute literalism</note>. Thus, when it is said that we ought to be perfect, just as our Father who is in heaven is perfect, everyone understands that the word "perfect" cannot be so pressed as to signify an absolute equality, because this cannot be performed even by the most pious men. This would be the case if they were not closed off even to our enemies: just as God does good not only to the good but also to the evil." The learned men who have made a dedicated effort to demonstrate the excellence of Christian ethics, and who have defended it against the objections of the Deists <note>Those who believe in God based on reason but reject supernatural revelation</note>, have shown all these things at great length.

IV. All interpreters, no matter which sect they belong to, follow a specific rule when they see imperfections attributed to God—for example, eyes, hands, etc.—or when He is thought to have commanded or caused moral evils if one looks only at the literal letter. In such cases, they trace every saying back to the genuine concepts of the Divine and His perfections. The very same thing must be done in this matter. Natural law, when dealing with the duties of a Christian, must be considered the primary norm. Certainly, no obligation is given for things that are morally impossible. We must always see whether the words themselves existing in the sacred text, through the rules of correct interpretation, cannot carry a meaning that agrees with the decrees of reason and the general precepts of the Law of Nature. The learned men who have dedicated themselves to explaining the rules of sacred philology <note>The study of language in historical sources</note> have shown this in more than one example, to say nothing of the scholarly interpreters who were equipped with skill in grammar, criticism, and the art of thinking. In this case, something must certainly be attempted, since we are dealing with the very first foundations of natural religion, which must always be kept sound and protected, unless we wish to surrender to the enemies of the Christian religion.

Other things, however, are such that they ought to be applied indiscriminately to everyone who wishes to be a student of Christian discipline...
