...ought to be applied. Indeed, it is of the greatest interest to have attended to these things. To be sure, that divine sermon was delivered and written in such a way that it is sometimes doubtful whether the precepts given there belong to all followers of Christian discipline, or whether they should be referred specifically to the Apostles. See what learned men have noted here and there, to say nothing of the Interpreters; for example, *Saurin* <note>Jacques Saurin (1677–1730), a celebrated French Protestant preacher</note> observes this in his work on the *Old and New Testament, Volume IX*; also in the *German Library, Volume XXVI, page 146*, and the *British Library Volume XXIV*, to say nothing of others.

VI. Just as certain unique duties were drummed into the Apostles who were to perform the duties of Christ’s public envoys—duties which do not pertain to all Christians indiscriminately—so likewise it must be observed in what times certain duties were to be diligently enjoined. Thus our most holy Savior had said that those who present themselves as genuine followers of his doctrine ought to be ready at every moment to leave their country, their wives, and to endure every adversity that comes under the name of "the cross." These things, without doubt, are not to be understood as if they must be endured in all times and places such that no one can be a Christian in name without suffering these evils. Rather, these are to be interpreted according to the circumstances of that time in which they were spoken. No one at that time could be a true follower of Christ unless he was prepared to sacredly keep those harsher precepts. For as soon as someone gave their name to the Christian religion, they were utterly hated by their own people and had to expect immediate death at any hour. The first confessors of the truth after Christ’s departure were subject to the same fate, which is abundantly clear from church history. Today, the same thing happens to those among the Heathens who leave paganism and cross over into the camp of the Christians. See the accounts of most excellent men concerning the propagation of the Christian religion among the *Malabars* <note>Refers to the Malabar Coast of India, where Lutheran missionaries like Ziegenbalg were active</note>, where you will find very frequent examples of this thing. But Christians in a time of peace and quiet do not have to endure these evils. Meanwhile, nothing should be more welcome to them than the study of piety and religion and the highest constancy in persecutions, so that if persecution rushes in, they ought to be ready to suffer anything for religion rather than admit superstitious opinions, errors, and views hostile to God for the sake of their own comfort.

VII. Finally, if a Deist, after weighing everything that learned men have brought forward to defend Christian ethics, still does not think he is satisfied, he ought nevertheless to grant a place for equity <note>fairness or justice</note>, and not—for the sake of his own wicked impulses—reject the moral precepts just as he finds them pleasing and...

The author distinguishes between rules meant specifically for the Apostles during times of persecution and general moral guidelines for Christians living in times of peace.</summary>

# MEDITATION XII

<page-num>544</page-num>

...it is established <note>original: "tum est"</note> to interpret: for in this way, not only the force and obligation of *Christian Ethics*, but also of the Law of Nature, would be subverted. It is certainly not within our power to wish to mold the obligation of moral laws according to our own whim. If that which seems harsh and extraordinary to some were removed, there would still remain firm those duties to be performed toward God, our neighbor, and ourselves, which are explained by the teachers of Natural Law <term>Natural Law: a system of ethics held to be inherent in human nature and discoverable by reason</term>.

It remains, finally, for us to arrive at the second part of the *Deists’* <note>Deists were 18th-century thinkers who believed in a creator God but rejected revelation and miracles</note> objection, about which (because we have said more in the dissertation on *Fanaticism as an Objection to Protestant Assemblies*) we think we should discuss briefly here. To be sure, the Deists complain about certain obscure and mystical expressions which occur partly in the sacred discourses of our Savior <note>original: "Soteris"</note> himself, but much more in the letters of the Apostles. In their opinion, moral precepts—which are given to all who take the name of the Christian religion—ought to be plain, easy to grasp, and suited to the intellects of all people. To resolve this objection, we believe the following points should be noted. 

I) Indeed, we do not deny that this objection is not entirely without merit; *Celsus* <note>A 2nd-century Greek philosopher and opponent of early Christianity</note> already pressed this point in his time, as noted in *Origen, Book VI, Section V, of Mosheim’s version, page 655.* <note>Johann Lorenz von Mosheim (1693–1755) was a famous German church historian who translated and commented on Origen's "Against Celsus"</note> Even the most learned *Interpreters of Holy Scripture* among Christians sometimes hesitate when they search for the true sense of obscure words. On one hand, care must be taken lest the force of metaphorical and obscure meaning, which the words themselves carry, be diminished beyond measure; on the other hand, the speech must not be so pressed that a meaning arises from it that is either entirely unintelligible, fanatical <note>original: "enthusiasticus"</note>, or binding one to the impossible. For experience shows that errors are committed both in excess and in deficiency.

II. To that end, effort must be given by those who read Revelation, especially the New Testament, so that they first have an accurate knowledge of the principal dogmas contained within it. For without this, they will hardly be able to form a sound judgment regarding moral precepts drawn from the discipline and dogmas of the Christian religion itself. The more they understand these, the clearer the phrases used by the sacred Writers will appear. If someone rightly understands the decrees of *Plato*, or of the *Platonists*, the *Stoics*, and other Philosophers, he holds the key to understanding certain obscure sayings expressed in metaphorical words. Furthermore, there are few writers who deal with certain dogmas and moral duties in whose work no obscurity of words occurs at all.

III) It is most just that all consequences be explained according to the nature of these dogmas, whether expressed in a plain or metaphorical style...

<column-break/>

<page-num>545</page-num>

-># ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF<-

...established <note>original: "rata"</note>. All the ancient philosophers often use turgid speech when they wish either to instill their teachings in others or to explain the wonderful efficacy of their doctrine. Even Christian Teachers, who take it upon themselves to pass down the true character and nature of Christian Ethics, often speak so obscurely and perplexingly that the common people do not understand the force of the words, while the more learned can only extract the sense lying beneath the words by applying sharp meditation. 

Truly, this error is to be censured more in recent writers than in the original authors who handed down the dogmas and precepts of the Christian religion. For the latter were not so concerned with style, nor were they sharply intent on defining every single word; the former, however, wish to be seen as Interpreters of the Apostles, having touched with a needle <note>i.e., identified with precision</note> the true sense of the words lying hidden under certain wrappings; and yet they more than once succeed only in pouring greater darkness over the words used by the Apostles themselves. This happens especially to those writers who affect a reputation for some sort of rare piety, but, being destitute of skill in the art of logic and the cultivation of the mind, nevertheless imagine themselves to be wiser than others in divine matters and in things which contribute most to Christian practice. The writings of these men certainly do more harm than good, because not only people inclined toward unbelief, but even sensible men, cannot help but be offended.

IV. If translations are not sufficient for understanding the phrases occurring here and there (although we think that those things pertaining to the study of piety are sufficiently and clearly enough handed down), one must take refuge in those who have dedicated their labor to explaining the style of the New Testament, clarified its more obscure phrases, and declared them in plain words. For just as Greek and Roman writers enjoy their own idioms—for example, the type of speech of *Cicero* is one thing, and that of *Tacitus* another—so it is well known that the style of the New Testament teems with Hebraisms <note>Greek grammar or vocabulary influenced by Hebrew or Aramaic</note>. Therefore, if a Deist burns with such a great desire to know the genuine sense of obscure phrases, it is necessary that he partly possess an accurate knowledge of the dogmas of the Christian religion, and partly make the style of the sacred Writers familiar to himself; if he does this, most of those obscurities will vanish.

V. Often the sacred Writers, especially the Apostles, use phrases that rest upon a certain spiritual sense, and which only he understands more accurately who is animated by a similar affection of the mind. Thus, whenever the Apostle Paul says: *I have been crucified with Christ, but I live, etc.* <note>Galatians 2:20; original: "Ego crucifixus sum cum Christo, vivo vero &c."</note>, he understands these words better who discovers the saving effects of the love of Jesus Christ in himself, than he who merely sticks to the outer shell <note>original: "cortici"</note> of the words and never discovers any movements of Christian piety in himself; although...

He warns against modern interpreters who lack logic and only make the text more confusing through their attempts at "rare piety."</summary>

# MEDITATION XII

<page-num>546</page-num>

...at the same time we do not deny that something unique could have happened to Paul in this regard, which cannot be said of all the godly in terms of their sense of internal experience. Meanwhile, since that singular joy—which was infinite in Paul’s soul—was undoubtedly supported by the most certain reasons, it can also be expressed in plain words: for a sensation is one thing, and the solid persuasion of the mind regarding the possession of certain gifts, joined with joy, is another.

VI. In this case, the Deists <note>original: "Deistæ"</note> ought to follow the rule that all interpreters approve: namely, that obscure phrases are to be interpreted by clearer ones. Thus, if anyone reads the writings of *Plato* or the *Stoics*, he can easily acquire for himself the sum of the general opinions which these men handed down. However, where he gets stuck on some more obscure passage, either that passage must be set aside for a while, or, if he wishes to shed some light upon it, he must do so in accordance with the clear teachings found here and there elsewhere in the writings of these philosophers. The same must be done in the interpretation of the New Testament. There are many duties to be observed toward God, our neighbor, and ourselves, which are set forth in the plainest words, so that there is no need for long and rambling interpretation.

VII. If anyone has seriously set his mind to perform the duties which the Christian religion prescribes—even if he does not understand everything or is unable to adapt everything to his own state—he can nevertheless please God. There are passages here and there that give even the learned a difficult time; yet this does not prevent one from understanding all the other things that must necessarily be performed. The same happens in other disciplines: for example, the general precepts of Natural Law and Medicine are easily grasped, but when it comes to their application, even the best practitioners often hesitate. God looks primarily to the sincerity of the heart. Where this is present, the principal requirement of a Christian man is also at hand. Common folk and the unlearned <note>original: "$\alpha\pi\alpha\iota\delta\epsilon\upsilon\tau o\iota$" (apaideutoi)</note> would be most miserable if they were to lose the hope of attaining salvation simply because they did not understand many of the more obscure passages of the New Testament. Since there are infinite degrees both of the knowledge of divine things and of the performance of the duties which religion prescribes, God will judge everyone according to equity and the circumstances in which they were placed; and He will even look to a person's will as to whether they intended to perform those precepts or not. A passage from *Peter Martyr* <note>Pietro Martire Vermigli (1499–1562), a Reformed theologian</note> in his *Commentary on the 1st Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 10, verse 11*, is very fitting here; the words read as follows: *It is a wretched thing, when we have so many clear and open things in Holy Scripture concerning faith, hope, charity, and the duties of the other virtues, in which nothing is obscure, that we leave those things utterly neglected; and*

---

<page-num>547</page-num>
<header>ON THE CAUSES OF UNBELIEF</header>

with such superstition, desire to pursue those things which are uncertain and contribute less to salvation. The Devil takes care of this: that people labor intensely over infinite and useless questions, while the necessary things are cast aside instead of being kept.*

VII. <note>The original text repeats the number VII for this new section.</note> Finally, the Deist must take care lest, in the interpretation of Holy Scripture, he follow his own emotions rather than the genuine rules of interpretation. In this matter, emotions are the worst advisors. The question here is not how pleasant or agreeable to the emotions a particular meaning may be, but how true it is. *No one* (says the late, celebrated *Werenfels* <note>Samuel Werenfels (1657–1740), a Swiss theologian known for his work on hermeneutics</note> in his *Dissertation on the Goal of the Interpreter*) *sins more gravely in this regard, or wanders more dangerously from the true goal of the interpreter, than those who seek a pretext for impenitence in the divine book—in which everything tends toward the sanctification of man—or an extenuation of the vices to which they are addicted, and a strengthening of the soul in that carnal security in which they lie buried. These are the ones of whom Peter rightly says that they twist the scriptures to their own destruction <note>A reference to 2 Peter 3:16</note>. Such were those of old who, abusing Paul's doctrine on the justification of man through faith, neglected all study of good works and holiness as if it were superfluous; these people indeed seem to have driven James to the point where he thought the Evangelical doctrine should be set forth in words that appeared, on the surface, contrary to Paul.* Such were the many Libertines and Antinomians <term>Antinomians: those who believe that under the gospel, the moral law is not binding because grace alone saves</term> of every age, both theoretical and practical, who interpreted the doctrine of grace brought through Christ (and the abolition of the Law of Moses) as if Christ had introduced unbridled license through the Gospel. Thus far the celebrated theologian. But if the Deist is willing to give an open ear to these warnings which we have given concerning Christian doctrine and its precepts, we do not doubt that he will give his name to the Christian religion, or at least judge it worthy of more diligent inquiry through further examination. And here we put an end to our meditations on the causes of Unbelief, and we heartily pray that this thin labor may contribute something toward—if not removing the vice of Unbelief (which cannot be hoped for given the great diversity of minds and the corruption of the human race)—at least repressing and diminishing it.

## MEDITATION XII.

<page-num>548</page-num>

...he judged that the evidence for the Holy Trinity <note>original: "S. Trinitatem"</note> taken from the Old Testament was not sufficiently solid, and for that reason, he was ridiculously criticized as if he were favoring Judaism.

II. The opinion of the celebrated John Locke <note>original: "Lokii"</note> regarding fundamental articles of faith is, in fact, highly consistent with the truth, and it does not favor the Socinians <note>A group who denied the Trinity and the full divinity of Christ</note>.

III. The incomparable men Erasmus and Grotius <note>Desiderius Erasmus and Hugo Grotius, famous humanist scholars</note> brought more light to the understanding of the New Testament than most of the Fathers of the ancient Church.

IV. The variant readings of the New Testament do not detract from the truth of the Christian Religion, nor do the many "pseudepigrapha" <note>Spurious or forged writings falsely attributed to apostles</note> that were scattered here and there shortly after the passing of the Apostles.

V. That no one has jurisdiction over the consciences of men is a truth as demonstrable as any usually proven by theologians.

VI. Weak arguments for the existence of God or the truth of the Christian Religion should be eliminated from theological systems, because they usually bring more harm than benefit.

VII. It is clear enough from the most transparent passages of the New Testament that our only and most certain hope and cause of salvation is placed solely in the ransom <note>original Greek: "λυτρῳ" (lytrō)</note> of our Savior.

VIII. Since the countless small disputes and controversies stirred up in the Christian Church contribute greatly to increasing the vice of unbelief, it is the duty of wise theologians to take up the refutation of only the most serious errors that are harmful to piety.

IX. In the Zurich Gymnasium <note>A school of higher learning</note> and Church alone during the time of the Reformation <note>original: "Emendationis Sacrorum," literally 'the improvement of sacred things'</note>, there were more learned men fit for correctly explaining the Holy Scriptures than in the whole of Italy combined. And indeed, those men—though very wise in other matters and most skilled in the Latin language—such as Sadoleto, Bembo, Contarini, and Pole, were like infants regarding this subject when compared with Zwingli, Bullinger, Bibliander, Pellikan, Leo Juda, Ceporinus, Collin, and others. To prove this, one need only inspect the published and unpublished monuments of the genius of these great men.

X. Those who explain the writings of the Evangelists and Apostles according to the analytical laws of philosophers cast darkness upon the Holy Scriptures rather than light.

### Sect. I.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' set within a square frame featuring a classical archway and a leafy tree.</image-desc>
Among the learned, there is no one who would rashly doubt that an accurate knowledge of the deeds once performed among the Philosophers, and the opinions they professed, contributes greatly to the progress of Learning and Wisdom. For even if I were to say nothing of how all those things which can be said in praise of *History* in general also apply to *Philosophical History*, there are many things which, by a certain singular reasoning, demonstrate its *excellence*. It brings back the [deeds and thoughts] of the ancients...

# MEDITATION ON THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION COMPARED
### WITH THE PHILOSOPHY OF SOCRATES

...and the thoughts of modern scholars concerning God, His virtues, the origin of the visible world, and the strengths and weaknesses of the human mind. It describes the fates of both true philosophers and those who consult a "mad wisdom" <note>original Latin: "insanientis Sapientiae"</note>; it recounts the noble discoveries of the former and their lives shaped by virtue, while detailing the verbal battles, pride, and intellectual games of the latter. All these matters are arranged so that they bring more utility to a mind eager for truth than those things which are most highly regarded in *Civil History*. For in the *History of Nations*, the *Lives of Emperors* and *Military Leaders*, and deeds done well or poorly in peace and war, fill every page. However, very few of those who devote themselves to literature—even if they weigh everything with the greatest care—can reap solid fruit from such records. Every condition of life requires its own specific supports and precepts. For a man who spends his whole life in study, the *Example of a learned and pious man* confers more utility toward properly maintaining the role he fulfills than the contemplation of even the most eminent virtues with which this or that *Military Leader* was ennobled. 

Truly, a *Philosophical History* supplies the lover of truth with many arguments for leading the soul away from depraved pursuits and errors, and toward the love of virtue and truth; thus, it wonderfully perfects the mind and bathes it in pleasure. Anyone who unfolds the writings of the ancient philosophers (to say nothing now of the moderns) will be persuaded of what I have said even if I remain silent. This has been sufficiently proven by men most well-versed in these letters: *Cudworth*, *Stanley*, *Ménage*, *Jonsius*, *Heumann*, *Brucker*, and others whose names are widely known. <note>These men were 17th and 18th-century pioneers in the "History of Philosophy," a discipline that sought to categorize the development of human thought.</note> 

However, there is no weightier argument than this: that such history contributes marvelously to demonstrating and defending the Excellence and divine origin of the Christian religion. The *Skeptics* <note>original: "Increduli"</note> are accustomed to extolling reason and its power with the highest praises. They constantly laud *Philosophy*, which they believe imposes no mysteries—that is, in their view, dogmas contrary to reason—to be believed. They profess that nothing is so excellently stated in Revelation that reason itself could not have discovered it. Therefore, they argue one must recur to reason alone in matters of belief, while all else is owed either to ignorance, superstition, or the frauds of priests. But he who cultivates *Philosophical History* is taught by the clearest examples how much reason is worth, and what its strength and its frailty are at the same time. We do not appeal here to the common people, who are led by even the slightest suspicions; nor to the monstrous rites of the Heathens; nor the silly decrees of priests; but rather to the opinions and dogmas of men endowed with the highest intellectual power, men devoted throughout their whole lives to the study of seeking the truth. Indeed, we appeal to those among Christians who, by their sharpness of wit and their skill in philosophical 

<column-break/>

matters, are by everyone's confession most celebrated, and who at the same time examined the Christian religion with the most piercing zeal. They all confess that, aided by divine Revelation, they attained more accurate notions of divine things: that Revelation supplied the most solid arguments for illustrating and demonstrating truths known by nature. Indeed, they admit they were very often driven to take refuge in divine Revelation as if in a "sacred anchor" <note>original Latin: "sacram quandam anchoram" - an idiom for a final or most reliable resource</note> in doubtful matters. Let those who doubt this read the writings of the greatest men—*Werenfels*, *Locke*, *Clarke*, *Leibniz*, *Turrettini*, *Le Clerc*, *Stillingfleet*, to say nothing of many others—and if they possess any sharpness of mind and love of truth, they will perceive what Revelation contributes to the perfecting of reason.

It has pleased me also, according to the strength of my own mind, to exhibit a specimen of this matter by the *Example of Socratic Philosophy compared with the Christian Religion*. Beyond the fact that the subject of this inquiry is most grave, I was invited to undertake it by a certain singular occasion, which I will briefly relate. 

Some time ago, while traveling, a conversation arose among those using a public carriage <note>original Latin: "communi vehiculo" - likely a stagecoach or mail coach</note> concerning a certain book published at the time, in which the author wished to demonstrate the Excellence of the Christian religion. *One of the companions*, a *Young Man* of upright character and keen intellect, judged the book quite skillfully; however, he added that all those who wrote such books were wasting their time. He claimed that no one had yet been found who could prove the necessity of any Revelation with clear arguments; that the precepts of reason and the cultivation of philosophy were sufficient for living well and blessedly. He appealed especially to the *Philosophy of Socrates*, claiming it encompassed everything that could serve to improve the human mind. He argued that this Incomparable Philosopher not only recognized the *Ruler and Governor* of this Universe but also brought forth the most wholesome precepts especially necessary for the improvement of the human race, and exhorted everyone to love virtue. If men had only lent their ears and obeyed his words, he argued, they would have been eternally happy. He claimed that the *Christian Religion* had not brought forth more effective arguments for cultivating virtue; rather, it should be attributed to fortune and superstition that such a great multitude of men approved its decrees, since in it—beyond the precepts known through reason—there is nothing that can satisfy a discerning mind. He complained that it spoke of miracles and Mysteries which clearly conflict with the principles of right reason, and so forth. 

As is usual in such familiar conversations, I countered many of his points, to which he replied with others that I do not intend to repeat here. What he said remained deeply fixed in my mind, and I meditated on this subject more than once. Since, however, for some years I have studied more diligently than before...

# MEDITATION ON THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION COMPARED
-> WITH THE PHILOSOPHY OF SOCRATES <-

...before I unfolded the systems of the Ancient Philosophers regarding divine matters, I took it upon myself to subject that controversy to examination in a specific dissertation. I did this certainly not with the intent of believing that I would prove the Excellence of the Christian Religion with a greater force of demonstration than has been done until now—for I measure myself by my own foot <note>original: "meo enim memet pede metior" — a Latin idiom meaning to know one's own limitations or to judge oneself by one's own standards</note>, and I know very well what a man of humble talent I am—but rather to show that I am among those who believe that nothing is more excellent than the Christian Religion, and to induce others to love it to the best of my abilities.

I offer this specimen—whatever its quality and perhaps perishable (though I have written it as if it were not)—to you, Distinguished Ulrich, as a **token** <term>original: τεκμήριον (tekmērion); a sign, proof, or convincing token of friendship</term> of the Love and Veneration with which I regard you. My reasons for this are most weighty. I shall say nothing of the singular favor with which you have treated me since my early youth; nothing of the excellent precepts and advice with which you imbued my mind; nothing of the fatherly affection you have shown me for a long time now, and still show. I will not recount your outstanding merits in Sacred and Literary matters. For everyone knows that you are to be numbered among the primary Ornaments of our Switzerland. This much only I will say: there are very few (if I set you aside) who have looked more deeply into the divine power and excellence of the Christian religion, or who have proven the excellence and admirable efficacy of Christ's teachings with a greater strength of argument, or fixed them more firmly in the minds of men. Witnesses to this are all those who heard you speaking in public, not without amazement, and who more than once felt that **sting** <term>original: κέντρον (kentron); literally a 'sting' or 'goad'. This refers to the lasting, piercing impact a powerful orator leaves on the listener's conscience</term> which you left in their souls. Witnesses are those most weighty Sacred Sermons, which are in everyone's hands and have been received widely throughout the World with the applause of the learned and the pious. Who, then, could judge better of the excellence of that divine Religion? Who could perceive the excellence of its precepts more certainly than he who makes it his sole aim, both publicly and privately, to urge men toward embracing and loving it with the gravest arguments, and who shows himself a Leader by his very work? I do not wish to further diminish your virtues through the fault of my own meager talent; I know your modesty, which is the principal Ornament of all your virtues, for you are accustomed to do nothing for ostentation, but to refer everything to conscience. Yet you cannot prevent me from using every given opportunity to sing your praises and show how much I esteem the Distinguished Ulrich. Receive, therefore, with a serene countenance, this sample of my affection for you, such as it is. One who lacks a great sacrifice of a hundred oxen <note>original: "Hecatombe". The author uses a classical metaphor: a poor man who cannot afford a massive sacrifice (hecatomb) should at least offer a rooster (the "Gallum" mentioned in text) as a sincere gesture</note> ought at least to offer what he can. If I should stumble anywhere, or reason less correctly, you shall lead me back to the path. I will follow your gentle admonition. But now to the matter at hand.

---

### II.

II. Before we begin the comparison between the Christian Religion and the Philosophy of Socrates, certain things must be cautioned in advance. First, this comparison is established on the fairest terms. The question is not what this or that Distinguished Philosopher, aided by the light of Revelation, could have achieved in explaining and demonstrating the principles and dogmas of Natural Religion; but rather what was achieved by a Man of piercing intellect who, though destitute of Revelation, nevertheless cultivated his talent as much as he could. We admit that modern Philosophers, aided by divine Revelation, can construct systems of Natural Theology that agree exactly with the precepts of reason; for those who have been imbued with the principles of the Christian Religion from early youth, and have simultaneously cultivated their reason with all their might, connect the notions which the Holy Scriptures suggest regarding God and divine things so aptly with those things known by reason alone, that they eventually believe they discovered all these things solely by the aid of reasoning. Such is the religion of most of those who are called **Deists** <term>original: Deistæ; 18th-century thinkers who believed in a creator based on reason but rejected supernatural revelation</term>. Raised on the dogmas and precepts of the Christian religion, they subject the main points of natural theology to examination, and, unmindful of what they have received from elsewhere, they attribute everything to the powers of their own reason. It is only fair, however, that in this comparison we listen to those who indeed devoted themselves most diligently to the contemplation of divine matters but were devoid of the light of any Revelation. 

II. Unbelievers contend that to lead a good and happy life, it is enough if one lives according to reason. They say there is no need for one to believe certain unusual decrees of the Priests; all that is required is a probity of life, as exact as can be achieved in this darkness of worldly affairs. They repeatedly object to the Pride of Philosophers, their itch for quarreling about matters of no importance, the depraved pursuits of the mind, and so on. But such men are not Philosophers in the true sense of the Name. We shall therefore oppose them with a most excellent Man and a Philosopher of a more upright example: namely, Socrates. He called Philosophy down from heaven to earth; he did not dispute about abstruse matters that exceed the power of the human mind; he was not a subtle Geometrician, or a Metaphysician, or a fabricator of technical terms; but rather one who did everything with the goal of improving the morals of men. He did not impose many dogmas on his disciples to be believed, nor did he use his authority to bring those into his opinion whom he could not win over with reasons. Furthermore, he was a Philosopher not given to pleasure, nor ambition, nor greed, nor other foul affections of the mind. All fair judges of such matters confess that such a man is most fit for investigating, explaining, and proving the precepts of reason. The Life of Socrates, says Marcus Erasmus, to me seems nothing else...

III. In this comparison, I will not imitate the Rhetoricians, who—to achieve their aim without regard for equity and truth—either exalt to the heavens with praise what they wish to defend while wrapping in silence those things that seem contrary to the goal they seek; or they so disparage those things they intend to blame that they keep no moderation at all, nor make any mention of things that could bring true honor. I will confess, therefore, that Socrates was a man of the most eminent virtues—a most good, wise, and excellent man. I will either wrap in silence, or give no credit to those things which certain less-than-fair Judges, such as *Athenaeus, the Epicureans, and Aristophanes*, have brought forward against him. On the contrary, we will by no means keep silent about the praises that Sensible Men have heaped upon him, so that all who examine the matter without partisan zeal may confess that we have acted candidly, and have forgotten nothing that could serve to illustrate the fame and virtues of the man, as far as brevity allows. IV. Finally, we shall compare the philosophy of Socrates with the Christian religion, insofar as it is contained in the books of the Old and New Testaments, and not in this or that System of Theology. For after Christians split into factions, many things were added to Religion from various principles which have receded from its primitive simplicity. We demand, therefore, that our statements be traced back to the clearest fountains of Revelation, and that what we bring forward concerning the doctrine of Christ and the Apostles be measured against the rules of correct interpretation. For in this brief inquiry, we could not bring forward individually every passage on which we rely. (*)

Plutarch advises this in *On Curiosity* <note>original: "περι πολυπαγμοσυνης" (peri polypragmosynes)</note> page 307: that the end of it (he is speaking of the Philosophy of Socrates) was to recognize one's own evils and be rid of them. Furthermore, not only the Athenian commoners but also those born of a nobler class were imbued with religious prejudices and stubbornly adhered to the publicly accepted worship. Therefore, these preconceived opinions about their ancestral worship had to be removed, and the genuine principles of Religion instilled through a clear method adapted to everyone's capacity. But *Socrates* almost always used a perpetual *Irony* <note>Socratic irony: a method of feigning ignorance to entice others into statements that can then be challenged</note>. However, this method is first of all difficult to grasp, and not suitable for convincing the common people. It must be firmly held that the question is not whether this method is suitable for blunting the Sophists <note>Sophists: professional teachers in ancient Greece often accused of using clever but fallacious arguments</note>; but whether that method ought to be employed by One who wishes to call back everyone from errors and lead them to the knowledge of truth and the love of virtue—which we deny. For either he who reasons in this way argues only *from concessions* <term>original: "ex concessis"; arguments based on what the opponent has already admitted</term>, or *from evident and immovable principles*. If the *former*, such an argument proves nothing other than that from a certain conceded proposition, some consequence can be drawn which the opponent either has not yet seen or has so far refused to admit. Meanwhile, however, he who is forced, even unwillingly, to concede such a proposition, does not yet see where he has erred, or is ignorant of why he should give his approval to this opinion rather than another. If it is the *latter*, all principles must be known with the greatest exactness, and the continuous connection of the propositions must be weighed most attentively, since he who wishes to lead us to concede some proposition can easily commit a gap in reasoning. Furthermore, the listeners must attend to all the consequences; and having instituted a comparison of what they have conceded with what the speaker wishes to infer, they are forced to turn and return each thing in their mind more than once. Indeed, they must attend not only to the force of individual propositions and the connection of the whole reasoning, but also to the words themselves, which are no small cause of errors. However, the common people are mostly unfit for conducting such an Examination, nor do they even have the time for weighing such reasonings. A clear and naked proposition of truth, without the windings of a longer reasoning, convinces the minds of the common people more than an artfully sought-out argument. All who apply their minds to instructing such people experience this: not once must even the clearest propositions be repeated and hammered in...

...believed, without doubt, that either all or most of their disputes were of no weight; that they debated rather over who was more learned, more perceptive, or more talkative, than over what might lead to the Benefit of Society and the Salvation of men. At the very least, the common people could hardly distinguish a Sophist <note>The Sophists were professional teachers in ancient Greece often accused of using clever but fallacious reasoning to win arguments for money.</note> from a Philosopher of true standing, such as *Socrates*. By what logic, then, could it happen that the Athenian people would give a listening ear to *Socrates*—who used irony almost constantly—and obey his words, if the other Sophists, who were vast in number, were constantly making a noise with their own tricks? Without doubt, if the public happened to be present at such a dispute, they believed either that both sides were merely talkative men, or that we simply cannot know what is true or false. *Socrates* himself admits this quite clearly in Plato’s *Phaedo* (page 37), for after saying that men can easily be led to hate both reason and other men, he continues:

> And especially those who spend their time in contradictory arguments—you know that in the end, they think they have become the wisest of all and have alone understood that there is nothing healthy or firm in either things or arguments. But all things that exist are simply turned upside down, just as in the Euripus <note>The Euripus is a narrow sea channel in Greece famous for its violent and unpredictable currents that change direction many times a day. Instead, out of distress, he might gladly shift all the blame from himself onto the arguments, and for the rest of his life continue to hate and revile them, thus being deprived of the truth and knowledge of reality itself."

It is indeed true that *Socrates* was not a Sceptic <note>Sceptics were philosophers who believed that certain knowledge is impossible.</note>, contrary to what the illustrious *Huetius* <note>Pierre Daniel Huet (1630–1721), a French bishop and scholar who argued that Socratic philosophy led directly to skepticism.</note> contends, whose reasons we examine elsewhere. When Socrates saw him thus disposed, he no longer troubled him with clever arguments, but most clearly and simply explained everything to him that he thought a man ought to know and study.*

Therefore, he was not in a hurry to make his listeners subtle, industrious, and ingenious, but thought it necessary to make them moderate first; for he judged that those who possessed such mental power without moderation would be more harmful and more capable of doing evil. From this passage it is clear: 1. It is very true, as I said, that many were alienated from him by the method of disputation he used. 2. That method was employed by him primarily to blunt the pride of the Sophists, and only when the swelling of vain opinion was set aside did he simply advise what needed to be said. 3. Few could be corrected in this way. For who does not know that it is nearly a miracle to lead a Proud and puffed-up man to the pursuit of a moderate mind and the confession of ignorance? From all these points, we conclude that the teaching method used by *Socrates* was less suited for recalling the minds of the Athenians from error and making them better.

# MEDITATION ON THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION COMPARED
<note>original: MEDITATIO DE RELIG. CHRIST. COLLATA</note>

...properly understand a longer and slightly more difficult line of reasoning; moreover, they suffer from a lack of time to undertake such an examination, being distracted by the business required to endure this life. Even if they were not hindered by these things, laziness would still prevent them from sticking with such an investigation for long; especially since prejudices about Religion and corrupt affections of the soul repeatedly distract the mind from properly weighing the truth. Furthermore, if we contemplate the character of the Jews—to whom our *Savior* was sent to lead back to the path of truth—we will see that their temperament was very little capable of perceiving an accurate logical demonstration. They stubbornly clung to their rituals and appealed to the oracles of the Old Testament and rashly adopted traditions rather than subtle reasoning. Finally, if our *Savior* had used this philosophical method, he might indeed have been regarded as an excellent Philosopher, but by no means as the promised Messiah.

Therefore, most rightly and wisely, our *Savior* neglected this method. He did not use that constant *Irony* <note>Socratic irony: a technique where a teacher pretends to be ignorant to expose the flaws in another's logic.</note> in which *Socrates* delighted, by which he would have alienated the minds of the Jews from himself and been counted among the *Sophists*; for even among the Jews at that time, as learned men have observed, there was a *disputatious* <note>original: "disputax"</note> class of men. Finally, he did not use a certain *Analytical* method, starting from innate ideas and progressing to prove what he intended; just as some in our own time are accustomed to breaking down and resolving the most simple speech of Christ and the Apostles into the tiniest parts. You find nothing here that tastes of artifice, nothing that tastes even slightly of the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to Scholasticism, the formal, highly structured university method of theology and philosophy.</note>. Everything (to use the words of the most excellent Genevan theologian, J. A. *Turrettini*) is plain and easy, drawn from nowhere else but common usage and accepted speech. Similes and parables are taken from obvious things, as if from the street corner. Arguments and reasonings are not those which affect the learned alone, but whose force even a peasant or an uneducated man <note>original: "idiota" – in this context, a person without formal academic training.</note> can recognize. All these things are so wisely fitted to their places that they subject even the most sublime matters to the senses themselves. Thus, that divine *Sermon* which he gave on the mount is an outstanding specimen of this; in which alone, he proposes whatever *Socrates* and the most celebrated of the Philosophers held of any value—as if contracted into a Summary—in sweet and pathetic, yet clear and transparent speech. Our Savior sometimes used parables and similar things sought from common use, so easy to grasp that it can hardly be conceived how a man, even moderately attentive, could have been ignorant of the meaning. I cannot restrain myself from adding the most elegant words of M.

# COMPARED WITH THE PHILOSOPHY OF SOCRATES
<note>original: COLLATA PHILOSOPHIA SOCRATIS</note>

*Erasmus*, which appear in that golden little book, the *Compendium on the Method of Reaching True Theology*, page 137:

> *There is no kind of teaching (he says) more familiar, nor more effective, than through the Comparison of Similes: Christ takes these from the most common things, as he wished his doctrine to be as popular as possible. For who has not seen seed thrown into the ground? Who has not watched fishermen casting nets? Who does not know that pruned branches wither? And he wonderfully renews these common things, adapting them to his Philosophy. It is for the few to discuss the most clever subtleties of the Scotists <note>The Scotists were followers of Duns Scotus, known for extremely complex and "subtle" medieval theology.</note>: in these [parables], it is easy for anyone to philosophize. You see the rising Sun and are cheered; what pleasure would you feel if that Sun of Righteousness <note>A traditional title for Christ.</note> should rise in the eyes of your heart? A disease of the body is a troublesome thing; how much more troublesome is a disease of the soul? You shudder at the contagion of a bodily plague; much more is the contagion of pestilential morals to be avoided. A garden blooming with every kind of flower and tree seems an elegant thing to you; what a spectacle is a soul green with innocence and overflowing with every kind of virtue? You see a serpent, and you have an example of Christian prudence; you see a dove, and you have an image of Christian simplicity; you see a deer, and you have a symbol reminding you that the divine scriptures are to be greedily sought, etc.*

Thus says *Erasmus*. Yet he [Jesus] wonderfully tempered all these things according to the requirements of the times and the people; he did not pour out everything that was to be believed in one rush, nor did he suggest everything to everyone at the same time. Rather, he opened the feelings of his mind and the divine Words to his disciples and the future propagators of the Christian Religion at intervals, putting some things off for other times and other states of their minds. But above all, he took care to prepare their minds to accept their fates—or to speak more clearly, he wanted them to lay aside the prejudices of their Sect and uproot the corrupt desires of the soul; persuaded that only then would the mind perceive the divine character of the Christian Religion. Hence the sum of his exhortations was this: *Change your minds, and have faith in my Gospel.* <note>The Latin "mentem mutate" (change your mind) is a literal translation of the Greek "metanoeite," usually rendered as "Repent."</note>

It is true that *Socrates*, by those continuous questions, wanted to lead men to self-knowledge and the study of a moderate mind. But since he used a certain accurate reasoning, exact according to the rules of the School, and wanted to lead even the unwilling to a confession of ignorance, it happened that many either did not understand the connection of the reasoning or were alienated from him, believing that he only acted to confound others and show off his supreme skill in disputing. This method of our divine Savior, however, was tempered for all temperaments, which the simple could follow and the learned could not despise. The disciples and the Apostles, the propagators of his religion, trod the same path.

# MEDITATION ON THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION COMPARED
<note>original: MEDITATIO DE RELIG. CHRIST. COLLATA</note>
<meta>catchword: netai</meta>

...to omit: yet sometimes they proved certain momentous Chapters of Religion more accurately with many arguments; especially when, among those who had given their faith to the Christian Religion, many arose who wandered from the simplicity of that divine doctrine and attempted to disturb others. But if the Apostles occasionally used allegories, those were brief and easily understood by the people of those times, though they seem more unusual to us who are devoted to other disciplines and accustomed to a different language and different customs. He who considers these things attentively and has a clear perspective on the nature of the human spirit will, unless I am mistaken, confess that while the method of **Socrates** might have been more subtle if one looks at philosophical *precision* <note>original: ἀκρίβειαν (akribeian)</note> in teaching, the method used by **Christ** and the **Apostles** was far more suitable and excellent for the reformation of the human race.

**V.** The excellence of the Christian Religion is further evident from the fact that **Christ** and the **Apostles** by no means shrouded in silence, tolerated, or much less approved of opinions that fought against the eternal salvation of men. **Socrates**, however, did not publicly reject the superstition prevailing at that time, nor the harmful opinions concerning the Gods and their worship, but even confirmed them by his own example. One who wishes to call men back from the most pestilential errors and lead them to a worship worthy of God ought to propose clearly and straightforwardly all those things that can hinder men from worshipping God rightly. A correct sense of God and a genuine contemplation of His attributes are the foundation of all worship and religion. If, therefore, such a man knows that those whom he wishes to reform either do not know God as the Supreme Ruler of the world, or hold opinions of Him that are contrary to His most Holy Nature and virtues, it befits him to strive with the greatest effort to tear those ideas out of their minds by the roots and teach more correct things, taking no account of those who disagree, nor of the publicly accepted religion, nor of danger. Yet **Socrates** did not reject the worship of the Gods, nor the Oracles, nor Sacrifices, nor divination, as we shall now show. *Xenophon, at the beginning of the Memorabilia, page 441, Basel Edition,* says in defense of Socrates:

"First then, as for the claim that he did not believe in the Gods whom the city believes in, what evidence did they ever use? For he was clearly seen sacrificing, often at home, and often on the common altars of the city." <note>original: Πρῶτον μεν ἐν, ὡς ἐκ ἐνόμιζεν, ὃς ἡ πόλις νομίζει Θεὸς, ποίω ποτ' ἐχρήσαντο τεκμηρίῳ ; θύων τε γὰρ φανερὸς ἦν, πολλάκις μεν οἴκοι, πολλάκις δὲ ἐπὶ τῶν κοινῶν τῆς πόλεως βωμῶν.</note>

<note>original: CUM PHILOSOPHIA SOCRATIS.</note>

...to those who ask how they should act, whether concerning sacrifices, or the veneration of ancestors, or any other such matters. For the Pythia declares that those who act according to the law of the city <note>original: νόμῳ πόλεως (nomō poleōs)</note> are acting piously. And Socrates did so himself and exhorted others to do the same; those who acted otherwise, he considered to be meddlesome and foolish." <note>original Greek: ἥ τε γὰρ ἡ Πυθία νόμῳ πόλεως ἀναιρεῖ ποιεντας εὐσεβῶς ἂν ποιεῖν. Σωκρατης τε οὕτως καὶ αὐτὸς ἐποίει, καὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις παρῄνει, τὰς δε ἄλλως πως ποιοῦντας, περιέργες καὶ ματαίες ἐνόμιζεν εἶναι.</note>

He opens his mind even more clearly on this business on page 510, which for the sake of brevity I will give in English only. "Tell me," he says, "O **Euthydemus**, what kind of thing do you think piety is?" And he replies: "A most excellent thing, by Hercules!" "Can you say what kind of man is a pious man?" "To me," he says, "that man seems to be pious who follows the Gods with veneration." "Is it permitted to honor the Gods in whatever way each person wishes?" "No," he says, "but by the law which has been set forth, defining what is appropriate to do." "Whoever, therefore, acts according to the laws, does he know in what way he ought to venerate the Gods?" "I think so," he says. "He, therefore, who knows how to honor the Gods, does he not think this ought to be done in any other way than as he knows it?" "By no means," he says. "Is there anyone who honors the Gods differently than he thinks he ought to?" "I certainly do not think so." "He, therefore, who holds to the laws established concerning divine worship, does he indeed honor the Gods according to the laws?" "Most strongly," he says. "He who therefore honors the Gods according to the laws, does he honor them as he ought?" "Why not?" "He who honors as he ought, is he pious?" "Highly so." "He, therefore, who knows the laws established concerning divine worship, may be rightly defined by us as pious." "So," he says, "it seems."

From which passages it is clear that **Socrates** not only did not wish to subvert the received worship, but even thought those who felt and acted otherwise were insane. But does this befit a Philosopher, or an honest Man? Can the reformation of the human race be expected from such a one? Should worship be tempered according to the law of the City, or rather to the eternal Ideas we have of God? How much better it would have been if he had said roundly that worship must be exhibited to the One, the One, I say, Creator and Governor of all things! Truly, here he did not stand by what he confessed of himself in the *Crito*: "I," he says, "not only now, but always, have been the kind of man who obeys none of my own except the reason <note>original: λόγῳ (logō)</note> which, as I reason, appears best to me." <note>original: Ἐγω, inquit, ἐ μόνον νυν, ἀλλα καὶ ἀει τοιατος, οἷος των ἐμων μηδενι ἄλλῳ πειθεσθαι ἢ τῳ λογῳ ὃς ἄν μοι λογιζομένῳ βελτιστος φαίνηται.</note> Certainly, if this is to be placed as an Axiom, that worship must be exhibited to God *according to the law of the city*...

# MEDITATION ON THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION COMPARED
<note>original: MEDITATIO DE RELIG. CHRIST. COLLATA</note>

...even the most absurd thoughts and opinions about God must be approved, and a detestable worship must never be abolished. In this way, someone can be an *Atheist* or a *Sceptic* and yet simultaneously repeat over and over that the ancestral worship should not be changed at all. Thus, Sextus Empiricus, on page 560 of Fabricius's edition, says of his Sceptic: *For perhaps the Sceptic will be found more secure and steady than those who philosophize differently: since he professes there are Gods in accordance with ancestral customs and laws, and does everything that pertains to their pious worship.* <note>original: Τάχα γὰρ ἀσφαλέστερος... συντεῖνον ποιῶν.</note> Regarding this, the Illustrious Editor rightly says in his notes: *It is foolish and completely removed from philosophical certainty <term>asphaleia: a state of being firm or secure in one's knowledge</term> to profess that Gods exist and that he worships them, not because he is securely persuaded by undeniable reasons, but "according to ancestral customs and laws"; he would thus just as securely profess any Chimera <note>A mythical monster, used here to mean a ridiculous or impossible idea.</note> and follow it with worship, if it were so received by custom and established by ancestral laws.* 

Who then will not confess that Socrates sinned gravely? For he was either convinced that the publicly accepted worship was false, or he was ignorant of it. If he was convinced it was false, why did he not openly confess this and, as much as was in his power, exhort everyone to offer worship to God alone? If he was ignorant of it, he was unfit to instill a pure religion in men. I know that Plato, in the *Eutyphro* and the second book of the *Republic*, asserts that Socrates disapproved of what the Poets had invented about the Gods. But can he who wants the Gods to be worshipped according to ancestral rites rightfully blame those who constantly adhered to the accepted opinion? For those who worshipped the Gods as was received by law could say that, regarding the *Worship of the Gods*, this must be held as an axiom: *One must not recede even a hair's breadth from ancestral worship.* 

What could this "best of men" <note>A common honorific for Socrates.</note> have replied here that could satisfy a lover of truth? For if he had said that he rejected only the coarser opinions of the common people about the Gods, the response was ready at hand: that the religion of the common people, or the religion publicly established by law, must be followed; therefore, even by *his own principles*, nothing here should be changed. If he had something else in mind, it should have been brought out into the open. From the passages cited above, it is clear enough that Socrates did not reject the authority of the Oracles; for he referred the rule of worship to the responses of the Oracles. Moreover, it is well known that these contributed much to increasing superstition; the gathering of people at them was great, and their authority was immense. However, most learned men—such as van Dale, Fontenelle, and Basnage—have so clearly proved that everything in those Oracles was composed for fraud, that hereafter few

And he accused others who do something contrary to the signs from the Gods, guarding themselves against the ill-repute among men. He himself looked down on all human things in comparison to the counsel from the Gods.* <note>original: Εἰ δὲ τι δόξειεν αὐτῷ... πρὸς τὴν παρὰ τῶν Θεῶν συμβουλίαν.</note> That is, if he ever thought anything was being shown to him by the Gods, he would have been less likely to act against those signs than if someone had tried to persuade him to accept a blind leader on a road instead of one who could see and...

...a path for the ignorant instead of the one who knows. Moreover, he accused those of folly who, by being wary of human opinions, acted against the things the Gods advised. The same author in Book IV, page 504 says: <note>original: "Το δὲ καὶ ἐξ ἀδυνάτων μὲν τὰ συμφέροντα προνοεῖσθαι... ᾗ ἂν ἄριςα γίγνοιτο." This is a reference to Xenophon’s *Memorabilia*, where Socrates discusses how the gods help humans through signs.</note> *But that, he says, when the foresight of beneficial things is impossible for us regarding the future, they themselves assist us through divination for those who inquire, showing the outcomes and teaching how things may best happen—this is a sign of great Love.* You see that Socrates by no means neglected divination; and although he perhaps spoke differently than he felt, it is clear nonetheless that he never wished to publicly criticize it. Moreover, it is so well known that this "theatrical performance" <note>original: "Histrioniam," referring here to the outward performance of religious rituals without internal belief.</note> did much to increase superstition that nothing more need be said. Hence Cicero rightly thought that such study should be overturned, even though in his own practice—just like Socrates—he had decided to change nothing. If we gather all these points into a summary, we must confess that Socrates fulfilled the duties of neither a Philosopher nor a Good Man, so long as he not only failed to subvert these pillars of Superstition, but even approved of them by his own authority. For if these had been removed, the path would have been paved for a purer worship. But while they remained, there was no hope of obtaining a better and more improved worship among men. However, among others, the very ingenious **Vayerius** <note>François de La Mothe Le Vayer (1588–1672), a French philosopher known for his skepticism and his work *On the Virtue of Pagans*.</note> intercedes on page 592, saying:

> His idolatry is poorly proven by the terms his disciples used in their apologies, when they wrote that he had innovated nothing in the matter of Religion, having always lived in this regard like the others, and practiced Sacrifices as they were then in use. For already their own self-interest and the fear of the hemlock <note>The poison used to execute Socrates after he was convicted of impiety and corrupting the youth.</note> may have made them speak in that manner. Besides, there is reason to say that Socrates, who had only implicit faith, was content to recognize a single God in the law of nature, without wishing for that reason to disturb the public government by the introduction of a new worship, which he could not use without violating the laws of the State: and that, if he sacrificed to some Athenian divinities, it was likely through a cloud of recognition of the powers of the one God, whom he adored under different names.

But the learned Vayerius defends this otherwise excellent man poorly: First, because we cannot know what Socrates felt or did from any other source than the testimony of his disciples; how then will it be clear that they were merely serving the needs of the time in this part? Second, by the very fact that Socrates followed his ancestral worship, he fulfilled the duty of neither a Philosopher nor a Wise Man

and as far as it appears, the most learned Vayerius himself would have attempted nothing to subvert the idolatrous worship of the Roman Church. Surely, where the authority of the Church is so great, both conscience and Philosophy carry little weight. Third, even if he had something else in mind while he worshiped the Gods of the Athenians, he still cannot be excused; for in the cause of religion, one is not permitted to "act a part" and pretend one thing while believing another, especially in those matters which regard the pure worship of God, and which cannot be hidden without offense to God and men.

->VI.<-

But our divine **Savior** departed very far from this path. When he appeared to the world, the state of the **Jews** was no less depraved than that of the **Gentiles**. The Jews, to be sure, possessed a divine Revelation contained in the writings of **Moses** and the **Prophets**, which they had nonetheless so neglected that only a thin shadow of true religion remained; they had wonderfully corrupted those things pertaining to the true worship of God with various traditions. Hence, having despised the most momentous truths that lead to a piously lived life and the attainment of supreme happiness, they pursued those things which can be easily performed without the improvement of the mind. Our **divine Savior** by no means tolerated these things; he called them back again to the Law and the Prophets. He repeatedly emphasized that true piety consists in the purging of the soul from depraved affections and in a way of living exacted according to the will of the Deity. He said it was not to be asked whether they worshiped God in Jerusalem or on the mountain of Samaria, but whether they did so with a true conversion of the mind toward the everywhere-present God. He said it helped them little that they were descended from **Abraham**: for he alone pleases God who uniquely pursues piety after the example of Abraham. He publicly taught that he was the **Messiah**, the sole hope of the Faithful and the unique Cause of our reconciliation with God, although he was hardly ignorant of how foreign this was to the opinions of the majority.

Since the leaders of even a very impure Religion are everywhere very powerful, and tenaciously defend opinions once they are received, and commonly obtain the favor of those in whose hands the summit of power rests, it can easily happen that men who love truth less—deterred by the fear of offending them—do not attack the received profession of public Religion with the fervor that is proper. Instead, they only whisper among their friends and laugh at it behind closed doors. But our **divine Savior** publicly rebuked the **Pharisees** <note>A Jewish sect known for strict adherence to traditional and written law, often criticized in the New Testament for hypocrisy.</note>, a pestilential class of men entirely shaped to the spirit of the age, and he depicted their morals to the life, showing them to be the primary cause of a religion so greatly disfigured and of morals...

...and he pronounced that the cause of the most depraved men existed even in the midst of the crowd. Although he easily foresaw that those **Performers** <note>original: "Histriones"; refers here to the religious and political leaders who acted out roles of piety while plotting against Jesus.</note> would prepare everything for His destruction, He never turned away from His most holy purpose. **He** did not wish for God to be worshiped *according to the law of the city* <note>original: "νόμῳ πόλεως" (*nomō poleōs*). This was the Socratic principle of following local religious customs regardless of personal belief.</note> as Socrates did. He did not want the things that belong to God to be given to others. He believed that a wound so grave and deeply embedded should not be nourished with ointments but must be removed entirely, even cut out with a sword, lest the healthy part also be dragged down. Similarly, the **Apostles** followed **His** example. And to speak now of the pagans alone, in the very flourishing city of the Athenians, they preached the **sole Ruler of the world**, publicly criticizing the worship of the Gods. This was despite the useless snarling of the "Consultants of Insane Wisdom" <note>A sarcastic reference to the Stoic and Epicurean philosophers of the time.</note> who, although following very different methods of philosophizing, nevertheless conspired together to defend superstition and established rituals. These **unlearned men** <note>original: "ἀπαίδευτοι" (*apaideutoi*). A reference to the Apostles being seen as uneducated by the standards of Greek philosophy.</note> argued—yet with more sincerity than the greatest philosophers—concerning God and His virtues, and the nature of a pure worship pleasing to God. They did this even though they were well aware that those philosophers considered themselves the only ones who were wise and who knew what was true and right. These men did not wish to serve the convenience of the times or to tolerate those things that seemed "immovable." Nay, what is more, since they were persuaded that faith in our Savior and other heads of religion connected to these were necessary beliefs for obtaining salvation, they professed them publicly. Nor could they be deterred from this most excellent profession of religion by any threats or the heat of persecutions, even though they knew full well that perverse men would receive such matters with mockery. Hence, they spoke of the resurrection of our bodies—a dogma entirely unknown to the Pagans—not only in the presence of philosophers but also to men of the highest dignity. They spoke with such gravity and confidence that it was easily apparent that these most excellent and pious men were deceived neither by the dreams of a deluded mind nor by subtle sophistries. The Athenians and other pagans veiled their **mysteries**, or rather their foul and ridiculous delusions, from the common people and only revealed them to the Initiated. The **Apostles**, just as they wisely and purely explained **the depths of God**, <note>original: "τὰ βάθη τοῦ Θεοῦ" (*ta bathē tou Theou*); see 1 Corinthians 2:10.</note> so they repeatedly said they were sent by the divine Savior for this very purpose: to bring into the light things that had been obscured by the vice of the ages and to announce to all mortals what the world had hitherto been ignorant of. By this means, at last, religion certainly took on another face. With divine grace assisting, the superstition that had flooded the world was forced to depart and give way to the most excellent way of worshiping God—something which not even the most subtle philosophers were ever able to achieve. It is true, meanwhile, that the **Apostles** tolerated certain things among the Jews and Gentiles, and they did not force them to immediately cast off all the rituals to which they were

first accustomed. They wisely bore with things that could be tolerated without the loss of salvation. But from the very start, they taught everyone what the true nature of Religion consisted of. And whenever they spoke of the mysteries of the Christian religion, they simultaneously demonstrated their **divine fitness**. <note>original: "θεοπρεπείαν" (*theoprepeian*); the quality of being worthy of or appropriate to God's nature.</note> Nor did they enjoin any **Discipline of the Secret** <term>Disciplina Arcani: a historical practice in the early Church where certain rituals and doctrines were kept hidden from non-believers and catechumens.</term> regarding dogmas and rituals to be observed; such a thing was only introduced in following centuries, not without damage to pure Religion. For I cannot approve (to say this in passing) the opinion of certain learned men who think that the restoration of this *Discipline of the Secret* would be highly beneficial to the modern state of Religion, given the daily emergence of so many **scoffers** <note>original: "ἐμπαικταῖς" (*empaiktais*); mockers or deriders of faith.</note> of religion. For we must either say that there are mysteries in the Christian religion that fight head-on with the most evident principles of reason, or that they are truths which, while surpassing our grasp, are not at all contradictory but are worthy of God. No one who has examined the Christian religion without partisan zeal will assert the former, nor do learned men suggest it. We concede the latter, certainly; but nothing is imposed here as a belief that perceptive men, well aware of the weakness of the human intellect, cannot admit. I speak, however, of the mysteries handed down in the Holy Scriptures, and not of those which have been fabricated by the Papists. At the very least, it is well known that through this "discipline" [of secrecy], the simplest signs of divine grace were transformed into a kind of theatrical performance.

We willingly concede, therefore, that this **Greatest of Men** <note>Referring to Socrates.</note> recognized the principal heads of natural religion <note>Natural religion refers to truths about God that can be discovered through human reason alone, without the help of the Bible.</note> and in this regard surpassed many other philosophers. 

If, however, we contemplate the decrees of the Christian religion without partisan zeal, either I am vehemently mistaken, or it has surpassed the philosophy of *Socrates* in many ways. First, those very things which can be known about God through reason alone, Revelation opens more clearly and evidently for the persuasion of all. For it exhibits magnificent notions concerning God; it presents God to us as **eternal**, **independent**, the **Founder of All Things**, producing all things by His nod alone; **Most Wise**, **Omniscient**, **Most Just**, **Merciful**, **Providing for all things, great and small**, **Preserving** and **Governing** all, especially fostering the pious, performing all things for the salvation of man, prescribing the most equitable laws for the human race, and so on. Nothing can be thought of so excellently, much less said about God, which the Christian religion does not repeatedly emphasize. I do not wish to prove these things with the very words of Scripture, since they are most familiar to all who acknowledge its divine origin. Let the books of the Old and New Testaments be compared with the writings of Plato and Xenophon, and once the examination is begun, it will be clear which doctrine offers more excellent thoughts regarding God and divine matters. 

Yet, even if the philosophy of Socrates taught us what can be known of God from reason no less correctly than the Christian religion, it nonetheless lacks those most excellent **incentives to Piety** which the Christian religion supplies. To love virtue, the most effective arguments must be brought forward, by which men are drawn to its study. If you take away the rewards, the love of virtue perishes. This is necessary because of the depravity of the human will, which is so great that, unless it is fortified by certain protections in the pursuit of virtue, it is very easily carried away headlong. For either no one, or very few mortals, are moved by

virtue alone and its own excellence. Indeed, if we wish to speak the truth, unless there is a certain or highly probable hope of a reward for virtue, it can hardly be conceived how the contemplation of virtue could have such power over the minds of men that, having suppressed the most vehement passions, they would cling to virtue. One must live agreeably to reason; one must work for virtue. This is so. But why? Because it is agreeable to reason. If I ask again, the same answer will be repeated. It is, moreover, extremely difficult to show that the precepts of reason have any force of **divine law**; whoever doubts this should read the *Doubts Concerning Natural Law* by the most consulted and learned *Hombergius*, a jurist of Marburg. 

Finally, it is added that everyone sees that those who love virtue are not always the most fortunate of all. The most acute *Locke* speaks elegantly in the treatise titled: *That the Christian Religion is very Reasonable* <note>The original French title cited is *Que la Religion Chrétienne est très-raisonnable*, referring to John Locke's 1695 work, *The Reasonableness of Christianity*.</note> on page 326: *In truth,* he says, *the Philosophers extolled the beauty of Virtue. > Fortune, rejoicing in her cruel business, and
> persistent in playing her insolent game,
> shifts her uncertain honors,
> kind now to me, now to another.
> I praise her while she stays; but if she shakes
> her swift wings, I resign what she gave, and wrap 
> myself in my virtue, and seek honest
> poverty without a dowry.

I do not deny that philosophers and poets sometimes spoke of themselves in this way. But it is one thing to say, another to do. Anyone who knows the character of *Horace* will find it difficult to persuade himself that virtue alone had such power over his mind that he was willing to endure the most difficult things for the sake of virtue alone. *Cicero* also more than once asserted with the Stoics that virtue is content with itself for living well and blessedly. Suppose, therefore, that Socrates, moved by the excellence of virtue alone, lived according to reason; yet it is clear that very few could have followed this man of most eminent virtues with equal steps in this racecourse of virtue. For, good God! how much time is required to persuade men—who have neither the talent nor the time to examine such things—that nothing is more excellent than virtue, and nothing more worthy of our love. Socrates, however, could not bring other arguments to persuade the minds of the Athenians as long as he himself spoke hesitantly about rewards and punishments after death. 

This we shall now prove with very clear testimonies. I will not place my trust in Lucian, <note>Lucian of Samosata, a Roman-era satirist known for mocking philosophers.</note> who in the *Dialogue of Menippus and Cerberus* (Volume I, page 307, Graevius edition) claims that Socrates approached death with great fear; instead, I will bring forward the words of his own disciples and supporters. "But now the hour is come to go away, I to die and you to live. A little earlier in the same *Apology* he says: 

"For death is one of two things: either it is like being nothing, and the dead have no sensation of anything; or, according to what is said, it happens to be a certain change and migration of the soul from this place to another place. ### VIII.
I will add here another incentive for the study of piety, which emerges from the very nature of the Christian religion and abundantly demonstrates its excellence. Since the human soul obeys the precepts of religion with difficulty, all arguments must be brought forward by which it may be induced to love virtue. Socrates, beyond what right reason teaches, could bring nothing into the discussion; nor could he, as we have heard, promise the certain hope of blessed immortality to the upright. The Christian religion not only draws arguments from the *perfections of God, the creation and preservation* of all things, and the innumerable benefits bestowed upon the human race, but primarily from the *Magnificent Work of Redemption* (Luke 1:74, 1 Corinthians 6:20, and many other places). To that end, it brings back to our memory the *miserable state of the human race, the atrocity and punishment of sin, the incredible love of God toward us, and the wisdom of Christ our Savior*,

<column-break/>
