<meta>catchword: nita-</meta>

*his innocence, the bloody death endured for man, the power and incredible weight of this death, his promises—which surpass all our merit and all power of the intellect—and finally the goods overflowing upon us, which are extraordinary, lasting, and will bring eternal happiness.* These incentives are not simply proposed, but are repeated and instilled in a way that is most suitable for moving the souls of men. I do not wish to expand upon or demonstrate these things further; the excellent *Werenfels, the eternal glory of our Switzerland, proves this in his own manner—that is, solidly—in Theological Dissertation VII.* <note>Samuel Werenfels (1657–1740) was a Swiss theologian known for his moderate views and influential writings on the interpretation of Scripture.</note> This only must be observed: that these *incentives* are suited to the grasp of everyone, practically standing out before the eyes, most effective for softening the souls of even the most perverse, and strengthened and confirmed by the examples of those who professed that religion and felt its power. I know what the *unbelievers will say here*: they will answer that these incentives I have mentioned are drawn from the *Mystery of the Holy Trinity and Redemption*; *these things, however, surpass human understanding*; and from a matter whose notions are clearly obscure, arguments for piety cannot rightly be drawn. They would argue that *Socrates argued from things that reason can grasp, but no one is obligated to do the impossible.* To these things, I note the following: First, we admit that these mysteries cannot be grasped by us; it is enough that they are not absurd or contradictory. We believe in One God; both reason and revelation teach this. We believe, furthermore, that in this unique and most perfect Being, there is something we call the Father, something we call the Son, and finally something we call the Holy Spirit; we are entirely ignorant of the manner of this thing. We believe, furthermore, that God was manifested in the flesh—to speak with Holy Scripture—in a certain unique way not sufficiently known to us men. Second, those incentives are by no means drawn from what we do not know regarding the ineffable nature of God and the mysteries, but from what men *can* understand. *The Triune God, insofar as He is considered as good, merciful, wise, and just*, is the object of adoration and worship, not insofar as He is some unspeakable Being whose inner nature we cannot know. For it is only by the former reasoning that God is *worthy of reverence*. <note>original Greek: σεβασμιος (sebasmios), meaning venerable or worthy of worship.</note> Thus Holy Scripture relates that Christ redeemed us with his blood, made satisfaction for us, and acquired life and immortality; it by no means argues from the ineffable union that occurred between God and human nature. That God the Father wishes to make the pious eternally happy through Christ, that the Holy Spirit changes the minds of men and brings help in adversities, etc. It is proper, therefore, that we flee to Christ and implore the grace of the Holy Spirit, but it does not argue from the manner of the Mystery of the Holy Trinity—

...of the Trinity. <note>original: "trinitatis"</note> 3. If no *incentives* <note>The author uses "incentiva" to mean "motivations" or "stimuli" for moral behavior.</note> to pursue virtue were effective unless they were drawn from things whose nature and manner we understood exactly, it would follow that even the *incentives* that reason provides regarding the worship of God would be worthless. Reason says that God is to be praised. Why? Because He is the Creator and Preserver of all things. But do we know by what method God was able to produce the visible universe by the sole command of His will? Thanks are to be given to God because He heaps countless benefits upon us daily; but has the mechanism of His preservation and His operation upon our bodies and minds been fully understood? Even those who believe only reason should be heard think it can be proven by reason alone that we are bound to live according to reason, even though that argument does not rely on "mathematical <term>precision</term>" <note>original: "ἀκριβεια" (akribeia). Therefore, although we may not correctly perceive the logic and nature of those mysteries, it is sufficient that, *insofar* as they can be grasped, they contain within themselves the *most effective incentives* for piety.

IX. We have proven the *excellence of the Christian religion*, when compared with the philosophy of Socrates, based on the *incentives for piety* which the Christian religion brings forward and which the philosophy of *Socrates* lacks. Furthermore, this *excellence* will become clear if we show that the *Christian religion shows the most certain way to make God favorable, whereas the philosophy of Socrates does not*. I prove this from the fact *that Socrates was unable to show that God is willing to return to a state of grace with a sinful human being*. To be sure, *Socrates* could conceive of God as a being who is most good, merciful, and placable, not prone to anger, vengeance, or moodiness: and thus that God could, if He wished, return to grace with one who wanders. But how did he know for certain that God *wills* this? He believed that one must live according to reason, that we must align all the desires of the soul with the nod of the Divine Power, and that we must be modest, temperate, placable, and lovers of peace; that we must resist the wicked affections and pursuits of the soul, and uproot from the heart all desires contrary to the will of the Divine, so far as it can be known. But if he looked deep within himself, he had to confess that he had many times turned away from the true and the right in his thoughts and actions. For the passions of the soul are too vehement to be broken even by the most evident reasonings; he did not know, therefore, whether God would be willing to forgive him for all those aberrations. You might say that Socrates could have believed that the *most kind Divine Power* would forgive errors that human nature is poorly equipped to avoid, and that it is enough if one keeps the decrees of reason according to one's strength. But who can safely determine to what degree the proba-

-bility, so to speak, of future forgiveness should be extended? Who can define how many sins God is going to pardon, or not? This is certainly the task of those who are skilled in the art of haggling with God. Therefore, a man who listens to reason alone cannot have a certain confidence, built upon immovable arguments, that God will return to grace with him. Let us suppose, however, that *Socrates*, shaped by many exercises in the love of virtue, was persuaded by *certain arguments* that God wished to return to grace with him, to forgive the errors he committed, and to make him a sharer in blessed immortality. This certainly would have been of little use to others who could in no way be compared to him. By the consensus of almost all antiquity, it is established that *Socrates* was endowed with extraordinary gifts of the mind. Even if he had progressed to such a degree of perfection that he could have hope for future happiness, others could perceive no comfort from this state of Socrates, especially since he asserted that, properly speaking, virtue cannot be taught, but that the seeds of virtue are implanted only in great men by a "certain <term>divine portion</term>." <note>original: "θειᾳ quadam μοιρᾳ" (theia moira). But in that darkness of the times, who could hope that many would progress so far in virtue? Who could uproot from the minds of those men all preconceived opinions about the way of worshipping God and the study of genuine piety, break the power of a depraved will, and instill in their minds the excellence of virtue, of which only some very slight and vanishing examples were available? But what need is there for words? *Socrates* himself, entangled in doubtful matters, more than once signified clearly enough that it was to be desired that God would teach mortals in some more evident way what would please Him most. In the second *Alcibiades* <note>A dialogue attributed to Plato, though its authenticity was debated even in the early modern period.</note> near the end, after he has taught that justice and wisdom belong to wise men, and that those are wise and just who understand what is to be done and said before gods and men, he continues as follows on page 232:

Socrates is pointing out human ignorance regarding what is truly beneficial, suggesting the need for divine revelation.</note>

**Socrates:** ...Indeed. Do you see then, that it is not safe for you to go to the god to pray, lest it happen that he hears you speaking impiously and accepts nothing of your sacrifice? And perhaps you might even suffer some other misfortune. It seems best to me, therefore, to remain silent. For as for the prayer of the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans, known for their brief and stoic prayers.</note>, because of their greatness of soul—which is the most beautiful name for what is actually ignorance—I do not think you would want to use it. It is therefore necessary to wait until one learns how one ought to behave toward the gods and toward men. **Alcibiades:** When then will this time come, O Socrates, and who is the teacher? For I think I would most gladly see this man, whoever he is. **Socrates:** This is he who cares for you. But it seems to me, just as Homer says Athena took away the mist from the eyes of Diomedes <note>A reference to the *Iliad*, where the goddess grants a hero the ability to distinguish gods from men on the battlefield.</note>, which happened to be there, so that he might then see clearly through which things you are to know both evil and good. For now, you do not seem to me to be able to do so. **Alcibiades:** Let him take away the mist, if he wishes, or anything else. For I am prepared to avoid nothing of those things commanded by him, whoever that man is, provided I might become a better person. **Socrates:** But truly, he has a wonderful eagerness for your well-being. **Alcibiades:** Then it seems best to me to postpone the sacrifice until that time. **Socrates:** And you are right to think so. For it is safer than running such a great risk. **Alcibiades:** But how, O Socrates? Since you seem to have advised me well, I will place this crown upon you. To the gods we will give crowns and all other customary things when I see that day has arrived. And it will arrive before long, if the gods are willing.

->that is, from the version by Marsilio Ficino.<- <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499) was a celebrated Renaissance scholar who translated the works of Plato from Greek into Latin.</note>

I desire nevertheless to hear from You, what you yourself think in these matters. **Alcibiades:** To me indeed, O Socrates, it seems no different than it does to You and to God; for it would not be right for me to disagree with God. **Socrates:** Do you remember saying that you were tossed about in great doubt and danger, lest you deceive yourself by occasionally wishing for evils instead of goods? **Alcibiades:** I remember. **Socrates:** Do you see then that it is not safe enough for you to proceed to prayer, lest perhaps God, hearing you praying for a curse, rejects your sacrifices, and you report back some other accidental misfortune? It seems to me, therefore, worthwhile to keep quiet: for I do not think you wish to use the prayer of the Lacedaemonians on account of their "greatness of soul," for that is the most honorable name for all those things by which foolishness is signified.

<header>WITH THE PHILOSOPHY OF SOCRATES.</header>

Therefore it is necessary to wait until it is learned how one should conduct oneself toward God and toward Men. **Alcibiades:** When will that be, O Socrates, and who is the Teacher? For most joyfully would I recognize this man, whoever he shall be. **Socrates:** This is He who has care for you. But it seems to me—just as Homer says Minerva <note>The Roman name for Athena.</note> took away the mist from the eyes of Diomedes so that he might discern God from man—so too it is necessary first to take away from your soul the darkness with which it is now flooded; then to bring those things closer through which you may distinguish whether something is good or evil, for now you seem unable to do so. **Alcibiades:** Let him take away the mist, whether he wishes, or whatever else. For I am prepared to omit nothing at all that he shall command, whoever he may finally be, provided I myself shall emerge better. **Socrates:** And He provides for you in a wonderful way. **Alcibiades:** In that time, therefore, I judge it will be best to defer this Sacrifice. **Socrates:** And rightly indeed; for it is safer than subjecting oneself to such great danger. **Alcibiades:** So it is, O Socrates. Meanwhile, however, since you seem to have counseled me well, I place this crown upon you. To the gods we will offer crowns and all other proper things only then, when I know that day has arrived. Moreover, it will arrive as soon as the gods are willing.

If someone should contend that it is by no means proven by this reasoning that Socrates recognized the necessity of revelation, I would not wish to argue with him *about words*. <note>original: "de Verbis"</note> For since, as is clear from this passage (to say nothing of others), *Socrates* believed that men would be most happy if God himself taught men the way He wished to be worshipped, it is sufficiently plain that a certain extraordinary Revelation seemed to this Most Excellent Man to be a Work most worthy of God.

<margin>(*) I have better explained my mind on this argument in the *Dissertation on the Causes of Incredulity*.</margin>

(*) Since, therefore, the Christian religion openly delivers the method of appeasing God, who could not have greater confidence in rendering God propitious to himself? Especially since the way to achieve this is not to be sought through long reasoning. For *Jesus Christ* Himself interposes His own faith, promising that no one will undergo condemnation who flees to Him as a **Sacred Anchor**. <note>A common metaphor in the early modern period for a final, secure hope or refuge.</note> He will grant pardon to all who confess and deplore their errors, provided they renounce them for the future. But if an upright man should plead his own weakness, Christ testifies that, on account of the infinite <term>excellence</term> <note>original: "ὑπεροχὴν" (hyperochen). This refers to the overflowing abundance or pre-eminence of Christ's merit.</note> of the merit He performed, He will forgive the pious for all their sins, even the most serious, and will not impute them to anyone who has applied themselves to the study of piety. Who, then, does not see the excellence of the Christian Religion in this regard? As *Lactantius* rightly says in *Divine Institutes*, Book I, Chapter I: *Because it could not happen that divine reason should become known to man through himself...* <note>Lactantius (c. 250–325 AD) was an early Christian author who argued that human reason is insufficient to reach divine truth without revelation.</note>

[...continued from the previous page] God did not allow man, when seeking the light of Wisdom, to wander any longer or to roam through inextricable darkness without any result for his labor; He eventually opened man's eyes and made the knowledge of truth His own gift. He did this so that *He might show that human Wisdom is nothing* and point out the way to attain immortality to those who were wandering and straying. Nor did He only clearly show the certainty of this Reconciliation of man with God, but He also brings everything into the open which can serve to introduce and extol the divine fitness <note>original: *theoprepeian*, a Greek term meaning that which is suitable or worthy of the nature of God</note> of such a great benefit. To that end, Revelation shows the *most wretched condition of men without Christ, and the impotence of the powers of the human mind, even in men who were otherwise most wise.* It calls us to recognize the *necessity and utility of such a reconciliation,* and vividly depicts the *infinite Goods joined with it.* What, then, can be more welcome to a man mourning the atrocity of his sins and feeling the silent lashes of conscience, than to see clearly to whom he can safely flee—one who will provide relief in narrow straits? Could sacrifices, or ritual washings, or the other things which the Athenians observed according to their laws of worship, bring such confidence or such *joy*? Indeed, *Socrates* speaks differently to those who were anxious about whether they would obtain pardon from God, even if they had worshipped Him to the best of their ability. 

In *Xenophon's Memorabilia, Book IV, page 505*, when *Euthydemus* <note>A young follower of Socrates often depicted as seeking political success through learning</note> had said that he was quite concerned that he might be neglecting the Gods, and grieved because no man could return thanks worthy of the benefits the Gods provide, *Socrates* replies: 

<note>original Greek: Ἀλλὰ μὴ ἀθυμει ἔφη, ὦ Ἐυθύδημε. ὁρᾷς γὰρ ὅτι ὁ ἐν Δελφοῖς Θεὸς...</note>
"But do not be discouraged," he said, "O Euthydemus. For you see that the God at Delphi <note>Apollo, whose oracle was the central authority on religious practice in Greece</note>, when someone asks him how he might please the Gods, answers: 'By the law of the city.' And the law everywhere is surely that everyone should please the Gods with sacrifices according to their ability. How then could anyone honor the Gods better and more piously than by doing so as they themselves command? But is it necessary to hold back nothing of one's power? For when someone does this, he clearly does not honor the Gods. One must therefore honor the Gods without failing according to one's ability, and be confident and hope for the greatest goods. For one would not be wise to hope for greater things from others than from those who are able to help the most. Nor would it be otherwise more fitting than if he should please these; and how could he please them more, or perhaps most of all, than by obeying them?" 

That is to say: *One should not grieve on that account, he says, O Euthydemus. For you see the Delphic God responding to those who ask in what way anyone may do what is pleasing to the Gods: "By the law of the State." For the law everywhere is such that each person pleases the Gods with sacrifices according to his means. By what means, therefore, can anyone honor the Gods better or more piously than in the way they themselves prescribe? It is necessary, therefore, not to omit anything possible (for whoever does this, neglects the Gods), but to honor the Gods in this way, and to hope—*

—and to hope for the greatest goods from them. For who of sound mind would hope for greater things from anyone else than from the Gods, who are able to benefit us the most? Indeed, it is necessary for him who pleases them to hope for these things from them; and he will please them who obeys them as much as possible.

**X.** But Revelation does not only show the way to make God favorable; it also promises and exhibits sufficient Strength to pursue virtue. *Socrates* could demonstrate the excellence of virtue, exhort men to love it with various arguments, and even show by his own example what power it has in the souls of men. These things are indeed distinguished; but that Greatest Man could not go further. Most mortals are led not by reason, but by depraved pursuits and affections, so much so that the most excellent precepts must generally yield to the violent and headlong desires of the soul. Even those who are flooded with a greater light than *Socrates* experienced this very often. Add to this a weak knowledge of God, obscured by the fables of the Poets and Priests <note>original: *sacrificulorum*, often used disparagingly for those who performed superstitious rituals</note>; the preconceived opinions of the Athenians about never changing public worship; and the habit of seeking God not in pure love, but in external rites—which both *Socrates* and *Plato* confirmed by both their teaching and their example. 

Hence, learned men among the Gentiles sometimes confessed and deplored that wretched state of human minds, although they themselves were ignorant of how they might bring a remedy. *Cicero* vividly depicts this state in his *Tusculan Disputations, Book III, Section 2*: 

> Nature has given us small sparks [of light], which we—quickly corrupted by evil habits and opinions—extinguish so thoroughly that the light of nature nowhere appears. For there are innate seeds of virtues in our characters; if they were allowed to reach maturity, nature itself would lead us to a blessed life. But now, as soon as we are brought into the light and received [into society], we are continuously involved in all depravity and the greatest perversity of opinions; so that we seem to have sucked in error almost with our nurse's milk. When we are returned to our parents and finally handed over to teachers, we are then imbued with such various errors that truth yields to vanity, and nature itself yields to confirmed opinion. The Poets also join in: since they present a great appearance of learning and wisdom, they are heard, read, and cling deeply in our minds. But when the people—acting as if they were some great Master—and the whole multitude from every side consenting to vices is added to the same, then we are clearly infected by the depravity of opinions and revolt from nature.

I omit other passages which are found everywhere. However, just as the character of human nature was in *Cicero’s* age, so it was also in the time of *Socrates*. Therefore, that Best of Men could not promise divine help to relieve the impotence of nature and break the hardness of the heart. Revelation is needed to prove that God...

...by some help granted from heaven, He will aid those who love uprightness. I know that those who hope to attain happiness under the sole guidance of reason reject divine help of this kind, and assert that a heavenly inspiration of this sort into the minds of men cannot even be conceived. But it is necessary for such men to prove that such an inspiration—which theologians are accustomed to call the **grace of God**—is absolutely impossible, which I believe they will never accomplish. Why do they themselves concede that God not only created the entire Universe, but also still preserves it? Do they see the operation of God better in a plant or in animals than in a creature endowed with reason? Should we deny that God can do this simply because we are ignorant of the manner of this operation? How many most obvious things would have to be denied if this method of reasoning were valid! Truly, Socrates himself would be able to refute them in this regard. In Xenophon's *Memorabilia*, Book IV, page 505, he proves that God cares for all things, the greatest and the smallest, even though His operation is invisible. <term>Furthermore</term> <note>original: ἀλλὰ μὴν</note>, he continues: <term>Indeed, the soul of man, if anything else human does, participates in the divine nature. For it is manifest that it rules in us, yet it is seen not at all. Which when someone considers, he ought not to neglect invisible things, but from those things which happen, their power being known, let us honor the Gods with respect.* In Book I, page 453, Socrates asks Aristodemus whether he thinks the most elegant order of the universe arose from a cause lacking intelligence. *Aristodemus* replies: <term>By Zeus, no! For I do not see the masters, just as I see the craftsmen of the things produced here. For you do not even see your own soul, which is the master of the body; so that according to this, it is permitted for you to say that you do everything not by judgment, but by chance.</term> <note>original Greek: Μὰ Δί’ οὐ γὰρ ὁρῶ... ἀλλά τύχῃ πάντα πράττεῖς.</note> *I think so indeed, by Hercules. For I do not see those who order these things, as I see those who manufacture the things that are made in this world. Nor do you see your own soul, which rules in the body, so that according to this you may say that you do all things not by reason, but by chance.* In the *Theaetetus*, page 120, Socrates says: <term>There are the uninitiated, who think nothing else exists except what they can grasp tightly with their hands. Anything invisible they do not accept as being part of existence.</term> <note>original Greek: εἰσι δὲ οἱ ἀμύητοι... ὡς ἐν οὐσίας μέρει.</note> They are profane, who think nothing else exists but what they can hold in their fist—whatever is truly invisible, they by no means count among the number of things that exist. So speaks Socrates, a man most skilled in the art of reasoning. Since, therefore, Revelation not only promises such divine help for pursuing virtue and attaining happiness, but also exhibits it in its very operation, everyone can see that it excels the philosophy of Socrates in many ways, which could never promise such things...

...such things. Moreover, no one who reads the Revelation—no matter which sect of disagreeing Christians they may follow—can deny that *Christ Himself* promised such help to upright men, and indeed granted it in his very work. Our most Holy and most Benign Savior promises that He will grant greater light to those eager for the truth, that He will confirm the fleeting and changeable efforts of upright men, that He will teach every truth necessary to be known, protect them kindly, strengthen the weak but simple and sincere, hear the prayers of the afflicted, not frustrate their hope and trust in the least, provide comfort to the distressed, and indeed bring it about that in the end **all things yield to the salvation of the pious**. All these things He also fulfilled in His very work, so much so that a total <term>transformation</term> <note>original Greek: καταστροφῇ (katastrophē), here meaning a final resolution or great turning point in affairs</note> of things arose, concerning which we speak below. If, therefore, we collect everything we have said about the doctrine of Christ into a sum, it will be clear that the Christian religion excels the philosophy of Socrates as much as possible. (*)

**XI.** Let us now compare Socrates himself with our divine Savior and His disciples, and in this part of the comparison also, the singular excellence of the Christian religion will shine forth. We confess above all that Socrates was a man of the most eminent virtues. We confess that, by the consensus of almost all learned men and the judgment of all Greece (to make Cicero's words my own), he was easily the foremost of all in prudence, sharpness, charm, and subtlety, as well as in eloquence, variety, and abundance, in whatever direction he turned himself. We shall, therefore, detract nothing from his praises. Indeed, we believe it was not done without Divine Will that Socrates, amid the most corrupt morals of the Athenians, set aside more abstruse contemplations and commended above all the study of virtue. Let us even concede that what he wrote of himself in the *Apology* in Plato, page 12, is true: <term>For I go about doing nothing else but persuading you, both younger and older, not to care for your bodies or your money first, nor for anything else so strongly as for your soul, so that it might be as excellent as possible; saying that virtue does not come from money, but money and all other goods for men, both privately and publicly, come from virtue.</term> <note>original Greek: οὐδὲν γὰρ ἄλλο πράττων... καὶ ἰδίᾳ καὶ δημοσίᾳ.</note> Meanwhile, I cannot deny that some seem to me to have run beyond measure in their praises of Socrates. *Marsilio Ficino* said he was a precursor (**) of Christ; and that saying of *Erasmus* in the "Sober Feast" is well known: *I can scarcely restrain myself from saying: [Saint Socrates, pray for us].*

# MEDITATION ON THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION COMPARED
### WITH THE PHILOSOPHY OF SOCRATES

<page-num>584</page-num>

I might even say: *“Oh Holy Socrates, pray for us.”* <note>original Latin: "O Sancte Socrates ora pro nobis." This famous phrase is often attributed to the humanist Erasmus, expressing deep respect for Socrates' Christ-like morality.</note> Tanneguy Le Fèvre, in his *Life of Aristippus*—which he translated from the Greek of Diogenes Laertius into French and illustrated with certain notes—adds the following after mentioning that *Socrates did not accept money for his teaching*:

> “This is exactly what Jesus Christ said to his dear Friends: <term>freely you have received, freely give</term> <note>original Greek: δωρεαν ελαβετε, δωρεαν δοτε; see Matthew 10:8</note>. Thus, there has never been a man—I mean a man who is simply a man—who so closely resembled Jesus Christ as Socrates.”

I do not wish to repeat the excessive praises of others. However, learned men primarily point to the **Delphic Oracle**, by whose decree Socrates was called the wisest of all men. They point to his <term>Genius</term> <note>From the Greek "daimonion," a personal guiding spirit or inner voice that Socrates claimed warned him against making mistakes.</note> granted to him by divine favor as a perpetual companion of his life, from which it appears that he was raised above the common human lot. Finally, they add that Socrates underwent death for the glory of the **One God** with a most constant soul and a serene countenance. 

However, these matters must be investigated a little more precisely before that comparison can be properly established. First, regarding the decree of the Oracle, it is highly doubtful whether the <term>Pythia</term> <note>The high priestess of the Temple of Apollo at Delphi who delivered the oracles.</note> actually pronounced this. We are now better instructed concerning the reliability of Oracles than to attribute anything to the divine counsel of God. These Oracles were merely the fraudulent mouths of priests; nothing more should be sought there. Socrates himself asserts in his *Apology* that his friend Chaerephon (who was already dead at that time) heard this decree from the Pythia. Yet, if we weigh the character of those priests, it is hardly credible that such a testimony was offered to Socrates. Such priests are usually less inclined to favor those who depart even a fingernail's breadth from the publicly accepted Religion and who excel in moral integrity. 

Therefore, the opinion of the most noble François de La Mothe Le Vayer does not seem likely to me; he thinks the Oracle granted this praise to Socrates because he better cultivated the doctrine of morals and inflamed everyone with the study of virtue. I would rather believe that the priests, perceiving his incredible strength of mind, praised him because they saw that he did not at all despise the Oracles themselves, nor did he interfere with the Athenians clinging to their publicly accepted worship. But there is no need for conjectures when the reliability of the narrative itself can be rightly doubted. This last point was elegantly shown by the man of most polished erudition, Christoph August Heumann, in his *Philosophical Acts, Volume 3*. Whatever the case, we do not deny that Socrates was a man most wise for his time; even without the response of an Oracle, everyone who has weighed the thoughts of that Great Man will admit this (for we care nothing for the futile rhetorical flourishes of Lactantius). 

Secondly, I do not intend to bring forth many things regarding his *Genius*. The distinguished theologian Gottfried Olearius, <term>now among the saints</term> <note>original Greek: ὁ νυν ἐν ἁγιoις; a respectful way of saying he has passed away.</note>, examined this matter learnedly in his erudite...

<page-num>585</page-num>

...dissertation written about the *Genius of Socrates*. I shall only report the opinion of those who think that a good <term>Spirit</term> <note>Latin: Daemon / Greek: Daimonion</note> was granted to Socrates from heaven, so that our comparison might become more illustrious. Maximus of Tyre, at the beginning of his 26th dissertation, speaks thus:

> *“Do you wonder that a divine spirit attended Socrates—a friend and a foreteller of the future, a constant companion of his life and a guest of his mind? A man who was most pure in body, best in soul, most perfect in his way of living, most sweet in speaking: who walked piously with God and holily with men.”*

Maximus maintains that this Spirit was a certain substance intermediate between Gods and men. As for the benefit this divine companion brought to Socrates, Maximus describes it thus: 

> “If indeed a man—who is of a most noble nature and appropriately tempered by education, always devoted to true wisdom, and not lacking the help of fortune—should obtain this from the Immortal God: to be held worthy of the company of this Spirit of whom we speak; will it seem strange or unworthy of belief that he was able to foresee the future as much as was sufficient for him? This was not so that he might give Oracles to the Athenians deliberating on the evils of Greece, or to the Spartans consulting on an expedition, or if someone about to compete in the Olympic games or in a trial should ask about Victory, or a greedy man about riches... For these are small matters for which men daily weary the Gods. It is not that the God of Socrates was perhaps ignorant of these things, since he was not ignorant of future events... But Socrates obtained this from the conversation of this God, whom he contemplated with his mind, above all others: that he might first establish his own life honorably as the companion of such a great Divinity; and then, whenever necessity required, he might offer himself to others without envy.”

And after a few intervening words:

> *“That Spirit of Socrates was simple, private, and common: which, when Socrates thought to cross a river, used to call him back; or when he set out to love Alcibiades <note>A prominent and controversial Athenian statesman and general who was a student of Socrates.</note>, it persuaded him to delay; or when he prepared a defense, it did not permit it; or when he decided to die, it did not struggle against him.”*

Afterward, Maximus maintains that a genius of this kind is granted to all who excel in Virtue. 

> “These are they,” he says, “whom a divine nature assists, whose lives it promotes, whom it protects and defends with its own hand. For it saves some by omens, others by auguries, these by dreams, those by warnings, and others by sacrifices. For it cannot be that the human mind, such is its weakness, should...”

<page-num>586</page-num>

*...especially since this second life, in the thickest darkness, and amidst the great and constant tumult and noise of all present evils, must necessarily be disturbed by them, yet it achieves all things by the power of reason. Finally, at the end of this dissertation, Maximus <note>Maximus of Tyre, a second-century Platonic philosopher known for his lectures on Socrates.</note> speaks thus: "Great is their number."*

> For thrice there are a thousand through the earth's most fertile kingdoms,
> An immortal race, the servants of Jove. <note>original: *Ter sunt mille etenim...* This is a Latin translation of Hesiod’s *Works and Days*. While the Latin here says "thrice a thousand" (3,000), Hesiod's original Greek usually specifies "thrice ten thousand" (30,000) guardian spirits.</note>

*Some of these heal diseases, others give counsel in doubtful matters, others announce hidden things, others assist in the practice of the arts; others again are Companions. Some are of the city, others of the countryside; some are of the sea, others of the land. Each in turn inhabits a different body. This one dwells in Socrates, that one in Plato, that one in Pythagoras, another in Zeno, another in Diogenes: for me, as many as there are human dispositions, so many are the kinds of Spirits.*

> For like gods, often in the likeness of foreign settlers,
> Having put on any body, they traverse the lands. <note>original: *Namque Dei similes...* This is a Latin translation of a passage from Homer’s *Odyssey* (17.485), describing gods wandering the earth in disguise to observe human behavior.</note>

But truly, if you show me an impious soul, know that it has neither an Inhabitant nor a protector of its life. Thus far *Maximus*. I will not inquire into those things which *Maximus* tells of the various kinds of Angels; one may compare on this matter the notes of that most eminent man, *Jean Le Clerc*, on *Genesis 18* and Section VII of his dissertation on *the destruction of Sodom*, likewise the great *Hugo Grotius* on *Matthew 18:10*. Nor will I call into doubt what *Maximus* relates concerning the *Genius of Socrates*. I had once believed that Socrates—who thought that men of superior talent were born by a certain <term>divine allotment</term> <note>original Greek: θείᾳ μοίρᾳ (*theia moira*); the idea that excellence is a gift from the gods rather than purely learned.</note>—had concluded, from the singular sharpness of his intellect and his zeal for virtue, and even from his mind's fitness for enduring anything, that all these things had happened to him not without the care of the Divine and the guardianship of a Spirit. I believed others were also easily led to that opinion because they saw that, even with all their effort, they remained far below the virtues of this Great Man. I was confirmed in that opinion because I knew a certain famous man of great authority who, near the final days of his life, most firmly believed that all his success in business was to be ascribed not to his talent, the favor of others, or his own authority, but to a certain familiar Angel. But I will set aside this conjecture, and I will suppose, for the sake of those who—not without cause—esteem Socrates highly, that a certain good Spirit, a Companion of his life, happened to this Great Man. The most eminent *Jean Le Clerc* also conceded to this opinion in his *Philological Forest*, chapter 3.

### XII.
But even if we concede all these things, the supreme excellence of the Christian religion will nevertheless be evident from a comparison between Christ and the Apostles.

<column-break/>

<page-num>587</page-num>
<header>WITH THE PHILOSOPHY OF SOCRATES.</header>
<sig>Eeee 2</sig>

First, for *Maximus* himself concedes that such a Genius was granted not only to *Socrates*, but to all outstanding men, for example to *Plato*, *Zeno*, and others. But that *Plato* and that *Zeno*, notwithstanding that perpetual companionship of a Spirit, wandered miserably in error in many things, produced strange monsters of the intellect, and were merely "animals of glory" <note>A common Latin expression (*animalia gloriae*) for those motivated by vanity or the pursuit of fame rather than truth.</note>, nor did they apply their minds to the moral improvement of the human race. Second: the duties of that Spirit of Socrates were those which *Socrates* could have performed by the help of his own talent, with few exceptions—which nevertheless were not of such importance that a Spirit should be granted from heaven. For instance, it does not permit him to cross a river, it bids him to delay his love for *Alcibiades*, and so on. *Plutarch, in "On the Genius of Socrates," page 831*, introduces *Theocritus* speaking thus: 

"But as for the Genius of Socrates, my friend, shall we consider it a fable? To me, just as Homer makes Minerva present to help Ulysses in all his hardships, so the Genius of Socrates seems to have joined to him from the very beginning a certain vision of life to go before him; this vision, preceding Socrates, brought light to obscure matters and those not penetrable by human reason. Just as the Genius often spoke to him, directing the purposes of his mind by a certain divine instinct. Most of these and the most significant instances one may learn from Simmias and other companions of Socrates. While I was present, when I was going to the seer Eutyphron, Socrates—as you remember, Simmias—was walking up toward the Symbol and the house of Andocides, while simultaneously questioning Eutyphron. Suddenly, however, he stopped, and persuading the others to stand still as well, he stayed there for a long time. Then, turning around, he went away through the street of the cabinet-makers, and called back his companions who had gone ahead, indicating that he had been warned by his Genius to turn aside this way. And most of them indeed turned back with him, among whom I myself stayed close to my Eutyphron. But certain young men, proceeding straight ahead—doubtless to refute the Genius of Socrates—took with them Charillus the flute-player, who had himself come with me to Athens to see Cebes. When they were walking through the street of the Sculptors near the law courts, a herd of swine covered in mud met them. Because of the great number of the pigs, and since there was no space for the men to step aside, they knocked some down by their charge and stained others with filth." *Charillus* even came home with his legs and clothes full of mud, so that they laughed when they wanted to mention the Genius of *Socrates*, which never leaves a man and never neglects him. Thus far *Plutarch*. Now, whether this matter was of such great importance that that Spirit should intercede here, anyone can easily see. But whatever the truth of this may be, it is certain that the Genius of Socrates did nothing that could contribute anything to the improvement of the human race, so that I cannot think so highly of this Spirit. For why did it not drive Socrates toward his preconceived notions about the Gods...

Why did He [God] not strike **Aristophanes**, <note>A famous Athenian comic playwright who lampooned Socrates in his play *The Clouds*, contributing to the public's negative perception of the philosopher.</note> that notorious scoundrel, with some disease during the very performance of a comedy, so that everyone might clearly perceive that **Socrates** enjoyed a closer communication with the Deity? Or what benefit, after all, flowed to the human race from that constant companionship of his Spirit-Guide? Was it finally brought about through him that the most pestilential superstition, which had invaded all minds like a wasting disease, either vanished entirely or spread less widely? Were his disciples not only persuaded of the divine mission of **Socrates** by this very thing, but also moved to subvert superstition?

Thirdly. If we compare **Christ** and the **Apostles** in this regard, we shall hear of far more excellent things. **Christ** our Savior was not born without a miracle; he was born by the will of God, born in such a way that his marvelous coming was announced long before, not by some deceptive Oracle, but by divine Revelation. God Himself performed stupendous miracles to signify this illustrious coming, such as the appearance and path of an unusual star, the arrival of the **Magi** <note>The "Wise Men" from the East.</note> stirred up for that purpose, and so on. He was born of a Virgin in a manner inexplicable to us humble mortals, yet by no means impossible. Indeed, either the entire narrative concerning **Christ** is utterly false, or that coming was not without the Divine Will. Here, no oracles of doubtful faith have any place; for the most bitter enemies of Christ themselves, the **Jews**, could not undermine the force of these predictions. 

But we do not wish to dwell on this argument. **Socrates** had a "genius," <note>original: *genium*. Referring again to his *daemon* or guiding spirit.</note> a perpetual companion of his life and a silent monitor. **Christ** was the eternal Wisdom of God, the *Word* <note>original: *ὁ λογος* (ho logos). The author contrasts the philosophical "Logos" of Plato with the divine "Word" of the Gospel of John.</note>—not that fictitious one of **Plato**, but the eternal one, more excellent than the Angels themselves, indeed, God Himself. But it is not necessary for us to assume that most solemn truth in this comparison. It is enough that **Christ** was furnished with a singular and most perfect Wisdom, which not even his enemies could deny. He had no need of a "genius" of that sort. For He Himself knew the innermost and most hidden thoughts of men; He was not ignorant of many things; He was driven to act by no depraved affections; being free from every stain and crime, He could appeal to the

Fourthly. Since even the most excellent precepts and examples are little valued by those who are not lovers of truth; and since there are very few who know the true value of things and attend to the warnings of the most excellent men—impeded as they are either by stupidity or depraved interests—our Savior performed very many miracles in the midst of the crowd, in the presence not only of friends but also of enemies; and thus men were compelled, even against their will, to confess that He was sent from heaven to amend the human race. No one is ignorant, however, that miracles—real miracles, I mean—cannot be performed by men alone. I will not ask now whether they can be performed by substances inferior to God, which is the opinion of many most learned men; it is enough that these very men confess they cannot happen without the will of the Deity, and that they cannot be permitted by God except to confirm truth and piety. 

Therefore, even if I were to grant most fully that God permits miracles to be performed by the help of angels, it is nevertheless clear that **Christ** far surpassed **Socrates**. The **Later Platonists, Iamblichus, and Porphyry** <note>Neoplatonist philosophers who sought to revive pagan spirituality in the face of rising Christianity.</note> ascribe many miracles to **Pythagoras**; if we believe **Philostratus**, **Apollonius** <note>Apollonius of Tyana, a 1st-century pagan philosopher and wonder-worker often compared to Jesus by anti-Christian writers.</note> also performed many. If that spirit-guide was granted by divine power, it nevertheless could not lead the Athenians to be firmly persuaded of this matter; anyone can claim some private spirit for himself, and whether that is true or false is not only difficult for others to see and know, but those very people who boast of such things, if they examine everything more subtly, are forced to take refuge in a *suspension of judgment*. <note>original: *εποχην* (epoche). A skeptical term for the state of mind where one neither denies nor affirms a claim.</note> It is especially difficult for the common people—whose interests God wishes to consult as much as possible through such unusual things—to conduct an accurate examination. Hence it happened that even the ancients themselves disputed among themselves about this Demon.

...against the Pharisees, who raised a scruple; yet they themselves, when they ascribed these miracles to some malignant Demon, not only betrayed an impudent boldness, but by this very detestable calumny confessed that the miracles of Christ were greater than human power and not fashioned by art. I know that *Spinoza* asserts that miracles cannot happen because they are against the laws of nature—that is, in Spinoza's mind, they would be against God Himself or the world existing by the necessity of nature. But that <term>shuffler<note>original: *Tenebrio*—literally a 'darkling' or someone who works in shadows; a pejorative term for a person who avoids the light of truth, here applied to Baruch Spinoza.</note></term> could not demonstrate that the laws which Philosophers call "natural" are absolutely necessary, such that another order of the world, or other laws regarding the motion of the Planets, etc., could not exist. But if those laws are arbitrary—though established most wisely—what prevents God from acting against them at some time, especially if we see by the work itself that God had the weightiest reasons for changing them? If, by a divine lot, a **Genius** <note>The author uses the Latin *Genius* to refer to the *daemonion*, the private "divine sign" or voice that Socrates claimed warned him against certain actions.</note> was granted to *Socrates* contrary to the usual order, even if only for the purpose of having him abstain from certain harmful things, is it not even more worthy of God to use unusual methods to uproot Idolatry and establish the purest worship among men hedged in by foul darkness? Indeed, it was necessary for God to act in this way, and no other. A prudent and Wise man, if he cannot achieve the most excellent goal he intends by a well-trodden path, is moved by a certain noble impulse to seek a path hitherto unusual, and leaves nothing untried to obtain his most praiseworthy purpose. God, without doubt the Wisest, after He had achieved nothing among the gentiles through the precepts provided by reason, not only declared His will by an extraordinary means but also added stupendous miracles, most fit for confirming a most excellent doctrine. He who did not have faith in these miracles *ought to be numbered among the portents*. But why should I prove with many words that Christ surpassed *Socrates* in so many ways? The *disciples of Christ* themselves—men cultivated in no disciplines, ignorant of Philosophical subtleties, fishermen, enduring life by the work of their hands—excel *Socrates* in many ways; not indeed in the clarity and sharpness of their wit, but in the abundance of gifts bestowed from heaven, in miracles, and in the innocence of their lives, which excels all academic learning. Before they had given their name to Christ and committed themselves entirely to be shaped by his discipline, they were not at all distinct from the rest of the crowd of men; but as soon as they handed themselves over to his divine discipline, they were totally changed. In the beginning, they did err in certain matters, not yet being capable of understanding the heavenly doctrine in all things. They did not boast that they were instructed by some "Genius"; but they were equipped with the power of performing miracles, which struck the eyes of men more vehemently than some

<column-break/>

<page-num>591</page-num>

unknown companion spirit could, or the most accurate method of reasoning, which cannot be properly weighed by the common people. Furthermore, in place of a "Genius," they were <note>original: *pheromenoi hypo pneumatos hagiou* (Greek: Φερομενοι ὑπο πνευματος ἁγιου)</note> "carried along by the Holy Spirit," whose operations, though we may understand them with difficulty, we nevertheless cannot deny. The force of this divine Operation exerted itself especially when they were suddenly adorned with an unusual faculty of understanding and speaking languages which they had never learned, to the astonishment of all. Good God! into what admiration the Athenians would have been swept if *Socrates*, besides the probity of his life, had been equipped with miracles and had demonstrated by the work itself for what purpose God had granted him such a Demon? By the help of these miracles, however, those disciples propagated that heavenly doctrine with the greatest success, and they recalled the Idolaters no less than others wandering from the true and pure worship of God. That *Divine Spirit* which they received did not only restrain them from seeking certain places, but exhorted them to undertake the most difficult Journeys here and there. Moved *by this impulse*, they attempted, suffered, and executed everything for the propagation of the Christian Religion, even despising the most violent and exquisite pains. Nevertheless, Divine Providence also watched over their endeavors so that, fortified by the protection of angels, they were delivered from the most present dangers of life. Compare, therefore—to say nothing further of doctrine—the *Genius of Socrates and its operations* with the miracles of the Apostles, the gifts of tongues, and the protection of God which they enjoyed; and either I am vehemently mistaken, or it will be most clearly established that Socrates, otherwise a great man, is far inferior to the Apostles.

XIII. But there are still other things that prove this very point. For first, *Socrates could not speak as a Legislator* [Lawgiver] whose precepts had the power of binding. He reasoned about the excellence of the virtues and recommended them to the Athenians; he even proved their utility and honesty. But he could not show that the Athenians were bound by these precepts. The decrees of other Philosophers stood in the way, to which the Athenians granted much weight; their reasonings had no less weight than those of Socrates. None of them could persuade men by his own *authority* that he was sent from heaven to amend mankind, and that the laws he recommended should be considered as divine. It is true that most of the precepts of *Socrates* were most equitable and agreeable to reason, and thus far all who perceived their force were bound to compose their manners according to them; but since *Authority* consists not only in enjoining those precepts, but in presenting them as the will of the Deity from heaven...

the power of commanding, was lacking in *Socrates*, nor could he, by his own authority, promise rewards and inflict punishments; thus, much of the strength and excellence of his precepts was lost. To this is also added the opinion of *Socrates* regarding virtue. He asserted, as is well known, that virtue could not be taught, but that the seeds of virtue were implanted in the minds of men by a certain <term>divine lot<note>original: *theia moira*—a Greek phrase meaning a divine portion or dispensation, implying that virtue is a gift from the gods rather than a learned skill.</note></term>, which are nevertheless granted by the Gods to only a very few. *Protagoras*, however, the famous <term>Sophist<note>A class of professional teachers in ancient Greece who were often criticized by Socrates and Plato for prioritizing rhetoric and winning arguments over absolute truth.</note></term> who lived in Athens during the time of *Socrates*, taught the opposite, as is clear from *Plato's* dialogue which bears the name of *Protagoras*. In it, he openly says: "The Athenians thought that virtue was not implanted by nature, nor by spontaneity, but could be taught, and was acquired by care by those who possessed it." <note>original: ὅτι ἀρετὴν οὐ φύσει ἡγοῦνται εἶναι, οὐδὲ ἀπὸ τοῦ αὐτομάτου, ἀλλὰ διδακτόν τε καὶ ἐξ ἐπιμελείας παραγίγνεσθαι, ᾧ ἂν παραγίγνηται.</note> I shall not ask whether this opinion agrees with the views of other Philosophers or not. The famous <term>Jean Le Clerc<note>original: *Cl. Clericus*—referring to the influential 17th-century Swiss theologian and scholar known for his work in biblical criticism and philology.</note></term> discusses this in his *Philological Woods*, page 166. It is enough that the same eminent man confesses that to many who read the thoughts of *Protagoras*, it will seem that *Protagoras* reasons better than *Socrates*. It is clear at least from this that either *Socrates* departed from the common and received opinion, or at least spoke in such a way that others thought he felt far differently than the rest of the Athenians. And in this way, *Socrates*, even if unwillingly, brought it about that those who were already immersed in vices might take some protection from his view; for such men hear nothing more gladly than those things which can prove the extreme difficulty of cultivating virtue. For they think it can then be necessarily inferred that it is not situated in their own power to follow virtue. At the very least, it is certain that the common people of Athens could not resolve that dispute between *Socrates* and *Protagoras*. And yet the matter was of no small importance: *Protagoras* could offer the appearance of an upright man and a lover of virtue by this assertion, while *Socrates* appeared as a Sophist, ready to tear down anything. Furthermore, the morals of the Athenians were most depraved, and nothing was more necessary than that the opinions which were adverse to the study of virtue should be removed from their minds, and instead, a certain supreme desire for seeking virtue should be injected. This, however, is obtained among other things if it is shown that the precepts of reason, when rightly weighed, are *easy to observe*. But the opinion of *Socrates*, at least in appearance, put a brake on the study of virtue. *Socrates* did not indeed deny, as is clear from *Xenophon*, that education and instruction contribute something to the study of virtue; but he who has once loved vices rather believes those things which conspire with the desires of the mind than those things which are said. If, however, *Socrates* had studied the reform of the human race—

—emendation, he should have sought to promote it as much as was in his power, and he ought to have avoided everything that could give any protection to errors and vices. Secondly, *Socrates*, *if we are willing to admit the truth*, did not suffer death for the confession of the *one Ruler of the World*. Most people think highly of *Socrates* for this reason and extol him to the heavens with praises because he met death with a most constant mind, and indeed for the love of the Deity. But he who reads the counts of the accusation and the defense of *Socrates* itself attentively will observe that this was by no means the cause of his death. We have already observed in the previous sections that *Socrates* not only did not reject the publicly accepted worship, but even asserted it should be followed. From the *Apology* which is read in *Plato*, it is clear that there were two kinds of accusers against him: the *first* accused him of curiously prying into what is in the heavens and under the earth, and that by reasoning he made the worse cause seem the better. Among these, *Aristophanes* seems to be counted, the main points of whose accusation come down to this. The *later* accusers said he corrupted the youth and introduced new Gods. We shall not dwell on the former, but we shall examine what *Socrates* replied to the latter. Plato, in the *Apology*, records his defense, which is nevertheless so equivocal that it is clear enough he did not wish to openly reveal what he felt: everything comes down to the point that he could not deny the Gods, since he worshipped <term>Daemons<note>original: *Dæmones*—in Greek philosophy, these were not evil spirits but intermediary divine beings or tutelary spirits. Socrates claimed to be guided by such a "divine sign."</note></term>. But why did that great Philosopher, who said the safety of the citizens was of such great concern to him, not <term>call a spade a spade<note>original: *Scapham Scapham appellavit*—literally "call a boat a boat," a Latin idiom for speaking plainly and directly.</note></term>? Why did he not confess that he acknowledged only One and Supreme Lord of the world, and was ready to suffer any extremity for this opinion? He does assert on page 12 of the *Apology* that he will exhort men to the study of virtue until the end of his life: "And as long as I breathe and am able, I shall not cease from philosophizing, and from exhorting and showing you, whomever of you I happen to meet, saying in my usual way: 'O best of men, since you are an Athenian, a citizen of the greatest city and most famous for wisdom and strength, are you not ashamed of devoting all your care to how you may have as much money and glory and honor as possible, while you neither think of nor care for prudence and truth and the best state of your soul?'" <note>original: Καὶ ἕως περ ἂν, ἐμπνέω καὶ οἷός τε ὦ, οὐ μὴ παύσωμαι φιλοσοφῶν. Καὶ ὑμῖν παρακελευόμενός τε καὶ ἐνδεικνύμενος: ὅτῳ ἂν ἀεὶ ἐντυγχάνω ὑμῶν, λέγων οἷάπερ εἴωθα. ὅτι ὦ ἄριστε ἀνδρῶν Ἀθηναῖος ὤν, πόλεως τῆς μεγίστης καὶ εὐδοκιμωτάτης εἰς σοφίαν καὶ ἰσχύν, χρημάτων μὲν οὐκ αἰσχύνῃ ἐπιμελόμενος, ὅπως σοι ἔσται ὡς πλεῖσα, καὶ δόξης καὶ τιμῆς, Φρονήσεως δὲ καὶ ἀληθείας, καὶ τῆς Ψυχῆς, ὅπως ὡς βελτίστη ἔσται, οὐκ ἐπιμελῇ, οὐδὲ Φροντίζεις &c.</note> But if such a great desire for propagating virtue was in him...

The reason for this was why he himself kept a deep silence here before the Judge regarding the worship of the One Deity, without which no virtue worthy of the name can exist. I know that many errors exist about which learned men dispute most sharply among themselves, which nevertheless usually bring no harm to salvation. But absurd opinions about God must be entirely uprooted from minds before a pure worship of God can be implanted in them. Yet *Xenophon* at the beginning of his *Memorabilia*, and *Plato* himself in his *Apology*, testify that *Socrates* by no means despised the Gods. *Jean Le Clerc* <note>original: *Joh. Clericus* — a prominent 17th-century theologian and scholar.</note> indeed attempts to defend him in this part to some extent, saying on page 205 of his *Philological Forest* <note>original: *Sylv. philolog.*</note>: "But I would truly think that *Socrates*, *Plato*, and other Philosophers, under the names of the Greek Gods—though they were dishonored by shameful fables—worshiped holy and eternal natures as they understood them, which were far more excellent than human ones, and to which they thought the name of God truly applied. Therefore, by the name of *Jupiter* in their discourses, one should understand **that Highest Deity** <note>original: *Summum illud Numen*</note>, of whom he speaks in the *Timaeus* (page 350) where he calls himself the Creator of the other Gods; but by the names of the remaining Gods, those who sprang from Him—that is, all the inferior Gods. The deities of the common people were nothing but the mere names of fictitious Gods, who neither were Gods (that is, better than human nature) nor had ever been; therefore the Philosophers thought they could use those same names to signify the invisible and everlasting minds which, as they believed, embraced all things with their providence, administered them wisely, and were benevolent toward the human race." Thus far speaks that most eminent man, *Le Clerc*.

But who does not see that this excuse is flimsy, and that the public worship of the Gods was thus reinforced? Nor do I see with what integrity *Socrates* could have used those names if he believed that worship belonged to God alone. If, however, he understood such inferior Deities by the name of 'Gods,' why did he not openly confess it? Why did he cry out that public worship must be retained by any means? Can it be said that he burned with a certain Zeal for the glory of God, he who plays with equivocations in the gravest of matters? But this is especially strange: that while in his *Apology* he spoke not as a defendant or a suppliant, but as the master and lord of his Judges—and thus by this method stirred up the minds of the Judges against himself—he nevertheless chose to keep a deep silence about those things which not even the most exquisite tortures could prevent a man who loves truth and virtue from bringing into the open. What shall I say about the cock which, when he was close to death, he ordered to be offered to *Aesculapius*? <note>Aesculapius (Asklepios) was the Greek god of healing. Socrates' last words were famously: "Crito, we owe a cock to Aesculapius; pay it and do not neglect it."</note> There are those who think that by this means he wished to mock the accepted worship. *Dacier* <note>André Dacier, a French classical scholar.</note> says thus on page 328 of his translation: **"Here the cock is the symbol of life. Aesculapius is the emblem of the Physician. Socrates means by this that he is returning his soul into the hands of the true Physi-"** <note>original: *Ici le coq est le Symbole de la vie. The most learned *Havercamp* <note>Sigebert Havercamp, a Dutch scholar.</note>, in his erudite *Observations on Tertullian’s Apology* (page 380), brings forward the image of an engraved gem which seems to represent *Socrates* sacrificing a cock upon an altar. The opinion of *Havercamp* concerning this sacrifice of *Socrates* is this: "Certainly," he says, "you know why he wished a cock to be sacrificed to him [Aesculapius], as one who had now recovered, being about to migrate from this frail and sickly life to a better one; punished in the estimation of his enemies, but finished by his own judgment—as is elegantly said of Theramenes by Valerius Maximus, Book 3, Chapter 2."

But even if we were to admit this most kind interpretation, I still do not see by what reasoning *Socrates* could be excused. He was at the threshold of death; only his friends were present. These men undoubtedly knew what he felt about the Gods; to what end, then, did he conceal the thoughts of his mind and speak obscurely? Do we believe that if the common people of Athens heard this command given by *Socrates* to his friends, they would have believed *Socrates* intended what those learned men claim? Would they not rather have believed that *Socrates* persisted in the accepted worship until the end of his life? Did it befit a Philosopher such as *Socrates* was to play games in a serious matter? How much better it would have been if, in prison, he had encouraged his friends with all the strength of arguments to offer worship to the one God, and never to allow themselves to be led away from defending this opinion!

The true cause of his condemnation, therefore, was not a constant confession of the unity of God. The famous *Le Clerc* honestly admits the cause of death in the place cited, page 217, saying: "He had offended the Athenians because he had quite often proven the ignorance of those who thought themselves most learned, and had rebuked the depraved morals of others, condemning them as much by words as by deeds. By his conversations, he had brought the youth to the point where they understood that many things had been established by their ancestors in the administration of the Republic with little wisdom, and that many things were being done wrongly at that time. Finally, he had shown that the poetic fables, upon which the ancient religions rested, were fatal to morality." Thus says *Le Clerc*. I will not say now that *Socrates*, in my opinion, acted very badly because he did not wish to defend himself, and refused to lend an ear to his friends when they urged him and showed him a way to escape. But these things must be examined in a special dissertation and vindicated against *Maximus of Tyre*.

XIV. However, the method of *Christ* and the *Apostles* was entirely different in this regard. *Christ* not only instilled laws most agreeable to reason and exhorted everyone to follow them; but as a Lawgiver, He set forth His own precepts and doctrine. **"But I say to you,"** He used to repeat to the *Jews* who were wrongly interpreting the sense of the divine oracles. Nay, He openly announced to everyone that God one day, when he had been appointed as judge—

the day of judgment was to come, when He would judge everyone according to the decree of the word He had proclaimed. He asserted that He was sent from heaven to save humanity. He appealed to a doctrine that was in harmony with divine oracles. He confirmed this doctrine with stupendous miracles. He spoke as a **Lawgiver**, who held the **Supreme Right** <note>original: *Jus Summum*</note> over all people because of the preeminence <note>original: *hyperochēn* (ὑπεροχὴν) — meaning excellence or superiority</note> of His infinite perfection, the Creation, and the undertaken Work of Redemption. He commanded the spirits themselves and showed that He was their Lord; and so that they might believe this more easily, He proved more than once that even the very thoughts of men were known to Him. He even publicly declared that He would suffer an ignominious death to acquire eternal happiness for mankind, but at the same time, He would emerge into the upper air by His own power. Moreover, He performed this very thing. 

Hence, by the highest right, He could exhort anyone to embrace His doctrine, subject all who despised His divine Decrees to damnation, and exercise the severest judgments upon the perverse. Now, what method more worthy of God can be devised for the correction of men? What could more vehemently stimulate mortals toward virtue than the presence of such a Lawgiver, who is able both to save and to destroy? Who will not yield to His Authority—He who flourishes in innocence of life and admirable doctrine, who confirms His words with miracles, and who commands the entire Universe of things; who seeks death for the benefit of the human race; and who, by His resurrection, displays the strongest argument of His divine mission, and finally demonstrates how much power He has over the minds of men and their actions by granting His most faithful companions gifts from heaven, and exercises His most immediate judgments upon His enemies? I call upon the conscience of all: is there not a greater power in **Him** to lead men away from perverse pursuits and to promote virtue than in a sharp-witted Philosopher who is merely conspicuous for his uprightness of character? 

Furthermore, by other arguments, our divine Savior demonstrated how much the Salvation of men was His concern. He not only exhorted everyone to the most chaste worship, most worthy of God, but He also burned with a zeal for the glory of God, which you would seek in vain in Socrates. To that end, He traveled here and there to win back those wandering from the path of truth. He demanded from men not only a character conformed to the laws of right reason, but also a sincerity, a most exact piety, spread through their whole being. For the nature of the divine Philosophy which He proclaimed—to make the words of **Desiderius Erasmus** <note>Erasmus of Rotterdam, the famous Renaissance humanist and theologian.</note> my own—is situated in the affections more truly than in Syllogisms; it is a life rather than a disputation, an inspiration rather than Erudition, and finally, a transformation rather than mere reason. From this, it happened that the Priests of Religion, in

in providing the principles of natural causes; but individually, they had either no care, or very little, for the improvement of the mind. So far were they from cultivating the study of virtue themselves—to which Socrates exhorted every individual—and recommending it to all, that this most noble part of **Philosophy** was all but entirely neglected. Plato and Aristotle spoke so obscurely about the supreme Lord of all things that we can only with difficulty grasp their meaning. This same Plato did not think at all that the publicly received worship should be changed. In the *Epinomis* <note>A dialogue traditionally attributed to Plato or his student Philip of Opus, discussing the path to wisdom and the nature of the cosmos.</note> he openly professes this: 

*The legislator of all these things <note>original Greek: "τουτων παντων ὁ νομοθετης..."</note>, whoever possesses even the slightest mind, will never dare to innovate regarding the worship of God, which does not have a clear path, nor turn his city toward it; nor will he prevent those things which the ancestral law has dictated concerning sacrifices, knowing nothing at all about them, just as it is not possible for mortal nature to know anything certain about such things.* 

That is to say: *The Legislator of all these things, who has even the least bit of mind, will never innovate anything. For he will take care not to turn his city toward a new, less certain religious cult. Nor will he dare to move those things which have been established by ancestral law or custom regarding the practice of sacrifice. For he ought to know that it is not possible for mortal nature to know anything certain about these matters.* 

In Aristippus <note>A pupil of Socrates and founder of the Cyrenaic school, which focused on pleasure as the highest good.</note>, the traces of those truths that are the most momentous of all have vanished. Not one of them burned with any Zeal for the glory of God; instead, they either gaped after pleasures or devoted their leisure to literature for the sake of delight. Furthermore, they shamefully neglected those things which could work toward the improvement of the human race. Hence, Socrates himself distrusted his own disciples and the propagation of his doctrine. Hear him speaking thus before his Judges in the *Apology* found in Plato, page 12:

*For if you kill me, you will not easily find another such as I <note>original Greek: "Ἐαν γαρ με ἀποκτεινητε..."</note>, even if it is a somewhat ridiculous thing to say—one attached to the city by God, just as to a horse, great and noble indeed, but due to its size rather sluggish and needing to be stirred up by some gadfly <note>term: "gadfly" (mūops/μύωψ) — Socrates famously used this analogy to describe his role in irritating the "sleepy" state of Athens into thinking critically.</note>. Such a one God seems to have added me to the city to be, who, awakening and persuading and reproaching each one of you, does not cease to sit near you all day long everywhere. Another such will not easily arise for you.* 

That is to say: *For if you kill me, you will find no other such person, truly—even if perhaps that saying is ridiculous—provided to your city by God, like a certain great and noble horse, but sluggish by its very bulk, and needing to be excited by some gadfly: such a one as God seems to have added to the city, who, awakening and advising and rebuking individuals, does not cease to assist you the whole day. You will not easily find another such, O Men of Athens.* It is true that the Athenians soon regretted killing such a man; it is also true that certain people paid the penalties for that reason.

Plutarch, in *On Envy and Hatred*, page 556, says: *Those whose slander oppressed Socrates were so hated by the Citizens as extremely evil, and so shunned, that they would neither light a fire for them, nor answer their questions, nor use the same water in the bath, but would order the servants to pour out the water they had washed in as if it were polluted—until those men, unable to endure the hatred, hanged themselves.* 

So says *Plutarch*, a most serious author. But neither he nor others testify that the Athenians adopted different morals or received a worship more worthy of God. In a word, the doctrine of Socrates had no greater power over the minds of men than any other method of philosophizing. Certainly, as far as history stands, the Athenians by no means rejected superstition. The disciples and followers of Socrates philosophized, each according to his own natural disposition, and miserably wasted their time in empty disputes. No one—no one, I say—exhorted the others to offer a pure worship to God; no one was willing to meet death for the glory of the **one** God. Most were flatterers, soft and argumentative, seekers of worldly glory. 

Now, who would believe that other men would devote themselves to virtue, bid farewell to depraved pursuits, and change their minds under *such* leaders? Who could expect hope for better times from the Priests <note>original: *Sacrificulis* — literally "petty sacrificers," used here dismissively of pagan priests.</note>, men who were as ignorant of divine matters as they were addicted to the most pestilential Superstition? Hence, a most foul Superstition flooded the world, and all things were verging toward ruin, until Divine Goodness brought a remedy to the human race through a certain extraordinary aid.

XVI. Our Savior Himself performed this. For He not only lived a most holy life, most worthy of God, and not only showed His power through miracles and the force He exerted on the minds of men; but He also predicted that neither the gates of hell, nor the violence of Tyrants, nor the heat of torments would prevail against the progress of the most Holy Religion. With this hope, He lifted the fearful and anxious minds of His disciples regarding the future, and promised an infinite reward for constancy. They, although they were timid at the start—one even being the betrayer of the best Master, another shamefully falling by trusting his own strength more than was right—nevertheless, with one single exception, came together as one, defending the discipline handed down by the Master with a brave heart. Nor did they allow themselves to be dragged away from defending the most holy Religion by any force of threats or persecutions. That very Peter, who a few days before had shamefully deserted the Master for fear of death, when called before the **Sanhedrin** <note>original: *Synedrium* — the supreme council or court of the Jewish people.</note> of the Jews, said to those high priests to their faces: *This very Jesus, whom you fixed to a cross, has been called back from death, and of this matter we are witnesses.* Moreover, all were [strengthened] by the gift of miracles...

# MEDITATION ON THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION COMPARED
