...and gifted from heaven with the knowledge of languages, they traveled everywhere. Driven by a noble impulse, amidst a thousand labors and persecutions, and with no regard for glory or profit, they invited all to embrace the Divine Religion. This doctrine held such power over the souls of men that the old and the young, the learned and the unlearned, and people of both sexes rushed eagerly to profess and defend it, establishing a life most worthy of God and of reason. Neither preconceived opinions—swallowed, as it were, with their mother’s milk—nor the tears of their dearest loved ones, nor the comforts of this life, nor even exile could stop them from protecting that Religion; indeed, what is more, not even the most **exquisite tortures** <note>In this context, "exquisite" refers to carefully designed or intense pains.</note> could terrify them. From this, they hurried toward martyrdom with a serene brow and an undaunted spirit, and sometimes even more quickly than necessity itself demanded. 

I know that some will say that superstition also contributed much to this; they will appeal to the arguments brought forward by the most learned *Dodwell* <note>Henry Dodwell (1641–1711), a scholar who questioned the traditional number and motives of early Christian martyrs.</note> in his dissertation on the *Causes of Martyrdom*. I will concede, if they wish, that some were carried away either by stubbornness or an excessive desire for martyrdom and suffered death with such an intrepid spirit without sufficient reason; but human nature itself—which does not usually stir up intense pains for itself without cause—scarcely allows us to believe that all, or even most, reached such a level of constancy moved by these reasons alone. Human nature was the same then as it is now. We flee from those things that tend to cause pain, especially if no benefit is attached. Ecclesiastical history teaches us well enough that many, in the heat of persecution, either consulted their own safety by flight or spoke differently than what they held in their hearts. Most people are devoted to a Religion without deep reason in those places where they can live securely without fear of persecution; but it can hardly be believed that men would endure the most exquisite tortures, which they could easily avoid, without cause. 

*Lactantius* <note>An early Christian author (c. 250 – c. 325) often called the "Christian Cicero" for his eloquent Latin.</note> rightly says in *Book V, chapter XIII*: *If women fall away due to the weakness of their sex (for sometimes those critics call this a superstition of women and old crones), surely the men are wise. If children or youths are improvident because of their age, surely the mature and the old possess a stable judgment. If one city were foolish, surely the others, which are innumerable, cannot all be mad. If one province or one nation lacks foresight, all the others must necessarily have an understanding of what is right. Since the divine law has been accepted from the rising of the sun even to its setting, and every sex, every age, nation, and region serves God with one and the same spirit, and since there is the same patience everywhere and the same contempt for death, they ought to have understood that there is some reason in it, which is not defended even unto death without cause; that there is some*

*foundation and solidity, which does not merely prevent that religion from being dissolved by injuries and harassment, but increases it always and makes it firmer.* 

It is true that many of the Christians, and a great part of them, were simple and **uneducated** <note>original Greek: "απαιδευτες" (apaideutes)</note> men. But those men are often burdened by a smaller mass of preconceived opinions than the Learned. For the Learned are mostly captured by the empty **distortions** <note>original Greek: "στρεβλωσει" (streblosei) – referring to the "twisting" or "torturing" of logic in complex debates.</note> of disputes and, hedged in by various doubts, they seek a thousand cracks through which to slip away; nor do they burn with such zeal for the glory of God. Even *Erasmus*, a man otherwise great, confesses in his letters that his own temperament was unfit for achieving the glory of martyrdom. However, the objection of those men <note>referring to critics of the "unlearned" Christians</note> supposes that to obtain salvation and perceive the true nature of Religion, there is a need for some systematic knowledge of all those propositions about which the Learned dispute among themselves—which I do not believe at all.

The purging of the soul from evil affections, a solid persuasion of the divinity of the Christian Religion and its nature and character, the love of Christian virtues, and an ardent desire to please God and live in accordance with this Religion, accomplishes more than a knowledge of all the reasons and objections concerning specific chapters of Religion that are debated among the families of disagreeing Christians. These very things were rarer in the first and most ancient times than in our own century, in which almost no lifetime would suffice to learn, let alone examine, the controversies that have arisen little by little.

I am speaking, however, of the common people, not of the Teachers, who ought to be equipped with a greater knowledge of divine matters. But if you now add that the first Teachers of this heavenly truth were men who were not refined by any academic disciplines, unskilled in the art of reasoning correctly according to the laws of the philosophers, and fortified by no human authority or protection, it will become even more evident that the progress of this Religion was plainly admirable.

For if they had been men equipped with the greatest sharpness of wit, refined in various languages and disciplines, and adapted to the spirit of the age, those to whom this most Holy Religion is displeasing would have something to object to; they could say that such men could easily deceive the simple. But God, in His infinite Wisdom, chose others. *Ludovicus Vives* <note>Joannes Ludovicus Vives (1493–1540), a Spanish humanist and student of Erasmus.</note> speaks elegantly on this subject in *Book II, On the Truth of the Faith*:

> God (he says) sent very few to very many, the unrefined to the most expert. For the world was refined in wits and arts, if ever it was, so that no one could suspect a deception had been made or that men had been captured by a trick; He sent infants to the most eloquent and silver-tongued, He sent the simple to the crafty, the unarmed to the armed, the peaceful to the warlike, the poor to the empire of the Roman people. It was fitting that there be such humility in those first builders of this edifice, lest they themselves, by human strength...

To Jesus Christ our Savior, therefore, we owe the fact that the better part of the world possesses a religion most fitting for God, most worthy of God—a pure worship purged from every stain of superstition. Even if this Religion is occasionally obscured here and there by various dross of human ingenuity from idle men, its divine Origin and admirable beauty still shine forth sufficiently if it is rightly weighed; indeed, nothing more excellent, nothing more suited to perfecting the human mind, can be imagined. We rightly wonder and stand amazed, therefore, that **men of barbarian speech have conquered the eloquence of Greek speech, and that skillfully adorned myths have been utterly driven out, and the grammatical errors of fishermen have dissolved the Attic syllogisms** <note>original: "βαρβαροφώνους ἀνθρώπους τὴν ἑλληνικὴν εὐγλωττίαν νενικηκότας... piscatorumque soloecifmis dissolutos fuisse atticos Syllogismos." Without Christ and the Apostles, every religion would have degenerated into mere absurdities, darkness, and the ravings of idle men; without them, the most excellent Philosophers would have brought a remedy in vain through their reasoning to a most stubborn disease that had pervaded every vein. Whether you ascribe that happy success of the Christian Religion to divine Goodness or to the excellence of the doctrine itself, it is clear enough that it had a greater force in the souls of men than the most accurate reasonings of *Socrates* and the most celebrated Philosophers.

I know that some will propose a difficulty of no small weight. To diminish this efficacy of the Christian Religion, they will surely appeal to the *lives of the many who are called Christians*, which are so contaminated by vices that we can hardly believe that Religion has taken root in their souls. If only we could as easily deny the fact itself as we can show that the causes of this perversity in no way prevent the efficacy of the Christian Religion from being admirable in changing the souls of men for the better. But since this most serious question cannot be examined in this place, I refer those who raise this question to the *fifth dissertation of the Distinguished Theologian Werenfels* <note>Samuel Werenfels (1657–1740), a Swiss professor known for his moderate and logical approach to theology.</note>, in which he proposes and discusses this very objection; and I add this Excellent Man’s friend, *Osterwald—likewise a Pious and Perceptive Theologian* <note>Jean-Frédéric Osterwald (1663–1747), a Swiss pastor famous for his "Treatise on the Sources of Corruption," which addressed why Christians often lived immoral lives.</note>—who responds at length to this same objection in that golden little book, which should be diligently studied by any candidate of Theology, *On the Sources of Corruption Spreading Among Christians*.

<page-num>603</page-num>

...termines. We add only this: we by no means disparage the Philosophy of *Socrates* because so few have lived their lives according to its standard. Rather, we contend that, however great its excellence may have been, it is nevertheless placed far below the dignity of the Christian Religion—not only in respect to the efficacy sought from the character of the Religion itself, but also because of the Divine aid which God supplies to those who desire from their heart to live in accordance with that Religion. 

In the meantime, we too *grieve* that, in such a great light of Truth, so few are found who model their lives after this most excellent Religion. We *grieve* that men wish to dispute about Religion, yet refuse to observe its most holy precepts. We *grieve* that in our own time, we can by no means appeal to the *most corrected morals of Christians as the most certain Argument for the Christian Religion*, as we read was done in former times <note>Ancient Christian apologists often pointed to the moral superiority and brotherly love of early Christians as proof of their faith’s truth.</note>. But these things do not prevent that divine Religion from exerting its power in the souls of many. For there are, praise be to God, not a few who feel its divine power; and those who do not yet feel it nevertheless confess that the Religion itself, viewed in its own light, is the most excellent of all. 

From this we finally conclude that the Christian Religion—whether we weigh the character of its doctrine and precepts, or its Author and disciples, or finally its Success—stands much higher than the *Philosophy of Socrates*. And these, Venerable *Huldrich* <note>Likely Johann Jakob Ulrich (Huldrichus), a Swiss theologian and contemporary of the author.</note>, are what I have meditated upon concerning this argument; certainly for no other purpose than to extol the excellence of the Christian Religion, of whose divine origin I am most fully persuaded, and, if possible, to lead men to love it. For I should consider that I have lived long enough if this thin labor of mine directed even one person, freed from errors, toward the heavenly journey. If I have performed less rightly than I ought, you will at least praise the Will. But I shall not add another word. Farewell.

He then invited me to a suburban villa, saying that *Fronto*, *Laelius*, and *Beatus*—all learned and eloquent men—would be coming to the same place. I agreed without delay, and while we were talking, we finally arrived at the villa. We went out into the meadow, and there, as a soft breeze blew, we sat in a circle at the roots of the trees; soon, vessels of beer were at hand, along with that divine tobacco <note>original: "herba Nicotiana." Tobacco was often referred to in 17th- and 18th-century Latin as the "Nicotian herb."</note>. They imposed upon *Phileleutherus* the duty of questioning each person in order and examining the opinions proposed to the group.

common. But since those forms <note>original: "species," referring here to the "sensible species" or mental images that Scholastic philosophers believed objects emitted</note> are corporeal <note>physical or bodily</note>, they must first be made spiritual by the **agent intellect** <term>agent intellect: in Aristotelian thought, the active part of the mind that "strips" the physical nature from a sensory image to make it an abstract concept</term>; once this is done, they are presented to the **passive intellect** <term>passive intellect: the part of the mind that receives and stores these processed concepts</term>, and thus the passive intellect possesses the *Ideas* of physical things.

*Phileleuthes.* I follow your meaning; but since I do not fully understand everything, you will permit me to inquire more carefully about the details.

*Fronto.* Ask freely.

*Phileleuthes.* Are those images <note>original: "simulacra"</note> that flow from objects actually parts of the objects themselves? For example, is the image of the tree you are looking at right here a part of the tree itself?

*Fronto.* So it would seem.

*Phileleuthes.* How is it, then, that a tree placed at a crossroads does not shrink, even though a great multitude of these images are carried from it every day to those who see it?

*Fronto.* Their abundance is so great that a decrease can hardly be noticed.

*Phileleuthes.* I certainly do not grasp by what logic parts can be taken away from any substance daily without detriment to the whole.

*Fronto.* Those forms are exceedingly minute.

*Phileleuthes.* But if those forms are so tiny, how is it that they can truly represent the objects themselves? For example, we all see that this tree placed here before our eyes is quite tall.

*Beatus.* Perhaps those images are able to speak and announce to the mind that, although they are endowed with a very tiny shape, they nevertheless represent very large objects.

*Phileleuthes.* But then they would be lying.

*Fronto.* Do not mock me, *Beatus*, for we are philosophizing.

*Phileleuthes.* These forms must be not only exceedingly minute, but also exceedingly fast, since they cover several miles in a very short space of time. I am thinking right now of a certain learned man living in England; at this very moment, therefore, that image—without even being called—has flown to me, having crossed the sea and traveled across Germany.

*Fronto.* But celestial rays <note>light from the stars and sun</note> move with similar speed.

*Phileleuthes.* It is a wonder, however, that those forms, measuring out such vast stretches of earth, are nowhere hindered, nor do they get mixed with others flying every which way.

*Fronto.* Many things are true for which we cannot provide a full explanation.

*Phileleuthes.* But I think you have not yet demonstrated the existence of those images; however, I will grant what you ask for now: let me ask you, do you have an idea of mercy or of temperance?

*Fronto.* I certainly do.

*Fronto.* I should think not.

*Phileleuthes.* Yet the idea of mercy is fixed in your mind.

*Fronto.* It is.

*Phileleuthes.* Therefore, we can acquire ideas of things without these "images": for you either contemplate the idea of temperance as an abstract idea, or as an idea composed of many individual instances. If in the first way, then I do not know by what logic that form could represent a thing that exists only in the intellect; if in the second way, it simply cannot be conceived how a composite idea of temperance can be presented to the mind from many individual images that have nothing in common with each other.

*Beatus.* Perhaps a completely different kind of image is carried to *Fronto* than to us.

*Phileleuthes.* You seem to have guessed well, *Beatus*; I have remained ignorant until now that an "agent intellect" was present within me, yet *Fronto* ascribes a marvelous strength and power to it. I ought to conceive of things as they are, yet I do not feel it lies within my power to make a purely corporeal thing spiritual. *Fronto.* Without a doubt.

*Phileleuthes.* But if your agent intellect makes the image of, say, a mountain, into something spiritual, should it be inferred from this that the mountain exists as something spiritual?

*Fronto.* Not at all.

*Phileleuthes.* Then what good is the "form" of the mountain brought to us?

*Fronto.* Because without it, we cannot present the mountain to ourselves.

*Phileleuthes.* But that "form" has nothing in common with the mountain existing outside of me. Furthermore, I do not know how the agent intellect can perceive things as they are, while the passive intellect cannot. For example: I see a bird; an image of it is carried toward some sense near you. Before the agent intellect can make that image of a bird spiritual, it must already know that this image represents a bird and not a flea. If this is the case, we have the ideas before they even arrive, which seems absurd. If the agent intellect does not already have the images of objects, it will offer squares instead of circles to the passive intellect. But if, on the other hand, the passive intellect can know not only the nature of the images...

...but as for knowing what reality they refer back to, I simply do not know to what end that **agent intellect** <term>agent intellect: in medieval philosophy, the part of the mind that transforms physical sensations into abstract concepts</term> was given to us. However, another doubt has occurred to me, which, with your permission, I shall bring forward. If all **sensory images** <note>original: "species"</note> carried to us from objects are made spiritual, I do not see by what logic the mind can judge that physical bodies exist outside of us; for that thing which I contemplate is purely spiritual, yet I am bound to judge things as they are presented to the mind. From this it follows, in my opinion, that no one can say for certain whether the image offered to the soul is a physical body or not. These things, my dear *Fronto*, make it impossible for me to **give your opinion my vote of approval** <note>original: "album calculum adjicere," literally "to add a white pebble," an ancient Roman way of voting in favor of something</note>; I do not say it is false, but I cannot deny that it seems so to me.

*Fronto.* This argument is more obscure than I imagined. On another occasion I will submit the question to a more careful examination; meanwhile, I am very eager to know which opinion is more pleasing to the rest of you.

*Phileleuthes.* I will say nothing for now regarding God, the mind, and all creatures endowed with reason; no mortal, if he follows your opinion, will be able to explain how physical images can be transferred from them to us. But I see our friend *Paulus* is ready to speak; come then, *Paulus*, you shall be our **oracle** <note>original: "Apollo," the Greek god of prophecy and wisdom</note> in this matter.

*Paulus.* I take an entirely different path, my dear *Fronto*, nor could I ever digest your opinion, having been taught better by the **most noble Descartes** <note>René Descartes (1596–1650), the French philosopher who argued that mind and body are completely different substances</note>, who is, as you know, the **supreme restorer of philosophy**.

*Phileleuthes.* What, then, do you think *Ideas* are?

*Paulus.* I shall trace the foundations of my opinion from a bit deeper. The mind, according to me, is a thing entirely separated from every stain of the body; everything required to constitute it is achieved by pure thought alone. Within it, two faculties especially shine forth: namely, the faculty of understanding and the faculty of willing. These faculties belong to the nature of the mind, because without them no mind can be conceived. However, whether the mind thinks about this or that specific thing does not belong to its essence, but is merely a **mode** <term>mode: a specific state or "way of being" of a substance, like the shape of a piece of wax</term> or an accident of the mind; and this perception of the mind is itself called an *Idea*. Hence, an *Idea* is to me nothing other than a certain way of thinking. Thus, *perception, sensation, and idea* will be one and the same thing; they are distinguished only by their relationship. That is, every individual thought can be considered either insofar as it is a modification of the mind, or insofar as it refers to some thing existing outside the mind.

*Phileleuthes.* You contend, then, that the nature of the mind is comprised of thought alone?

*Paulus.* That is so.

*Phileleuthes.* How do you know this?

*Paulus.* Because whatever I discover within the mind can be referred back to thought.

*Phileleuthes.* Do you then discover in the nature of the mind a power to represent physical things?

*Paulus.* I feel this intimately.

*Phileleuthes.* I am not asking whether you feel that you have that faculty; but rather, whether you find anything in the nature of thought that has any **congruence** <note>original: "convenientiam," meaning a shared quality or likeness</note> with the physical things that ideas represent. For example: do you find anything in the mind that has a congruence with the shape of a table?

*Paulus.* I find nothing.

*Phileleuthes.* Why, then, do you assert that the idea of a table is a modification of the mind?

*Paulus.* Because the nature of the thing demands it.

*Phileleuthes.* Why so?

*Paulus.* Consider this tree: the idea of it is observed by our soul, yet the tree itself is not within us; nor does the movement of the brain have anything in common with the tree. It is necessary, therefore, that the idea of the tree be in the mind.

*Phileleuthes.* Therefore the mind has something in common with the body—that is, the tree.

*Paulus.* It has nothing, as you have already heard.

*Phileleuthes.* If the mind has nothing in common with the tree, it follows that the mind cannot represent the tree. It follows that the modification of the mind and the idea of the tree are distinct things. I have always heard this axiom to be true: **no one gives what they do not have** <note>original: "nemo dat quod non habet," a legal and philosophical rule implying that a cause must contain the qualities it produces in an effect</note>. If, according to your opinion, the mind is pure thought—whether you consider its nature, its properties, or its modes—it could never possess the shape of a tree.

*Paulus.* You are confusing imagination with perception; imagination draws something from the body, but perception does not.

*Phileleuthes.* I see no confusion. By the <term>Facultatem imaginatricem</term> <gloss>imaginative faculty</gloss> I mean that power of the mind by which we can make the ideas of absent objects present to the soul. This image, which is present to the soul, is either a mere modification of the mind, or it is something different from perception. If the former, the mind will have something in common with the body it represents, because it refers to a sensible thing endowed with shape; if that image presented to the mind is something different from the mind's perception, it follows that the idea and the modification of the mind are not one and the same.

*Paul.* But a certain motion of the brain is present during imagination.

*Phil.* Even if this were entirely true—though it could be doubted—it would not help your case. You admitted earlier that a specific brain motion has nothing in common with this or that body, such as a tree. From this, one must necessarily conclude that perception—or a certain **modification of the mind** <term>modification of the mind: a change in the state or "shape" of the soul, a common term in 17th-century philosophy</term>—and an "idea" are not one and the same. Moreover, it is one thing to know that I see a tree, but quite another to have the image of the tree itself presented to the soul. You might call the former a modification of the mind, but not the latter.

*Paul.* I see this opinion is pressed by some difficulties; yet I always thought that by establishing a distinction between imagination and **pure perception** <term>pure perception: the mind's direct intellectual awareness, independent of the physical senses</term>, as the Philosophers say, all doubt could be removed.

*Phil.* Let us take another example to see if we can shed light on this argument. Let us take, for instance, the idea of **temperance** <term>temperance: the moral virtue of moderation or self-restraint</term>. When you think about temperance, is this thought a modification of the mind?

*Paul.* It is.

*Phil.* You surely know what is required to constitute the nature of this virtue.

*Paul.* I know it well.

*Phil.* I ask you then: how can a single modification of the mind represent things distinguished by different properties all at once?

*Paul.* This idea is what they call in the schools a **collective idea** <note>original: "collectiva," a concept that groups multiple distinct parts into a single whole</note>.

*Phil.* So be it. Yet, according to you, it is a modification of the mind—and only that. I do not understand how a single modification can represent distinct things in one single moment, so to speak. But lest I state my feelings unclearly, I will use another example. When you open your eyes, do you not see many objects at once?

*Paul.* I see the sky, water, trees, villas, and other things.

*Phil.* Are not the ideas of those objects very different from one another?

*Paul.* They are different.

*Phil.* Then how can the mind—which is a most simple thing—reflect the ideas of such diverse objects? Do you believe it possible for one and the same body to move in such a way that it is simultaneously a square, a circle, an ellipse, and a cone?

*Paul.* I do not think so; meanwhile, you must remember that the nature of the mind is not sufficiently known.

*Phil.* You say rightly; but that does not mean one may affirm just anything about it. What I have said so far proves either that there is something in the nature of the mind that can take on the shape of a body, or that perception—or a "modification of the mind," as you usually say—is something different from an idea. You refuse to admit the former, so it seems the latter must be said. But there are other things, my dear Paulus, which persuade me that your opinion is built on no foundation.

*Paul.* Bring them forward then; I will listen.

*Phil.* You said above that perception, sensation, and idea are one and the same thing: namely, a specific operation of the mind.

*Paul.* I still feel that way.

*Phil.* Let us set aside perceptions for now and speak of **sensations**. When you taste sugar or use vinegar, do you feel something?

*Paul.* Who would deny it?

*Phil.* Is this sensation a modification of the mind?

*Paul.* It is.

*Phil.* Do you then have an "idea" of the sweetness perceived when you use sugar?

*Paul.* I do not have an idea, but I feel it at least.

*Phil.* Therefore, sensation and idea differ; thus, modifications of the mind and ideas are different things. Again, if your finger is hurt by a knife, do you not feel pain?

*Paul.* Indeed I feel it, and recently I experienced this more than enough.

*Phil.* This troublesome sensation is undoubtedly a certain affection of the mind, which you call a modification.

*Paul.* It is.

*Phil.* Does this sensation, then, exhibit an "idea"—either of the pain or of the knife?

*Paul.* It does not.

*Phil.* Therefore, an idea and a sensation are not one and the same. By the consensus of all Philosophers, we have no "idea" of sensations; hence, if asked what "sweet" is, or what "bitter" is, we can answer nothing. According to you, that which is within us is confused with the perception of things placed outside of us. When we are hurt by a knife, we feel the pain exists within our mind; but when we see a tree, we cannot judge that the tree is within our mind. For we are conscious that the tree we contemplate is outside of us. Indeed, if the truth be told, my dear Paulus, this opinion of yours [contradicts] the teachings of your most **noble Teacher** <note>The text cuts off here at "Præcepto-," but the catchword "ris" indicates the full word is "Præceptoris" (Teacher's). <summary>In this dialogue, Phileleuthes argues that 'ideas' must be distinct from 'mental modifications' or 'sensations,' using the examples of complex virtues, simultaneous visual objects, and the physical sensation of pain to prove that the mind's internal states do not match the nature of external objects. He highlights the paradox of how a simple mind can represent many complex things at once and distinguishes between the 'feeling' of a sensation and the 'idea' of an object.</summary>

...is contrary to reason; for on one hand, you are judging a thing of which you do not have a clear concept, and on the other, you attribute something to the mind that conflicts with the very nature of a thinking thing. Both of these are contrary to the teachings of Descartes.

*Phil.* Since this idea representing the mountain is nothing other than a **modification of the mind** <term>modification of the mind: in 17th-century philosophy, this refers to a specific state or "mode" the soul takes on, similar to how a piece of wax can be shaped into different forms</term>, something of a "shape" must necessarily exist within the mind. A "clear and distinct perception" is the **Criterion of Truth** <term>Criterion of Truth: the standard by which we decide what is true; for Descartes, anything we perceive clearly and distinctly must be true</term> according to Descartes; and I feel clearly and distinctly that my soul has the faculty to behold various ideas.

*Phil.* But that is not what is being asked, my dear *Paul*. Philosophers of every sect agree that the mind contemplates the ideas presented to it in some way or another. The question is whether those ideas are modifications of the mind itself, or something else entirely distinct from the mind.

*Paul.* Do you then think it is impossible for God to bring it about that, on the occasion of a movement in the brain, an idea is stirred up in the mind?

*Phil.* That is not the question either. So far, we are not arguing about the *origin* of ideas, but about their *nature*. But since I see you are quite stubborn in defending your Master’s opinion, here is a **horned syllogism** <term>horned syllogism: a dilemma or "argument with two horns," where both choices lead to a difficult or absurd conclusion</term>! Either an idea representing a thing existing outside of us is present in *all* modifications of the mind, or only in *some*. If an idea is attached to every modification of the mind, it follows that not only are ideas joined to all our sensations, but that even the pain or pleasure we feel exists outside of us—which is absurd. If ideas are present only in certain modes of thinking, it follows that a specific mode of thinking and an "idea" are distinct from one another, not just by mental abstraction, but in reality.

*Paul.* You are pressing the points you already mentioned above.

*Phil.* I am, but I do not remember you bringing forward anything that unties the knot. Perhaps *Beatus* will shed greater light on this argument. For to tell you the truth, I still do not know what an "idea" actually is.

*Phil.* You would do us a great favor, then, if you would explain his opinion to us and bring forward the arguments upon which it rests.

*Beat.* I will do what I can. That learned man thinks that **we see all things in God** <term>Vision in God: Malebranche's famous doctrine that human beings do not see physical objects directly, but rather perceive the ideas of them as they exist within the mind of God</term>; that our mind is most closely joined with God; and that in God, who created all things, are the **Archetypes** <gloss>original patterns or models</gloss> of all things. He believes ideas of these things are impressed upon the mind—or rather, offered to be contemplated within the nature of God—whenever our brain is affected in a certain way by external objects. I will soon provide the arguments by which Malebranche proves his opinion; for now, let it suffice to describe the opinion itself.

*Phil.* I do not quite understand what you mean. With your permission, I will ask one or two questions so that I might properly grasp this opinion, which is difficult to catch. You said that we see all things in God, and that He contains within Himself the **prototypes** <gloss>first models</gloss> of all possible ideas.

*Beat.* That is correct.

*Phil.* Are those ideas which are in God, and which He offers to us for contemplation, the very most perfect nature of God itself, or something distinct from God?

*Beat.* The question is not so much *how* ideas are in God, but whether we can contemplate them in God. Therefore, it matters little to me what you decide regarding how ideas exist within God.

*Phil.* Let us suppose that the ideas we are said to contemplate in God are nothing other than the divine essence itself, modified in a certain and determined way (as they say in the schools) so that it represents this or that object. For example: I see this tree; on the occasion of this tree, God offers the idea of a tree for me to contemplate within His own nature. Is the idea of a tree distinct from all other objects?

*Beat.* It is. What follows from that?

*Phil.* Therefore, the most perfect nature of God must have something in common with a tree.

*Beat.* It has nothing in common with it.

*Phil.* How then can you distinguish the idea of a tree from the idea of a house?

# DIALOGUE ON THE NATURE OF IDEAS.

**Phil.** ...how can I? An idea of either thing is a certain **modification of the most perfect divine nature** <term>modification of the divine nature: the idea that specific thoughts or things are just different "modes" or "shapes" of God's own infinite essence</term>. But if that most perfect thought of God is one and the same, whether it refers to a tree or a house, I do not know how I could distinguish between them. If, however, that most perfect modification of the divine mind, insofar as it refers to a tree, is distinct from the one that represents a house, then something must be contained in the most perfect nature of God that has a relationship with a body—that is, with the tree or the house. For although all things exist in God in the most excellent way, we cannot understand them otherwise than by a certain comparison established with the nature and properties of our own minds. But as you heard above, no one can understand by what logic a mind, separated from all bodily mass, can nevertheless represent a material thing. Therefore, if you say that the ideas of God are nothing but modifications of the most perfect divine nature, you fall into the same difficulties when the conversation turns to the ideas of bodily things.

**Beat.** I never said that I would explain the way in which God understands.

**Phil.** Yet you thought there was nothing absurd in saying that the ideas the mind contemplates are nothing but modifications of the divine nature and essence. But suppose those ideas are something different from the most perfect nature of God; I ask you, how can we assert that we "contemplate all things in God" when it cannot even be known for certain whether they are in Him? Or what, finally, are those ideas, and where are they, if you separate them from that most perfect nature of God? I know the Philosophers say that there is an **intelligible world** <term>intelligible world (mundus intelligibilis): a conceptual realm of pure ideas or truths that exists in the divine mind, accessible to reason rather than the physical senses</term> in God, and that He contemplates it perpetually; but if you ask where that world actually is, you will hear that it is God Himself. After they have said many things about it, you will ultimately be taught nothing other than that God has ideas of all things. And so, you understand the matter no better than before. However these things may be, there are other points that prevent me from subscribing to your opinion. I ask you, my dear *Beatus*, what do you understand by "body"?

**Beat.** We are discussing ideas, and you ask about the body; nevertheless, I will tell you: a body is a substance extended in length, breadth, and depth.

**Phil.** I am not asking what properties matter is primarily equipped with, but what it *is*.

**Beat.** A body is nothing other than a gathering of infinite parts, each of which constitutes a body.

**Phil.** You answer correctly. Let us then suppose any body is divided into a thousand parts, and let us take the thousandth part of that body; I ask you, what do you understand by the name of this "part"?

<meta>Catchword: Beat.</meta>

<column-break/>

**Beat.** Nothing other than a body consisting of innumerable smaller corpuscles.

**Phil.** Since, therefore, every composite must necessarily consist of simple parts, and every body—no matter how thin—is not simple, it is necessary that the most subtle corpuscles must eventually be resolved into something simple.

**Beat.** That is so; and this simple thing is an **atom**, or if you prefer, a **monad** <term>monad: from the Greek 'monas' (unit); in 17th and 18th-century philosophy, it refers to a fundamental, indivisible point of existence that makes up the universe</term>.

**Phil.** Is an atom or a monad a body, or a spirit?

**Beat.** Neither.

**Phil.** What is it then?

**Beat.** I do not know; it is enough that by reasoning, one must necessarily arrive at that point.

**Phil.** But if we are ignorant of this, then we do not truly know what a body is.

**Beat.** Where are you wandering? I thought you were going to speak about *ideas*.

**Phil.** That is what I am doing. God has ideas of all things, and indeed in the most perfect way; we contemplate all ideas in God; therefore, we have the most perfect ideas of all bodies.

**Beat.** I have already said that this is false.

**Phil.** How then can we contemplate the ideas of things in God, if our ideas of bodily things are imperfect? Certainly, there is no third option: either the ideas of all things—if we contemplate them in God—are most perfect, or we do not contemplate all things in God. Since you deny the former, you must necessarily admit the latter.

**Beat.** You are mistaken. God, in this matter, accommodates Himself to **human weakness** <note>original: imbecillitas humana</note>.

**Phil.** I do not understand what these words mean.

**Beat.** God knows that humans are finite, and not capable of knowing things perfectly; therefore, He presents ideas to be contemplated in a way that suits their natural talent.

**Phil.** Are the ideas of one and the same thing in God therefore diverse? For example, does He have an idea of the mind (1) as a most subtle air, or (2) as a nervous fluid, or (3) as a thinking thing?

**Beat.** Not at all.

**Phil.** Therefore it must be said: either we do not see all things in God, or our ideas are most perfect—the same as those God Himself contemplates. Since the latter is false, by your own admission, you must see for yourself what should be thought of your hypothesis. But the idea of the body brings something else to my mind, *Beatus*. You know that most of our ideas are composite.

### DIALOGUE ON THE NATURE OF IDEAS.

*Phil.* I know.
*Phil.* Ideas of virtues and vices, insofar as they are not considered as mere abstractions but as being composed of many singular ideas, are composite.
*Beat.* Who would doubt it?
*Phil.* Therefore, we contemplate them in God.
*Beat.* Without a doubt.
*Phil.* If, therefore, I hold the idea of fornication present in my mind, along with everything that completes this vice, do I see that idea in God?
*Beat.* Far be it! <note>original: "Absit"</note>
*Phil.* Where, then, does the presence of that composite idea come from?
*Beat.* One must philosophize with purity; use another example.
*Phil.* You know all the things required to describe anger, which is a brief madness. <note>original: "ira, qui brevis furor est," a common Stoic definition of anger popularized by Horace and Seneca</note>
*Beat.* I know them.
*Phil.* If, therefore, I see everything contained in the idea of this vice in God, one must necessarily conclude either that the most foul things are seen in God, or that what you say is false: that we see all things in God.
*Beat.* Do not imitate those who are accustomed to press their opponents with consequences born of malice.
*Phil.* I am not saying these consequences are believed by you, but I am explaining what seems to follow, in my opinion, from the principles you have laid down.
*Beat.* The ideas of those vices are abstract.
*Phil.* I know they can be considered that way; but that is not the issue. The question is whether all the singular ideas from which that collective idea is composed are in God, and can be seen in Him by the human mind. Whatever you say, you will be caught; indeed, I will say more, my dear *Beatus*: if we see all things in God, then all foolish imaginations, visions, and the phantasms of those who are delirious must be said to be seen in God.
*Beat.* Remember, however, that such objections should be raised more sparingly against men of standing.
*Phil.* These conclusions can necessarily be drawn from your opinion, or from that of *Malebranche* <term>Malebranche: Nicolas Malebranche (1638–1715), a French priest and philosopher who famously argued that humans do not perceive the world directly, but rather "see all things in God"</term>, if you prefer. *Beat.* I see where you are heading, but assume whatever you wish; I appeal to the arguments.

—I ask, from where then do those most impure images and things most hostile to God—which are often thrust upon the pious and miserably tear at their minds, and which they often attempt in vain to put to flight with the most ardent prayers—trace their origin?
*Beat.* These images are to be attributed either to one's physical temperament or to some evil spirit.
*Phil.* But in that case, we would not be seeing "all things" in God. Suppose, on the contrary, that those ideas are shown to us because we wish to view them. But since you appeal to arguments, these matters must be passed over in silence. However, I would like to ask one thing of you before I hear those arguments of yours. Surely you believe, without doubt, that humans are equipped with five senses, and you do not doubt that the Author of the human race had the wisest reasons why He fashioned humans in this way.
*Beat.* Who is so foolish that he would not admit this?
*Phil.* Do we, properly speaking, see with our eyes or hear with our ears?
*Beat.* No; for God offers the ideas of objects in Himself to be contemplated.
*Phil.* So, we see the idea of a tree placed before us in God?
*Beat.* We see it.
*Phil.* But if humans were made of hard marble, and the power of understanding were added to it, could we similarly contemplate the ideas of objects in God?
*Beat.* We could.
*Phil.* Therefore, I see no reason why *God* gave us eyes for seeing. I am deceived every day when I think that, by the help of the external senses, representations of things are carried to the mind; I do not know what so many objects existing outside of me mean, none of which, properly speaking, I can contemplate. I am deceived when I conclude from the wonderful structure of the external organs that they were made for the best and wisest purpose by the Creator of all things; yet you said above that the senses were granted to us by the best Divinity not without the weightiest reasons.
*Beat.* I have already said above that it is not necessary to satisfy every difficulty; it is enough if this opinion can be proved by clear arguments.
*Phil.* But if the opinion, viewed in itself, is absurd, will you make it beautiful, solid, or anything else by your arguments?

### DIALOGUE ON THE NATURE OF IDEAS.

*Paulus.* Let us hear his arguments; he will hardly escape your snares, *Phileutherus*.
*Phil.* Produce those solid arguments then, *Beatus*.
*Beat.* My first argument is drawn from the propriety of the *Divine Virtues*. It is fitting for a most wise and perfect Being to achieve all things—especially momentous ones—through the simplest principles and methods. Where a thing can be done by a shortcut, a wise person will not use circuitous routes. Now, God can more easily display the ideas of all things to the human mind to be contemplated within Himself than He could create the mind in such a way that He would then be required to produce those ideas in the mind whenever objects happen to be present.
*Phil.* I have heard the argument. To understand its force, I ask you: when God wishes to create something, does He consider only His own power, or does He simultaneously contemplate the ideas of the things to be made and take them into account as well?
*Beat.* Without a doubt, both are observed by the most perfect mind.
*Phil.* Did God, therefore, see that it was possible—in the administration of all future things, especially those that are contingent <note>Events that may or may not happen, depending on free will or chance, rather than necessity.</note>—to reach the goal of His works through the paths you call "simplest and shortest"? For example, before God created the human race, did He not have the ideas of the Jewish people, of the best laws, of the fates of a nation prone to idolatry, of the precepts of the Christian Religion, and so on?
*Beat.* He did.
*Phil.* But does the way to reach eternal happiness seem to you to be equally "easy" in the *Old* and *New Testaments*?
*Beat.* It does not seem so.
*Phil.* Therefore, God does not always employ those means for reaching an end which seem simplest to *us*. Otherwise, God would have impressed the ideas of all things necessary for knowledge upon all men, and would have so disposed everyone toward living piously by His power that they could not have strayed from the true and the right even in the smallest matters.
*Beat.* Yet it seems contrary to the divine virtues to say that He does not use the simplest means to reach the goal He intends.
*Phil.* When you speak of the administration of all things, you must not consider the divine virtues alone in the abstract—as we say in the schools <note>A reference to "Scholasticism," the traditional philosophical and theological system taught in medieval and early modern universities.</note>—but you must join them with God's wisdom, in which all properties of things, circumstances, connections, and outcomes are understood together.

### DIALOGUE ON THE NATURE OF IDEAS.

*Phil.* No mortal can do this. From this I conclude that we little men <note>original: "homunciones," a diminutive suggesting the insignificance of humans compared to God.</note> discuss the simplicity of God's ways in vain. Who, for instance, shall judge whether some magnificent building could have been constructed by an easier and more concise method if the reasons the Master of the building had are entirely unknown to him? As for God, the variety and multitude of His thoughts is immense; the number and diversity of things to be managed is countless. The principle of divine administration rests upon the diverse nature, constitution, and ends intended for these things by the most wise Deity. Nor is God's care focused solely on this tiny little point we call Earth; there remain immense orbs in the vast universe, over whose governance the adorable Rector of the world keeps watch. We clearly know scarcely a fraction of these things, since all things are interconnected, and only the outcome of the final day will at last teach us the reason for the whole of divine administration, insofar as it concerns us to know it. Nor is it necessary, my dear *Beatus*, for us to call upon various examples occurring in the kingdoms of Nature and Grace to prove what I am saying; for the very thing we are disputing may serve as an argument. You think nothing could be simpler for knowing objects than if God offers us the ideas of objects to be contemplated in Himself; but I would believe the same thing could have been done most simply if God had adorned the mind with the faculty of exciting ideas. Since God could do both with equal ease, who shall be the judge between us and settle the suit? To know this, one would need an extraordinary revelation from God. Since this can be expected by no one, it seems rash to conclude: "this or that thing should have been done differently, because according to my opinion God could have produced it by a far easier method." Or, I ask you, why did God attach a body to our mind, by which it is often hindered in its reasoning, when—if it is lawful to reason this way—God could have impressed the ideas of all things even without it? Why did He give external senses, and yet, according to you, offer all bodies to the mind to be contemplated in Himself? I could bring forward infinite examples which would most evidently demonstrate our ignorance regarding this argument, were it not for the fact that we must be mindful of the time. Forgive me, then, if I say that your argument seems to me to be entirely weak.
*Beat.* Hear then another argument, far stronger than the first, in my opinion.
*Phil.* I shall listen gladly.

with respect to his knowledge, he depends on God. This view is, without doubt, more consistent with the virtues of God than if it were said that the mind produces ideas by itself, or has the power to draw them out on the occasion of encountering objects. For in this way, man recognizes that he depends entirely on God in all things, and at the same time, the Majesty of God is most greatly exalted. Hence, the Holy Scriptures also confirm this opinion, as Paul testifies in 2 Corinthians 3:5. <note>original: "Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as of ourselves; but our sufficiency is of God."</note>

*Phil.* I do not know what you understand by the word *depend*, when you say it is necessary that, with respect to all knowledge acquired through ideas, man depends on God.

*Beat.* By this word I mean to signify that, properly speaking, neither minds nor bodies act, but that God fashions all ideas in the mind and produces all actions; for if this were denied, creatures would not depend on God.

*Phil.* I do not see by what reasoning God’s independence <note>Phileutherus likely means God's status as the only independent being, or rather, the creature's dependence on Him.</note> would be denied if it were said that man can stir up ideas and act in some way with respect to his will. *Beat.* Nevertheless, it is more fitting to the divine virtues if we say that creatures can do absolutely nothing at all.

*Phil.* I am so far from granting this that I would instead assert that this claim is contrary to all of God's virtues. For if the mind contemplates all ideas in God, and if all sensations and inclinations of the will are the effects of Almighty God, then we are truly *wooden puppets moved by the strings of another* <note>original: "alienis nervis mobile lignum," a quote from the Roman poet Horace, Satires 2.7.82, suggesting humans would be mere marionettes without free will.</note>, nor do we differ one bit from a stone or a tree trunk. It would follow that natural and supernatural religion, which most clearly teach the opposite, were devised to deceive man, etc. etc.

*Beat.* Do not be carried away by the heat of the dispute; judge this argument with a calm mind.

*Phil.* If you wish, I will prove the force of my conclusions as clearly as mathematicians are wont to do; but that would lead us further than the limits of our time permit. I say only this: even if you most strongly wish to defend that dependence of the creature, it can be done just as easily by saying that God stirs up ideas in our minds on the occasion of objects, as by contending that God offers them to be contemplated in Himself. Hence, the defenders of the *System of Occasional Causes* <term>Occasionalism: The philosophical theory that created substances cannot be efficient causes of events. Instead, all events are taken to be caused directly by God.</term>, as it is called, proceed by the path I have mentioned. You are arguing at least from utility, a method of debating that is liable to innumerable difficulties.

that it exists, and has its origin from another far more powerful being, whether the idea of the moon is already in God or in my mind? Since there is nothing in the idea of the moon that can be confused with the idea of God, I conclude—from wherever that idea may have arisen—that I do not exist for the sake of the moon; but so that, having known the existence of the moon, I may proclaim God’s infinite Power, Goodness, and Wisdom. Suppose that the idea of God, like that of all things, is impressed and engraved upon the mind from the very moment of conception; it will necessarily follow that the idea of God, as the first and eternal cause, will be different from the ideas of contingent <note>A "contingent" thing is something that does not have to exist, unlike God, who exists by necessity.</note> things. From this, it will be easy to conclude that God himself must be considered as the cause of the existence of the remaining Beings. You see, therefore, that with respect to divine glory, it is all the same whether the mind was so created by God that, on the occasion of objects, it can bring forth ideas from its own—so to speak—bosom. <note>original: "sinu." This is a metaphor for the mind's internal capacity to generate thoughts.</note> Therefore, that danger you think hangs over all those who do not believe ideas are seen in God is vain, as you imagine they will seek a refuge of trust and love in the objects of created things as if in a first cause. At the same time, you see that your Malebranche <note>Nicolas Malebranche (1638–1715) was a French priest and philosopher who famously argued that we "see all things in God."</note> has said nothing except what is said in all the systems of the Philosophers regarding this argument. All cry out that the mind ought to be stirred by the contemplation of creatures to celebrate the divine virtues. Since, however, I see that you have Malebranche’s book *On the Search for Truth* at hand, please open Book III, Chapter VI, and read what pertains to this in a loud voice, so that the others may also hear this great mystery.

*Beat.* I will read it. The words to which you point your finger sound like this: 
> <note>original: French</note> It is impossible for God to have any other principal end for his actions than himself: this is a notion common to every man capable of some reflection, and Holy Scripture does not allow us to doubt that God made all things for himself. It is therefore necessary that not only our natural love—I mean the movement he produces in our Spirit—tend toward him, but also that the knowledge and the light he gives it make us know something that is in him: for everything that comes from God can only be for God, and he cannot make a Spirit to know his works unless that Spirit sees God in some way while seeing his Works; so that one can say that if we did not see God in some manner, we would see nothing, etc.

*Phil.* These words either mean absolutely nothing and are thus what the French call a "play on words," <note>original: "un jeux des mots" (archaic French spelling for *un jeu de mots*).</note> or they express what everyone says: namely, that the contemplation of creatures excites in the mind the most perfect ideas...

<summary>In this portion of the dialogue, Beatus and Phileutherus debate whether human knowledge is found within God or within the human mind. Beatus argues that perceiving ideas "in God" is the only way to ensure our focus remains on the Creator, while Phileutherus maintains that studying the created world naturally leads a rational mind to praise God regardless of where the ideas originate.</summary>

### DIALOGUE ON THE NATURE OF IDEAS.

...of the most perfect virtues of God, and to that end God, the Best and Greatest, <note>original: "O. M." or "Optimum Maximum," a traditional title for the deity.</note> subjected a series of the most beautiful things to the eyes of men; if you wish to call this *seeing God in his works*, I do not object. But it does not follow from this that the ideas of all things are seen in God.

*Beat.* Yet this opinion seems to extol the infinite preeminence <note>original: "ὑπεροχὴν" (hyperochēn). This refers to God’s absolute superiority over all created things.</note> of God more than the opinions of others.

*Phil.* It seems so, indeed, if you attend to the words and not the meaning of the words; for if I am not mistaken, I have shown abundantly how many difficulties this opinion is subject to. But even if I granted you everything, we would have gained nothing so far; for the question always remains: what is an idea?

*Beat.* There are many things I could add, but I fear someone might think me more talkative and persistent than the nature of our conversation requires; I gladly hand over the duty of speaking to others. Meanwhile, thirst presses upon my throat, and since Bacchus, the giver of joy, <note>Bacchus is the Roman god of wine.</note> is present, let us drain the foaming bowl, my friends.

*Paul.* I have certainly perceived more pleasure from this one draft than from your entire dispute *on the nature of ideas*; but we must also hear our friend *Lelius*. Perhaps he will wring an agreement from *Phileleutherus* and ensure that in the future he cannot flee to his suspension of judgment. <note>original: "ἐποχὴν" (epochēn). In ancient philosophy, this was the practice of withholding one's consent or judgment when faced with equal arguments on both sides.</note> What, then, do you think, *Lelius*, about the subject of our dispute?

*Lelius.* I have listened with pleasure so far to the arguments you have made on both sides; the opinions *on the nature of ideas* brought forward thus far seem ingenious rather than true. Meanwhile, to tell the truth, it is easier to say what ideas are not, than what they are. However, so as not to be entirely without a contribution, <note>original: "ἀσύμβολος" (asymbolos). Literally, one who does not pay their share of a bill or contribute to a communal meal.</note> I will say which opinion seems to me the most probable of all.

*Phil.* You will make us happy, *Lelius*, if you share your opinion on this subject with us.

*Lelius.* In this matter, I think we must primarily attend to those things that anyone feels when looking deep within themselves. And yet it is certain to those who attend to what happens within us, that ideas are created or produced by the very will of man upon the occasion of certain movements of the brain.

*Phil.* Does this production of ideas happen with the mind knowing and willing it, or rather against its will?

*Lelius.* Willing it.

*Paul.* When the mind wants to form such ideas, does it want in a general way that ideas be present, or is it required that *this* idea, and no other, be at hand?

---

### DIALOGUE ON THE NATURE OF IDEAS.

*Lelius.* Without a doubt, it must want the latter.

*Phil.* Therefore, the mind has an idea of the thing it wants to be present *before* it wants it to be present—which is a contradiction?

*Lelius.* You do not grasp the matter correctly; it is enough that the will is present, and once it is set, the idea is formed.

*Phil.* No mortal understands how a craftsman could construct a specific and defined machine unless he first has a preconceived image of the thing to be made in his mind. Ideas, according to you, are representations of things; it is necessary, therefore, for the will to want not just *any* idea to be present, but for *this or that* specific idea to be present, conforming to the object. But if the will can create ideas at its pleasure, why does it happen that many ideas are present to us against our will?

*Lelius.* Because the mind often does not attend to the decrees of its own will; hence it does not know that it wanted to bring forth this or that idea.

*Phil.* Then there is plainly no cause for why ideas are present; yet I have thought until now that nothing happens without a cause.

*Lelius.* The will is the cause.

*Phil.* But the will, unless it is directed toward a certain object, cannot be said to "will" anything.

*Lelius.* I will explain the matter with an example. Do you see here a bird sitting in a tree?

*Phil.* I see it.

*Lelius.* On the occasion of this object being brought to the senses, our brain is moved in a certain way; once the brain is moved, the will wants an idea suitable to the object—that is, the bird—to be present. Because the will wants it, it is there.

*Phil.* But the idea of this bird was present to my mind before any inclination of the will intervened; for as soon as I lifted my eyes to the tree, I saw the bird sitting in the tree whether I wanted to or not <note>original: "volens nolens."</note>. Therefore, the will cannot be called the cause of this idea.

*Lelius.* We cannot distinguish the moments of time closely enough.

*Phil.* There is no need for a distinction of time; just open your eyes, and the ideas of objects will be present even against your will.

*Lelius.* Hear another example, which proves my opinion more than enough. When I sit at home in my study, <note>original: "Muſeo." In the 17th century, a "museum" was often a private library or room dedicated to study and the arts.</note> I often close my eyes so that I am not hindered by a variety of objects while meditating; then I want these or those ideas to be present, and behold, for the most part, they are at hand at my command. You see, therefore, that ideas are present at the command of the will before the objects themselves are pressed upon the senses.

<summary>This portion of the dialogue features Lelius proposing that ideas are products of the human will triggered by brain activity, while Phileleutherus counters that we often perceive things involuntarily, suggesting the will cannot be the sole cause of our mental representations.</summary>

<meta>This page continues a dialogue concerning the nature of ideas. Philo (the skeptic/rationalist) is debating with Lelius (representing a more theological or Cartesian view) about whether the human will is the cause of our mental ideas, or if they have a different origin entirely.</meta>

<page-num>626</page-num>

### DIALOGUE ON THE NATURE OF IDEAS.

*Phil.* I do not call the matter itself into doubt; but this example by no means proves the point in question. For we are not asking whether we know and feel that ideas are often present through the intervention of our will, but whether the will is the *cause* of those ideas, and whether, assuming this is true, it becomes clear what an "idea" actually is. It is not established by any argument to me that my will is the cause of my ideas, since countless ideas are absent that I would wish to be present. But I will concede for a moment that a power to produce ideas exists within the mind or the will; it remains to be explained by what logic the will draws certain ideas out from the "bosom of the mind," so to speak. For example, I want the idea of a parrot to be present to me; I ask, what is the connection between the idea of a parrot and the inclination of the will, and why is the image of a parrot ready at hand, and not that of a cat? It seems reckless to me to affirm any proposition when we see no connection between the two ideas of the proposition. In short, all our ideas arise through *sensation* and *reflection* <note>original: "sensationem & reflexionem." These are the two sources of knowledge identified by the philosopher John Locke.</note>; as far as sensations are concerned, there is no operation of the will; regarding reflection, the will does indeed play a part, but in such a way that we remain ignorant of how it places those ideas before the mind.

*Lel.* I believe that if a fact itself is certain, the fact should not be called into doubt just because of the *manner* in which it occurs. For instance, I know that the members of our body move at the command of the will; we are ignorant of the manner, yet we believe this no less constantly.

*Phil.* There is no doubt that our limbs move when our will intervenes; but there is no dispute about this among the disagreeing families of philosophers. This alone is asked: what is the connection between the inclination of the mind and the movement of the body? Does the mind do this, or God, or some third substance, etc.? Similarly, I know that certain ideas are present on the occasion of the will; but it is asked whether the will produced those ideas, and what they finally are. Since this has not yet been clearly explained to me, I think nothing should be defined recklessly.

*Lel.* Something divine <note>original Greek: "ΘEIOY τι" (theiou ti).</note> undoubtedly intervenes here, and unless I am mistaken, it is not at all absurd to say that God formed all the minds He created in such a way that they can draw from their own bosom all the ideas that will correspond to the future movements of the body.

*Phil.* This also seems to me to be not without difficulty. For either you must say that all ideas corresponding to the movements of the body, and all other ideas, are innate <note>term: "innate" (existing in the mind from birth rather than learned from experience).</note> to the mind, or that a faculty has been granted to the mind to produce them at pleasure when necessary. If you say the former, you will find it difficult to explain why we are brought into the light of the world in total ignorance of all things; why there is a need for so many exhortations and instructions; why there is such a diversity of talents; why

---

<page-num>627</page-num>

### DIALOGUE ON THE NATURE OF IDEAS.

we are unwillingly ignorant of so many things; why animals themselves, coming forth for the most part into the light of day, surpass infants in sagacity; why certain nations are so brutalized by savagery, and so on? Even if you had explained all these things, it would still remain for you to say what those ideas finally are—whether they are certain intellectual substances, such as *Plato* once imagined, or whether they are certain accidents. Whatever you say, you will see it shrouded in darkness. But if you believe that ideas are created by the mind itself at every single moment, this itself must be proven by arguments. You have already heard something of what their value is; the force of your entire argument comes down to this: "I feel that ideas are sometimes present at the command of my will; therefore, the will is the builder of all ideas." I do not see the force of this inference. Certainly, if the will could create ideas at pleasure, it would have much more power to call back before the mind ideas that were once present; yet everyone experiences that nothing is more false than this assertion—especially those who have read many things.

*Lel.* Perhaps the nature of the brain is such that ideas cannot always be ready at hand.

*Phil.* But if the will can form ideas at pleasure, I do not know how the brain could be an obstacle to the will; nor is it permitted to cover conjectures with more conjectures so they do not leak away. If I were to concede this, however, I would ask you to show me some connection between ideas, the will, and the brain.

*Lel.* Look, I conceive of it this way: God saw from eternity the connections of all things and events; He knew which movements would arise in the body and which ideas would likewise arise. Therefore, He created the mind endowed with the faculty of bringing forth ideas suitable to the state of its affairs; the connection of those things, therefore, is to be sought in the will of God.

*Phil.* I actually thought you were going to show me the connection between the brain, the will, and ideas. The question is not whether some most powerful and wise substance, whom we call God, formed man so that he can form ideas about things; but rather what those ideas are, and by what means they are present to the mind. I would like you to know this, and to that end we have spent our time talking thus far. It is not necessary, therefore, to immediately appeal to the decrees and the will of the Deity, unless you think that "philosophizing" simply means saying that God willed it so for things we cannot account for. If you say a hundred times that God willed that the ideas of objects be present to the mind, and that this connection must be sought in God's wise will, it is still not clear what *ideas* are—which is the one thing we have been looking for.

*Lel.* But in this way, one could dispute both sides of any argument, and the scholar would not differ much from the fool.

<header>DIALOGUE ON THE NATURE OF IDEAS.</header>
<meta>catchword: DISSER-</meta>

*Phil.* It by no means follows from this that everything can be disputed in such a way; there are many indubitable things which can be denied by no one who is of sound mind. Thus, Mathematicians and Metaphysicians can demonstrate many things most evidently, because they rely on abstract and clear ideas. Therefore, those things which can be certainly demonstrated must be distinguished from those which are equipped only with certain degrees of probability, or clearly with mere conjectures. Meanwhile, it is true that many have acquired the reputation of "Learned Men" who, nevertheless, are often no wiser than the peasants themselves. Peasants are ignorant of many things, and they admit it; many of the Learned do not know those things any better, and yet they wish to seem to know—in which case the peasant is the wiser. Much more is required for the solid knowledge of any matter than is commonly believed. Hence the celebrated Werenfelsius <note>Samuel Werenfels (1657–1740) was a prominent Swiss theologian and professor at Basel, known for his critiques of empty academic pretense.</note>, the eternal glory of our Switzerland, is accustomed to write this prudent and most true maxim in the *Alba Amicorum* <note>term: "Alba Amicorum" (Friendship Books) — popular in the early modern period, these were personal autograph books where friends and famous scholars would write signatures, mottos, or short verses.</note>: *Those finally seem to themselves to know the most, who do not know what it is to know.* <note>original: "Illi demum sibi plurima scire videntur, qui nesciunt, quid sit scire."</note> I do not call that man learned, my dear *Lelius*, who has a memory stuffed with countless words—often signifying nothing—and thinks the secrets of all sciences are stored in the cabinet of his heart. Rather, I think him worthy of the name who knows those things which are required for living well and happily; who knows that he is utterly ignorant of many things, knows a few with certainty, and many only with probability; who, because of whatever apparatus of learning he possesses, neither lifts his crest <note>note: a metaphor for being prideful or arrogant, like a rooster.</note> nor despises a neighbor who perhaps is equipped with less knowledge of things, nor insults one who is doubting or wandering in certain errors, but, mindful of the weakness of the human mind, can bear all men with an equal spirit. If I were to say these things in a crowd of certain "Learned Men," I know well enough that I would earn no favor from them; but I know those with whom I am now dealing. Our conversation about *Ideas* and their nature has, I think, sufficiently shown that the limits of our knowledge are very narrow. *Ideas* are the foundation of all our science; and yet, as far as it seems to me, we are ignorant of what they are. Perhaps we shall finally know then, when our mind is surrounded by eternal light; however, I do not object if others feel differently about this.

*Paul.* But I see the rooftops of the villas smoking everywhere, and longer shadows falling from the high mountains <note>original: "At video passim villarum culmina fumare, majoresque cadere altis de montibus umbras." This is a playful reference to the closing lines of Virgil’s first Eclogue, signaling the end of the day and the conversation.</note>; let us rise, friends, and head for the city. We have heard enough about *Ideas*, and my stomach is not fed on *ideas*, but on food; I hasten, therefore, to dinner.

*Beat.* Let us go.

*Phil.* Farewell, my most delightful companions.

*Fronto.* Farewell to you as well, most friendly Phileleutherus.

# EPISTOLARY DISSERTATION
### CONCERNING THE
# VALUE OF THE ART
# OF RHETORIC
### TO A MOST FRIENDLY MAN
## L. CANDIDUS.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'M' showing a landscape with a winding path through hills and shrubs under a cloudy sky.</image-desc>
You remember, excellent *Candidus*, in a recent gathering of friends, after various conversations were held among us—as is usually the case—that we happened upon the subject of *Eloquence*, its genuine sources, and the powers it has over the minds of men. Concerning the praise of Eloquence itself, there was, as you know, no divorce of opinions among our friends. Regarding its forces and power, there was slight disagreement; but regarding the sources from which this Eloquence must be drawn, as is the way with human temperaments, there were diverse judgments. Most people discussed at length the excellence and wonderful utility of the *Art of Rhetoric*, and its singular power to sway the minds of men. They argued that this art was the reason why, among the ancient Greeks and Romans, so many excellent Orators flourished, whom the most learned men admire today. I, however, although I had heard the opinions of the others, indicated clearly enough that I was devoted to a different view, and I contended that the Art of Rhetoric—just as it is commonly taught as a specialized science in the Gymnasiums <note>term: "Gymnasiums" — in this context, higher-level secondary schools or preparatory colleges focusing on classical learning.</note>—contributes little or nothing to obtaining Eloquence worthy of the name. But since this opinion seemed paradoxical not only to you but also to others, and the time for departing was pressing, you asked me to open my mind a little more fully on this argument, and as a sort of "penalty," to cast onto paper the thoughts I had meditated on at home...
