<page-num>630</page-num>
# LETTER ON THE VALUE OF THE ART OF RHETORIC.

...soothing me with the hope that you will subject this opinion of mine to a most fair examination, and if my discourse commends itself with some probability, you will not deprive me of due praise. Although this opinion of mine may seem paradoxical to some, it will harm no one. For we are not dealing here with <term>Articles of Religion</term><note>The fundamental dogmas or essential doctrines of a church, which were legally and socially dangerous to challenge in the 18th century.</note>, an argument in which, if someone departs from the path trodden by others and treads a new one, he is suspected of <term>Heresy</term><note>From the Greek 'hairesis' meaning choice; here referring to the defense of a grave religious error.</note>. The only question here is whether the **Art of Rhetoric**, as it is commonly taught in the Schools, contributes anything to obtaining true **Eloquence**, or not. Nor am I one who thinks this art should be banished from the Academies and Gymnasiums. Hence, there is no reason for the Professors of this art to be angry with me; for as far as I am concerned, they may teach this art with impunity and enjoy their salaries. But if my opinion displeases my friends, it will at least give them an opportunity to examine this argument a little more accurately. Concerning you, my dear **Candidus**, I promise myself much in this argument; for your sharp intellectual power and your fairness in judging the opinions of others are well known to me. But putting these things aside, I approach the matter itself. Right from the beginning, in setting out and proving my opinion, I will not argue in the manner of a Rhetorician, but of a Philosopher using <term>Syllogisms</term><note>A logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two shared premises (e.g., All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal).</note>. Thus I reason: If, without any knowledge of the **Art of Rhetoric**, all those things can nevertheless be obtained which are required to achieve a manly and genuine **Eloquence**, it follows that the Art of Rhetoric is a discipline we can easily do without. But the former is true. Since you will not deny that the <note>original: "Consequentiam majoris propositionis"</note> logical consequence of the major premise is legitimate, all my labor will consist in establishing the minor premise.

---

<note>(*) Before I had made up my mind to commit my thoughts on this subject to the press, I shared this letter—according to the custom accepted among friends—with **L. Candidus**, for the purpose that he might not only understand my opinion clearly but also subject it to examination and sincerely indicate what he thought should be noted. For I thought that in this way, greater light would be brought to this argument. He therefore sent me certain "strictures" (critiques), which I have placed below the text along with my response, so that the flow of the discourse in this letter is not too disturbed. First, therefore, he opposes my Syllogism with another, intended to demonstrate that if my logic had any value, it would simultaneously prove that an Orator could also do without a knowledge of the **Art of Logic**. His words are as follows: "If, without any knowledge of the art of logic, all those things can nevertheless be obtained which are required for the knowledge of the true and the false, it follows that the art of logic is a discipline we can easily do without. But the former is true."</note>

**I** indeed concede (to use the words of **Cicero** in his speech *For Archias* with a slight change) that there have been many men of excellent talent and virtue who, by a nearly divine quality of nature, were eloquent through themselves alone; and I add this, that more often nature without the skill of the art of logic has contributed much to the praise of eloquence. At the same time, however, I contend that when a skill in the art of logic is added to an exceptional and illustrious nature, then that "something" remarkable and singular emerges. Cicero acknowledged this elsewhere, namely in his work *Brutus*, where he said that the practice of Civil Law existed among many, but the *art* of it existed in **Servius Sulpicius** <note>A famous Roman jurist and contemporary of Cicero.</note> alone; which he could never... <meta>catchword: never...</meta>

<column-break/>

<page-num>631</page-num>
# LETTER ON THE VALUE OF THE ART OF RHETORIC.

...have achieved by the knowledge of law alone, unless he had additionally learned that art which teaches how to distribute the whole matter into parts; to explain what is hidden by defining it; to clear up what is obscure by interpreting it; first to see ambiguities, then to distinguish them, and finally to have a rule by which the true and the false might be judged, and what consequences follow from certain premises and what do not.

<margin>2.)</margin> But since the question here is what must be provided to all who wish to acquire true Eloquence for themselves, without regard for those who are endowed with a certain natural goodness of talent and excellent judgment without the cultivation of various disciplines (whose number, however, is <note>original: "albis corvis rarior"</note> **rarer than white crows**), I confess I cannot see how anyone can achieve the praise of a genuine Orator and discourse properly on matters of the greatest importance without a more accurate knowledge of the **art of thinking**. I say "genuine," for I am not unaware that many have obtained that praise among the common people and those ignorant of things without this art; however, that is not what is being disputed here.

<margin>3.)</margin> For the knowledge of the true or the false, there is required above all an accurate knowledge of the argument itself which is to be treated, which is to be drawn not from logic, but from the disciplines from which the argument is sought. Logic only weighs whether the matter proposed is precise according to the true laws of reasoning or not; therefore, knowledge of many things can be obtained without Logic, but it is the skill of the art of thinking that teaches whether the things brought forward are worthy of our assent.

---

<note>(**) The distinction between the **Philosophical** and the **Oratorical** framework—which is nevertheless essential—is not observed here; for the former intends only this one thing: that the pure intellect be convinced; but the latter is permitted to claim the whole man for itself.</note>

**Response:** I do not see that "essential distinction" between a discourse to be treated Philosophically or in the manner of Orators. For whatever must be performed by an Orator, when dealing with an argument that must be either explained or persuaded to others, I think the same must also be done by him who wishes to play the part of a Philosopher. We are not talking here about Metaphysics or Mathematics, but about **Theological**, **moral**, or **historical** truths, which do not exceed the capacity of the readers or listeners. Suppose, for example, the task is to commend some virtue. Here, the Philosopher and the Orator must perform the same task: namely, they are bound to exhibit an accurate idea of that virtue, to propose its true characteristics clearly, to commend its effects, excellence, dignity, and utility, and thus to instill it into the minds of the audience. Therefore, both must be performed by the Orator; namely, he must not only represent the genuine nature of the thing to be commended in the accepted manner of a Philosopher, but also induce its embrace with the weightiest arguments. I would believe that this cannot be performed unless the notions are repeated from the very character, nature, and dignity of the thing proposed. Arguments sought from the honorable, the useful, and the pleasant must be dug out, so to speak, from the very "innards" of a thing that is sufficiently known and proven.

it will appear how little that much-repeated skill in the <term>Art of Rhetoric</term><note>The formal study of persuasion and style, a cornerstone of classical education.</note> contributes to this. In my opinion, there are only three things required to achieve this. *The first is*: That the Orator understands correctly and accurately the nature and true character of the argument he must discuss—whether it is to be explained, proven, and recommended, or rejected and discouraged; whether it concerns a theological or philosophical argument; or whether it pertains to <term>Civil Law</term><note>Roman law or the legal system of a state.</note>, <term>Natural Law</term><note>A system of right or justice held to be common to all humans and derived from nature rather than the rules of society.</note>, or even history. He must have a clear view of all the foundations upon which the argument rests and its entire complexity; and finally, he must know well what difficulties the material is subject to, and how much help can be brought to dissipate and remove them. This is the first and most important thing required of a learned Orator in my opinion, so much so that if this one thing is missing, everything else that might be added is vain and of little use. From this, it is also clear that those who wish to prattle about any subject whatsoever will never attain the praise of true Eloquence. For how much is required to obtain a solid and accurate knowledge of even a single science is known to all who have a clear understanding of what it means to truly "know" something. *The second is*: That he proposes the matter itself in a pure, clear style, suited and adapted to the material being handled, and speaks in such a way that, according to the advice of **Quintilian**<note>Marcus Fabius Quintilianus (c. 35 – c. 100 AD), a Roman educator and rhetorician whose "Institutes of Oratory" was the standard textbook on the subject.</note>, the listeners—provided they are capable of understanding the matter—cannot fail to understand him. For *although* there is no inherent power in the style itself (properly speaking, as a collection of words and phrases) to either prove or reject an argument, it nevertheless contributes not a little to winning favor for the Orator; indeed, the arguments themselves are heard with greater pleasure and are accepted by those who are skilled in the elegance of the language the Orator uses. (*) But whatever becomes of that, nothing is more suited to the common crowd,
<meta>catchword: indeed</meta>

---

*The question is asked here: whether the Orator cannot help and direct his knowledge concerning the matter to be spoken of by the rules of Rhetoric?*

**Response:** I truly believe that Rhetorical Rules can do nothing to help the knowledge of a matter that is to be properly discussed. Knowledge of a thing must be drawn from the disciplines from which the argument is taken: the <term>Art of Logic</term><note>The study of valid reasoning and the structure of arguments.</note> commands the arrangement of the argument according to accurate laws of method; finally, the style must be pure, clearly elegant, and tempered to the nature and dignity of the argument. If these are present, I believe everything required to handle an argument properly is at hand.

---

(*) *<note>original: "Σαφήνεια"</note> Clarity is the Orator’s chief gift; but not the only one: and a speech admits a greater perfection while preserving clarity.*

**Response:** I would easily concede that a Speech is not completed by clarity of language alone: for one can speak elegantly and clearly and yet be a backward Orator. For where the legitimate treatment of the theme is missing, it is in vain that protection is sought in the clarity of language—

<header>LETTER ON THE VALUE OF THE ART OF RHETORIC. 633</header>

indeed, if we wish to confess the truth, it is suited to everyone, as it is appropriate for a speech to be set forth in clear language. *The third* and final requirement for attaining true Eloquence and fulfilling the duty of a learned Orator is this: that one not only sets forth and proves the subject at hand with clear language and the weightiest arguments, but also that he arranges what he is about to say in a harmonious order, according to the legitimate rules of the <term>Art of Thinking</term><note>Another term for Logic, specifically focused on the internal process of reasoning.</note>. He must know what should be placed first, what second, and so on in order, showing the weight of the arguments brought forth piece by piece, discarding everything that does nothing to prove the case, while preserving all those things that can place the subject of the discussion in a clear light. In my opinion, all things required for the duty of a genuine Orator should be referred to these three heads. Therefore, it can be obscure to no one where the true resources should be drawn from to fulfill the Orator's duty. *The first* resource is certainly placed in an accurate knowledge of the <term>Language</term><note>original: "Idiomatis"</note> that is to be used; to obtain this, when speaking of languages that are no longer in use today, more is required than is commonly thought. *The second* depends on an accurate knowledge of this or that discipline. *The third* resource must be drawn from the art of thinking itself and the rules it prescribes. From this, the learned reader will easily conclude that there are few Orators of true renown; for either most do not exactly understand the Theme they take up to handle, or they use a style so tangled and obscure that, although they may have equipped what was to be proven with sufficiently brilliant arguments, they nevertheless disturb and confuse the minds of the Listeners by the very barbarity and obscurity of their Speech; or finally, they are unskilled in the <term>Art of Reasoning</term>, plainly neglecting order in their logic, and drawing up their line of arguments in a backward fashion. I will not repeat now what I warned above: namely, that it is manifest from what has been said that those who wish to prattle about any things whatsoever (often differing from each other as much as the whole sky) can never carry away the praise of men endowed with masculine and genuine Eloquence from learned and experienced men. Therefore, one must stick to learning only a few disciplines, and their precepts must be known most accurately. Hence, even **Cicero**<note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BC), the Roman statesman and orator often considered the greatest master of Latin prose.</note> himself seems to me to have erred, who in his writings on this subject demanded more from an Orator than

it is sought: for a Speech receives greater perfection through the accurate treatment of the argument, through the legitimate arrangement of arguments, and finally through not only the clarity of the style, but also its purity, elegance, and use appropriate to the theme.

which can happen to a man—namely, such a great skill in very diverse things—rightly seems to exceed the capacity of the human mind. Therefore, everyone should "live within themselves" <note>original: *Secum ergo quisque habitare debet*; a call for self-awareness and focus on one's own strengths.</note> and exert all the strength of their talent to adorn the discipline they have cultivated above others. For what good do the categories of <term>Invention</term> <note>original: *loca Inventionis*; the "places" or methods used to find arguments in a speech.</note> supplied by <term>Rhetoricians</term> do for me when I am about to speak properly on some matter? But there will be a more convenient place to speak of these things below. Those who attribute much to the <term>Art of Rhetoric</term> are accustomed to appeal to its wonderful power, which they say it has not only over the minds and imaginations of men, but even over the human body itself.

You know that in our meeting many examples were brought from ancient and modern history to prove this, and daily experience was appealed to. I do not deny these things, but rather gladly admit them; yet I deny that this power and effectiveness in persuading arises from the science of the art of <term>Rhetoric</term>. Instead, it must be traced back to a threefold source: namely, the character and nature of the proposed argument; the elegance of the style and a way of speaking proportioned to the material; and finally, from the arrangement and order of the arguments. So that this may be better understood, we must attend *first* to the argument itself that the <term>Orator</term> takes up to treat; 2.) to the nature and diversity of persuasion; and 3.) to the character of minds and the various states of men. Regarding the argument itself, whatever its nature may be, it must either be proven and suggested, or disproven and discouraged. Now, an <term>Orator</term> can and should achieve this only through arguments; and without these, one cannot conceive how a persuasion worthy of the name could be born in the minds of men. This is true not only when it comes to commending truth or refuting error, but also when emotions must be stirred up or suppressed. Arguments are either those that shine with their own light, so that all who are skilled in the subject cannot help but grant them their assent; or they are those equipped with different degrees of probability according to the nature of things; or finally, it is necessary that the <term>Speech</term> be supported by false arguments or those that prove nothing. If a <term>Speech</term> is equipped with such clear and solid reasons that the Readers or Listeners—being knowledgeable of the matters proposed—attend only to the arguments and the nature of the matter, then assent cannot help but

arise in their minds. If to these are added purity and beauty of style, as well as a fitting arrangement of arguments, minds are rendered more attentive to hearing the arguments calmly and weighing them properly. (*) But only arguments can effect true persuasion. Thus, although a <term>Mathematician</term> about to demonstrate a geometric proposition might use a "barbarous" style <note>Meaning a style that is unpolished or lacks literary refinement.</note>, he would still convince a person skilled in the art, because the nature of this discipline is such that it cannot help but force assent from one who understands it. A <term>Speech</term> also produces true persuasion when it is equipped with more or fewer degrees of probability: for when the argument itself is of such a kind that it cannot be raised to geometric certainty—for example, in a historical narrative—one must be satisfied with probable reasons; the more or fewer they are in number, the greater or lesser the assent will be, and thus the persuasion will be stronger or weaker. But we always assume that the Listener or Reader attends to the arguments and has enough capacity to feel and judge the force of arguments that are more or less probable. Finally, if the speech is such that it is built on no reasons, or at least silly ones, and consists of mere verbal noise and "foot-and-a-half-long" words <note>original: *sesquipedalibus verbis*; a classical reference to pompous, overly long words.</note>, then I assert it is impossible for true persuasion to arise in the minds of those reading or hearing. <meta>This page continues the author's argument that true eloquence is rooted in logical clarity. Having previously dismissed the empty "figures" of traditional rhetoric, the author now addresses the common observation that illogical, bombastic speakers often succeed where rational speakers fail.</meta>

<page-num>636</page-num>
->### LETTER ON THE VALUE OF THE ART OF RHETORIC.<-

It is often observed, however, that a speech equipped with solid arguments—those that are either most evident or highly probable—frequently has little or no power over the mind. Conversely, an actor or a braggart <note>original: *thrasonem*; a reference to Thraso, the boastful soldier from Roman comedy, used here to describe a pretentious speaker.</note> who uses nothing but bombastic words <note>original: *ampullis verborum*; literally "jars of words," referring to inflated or puffed-up language.</note> often extorts agreement from men. Before I respond to this directly and uncover the causes of this human failing, we must *secondly* attend to the distinction between true and legitimate persuasion. **Legitimate persuasion** is that which arises from a careful comparison of ideas and the connection that exists between propositions. Thus, if a reader or listener is skilled in the language the orator uses, even if the speech itself lacks purity and elegance, they will not only understand the meaning of the things proposed but will also be able to explain them in their own words. For instance, when someone understands what virtue and duty are, they will easily see that there is a natural connection between the two; in such a case, the persuasion will be *legitimate*.

**Persuasion in name only**, however, occurs when men do not understand the argument itself, or understand it only very imperfectly. This happens if they are merely stunned by the sounds of voices; if they do not focus their mental powers on understanding things correctly; or if they are unskilled in the art of reasoning. Yet, in matters either plainly unknown or poorly perceived, they acquiesce to the mere sounds of words and imagine that they believe, though they cannot explain what they believe when questioned, since they were either unable or unwilling to weigh the matter. This is the evil produced by "Eloquence" in name only.

The most learned *Author of the Parrhasiana* <note>Referring to Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), a famous Swiss scholar and critic. *Parrhasiana* was one of his major works of criticism.</note> noted this long ago on *page 87*. Among other things, he says:

*The first defect is that those who allow themselves to be moved by a multitude of words, by bad reasons, or by thoughts that have nothing to do with the subject, are indeed dazed by the noise of the words and the great number of thoughts: but they understand nothing of the matter. Even though they imagine they have gained much from discourses of this nature which they have heard or read, they cannot say what they contain, nor reduce them to certain clear and followed headings. Everything is confused, everything is overturned in their minds; and as connection and order are of infinite use to the memory—which becomes troubled and erased without their help—these people have soon forgotten what they had read or heard.* <note>The original text provides this quote in French.</note>

Having weighed this distinction between legitimate and false persuasion, it will be easy to respond to your objection. It is true that many are not persuaded by the most evident and certain reasons; but the question is not what even the best arguments can or cannot achieve in the minds of this or that person, but what they ought to achieve by their very nature.

<meta>catchword: Certainly</meta>

<page-num>637</page-num>
->### LETTER ON THE VALUE OF THE ART OF RHETORIC.<-

(*) Certainly, if you depart from reasons and arguments, there is nothing that can excite true persuasion in the mind. The reasons for this quite clear fact can be easily rendered. To be sure, many men are not moved by the most solid arguments, either because they cannot understand the nature of the argument, or because they do not want to. A weakness of intellect prevents many from allowing the weightiest reasons to exert any force on their minds; many are unskilled in the art of reasoning and meditation; others are simply stunned by a heap of words and various figures. Is it any wonder that even the most solid arguments do not extort agreement from men of this sort? Others, however, refuse to yield to arguments because, due to a flighty nature, they are not accustomed to weighing things, being dragged by a certain rapidity from the contemplation of one object to another. In others, corrupt passions stand in the way. You could argue a hundred times against greed, lust, and so on, and you will not move a man devoted to these vices even a tiny bit. On the other hand, men can...

<sig>Llll 3</sig>

---

(*) <margin>You say: "One must certainly consider not what a philosophical demonstration <term>philosophical demonstration: a formal logical proof used in academic philosophy</term> ought to achieve by its nature, but what it actually achieves among the majority of men. For it is of great importance that the greatest part of men, and not just a few philosophers, be persuaded of these or those truths. If this persuasion cannot be obtained through the evidence of demonstration because of the incapacity of the many, is there not some other method of persuasion?"</margin>

**Response I:** I think your words must be taken with a grain of salt <note>original: *cum grano salis*</note> when you contend we should look at what a demonstration achieves in the majority rather than its nature. If this were universally true, the most excellent part of the art of speaking—which is perfected by the gravity and weight of arguments—would perish. For who does not know that the majority of men are stunned by words? They take a semi-fanatic for a distinguished orator; they are moved by the shallowest reasoning, analogies, and bombastic words; they understand the matters themselves either not at all or obscurely; they do not attend to the force of arguments; or finally, they are prevented by a tide of passions from wanting to recall the orator’s points to their minds. If a speech must be tempered to their taste, then it seems to me that Rhetoric—even that written by the most excellent man—is finished.

**II:** When we speak of <term>philosophical demonstration</term>, we are not talking about metaphysical or mathematical proof, which exceeds the capacity of most listeners, but about **moral demonstration**. This is the kind of proof that all people are bound to understand if they are capable of knowing religion or the duties common to all men. This demonstration rests on evident or probable reasons, which we believe are arranged so that they can be understood by anyone who is attentive and not entirely dull.

**III:** An orator can obtain the persuasion that ought to arise from moral demonstration if they choose a subject-matter tempered to the intellects of all; if they use arguments that are clear and easy to grasp; and if they strive with all care to avoid obscurity, ambiguities, wordplay, and affected loftiness in their style. Indeed, all who prepare themselves to speak on matters of religion or common duties must, before all else, believe and be persuaded that men who attend properly to arguments and incentives can perceive the force of the truth presented. Unless you assume this, all speeches will be in vain.

<summary>This page distinguishes between "legitimate persuasion" based on logic and "false persuasion" based on emotional wordplay, arguing that while many people are swayed by bombast, a true orator must rely on "moral demonstration" that appeals to common human reason.</summary>

men are led to some form of persuasion, though it be imaginary and vain, for various reasons. They often find something in the face and gesture of the Orator that seems to add weight to his words. Hence, even the mute and the mimes invite men to agreement; for others, where arguments fail, the emotions seize them. The common people, and those like them, marvel at and praise a speech even if it is provided with no solid arguments, clothed in no elegance of language, and protected by no order or artifice; indeed, they often praise it more the less they understand the argument.

Strictly speaking, a wise man ought to be led to approve or reject something by reasons alone. And how, finally, could it be that these speeches of Generals could excite a true and solid persuasion in the minds of soldiers, when it is manifest that they are for the most part built upon false and fictional arguments? For they primarily bring forward those things which can shake fear out of their minds—even if without cause—while they press all other things into deep silence. Highly learned men, well-versed in this subject, noted this long ago. *The most learned Jean Le Clerc* <note>original: "Eruditissimus Clericus"; Le Clerc (1657–1736) was a famous Swiss theologian and scholar</note> in Part II, Section I, chapter XVI, page 319 of his *Art of Criticism*, pronounces on this matter in the following way: *If we seek the reason (he says) why we are so drawn to figures of speech, we will find that it is of such a kind that it necessarily produces obscurity. Figures add such force to an argument that is adorned by them because they show the listener or reader only that part of it which is most fit to move him; all those things which could stop that emotion are removed, or rather, hidden.* If a soldier must be encouraged to fight, the horror of death—which is naturally in everyone—is pressed into deep silence, as is the extreme caution that ought to be used when it comes to shedding human blood, and other things which a wise man would then seriously weigh. He abstains from ominous words of that sort. Glory is proposed to the soldier, as is the victory to be won, wealth to be gathered from spoils, rewards, honors, etc. By these means, it happens that he turns his mind away from those former concerns and, intent on these others, becomes eager to undertake a task that is in itself the most foul of all: the work of a most dreadful executioner against the Innocent. An example can be found in the Speech of Caecina in Tacitus's *Annals*, Book I, Chapter 64. When the soldiers were terrified by the difficulty of the paths, a setback in battle, the loss of baggage, and the fear of the looming enemy, he showed them that their only safety was in arms; they must stay within the rampart, then break out, and by that breakout reach the Rhine. He warned that if they fled, more forests, deeper swamps, and the cruelty of the enemies remained. But for the victors, there would be honor and glory, things dear at home and honorable in the camp. Tacitus adds that he was silent about the adversities, whether present or future, so that their terror would not be increased by the image of past slaughter, nor would a similar fate be feared for the future. So says *the famous Le Clerc*. But, you say, they nevertheless fought bravely for the most part after hearing these speeches. This is true: but how many battles were fought in the past, and are fought today, which the soldiers entered without being moved or incited by any speeches from their Generals? And yet those same soldiers fought spiritedly—

---

<page-num>641</page-num>
## LETTER ON THE VALUE OF THE ART OF RHETORIC. 641

—or rather, whether they wanted to or not, they were forced to resist the enemy, and they protected their lives as much as they could. Often both the Generals of war and the soldiers know, and indeed know well, that the war they are waging is unjust; but because they generally regard the just and the unjust as equal, because they cannot flee due to fear and necessity, or because they persuade themselves that by this way, and no other, can they conveniently provide themselves with food and clothing, or they long for rich booty, etc. Once the signal for battle is given, they rush spiritedly into the fight. Now, do you think the soldiers believe for that reason that they had to fight so fiercely for entirely legitimate causes? Can persuasion in the mind of the same man be solid and foolish at the same time, being built on no reasons at all? If anyone wanted to conclude that because men are often moved by foolish reasons and an empty noise of words, there is equal efficacy in all reasons—whether solid or weak—that person would deservedly be laughed at by all people of sound mind. From this it is clear that a distinction must rightly be made between "true persuasion" and "imaginary persuasion." You must also remember, my dear *friend* <note>original: "Candide," likely referring to a "candid reader" or a specific correspondent</note>, that genuine Eloquence is only the fruit of true Erudition; only Erudition and an accurate knowledge of a certain theme supply the arguments that necessarily flow from the nature of the material to be treated. From that, finally, is born that true persuasion, that splendid light in the minds of men. Other things have little weight in extorting assent from a perceptive man. As for the emotions, I do not deny that men are greatly moved by them to act in one way or another; therefore, it is also the Orator's duty to learn by what method he can stir them up or calm them down. But that should only be done after the argument itself has been properly explained and proved with solid reasons. In this way, the Orator can have hope that his incitements will exercise their power on minds illuminated by the light of truth. *To this end* (I use the words of the most celebrated *Werenfels* <note>Samuel Werenfels (1657–1740), a Swiss theologian known for his work on oratory and hermeneutics</note>, who beautifully understood what an Orator must provide and demonstrated it by his own example): *the art of stirring and calming emotions is not best understood by one who has grown old in learning the rules of Rhetoric, but by one who has learned to know himself first, and then other men, as deeply as possible, both through perceptive attention and long experience.* (*) Truthfully—

<note>
(*) This is precisely what a genuine system of the art of rhetoric ought to explain: by what reasons these or those emotions can be stirred, and by which they can be calmed. Common Rhetoric books do not teach this, and if they do hand down anything of the sort, it is borrowed from elsewhere. To achieve this, the character of men must be properly understood; the origin and nature of the emotions must be drawn from the wide fields of Philosophy; one must spend time with wise men and those who are most powerful in speaking; and one must study the books of the most excellent men, which [abound] with examples and speeches...
</note>

<summary>The author argues that military oratory is often a form of manipulation that hides the grim reality of war to incite soldiers, contrasting this "imaginary persuasion" with true eloquence based on logic and deep knowledge. He concludes that a real orator must understand human psychology and philosophy rather than just following dry rhetorical rules.</summary>

...most famous is that ancient saying of Solon: <note>original: "τον λογον εἰδωλον εἰναι των ἐργων"</note> "speech is the image of deeds." And that of Plato: <note>original: "Οἱος ὁ λογος, τοιουτος ὁ τροπος"</note> "As the speech is, so is the character." <note>original: "Qualis Oratio, talis vita" — literally "As the speech, so the life."</note> To that end, he who wishes to fulfill the duty of an Orator with praise, and to sway the minds of other men through speech, ought above all else to descend into himself. He must learn his own mind and temperament, and discern by what reasons and incentives his own emotions are stirred or restrained; then, indeed, he ought to transfer these insights to other men. Certain emotions are common to all men, while others are private to individuals: compare the Excellent *Pope’s Essay on Man, Epistle II.* <note>Alexander Pope (1688–1744); his "Essay on Man" was a highly influential philosophical poem in the 18th century.</note> From what has been said so far, it is simultaneously manifest that the so-called "art of rhetoric" contributes nothing, or very little, toward obtaining that true Eloquence. For how do those <term>topical locations</term> <note>Loci topici: traditional categories in logic and rhetoric used to find arguments, such as "cause," "effect," or "definition."</note> regarding *notation, efficient cause, form, matter, and end* help me to speak properly on a grave subject? Is not a knowledge of the idiom and an accurate understanding of the theme to be treated sufficient? What of those anxious precepts concerning the "invention" of themes? Or regarding figures of speech and thought? Emotion itself will teach the one speaking which words he should chiefly use to express the feelings of his mind. Those "figures" are like technical terms, which can be learned without the art of rhetoric. Among the most recent teachers of the art of rhetoric, the celebrated G. C. Myllerus <note>Gottlob Christian Miller (1712–1763), a German theologian and rhetorician.</note> should be mentioned. He says the following regarding rhetorical figures in his *The Wisdom of the Orator Systematically Outlined, page 101:*

*Perhaps, he says, those who remember their old rhetorical school-knowledge might demand from us a special treatise on the Figures. Yet we release ourselves from such a duty, which consists of the recitation of many names and yet does not help achieve the goal of teaching others figurative language; primarily, the Figures are the language of Emotion. This [emotion] will teach everyone their own nature better than art. If the naming of the Figures still has any use at all, it manifests itself in the judgment of the language of a passion, so that one can label such things by name.*

Indeed, the frequent use of these figures cuts off the force of arguments and causes men to be stup-

<margin>
...having used eloquent speech, they treated matters of the greatest importance not without use. But the sterile little precepts of the art of rhetoric, born in the shadows of men, have very little value. These things, however, which I have brought forward thus far, I gladly permit to be judged by you, my dear Candidus, and the learned crowd of friends. For the rest, I do not deny that it is sometimes permitted for one or many to use a fictional speech where necessity demands. The Interpreters of Natural Law deal with this at greater length when they explain the duties of those engaged in conversation. But the art of rhetoric hands down no rules concerning these.

<meta>catchword: tout</meta>

-efied by words and their various combinations. Those figurative speeches are the effects of the imagination. This, however, very easily leads the Orator away from the rules of genuine Eloquence, and it is not in everyone's power to restrain it within limits. The celebrated *Barbeyrac* <note>Jean Barbeyrac (1674–1744), a famous jurist who translated the sermons of the English Archbishop John Tillotson into French.</note> expressed this elegantly in the preface to the second volume of the Illustrious *Tillotson's* Sermons: *However little (he says) one lets go of the reins of the imagination, it never fails to outrun Judgment. It is a fiery horse, but skittish or blind: If one does not have a very firm hand and is not perpetually attached to regulating its steps, it can only lead us across fields, and make us stumble heavily, or throw us into a precipice. The grossest errors, the most absurd thoughts, the most frivolous reasonings, slide in easily by favor of a bold figure, a pompous description, an assemblage of metaphorical expressions and ingenious turns, or a well-cadenced period. Instead, if things appeared in their natural state and stripped of foreign ornaments, all this false brilliance vanishing, their deformity could not be hidden. The character of truth is an amiable simplicity: as she needs only herself to instill herself into minds, she asks only for the natural ornaments that suit her, and which let her be seen clearly as she is.* What she has that is most noble and great is always very far removed from "swelling" [bombast]. What I have said so far regarding the nature of true Eloquence and the meager use of the art of rhetoric, I will confirm by the testimony of a man who held the laws of both reasoning and speaking in the most accurate regard. This is the Illustrious Locke, <note>The author is quoting from a French translation of John Locke’s "An Essay Concerning Human Understanding."</note> who in *Human Understanding, Book III, Chapter X, page 641 and following, Basel Edition,* discusses it thus: *Since what is called wit and imagination is better received in the world than real knowledge and dry truth, one will have trouble looking at figurative terms and allusions as an imperfection and a true abuse of Language. Admit that in discourses where we seek rather to please and divert than to instruct and perfect the judgment, one can hardly count as faults these sorts of ornaments borrowed from figures. But if we wish to represent things as they are, we must recognize that, except for order and clarity, all the art of Rhetoric, all these artificial applications and figures made of words according to the rules that Eloquence has invented, serve no other purpose than to insinuate false ideas into the Mind, to move the passions, and thereby to seduce the Judgment; so that they are, in effect, perfect deceptions. And consequently, it is in vain for the art of Oratory to seek acceptance or even admiration...*

All these different traits—it is beyond doubt—must be absolutely avoided in all discourses intended for instruction; one cannot but regard them as great defects, whether in the language itself or in the person who employs them wherever truth is at stake. It would be useless to state here what these rhetorical turns are, or how many different species of them exist: the books on Rhetoric, with which the world is abundantly provided, will inform those who are ignorant of them. One thing only I cannot help remarking is how little care and interest men take in the *preservation* and advancement of truth, since it is to these fallacious arts that the first rank and rewards are given. It is, I say, quite visible that men love dearly to deceive and to be deceived, since Rhetoric—this powerful instrument of error and deceit—has its salaried Professors, is taught publicly, and has always enjoyed a great reputation in the world. This is so true that I do not doubt that what I have just said will be regarded as the effect of extreme audacity, not to say of an unexampled brutality. For Eloquence, much like the "fair sex," <note>original: "beaux Sexe." A common 18th-century metaphor comparing the persuasive, ornamental, and sometimes "fickle" nature of rhetoric to contemporary social views of women.</note> possesses charms too powerful for one to be permitted to speak against her: and it is in vain that one would uncover the faults of certain deceptive arts by which men take pleasure in being deceived.

Thus says that famous philosopher. <note>This preceding section in French is a close paraphrase of John Locke's *An Essay Concerning Human Understanding* (1689), Book III, Chapter 10, where he critiques rhetoric as a tool for deception.</note> From this we also see, young men, that although students have often committed the entire art of rhetoric to memory, when they ought to discourse properly upon some subject, they hesitate and seek help from Rhetoric in vain. The reason is readily apparent: for either they are not capable of "style"—that is, the art of speaking purely, neatly, and clearly—or they have only a superficial knowledge of the argument they are to treat; or finally, they are ignorant of the art of thinking and the proper laws of method. Hence, such Orations are for the most part composed either by the Professors of rhetoric themselves or by friends. Or, if the youths themselves apply their minds to writing, you will find everything so obscure, so poorly connected, and furnished with such weak arguments, that you will easily perceive the good fellows have tormented themselves in vain. I said above that Eloquence is the fruit only of true Erudition. <note>Erudition: broad, deep learning across multiple disciplines.</note> From this, in my opinion, it follows that young men should only be led to deliver Orations at a more mature age; certainly only at that time when we can be persuaded, not without reason, that they have thoroughly learned the art of logic and rightly understand the subject of which they are to speak. This latter point can easily be established by a Professor through private conversations. It is also evident from this that certain masters of the art of rhetoric act ridiculously...

<sig>Mmmm 3</sig>

...who prescribe such themes for their students to pursue in writing which are plainly unknown or little known to them. Thus I remember, once, a fifteen-year-old student was forced by necessity to deliver an Oration on the *Essenes*, <note>A Jewish sect of the Second Temple period. The author argues a teenager would have no context for such a complex historical and theological topic.</note> whose very name the youth had never even heard, let alone being able to speak properly of their origin, dogmas, and rituals. It is manifest, moreover, from what I have said, that true Orators are very rare. I am not one who would wish, or even be able, to snatch away the crown that clings with much praise to the heads of the most famous men of Greece and Rome—to say nothing of many moderns. But when I consider how little care the Ancients had for the "art of thinking," and how entirely they were occupied in cultivating <term>Dialectics</term>, <note>Dialectics: here referring to the Scholastic or Sophistic method of arguing for or against any position regardless of the truth.</note> I begin to think that their Eloquence has been praised beyond measure. For it is well known that their Dialectic consisted in this: namely, that they would dispute on either side of any argument without any regard for the truth. Indeed, some went so far as to say that it was permitted for a Rhetorician to use openly false arguments. They taught, as *Titius Castratius* <note>A Roman teacher of rhetoric mentioned in the works of Aulus Gellius.</note> attests in *Gellius, Book I, Chapter IV*, that it is permitted for a Rhetorician to use false, deceitful, and catchy sentiments, provided they are plausible and can creep in by some trickery to move the minds of men. Therefore, he said it was a disgrace if one should leave anything in a bad cause undefended or unattacked. See the famous Le Clerc <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), a famous Swiss theologian and scholar.</note> treating this subject at greater length in his *Art of Criticism, Chapter XVII, Part II, Section I*, to which you may add the brilliant Lucian’s <note>Lucian of Samosata (c. 125 – 180 AD), a satirist who mocked the hollow rhetoric of his day.</note> little book on the *Precepts of Rhetoricians*.

This, my *dear friend*, is my opinion on the use of the art of Rhetoric. If you think I have erred, it only remains for you to teach me better things. Before I put an end to this letter, I shall transcribe two passages from the ancient Greeks (since I know you are captivated by the reading of them) regarding this subject. The first is from *Myson* in *Diogenes Laertius*. He, on page 96, speaks thus: <note>original: "Δει μη εκ των λογων τα πραγματα, αλλ’ εκ των πραγματων τους λογους ζητειν..."</note> "One must not seek things from words, but words from things; for things are not completed for the sake of words, but speech exists for the sake of things." The second is from a fragment of an uncertain Poet, which the illustrious and *Great Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), a foundational Dutch jurist and scholar.</note> brought forth in his excerpts from the Tragic and Comic Poets, page 461. The words sound thus: <note>original: "Ω παι γενοιτ’ αν κωι λεγομενοι ευ λογοι ψευδεις..."</note> "O Son, often a polished speech is false. Meanwhile, truth is overcome by charming deceits: but this is not therefore the best thing, but rather one's nature and virtue. I will admit he who is strong in tongue is learned; but yet I have thought, and think now, that facts are always to be preferred to words."

So, farewell my friend, and continue to favor me.

### Section I.

<image-desc>Decorative square woodcut initial 'Q' with foliate scrolls and floral patterns surrounding the central letter.</image-desc>

As soon as—by God's will and merciful guidance, and with the support of the *most Distinguished and Celebrated Presidents of this Illustrious Academy*—I was appointed to the instruction of the more sacred disciplines, I clearly perceived that I had been given the duty not only to explain, both publicly and privately, the most holy decrees and precepts of the Christian Religion with the zeal, clarity, and solidity of the best literature, and where necessary, to defend against the clever tricks <note>original: "strophas." Refers to rhetorical or logical evasions used by opponents.</note> of dissenting arguments; but also, in accordance with the laudable custom of our ancestors for public exercises, to explain and prove such chapters of Theology as might recommend themselves by their weight and utility. Therefore, I had determined within myself that as soon as time permitted, I would apply my mind to the elaboration of a serious subject. However, after it was announced how many labors I was to endure in a short space of time, and when I felt at once how many and how great were the tasks arising from the very nature and promotion of this new office, I saw that all the time and leisure for properly conducting a new inquiry had been snatched from me. I looked about, therefore, to see if there was anything stored in my desks that was neither entirely foreign to our purpose nor unworthy of the persona which I now, by the grace of God, sustain. I discovered among other things which I had scribbled on paper while I had some leisure, an *Historical and Theological Dissertation* written by me, which—if not for its erudition—might perhaps recommend itself by the novelty of its argument, and would not be entirely foreign to my office. Therefore, since not my will, but time and leisure failed me for offering other things, I submit this work to your judgment, *Most Distinguished and Celebrated Presidents*, with all due respect, and I pray that you may be willing to judge kindly of this first specimen, such as it is. I promise at the same time that in the future I shall expend every effort and diligence so that I may offer other chapters of sacred discipline more closely suited to the Students of Holy Letters.

II. In writing about the Visions which are said to have occurred to certain Christians in the first four centuries after the passing of Christ and the Apostles, I advise before all else that I will not be dealing with the origin, nature, or certainty of Visions, nor the method of distinguishing them from other fantasies; nor will I treat the Visions that were offered to many in the Old and New Testaments. For this would be entirely foreign to the goal we have set for ourselves. We shall do this one thing: inquire into what should be thought about the majority of Visions mentioned by the writers of Ecclesiastical History in the first centuries after the passing of Christ and the Apostles. That this subject has not yet been sufficiently thrashed out by Learned Men will be evident if the Educated Reader compares these meditations of ours with the labors of others.

Since, however, the Learned go in different directions regarding this matter, and Men of great name not only fiercely defend most of the Visions said to have happened to Christians of the first centuries, but also think that those who call many of them into doubt detract much from the excellence of the Christian Religion; I see clearly that two things must be performed by me before I come to individual examples. The *first* is to state in what spirit I believe the writings of the ancient Teachers of the Christian Church should be read, and what authority they hold with me. The *second* is to bring forward certain rules according to which, as a standard, I have weighed and examined those Visions.

Regarding the *first* point, the Teachers of the Church, whom they call *Fathers*, can be considered in a threefold respect: namely 1.) as *Men*, 2.) as *Christians*, and 3.) finally as *Scholars* who shared their thoughts on various matters, especially sacred ones, with others. If I consider them as *Men*, I think everything should be attributed to them that usually happens to human nature. Therefore, the Fathers are equally subject to all infirmities as other men. It would not be necessary to advise this, were there not learned men so infatuated by the authority of the Fathers that they extol them beyond the human lot. By this very act, however—as experience has taught—they have detracted from their reputation rather than added to it. It is necessary, therefore, that above all we remember the Fathers were *Men*. By this it will be established that all things could happen to them which we know to have

<column-break/>

<page-num>649</page-num>
<header>ON THE VISIONS OF THE FIRST CHRISTIANS.</header>
<sig>Nnnn</sig>
<meta>catchword: ho- (ctissi-)</meta>

happened to men of our own age. Whatever is accustomed to be born from the nature and character of the intellect, will, appetite, and temperament, or from education and training—whether they be good or bad—all those things, I think, must be asserted as being able to happen even to the *Fathers*. I do not think any man of sound mind will stir up a controversy with me over this.

I pass, therefore, to the second respect. Namely, the *Fathers* can be considered as *Christians*, that is, as those who embraced the decrees of the Christian Religion as divine. In that respect, all students of the most holy discipline, if indeed they were devoted to it from the heart, are to be praised; for there is no doubt that they acted most rightly and wisely who gave their name to the most holy and excellent of all Religions. However, Christians can conveniently be divided into three classes. There are *First* those who have nothing but the name, and are thus either contaminated by crimes or are mere Hypocrites; in the *second* class you may place those who can indeed be called pious, but are at the same time subject to many infirmities, whether you look at their knowledge or their actions; there are *finally* those who stand out for their singular zeal for piety. In light of this threefold respect, it will be admitted by the sensible that the *Fathers*, as Christians, must be judged in different ways. The standard according to which they must be judged are the eternal laws of truth and virtue, elicited both by reasoning alone and handed down by Christ and the Apostles in the sacred writings. Therefore, when looking at the first character I find that some *Father* gave only his name to the Christian Religion, but in life and morals basely fell away from the most holy rule of discipline, I think a spade should be called a spade <note>original Latin: *scapham scapham appellandam esse*</note>; for natural and divine laws are not accustomed to change according to the diversity of times and regions. If those *Fathers* are pious, but subject to many blemishes—whether you look to the intellect or the will—they must be judged similarly to how it ought to be done for Christians of our own age: things worthy of praise are to be praised and followed; sins which human nature takes little care against are not to be excessively exaggerated, nor yet at the same time approved. It is most manifest that people have very often sinned in this regard. A shameful error of some *Father*, or an uncontrollable emotion, is excused by their other admirers; but where someone from the moderns has stumbled against that same stone, it is a heresy, or a vice to be marked with a black coal <note>original Latin: *atro carbone notandum* — a Roman expression for something judged as bad, unlucky, or worthy of condemnation.</note>. Certainly, if the admirers of the *Fathers* were willing to see as sharply into the vices of the *Fathers* as is done with the Writers and Teachers of our own age, I do not know in what place many of them would have to be held. Finally, where it is clear that some *Father* shone with singular virtues, and ho...

<header>ON THE VISIONS OF THE EARLY CHRISTIANS.</header>
<meta>catchword: in</meta>

One who has constantly adhered to the precepts of the most upright discipline, as far as is possible in this cloud of worldly affairs, is to be extolled with worthy praise. However, I think the following points must be observed: First, when the virtues of the <term>Patres</term> <note>Latin: "Fathers"—referring to the influential leaders and writers of the early Christian Church.</note> are to be judged, they must be weighed according to the standard of right reason and Revelation. If you depart from this rule, everything is surrounded by darkness. Many, when they judge the virtues of the Fathers, seem to hold the **Paradoxes of the Stoics** <note>The Stoics were ancient philosophers known for extreme moral rigor; the author suggests some people judge the Fathers by these harsh standards rather than by Christian teachings.</note> as the standard for their judgments rather than the decrees of right reason and the precepts of Christ. 2.) Where neither the laws of reason nor revelation insist upon or demand certain actions, but those same actions arose from ignorance, superstition, or temperament, those actions are neither to be praised nor represented as an example for other Christians to follow. 3.) Since piety does not prevent a person from being able to err—and it is well-established that many errors regarding theoretical and practical principles were committed by Fathers otherwise flourishing in the praise of piety—it is right and permissible for anyone to challenge those errors, as has been shown by very learned men, especially **Daillé**, **Whitby**, **Le Clerc**, and **Barbeyrac**. <note>These were 17th and 18th-century scholars known for their critical approach to the authority of the early Church Fathers.</note> 4.) Although we do not deny that many Christians shone with greater virtues—namely piety, sincerity, and zeal for the glory of God—the closer they were to the times of the Apostles, with God sharpening their virtues through a sad fate <note>Referring to the era of persecutions and martyrdom.</note>, it must not be thought that they were devoid of all errors and blemishes, or that no one is truly pious unless they have been exercised in the same way. From this it follows that singular actions, to which they were called by a singular dispensation of divine providence, are not to be held as a universal rule for all Christians to imitate. For while the true love of God is one and the same, though it exerts itself in various ways, everyone in whose heart that affection resides is to be considered truly pious, even if the virtues of others shone more brightly according to the requirements of their times.

Finally, in the third place, I consider the Fathers as **Learned Men**, or public Teachers, who wished to communicate their thoughts on various matters, especially sacred ones, with others. And here again, they either report events, or they reason about divine and human things as Philosophers, or finally, they perform the duty of Theologians. When they play the part of **Historians**, they either make mention of things done in their own age in the State or the Church, or they report those things which have been handed down by others. If they discourse on things done in their own age, I ask whether they are eye-witnesses or "ear-witnesses" <note>original: "testes... auriti"—meaning those who heard about events from others rather than seeing them.</note>; whether the things viewed in themselves are credible or not; whether they have conceded anything to prejudiced opinions; and what other things are required in 

<column-break/>

<page-num>651</page-num>

<sig>Nnnn 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: How (Quam)</meta>

in examinations of that kind. If, however, they make mention of things done before the times in which they themselves lived, then I see whether the records to which they appeal have survived to our age or not. If the former is true, I think those things said by those Fathers should be compared with the records of those writers, and it must be seen whether they correctly grasped the mind of the authors or not; whether they added or subtracted anything from them; and so forth. If the latter is true, it can only be said with difficulty whether they followed the mind of the authors in all things; meanwhile, it should be looked into whether others make mention of those same writers or not, etc.

If the Fathers act as **Philosophers**, nothing else is required than that we weigh their reasonings according to the standard of right reason. For since the Fathers had no other instrument for weighing the reasoning of men than we do—and the objects of Philosophy, whether looking toward Mathematics and Physics or toward moral disciplines, have always been the same—indeed, in the judgment of all who are wise, they have been more correctly weighed by moderns, everyone sees that it is permissible to refute Fathers who reason less correctly and to weigh their arguments. However, since it is well-known that most of the Fathers of the first centuries were captivated by a love for **Pythagorean-Platonic Philosophy**, it can easily be judged what kind of Philosophers they were. For this philosophy was resting on no certain principles; it promised sublime things in appearance, but if you inspect the matters themselves, it contained nothing but uncertain, vague, and even foolish decrees. (*) Finally, if the Fathers deal with **sacred matters**, nothing is easier—if you bid all prejudiced opinions to be gone for a while—than to know for certain whether their opinions agree with the Holy Scriptures or not, and how much should therefore be attributed to them in this part. Theologians either interpret the Holy Scriptures, or explain the decrees of the Christian Religion, or challenge dissenters, or finally, they hand down and confirm the precepts of the Christian Religion pertaining to morals. Therefore, when the Fathers explain the Holy Scriptures, one must walk with them into the field of **Philology** <note>The study of language and literary texts.</note> and see whether they rightly perceived the nature and character of the Greek and Hebrew languages. Since the general rules of Grammarians and Critics are the same among everyone, and thus the Fathers ought to have required their interpretations to meet that standard no less than we do, it is manifest that the Fathers are to be followed where they reason agreeably to those rules, but are to be deserted where they err and bring forward foolish interpretations.

(*) The most learned man, and my very dear friend, **Johann Jakob Brucker**, is worthy to be read on this subject in his *History of Philosophy*, Volume IV, part II. <note>Brucker was a pioneer in the history of philosophy, known for his critical view of how Neoplatonism influenced early Christianity.</note>

# ON THE VISIONS OF THE EARLY CHRISTIANS

No learned person today is ignorant of how disgracefully—and indeed how very frequently—the <term>Patres</term> <note>Latin: "Fathers"—the influential leaders and writers of the early Christian Church.</note> were occupied with this argument, nor how many clumsy and convoluted explanations and allegories they devised.
&emsp;Since the Holy Scripture is the sole and infallible rule of what is to be believed, it is necessary that we examine the dogmas of religion handed down by the *Fathers* against it, as if against a <term>touchstone</term> <note>Original Latin: "lydium lapidem," literally a "Lydian stone," used to test the purity of gold.</note>. Since we are today equipped with equally good—if not better—tools for explaining and drawing out the meaning of the divine oracles, and since the sacred book is in everyone's hands, it will not be difficult to judge whether or not the *Fathers* depart from the decrees of the Prophets, Christ, and the Apostles. Therefore, where it is clear that they follow preconceived opinions accepted from their youth, or views based on false interpretations, they are deservedly to be criticized; but where they draw their decrees from the clear fountains of Revelation, they are to be approved.
&emsp;If the *Fathers* "enter the arena" <note>A metaphor for engaging in public theological debate.</note> against the **Heretics**, we must see whether they properly weighed the points of controversy and represented the opinions of the Heretics candidly and sincerely; whether they attacked their opinions with weighty and solid arguments; and whether or not they exaggerated the heretics' errors or used various tricks born of spite, and so forth. If the opinions of the Heretics are known and understood, this examination can be easily completed. One need only compare the arguments of the *Fathers* with the decrees of right reason and Revelation; and here, according to whether they performed their duty well or otherwise, we judge that the *Fathers* should be praised or blamed. It is to be lamented, however, that the writings of most of those men—and the most ancient of the so-called Heretics—have perished. Because of this, it is difficult to define what those men actually thought. If the *Fathers* attributed nothing false to these men, we would have to conclude that most of them (and the most ancient ones) were impostors or fanatics. But experience shows that the slightest erroneous opinions were often regarded by the *Fathers* as the gravest errors, and many things were wrongly attributed to those in error.
&emsp;Finally, where the *Fathers* deal with the precepts of the Christian religion, we have at hand not only the laws of eternal truth and virtue, but the precepts and decrees of Christ himself, the infallible Teacher. If the *Fathers* adapt their precepts to this standard, they are pleasing. If, however, they merely play the rhetorician and pass judgment on Christ’s commands based on the clumsy opinions of philosophers; if they urge certain precepts beyond measure; if they defend superstitious opinions and customs against the eternal rules of truth and right... 
<meta>catchword: que</meta>

<column-break/>

<page-num>653</page-num>
# ON THE VISIONS OF THE EARLY CHRISTIANS

...ness, then we bid the Fathers "keep their business to themselves" <note>Original Latin: "res suas sibi habere jubemus"—a Roman legal formula for divorce, here used as a scholarly dismissal of their authority on those specific points.</note> and we adhere firmly to the decrees of right reason and the precepts of Christ.
&emsp;With this mindset, and according to the laws stated above, I have been occupied thus far in reading the *Fathers*. Whether I have done so rightly or wrongly, let *Learned Men* and those skilled in these matters judge. I at least believe that by acting in this way, I neither detract from the authority of the *Fathers* nor attribute more to them than is fair—though everyone who has even a slight taste for the history of scholarly affairs knows that errors have often been committed in both directions.
&emsp;III. But it is time for me to say what method I used in evaluating the **Visions** that are said to have occurred to certain Christians of the primitive Church. To that end, I will set forth in order certain rules that I thought should be observed, and I will confirm them in the examples that follow:
&emsp;*This is the first rule:* Visions could happen—and in actual fact did happen—to Christians in the first centuries after the departure of Christ and the Apostles. Since nothing can be shown on the part of God, nor on the part of man, to prove either that visions are impossible in themselves, or that God was unwilling to grant such things after the passing of Christ and the Apostles, there is in our opinion nothing to prevent us from asserting that visions could happen to Christians just as they happened to those who lived in the age of the Prophets, Christ, and the Apostles. Indeed, since brilliant testimonies can be brought forward regarding certain individuals, it would be rash to wish to outlaw them all entirely.
&emsp;*The second rule:* Since visions are to be numbered among miraculous gifts, and since God does not usually perform miracles without extreme necessity, it must not be asserted that a vision happened to this or that person unless the gravest reasons persuade it. I do not think anyone will move to dispute this rule with me; *Theologians* of almost all sects, when occupied in the interpretation of the *Holy Scriptures*, are accustomed to stress this very point. If this is to be observed in those places where **divinely inspired men** <note>Original Greek: θεοπνευστοι (theopneustoi), meaning 'God-breathed' or inspired by the Holy Spirit.</note> speak, it is much more to be observed when men not endowed with this gift tell such things about themselves or others—especially since it is well known how easily the tricks of the imagination are confused with true *Visions*.
&emsp;*The third rule:* There is no need for an extraordinary vision to reveal those things that can easily be learned by anyone either from reason or from revelation. Since the all-wise God does nothing in vain, and since the general precepts for living rightly and the decrees necessary to know for salvation are easily available to anyone from the reading of the *Holy Scriptures*, it is hardly credible that God would use unusual methods.

<meta>catchword: God</meta>

*Fourth: Visions that involve propositions that are clearly false and contradictory, or contrary to the virtues of the Deity and to clear Revelation, cannot be of divine origin.* I do not think it necessary to prove the fairness of this assertion with many words. Contradictory propositions provide no meaning, and therefore cannot be believed. Those that are false and contrary to the divine virtues and clear Revelation cannot have God as their Author, unless you maintain that God can enjoin things contrary to Himself and His own nature at the same time—a thought that is impious even to conceive of God.

*Fifth: Visions that are brought forward to prove the private opinions of some sect—especially if those opinions are false, or even if they are true but easily known from Revelation alone—are deservedly suspected of falsehood.* For since God, by His very nature, cannot instill false propositions into mortals, and since particular propositions (even if true) can be easily perceived from Revelation, we see no reason why God would use Visions to confirm such specific truths over which Christians are accustomed to contend among themselves.

*Sixth: If anyone boasting of heavenly Visions is caught having erred more than once, credit is withdrawn from the rest of the Visions which he says happened to him, even those that contain nothing false.* For he who could be deceived two or three times, and took the delusions of his own brain for a heavenly vision, could also have been deceived in the rest. At the very least, this makes it difficult for us to distinguish true Visions from false ones. For if this could happen to the very person who narrates that such things happened to him, what wonder is it if others, not without reason, doubt the truth of his Visions?

*Seventh: Visions which, viewed in themselves, contain nothing absurd or contrary to divine virtues, but are nevertheless clothed in many mythical and silly circumstances, are suspected of falsehood.* When those who claim that Visions happened to them, or those who tell of them happening to others, add most obvious fables to their narration, they thereby cause us to regard them either as impostors or as gullible men. It could indeed have happened that a Vision occurred to this or that Christian, which, when told to another, was augmented with many fables; but since we have no witness other than the one who mixed fables with the truth, we cannot discern the true from the false, and for that reason the narrator, whoever he may be, is suspected of fraud.

*Eighth: If it is established from the entire way of life and the opinions of a man boasting of Visions that he is a fanatic <note>In this context, a "fanatic" refers to someone whose religious fervor is driven by an overactive imagination rather than reason or sound doctrine.</note>, follows the heat of his imagination, and always pursues things that are singular and unusual, it is hardly credible that Visions occurred to him from*

God. Since God is accustomed to produce visions and miracles not merely for the sake of one man, but usually for the sake of others as well; and since a fanatic man cannot easily distinguish the inventions of his own brain from a true vision, and other men, having detected so many proofs of a delirious mind, can hardly have faith in a man boasting of such things, it does not seem to agree with divine Wisdom to offer certain sights to such a man through a miracle.

*Ninth: A man who produces various signs of imposture regarding himself, and who is not ashamed to narrate the falsest things when dealing with other matters, deservedly loses all credibility when he narrates that Visions happened to him.* There is no need for us to prove with many arguments how fair and agreeable to reason this rule is.

*Tenth: He who narrates that a certain divine <term>theama</term> <note>Original Greek: "θέαμα," meaning a spectacle, sight, or something seen.</note> was offered to someone born long before him, of which those who lived in that same age and could have known the matter well make no mention at all, is deservedly suspect.* This rule is used by almost all writers of Ecclesiastical History when examining the narrations of the ancients, and it can and should be applied most rightly here.

According to these rules, learned Reader, I have instituted my examination of the Visions of the Christians. I know that they are not always infallibly certain, nor do they necessarily extort assent from everyone. In the meantime, if you weigh them according to the laws of probability handed down by the masters of the art of reasoning, I am either mistaken, or there will be nothing greatly worthy of censure. No one will expect mathematical <term>akribeia</term> <note>Original Greek: "ἀκρίβεια," meaning precision, exactness, or strict accuracy.</note> from us in this argument. But if I have been deceived in the application of examples to these rules, a prudent and fair man will judge that it was not done with bad intent. If anywhere, it is certainly prone to error here. Often the manifold circumstances, which could have provided much light for confirming some narration, are not at hand. Nor does it escape anyone that mortals can be variously deluded by nocturnal Visions, by temperament, and by silly superstition. To say nothing of the manifest frauds detected so very often among the ancients as well as the moderns, who does not know how many forged books were devised by malicious men in the early centuries? Errors were often joined with piety. In a word: we are not dealing here with the Visions mentioned in Holy Scripture, but with sights said to have happened to men who, just like us, could have been fascinated by false images. Not to mention that most of the things narrated here were not committed to writing by those to whom they happened, but by others, of whose faithfulness we cannot always be persuaded. The Apostle is the authority that the gift of prophecy must remain until the very last coming of the Lord.
