...complete healings, and they see certain things according to the [divine] will regarding the future. And though Celsus <note>A 2nd-century Greek philosopher who wrote the first comprehensive intellectual attack on Christianity</note> may mock what is about to be said, or the Jew whom he has introduced, nevertheless it shall be said: that many have come to Christianity as if against their will. Some Spirit suddenly turned their governing mind <note>original: "ἡγεμονικόν" (hegemonikon) — the Stoic term for the commanding faculty of the soul</note> from hating the Word to being willing even to die for it, by presenting them with visions either while awake or in a dream. For we have recorded many such things; if we were to write them down as having occurred in our own presence and sight, we would be laughed at loudly by unbelievers, who would suppose that we, like those they already suspect, have fabricated these things and done so ourselves. But God is witness to our conscience, that we do not wish to report false things through any [private] deceit, but to establish the divine teaching of Jesus through various manifestations of power.

-> i. e. That is to say: <- 

Even today, traces of that Holy Spirit, who appeared in the form of a dove, are preserved among Christians; they cast out demons, perform many healings, and foresee future events by the will of God. Though Celsus may mock what is said, or the Jew brought forward by him, it shall nonetheless be stated: many were drawn to the Christian religion almost against their will, a certain Spirit suddenly changing their intellect from the hatred by which they were held toward the Word, so that for its sake they did not hesitate to meet death, after visions were offered to them either while sleeping or waking. For we see many such things, which if we were to mention only those performed in our presence, the infidels would raise a loud laugh, thinking that we also, like those of whom they are wrongly suspicious, were making them up. But God is the witness of our conscience that I am trying to commend the divine doctrine of Jesus Christ not with false anecdotes, but with various examples of found truth.

These are the primary passages by which it is proven that the miraculous gifts <note>original: "dona miraculosa"</note> did not fail the Christian Church after the departure of Christ and the Apostles. The only question is whether the number of such blessings was as great as those testimonies seem to imply. There are those who think the Fathers gave some weight to uncertain rumors and were sometimes rhetorical when they spoke on this subject. Among them is the most learned Le Clerc <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), a famous theologian and critic known for his rational approach</note>, who in his *Ecclesiastical History, page 681*, after relating the words of Irenaeus <note>An early Church Father and bishop of Lyon (c. 130–202 AD)</note>, breaks out into these words: "While no one would maintain a total denial of faith in these things, nevertheless, whatever good men heard from others and easily believed in those times—when credulity was held as a virtue—it does not follow that those things are therefore true. In that time, no one considered it a violation of religion to use hyperbolic speech for the honor of God and the salvation of men." These words have vehemently displeased many. For this reason, the celebrated Kettner, in his dissertation on the remnants of miracles and visions after the Apostolic times, is indignant at that most erudite man:

> "He speaks," Kettner says, "disparagingly of Saint Irenaeus, a listener of Polycarp and a Father near to the 

<column-break/>

> Apostles' times, and renders his faith suspect; yet Tertullian called him the most curious explorer of all doctrines, and Eusebius called him a most worthy witness and a defender of the right Catholic doctrine. Surely there is no reason to suspect that Saint Irenaeus wished to lie about a matter so recent and manifest."

But I, (I.) along with many others, cannot follow the force of that inference; namely, that because *Irenaeus* was, according to *Tertullian*, a most curious explorer of all doctrines, and according to *Eusebius*, a defender of the Catholic faith, he therefore could not have erred regarding the multitude of miracles and visions. Since *Irenaeus* could not have known everything that happened in every place, he could easily have lent his faith to those things said by others in praise of the Churches. Nor had *Le Clerc* said that *Irenaeus* had lied on purpose, but that he, with others, often used hyperbolic speech when the conversation concerned the progress of religion confirmed by miracles. He could have described the constancy in the profession of the Christian religion, the trust in God, and the zeal for the glory of God—virtues in which we do not deny the Christians of the first age shone—or represented things handed down by others as if everything had been done outside the order of nature. Certainly, in the following sections, we shall show that the martyrs themselves were sometimes delighted by figurative and hyperbolic expressions. 

But (II.) since many attend not so much to *what* is said as to *who* says it, I shall bring forward the testimony of a theologian who is, in everyone’s judgment, most modest; one who, speaking of these miraculous gifts of the early times, opens the sentiment of his mind no less heartily and openly. And that is *Herman Witsius* <note>A prominent Dutch theologian (1636–1708) known for reconciling different theological factions</note>, whose words are found in his *Miscellanea, Vol. I, Section XIV, page 371*, and they sound like this:

> "However much," he says, "we see many things narrated with great confidence, I nonetheless do not think it a sin to subject them to a more accurate examination. It seems to me thus: that at the beginning of the Gospel, the Best and Greatest God granted to the Church Prophets acted upon by His Spirit in a singular way, who together with the Apostles, and indeed for some time after their departure from the earth, watched over the propagation of the saving doctrine and confirmed their mission with wonders; for the condition of those times seemed to require this entirely. Nor do I deny that such distinguished men of God existed even in the third and fourth centuries of the Christian era: for it would be hard to strip all faith from the pious Fathers when they constantly narrate such things about the men of their own age and their own acquaintance. Nevertheless, I do not think it necessary for that reason that we should admit everything without discrimination. The style of most of the Fathers was adapted to a declamatory <note>A style of speech meant for rhetorical effect rather than literal reporting</note> way of speaking, prone to hyperbole..."

...that the kingdom of Christ should stand bodily upon the earth. *Papias* <note>Papias of Hierapolis (c. 60–130 AD), an early Christian bishop whose works are mostly lost but quoted by others</note> seems to have held these opinions based on misunderstood narrations from the Apostles. He failed to see that those things were spoken by them in a certain hidden sense and for the sake of example. Indeed, he was endowed with a quite mediocre intellect, as may be gathered from his writings. Nevertheless, he provided the occasion for the same error to many ecclesiastical writers after him, who defended his opinion because of the man’s antiquity—such as *Irenaeus* <note>Irenaeus of Lyons (2nd century AD), a prominent theologian who wrote against heresies</note> and whoever else stood as a supporter of the same opinion. From this testimony of *Eusebius* <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), the "Father of Church History"</note> it is established: **a.)** that this *Papias* was a man of small judgment, and thus prone and inclined to accepting any fables and trivial traditions. It is true that the same *Eusebius*, in chapter 36 of the same book, calls the man a "most learned and eloquent man." But *Valesius* <note>Henri Valois (1603–1676), a French scholar and editor of Eusebius</note> testifies that this praise is absent in the manuscript codices he consulted, nor is it read in the version by *Rufinus*. **b.)** It is clear that *Papias* did not hear the Apostles themselves, but only their disciples; hence any uncertain and portentous narrations were snatched up by him, as *Eusebius* himself admits. **c.)** Therefore, it is no wonder that a man intent only on traditions was very often deceived. **d.)** The narrations of *Papias* itself were greedily seized upon by writers of the following age, who were captured by a prejudice in favor of antiquity. Is it any wonder, then, that in the second century, when *Irenaeus* lived, many things were rashly boasted regarding miracles? *Grabe* <note>Johannes Ernest Grabe (1666–1711), a scholar who published fragments of the early Church Fathers</note> himself, a great admirer of the Fathers, who wishes to vindicate the reputation of *Papias* in part II, page 28 of his *Spicilegium*, cannot deny that the judgment of *Eusebius* is true. For on page 29 of the cited place, he speaks thus: „Nevertheless, those few fragments preserved for us seem to show, in part, that excessive simplicity of mind which Eusebius noted in Papias.“ Then he brings forward the fragment itself, which exists in *Irenaeus, Against Heresies, Book V, Chapter 33*; it sounds like this: „The Elders remember, those who saw John the disciple of the Lord, that they heard from him how the Lord used to teach about those times and say: The days will come in which vines shall grow, each having ten thousand branches, and on one branch ten thousand arms, and on each shoot ten thousand clusters, and in each cluster ten thousand grapes, and each grape, when pressed, will give twenty-five measures <note>original: "metretas," an ancient Greek liquid measure roughly equal to 9 gallons</note> of wine. And when one of the Saints shall take hold of a cluster, another will cry out: I am a better cluster, take me; bless the Lord through me. Similarly, a grain of wheat will generate ten thousand ears, and each ear will have ten thousand grains, and each grain five two-pound weights <note>original: "bilibres," a weight of two Roman pounds</note> of clear, clean flour; and so on with the rest...

...of the fruits, and seeds, and grass according to the harmony following them. And he added, saying: 'These things are believable to those who believe.' And when Judas the traitor did not believe and asked, 'How then shall such growths be brought to pass by the Lord?' the Lord said: 'Those who come into those times shall see.'“ After *Grabe* had related the opinions of Christians and Jews concerning the second coming of Christ, he said: „Whatever may be determined about the matter itself, which I leave to the judgment of pious and learned theologians, certainly the manner of proposing it is so different from the character of the sayings of Christ which the Evangelists recorded, that I can hardly persuade myself that those other things flowed from the mouth of our Savior.“ *Massuet* <note>René Massuet (1666–1716), a Benedictine editor of Irenaeus</note>, however, simply says in his notes to *Irenaeus* on page 333, that he <note>Papias</note> received them „either from certain dreams of the Apocrypha, or from spurious traditions.“ What wonder is it (I repeat) if a man spread among the common people many foolish and strange things as if received from the disciples of the Apostles? What wonder if the men of the following age were hardly able to distinguish true traditions from false ones? **IV.)** (*) Something must be noted regarding the cited passage of *Origen* <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253 AD), an early Christian scholar and theologian</note>: for he says that many, inflamed with love for the Christian religion, underwent martyrdom for it. Yet he says the contrary in Book III, page 116: „Few, at various times and quite easily counted, have died for the Christian worship of God.“ <note>original Greek: Ὀλίγοι κατα καιρȣς καὶ σφοδρα ἀριθμητοι ὑπερ της των χρισιανων θεοσεβειας τεθνηκασι</note> *Dodwell* <note>Henry Dodwell (1641–1711), an Anglo-Irish scholar</note> had already produced this passage in his *Dissertation on the small number of Martyrs, Thesis VII*, to prove that such a great multitude of martyrs did not exist in the first centuries as is commonly believed. *Ruinart* <note>Thierry Ruinart (1657–1709), a French monk who defended the traditional accounts of martyrs</note> responds in his *General Preface to the Acts of the Martyrs, Section 22*, thus: „But by these words Origen intends nothing other than that the persecutions stirred up against the Christians were not so bitter that they were utterly...“

...that the Christians could have been wiped out, and that in truth only a few suffered if compared to those who survived. However, the most learned *Clericus* <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), a famous theologian and scholar</note> long ago cautioned in his *Select Library, Vol. XXVI, p. 18*, that the words "many" and "few" are relative terms; thus, that dispute between *Dodwell* <note>Henry Dodwell (1641–1711), who argued that there were fewer martyrs than usually claimed</note> and *Ruinart* <note>Thierry Ruinart (1657–1709), who defended the high number of early Christian martyrs</note> cannot easily be settled by the words of *Origen* <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–253 AD), a foundational Christian scholar</note> alone. (*) But there is also another passage from *Origen* produced by *Dodwell* on another occasion in his *Dissertation IV: On the Visions of the Early Christians*, which seems to prove clearly enough that there was not such a great abundance of heavenly (namely, extraordinary) gifts as some claim. The words of *Origen* in *Book III: Against Celsum* sound like this: <note>original Greek: Σημεῖα δὲ τὰ ἁγία πνεύματος κατ' ἀρχὰς μὲν τῆς Ἰησοῦ διδασκαλίας, μετὰ δὲ τὴν ἀνάληψιν αὐτὰ πλείονα ἐπιδείκνυτο ὕστερον δὲ ἐλάττονα. πλὴν καὶ νῦν ἔτι ἴχνη ἐστὶν αὐτῶν παρ' ὀλίγοις τὰς ψυχὰς τῷ λόγῳ καὶ ταῖς καθ' αὐτὸν πράξεσι κεκαθαρμένοις.</note> "Signs of the Holy Spirit were shown at the beginning of Jesus' teaching, and more after his ascension, but later fewer. Yet even now there are still traces of them among a few whose souls have been purified by the Word and by actions consistent with it." Certainly, this passage clearly testifies that the number of men endowed with unusual gifts was small at that time. When *Origen* says in the passage cited above that many were drawn to the Christian religion almost against their will—their intellect being suddenly changed by some spirit—this must undoubtedly be understood as referring to those Gentiles who had already acquired some knowledge of the Christian religion. Otherwise, it could hardly be believed that God would deign to favor an ignorant man with a miracle of such unusual favor.

V.) Finally, those things which happened in the second century on the occasion of *Montanus* <note>Montanus was the founder of Montanism, a movement that emphasized new prophetic revelations</note> seem to suggest that the testimonies regarding the multitude of miracles cited above should not be pressed too hard. For it is well known that *Montanus* and his associates, in order to seek fame and reputation, appealed to wonderful *Visions and raptures*. However, it is not probable that *Montanus* would have consulted his reputation in this way if these gifts had been so frequent among everyone indiscriminately. That is one point; the second point I urge is this: namely, that those who entered the arena to argue against *Montanus* did not appeal to that supposedly great number of extraordinary gifts. Neither point proves that these wonderful effects had entirely ceased in the second century or were very rarely perceived; but this one thing seems to be shown: that the abundance of those unusual gifts was smaller in number than is commonly believed. *Joannes Clericus, a most learned man, in his Church History...*

(*) The truth is, (he says) that the words "few" and "many" are relative terms, whose meaning is ambiguous depending on the subjects to which they refer. Thus Origen could have used the other term while speaking of the same thing in different regards; but it is very difficult, if not impossible, to mark today with any precision the boundaries he set in his mind between the "few" and the "many." <note>This note was originally in French.</note>

*...History, page 679, for the year 157, says* that the *Montanists* reproached the more orthodox Christians for not having prophets among them. If this could be proved by clear testimonies, it would be highly probable that the gift of prophecy and miracles was extremely rare at that time. To prove this, he appeals to *Eusebius, Church History, Book V, chapter 17*, and to *Epiphanius*. But in neither is what the learned man intends clearly designated. Lest I seem to have said this in vain, I will bring forward the words of the Anonymous author found in *Eusebius* at the cited place. They sound like this, from the version by *Valesius* <note>Henri Valois, the editor of Eusebius mentioned on the previous page</note>: "In the same book he also makes mention of a certain writer, *Miltiades*, who wrote a book against the aforementioned heresy. For having cited certain words of those heretics, he then writes: 'When I found these things in a certain book of theirs against our brother *Miltiades*, who had taught in a specific work that a prophet ought not to speak in ecstasy <note>The term "ecstasy" here refers to a trance state where the person loses their reason or self-control</note>, I made a summary of it.' Then a little later in the same book, he enumerates all the prophets of the New Testament, among whom he reckons a certain *Ammia* and *Quadratus* in these words: 'But the false prophet,' he says, 'speaks in a false state of mind, which is accompanied by license and audacity, starting indeed from spontaneous ignorance, but ending, as I have said, in involuntary madness. They could never demonstrate that any prophet, either in the Old or New Testament, was inspired by a spirit of this kind—not *Agabus*, not *Judas*, not *Silas*, nor the daughters of *Philip*, nor *Ammia of Philadelphia*, nor *Quadratus*, nor certain others who, they will preach, have nothing to do with them.' Then, after a few words, he speaks thus: 'For if indeed, as they preach, those women of *Montanus* succeeded to the grace of prophecy after *Quadratus* and *Ammia of Philadelphia*, let them show us who among them succeeded *Montanus* and the women. For the Apostle [Paul] testifies that the gift of prophecy must remain in the whole Church until the final coming of the Lord. But they can show no one at all, even though it is now the fourteenth year since the death of *Maximilla* <note>Maximilla was one of the two primary prophetesses associated with Montanus</note>.'" Thus he says.

*Epiphanius* <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310–403 AD), a bishop known for his "Panarion," a refutation of many heresies</note>, in *Heresy XLVIII, page 402, following the edition of Petavius*, says thereafter: "The *Phrygians* <note>Another name for the Montanists, as the movement started in Phrygia</note> therefore (he says) accept both the Old and New Testament. They approve of the resurrection of the dead. But they preach a certain *Montanus* as a prophet, along with *Priscilla and Maximilla*, as prophetesses: by clinging to whom they turn aside from the right path. For they feel the same way as the Catholic Church regarding the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: but they have separated themselves from its communion because [they have given heed to] spirits of error and doctrines..."

> “...they follow demons. For they say, ‘We must receive heavenly gifts.’ Indeed, the Catholic Church has received gifts from God, but they are true gifts, confirmed by the authority of the Holy Spirit, the Prophets, the Apostles, and the Lord himself. Look, by that very fact which they propose for themselves, they are openly convicted of being unable to obtain that which they claim with such contentious ambition. For if those heavenly gifts are to be received, and it is fitting for the Church to be endowed with them, why have they had no more prophets after **Montanus**, **Priscilla**, and **Maximilla**? <note>Montanus (2nd century) was the founder of Montanism, a movement that emphasized new prophetic revelations. Priscilla and Maximilla were his two primary prophetesses.</note> Has the divine gift been exhausted? But in the Catholic Church, it is by no means exhausted. Far from it! But if the Prophets prophesied to some extent and now cease to prophesy, it follows that not even **Priscilla** or **Maximilla** uttered any oracle according to the apostolic prophecies which are received in the Church. Therefore, their madness is constrained on both sides. For they must either show some prophets after **Maximilla**, so that the grace they boast of does not seem extinct, or **Maximilla** and her associates must be judged under the name of a **False Prophetess**, since they were not afraid to admit the inspiration of error sent by demons—rather than the Holy Spirit—after the prescribed time of the prophetic gift and office had passed, and thus to mock their listeners.”

Thus far *Epiphanius*. <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 315–403), a bishop known for his fierce opposition to heresies.</note> From these testimonies it appears: 1.) That extraordinary gifts were not entirely lacking in the Church at the time of *Montanus*, although *H. Dodwell*, in his *Dissertation on Visions*, mentioning the testimony brought from *Epiphanius*, thinks that what he said did not suit the century of *Epiphanius* and was unskillfully copied from an older writer. At the very least, it agrees with the things narrated in *Eusebius*. 2.) None of the writers he mentions worked specifically to show that there was a very great abundance of miracles and prophetic gifts, which they probably would have done if they had wished to tear down the boasted prophecies of *Montanus* and the resulting dignity sought for his associates. 3.) *Eusebius* mentions *Apollinaris*, *Miltiades*, *Apollonius*, and *Serapion*, and presents fragments from them. All of them reject ecstatic visions and attribute them to the arts of a demon; they object to many other things, but nowhere do they fight their enemies equipped with any notable display of portents. 4.) *Miltiades* mentions only six prophets from the age of the Apostles onward, to which he adds certain others; he surely would have fought against *Montanus* with a much larger number if those extraordinary gifts had been so frequent. What *Miltiades* discusses regarding the gift of prophecy lasting forever in the Church is false, unless by the name of **Prophets**

he understands the learned and pious interpreters of Holy Scripture, regarding which the discussion by the famous *Le Clerc* (page 679 ff. of his *Ecclesiastical History*) is worth reading. To return to our path, then, we assert that in the first centuries after Christ's departure, miraculous gifts were not lacking in the Christian assembly; but at the same time, they were fewer in number than is commonly reported. ### V.

But let us come finally to the *Visions* themselves, which are suspected of being false not without cause. In the Apostolic century—that is, the *first*—it is said that *Hermas* lived, regarding whose book there are various judgments by the Ancients and Moderns. Most learned men, such as *Cotelerius* (*Apostolic Fathers, Vol. I, p. 68*) and *Pearson* (*Vindication of Ignatius, Book I, ch. 4*), have collected these. I will say nothing of *Ittig*, both *Basnages*, and others. We have already said above that these foolish little books were held in high regard by *Clement of Alexandria*, *Irenaeus*, and *Origen*. Others do not value him so highly, yet they think some price should be placed on the book due to its venerable antiquity. To me, those who think the author of the booklet was a *fanatic* seem to have the most correct opinion of all. *Blondel*, certainly, in his *Apology for the Opinion of Jerome (pp. 16, 17)*, calls him a masked *prophet and dreamer*. The famous *Mosheim* in his *Institutes of Ecclesiastical History*...

---

(*) A new controversy regarding the miracles of the first centuries was stirred up several years ago by the most celebrated *Middleton, Librarian of Cambridge University*. <note>Conyers Middleton (1683–1750), whose "Free Inquiry" argued that miracles ceased with the Apostles.</note> He contends that after the departure of the Apostles, no miracles were performed either by the leaders of the churches or by the common crowd of followers of our Savior. For if this were once granted, the learned man says, full faith would have to be given to the portents said to have been performed in the third and fourth centuries. Now, it is well known that most miracles of this time are so filled with fabulous narrations that a man who loves the truth cannot admit them. But those who follow the common and received opinion retort with two main points. The first is: it does not follow that because true miracles were performed by Christians in the second century, the portents of the 3rd and 4th centuries must also be admitted. The second: they say care must be taken lest historical faith be abolished. For authors most worthy of trust testify in the clearest words of that age that in the second century, miracles of a true name were performed by Christians. I do not make this controversy my own here, since I have not yet unrolled the booklets written by either side, but have learned these things from the *Journals of Learned Men*. Yet if there is room for conjecture, I would believe this controversy will have the same outcome as the dispute over the fewness or plurality of the first martyrs of the Christian Church. The most learned *Dodwell* set out to prove that there were far fewer martyrs in the first age of the Church than is commonly thought; and those who stand by the common opinion, chief among whom was *Ruinart*, had to admit this; yet at the same time, the supporters of *Dodwell* had to admit that in establishing the fewness of martyrs, he overstepped the boundaries set for historical truth. It is clear from these controversies that learned men who examine received opinions with industry in the pursuit of truth are to be praised rather than blamed, since from mutual concerts of this kind, a new light is always kindled for the truth. For the rest, as far as the last controversy is concerned, one should consult the learned dissertation of *P. Casto Innocente Ansaldi, On Martyrdom without Blood, published in Milan, 1744*.

On page 78 of the first edition, he judges it thus: *The Shepherd of Hermas* is the writing of a fanatic <note>original: "hominis fanatici"</note>, of whom I am certain that he often did not understand what he was saying; indeed, the heavenly spirits in his work sometimes chatter more foolishly than our own porters. *Jean Le Clerc* <note>A 17th-century theologian and scholar known for his critical approach to historical texts.</note> says regarding the year of Christ 69: *“If the things he relates about the Visions offered to him by Angels were true, this book would have to be admitted as almost Prophetic, as was done by Irenaeus, who honors it with the name of Scripture; but if they are false, it must be numbered among those who believed the common people could be led to piety by 'pious frauds,' as they call them—a plan that can be approved by no one of even slight prudence.”* That this latter view is most probable will be established from the evidence we shall bring forward. There are, moreover, two primary reasons that lead me to believe the Visions contained in the little book are false; the first is that most of the Visions said to have happened to *Hermas* contain only matters very easy to know; the second is that it would have to be said that these Visions were given to him by God to confirm false things. Both will be established by the introduction of examples.

The complete book consists of three parts. The first is titled *Visions*; the second, *Mandates*; the third, *Similitudes*. Let us first discuss the Visions. In the first Vision, *Hermas* relates that the man who had raised him had sold a certain girl in Rome. After many years had passed, he saw her again and loved her like a sister; and when he later saw her washing in the river Tiber, he reached out his hand to her and said in his heart: *“How happy I would be if I had been allotted such a wife, both in beauty and in character.”* This alone (he says) and nothing further did I think; afterwards, while he was at prayer, he relates that these things happened to him: *“While I was praying, heaven was opened, and I see the woman whom I had desired greeting me from heaven and saying: 'Hail, Hermas.' Then she, smiling at me, said: 'The desire of wickedness rose up in your heart. Does it not seem to you an unjust thing for a righteous man if an evil desire rises in his heart? *walking correctly, he will have the Lord favorable to him in every matter. But those who think wicked things in their hearts bring death and captivity upon themselves, especially those who love this present world.”* Thus says *Hermas*. Let the following points be observed here:

1.) *Hermas* asserts that upon seeing the woman, he said nothing else than that he would have been happy if he could have obtained such a wife as she was. If he did nothing more than this, he did not sin; he had, as will be clear from what follows, a talkative and morose <note>original: "loquacem & morosam"</note> wife; therefore, he could say without any crime that he would have been happier if he could have married one adorned with virtues. Yet for this very thing, he is rebuked by the woman received into heaven. Either *Hermas* lied, therefore, when he asserted he said nothing else than what we reported, or it is false that a divine Vision happened to him for that reason.

2) That Lady received into heaven is said in the following parts to be sometimes the Church, and sometimes Christ. But how, I ask, can anyone burn with carnal love for the Church?

3.) Let us suppose that an evil desire invaded a good man; is there any need for an extraordinary Revelation to teach him that the love of another man's wife or woman is evil? Was Hermas ignorant of the words of Christ in Matthew 5:27? <note>"But I tell you that anyone who looks at a woman lustfully has already committed adultery with her in his heart."</note> Was he so stupid that he could not know what even the wiser Pagans <note>original: "Gentiles"</note> had beautifully understood?

4.) Soon, in Section II, another woman appears—an old woman, in fact—who brings solace to the sad *Hermas*, and among other things says: *“Perhaps the desire for her rose in your heart. And indeed, in the servants of God, such a thought brings sin. For this thought ought not to be found in a Servant of God, nor should a proven Spirit desire an evil work—especially Hermas, who is continent from every wicked desire, and is full of all simplicity and great innocence.”* If *Hermas* is free from every evil desire, why is he rebuked after all?

5.) Nay, what is more, that old woman asserts that God is not angry with *Hermas* himself, but with his house—that is, his wife and children. Therefore, it must be that one or the other of these women, who were thrusting these Visions upon him, was lying.

6.) Section III reports that this heavenly rebuke was made so that he might correct his disobedient children. But is a Vision needed to instill such a duty into a man of sound mind?

In the second Vision, that old woman appeared again, and the sole cause of this miraculous Vision was so that *Hermas* might know that the talkativeness of his wife and the ruined morals of his children must be restrained. Apparently, there is need for a portent <term>portentum</term> <note>A miraculous sign or supernatural omen.</note> for this. b.) Is it possible, then, that not even heavenly souls—let alone men—can distinguish forged books from genuine ones? In Section IV, *Hermas* says: *It was revealed to me, brothers, while I slept, by a handsome Youth, saying to me: That old woman from whom you received the little book, who do you think she is? And I said, the Sibyl <note>The Sibyls were legendary prophetesses in the ancient world; "Sibylline" books were often forged in this era to support various religious views.</note>. You err, he said, she is not. Who is she then, Lord? and he said to me, She is the Church of God; and I said to him: Why then is she an old woman? Because, he said, she was created first of all things, therefore she is old, and for her sake the world was made.* Three things should be noted here. The first is: Hermas thought the old woman presented to him was the Sibyl, which shows the man flourished around the middle of the second century. For it is the nearly unanimous opinion of the most learned men that the eight Sibylline books were manufactured by an impostor between the years 138 and 167. See *Le Clerc*, Ecclesiastical History for the year 131; *Blondel* in his French work on the Sibyls; *Prideaux*, History of the Jews, etc., Volume II, book 9, page 757 of the German edition in quarto. Second: Good *Hermas* thought the Sibylline books were of divine origin. Certainly, unless he had believed this, he would never have persuaded himself that some Sibyl had spoken to him from heaven. Third: He falsely asserts that the Church was created first; where, pray tell, is this handed down in the Sacred Scriptures?

Let us proceed to the *Third Vision*. Generally, it should be noted that here and in what follows, *Hermas*, seeking the meaning of the offered Visions, is rebuked by that old woman as if he were talkative, peevish, and stubborn. But for what purpose are such extraordinary Revelations made if they are not meant to be understood, and why are those who desire explanations worthy of such sharp censure?

In Section I of this third Vision, it is revealed through a Vision to *Hermas* that the steadfast Confessors and Martyrs of the Christian religion will carry away remarkable glory and sit at the right hand of God, though other pious people will not. But besides the fact that an extraordinary Revelation is not needed to prove that Confessors of a most holy religion will receive a reward worthy of their piety, the author seems to have been imbued with the opinions received at that time concerning the extraordinary privileges which Martyrs were to enjoy in the future age: on this argument, see *Henry Dodwell's* Cyprianic Dissertation XII.

In Section IV of this Vision, *Hermas* asks: *Those six young men who are building, who are they, Lord? These are the Angels of God, who were first established, to whom*

to whom the Lord delivered His entire creation, to organize, build, and rule over that creation. For by this the structure of the tower shall be finished. These things are an insult to God and Christ. Here *Cotelier*, otherwise most eloquent whenever there is even the slightest opportunity to defend this foolish man, remains silent. *Papias* <note>An early 2nd-century bishop whose works are mostly lost and who was often criticized for being too literal or imaginative.</note>, a writer of similar mettle, asserted the same, as seen in *Grabe's* Spicilegium, Volume II, page 33. In Section XIII of the third vision, it is said the world is contained by four elements <note>The ancient theory that everything is made of earth, air, fire, and water.</note>. A quote from the Roman poet Horace, used here to mean "I don't believe a word of it."</note>

After *Hermas* had seen a beast of immense magnitude in a Vision, a virgin (whom *Hermas* persuades himself was the Church) said: *You have escaped well, because you cast your loneliness and anxiety upon the Lord, and opened your heart to Him, believing that you can be saved through no other than His great and honorable name.* Because of this, the Lord sent *His Angel, who is over the beasts, whose name is Hegrin, and he shut its mouth so that it would not tear you apart.* It is manifest that the Author is <term>Platonizing</term> <note>original: "πλατωνίζειν" (platonizein) — adopting the philosophical style or ideas of Plato.</note> here. Hence it is no wonder that the book of *Hermas* pleased *Origen* <note>A famous 3rd-century theologian often criticized for his allegorical and philosophical interpretations.</note>, who was imbued with foolish opinions of this sort tending toward superstition. In the rest of these Visions, under the figure of monstrous beasts, nothing else is denoted than the heavy afflictions about to come upon the pious Confessors of Religion. But this could easily have been known without Visions, and Christ had long ago foretold what was to come.

...are said to have happened to him through extraordinary Visions. In the prologue, he says that the Angel of Repentance appeared to him.

The first Mandate deals with faith in God. This precept commends itself by its simplicity, it is true; but it is of such a nature that a vision is not necessary to recognize and accept it. It sounds like this: *“First of all, believe that God is one, who created and perfected all things, and made all things out of nothing. He alone contains all things, and is himself immense <note>original: "immensus"; in this context, it means infinite or immeasurable.</note>. He can neither be defined by words nor conceived by the mind. Believe therefore in him, and fear him: and in fearing him, exercise self-restraint. Keep these things and cast away from you all wickedness, and put on the virtue of righteousness, and you shall live to God, if you keep this commandment.”*

In Mandate II and III, he teaches that slander and lies must be avoided. As if a Vision were needed to accept this! It is strange, however, that this same *Hermas* confesses in this very place that he had lied throughout his whole life. For how, I ask, can these things be reconciled with the simplicity, piety, and sincerity attributed to him above through the heavenly Vision? Who will persuade us that a man accustomed to lies could not have fabricated Visions?

In Mandate IV, he says: *“A man whose wife is caught in adultery can and ought to put her away, but he himself also commits adultery if he marries another while the former is living.”* But by what argument, finally, will *Hermas* prove this? Since the essence of the marriage contract itself is violated by such fornication, and the innocent party contributed nothing to the violation of this contract, why should it not be permitted to enter into a new contract with another? Read Chapter IV of the most learned *Barbeyrac’s* <note>Jean Barbeyrac (1674–1744), a famous jurist who was often critical of the moral philosophy of the early Church Fathers.</note> "On the Morality of the Fathers," where he attacks the inept little arguments of the Fathers on this subject at length. *Cotelerius* <note>Jean-Baptiste Cotelier, a 17th-century scholar of early Christian texts.</note> indeed says in his notes on this passage that this opinion of *Hermas* is truly orthodox—that is, as he himself explains, consistent with the decrees of the <term>Synod of Trent</term> <note>A major 16th-century Roman Catholic council that defined church doctrine in response to the Reformation.</note>. It seems the Angels in heaven were eager to confirm the decrees of the most holy Synod many centuries in advance through Visions! We know various other opinions and decrees which can be read in <term>Böhmer</term>, <term>Thomasius</term>, and <term>Bingham</term> <note>All prominent 17-18th century scholars of ecclesiastical law and history.</note>. But the decrees and precepts of Natural Law, of Christ, and of the Apostles, are broader than the opinions of the Fathers, which were built on no firm arguments. See what the cited *Barbeyrac* discusses on this subject in his notes to <term>Pufendorf’s</term> <note>Samuel von Pufendorf, a leading 17th-century philosopher of natural law.</note> "On the Law of Nature and Nations," Book VI, chapter I, 1734 edition. Therefore, that Vision cannot have God as its Author.

In the same Vision IV, or Mandate IV, that Angel—given as a perpetual companion to our *Miracle-monger*—says that he is not only the Overseer of Repentance, but also gives understanding to all who repent. In Mandate VI, page 93, he asserts that a good and a bad Angel are given to every human being. This foolish opinion can be proved neither by the laws of right reason nor by the testimonies of Holy Scripture. Indeed, this assertion clearly conflicts with the divine attributes. *Menander the Comic Poet* <note>An ancient Greek playwright (c. 342–291 BCE).</note> recognized this, whose verses from an uncertain comedy are these:

->A guardian spirit stands by every man<-
->As soon as he is born, a guide for his life<-
->A good one. For it is wrong to believe an evil<-
->Spirit exists to harm a good life. For in all things<-
->God must be good.<-

This is, as translated by *Grotius* <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), the Dutch legal scholar and poet who translated many Greek works into Latin.</note>:

> A presiding Spirit follows every single man,
> As soon as he is brought forth, who sets the omen of his life;
> A good one, certainly: for it is a sin to believe an evil spirit
> Inhabits a good life: for he who is God
> Must also be good.

*Cotelerius*, after he had brought forward the agreeing testimonies of many Fathers—indeed even of Jews and Muslims—finally admits (which is surprising) that the Holy Scriptures are silent about these things, and even that many of the Fathers go in the opposite direction. In Mandate VIII, the Angel solemnly teaches that evil things are to be avoided, but good things are to be done. Certainly, it takes an angelic wit to know such things!

In Mandate XII, *Hermas* says to the Angel: *“I know that you will shatter every power of the Devil.”* But do these things agree with the Decrees of the Christian Religion? VI. But let us proceed to the visions which are said to have occurred to certain Christians in the second century. However, since many of those to whom such visions are said to have happened were martyrs who shed their blood for the truth of the Christian religion, and since many people persuade themselves that such men could suffer nothing of human weakness, we think a few things should be mentioned in advance regarding the Acts of the Martyrs and the martyrs themselves, lest we seem too bold in our judgment. 

1.) Indeed, as *Ruinart* himself admits in his *General Preface to the Sincere Acts of the Martyrs, Section VII and following*, the first among the ancient teachers of the Church to collect the acts of the ancient martyrs was *Eusebius, Bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, a writer of the 4th century*. But his book, which he had titled <term>Collection of the Ancient Martyrs <note>original: "ἀρχαίων Μαρτύρων συναγωγήν"</note></term>, and which was said to have encompassed the oldest Acts, has perished through the injuries of time. (*) 

2.) Since superstition grew strong in the fourth century, it is uncertain whether many things were not rashly added to the ancient Acts. 

3.) It will be established by examples cited below that certain things were added even to the oldest Acts of the Martyrs. 

4.) *Ceraunius, Bishop of Paris, a writer of the 7th century*, followed *Eusebius* in collecting the Acts of the Martyrs. But who does not know what the state of the Church was in that century? Regarding *Symeon Metaphrastes* <note>A 10th-century Byzantine official and author known for rewriting the lives of saints to make them more "edifying."</note>, who collected the Acts of the Saints sought from everywhere into one volume, *Ruinart* himself testifies on page 11 of his preface that he interpolated several of them with various additions and, when the old records were lacking, forged a few new ones by his own effort <note>original: "proprio Marte cuderit"</note>. I shall say nothing of more recent collectors of such Acts. 

5.) Furthermore, the acts of even the most ancient martyrs were recorded by private individuals, of whose good faith and character we cannot be sufficiently certain. 

6.) Since the martyrs themselves were unable to record the circumstances of their suffering and death, and since the spectators who were present could not observe every detail due to the heat of the persecution, it could not have happened otherwise than that the narrative was rendered inconsistent and uncertain by various traditions collected from here and there. Lest I seem to have said these things without cause, I shall appeal to *Ruinart* himself, who strove with as much zeal and diligence as possible

These ACTS were, as we have already said, either excerpted from public records <note>meaning official Roman court transcripts</note>, or composed by some Christians who had been present at the interrogations of the martyrs; or, if by chance they could be obtained in neither way, if it were known from public report or certainly from older men who had lived during the time of the persecutions, all these things were collected into one, so that at least some of the deeds of the martyrs might become known. But when, a little later, almost all the provinces of the Roman Empire were devastated and occupied by Barbarians, even those Acts perished, and others were subsequently substituted for them, which do not reach the authority of the former, much less the sincerity of the originals. These are the ones that occur everywhere in manuscript and printed codices, which, although they do not attain the purity of the first Acts and are mostly full of errors regarding persons and dates, I nonetheless believe should not be entirely rejected. To these must be added those Acts which are sincere in substance but have been rashly violated by unskilled men, who added miracles to the earlier Acts or debates between the martyrs and tyrants, by which they thought they might better celebrate the courage of their martyrs; although because of this, such monuments have lost their authority among learned men, even if sparks of the former sincerity may be seen shining out here and there in them. Care must be taken, however, that those Acts are not placed in this category which are entirely sincere but have a short preface fixed at the beginning or a closing statement at the end in which the completion of the martyrdom is explained. For since public Acts usually ended immediately with the passing of the sentence, and the death of the martyrs was not recorded in them (unless by chance they died during the interrogation itself due to the bitterness of the torments), Christians supplied this later, either during the time of persecution itself or at least when such monuments were first collected into one. But the authority of the Acts themselves is in no way diminished by this. *And on page 12:* Truly, the Acts of the Martyrs, which ought to have been clarified by so many collections and various editions, have come forth less sincere the more often they were transcribed or printed. For some of these collectors interpolated them with various additions; others recorded..."

„ ...erased some things that they disliked in those Acts; or even, so that the
„ writing might seem more polished, they dared to change the authentic and pure
„ style, than which certainly nothing in sacred antiquity ought to be held more
„ holy. But those who set out to present those old monuments as they are

„ volume the deeds of all martyrs and confessors alike—the doubtful or false

„ that it became a work of several and indeed massive volumes, so that only a 
„ few Acts are contained therein, and indeed so mixed with doubtful and false
„ elements that they cannot be distinguished without great labor, even by
„ more discerning men.„ Thus far the most learned *Ruinart*. I could point out many things regarding this speech, if I were currently engaged in investigating by what method the authentic Acts of the Martyrs might be distinguished from the interpolated ones. But I will point out this one thing, which is the heart of the matter: namely, *Ruinart* takes great care to teach that faith should not be withdrawn from the authentic Acts of the Martyrs on account of the many fabulous and invented stories and wonders stitched onto the true Acts by certain impudent writers. But if these idle men were not ashamed to devise miracles to exaggerate the deeds, how then can we be certain that nothing was mixed into the narrative other than what was actually said or done by the martyrs themselves? It will become clear below, through the introduction of specific examples, how serious the reasons for doubting the authenticity of even the most ancient Acts often are. In the meantime, one may consult what the most learned men *Jean Le Clerc in his Choice Library <note>original: "Bibl. Select."</note>, Volume 26, page 181 and following, and Jacques Basnage in his History of the Church, Volume II, page 1068 and following,* have noted on this subject.

As for the martyrs themselves, it should be known that 1.) they were men, subject to infirmities just like other mortals. 2.) They could, therefore, be pious and yet err regarding many theoretical propositions relating to Religion. For piety does not make anyone infallible in judgment. 3.) He is properly to be called a Martyr who, under the pressure of necessity, freely and constantly defends the divine origin of the Christian Religion and confirms it with his blood when he can no longer consult his conscience in any other way. 4.) It is certain that many among the Christians, where it was not necessary and where there was an opportunity to avoid danger, rushed forward to carry off the glory of Martyrdom, or even voluntarily provoked the most severe punishments upon themselves. See what the illustrious *Pearson in his Defense of Ignatius <note>original: "vindic. Ignat."</note>, part II, chapter X, section 5,* has collected regarding this last point. 5.) Just as it has happened to other pious people, namely that they have confused a good and pious state of mind with the extraordinary operations of God,

<column-break/>

### 677

# ON THE VISIONS OF THE EARLY CHRISTIANS.

the same could also happen to the martyrs. Often, those things which they agitated within themselves with an anxious mind at night, or desired with a certain vehement impulse of the soul, they were able to believe—upon waking from sleep—had truly happened to them, not without a miracle. By this, however, it is not denied that either God was present to them with singular favor, or even sometimes strengthened their minds against the fear of death through Visions. 6.) Since, however, the collectors of the Martyrologies (as *Ruinart* himself confesses) rashly added many wonders and extraordinary sayings and deeds to the Acts of the Martyrs, it is always doubtful whether this or that Vision truly happened to the Martyr or not. 7.) Furthermore, I contend that those who think God always performed miracles for the sake of the most ancient Martyrs detract from the excellence and efficacy of the Christian Religion and divine grace rather than adding to it. Certainly, all who have spoken for the truth and divinity of the Christian Religion bring forward, among other things—and indeed most correctly—that in the first centuries after the passing of Christ and the Apostles, faith held such weight in the souls of Christians that they not only willingly said farewell to those things which mortals consider primary, but also accepted tortures and death itself with a constant mind. If, however, constant miracles were needed to endure these things, it takes away much from such a great virtue and such a most salutary persuasion. 8.) Whatever the case may be regarding this, it is lawful and permissible to weigh the words and deeds of the martyrs against the eternal rules of reason and Revelation; as long as we do not depart from these, there is no place for error or danger. 9.) Just as a lighter error or infirmity is always to be forgiven, so also the piety and other virtues of the Martyrs are to be praised and imitated. Yet, in this, one must always look to the matter itself for which they suffered the hardest things, rather than to the impulse itself or the desire for suffering, which was sometimes not sufficiently tempered by the precepts of Christ and the decrees of reason concerning self-preservation, as the Acts of the Martyrs testify, and as we shall show below with one or two examples. We wished to advise these things concerning the Acts of the Martyrs and the martyrs themselves for the reason that it will be useful to have observed these things in what follows, where there will be talk of their Visions.

VII. Among the most ancient and most worthy of attention of the Acts of the Martyrs are to be counted the Acts of the Martyrdom of *Ignatius* and *Polycarp*. According to *Ruinart*, *Ignatius* suffered in the year 107. There is a triple edition of the Acts of the Martyrdom of *Ignatius* in the works published by *Cotelerius*. The first is Greek-Latin, published by *Ruinart*; the second is by the <term>Metaphrast <note>Symeon Metaphrastes, a 10th-century Byzantine author known for rewriting lives of saints into a more polished style.</note></term>; and finally, the third is an ancient Latin version, first brought to light by <term>Ussher <note>James Ussher (1581–1656), Archbishop of Armagh, a famous scholar and chronologist.</note></term>. We shall stand by the edition of *Ruinart*.

...Greek-Latin. Regarding the sincerity of these Acts, Jacques Basnage <note>original: "J. Basnage"</note> in his *History of the Church* (Vol. I, p. 101) and Samuel Basnage in his *Ecclesiastical Annals* (Vol. II, p. 17) doubt them vehemently. Grabius also admits they were interpolated <note>meaning "altered or expanded with later additions"</note> in his *Spicilegium* (Vol. II, p. 22), whose words we will soon cite. The arguments of these learned men are of such a nature that they cannot be fully satisfied in every respect. This fact certainly carries no small weight in excusing us when we assert that the truth of the visions said to have occurred to Ignatius’s companions can be doubted. But let us see what should be thought of the vision granted to Ignatius’s companions. In Section VII of the Acts edited by Ruinart, these companions speak as follows in this version: *“These things indeed occurred on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January, that is, the twentieth of December, during the second consulship of Sura and Senecio. Having been eyewitnesses <note>original: "αυτοπται" (autoptai)</note> of these events, we spent the night at home in tears, and when, with knees bent, we had prayed to the Lord with many petitions to make us, in our weakness, more certain of those things which had previously been done, and had slept for a little while; some of us suddenly saw the Blessed Ignatius standing and embracing us; others again beheld him praying for us; while others saw him dripping with sweat, as if arriving from a great labor, and standing before the Lord with much joy. When we had seen these things and compared the sights of our dreams, we glorified the Blessed Man, and we have made known to you both the day and the time, so that gathering at the time of his martyrdom, we may bear witness to our communion with the Athlete and noble Martyr of Christ, who trampled the Devil underfoot, etc.”* Regarding this, the following points should be observed: 1.) This narration, as noted by Ussher <note>James Ussher, a 17th-century archbishop and scholar</note>, was made by Philo and Agathopus, companions of Ignatius from Syria. 2.) It is not at all probable that this vision was granted for the sake of these companions. For did they need to be persuaded of the truth of the event—that is, that Ignatius truly suffered? This would have been foolish, as they were eyewitnesses. Did they perhaps doubt the piety of Ignatius and his attainment of happiness in the future life? Yet at the beginning of the narration, they had extolled him to the heavens with praises for his piety. Perhaps they wished to test through this vision whether God approved of his singular ardor for martyrdom or not? This is the conjecture of Jean Le Clerc <note>original: "J. Clerici"</note> on this passage. But if those companions had devoted themselves to prayer with that intention, it is simply not believable that God would satisfy their desire through a miracle. For he would have thus confirmed a matter that many could easily have abused. We do not, of course, doubt the piety of Ignatius. But from these Acts of Martyrdom, and especially from the letters—particularly the one he wrote to the Romans—it is more than clear enough that the good man was carried away by an excessive love of martyrdom. Hence, he labors so hard to prevent his Roman friends from hindering him as he marches with quick steps toward the glory of martyrdom, or from doing anything that might stand in the way of his most burning desire.

<column-break/>

But God is not accustomed to performing miracles for those impulses which are suggested by an affection not sufficiently tempered by reason and the precepts of the Christian religion. I know that such free judgments are displeasing to the admirers of the Church Fathers, but they are not so to those who are accustomed to examine all the words and deeds of mortals according to the eternal laws of truth. The celebrated Weismann, in his *Ecclesiastical History* (Vol. I, p. 116), after citing Basnage's opinion on the martyrdom of Ignatius—which agrees entirely with mine—breaks out in these words: *“Where, I ask, are we when we blame those things which should be most singularly praised? He must be ignorant of antiquity, as Du Pin most correctly says, who denies that the first Christians were incensed with a zeal for martyrdom; and he is a most wretched theologian who would disparage it.”* Thus says Weismann. But I would have preferred arguments instead of examples; an example that resolves one dispute by creating another achieves nothing. <note>original: "nil agit exemplum quod litem lite resolvit"</note> Cotelier, in his notes on Ignatius’s *Epistle to the Romans*, and Ruinart after him, seeking to excuse that singular desire of Ignatius, appeal to the examples of other martyrs. But is this to reason or to prove? All points return to this: 1.) God has implanted in man the desire for self-preservation. 2.) God, therefore, wills that we study to preserve life by every means, and that we do all that can be done to place it in safety. 3.) The laws of nature do not conflict with the precepts of the Christian religion. 4.) Christ himself commanded his disciples not to expose their lives rashly to dangers, and if they should ever be unjustly sought for death, to flee from one city to another if they could (Matthew 10). 5.) Martyrdom in itself, nor even the desire for it in itself, can please God, since someone can undergo death for a most foul error, as is evident from the example of the Marcionites <note>an early Christian dualist sect deemed heretical</note> and others; nor can God approve of any action unless it is done according to the rule of reason and the precepts of the Gospel. 6.) Therefore, only that martyr is to be praised who is persuaded of the truth of the Christian religion and is cast into such circumstances that he cannot satisfy God and his conscience in any other way than by a constant and free confession of the truth, even if joined with exquisite <note>meaning "intense" or "refined"</note> torments and the loss of life. 7.) On the contrary, he who does not escape traps when he could; who calls down dangers upon his own head without necessity; who desires to meet death when no necessity urges it; who spurns the help of others—that man, though he may otherwise be a good and pious man, is nevertheless not to be praised, even if he sheds his blood, although it is believable that God will interpret that weakness in a favorable light. But if we read these Acts of Martyrdom, and especially the *Epistle of Ignatius to the Romans*, diligently and attentively, it is sufficiently...

...it seems clear enough that *Ignatius* could have preserved his life at that time, and thus could have continued to be of service to the Church of Antioch. If, however, we are mistaken in this, and there was no way of escaping, no one will fail to praise the constancy of that Blessed Man. But if this were the case, I certainly do not see the reason why those companions should have had to expect a miracle from God. Therefore, there was no reason for the famous *Weismann* <note>Christian Eberhard Weismann (1677–1747), a Lutheran church historian</note> to think that the most learned *Basnage* <note>Jacques Basnage (1653–1723), a prominent Huguenot historian</note> spoke in an unseemly manner regarding his martyrdom. But lest anyone think that I am pleading the case of the famous *Basnage* without reason, I will provide his very words: for the most learned man is intent on proving that the *Letter of Ignatius to the Romans* is rightly suspected. Among other reasons he brought forward to prove this, there is one drawn from the very subject matter of the Letter. 

> "I am not examining," (he says in *History of the Church, Vol. I, page 121*)
> "the interrogation of Ignatius at all, in which he makes an equivocation to the Emperor regarding his name *Theophorus* <note>original: "Porte-Dieu" (God-bearer). Ignatius was famously called Theophorus, which can mean either "God-bearer" or "borne by God."</note>, concluding from this that he cannot have a Demon: But how could Ignatius, condemned by the mouth of the Emperor, believe that it was easy to protect him from death, and pray to the Romans not to do so? This seems to offend common sense and Religion; for neither the People nor the Magistrates of Rome could save the life of a man condemned by the Prince, and sent from so far by his order to be torn apart by beasts. It was even more impossible for Christians, in the heat of the persecution, to prevent the execution of the Imperial Sentence. Religion is offended by it: for whatever ardor one has for Martyrdom, one must wait for what Providence ordains, without opposing the means it has to protect us from punishment. However, not only does Ignatius want to die, and warns the Romans from afar for fear that they might oppose his execution; but he begs them to flatter the beasts so that they might tear him apart. This is a new way to excite the cruelty of Tigers and Lions, by flattering them; at the very least, this is not the Spirit of Christianity, and these things would be a stain on the life of St. Ignatius, if they were true." 

Thus far *Basnage*. To this I will add—since authority and testimonies are more suited to the temperaments of some than are logical reasons—the judgment of a most learned man, one who accurately weighed what the laws of nature and the precepts of the Religion handed down by Christ require. This is the famous *Barbeyrac* <note>Jean Barbeyrac (1674–1744), a famous jurist known for his work on natural law</note> in his *Treatise on the Morality of the Fathers*, chapter VIII, page 125, speaking thus of this Martyrdom of *Ignatius*:

> "With regard to St. Ignatius, whose example Father *Ceillier* <note>Rémy Ceillier, a Benedictine monk and historian</note> again alleges, one cannot deny that he desired Martyrdom

> "with an extreme ardor: and all that one can say to excuse him is that he was already captured, so that there was no appearance that he could avoid death. But miracles are not to be multiplied without necessity. Here, however, there is clearly no necessity. If those companions were Christians, as they were, they could have found enough protection against grief in the Decrees of the Christian religion. *Secondly*, the image of a most beloved man could have been observed by those dreaming without a miracle. *Thirdly*, if whatever God *can* do must immediately be said to have been done in actual fact, then faith must be given to almost all <term>Legends</term> <note>original: "Legendis". I would wish, therefore, *Fourthly*, to note that the narrative of those companions can in no way be reconciled with Chronology, which the most learned men *Le Clerc, Pagi, Lloyd, Basnage, and Noris* <note>A list of prominent 17th and 18th-century historians and chronologists</note> have proved.

> And these (he says in *Spicilegium, Vol. II, page 22*) are the Acts, or rather the Passion, of the Holy Martyr Ignatius, published from a double Latin manuscript. First by Ussher <note>James Ussher (1581–1656), Archbishop of Armagh, famous for his biblical chronology</note>, who concluded in his Preface that at least the final part was written by Philo, Gaius, and Agathopus—who followed the blessed Martyr from Syria all the way to Rome—based on the following phrases: *We were led away unwillingly, groaning over the separation that was to come; we met the brothers filled with fear and joy.* Having become witnesses of these things ourselves, etc. I, on the contrary, judge the earlier parts written in both Latin manuscripts to be genuine and ancient, but I think the final part of Ignatius is spurious and sewn on by some interpolator; partly because it is missing in one of the manuscripts, namely the Cottonian <note>A reference to the library of Sir Robert Cotton</note>, and partly because it contains <term>inconsistencies</term> <note>original Greek: ἀσύστατα (asystata)</note> and falsehoods. Indeed, these words of the Holy Man seem to openly contradict each other, which in Ussher’s Latin text read: *Having become witnesses of these things ourselves with tears, and staying awake at home all night, and praying much with kneeling and prayer to the Lord to confirm us, who are weak, concerning the things done before.* For if these witnesses had seen these things with their own eyes, what need was there to ask God for further certainty about them? Moreover, it appears to be false that these events are said to have happened when *Sura and Senecio were consuls for the second time* <note>The Roman consuls for the year 107 AD</note>, that is, in the year 107 of the common Christian era, as one can learn from Ussher's notes. I say this appears to be false because it is established from the Acts themselves that Ignatius was condemned by the Emperor Trajan when he came to Antioch during the expedition undertaken against the Parthians. But two distinguished masters of chronology, Henry Norris in his *Consular Letter, page 72*, and Antoine Pagi in his *Historico-Chronological Critique of the Annals of Baronius for the year 115*, have excellently proved that the Parthian war only began in 112 AD. To these is added a third, the prince of chronologists of this time, whom I should have named first: the Very Reverend William *Lloyd*, now Bishop of *Worcester*; while some think it happened a little earlier and others a little later, almost everyone agrees it happened after 112 AD. Thus says *Grabe*.

The same author writes that this vision was granted not for the sake of his companions, but for his friends living in

Rome. And these points may suffice to prove that faith should not be rashly granted to those visions narrated in these *Acts*.

There are learned men who contend that visions occurred to *Ignatius* himself. I certainly do not deny that this could have happened. I only doubt whether the passages brought forward to prove it signify this clearly enough. The celebrated *Kettner* <note>Friedrich Ernst Kettner (1671–1722), a German theologian</note>, in his Dissertation cited above, appeals to the *Epistle of Ignatius to the Trallians*, in which (at *Section V, page 23 of Le Clerc’s edition*) the Blessed Martyr speaks thus:

> Am I not able to write to you of heavenly things? But I fear lest I should inflict harm on you who are infants; so forgive me: lest, being unable to take them in, you be choked. For even I, though I am bound in chains, am not for that reason able to understand heavenly things, and the placements of the angels, and the gatherings and constitutions of the principalities, things visible and invisible; I am not yet a disciple because of this: for many things are lacking to us, lest we be distant from God.

From the eleventh chapter of the *Vindication of the Letters of Ignatius*, written by the illustrious *Pearson* <note>John Pearson (1613–1686), Bishop of Chester and a defender of the Ignatian epistles</note>, it is clear that *Daillé* <note>Jean Daillé (1594–1670), a French Huguenot who argued the Ignatian letters were forgeries</note> attacked this very part of Ignatius's speech, thinking that Ignatius had exceeded the limits of modesty by claiming for himself things granted to no mortal. Let us bring forward Pearson's own words.

> The first violation of modesty (according to Daillé, that is) is that he claims knowledge of <term>super-heavenly things</term> <note>original: super-caelestium / ἐπεράνια (eperania)</note>. As if no knowledge of super-heavenly things were suitable for a Christian man, and indeed a Bishop taught by the Apostles. Are the "heavenly things" mentioned so many times by the Apostle [Paul] such that Christians could know nothing and write nothing of them? These things seem strange to me: and yet because of this one sentence, this modest writer is said to depart from modesty on two counts. First, he attributes to himself things granted to no mortal man. I deny this, I utterly deny it. He says he "thinks many things in God"; is this granted to no mortal? Or is it not rather required of all Christians? All are called to wisdom in God, and indeed much wisdom: especially him whom St. Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), a prominent Church Father and Archbishop of Constantinople</note> does not fear to call "a teacher of equal weight to Peter." He says he is able to write things that the *Trallians* could not grasp. Is this granted to no mortal? It does not appear that the knowledge of the *Trallians* at that time was yet so great. Furthermore, when he made mention to the *Smyrnaeans* of super-heavenly and visible and invisible things, he immediately added: *He who takes it in, let him take it in.* Finally, he defines these heavenly things more clearly when he says he can understand "the locations of the angels and the assemblies of the principalities." Yet it is not clear that these are the sorts of things no mortals know. Perhaps we do not correctly understand what the Epistle...

<meta>This page continues the author's critical examination of the visions attributed to St. Ignatius of Antioch. <page-num>684</page-num>
-> ON THE VISIONS OF THE EARLY CHRISTIANS. <-

> "...what the Writer of the Epistle intended by those words, and that he did not understand those things which he wished to signify by these words, etc." 

So says the illustrious **Pearson** <note>John Pearson (1613–1686), Bishop of Chester and a major defender of the Ignatian epistles</note>. But from the evidence brought forward by this *most learned man*, it is clear enough that he is turning every which way and exerting every effort to ensure that the honor of **Ignatius’s** Epistles remains intact. First, he says that knowledge of "heavenly things" is available to all Christians; yet soon after, he says we do not know what **Ignatius** intended by these words. But if this is the case, why should it be said that all Christians "know" that which even we do not understand? Certainly, I am persuaded that if **Ignatius** were asked what he understood by <term>arrangements of places</term> <note>original Greek: τοποθεσίας (topothesias)</note> and <term>ruling assemblies</term> <note>original Greek: συστάσεις ἀρχοντικὰς (systaseis archontikas)</note>, he would scarcely, if at all, have been able to answer. 2.) Again, the same **Pearson** appeals to **Chrysostom** to prove that **Ignatius** learned both "spoken and secret things" from the Apostles. Yet, after citing the words of **Chrysostom**, he says: *In the excerpts of Clement from the "Eastern Doctrine" <note>original Latin: ex orientali doctrinâ</note>—which surely could not have been unknown to Ignatius—certain things are related concerning the various duties and dignities of the Angels.* If we concede this to the *Illustrious Man*, it follows that Ignatius drew these descriptions neither through a Vision nor through Apostolic instruction, but from the foolish opinions of that age. And certainly, this last conjecture of the most learned man is the most consistent with the truth. For it is well known that the Pythagoreans, Platonists, and the Heretics of the Apostolic age prattled much and rashly about the Orders and Offices of Angels and Demons, so much so that learned men think, not without cause, that **Paul** was pointing his finger at these things in 1 Timothy 1:4. See **Porphyry**, *On Abstinence* <note>original Greek: περὶ ἀποχῆς (peri apoches)</note>, Book II, Section 37 and following, in the edition by **Holstenius**. 3.) Since God revealed nothing clearly even to the Apostles themselves regarding the various offices and seats of the Angels, is it credible that God would teach **Ignatius** about these things through Visions?

The other passage to which the famous **Kettner** appeals appears in the *Epistle to the Philadelphians*, where in Section VII, page 32, he speaks thus: 

> *“For although some wished to deceive me according to the flesh, yet the Spirit is not deceived, being from God. For it knows whence it comes and whither it goes, and it rebukes secrets. I cried out while I was present, I spoke with a loud voice, the voice of God: 'Pay attention to the Bishop, and to the Presbytery, and the Deacons.' But some suspected that I said these things because I foreknew the division of certain people. But He is my witness, in whom I am bound, that I did not know this from human flesh; but the Spirit announced it, saying these things: 'Do nothing without the Bishop.'”*

But even this passage does not prove that he was taught this proposition—"Do nothing without the Bishop"—through a Vision. For in the *Epistle to the Trallians* (Section II), to the *Philadelphians* (Section VII), and to the *Magnesians* (Section IV), he repeats and emphasizes this same point again and again, but as...
<meta>catchword: as...</meta>

<page-num>685</page-num>
-> ON THE VISIONS OF THE EARLY CHRISTIANS. <-

...as if it were an Apostolic precept. Hence, even those who fight for the *Ignatian* Epistles (among whom the Illustrious **Pearson** stands out) defend themselves by appealing to Apostolic tradition—not extraordinary Visions—to excuse the magnificent things said about Bishops in the *Epistles of Ignatius*. And certainly, if **Ignatius** was taught that such great honor should be given to Bishops either from the Epistles of the Apostles or from familiar social interaction with the Disciples of the Apostles, it is useless to appeal to Visions. See what **Ussher** discusses on this argument in *Dissertation on the Epistles of Ignatius the Martyr*, etc., Chapter X, page 22; found in **Cotelerius's** *Apostolic Fathers*, Volume II. Certainly, among the chief reasons that make the Epistles of **Ignatius** suspect, I include this exaggeration of Episcopal power. We do not read such things in the words of Christ or the Apostles. I know what learned men answer. But the nature of our project does not allow us to deal with these matters at length, and they have been sufficiently debated by most learned men.

**Socrates** in his *Ecclesiastical History*, Book VI, Chapter 8, asserts that **Ignatius** was taught the art of singing hymns antiphonally <note>singing back and forth in alternating groups</note> through a Vision: 
> *“It must further be told (he says) whence that custom of singing hymns alternately in the Church took its beginning. Ignatius, the third Bishop of Antioch in Syria after the Apostle Peter, who also lived familiarly with the Apostles themselves, once saw Angels celebrating the Holy Trinity with hymns sung alternately, and he handed down to the Church of Antioch the manner of singing which he observed in that Vision. From there, that tradition spread to all the churches thereafter.”*

But how uncertain this tradition of **Socrates** is has long since been shown by the learned. See the evidence brought forward on this subject by **Bingham** in *Antiquities of the Christian Church* <note>original Latin title: Origines Ecclesiasticae</note>, Book XIV, Chapter I, Section XI, page 14 and following, in the Latin edition.

VIII. We proceed to the Visions of **Polycarp the Martyr**, who, according to **Ruinart**, laid down his life for the truth of the Christian religion around the year 166 (or according to **Ussher** and **Pagi**, in the year 169). The leaders of the Church of **Smyrna** record that two Visions occurred to **Polycarp**. Regarding the first, they speak thus on page 198 in **Cotelerius**: 
> *“But so great was the tumult in the stadium that no one could be heard. Furthermore, as Polycarp was entering the stadium, a voice came from heaven: 'Be strong and play the man, Polycarp!' <note>original Greek: ἴσχυε καὶ ἀνδρίζου πολύκαρπε (ischye kai andrizou polykarpe)</note> And indeed, no one saw the one who emitted the voice, but those of our people who were present heard the voice.”*

My reasons for doubting that God sent this voice through a miracle are as follows. 1.) By the testimony of those who were present, the tumult was extremely loud, and **Polycarp’s** mind was distracted by various thoughts; hence he could hardly hear a voice or distinguish it from the voice of a man. Hence, not even in the Epistle itself...
