...she herself <note>referring to the church or the account</note> affirms that **Polycarp** heard a voice. But if God had wished to strengthen him through a miracle of a heavenly voice, He would have sent it at that precise moment in such a way that there could be no reason to doubt that He wished to be present to him in an extraordinary manner. 2.) The Blessed Man was burning with a singular desire to obtain Martyrdom, and he placed all fear of tortures under his feet. 3.) There is no reason why we should doubt that God was present with His grace and singular favor to a Man most devoted to the Christian Religion. Therefore, it was not necessary that a spur be added by a miracle to a man who was running toward the glory of Martyrdom of his own accord. 4.) We do not wish to deny that the Spectators of this Tragedy heard that voice; but how could they be persuaded—without a new miracle—that among such a noise, that voice had fallen from heaven? Finally, those things which pertain to both matters, as we shall soon hear, cause us to doubt whether those things said about his Visions are true or not.

The second Vision, which is narrated in that Epistle of the Smyrnaeans to have happened to **Polycarp**, is this: *While he was praying (say the Smyrnaeans) three days before he was captured, a Vision was offered to him. He saw his pillow being consumed by a conflagrating fire. Then, turning to his companions, he said prophetically: "It is necessary for me to be burned alive."* But even this Vision is not placed beyond the risk of doubt. 1.) **Eusebius** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), the "Father of Church History"</note> in *Book IV, chapter 15*, narrates that this Vision happened to him while praying, but at night in a deep sleep. Yet it could naturally happen that this occurred to him in dreams. The same **Eusebius** omits that "prophetic" element which is in our Text. 2.) When the Proconsul had said, *“I beseech you by the geniuses, or by the other gods, or I will deliver you to the fire,”* **Polycarp** responds: *“It shall not be,”* <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἔσαι (ouk esai)</note> etc. But if he had believed that God had certainly signified to him through a Vision that he was to be extinguished by fire, he ought to have desired that which was the spontaneous will of God. 3.) The truth of the Vision can be doubted because God, through a miracle, had prevented him from being consumed by the fire. For hear how the Smyrnaeans speak, in *Section XV* and following, in the works of **Cotelerius** <note>Jean-Baptiste Cotelier (1629–1686), a French scholar of early Christian texts</note>: *“And after he had sent forth his 'Amen' and completed the prayer, the men or Ministers of the fire lit the fire. But when a huge flame burst forth, we saw a great miracle—we to whom it was granted to see, who were reserved for this purpose, that we might announce to others what happened. For the fire, presenting the appearance of a vault, like a ship’s sail filled and bellied out by the wind, surrounded the body of the Martyr on all sides; which indeed, placed in the center, did not seem like roasted flesh, but like baked bread, or like gold and silver glowing in a furnace. Indeed, we smelled such a great fragrance, as if frankincense or some other precious spice had been burning. At last, therefore, the wicked ones, seeing that his body could not be consumed by the fire,”* order—

—ordered the executioner <note>original: confectorem; literally "the finisher," a term for the official who delivered the death blow</note> to approach nearer and to hide his dagger up to the hilt [in Polycarp's body].

4.) This miracle concerning the fire not consuming **Polycarp's** body was said to be for the sake of the infidels. But the pagan Centurion finally burned the body placed in the midst of the fire, as is signified in *Section XV*. Certainly, this would have cast the Spectators into doubt rather than making them believe a miracle had occurred. For they saw the fire did not harm the body of the Blessed Man. And this could have led the pagans to believe that God took singular care of the man, and even that His decrees could not be evil. Yet the same people soon see, through the Centurion, that it was brought about that the body—hitherto untouched and not reduced to ashes—was entirely dissolved. From this they rightly ought to have suspected that the event happened not through natural means, but through natural yet unknown causes, and that the flames had been in vain. Who, however, would believe that God is so lavish with miracles that He would produce portents in circumstances of this kind? 5.) It is said a dove emerged from his body. Regarding this portent, however, **Ruinart’s** manuscript <note>Thierry Ruinart (1657–1709), editor of "Acta Martyrum"</note>, **Eusebius**, and **Rufinus** are silent...

Rufinus, or rather Nicephorus <note>Nicephorus Callistus, a 14th-century church historian known for recording many legends</note> himself, was an exceedingly credulous man. It is therefore necessary that this was added to the *Letter of the Smyrnaeans* by some impostor. *Prudentius* <note>A Roman Christian poet (c. 348–413 AD)</note> relates a similar fable in his third hymn on the *Martyrdom of Saint Eulalia*, saying:

->From there a dove suddenly springs forth,<-
->Whiter than snow, from the martyr's mouth,<-

For the various opinions of the learned regarding that dove having emerged, as they say, from the body of the Martyr, see the *Bremen Library*, Class III, volume 3, page 429 and following.

6.) It is said that such a great force of blood flowed out from his body that it extinguished the fire. But from where could so much blood come from an aged and worn-out body? Did God by a miracle increase the Martyr's blood? If this is true, and it was done by a miracle so that the fire would be extinguished, why then did He permit the Centurion to finish the deed? 7.) Finally, that fragrant odor of the Martyr’s body, which the spectators are said to have inhaled with greedy nostrils, shows clearly enough what value should be attributed to those miracles. Certainly, neither physical nor moral causes can explain this wonderful effect. In the legends of the *Monks* of the following age, such things are reported in great number; but they are believed only by those who have no brain. Did God really wish to show by this odor that the bodies of Martyrs are formed from an entirely different material than those of other men? Everyone knows this to be false. Did He wish to prove that the steadfast <term>confessors</term> <note>Those who suffered for the faith but did not necessarily die</note> of the Religion of Christ please Him greatly? But even this was sufficiently known and understood by Christians without these aromatic particles. If we reduce all these things to a sum, there are no slight reasons why we should doubt the narrated miracles no less than the Visions. I know some will say with *Ruinart* <note>Thierry Ruinart (1657–1709), a Benedictine monk and scholar who compiled acts of the martyrs</note> that the certain must be distinguished from the uncertain, and that the Visions should not be called into doubt just because they are suspected of falsehood due to those portents. But who, I ask, will guarantee us that men who were not ashamed to sew empty fables into the *Letter of the Smyrnaeans* restrained themselves from inventing Visions? At least no sensible person will, I believe, find fault with me if, until I am better instructed, I frankly confess that those Visions are highly suspect to me. (*) <meta>catchword: But</meta>

But the leaders of the Church of Lyons and Vienne <note>referring to a famous letter describing the persecution in Gaul in 177 AD</note> also mention other Visions made at this time to a certain *Attalus*, as recorded in *Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, Book V, chapter 3*. The words sound like this from the translation of *Valesius*: *A certain Alcibiades, one of the number of those martyrs, followed a harsh and squalid way of life; admitting no food at all but bread and water, he had been accustomed to eat only that until that time. And when he was placed in prison and wished to retain the same way of living, it was revealed to Attalus after the first combat he had performed in the Amphitheater, that Alcibiades was not doing rightly or in order, as he was making no use of the creatures of God, and was becoming an example of scandal to others. Therefore, Alcibiades obeyed, and from then on began to use all foods indiscriminately, giving thanks to God.* For divine grace had not abandoned them. But they had the *Holy Spirit* as their counselor. So speak those brothers of *Lyons*. I cannot believe that such an admonition was truly given to *Attalus* through an extraordinary Vision. For God never performs miracles for the sake of men when they can be warned about a matter by common sense. *Alcibiades*, if he could not sufficiently refresh his strength with bread and water, could have well understood by the guidance of reason alone that the foods kindly shared by the brothers were not to be rejected. The examples of other <term>Confessors</term> were present. And if neither reason nor the examples of the pious brothers had sufficed, the exhortation of *Attalus*, a strenuous confessor of the truth, could have moved him even without a Vision. I do not doubt, indeed, that *Attalus*, touched by a singular love for *Alcibiades*, thought that this desire to persuade him of better things was an admonition of the *Holy Spirit*, especially after he had seen the man stubbornly persevere in a squalid and harsh way of life, and wish to macerate himself without necessity; but I cannot believe that an extraordinary Revelation was made to *Attalus* for this very purpose, for the reasons I have stated. Certainly, faith must be given to all portents and miracles if we admit such things even once.

*Tertullian* lived in this second century, and in his writings, he makes mention here and there of Visions which are said to have happened to certain Christians. But we cannot attribute much to these, partly because he had a mind clearly prone to *fanaticism*; and partly because he was for a long time addicted to <term>Montanism</term> <note>An early Christian movement emphasizing new prophecy and ecstatic visions, later declared a heresy</note>; moreover, it is well known that *Montanus* and his associates boasted of perpetual Visions, which were justly suspected of fraud; and I will not even mention that it can hardly be determined with certainty which books he wrote while imbued with the errors of *Montanus*, and which he wrote when following the opinion of those who think more rightly. follows the nature [of his temperament], and almost never uses a clear style, but rather exaggerates beyond measure whatever he wishes to praise or condemn; he can scarcely be distinguished from a fanatic <note>The author uses "fanatic" in the 18th-century sense: someone whose religious fervor overrides their reason</note>. For how can we understand his flowery speech when he speaks of divine matters, and distinguish him from a man who has been seized by a kind of "Enthusiasm"? Indeed, it has been a long time since learned men, by almost unanimous consent, warned that *Tertullian* labored under this very disease. Let it suffice to bring forward the judgments of two most distinguished men regarding the character of *Tertullian*. *The first is from Nicolas Malebranche*, a man, as is well known, of the sharpest intellect, who in *Book II, chapter 3, of "The Search after Truth"* depicts the man’s disposition thus:

> "Tertullian (he says) was indeed a man of profound Erudition, but he had more memory than judgment, more penetration and extent of imagination than penetration and extent of spirit. Finally, one cannot doubt that he was a visionary in the sense that I explained before, and that he had almost all the qualities that I have attributed to visionary spirits. The respect he had for the Visions of *Montanus* <note>Montanus was a 2nd-century prophet who claimed new revelations; his movement, Montanism, was later declared heretical</note>, and for his Prophetesses, is an incontestable proof of the weakness of his judgment. This fire, these outbursts, these enthusiasms over small subjects, sensibly mark the disorder of his imagination. How many irregular movements are in his hyperboles and in his figures? How many pompous and magnificent reasons, which prove nothing but by their visible brilliance, and which persuade only by stunning and dazzling the mind."

*The second is from Jacques Basnage*, who in *History of the Church, Vol. I, Book IV, chapter 3, page 177*, judges his character thus:

> "Tertullian had a fortunate genius, he possessed a vast Erudition, his style was lively and tight; all his periods were as much sentences as proofs of what he advanced, but often he overstretched them, and by overstretching them they became false. One finds in his Works a great number of traditions and rites which would have remained unknown without him; he was an ardent defender of the truth, but he abandoned himself too much to the fire of his imagination, which carried him away and prevented him from reasoning justly. Finally, he had the misfortune to give into the Visions of the Montanists, whose fasts and austerities had dazzled him: he has given us thereby a very sensible proof that great men often fall into great weaknesses."

*So says J. Basnage*. And from this it has happened that even those who strenuously plead the cause of the Visions granted to the ancients nevertheless refuse to use the authority of *Tertullian*. *Dod-*

# ON THE VISIONS OF THE EARLY CHRISTIANS

Among other things, it is well established that he <note>Tertullian</note> is not to be trusted on this very account: that he was a follower of the Montanist <note>The Montanists were a 2nd-century Christian movement led by Montanus, who claimed to receive direct prophecies from the Holy Spirit.</note> faction; it is clear enough what we should think of the visions of Montanus and his followers. I believe they were mere impostures, and those who lived in that age believed the same. I will not deny, for my part, that one or two things were falsely attributed to *Montanus* and his disciples out of envy—for example, that *Montanus* said he himself was the Holy Spirit, and other such claims. Meanwhile, everyone agrees on this: that the boasted visions were mere impostures, which they proved by various reasons. For instance, that *Montanus* had dyed his eyebrows and hair with makeup; that a profane spirit had driven them into insanity and strange raptures; that *Maximilla* (according to Epiphanius in *Against Heresies, Book 48, Section 2*) had prophesied of herself that after her there would be no other prophetess, but rather the consummation of the world; that *Montanus* had established salaries for his prophets and a kind of trade under that pretext; that those poor women <note>Maximilla and Priscilla, the leading prophetesses of the movement.</note> had left their husbands when they took up the office of prophetesses; that they were also entirely intent on scraping together greed and money by whatever art possible; and that they had taught "contrary to the custom handed down and the succession of the church from above" <note>original: "παρα το κατα παραδοσιν και κατα διαδοχην ανωθεν της εκκλησιας εθος"</note>, etc. And so we do not seem to say these things without cause, testimonies must be brought forward by which this very point is proven. And here I shall follow the tracks not of an Epiphanius or a Jerome, but of the ancients, whose fragments Eusebius has preserved. These testimonies are produced by *Eusebius in Book V, chapters 16–20.* We will select certain parts relevant to our purpose. In *Chapter 16 of the cited book*, Eusebius mentions a certain anonymous author who, having clashed with the Montanists, later committed what was said to paper. He writes as follows: *Therefore, the stubborn assembly of those people against the Church, and the new heresy of a destructive schism, has this origin. There is said to be a certain village in Mysia, bordering Phrygia, named Ardaba. In which they say a certain Montanus, one of those who had recently been enrolled in the number of the faithful, being seized by an immoderate desire for the first place, first gave access to the opposing Spirit under Gratus, the Proconsul of Asia; being filled by a Demon, he suddenly began to be shaken by a certain frenzy and mental ecstasy, and to speak certain new and unheard-of things; raving and predicting future things contrary to the custom and institution*

of the Church handed down by the ancestors, and extended thereafter by continuous succession. Furthermore, of those who at that time had heard the man’s counterfeit speeches, some indeed—indignant as if at one possessed and demonic and driven by a spirit of error and exciting disturbances among the people—rebuked him and forbade him to speak further. For they kept in mind the distinction marked out by the Lord, and the threats by which we are commanded to observe the arrival of false prophets vigilantly and solicitously. Others, however, as if elated and puffed up by the Holy Spirit and the grace of prophecy, and having entirely forgotten the distinction shown by the Lord, voluntarily invited that infatuating and flattering spirit, the seducer of the common people, to speak, being captured by its allurements and led into fraud. By this art, or rather by this fraud and craftiness, the Devil—devising destruction against those who were not obedient to the Lord’s word—when he was undeservedly worshipped by them, gradually aroused their minds which were turning away from the true faith and oppressed by sleep, and inflamed them more vehemently. Indeed, he raised up two other little women and filled them with a counterfeit spirit; so that they too, just like that one mentioned above, spoke certain insane, untimely, and strange things. And that spirit declared those who delighted in such things and were swollen with pride to be "blessed," and inflamed them beyond measure with the magnitude of his promises. Sometimes, however, using conjectures and arguments worthy of belief, he openly condemned them, so that he might also appear to be rebuking them. He refutes the falsehood of these prophecies with these words: *Has not this lie (he says) appeared manifest to all? For from the death of Maximilla until this day, more than thirteen years have already passed, and yet there has been no war, either local or universal, in the lands.* The same anonymous author—whom *Eusebius* later reports in *Chapter XVII* to have been *Asterius Urbanus*—lists in the same book all the prophets of the New Testament, among whom he reckons a certain *Ammia* and *Quadratus* with these words: *The false prophet, however (he says), in a false mental ecstasy, whose companion is license and audacity, taking his beginning from a spontaneous ignorance, ends in an involuntary madness, as I have already said.* They will never be able to demonstrate that any prophet in either the Old or New Testament was inspired by a spirit of this kind. In *Chapter 18*, "Apollonius the Churchman," a writer, judges Montanus thus: *But who is that new Teacher? His works and doctrine betray him clearly enough. This is he who [taught the dissolution] of marriages...*

> "He taught divisions, he who imposed laws of fasting; who named Pepuza and Tymion <note>Small, obscure towns in Phrygia (modern-day Turkey) that Montanus claimed would be the site of the New Jerusalem.</note> (small towns in Phrygia) 'Jerusalem,' so that he might call people there from everywhere. He appointed money collectors; he cleverly masked the greedy pursuit of gifts under the name of 'offerings'; he provides salaries for those preaching his doctrine, so that his doctrine might thrive through the foul gluttony of the belly."

Regarding the Prophetesses of **Montanus**, he <note>Apollonius, an early Christian writer who wrote a treatise against the Montanists.</note> speaks a bit later in this manner: "We have shown, therefore," he says,

> "that these leading Prophetesses, as soon as they were filled with the spirit, left their husbands. When I see a Prophetess receiving gold, silver, and precious clothes, how shall I not reject her?" and a little later concerning a certain man from their number, whom they consider among their 'confessors' <note>Those who suffered for their faith but were not killed.</note>, he says: "Moreover, **Themison**, masked by a showy greed, did not endure the sign of confession <note>original: 'confessionis signum non pertulit' — meaning he failed to actually suffer for the faith.</note>, but threw off his chains by paying a large sum of money. While he should have acted more modestly and submissively thereafter because of that, he dared to offer himself as a Martyr, and following the example of the Apostle, he wrote a 'Catholic Epistle' to instruct those who had been more faithful than himself; he championed the new doctrine and finally spoke impiously against the Lord, the Apostles, and the Holy Church." Again, regarding another from the number of those whom they venerate as Martyrs, he writes: "But not to speak of too many, let him answer: who is it she feasts with, who is himself adored by many? There is no need for us to speak of his robberies and other crimes for which he was punished, especially since they are contained in the public records. Which of them then forgives the other's sins? Does the prophet forgive the Martyr's prophecies? Or the Martyr the Prophet's greed? For since the Lord commanded: 'Do not possess gold, nor silver, nor two tunics'; these people, on the contrary, have seriously sinned in possessing forbidden things. We will demonstrate that those they call Prophets and Martyrs collect money not only from the rich but also from beggars, orphans, and widows. If they trust their innocence in this regard, let them stand and debate these things with us; or if they are convicted, let them at least stop sinning in the future. — Furthermore, it is necessary that all fruits and actions of a prophecy be tested. Tell me, does a prophet dye his hair? Does he paint his eyes with antimony <note>original: 'stibio' — a dark mineral used as eyeliner in antiquity.</note>? Does he strive to be adorned? Does a prophet play with tables and dice?

> "Does he lend money at interest? Let them frankly confess and answer whether it is permitted to do these things or not. I will prove that these things have been done among them."

Thus says *Apollonius*. If we were writing a critical history of *Montanism*, not only these but other testimonies would need to be diligently examined. For anyone can see that some things were said out of hatred for *Montanus*, and others are clearly weak and devised to stir up envy against the *Montanists*. But the nature of our purpose does not allow this. Most of what I could bring forward has already been noted by the most learned men: *Rigaltius* in his preface to *Tertullian*, *J. Le Clerc*, *S. Basnage*, *Arnold*, and *Weismann*. We say this one thing: the enemies of the *Montanists* rashly and without sufficient reason ascribed the prophecies they boasted of, and the Visions, to the Devil. Certainly, if *Montanus* and his followers were such as their adversaries say they were, it should rather be said that black bile <note>original: 'atram bilem' — according to the medical theory of the four humors, an excess of black bile caused 'melancholy' or madness.</note> disturbed their brains, and that some of them were impostors. Hence those Bishops did wrong who wanted to cast out Demons from the *Montanists*. For I have no doubt that the *Montanists* would have raved more after the exorcism was applied than before. Certainly, this gave the simpler folk an occasion to imagine great things about those imaginary prophets, and to think lowly of their own Bishops. What was done with the *people of the Cevennes* <note>original: 'Cebennatibus' — a reference to the 'Camisards,' French Protestants in the early 1700s who claimed prophetic visions; the author is comparing the ancient Montanists to these modern 'fanatics.'</note> in the memory of our fathers is very well known. It is enough for us that no argument is present to say that the boasted Visions of the *Montanists* were of divine origin. God does not usually perform miracles to amend Church discipline. But here the question was solely about rigor toward those who lapsed, fasts, marriages, etc. To arrange such matters is for wise Church Moderators. But enough about the Visions of the *Montanists*. ### COROLLARIES <note>In an academic setting, these are concluding propositions or "takeaway points" that the author is prepared to defend in debate.</note>

I. *Rightly, and not without the weightiest of reasons,* the Psalmist <note>Referring to the author of the Psalms, traditionally King David.</note> *asserts in Psalm 14 that he is a fool who either thinks in his heart or professes with his mouth that there is no supreme Deity.*

II. *Although, as* Paul *testifies in his letter to the* Romans, chapter 1, verses 19 and 20, *that which can be known about* God *was also known to the* Gentiles <note>Non-Jewish people of the ancient world.</note>; *it does not yet follow from this that ideas about* God *are engraved and imprinted on all minds.* <note>The author is engaging in a philosophical debate about "innate ideas"—whether we are born with the concept of God or learn it from the world around us.</note>

III. *The whole universe and its individual parts—whether we consider the heavens, the earth, humans, animals, and plants; or finally, the order, beauty, harmony, and use of each—prove that not only were all things made and arranged by a most wise, good, free, and powerful* Artisan <note>A common Enlightenment-era term for God as the "Great Architect" or "Clockmaker."</note>, *but that these same things are still preserved and governed by Him with singular care. Hence, not only reason, but Revelation especially, leads us to duly celebrate the divine virtues visible in the administration of the world. See* Psalm 8:4-5, Psalm 19:1, Psalm 145:15-16.

IV. *Granted that reason provides sufficiently probable and clear arguments to prove that human minds are free from death <note>meaning the soul is immortal</note>; it is nevertheless certain that the Christian Religion adds the greatest weight to this argument.*

V. *We assert that Moses is not only the* Author of the Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Bible.</note>, *but we also contend that he is a most trustworthy envoy of* God, *contrary to what a recent* author—*and a most impudent one at that—of the book titled* The Malabar Princesses <note>original: "Les Princesses Malabares." This was a satirical work by Guillaume-Hyacinthe Bougeant (1734) that used an allegorical story of a distant land to critique the history and foundations of religion.</note> *did not blush to profess.*

VI. *Neither the books written in great number by impostors after the passing of* Christ and the Apostles, *and spread among the common people under the names of holy men, nor the varying readings of the* New Testament, *detract at all from the divine origin of the Christian Religion.*

VII. *Miracles are certain and infallible signs of true doctrine delivered by divine authority.*

VIII. *The opinion of* Woolston <note>Thomas Woolston (1670–1733), an English theologian who gained notoriety for arguing that the miracles of the New Testament were not historical facts but mere allegories.</note>, *who turned all the miracles of the* New Testament *into mere allegories—which recently caused such an uproar in* England—*is foolish and unworthy of a learned man.*

IX. *Holy Scripture is sufficiently clear and transparent in those things which are necessary to be known and done to attain salvation.*

X. *To correctly understand the Holy Scriptures and to settle controversies*

## HISTORICAL AND THEOLOGICAL DISQUISITION
### CONCERNING
# VISIONS,

### Which are said to have occurred to certain Christians during the first four centuries after the passing of Christ and the Apostles.

## THE SECOND PART.

### Section IX.

<image-desc>Large decorative drop cap 'P' inside a square frame featuring ornate foliage and scrolling patterns.</image-desc>
We proceed now to the 3rd Century, in which many visions of this kind are recorded to have happened to Christians, and especially to Cyprian <note>Thascius Caecilius Cyprianus (c. 210–258 AD), the Bishop of Carthage and an important early Christian writer.</note>. At the beginning of this century—specifically in the year 202 AD—Ruinart <note>Thierry Ruinart (1657–1709), a Benedictine scholar who edited the "Acta Primorum Martyrum," a collection of early martyr accounts.</note> places the passion of Perpetua, Felicitas, and Saturus. However, learned men disagree among themselves, not only regarding the collector of these *Acts of the Martyrs*, but also regarding the religion to which those martyrs were devoted. Valesius <note>Henri Valois (1603–1676), a French classical scholar.</note> contends that the collector of these *Acts* was a Montanist <note>A follower of Montanism, an early Christian movement that emphasized new prophetic revelations and strict asceticism, often viewed as heretical by the mainstream Church.</note>; furthermore, both Basnages <note>Referring to the Protestant historians Samuel and Jacques Basnage.</note> prove with arguments that are not to be despised that not only the collector of the *Passion*, but the martyrs themselves, were devoted to the opinions of Montanus. On the other hand, Ruinart and H. Dodwell <note>Henry Dodwell (1641–1711), an Anglo-Irish scholar and theologian.</note> deny both claims. It is difficult to settle the dispute from the visions themselves and the sayings of the martyrs; their words are not inconsistent with those made by the Montanists. But orthodox women could also speak in such a way. Since we must consider not only whether such things truly happened to certain people, but also whether those visions were of such a nature that it was worthy of God to offer them to humans, it will be all the same to us whether those women followed the camp of Montanus or that of the Catholics <note>In this context, "Catholic" refers to the "universal" or "orthodox" mainstream church of the time, as opposed to sectarian groups.</note>, although we do not find it difficult—

(*) Joseph Augustine Orsi <note>1692–1761, a Dominican theologian and later Cardinal.</note>, Lecturer of Sacred Theology, published an apologetic dissertation in Florence in 1728 concerning the orthodoxy of Perpetua, Felicitas, and their fellow martyrs against Samuel Basnage. In this work, he wished to prove with many learned arguments that Perpetua and Felicitas, along with their fellow martyrs, were clearly foreign to the error of Montanism. The matter does not seem to be of such great importance that I should examine individually all the arguments by which he wished to prove his opinion. It is enough for me that this most learned man confesses that the author of this compilation of martyrdom was devoted to the sect of Montanus; which is evidence to me that the martyrs themselves were not far removed from those opinions which Montanus and his followers defended. If someone devoted to the Roman Church were to set forth the martyrdom of a person recorded in the Protestant assembly and used those phrases which are accustomed to be used by the Protestants themselves, everyone would conclude that he was inclined toward that mind. The most learned man [Orsi] indeed asserts that the phrases used by the compiler of these martyrs are orthodox. But I would ask of him to explain in what that orthodoxy is situated. How much "Fanaticism" differs from "Montanism" is known to those who have examined the systems of both.

Section 21. Concerning *Perpetua*, the Anonymous Collector says: The others indeed stood motionless and received the sword in silence; much more so *Saturus*, who had also ascended the ladder first, was the first to give up his spirit, for he was also supporting *Perpetua*. But *Perpetua*, so that she might taste something of the pain, cried out when she was pierced between the ribs, and she herself placed the wavering right hand of the <term>apprentice gladiator</term> <note>original: "Tirunculi"—a novice gladiator in training</note> against her own throat. Perhaps such a great woman could not have been killed otherwise—because she was feared by the unclean spirit—unless she herself had willed it. Thus far the Collector of that Martyrdom.

It is helpful to note certain things regarding what has been said so far. And (1.) indeed, let no one be surprised if we doubt the visions reviewed thus far. Men far sharper and more learned than I have doubted them. The illustrious *Jacques Basnage* <note>A prominent 17th-century French Protestant theologian and historian</note>, a most fierce defender of the Christian Religion in other matters, did not hesitate to count *Perpetua* among *fanatical women*. We wish to detract nothing from the virtues of those Martyrs. We praise their singular constancy in bearing evils, and the confidence which they had in God. But we do not think that, for that reason, everything they said and did must be admitted without examination. If anyone thinks that extraordinary and divine revelations happened to these Martyrs, we willingly and with an even mind allow him to enjoy his own judgment. Why we think otherwise is due to reasons that are not slight, as we believe, whether we look to the author of these *Acts* or to the visions themselves. As (2.) pertains to the Author himself, *J. Basnage* proved by no contemptible reasons that he was addicted to the *Montanist sect* <note>A 2nd-century Christian movement that emphasized new, ecstatic prophecy and rigorous asceticism, often viewed as heretical by the mainstream church</note>. Let the reasons be read in his own work, Volume 2, page 1062 of the *History of the Church*. However, even if someone thinks the reasons brought forward by that learned man are not above all exception, it is nevertheless certain that many traces of lazy credulity are found in this very narrative. I will say nothing now (as is sufficiently clear from the preface prefixed to the *Acts*) of how the man strives with all his might to persuade us that miracles and visions can still happen in his time, that is, in the year 202 AD—a matter for which no one sees a reason why he should have labored so anxiously. Furthermore, he attributes many things to these Martyrs which are far from being likely. Such as: (a) that *Perpetua* was dyed in the holy font of baptism only a few days before she was cast into prison, and yet she enjoyed familiar conversation with God. If he only meant that this pious woman had embraced God with sincere

love, and had implored His help through prayers constantly poured out to God, there would be nothing we would not most willingly believe. But that God would grant perpetual visions to a woman not yet sufficiently taught in the Decrees of the Christian Religion can hardly be admitted. God is accustomed to accommodate Himself to the capacity of minds, and does not demand more than human natures can bear. A pious affection, joined with the knowledge of things necessary to be known for salvation, was sufficient to sustain the soul in adversity and to fortify it against dangers. But how a woman, who had not yet sufficiently perceived the character and nature of the Christian Religion, could have distinguished a mere dream from an extraordinary vision, is difficult to say.
<margin>(b) Page 95 of the *Acts* asserts: *Perpetua, having had a vision about receiving a small piece of cheese, and having woken from sleep, was still chewing I know not what sweet thing.*</margin>
Regarding these words, *Holstenius*, *Possinus*, and *Ruinart* <note>Prominent 17th-century scholars and editors of hagiographical texts</note>—the most fierce defenders of these visions—are silent. It is manifest, however, either that *Perpetua* was deceived, or that the Collector of these *Acts* lied on purpose. For if these things happened to her while dreaming through a true vision, by what means can she finally be said to have been eating something after being woken from sleep? Does it not follow from this that she did not have a clear view of the nature and character of a true vision? Unless perhaps you say (which would nevertheless be absurd) that a piece of cheese was actually given to her by Christ; yet how that could have contributed to fortifying the soul against encroaching dangers, we do not see. These things recall to my mind those events which once took place in *Bremen* regarding a paralyzed woman, whom I myself had seen and had questioned about the nature of the vision offered to her. ...so that she might be thrown to be torn apart by all sorts of beasts indiscriminately. Surely the Collector would not have brought these things forward to trumpet the praise of this Martyr if he had possessed an accurate knowledge of the Christian Religion. (*d*) He relates, furthermore, that *Perpetua*, after being tossed here and there by a cow, pinned up her scattered hair, lest—as he adds—she should seem to be mourning in the midst of her glory. Is it truly believable that a pious woman, placed in the very heat of her passion, would be anxious about arranging her hair, or would believe that her glory would be diminished if her hair were not properly set? Even more incredible is that *Perpetua*, having been tossed and wounded by a cow for a long time, was as if she had been lulled into a very deep sleep, having no sense of pain, and even being unaware until then that she had been attacked by a cow. I do not doubt that God can and usually does bring solace to pious souls in the midst of exquisite torments; but it is difficult to believe that they feel absolutely no pain during the torments, or are completely unaware that they are being tortured. (*e*) At the end of his narration, the Collector reports that it is believable that the woman could not have been killed in any other way than the one in which it happened. From this, the inept credulity of the man is apparent. *Perpetua* herself thought she would first be thrown to the beasts and thus pour out her wretched life; what, then, would have finally stood in the way of her dying by God's providence? Naturally, [he claims] because she was feared by the unclean spirit, she could only be killed by a sword driven into her throat. An extraordinary reason! (*f*) Regarding the same *Perpetua*, he says at the end that, so she might taste some pain, she placed the wandering right hand of the <term>apprentice gladiator</term> <note>original: "Tirunculi"—a novice gladiator in training</note> to her own throat

What the final scene of this story was, I shall add here together with the <term>evaluation</term> <note>original: "ἐπικρίσει" (epikrisei)—judgment or critical assessment</note> of this most distinguished Theologian, who was most favorable to us while he lived. This ought not to be neglected by me, so that you may see that my opinion has gained no small strength—which I have declared more than once—that whatever happened to her must be attributed not to some extraordinary miracle, but to the operation of nature, albeit a rarer and more obscure one. Let those attend to this who refer those things, the causes of which they are ignorant of, safely among the prodigies; and let them beware of selling the phantasms and dreams of their own unhealthy brains as visions presented by God. Would that in ancient times little stories of this kind had been so discussed and weighed by the scales of a holier wisdom. How small do we think the number of miracles would be which that dark and witless age attributed to its little saints? So says that famous Theologian.*

...to her own throat. If the Anonymous author was himself a spectator, how did he know that the pious woman had felt no sense of pain before being touched? Why does he praise what certainly ought not to be praised? She ought to have waited for the fatal stroke with constancy of mind, rather than, like a rabid person, moving the sword to her own throat. From this, one can judge what should be thought of *Holstenius’s* note on this passage, which says: *The gladiators used to do out of fury and madness what St. Perpetua did piously and generously, by Divine instinct.* (*)

(3.) If we turn our minds to the visions themselves, we shall find in them, in my opinion, nothing that could not have happened to these Martyrs in sleep according to the accustomed order of nature, and which therefore compels us to say that God instilled these visions through a miracle. The sum of them comes to this: *That Christians thrown into prison, if they were not going to deny the Christian religion, would suffer death, but on account of their constant confession of the truth, they would carry away a singular glory in heaven.* These men could believe these things without visions. Nor is it believable that they would ever have given their name to the Christian religion unless they had been most thoroughly persuaded of the great reward and happiness of the future life. And yet, as we have often warned, God is not accustomed to pour out miracles without cause. But (2.) other things are added in these visions which can prove they were a mere dream, not an extraordinary revelation. *Perpetua* asserts, as we heard above, that she freed her seven-year-old deceased brother from <term>limbo</term>, or <term>purgatory</term>, or if you prefer, from hell itself by her prayers; which opinion, although ancient, is false and contrary to the Holy Scriptures; and therefore not...

<sig>Vvvv 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: therefore not</meta>

<note>
(*) *The illustrious Pearson, in "Vindications of Ignatius," Part II, Chapter IX, not only praises this very action of Perpetua but also wishes to confirm his opinion by the example of other Martyrs of the primitive Church. But examples that "resolve one dispute with another dispute" accomplish nothing. It is one thing to say that unusual actions of this kind by Martyrs should not be attacked, but should be interpreted kindly because of the piety and zeal for the glory of God with which they were inflamed; it is quite another to assert that these same "heroic virtues" (if you wish to call them that) should be set forth and praised as an example for every single believer to follow in a time of persecution. We deny only this last assertion, and we have brought forward the principles on which our opinion rests in the first part of this Exercise, Sections VI and VII. From the huge number of examples to which the illustrious Pearson appeals in the cited place and praises them, I will bring forward only one. Especially famous (to use Pearson's own words) was the name of the Martyr Phocas, who, having by chance received the officers as guests who were telling him they had been sent to kill Phocas, promised he would show them Phocas the next day. Standing by the place already prepared for his burial, he said to them: "I am that Phocas." When they then hesitated, he added encouragement to their minds to kill him. "He spoke, he persuaded, he suffered, and having been beheaded, he was offered as a sacrifice pleasing to God." Thus Pearson. Whether, however, this action is to be so greatly praised, let the judgment rest with learned and pious readers.*
</note>

The author further argues that her visions, such as praying a brother out of purgatory, are biblically unsound and likely just natural dreams reflecting the prisoners' anxieties.</summary>

The Anonymous Collector, acting as the interpreter of the vision, says: she trampled the head of the Egyptian because she was singing psalms. But is singing hymns the same as fighting with the Devil? If fighting with the Devil is nothing else than standing bravely for the truth of the Christian Religion, then to what end was the Egyptian man represented in the vision? In the vision, she saw at one moment that she would fight with beasts, and at another with the Devil; yet the kind of death she would undergo was not revealed to her. <note>The following is translated from the original French.</note> *Is one not truly edified by reading these much-vaunted Acts, and seeing a Christian woman who becomes a boy, who struggles with fistfights, and who crushes the head of an Egyptian by taking it in her hands? These same ecstasies are seen in Perpetua’s sleep; the ridiculousness is not lacking, since she changed her sex there, becoming a male, and young boys came to rub her with oil. Finally, I do not know whether a vision was necessary to warn Bishop Optatus about correcting the common people who were fostering factions. These points seem sufficient to me to relegate these visions to the category of suspect Revelations.

He most urgently finished and faithfully dedicated the Basilica which his predecessor had faithfully begun. <meta>catchword: narrat</meta>

through miracles, priests and monks wished to secure grace and honor for relics when they could not do so through reason. *The spirit of vision* (so says J. Basnage in his *History of the Church*, page 1152 seq. Vol. II) <note>Jacques Basnage (1653–1723) was a celebrated French Protestant theologian and historian. The following passage is translated from the original French.</note> *and of miracles, contributed not a little to give currency to the veneration of Relics and Martyrs. On one hand, men run after the miraculous, with which they are enamored to excess; and on the other, it is almost impossible not to carry one's respect beyond just limits for the instruments that perform miracles. The discovery of Relics was made by means of some Revelation and established by a series of miracles. Instead of imitating the wisdom of God—who does not compromise His Omnipotence at every moment, and who would make it contemptible if He accustomed men to see it deployed for trivial subjects or to labor for the glory or satisfy every whim of a creature—there is nothing of which a more lavish profusion has been made than miracles. They are handed out with the same ease that God would produce them if such frequent miracles accorded with His wisdom. Unfortunately, even into sincere devotion there slips a trait of self-love, which leads good people to believe not only that God is interested in a religion He loves ardently, but that He must enter into their views and their thoughts to enhance the brilliance and glory of the Church. If those who sincerely love God fall into this fault, what must one think of the superstitious? Not only does such a person imagine that God loves Religion and the Church and interests Himself in his particular devotions, but that God almost never fails to authorize them by some miraculous event that brings shame to those who mock or despise him. Or rather, since voluntary devotions—the veneration and worship of Saints—cannot be established by Scripture, which directly opposes them, and since moreover there is no proof drawn from reason and common sense that can show a dead body and bones are worthy of veneration, one is forced to have recourse to miracles. One must show God speaking and teaching beyond His Scriptures, violating all natural laws in order to authorize a devotion different from that which common sense dictates and which He Himself established in His Word.* Thus that learned man speaks truly. Let these things, once said regarding relics confirmed by visions, suffice; nor in what follows shall we uselessly waste precious time examining visions made for the purpose of commending Relics.

*Ruinart* <note>Thierry Ruinart (1657–1709), a Benedictine scholar and editor of the "Acts of the Martyrs."</note> narrates this from *Eusebius’s Ecclesiastical History, Book VI, Chapter X.* The history, or rather the fable in my opinion, sounds like this according to the version by Valesius <note>Henri Valois (Valesius), a 17th-century scholar who produced a standard edition of Eusebius.</note> found in Eusebius: "But when, on account of extreme old age, he (namely Narcissus) could no longer perform his ministry, a divine dispensation called the aforementioned Alexander—who was bishop of another church—to share the priestly office with Narcissus, by means of a certain Revelation which appeared to him in a dream." Admonished by this Vision as if by a divine oracle, **Alexander**, who had first been ordained a Bishop in Cappadocia, set out for Jerusalem for the sake of both praying and seeing the holy sites. The brethren of that Church received him most kindly and did not allow him to return to his homeland thereafter. For another revelation had also been seen by them in a dream, and a most clear voice was heard by those who were eminent for holiness among them; it signaled to them that they should go outside the gates of the city and receive the Bishop destined for them by God. When they had done this, with the consent of the Bishops of neighboring Churches, they compelled him to remain with them from then on.

**Rufinus** <note>Tyrannius Rufinus (c. 340–410 AD), a monk and historian who translated and expanded Eusebius’s work into Latin.</note> in his *History, Book VI, Chapter 8*, tells the story in such a way that it appears even more miraculous to the reader. For after he noted that **Alexander** had arrived in Jerusalem, he adds these details: "It was clearly shown by the Lord, not only to the Blessed Narcissus himself, but also to many others among the people through Revelations, that they should keep him as Bishop in that Holy Place. Furthermore, what was more terrifying than all the rest: on the day when Alexander’s entry into the City was announced, and a great multitude of the brethren went out to meet him beyond the gates, a Voice from heaven was most clearly made to all those listening: 'Receive the Bishop who is destined for you by God.' And when the dispensation of God had been clearly declared to them by all these signs, the Bishops of the neighboring cities, having learned of everything that was being done concerning him by the judgment of God, compelled him by necessity to reside there."

Concerning these things, we advise the following: (1) We do not doubt that Narcissus and Alexander were men flourishing in piety and other virtues; but we do not think that everything narrated about them must be accepted for that reason. (2) *Eusebius, in Chapter IX* of this book, says: *The inhabitants of that parish commemorate many other amazing things about Narcissus, as if handed down from the succession of the brethren.* <note>original: "Πολλα μεν οὖν καὶ ἄλλα παραδοξα οἱ της παροικιας πολιται ὡς ἐκ παραδοσεως των κατα διαδοχην ἀδελφων τῶ Ναρκισσῶ μνημονευουσιν."</note> Behold the fountain and origin of the miracles from which **Eusebius** drew his narrative! Clearly, the inhabitants told many things about their Bishop, whom they held in the highest regard, and these stories, as usually happens when tradition enlarges everything, were later multiplied. I refer here to the miracle that Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), known as the "Father of Church History."</note> mentions immediately: namely, the miraculous changing of water into oil. (3.) The events related in this same ninth chapter concerning Narcissus <note>Narcissus of Jerusalem (c. 99–216 AD), a bishop celebrated for his longevity and holiness.</note> prove that not all actions of such men should be imitated. For after saying that certain wicked men, conscious of their own crimes, had cast a very heavy slander upon him and even wanted to gain belief through oaths and lies, Eusebius continues: *“But however much they swore, no one from among the number of the faithful believed them, because the restraint of Narcissus and the sanctity of his life, perfect in every measure of virtue, had always been seen and proven by all.”* Yet Narcissus, *“unable to bear the infamy of the rumors, and because he had long been held by a love for the philosophical life, abandoned the congregation of the Church and hid for many years in the wilderness and remote fields.”* Would it not have been more righteous for the Bishop to have managed the care of his Church and dissolved the slanders by the integrity of his life, especially after he noticed that no one believed the slanders spread against him?

I might say the same of Alexander himself, who, while Bishop of Flaviadis in Cappadocia, traveled to Jerusalem both for the sake of prayer and to visit the holy sites. It would have been better if he had stayed at home with his flock and prayed there. It seems that even then, many Bishops were seized by a certain superstitious love for the "Holy Land." (4.) As for the visions themselves, said to have been granted to Narcissus, Alexander, and others, they do not seem likely to me—not only because Eusebius relies solely on tradition, but because of the matter itself. Surely, without an extraordinary vision, the brethren could have substituted another for Narcissus when he was no longer able to perform his ministry due to his age. After he had fled to deserted places, the neighboring Bishops (according to Eusebius in Chapter 10) *“substituted Dius in his place, then Germanion, and finally Gordius.”* Why could they not have done the same now without a revelation?

Add to this that Eusebius himself confesses in Book VI, Chapter 8, that *Alexander* was famous for his noble confession of faith <note>A "confession of faith" refers to Alexander being imprisoned or tortured for his beliefs during a period of persecution.</note>. Was this not cause enough, and more, for the brethren in Jerusalem to ask him to accept the Bishopric of Jerusalem, leaving his own see? It is more remarkable that Eusebius, in the cited passage, says in so many words, *“He was promoted to the aforementioned Bishopric on account of his noble confession of the Christian faith,”* making no mention of Revelations. From this, it is clear enough what should be thought of the judgment of Valesius <note>Henri Valois (1603–1676), a French classical scholar and historian.</note>, who on this point is more pleased by the narrative of Rufinus <note>Tyrannius Rufinus (c. 345–410), who translated and expanded upon Eusebius’s history.</note> than that of Eusebius. The second: the authors of the narrative wanted to defend this election, which was made against the <term>Ecclesiastical Canons</term> <note>Church laws or regulations established by councils.</note>, with Divine visions. Two things (to use the words of *Ruinart* <note>Thierry Ruinart (1657–1709), a Benedictine monk and scholar who compiled the "Acts of the Martyrs."</note> following *Valesius*) *“were committed against the rules of the Church: first, that Alexander was transferred from one see to another; and second, that he was substituted for—or at least joined to—a Bishop who was still living.”* No example of such an act had previously occurred in the Church at that time. Whatever the cause of this narrative may be, nothing forces us to believe that God intervened here through a miracle.

To the narrative of the deeds of *Alexander* and *Narcissus*, *Ruinart* joins the *Acts of the Martyrdom of St. Pionius*. Exactly when he underwent martyrdom is not entirely certain. *Petavius*, *Scaliger*, and *Pearson* think it was in the time of *Marcus Aurelius*; while *Baronius*, *Ussher*, and *Valesius* believe it happened in the age of *Decius* <note>Mid-3rd century AD</note>, and *Ruinart* himself adds his support to this latter group. This *Pionius* is also said to have had a vision. Therefore, the day before the birthday of the Martyr Polycarp arrived, while he was devotedly persisting in fasts with Sabina and Asclepiades, he saw in his sleep that he was to be captured the following day. Since he recognized these things clearly and without doubt, because the vision appeared so vividly, he placed a rope around his own neck and those of Sabina and Asclepiades. Thus, when those who were to bind them arrived and found them already bound, they would know they were doing nothing new, and would understand that they were not to be led like the others who were tasting the sacrifices; since the chains had been put on before they were ordered, as both a testimony of faith and a sign of their will.”* So say the *Acts*. The vision itself is so constructed that it cannot easily be persuaded to any man of sound mind that God is its author. Pionius, as the acts testify, was a pious, intrepid man; indeed, he is said to have foreseen the encroaching evils. What cause was there, then, for God to teach him through a miracle that he was to be captured? Nor do I know why he placed a rope on his neck and that of Sabina: surely, he says, so that those who were about to capture him would know they were doing nothing new. But certainly those men, seeing a rope thrown around his neck, could believe nothing other than that Pionius either wished to lay violent hands on himself or was out of his mind. Could that rope thrown on the neck exhibit a testimony of faith? Nonsense!

XI. But let us come to the most celebrated Doctor and Martyr of the Church, *Caecilius Cyprian*, Bishop of Carthage. It is a common opinion that many visions occurred to him. We shall examine how truly this was done with care and without party zeal. We heard above that *Herman Witsius*, a most modest theologian, doubted many of them; he is followed by the most celebrated *Le Clerc* <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), a famous Genevan scholar.</note> in his life of our *Cyprian*, written in French. Indeed, even Bishop *Fell* <note>John Fell (1625–1686), Bishop of Oxford and editor of Cyprian's works.</note> himself, the editor of the Oxford edition and a sharp defender of the Fathers, confesses in certain places, not obscurely, that he does not admit them all indiscriminately. On the other hand, the most learned *Dodwell* <note>Henry Dodwell (1641–1711), a non-juring scholar and theologian.</note>, in *Cyprianic Dissertation IV*, not only sharply defends all the visions of the Blessed Martyr, but even goes so far as to say that all those who deny their divine origin are profane. We shall clearly prove, however, that here in this argument, as elsewhere, this man—otherwise most learned—allowed himself to be carried away by an excessive zeal for antiquity. And how, finally, do these things hang together: this or that learned man doubts, and indeed for serious reasons, whether all the visions *Cyprian* is said to have had are divine and extraordinary; therefore, this man, otherwise honest and even a lover of religion, favors impiety? Oh, what an unjust law learned men make against themselves, judging others so boldly! *Dodwell* himself, when he had published his dissertations on the small number of martyrs and the causes of martyrdom, experienced how vehemently those works displeased certain English prelates, who thought that material for triumphing was thus given to the Deists. > <margin>He belonged formerly to the Church, which produced about twenty-three pounds Sterling per year. He never wished to receive this portion of his income. He had half of it distributed to some of his relatives, and the other half to four widows and an orphan. Some other examples of the charity of Mr. **Dodwell** are reported, of which I shall say nothing. But I must not omit that, a few days before his death, he sent for Mr. **Brokesby** at night to tell him that he had thirty guineas in a purse, and that he wished half of it to be given to the poor children of his parish who came to Catechism, and the rest to other indigent persons. When he had some work printed, he asked for money from the booksellers only to give it away as charity. It was usually to needy clergymen that he distributed this money. He took care to give good advice to young students so that they might make themselves capable of serving the Church and the State. He reminded his friends of things regarding their salvation. We are told on this occasion that a certain learned man being ill, Mr. **Dodwell**, who suspected him of indifference in matters of religion, wrote to him, among other things, that the **Siamese** <note>Used here as a generic reference to distant non-Christians; the implication is that those who have never heard the Gospel are more excusable than Christians who ignore it.</note> would be more excusable on the Day of Judgment than Christians who do not act according to their principles. He was always ready to satisfy those who consulted him on some point of literature or on cases of conscience. He traveled on foot so that he could read while walking; and the books he carried then in his pockets were the *Hebrew Bible*, the *Greek New Testament*, the *Liturgy of the Church of England*, the *Imitation of Jesus Christ* by **Thomas à Kempis**, the *Meditations of St. Augustine*, etc. He was sometimes so burdened by them, even by large quartos, that one of his friends said jokingly that he had portable shelves under his great cloak, where he arranged them as if in a cabinet.</margin>

Finally, the Illustrious **Burnet**, Bishop of **Salisbury**, after showing more than enough in a letter given to **Dodwell** himself how much certain opinions defended by him displeased him, nevertheless praises his piety, saying in the place cited on page 92: *“You are learned, and you have led an irreproachable and even exemplary life.”* <note>original: "Vous êtes Savant, & vous avès mené une vie irréprochable, & même exemplaire." *“To us also,”* (he says) *“the least and the last, how often it has been revealed, how frequently and clearly it has been commanded by the condescension of God: That I should constantly protest and publicly preach that our brothers who have been freed from the world by the Lord’s summons are not to be mourned, since we know they are not lost but sent ahead; that in departing they precede us, as those who are traveling or sailing are wont to do; that they should be longed for, not lamented, and that black garments should not be taken up here when they have already taken up white robes there; that no occasion should be given to the Gentiles to deservedly and rightly reproach us, that we mourn as extinguished and lost those whom we say are living with God, and that we do not prove by the testimony of our heart and breast the faith which we utter with words and voice?”*

I do not know by what reasoning the brothers, being persuaded of the truth of the Christian religion, could have doubted whether pious men carried off by a pestilential disease had passed into blessed immortality, and whether their grief should be indulged to such an extent. Even granted that some, touched by the loss of their loved ones, exceeded the limit in their sorrow, was a singular Revelation finally necessary to recall them? Were there not the weightiest arguments at hand, known to neither **Cyprian** nor the brothers? See what **J. Le Clerc** thought of this Revelation of **Cyprian** in the *Life of Cyprian* written in French, page 317 and following. In Epistle XI, the Blessed Martyr relates several visions made to him. In this letter, he exhorts them to constant prayer. Among other things, he speaks thus on page 24: *“For you ought to know what more persuaded and compelled me to write these letters to you (just as the Lord deigns to show and reveal; it was said in a vision: ‘Ask and you receive’).”* <note>original: "Petite & impetratis." A Latin rendering of the biblical promise "Ask and it shall be given to you."</note> Indeed, a command was then given to the people standing by that they should ask for certain persons designated to them. But in asking, there were discordant voices and differing wills; and this greatly displeased Him who had said, *“Ask and you receive,”* because the inequality of the people disagreed, nor was there a single and simple consensus of the brothers, and joined concord, since it is written: *“God who makes those of one mind to dwell in a house.”* And again: *“But I say to you, that if two of you agree on earth, concerning anything whatsoever you shall ask, it shall happen for you from my Father, who is in heaven. For if two of one mind can do so much,”*

Long ago we would have obtained from divine mercy what we seek, nor would we have fluctuated so long in this danger to our safety and our faith. **Cyprian** <note>Saint Cyprian was the Bishop of Carthage in the 3rd century, known for his writings on church unity.</note> wishes to show that one must not only be free for prayer strenuously, but that this must be done with united forces; however, he suggests that the seeds of dissension stand in the way of many of the common people doing this, and for this reason, God does not always hear those who pray. But can these things not be known without an extraordinary vision? Furthermore, it must be added what **Le Clerc** <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), a famous Genevan theologian and scholar known for his critical approach to history.</note> most rightly advises here, saying on page 252 of the *Life of Cyprian*: *Cyprian does not say (thus I translate from the French edition) that this diversity of opinions, into which the common people were distracted, had been revealed to him from heaven, nor that he had been taught by the same extraordinary way that God was offended for that reason. Whence it cannot be held for certain, as **Dodwell** <note>Henry Dodwell, the scholar discussed on previous pages, who often defended the authenticity of early Christian miracles.</note> asserts, that our Bishop had perceived the thoughts of the common people through revelation. He could have known them from the talk of the people themselves; moreover, from the outcome and from scripture, he could have known that it displeases God that they were so little in accord with one another regarding the matter of their prayers. Whence it is probable that Cyprian could have mistaken a natural dream for an extraordinary Revelation.*

The second vision follows. *Indeed (he says) these evils would not even have come to the brothers if the brotherhood had been animated as one. For this too was shown: that the Master of the House was sitting with a young man <note>original: "juvene"; likely referring to Christ</note> sitting at his right hand, which young man—anxious, and with a certain sadness mixed with indignation—was sitting with his hand supporting his jaw with a mournful face. But another, standing on the left side, carried a net, which he threatened to cast so that he might catch the surrounding people; and while the one who saw it wondered what this might be, it was said to him: that the Youth, who sat thus at the right hand, was saddened and grieved because his precepts were not being observed; but that one on the left exulted because an occasion was given to him to take the power of venting his rage from the Master of the House.* This was shown long before the storm of this devastation <note>referring to the Decian persecution of Christians</note> arose. *And we saw fulfilled what had been shown: that while we despise the Lord's precepts, while we do not keep the healthy commands of the law given to us, the enemy received the power of doing harm, and covered those who were less armed and less cautious for resisting with the cast of his net.* The argument of the whole vision comes down to this: men who neglect God's commands are exposed to the insults of the Devil, and as persecution rushes in, this very thing has been confirmed by the example of many. However, this Revelation is far too vague. **Cyprian** could easily have known without a revelation that men devoted to pleasures and unmindful of God's commands would stir up harmful dangers for themselves, and would not be properly

<margin>The famous Le Clerc's words</margin> (*) The defenders (he says) of the visions of St. Cyprian suppose that he had this revelation at a time in which one could not humanly foresee whether the persecution would last or not; but he says nothing of this, and he proposes this Revelation like all the others with much obscurity, without joining to it almost any circumstance. But even if one could not have foreseen the end of the persecution—which one cannot know unless one had lived in that time—one could always say that one easily dreams of what one ardently desires, and that when one extremely wishes to have Revelations, one easily takes one's dreams for Prophecies. And as soon as some person of consideration is found who imagines that he has visions, his heated imagination makes him have them at every moment, and causes many to believe also that God does not disdain to converse with them. One can fall all the more easily into this thought because St. Cyprian adds that God had also deigned to reveal to him that it was necessary to eat and drink very little, for fear that the Spirit, already elevated by a divine vigor, should be weakened by the attractions of the world. A precept as general as that one would have no need of a new Revelation; and God, who never squandered them upon the ancient Prophets, would have used them then in an entirely new manner.

But everyone who understands the institution of the Holy Supper <note>The Eucharist or Communion.</note> handed down by Christ knows this is false. It is true that the custom of mixing wine with water was ancient enough, as **Bingham** <note>Joseph Bingham (1668–1723), an English scholar of Christian antiquities.</note> shows in *Antiquities of the Christian Church*, Vol. VI, Book XV, Chapter II, citing the testimonies of **Irenaeus**, **Justin Martyr**, and the author of the *Apostolic Constitutions*. The modern Greek Church still observes this rite, as **Rycaut**, **Heineccius**, and **Elsner** prove. But there is no express command of Christ on this matter. Even if Christ had most especially taught us by His own example that wine used in the Holy Supper should be tempered with water, was a new vision really necessary to prove it? I will say nothing now about the forced interpretations of many passages of Holy Scripture by which he wanted to confirm his opinion—which was, of course, presented as a vision. <margin>(1)</margin> ...it seems that some found these visions ridiculous and foolish, but primarily those who preferred to believe against the priests rather than believing the priest, etc. From these citations, it is clear that **Cyprian** <note>St. Cyprian (c. 210–258 AD), Bishop of Carthage and an important Early Christian writer.</note> wished to suggest that the election of Bishops in that era occurred through some extraordinary divine method. However, anyone who paid even the slightest attention to the actual process of election could easily see that this was false. The worst part was that **Florentius** <note>A critic or rival of Cyprian who questioned his authority.</note> could have used this same argument against Cyprian himself. <margin>(2)</margin> It is well established that the constant boasting about visions caused certain people—those with a "keen nose" for the truth—to doubt the reality of those visions, and for good reason. Cyprian’s refutation of these skeptics is certainly weak; he merely claims that these visions only seem foolish to those who would rather trust rumors against a priest than trust the priest himself. It is as if every word spoken about priests must be accepted as a divine oracle with blind consent. <margin>(3)</margin> It is therefore believable that Cyprian intentionally fabricated this vision to strengthen his own authority; unless, perhaps, you argue that those who think more kindly of him are right—that Cyprian viewed anything he did with a good heart and judged to be right and praiseworthy as a "vision granted from heaven." In that sense, no good person is ever without "visions." But lest I seem to judge this vision too harshly, I will present the judgments of others here. **Rigaltius** <note>Nicolas Rigault (1577–1654), a French classical scholar and jurist who edited the works of Cyprian.</note> speaks thus: *“Here he also makes use of appearances and visions—a weapon for crushing adversaries that was most powerful in the hand of Cyprian, an excellent and divine man, though otherwise it would be vain and futile.”* <note>original: "hic etiam utitur ostensionibus & visionibus, telo ad conterendos Adversarios..."</note> For even a clever rhetorician or a crafty sophist could devise such visions perfectly suited to his cause to deceive the unwary and the simple. **Fell** <note>John Fell (1625–1686), Bishop of Oxford and editor of Cyprian’s works.</note> briefly, though with less confidence in the case, judges it so: *“But if Pupianus <note>A critic who wrote a letter to Cyprian questioning his character.</note> believed it right to trust rumors, it is only fair that he should not be angry at Cyprian for trusting dreams.”* It is remarkable how the prejudice of authority carries away even the most learned men, so that they do not dare to speak their true opinions openly! For what does Rigaltius mean by a “Divine man”? Does he mean a good and pious man? Even a good and pious man can be carried away by emotion and add the weight of a firm conviction to a slight opinion or a play of the imagination. Or does he mean a man endowed with a perpetual gift of Inspiration? But it first had to be proved that Cyprian was adorned with this gift, rather than simply taking it for granted. Fell’s explanation, if I understand anything, comes down to this: since Pupianus was allowed to trust any little story harmful to Cyprian’s reputation, Cyprian could similarly use fictional visions against Pupianus to suppress him. Whether this defense is honorable for the Bishop of Carthage—or for the Bishop of Oxford, who would elevate the dignity of the episcopal office beyond measure—is for others to judge. For us, the candor of **Jean Le Clerc** <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), a famous Genevan theologian and scholar known for his critical approach to church history.</note>

In **Letter 32**, he says that the "divine votes" preceded the ordination of **Aurelius**. From this, conclude that the ordinations of the clergy—not only of Subdeacons and Presbyters, but even of Lectors—were already considered not secular, but sacred, to the point that they were almost signaled [by God].

> (\*) <note>This section translates the original French footnote into English.</note> If these dreams (he says) were good for **St. Cyprian**, who had them, they could not have much force against his adversaries, because they were not obliged to believe what he said without proof—that he was making God say his own opinions, which experience refuted. He could have added: speaking of himself. It appears everywhere that our Martyr believed that as soon as a man was elected Bishop, it was a sign that God approved of him, and that as long as he remained attached to the majority of Bishops, no one had the right to accuse him. He expresses himself in terms so general and so positive that one cannot doubt that this was his principle, despite whatever inconveniences it might be subject to.
