...that some divine occurrence might happen before their ordination. If **Rigaltius** <note>Nicolas Rigault (1577–1654), a French classical scholar and editor of Cyprian’s works.</note> had wished to speak plainly, he would have said that **Cyprian** was either deceived by certain passages of Scripture—especially the Old Testament—or deluded by a vain opinion, believing that perpetual visions were necessary to fulfill the office of a Bishop. And what does Rigaltius's ambiguity mean when he says that signs *almost* <note>original: "Fere"</note> occurred before the ordination? If they *almost* occurred, then they did not *truly* occur; in that case, Cyprian was merely using rhetoric and wished to impose upon his Clergy—or, if that seems too harsh, he was at least deceived himself.

In the preceding letter (which is the 39th according to the chronology of **Pearson** <note>John Pearson (1613–1686), Bishop of Chester and a renowned scholar of the early church.</note>), he informs the Church of Carthage about the ordination of **Celerinus** as a Lector. He speaks of this election in the following way:

> *Exult and rejoice with us (he says) upon reading our letter, in which I and my colleagues who were present report to you that Celerinus, our brother, glorious alike in virtues and character, has been joined to our Clergy not by human favor, but by divine dignity. When he hesitated to consent, he was compelled by the admonition and exhortation of the Church itself in a vision by night, so that he would not refuse our persuasion; for it was neither right nor fitting that one whom the Lord had so honored with the dignity of heavenly glory should be without ecclesiastical honor.*

Let the notes of Rigaltius on this passage be consulted again. Among other things, he says: *One should also note here the industriousness of Cyprian, who uses the efficacy of visions so smoothly.* Rigaltius follows a metaphorical way of speaking so that he might seem to say something in Cyprian's defense. However, if Celerinus, though adorned with such great virtues, could not be moved by reason while awake to undertake this office, how could a phantom of the "Church" presented to his imagination at night achieve this—and indeed, without reasons? Perhaps the abstract idea of "the Church" holds a singular power over certain temperaments. But to speak seriously, this vision carries no appearance of probability. There was no lack of men in **Africa** and **Italy** who could perform public duties if one or two happened to decline; nor was there such a need for singular visions and miracles to rouse men to seek Ecclesiastical offices. It is more than sufficiently clear that Cyprian, being absent, wished to persuade the Presbyters and the people that whatever he had undertaken with good intentions was confirmed by divine visions and revelations. Hence, in Letter 59, he extols the authority of Bishops beyond all measure, asserting that all heresies are born because Bishops have not been obeyed. To not listen to a Bishop, he claims, is the same as despising the decrees of God. I will not even mention what a wretched interpreter of Scripture Cyprian is, appealing to passages of Holy Scripture to defend an inept opinion which actually concerns—

<meta>catchword: other [aliis]</meta>

---

<page-num>725</page-num>
->### ON THE VISIONS OF THE EARLY CHRISTIANS.<-

—other matters entirely. I will say only this: he "cuts down his own vineyards" <note>An idiom meaning he undermines his own argument.</note>. It is well known what was debated and transacted between **Stephen**, the Bishop of Rome, and **Cyprian** regarding the baptism of Heretics. According to Cyprian’s principle, obeying a Bishop is the same as obeying Christ or God. This being granted, it necessarily follows that contradictory things must be followed by the force of the Divine will: for one Bishop <note>Cyprian</note> decreed that Heretics must be baptized again, while the other <note>Stephen</note> decreed they must not. What could be more absurd than this assertion? 

In Letter 61, he contends that **Cornelius** <note>Pope Cornelius (died 253 AD).</note> was made Bishop of Rome by a unique Providence of God, even though it is clearer than the midday sun that the Roman and African Bishops and Clergy raised Cornelius to that dignity. **Baronius** <note>Caesar Baronius (1538–1607), a Cardinal and historian who wrote the *Annales Ecclesiastici*.</note> noted this well and turned it to his own advantage <note>To support the idea of divine appointment for Popes.</note>, for which he was rebuked by the **Bishop of Oxford** <note>John Fell (1625–1686), who edited Cyprian’s works.</note>, who said: *The most illustrious Annalist [Baronius] thinks he was designated by some divine sign. But it is not our place to forge miracles. He is said to be elected by the judgment of God who is the kind of man the law requires for the undertaking of that office.* 

This explanation, although favoring our side <note>The Protestant/critical view.</note>, is not consistent with Cyprian’s style. His actual words sound like this:

> *Cornelius was made Bishop by the judgment of God and His Christ, and by the testimony of almost all the Clergy, by the vote of the people who were then present, and by the college of ancient Priests and good men:*

and a little later: *Then, afterwards, he undertook the Bishopric not by canvassing or extortion, but by the will of God, who makes priests, etc.* Thus says the **Reverend Fell**: I am persuaded that this man <note>Fell</note> would have interpreted Cyprian’s words very differently had he not seen Baronius seeking an argument from them to establish the authority of the Pope. Therefore, that paraphrase seems to have arisen from partisan zeal. For if Cyprian had wished to say nothing more than that Cornelius had been elected according to the canons, it would have been enough to appeal to the consent of the excellent men who favored this promotion; but he goes further and appeals to the will of God and Christ. For this reason, we can rightly say that Cyprian, by using rhetoric concerning the authority of Bishops, contributed greatly to the pride of the Roman Bishops and the innumerable evils that followed. To this you may also refer his discussions on excommunication. Hear how he responds in **Letter 4** to **Pomponius**, who was consulting him about certain disobedient people:

> *Let them not think (he says) that the logic of life or salvation remains for them among other things, if they refuse to obey Bishops and Priests; since in Deuteronomy the Lord God says: And whatever man acts in pride...*

For they cannot live outside, since the house of God is one, and salvation can belong to no one except in the Church. The third Epistle <note>Actually refers to Letter 4 in many modern numbering systems, or Letter 3 to Rogatianus.</note> speaks even more boldly. When the **Illustrious Böhmer** <note>Justus Henning Böhmer (1674–1749), a celebrated German canon lawyer and historian.</note> had brought forward these passages in his learned book cited above, he rightly adds on page 209: *In the passage cited, he [Cyprian] heaped up all the arguments, authority, power, and honor he could find in the Old Covenant to vindicate the Priests, for no other purpose than because he believed that the same authority and power—which among the Jews was nearly royal—should also be granted to Bishops. For he saw them as similar to the High Priests and Supreme Pontiffs in the Jewish Republic, so that all their rights could and should be applied to them. From this persuasion, the power of Bishops was immensely increased, and thereafter the affairs of Christians, which from the beginning conformed to the institutions of the Jewish Synagogues, began to be modeled entirely after the liturgy of the Jewish temple.* Thus says the Illustrious Böhmer. By what means the spiritual or metaphorical sword was truly changed into a real one by the Bishops in the following centuries is, alas, well enough known <note>A likely reference to the later use of secular force and the "two swords" doctrine to enforce religious orthodoxy.</note>.

And these things which we have brought forward so far might suffice for a **Discerning Man** to pass judgment on the value of the visions offered to Cyprian. However, lest we seem to have omitted anything that might serve to examine those visions, come, let us hear how the most learned **Dodwell** <note>Henry Dodwell (1641–1711), an Anglo-Irish scholar who defended the antiquity of the episcopal system.</note> proves that truly divine visions happened to him.

First, he appeals to *Letter 10*, in which Cyprian ascribes his retreat <note>During the Decian persecution (c. 250 AD), Cyprian fled Carthage and governed via correspondence.</note> to a Revelation. *And you shall hear everything, when the Lord makes me return to you, He who commanded me to withdraw.* But I deny that this is an indubitable sign of an extraordinary revelation having been made. For since Christ himself in the Gospel enjoined his disciples that, if persecution were imminent, they should move from place to place if they could, **Cyprian** could have said the Lord commanded this in that sense. The love of life and the laws of prudence could have sufficiently stimulated and induced him to this. Furthermore, **Pontius** <note>Pontius the Deacon, Cyprian’s biographer.</note>, the writer of Cyprian’s life, to whom Dodwell appeals on page 5, adds many and various reasons for this retreat—all of which are hollow if he was moved to seek retreat by a direct Revelation.

*Secondly*, **Dodwell** cites the words of **Cyprian**, in which he says he is chastised by nocturnal and diurnal visions because the Priests, without consulting him, had granted peace to the lapsed <note>term: "lapsed" (Latin: *lapsi*). Christians who renounced their faith or performed pagan sacrifices under the pressure of Roman persecution.</note>. But will anyone persuade himself that God would even provide visions on account of the canons of Church discipline, which must be moderated according to the circumstances of the time? Did not **Cyprian** himself eventually think that one should retreat from excessive rigor toward the lapsed? Must we believe, then, that this man enjoyed perpetual and never-interrupted visions? Certainly, his entire opinion regarding Church discipline rested on poorly understood passages of Scripture, not on visions. See the **Illustrious Böhmer** in the place cited above.

Furthermore, **Dodwell** calls to his aid those things which **Cyprian** narrates in *Letter 43* concerning the five Priests who were followers of **Felicissimus's** faction and were represented, as it seems, through a vision. Specifically, five Priests, aided by the faction of **Felicissimus**, began to alienate the minds of many from **Cyprian**. These dissensions had prevented him from being able to come to Carthage before the feast of Easter, fearing—as he had been warned—lest his presence increase the tumult and provide the pagans an opportunity for insulting the Christians. He therefore wrote this Letter to the entire congregation, and he not only exhorts them to adhere constantly to him, but also vehemently inveighs against his adversaries, desiring to make them hated in every way; indeed, he seems to assert as if he had seen those five Priests in a vision, conspiring with the Nobles <note>original: "Optimatibus"</note> who were attacking the Christian Religion. Cyprian's words sound like this:

> This is another persecution, and another temptation: and those five Priests are nothing other than those five leaders who were recently joined to the Magistrates by the edict.

**Pamelius** <note>Jacques de Pamèle (1536–1587), a Flemish theologian and editor of Cyprian.</note> explains these words thus: *It seems to me he alludes to some vision, in which the five leaders appeared with the Magistrates, who together published the edict against the Bishops.* This interpretation pleases **Dodwell**, because it favors his purpose. But I detect no trace of any vision in these words. To me, it seems rather that the Bishop is using an argument drawn from hostility. Namely, he wants to make those five Priests hated, as is evident from the whole Letter. Therefore, to achieve this, he compares them with the Governors and Proconsuls of the Provinces among the Heathens, who declare war on the Christian Religion and persecute Christians. But who, finally, would believe that God, in order to kindle and increase anger against Priests in the mind of **Cyprian**, would have brought this about through a miracle? And why do only the Priests, and not **Felicissimus** himself, appear in that vision? **Rigaltius** <note>Nicolas Rigault, another editor mentioned on the previous page.</note> likewise [considers it] a vision...

## XII.

But let us come to others. In the same times that Cyprian flourished, *Dionysius of Alexandria* <note>Bishop of Alexandria (d. 264 AD), known for his moderate stance on church discipline and his scholarly approach.</note> was famous. He, in a letter to *Philemon*, a Priest of the Roman Church, which is found in *Eusebius's Ecclesiastical History, Book VII, Chapter 7*, relates the following:

> *Indeed (he says), I applied my labor to learning the books and traditions of the Heretics; for a time defiling my soul with their execrable opinions; yet perceiving this benefit from them, that I might refute them silently within myself, and detest them much more than before. And when a certain brother from the order of Priests prohibited me, fearing lest I might be mingled with the filth of their wickedness—indeed saying that my mind would be contaminated, and quite truly so, as I myself felt—I was confirmed by a vision sent from heaven. And a voice brought to my ears spoke clearly to me in this way:* Read everything that comes into your hands. For you are capable of inquiring into and examining individual things: and by this occasion you were first impelled toward the faith of Christ. *I embraced that vision, as one that agreed with the Apostolic voice, which addresses the very strong in this way:* Be skilled money-changers. <note>Original: "Estote periti Nummularii." This is a famous "agraphon"—a saying attributed to Jesus or the Apostles that is not found in the standard Gospels.</note>

<margin>(*) Concerning the origin of the practice of proscribing the books of Heretics and Pagans in the Christian Church, see *Paolo Sarpi's History of the Council of Trent*, Volume II, page 150. *Amsterdam* Edition.</margin>

(*) Cannot any man of sound mind understand without any inspiration that the errors of Heretics cannot be rightly refuted unless their writings are read? Who then will believe Dionysius in these matters? I could easily believe that the good man, touched by empty anxiety and fear while reading such things, sometimes thought a voice happened to him while meditating or sleeping; but I cannot be led to believe that a miracle intervened. (2.) From the example of Dionysius, and the Priest of whom he makes mention, it is clear how early a hatred toward dissenters was bred in the Orthodox,

And the outcome of events later declared that this was the work of Divine Providence. For perhaps we were not useless to some people.*

<page-num>732</page-num>
<header>->ON THE VISIONS OF THE EARLY CHRISTIANS.<-</header>

the good disposition of his mind—as we previously noted in the example of reading the books of the Heretics—for an unusual and extraordinary command from God, it could easily have happened that what was actually done through his own prudence, he attributed to the singular and miraculous protection of God. The latter point is this: the words, <term>ὧδε ἄθεος πεποίημαι τὴν ψυχὴν</term> <note>original Greek: "thus I have made my soul godless"</note> can signify that he always weighed within himself, in the fear of the Lord and having invoked His name, whether the traps of the persecutors ought to be fled or not. Certainly, we have said elsewhere that *Christ* himself enjoined his disciples that, if it could be done without detriment to illustrating the truth, they should withdraw from one place to another.

The same *Eusebius* <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, the 4th-century "Father of Church History."</note> in Book V, Chapter 28, quoting from an *Anonymous author*—whom some think to be *Caius*—relates the following regarding the confessor *Natalis*. There was (he says) a certain *Natalis* (*) by name, a Confessor <note>A "Confessor" was a Christian who suffered for their faith during Roman persecutions but was not executed.</note>, who lived not so long ago, but within our own age. This man was by chance led into deception by *Asclepiodorus*, and another man, *Theodotus the Money-changer*. Both were disciples of that *Theodotus the Tanner*, who was the first to be removed from the communion of the Church by *Victor*, the Bishop at that time, because of this doctrine, or rather, this madness. These men persuaded *Natalis* to be appointed as the Bishop of their heresy in exchange for a salary; namely, on the condition that he would receive one hundred and fifty denarii from them every month. Having thus joined their party, he was often rebuked by the Lord in his dreams. For the most merciful God, and our Lord Jesus Christ, who had been a witness to his sufferings, did not wish him to perish outside the Church. But when *Natalis* neglected such nocturnal visions, being enticed by the honor of the high seat among them and by the desire for base gain (which is the ruin of many mortals), he was finally beaten with whips and most severely lashed by holy Angels throughout the entire night. So much so, that rising at the first light of dawn, he put on sackcloth, sprinkled himself with ash, and immediately threw himself with tears at the feet of Bishop *Zephyrinus*, prostrating himself at the tracks not only of the Clergy, but even of the Laity; and by his weeping, he moved and shook the very Church of the merciful Christ, which is itself merciful. And using many prayers, even showing the welts from the lashes which he had endured for the confession of *Christ*, he was at last barely admitted back to communion. Thus says that *Anonymous author*.

However, we consider that vision to be doubtful (1) because the reliability of this author is not well known, nor is it established whether he received what he narrates from *Natalis* himself, or whether he placed his faith in the narration of others. (2) It is not probable that Heretics are recalled to a better mind by visions. Reasons and arguments alone are sufficient to recognize the nature of some error.

<meta>catchword: nature (ram)</meta>

(*) In the Summary of this investigation, which was sent before the first part, the name *Attalus* crept in by error instead of the word *Natalis*; I pray the Kind Reader to correct it or forgive the mistake.

<page-num>733</page-num>
<header>->ON THE VISIONS OF THE EARLY CHRISTIANS.<-</header>

(3.) If God had wished to perform a miracle, then he would have brought it about that He first rooted out the desire for gain from his soul, rather than recalling him to a better mind only after he had shamefully fallen. (4.) If it is true that the man was warned by nocturnal visions—and divine ones at that—to confess his error, it is scarcely probable that God would judge him worthy of angelic punishments to compel him to finally renounce his error. (5.) Finally, how did *Natalis* know they were Angels who were beating him with whips? Where had he ever heard that Angels are the Torturers of Heretics? And if he knew they were Angels, how did he know this was being done solely because he had lapsed into heresy? Perhaps one might guess that these things were handed down concerning *Natalis* in imitation of what is said about *Paul* in 2 Corinthians 12:7. (*) (6.) If I weigh those things which the *Anonymous author* narrates concerning those Heretics in the following passages, it is not far from the truth that some of the orthodox handed down such things about *Natalis* for the purpose of bringing some glory to the orthodox doctrine, while rendering the Heretics hated. The words of the *Anonymous author* are these: *They boldly corrupted the Holy Scriptures, and rejected the rule of the primitive faith.*

<meta>catchword: Chri-</meta>

---

(*) I think that the uncertain narrations of the Ancients concerning nocturnal and daily beatings, which Angels (especially evil ones) are said to inflict on the pious, arose from this difficult passage. In the *Life of St. Anthony* written by *Athanasius*, there is frequent mention of such angelic beatings. In the Legends of a later age, where everything is increased by fictional narrations and miracles, Demons are very frequently brought onto the stage receiving the saints with horrific whips. These things, however, smack of fables. And this is the one reason why the author of the *History of the Popes* written in the French language, on page 48, rejects the narration of *Caius*. I saw recently, while doing other things, that the Reverend Bishop *Bull* <note>George Bull (1634–1710), a famous Anglican theologian.</note>, in his *Judgment of the Catholic Church* concerning the necessity of believing that our Lord Jesus Christ is the true God, Chapter III, page 27 (Grabe’s edition), wished to vindicate the truth of this narration. The words of that Most Learned Man sound thus: *Otherwise, as far as the repeated visions are concerned, in which the Lord Jesus himself is said here to have shown himself as the avenger of his divine Majesty and to have punished the madness of the lapsed Confessor; no one will easily reject them as fictions who observes that the Confessor himself narrated these things about his own most shameful fall, while seriously performing penance in the Church before many witnesses, whose faith the most serious Writer of this History appealed to as mostly still surviving. Thus says Bull.* We reply with two points. The first is, it is not explicitly said by the Author that these things were spoken before many witnesses in a meeting of the Church. The second: we do not deny that *Natalis* publicly confessed his error; nor do we call into doubt what the Confessor narrates concerning the anguishes of his conscience. This one thing is investigated: whether truly divine visions happened to him in his sleep, and whether he was beaten by Angels with whips. He could have been tormented day and night because of the foul error and fall into which he fell due to greed, without the whips of Angels and the warnings of nocturnal visions. For what is more contrary even to the first Elements of Religion than to patronize an error, which we ourselves confess to be deadly, for the sake of some base gain? Could *Natalis* not easily have been convicted of the atrocity of this crime without nocturnal visions? Furthermore, this same *Caius*, in his dispute against Proclus the Montanist, wishing to prove the excellence and dignity of the Catholic Church, appealed to the Holy Bodies of Peter and Paul preserved at Rome; concerning which *Spanheim* in his *Four Dissertations, 1* should be consulted.

<meta>This page continues the critique of heretical groups who favored secular logic over scripture, specifically focusing on the followers of Theodotus. It then transitions to a famous account from Eusebius regarding the martyrdom of Potamiaena and the miraculous conversion of the officer Basilides through a vision.</meta>

<page-num>734</page-num>
<header>->ON THE VISIONS OF THE EARLY CHRISTIANS.<-</header>

They were ultimately ignorant of Christ himself, not seeking what the sacred scriptures teach, but instead busily meditating on what kind of syllogistic figures <note>A syllogism is a form of logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises (e.g., All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal).</note> might be found to confirm their own impiety. If anyone should confront them with a passage of divine scripture, they examine whether a connected or disconnected type of syllogism can be constructed from it. Having abandoned and cast aside the sacred scriptures of God, they study geometry; for they are of the earth and speak of earthly things, and they ignore him who came from heaven. Thus, the geometry of **Euclid** is diligently cultivated among some of them. **Aristotle** and **Theophrastus** are held in the highest admiration. **Galen** <note>Galen was a famous Greek physician whose works dominated Western medicine for centuries; here, the author suggests the heretics treat his scientific writings like scripture.</note> is even worshipped by some. Furthermore, what is the point of saying that those who abuse the arts and disciplines of infidels to establish the opinions of their heresy, and who adulterate the most simple faith of the divine scriptures with the subtle craftiness of impious men, are far removed from the faith? So says the *Anonymous Author*.

It is likely that men educated in these letters would have elected a Bishop who was also captured by a love for such disciplines. However, it is exceedingly difficult to believe that men adorned with such intellect, and devoted to these studies, were going to be recalled from their errors by nightly visions. If, however, **Natalis**, being unlearned in philosophical letters, attached himself to this faction out of mere greed for gold, he could have been recalled to a better mind by the stings of conscience without a miracle. Whatever the case, this is certain: the Author of the *Apostolic Constitutions* <note>A 4th-century collection of ecclesiastical law; <term>Constitutio Apostolica</term></note>, who seems to have lived in this century, did not recommend the reading of such books to Bishops and the whole Clergy. See *Apostolic Constitutions*, Book I, Chapter VI, and the notes by **Cotelerius** there.

The same **Eusebius**, after he had narrated many remarkable things at the beginning of Book VI, Chapter II and following, regarding the virtues of **Origen** <note>Origen of Alexandria was one of the most influential and prolific early Christian theologians.</note> and his disciples—some of whom even suffered martyrdom—mentions the wonderful conversion of **Basilides**, one of the officers who had led **Potamiaena** to execution. She was a woman not only of elegant beauty and most chaste life, but also most pious and a lover of truth. Eusebius tells the story thus:

Immediately, therefore (he says), by the sentence of the Judge, **Basilides**, one of the officers, leads her away to execution. And when the crowd tried to harass her and mock her with obscene words, Basilides drove back those who were insulting the virgin and showed many signs of mercy and humanity toward her. She, freely embracing the man’s kindness toward her, told him to be of good heart: for she said that after her death, she would obtain his salvation from the Lord, and would shortly repay the benefits he had bestowed upon her. When she had said this, as boiling pitch was slowly and gradually poured over various parts of her body from the soles of her feet to the very crown of her head, she is recorded to have endured death with a steadfast mind, and in this manner indeed...

<meta>catchword: nevertheless</meta>

---

<page-num>735</page-num>
<header>->ON THE VISIONS OF THE EARLY CHRISTIANS.<-</header>

nevertheless, this most noble virgin finished her struggle. Shortly thereafter, however, when **Basilides** was being forced by his fellow soldiers to take an oath for some reason, he affirmed that it was entirely unlawful for him to swear, because he was a Christian, and he professed this openly. At first, they thought the man was joking. But when he asserted it constantly, he was led to the Judge, before whom he professed the constancy of his faith and was cast into chains. When certain brothers in the Lord heard him and asked the cause of that sudden and unexpected conversion, he is said to have stated that **Potamiaena**, appearing to him at night on the third day after her martyrdom, had placed a crown upon his head, and said that she had prayed to the Lord on his behalf and had obtained what she asked; and that not long after, he himself would depart to the heavens. After this, having received the seal of the Lord <note>The "seal" refers to the sacrament of Baptism.</note> from the brothers, he gloriously confessed Christ the next day and was beheaded. Several others among the citizens of Alexandria are also recorded to have suddenly crossed over to the faith of Christ at that same time, whom **Potamiaena**, appearing in dreams, had provoked to do so. So says **Eusebius**.

However, the following points prevent me from considering this narrative to be beyond all exception. 
(1.) **Eusebius** says in Chapter II that he had the things he was about to narrate concerning **Origen** partly from Origen’s letters, and partly from disciples who flourished in his own age. Since, however, Eusebius does not produce the actual words of Origen contained in those letters, it is believable that he heard it from those who, in his own time, held Origen in great and indeed deserved esteem. But many things could have been said about Origen from the year 210 (when that most excellent woman is said to have suffered martyrdom) until the time of Eusebius, which might be plainly uncertain and doubtful. 
(2.) **Eusebius**, making mention of the unusual conversion of Basilides, says: <term>λεγεται ειπειν</term> <note>original Greek: "it is said that he said"</note>—meaning "it is reported that he said." 
(3.) There exists in the *Lausiac History* of **Palladius**, Bishop of Hellenopolis, Chapter 3, a short narrative of the martyrdom of **St. Potamiaena**, which the blessed **Isidore** professes to have learned from **Antony**. Now, he mentions the pitch into which she is said to have been cast, but he makes absolutely no mention of the singular conversion of **Basilides**. But who would believe that **Antony**, being of such a character, would have suppressed such a memorable matter in silence if there had been a constant report of this thing? See the History of **Palladius** in **Ruinart’s** *Acts of the Martyrs*, page 123. 
(4.) I do not doubt that the image of that most pious woman remained in the minds and eyes of the citizens, as if exhorting them to run the same race of constancy; but that she herself, having left the seat of heavenly glory—even if she had been adorned with a most glorious body, which she had not yet put on—stood by those Alexandrians, I can hardly persuade myself. Certainly, how she herself, having been received into heaven in spirit, could exhibit herself to be seen, I do not understand. But if you say...

<meta>This page continues the critique of accounts regarding miraculous visions during the early Christian persecutions. Having just discussed the martyrdom of Potamiaena and the officer Basilides as recorded by Eusebius, the author now challenges the necessity and probability of such miracles for the conversion of witnesses.</meta>

<page-num>736</page-num>
<header>->ON THE VISIONS OF THE EARLY CHRISTIANS.<-</header>

To the argument that God, through a miracle, displayed her <note>Potamiaena, a famous martyr of Alexandria.</note> to the people of Alexandria to be seen, so that, being set on fire by her image, they might be more eager to undergo martyrdom, I respond: this is also not probable. For since the Alexandrians were eyewitnesses <note>original Greek: αὐτοπταὶ (*autoptal*)</note> of her incredible constancy, they could have been incited to imitate such great virtues without a miracle. Certainly, as I have said more than once, God is not accustomed to performing miracles without necessity. (5.) That officer **Basilides** was a man estranged from the Christian religion. How, then, could he be so persuaded of the divine origin of the Christian religion by that vision alone that he was immediately ready to undergo martyrdom for it? Is he truly a martyr who seeks death when he is not yet properly persuaded? If you say that the man, having the admirable constancy of **Potamiaena** deeply recalled to his mind, was taught the truth of the Christian religion and, finally perceiving the excellence of heavenly discipline, shed his blood for it, then there was no need for that miraculous apparition. Certainly, this narrative relied on the opinion accepted at that time: that saints after death pray to God for the living, and that their prayers carry the greatest weight.

The things which **Eusebius** narrates in *Book VII, Chapter XXIX* concerning the singular election of **Fabian**, Bishop of Rome, do not belong here. See what the most learned men **Hase** and **Heumann** judge concerning this history in the *Bremis Library, Class III, page 435.* <note>Eusebius recorded that a dove landed on Fabian's head during the election, signifying he was God's choice; the author here dismisses it as irrelevant to the current discussion of visions.</note>

Let us return to the visions of the martyrs of this century. **Ruinart** <note>Thierry Ruinart (1657–1709) was a Benedictine scholar who published a famous collection of "Sincere Acts" of the early martyrs.</note> records, under the year 259, the *Acts of the Martyrdom* of **Fructuosus** the Bishop, and the Deacons **Augurius** and **Eulogius**. The parts relevant here sound like this (quoted from page 221): Therefore, having been placed in the arena of the Amphitheater (namely, **Fructuosus**), when he was already close to entering into an unfading crown rather than a punishment, even though the soldiers <note>term: *beneficiariis* - soldiers who enjoyed certain privileges or exemptions; here acting as guards.</note> were watching as part of their duty, our brothers heard him, as the Holy Spirit equally warned and spoke through him. **Fructuosus** the Bishop said:

> "A Pastor shall not be lacking to you now, nor can the charity and the promise of the Lord fail, both here and in the future. For this which you see appears as the weakness of a single hour."

Having thus consoled the brotherhood, they entered into salvation: worthy and happy in their martyrdom itself, they felt the fruit of the Holy Scriptures according to the promise. They stood like **Ananias**, **Azarias**, and **Misael** <note>These are the Hebrew names of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, who were thrown into a fiery furnace in the Book of Daniel.</note>, so that even in them the divine Trinity might be perceived. Indeed, as they were each placed in the fire, the Father was not absent, the Son brought help, and the Holy Spirit walked in the midst of the flames. And when the bands with which their hands had been bound were burned away, mindful of the Divine Prayer and their usual custom, they joyfully knelt down. Secure in the resurrection and standing as signs of the Lord’s Trophy, they prayed to the Lord until they together

---

<page-num>737</page-num>
<header>->ON THE VISIONS OF THE EARLY CHRISTIANS.<-</header>

poured out their souls. After this, the usual wonders of the Lord were not lacking, and heaven was opened to the sight of our brothers **Babylon** and **Mygdonius**, who were of the household of the Governor **Aemilianus**. They even showed to the daughter of the same **Aemilianus**, their mistress according to the flesh, the Bishop **Fructuosus** with his Deacons; they were still wearing the bonds with which they had been tied, remaining as they ascended into heaven crowned. And they called out to **Aemilianus**, saying: "Come and see those whom you condemned today, how they have been restored to heaven and to their hope." However, when **Aemilianus** came, he was not worthy to see them.

The brothers, however, were sad, or rather sustained the anxiety of being left behind without a Pastor; not that they grieved for **Fructuosus**, but rather they missed him, mindful of everyone’s faith and struggle. When night fell, they came quickly to the Amphitheater with wine to extinguish the half-burned bodies. This being done, each person collected the ashes of the same martyrs as they were able and claimed them for themselves. But even in this, the wonders of our Lord and Savior were not lacking, so that faith might be increased in the believers and an example shown to the little ones. For it was fitting that the martyr **Fructuosus** should prove in his own subsequent passion and the resurrection of the flesh what he had promised in the Lord and our Savior during his life by teaching through the mercy of God. Therefore, after his passion, he appeared to the brothers and warned them that they should restore without delay what each through charity had taken of the ashes, and see to it that they were buried together in one place. To **Aemilianus**, who had condemned them, **Fructuosus** likewise appeared together with his Deacons; he was in the robes of the promise, both rebuking and insulting him, saying it had profited him nothing that he believed those whom he saw in glory were stripped of their bodies in the earth to no purpose. So say the *Acts*.

How "sincere" these *Acts* are can be clear to any sensible person from the narration of the circumstances themselves. I have no doubt that **Fructuosus** suffered martyrdom with his Deacons; but I do not believe all the circumstances added here are true. **Ruinart** indeed appeals to **Augustine** and **Prudentius**, who made mention of these martyrs. But these Fathers were born a full hundred years after this martyrdom. For **Augustine** was born in the year 354, and **Prudentius** in 368; in the span of those years, many things could have been added, and were indeed added by those who came after. **Prudentius** himself, in his book *On the Crowns*—in which he sang hymns in praise of the martyrs—confesses that consuming time and the furies of the Gentiles destroyed many *Acts* of the martyrs. Hence he says in Hymn I, verse 73:

> "O rusty forgetfulness of silent antiquity!
> Those things are envied us, and even fame itself is extinguished,
> For a blasphemous henchman once took away the records."

<meta>This page continues the author's systematic critique of early Christian "Acts of the Martyrs." Having previously examined the accounts of Potamiaena and Basilides, the author now turns his skeptical eye toward the 4th-century accounts of martyrs in North Africa and Spain, specifically focusing on the Acts of Fructuosus and the visions of James and Marian recorded by Ruinart.</meta>

<page-num>738, 739</page-num>
<header>->ON THE VISIONS OF THE EARLY CHRISTIANS.<-</header>

It is well known, moreover, that the writers of the 4th century were far too lenient in accepting these matters, as **Henry Dodwell** himself admits in his *Irenic Dissertations 2*, Thesis 55, page 195. (2.) The circumstances themselves show that the authors did not consider it a sin to add fables to religion. It is said that the Holy Spirit walked in the middle of the fire <note>This refers to the martyrdom of Fructuosus, where the fire allegedly did not burn the martyrs' bonds or bodies initially.</note>, which is either absurd or must be understood in a metaphorical sense. (3.) It is said that **Babylon** and **Mygdonius** saw **Fructuosus** ascending into heaven, but **Prudentius** <note>A Roman Christian poet (c. 348–413 AD) who wrote hymns about martyrs.</note> in verse 121 mentions only one witness. Furthermore, the same **Prudentius** makes no mention of the martyrs threatening **Aemilianus**. (4.) That **Aemilianus**, an enemy of the Christians, had two Christians (whom the authors of the *Acts* call "brothers") in his close company, shrinks from all likelihood. (5.) That the three martyrs were seen snatched up into heaven while the stakes to which they had been bound remained behind is a fable. (6.) The rebuke delivered from heaven against **Aemilianus** is no more credible. (7.) One might say the same regarding the warning to collect the ashes. **Samuel Basnage** <note>A 17th-century Protestant historian.</note> rightly adds to these:

> Truly, such is the labor of the gods above; such care disturbs their peace. <note>original: *scilicet is superis labor est, ea cura quietos sollicitat* — a quote from Virgil’s *Aeneid*, used here sarcastically to suggest that God would not bother with such trivialities.</note>

There follow in the collection of **Ruinart** <note>Thierry Ruinart (1657–1709), a Benedictine scholar who compiled "Sincere Acts of the Martyrs."</note> the *Acts of the Martyrdom of James, Marian, and others in Numidia*. The year in which these things are said to have happened is 259. On page 225 and following in Ruinart, the visions said to have occurred to **James** and **Marian** are recorded, but they are of such a nature that they could have happened naturally without a miracle. Specifically, everything comes down to this: that the martyrs would be honored with singular distinctions in heaven, which is why **Marian** saw **Cyprian** <note>St. Cyprian, the famous Bishop of Carthage.</note> the martyr at the right hand of the Judge. I will at least provide the vision of the soldier **Aemilianus**, from which the value of the others can also be judged. The words read as follows:

*Aemilianus, having lain down for sleep at midday, and having soon shaken off his rest, revealed to us these secrets of his vision: "As I was being led," he said, "from the prison, a pagan man—that is, my brother by blood—met me. Being quite curious about our affairs, he inquired in an insulting voice, asking how we were faring in those penal shadows and in the middle of the prison. To him I replied: 'The soldiers of Christ have the brightest light in the darkness, and in their fasting they have the satisfying food of God’s word.' And when he heard this, he said: 'Know that for all of you who are held in prison, if you persist stubbornly, the death penalty awaits you tomorrow.' But I, who feared he might be playing a trick with a fabricated lie, wanted to confirm my desire: 'Truly,' I said, 'will we all suffer?' And he, affirming it again, said: 'The sword and blood are near for you. But I would like to know whether for all of you who despise life, distinct rewards or equal heavenly gifts are paid back?'"*

<column-break/>

*"To him I replied: 'I am not fit to offer a judgment on so great a matter. — Look up,' I said, 'to the heaven for a little while; you will see an innumerable crowd of twinkling stars. Do all the stars shine with an equal honor of light? And yet, there is light for all of them.' At this, that curious man found something to ask again. 'Therefore, if there is any distinction,' he said, 'who among you are more powerful in deserving God’s pleasure?' 'Surely,' I said, 'two above the others, whose names are not to be told to you but are known to God.'* Finally, as he pressed harder and scrutinized more annoyingly: *'These are they,' I said, 'who, because they conquer more with greater difficulty and rarity, are more gloriously crowned; and it is because of them that it is written: it is easier for a camel to enter through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdoms of heaven.'"* Thus spoke that soldier. These things are certainly more consistent with a simple narrative than with a heavenly and extraordinary vision. So it would be quite surprising if a miracle had intervened here. Everything comes down to this: there will be degrees in the future life, and martyrs will receive an eminent degree of dignity. These things can surely be known without a vision. Moreover, it is strange that a pagan man was so concerned about these degrees of reward.

In the following Section IX of these *Acts*, these things are said of a certain one of the martyrs: *"And behold, one of our brothers standing by turned the eyes of all the pagans toward himself, because already, through the grace of his approaching passion, Christ was shining back in his mouth and face."* By what reasoning these things can be explained, I confess I am unable to understand.

In Section XII, the following is said of certain martyrs: *Then, their eyes being veiled according to custom under the stroke of the sword, no darkness nevertheless closed the vision of their free mind, but a generous and inestimable splendor of immense light shone forth. For many, together with the brothers standing near them, although the physical eye was not open to sight, nevertheless spoke of seeing marvelous things; and that there appeared to them horses from above, white with a snowy color, upon which were carried young men dressed in white.* <note>original: *candidati* — "candidates," referring to those wearing the white toga of light or purity.</note> Nor were there lacking from that same number of martyrs those who could testify to the report of their colleagues with their ears, recognizing the heard neighing and sounds of the horses. It is strange by what reasoning they could perceive the noise of horses with their ears, when those horses were presented only to their imagination, and not to their external senses. One would have to say a double miracle intervened, and indeed only for the purpose of proving that the martyrs would obtain great glory—a thing which no Christian would have doubted before their martyrdom. Yet all those visions tend toward declaring this one thing. Likewise, on page 232, Section VII, the **Vision** said to have happened to **Victor** is of the same theme. There remain, as far as this century is concerned, the visions which occurred to **Gregory Thaumaturgus**... <note>Gregory "The Miracle-Worker," a 3rd-century bishop famous for his visions and wonders.</note>

<margin>(*) Read only what **[Gregory of] Nyssa** <note>A 4th-century theologian and Bishop of Nyssa.</note> babbles without shame in his *Oration on the life of this Gregory* regarding the demons cast out of pagan temples by **Gregory**; about a massive boulder moved from one place to another by a single word; about a lake reduced to dry land by that same verbal power; and about **Gregory’s** staff being changed into a tree. From this, it will be easily established what sort of nonsense the rest will be. Furthermore, I have no doubt that those visions, which were boasted of everywhere among Christians, ensured that the Platonic philosophers of this and the following century—**Plotinus**, **Iamblichus**, **Porphyry**, **Proclus**, **Syrianus**, and others—did not hesitate to claim similar divine powers for themselves. The most learned and dear friend **Johann Matthias Gesner** <note>original: "Brukerus," likely referring to Johann Jakob Brucker, author of *Historia Critica Philosophiae*.</note> diligently collected testimonies on this matter in his *History of Philosophy, Volume III*.</margin>

...events are said by **Nyssenus** <note>Gregory of Nyssa.</note> to have happened to the **Miracle-worker** <note>Gregory Thaumaturgus (c. 213–270 AD), known for his alleged supernatural powers.</note>. But since anyone with any sense can easily perceive that this life of the **Miracle-worker** is filled with countless fables, I will not waste time examining the visions of this Father. **Henry Dodwell** himself, a strenuous defender of the Church Fathers, speaks thus in his *Cyprianic Dissertations, Dissertation IV, Section XVI*: *That single life of Gregory the Miracle-worker, a disciple of Origen, written by Nyssenus, would provide a favorable argument here; were I not afraid that I would undermine the credibility of more certain records if I were to accumulate even more uncertain ones. Nyssenus did not draw those stories from contemporary records, but truly from oral tradition for the most part, and not even from a close source, but one removed by an interval of at least one generation.* (*)

XIII. We proceed, therefore, to the 4th Century, intending to present specimens of certain visions that are suspected of being false. However, we shall embrace what must be said in a shorter summary, partly because in this century everything is full of fables, and partly because very learned men prove—by the testimonies of the writers of this century, especially **Chrysostom** and **Augustine**—that miracles, those truly deserving of the name, ceased in this century. See what **Dodwell** discusses on this argument in his *Irenaic Dissertations II, Section LIX and LX*, and **Pfanner** in his *Treatise on Miraculous Gifts, Chapter VII*.

And here, indeed, the first place is claimed by the vision said to have happened to **Constantine the Great** while he was both awake and dreaming. **Eusebius** <note>The "Father of Church History" and advisor to Constantine.</note> tells the whole story in *Book I of the Life of Constantine, Chapters XXVIII* and following. For after he had said at the end of Chapter 27 that **Constantine** decided he should worship only the God of his father, he continues thus: *He began, therefore, to implore His help, praying and beseeching that He would make Himself known to him, and stretch out a helping hand in his present affairs. While the Emperor was praying and asking in such a suppliant manner, a certain wonderful sign sent from God appeared to him. Indeed, if it were told by anyone else, the listeners would not easily believe it. But since the Victorious Augustus himself related it to us, who are writing this history, a long time afterward—when, naturally, we had come into his acquaintance and familiarity—and since he confirmed the story with the sanctity of an oath, who hereafter will hesitate to believe this narrative, especially*

*since the time that followed confirmed its truth by its own testimony? During the midday hours, as the sun was sinking toward the west, he affirmed that he saw with his own eyes the trophy of a cross, fashioned from light, placed above the sun, with an inscription of this sort:* **By this, conquer** <note>original: "Τούτῳ νίκα" (Touto nika).</note>. *At that sight, both he and all the soldiers who were following him on some journey, and who had been spectators of the miracle, were vehemently astounded. Meanwhile, he himself, as he said, began to doubt in his mind what this specter might mean. While he was thinking and reflecting on it for a long time, night finally came. Then indeed, the Christ of God appeared to him in his sleep with that sign which had been shown in the sky, and commanded that he should use a military standard fashioned in the likeness of what he had seen in the sky as a saving protection in battles. Immediately at the first light of dawn, he rose and explained the whole secret to his friends. Then, having summoned workers in gold and gems, he sat in their midst and described the appearance of the sign to them in words, and ordered them to express its likeness in gold and precious stones.* Then, after describing the form of the cross in Chapter XXXI, **Eusebius** speaks thus: *The Emperor always used this saving sign as a defense against the opposing forces of any enemies; and he ordered other signs expressed in its likeness to be carried before all his armies.* Thus far **Eusebius**.

<margin>(*) To see what the Illustrious **Cuper** and the **Jesuits of Trévoux** judged concerning the opinion of this Great Man, see the *Biography of Fabricius*, page 262. The conjectures of learned men regarding these visions are varied. Some lean in neither direction. Others think **Eusebius** should be believed because the Emperor confirmed it with an oath. The late, celebrated **Fabricius** <note>Johann Albert Fabricius (1668–1736), a massive figure in classical and biblical scholarship.</note> accepts the event itself but refers it to natural causes, thinking that a cross appeared in a solar halo at that time (*Greek Library, Volume VI, Chapter I*). (*)

Finally, others categorize the whole matter among fables or military ruses, such as **Hornbeck**, **Oiselius**, **Tollius**, and **Arnold**. We join the opinion of those to whom these visions are suspected of being false. And here, arguments of two kinds are present. Some emerge from the circumstances of the narrative itself; others truly can be taken from the goal and intention of the alleged miracle. If we attend to the circumstances of the event, it will be clear from the very variety of the narrative that one can rightly doubt that daytime vision. Since **Samuel Basnage** <note>A French Protestant historian.</note> collected these reasons into one place (*Annals, Volume II, page 631*), I will present them here for the benefit of the reader. **Lactantius** <note>An early Christian author (c. 250–325 AD) who was an advisor to Constantine.</note>, who was appointed as tutor to **Crispus Caesar** and frequently enjoyed private conversation with **Constantine**, says not a single word about a daytime "Trophy of the Cross" formed out of light. He says only this (in *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, Chapter 44): *Constantine was warned in his sleep to mark the heavenly sign of God on the shields, and so join the battle.* <note>original Latin: "Commonitus est in quiete Constantinus, ut cæleste signum Dei notaret in scutis..."</note> What of this? Would he have passed over a daytime miracle of the cross in silence if he had known of it? Could he truly have been ignorant of it if it had appeared to **Constantine**? Would the miracle not have been spoken of to **Lactantius** just as much as to **Eusebius**? **Ruffinus** <note>A historian known for translating Eusebius into Latin.</note> increases the weight of the argument in his version of **Eusebius's** *History*: *Constantine sees, while in a deep sleep, the sign of the cross glowing with a fiery brilliance in the eastern part of the sky.* Therefore, the heavenly sign was presented to **Constantine** while he was sleeping, not while awake; and this was the tradition that reached the ears of **Ruffinus**. **Sozomen** <note>A 5th-century Church historian.</note> is likewise unaware of a daytime vision. **Constantine**, distracted by the cares of the war against **Maxentius**, *saw in his dreams* (so says **Sozomen**, Book I, Chapter 3) *the sign of the cross shining in the sky.* Furthermore, who would believe that the author of the *Panegyric* <note>A formal public speech of high praise.</note>—delivered in praise of **Constantine** long after the heavenly vision—would have suppressed such a public miracle? What theme in a Panegyric could be more fortunate or grand? Yet, regarding that omen, he maintains a profound silence. What of the fact that **Nazarius**, who in his Panegyric extols a miracle celebrated by obscure and uncertain rumor, mentions nothing of the shining cross? He says: *They say that in a certain Roman war, two youths appeared with horses, alike in beauty and strength; because they were more distinguished in fighting than the others, they were sought out by order of the Emperor to be rewarded, but when none were found, it was believed they were divine, because they had shared the labor so diligently but rejected the reward of the labor.... Be at ease, O most grave authors, concerning the religion of the writers; let us believe the deeds, which we now feel to be greater... once two youths were seen, but now an entire army.* Surely **Nazarius**, who narrates even fabricated or at least uncertain wonders, would not have passed over a public miracle so well known to the Romans. Finally, none of the pagan historians mention this most famous vision. Indeed, it is clear from **Gelasius of Cyzicus** that this daytime cross was a source of mockery to the pagans: *This narrative* (**Gelasius**, *Council of Nicaea*, Book I, Chapter 4) *seems to the infidels to be a fable and a fiction created for the sake of our doctrine.* But if a bright cross had been brought openly and publicly before the eyes of the Romans, it is a wonder that it was regarded as a fable by the pagans. Therefore, there are learned men who think the figure of the cross seen by **Constantine** was a dream sent by God. One of these is **Johannes Columbus** in his notes on **Lactantius**. After **Lactantius**, the inscriptions which **Constantine** ordered to be placed at Rome give credit to this nocturnal vision. So says **Samuel Basnage** <note>A prominent 17th-century Protestant historian.</note>. These testimonies cited by a most learned man are of no light weight. **Valesius** <note>Henri Valois, a 17th-century philologist and historian.</note> himself, from the Greek text,

<meta>catchword: not</meta>

<column-break/>

<page-num>743</page-num>
<header>ON THE VISIONS OF THE EARLY CHRISTIANS</header>

not without reason, conjectures that the vision occurred when the day was already declining. This much is certain: no one besides **Eusebius** mentions that wonderful vision. However, we shall argue even more strongly against that miraculous vision if we turn our mind to the purpose which God must be said to have intended by producing this omen. For one must either say that God, through that figure of the cross presented to **Constantine**—whether by day or by night—wished to signify that a cross made of gold, silver, or any other material, possesses incredible power against enemies and for removing various diseases of body and mind; or, at least, that God wished to call to his memory the bloody passion of **Jesus Christ** and its wondrous efficacy for taking away the sins of men. No sane person will believe the first. For in that way, God would have confirmed a most shameful superstition by a miracle. Without doubt, God foreknew how deeply rooted superstition already was in that century, and what power those with minds prone to superstition were accustomed to attribute to the sign of the cross. If, therefore, He had produced a remarkable omen to establish the power and efficacy of the cross itself (consisting of whatever material), He would have led **Constantine** into superstition, which is contrary to the most holy divine nature. Added to this is the fact that **Constantine** thought such things about the cross before the vision. For he asked God, as **Eusebius** testifies in Chapter 28, to provide a helping hand in his present affairs. Hence **Christ** Himself, seen by **Constantine** in sleep, ordered that he use this sign <gloss>as a protection against the encounters of the enemy</gloss> <note>original Greek: "πρὸς τὰς τῶν πολεμίων συμβολὰς ἀλεξηματι"</note>; and in Chapter 31: <gloss>The Emperor used this saving sign at all times as a defense against every opposing and hostile power.</gloss> <note>original Greek: "τούτῳ μὲν τῷ σωτηρίῳ σημείῳ πάσης ἀντικειμένης καὶ πολεμίας δυνάμεως ἀμυντηρίῳ διαπαντος ἐχρῆτο βασιλεύς"</note> It is therefore entirely false that God performed a miracle to confirm a foolish and superstitious opinion. But if someone should slide toward the other [argument], asserting that God wished in this way to recall to **Constantine's** memory the bloody passion of our Savior **Jesus Christ** and its incredible efficacy for taking away sins, even then he says nothing that would satisfy a lover of truth. For I will not mention that far more things are required to acquire a saving knowledge of the divine passion than a naked image of a cross can offer; I will even pass over the fact that the representation of any physical thing is of no use unless it is already known and understood what it signifies and for what purpose it was instituted to represent something. Finally, I will not say that **Constantine** was hitherto ignorant of the Christian religion; to pass over all these things, I say, **Constantine** could very easily have been taught about the whole Christian religion and this capital article of faith without a monstrous representation of a cross.

# ON THE VISIONS OF THE EARLY CHRISTIANS

**Constantine** had a father <note>Constantius Chlorus, who was known for being relatively tolerant of Christians compared to his fellow emperors.</note> who was harsh toward no one on account of their religion; his mother **Helena** was already devoted to Christian discipline; his family had been favored by Christians in various ways; and there were a great many men present who were well-versed in the Christian religion, from whom he could have received accurate knowledge on every point of heavenly teaching. What need was there, then, for some shadowy representation of the cross, presented to his imagination as a miracle? Furthermore, according to the testimony of **Eusebius** himself in Chapter 33 of his *Life of Constantine*, it was only after this vision was presented to him that the Emperor became a <term>catechumen<note>A person receiving basic instruction in the Christian faith before being baptized.</note></term> and was taught the first principles of the Christian religion. Why would it be necessary to offer a thing by a miracle that you do not understand, and whose nature and character you must later learn with no small effort? What has been said so far seems to me to be so well-founded that whether you defend the first or the second part of the proposition, you will find yourself laboring in vain.

<margin>(*) See the *Acts of Halle*, Volume 1, Observation 24, Section 8. <note>original: "Acta Halens." These were scholarly journals published in Halle, Germany, a center of 18th-century intellectual activity.</note></margin>

However, very learned men oppose us with the narrative of **Eusebius** and the oath of **Constantine**. But I would like them to consider the following points. First, **Eusebius** himself admits that **Constantine** only told him this marvelous story after a considerable amount of time had passed. But who could believe that a thing so wonderful, seen by the entire army in broad daylight, could have remained hidden from the Christians and from **Eusebius** himself for so long? Second, it is well known that **Eusebius** was a <term>panegyrist<note>A speaker or writer who delivers high praise; an "encomiast."</note></term> of **Constantine**, and he did not consider it a religious duty to avoid exaggerating the Emperor's individual actions and virtues. **Eusebius** might therefore have invented the story, as if it had been told to him by the Emperor, because he saw that it could greatly enhance the Emperor's praise. If you say that **Eusebius** had indeed known the history of this wonderful event beforehand and it was merely confirmed by **Constantine**, I respond: there was absolutely no need to confirm the conversation with the solemnity of an oath to prove a thing that was supposedly well known, and of which the entire army—both enemies and friends—could be witnesses. Third, it was an accepted dogma of that century: *To deceive and lie, if the matter of religion so requires, is a virtue.* <note>original Latin: "Fallere ac mentiri, si res ita postulet Religionis, virtutem esse."</note> The most learned **Mosheim** <note>Johann Lorenz von Mosheim (1693–1755), a famous German Lutheran church historian known for his objective approach.</note> asserts this very thing in his *Ecclesiastical History*, page 248, even though he himself appeals to the Prince's oath. Would it then be any wonder if **Eusebius**, as the perpetual flatterer of **Constantine**, had thought up such things himself? Even if one thinks such impudence could not be attributed to **Eusebius**, it has not yet been proven that the Prince’s oath necessarily implies that a miracle in the true sense of the word occurred here. For I will not even mention that the Prince was not always so scrupulous regarding such matters, as seems clearly evident from his dealings with **Licinius**; (*) he could have con-

<page-num>745</page-num>

# ON THE VISIONS OF THE EARLY CHRISTIANS

firmed with an oath a thing that, as he believed, he had seen, and thus he spoke in accordance with his own persuasion—even if it was erroneous—without necessarily sinning against the dictates of his conscience. 

Truly, I conceive of the whole matter in this way: **Constantine**, according to **Eusebius**, had for many reasons begun to feel less reverence for the pagan religion; he had heard the Christians boast that those who gave their name to that most holy discipline experienced the immediate care and protection of God; and above all, he heard much talk about the cross and the passion of Christ, and that they attributed great power to the sign of the cross. Furthermore, his mind was wavering and uncertain between hope and fear due to the outcome of the imminent battle. Therefore, at night, having fallen into sleep, he seemed to see that cross brought to him by someone as a most certain protection against the enemy. When he related to his friends what had appeared to him, the Christians—who wished him well—used the dream for their own cause, claiming that this had happened to him not without a miracle. Thus they encouraged him more and more to recognize that vision as a thing sent from heaven. I have no doubt that things could have happened in this manner. Certainly, I believe this interpretation of mine is subject to fewer difficulties than the commonly held one, which is full of miracles. But let everyone enjoy their own judgment. 

This very vision that is said to have happened to **Constantine** brings to my memory another which his mother **Helena** is said to have had. **Socrates** <note>Socrates Scholasticus, a 5th-century Greek church historian.</note> mentions it in his *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 1, Chapter 17. The historian tells the story thus: **Helena**, the Emperor’s mother—for whose sake the Emperor wished the town of **Drepanum**, which he had raised from a village to a city, to be called **Helenopolis**—came to **Jerusalem** after being warned by God in a dream. And when she found that ancient **Jerusalem** deserted, just "like a shed in a garden" <note>original Latin: "sicut pomorum custodiam." This is a quote from the Vulgate Bible, Isaiah 1:8, describing the desolation of Zion.</note> according to the prophecy of the Prophet, she began to search diligently for the monument of Christ, in which He was buried and rose again. She found it at last with difficulty, though with the help of God. I will explain in a few words the cause of this difficulty. 

Those who followed the faith of Christ after His death greatly honored that monument. But those who recoiled from the religion of Christ filled the place with a mound of earth and built a temple of **Venus** upon it. By placing a statue over it, they sought to utterly abolish the memory of the place. And this had indeed succeeded for them for a long time. However, the matter became known to the Emperor’s mother. Therefore, after the statue was cast down, the earth cleared away, and the site cleaned on all sides, she found three crosses in the tomb: one blessed one, on which Christ had hung, and two others on which the two thieves, who were crucified together with Him, had died. Along with these was also found the tablet on which **Pilate** had declared in various languages and scripts that the crucified Christ was the King of the Jews.

...had announced. But because it was uncertain which cross was the one being sought, the Emperor’s mother <note>Empress Helena, mother of Constantine the Great.</note> was affected by no small grief. However, the Bishop of Jerusalem, named Macarius, soon calmed her and dissolved all ambiguity through the power of faith. He sought a sign from God and obtained it. The sign was of this nature: a certain woman of that place, worn out by a long-lasting disease, was already at the very point of death. To this woman, as she was breathing her last, the Bishop ordered each cross to be applied one by one, most surely persuading himself that the woman would be restored to her former health if she touched the precious cross of the Lord. His hope did not fail him. For when two crosses were brought near, which were not the Lord’s, the woman nonetheless remained in the highest danger of her life. But when the third was applied, which was the true cross of the Lord, she who had been placed at the boundary of life and death immediately recovered and regained her former vigor. In this way, then, the wood of the cross was found. *Thus far, Socrates.* <note>Socrates Scholasticus, a 5th-century Church historian.</note>

However, all those who turn their minds to the customs of the century in which these things are said to have happened will admit that this "discovery of the cross" is deservedly suspected of being false. Thus, it is no wonder that for more recent writers—both of the **Basnages**, **Jean Le Clerc**, and especially **Dallaeus** <note>Jean Daillé (1594–1670), a French Protestant theologian known for his critical approach to the Church Fathers.</note> in his work *On the Object of Religious Worship of the Latins, Book V, Chapter II*—the narrative of Socrates has been exploded as a fiction. There are many reasons why these most learned men felt this way, of which I shall bring forward only a few.

The first and weightiest reason is taken from the silence of **Eusebius**. It is well known that **Eusebius** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, the "Father of Church History" and a contemporary of Constantine.</note> praised the actions of **Helena** and **Constantine** to the heavens. This Eusebius, I say, in *Life of Constantine, Book III, Chapter XXV*, reports how the Emperor commanded a temple to be built in Jerusalem at the holy site of the Lord’s resurrection; in *Chapter XXVI*, how the impious covered the tomb of the Lord with debris and placed idols over it; and in *Chapter XXVII*, he narrates the manifestation of the Holy Sepulcher. But he does not mention even a <term>grunt</term> <note>original: "γρῦ" (gru). A Greek idiom meaning "not even a syllable" or "not a word."</note> about the discovery of the cross. Who could believe that the Bishop of Caesarea would be ignorant of this, or would pass over in silence a matter that could do so much to increase the glory of **Helena** and **Constantine**? 

(2.) Why does he mention the tomb but not the cross? (3.) The same **Constantine**, in the same work by **Eusebius**, *Book 3, Chapter 30*, sent a letter to Bishop **Macarius** in which he discusses the building of the shrine of our Savior; here again he had the opportunity to mention the cross, but he remains profoundly silent on the matter. (4.) Moreover, **Eusebius** in *Life of Constantine, Book III, XXV* relates that the tomb of Christ was found before **Helena’s** arrival in the Holy Land. (5.) **Socrates** himself, after telling the story, says: <note>original: "Τοῦτο μὲν ἀκοῇ γράψας ἔχω. Παντές δὲ σχεδὸν οἱ τὴν Κωνσταντίνου πόλιν οἰκοῦντες ἀληθὲς εἶναί φασι."</note> "I have written this based on hearsay. But almost all who inhabit the city of Constantine say it is true." (6.) Those...

...who have faith in this story indeed appeal to several others, namely **Cyril**, **Ambrose**, **Sulpicius Severus**, **Paulinus**, **Rufinus**, and **Chrysostom**. But **Dallaeus** proves at length in the place cited that they are witnesses of no credibility. Among them stands out **Cyril**, who in his letter to **Constantine** on page 247 speaks thus: <note>original: "Ac tempore Deo dilectissimi..."</note> "And in the time of the most God-beloved and of blessed memory Constantine, the saving wood of the cross was found in Jerusalem, divine grace granting even the discovery of hidden holy places to him who rightly sought piety." But **Cyril** mentions **Constantine**, not **Helena**, nor does he explicitly mention the miracle. Furthermore, he lived during the reign of **Theodosius**, and like **Ambrose**, he was a marvelous lover of relics. This is clear from the fact that in his *Catechetical Lectures II. 7, X. 9, and XIII. 2*, he asserts that particles of the wood of the Holy Cross have been distributed through the whole earth. 

To ensure no fables were missing, **Paulinus of Nola** goes even further in *Epistle 33*, babbling thus about the cross: <note>original: "Quæ quidem crux..."</note> "Which cross, though made of unfeeling material, possesses a living power, so that from that time it provides its wood to the prayers of almost countless people daily in such a way that it feels no loss, and remains as if untouched, always whole for those who daily take pieces to venerate. But it surely drinks this rot-proof virtue and indestructible solidity from the blood of that flesh which, having suffered death, did not see corruption." What person of sound mind will finally give credit to such writers? Besides the authors cited, one may consult **Le Clerc’s** *Ancient and Modern Library, Volume XVI, page 113 and following*, and the *Acts of Halle, Volume I, Observation XXIII*. (*)

What I should judge regarding the visions of the good **Anthony** <note>Saint Anthony the Great, often considered the father of Christian monasticism.</note> will be easily judged by all sensible people. To be sure, **Athanasius** wrote a biography of **Anthony**, whom he held in the highest regard, that is completely full of <term>wonder-stories</term> <note>original: "τερατολογίαις" (teratologiais). Tales of monsters or supernatural marvels.</note>. Minds captured by perverse superstition delight in these little fables, not men who are accustomed to subscribe only to the decrees of reason and Revelation. I do not deny that **Anthony** was a pious man, as times were then, if what the ancients hand down about him is true. But that is no reason to have faith in every little story brought forward by **Athanasius**. Nor is it surprising that men such as **Anthony** were often deceived and took the phantasms of their imagination for inspirations. **Sozomen** in *Book I, Chapter XIII* says expressly of him: <note>original: "γραμματα οὐκ ηπισατο οὐδε εθαυμαζεν"</note> "He neither knew letters, nor did he value them." Such men often feed on visions in place of literature. (**)
