time, very little credit can be given to this narrative. To make this clear, I will bring forward certain points from this biography <note>original: "$\beta\iota o\gamma\rho\alpha\phi\iota\alpha$"</note>. At the beginning of this life, Athanasius asserts that he had a great concern for speaking the truth. Yet a mere reading of the booklet teaches that he either had little regard for the truth or was foolishly credulous. (2.) It is clear enough that Athanasius wanted to show the Monks how the monastic life ought to be properly established. See page 794 of the Benedictine Edition; hence on page 865, he advises them to read this narrative of the life diligently. From this, it is easily apparent that his aim was not to represent an accurate history of deeds performed, but to fashion an ideal image of a Monk, perfect in every respect.

Hence the most frequent appearances of the Devil, the familiar conversations held with him, the blows inflicted on Anthony by the same, and finally the miraculous power of the cross against the insults of the Devil. See pages 802, 806, 814, and 829. Anthony offers an exceptional method for discerning a good vision from a bad one. Hear it: *Let this be a sign for your security: when a vision presents itself, do not immediately fall down in fear, but whatever kind it may be, first confidently ask: "Who are you, and where are you from?" Then, if it is a vision of the saints, they will reassure you and turn your terror into joy; but if it is a diabolical one, it is immediately weakened when it perceives the firmness of the soul, for it is a sign of an unperturbed mind even to ask, "Who are you, and where are you from?"* On page 835, Athanasius reports that all kinds of wild beasts, while he was in a desert place, and Demons—as if in a formed battle line—attacked Anthony, but in vain; indeed, what is marvelous is that he rebukes the beasts with words, and they immediately obey. And at the beginning (these are the words of Athanasius, page 834): *The beasts of the wilderness, coming there for their own reasons, frequently harmed his crops and cultivation; he, having calmly caught one, said to them all: "Why do you hurt me when I have not hurt you? Depart in the name of the Lord; never come near here again." And from that time, as if fearing a command, they never approached that place.* No one, while reading this, will fail to recall that line of Phaedrus,

<margin>
> But if anyone wishes to slander us
> Because trees speak, not just beasts,
> Let him remember we are playing with made-up fables.
</margin>

Hence I wonder that the most learned Benedictine Monks, in the preface placed before this booklet by Athanasius, wanted to win some color of credibility for these foolish narratives. Hear how they plead the cause of Athanasius: *It remains for us to relieve one scruple of certain people who hardly believe so many sights, so many wonders, so many phantasms and portents of Demons as are read in this life; but in this matter, three things primarily must be considered. (1.) Whatever may be the case with these sights and phantasms of Demons, whether they be true or not, it is established from the testimonies of Chrysostom, Rufinus, Augustine, and Socrates cited above that many such things were recounted in the Life of Anthony written by Athanasius; therefore, that is of no weight in stripping the authorship from Athanasius. (2.) Although one should not rashly believe everyone speaking of visions and specters of Demons, since many especially delight in recounting such fables, it would be utterly rash to explode everything without distinction, especially since we read many such things in the Gospel—namely, Legions of Demons sometimes invading a single man, sometimes two thousand pigs—and we see the Devil approaching Jesus in a human form (as almost everyone thinks). Since God also foretold that those who believed in Him would cast out Demons in His name and perform other wonders, even greater than those He Himself performed; and since among almost all the most serious and learned Fathers, many such things are narrated. Therefore, it would not be the mark of a prudent person to count such things among old wives' fables solely because they are out of the ordinary, without taking the narrators into account. (3.) What is read here about the phantasms of Demons, the same things are found expressed in almost the same words in the Letter to the Bishops of Egypt and Libya near the beginning; where you will find many things so similar to these that you may easily recognize the same hand of Athanasius.*

Thus say those learned Monks. The space of the paper does not permit us to show in more detail how frivolous this apology is. We concede to the learned men that Athanasius is the author of this biography. But from that, we conclude that he either delighted in lies or was driven mad by foul and old-womanish superstition while he wrote these things. While the things narrated in Holy Scripture about the casting out of Demons performed by our Savior <note>original: "Soterem"</note> rest upon the most trustworthy witnesses and those moved by the Holy Spirit <note>original: "$\phi\epsilon\rho o\mu\epsilon\nu o\iota\varsigma$ $v\pi o$ $\pi\nu\epsilon\upsilon\mu\alpha\tau o\varsigma$ $\alpha\gamma\iota\omega$"</note>, the writers of the age in which Athanasius lived confess that miracles had generally ceased, and that many things had been recklessly devised by idle men to nourish and promote superstition. Who, then, of sound mind could demand that we have faith in these inept little stories? If this way of arguing used by those learned men were valid, then the most foul Legends would have to be received as the most certain histories in the future.

(4.) Anthony not only mixes conversation with beasts, but also sees souls traversing the air. While he sat on a mountain (so says page 841): *Raising his eyes, he saw someone being carried in the air, and there was great joy among those who went to meet him. Wondering at this, and proclaiming such a company blessed, he asked to learn what it was. Immediately a voice came to him, saying it was the soul of Amun, a Monk in Nitria. He had persevered in the state of an ascetic until death. And the mountain where Anthony was is a journey of thirteen days' distance from Nitria.* Those who were with Anthony, seeing the old man wondering, asked what it was, and heard: "Amun has just died." For he was well-known, because he frequently went there and many signs were performed through him. Unless the souls of Monks are of a completely different nature than those of other men, the good Anthony was deceived by this vision of his.

(4) Finally, regarding the vision mentioned by Sozomen, reasons for this vision can easily be given besides what we have said. Athanasius himself, on page 847 of this booklet, testifies that Anthony turned away from all dissenters—indeed, pursued them with the greatest hatred. He was unlettered <note>original: "Literarum erat rudis"</note>, and yet he repeatedly wanted to refute those in error. Experience of all ages shows that those who have never properly weighed the complexities of religious controversies are the most ready of all to persecute and attack others. Hence, the fervor against dissenters was always greatest among Monks, and especially the most ignorant among them, and it still is. Who, then, would wonder that Anthony, both while awake and dreaming, fought with heretics and saw what he had always desired with such great longing?

But let us set aside the visions of **Anthony**, and proceed to those said to have been presented to certain people during the impending death of **Emperor Julian**. <note>Julian (reigned 361–363 AD), known as "the Apostate," was the last pagan emperor of Rome who attempted to roll back the influence of Christianity.</note> **Sozomen**, in *Book VI, Chapter 2*, dealing with the death of the Emperor, relates the following: *Truly, as everyone affirms with one voice, a true narrative has reached us that He was destroyed by divine vengeance. On page 364 of Ruinart’s *Acts*, the Martyrdom of **Saint Vincent** is recorded for the year 304, described by an anonymous author—a man, as the entire *Acts* show, who was exceedingly credulous. To be sure, Ruinart appeals to **Augustine** and **Prudentius** <note>Prudentius was a Roman Christian poet (c. 348–413 AD) known for his hymns celebrating martyrs.</note> to win credit for these "monstrous tales." <note>original: "τε-ρατολογιαις" (teratologiais)</note> But besides the fact that **Augustine** himself was quite credulous, it appears from **Prudentius** himself that even then, credulous Christians were calling upon the help of Martyrs in tight spots; indeed, they even believed that Martyrs were "Patrons" of certain specific places. See Prudentius' first *Hymn*, verse 10. Also *Hymn II*, v. 457; *III*, 311; *IV*, 175 and 196; *V*, 545; *IX*, 97; *X*, 1139; *XIV*, 124. The same is confirmed by the disputes of **Vigilantius** and **Jerome**, <note>Jerome (Hieronymus) famously attacked Vigilantius for the latter's opposition to the veneration of relics and night vigils at tombs.</note> concerning which see Jerome’s *Works*, Vol. II, and those things said at the end of these *Acts*: *Finally, however* (so speaks the compiler of these Acts), *the disbelief of the unfaithful ceasing and the devotion of the faithful growing, the most blessed Martyr was raised from there to the honor of burial, carried with worthy reverence, and laid to rest under the sacred altar outside the walls of that same city of Valencia, where by his merits divine benefits are granted in many ways to the praise and glory of the name of Christ, etc.* 

Clearly, the goal of the entire narrative aims at proving that the body of the Blessed Martyr was preserved through various miracles for the purpose that his relics might be treated by Christians with "due honor"—that is, with divine honor. By this very fact, it is already clear enough how much credit the visions and miracles mentioned by the author of the *Acts* deserve. Certainly, he thinks meanly of the wisdom of God who says that He

<meta>catchword: mira-</meta>

---

performs miracles for such a trivial matter; and he detracts from His holiness who decides that He would use all kinds of portents to establish the cult of relics. 

However, so that the Kind Reader may rightly judge what the nature of those miracles was, performed to preserve the body of the Blessed Martyr **Vincent**, I will mention at least two. After the Blessed Martyr had suffered the most exquisite tortures but had not yet succumbed, **Dacianus** the Prefect said to his attendants: *"Seek out a dark place, crushed by the weight of the earth, removed from all public light and condemned to perpetual night—a prison within the prison, specifically for his crime. There, heap up sharp shards of broken pottery everywhere, so that whatever part of his lying body touches the jagged edges, it may press in with unpolished stings, and the very turning of his sides may be renewed as punishment; so that, in shifting his limbs to escape pain, they always strike against it. Furthermore, with his feet broken on the wooden rack and his legs pulled apart, let the rebel against the Princes expire with his limbs torn asunder. Then leave him shut in the darkness, where he may not even breathe the light with his eyes. Let no man be left there, lest he be encouraged even by the company of some conversation."*

The servants fulfilled what the judge commanded without delay and shut away the most strong athlete of God in that horrific dungeon. But when the first quiet of the night had loosened the tired limbs of the guards as sleep overcame them, what Dacianus had intended as a most heavy punishment of death was divinely changed into glory. The night of that prison received eternal light; candles shone, radiating brighter than the glow of the sun; the tightened grip of the wooden stocks burst open; and the roughness of the pottery shards became the joy and softness of fragrant flowers. Refreshed by these, the most invincible athlete of God exulted with joy, singing a psalm and a hymn to God. And so, that horrible solitude was relieved by a crowd of Angels, surrounded by a troop of whom the distinguished Martyr was cherished with venerable service and soothed by their speech. 

*"Recognize, O most invincible Vincent,"* they said, *"for whose name you have faithfully fought; He Himself truly keeps the prepared crown for you in the heavens, He who made you a victor in your punishments. Be secure now, therefore, regarding your reward, because soon, having laid down the burden of the flesh, you shall be added to our Company."* 

From this, praises were given to God, and the modulated sweetness of the angelic voice, sounding like an organ, spread far and wide. The guards, suddenly disturbed, were terrified; and as if thunderstruck by a powerful stupor, they hurried to explore the miracle more certainly. They went to the closed doors and, peering through the cracks, they saw the ministers of the deity shimmering with celestial beauty: the hellish cavern, <note>original: "antrum tartareum"</note> previously horrible with shadows, was shining with immense light; the sharp points of the pottery shards were blooming with many flowers; and the holy Martyr of God, with all his bonds loosened, was walking and singing psalms.

Those who were soon struck by divine terror and respect, having abandoned the error of paganism, faithfully gave themselves to the Christian Religion, desiring now to pay their changed devotion and service to Him whom they had previously persecuted even unto death. After the Blessed Martyr had died in his bed, **Dacian** <note>Dacian was a Roman governor in Hispania known for his brutal persecution of Christians, particularly during the reign of Diocletian.</note> wished to vent his rage upon the corpse, but even so, he achieved nothing despite much effort. Hear the narration of this Nilus and marvel at his ingenuity: *Awareness of his departure having already conquered and confused him,* he says, *Dacian said: if I could not overcome him while living, I will punish him even when dead. There is no spirit to resist, no soul to strive for victory; there is no contest with an empty body.* I shall rage with new punishments against the bloodless limbs of the abandoned body. Throw him, he said, into the open field, with no obstacle to defend him, so that the lifeless corpse, lacking the honor of burial and being utterly consumed by wild beasts and birds, may not appear, lest perhaps the Christians, taking his remains, claim the dignity of a Martyr for themselves: *The venerable body, therefore exposed to punishments without covering, is again honored by angelic watches and services. No hand of man, which perhaps could have been corrupted, guarded it; nor did the pious compassion of the saints, which would have benefited only you, rejoice in the Martyr in common. And I think for this reason human services were denied by divine instinct, so that divine protection might not seem to be lacking in any way.* And so a crow, a slow and very lazy bird, sitting not far off, demonstrating the habit of a mourner by its dark appearance, when it drove away from a distance with a certain force of its swift and fearsome wings the other birds that approached, suddenly drove away a huge wolf in its path, even while it was not moving slowly, from the body. But the wolf, with its neck turned back, remained stunned at the sight of the sacred body, and, as we believe, marveled at the angelic protection. A story of antiquity has now been returned to us by a similar bird. For he who before had brought food in his full beak to **Elijah**, now performs the commanded services for **Vincent the Martyr**. <note>The author is comparing the crow guarding St. Vincent of Saragossa to the ravens that fed the prophet Elijah in the wilderness (1 Kings 17:4-6).</note> Thus says that *Trifler* <note>original: "Nugator" — a dismissive term the author uses for the hagiographer.</note>. It is a wonder that a man such as **Gregory** was not ashamed to enroll him in the number of Martyrs, or rather, what is even more, to invoke him. See the words of this Rhetorician on page 485, Section VII, in **Ruinart**. A Martyr of similar grain was **Abdas**, or **Abdaa**, laying waste by fire to a temple of the Persians sacred to fire; concerning which matter see **Theodoret’s** *Ecclesiastical History, Book V, Chapter 39.* How rightly that was done, and how much he sinned against the first precepts of Natural Law <meta>catchword: he</meta>

By way of a finishing touch, I will add a vision which is said to have happened to **Augustine**, hitherto devoted to the sect of the Manichaeans, but drawn over to the side of the Catholics by some sudden vision. **Augustine** himself tells the story in his *Confessions, Book VIII, Chapter XII. I (he says) threw myself down under a certain fig tree, I know not how, and gave free rein to my tears, and rivers broke forth from my eyes, an acceptable sacrifice to You. And indeed not in these words, but in this sentiment I said many things to You: And You, O Lord, how long? How long, Lord, will You be angry unto the end? Do not remember our ancient iniquities. For I felt that I was held by them, and I cast out miserable cries: How long, how long, tomorrow and tomorrow? Why not now? Why is there not an end to my uncleanness in this hour? I said these things and wept in the most bitter contrition of my heart. And behold, I hear a voice from a neighboring house with a chant saying, and frequently repeating, as if of a boy or girl, I know not: TAKE UP AND READ, TAKE UP AND READ <note>original: "TOLLE, LEGE, TOLLE, LEGE"</note>. And immediately, with my countenance changed, I began to think most intently whether children were not accustomed to chant such a thing in some kind of game: nor did it occur to me at all that I had heard it anywhere. And with the impulse of my tears repressed, I arose, interpreting it as nothing else than that it was divinely commanded to me that I should open the book, and read what I found in the first chapter. For I had heard concerning Anthony, that from a Gospel reading, which he had happened upon, he was admonished, as if what was being read was being said to him: Go, sell all that you have, and give to the poor, and you shall have treasure in heaven; and* <sig>Ccccc 2</sig> <meta>catchword: come</meta>

For neither did the divine Apostle, when he had come to Athens and had seen the city given over to the worship of Idols, overturn any altar of the Gods who were worshipped by them, but he refuted their error with words and demonstrated the truth.

“Come, follow me,” and by such a divine utterance I was immediately turned toward you. Therefore, I hurriedly returned to that place where Alypius <note>Alypius of Thagaste was Augustine’s lifelong friend and later the Bishop of Thagaste; he was present during Augustine's conversion in the garden at Milan.</note> was sitting; for I had placed the book of the Apostle <note>Referring to the Epistles of St. Paul.</note> there when I had risen from that spot. I snatched it up, opened it, and read in silence the chapter upon which my eyes first fell: *Not in reveling and drunkenness, not in lust and wantonness, not in strife and jealousy, but put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh in its concupiscences.* <note>original: "Non in commessationibus & ebrietatibus, non in cubilibus & impudicitiis, non in contentione & aemulatione, sed induite Dominum Jesum Christum, & carnis providentiam ne feceritis in concupiscentiis." This is Romans 13:13-14.</note> I did not wish to read further, nor was there any need. For immediately upon the conclusion of this sentence, as if a light of security had been poured into my heart, all the shadows of doubt fled away. Then, having inserted either a finger or some other mark, I closed the book and, with a now tranquil countenance, indicated this to Alypius. But he, in turn, revealed what was happening within himself, which I did not know: he asked to see what I had read. I showed him, and he attended even to what followed, which I had not read and did not know. What followed was: *But receive him who is weak in faith.* <note>original: "infirmum autem in fide assumite." Romans 14:1.</note> This he applied to himself and opened his heart to me. And by such an admonition he was strengthened. 

In place of a commentary on this vision of *Augustine* and his sudden transformation, I shall provide not my own words, but those of the most learned *Jacques Bernard*, <note>Jacques Bernard (1658–1718) was a French theologian and journalist known for his critical approach to history and religion.</note> translated from the French language into Latin, which appear in the *News from the Republic of Letters, March 1703, page 259 and following*: *Augustine himself (thus speaks the learned man) narrates the singular circumstances of his conversion in his Confessions. Some will persuade themselves that these things could not have happened without miracles; others, however, will think Augustine was deceived by superstition. That voice, which he heard so often, crying "Take up; Read"; that method of first opening the Holy Scriptures at the place that offered itself, and the plan of composing his actions according to its sense, will be suspect to a prudent man. Such a man is not ignorant that if God wishes to change the mind of a person through the grace of the Holy Spirit, He offers and instills at the same time the most weighty reasons, which are beyond any exception. Often through <term>philautia</term> <note>original: "φιλαυτία"; Greek for "self-love" or "conceit."</note> a man is led to believe that God has changed the laws of nature for his sake, and he uses the example of Paul, who was led to the confession of the Christian religion in an unusual way, to add weight to his own persuasion. I do not say these things with the intent of believing that Augustine deliberately wished to deceive his readers. I would believe that he narrated in good faith whatever happened here, just as it appeared to him. But even the holiest men are not immune to every danger of error. He did not wish to deceive us, but he himself could nonetheless have been deceived. Thus says the most learned Bernard.* 

I do not deny that the opinion of this *learned man* greatly pleases me. Yet, lest I seem to follow him with blind assent, I shall bring forward other reasons that have come to mind while meditating on this subject. And (1.) indeed, let the reader remember that heavenly voice, at whose command *Augustine* is said to have opened the Sacred Book, according to 
<meta>his own</meta>

*Augustine’s* own interpretation, intended only this: that he should bid farewell to the depraved pleasures by which he was held captive, and not only give his name to Christ, but also conform his life and character according to the most holy and chaste precepts of discipline. To be sure, *Augustine* looked upon verses 13 and 14 of Chapter XIII of the Epistle to the Romans, where these words appear: *Let us walk honestly, as in the day; not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness, not in strife and envying. But put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh, to fulfill the lusts thereof.* <note>original: "ὡς ἐν ἡμέρᾳ εὐσχημόνως περιπατήσωμεν, μὴ κώμοις καὶ μέθαις, μὴ κοίταις καὶ ἀσελγειαῖς, μὴ ἔριδι καὶ ζήλῳ. Ἀλλ’ ἐνδύσασθε τὸν κύριον Ἰησοῦν χριστὸν, καὶ τῆς σαρκὸς πρόνοιαν μὴ ποιεῖσθε εἰς ἐπιθυμίας."</note> But who would believe that *Augustine*, being not ignorant of the Christian religion and well-versed in the philosophical writings of the ancients, did not know how shameful, indeed detestable, the crimes mentioned by the Apostle are? Even the Gentiles themselves, using the guidance of reason alone, had discovered the foulness of such actions. Hence, the vices prohibited in this verse were condemned by *Pythagoras* in his "Golden Verses" from verse 9 onward. To what purpose, then, is a miracle needed to recall to mind those things which can be known by anyone of sound mind without long meditation? 

(2.) The difficulty increases if we weigh those things which he himself narrates in his *Confessions*. Surely he confesses that he was seized by impure love, and that in his eighteenth year a little boy named *Adeodatus* was born to him from a concubine. See *Confessions, Book III, Chapter I.* For this reason, was he not already saddened at that time, even if not sincerely enough? Indeed, did he not shrink from the lost morals of the students of his age? If the young *Augustine* already recognized then that he had done poorly by contaminating his mind and body with impure loves, surely he could have been taught about the foulness of the crimes mentioned by the Apostle Paul even without an extraordinary revelation. 

Finally, (3.) he himself explains at length concerning the morals of the *Manichaeans* <note>The Manichaeans were a major dualist religious movement that taught a struggle between a good spiritual world of light and an evil material world of darkness. Augustine was a member for nine years before converting to Christianity.</note> in Chapters XIX and XX, showing to what foul and most shameful crimes the *Manichaeans* were addicted, and he testifies that this was the primary cause of his departure from this sect. I will not examine whether he fashioned any of this out of pure hatred for the *Manichaeans*, as the most erudite *Beausobre* <note>Isaac de Beausobre (1659–1738), a Protestant theologian who wrote a definitive critical history of Manichaeism.</note> suggests in his *Critical History of Manichaeism, page 227 and elsewhere.* Does it not follow from this, by the legitimate laws of consequence, that even without a miracle *Augustine* could have detested the foulness of those crimes which are condemned by the Apostle? What need was there, then, for that unusual voice: **TAKE UP, READ; TAKE UP, READ**? <note>original: "TOLLE, LEGE, TOLLE, LEGE"</note> If anyone should say that in the cited verses of the Apostle, it is not only shameful crimes that are condemned—the foulness of which *Augustine* could easily have recognized—but that one must also consider the command *to put on the Lord Jesus Christ*, I respond: not even that proves—

...to prove that there was a need for an extraordinary Revelation. Soteris nostri"</note> is required, joined with a love for Him, as part of the Christian religion. Hear how the very learned Benedictine Monks <note>This likely refers to the Maurists, a congregation of French Benedictines known for their high standards of scholarship and their definitive editions of the Church Fathers.</note> speak of this matter in Book I, Chapter 2 of the *Life of Augustine*: *Augustine certainly professes that the Christian Religion was implanted in him as a boy by his parents, and that he was a Catholic Christian before he fell into the errors of the Manichaeans.* <note>The Manichaeans were followers of a dualistic religious movement that viewed the world as a struggle between a good realm of light and an evil realm of darkness.</note> *Even as a boy, he had heard of eternal life, promised to us through the mystery of the incarnation of the Lord our God, who came to heal our pride with his humility. Thus, even then he believed in Christ, as did his mother and the whole household, with the exception of his father alone; yet the father's wicked plans and encouragements were never able to overcome the right of maternal piety in Augustine's soul.* Second. Before that marvelous conversion, he had heard the sacred sermons of *Ambrose* delivered in public, which had such power over his mind that he decided to leave the *Manichaeans* and remain a catechumen <note>A convert to Christianity receiving basic instruction before baptism.</note> in the Catholic Church until something certain should shine forth to him. Indeed, by hearing the public prayers more and more, he understood and approved the truths of the Catholic Church, as the same Monks teach in several places in Chapters 2 and 3 of Book II of the *Life of Augustine*. From this also, as is taught in Chapter 4 of this life, he began most diligently to read the Holy Scriptures, especially the epistles of *Paul*. Who could believe that *Augustine*, taught from childhood in the mysteries of the Christian religion, moved by the sacred orations of *Ambrose*, and intent on the reading of Holy Scripture, could not—without a miracle—grasp and perceive that a Christian in more than name is required to have not only faith in Jesus Christ, but also a life consistent with the most holy discipline? Third. Therefore, he listened to them zealously, curiously investigated all their fictions, rashly gave them his faith, and even urgently persuaded others of them as best he could, defending them stubbornly and spiritedly against others. Nor did success fail his counsel and rash endeavor, to such an extent that he acknowledges with grief that he had laid waste to the Catholic faith with a most wretched and furious loquacity. ...the Book, it is narrated that *Augustine*, having compared the truth of the arguments of both sides, soon detected the errors of the *Manichaeans*. But how, I ask, could *Augustine* have attacked the Catholic truth (as it was called at that time) with arguments, and drawn others to his own opinion, if he had been plainly ignorant of the chief decrees of the Christian Religion? If he was not ignorant of them, what need was there for an unusual light to finally perceive them? Added to this is the fact that he himself, in the same place—namely *Confessions* Book VIII, Chapter 12, where he mentions this conversion—confesses that he was stung by the crimes he had committed and the errors of his heart, and that he watered his face with tears; which, according to *Augustine's* own principles, was already a sign of conversion. Finally, those very things which *Augustine* had written concerning miracles warn us that we should not easily give credit to narrations of this kind without the weightiest reasons. For on one hand, in many places, he asserted that after the truth of the Christian Religion had been so greatly proved, there was no need for miracles; he had maintained that they had ceased in his time and were not a clear and infallible sign of true doctrine, especially when the discussion was against the *Donatists*. <note>A schismatic group in North Africa that argued the church must be a church of saints, not sinners, and that sacraments administered by "traditores" (those who handed over scriptures during persecution) were invalid.</note> The places in which he expresses his opinion in this way are extant everywhere, and have been cited in abundance by *Protestant Theologians* in their disputes with the doctors of the Roman Church. On the other hand, it is well enough established that *Augustine* was too credulous in this matter, and often allowed himself to be carried away by the torrent of superstition that had gained strength in his age. Many examples can be brought from his writings. Compare these with the things brought forward on this subject by the *most learned Lenfant* in his *Preservative against Reunion with the See of Rome, Volume III, Letter 14*. Anyone will easily perceive what can be gathered from these things in favor of our opinion. For if we can easily explain the conversion of *Augustine* without such a miracle; if in his age either no miracles or very few were performed; and if *Augustine* rashly gave credit to false narrations about miracles performed through relics, we can hope that those who are lovers of truth and right will not wonder if they do not rashly assent to his own narration, but rather believe that he...

### SUPPLEMENT <note>original Greek: "Epimetron"</note>

## Of Theological Theses.

I. They err gravely who say that it is a matter of indifference which Religion we uphold.
II. The distinction of the Articles of Religion into Fundamental and non-fundamental, which all Protestant Theologians are accustomed to make, is solid; it rests not only on the authority of Holy Scripture but is easily proven from the character and nature of Religion and the human mind.
III. Since the Apostle Paul, in the Epistle to Titus Chapter 1, verse 1, calls the Christian Religion the "acknowledgment of the truth which is according to godliness," it follows necessarily that articles of Religion are of greater or lesser weight according to whether they contribute more or less to the exciting, fostering, and perfecting of godliness <note>original: "pietatem," often translated as piety or godliness.</note>. Conversely, an error is either lighter or heavier depending on how much it hinders the pursuit of godliness.
IV. That a person is justified by faith through the most perfect merit of Christ by the mere grace of God is the most attested voice of Holy Scripture. See Acts 13:38–39; Romans 3:24–25, 28; Ibid. 4:5; Ibid. 5:1; Galatians 2:16; Ephesians 2:4–5, 7, 8–9; 2 Timothy 3:15, etc.
V. Whether you call this faith—that true and saving faith which Theologians call "justifying"—a "necessary condition" <note>original: "causam sine qua non"</note>, a divine virtue, or an 

<meta>catchword: instrumental</meta>

<column-break/>

<page-num>761</page-num>
<header>ON THE VISIONS OF THE EARLY CHRISTIANS</header>

instrumental cause, or finally a condition, it is all the same, provided these two things are firmly held: First, that the unique and only most perfect cause of our justification is the obedience and satisfaction of our Holy Savior <note>original: "S. Soteris"</note>; Second, that faith itself is not of such dignity and excellence that it has the character of merit in itself.
VI. Moreover, since that true and saving faith cannot exist without serious repentance and love of God and neighbor, according to Galatians 5:6; Ibid. Chapter 6:15; 1 Corinthians 7:19: it is manifest that only those in whom there is a serious pursuit of godliness can boast of possessing such a great Good.
VII. When our best Teacher and Master, Jesus Christ, examined his disciple Peter for the Holy Ministry (as we are accustomed to speak today), He proposed this question to him above all and repeated it three times: *Peter, do you love me?* From this we conclude that a sincere love for Christ is a requirement for a Pastor. See John 21:15, 16, 17.
VIII. Although we do not deny that wicked Ministers of the Word of God are the causes of infinite evils in the Christian assembly, we nevertheless rightly reject the opinion of those who deny that a Minister of the Church can be legitimate unless he is reborn <note>original: "regenitus". This refers to the debate over whether the personal holiness of a priest affects the validity of the sacraments they perform.</note>. For this opinion is most suited to disturbing peace in the Church and dissolving its order and unity.
IX. Although an erring conscience binds one no less than a correct one, it does not yet follow from this that the erring person is always free from blame.
X. If Christians—and especially public Teachers—would spend as much diligence and effort in praising and celebrating, in mind, word, and deed, the divine virtues clearly shining forth from the works of Creation, Providence, and Grace, and in uprooting the vices spreading everywhere from the souls of men, as they spend labor and study in investigating the individual reasons of the divine counsels regarding the permission of moral and physical evil, and in arranging the Decrees of God into order, the state of the Christian Commonwealth <note>original: "Christianae Reipublicae"</note> would be far better and happier.
XI. The passages of John 1:1 seq.; Acts 20:28; Romans 9:5; 1 Timothy 3:16; 1 John 5:20; to say nothing of others, most clearly prove the divinity of Jesus Christ.
XII. Against the fear of death and the encroaching evils of this life, we find the best and most effective defense in the Decrees and precepts of the Christian Religion in general; and specifically, in the serious, attentive, and pious meditation on the bloody death of Christ, our Savior.

# DISCOURSE
## ON THE
### ATHEISM ASCRIBED TO PLATO.

->James Zimmermann sends many greetings to the most illustrious and learned man, Jacob Brucker.<-

---

<image-desc>An ornate woodcut decorative initial 'J' featuring a landscape scene with a traveler walking past trees and a building in the distance, framed by floral scrolls.</image-desc>

I ask for you as my judge, Reverend Sir, in a controversy that requires your particular expertise. Plato himself—exalted to the heavens by the praises of both the ancients and the moderns—stands accused of Atheism, that most pestilential of errors, and he is not being accused as just one of the common crowd of philosophers. He is accused not by obscure men who occasionally assault heaven itself with their folly to appear wise, but by most celebrated men of the sharpest intellect: Pierre Bayle <note>A French philosopher (1647–1706) famous for his *Historical and Critical Dictionary*, known for his skepticism and complex views on religion.</note> and Nicolaus Hieronymus Gundling <note>A German jurist and philosopher (1671–1729) who often took controversial or heterodox positions in intellectual history.</note>. Against these men, I have taken up the cause of defending Plato. But who can judge this whole matter more perceptively than you? You have not only crawled through every corner of ancient philosophy, but through long study, you have become most intimately acquainted with Plato himself. This is evidenced not only by your most refined book, in which you excellently explained the opinions of the ancients and moderns regarding Ideas, but also by many most elegant dissertations inserted into the *Journals of the Learned*. I therefore offer this defense of Plato to be judged by you as a specimen of my future labor. I hope you will subject it to the most rigid examination and candidly reveal what you think of it; my mind is held by no partisan zeal in this dispute. I am not among those who strive to pull the ancients over to their own opinion at every turn and admire everything simply because it is old. But I also depart from those who are only struck by what is new and recent, believing that the ancients were merely "mushrooms" <note>A Latin idiom (*fungi*) used to describe people who are dull-witted or foolish.</note>.
<meta>catchword: just as</meta>

<page-num>763</page-num>
<header>ON THE ATHEISM ASCRIBED TO PLATO.</header>

It is just as well to me whether the truth was uncovered by Plato, Zeno, or someone like Locke or Leibniz. Just as I do not wish to increase the number of atheists, I do not wish to decrease it. I have indeed undertaken to write a defense of illustrious men who were falsely suspected of atheism, but in such a way that I do not depart even a finger's breadth from the eternal laws of truth, insofar as they are clear to me. And lest I perhaps err in this part, I will offer more than one specimen of how I defend the ancients and moderns to be examined by the learned, for the purpose that, being warned by their observations if I have erred anywhere, I may be able to examine everything more accurately in the future. It will now be yours, *most learned Brucker*, to discern whether I have rightly defended Plato or not. Therefore, present yourself as a judge who is as severe as he is candid. Meanwhile, I shall be mindful of that saying of Quintilian: *One must pronounce judgment on such great men modestly and with circumspection, lest, as happens to many, they condemn what they do not understand.* <note>original: "De tantis Viris modeste & circumscripto Judicio pronunciandum, ne quod plerisque accidit, damnent, quæ non intelligunt." Quintilian, *Institutio Oratoria*, Book 10, chapter 1.</note> But now I come to the matter itself.

II. I have said that men most flourishing in the praise of learning, Pierre Bayle and N. H. Gundling, argue that Plato is guilty of Atheism and indeed of Spinozism <note>The philosophy of Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677), which identifies God with the totality of the universe (pantheism), often equated with atheism by his critics.</note>. It is well known, however, that Spinoza asserted that only one substance is given, and that this substance is God. Therefore, to show the contrary, I will prove by the testimonies of others as well as of Plato himself: 1. *that this famous prince of wisdom recognized some eternal, most wise Being, whom we call God*; 2. *that he skillfully distinguished that Divinity from matter*; 3. *that he joined Him to matter by no necessary bond*; 4. *that he attributed to God supreme freedom and command over matter*; 5. *finally, that he professed the providential care of the most wise God over all things.* Once these points are duly proven, I will examine accurately and at length the reasons brought to the contrary by the most learned men I have just cited, especially the most celebrated Gundling.

III. Let us therefore bring forward in the first place the testimonies of the Ancients, asserting that *Plato* recognized an eternal and most wise Being, whom we call God. *Plutarch* <note>Greek historian and essayist (c. 46–120 AD).</note> in *The Opinions of the Philosophers*, Book I, chapter 7: *Socrates and Plato [held] the One, of a single nature, self-existent, monadic, and truly good. All these names tend toward Mind; Mind is the one God, a separate form, that is, unmixed with all matter, entangled with nothing that can suffer.* <note>original Greek: Σωϰράτης ϰαὶ Πλάτων τὸ ἓν τὸ μονοφύες, ϰαὶ αὐτοφύες, τὸ μοναδιϰὸν, τὸ ὄντως ἀγαθὸν... Zimmermann provides the Greek followed by a Latin translation.</note> *Apuleius* <note>Author and Platonist philosopher (c. 124–170 AD) who wrote *On the Doctrines of Plato*.</note> in *On the Doctrine of Plato*, page 368: *Regarding God, he thinks that He is incorporeal. He is the one,* he says, *immeasurable* <note>original Greek: ἀπεριμετρος</note> *of things—*

Zimmermann begins by compiling evidence from ancient sources—including the church fathers and early biographers—to demonstrate that Plato held a firm belief in a singular, divine Creator, positioning this against the materialist "atheism" of his day.</meta>

...and father, the creator of all, blessed and making blessed, the best, lacking nothing, himself bestowing everything. Indeed, he pronounces him celestial, internal, unnamable, and as he himself says, <note>original: ἄῤῥητον, ἀκατανόμαστον</note> *ineffable and unnamable*; whose nature it is difficult to find, and if found, cannot be declared to the many. *The author of the Philosophumena, chapter 19:* <note>This refers to a work by Hippolytus of Rome (c. 170–235 AD) that catalogs ancient philosophies to refute heresies.</note> <note>original: Πλάτων ἀρχὰς εἶναι τὰ πάντος Θεὸν καὶ ὕλην καὶ παράδειγμα. Θεὸν μὲν τὸν ποιητὴν καὶ διακοσμήσαντα τὸδε τὸ πᾶν καὶ προνοούμενον αὐτῶ.</note> *Plato says the principles of all things are God, Matter, and the Pattern. God is the creator who ordered this universe and provides for it.* *Diogenes Laertius, Book 3:* <note>A 3rd-century biographer of Greek philosophers.</note> <note>original: δὺω δὲ τῶν πάντων ἀπέφηνεν ἀρχὰς, Θεὸν καὶ ὕλην, ὃν καὶ νοῦν προσαγορεύει καὶ αἴτιον.</note> *He showed two principles of all things: God and Matter, which he also calls Mind and Cause.* *following page:* <note>original: τῆς μὲν ὅλης γενέσεως αἴτιον εἶναι τὸν Θεὸν, ὅτι πέφυκεν ἀγαθοποιὸν εἶναι τὸ ἀγαθὸν.</note> *Of all generation, God is the cause, because the good is naturally inclined to do good.* *Maximus Tyrius* <note>A Platonist philosopher and rhetorician of the 2nd century.</note> in his entire first dissertation is concerned with proving that, according to Plato’s mind, God exists and is incorporeal. I do not wish to cite other passages, especially from the Church Fathers, confirming the same thing, but we shall hear from Plato himself. *In Book 10* <note>of the *Laws*, Plato's last and longest dialogue</note> almost from the beginning, he complains about the contempt for the Divine; he says those who act and speak impiously toward the Gods are either those who deny that Gods exist, or those who, while they think Gods exist, nevertheless judge that they do not care for human affairs; or thirdly, even if they exist and care for humans, they believe they are easily appeased by prayers and sacrifices. He simultaneously warns wisely that one should act toward such men with arguments, not with force. He then argues for the existence of God from the order of the universe and the common consensus of all men *on page 604:* <note>original: πρῶτον μὲν γῆ καὶ Ἥλιος, ἄστρά τε τὰ ξύμπαντα, καὶ τὰ τῶν ὡρῶν διακεκοσμημένα καλῶς ἔτως, ἐνιαυτοῖς τε καὶ μησὶ διειλημμένα, καὶ ὅτι, πάντες Ἕλληνες τε καὶ βάρβαροι νομίζεσιν εἶναι Θεοὺς</note> i. e. *First, the Earth and the Sun, all the stars, and the seasons so beautifully ordered, divided into years and months; and that all Greeks and Barbarians alike believe there are Gods.* On the following page, he rejects the opinion of those who assert that all things come to be by either chance or nature.

*ATHENIAN:* <note>The speaker in Plato's *Laws* who represents the philosophical perspective.</note> Some say that all things which are coming to be, will be, or have been made, are made by nature, or chance, or art.
*CLINIAS:* <note>A Cretan politician and one of the interlocutors in the dialogue.</note> And they say it rightly.
*ATHENIAN:* Therefore let us follow them and inquire what they mean.
*CLINIAS:* By all means.
*ATHENIAN:* They say that the greatest and most beautiful things are made by nature and chance, but the smaller things by art; and they say that art, having received from nature the generation of great and primary works, fashions and fabricates all the smaller things which are called "artificial" by everyone.
*CLINIAS:* How do you mean?
*ATHENIAN:* I will say it more clearly. Fire, water, earth, air—they say all these exist not by art, but by nature and chance. The bodies which follow these—the earth, the sun, the moon, and all the stars—they say were made from these things, which are entirely lacking in soul; each thing being driven by its own force...

<meta>catchword: driven</meta>

<page-num>765</page-num>
<header>ON THE ATHEISM ASCRIBED TO PLATO.</header>

...driven and carried along, each according to its own nature—the cold with the hot, the dry with the moist, the soft with the hard, and all opposites with opposites—they met by chance and were necessarily blended together. In this way, the heaven and all that is in it, as well as animals and plants and the seasons, were produced—not through intellect, nor through some God, but by nature, as we said, and chance. Plato rejects this opinion and contends that all things were rather made by art <note>term: art (Latin *ars*, Greek *techne*). Here, it means "intelligent design" or "craftsmanship," as opposed to blind material forces.</note>, and indeed by a twofold argument. The first he takes from the nature of bodies and their disposition, the second from the origin of motion. The first appears on *page 606:*

> *ATHENIAN:* I would say now, it seems, a certain argument that is almost unusual. That which is the first cause of generation and decay of all things—this those speeches which have produced the impious soul have declared not to be first, but later. But that which is later, they say is first. From this they have erred concerning the true essence of the Gods.
> *CLINIAS:* I do not yet understand.
> *ATHENIAN:* My friend, it seems that almost everyone is ignorant of what the soul happens to be and what power it has. Regarding its other qualities, and especially its generation, it is among the first things, having come into being before all bodies, and it rules over all their change and every rearrangement. If these things are so, must not the things related to the soul necessarily have been born prior to those belonging to the body, since the soul is older than the body?
> *CLINIAS:* It is necessary.
> *ATHENIAN:* Therefore, opinion, care, intellect, art, and law would be prior to hard and soft, heavy and light. And indeed, the great and first works and actions would belong to art, being among the first. But things that are "by nature" and "nature" itself (which they incorrectly name) would be later and governed by art and mind.
> *CLINIAS:* How so?
> *ATHENIAN:* They do not correctly wish to call "nature" the generation concerning the first things. But if the soul appears as first, and not fire or air, then the soul, having been generated among the first things, would most rightly be said to exist preeminently "by nature"—if someone demonstrates that the soul is older than the body, but otherwise not at all.
> *CLINIAS:* You speak most truly.

*Ficinus* <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the Italian humanist who first translated the complete works of Plato into Latin.</note> translates these things as follows: *I will say now this new and almost unheard-of reasoning. That which is the first cause of generation and corruption of all things, those speeches which have made souls impious have affirmed to be not first, but a later creation. But that which is truly later, they say is prior. Wherefore they have been ignorant of the true substance of the Gods. CLIN. I do not yet understand. ATH. What the soul is like and what power it has, almost all seem to have been ignorant of, both in other respects and in regard to its generation, for it was born before all bodies, and it is the prince of all transformations and the order of bodies. If these things are so, must not those things which are proper to the soul itself necessarily be prior to those which pertain to the body, since the soul itself is older than the body. CLIN. It is necessary. ATH. Therefore opinion, care, intellect, and art, and law, before hard...*

...hard and soft, heavy and light, come before them. Therefore, the great and primary works, and the operations of art themselves, will be foremost; whereas those things which are "by nature" and "nature" itself (as they incorrectly call it) are secondary, and follow after art and intellect. **CLINIAS:** Why incorrectly? **ATHENIAN STRANGER:** Because they want to say that "nature" is the generation concerning first things, and they prioritize bodies. If, however, it appears that the soul exists first—and not fire or air—the soul itself will most rightly be affirmed to be older than the body. It will follow that "nature" consists of this very thing, if it is established that the soul is more ancient than bodies; otherwise, it is not so at all. **CLINIAS:** You speak the truth. <note>This is a translation of a dialogue from Plato’s *Laws*, Book X, where the "Athenian Stranger" argues against materialists who believe the physical elements came before the soul.</note> The second argument is sought from the origin of motion. For the sake of brevity, I will provide it only in English. <note>original: "latina" - The author originally provided it in Latin.</note> When one thing is moved by another, and that again always by another, will there be among such things something that is moved first? But how can that which is moved by another be the first of those things that are moved? Surely that is impossible. But when something moving itself also moves another, and that other moves something else, and thus many things are moved in succession—will there be any other beginning of the whole motion than the change of that which moved itself? **CLINIAS:** That is excellently said and must be granted. **ATHENIAN STRANGER:** Furthermore, let us ask ourselves and answer ourselves: If, in some way, all things stood still together (as many such people dare to say), which motion would necessarily arise in them first? Surely that by which a thing moves itself; for motion depending on another will not occur until some other change has fallen upon them. Therefore, it is necessary to confess that the beginning of all motions and the first motion—which exists both in things standing still and in those now moving—is that by which a thing moves itself; whereas the second is that by which a thing is changed by another and moves others. And after a few intervening words, he concludes thus: **CLINIAS:** You assert that to be moved by itself is the definition of that substance which we all call by the name "Soul." **ATHENIAN STRANGER:** Indeed, I do. If this is so, do we still require it to be more sufficiently demonstrated that the soul is the same as the first generation and motion of things that are, and that will be, and again of all things contrary to them? Since it has appeared to be the cause of all transformation and motion in all things. **CLINIAS:** Not at all. For it has been most sufficiently shown that the soul is older than all things, since it is the principle of motion.

IV. In my opinion, these points could suffice to demonstrate that Plato recognized a most wise Ruler of the Universe. But here **Pierre Bayle** <note>A 17th-century French philosopher known for his *Historical and Critical Dictionary*; he often argued that a society of atheists could be virtuous and questioned traditional proofs of God's existence.</note> intervenes and objects with two points, which must first be examined. In his *Continuation of Diverse Thoughts, chapter 25*, he is intent on breaking down that argument taken from the universal consent of nations, and among other things, he warns that by the same reasoning, polytheism is proved rather than the existence of one and the same eternal

Deity. To that end, he brings forward the testimonies of Cicero, Seneca, Maximus of Tyre, and Plato. *It is clear (he says on the occasion of Maximus of Tyre’s testimony) that he considers the divine nature as a species, which has under it a great number of individuals, and he claims that this is the opinion of all peoples. And after a few words:* <note>original: French "Il est clair... Savez-vous bien comment Platon a combatu les Athées? Ce n'est pas en leur prouvant qu'il n'y a qu'un Dieu, c'est en leur prouvant, qu'il y a des Dieux"</note> *Do you know well how Plato fought the Atheists? It was not by proving to them that there is only one God; it was by proving to them that there are Gods.* He then cites Book X of the *Laws*, from which I have argued. I do not wish to dispute the value of this argument; I say only that both Maximus of Tyre and Plato produced "Gods" on the stage for the sake of the argument, which is clear enough from the method by which they prove that Gods exist. **Maximus** says: <note>original: ἐν τοσέτω δη πολεμῳ... Θεος εἷς παντων βασιλευς καὶ πατηρ καὶ Θεοι πολλοι, Θεε παιδες, συναρχοντες Θεῳ</note> *In so much war, faction, and discord, you may see one law and speech in every land in agreement: that* **Note:** *there is one God, king and father of all, and many gods, children of God, co-rulers with God.* And a little later: *In this, the Greek agrees with the Barbarian, the inland-dweller with the islander, the wise man with the fool.* So that if you proceed to the furthest shores of the Ocean, here too you will find Gods, <note>original: τοις μεν ἀνιζοντες ἀγχι μαλα, τοις δε καταδυομενοι</note> *rising very near to some, and setting for others*; who rise not far from some and set for others. You see here, surely, that "the God who is King of all" is most clearly distinguished from the Gods who set and rise. For those "Gods" are the sun, moon, and stars. Hence, at the end of this first dissertation, he says: *Let that great King sit on high, and let him prescribe laws to his willing people, by which they may remain safe and protected. But let many Gods be sharers in his kingdom, some of whom are seen, while others cannot be beheld by the eyes.* You see again that "Great King" most clearly distinguished from the rest of the crowd of Gods. But who are those "visible" or "unseen" Gods? Are they perhaps, as **Bayle** wants, individuals of the same species? I shall answer in the words of the most learned **David**: <note>Likely referring to a Neo-Platonic commentator.</note> The *visible* Gods, he says, are the *natures of the stars*. We perceive the celestial Gods, says **Apuleius** in *On the God of Socrates, page 41*, partly by sight; others we track by the intellect. And indeed, we discern by sight:

> You, O brightest lights of the world,
> [who lead the passing year through the sky] etc. <note>A famous quote from Virgil’s *Georgics*, referring to the Sun and Moon.</note>

In the same number of visible Gods are the other stars, which you, who agree with Plato, have situated. To **Alcinous** <note>A 2nd-century Middle Platonist philosopher.</note> in chapter 14, the stars are also *intellectual animals and gods.* To **Philo the Jew** in *On the Creation of the World, page 4*, they are *sentient gods.* For they believed them to be endowed with a soul, and indeed a most excellent one, whence **Plato** in the *Epinomis* says: <note>original: Θειον γενος ἀστρων σωματος μεν τυχον καλλιστ, ψυχης δε εὐδαιμονεστατης</note> *The divine race of stars, having obtained a most beautiful body and a most happy soul.* **Origen** was of this opinion (see P. D. Huet’s *Origeniana*, Book 2, question 8). In the number of *unseen* Gods were those twelve whose names were compressed into two verses by **Ennius**: <note>Quintus Ennius, an early Roman poet. The verse listed the twelve Dii Consentes.</note> *Juno, Vesta, Minerva, Ceres...*

While the previous page examined the arguments from motion in Plato's "Laws," this section addresses the criticisms of the Enlightenment philosopher Pierre Bayle and turns to the "Timaeus" to demonstrate Plato's belief in a single, supreme Creator.</meta>

<page-num>768</page-num>
<header>ON THE ATHEISM ASCRIBED TO PLATO.</header>

...and others. Apuleius, in *On the God of Socrates*, page 42; so far Davis. However, this is especially clear from the entire discourse of Maximus of Tyre <note>original: "Maximi Scopi," likely referring to Maximus of Tyre, a second-century philosopher</note>; he wishes not only to prove that God exists, but also that He is most distantly removed from everything that strikes the senses—indeed, that He cannot even be fully grasped by the mind. Hence, in his 18th dissertation, he called God the **"anonymous legislator"** <note>original: ἀνώνυμον νομοθέτην</note> because of the majesty and excellence of the divine nature. Yet those vast bodies floating in the heavens can be seen not only by philosophers but by any common person.

The same can essentially be answered regarding Plato: for he not only skillfully distinguishes the **"generated god"** <note>original: γεννητὸς Θεὸς – referring to the created universe or celestial bodies</note> from the supreme Ruler of the universe (as we shall prove below), but in the cited passages he argues from the order of the universe, the nature of corporeal things, and the origin of motion—things which certainly do not imply a plurality of equal causes.

Another objection raised by Bayle is found in the same book, page 351. *He says,* "People will quote excellent passages to you where Plato spoke of God very holistically; but look for the books where he spoke as a physicist, and not as a moralist or politician. You will find a gibberish and appalling impieties in his philosophical theology, if you can dissect it, and you will not find the real unity of any thing."

I freely admit there are many things in Plato's philosophy, especially where he deals with divine matters, that appear sublime on the surface but are actually either commonplace or signify nothing at all; many things are even directly contradictory. However, I deny that the existence and **Unity of the Supreme Deity** cannot be proven from his works. Furthermore, it is true that Plato does not treat physical dogmas in his books on the *Laws*, yet in this very tenth book of the *Laws* he argues for the existence of God, as do all those who strive to demonstrate this fundamental truth—even if he does not follow the method of reasoning used by modern philosophers such as Clarke, Wolff, and others highly skilled in the art of correct reasoning.

But lest those who consider all the decrees of the great Bayle as oracles think I am avoiding the test, I appeal to Plato's *Timaeus*, which I believe is what Bayle primarily had in mind. For the sake of brevity, I will cite most of this from the Latin version by Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the priest and scholar who first translated Plato's complete works into Latin</note>. On page 708, Plato begins to speak about the Origin of all things:

"We pray to the gods and goddesses," *he says,* "primarily that we may say things that please them, and secondly, that we may be consistent with ourselves. As far as the gods are concerned, let our prayer be thus. But as for us, we must ask that you may easily follow along, and that I may complete the matter at hand according to the purpose of my mind. First, it seems to me that a distinction must be made: **what is that which always is, lacking generation; and what is that which is indeed generated**..."

---

<page-num>769</page-num>
<header>ON THE ATHEISM ASCRIBED TO PLATO.</header>

"...but never truly exists? The former can be perceived by the intellect through the investigation of reason, since it is always the same. The latter is reached by opinion through irrational sensation, as it is born and perishes and never truly exists. Now, whatever is generated is necessarily generated from some cause. Indeed, it is impossible for anything to arise without a cause. Therefore, whenever the **Craftsman** <note>term: Opifex – Plato's 'Demiurge' or world-maker</note>, in the construction of some work, looks toward that which always remains the same, and using such an example, draws out its idea and power into the work, that entire work must necessarily be beautiful; but when he looks toward that which is created, it is not beautiful at all.

Let us therefore name this whole universe 'Heaven' or 'the World' <note>original: "Mundum"</note>, or whatever other name it enjoys. Regarding this, we must first consider what must be investigated above all in the question of the universe: Whether it has always existed without any beginning of generation, or whether it was created, taking its start from some beginning. It is certainly seen and touched and has a body. All such things move the senses. Things that move the senses are perceived by opinion through sensation. It is clear that such things are generated and have been created. Now, we have asserted that whatever is generated must necessarily be generated by some cause. **To find the Maker and Father of this world is difficult, and when you have found Him, it is impossible to declare and speak of Him to the common people.**

Again, it must be considered whether the Builder of the World imitated an **Exemplar** <note>term: Exemplar – the eternal 'Form' or 'Idea' used as a blueprint</note>; that which is always the same and similar, or that which was generated. Surely, if this world is beautiful and its Craftsman is good, He certainly wished to imitate the eternal Exemplar. If otherwise—which is a sin even to say—He followed a generated exemplar instead of an eternal one. Since the world is the most beautiful of all generated things, and its Author the best of all causes, there is no doubt that He followed the eternal Example. Thus, having been generated, it was made according to that which can be understood by reason alone and remains immutable. From this it follows that this world must necessarily be an image <note>original: "simulacrum"</note> of something else."

After a few brief remarks, he reveals the cause that moved God to undertake such a great work. "Let us say, then, for what reason the Author of things established generation and this Universe. **He was good. And in one who is good, no envy ever arises regarding anything. Being free from this, He desired that all things should become as much like Himself as possible.** If one were to accept this as the most principal and sovereign origin of generation and the world from wise men, he would accept it most rightly. For God, wishing all things to be good and nothing to be bad insofar as it was possible, took up all that was visible—which was not at rest but moving in a discordant and disorderly fashion—and brought it from disorder into order, judging the latter to be altogether better than the former. For it was not, nor is it, lawful for the Best to do anything except the most beautiful."

On page 711, he says that God alone is eternal, and all other things are fleeting and changeable. Days, nights, months, and years...

<meta>This page continues the defense of Plato against accusations of atheism. Having previously addressed his views on motion and the soul, the author now examines Plato's "Timaeus" to demonstrate his conception of God as an eternal, incorporeal being distinct from the material world.</meta>

which did not exist before the heavens; then, as the world was being born, He commanded them to be born, all of which are parts of time. And yet "was" and "will be," which are forms of time brought into being, we do not correctly assign to the eternal substance. For we say of that substance: "it is," "it was," and "it will be." But in truth, only **"to be"** belongs to it. We ought to refer "to have been" and "to be hereafter" to the generation that proceeds in time. For those two are certain types of motion. However, because the eternal substance remains always the same and immobile, it never becomes older or younger than itself, nor has it been so until now, nor will it be in the future; nor does it receive any of those things to which corporeal and mobile things are subject by the very condition of their generation. p. 712.

He states that the sun, stars, etc., were produced for a certain purpose on page 713 and following. He grants, indeed, that God had certain ministers in the adorning of the Universe, but that He nevertheless holds Sovereignty over all. Hence, he introduces the Father of the Gods speaking thus on page 481: <note>This is the famous speech of the Demiurge from Plato's *Timaeus* 41a-b.</note> *“Gods of gods, of whom I am the Maker and Father of works, which, having been brought into being through me, are indissoluble so long as I will it. Every bond, indeed, can be dissolved. But it is the mark of an evil will to desire to dissolve that which has been beautifully composed and is in a good state. Therefore, because you have been generated, you are not indeed immortal, nor are you entirely indissoluble. Yet you shall not be dissolved, nor shall you meet the fate of death. For my will is a greater and more powerful bond for the preservation of your life than those knots by which you were bound together at the time you were being brought forth.”* <note>original Greek: "Θεοι Θεων, ὧν ἐγω Δημιουργος... οἱς ὀτ' ἐγιγνεσθε συνεδεισθε."</note> i.e. *Gods of gods, of whom I am the Craftsman and Father, attend to this. The things which have been made by me, because I so will it, are indissoluble. For everything that is bound can be loosened. But it is the act of an evil one to wish to dissolve what is beautifully composed and fares well. Wherefore, because you were created, you are not indeed immortal, and you are not indissoluble. Yet you will never be dissolved, nor will you undergo the fate of death. For my will is to you a greater and more excellent bond for the guarding of life than those connections by which you were bound together then, when you were being born.* Page 715 and following, he demonstrates the infinite wisdom of God from the eyes, heart, lungs, etc., which I shall not transcribe for the sake of brevity. I note only those things which he excellently asserts on page 726. Just as we said from the beginning, when these things lacked order, God instilled into each thing—both in relation to itself and to others—a measure and a rule of proportion, insofar as each was able to receive it. At that time, truly, there was no order, except perhaps by some chance participation; nor was there then anything that could rightly be called water, fire, or any of those things which are now named among us. But He first adorned all these things, and then from them He established this Universe as a single living being, containing within itself all living things, both mortal and immortal. These points, unless I am mistaken, prove as much as possible that Plato recognized an eternal, most wise, and most Good Being.

V. We will therefore prove in the second place, that Plato neither confused God with matter,

<column-break/>

<page-num>771</page-num>
<header>ON THE ATHEISM IMPUTED TO PLATO.</header>

nor established that only one substance is given in the Universe. This is evident from those passages in which God is said to be most distantly separated from all matter. In addition to the passages from Plato and Plutarch, we will now support this with other testimonies. Maximus of Tyre, in his 1st dissertation, when about to explain what God is according to the mind of Plato, begins from the nature of sensible things and then concludes that God is nothing of that sort, because all bodies are imperfect and subject to perpetual change: *“It remains, then, as if having led the mind up to a certain sublime citadel, to establish God there as the founding-city.”* <note>original Greek: "λειπεται δη ὥσπερ εἰς ἀκροπολιν ἀναϐιϐασαμενος το λογω τον Θεον, ἱδρυσαι κατα τον νυν αὐτον ἀρχηγοπολιν."</note>

The remaining conclusion is, therefore, that we should place God in the sovereign intellect, as if in some high citadel. Alcinous <note>A Middle Platonist philosopher, likely 2nd century AD.</note>, in chapter 9, is entirely devoted to demonstrating that God cannot be a body. Since (he says, according to the version of Ficino) God has no parts, He is moved neither according to place nor according to alteration. For if He suffers change, He must be changed either by Himself or by another. If by another, that other would surely be more powerful. If by Himself, He would migrate either into something worse or into something better; but both are impossible. From all of which it is clear that He is incorporeal. Nevertheless, from those things which will be added, the same will also be evident. If God were a body, He would consist of matter and form, because every body is a certain composite of matter and form together, which is indeed rendered similar to the <term>Ideas</term> <note>The perfect, eternal archetypes in Plato's philosophy.</note> while participating in them by some ineffable reason. But it is absurd for God to be composed of matter and form; for then He would be neither simple nor a first principle; for which reason God is incorporeal.

Furthermore, if He is a body, He consists of matter. Therefore, He is either fire, or air, or earth, or water, or something fashioned from them. But however it may be, He would not be the principle at all; He would be posterior to matter itself, if indeed He were made from matter—which things, since they are wicked to suggest, it is necessary that God be incorporeal. For if He is a body, He can be destroyed, He is created, and He is subject to transformation. Yet none of these things apply to God. Timaeus Locrus, whom Plato seems to have followed in these matters, says in *On the Soul of the World*, page 549, Gale’s edition: *“As for God, only the mind sees Him, the eternal leader and parent of all these ideas.”* <note>original Greek: "Θεον δε, τον μεν αἰωνιον νοος ὁρη μονος, των ἁπαντων ἀρχηγον καὶ γενετορα ἰδεων."</note> Furthermore, only the mind sees God in all these truly existing things, as the prince, author, and Parent of them all.

But not only did Plato assert that God is the most excellent mind, he also distinguished Him from matter, which he thought was simultaneously eternal; and thus he believed that not only one substance was given. This is proven by the very frequent distinction made by Plato and his followers between **intelligible things**, which truly are, indissoluble, and divine, <note>original Greek: "τα νοητα, ὄντως ὄντα, ἀδιαλυτα, Θεα"</note> and **generated things**, which are not [truly] being, and are perceived by the senses. <note>original Greek: "τα γιγνομενα, μη ὄντα, αἰσθητα"</note> Plato himself asserts in the *Statesman*, page 174, that the former belong to divine things alone: *“to remain always in the same state and in the same way, and to be the same, belongs only to the most divine of all things.”* <note>original Greek: "ὀτι κατα ταὐτα καὶ ὡσαυτως ἐχειν ἀει καὶ ταὐτον εἶναι τοις παντων Θειοτατοις προσηκει μονοις."</note>

Here, the author examines Plato's relationship with matter, arguing that while Plato believed matter to be eternal, he still viewed God as a free and sovereign agent distinct from it.</meta>

<note>original: "σωματος δε φυσις οὐκ αὐτης της ταξεως"</note> The nature of the body is not of that same order: *To be always the same and according to the same things, and to behave in the same way, belongs only to the most divine of all things; however, the nature of the body is not possessed of this order.* **Laertius**, representing the mind of **Plato** in Book 3: <note>original: "αἰσθητον μηδεποτε ἐν τῳ ποιῳ μηδε ποσω διαμενον, ἀλλα ἀει ῥεον καὶ μεταβαλλον. Νοητον δε ἐξ ὁ μηδεν ἀπογινεται μηδε προσγινεται"</note> *That which is sensible never remains the same in quality or quantity, but is always flowing and changing. But the intelligible is that from which nothing is taken away and to which nothing is added.* 2. Among the principles of Plato, the ancients report that all things refer back to **God, matter, and the idea**; <note>original: "Θεον, ὑλην, ἰδεαν"</note> for I do not care for Laertius, who established only two: **God and matter**. However, **Plato** not only most clearly distinguished God and matter, but also maintained that both were eternal. The author of the *Philosophumena* <note>A work on refuting heresies, often attributed to Hippolytus of Rome, but here cited as an anonymous source.</note> on page 111 says: *that matter is a principle and co-eternal with God.* <note>original: "την μεν ἐν ὑλην ἀρχην εἶναι καὶ συγχρονον τῳ Θεῳ"</note> **Plutarch**, in *On the Generation of the Soul in the Timaeus* on page 1014, says: *concerning the substance and matter from which the world was made, it was not created, but was always underlying the Creator for its arrangement and ordering, and for its transformation into a likeness of Him (as far as was possible to provide); for generation did not come from that which was not, but from that which was not well, nor sufficiently, disposed.* The substance and matter *from which the world was made, was not born but was always subject to the Creator, offering itself to be disposed and ordered, and to be shaped into his likeness, as much as was possible.* For the world did not emerge from that which was nothing, but from that which was not beautiful, not right, or not perfect. I know that the younger Platonists—**Plotinus, Porphyry, Iamblichus, Hierocles**—and among the more recent, the **Famous Cudworth**, <note>Ralph Cudworth (1617–1688), a Cambridge Platonist who tried to reconcile Plato with Christian doctrine.</note> assert that according to the mind of **Plato**, the world was created by God; but the most learned men **J. Thomasius and Ch. Wolf** <note>Jacob Thomasius and Christian Wolff, influential German philosophers and historians of philosophy.</note> have already brought forward most evident passages to the contrary. Let it suffice for us to have shown that Plato separated God from all matter, and thus asserted that more than just one substance exists. (*)

VI. I believe those who are skilled in Platonic philosophy will grant me these points without difficulty; but they will call this into question above all: whether **Plato** joined God to matter by any necessary bond. It must therefore be proved (3) that *God, according to the mind of Plato, is joined to matter by no necessary bond.* To demonstrate this, I will prove (a) *that God, in Plato's view, is free; (b) that He intended certain ends in the adornment of the Universe; (c) that God commands necessity; (d) that our mind is most free, and capable of punishment and rewards; (e) that the destruction of the world depends on the most free will of God.* From which it will necessarily follow that God is joined to matter by no necessary and immutable bond. But before I prove these points one by one,

---
(*) In a singular and very learned dissertation, the **Magnificent Chancellor of Göttingen, Mosheim**, <note>Johann Lorenz von Mosheim (1693–1755), a famous church historian.</note> proved that no one among the Gentiles <note>Meaning the non-Christian or "pagan" philosophers of antiquity.</note> professed the creation of the world out of nothing.

<column-break/>

<page-num>773</page-num>
