<sig>Eeeee 3</sig>

this must be warned in advance. Namely, that **Plato** conceded that matter is eternal, and in that he erred along with most of the ancients; for the greatest difficulties arise concerning the operation and sovereignty of God over matter once the eternity of matter is posited, especially if all the consequences that follow from it are pressed. However, I would hardly think that anyone should be classified among the atheists for that reason. For he who skillfully distinguishes God from matter, attributes the production of the world to God alone, ascribes to God the highest wisdom and other virtues worthy of the Divine—upon which all worship of God and reverence for laws rests—and furthermore pronounces our mind to be most free, is in my opinion free from the charge of atheism. Especially if we consider how difficult it is to prove by reason alone that God created all things out of nothing. Yet **Plato** acknowledged all these other things. I will therefore prove (a) *that God, according to the mind of Plato, is most free.* This is evident from the state of matter before God adorned it. Truly, matter, as is clear from the passages cited above, was *something formless and disordered* <note>original: "ἀμορφον τι καὶ ἀτακτον"</note>; it could have remained in this state through all eternity, and there would have been no distinction of things and creatures. God could also, according to the mind of **Plato**, have contemplated that matter—which was most distinct from Himself—throughout all eternity. However, since various species of creatures arose, which cannot be traced back to the nature of matter in the mind of **Plato**, one must have recourse to the most free will of the supreme Moderator of things. Nor do I see any shadow of necessity here. Take away the eternity of matter, and there will be little or no diversity of opinion between the views of **Christians and Plato**, at least in this part. According to us, the most wise and good God willed to produce or create the Universe outside of Himself, compelled to it by no internal or external necessity. The ideas of all possible things were present to God, and finally He willed the existence of that complex of things which we call the world, in accordance with those ideas which He had pre-formed for Himself. God, according to **Plato**, was distinct from matter. He saw that matter was a rude and undigested mass. God willed to make it most beautiful. Therefore, moved by his own accord and the goodness of his nature, He reduced it into order, which **Plato** recounts at length in the *Timaeus*. From this, finally, by the will of the same God, arises this world, this most beautiful series of things. Who, then, sees necessity in this system? But you say: necessity arises because of the eternity of matter, for God made it beautiful and perfect "according to its power" <note>original: "εατα δυναμιν"</note>, as far as it would allow. It is so. But before God moved his hands to the work, He was nevertheless free; He could have left matter in that confused state: matter could not force God to act.

...could, which is sufficient for now. Consider our own system. God was free whether he wished to found the world or not; he produced the world freely. Once that most perfect will decided to produce this world, he could not act inconsistently with the ideas which he had pre-formed of it, even though he foresaw that a certain imperfection would take place in respect to us. I have no doubt that God could have created a world in which no imperfection at all would have occurred; for he can do all things that do not involve a contradiction. Yet, by God's will, a world arose in which some imperfection has a place. If you ask, from where did this imperfection arise? Plato fled to the depravity <note>In this context, "depravity" refers to a natural defect or resistance in raw matter, rather than a moral failing.</note> of already pre-existing matter, which hindered him from founding all things in the most perfect way. We [Christians] say that all things were created most perfectly by God, but that partly the varied concatenation <note>The interconnected chain or linking together of causes and effects.</note> of matter, and partly the depraved pursuits of human minds, are the cause for why this world we inhabit is not free from all imperfection. Nevertheless, its beauty must be judged from the **Harmony of the Universe**. Meanwhile, we willingly confess that the Christian system is far to be preferred over Plato's system. Yet it is clear from these points that God, according to Plato's mind, was by no means coupled with matter by some necessary bond, which for now is enough for our purpose.

VII. Let us pass to the second argument, which proves that God was joined to matter by no necessary link. We seek to prove this from the fact that Plato most clearly asserted that God founded all things for certain ends <note>Plato argues for "teleology," the idea that everything in nature is designed for a specific purpose or goal.</note>. He who, before he acts, prudently contemplates the connections of all things and intends the wisest ends, is one who acts most freely; but he who cannot help but act and merely follows the force of things must be said to be dragged along rather than to act freely. We shall prove, therefore, by the testimonies cited, that God (in Plato’s view) prefixed the wisest ends for himself in the adornment of the universe. I have already brought forward passages above in which Plato explicitly denies that all things were made by nature or fortune; I brought forward places where he testifies the eye was made for seeing, etc. In Book X of the *Laws*, page 610, after he had asserted that God cares even for the smallest things, he continues: <note>original Greek: "Πείθωμεν τον νεανιαν... Εις μερισμον τον ἐσχατον τελος ἀπειργασμενος, ὡν ἐν και το"</note> *Let us persuade the young man with these words: that for the one who cares for the whole, all things are ordered toward the salvation and virtue of the whole. In these things, each part also, according to its power, suffers and acts what is fitting. For each of these, there are rulers appointed over even the smallest affection and action, having worked out the goal to the furthest distribution...*

<column-break/>

<page-num>775</page-num>
<header># ON THE ATHEISM IMPUTED TO PLATO.</header>

*...and even your own part, O miserable man, is one small piece which always stretches toward and looks to the whole, even though it is very small. But it escapes you that every generation of individuals happens for the sake of that whole, so that the existence of the universe might be happy. Its substance is not for your sake, but you were made for its sake. For every physician and every skilled craftsman works all things for the sake of the whole, stretching toward that which is best in common; he works on the part for the sake of the whole, not the whole for the sake of the part. But you are annoyed, being ignorant of how that which is best for you happens for the sake of the universe, and for you as well, according to the power of our common origin.* <note>The author provides a Latin translation of this Greek passage by Marsilio Ficino, the famous 15th-century scholar who reintroduced Plato to the West.</note> Truly, that most elegant passage shows most clearly that God, according to Plato, not only ordered everything with singular wisdom, but also applied his mind to correctly perfecting the **Harmony of the entire Universe**. The same is clear from a lengthy passage in the *Timaeus*, page 709 (see Ficino). *God,* he says, *wishing to make this world most similar to that which is most beautiful and absolutely perfect among all things that can be understood, made it one single living being, containing all creatures within its limits according to their nature.* Read the following parts which look to the same point. It is true that Plato always supposes the eternity of matter, but since the connection of bodily things is not founded in Matter itself, and God not only foresaw the concatenation of all things in that intelligible world but also willed to found it, "iron necessity" <note>The idea that the universe exists by cold, mechanical fate rather than divine choice.</note> is surely exiled. From this it also happened that the **Younger Platonists** <note>The Neoplatonists of late antiquity, such as Iamblichus.</note>, in response to objections about the origin of evil, fled to that Harmonic disposition of things. **Iamblichus**, in *On the Egyptian Mysteries*, Section I, chapter 18 (Gale's edition), says: *And there might be something...* <note>original Greek: "Γενοιτο δ' αν τι και το"</note>

...such a thing exists in the harmony and mixture of the whole, so that the same things which are a source of salvation for the whole and the universe—because of the most perfect nature of the things within it and those in which they exist—are nevertheless harmful to the parts because of a partial lack of symmetry. In the movement of the whole, all the revolutions within the entire world-order are preserved in the same way, yet in the movements of the parts, one part is often crushed by another. We see this same thing happen in a dance, and so on. <note>original: "τοιουτον ἐν τῃ τ8 παντος ἁρμονιᾳ..." This Greek passage and its Latin translation below argue that the "evils" we see are actually necessary for the greater harmony of the cosmos.</note> Indeed, in the harmony and mixture of the Universe, it can happen that the same things which are beneficial to the whole Universe—due to the suitability and perfection of those things which receive and are received—are meanwhile harmful to the individual parts because of particular weaknesses. To speak of the movements of the universe: certainly all the circular rotations of the spheres preserve the world as a whole in a similar way, even while one part may be struck by another. We see this often happen in choral dances, where the beauty of the entire chorus is maintained even if a toe or a foot is occasionally stubbed. <term>Maximus Tyrius</term> <note>A Greek philosopher and rhetorician of the 2nd century AD.</note> in his 25th Dissertation, regarding the question <term>since God does good, where do evils come from?</term> <note>original: "τε θεω τα ἀγαθα ποιυντος, ποθεν τα κακα"</note>, attributes moral evil to the <term>power of the soul</term> <note>original: "τη της ψυχης ἐξυσια" — meaning free will or the soul's independent capacity.</note>, but physical evil to the condition of corrupted matter. Having brought these points forward, he continues on page 259 of Davis’s edition:

<note>The following is a quote from Maximus Tyrius using a famous analogy of a craftsman at an anvil.</note>

"You see matter placed beneath a good Artificer <note>original: "Δημιουργῳ" (Demiurge). In Platonic thought, this is the divine craftsman who shapes the world.</note>; that which is beautiful comes from his art. But if the things on earth, being unmixed in themselves, suffer some discord, do not blame the art. For no intention of a craftsman is without art, just as no law of a legislator is unjust; and the Divine Mind is more unerring than human art. Just as in the manual labors of the arts, the art performs the primary actions by aiming at the goal, while other things merely follow the manual labor—not as works of art, but as 'suffering' or reactions of the matter—such as sparks flying from an anvil, or soot rising from a forge; these are necessary consequences of the work, but not the primary intention of the craftsman. In the same way, you must consider the sufferings that occur on earth—which we call the incursions of human evils—to be blameless on the part of the Artificer. These things are like necessary and following natures of the creation of the Whole. What we call evils and destructions, and over which we wail, **NB.** these the Artificer calls the 'salvation of the Whole.'"

Thus elegantly speaks <term>Maximus</term>. I know that certain learned men think that <term>Maximus</term> has wandered here from the opinion of <term>Plato</term>; but anyone who rightly weighs the cited passage of <term>Plato</term>, and compares it with what follows there, will perceive that <term>Plato</term> was devoted to this same opinion. And this is also the opinion of the most excellent philosophers of our own age, <term>Leibniz and Wolff</term> <note>Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646–1716) and Christian Wolff (1679–1754), famous for their "Theodicy" or defense of God's justice in an imperfect world.</note>. In

this, however, they disagree: <term>Leibniz</term> seeks the traces of that imperfection not in matter, but in the eternal ideas of possible things themselves—a matter we are not dealing with now. It is enough that, according to <term>Plato’s</term> mind, God formed all things for the wisest ends and looked toward the Harmony of the entire Universe of things; from this it is clearly inferred that God is not bound by an unbreakable chain to matter.

VIII. (c) The third argument, by which it is proved that God was not constricted by the bonds of matter according to <term>Plato’s</term> mind, we take from the fact that <term>Plato</term> asserts that God commands matter and the necessity that arises from it. If God exercises his force and power upon matter, yet is not forced by it to act in this or that way, it follows that he is in no way [servilely] joined with matter. We shall prove this again with <term>Plato’s</term> own words. But let us first see what <term>Plato</term> understood by the names of "Necessity" and <term>Fate</term>. <term>Plutarch</term> <note>A Greek historian and Platonist philosopher.</note> in *On the Opinions of the Philosophers*, Book I, chapter 26, <term>concerning the essence of necessity</term>, says regarding Plato: "Plato brings some things under Providence, and others under Necessity." In chapter 27, <term>concerning Fate</term>: "Plato admits Fate in regards to human souls and lives, but he also introduces a cause that comes from ourselves." In chapter 28, <term>concerning the essence of Fate</term>: "Plato calls the nature of the universe an eternal reason and an eternal law." From these passages it is clear that: 1. <term>Plato</term> attributes certain things to the freedom of the mind; 2. He calls "Necessity" either matter itself viewed in isolation, or the will/operation of God which circumscribes matter within certain limits.

<term>Apuleius and Alcinous</term> <note>Later commentators and teachers of Platonic philosophy.</note> agree with <term>Plutarch</term>. The former says in *On the Doctrines of Plato*, page 374: "<term>Plato</term> thinks that not all things are to be attributed to the lot of <term>Fate</term>. For he defines it thus: **Divine Providence is the decree that preserves the prosperity of that for whose sake it undertook such a duty; Fate is the divine law through which the inevitable thoughts and undertakings of God are fulfilled.** Hence, if anything is done by Providence, it is also done by fate; and what is determined by fate must be seen as undertaken by Providence." And after a few intervening words: "Indeed, he thinks not everything should be referred to the force of Fate: but that there is something in us, and something in fortune. He confesses that the unforeseen accidents of fortune are unknown to us. For something unstable and rushing in often interrupts things that were undertaken with counsel and meditation, which does not allow the contemplated things to reach their end." <term>Alcinous</term> is even clearer in chapter 26: "Fate says that if any soul chooses such a life, it will perform these certain actions..."

<meta>This page continues the defense of Plato against the charge of atheism or "blind necessity." The previous discussion likely focused on how Plato distinguishes between God's will and the constraints of the material world. Here, the author uses the *Timaeus* to prove that Plato believed God has supreme power over matter and that human free will exists within a framework of divine order.</meta>

<page-num>778</page-num>
<header># ON THE ATHEISM IMPUTED TO PLATO.</header>

"If the soul chooses such a life, this consequence will follow. The soul is without a master, and it is in its own power to act or not to act. There is no compulsion regarding this. But that which follows the action will be completed according to fate. For example: if Paris carries off Helen—an act within his own power—it will follow that the Greeks will wage war against the Trojans over Helen." <note>original Greek: "δε ἵνα, ἀυτη ἕψεται...". This is a standard middle-Platonic explanation of fate: human choice is free, but every choice triggers a set of fated consequences.</note>

He says that Fate means that if the soul chooses a life of a certain kind and performs such actions, these consequences will follow it. Therefore, the soul is free, and it lies within its power to do or not do those things; it is not driven to them by any necessity. However, that which follows in that sequence is fulfilled by fate. Just as from the fact that Paris will carry off Helen (which was indeed a free act for him), it will be a consequence that the Greeks wage war against the Trojans on behalf of Helen. But we must bring forward passages from Plato himself to make this very point manifest. After he had said in the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s famous dialogue on the creation of the universe.</note>, page 716: "The lover of mind and knowledge must seek the primary causes of a wise nature; and those others which are necessarily moved by others, but which move others as secondary causes, must be considered differently." After this, he explains why the ears and eyes were given by God, and adds this on page 484:

"The things already discussed, with few exceptions, have shown the works fashioned by Intellect. But we must also place beside them in our account the things that come about through Necessity. For the generation of this world was mixed, being born from a combination of Necessity and Intellect. But since Intellect ruled over Necessity by persuading her to lead most of what comes to be toward the best, in this way and for these reasons, this Universe was constructed in the beginning, with Necessity yielding to wise persuasion." <note>original Greek: "Τα μεν ἐν παρεληλυθοτα...". This famous passage argues that God (Intellect) does not use force, but "persuades" the chaotic material world (Necessity) into an orderly cosmos.</note>

Having brought these points forward, he proceeds to explain the origin and nature of bodies, from which it is clear that Plato calls the bodies themselves "necessity," and that God has dominion over them. In the same *Timaeus*, page 709:

> Since, indeed, (he says) the world was to be corporeal, visible, and tangible, and nothing can be seen without fire, nor can anything be touched without something solid, and nothing is solid without earth, therefore in the beginning of this work God first created fire and earth. But two things alone cannot fitly hold together without a third; they require some intermediate bond between them both, and he said this bond was air and water. Since the world required solidity, and solids are always joined not by one but by two means, God placed air and water between fire and earth, and compared them to one another as far as possible, so that as fire is to air, so air is to water; and as air is to water, so water is to earth. From this conjunction, the world was thus constituted,

<meta>catchword: so</meta>

<column-break/>

<page-num>779</page-num>
<header># ON THE ATHEISM IMPUTED TO PLATO.</header>

so that it might be seen and touched. From this, the world embraces itself in a bond of harmonious friendship, and fits together so aptly that it cannot be dissolved in any way except by the same one who bound it. From these words, it is clear not only that God, according to Plato's mind, wisely joined all things together, but also that God has supreme power over matter. In the same place, page 492:

"God is capable of mixing many things into one, and again of dissolving one into many, as he is both knowing and powerful at once. But of men, no one is capable of either of these, neither now nor ever in the future. All these things, then, which were at that time produced by necessity, the Maker of the most beautiful and best took up among the things coming into being, when he was generating the self-sufficient and most perfect God <note>In the *Timaeus*, Plato refers to the living Universe itself as a "created god."</note>, using the causes relating to these things as ministers, but himself arranging the good in each. One must distinguish two kinds of causes: one necessary, the other divine. And one must seek the divine in all things for the sake of a happy life, so far as our nature allows; but the necessary cause for the sake of those other things... <gloss>and with a few words intervening:</gloss> for as was said at the beginning, when these things lacked order, God instilled in each thing, both in relation to itself and to others, such measures as it was possible for them to be proportional and symmetrical. For at that time, none of them shared in order except by chance, nor was there anything worthy of the names now used, such as water and the others. But first he ordered all these, then from them he constructed this whole, one living being containing within itself all living beings, both mortal and immortal." <note>original Greek: "Θεος μεν τα πολλα εἰς ἑν ξυγκεραννυναι..."</note>

Marsilio Ficino <note>A famous 15th-century philosopher who first translated the complete works of Plato into Latin, making them accessible to the Renaissance.</note> translates these things thus:

> God is sufficient to collect many into one, and again to produce many from one. For he knows and can do so at the same time. But no man is able to do either, either now or ever. All these things, indeed, being then naturally produced from necessity, that fabricator of the most beautiful and best work took them up in those things which were being born, when he generated the God sufficient in himself and most perfect: using causes as ministers to these things, but himself acting in each for what was well-arranged. For it is fitting to distinguish two species of causes. One indeed necessary, the other divine. And to seek the divine in all things, so that we may obtain a blessed life, as far as is possible for our nature, and also to search out the necessary cause for the sake of those things. As we said from the beginning, when these things lacked order, God gave to each, both toward itself and toward others in turn, a measure and a logic of proportion, as far as each was able to receive it. Then indeed there was no order unless perhaps by some chance; nor was there anything then that could rightly be called water or fire, or any of those things now named among us. Verily, he first adorned all these things, then from them he constituted this universe, one animal, containing within itself all animals, mortal and immortal.

<margin>(d)</margin> IX. To make this even clearer, I shall add two arguments. The first is that Plato not only denied that God could in any way be the cause of evil, but he also asserted that our mind is entirely free, and capable of both punishment and reward. In Book X of the *Republic*, page 472, he writes: "Virtue is without a master; as one honors or neglects it, so shall one possess more or less of it. The fault lies with the chooser; God is blameless." <note>original Greek: ἀρετὴ δὲ ἀδέσποτον... Θεὸς ἀναίτιος. This famous passage emphasizes that moral character is a result of individual choice, not divine decree or fate.</note> In Book II of the *Republic*, page 430: "Therefore God, since He is good, would not be the cause of all things—as many claim—but He is the cause of a few things for men, and of many things He is not the cause. For our good things are far fewer than our evils. And for the good things, no other cause must be assigned than God. But for the evils, one must seek any cause other than God." <note>original Greek: ἐδ᾽ ἄρα... ὁ Θεὸς, ἐπειδὴ ἀγαθὸς... Των δὲ κακων ἀλλ᾽ ἢ τὸν Θεὸν.</note> In the following passages, after he had criticized Homer for representing God as the cause of both good and evil, he adds: "That God, who is good, is the cause of evil to anyone, must be rejected entirely; nor should anyone be permitted to say this in his city, if that city is to be established with good laws. Furthermore, no one should be allowed to hear such things—whether young or old, whether in verse or prose—as they are neither holy to speak, nor useful to us, nor consistent with themselves." The followers of Plato maintain this same view, such as Maximus of Tyre in *Dissertation 30*, page 313: "God gives nothing that is not beautiful." <note>original Greek: ἐδεν των μη καλων διδωσι Θεος.</note> The illustrious Mosheim <note>Johann Lorenz von Mosheim (1693–1755), a famous Lutheran church historian known for his objective approach.</note> recently noted with great learning in his dissertation on the Church being disturbed by the later Platonists, that Proclus, Plotinus, and Ammonius fought most fiercely against fate and necessity, and that no one granted greater power to human freedom than the Platonists. It is not necessary to bring forward more examples. But someone might perhaps object, as we have already confessed above, that Plato sought the origin of evil in matter, and thus the difficulty is not removed; for, according to Plato's opinion, God adorned matter and formed all things from it. I respond that the question is not whether Plato satisfied all the difficulties that arise concerning the origin of evil—for we willingly concede that he did not achieve this. Whoever thinks he can easily extricate himself from these tangled mazes of doubt should read the thoughts of the most subtle philosophers of our own age, such as Bayle, Leibniz, Clarke, and others, on this

subject, and he will perhaps judge Plato’s error more mildly. It is enough for us that Plato explicitly asserted that sins have their origin in the free will of the mind, and that God is the author of nothing but good. Those things called "physical evils" do indeed arise from matter, but by God’s will, these turn out for the good of the upright man. For he speaks most clearly in Book 10 of the *Republic*, page 670: "Thus we must think of the just man, that whether he is subject to poverty, or diseases, or any other of those things that seem to be evils, these will ultimately lead to some good for him, whether he is living or dead. For he is never neglected by the Gods, whoever strives to become just and, through the duties of virtue, to become as like to God as is possible for a human." Perhaps Plato, who could not conceive of creation out of nothing, feigned that matter was eternal and the source of evil out of reverence for the Divine. Indeed, Justin Martyr <note>An early Christian apologist (c. 100–165 AD) who often looked for "seeds of truth" in Greek philosophy.</note> thinks so in his *Exhortation to the Greeks*, page 19: "He said that matter was uncreated, so that he would not seem to call God the maker of evils." <note>original Greek: ἀγέννητον τὴν ὕλην ἔφησεν εἶναι, ἵνα μὴ δόξῃ Θεὸν τε κακῶν ποιητὴν εἶναι λέγειν.</note> Although it follows necessarily from the method of philosophizing he followed that our mind is free, we shall nevertheless bring forward some testimonies proving the same point clearly. In the *Epinomis*, page 639, he says: "The things that exist are two: one is the soul, the other the body; and there are many of each, yet they differ from one another... The soul differs from the body in that we shall find the one has mind, the other is mindless. The one rules, the other is ruled. The one is the cause of all things, while the other is the cause of no passion." <note>original Greek: Τὰ ὄντα εἶναι δύο... τὸ δὲ ἀναίτιον πάσης πάθης. In Platonic thought, "passion" or *pathos* refers to being acted upon or suffering an external influence.</note> He does acknowledge in this very Dialogue that a certain necessity exists in the mind, but only regarding those things which are evident, and which the mind perceives, so to speak, in a single glance. "The necessity of a soul possessing intellect," (these are Plato's words) "is the greatest of all necessities. For leading, not being led, it governs. But when the soul, which is the best thing, is perfected by counsel according to the best intellect, the result occurs by necessity, and not even adamant could be more solid or immovable." See the same *Epinomis* page 640, Eusebius's *Preparation for the Gospel* Book 12, chapter 28, Maximus of Tyre’s *Dissertation 25*, and what we have cited above regarding fate and necessity. Moreover, I shall not prove with many words that the mind is capable of punishment and reward, since the passages are very well known. See the *Apology of Socrates*, Book X of the *Laws*, and the *Phaedo*.

<page-num>782</page-num>
# ON THE ATHEISM IMPUTED TO PLATO.
<meta>catchword: mon,</meta>

X. <margin>(e)</margin> The second argument, and indeed the final one by which we prove that, according to the mind of **Plato**, God is in no way joined to matter, we derive from Plato’s opinion regarding the destruction of the world. For he asserted that the world could only perish by the sole will of God, if indeed it were ever to be destroyed. In the preceding sections, I have shown that the origin of all things—or at least the production of already existing matter and its most wise arrangement—must be ascribed to God alone according to the mind of **Plato**. From this, it follows that the destruction of this most skillfully crafted machine, if any were to occur in the future, must be attributed to the same supreme Governor of things. If God were constrained by an inviolable necessity or by the chains of matter, it would be pointless to ask whether the world could be destroyed by God’s will; for everything would be unable to happen otherwise, and all liberty would be banished. Just as all things would have arisen by a certain blind necessity, so they would be unable to remain otherwise. Such a necessity of all things finds a place in the system of **Spinoza**, but least of all in that of **Plato**. According to the mind of **Spinoza**, it was as necessary that I should have been born in Zurich and not elsewhere as it is necessary that the three angles of a triangle be equal to two right angles. <note>Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677) was a philosopher who argued for a form of pantheism where everything happens by logical necessity, leaving no room for divine or human free will.</note> According to his system, I cannot be destroyed, since my mind and my body are parts that exist just as necessarily as God exists, of whom I am a part. In the system of **Plato**, the origin of all men and all creatures must be attributed to the most free will of God and his ministers. Therefore, by His will, all things are returned to the ancient Chaos; by His will, they remain.

There is a celebrated passage of **Plato** in the *Timaeus*, page 481: <note>original Greek: Θεοι Θεων, ὧν ἐγω Δημιουργος... "Gods of gods, of whom I am the Maker and Father, listen to these things. Those things which have been made by me are indissoluble, provided I will it so..."</note> *Gods of gods, of whom I am the Maker and Father, attend to these things. Those things which have been made by me, because I so will it, are indissoluble. For indeed everything that is bound can be loosened. But it is the mark of an evil being to wish to dissolve that which is beautifully composed and fares well. Therefore, because you have been generated, you are not indeed immortal or entirely indissoluble. Yet you shall never be dissolved, nor shall you undergo the fate of death. For my will is a greater and more excellent bond for the preservation of your life than those ties by which you were bound at the time you were being brought into being.* In a similar manner, he speaks in the same *Timaeus*, page 709 of the Ficino edition, a passage which we cited above on pages 25 and 26. **Plutarch** also explains the mind of **Plato** in this way in *On the Opinions of the Philosophers*, Book II, chapter 4: <note>original Greek: Πυθαγορας καὶ Πλατων γενητον ὑπο θεου τον κοσμον...</note> *Pythagoras and Plato thought the world was made by God, and as far as its nature is concerned, it is subject to destruction because it is corporeal and thus exposed to the senses; however, it will not perish, because providence and God hold it together.*

**Maximus Tyrius**, in his 29th dissertation, page 309, wishing to prove that it is by the will of God that the world does not slide back into ancient Chaos, says: <note>original Greek: ἀνευ τε ἀληθες μηθε μαθων...</note> *Therefore, without truth, believe neither the too-poetic myths nor the words of philosophy. ->The soul of Achilles, and that of man-slaying Hector<-

*And that his right hand lifted the yoke.* For I see that their fate nods in unison with the right hand of Jove. <note>original Greek: ἐ γαρ ἐμον παλιναγρετον... "For what I have nodded with my head shall never be changed, nor be false, nor fail of its end."</note>

> Shall never be changed, nor be false, nor fail of its end.

I understand the nods of Jove, by whose benefit the earth remains, the sea is poured out, the air flows, fire moves upward, the heaven turns in its orbit, animals are created, and trees are born. <meta>This page continues the author’s defense of Plato’s theology. Having previously established that Plato viewed God as a free creator, the author now addresses the mechanism of Divine Providence. He explains how Plato used "ministering" deities or forces to govern the world, a concept he defends against the charge of atheism by comparing it to the "Plastic Natures" discussed by contemporary 17th-century scholars. He concludes by providing a point-by-point contrast between Plato’s philosophy and the "detestable" views of Baruch Spinoza.</meta>

# ON THE ATHEISM IMPUTED TO PLATO.

And of all the most transcendent Gods: who not only ordained the celestial gods <note>original: "Deos cœlicolas"</note>, whom he scattered through all members of the world for protection and glory; but also, by his nature, he produced mortal Gods <note>The author likely refers to human beings or rational souls</note>, who excelled other earthly living creatures in wisdom, for the longevity of time. Having established laws, he handed over to the other Gods the arrangement and protection of the remaining things which must necessarily happen every day. From this source, the Gods of "secondary providence" so diligently maintain the Providence they have undertaken that all things, even those shown to mortals from heaven, maintain the immutable state of the paternal order. 

Yet it must not be thought that anything is withdrawn from divine Providence simply because Plato maintains that God does not govern all things immediately <note>meaning "directly" or without intermediaries</note>. For those most illustrious men, **Cudworth, Le Clerc, and Ray**, who defend the existence of certain <term>Plastic Natures</term> <note>These were "formative forces" proposed by 17th-century philosophers to explain how nature operates under God's general laws without God having to personally move every atom</note>, which God uses in the government of the Universe (especially in the production of plants, etc.), by no means deny that all things are subject to God’s command, but only that He uses their ministry. 

Plato thought similarly, as is clear from the cited passages. For he thought it was unworthy of the Majesty of such a great Divinity to perform and care for all things through Himself directly without certain ministers. So speaks **Apuleius** expressly in *On the World*, page 353: "But if it is unbecoming for any man," he says, "or for any King, to provide for and perfect all things through himself, it will be much more unsuitable for God." 

**Maximus Tyrius**, a Platonist, defends this same divine Providence against Epicurus <note>The philosopher Epicurus was often accused of atheism because he taught that the gods do not involve themselves in human affairs</note> in *Dissertation XXV*, page 257: 

> The mind, being unbreakable and tireless, and reaching into all natures with incredible speed, like a glance of the eye, adorns everything it touches. Just as the solar rays, when they fall upon the earth, illuminate everything they catch. But as to what the manner of this "touching" is, I am not able to say, but **Homer** hinted at it quietly: 

>> He spoke, and the son of Saturn <note>Zeus</note> nodded with his dark brows.

> Together with the nod of Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note>, the earth stood firm, and whatever the earth brings forth; the sea stood firm, and whatever the sea produces; the air stood firm, and whatever the air carries; and the heaven stood firm, and whatever is moved in heaven. These are the works of the nods of Jove. Thus far I require no oracle. I have faith in **Homer**, I believe in **Plato**, and I pity **Epicurus**. 

That is to say: *Whose mind is solid and incorruptible, is never divided, but with incredible velocity—as if with a single glance of the eye—whatever it touches, it adorns and illustrates. Not otherwise than the solar rays, where they have fallen upon the earth, illustrate whatever part of it they have invaded. How, however, that happens,*

---

# ON THE ATHEISM IMPUTED TO PLATO.

*is not easy for me to say; Homer nevertheless secretly hinted at it when he said:*

> He had said these things, and the Saturnian Offspring <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note> nodded with his dark eyes.

Along with the nod of Jove, the earth stood firm, and whatever the earth nourishes; the sea stood firm, and whatever the sea produces; the air stood firm, and whatever the air carries; the heaven stood firm, and whatever is moved in heaven. The nod of Jove perfected all these works. Thus far I require no oracle. I hold faith in **Homer**, I believe **Plato**, and I pity **Epicurus**. 

And so, unless I am mistaken, I have proven point by point that Plato retreated very far from the detestable opinion of **Spinoza** <note>Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677), whose pantheistic view that God and Nature are the same was frequently equated with atheism by his contemporaries</note>. However, so that this may be more clearly seen, I shall briefly set forth the summary of my reasoning, and by adding the very words of Spinoza himself, I shall show how his dogmas and those of Plato fight against each other with opposing fronts.

1.  **Spinoza** asserted that only one substance is given. *Ethics, Part 1, Proposition 14:* "Besides God, no substance can be given or conceived." *Prop. 15:* "Whatever is, is in God, and nothing can be or be conceived without God." **Plato** asserted that besides God (the supreme mind), matter is given, as well as demons and other substances.

2.  **Plato** believed that God set Himself freely to the task of adorning and founding this world. **Spinoza** says all things follow from the necessity of the divine Nature. *Ibid. Prop. 16:* "From the necessity of the divine nature," he says, "infinite things in infinite ways (that is, all things which can fall under an infinite intellect) must follow."

3.  **Plato** professed that God had most wise "ends" <note>final causes or purposes</note> in the production of all things. **Spinoza** rejects all ends. In the appendix to *Prop. 36*, he lists this among prejudices, saying: "All the prejudices I here undertake to indicate depend on this one: namely, that men commonly suppose that all natural things act, like themselves, for the sake of an end; indeed, that God Himself directs all things toward some certain end."

4.  **God**, according to the mind of **Plato**, acts freely, not necessarily. In **Spinoza**, God is bound by the iron bond of necessity. *Prop. 33:* "If things," he says, "could have been of another nature, or determined to operate in another way, so that the Order of nature was different: then the nature of God could be other than it now is." *Prop. 35:* "Whatever we conceive to be in the power of God, is necessarily." *Prop. 32 simply says:* "God does not operate from freedom of will."

5.  **Our mind**, in the system of **Plato**, is free; in **Spinoza**, it is necessary. *Ethics, Part 2, Prop. 48:* "In the mind there is no absolute or free will. But the mind is determined to will this or that by a cause, which is also determined by another, and this again by another, and so on into infinity."

Just as the entire universe is *Spinoza's God*, all things flow from it with an inviolable necessity; thus, it is not even necessary to prove that, according to the mind of *Spinoza*, the universe cannot be subject to any change or destruction. Plato, however, ascribes the destruction of the world (if any were to occur) to the will of God. From all these points joined together, we conclude that Plato is very far removed from the opinion of *Spinoza*, and therefore can by no right be accused of Atheism.

XII. Let us now examine the arguments which the most celebrated man *N. H. Gundling* <note>Nicolaus Hieronymus Gundling (1671–1729) was a German jurist and philosopher known for his skeptical and eclectic approach to the history of philosophy.</note> has brought forward to prove that Plato went over into the camp of *Spinoza*. His reasons exist partly in his *Otia* <note>original: "Otia," likely referring to Gundling's "Otia, seu varii generis exercitationes ad rem litterariam spectantes"</note>, fascicle 2, and partly in a unique dissertation inserted into the *New Library* <note>original: "novæ Bibliothecæ"</note> published at Halle. Since his *Otia* is not at hand, but the illustrious *Wolff* <note>Christian Wolff (1679–1754), a central figure of the German Enlightenment who wrote extensively on Plato and Manichaeism</note> has faithfully, as I believe, cited the reasons of that renowned man in his *Manicheans before the Manicheans* <note>original: "Manich. ante Manicheos"</note>, page 142, I will first cite and weigh those, and afterwards I will subject the dissertation inserted in the *New Library* to examination, and bring forward the doubts of *Bayle* <note>Pierre Bayle (1647–1706), author of the famous "Historical and Critical Dictionary," which was often skeptical of ancient theology</note> which he raised here and there. The illustrious *Wolff*, after stating in the cited passage that the most learned *Gundling* thinks the *Spinozistic* system is not different from the Platonic, proceeds thus:

> "This indeed is the reason for his thinking this way: because Spi-
> noza devises one substance out of God and matter; and the same
> thing happens as soon as Plato’s God joins himself with matter,
> whether that happens with the fullest liberty and greatest will, 
> as Plato maintains, or by necessity, as the Stoics contend."

The illustrious *Wolff* responds that the God of Plato, in the creation and formation of this universe, does not—according to the force of Platonic phrases—join himself with and mix with matter so much as he approaches it to shape it like a <term>απο μηχανης</term> <note>original: "apo mēchanēs," meaning "a god from a machine" or "deus ex machina." In this context, it refers to a deity who intervenes from the outside rather than being part of the material itself.</note>. And in my opinion, the illustrious *Wolff* responds most correctly; for by no reasoning can it be seen how God becomes a single substance with the world as soon as God prepares himself to adorn matter. No mortal would say that an artisan (to whom *Plato* also compares God) becomes a single substance with the building as soon as he applies his mind to working the material. In the closest conjunction of mind and body, a Union takes place, yet no one would say the mind and body therefore become a single substance. Matter, before God adorned it, was a substance according to the mind of *Plato*, and indeed an eternal one; furthermore, God was a substance in the most excellent degree. But how can the most diverse things become a single substance? Certainly, if *Spinoza* had maintained that matter is a substance and eternal, but that God, as a most wise and free Being, applied his mind to adorn-

ing it, no one would ever have asserted that he removes all Divinity; but since he professed that all things which exist constitute only a single substance, and claimed that this substance is God, he fell into detestable error. Indeed, in my opinion, even the most excellent systems of the modern philosophers would have to be called pure and simple *Spinozism* if the most free conjunction of God with matter proved it. In the system of Christians, a certain conjunction of God with the world takes place, but it is by no means necessary; rather, it is most free. We suppose that God willed to build the world or create it from nothing; we assert that the ideas of the things to be built were in the mind of God; we affirm that God governs the world according to certain laws not founded in the nature of matter; indeed, he sustains it by a certain continuous and uninterrupted conservation so that, without his perpetual care, all things would slide back into the ancient Chaos, or rather into nothingness. From this, God and matter would undoubtedly become a single substance if even the most free conjunction—even with the properties of each substance remaining safe—were sufficient for this. However, we have produced above, unless I am mistaken, the most evident passages from *Plato* which prove that the will of God was most free regarding the shaping of matter. recognized only a single substance; other substances—minds, bodies, and so on—are nothing but modifications of that single substance he imagines. In fact, no reason can be given why *Plato* would have set a soul of this kind over the world, except to avoid joining the highest and most excellent God more closely with matter than he thought was fitting. But the distinguished scholar *Gundling* says that this "World Soul" comes from the Mind, and the Mind comes from God, and therefore these individual things do not differ. However, even if I were to grant that this was *Plato’s* view—though, as will be clear from what is said below, there are just reasons to doubt it—I do not yet see how, even if all these points were granted, it would follow that there is only one substance, or that God is joined to matter by a necessary bond. Let us suppose that the Mind arose from God through a certain emanation, and the Soul from the Mind: does it follow that the Mind, Soul, and God are therefore only one substance? Who among them has so far explained the manner of this emanation, which the distinguished gentleman assumes, according to the mind of those philosophers? 

Certainly, God can be considered as a "most sufficient Being" <note>original: "Ens aliquod sufficientissimum"</note> from whom all minds have emanated, and who subsist in God—not as parts of the essence of God, or as if the essence of God were torn apart by these emanating things, but as things very distinct from God, yet subsisting in the infinite and inexpressible Nature of God. But how, he will ask, can these things be understood—that something can be "in God" and yet be able to emanate without harm to the divine perfections? I admit that I do not clearly and evidently conceive the manner of this emanation; yet, I can see that this opinion is not so dangerous and absurd as has been claimed. Indeed, I am easily persuaded that certain ancient and even modern philosophers could establish a theory of emanation which, in their judgment, would bring no imperfection to God. Do we perceive any better or more clearly how, once the will of God was established, the immense mass of sensible things arose, moved, grew, and was directed toward certain ends? 

Therefore, even if that Mind emanated from God in the highest degree, and the Soul from the Mind, and even if it were granted that this involves some imperfection, it nevertheless remains most clearly established that the supreme Mind is distinct from the world. Thus, there will not be only one substance, but very diverse and distinct ones, which is clear enough from the attributes of those two substances. Even if you suppose that not the Soul, but God Himself is joined with matter, what the distinguished gentleman intends still does not follow. For the question arises concerning the *mode* of the Union. In the system of *Spinoza*, all things—that is, both minds and bodies—joined together, make up that single substance which he calls God.

<column-break/>

But above, in the clearest passages, I have shown that according to Plato, the Mind or God is most distantly separated from matter, and that God prepared himself most freely to adorn matter. From this it follows that, notwithstanding that conjunction, God and matter remain substances as different as the heavens are from the earth. Therefore, in my opinion, one would have to produce passages in which Plato asserted that only one substance is given, or that minds and bodies are only "modes" of God, or that all things arise from God by a certain absolute necessity. But the entire face of Platonic philosophy cries out that this cannot be provided. 

3. *The distinguished gentleman says that Plato called the world an "animal."* <note>In this context, "animal" refers to its literal Latin meaning: a living thing possessing an "anima" or soul.</note> This is true; he called the world a "most beautiful animal." In what sense Plato did this is clear enough to anyone who reads Plato's *Timaeus* attentively (see page 708 and following in Ficino’s version) <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499) was the primary translator of Plato into Latin during the Renaissance; his version was the standard reference for scholars in the 1700s.</note>. Everything comes down to this: 
1. God wanted to create a most beautiful work. 
2. He wanted to provide a substance endowed with reason and sense, which is superior to inanimate things. 
3. Before God set His hand to it, matter was not only a "crude and undigested mass" <note>original: "rudem indigestamque molem"</note>, but was also destitute of all sense. 
4. Therefore, God adorned the world, and the stars especially, with various intelligences; hence the world is like a living being, and is most beautiful. 
How these points serve to prove that *Plato* established only one substance, or that God is joined to matter by a necessary bond, I do not see. If God is distinct from that "animal" according to the mind of *Plato*, this ought to be enough for us. Even if *Plato* had called God "the Animal" insofar as He is joined with the world, this title still should not be taken in a bad sense, unless it could be proven at the same time by the most evident reasons that a Spinozistic meaning lies beneath it, or at least that the highest imperfection is thus attributed to God. But it is well known that different sects use the same word in different ways; Plato could therefore have diverged from the impious opinion of *Spinoza*, even if he had understood God and the world taken together by the name of "animal." 

4. The distinguished Gundling objects that *Plato called the world "God."* The celebrated *Wolff* <note>Christian Wolff, the Enlightenment philosopher, who was often a target of the same accusations of "Spinozism" as Plato.</note> demands that the passage be shown to him, and indeed a most clear passage exists in the *Timaeus*, page 478, where he calls the world "God" twice: "This then was the entire plan of the God who exists forever, reasoned out concerning the God who was one day to exist: he made it smooth and level, equal in every way from the center to the extremities, a whole and perfect body composed of perfect bodies." <note>original Greek: οὗτος δὴ πᾶς ὄντος ἀεὶ λογισμὸς Θεοῦ, περὶ τὸν ποτὲ ἐσόμενον θεὸν λογισθεὶς, λεῖον καὶ ὁμαλὸν πανταχῇ τε ἐκ μέσου ἴσον καὶ ὅλον, καὶ τέλεον ἐκ τελέων σωμάτων, σῶμα ἐποίησε.</note> Therefore, when *God*, who always is, thought about a God who would exist at some time, he made it smooth and equal, and even from the center to the top, a whole and perfect body out of whole and perfect bodies. And after a few intervening words, he says: "And so, for all these reasons, its Maker made the world a blessed God." But for that reason...

Nevertheless, the philosophy of *Plato* suffers no detriment; for besides the fact that the word <term>God</term> <note>original Greek: Θεὸς (Theos)</note> has various meanings, and "God" may denote everything that is excellent in its own kind—as that most eminent man, *Jean Le Clerc*, showed in an entire chapter of his *Art of Criticism (Part II, Section 1, Chapter 3)*—it appears most clearly that *Plato* in these passages not only most clearly distinguishes the supreme God from that which was ultimately to be created (namely, the world), but he also calls the same supreme Ruler and Maker of the world a <term>begotten god</term> <note>original Greek: Θεὸν γεννητὰ (Theon gennēta)</note> and subjects him to the command of God. From this, it is certainly clear enough that this title cannot be pressed too hard. And these are the principal arguments of the distinguished *Gundling*, as the distinguished *Wolf* has cited them. Thus far the distinguished man <note>referring to Gundling</note>, from whose words it is clear what he has taken upon himself to demonstrate. We could simply deny all these points and appeal to the arguments made previously, for the claims the distinguished man brings forward here are supported by no clear passages from the Ancients—unless perhaps you except a passage from *Timaeus of Locri*, from which he, along with *Pierre Bayle (Continuation of Diverse Thoughts, p. 345)*, repeats this most serious accusation. Therefore, it is my sole duty thus far to carefully weigh the passage of *Timaeus of Locri*, upon which the distinguished man's entire accusation rests, as will become clear from what follows. However, I cannot help but first bring forward the very prudent opinion of the venerable and most learned *J.F. Reimann*, which appears in his *Universal History of Atheism, pages 161–162*. The suspicion of the most celebrated *Gundling* (so the distinguished man speaks) rests on only a single passage, and indeed a passage of such a kind that it is not properly *Plato's*, but belongs to *Timaeus of Locri, the Pythagorean*, whom *Plato* introduced as the speaker in that place. *Plato* is even said to have compiled this Dialogue from Timaeus's own booklet, if we believe *Timon the Sillograph* as quoted in *Gellius (Attic Nights, Book 3, Chapter 17, page 112)*. If *Plato* were to return to life, he would perhaps no more acknowledge Timaeus’s opinion as his own than *Euripides* would acknowledge the character of the Cyclops, or *Cicero* that of Velleius. Add to this that the passage is the most obscure in the entire dialogue, and it does not contain <term>literally</term> <note>original Greek: kata rēton</note> what the most learned man attributes to *Plato*. Rather, it is drawn from it only by a logical consequence—one which *Timaeus* perhaps did not foresee, or if he did, he believed it could be softened by a convenient interpretation. Indeed, not every connection of God with the world involves *Spinozism* <note>The philosophy of Baruch Spinoza, often accused of pantheism—the belief that God and the universe are one and the same substance.</note>, but only that connection which is said to be necessary, essential, and eternal. And even if we grant that this passage is such that something could be carved out of it to the prejudice of *Plato*, there are nonetheless six hundred other passages that plainly teach the contrary. Even in this dissertation of *Timaeus*, several things are read which make it clear that he distinguished the Soul of the World from God, and was as far removed from *Spinoza* as, they say, the whole of heaven. It is consistent with fairness to reveal the mind of an author not from only one passage, but from many, and to clarify his <term>difficult passages</term> <note>original Greek: dysnoēta</note> by means of those that are easier and clearer; and also to interpret those things which were poorly said in the best possible light, as far as can be done. Thus far *Reimann*. In my opinion, these warnings should not be neglected, precisely because we are not dealing with a trivial error, but with Atheism—an accusation that should be attributed to no one without the most evident reasons. The learned men who disagree with me cannot, of course, harm *Plato* with this accusation, as he has long since "departed to the many" <note>An ancient euphemism for dying.</note>, but they can sometimes harm the living by their example. For alas! even today, in such a great light of letters, there are many who twist some obscure and

But let us now examine the principal passages of *Timaeus of Locri*, which can shed light on this controversy. On page 543 of Gale’s edition, at the beginning of the work, he says: <term>that there are two causes of all things: mind, for those things which arise through reason; and necessity, for those things that exist by force according to the powers and faculties of bodies.</term> <note>original Greek: duo aitias eimen tōn sympantōn. Noon men tōn kata logon gignomenōn, anankan de tōn bia kattas dynameis tōn sōmatōn.</note> *That of these things—that is, of the nature of good things—the best is a certain principle of the best things and is called God.* <note>The author provides a Latin translation of the Greek: "Harum rerum, id est, naturae bonorum, optimum esse quoddam rerum Optimarum principium & Deum vocari."</note> You have here, first, <term>mind</term> <note>Greek: noon</note> as the cause of things endowed with intelligence; second, <term>necessity</term> <note>Greek: tēn anankēn</note>, by which name Matter and those things arising from its various dispositions are denoted in the Platonic sense; third, the first and most excellent cause of all things, <term>God</term> <note>Greek: Theon</note>. Ta de sympanta, idean, hylan, aisthēton te, hoion ekgonon tetōn"</note> he says that the Idea is: <term>an intelligible pattern of things that are born, and that matter is unbegotten and immobile</term> <note>original Greek: noaton paradeigma tōn gennomenōn, materiam agenaton kē akinaton</note>; it is nowhere either born from or expelled from the essence of God. He says the same is <term>a mold and a mother, and the site and producer of the third essence</term> <note>original Greek: ekmageion kē matera, ithanan te kē gennatikan tas tritas ousias</note>; furthermore, he calls it <term>formless and without shape</term> <note>original Greek: amorphos kē aschēmatisos</note>. On the following page, 545, he again attributes eternity to the same, saying: <term>before the heavens were made, Idea and Matter existed in reason, and God was the Creator of the better thing.</term> <note>original Greek: prin ōranon genesthai, logō ēn idea te kē hyla, kē ho Theos Dēmiourgos tō beltionos.</note> If we weigh all those phrases used by *Timaeus*, it is easily apparent that Matter seems to *Timaeus* to be eternal, passive, and disordered; but no one will easily observe it being "expelled" from the bosom of God as a part of God. It is considered as something not only distinct from the Parent of the best things, but also from the Idea itself, or the intelligible world. Furthermore, it is subjected not only to the command of God, but also to the Idea, which on page 445 he considers as a Father. The world is indeed considered <term>as it were an offspring</term> <note>original Greek: hoion ekgonon</note> of Idea and Matter, which finally came into being when the singular power and most free will of God intervened. Hence on the same page, 545, *Timaeus* speaks thus from Gale’s version: *Since therefore the ancient...*

...is more excellent than the younger, and that which is ordered is more excellent than the disordered. Since God is surely good and saw that matter received form and changed in various ways, yet remained disordered, He saw also that there was a need for Him to reduce it into order, and to establish it from indefinite mutations into a certain and defined state; so that the distinctions of bodies might correspond to one another by mutual reason, and not receive vicissitudes back and forth at random. *He then made this world from all matter, establishing it as the very limit of true nature,* <note>original Greek: Εποίησεν αὖτις, ὧν τὸν δὲ κόσμον ἐξ ἁπάσας τὰς ὕλας, ὅρον αὐτὸν κατασκευάξας τᾶς τῶ ὄντως φύσιος</note> that is: *God therefore created this world from all matter, and circumscribed and defined the nature of the universe as its very boundary* (page 546). Therefore, when God wished *to produce the most excellent offspring* <note>original Greek: άριστον γένναμα ποιεῖν</note>, he made this "begotten God" <note>The "begotten god" refers to the physical universe itself in Platonic thought, viewed as a living, divine being.</note>, never to be destroyed by any cause except by God; concerning this same world on the same page, he says: *it is the most excellent of things born, since it came into being by the most excellent cause, looking not at some examples produced by the craftsmanship of hands, but at that Idea and intelligible essence.* <note>original Greek: κράτιστος ἐστὶ τῶν γεννάτων, ἐπεὶ ὑπὸ τῶ κρατίστω αἰτίω ἐγένετο, ἀφορῶντος ἐκ χειρόκματα παραδείγματα ἀλλ’ ἐς τὰν ἰδέαν κη’ ἐς τὰν νοατὰν ὁσίαν</note> Here I would like it to be observed that Timaeus asserts that God reduced the world into order, that He made the world, and that both the origin of its existence and its continuation are attributed to His will; finally, that it was made according to the most perfect Model. All of these things signify not at all a certain "expulsion" or "outflowing" from the essence of God, as the <term>Distinguished Man</term> <note>Clarissimus Vir, referring to Nicolaus Hieronymus Gundling.</note> supposes.

On page 548, he treats the Origin of the World Soul, where again no "expulsion" takes place. *But the Soul of the world,* he says, *God implanted in its center and led it out to the exterior, veiling the whole world with it, having mixed it as a certain temperament of both indivisible form and divisible essence, so that one certain temperament might exist from these two, into which He mixed two powers, the principles of motions: namely, that of the Same and that of the Other.* <note>original Greek: Τὰν δὲ... τῶ κόσμω ψυχὰν μέσοθεν ἔξαφας ἐπάγαγεν ἔξω... This refers to the Platonic concept of the World Soul composed of the "Same" (constancy) and the "Other" (change).</note> Regarding the same page (549), he says: *God did not ordain this Soul last, after the bodily essence itself, but created it more ancient.* Although certain things concerning the nature of this soul are somewhat obscure, it is nevertheless clear: 1. that it is distinct from God, and 2. that it was ordained by God Himself for certain ends and remains subject to His Command. On the same page, Timaeus speaks of God thus: *But God, the eternal mind, alone sees the Leader and Father of all these things.* <note>original Greek: Θεὸν δὲ, τὸν μὲν αἰώνιον νόος ὄρη μόνος, τὸν ἁπάντων Ἀρχάγον κη’ γενέτορα τετέων.</note> On page 551: *God ordained time along with the world itself.* For there were no stars before ti—

And these are the principal doctrines contained in this booklet of Timaeus of Locri; yet, such is the weakness of my intellect, I have not been able to find there that which the <term>Distinguished Man</term> deduced from it: namely, that matter was "ejected from the bosom of God." Hence, I do not think it necessary to respond at length to those corollaries which he deduced from this hypothesis, since they are fortified by no open testimonies. I should believe that the <term>Distinguished Man</term> (and if I err in this, he will grant me pardon) was moved to maintain this opinion not so much by the authority of Timaeus of Locri as by that of Bayle or Souverain. The latter, in his *Platonism Unveiled*, page 93, speaks thus: *Timaeus of Locri, from whom Plato drew his doctrine, first posits a very good principle. Next, he distinguishes three orders of things: 1. The Idea, or the form which is eternal in God, and which is the perpetual Model of all things begotten and subject to change; behold the first Word, the internal and intelligible Word. 2. Matter, by which he understands that substance which God pushed out of His bosom, destitute of form, and which others have called the second Word, or the uttered Word. 3. Having considered the Idea as the Father, and matter as the Mother, he claims that from these two principles a third is formed, which is the Son, which he calls the "sensible" thing, or the world.*

From this, however, the Distinguished *Gundling* argues that *Plato* was a follower of *Spinoza’s* opinion. *Bayle* speaks similarly, citing passages from *Souverain*:

->Have you ever read anything more monstrous? <note>translated from original French</note> Is the world not here formed from a substance that God pushed out of His own bosom? Do you not have there all the horrors, all the monstrosities of the "soul of the world"? More wars among the Gods than in the writings of the Poets? The Gods as authors of all the sins of men? I hear here a rhetorician declaiming beautifully, but certainly not a philosopher reasoning accurately. *Bayle* ought first to have examined the passage of *Timaeus* to which *Souverain* appeals according to the genuine rules of interpretation, rather than immediately trusting *Souverain’s* authority. Secondly, he should have compared the thoughts of *Timaeus* with those of *Plato*, and skillfully inquired whether *Plato* felt the same or not; only then would it have been permissible to press the consequences in one direction or the other. But *Bayle* performs this not at all; instead, he immediately appeals to *Gassendi*, who brought forward passages from *Plutarch* and *Plotinus*. However, since the Distinguished *Gundling* likewise appeals to *Gassendi* and *Plutarch* in the following pages, we shall examine those in their proper place.

Indeed, if you wish, into three. **Protarchus:** In what way? **Socrates:** Let us take some of those things that have just been said by us. **Protarchus:** Which ones? **Socrates:** I was saying that God showed, among the things that exist, one to be the infinite, and the other to be the limit. **Protarchus:** Entirely so. **Socrates:** Let us then set down those two as Species: and the third as one mixture composed of both. Yet I seem quite ridiculous while I strive to divide and enumerate these things by species. **Protarchus:** What are you saying, my good man? **Socrates:** It is clear that a fourth kind is still needed. **Protarchus:** Which one? **Socrates:** Consider the cause of the mutual mixing of those things; and set that down as a fourth besides those three. 

Since these things may be less than clear, we shall hear Plato himself explaining his mind more openly in the following parts, as he is the best interpreter of his own words. For the sake of brevity, however, we shall follow the version of Ficino, which the Distinguished Man <note>Referring to Nicolaus Hieronymus Gundling, the critic the author is refuting</note> considers sufficiently accurate. On page 87, Plato explains—or at least relates—what he understands by the names of the "finite" and the "infinite." Socrates says: "Whatever things admit of 'the more' and 'the less,' of 'vehemently' and 'mildly,' of 'too much' and suchlike, must all be reduced to the one genus of the infinite <term>infinite</term> <note>In this context, it refers to the Indefinite or that which has no inherent boundaries, like heat or cold</note>, just as we said above, asserting that all things which are divided and dispersed ought to be collected into one, and marked according to a single power, as if a single nature. But those things which do not accept such qualities, but rather their opposites—first, the equal itself and equality, and after the equal, the double, and every proportion that number has to number and measure has to measure—all these, I say, we shall rightly refer to the genus of the finite <term>finiti</term> <note>The Limit or that which imposes order and proportion</note>." 

Later, on page 88, Socrates explains the third kind, saying: "Mix the infinite with the offspring of the limit." **Protarchus:** What do you mean, and how? **Socrates:** It does not allow the offspring of the equal and the double, and whatever things are different, to be contrary and hostile, but by making them commensurate and harmonious, it produces number. **Protarchus:** I understand. For you seem to me to be saying that, if these things are mixed, certain generations will arise from each of them. **Socrates:** And I seem so rightly. Finally, he prepares to apply himself to the fourth kind, and at the same time opens up the whole matter. "See then," says Socrates, "whether it does not seem necessary that whatever is born, is born through some cause." **Protarchus:** To me, clearly. For how could it happen without one? **Socrates:** And the nature of the "efficient" <note>The active force or creator</note> differs from the "cause" in name only; the efficient and the cause shall rightly be called one. **Protarchus:** Rightly. **Socrates:** Furthermore, that which is made and that which is born will differ only in name. **Protarchus:** Certainly. **Socrates:**

That which is the efficient always precedes and leads by nature; that which is made and born from it follows it. **Protarchus:** Exactly. **Socrates:** Therefore, the cause is not the same, but something else than that which serves the cause for generation. **Protarchus:** What prevents it? **Socrates:** Have not the things generated themselves, and the things from which all things are born, provided us with three genera? **Protarchus:** Most certainly. **Socrates:** But we set the Craftsman <term>Opificem</term> of all these things as the fourth, and we call him the Cause, as being something other than those things demonstrated to be sufficient. **Protarchus:** We set him down without doubt. **Socrates:** But now it is proper, since those four are distinct, that we enumerate them individually, so that we may better remember each one. **Protarchus:** By all means. **Socrates:** First, therefore, I say the Infinite; second, the Limit; third, the essence born and mixed from these; fourth, the cause of the mixing and generation—if I call it the fourth, shall I have erred? **Protarchus:** Not at all. 

On page 89, Plato applies these things to pleasure and wisdom, intending to show that neither is pleasure the whole of good, nor pain the whole of evil. For what you were just saying, O Socrates, seems profane to me; but to confess that all these things are adorned by this mind is an opinion worthy of the sight of the world, the sun, the moon, and the other stars, and finally the whole celestial circuit; nor would I ever dare to speak or feel otherwise about them. 

He asserts the same on the following page. Let men more perceptive than I, therefore, judge whether it can be firmly concluded from the cited passage of the *Philebus* that matter was expelled from the bosom of God. I, to say simply what I feel, see neither a footprint nor a shadow of this thing, let alone that the objection sought from there should commend itself with any appearance of probability.

<meta>This page continues the author's argument against the "Famous Man" (likely Nicolaus Hieronymus Gundling) regarding Plato’s view on the origin of the world. In the previous section, the author examined the *Philebus* to show God as a distinct Cause. Here, he addresses whether Plato believed in creation from nothing or "emanation" (the idea that all things flow out of God’s own substance), and explores whether Plato thought the world was eternal.</meta>

<page-num>8002</page-num>
<header>ON THE ATHEISM IMPUTED TO PLATO.</header>
<meta>catchword: „ argue</meta>

> "...this, the Platonists call emanation."

Briefly, I offer three warnings regarding these matters. First, I believe those who think that matter was created out of nothing <note>Latin: *ex nihilo*</note> according to the mind of Plato are mistaken; however, in the meantime, many passages from Plato's writings could be cited from which it could be inferred with a greater appearance of probability that the world was created out of nothing, rather than that all things arose from the infinite essence of God. 

2. I am surprised that the Distinguished Man <note>Referring to Gundling</note>, as soon as he denied that Plato believed in creation from nothing, asserted that he professed an emanation of all things from God. For there is a third option: namely, by establishing two eternal principles of things. That this was a familiar assertion of the ancients is shown, among many others, by the illustrious *Wolfius* <note>Christian Wolff (1679–1754), a preeminent German philosopher of the Enlightenment who argued that many ancients believed in both an eternal God and eternal matter.</note>, from whom the Distinguished Man departs concerning this controversy. It is not necessary, therefore, for us to explain the logic of this Emanation to the Distinguished Man, for so far he has demonstrated by no testimony that Plato believed in this emanation of matter. Even if Plato or others could not explain the manner of it, would it therefore follow that it is false? I should hardly think so. No one has clearly explained by what reasoning all things were made from nothing, yet we firmly believe it. 

3. It seems beyond doubt to the Distinguished Man that Plato considered God as something extended, or as a "whole," and so forth. To me, however, and to others, as we are but men, these things seem not only doubtful but utterly false. So many excellent passages of the Ancients speak of Plato's God as not extended and not solid, that after those which I have cited above, there is no need to add more. Certainly, if Plato had conceived of God like a "whole" that had separated matter by internal motion, what need was there to imagine that matter is by its nature unfit for motion? How could he have adorned it once it was thrust out from his own bosom? For what purpose would Plato have fashioned the "intelligible world" and the "soul of the world"? If these things which Plato asserts about the adorning of the world are nothing but pure fictions, then it must be shown to us in what place he spoke clearly and transparently about that Emanation. I know that nothing is so absurd that it has not been said and defended by some philosopher; I am not ignorant of Plato’s talent, which was most suited for fashioning marvelous <term>monstrous tales</term> <note>original Greek: τερατολογίας (teratologias), referring to the telling of wonders or myths.</note>. But without the most evident arguments, I think an absurd opinion should be ascribed to no one. Furthermore, I do not wish to dispute here how much the Egyptians and Stoics agreed with Plato's decrees; the question is only Plato’s mind and opinion. The Distinguished Man continues on page 12, saying:

> "Plato's God exists with matter <note>Greek: ὑλῃ (hyle)</note>, but which he brought forth from eternity <note>Greek: εξ αιωνος (ex aionos)</note> and with
> "which he joined himself again and from eternity, like a spider with its web. These 
> "last words 'from eternity' perhaps will not please those who shrink from them. 'In 
> "time,' they say, 'it was done, and freely.' But I fear lest those who thus ar-

Gassendus <note>Pierre Gassendi (1592–1655), a French philosopher and scientist who sought to reconcile Epicurean atomism with Christian doctrine.</note> certainly affirms, not without reason, that all are mistaken who believe that Plato's matter and soul were brought into effect before the world. It occurs here not so much 'prior in time' as 'prior in nature.' Whatever the Platonists depict in the mind indicates a mental abstraction, but nothing in reality. That you may perceive this more clearly, suppose you place your foot in the dust; you will have, I believe, an eternal footprint: but when? Indeed, I ask you now not to think of it as prior in time. Aristotle stated without evasion: the world is eternal—a fact which Plato often hid under his own mental abstractions. Alcinous <note>A 2nd-century Middle Platonist philosopher.</note> says plainly in chapter 14: *When he says the world is generated, it is not to be understood as if there were once a time in which the world did not exist; but rather because it is always in a state of becoming, and reveals a certain cause more fundamental than its own existence. Furthermore, the Soul, which has always existed, God does not 'make' for the world, but rather 'adorns' it.* <note>original: "ὁταν δε λεγη γεννητον ειναι τον κοσμον..." (Alcinous, Handbook of Platonism)</note> Since he wants the world to be 'begotten,' it must not be thought that he wanted this: that there was some time when the world was not; but because it persists always in a state of generation, and indicates that there is some more excellent and principal cause of its essence. Moreover, the soul of the world, which always was, is not created by God but only adorned. Similarly, Apuleius <note>Lucius Apuleius (c. 124–170 AD), author of "On the Doctrines of Plato."</note> in Book I on the teachings of Plato, reveals the mind of the Master: *And indeed he says this world is now without a beginning: at other times he says it has an origin and was born. However, he says it has no commencement or beginning for this reason: that it has always been. But it is seen as 'born' because it consists of those things—the nature and substance of the whole—which have obtained the quality of being born.* From which it is aptly gathered how little credit should be given to the argument of those who contend that because Plato called the world 'generated' <note>Greek: γεννητον (genneton)</note>, the same was made in time."

Thus the Distinguished Gundling continues after Bayle <note>Pierre Bayle (1647–1706), author of the "Historical and Critical Dictionary."</note> in *Diverse Thoughts* <note>Referring to Bayle's "Pensées diverses sur la comète."</note> page 346. To these things I note the following: 1. It is false that matter was joined with God from eternity, as I have abundantly shown above (unless I am mistaken), nor does the authority of Gassendi (otherwise a most great Philosopher), being destitute of the most evident reasons and testimonies, delay us much. 2. Nor do we have faith in Apuleius and Alcinous, who depart from Plato's genuine opinion. We know that Plotinus, Taurus, Porphyrius—when they could not solve Aristotle's arguments for the eternity of the world, nor yet wished to admit that Aristotle had perceived things more correctly than Plato—devised a reasoning (the words are of G. Vossius <note>Gerardus Johannes Vossius (1577–1649), a Dutch scholar of great influence.</note> in *On the Sects of the Philosophers* ch. 12, p. 70) by which both would seem to have felt the same. For they say that Plato, when he says the world is 'generated,' is not speaking of a world generated according to a beginning in time (in which way Aristotle and others understood Plato), but of...
