Having previously argued that Plato saw God as a distinct "Cause," the author now explores the relationship between God, the world, and time, specifically addressing whether a belief in an "eternal world" necessarily implies atheism.</meta>

principle according to cause: so that the world is said to be from God, just as light is from the sun. Thus far *Vossius* <note>Gerardus Vossius (1577–1649), a Dutch classical scholar.</note>. *Stillingfleet* <note>Edward Stillingfleet (1635–1699), an influential English theologian and author of *Origines Sacrae*.</note> observed the same in his *Origines Sacrae, Book 3, chapter 2, page 868*. *Augustine* expressed their view with an elegant simile in *The City of God, Book X, chapter 31*:

> For just as the Platonists say, if a foot had been in the dust from all eternity, there would always be a footprint beneath it; yet no one would doubt that the footprint was made by the one stepping. Neither would one be prior to the other, even though one was made by the other. So, they say, both the world and the gods created within it have always existed; the one who made them always existed, and yet they were made.

But I would wish it to be proven that **Plato** himself held this opinion; for not only is God called by **Plato**: "The maker and father of the universe," <note>Original Greek: Ὁ ποιητης καὶ πατηρ του παντος</note> but specifically in *The Republic, Book X*: "The one who fashioned the earth, the sky, the gods, and all things in heaven, and those in Hades, and everything under the earth." <note>Original Greek: Ὁ γην, ουρανον, καὶ Θεους, καὶ παντα τα ἐν ουρανω, καὶ τὰ ἐν ἅδου, καὶ ὑπο γης ἅπανta ἐργασαμενος.</note> We clearly perceive **Plato's** mind if we attend to what he said concerning time. We observed above that **Plato** in the *Timaeus* mostly followed the thoughts of *Timaeus of Locri* <note>A Pythagorean philosopher whom Plato uses as a character; the author treats him as a historical source for Plato’s ideas.</note>. He, on page 551 and following, reasons on this matter thus:

> These are the parts of time, which they call circuits, which God ordered along with the world. For there were no stars before the world; and therefore no year, nor seasonal circuits, by which this created time <note>or "world," depending on the manuscript reading</note> is measured. But time is the image of uncreated time, which we call eternity. For just as this Universe was created according to the Pattern of the intelligible world; so also was this time established with the world by the Creator according to eternity as a kind of Pattern. <note>Translated from the provided Greek: χρονω δε τα μερεα... συν κοσμω ἐδαμιεργηθη.</note>

Here *Timaeus* says clearly enough that the stars arose together with time, and likewise that time was established by the Creator according to eternity. **Plato** concedes to the same opinion in the *Timaeus*, page 711 in *Ficino's* <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), whose Latin translation of Plato was the standard for centuries.</note> version:

> Moreover, days, nights, months, and years, which did not exist before the heavens, he ordered to be born then as the world was being born; all of which are parts of time. Furthermore, "was" and "will be," which are forms of created time, we incorrectly assign to the eternal substance. For we say of it: "it is," "it was," and "it will be." But in truth, only "it is" belongs to it.

And in the following:

> Time was made together with the heavens, so that, having arisen together, they may also be dissolved together, if any dissolution should ever happen to them; and it was made according to the pattern of the eternal nature so that this world might be as similar to that superior one as it <meta>catchword: can</meta>

<column-break/>

# DE ATHEISMO PLATONI IMPACTO. 8005

can possibly be. And this opinion certainly harmonizes agreeably with the rest of **Plato's** dogmas. For he teaches that matter was at first <term>formless and unshaped</term> <note>Original Greek: ἀμορφος καὶ ἀσχηματισος. This refers to the "receptacle" of matter before the Creator gives it structure.</note>; he teaches that it was made according to an eternal pattern; he argues from the order of things to demonstrate the existence and Providence of a most wise Being; and he skillfully distinguishes eternity, which belongs to God alone, from time. All these things, in my opinion, sufficiently testify that according to the mind of **Plato**, the world did not arise from eternity. I know the Distinguished Man <note>Referring to the opponent, Gundling.</note> flees with *Bayle* <note>Pierre Bayle (1647–1706), a skeptical philosopher who often highlighted contradictions in ancient thought.</note> to some kind of mental abstraction, but it must first be demonstrated by the clearest testimonies that **Plato's** opinion on this business is such that it cannot be understood without some supposed abstraction of the mind.

3. But even if we were to grant the Distinguished Man that **Plato** believed the world arose from eternity, it would still not follow from this that **Plato** was an Atheist. For it is one thing to assert that the world existed from eternity of itself, and another that the world arose from eternity by the will and omnipotence of an Intelligent Being. Those who defend the former are undoubtedly Atheists, but not those who defend the latter; for they concede an eternal and most wise cause of the world, even if they simultaneously maintain that the same cause produced the world from eternity. The most learned *Clarke* <note>Samuel Clarke (1675–1729), an English philosopher famous for his "A Discourse Concerning the Unchangeable Obligations of Natural Religion."</note>—a man suspected by no one in this regard—observed this before me in his *Demonstration of the Existence of God and Revealed Religion, page 45, Volume I*:

> "I agree," he says, "that the opinion of the eternity of the world is incompatible with common sentiment: yet since the defenders of this opinion did not believe it incompatible with the belief in an eternal, all-powerful, and all-wise Being, the Author and Creator of the Universe: and since the arguments they used to defend their sentiment are much better suited to overthrew the necessary existence and independence of the material world than to establish it, what is more unjust and unreasonable than the claim of our modern Atheists, who deck themselves in the Authority of these ancient Authors, and cite them as having been on their side? Who does not see, in fact, that it is in vain for them to cite what these Ancients said about the eternity of the world, while they cannot show that they also denied the existence and supreme power of an eternal intelligence?" <note>Translated from the author's French quote: "Je conviens, ait ille, que l'opinion de l'éternité du monde..."</note>

Thus says *Clarke*, than whom no one has subverted Atheism with a greater weight of arguments.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into whether Plato’s philosophy aligns with atheism or pantheism. The previous page discussed the "eternity of the world" and the distinction between the Creator and the creation. Here, the author examines the "soul of the world" (anima mundi) and the views of scholars like Vitringa and Gundling regarding the unity of God and matter.</meta>

# 8006 ON THE ATHEISM IMPUTED TO PLATO.
<meta>catchword: with</meta>

The most learned Vitringa <note>Campegius Vitringa (1659–1722), a prominent Dutch theologian and Hebraist.</note> has already observed that the Craftsman of the world is not different from the mind of God. The same being who is sometimes called the Craftsman is likewise called the Mind: he adds further, that the mind is not in reality distinct from the soul of the world, but is conceived as separate only by a logical distinction: just as we daily consider the will and the intellect as separate things, even though it is one single mind that understands and wills. Hence Plato called it the soul and the Spirit, which is the same as the mind. The distinction that occurs here seems, again, to be an invention. It is called <term>mind</term> <note>Original Greek: νους (nous). In Platonism, this refers to the higher intellect or divine reason.</note> when it understands and executes; therefore, just as the will cannot be seen without the intervention of the body, so the soul of the world—to which he added its own <term>substance</term> <note>Original Greek: ὑποστασιν (hypostasis). This refers to an individual existence or underlying reality.</note>—is nothing other than the Spirit of the mind and of the supreme God, diffused and extended through the Universe, like the "subtle matter" of Descartes <note>René Descartes (1596–1650) proposed that the universe was filled with a "subtle matter" that transmitted forces, as he did not believe in a vacuum.</note>. Once these points are established, it surely follows that Plato’s God, the Universe, matter, the mind, the soul, and the world appear to be only different names for one single thing. Lest this be thought a fiction of my own making, I cite Plutarch, who agrees with us excellently in his book *On the Procreation of the Soul*:

> All of them equally believe that the soul was not created in time, nor is it of a generated nature, but that it possesses several powers; Plato, for the sake of theoretical study, analyzes its essence into these powers, assuming it to be generated and mixed. He thought the same regarding the world: although he knew it was eternal and never born, he saw it was not easy to understand how it was composed and governed unless one assumed its origin and the coming together of its generating causes from the beginning; thus he insisted on this path and method.

Thus says the illustrious *Gundling* <note>Nicolaus Hieronymus Gundling (1671–1729), a German jurist and philosopher known for his eclectic and often controversial views.</note>.

The Illustrious Gentleman <note>Referring to Gundling.</note> wishes to show that the God of *Plato*, the Universe, matter, the mind, the soul, and the world are one and the same thing, distinguished only by different names; and to prove this, he appeals to *Vitringa* and *Plutarch*. We do not wish to prove in this place that the universe and matter are distinct from God, for we have proved this above, and no clear testimony has yet been brought forward by the Illustrious Gentleman to establish that matter either emanated from the essence of God or is connected to Him by an insoluble bond—

<column-break/>

# 8007 ON THE ATHEISM IMPUTED TO PLATO.
<meta>catchword: argu-</meta>

—much less that God Himself is some sort of most subtle body, so that the conclusion of the Illustrious Gentleman cannot help but falter. Having noted these things, we shall show three points: *first*, that the hypothesis of the Illustrious *Vitringa*, even if it were entirely certain, does nothing to establish the opinion of the Illustrious Gentleman. *Second:* that the soul of the world is in fact distinct from God, the Craftsman of all things. *Third:* that the testimony of *Plutarch* is improperly drawn into this argument.

Regarding the first point, it is true that the Illustrious Theologian <term>now among the saints</term> <note>Original Greek: του νυν ἐν ἁγιοις. A pious formula referring to the late Vitringa.</note>, Vitringa, thought that the opinion of *Suverenius* <note>Likely Jacques Souverain (d. 1699), a French author who wrote on the "Platonic Trinity" and how it influenced Christian dogma.</note> concerning the Platonic trinity was not far from the truth. Suverenius argued that Plato intended to designate three of God’s more excellent properties that shone forth in the Creation of this Universe: namely, His goodness, wisdom, and power. I have read the booklet of *Suverenius* carefully, but I could not see that this opinion was fortified by invincible reasons and testimonies sought from *Plato*. However, let us suppose this opinion is true; it would follow that everything said about the soul of the world must be explained and interpreted in accordance with this view. God, insofar as He is considered the Craftsman of all things, was moved by His goodness (according to the mind of *Plato*) to adorn this universe. He directs the same Universe toward the wisest ends and, finally, by His power, He not only looks out for all things, both great and small, but also works most effectively within them. Therefore, whatever is said concerning the operations of the soul of the world in this universe ought to be explained more gently according to this opinion. For example, it is said that the soul of the world is "infused" into matter. Under *Suverenius’s* hypothesis, this cannot be explained otherwise than that God, by His infinite and unsearchable power, preserves the mass of matter at every moment, and moves and makes fruitful what He has preserved. For we also are accustomed to understand phrases that at first glance seem harsher—for example, that "God dwells in us," or that "we are in God, live, and move"—as referring only to the various operations of God in the kingdom of Nature and Grace. Thus, far from this system supporting the Illustrious Gentleman’s opinion, it rather destroys it. For God will be distinct from matter and from the world. Matter is eternal, but God adorns, directs, and moves it—ideas which are entirely abhorrent to the opinion of *Spinoza* <note>Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677) famously argued for pantheism, the idea that God and Nature are the same substance.</note>. But the conclusion of the Illustrious Gentleman is plainly different. Specifically, he supposes that this soul of the world is a most subtle matter, and that this same matter, together with the Ruler of the Universe and the <term>Word</term> <note>Original Greek: λογῳ (logō). In this context, the divine Reason or Word through which God acts.</note>, makes up one single substance. But from where does the Illustrious Gentleman prove this? Certainly, if the soul of the world denotes nothing but the power of God, then the idea of it being "subtle matter" is finished. If, however, the soul of the world is nothing but most subtle matter, it fights diametrically against the system of *Suverenius*. Indeed—

The author refutes Gundling’s claim that Plato was a materialist by arguing that terms like "soul of the world" refer to God's divine attributes and power rather than God being composed of physical matter.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the critique of arguments that attempt to reduce Plato’s philosophy to a form of materialism or atheism. Specifically, it addresses the "Illustrious Man" (likely Nicolaus Hieronymus Gundling or a similar contemporary scholar) who argued that Plato's "World-Soul" is merely "subtle matter" identical to the divine essence. The author here begins to provide evidence from Plato's *Timaeus* and other ancient sources to prove that the World-Soul is a distinct, created entity subordinate to the supreme God.</meta>

# 808 ON THE ATHEISM IMPUTED TO PLATO.
<meta>catchword: ani-</meta>

The argument of the Illustrious Man <note>Latin: Clarissimi Viri. A polite academic shorthand for a contemporary scholar whose views are being debated.</note> proves more than it ought to prove, and therefore it proves nothing at all: for it would prove that in *Plato's* system, no intelligent substances could have any place whatsoever. For if we believe him, Matter was expelled from the essence of God; the soul of the world is the most subtle matter, and this same soul constitutes a single substance with the first and second principles. Therefore, all things that exist would be nothing but bodies. This opinion is contradicted by the clearest testimonies of the Ancients. The Illustrious Man takes various opinions as granted and properly proved, and argues from them while neglecting the clearest testimonies which ought to be presented here above all. It must be proven that the soul of the world is nothing but the most subtle matter; it must be proven that the first and second principles are not distinct from the soul of the world; it must be proven that *Plato's* first and second principles are nothing but subtle matter; but we do not wish to dwell on these points any longer. We shall only prove, in the second place, that the soul of the world, according to *Plato's* mind, is a substance distinct from God. We have already cited above in Section 13 the very clear passage from *Timaeus of Locri* <note>A Pythagorean philosopher to whom a treatise on the World-Soul was attributed; Plato's *Timaeus* is modeled after his ideas.</note>, from which it is evident that the soul is subject to the will of the Governor of all things and is distinct from God. We shall now show the same from *Plato* himself. In the *Timaeus*, page 478, *Plato* speaks thus:

<note>Original Greek: οὗτος δη πᾶς ὄντως ἀεὶ λογισμὸς Θεοῦ, περὶ τὸν ποτὲ ἐσόμενον Θεὸν λογισθεὶς, λεῖον καὶ ὁμαλὸν, πανταχῆ τε ἐκ μεσοῦ ἴσον καὶ ὅλον καὶ τέλεον ἐκ τελείων σωμάτων, σῶμα ἐποίησε. Ψυχὴ δὲ εἰς τὸ μέσον αὐτῆς θεὶς, διὰ παντὸς δὲ ἔτεινε, καὶ ἔτι ἔξω τὸ σῶμα αὐτῇ περιεκάλυψε</note>
"This, then, was the whole reasoning of the eternally existing God, when he reasoned concerning the god who was one day to exist: he made it a body, smooth and even, everywhere equidistant from the center, whole and perfect, consisting of perfect bodies. And having placed the Soul in the middle of it, he extended it through the whole, and even covered the body on the outside with it," etc., a few lines later:
<note>Original Greek: Διὰ πάντα δη ταῦτα, εὐδαίμονα Θεὸν αὐτὸν ἐγεννήσατο. Τὴν δὲ δὴ ψυχὴν, ἐκ ὡς νῦν ὕστεραν ἐπιχειροῦμεν λέγειν, οὕτως ἐμηχανήσατο καὶ ὁ Θεὸς νεωτέραν.</note>
"For all these reasons, he generated him [the world] as a happy God. But as for the Soul, God did not make it younger than the body, as we are now attempting to say."

On page 470, he speaks again in a similar manner. After the whole constitution of the soul was completed according to the mind of that Creator, he says: "he immediately fashioned all that is corporeal within it, and joining center to center, he coupled them together with a fitting harmony. But she [the soul], reaching out from the center all the way to the extremities of heaven, and wrapped around it from the outside, turning herself within herself, gave a divine beginning of an eternal and wise life for all time. And while the body of the heaven was made visible, the soul escaped the gaze of the eyes; she is a partaker of reason and harmony, made by the best of all eternal and intelligent things, being herself the best of all things that have been generated." And later he adds these words: *“When, therefore, that Father who generated it perceived that this beautiful image of the eternal Gods, which he had made, was moved and lived, he was delighted with his work; and led by this joy, he thought to make the work even more similar to that first Exemplar.”* From which, in my opinion, it appears clearly enough that the ani-

animal soul of the world is distinct from God, the Author of all things, and is subject to His command; it is nothing other than a certain force quickening all things, similar to the <term>Plastic Nature</term> <note>A term used by 17th-century philosophers like Ralph Cudworth to describe an unconscious but divine-like creative force in nature that carries out God's plan.</note> which certain Illustrious Men have imagined, and which *Virgil* elegantly described in the 6th book of the *Aeneid*. 

But (as we said we would prove in the last place) even the passage from *Plutarch* does not help the Illustrious Man. At the beginning of this dissertation, *Plutarch* brings forward the words of *Plato* concerning the soul of the world and its diverse mixture, adding that interpreters go in different directions. He offers the opinions of two most excellent philosophers, *Xenocrates* and *Crantor of Soli*; that the former said the soul is a *self-moving number*, while the latter said the soul is mixed from two natures, one of which is perceived by the mind, and the other is based on opinion and inherent in the senses. After he had clearly set forth their meaning, the words cited by the Illustrious Man follow. But he immediately adds a refutation himself, saying: 
<note>Original Greek: Ἐμοὶ δὲ δοκεῖ τῆς Πλάτωνος ἀμφότεροι διαμαρτάνειν δόξης εἰ κανόνι τῷ πιθανῷ χρῆσθαι, οὐκ ἰδία δόγματα περαίνοντας, ἀλλ’ ἐκείνῳ τί βουλομένῳ λέγειν ὁμολογούμενον.</note> 
that is, *"To me, if probability is to be held as the rule of judgment, both seem to have wandered from the opinion of Plato; if the intention is not to arrange their own beliefs, but to say what is consistent with Plato’s sentiment."* In the following pages, he sets forth and strives to defend his own opinion at greater length. We do not wish to discuss here what should be thought of that opinion; let it suffice for us that the words cited by the Illustrious Man are foreign to *Plutarch's* own mind. 

The Illustrious Man continues:

> I warn again and again that Plato’s Creation is not a creation out of nothing, but at most an emanation. In this, those who think the Idea is not separated from God's intellect come to our aid from the opposite side. For in this way, the first and second principles coincide. The Idea, then, will be nothing but an attribute of the supreme principle, even though Plato speaks of it as if it were a separate person. Whichever way you turn, his trinity will either turn out to be a monster, or it will be called only a nominal trinity: for if you make the Idea distinct from the first Being, then all the remaining ideas emanating from the Idea and the Exemplar will exist separately—an objection Aristotle made against his Master, which contains an absurdity. But if you depict the Idea in your mind as an attribute expressing the wisdom of God, you will have not two principles, but one. The only doubt is whether the soul of the world is distinct from God and the mind? I do not doubt that the soul of the world is <term>consubstantial</term> <note>Original Greek: ὁμοούσιος (homoousios). A key theological term meaning "of the same substance," famously used in the Nicene Creed to describe the relationship between God the Father and the Son.</note> with the Father of all things, or that it is another of his attributes indicating power. If the former, the world will be divine or a third God. If the latter, you will not have three principles, but one connected with matter, and either entangled or joined with it.

<meta>This page continues the author's defense of Plato against charges of atheism and Spinozism (the idea that God and the universe are the same thing). The previous page established that the "Illustrious Man" (the opponent) wrongly equates Plato’s World-Soul with God’s own essence. # 810 ON THE ATHEISM IMPUTED TO PLATO.
<meta>catchword: than</meta>

> >> In the *Timaeus*, he speaks these words: "But he [the Creator] fashioned the soul to be prior to and older than the body in both its origin and its excellence, to be its mistress and ruler over that which is ruled, and he composed it from these elements and in this manner. From the indivisible substance that is always the same, and from that which becomes divided among bodies, he mixed a third type of essence between the two, belonging to the nature of the Same and of the Other; and in this way, he established it in the middle of the indivisible and the divided among bodies. And taking these three existing things, he mixed them all into one form, forcibly harmonizing the nature of the Other—which was difficult to mix—into the Same." <note>This is a famous passage from Plato's *Timaeus* (34b–35a) describing the "recipe" for the World-Soul. The author provides both the original Greek and a Latin translation in the source text.</note>

I respond: 1. That matter *emanated* from God according to Plato’s opinion is indeed assumed so far, but it is not proven. 2. Whether the <term>logos</term> <note>Greek for "word," "reason," or "plan"</note>, the idea, is something distinct from God, or God himself—insofar as God thinks in this or that way, as the moderns speak—I would not wish to define just yet. Most learned men stand on both sides of the issue. The former view [that Ideas are distinct from God] is defended by *Aristotle, Plutarch, Philoponus, Plotinus, Petavius*, and others; the latter [that Ideas are within God's mind] is held by *Proclus, Seneca, Cicero, Augustine, Vossius, Gale, Sc. Agnellus*, and so on. But let us suppose, along with that Illustrious Man, that this idea or <term>logos</term> is nothing but an attribute of God; even then, we do not perceive a "monstrous" or merely "nominal" Trinity. Let us suppose *Plato* said that the ideas of all things are in God, and indeed from God himself, like certain singular, distinct substances; is this supposition so monstrous? In my opinion, it is utterly immense, and we can hardly define what ideas are, let alone how they might exist in God. Perhaps those who say that ideas are nothing but modifications of God's essence are pressed by no fewer difficulties than those who defend them as certain immutable substances distinct from God himself. At least I do not understand how the divine essence can be "modified" so that the idea of a tree, a fish, a house, etc., arises. But if that <term>logos</term>, or idea, is an attribute of God, it is not yet merely "nominal." For the soul of the world is present, which *Plato* considered as <term>something divine</term> <note>Greek: Theon ti</note> because of the power it exerts in this universe. 3. The Illustrious Man

Furthermore, all who examine Plato's thoughts on that world-soul will admit that they are so perplexed that explaining what he meant is, if not impossible, at least extremely difficult. Clear arguments cannot be drawn from an obscure principle or proposition. We see this: that the soul of the world is tempered from body, mind, and a certain third substance. # 812 ON THE ATHEISM IMPUTED TO PLATO.

The eternal Glory of our Switzerland <note>Likely referring to a Swiss scholar like Johann Bernoulli or Jean-Alphonse Turrettini</note> once replied to those objecting that an atom must be either body or mind, by saying that an atom is neither mind nor body, but simply an atom. In a similar way, I say that *Plato's* World-Soul is not a body, nor is it a mind, but it is the World-Soul—that is, something he himself did not fully understand. It would have been better if he had not spoken about things he was ignorant of. However, his genius was more suited to bringing forth the fictions of the brain than to bringing truth to light through clear reasoning. Meanwhile, it is enough for us that this World-Soul was distinct from God Himself in *Plato's* mind, even though the Illustrious Man has supposed the contrary until now.

> "What gave grace to Plato’s hypothesis," (the Illustrious Man continues on page 21), "is that he speaks of God and the World-Soul as if they were distinct <term>Persons<note>Plato uses the concept of 'hypostasis' to describe these distinct realities.</note></term>. > "...the principle of the race from the Bosom of the Parent. It does not hurt this reasoning to say that contrary faculties were reported or received from there: for it is a common trait of Atheists to admit contrary and repugnant things." The Illustrious **Wolf** <note>Christian Wolff (1679–1754), a major German Enlightenment philosopher who sought to reconcile reason and revelation.</note> asserts that matter, according to the mind of **Plato**, has existed of itself from eternity. This Illustrious Man <note>Referring to Gundling, the opponent in this debate.</note> proves this to be false with no actual argument. Wolf brought forward the clearest passages by which that opinion might be firmly proven; moreover, in my opinion, he rightly refuted **Plutarch**, who asserted that **Plato** established a certain soul which agitated matter before God set his hands to the work. For this opinion rests neither on the testimonies nor the principles of **Plato**. **Plutarch** could not conceive how that matter could be agitated by a varied and confused motion without an external cause; thus he immediately concluded that **Plato** assigned it an external cause, namely a soul. But this way of arguing is weak. It would follow that **Plato** would not have been consistent with himself if he had not supposed a soul to be the cause of this turbulent agitation. Therefore, he supposed it. For he who could establish that matter is eternal of itself could also ascribe to it some principle of motion. On the contrary, the Illustrious **Wolf** has rightly interpreted the mind of **Plato**. Matter, before God reduced it into order, was confusedly moved according to **Plato's** mind, yet it is nowhere evident at the same time that he called the cause of this motion (which preceded the adornment of the world) a "soul." Whence, of necessity, the Illustrious **Wolf** had to conclude that **Plato** believed matter was endowed with a certain power of moving itself; he therefore attributed nothing false to **Plato**, but relies only on testimonies, which must be insisted upon in the explanation of the Ancients. But, says the Illustrious **Gundling**, there is an "active Force" in God. This Illustrious Man understands this according to the mind of **Spinoza**, whose opinion he thinks **Plato** followed. But this supposes that matter emanated from God, and that Plato’s God consists of some most subtle matter—assertions which, as we proved above, are repugnant to the clearest testimonies of the Ancients regarding the philosophy of **Plato**.

# 818 ON THE ATHEISM IMPUTED TO PLATO.
<header>ON THE ATHEISM IMPUTED TO PLATO.</header>
<meta>catchword: in a way</meta>

**Spinoza's** <note>Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677), whose philosophy was often equated with atheism because he identified God with Nature.</note> opinion conflicts [with this]: that opinion will be both erroneous and yet not so dangerous. But the manner of emanation may displease the Illustrious Man <note>Referring to Nicolaus Hieronymus Gundling, the opponent in this debate.</note>, and it displeases us too. But who, nevertheless, will be able to prove that in a most perfect God there cannot be certain intelligent substances smaller than God, yet not belonging to the most perfect essence of God? Do we adequately know the essence of God and His nature? The Illustrious and most learned **Le Clerc** <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), a famous Swiss theologian and scholar.</note> used to say that God is a Being who includes in Himself the properties of all things—both of bodies and of spirits, and perhaps a thousand other substances that are hidden from us—because of which definition the followers of **Descartes** <note>René Descartes (1596–1650); his followers, the Cartesians, insisted on a strict separation between mind and matter.</note> harshly criticized him. 

But he who rightly weighs all things, and who knows how weak our knowledge is regarding the intimate essence of things, will insult no one. In truth, we only stammer about the nature of God; and what shall I say about the nature of God? We dispute about the nature of our own mind, and we will dispute until the end of the ages. What wonder is it, then, if we are ignorant of the abyss of divine perfections, or if we do not know by what reasoning things can be "in" God and yet not belong to His Essence? 

Perhaps the Illustrious Man will say that the dispute here is not about the nature of God, but a question of how something more imperfect, such as the **World-Soul** <note>original: "anima mundi"; the vital principle that Plato believed gave life and order to the universe.</note>, can emanate from God. What if we grant that **Plato** is no less ignorant than we are? Has it therefore now been proven that the World-Soul is a part of God? I would least believe so. It must be proven that God, in His infinite essence, can embrace nothing except what necessarily belongs to His essence. Who knows whether God willed from eternity that certain intelligent substances exist in Himself—in a way unsearchable to us little humans—eventually to be sent out from God in their own time, not indeed as emanating parts of God (by whose emission God would be no less perfect than before)? 

Commonly, philosophers say that the **Ideas** <note>Platonic Ideas or Forms: the eternal, perfect patterns of all things.</note> of all things are in God, and that they are eternal and immutable; yet, in the judgment of modern thinkers, they are not distinct from God Himself. Therefore, God will contain in Himself something that, to some extent, does not belong to His most perfect Essence. God indeed thinks and acts most perfectly; but if those Ideas are "something" rather than "nothing," God’s thought—insofar as it refers to an imperfect thing, for example, a triangle—will by that very fact not necessarily belong to the Essence of God. For who will say that God thought about the production of this or that atom from eternity by the same necessity that He Himself is eternal and exists by the necessity of His own nature? If those Ideas are the immediate object of God's contemplation—not existing "in" God, yet joined to God like some "intelligible world"—we can hardly conceive what they are or how

they can be eternal, yet not belong to the Essence of God. 

But it helps to illustrate the matter with an example that pertains more closely to the subject. We Christians believe in the **Holy Trinity**—not as a mere name, but as something involving a distinction. We say the Son is from the Father from eternity, and with Him, the Holy Spirit proceeds from both, yet is equally eternal and most perfect. But who can explain the manner of this distinction? In a word: whichever way the Illustrious Man turns, he can hardly prove that the emanation of any intelligent substance from God implies a "tearing apart" of God's infinite nature. It is necessary that he provide a clear and adequate definition of the nature of God, and only after this is performed can the reasoning of that emanation be properly discussed. 

If, however, the Illustrious Man argues that this **World-Soul** arisen from the Mind is similar to the "subtle element" of **Descartes** <note>Descartes proposed a "subtle matter" that filled all space; the author is arguing Plato's World-Soul is spiritual, not physical like Descartes' element.</note>, and thus seems to be a body arisen from a body, I will appeal to all those things we said above regarding the nature of the body according to the mind of **Plato**, and likewise regarding God as the most wise Founder of the universe, etc. 

Having noted these things in general, I will respond in the name of the Illustrious **Wolf** <note>Christian Wolff, the philosopher being defended.</note> to the questions proposed. "What is derived, I ask?" asks the Illustrious Man. A certain intelligent essence, the **World-Soul**, is derived from the **Mind** <note>original: "mens"; often referring to the 'Nous' or Divine Intellect in Platonic thought.</note>, and that Mind from God the Ruler of all things—something divine from God, but not as a part from a whole. However, I am ignorant of the *manner* of it, because the nature of God is not intimately understood by me. "Is God divided?" Not at all, I say. From the mind of **Plato**, God is not a body, not something divisible that has parts; rather, that Mind or Idea arose from God and emanated from the infinite essence of God. Since I, a creature circumscribed by the narrowest limits, am not capable of grasping that infinity, I cannot determine the manner, yet I cannot assert it to be impossible. 

The testimonies of the Ancients—on which I solely rely in the explanation of philosophical systems—forbid me to believe that this reasoning of emanation attributed to **Plato** is a mere abstraction of the mind. I also strive to conceive of things distinctly, but here I both acknowledge and profess that the matter cannot be sufficiently conceived. I do not wish to dispute merely so that I may win and protect a distinction once snatched up; that is for boys, not for men. But I cannot deny that some distinction of degrees of perfection is given in the three principles that **Plato** established, although I do not sufficiently understand it. I do not understand how extension arises from an atom or a **monad** <note>term: Monad. A fundamental, indivisible unit of existence, used here to show that even in physics, we accept things we can't fully explain.</note>, yet I know from elsewhere that matter is indeed composed from them. I also hold it as certain that God always remains the Same—that is, most perfect—even if something emanates from the infinite Essence of God. Some external cause—namely God—to adorn matter...

This is how I would respond to that Illustrious Man <note>Referring to Nicolaus Hieronymus Gundling (1671–1729), the scholar whose accusations of "Platonic Atheism" the author is refuting.</note>, though I do not doubt that the most learned *Wolff* <note>Christian Wolff (1679–1754), a major German Enlightenment philosopher who also faced accusations of Spinozism/Atheism.</note> would have responded with even greater clarity and weight of argument, had he wished to take up the pen. But if the strength is lacking, the will is still to be praised.

XVIII. On page 25, the Illustrious Man says that not only are those people atheists who claim the emanation of all things from God is necessary, but also those who defend the eternity of matter. He then brings forward the testimony of men who are, without controversy, most learned—*Bayle* <note>Pierre Bayle (1647–1706), a French philosopher known for his skeptical "Historical and Critical Dictionary."</note> and *Basnage* <note>Jacques Basnage (1653–1723), a French Protestant historian.</note>—who assert that everyone who defends the eternity of matter is weighed down by the greatest difficulties. As an example, he brings forward certain points raised by *Bayle*, from which he concludes that *Plato* did not advocate for the eternity of matter (or two eternal principles of things), but rather for the emanation of all things from God, and was thus devoted to the opinion of *Spinoza*. It falls upon the Illustrious Man to prove that everyone who asserts the eternity of matter "removes God" <note>i.e., acts as an atheist</note>, even if they acknowledge a Ruler of the Universe who looks out for all things. On the other hand, we concede that he who thinks all things have necessarily arisen from the necessity of an infinite nature subverts all religion. But that *Plato* was devoted to this opinion, the Illustrious *Gundling* has not proven with arguments that could draw me into agreement. I can by no means approve of the conclusion just brought forward by the Illustrious Man: namely, that "the opinion of two eternal principles is hedged in by many difficulties, therefore *Plato* by no means defended this system, but rather the emanation of all things from God." This method of reasoning is not at all safe; to say "this or that opinion is absurd, therefore—ignoring even the clearest evidence—it must be denied that a learned man believed it." For how many absurd hypotheses, I ask, subject to the greatest difficulties, have scholars both ancient and modern not only confessed but even fiercely defended? How many men are there, by no means unlearned, in the Roman Church who believe (or at least say they believe) that ridiculous and monstrous dogma of Transubstantiation <note>The Catholic doctrine that the bread and wine of the Eucharist become the literal body and blood of Christ.</note>, to say nothing of others? Therefore, *Plato* could also have established two principles of things, even if this opinion is subject to many doubts. The Illustrious Man himself affirms that the emanation of all things from God is pressed by no fewer difficulties; why then was it necessary for *Plato* to turn himself toward embracing that opinion? If we wish to interpret the philosophy of Plato according to our own whim, ignoring the testimony of the ancients, it could be proven—not without a show of truth—that he

believed in Creation out of nothing. But one must not depart from the eternal laws of truth. Nor should an opinion built upon solid arguments be abandoned because of certain difficulties. We believe that God made the world out of nothing <note>Latin: ex nihilo</note>, and rightly so. Yet if we weigh this opinion of ours, there are many things here that cause trouble: we are disturbed by the innumerable evils with which the world is as if flooded—evils which the most eloquent Father *Bayle* pressed with a great display of learning that was surely quite unnecessary. If we turn ourselves toward God Himself, we cannot clearly see by what means a most perfectly thinking Being could produce that huge and infinite mass of matter by will alone; that [axiom] of *Spinoza* comes to mind: "things which have nothing in common with each other cannot act upon each other," etc. But we do not for that reason desert that opinion, which is strengthened by the most evident arguments. For we think, and indeed with the highest reason, that a system resting on invincible demonstrations, but pressed by certain difficulties arising from the weakness of our own intellect, must be constantly defended. In a similar way, *Plato* could have believed that the opinion of two eternal principles <note>The idea that God and Matter have both always existed, rather than God creating Matter.</note>, though subject to many doubts, was nevertheless to be preferred to any other, since better options did not occur to him. Perhaps he did not see every sharp point of the consequences; perhaps in many things we do not rightly understand his mind. In a word: the system of two eternal principles teems with many errors, but it does not involve open Atheism.

Those of my works which have proceeded from me are indissoluble, if I will it." These words sufficiently declare that the Works of God seem immortal in the same way as the Gods born of God are immortal. This is what he means. But the little words "if I so will" do not signify freedom, but a necessary perseverance. He who is shut in a room also "wills" to stay in it, even if freedom...

"...the freedom to leave is lacking. But here, the freedom to depart is indeed lacking, because otherwise the form beloved by God would be destined to perish, and the soul of the world, necessarily emanating, would have to be drawn back to God. From which it is clear that Laertius <note>Diogenes Laertius, the 3rd-century biographer of Greek philosophers.</note> rightly included among the doctrines of Plato that *the world remains incorruptible, because it is not dissolved into God.* <note>Original Greek: ἀφθαρτον διαμενειν τον κοσμον, δια το μη διαλυεσθαι εις Θεον.</note> I do not care for other interpretations, because they do not cohere with the rest of Plato's teachings. Whatever he says regarding the natural corruption of the world pertains once again to a distinction of the mind." The whole controversy, therefore, comes down to this: whether the world is joined to Plato's God by some insoluble bond, such that the world cannot help but exist perpetually, or whether that world, having been most freely founded by God, is also destined to endure by that same God’s will. The Illustrious Man <note>Referring to the author's opponent, likely Gundling.</note> defends the former; we defend the latter. He reasons partly from the principles laid down above, and partly from testimonies. The principle of the Illustrious Man from which he reasons is this: that all things emanate from God, and that the world together with God, according to the mind of *Plato*, completes one and the same substance; if this were granted, the world would undoubtedly be eternal. Unless I am mistaken, we have already sufficiently shown above that this "emanation" of matter from God, and its "necessary" conjunction with God, is attributed to *Plato* in vain. I will not repeat what was said before, but will examine the testimonies brought forward by the Illustrious Man and confirm my own opinion with others. On page 708 of the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue concerning the creation of the universe.</note>, the sole cause for the production of all things is established as *goodness, not necessity*. *Let us say*, says *Plato*, *for what reason the Author of things established generation and this universe. He was good. And he who is good is never touched by any envy regarding any matter.* And a little later: *If anyone receives this as the chief cause for the birth of the world from wise men, he shall receive it most correctly.* In the same work, page 709: *the body of the world cannot be dissolved in any way, except by him by whom it was bound together.* I have already cited the words to which the Illustrious Man appeals in *Section IV, page 846.* In that passage, observe: first, the title of God as *God of Gods* <note>Original Greek: Θεος Θεων.</note> and *Demiurge* <term>Demiurge: from the Greek 'dēmiourgos', meaning a craftsman or artisan; in Platonic philosophy, the creator of the physical world.</term>. Second, that all things which have been founded are dissolvable, but are not dissolved because God wills it so. Third, that God does not dissolve them because it would be unbecoming of God to dissolve that which he made most beautiful. In the system of *Spinoza* <note>Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677), whose philosophy was often equated with atheism because he identified God with Nature/Substance.</note>, none of these things can have a place; there is no free *Demiurge* here. Rather, just as all things have arisen from the infinite nature of God, so also they cannot but remain. Hence, the interpretation of the words *By my will* <note>Original Greek: Ἐμε θελοντος.</note> is extremely distorted. For from where is that "necessity" to be derived? Moved by goodness alone, he formed a system of most beautiful things; his will, not some brute necessity, is said to be the cause of the world's duration. The analogy brought forward by the Illustrious Man merely "resolves one dispute with another dispute"; for where is it asserted

that God is enclosed within the world? He who cannot leave a room even if he wanted to cannot properly be said to "will" to stay. He wills it because he cannot do otherwise; he wills it, but not freely—he is compelled. But according to *Plato*, God prepared himself freely to produce the world; the world, considered in itself, can be dissolved, but God wills not to dissolve it on account of its beauty. Nothing else can be elicited from the words of *Plato* and the connection of his whole system. *Freedom is lacking*, says the Illustrious Man, *because the beloved form would perish*; but these words mean nothing other than that God, because of the beauty of the work, does not wish to destroy the world he freely founded. Now, should he who does not wish to delete some most elegantly composed Poem because of the beauty of the work be said to have done this compelled by some necessity? Those very reasons drawn from beauty imply a certain wisdom, and by no means some inescapable and iron necessity. Nor does the other reason of the Illustrious Man fit any better—namely, that God does not wish to destroy the world lest the "world-soul" have to be retracted back into God. There is plainly no trace of this interpretation; it rests on mere supposition, which we have sufficiently refuted above. And how, finally, could the soul of the world be retracted if it and the world together make up a single substance? Who would be the one retracting it—God? But God is the same as the world, if we believe the Illustrious Man; where, then, is it retracted to, if God is joined to the world in an insoluble bond? Also resting on mere supposition are the things the Illustrious Man says about the world: namely, that it is immortal in the same way as the "Created Gods" <note>Referring to the celestial bodies or stars, which Plato treats as divine beings.</note> are immortal, silently supposing that those gods, or Daemons, and the stars emanated from the nature of God by necessity, and thus, in the same way, the world cannot but remain. These things are contrary to the most open words of *Plato*; for he says on the same page 713 in the *Timaeus*: *After all were born, both the Gods who revolve in the heaven and those who become visible to our eyes only as far as they themselves wish, then the generator of the world spoke to them thus: Gods of Gods, etc.* and after a few intervening words: *Wherefore, because you have been generated, you are not indeed immortal or altogether indissoluble. Yet you shall never be dissolved, nor shall you undergo the fate of death. For my will is a greater and more excellent bond for the preservation of your life than those bonds by which you were bound at the time you were being born.* It is clear from those words that the Daemons and the stars, which are called gods, are said to be mortal and dissolvable when considered in themselves, and are by no means propelled out of the essence of God; therefore, similarly, the world considered in itself is dissolvable, but remains so because God Wills it. The cause of this matter is therefore repeated: it is not from the necessity of God's nature, but from his free

The former, on *page 546 of Gale’s edition*, says this: <note>Original Greek: βουλόμενος ὧν ἄριστον γένναμα ποιῆσαι, τοῦτον ἐποίει Θεὸν γεννατόν, οὔποκα φθαρησόμενον ὑπ᾽ ἄλλω αἰτίω, ἔξω τω αὐτὸν συντεταγμένω Θεῶ, εἴ ποκα δήλει αὐτὸν διαλύειν.</note> "Wishing, therefore, to produce the most excellent offspring, he made this a created God [the world], never to be destroyed by any other cause, except by that same God who composed it, should he ever wish to dissolve it." The latter [Plutarch], however, in his *Opinions of the Philosophers, Book 2, chapter 4*, writes: <note>Original Greek: Πυθαγόρας καὶ Πλάτων γεννητὸν ὑπὸ Θεοῦ τὸν κόσμον, καὶ φθαρτὸν μὲν ἐπὶ τῇ φύσει, αἰσθητὸν γὰρ εἶναι διὰ τὸ σωματικόν, οὐ μὴν φθαρησόμενόν γε προνοίᾳ καὶ συνοχῇ Θεοῦ.</note> "Pythagoras and Plato say the world was created by God, and while it is corruptible by its nature (for it is perceptible because it is physical), it will nonetheless not be destroyed, thanks to the providence and preservation of God." I do not wish to defend the passage from *Minucius Felix* <note>An early Christian apologist.</note> which *the Illustrious Thomasius* cited, since a simple denial is needed; one must look for nothing but a distinction of the mind in Felix's words. As for the rest, which the Illustrious Author repeats again regarding the emanation of all things from God, we do not wish to refute them, as that has been done abundantly in the preceding pages. He finally concludes his dissertation by saying:

> "In my opinion, there is nothing venerable in Plato’s teaching, nothing solid, nothing divine. Errors clamor from every side: Atheism <note>Original: *Atheotes*</note> itself lurks in these inner shrines."

As far as I am concerned, I willingly confess that *Plato* was a philosopher endowed with a most vast power of imagination, and by no means a precise reasoner. I acknowledge that he brought forth many doctrines that appear sublime but are in fact trivial and very often erroneous, and that he shrouded even the clearest matters in darkness with an abstruse and metaphorical style of speaking. However, I deny that he was an atheist or an open enemy of all religion. By what right I have made this claim, it will be for you, *Most Distinguished Brucker*, <note>Johann Jakob Brucker, a famous 18th-century historian of philosophy.</note> to determine. Your judgment on either side remains. To me, the authority of your simple disagreement will be just as pleasing as your approval. Farewell.

->Given from my Study in Zurich<-
->May 24, 1728.<-

### To the Man Most Preeminent in Piety, Learning, Nobility, and Finally, Integrity,

# JOHANN CONRAD ZIEGLER,

### of Schaffhausen, a Singular Friend.

->This Apologetic Dissertation, as a token<-
->of a grateful mind and a monument of friendship,<-
->is given and dedicated by<-
->**JACOB ZIMMERMANN.**<-

---

You will no doubt wonder, *Most Excellent Man*, how it happens that I inscribe this Apologetic Dissertation to YOU. For you are a man most foreign to all strife, and you desire nothing more than that—setting aside those empty disputes in which the learned miserably waste their most precious time—all men should strive to be persuaded of the most momentous things and devote their whole lives to virtue. In your profound leisure, you devote yourself to the study of seeking truth, yet in such a way that you maintain moderation in wisdom—a thing which is most difficult. You strive with all your might so that, through the most eager pursuit of virtue, you may march with swift steps toward a blessed immortality. This is your business, this your leisure, this your labor, and this your rest. In these things you place your waking hours, and in these even your dreams. Justly, therefore, will you wonder that this argumentative dispute, destitute of both weight of matter and brilliance of style, is offered to YOU. But I, my dear *Ziegler*, praise you and declare you blessed; indeed, I count it among *your most eminent virtues* that you know the true value of things. For I do not, like many, envy others the good that I myself lack; on the contrary, I feel a certain sense of pleasure if I see those things which are denied to me abounding in my friends. Very few mortals know for what purpose the Best and Greatest God joined the mind—than which nothing more excellent has been given to us—into this tiny little body. Many think they were born for this: to waste time on things that will benefit nothing, to strain their food, to ensure the belly is well-served, and so on. Here...

<meta>This page concludes the introductory dedication to Johann Conrad Ziegler and begins the formal "Vindication" (defense) of Zimmermann’s earlier work on Plato. It bridges the personal correspondence of the author with his scholarly response to the criticisms of Nicolaus Hieronymus Gundling.</meta>

...is the custom of humble minds. Those who are of a more excellent nature think they have only then properly fulfilled their duty, and judge themselves to have truly lived, if they know many things—even if those things are of no use or very little—if they can speak on all subjects, if they are praised, celebrated, and "fly through the mouths of men," <note>A classical idiom (originally from Ennius) meaning to become famous or a household name.</note> and if they surpass others either in the dignity of their offices or the splendor of their learning. Very few purge their minds of prejudiced opinions and depraved pursuits; very few rightly recognize the most momentous things and devote themselves with sharp zeal to virtue, which stands above all even the most noble sciences, and spend that brief and fleeting time in pursuing and cultivating it. Finally, very few seem to themselves to be sufficiently wise only when they know those things which the Best Teacher <note>Likely referring to God or Christ as the ultimate instructor.</note> wished us to know, and do those things without which we cannot be blessed. Since you meditate on these things day and night—since you place all your care and meditation in this—who will deny that you are truly Learned, truly Wise, and truly Happy?

"What then," you will say, "does your Plato have to do with me? Why this examination of your disputes?" Listen, my dear Ziegler. It has been a long time since I have been in your debt. Infinite are your favors toward me, by which you have bound me to you. I love you, and I can say why. I wished, therefore, since better things are not at hand, that at last some monument of my love for you should exist—a light and small one, to be sure, yet a monument nonetheless. Those who lack incense must offer milk in prayer. <note>A proverbial expression meaning that one should offer what they can afford, even if it is a humble gift, provided it is sincere.</note> Look, therefore, not so much at the thing itself as at my spirit. Even parents look upon the attempts of their children with fair eyes, even if the maturity of genius is lacking throughout. It is better to test in small things what one's strengths can do and what they refuse to bear. Not everyone dares to trust themselves to the deep sea; it pleases the timid to have skirted the shore. Meanwhile, just as I will never forget your favors, so too will I never forget your advice. As often as I think of you—and I think of you very much—so often is my soul kindled toward virtue. Your well-known modesty, which even an enemy would admire in you, forbids me from adding more here. Receive, therefore, with a serene mind, this whatever-kind-of token <note>original Greek: Τεκμηριον (tekmerion), meaning a sign, mark, or proof.</note> of friendship, and never cease to love your Zimmermann.

->Farewell.<-

# VINDICATION OF THE DISSERTATION
### CONCERNING THE
# ATHEISM OF PLATO
->Against those things which, in parts 43 and 44 of the *Gundlingiana*,<-
->were very sharply noted by<-
->**DR. NICOLAUS HIERONYMUS GUNDLING,**<-
->Jurist of Halle, and Privy Councilor to His Holy Royal Prussian Majesty.<-

->By the celebrated **SAMUEL WERENFELS**<-
->Epigram LXII.<-

> *That all should feel the same*
> *in every tiny detail*
> *is impossible, nor is it required.*
> *But that I should bear with him who cannot*
> *believe whatever I believe,*
> *is possible, and is required.*

->Section I.<-

A year has passed, and some time over, since I composed the *Dissertation* on the *Atheism of Plato*; my very close friend Schelhorn, <note>Johann Georg Schelhorn (1694–1773), a German theologian and historian of literature.</note> out of his affection for me, included it in the ninth volume of the *Literary Amenities*. <note>Original title: Amænitatum Litterar. (Amoenitates Litterariae).</note> My intention was to show by this specimen, such as it was, the method by which I would defend those of the ancients who had been accused of atheism. I signaled at the same time, quite clearly, that it would be most welcome to me if learned men would offer warnings, either publicly or privately,

<margin>X</margin> ...they might be, or what they might find lacking in this preliminary sample: for I am not so caught up in myself as to think that, without the warnings and advice of others, I could rightly perfect and adorn the work I am planning—namely, an *Apology for Illustrious Men Falsely Suspected of Atheism.* <note>An "Apology" in this historical sense is a formal written defense of someone's character or ideas.</note> For here a most vast field opens up before me. <margin>X</margin> Nor is it merely a matter of reasoning; rather, the philosophical systems of the Ancients must be properly looked into; one must attend no less to the facts than to the words. The monuments of the ancients, sometimes most obscure, must be unrolled, and their thoughts reduced to a summary. Modern authors must be read, who have explained the decrees of the ancient experts in wisdom with no small care. We must take care lest we be deceived by a zeal for antiquity, by prejudiced opinions, by bad interpretation, or by love for a particular sect, to say nothing of other dangers. No one fails to see that all these things demand great attention and tireless reading. I believed nothing less, however, than that instead of help and advice, I was going to provoke the anger and indignation of others against me. It was not my intention in this sample to hurt anyone or to seek adversaries without necessity. My mind is most averse to *disputes*. <note>The author uses the Latin "litibus," referring to legalistic or bitter academic quarreling.</note> By a certain divine providence <note>original: "Θείᾳ quadam μοίρᾳ"</note> from my very youth, I have loved the pursuit of a moderate mind, and I love it still. I even consider time to be too precious to be wasted on useless bickering. Of disputes, word-wars <note>term: "logomachiarum," a common scholarly term for arguments that are merely about the choice of words rather than substance.</note>, and controversies, there is more than enough. It is true, I examined in the second part of my dissertation the *arguments of the Renowned Gundling, by which he wished to prove that Plato was a follower of Spinoza’s opinion.* <note>Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677) was often accused of atheism or pantheism; comparing an ancient philosopher to him was a serious charge in the 18th century.</note>

I thought that a learned man, and one most loving of the freedom of thought, would hardly interpret a modest examination of his thoughts in a bad light, but would bear this slight disagreement with a calm mind, and if I had slipped anywhere, would demonstrate the cause of the error without bitterness. <margin>X</margin> I believed this to be most fair for many reasons. The matter we are debating is a *problem*, as Gundling himself admits. It does not concern the chapters of Religion connected with salvation, but a question of no great importance. It is not of the greatest interest to the sacred assemblies, nor to the Republic of Letters, <note>A common term for the international community of scholars and intellectuals.</note> nor to me, whether *Plato* was an atheist or not. Moreover, I believe it is quite tasteless to dispute in such a question, or to make such a "grand tragedy" of it, <note>original: "paratragædiari"</note> as if it were the most momentous thing of all. It has been a long time since wise men categorized those who rage against others over a slight disagreement among those whom the French call *Pedants*. I thought this was most fair because I have detracted nothing from the reputation or the erudition of that *Renowned Man*, because I brought forth my thoughts most modestly, and because I did not omit the titles in their proper places which the ears of some people enjoy, and because I showed myself to be most ready—

—and finally, I showed myself ready to listen to better things if indeed I had erred, and to embrace the truth with "both hands," as they say. But my opinion deceived me. He did indeed subject my dissertation to an examination, but in such a way that I have the most just causes for complaining about him. *For his dissertation is full of accusations, taunts, and rude wit. He reproaches me for ignorance, stupor, and stupidity; finally, he omits nothing that could signify a lack of self-control and an intolerable pride. Whether I have deserved these things, and whether this way of acting is worthy of the age, erudition, and reputation of the Renowned Gundling, let prudent men who are free from partisan zeal judge.* Thus far, I consider that nothing can bring literature into greater contempt than if those who ought to surpass others in modesty, fairness, and prudence imitate laborers and peasants, who strive to achieve with insults what they cannot achieve with arguments. I shall not return like for like. *The MANNERS OF CLOISTERED SCHOLARS* <note>original: "UMBRATICORUM DOCTORUM," referring to scholars who stay in the "shadows" or "shade" of the academy rather than engaging with the real world.</note> *displease me greatly.* I will examine *without bile* <note>original: "sine bile," meaning without bitterness or anger.</note> the reasons which he brought forth against my opinion; I will discuss the foundations upon which his system rests; I will not forget those things which do not pertain to the heart of the matter, but by which he wished either to subvert my opinion or twist it into a foreign meaning; finally, if any "knot worthy of a deliverer" <note>A classical idiom (from Horace) referring to a problem so difficult it requires a hero or a god to solve it.</note> occurs in the 31st of Gundling's Dissertations, I will give my effort to solve it, not to make it worse.

II. Before I approach the matter itself, two things must be mentioned beforehand. The first regards those things which Doctor Gundling warns about near the end of his *Dissertation*. *Namely, he thinks that those who strive with all their might to free the Ancients from the charge of atheism act incorrectly; he says it is strange that those who labor to show how much poison lurks in the system of the Ancients are disapproved of, even though by everyone's confession they failed shamefully in their other doctrines; he says the Apostle Paul himself said that the Wise among the Gentiles were deluded by vain sophisms; and that he could purge Spinoza himself by the same reasoning with which many defend the Ancients, etc.* Since these things touch not only me, but men far more excellent and learned than I, I could use many testimonies of Renowned Men—*Cudworth, Le Clerc, Fabricius,* and others—to ward off this ill-will from myself. <note>Ralph Cudworth, Jean Le Clerc, and Johann Albert Fabricius were major 17th/18th-century scholars known for their deep study of ancient philosophy.</note> But since I must strive for brevity here, I will omit this labor, intending to insert those things into my future work, God willing—not indeed with the intent of adding weight to an error by the authority of others, but for the sake of those who disagree with me. For there are men so perverse that as soon as they hear that a defense of men with bad reputations is being undertaken, they interpret this project maliciously: there are those who think...<margin>X - think</margin>

...they believe that the more they disparage the decrees of the Ancient Philosophers, the greater the honor and ornament added to the Christian Religion; then finally, those who, carried away by an excessive admiration for Pierre Bayle—a man of truly great genius—strive with all their might to refer almost all the most celebrated philosophers of the East, Greece, and Latium <note>original: "Latii"; referring to Rome/Italy</note> to the rank of Atheists. These latter thinkers believe that others who disagree in this matter are equipped neither with knowledge of Ancient Philosophy, nor with great judgment, or the skill to examine a System. However, so that I may satisfy Mr. Gundling in some part here, I will briefly state the method I shall use in this argument.

III. And first, indeed, I do not approve of those who scrape together everything from the ancient Philosophers, Poets, and others, which seems correctly said by some external appearance of words, but which, when examined a little more accurately, either has a far different sense or involves manifest impiety. The ancient Fathers of the Church sinned in this more than once; they, either through a lack of examination or through partisan zeal, snatched up whatever they could find here and there to defend their own opinions. It is well known what happened in the Disputations concerning the Trinity. Many moderns have also sinned, whom there is no need to review. Therefore, the complaint of learned men in this regard is just. Second, I disapprove of the opinion of those who reject the system of those who count most of the Ancients as Atheists only because it seems contrary to certain principles accepted by some Theologians. Surely one must never argue in this way: "This opinion, if it were true, would oppose our hypotheses and our cause; therefore, it must be denied and refuted." The principles of Natural and Revealed Religion are built upon more solid foundations than to be brought into danger even if we granted that atheism to most of the Ancient Philosophers. The Ancients may have reasoned poorly, they may have been delirious, they may have fallen into monstrous opinions; this in no way touches the unshaken reasons by which we can prove the foundations of the Christian Religion according to the most rigid laws of correct reasoning. Third: I think no one should be accused of Atheism—than which no more pestilential error exists—without urgent necessity, whether they be ancient or modern, Gentile or Christian. For we know what evils are usually joined with this accusation: <margin>+</margin> often the most excellent and innocent men have had to desert the sweet soil of their Fatherland, their wives, and the most faithful pledges of their love, and move into exile, to the pyres, or to the mines. <note>The "mines" refers to a form of penal slavery or forced labor common in antiquity and early modern legal punishments.</note> To be sure, accusers cannot harm those ancient Philosophers in this way,

<column-break/>

<page-num>831</page-num>
<header>ON THE ATHEISM OF PLATO.</header>

but they usually stir up harmful danger for the living. For alas! in this most literate age, there are many who do not fear to charge the most celebrated and innocent men as guilty of the most shameful error. Fourth: Moreover, I believe no necessity of charging the ancients with Atheism is imposed upon us when (a) the connection of the whole System is not clear, or (b) it is clear, but there are plain testimonies brought to the contrary by the most serious and skilled experts in Philosophical history, which give a far different face to the System, (c) or where there is an equilibrium of reasons brought on both sides, (d) or a single testimony while others otherwise skilled in the matter keep a deep silence, (e) or finally if the words the Ancients use are so perplexed that they have neither defined what power they have, nor can we bring light from elsewhere. Where these things are clearly detected, I believe the laws of equity demand that we assert nothing rashly. In the System of Spinoza, none of these things have a place. He employed definitions, axioms, clear propositions, and corollaries, so that all who do not wish to drag his thoughts into a foreign sense by zeal can easily see the connection of the whole System. But in the examination of the opinions which the ancient Philosophers brought forward, those things I mentioned occur very frequently. I will demonstrate this in its proper place with very clear examples. Meanwhile, let those things be added which the most distinguished and close friend, Johann Jakob Brucker, learnedly advised on this argument in the first part of his *Vindelic Leisure*. <note>original: "Otii Vindelici"; a work by Brucker published in 1729.</note>

IV. At the same time, I do not wish to deny that for many reasons the opinion of those who, neglecting those cautions I have brought forward, refer most of the Ancient Philosophers to the number of Atheists, is displeasing to me. For first, it harms good literature. For a long time, most excellent men have complained that historians, poets, and comedians are indeed read by young men, but the Philosophers are mostly neglected. Yet these same people simultaneously confess that nothing more excellent can be read among the Ancients than the writings of Plato, Xenophon, the Stoics in general, etc. But if all their thoughts concerning God and divine things involve pure and simple Atheism, these books ought to be shaken out of the hands of honorable young men; for they ought to attend not only to the words, but especially to the sense. It is better to be ignorant of the Greek and Latin languages than to drink the poison of Atheism from youth itself. When Jean Hardouin asserted that almost all the monuments of the ancients, with very few exceptions, were fabricated and born only the day before yesterday, <note>Hardouin was a Jesuit scholar famous for his eccentric theory that most classical texts were medieval forgeries.</note> not without cause did learned men, and among them the distinguished La Croze, think that this Jesuit (and perhaps other associates) was acting so that those ancient monuments of the elders, which contribute to the Christian Religion...

He warns that these accusations can harm modern scholarship and discourage the study of classical literature.</summary>

# VINDICATION OF THE DISSERTATION

...[they] do much to support these claims; if these arguments are shaken from the hands of Christians, then impiety and superstition might triumph. Far be it from me to hold those most learned men—who refer most of the Ancients to the Catalog of Atheists—guilty of so great a crime; yet I would not think it entirely groundless to fear, as some do, that the study of more refined Literature may suffer some harm. At the very least, the study of more rigorous Philosophy, in my opinion, is significantly hindered. There will be a lack of those who would offer advice, *if there is danger in having offered it, as Darius says in Curtius.* <note>original: "si suasisse periculum fit, inquit Darius apud Curtium"; a reference to the historian Quintus Curtius Rufus regarding the Persian King Darius III, suggesting that when it is dangerous to speak the truth, wise counselors remain silent.</note> Indeed, there will be a lack of those who, at the cost of their eyes and with a contempt for pleasures, would devote all their strength to the study of seeking the truth, if after so many exhausting labors they can expect almost no other reward than to be accused of the most poisonous errors and exposed to the envy of all—especially if they depart a little too far from received opinions. Added to this is the fact that, in this way, the *divine power of reason* is weakened quite a bit without necessity. I willingly concede that notions about God and divine matters have been wonderfully corrected and illuminated by the light of the Christian Religion and experience; however, I cannot persuade myself that the *power of reason is so weak* that almost all the ancient Philosophers, who were possessed by a most sharp zeal for truth throughout their entire lives, fell into Atheism and saw no crack through which to escape. This seems to me an injustice against the *Author of Reason* himself. I do not know by what reasoning those men should be called <term>without excuse</term> <note>original: "ἀναπολόγητοι"; a term from the New Testament (Romans 1:20) implying that humans are responsible for recognizing God through creation</note> who, having applied all diligence, were yet scarcely—or not at all—able to perceive that a Deity exists, distinct from the visible universe. At the very least, that conclusion which Pierre *Bayle* <note>A famous French philosopher known for his skeptical and encyclopedic "Historical and Critical Dictionary."</note> urged with a great appearance of erudition—namely, that reason is so constructed that in divine matters it can indeed subvert everything but find nothing certain—is wonderfully confirmed. It seems especially harsh to me to assert, as *Mr. Gundling* does, that all who do not establish creation out of nothing must necessarily flee to the emanation of all things from the divine essence. He knows very well with how many difficulties this very doctrine of the creation of all things out of nothing is hedged; he knows the efforts of *Pierre Bayle*; he is not ignorant that among Christians themselves there are many who think that neither from the word <term>Created</term> <note>original: "bara" (Hebrew: ברא)</note>, nor from <term>To create</term> <note>original: "ktizein" (Greek: κτίζειν)</note>, nor from other places in the *Old and New Testament* can it be proven that all things were produced out of nothing. Yet these very people are most persuaded of the existence of the Deity. I cannot, therefore, deny that for the reasons brought forward, I am of the opinion of those who think that one should deal more mildly with those ancients: yet I will willingly listen to those teaching better things, here as in other matters.

***

# ON THE ATHEISM OF PLATO.

V. *Another point to be noted is this:* Mr. *Gundling* complains more than once that I have nowhere defined what I mean by the name *Atheism* in my defense of Plato. This is true. But I thought it was not at all necessary to provide a definition of Atheism in general. *The question is: was Plato a follower of Spinoza’s opinion, or not?* <note>Baruch Spinoza was often accused of atheism because he identified God with Nature (Pantheism), a view the author is trying to distinguish from Plato's.</note> To that end, I reduced *Spinoza’s* opinion to two main points: namely, that there is only one substance, and that this substance is God. I proved, however, not only that Plato completely distinguished God from matter, but also that he joined matter to God by no bond. I know there are Atheists who depart from *Spinoza’s* opinion, but *that* was not the subject of the present dispute. The question is only whether my arguments are so constructed as to prove that Plato was far removed from *Spinoza’s* opinion. Therefore, it is in vain that it is repeated more than once that some external cause, distinct from matter and the world, is required. For the very facts cry out that this was the goal of my arguments. I say only this: I cannot give the name of "Atheist" to one who acknowledges a most perfect Deity, and one who is most good and most free; who extols the other virtues worthy of such a Deity; who concedes to God right over matter; and who says He provides for the whole Universe—even if, at the same time, he professes the eternity of matter. For either it must be said that all errors concerning the nature and virtues of God subvert all worship of the Deity, or only some of them. The former is clearly harsh. Very few mortals can raise their minds to contemplate those sublime *Categories of divine perfections*. *When the intention, sharpness, and memory of the human mind reaches Him; as if all paths were removed and consumed, it stops, hesitates, and fails: nor is there anything further where it can go*, as *Lactantius* <note>Early Christian author known as the "Christian Cicero."</note> elegantly says in Book V, Section 7. Furthermore, all our reasonings about God and His perfections rest on a certain comparison established between our own perfections and the divine virtues. But who does not know how easily we can err in this part? Therefore, those errors concerning the divine attributes are fatal which directly prevent us from being able to venerate and worship the Supreme Deity. Thus, for example, whoever would take away all freedom from God and transform Him into some cause acting with blind impulse, would undoubtedly subvert an attribute by which all Religion and reverence for laws would be removed at the same time. I confess that those who suppose the eternity of matter harbor an opinion that cannot be rightly reconciled in all ways with the divine virtues; however, I am most doubtful that it can be properly proven that this opinion is so constructed as to subvert the entire existence of the Deity.

He specifically refutes the idea that Plato's philosophy should be equated with Spinoza's pantheism.</summary>
