VI. Nevertheless, Dr. Gundling <note>Nicolaus Hieronymus Gundling (1671–1729), a German jurist and philosopher known for his eclectic and often controversial views.</note> holds this view. In Section 97, he speaks as follows: *I have judged, and not without merit, that those who admit and defend the eternity of matter fall, by a steep and easy slide, into* atheism <note>original: "ἀθεότητά"</note>. *Zimmermann, on the contrary, argues: The reasoning that settles it for me is reduced to this: God would be so compelled that he either touches and fashions matter like a wood-worker <note>original: "faber lignarius"</note>, leaving behind a work that would perish in a light wind; or he pours himself into the matter so that he might consist and persist within it. A God fashioning a perishable work is not God, because that is repugnant to his infinite perfection; and an imperfect God, meanwhile, will not be God. If, however, the Divinity flows in, or pours himself into the produced thing, God will be confounded with the world; the world itself will be God, and God the world: Which Was To Be Demonstrated.* To this, that Man of Most Elegant Genius <note>A complimentary reference to Gundling.</note> adds: *What of Zimmermann? Does he speak or is he silent? He is silent; and at last, loosening his tongue, he responds by contradicting, and declares that he cannot agree with me.* Let Dr. Gundling see whether the following points are satisfactory: and first, indeed, I would wish it to be noted that I have nowhere asserted that those who uphold the eternity of matter cannot easily slide into Atheism. I only said this in Section 18, page 958: *It will fall to the Distinguished Man to prove that all who uphold the eternity of matter do away with God, even though they acknowledge a Governor of the universe who provides for all things.* The question, therefore, is not whether they *can* slide into Atheism, but whether they are Atheists *in the true sense of the Name*, and by that very fact do away with the Deity because they uphold the eternity of matter. 2. Moreover, the cited dilemma proves this least of all. Regarding the latter member—namely, the infusion of God into matter—I shall say nothing. Let us examine only the first part, which is the proper subject of discussion. God, says *Gundling*, will be compelled to fashion matter and leave behind a work that will perish in a light wind. But *first*, he ought to have added that God, before he applied his mind to working the matter, was *free*; he could have left that eternal matter in confusion, and thus was compelled by no necessity, either intrinsic or extrinsic, to adorn the matter. But if reasons now be added, drawn either from the goodness or the wisdom of God, it is clear that it can in no way be said that God was compelled by a certain necessity to fashion the matter. 2. If God wishes to adorn eternal matter, it is asked by what right he can act upon eternal matter, and how he can execute *that right*. As far as the *latter* point is concerned, the question comes to this: how an intelligent substance can move matter and adorn it. However, this difficulty occurs no less in the system of those who uphold the eternity of matter than of those who believe in creation out of Nothing. For no one so far has been able to explain that link which comes between the will—

<meta>catchword: will-</meta>

---

<page-num>835</page-num>
<header>ON THE ATHEISM OF PLATO.</header>

—of an intelligent substance and the motion of matter. But as for the *former* point, there is a greater difficulty in the system of those who acknowledge the eternity of matter. For those who affirm that God produced all things out of nothing assert, by that very fact, that God has a right over the matter established by himself. But he who upholds the eternity of matter cannot give a cause for this power which God claims for himself. And the Ancients—*Simplicius, Hierocles, Tertullian*—pressed this point no less than the Moderns—*Bayle, Jaquelot*, and others. I will produce a single passage from *Hierocles*, already cited by *Bayle* and others. *Why indeed,* he says, *would he attempt to arrange those things which he did not establish, since an entirely good order exists in them by their own unbegotten nature? For if anything is added to that which is unbegotten and self-subsisting, it will happen against its nature. But that which is brought about against nature is corrupted; wherefore it is not at all good for the said matter to be adorned, if indeed it be unbegotten not only in time, but also without a cause.* <note>original Greek: "Τί γὰρ ἂν μάθων... ἀπὸ τᾶ αἰτία." Zimmermann provides a Latin translation in the text, which I have rendered here into English. Hierocles was a 5th-century Neoplatonist who argued that if matter is eternal and uncaused, God has no "business" or right to change its natural state.</note> *Bayle* <note>Pierre Bayle (1647–1706), author of the influential "Historical and Critical Dictionary."</note> urges the same difficulty even more strongly; yet we do not wish to cite his very words. It is clear, therefore, that the whole difficulty consists in this: that the supporters of two eternal principles cannot show by what right God can change a thing that is eternal in itself. But are they therefore Atheists who assert this? Do they deny that God fashioned the matter because they cannot explain by what right he did so? *Plato*, who acknowledged the eternity of matter, concluded from the order of the universe that there is an eternal and most wise cause; he asserted that God, moved by goodness alone, prepared himself to adorn the matter. He therefore *acknowledged* a first, most wise, and best cause; he *acknowledged* that matter is inert of itself, though eternal; he *acknowledged* that the entire order of this visible universe of all things must be ascribed to the Deity alone. These things sufficiently show that the eternity of matter did not prevent him from both acknowledging God and ascribing the most excellent virtues to him. We believe that God made matter out of nothing, and most rightly indeed. But as soon as we wish to show in what manner that immense mass of sensible things arose, or what the link is between the will of an intelligent being (even an infinite one) and the origin of matter and its adornment, we are stuck. Yet our arguments do not therefore lose their weight—

# VINDICATION OF THE DISSERTATION

<page-num>836</page-num>
<header>VINDICATION OF THE DISSERTATION</header>

...we rightly believe. In a word, it is an error, and indeed a most grave one, to assert that matter is eternal, but it is not likewise atheism. 

3. But let us directly consider the argument of Dr. Gundling. He claims that if God fashions a world from eternal matter, then he must necessarily leave a work destined to perish to the "light wind." But why is that world said to be "destined to perish"? Is it **in respect of the matter** <note>original: "respectu materiæ"</note> from which it consists, or **in respect of the will** <note>original: "respectu voluntatis"</note> of Him who wishes it to change and perish? According to the minds of those who defend its eternity, matter cannot perish. In our own System, the world, viewed in itself, can perish; however, it does not perish at all because of the will of the Founder. Plato likewise said the world would not **perish** because of the most excellent will of the Divinity <note>original: "Numinis"</note>. 

But how will it be proved that a God fashioning a perishable work is not God? God remains most perfect and most good, even if he has fashioned a world which, viewed in itself, could perish and return into nothingness. The question, therefore, is only whether God, who fashioned eternal matter, can preserve that same matter so that it does not perish. But what, according to the opinion of those who say God can adorn eternal matter, prevents Him from preserving it? For *Gundling* supposes that God can adorn eternal matter; if he can do this, he can also protect that which has been adorned. Does he perhaps wish to claim that God takes no account of it? But from where, finally, will he prove this? 

If he had repeated the reasons of *Bayle* <note>Pierre Bayle (1647–1706), a French philosopher known for his skeptical inquiries and influential "Historical and Critical Dictionary."</note> by asserting that God can have no power over matter to which he gave neither existence nor essence, then the difficulty would have been far greater. But in this argument which he brings forward—though presented with **much pompous display** <note>original: "μετα πολλης Φαντασιας"</note> according to his custom—there is clearly no force for proving that those who assert the eternity of matter should be counted among the Atheists. I will not say more now regarding the "imputation of consequences"—where one must look not only at what follows from the structure of a system, but also especially at what flows from the actual opinion of the one defending such a system. Nor will I repeat what others have long since pointed out: how difficult it is for our minds to conceive of **creation out of nothing** <note>original: "creationem ex nihilo"</note>; how many otherwise excellent and most sagacious men have believed that God formed the world from some already pre-existing matter; and that in revelation, "creation out of nothing" is not clearly handed down. For these things are very well known.

VII. But let us come at last to the matter itself. To that end, I will first repeat the arguments I brought forward in my dissertation, and I will explain and vindicate them further. 2. I will directly examine the **System of Dr. Gundling**. 3. I will add certain things that serve to illustrate this matter. I proved by the following reasons that **Plato** was not an adherent of **Spinoza's opinion** <note>Referring to Baruch Spinoza’s pantheism, which identifies God with the universe/nature.</note>:

...by the following reasons: 1. **This celebrated High Priest of Wisdom recognized some eternal and most wise Being, whom we call God.** 2. **He skillfully distinguished that Divinity from matter.** 3. **He joined Him to matter by no necessary bond.** 4. **He attributed to God the highest freedom and command over matter.** 5. **Finally, he professed the providential care of the Most Wise God over all things.** 

I will therefore repeat each proposition and vindicate them against the exceptions of **Dr. Gundling**. Since, however, the **State of the Question** <note>original: "Status Quæstionis"</note> returns to this: **Whether indeed Plato recognized two eternal and self-subsisting substances—namely God, an eternal, most wise, and most good Being; and extended, divisible matter, entirely different from God, connected by no bond, and in no way a participant in the divine essence—or not?** I shall labor at length in examining this. 

For Dr. Gundling denies that matter is a substance in the system of **Plato**. In **Section 54**, he says: *matter by itself is not a Being, but an accident, by no means a substance.* In **Section 55**: *For Plato never passed off matter as a substance, where matter is bare and is conceived without divinity.* I will remain silent about other places in which he repeats the same. Most diligently, therefore, one must examine what **Plato** felt concerning **God** and **matter**, so that it may become more evident whether **Plato** held matter to be a substance just as much as God.

VIII. I would wish, however, before all else, that it be observed that **Plato and the Platonists** speak of the nature of God in such a way that they openly testify that **God surpasses almost every grasp of our mind**, and, to speak with the Schools, **transcends all categories** <note>The "categories" are the fundamental ways of classifying being, famously defined by Aristotle.</note>. Indeed, I would not deny that **Plato** sometimes speaks ambiguously and covertly about this most grave topic, according to the custom of the Ancients, who hid certain things from those not yet initiated; yet no one would deny that the difficulty of the thing itself, and its almost impenetrable obscurity, also contributed much to this—especially if one considers the thoughts of others who were themselves most skilled in Platonic philosophy. Thus **Proclus** <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensive commentaries on Plato.</note> says in **Book II, chapter 11**: **Let us praise him, not by saying that he established the earth and the sky. ...saying that heaven and earth were created by him, or that souls and animals were brought forth; for he did indeed bring these forth, but among the last things. *Let us praise him, because before these things he created every genus of intelligible Gods, every genus of intellectual ones, all those above the world, and all the Gods in the world; for he is the God of all Gods, the Unity of unities, above the first impossibilities, more ineffable than all silence, more unknown than all existence: Holy among the Holy, and hidden even from the intelligible Gods.* <note>The author is quoting a Latin translation of a Neoplatonic-style prayer or description of the divine hierarchy.</note> Maximus Tyrius, in his 38th dissertation, page 403, speaks similarly of God: <note>Maximus of Tyre was a 2nd-century Greek rhetorician and philosopher.</note> *For God, the Father and Creator of all things that exist, is older than the sun, older than the heaven, greater than time and eternity and all flowing nature; a nameless lawgiver, an unutterable voice, and invisible to the eyes.* <note>original Greek: "Ὁ μὲν γὰρ θεὸς ὁ τῶν ὄντων πατὴρ καὶ Δημιουργὸς ὁ πρεσβύτερος μὲν ἡλίου, πρεσβύτερος δὲ οὐρανοῦ, κρείττων δὲ χρόνου, καὶ αἰῶνος, καὶ πάσης ῥεούσης φύσεως, ἀνώνυμος νομοθέτης, καὶ ἄῤῥητος φωνὴ, καὶ ἀόρατος ὀφθαλμοῖς."</note> The most learned Davis observes in the same place that the ancient Christians agreed with this same opinion. These passages most clearly show that, according to the mind of Plato and his followers, God is a substance—considered analogically as having something in common with us, insofar as we cannot speak otherwise due to the poverty of language and the sublimity of the subject itself; yet in truth, if we wish to speak the truth, He surpasses all capacity of our mind. Everyone who meditates accurately on the nature of God and abstracts the mind from all things joined to us with some imperfection will easily observe this. From this, in my opinion, it can rightly be inferred that Plato not only held God to be a substance, but also thought that all things which exist besides God, when compared with Him, do not even deserve the name of substance. It also follows that Plato was so far from saying that God was composed of some subtle or fluid matter, that he instead asserted He was something more excellent and noble even than our mind and its faculties. In the *System of Spinoza*, God is composed of infinite, most imperfect, most abject, most miserable substances, devoid of all sense. For as is the nature of the parts, such also is the nature of the whole. <note>The author contrasts the "transcendent" God of Plato with the "immanent" or "pantheistic" God of Baruch Spinoza, which he views as a collection of lowly material things.</note>

-tion of the Ancients, asserting that *Plato established two principles of all things: God and matter.* <note>original: "Θεὸν καὶ ὕλην"</note> We shall speak of his third principle in its own place. For that purpose, I have brought forward the testimonies of Plutarch, Maximus Tyrius, Diogenes Laërtius, and others. Now, the word *principle* <term>arche (ἀρχὴ): a Greek term meaning 'beginning,' 'origin,' or 'first principle'</term> in this place can denote nothing other than some real, constitutive principle or substance: for from those two, namely God and matter, they derive every apparent origin of all things. Sometimes they also called them *causes*. Thus Plato in the *Timaeus* says: *there are two causes, one necessary, the other Divine.* <note>original: "δύο αἰτίαι, τὸ μὲν ἀναγκαῖον, τὸ δὲ Θεῖον"</note> Moreover, they explain those principles in such a way that we cannot help but understand two diverse subjects. The author of *On the Opinions of the Philosophers* speaks distinctly on this matter. He calls God "the maker and orderer of this universe, and the one who provides for them," but matter he calls "all the underlying material." <note>original: "τὸν ποιητὴν καὶ διακοσμήσαντα τόδε τὸ πᾶν... πᾶσαν τὴν ὕλην ὑποκειμένην"</note> Furthermore, Plato calls *God* "incorporeal and formless and perceptible only to wise men," but matter he calls "shapeless and without quality until it receives shapes and qualities." Everyone who is free from partisan zeal sees that these things imply not a distinction of reason (as Dr. Gundling contends), but a real and essential distinction. Plutarch, in *On the Opinions of the Philosophers*, Book 1, chapter 2, shows most clearly what is to be understood by the name of *principles*. Let us take only the first example in which this word is used: *Thales the Milesian declared water to be the principle of all things.* <note>Thales of Miletus was a pre-Socratic philosopher often cited as the first Greek philosopher.</note> Who does not observe that the word *principle* can denote nothing other than a *constitutive principle, or substance*? I know indeed that Aristotle, in Book 4 of the *Metaphysics*, chapter I, offers various definitions of *principles*, but anyone who has rightly inspected the argument under discussion will easily see that in this place that word can be taken in no other sense. Similarly, the word *substance* <term>ousia (οὐσία): the Greek philosophical term for 'being' or 'essence,' usually translated as 'substance'</term>, which Plato and his disciples used when they spoke of God and matter, sufficiently shows that Plato held *God* no less than *matter* to be a *substance*. Timaeus of Locri, on page 548, calls the body a *divisible substance*. <note>original: "μεριστὴν οὐσίαν"</note> Plutarch, in *On the Procreation of the Soul in the Timaeus*, page 1014, says of Plato: *The substance and matter from which the world was made was not born, but was always underlying the Creator to offer itself for arrangement and ordering.* That is: *The substance and matter, out of which the world was made, was not created, but presented itself as always subject to the Maker to be disposed and ordered.* In this place, therefore, matter is called *substance*; the world is said to be made from it, and the same is distinguished from God. No *abstraction* has a place here, for the whole world was not made from an "accident," but from a *substance* of a true name. Let us hear, then, the testimonies of the Ancients on this matter. Therefore, some things are animate [living], others are without a soul [inanimate]. Without a soul, like stones, wood, and other things of that kind. Animate, like plants and animals. Now the animate excels that which is without a soul. In the animate, one part is vegetative, the other sensitive. Again, the sensitive is more excellent than the vegetative. In the sensitive, one part is rational, the other lacks reason. Again, the rational precedes that which lacks reason. But even in the rational soul, since it is like a certain whole heap (for the nutritive is in it, and the sensitive, and the motive, and the passive), that part excels which is called the intellective. Just as, therefore, the animate relates to that which is devoid of soul, so the intellective soul relates to the whole. From which it follows that the intellect is more excellent than that which is composed of all these parts. In which of these, then, shall we place the God of whom we treat? In that manifold heap? Lest God himself be made many. It remains, therefore, that we establish God as if in some sublime citadel, in the primary intellect. But I also see a twofold intellect. For one can understand, although it does not understand; the other actually understands. Yet even this is not yet perfect, unless it also understands always, and all things, and not some things at one time and others at another. So that he at last shall be the most absolute, who understands both always and all things at the same time.”* Having brought these points forward, he illustrates the matter by an example on page 15, saying: *“We know indeed that God is beautiful, and the most beautiful of all beautiful things; yet not a beautiful body, but that from which the body gets its...”*

*...its beauty comes. Nor is the meadow beautiful in itself, but rather it is beautiful because of that source from which the meadow’s beauty is derived. Finally, whatever we call beautiful in a river, or in the sea, or in the sky and the celestial Gods; all that beauty flows from that source as if from a perpetual and most clear fountain. Individual things possess as much beauty, stability, or longevity as they draw from that fountain, and they recede from beauty and tend toward their own destruction as much as they depart from it. If these things are enough, you have seen God. If not yet, by what image can He finally be conveniently expressed?* We see that Maximus <note>Maximus of Tyre (2nd century AD), a Greek rhetorician and philosopher who sought to harmonize various philosophical traditions under Platonism.</note>, *who was most skilled in Platonic Philosophy, removes from God everything that can be classified as matter, and ascends through a continuous ladder of Beings to that sublime object of our contemplation: namely, God. Because it is rather long, I will provide it only in English.* <note>The original text provides a Latin translation of the Greek.</note> *At this point it is right to ask, he says, in this manner: "Come, tell me, O soul, where is He who created such vast beauty, who brought forth such excellent life, who made the first essence? Do you see, O soul, beauty itself shimmering in all various forms? It is indeed beautiful to dwell there. But it is worthwhile for the soul already existing in beauty to investigate from where these things come, and from where they become beautiful. Surely the Author of all beautiful things must himself be none of them; otherwise, if He were any of them, He would be only a certain part. Therefore, He is neither a certain form of that kind, nor a certain power. Nor again is He all the things that exist there, both forms and powers; rather, He must stand above all powers and forms. He is therefore the principle itself, devoid of specific form—not indeed because He lacks form, but rather as the one from whom every intellectual form arises."*

*For that which has been made, if indeed it was being made, required something to be effected; and therefore it received its own form. But that which was made by no one was certainly not "made" into something. This, therefore, is none of the Beings, and yet all Beings: none indeed, because Beings are posterior to Him; yet all, because they are born from Him. Since He can do all things, what magnitude might He have within Himself? Or perhaps will He be immense? Truly, if He is immense, He has no magnitude. For magnitude only has a place in the outermost things. Now indeed it is necessary that the Creator of magnitude* NB. *not be a participant in magnitude. Furthermore, even that which is usually called the magnitude of essence is not any quantity. Without doubt, that which comes after Him can have magnitude. But His magnitude consists in the fact that nothing is more powerful than He, and nothing can be made equal to Him. For by which of His own things could anything be made equal to Him, since nothing possesses the same? Moreover, what is usually said—that God reigns through all ages and everywhere through the universe—signifies neither a measure in God nor, on the other hand, a vast immensity; otherwise, in what way would He measure the rest? Therefore, it is not fitting to imagine any shape in Him.* Thus far Plotinus; and the opinion of Plato agrees with all these points. In my *Dissertation on the Atheism of Plato*, I proved using Plato's own words that the Divinity, who is the cause of all things, is most wise and most good, and that He gave motion to all things and disposed everything toward certain ends. All these things are such that they most clearly reveal the properties of some intellectual substance. Plato reveals his mind even more clearly on this very matter in the *Phaedo*, page 31: *The question concerns the nature of the mind; Socrates asks whether the mind is of the same nature as the body.* <note>original Greek: ̓́Ιωμεν, δὴ ἐπὶ ταῦτα ἐφ᾿ ἅπερ ἐν τῷ ἔμπροσθεν λόγῳ. αὐτὴ ἡ οὐσία, ἧς λόγον δίδομεν τὸ εἶναι, καὶ ἐρωτῶντες καὶ ἀποκρινόμενοι, πότερον ὡσαύτως а̓εὶ ἔχει κατὰ ταυτὰ, ἢ ἄλλοτ᾿ а̓́λλως; αὐτὸ τὸ ἴσον αὐτὸ τὸ καλὸν αὐτὸ ἕκασον, ὃ ἐστι τὸ ὂν, μή ποτε μεταβολὴν ἡντινον ἐνδέχεται, ἢ а̓εὶ αὐτῶν ἕκασον, ὃ ἐστι μονοειδὲς ὂν αὐτὸ καθ᾿ αὐτὸ ὡσαύτως κατὰ ταυτὰ ἔχει, καὶ οὐδέποτε οὐδαμῇ οὐδαμῶς, а̓λλοίωσιν οὐδεμίαν ἐνδέχεται. Ὡσαύτως ἔφη а̓νάγκη ὁ Κέβης, καὶ ταυτᾶ γε αὐτὰ ἔχειν ὦ Σώκρατες.</note> i. e. *Let us now return to those things to which we withdrew in the earlier discussion. Cebes says, in the same manner, that these things always hold themselves according to the same conditions. Afterward, he [Socrates] classifies the soul and all intellectual things among those which are simple and always remain the same; but he classifies bodies among those things which can be touched, seen, and reached by the senses. After a few intervening words, Cebes proceeds as follows: "I believe indeed, O Socrates, that from this discussion, anyone—even the most unlearned or stubborn—would concede that the soul is, in every part and in every way, more similar to that which is always the same than to its opposite. But what of the body? It belongs to the other category. Consider it again in this way: as long as the soul and body are in the same place, nature commands the latter to serve and be subject, but the former to rule and dominate. According to these points, which of the two seems to you to be like the divine, and which like the mortal? Do you not think that the divine is such by nature that it rules and leads, while the mortal is such that it is subjected and serves?" "I certainly think so." "To which of these, then, is the soul similar?" "It is clear, O Socrates, that the soul is similar to the divine, and the body to the mortal." Finally, he reveals what follows from this: <note>original Greek: σκοπει δη εφη, ω Κεβης, ει εκ παντων των ειρημενων ταδε ημιν ξυμβαινει. τω μεν θειω, και αθανατω, και νοητω, και μονοειδει και αδιαλυτω, και αει ωσαυτως και κατα ταυτα εχοντι εαυτω ομοιοτατον ειναι ψυχην. τω δ’ ανθρωπινω και θνητω, και ανοητω, και πολυειδει, και μηδεποτε κατα τα αυτα εχοντι εαυτω ομοιοτατον αυ ειναι σωμα.</note> i.e. *Observe now, O Cebes, whether these things follow from all that has been said: Namely, that the soul is most similar to the divine, immortal, intelligible, uniform, indissoluble, and that which always remains the same as itself; while the body is most similar to the human, mortal, unintelligible, multiform, dissoluble, and that which never remains the same as itself.* <note>This is a foundational argument from Plato's Phaedo (80a-b) for the immortality of the soul based on its kinship with the divine.</note> I do not wish to bring forward other passages of Plato; for the entire face of Platonic Philosophy shows well enough that <term>the intelligible things</term> <note>original Greek: τα νοητα (ta noēta); refers to the realm of Forms or Ideas that can only be grasped by the mind.</note> are entirely different from <term>the sensible things</term> <note>original Greek: τοις αισθητοις (tois aisthētois); things perceived through the five senses.</note>. Therefore, if we examine the cited passages according to the laws of correct reasoning, we must necessarily conclude from them that God, the most excellent mind, is set apart from every stain of matter. Furthermore, if we unfold Plato's thoughts on matter from the other side, it will be clear that the properties of bodies, according to the mind of this Philosopher, are entirely different. It is well known that Socrates and Plato agreed with the opinion of Heraclitus <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher famous for the idea that "everything flows" (panta rhei).</note>, who asserted that matter is in a perpetual flux, unstable, and never remains in the same state. Besides this profound passage of Plato, there are innumerable testimonies to this fact. We shall be content with only a few. Laërtius, Book 2, on the opinion of Plato: <note>original Greek: αισθητον το μηδεποτε εν τω ποιω μηδε ποσω διαμενον, αλλα αει ρεον και μεταβαλλον, νοητον δε εξ ω μηδεν απογινεται μηδε προσγινεται.</note> *The sensible is that which never remains the same in quality or quantity, but is always flowing and changing; the intelligible is that from which nothing is taken away and to which nothing is added.* In the *Timaeus*, he speaks more than once of the body as a thing most imperfect...

...talks [about matter]. Sextus Empiricus, Book 3, chapter 5, page 142 of the Fabricius edition, testifies to the same: <note>original Greek: πας’ ο και Πλατων, inquit, γινομενα μεν, οντα δε ουδεποτε καλει τα σωματα.</note> *Wherefore Plato,* he says, *calls bodies things that are indeed becoming, but never truly "are."* See the notes of the famous Fabricius there. Eusebius relates the same from the mind of Plato in *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book XI, chapter 9, page 523, to say nothing now of the other followers of the Platonic Philosophy. (*) If, therefore, we gather these points into a summary and weigh what all authors testify concerning the nature and properties of matter in general, one can conclude nothing else than that there are two most diverse substances—the intelligent and the material—and thus, according to Plato's mind, there is not only a single substance, contrary to what the famous Gundlingius <note>Nicolaus Hieronymus Gundling (1671–1729), a German jurist and philosopher who was skeptical of traditional interpretations of Plato.</note> contends.

**XI.** Before we prove this thesis of ours further, let us hear what Mr. Gundling brings forward against our assertion in Section IV. He asserts that Plato’s distinction between the "intelligible" and the "sensible" proves nothing, for it does not yet follow that Plato did not confuse God with matter; he observes that intelligence is given in all things, and in <term>natura naturata</term> <note>Literally "nature natured"; a term later used by Spinoza to describe the world as a manifestation of God, rather than something created from nothing.</note>, and that the distinction occurs only in reason. But I did not wish to prove by this distinction that Plato did not confuse God with matter, but only this: that Plato accurately distinguished <term>the intelligible things</term> from <term>the sensible things</term>, and intended to denote two most distinct substances by those different names. Since this can be shown from the very words <term>substance</term> and <term>principles</term>, and likewise from the properties of both substances, it follows necessarily that those two kinds of substances are distinct in Plato's mind. That distinction of <term>natura naturans</term> <note>"Nature naturing" or creative nature.</note> and <term>natura naturata</term>, which Mr. Gundling insists upon, relies on the sense in which Spinoza used it. However, since matter in Spinoza’s system is a part pertaining to the Essence of God and is separated from God only by a mental abstraction, it must be proved from elsewhere that Plato distinguished matter from God in that sense. Whether Plato, like Spinoza, confused all things into one mass or substance, we shall see below...

...we shall look into below. In Section 102, Mr. **Gundling** <note>Nicolaus Hieronymus Gundling (1671–1729), a prominent German jurist and philosopher who often clashed with more traditional theologians.</note> wishes to prove that Plato's God consists of a fiery substance; he appeals to **Justin Martyr**, **Laërtius**, a fragment of **Atticus** found in **Eusebius**, and a **"Learned Frenchman."** Let us examine each one. The passage from **Justin Martyr** is found in his *Exhortation to the Greeks*, page 6, in which the **Blessed Martyr** says: <note>original Greek: Πλατων μεν γαρ, ως ανωθεν κατεληλυθως, και τα εν ουρανοις απαντα ακριβως μεμαθηκως και εωρακως τον ανωτατω θεον εν τη πυρωδει ουσια ειναι λεγει.</note> "For Plato, as if he had descended from heaven and accurately learned and seen all things there, says that the supreme God exists in a fiery essence." But in my opinion, it is one thing to say that God exists or dwells *in* a fiery substance, and quite another to say that God *consists of* fire. Justin said the former, not the latter. Hence, on the following page, the same author asserts that Plato established three principles: namely, God, matter, and the Idea. Meanwhile, certain Eastern peoples believed that God dwells in a kind of fiery substance. Holy Scripture says that God "dwells in inaccessible light" (1 Timothy 6:16); on this passage, one may consult **Vitringa**'s *Sacred Observations*, Book 5, chapter 16, page 216, and **Spanheim**'s notes on Callimachus, page 612. If we believe **Iamblichus**, the **Egyptians** and **Chaldeans** (these are the words of the Great Man **Jean Le Clerc** in his notes on Exodus, chapter 3, verse 2) observe that among the various forms under which natures superior to humans present themselves to be seen by men, one is fiery; they distinguish between different types of flame according to the excellence of the nature hidden beneath it. Thus, Iamblichus says in Section 11, Chapter 4 of *On the Mysteries*: <note>original Greek: το μεν των Θεων πυρ ατομον, αφθεγκτον εκλαμπει, καὶ πληροι τα ολα βαθη του κοσμου... Το των Αγγελων διηρημενον πυρ, πλην εν ταις γε τελειωταταις ιδεαις διαφαινεται.</note> "The fire of the Gods shines forth as indivisible and ineffable, and fills the entire depths of the world. The fire of the Archangels is also indivisible, but it is seen with a great multitude preceding it, surrounding it, or following it. But the fire of the Angels is divided, though it appears in a most perfect form." Doubtless, the Ancients, swept up in admiration by their contemplation of the sun and stars, believed nothing was more excellent than these; it was therefore probable, they thought, that God was adorned with such most splendid light as if by a <term>vehicle</term> <note>In Platonic philosophy, a "vehicle" (ochēma) is a subtle, quasi-material body that allows a pure soul or spirit to interact with the physical world.</note>. Perhaps they also thought that no substances were entirely free from every corporeal vehicle—an opinion held even by some moderns. Thus, quite recently, that most learned man and my very dear friend, **Louis Bourget**, in his *Philosophical Letters* published in Amsterdam, judged that all intellectual substances, except God, are clothed in some subtle body. Hence, as I would not wish to rashly reject this—

—reject it, so neither would I wish to approve it. (*) For even if Plato had believed that God, though separate from all matter, was nevertheless equipped with a certain most splendid light as a vehicle, he would indeed have asserted something that he could not prove with clear arguments, but he would not, for that reason, have confused God with matter. The passage from **Diogenes Laërtius** to which Mr. **Gundling** appeals is found in Book 3, page 87, in which **Laërtius** asserts that Plato said: <note>original Greek: Θεος μεν εν εχειν το πολυ πυρινες</note> "The Gods for the most part contain a fiery nature." But anyone who reads what comes before and after will easily see that this passage has absolutely nothing to do with the matter. The discussion there is about the stars, which Plato, as is well known, called "gods." Hence, immediately in what follows, he says that "the Earth is the oldest of the gods in heaven." I need not even mention that **Laërtius** most clearly distinguished God from matter according to Plato's mind. Thirdly, the famous **Gundling** appeals to an **Anonymous Frenchman**, who asserts that Plato, along with **Heraclitus**, professed that God consists of fire. Whether that learned **Frenchman** brought forward any evidence or not, I certainly do not know. But without evidence, authority is worth nothing in this context. It is indeed certain that **Heraclitus** believed matter and the world consist of a composition of the smallest and most rapid particles; but that he added no other principle is what we deny. So far at least, I have not seen any reversal of the arguments brought forward by the most famous theologian **Olearius**, <term>of blessed memory</term> <note>original Greek: ὁ νυν εν ἁγιοις (literally "who is now among the saints"), a formula used for the deceased.</note>. **Pierre Bayle**, indeed, in his *Supplement to Thoughts on the Comet*, page 495, holds the same opinion as that learned **Frenchman** and **Gundling**; indeed, he mentions the dissertations of the famous **Olearius** in his margin, yet he passes over the reasons brought by that celebrated man with a "dry foot" <note>A Latin idiom meaning to pass over something quickly or without addressing the difficulties.</note>. Finally, the last passage is found in **Eusebius**'s *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book 15, chapter 8, page 806; there, **Atticus the Platonist** <note>A 2nd-century philosopher who defended Plato against Aristotle.</note> disputes against **Aristotle**. Among other things, he says: <note>original Greek: ὁ μεν φησι τα κατ’ ουρανον την πλειστην ιδεαν εκ πυρος εχειν.</note> "For Plato says that the appearance of heavenly things is mostly made of fire." But everyone sees that the discussion is not about the nature of God, but about the stars. Hence, in his notes on this passage, the most learned **Viger** adds the following: "Plato in the *Timaeus*, page 530, established four ideas of living beings: the first, the **celestial race of gods**; the second, the **winged and air-borne**; the third, the **aquatic type**; the fourth, the **pedestrian and land-dwelling**."

> (*) The most learned **Mosheim** <note>Johann Lorenz von Mosheim (1693–1755), a famous church historian.</note> does not seem far from our opinion in his notes on **Cudworth**, page 1011, saying: "I am certain that Plato entirely abstracted God from this gross and mutable matter of which bodies consist; nor can I bring myself to agree with those who wish to persuade us of the contrary, simply to more easily count this philosopher among the Atheists. Yet, nonetheless, I hardly doubt that he made Him a participant in a certain most subtle, simple, and indivisible matter." See the rest in that place.

# VINDICATION OF THE DISSERTATION

<page-num>848</page-num>

Then, concerning the first [class of beings]: <note>original Greek: τὰ μὲν ἐν θείῳ, τὴν πλείστην ἰδέαν ἐκ πυρὸς ἀπεργάζετο, ὅπως ὅι λαμπρότατον ἰδεῖν τε κάλλιστον εἴη</note> "Of the divine kind, he made the greatest part from fire, so that it might be the most brilliant and most beautiful to behold." <note>This is a quote from Plato's *Timaeus* 40a, describing the creation of the stars/heavenly gods.</note> **Proclus** and **Alcinous** <note>Influential commentators on Plato from late antiquity.</note> add that **Plato** felt that most excellent body was fashioned from the "flower" and, as it were, the choice parts of the elements, yet in such a way that fire held the primary place in this mixture. Thus far says **Vigerus** <note>François Viger (1590–1647), a French Jesuit scholar.</note>. From these points, it is clear that the passages cited by **Mr. Gundling** by no means prove that God consists of fire.

XII. Before we prove that God, in the mind of **Plato**, is not joined with matter, we shall further prove that **Plato** did not believe there was only one single substance. **Spinoza**, indeed, asserted that there is only one substance, a single Deity, but this substance itself consists of infinite substances confused into one single mass. All individual bodies and intellectual substances are merely "modifications" of that great substance. It would be better to say, therefore, that an infinite number of substances make up the God of **Spinoza**, rather than saying there is only one. However, I proved in my *Dissertation* that, in **Plato’s** mind, there is one supreme, best, and wisest Deity. A French author of the *History of Pagan Philosophy*, published at **The Hague** some years ago (p. 119), proves the same with many testimonies from **Plutarch, Iamblichis, Plotinus, Porphyry,** and **Hierocles**. I do not wish to cite the passages themselves. I have proved, moreover, that God in the mind of **Plato** is separate from every stain of matter. This being established, it follows necessarily that **Plato** believed in more than one substance. For he distinguishes matter from this unique Deity with great care, and in such a way that he attributes eternal existence to it. I could prove this with testimonies from **Plutarch**, **Diogenes Laërtius**, and the author of the *Philosophumena* <note>A work refuting heresies, often attributed to Hippolytus of Rome.</note>: but a single testimony from **Timaeus of Locri** <note>A Pythagorean philosopher featured in Plato's dialogues.</note> suffices, which appears on page 544 of the *Mythological Opuscula*: <note>original Greek: Ταύταν δὲ τὰν ὕλαν ἀΐδιον μὲν ἔφα, ε' μὲν ἀκίνατον, ἄμορφον δὲ καὶ ἄυλαν, κ' ἀχημάτιστον, δεχομέναν δὲ πᾶσαν μορφάν.</note> "He said that this matter was eternal, not indeed movable [by itself], and of its own nature devoid of form and shape, yet receiving every form." If, therefore, God is not only distinguished from matter by **Plato**, but eternal existence and subsistence are also attributed to that matter, it follows necessarily that there is not only one substance in **Plato’s** thought. For if God were separate from matter only by a certain abstraction of the mind, why did everyone who explained **Plato’s** dogmas so carefully distinguish matter from God? Why is matter called the "receptacle" of all bodily things from which the world was fashioned, if it was not distinct from God? And how could matter, which subsists from eternity, finally become a substance

<meta>catchword: become</meta>

<column-break/>

<page-num>849</page-num>

only after God wished to adorn it? 2. In the *Laws*, Book X, page 880 and following, **Plato** proves at length that motion has its origin in a mind, and indeed a most excellent one; but that bodies are by themselves unfit for motion; he therefore distinguishes bodies from minds. For if God were distinct from matter only by an abstraction of the mind according to **Plato**, then it would follow necessarily that matter also has the power of moving according to **Plato**'s thought: yet this is highly impossible in **Plato**'s view: therefore, the former premise must also be false. 3. The same can be proven from **Plato's** opinion on the origin of evil. The doctrine of the origin of evil disturbed the Ancients in no small way. They did not dare to ascribe it to God, whom they knew well to be the best and most holy. They therefore threw the origin and cause of evil onto matter. **Plato** did the same, which learned men—**Thomasius, Wolf, Brucker,** and others—have proved with many testimonies. **Plato** himself should be heard, saying very clearly in the *Timaeus*: <note>original Greek: βεληθεις ό Θεος αγαθα μεν παντα, φαυλον δε μηδεν ειναι κατα δυναμιν.</note> "God wished all things to be good, and that there be no evil, as far as was possible by nature." Likewise in the *Theaetetus*, Volume I of his *Works*, page 176: <note>original Greek: αλλ' έτ' απολεσθαι τα κακα δυνατον, ὑπεναντιον γαρ τι τω αγαθω αει ειναι αναγκη.</note> "But it is not possible for evils to be destroyed, for it is necessary that there always be something opposite to the good." These quotes show more than enough that matter, which is the origin of evil for **Plato**, is entirely distinct from God, and thus there is not only one substance. For if matter were only distinct from God by a mental distinction, why would almost all philosophers in the world, and **Plato** especially, flee to matter [to explain evil]? Why would he so carefully have distinguished "the Good" from "Necessity"? Could not God have been called the cause of all evils just as much as matter, if those two principles had not been truly distinct from one another? I know **Mr. Gundling** objects that **Plato**, led by reverence for the Deity, denied that God was the cause of evils. But that reverence was undoubtedly based on the notions he held about the Deity. Since he himself speaks of God more than once in such a way that nothing more excellent could be said by a man lacking the light of Revelation, we must necessarily conclude that he did so for this reason: because he recognized matter to be a viler thing than could possibly belong to the nature of God. We have proved, therefore, if I am not mistaken, with clear arguments, that **Plato** recognized more than one substance, and thus is as far as possible from the opinion of **Spinoza**.

XIII. Let us proceed, therefore, and show that **Plato** did not confuse God with matter at all. In Section VI, page 851 of my *Dissertation*, I brought forward the following reasons. 1. That God, in **Plato's** mind, is free.

He is specifically refuting the scholar Nicolaus Hieronymus Gundling, who claimed that Plato’s God was bound by necessity (like Spinoza’s God) rather than acting with true freedom. Zimmermann is arguing that for Plato, God is a free agent who chooses to organize matter out of goodness, not because He is forced to.</meta>

# VINDICATION OF THE DISSERTATION

<page-num>850</page-num>

2. That He intended specific ends in the decoration of the entire universe. 3. That God commands necessity. 4. That our mind is free, capable of receiving punishment and reward. 5. That the destruction of the world depends upon the most free will of God. Against these individual arguments, **Mr. Gundling** brings forward certain points which must be examined. In Section 5, he says: *“Because it proves nothing against me that Plato’s God wanted to adorn, fashion, and form matter: in this, Spinoza likewise agrees with Plato. But Zimmermann is deceived when he mixes will with liberty, in the way we define it, and sells them as synonyms.”* But I would very much wish that **Mr. Gundling** had clearly shown in what way I confused will with liberty. For I cannot find a trace of this error of mine. I proved that God and matter are two substances, and indeed, according to **Plato**, coeternal. I proved that the origin of motion, according to **Plato**, is not to be sought from the body; I proved that from the contemplation of matter—which exists eternally by itself according to **Plato’s** mind—it necessarily follows that God could have restrained His mind from adorning matter. Yet He did adorn it, a decision which cannot be called anything but most free. By liberty, therefore, I understood 그 faculty of the divine mind according to which He can do something or not do it, effect something or not effect it; a faculty, therefore, removed from all internal and external necessity. That such a faculty was in God according to **Plato's** mind, the entire face of the Platonic System shows. Matter was eternal, subsisting by itself, <term>unformed</term> <note>original Greek: ἀσχημάτιστος (aschēmatistos), meaning without shape or arrangement</note>. God is the most excellent mind, separate from every stain of matter. Therefore, He could not be driven by necessity to act by matter itself, which according to **Plato** does not even possess motion. Yet God adorned matter according to **Plato’s** mind, and indeed according to the <term>pattern</term> <note>original Greek: παράδειγμα (paradeigma), the ideal model or blueprint</note> which was in the divine intellect. But just as the mere contemplation of an object does not introduce necessity, neither does a will moved by reasons subvert liberty. When, therefore, God applied His mind to adorning matter, He must be said to have done this freely, although not without reasons. A most noble <term>pattern</term> was before His mind. According to **Plato**, goodness was added to this. The reasons for crafting the world, therefore, are sought from the fittingness of the divine virtues. If anyone asserts that these reasons, being present to the intellect of God, introduce necessity, he must either maintain that God acts without reason, or establish that all reasons inclining the mind to act introduce absolute necessity—both of which are absurd. I do not know, then, where I have finally mixed will with liberty. **Jakob Thomasius**, a man most skilled in the history of philosophy, expressed my thinking with an elegant simile in his *Dissertation on the Stoic Conflagration of the World*,

<column-break/>

<page-num>851</page-num>
<header>ON THE ATHEISM OF PLATO.</header>

Dissertation 2, Section 10. **Plato’s** God, he says, is like a **Craftsman**, separated from his timber by a vast distance of paths. This craftsman, therefore, rests as long as he wishes; when the desire to exercise his art comes upon him, armed with an axe, he moves toward the timber and imprints his ideas upon it, as much as its suitability permits. Perhaps light will be shed on this very question we are dealing with by a comparison with the doctrine of the creation of all things from nothing. According to our view <note>The standard Christian theological view</note>, God was most free, compelled by no necessity of nature to create the world from nothing. Similarly, in **Plato’s** mind, God was most distantly separated from matter and freely applied His mind to adorning the world. In the mind of God, according to us, were the ideas of all possible things, and thus also of possible worlds. In Himself, according to **Plato’s** mind, God held (or at least looked upon) the most beautiful <term>pattern</term> of all intelligible things, to which all things were to be measured. God, according to us, could have existed through all eternity as most perfect and self-sufficient without the world, yet He wished to show the <term>pre-eminence</term> <note>original Greek: ὑπεροχήν (hyperochēn), meaning excellence or superiority</note> of His virtues. Therefore, He created the world from nothing. **Plato’s** God contemplated that rude and undigested mass, yet since He was good, He wished to adorn matter as much as He could according to the most beautiful model. Finally, He also did this, as the whole of **Plato’s** *Timaeus* most evidently shows. Moreover, just as God, according to us, did not make the world without a cause, but led by the wisest reasons (though not at all by necessity); so neither did **Plato’s** God craft matter either without a cause or by necessity, but moved by goodness alone. Therefore, in our view, God freely made the world from nothing; likewise, **Plato’s** God must be said to have freely crafted the world. In a word: take away the eternity of matter, and as far as the core of the matter is concerned, there will be no difference between the two systems. The question here is not by what right **Plato’s** God could have crafted matter, but what **Plato** himself felt, based on the testimonies of the Ancients, which must be insisted upon. Nor is the question whether **Plato’s** God always commanded matter according to His whim; for we confess that matter by no means always complied with the divine will, but only this: whether God, freely and compelled by no necessity, approached the task of arranging matter—which we assert has a place in the Platonic System. For just as a Craftsman can freely apply his mind to working matter, even if he later observes that a Mercury cannot be made out of just any piece of wood; so **Plato’s** God, most freely and moved by the goodness of His nature alone, approached the task of hewing out matter, even if in the process the very unsuitability of the matter stood in the way of Him being able to effect everything He wished. This assertion...

[...continued from previous page] does not conflict with the Omnipotence of God, but it does not make that primary will of God to adorn the world in the least bit necessary. From these points, it is clearly evident that I have not confused will and liberty in the slightest. But *Spinoza*, says *Mr. Gundling*, feels the same as *Plato*. I wish he had demonstrated this. *Spinoza, in Proposition 14*, says: *No substance can be granted or conceived besides God.* *Proposition 15: Whatever is, is in God, and nothing can be or be conceived without God.* *Proposition 16: From the necessity of the divine nature, infinite things in infinite ways (that is, all things which can fall under an infinite intellect) must follow.* *Proposition 17: God acts from the laws of his own nature alone, and is compelled by no one.* He demonstrates this Proposition thus: *We have just shown in Proposition 16 that infinite things follow absolutely from the sole necessity of the divine nature, or (which is the same thing) from the laws of that same nature alone; and we demonstrated in Proposition 15 that nothing can be or be conceived without God; but that all things <note>NB: "nota bene" or "note well"</note> are in God; wherefore nothing can exist outside of him by which he might be determined or compelled to act; and therefore God acts from the laws of his own nature alone, and is compelled by no one.* Which was to be demonstrated. Anyone can see that *Plato* and *Spinoza* harbor very different opinions: *Spinoza* acknowledges only one Substance; *Plato* acknowledges God and matter. *Spinoza* says all things follow necessarily from the nature of God, and thus the world itself; *Plato* introduces God as moved by goodness alone to fashion matter. However, I believe I have observed the cause that led *Mr. Gundling* to assert that I confused will with liberty. Specifically, he thought that in this part I followed the opinion of the *Famous and Most Excellent Philosophers, Leibniz and Wolff*, of which he himself thinks very poorly; in *Section 1* of his *Dissertation*, he says: *Spinoza, Plato, and Leibniz with their followers conspire in this part: none of whom thinks that "indifference" <note>In philosophy, "indifference" refers to the ability of the will to choose between two options without being predetermined by prior causes.</note> is included in the definition of liberty—namely, so that our mind might determine itself without a prior cause and <term>of its own power<note>original Greek: αὐτεξουσίως (autexousiōs)</note></term>.* But in this matter *Mr. Gundling* is mistaken. I employed the definition of liberty which the most rigid defenders of liberty maintain, so that I might not give my adversaries a cause to find fault without necessity. Furthermore, I do not wish to make that dispute my own. Yet I believe an injustice is done to these *Distinguished Men* when they are referred to the same class as *Spinoza*. *Mr. Gundling* could, however, clash in this area with the *Illustrious Wolff*, who knows best of all upon what foundations *Leibniz's* opinion on this argument was built.

perceived that all the actions of men are animated, and that they possess in themselves much virtue and much depravity; and because what has been made—soul and body—does not suffer destruction, yet is not eternal in the way the gods are (for if either of these were destroyed, all generation of living things would cease); furthermore, because he perceived that what is good in the soul is to help, and what is evil is to harm—having perceived all these things, I say, he [God] devised where each part might be located most effectively, best, and most easily, to provide victory for virtue and an impediment for vice in the universe, so that vice might not conquer.

If, therefore, we judge all these things by the laws of right reasoning, it is most evidently clear that Plato asserted: 
1. In God there was a **pattern** <term>paradeigma: a divine blueprint or ideal model</term> of the most beautiful things. 
2. He wished to build the world according to that **Exemplar**. 
3. God, being Most Wise, intended **ends** <note>purposes or goals</note> by looking both to the harmony of the whole universe and to the state of individual actions and men, insofar as individual things can contribute to the salvation of the whole. 

Hence he also compares God to a physician, who "works all things for the sake of the whole, striving toward what is best for the common good." <note>original Greek: "παντος ἕνεκα παντα ἐργαζεται προς τα κοινη ξυντεινων βελτιστα."</note> Should such a one not be said to intend ends? I should certainly think so. 

It is true that Plato asserts in this passage that man is a "tiny part" of the universe. *Spinoza* might say the same, but not in the same sense. **Plato** considers man as a substance entirely distinct from God, a substance created for certain ends, a substance for which God cares no less than for the universe. In the **System of Spinoza**, man is not distinct from God except by a certain "modification" (as the Scholastics say); he is a part of God just as necessary as God himself, and necessarily such as he is. Therefore, when two people say the same thing, they do not necessarily mean the same thing.

I say that God will be the cause, and it is never possible to be otherwise. For it could never become ensouled in any other way than through God, as we have declared. But because God is capable of this, all ease has come to Him: first, that every body and every mass has become a living thing; then, that it should be carried in this way, if he has thought it best. Now we speak a true word concerning all these individual things. It is one thing for the earth and the heaven, and all the stars and all the masses, not to proceed with accuracy year by year, and months and days, unless a soul were present with each or in each, and that all things produced should become good for all of you. # VINDICATION OF THE DISSERTATIONS

Let us consider, therefore, how it is possible for such a great mass to be carried around by any nature over such a long time. I assert, then, that God is the cause, and it cannot be otherwise. For a living being could not exist except through God, as we have declared. Since God is able to do this, it was easy for Him first to grant life to every body and magnitude, and then to lead them in the way He thought best. Finally, we wish this true opinion to be held concerning all these things: it is impossible for the earth, the heaven, all the stars, and the masses composed of them to be revolved through years, months, and days—and to do all good things for us—unless a soul were present to each or within them by such an exquisite reason. Indeed, it is fitting for a man, the lowlier he is, to trifle less with these things, but rather to strive to say something certain. If anyone says that the impulse of bodies, or their natures, or anything of this kind is the cause of this order and agitation, he will bring forward nothing clear. The later Platonists feel the same way. Plotinus, in the *Enneads* <note>The *Enneads* are the primary collection of writings by Plotinus, the 3rd-century founder of Neoplatonism.</note>, Book III, Chapter 2, Section 3, argues from the order of the universe and pronounces those people foolish who judge the whole by a part, and who say God did not arrange all things in order because they do not observe Him in this or that specific part. The same author, in *Ennead* IV, Book 4, Chapter 9, says:

> Jupiter <note>Plotinus uses "Zeus" to represent the World Soul or the ordering principle of the universe.</note>, adorning and governing and arranging all things, always possessing a royal soul and a royal mind, and a providence for how each thing should come to be, and an oversight over those things that are happening, and administering them in order, and having already wound through many and perfect cycles—how could he, in all these things, not have a memory of how many and of what kind the cycles have already been? And again, as he plans, connects, and thinks out how things should happen in the future, he would be the most mindful of all, just as he is the wisest Architect. 

<note>original Greek: "ὁ δὲ δὴ παντα κοσμῶν Ζεὺς... ὅσῳ καὶ Δημιουργὸς σοφώτατος."</note>

In Proposition XXXII <note>The author is quoting from Spinoza’s *Ethics*, Part 1.</note>, he says: *The will cannot be called a free cause, but only a necessary one.* From this, it follows by the first Corollary that *God does not act from freedom of will.* It follows 2nd: *Will and intellect relate to the nature of God just as motion and rest do; and absolutely as all natural things which (by Proposition 29) must be determined by God to exist and operate in a certain way.* Proposition XXXIII states: *Things could have been produced by God in no other way and in no other order than they were produced.* Proposition XXXIV: *The power of God is His very essence.* Proposition XXXV: *Whatever we conceive to be in the power of God, is necessarily so.* Proposition XXXVI: *Nothing exists from whose nature some effect does not follow.* 

He wishes to prove this last Proposition in this way: *Whatever exists,* he says, *expresses the nature or essence of God in a certain and determined way (by Prop. 25); that is (by Prop. 34), whatever exists expresses the power of God, which is the cause of all things, in a certain and determined way; and therefore (by Prop. 16) some effect must follow from it.* Thus it is proven. To these Propositions, he added an appendix in which he wishes to subvert various "prejudices" (as he calls them). Among those, on page 34, he mentions the common opinion of men who claim that *all natural things, like themselves, act for the sake of an end; indeed, that God Himself directs all things toward some certain end.* He then strives to subvert this opinion with certain arguments, and finally, on page 36, he speaks as follows: *To show now that nature has no end set before it, and that all final causes are nothing but human fictions, there is no need for many words.* 

"For I believe," he says, "that this is already sufficiently clear, both from the foundations and causes from which I showed this prejudice to have drawn its origin, and from Proposition 16 and the Corollary of Proposition 32, and furthermore from all those things by which I showed that all things proceed by a certain eternal necessity of nature and with the highest perfection." From these quoted words of Spinoza, it is clearer than the noon light that all "ends" (purposes) are banished by him, and that everything—in the mind of this Atheist <note>The author uses the term "Atheist" for Spinoza because Spinoza’s God is identical to Nature and lacks personal will or purpose, which conflicted with traditional religious views of the time.</note>—has arisen by necessity from the divine nature, and that he plainly disagrees with Plato. In my opinion, these things could suffice to prove that *Plato's God intended ends, which is not the case for Spinoza's.* But so that even the reluctant may feel the force of my arguments, I will add certain passages from Plato's *Timaeus* <note>The *Timaeus* is Plato's famous dialogue on the creation of the physical world.</note> which prove the same thing most clearly. "But if you remember, O Clinias—for you surely took notes—what was said then was indeed very true. And the greatest of those points was this: that the soul is older than every body. Do you remember? Or at least this much? For that which is better, more ancient, and more divine, is likely prior to that which is worse, newer, and more base; and in every way, that which rules is older than that which is ruled, and that which leads older than that which is led. Let us then accept this: that the soul is older than the body. If this is so, then that which is first in our origin would most likely have been present as the primary element. Let us then posit that the beginning of the beginning is more noble, and that we are most correctly approaching the greatest heights of wisdom regarding the generation of the Gods."

That is, from the version of Ficinus <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the influential Renaissance translator of Plato into Latin.</note>: *Remember, these things were said, O Clinias! Indeed, you received them then so that you ought to remember them, especially because they were established as most true. Of all things, this was held as greatest: that every soul is older than every body. Do you remember? Indeed, most certainly. For that which is better is also older, and that which is more divine is prior to the inferior and viler. And similarly, the Leader is prior by nature to the led, and the prince to the subject. Let us therefore admit that the soul is older than the body. If it is so, that which is first in generation likely preceded. Wherefore let us posit that the leadership and the beginning of the beginning are in a more decent state, and thus we most rightly enter into wisdom concerning the generation of the Gods.*

A most learned Frenchman, who a few years ago published a <term>History of Pagan Philosophy</term> <note>Likely referring to Isaac de Beausobre or another contemporary scholar publishing in the Hague.</note> at The Hague, after citing part of this passage of Plato, reasons thus on page 253:

"This can only be conceived by admitting a time when there were no bodies, unless by 'bodies' one understands 'arranged bodies': but as matter before its arrangement is no less a body than after God had formed it as it is, one can say with reason that if Plato did not think exactly, at least he expressed himself exactly when he said that God was before there were bodies. If this Philosopher had followed his principles, he would have believed that everything sensible had been drawn from nothingness."

<meta>catchword: Assen-</meta>

<header>ON THE ATHEISM OF PLATO.</header>

I agree with this most learned man. Meanwhile, since a candid man must never depart from the eternal laws of truth, I confess that the testimony cited proves nothing other than that God made bodies out of pre-existing matter; yet this itself suffices to prove that God was in no way restricted by the bonds of matter. The same can be proven from the origin of *motion*, which Plato ascribes entirely to God, especially in the *Timaeus*. These testimonies are too well known for me to bring them forward here. Let us hear, therefore, what *Dr. Gundlingius* <note>Nicolaus Hieronymus Gundling (1671–1729), a prominent legal scholar and historian who often criticized traditional views of ancient philosophy.</note> attempts against this argument. In *Section 54, page 257*, he rises up thus:

"Even if," he says, "we imagined that matter existed separately from God, or established that it was finally separated: Zimmermann would certainly find no protection. For the divine is again joined with matter: which will be the same as if it had always remained attached to matter." 

Nor will it protect him that he keeps saying the Platonic God *decorated all things*. For even Spinoza does not deny this. He acknowledges the beauty of the world, which is surely a most exquisite decoration. The question is, how does He decorate it? Whether as an immanent cause [inside the matter], or as an external efficient cause by His omnipotent virtue? The latter is clearly false, provided he persists in the correct opinion that the Platonic God did not create the world out of nothing. Therefore, that <term>ordering</term> <note>original: "διακόσμησις" (diakosmesis) — the act of arranging or beautifying the universe.</note> will flow from an internal and necessary principle that joined with matter—which in itself is non-being, that is, an accident, and by no means a substance. 

He [Gundlingius] proceeds to prove this last point from a passage of Porphyry's *Sentences*, 21, in which that Platonist speaks thus: *Matter is variable, infinite* (<term>boundless</term>) <note>original: "ἄπειρος" (apeiros)</note> *powerless, and therefore not a being, but* [(<term>not being</term>) <note>original: "ἐκ ὄν" (ek on)</note> *non-being. Nor is it non-being in the way that motion is, but a true non-being* (<term>true non-being</term>) <note>original: "ἀληθινὸν μὴ ὄν" (alethinon me on)</note>, *an image and phantom of bulk, because it is that which is first underlying bulk, powerless and a craving for existence* (<term>desire for subsistence</term>) <note>original: "ἔφεσις ὑποστάσεως" (ephesis hypostaseos)</note>. *Therefore, matter only then receives a constant and certain substance when form flows into it from divine virtue.* Whence the Platonists called it in itself <term>incorporeal</term> <note>original: "ἀσώματον" (asomaton)</note>, an observation by *E. Grabe on Irenaeus, page 28*.

Thus far Dr. Gundlingius. To these things I note the following:
1. It is the case that the Famous Gundlingius repeatedly supposes the very thing in question: namely, that matter was in God and emanated from Him. For nowhere has he brought forward a clear passage to prove this, as is obvious to anyone comparing the texts. It is likewise a mere and precarious supposition that God, after he approached the fabrication of matter, made one whole with matter. For we have proven that God and matter in the System of Plato are most diverse substances, and that God—freely, compelled by no necessity either internal or external—approached its decoration; which certainly implies no confusion [of their essences]. 
2. When I said that God *decorated* matter, by that very fact...

I have proved clearly enough, and indeed supported by the testimonies of the Ancients, that matter must be considered as a substance entirely distinct from God; I said God is like a craftsman who, of his own will, approaches the shaping of matter. And yet, in the opinion of all men, a craftsman is not one single substance with his material, even if he is occupied in perfecting and working upon it. No one who understands his system will believe that the same can be said of Spinoza’s God. For he openly admits that all things have arisen from the necessity of nature. Plato supposes a <term>paradigm</term> <note>original: "παράδειγμα" (paradeigma) — a model or pattern used by the Creator.</note> standing before God before the world was founded; he supposes the supreme Lord of all, moved by Goodness alone, approached the shaping of matter. Therefore, he openly rejects an immanent cause <note>An "immanent cause" is a philosophical term for a cause that remains within the effect, implying God and the world are the same. Plato's "external" cause separates the Creator from the creation.</note>.

3. It cannot be proved that matter, in Plato’s mind, is not a substance but an accident <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that can change without changing the essence of a thing; the author argues matter is a fundamental "substance," not just a property of God.</note>. In previous sections, we have already shown this opinion of <term>Dr. Gundling</term> <note>Nicolaus Hieronymus Gundling (1671–1729), a German jurist and scholar who often debated these points.</note> to be false based on clear passages. It is true that the Platonists sometimes called matter <term>non-being</term> <note>original: "οὐκ ὄν" (ouk on).</note>, but not in the sense that Dr. Gundling imagines. Namely, they called matter "non-being" when compared to intelligible things, because it was in constant flux and change, and because it would have no definite form without an external cause. That this was the Platonists' intention is taught by the very passage of <term>Porphyry</term> cited. For <term>Plotinus</term> appeals to him in the *Enneads*, Book III, Part VI, Section VII, page 310; for after he had brought forward these very words of Porphyry, he immediately adds: <note>original Greek: "καὶ ἑστηκὸς οὐκ ἐν φάσει... οὐ᾽ ἂν φεύγειν δυνάμενον."</note> that is: *Standing indeed, yet not in a state of rest; invisible in itself and escaping whoever wishes to see it; and when one does not look, it is then somehow present; but when one gazes more intently, it is not seen. Again, always appearing as opposites within itself: small and great, less and more, deficient and exceeding—a mere image, neither remaining nor able to escape.* The same author asserts in Section 10 of this book that matter, when quality is added, becomes <term>qualified matter</term> <note>original: "ποιαν ὕλην" (poian hylen) — matter that has taken on specific properties.</note>, that is, a certain and definite form which it previously lacked. Similarly, Plato says in the *Statesman*, page 174: <note>original Greek: "τὸ κατὰ τ᾽ αὐτὰ... οὐ ταύτης τῆς τάξεως."</note> that is: *To always be the same, in the same way, and to be identical, belongs only to the most divine of all things; but the nature of the body does not belong to this order.* Diogenes Laërtius asserts the same in Book 3, Sections 9 and 10, a passage we cited above. An even clearer one exists in the same Book 3, page 84: *He uses,* he says, *even contrary terms for the same thing. Thus, that which is subject to the*

<column-break/>

<page-num>863</page-num>
<header>ON THE ATHEISM OF PLATO.</header>

*senses, he calls both being and non-being: "being" because of its origin, but "non-being" because of its continuous change.* From which passages it is clear enough that matter was called <term>non-being</term> because it was subject to perpetual change and flux and was devoid of form. Hence Aquila translated that [Hebrew phrase] *tohu va-bohu* <note>The Hebrew phrase from Genesis 1:2 describing the world before creation.</note> as <term>emptiness and nothing</term> <note>original: "κένωμα καὶ οὐδέν" (kenoma kai ouden).</note>, and Theodotion as <term>empty and nothing</term>. But no one is ignorant of the fact that a raw and unformed mass is still a substance. It is certain that matter is sometimes called <term>incorporeal</term> <note>original: "ἀσώματον" (asomaton)</note> by the Platonists, but in no other sense than that it lacks a certain definite form. Hence they attribute the term <term>body</term> <note>original: "σώματος" (somatos)</note> to things reduced into a certain definite form, but the term <term>matter</term> <note>original: "ὕλης" (hyles)</note> to unformed material. Therefore, "incorporeal matter" is the same as "formless matter." (*) Hence Plotinus, page 310, says: <note>original Greek: "ἔστι μὲν οὖν... ἕτερα τῶν σωμάτων."</note> that is: *It is therefore incorporeal, since the body is subsequent and composite, and matter itself, along with something else, completes the body. For thus it obtained the same name according to the incorporeal genus, because both—namely Being and matter—are different from bodies.* If, therefore, matter is a substance even before God arranged it into order, and was freely adorned by God, it follows that God is joined to matter by no necessary bond. (**)

***

(*) The distinguished <term>Grabe</term> <note>Johann Ernst Grabe (1666–1711), a theologian and scholar of the early church.</note> cites a passage from <term>Irenaeus</term> entirely in support of our view, from which we have a new example of how shamelessly Gundling appeals to the testimony of others. For Grabe says, among other things on page 38 in the notes of Massuet's edition: *Nor will anyone doubt the said reading who looks at the source from which the Valentinians derived this hypothesis of theirs—I mean the doctrine of Plato, whom Origen, in the "Philosophumena" (not yet published at the time), says established three principles: God, matter, and the Idea; and regarding matter, according to his mind, he writes thus among other things:* <note>original Greek: "ἦν δὲ ὕλην... γενέσθαι σῶμα."</note> *that is, that matter was potentially a body, but not yet actually so; for existing as formless and without quality, once it took on shapes and qualities, it became a body.* Similarly, Diogenes Laërtius, Book 3, page 86, says of Plato's opinion: <note>original Greek: "εἶναι δὲ τὴν ὕλην... τὰ συγκρίματα."</note> *that matter was formless and infinite, but from it composite bodies were made.*

(**) If the distinguished Gundling had wanted to include the words that immediately follow the passage cited from Porphyry, he would have clearly seen in what sense Porphyry said matter was "non-being." For in this very Sentence XXI, he speaks thus: *small and great, less and more, deficient and exceeding, always becoming and never remaining.*
