### XVI. 

The fourth argument, by which I proved that Plato did not bind God with the chains of matter, is drawn from this: that he said our mind is most free, capable of punishment and reward, and that he further removed God as far as possible from the blame of any evil. I have proved this thesis of mine once again using passages from Plato, <term>Maximus of Tyre</term> <note>A Middle Platonist philosopher and rhetorician from the 2nd century AD.</note>, <term>Justin Martyr</term>, and <term>Eusebius</term>. Furthermore, I have shown that in <term>Spinoza's system</term> <note>The philosophy of Baruch Spinoza, often accused in the 18th century of being a form of atheism because it identified God with Nature and denied human free will.</note>, all freedom is exiled. What does Dr. <term>Gundling</term> <note>Nicolaus Hieronymus Gundling (1671–1729), a prominent German jurist and philosopher who was the author's intellectual opponent here.</note> say to this? In Section 50, he raises many objections against this argument, which we shall weigh in order. He claims that Plato does indeed ascribe freedom to the mind. He continues thus: *Spinoza deprives God of freedom. This latter point does not entirely agree with the truth. Spinoza denies absolute freedom to the mind; he says it is determined by causes, so that when several causes are present, it prepares itself for this or that.* It is a wonder that the Distinguished Man denies what is clearer than the midday sun. It is so certain that Spinoza strips all freedom from the mind that no one until Gundling has called it into doubt. I will not say now that Spinoza asserts that only one single substance is given, from which all things necessarily emanate; I will merely place the very words of this Atheist here, which are so clear that they cannot be twisted into another meaning without the most manifest distortion. In his *Ethics*, part 2, Proposition 48, he says: *In the mind there is no absolute, or free, will; but the mind is determined to will this or that by a cause, which is also determined by another, and this again by another, and so on to infinity.* In the <term>Scholium</term> <note>An explanatory note or commentary added to a text.</note> following the Demonstration, he speaks thus: *In this same way it is demonstrated that in the mind there is no absolute faculty of understanding, desiring, loving, etc. From which it follows that these and similar faculties are either entirely fictitious, or are nothing but metaphysical Beings or universals, which we are accustomed to form from particulars. So much so that the intellect and the will are related to this or that idea, or to this or that voli-*

> <note>original: "ὃ ἂν φεύγειν δυνάμενον... μικρόν ἐστι."</note> That which is able to flee is a deficiency of the whole. Therefore, whatever it promises, it lies. Even if it is imagined to be great, it is small. *That is: The small and the great, likewise the less and the more; the deficient and the exceeding; that which always exists, yet never remains, and yet cannot flee or slip away: the lack of all being. Therefore, whatever it promises, it lies, and if it seems to be great, it is small.*

<term>Porphyry</term> <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus.</note> opens his mind even more clearly in Section 33, speaking thus from the version by <term>Holstenius</term> <note>Lucas Holstenius (1596–1661), a German humanist and geographer who translated Porphyry.</note>: *These things are truly affirmed about the sensible and the material: that it is entirely extended or spread out, that it is changeable, that it subsists in alteration, that it is composite, that it exists through itself, that it is seen in place and bodily mass, and other things similar to these. But of True Being, which subsists through itself, these things are predicated: that it is always situated in itself, staying in the same way and according to the same thing, in its very substance, consisting in identity, being immutable according to substance, not composite, nor dissolvable, nor in a place, nor distended in mass.* Thus Porphyry speaks plainly according to my own view. Hence the learned Jesuit <term>Mourgues</term> <note>Michel Mourgues (1643–1713), a French Jesuit and mathematician.</note>, in his second Letter, not only concludes from this that the God of Plato's mind has nothing in common with matter, but also that from this very definition of matter by the Platonists, it can be proved that some most wise cause arranged matter into order.

The author argues Plato's "fate" isn't the same as Spinoza's "necessity."</note> according to Plato's opinion, the distinguished Gundling would still gain nothing unless he first proved that Plato understood "fate" to mean a certain inevitable and necessary connection of all things, by which all <term>contingency</term> <note>The possibility that things could happen otherwise; the opposite of necessity.</note> is subverted. that, by the force of some Decree, minds descend into bodies according to the mind of **Plato**; we also maintain that minds, whether created together with the world or newly brought into the light, are sent into our tiny bodies by the force of a Divine Decree; but from this it is by no means effected that minds therefore lose their freedom. mortal? And the founder of the Old Academy <note>Plato</note> will find himself in a bind <note>original: "aqua hærebit," literally "the water will stick," a Latin idiom for being stuck or at a loss</note>, just like Spinoza, when he is pressed with questions. Add this: why then are souls punished, if they are themselves a portion of the Gods and of the lower mind? I despair of ever receiving an answer that would satisfy me. I respond: 1. Concerning the origin of the human mind according to the opinion of Plato, that is not the question here. Neither Timaeus Locrus nor Plato clearly assert that minds are "clipped off" from the divine nature of the first principle, but rather that they are sent into bodies through the World Soul <note>original: "animam mundi"</note>. We shall investigate this more accurately below. But even if the mind arose from God or the World Soul according to Plato's thought, the question then is how it could abuse that freedom to perpetrate evil. Thus, the freedom of the mind is already presupposed, which is the proper subject of the question. For when Plato and his followers speak of the origin of moral evil, they flee for refuge to the free withdrawal of the mind from the good and the right; likewise, they say the body, the deceptions of the senses, and the heat of the passions are the cause of the depraved mind. Thus, the divine element does not tame the mortal because that divine mind is free, and can incline toward the good no less than toward evil; finally, minds are punished when they have abused their freedom. But you say, "In that case, God would be punishing himself." Yet it must first be proved that minds originating from God are, in Plato’s opinion, parts of a divisible Divine Essence consisting of parts. But we shall deal with this matter more fully below. We say only this: that Plotinus, in *Ennead IV*, part 3, chapter 1 and following, denies that our soul is a part of the World Soul. Hence in Section VII, page 376, he says:

> *That which was said in the "Philebus," however, which induces the suspicion that perhaps all souls are parts of the World Soul, does not actually mean what someone might think, but rather what was most useful for him at that time—namely, that the world is animate. For striving to prove this, he says it is absurd to say the heavens are inanimate when we, who have a body that is a part of the world’s body, have a soul. For in what way would the part have a soul if the whole were inanimate?*

Indeed, Plato's opinion is most clear in the *Timaeus*: where, once the World Soul has been made, others are subsequently born in the same mixing bowl; in which they too are mixed and made conformable to it, yet he assigns their difference through second and third degrees. As for what is said in the *Phaedrus*, that *every soul takes care of all that is inanimate: what is so strange about that? For what else governs, orders, and creates the nature of the body, if not the soul?* Thus far Plotinus. Therefore, just as we trace moral evil back to the notion of a substance which is free by its own nature, Plato and his followers argued similarly. Indeed, the origin of human minds is plainly obscure in almost every system.

Concerning the opinion of the Stoics on this point, I do not wish to deal with it here; I have examined this material at length in the *Dissertation on the Fate of the Stoics* inserted in the first volume of the *Bremen Museum*. However, since some have not correctly grasped my meaning and have misinterpreted it, I will state here what my goal was. Specifically, I by no means wished to prove that the Stoics were immune from all errors in this area. Nor did I wish to show by this example how the goodness and justice of divine Providence can be proven and defended according to my own opinion. Rather, I wished only to show this: that the common and accepted opinion of learned men—asserting that all things are bound by an inevitable chain of necessity according to the Stoics—is not built upon certain and unshakable reasons. Furthermore, from the decrees and principles of the Stoics themselves, which are placed somewhat inaccurately and in different ways, two contrary systems can be constructed: in one, 그 iron necessity would be exiled; in the other, it would not be far removed from the opinion of Spinoza on this matter. And I wished to show a specimen of the former system in the said Dissertation. For the rest, I have shrunk from the opinion of those who introduce an irrevocable necessity to all things and take away all freedom from God and our mind throughout my whole life, and I shrink from it still. Meanwhile, I have proved by the clearest testimonies that Plato subjected God to no necessity; since Gundling brings nothing against these, I do not wish to repeat them. Meanwhile, he contends that Plato said God is not the author of sin out of fear, but if we inspect the connection of the system, this most harsh consequence follows. I would wish that the Illustrious Gundling demonstrate this with clear arguments. I confess that I am still unable to see how this error follows from the principles of Platonic philosophy. Evil is either Moral or Physical. Plato's God is not the author of physical evil, but rather Matter is. For since he recognized the eternal existence of matter, and exerted his power upon it <term>κατα δυναμιν</term> <note>original Greek: "kata dynamin," meaning "according to [its] capacity" or "as far as possible"</note> only as far as that matter would allow, it follows necessarily that matter, not God, must be called the cause of physical evil, which obstructed him from being able to effect what he wished. Nor did Plato speak one way in his physical dialogues and another when he dealt with the laws. Moral evil, however, he everywhere traces back to the depraved nature of the human mind and its inclination toward vice. Spinoza’s system, however, is so constructed that whichever way you turn, you find no freedom anywhere.

XVIII. The fifth argument brought forth in Section 10 of my *Dissertation*, to prove that *Plato’s God is not joined with matter*, I have taken from Plato’s opinion on the destruction of the world. For he asserted that the world would endure not by the necessity of its own nature, but by the will of God. To prove this, I brought forward very clear passages from Plato, Plutarch, and Maximus Tyrius <note>Maximus of Tyre was a 2nd-century philosopher who lectured on Plato</note>, and I defended them in Section XIX against the objections of Dr. Gundling. He wishes to weaken my reasoning in Section CCI. He believes—*these are Gundling's words*—that just as Plato’s world was founded by a most free choice, it will likewise be dissolved by that same freedom, and that his "Wise Man" <note>Plato</note> established this in the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s famous dialogue on the origin of the universe</note> in the clearest words. "I," says Gundling, "if 'freely' means 'with no one forcing him,' grant what is said with both hands; for in this way *Spinoza* also acknowledges the world was produced 'freely.' But if, on the other hand, 'deliberation' is attributed to Plato’s Divinity, followed by an 'arbitrary choice,' I reject it." I respond: Dr. Gundling always repeats the same points, yet he ignores the clear passages of the Ancients, as if the question were a theme to be solved by reasoning alone. Plato’s God, as I have already proven above, freely made the series of most beautiful things which we call the world—I say, compelled by no necessity, whether internal or external—so freely that he could have neglected that immense and unformed mass <note>original: "indigestam molem," a reference to the raw state of matter before creation</note> through all eternity. However, these things cannot even be conceived without the prior deliberation of a most noble mind. There was present to God a certain "intelligible world" <note>The world of Ideas or Forms</note>; God contemplates this world. He saw that matter was a raw and unformed mass; he judged that order was superior to confusion; finally, moved by goodness, he applied his mind to reducing this matter into order. These things are found in almost as many words in the *Timaeus*. Now, where there is a constant contemplation of ideas and a free inclination of the will to execute a work, there, by the consensus of all men, deliberation has a place. But there was no necessity to found the world, neither in respect to God nor in respect to eternal matter; therefore, according to Plato's mind, we cannot show a cause for the founding of this world other than the free will of God. Let the passages cited in the *Dissertation* be inspected now, and I am most persuaded that they prove this opinion of mine. *That goodness*—so Dr. Gundling continues—*which the defender especially urges, is a necessary attribute of God, and if it impelled him, it impelled him necessarily; it impelled him from eternity, since there is never a time when goodness is not in him, nor can a moment be conceived in which he could fall away from goodness or not exercise it. From which it should rather be concluded that the Platonic world was founded necessarily and from eternity, because it cannot happen that God should be anything but the best, most perfect, harmful to no one, envious of none, and to all*

advantageous. The *illustrious Gundling* plays with the word *Goodness*: this word among philosophers is sometimes taken for an essential divine attribute, but sometimes (and most often) for a relative one. The name is borrowed from humans who are carried by an ardent zeal to serve the advantages of others. And it denotes the same thing as *Benignity* or *Beneficence*. But if God had willed to create no world and no men, but to remain in the supreme happiness which he enjoys, he could not be called "good" in the common sense, for there would have been no object outside of God to whom he could do good. Secondly, this word is taken for the *All-sufficiency* of God, through which he is the source of all perfection. And in this sense, without doubt, the goodness of God is an essential attribute. In whichever sense the *illustrious man* takes this word, it nevertheless does nothing for the defense or protection of his opinion. *Plato* supposed the eternity of matter; he contemplated it as a raw and unformed mass; he judged that order was superior to confusion; the most beautiful pattern <note>The "exemplar" or world of Ideas</note> was present, as was the intention of forming a most beautiful world. Yet even with all these things in place, there was no absolute necessity to demonstrate his goodness from all eternity. The Will of God is an essential attribute of God, and thus necessarily belongs to the nature of God; but it is not necessary that he execute the decrees of his will from eternity. For he is endowed with freedom and wisdom to bring all things to pass in his own time. According to our own belief, God created the world in time, yet he was good from eternity, and he also willed the best from eternity. If he were necessarily bound to do from eternity everything he considered good, then the world and all creatures would have to exist necessarily as well. But even suppose the world was founded from eternity according to *Plato's* mind, this would still take nothing away from the weight of our argument. The question is: if the world were to be destroyed, would it be destroyed by the will of the best God? Or if it is to endure, is it preserved because God wills it? *If you contend that either of these will happen by the will of God, it is clear that the world will not necessarily either perish or endure, but does so by God's willing it.* And yet *Plato* asserts that the world *will endure because God wills it*; its duration, therefore, is not to be sought in an absolute eternity of the world, but in the perpetual, most constant, and best will of Him who made the world, whether in time or from eternity. *Plato*, the Antagonist <note>Gundling</note> continues, in order to weave a history of natural things, expresses everything "in a human manner" <note>original: "ἀνθρωποπαθῶς"</note>, and by a circuitous route says what *Spinoza* explains more openly, substituting "perfection" for "goodness," from which everything would have necessarily flowed. But this is a mere supposition, which I do not wish to refute with many words; for it is apparent that the author, without necessity, is "slaving for his own hypothesis" <note>original: "τῇ ὑποθέσει δουλεύειν"</note>. I will prove by reason that, according to the mind of Christians, the world is absolutely eternal and necessary. For God had the ideas of all things, had the notion of the best world, and by the goodness of his nature, he desires and wills the best; Moses describes everything in a human-like way <note>original: "ἀνθρωποπαθῶς" (anthropopathos) — a term meaning "attributing human passions or feelings to God" to help humans understand divine actions.</note>. Therefore, the world was founded from eternity according to the opinion of Christians; indeed, it is just as necessary as God's goodness is his necessary attribute. But who does not see the weakness of this reasoning? *Mr. Gundling* refers me to *Section 149 of his dissertation.* Let us obey him. "Moreover," he says there, "the same God of Spinoza is the cause of all things, and he works from the absolute freedom of his will, forced by no one, but determined by himself alone: which is the definition of freedom found in Spinoza; upon which Proposition 16 then rests, where all things are said to follow from the necessity of the divine nature." But that man reads Spinoza with superficial attention and hardly understands him. For in *Proposition 17*, the Jew <note>Referring to Spinoza, who was of Jewish-Portuguese descent.</note> indicates that *to follow from the necessity of the divine nature* means the same as *from the perfection of the divine nature.* From which it is clear that Spinoza asserts that *God acted freely and was not forced, being moved only by his own perfection, and while he acted, he decreed.* Plato sings the same thing in the *Timaeus:* <note>Plato’s dialogue concerning the nature of the physical world and human beings.</note> "God acted," he says, "because he is good: nothing moves him from the outside; but perfection alone made him act, and at the same time decree." *But his decrees are immutable; from this flows Spinoza's Proposition 33: God could not have created the world otherwise than he decreed.* Spinoza’s causal expression is: *because he decreed to create it thus, he could not create it otherwise, lest God become changeable, or multiple Gods arise, willing different things.* Now let *Zimmermann* <note>Probably Johann Jakob Zimmermann, a theologian and contemporary.</note> see whether Plato believed that a different world could have been made by his God than the one he willed? So far *Gundling*. I would have believed that the *Illustrious Polyhistor* <note>original: "Polyhistori" — a title for a person of great and varied learning, here referring to Gundling.</note> either had a different copy of *Spinoza’s Ethics* than the common one at hand while writing this; or, carried away by an excessive desire to win the argument, wished to deceive readers who rarely look at the evidence to which he appeals. Inspection alone is needed to refute the falsehood of these statements. I. He says *Spinoza's God operates from absolute freedom of will, and that this assertion is the basis for Proposition 16.* But this is openly false. Among the definitions which he prefixed to his *Ethics*, the seventh is this: *That thing will be called free which exists from the necessity of its nature alone, and is determined to act by itself alone.* However, he does not mention this freedom by so much as a word until the Corollary to Proposition 17. But those things which precede Proposition 16 sound far different than *Mr. Gundling* would like. *Proposition 14* sounds thus: *Besides God, no substance can be given, nor conceived.* *Proposition 15:* *Whatever is, is in God, and nothing can be or be conceived without God.* 16. *From the necessity of the divine nature, infinite things in infinite ways (that is, all things that*

From those Propositions, the demonstration of *Proposition 17* is established, which is such: *God acts from the laws of his nature alone and forced by no one.* Demonstration: *We have just shown in Proposition 16 that infinite things follow absolutely from the necessity of the divine nature alone, or (which is the same thing) from the laws of the same nature alone; and in Proposition 15 we demonstrated that nothing can be or be conceived without God, but all things are in God; wherefore nothing can be outside him by which he might be determined or forced to act, and thus God acts from the laws of his nature alone and forced by no one.* Q.E.D. <note>original: "Q. E. D." (Quod Erat Demonstrandum) — "Which was to be demonstrated," a standard conclusion for a proof.</note> Corollary 1. Hence it follows 1. *that no cause is given, whether external or internal, which might incite God to act, besides the perfection of his own nature.* Corollary 2. It follows 2. *that God alone is a free cause. For God alone exists from the necessity of his nature alone, and acts from the necessity of his nature alone, and thus he alone is a free cause.* Who does not see that necessity of nature, laws of nature, and perfection of nature denote the same thing, and thus all things are very clearly traced back to the necessity of nature, which subverts all liberty? But where did Plato ever say such things? Surely the goodness of the will and the necessity of nature are not the same. Nothing from the outside stimulates Spinoza's God to act, because he himself is all things; the only substance. Outside Plato's God was eternal matter. Plato's God acted led by goodness: Spinoza's God by *perfection of nature*, that is, as he himself explains, by *necessity of nature*. Therefore, no free decrees have a place in God according to Spinoza's mind. It is therefore once again most false that Spinoza's Proposition 33 is built upon divine decrees. Proposition 32 sounds thus: *The will cannot be called a free cause, but only a necessary one.* Corollary I. *Hence it follows that God does not work from freedom of will.* Corollary II. *It follows secondly that the will and the intellect relate to God's nature just as motion and rest do; and absolutely as all natural things, which must be determined by God to exist and operate in a certain way.* Proposition 33, however, sounds thus: *Things could have been produced by God in no other way, and in no other order, than they have been produced.* But who is there who would not find a lack of honesty in *Mr. Gundling* when he says that Proposition 33 sounds thus: *God could not create the world otherwise than he decreed?* If this method of quoting is valid, I will undertake to prove anything. I will say nothing about the application of those Propositions. For I have shown more than enough that Plato, in this part, departs very far from Spinoza. For what he urges in *Section 101* clearly shows that it is impossible to show by legitimate laws of reasoning that the world, according to Plato's mind, will necessarily remain by the force of its own nature. *The dissolution,* he says, *of the world is neither going to happen, nor can it happen.*

Why then? For he says that this work of Plato is, in his opinion, the most beautiful thing, than which nothing more perfect could be imagined. Moreover, **The Good** <note>original: "τἀγαθὸν" (tagathon) — the supreme principle in Plato’s philosophy.</note> will certainly not destroy the most perfect thing, because it is that very perfection itself; and thus it will necessarily endure and retain its existence. From this it is clear that *Mr. Zimmermann* is being too troublesome and too literal while he stubbornly insists on that phrase **if I so will** <note>original: "ἐμοῦ θέλοντος" (emou thelontos) — a reference to the Timaeus 41b, where the Creator addresses the lesser gods.</note>. For the Platonic Divinity cannot will that what is most excellent be destroyed. Even if I were to grant all these points to *Mr. Gundling*, it still does nothing to destroy my own position. Suppose the world will remain and, according to Plato's mind, will never be destroyed; does it therefore follow that this will happen by necessity and without the will of God? Plato says openly that the world will remain **by God’s will** <note>original: "Θεῷ θέλοντος" (Theō thelontos)</note>; God is openly called the **Father and Creator** <note>original: "Πατὴρ καὶ Δημιουργὸς" (Patēr kai Dēmiourgos)</note> of all things; all those works are openly said to be **indissoluble if He so wills** <note>original: "ἄλυτα αὐτῷ θέλοντος" (alyta autō thelontos)</note>; the will of God is called that most excellent bond which would bind the world together. **Thus this one world stands by the proportion of a certain blessed and clearly divine bond** <note>original: "εἷς μὲν ὢν ὧδε ὁ κόσμος δαιμονίῳ δεσμῷ τὸ ἀνάλογον ἔσιν."</note>, as *Timaeus Locrus* says in *On the Soul of the World*, p. 555. Therefore, I do not cling to the literal letter, but I follow the sense of Plato. I follow those most excellent men *Timaeus Locrus, Laërtius, Plutarch, Maximus of Tyre*, and all who have explained the doctrines of *Plato*. The entire face of Platonic philosophy commands me to explain it thus: In the system of *Spinoza*, no such thing has a place. The **All** <note>original: "τὸ πᾶν" (to pan)</note>, which is Spinoza’s God, arose as if by a certain inevitable necessity, and so all things will remain. In this system, there is no **Rector of the World** who is widely distinct from the visible universe of things, by whose favor it might endure. Christians, *Mr. Gundling* continues, take a different approach; they are persuaded that a new and better world will be established by God, which Plato did not believe, marvelously fixing his mind and eyes upon his most beautiful "living animal" <note>A Platonic term for the cosmos as a living, rational being.</note>. But what follows from that? Just because Plato knew nothing of a new heaven and earth, did he assert that the world would endure by the power of its own nature? I should not think so. Just as that most beautiful series of things will exist in the future by the will of God according to the mind of Christians, so likewise the world of Plato, freely established by God, will endure by the will of God. This fact makes it so (as *Mr. Gundling* speaks again) that the world is established by at least a *hypothetical necessity* and will never perish. But if it were established by absolute necessity, it would also endure by absolute necessity. This is a strange reasoning by a most ingenious man. In the preceding pages, he wanted to prove that the world existed necessarily, that matter was thrust forth from the bosom of God, and that *Plato* felt the same as *Spinoza*. But now he maintains that the world will be indissoluble according to the mind of *Plato* by hypothetical necessity 

<meta>catchword: maintains</meta>

<column-break/>

<page-num>875</page-num>
<header>ON THE ATHEISM OF PLATO.</header>

maintains. But this very assertion fights diametrically against the opinion of *Spinoza*: for he professes the absolute necessity of the world. Therefore, if hypothetical necessity has a place, it follows as clearly as possible that the world has its origin from God; it follows that the world is not absolutely necessary; it follows that the world does not constitute a single substance with God, and thus *Mr. Gundling's* entire system is false and fabricated. For everyone knows that hypothetical necessity depends on the will of God. The things he adds about the "soul of the world" do nothing at all to the point. For he asks what the soul of the world—adapted and destined for this universe—would do if God willed to destroy the world. I am not worried about this; let our descendants take care of such things if they wish. It is enough that the world, by God so willing, is to endure according to the opinion of *Plato*. Where the soul of the world and the minds would migrate, and what dwellings they would have once the world was destroyed, would have to be asked of *Plato* himself.

XIX. Finally, the last argument by which I have proved that *Spinoza* differs from *Plato* is sought from the provident and most wise care with which God, according to Plato's mind, looks out for this universe. To confirm this assertion, I have brought forward passages from *Plato, Apuleius, and Maximus of Tyre*. In Section VIII, my very famous opponent differs from me; at the same time, I brought forward passages from the Ancients asserting that *Plato* attributed something to the necessity of matter and something to our freedom. Yet at the same time, he subjected everything to the command of one and the same most wise and powerful Rector. I do not wish to bring those passages forward again or repeat what has been said. Especially since *Mr. Gundling*, having neglected clear passages which should always be cited, reasons from mere suppositions. He wants to prove that everything happens by Fate according to the opinion of *Plato*, and yet in the meantime, he does not cite the passages of the Ancients concerning fate from Plato's mind. By **Providence** (I use the words of *Apuleius in On the Doctrines of Plato, p. 374*), *Plato* understands a divine judgment that preserves the prosperity of that for which he undertook such a duty. **Fate is a divine law through which the inevitable thoughts and undertakings of God are fulfilled.** Whence, if anything is managed by *Providence*, it is also done by *Fate*, and what is determined by *Fate* must be seen as undertaken by *Providence*. By "necessity," they understood, according to *Plutarch's* definition: **either matter, or the relationship toward matter in the act of creation** <note>original: "εἴτε μεν τὴν ὕλην, εἴτε δὲ τὴν ἐν τῇ ποιήσει πρὸς τὴν ὕλην σχέσιν." — Placita Philosophorum, Book I, ch. 26.</note>. Therefore, *Plato* acknowledges: 1. A most wise Mind distinct from the world. 2. That He acts according to **Logos** <note>original: "λογον" (logon) — Reason or Plan.</note>, or reasons and laws. 3. That the progress of things is rooted in the provident care of God. 4. That matter itself obeys the nod of divine Providence. These things certainly altogether remove the inevitable and blind connection of all things. Whence

It is easily apparent what should be judged regarding the definition provided by *Gundling* on page 241, Section 46. He says: *Fate is the decree of the divine mind, to which all things return as if to a remote cause, even if some things are done immediately by men and are believed to be done freely, or even by chance.* This is based on mere supposition, supported by no testimonies; he wishes to imply that all things follow from God, and that "freedom" is only asserted by Plato for the sake of appearances <note>original: "dicis causa" — a legal term meaning "for form's sake" or "pro forma."</note>. But this assertion fights both against the testimonies of the Ancients and against the harmony of the Platonic System. I cited the testimonies of the Ancients on page 862, in which they state most clearly that *Plato* did not attribute everything to fate, but granted much to freedom. All the Platonists repeat this same point. Thus *Plotinus* <note>A major Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 204–270 AD) who expanded on Plato's teachings.</note> on pages 274, 145, 141, 735, and 734. Hence, on page 231, he rejects the "fate" of the Astrologers because it is hostile to freedom. This also conflicts with the entire nature of Platonic Philosophy. For everything concerning the care of divine Providence in *Plato’s* mind can be referred either to bodies or to minds. *Minds*, according to Plato, cannot be necessarily impelled toward doing evil, but by their own intrinsic nature, they have the power of acting according to the variety of objects and desires. Over *bodies*, God does not have as much command as He might wish, according to *Plato’s* view <note>In Plato's Timaeus, the Creator (Demiurge) works with "necessity" or "pre-existing matter" which is sometimes resistant to perfect order.</note>. Therefore, no absolute necessity takes place here. Nevertheless, he appeals to *Cicero's Academica, Book I, Section VII*, speaking of the World Soul according to the mind of the old Academy in this way: *Moreover, all things that are in the world are parts of the world, and are held together by a sensing nature, in which perfect reason dwells, which is itself eternal. For nothing is stronger than that which might cause it to perish; they say this force is the soul of the world, and that this same thing is perfect mind and wisdom: which they call God, and a kind of prudence, as it were, of all things subject to it, looking after celestial things most of all, and then on earth those things which pertain to men: which they sometimes call necessity: because nothing can happen otherwise than has been established by it, within a sort of fatal and immutable continuation of eternal order: yet sometimes they call it fortune, because it produces many things that are unforeseen and unexpected to us on account of the obscurity and our ignorance of the causes.* Thus says *Cicero*. But what, finally, follows from this passage of *Cicero*? Hear *Mr. Gundling*: from this, he says on page 242, *it follows that that lower mind, which is in the world and its parts, provides for all things, and has other ministers serving it: demons and intelligences, even below the moon.* But if I were to admit this consequence, what will the *Illustrious Man* gain? Does it follow from this that in *Plato's* system everything is subject to brute necessity? Does all freedom go into exile? Does it follow that because the world soul is subject to the Ruler of all things and executes His decrees, the provi-

(*) By what right the illustrious Gundling appeals to Iamblichus will be clear from the following observations: 1. This most learned man contends that Thomas Gale <note>An English scholar who published a famous edition of Iamblichus in 1678.</note> observed, in that controversial passage of Plato, traces of the "emanation" of matter within God <note>The idea that matter is not created from nothing, but is a part of God's own being flowing outward.</note>. The words of Iamblichus to which Gundling refers are found in Section 5, Chapter 23, page 138 of Gale’s edition. They sound like this: *In the supreme causes of the universe, there is such an exuberance of power that it surpasses all others, specifically because it is present to all things equally and without hindrance. Therefore, by this reasoning, those things that are first of all shine down even to the last things, and immaterial principles are present to material things in an immaterial way. Let no one wonder, then, if we say that there is also a certain "pure and divine matter." For since this matter was made by the Father and Creator of all, it must be considered to have received a certain perfection of its own, suitable for receiving the gods. Furthermore, nothing prevents the higher things from diffusing their light to the lower things.* 

Now let us hear Master Gale’s commentary on this passage at the words "from the Father of all": *He touches upon a most debated question among the Platonists. If matter is unbegotten <note>i.e., eternal and not created.</note>, there will be two first principles; if it is begotten by God, how can it be foul and evil? Furthermore, what Plato’s opinion on matter was is certainly not clear enough in the "Timaeus"; for he seems to oppose matter to the Craftsman <note>term: Demiurgus (the divine worker/creator in Plato’s philosophy)</note> and distinguish it from him. But in the "Philebus," he says expressly that God "showed" <note>original: δειξαι (deixai)</note> the limit of beings and also the infinite. It is established that "matter" is understood by the word "infinite" <note>original: ἀπειριαν (apeirian)</note>. But note well: that God, for Plato, is not the Craftsman, but of a higher order.* Thus far Gale, who at the same time adds that Damascius and Julian agree with Iamblichus. Meanwhile, he advises reading Simplicius and Porphyry’s 21st Sentence. But who does not see that Gale thinks Iamblichus is departing from Plato's own opinion? 

2. Anyone hearing Gundling explain the passage in the *Philebus* would think that Iamblichus had explained that passage professionally, and had interpreted Plato's word "to show" <note>original: το δειξαι</note> through the word "to produce" <note>original: το παραγαγειν</note>. But nothing is further from the truth if we look at the text itself. For that passage in which the word "to produce" is used by Iamblichus (Section 8, Chapter 3, page 159) sounds like this: *Regarding matter, God also produced a material divinity from essentiality; the Craftsman God, receiving this as vital matter, fabricated the simple and impassible spheres from it, and organized the last part of it into generated and corruptible bodies.* From this it is clear that Master Gale does not translate the word "produced" <note>original: παρηγαγεν (parēgagen)</note> as "ejected from himself" or "caused to emanate," but simply as "produced and transferred." <meta>This page continues the author's philological defense of Plato's theology against the accusations of Nicolaus Hieronymus Gundling. The author is currently examining whether the Greek verb used by Plato implies a creation out of nothing or merely a "showing forth" of pre-existing matter.</meta>

...which is "to demonstrate" and "to effect," means to produce a thing out of nothing. Thus far the most learned Jesuit. — No one fails to see that, in this place, the question is rather about the genuine interpretation of the word *bara* <note>Hebrew: ברא; the primary biblical verb for "to create."</note>, than about the inherent nature and meaning of the word *anadeixai* <note>Greek: ἀναδειξαι; meaning "to show forth" or "proclaim."</note>.

XXI. Let us see, then, what that word *deixai* <note>Greek: δείξαι; to show or point out.</note> means. Without doubt, we must first attend to its primary meaning before we turn to a figurative one. The primary meaning of this word is *to show, whether the discourse concerns a physical object or a truth perceived by the mind*. It is not necessary to demonstrate this with many examples. *It signifies to declare with many words*. Thus Hesiod, in *Works and Days*, verse 502:

->Point it out <note>original: δειγνυε (deignyue)</note> to the servants, while it is still midsummer:<-
->It will not always be summer, build huts.<-

->i. e. Say (declare) to the servants, while it is still midsummer;<-
->It will not always be summer, build huts.<-

The scholar Graevius, in *Readings on Hesiod*, page 63, taught that the word *ostendere* <note>Latin: to show or hold out.</note> has the same meaning among the Latins. Thus Cicero in *Letters to Friends*, Book V, letter 12: *Since you have often "shown" me that you will record the plans and events of our times with the greatest accuracy—that is, you have said it, you have declared it*. So too Herodian, Book 3, chapter 13: *He "showed" <note>original: ἐδεικνυε (edeiknye)</note> the treasuries and temples to be full of wealth—meaning he declared in words that the treasuries and temples were full of money*. 3. It means *to exhibit, to produce, or to make*. Thus Aelian, *Various History*, Book XIV: *I am not accustomed to looking idly at statues and images, which the art of the sculptors "shows" <note>original: δεικνυσι (deiknysi)</note> to us—that is, the statues and images which the art of the molders exhibits to us*. Lucian, in *The Dream*: *That famous Phidias "showed" <note>original: ἐδειξε (edeixe)</note> Zeus—that is, Phidias exhibited Jove to be seen*. This word is even used in this sense by the Sacred Writers. Thus John 10:32 <note>The text incorrectly cites Job X, but quotes John 10:32.</note>: *Many good works have I "shown" <note>original: ἐδειξα (edeixa)</note> you from my Father*. Castalio translated these words thus: *Many excellent works, by the authority of my Father, have I produced*. Compare John 2:18 and 5:20, and the Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> version of Psalms 60 and 71:20. Indeed, in the same sense, those same translators of the Septuagint interpreted the word *bara* <note>Hebrew: ברא, "to create."</note> as *deixai* in Numbers 16:30. The Hebrew words sound like this: *The Lord will create <note>original: ברא (bara)</note> a creation*; the Septuagint: *But the Lord will "show" <note>original: δειξει (deixei)</note> a thing in a chasm*. The most learned Le Clerc translates it: *If he shall do a new thing*. They interpreted the word *bara* similarly in Isaiah 45:26, 41:20, and 43:15. Likewise, the word *enedeixato* <note>Greek: ἐνεδειξατο</note> in 2 Timothy 4:14 is rightly translated as *he exhibited* or *he did*. Now, if we consider the passage in the *Philebus* <note>A dialogue by Plato concerning pleasure and the good life.</note>...

<meta>catchword: attentively</meta>

<page-num>883</page-num>

...attentively consider it, it will be clear that the word *deixai* denotes nothing other than *to exhibit for viewing* or *visiting*. The *apeiron* is the infinite, and the *peras* is the finite. *A third thing mixed from both*, says Plato on page 159 of this *Dialogue*, is a single thing combined from these two. *The fourth he calls* the cause of the mutual mixing of these things. *Therefore, that first thing*, the *apeiron* <note>The "unlimited" or "infinite."</note>, is matter hitherto undigested and confused. *The Finite* <note>The "limit" or "peras."</note> is matter circumscribed by certain limits. *The third is the World itself, tempered by the soul of the world and endowed with life*. For he describes it more broadly on page 160: *But know that I call the third thing that one which is born from these, namely, the generation into essence from the measures established together with the term*. *The fourth will be God, the efficient cause, who made the visible world consisting of the finite and infinite*. Hence Socrates, on the same page, having brought forward those three, shows that it is necessary for a fourth to be added:

->But besides these three, he said, we must consider what the fourth genus is. This is a common discussion. For see if it does not seem necessary to you that all things that are generated are generated through some cause. Pro. To me, certainly; for how could they happen without these? So. Therefore the nature of the Maker differs from the Cause in name only; the Maker and the Cause may rightly be called one. Pr. Rightly. So. Furthermore, that which is made and that which is generated will differ only in name; is that not how we find it? Pr. Just so. So. Does not the Maker always lead by nature, and the thing made follows, being generated by the former? Pr. Entirely. So. Therefore the Cause is one thing, and that which serves the Cause for generation is another. Pr. Why not? So. Have not the things generated, and those from which they are generated, provided us with all three genera? Pr. Very much so. So. But that which crafts all these, let us call the fourth: the Cause, as it has been shown to be sufficiently different from those others. Pr. Let us call it so.<-

->i. e. But beyond these three, let a fourth genus remain to be discussed. This is a shared inquiry. See if it does not appear necessary to you that whatever is born is born through some cause. Protarchus: To me, clearly. For how could it be done without it? Socrates: And the nature of the Efficient Cause differs from the "cause" only in name; "efficient" and "cause" are rightly called one. Pr: Rightly. So: Moreover, the thing "done" and the thing "born" will differ in name alone. Pr: Certainly. So: The Efficient, by its nature, always precedes and leads; but that which is done by it and born from it, follows. Pr: Precisely. So: Therefore the cause is not the same, but something different from that which serves the cause for generation. Pr: What prevents it? On the previous page, the author began examining the Greek verb "deixai" (to show) to prove that Plato viewed God as a craftsman shaping pre-existing matter, rather than matter being an emanation or "outpouring" from God’s own essence, as his opponent Gundling claims.</meta>

<page-num>884</page-num>
<header>VINDICATION OF THE DISSERTATION</header>

...offered? <note>Referring to the previous page's discussion on the categories of existence.</note> **Pr.** Most certainly. **So.** Therefore, we place the Maker of all these things as the fourth category, and we call Him the "cause," since He has been demonstrated to be something distinct from the others and sufficient in Himself. **Pr.** We place Him there without a doubt. If, therefore, these points we have brought forward are rightly weighed, the sense of the controversial words is this: *God, as the efficient cause <note>The "efficient cause" is the agent that brings something into being or initiates change—in this case, the Creator.</note> in the construction of the world, exhibited to be seen the infinite and the finite—that is, raw matter circumscribed by certain limits.* This explanation agrees with the native meaning of the word <term>deixai (to show)</term>, with the words of Plato cited previously, and finally with the internal logic of the entire Platonic system. 

Now, if the explanation of Mr. Gundling is compared with mine, it will be clear that the meaning he attributes to Plato's words cannot be extracted either from the nature of the word <term>deixai</term> or from Plato’s own text. He contends that the word <term>deixai</term> means *to pour out, to expel—that is, to make or to emanate.* This, then, must be proven by clear examples. He brings forward two passages: the first from Diodorus Siculus, but he notes neither the chapter nor the page so that it might be more accurately considered. However, even if we assume that the phrase <term>a rain shown by Zeus</term> <note>original: "ὄμβρον ἀπὸ Διὸς δεδειγμένον"</note> means "a rain poured out by Jove," or what is the same, "produced," the word <term>deixai</term> would still not signify, by itself, something expelled or poured out from his own "bosom." It is clear that <term>that which was shown</term> <note>original: "τὸ δεδειγμένον"</note> was rendered as "poured out" by the translator simply because the subject is rain. We must look not only at what a word means when mixed with others, but also what it denotes on its own. (*) The second passage, certainly sought from Homer, proves nothing at all; for even if <term>the beech tree showed</term> <note>original: "φαγὸς ἔδειξε"</note> were the same as <term>it brought to light</term> <note>original: "εἰς φῶς ἤγαγε"</note>, it would still not mean the same as "it produced or brought forth from itself." 

This does not fit with Plato's words; for in the passage we cited, the efficient cause is so clearly distinguished from the finite and the infinite (and that which consists of both), that it cannot be said to be one and the same with them. It does not fit with Plato’s principles. For he everywhere posits a certain eternal matter that is <term>unformed</term> <note>original: "ἀσχημάτισον" (aschēmatiston)</note> and distinct from God, which, unless I am mistaken, we have clearly demonstrated above. I cannot help but repeat the words I used on page 917 of my dissertation after examining this passage of Plato: *Let men more perceptive than I judge whether it can be firmly concluded from the cited passage of the Philebus that matter was expelled from the bosom of God. To speak simply what I feel, I see neither a trace nor a shadow of this thing, let alone that the objection drawn from it should commend itself with any appearance of probability.* (**)

<header>ON THE ATHEISM OF PLATO.</header>

XXII. The second passage to which Mr. Gundling appealed was taken from Timaeus Locrus. He contends, following Souverain and Bayle, that this Timaeus Locrus asserts that matter was expelled from the bosom of God. I have said that Gundling followed Souverain or Bayle rather than Timaeus Locrus himself. They all appeal to him, yet they nowhere designate the place in which these words might be found. The learned gentleman does not deny that he consulted those two men; but he says he simultaneously unrolled Plato's *Philebus* and Iamblichus's *On the Mysteries of the Egyptians*, and thus observed that the decision should be sought from Plato’s *Philebus*. And this is the very passage subjected to examination in the preceding section, which is the foundation of his entire edifice. In my dissertation, from page 900 to 909, I weighed the short book of Timaeus Locrus and showed there is no protection for Gundling in it. All that Locrus teaches in this slim volume can be reduced to the following points: 
1. *God is the most excellent mind.* 
2. *Matter is infinite and eternal.* 
3. *There is a <term>Logos</term> (Reason) or <term>Pan</term> (the All), in which the <term>paradigm</term> (model) of the sensible world exists.* 
4. *There is a world-soul subject to the command of God.* 
5. *The Best God willed to shape <term>unformed</term> matter and to make from it the most beautiful living being.* 
6. *This was done by God's will through certain ministers.* 
7. *This world will be eternal because God so wills it.* 

These points are delivered as <term>self-contained</term> <note>original: "αὐτοτελεῖ" (autoteleis)</note> principles in this book. Everyone sees how they can consist with an eternal emanation of matter from the bosom of God <note>The author is being sarcastic here: it is obvious they do NOT agree with emanation.</note>. Let us see, however, what he brings against us from that book that might carry weight. In Section LX, page 273 and following, he speaks thus: *He will hardly fail to be an atheist who makes matter a participant in God, which [matter] is "the nature of the 'other' regarding bodies."* <note>Gundling is quoting Locrus here to argue that Locrus (and thus Plato) makes matter part of God's nature.</note> *For Locrus, the "other" nature is matter, just as the "same" expresses the divine nature.* In this, the Apologist <note>Gundling</note> will no doubt agree with us. Add to this the <term>economy</term> (arrangement) of natural things: *form, matter, and the sensible. But the power and <term>energy</term> from which form flows into matter, and by which matter accommodates itself to form, is in the mind of God, from which other things proceed like offspring, which he calls <term>progeny</term>.* <note>original: "γεννήματα" (gennēmata)</note> *What is not created is not made from nothing. What is not made from nothing buds forth from elsewhere, and the offspring is similar to the father and mother according to essence.* 

I respond: 1. It is nowhere said in this book that matter is a "participant in God." In the beginning, he posits <term>two causes of all things</term>: first, <term>those that come to be according to reason</term>; and second, <term>necessity regarding the powers of bodies</term>. Of these natural causes, he places God as the highest and primary cause, whom he calls the <term>origin of the best things</term>, the <term>leader of all</term>, and the <term>craftsman of the better</term>. Regarding matter, he says it is <term>without form</term> and <term>without shape</term>...

<meta>This page continues the author's refutation of Mr. Gundling’s interpretation of Platonic philosophy. While the previous page focused on the Greek verb "to show" (deixai), the author now examines the work of Timaeus Locrus—a Pythagorean philosopher whose writings were heavily used to understand Plato’s cosmology—to argue that the "offspring" of the universe is a result of God ordering pre-existing matter, not an emanation of God's own substance.</meta>

<page-num>886</page-num>
<header>VINDICATION OF THE DISSERTATION</header>

...receiving every form, <note>original: *δεχομεναν δε πασαν μορφαν*</note> [Timaeus] adds: *that it is divided among bodies and partakes of the nature of the other,* <note>original: *ταν δε περι τα σωματα, μεριζαν ειμεν και τας θατερω φυσιος*</note> meaning that matter is divisible around bodies, and *partakes of the nature of the other*; that is, matter, when looked at in itself, is raw and infinite, but when looked at as arranged into order, it is divisible. Naturally, when the **Idea** <note>In Platonic thought, the "Idea" or "Form" is the perfect blueprint used by the Creator to shape the world.</note> is added to matter, it becomes a partaker of *the nature of the other.* <note>original: *τας θατερω φυσιος*</note>

**2.** Mr. Gundling argues in vain over the word **offspring** <term>ekgonon (foetus/offspring)</term>, which he claims would mean the world proceeded out of God (if you listen to him); on page 544, Timaeus Locrus considers the world as <note>NB: Note Well</note> an **offspring** of those two—namely, of matter and the idea. For indeed, he considers matter as a **mother and nurse**, <note>original: *ματέρα και τιθαναν*</note> and further as eternal and formless, *receiving every form.* The **Form** <note>original: *το ειδος*</note> however, he says on page 545, *has the role of the male and the father,* <note>original: *λογον εχει ἀῤῥενος τε και πατρος*</note> and there are, he says, *three things that are the offspring of these.* The third thing is the essence that is born from these, like a child. From this, it is clear that the world is called an **offspring** because the operation of God was applied to formless matter, which, through the Idea, reduced matter into a specific form; hence matter is called *ordered* <note>original: *τεταγμένη*</note>. Nowhere, however, is it said that this "offspring" was expelled from the bosom of God; indeed, not even from the Idea, which is considered in the likeness of a parent. Therefore, if any "outflowing" takes place, the **perceivable world** <note>original: *το αισθητον*</note> came forth from matter (the mother), adorned with species by the Idea; but God is entirely distinct from the Idea, matter, and the world. Hence, on the cited page, he says: *God, being good, and seeing matter receiving the Idea and being altered.* <note>original: *ἀγαθος ὠν ὁ Θεος, ὁρων δε ταν ὑλαν δεχομεναν ταν ιδεαν και ἀλλοιυμεναν*</note> That is: God, because He is good and sees matter receive form and be variedly altered. Therefore, according to Timaeus Locrus's mind, God used the Idea to form matter; He by no means expelled matter from His own bosom; and why, I ask, would there be a need for an Idea if matter had already been lying hidden in the bosom of God? Or if all things had emanated from the nature of God by some unavoidable necessity? It is true that this "offspring" did not come from nothing, but it does not yet follow that it was expelled from the divine essence of God; for the mother of this offspring is present—namely, that eternal and **unformed** <note>original: *ἀσχηματιστος*</note> matter. This offspring is similar to the Parents who gave it origin: similar to the mother in its body or matter, but similar to the Idea or the **intelligible exemplar** <note>original: *νοατω παραδειγματι*</note> in its order and arrangement. This comparison cannot be pushed any further.

*What is the reason*, Mr. Gundling continues, *that he establishes something divine in the university of nature that remains, and which becomes the intelligible exemplar of the generations and changes in individual things? What is in individual things is not outside of them.* But from where, finally, is this reasoning sought? Timaeus, among the helping causes on page 544, places the **Idea**, **Matter**, and the **Perceivable**. He defines that Idea as follows: *And that which is unbegotten and unmoved, and alone, and of the same nature, the intelligible exemplar of things being born, as many as exist in change...* <note>original: *και το μεν ειμεν ἀγενατον τε και ἀκινατον, και μονον τε, και τας ταυτω φυσιος νοατον τε και παραδειγμα των γεννωμενων, ὁκοσα ἐν μεταβολα οντι*</note>

<meta>catchword: ...makes</meta>

---

<page-num>887</page-num>
<header>ON THE ATHEISM OF PLATO.</header>

*...it makes the Idea to be both spoken of and understood.* That is: *There is, moreover, in this universe of things, something that remains and is intelligible—the exemplar of generated things, which indeed are involved in a certain perpetual flux of changes.* In this way, among these vicissitudes of individual things, the constant and eternal exemplar is called the "Idea" and is grasped by the mind. Everyone can see that this **exemplar** <note>original: *παραδειγμα*</note> is to be perceived by the mind alone, and is distinct from the flowing things that exist outside of that exemplar and are in no way joined with it. That Idea is called the *exemplar of things being born, as many as are in change*; that is, *all flowing things, or all bodies which are in perpetual change, were made according to the immutable Ideas represented in that intelligible world.* Whatever, therefore, is *ordered* <note>original: *τεταγμενον*</note> in individual things must be traced back to that **Intelligible Exemplar**. 

Furthermore, [Gundling] denies that matter is called **unbegotten** <term>agennaton</term>; nor, says the famous Mr. Gundling, would Timaeus be consistent with himself if he had believed matter to be properly "unbegotten," since according to Timaeus's dictates, the everlasting principle called God is the principle of all things, including the mind (and what comes from the mind) as well as matter (and what follows it). Therefore, that same God both begot matter and expelled it from Himself like an offspring *out of a certain unmoved, formless, and unshaped state.* It is true that matter is not called "unbegotten" in this specific passage; however, it is called **mother**, **nurse of all things**, and it is called **eternal** <note>original: *ἀιδιος*</note>. The world is called **begotten** <note>original: *γεννατος*</note> and is considered as a kind of offspring; therefore, before God adorned it, it was "unbegotten"—not yet born, or rather, not yet arranged into order. For the world is said to be "born" when it is *ordered*, reduced into a certain and definite arrangement. This does not prevent God from being the author of all things at once; for since He Himself arranged matter into order and divided the unshaped matter into certain species, He can be said to have "begotten" the world. 

Hence, on page 545, Timaeus says: *God, when He saw matter receiving form and being altered in various ways, but nevertheless inordinately: He saw also that there was a need for Him to reduce it into order, and from indefinite changes to establish it into a certain and defined state.* Where, then, is there even a shadow of that "eternal expulsion from the divine essence"? If that word **to beget** <note>original: *γενναν*</note> so greatly displeases Mr. Gundling, let him take the words **to lead into order** <note>original: *εις ταξιν αγειν*</note> or **to make** <note>original: *ποιειν*</note>, which are used by Timaeus on this very page 545, and that fear will vanish. (*)

<meta>catchword: Which-</meta>

---

(*) Learned men have long ago observed that **to beget** <note>original: *γενναν*</note> and **to make** <note>original: *ποιειν*</note> are used interchangeably among the Greeks. Let the most learned **Clericus** <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), a famous Swiss theologian and biblical scholar.</note> be heard in his Commentary on Genesis 2:4. Just as the Hebrew word *yalad* <note>Hebrew: ילד</note>, he says, primarily means "he begot," and from there signifies "he made anything"; so also its derivative, which Moses uses here, signifies first generation, and then any procreation. Similarly among the Greeks, *gennan*, which is "to generate," commonly means **TO EFFECT** or **TO CREATE**.

<summary>This page defends Timaeus Locrus (and by extension Plato) against the charge of emanationism, arguing that describing the world as an "offspring" is a metaphor for God imposing order on eternal, formless matter rather than matter being "born" out of God's substance.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the author’s (Zimmermann’s) rigorous defense of his dissertation against the criticisms of Mr. Gundling. The debate centers on whether Plato believed matter was eternal and separate from God, or whether matter emanated from God’s own substance (a view that would link Plato to Spinozism or pantheism). Zimmermann continues to argue for the former, asserting that Plato viewed God as a craftsman working with pre-existing material.</meta>

<page-num>888</page-num>
<header>VINDICATION OF THE DISSERTATION</header>

The celebrated Mr. Gundling asks how matter could be mobile according to Timaeus, even before it was arranged into order by God. But what does this have to do with the matter at hand? Plato supposed many things that he could not prove. The question is simply what he *thought*. That famous *Timaeus* <note>Timaeus of Locri, the Pythagorean philosopher featured in Plato’s dialogue.</note> agreed with *Pythagoras* that all bodies are in a state of perpetual flux. I beg you, *he says*, to reveal how the offspring comes forth, and what the nature of the matter is. *You are being ignored.* And again, I say, he who is ignorant neither affirms nor denies. *Why then do you deny that it was expelled or secreted?* I ask the celebrated *Polyhistor* <note>A title for a person of great learning, here referring to Gundling.</note> in turn to explain how, by the will of God, the mass of sensible things arose; let him explain the connection that exists between the will of an intellectual Being and the existence and motion of bodies, and I will then explain to him how God was able to manufacture the world out of eternal matter. I confess that I do not know how the world was built by God according to the mind of *Plato*; but although I willingly confess my ignorance in this regard, I can nevertheless rightly assert that **matter was not cast out from the bosom of God**. Why is that? Because there is neither a *trace* nor a *footprint* of such a thing in the *Timaeus*; and because it does not follow from the principles of *Timaeus*. Therefore, what I know, I affirm; what I do not know, I leave in doubt. For it is permitted, if I am not mistaken, for *Mr. Gundling* to maintain that matter, according to the opinion of Christians, is not eternal; yet it was not propelled from the bosom of God, even though neither he nor anyone else can explain how, given the eternal will of the Deity, bodies came into existence and are still moved by that same will.

XXIII. I asserted in my *Dissertation* that it is most clearly evident from this book of Timaeus that Plato did not grant only a single substance, but asserted many; therefore, *Mr. Gundling* betakes himself to the soul of the world <note>original: *anima mundi*</note>, intending to prove from there that Plato recognized only one substance. *That (soul of the world), he says, the God of Plato "brought forth outside" <gloss>original: επαγαγεν εξω (epagagen exo)</gloss>: which is a sign that it lay hidden within the bosom of the divinity: then he covered the "entire universe itself" <gloss>original: αυτο ολον (auto olon)</gloss> with it, and gave to it something from an indivisible form and a divisible essence: the former is divine and indivisible; the latter is matter and divisible, so that by the intervention of motion, a second thing might be made, while in the meantime the one and the same might remain. Zimmerman—*

<note>The following is a supplementary note regarding the terminology of creation used by ancient authors.</note>

...and **Generation** <term>genesis</term> is the name for the action by which anything is made. Indeed, Plato in the *Timaeus*, where he disputes concerning the creation of the world, frequently confuses **to beget** <gloss>gennan</gloss> and **to make** <gloss>poiein</gloss>, **begotten** <gloss>gennēta</gloss> and **created** <gloss>genēta</gloss>, and **becoming** <gloss>genesis</gloss> and **existence** <gloss>hyparxis</gloss>. He calls the world **begotten** <gloss>gennēton</gloss>, and God the **Father** <gloss>Patera</gloss> no less than the **Cause** <gloss>aition</gloss>. Thus far Mr. Le Clerc. This is also proved by the translation of Cicero. For in his book *On the Universe*, he translates that most famous passage of Plato thus: *Then that God, who begat all things, speaks to the Gods. Listen to these things, you who are sprung from the seed of the Gods. Of these works I am the Parent and the Maker; those things made by me cannot be dissolved against my will, etc.* Where he called Him "Begetter," he immediately calls Him "Maker."

<page-num>889</page-num>
<header>ON THE ATHEISM OF PLATO.</header>

...Zimmermann calls this description obscure, although it fits Plato's mind like one egg fits another. It is true, I have said and I still say, that it is most obscure what *Timaeus* and *Plato* understand by the name "soul of the world"; and I still believe that we cannot correctly reason from those things which are, by the consensus of almost everyone, obscure. It is true that the description of the soul of the world which *Timaeus* provides exactly matches the description of *Plato*: but in my opinion, this is the same as if someone were to say that the nonsense word *blitri* <note>A term used by ancient logicians to signify a sound without meaning.</note> has a meaning no less clear than *Aristophanes’* *phlattotrattophlattotrat* <note>A nonsense sound mimicking the plucking of a lyre string from Aristophanes' comedy *The Frogs*.</note>. Certainly, the description of the soul of the world by *Timaeus* is just as obscure as that of *Plato*. Famous men, most skilled in the History of Philosophy, have long ago confessed that Plato is most obscure on this matter. *Plutarch*, a man of vast learning <note>original: *πολυμαθεστατος*</note>, confesses this at the beginning of his *Commentary on the Procreation of the Soul of the World*, which is described in Plato's *Timaeus*. *Sextus Empiricus*, in Book I, chapter 13, *Against the Grammarians*, page 283, says: *For where is there one among the haughty Grammarians who is able to understand Heraclitus or follow Plato when he says: From the essence which is indivisible and always remains the same, and from that which is divisible among bodies, he mixed a third type of essence from both, namely the nature of the Same and the nature of the Other.* Of the more recent authors, I will cite only *Burnet* in his *Philosophical Archaeologies*, Chapter 13, page 439, speaking thus: *This Platonic soul, he says, many interpreters of Plato have explained—Chalcidius, Proclus, and as many as have commented on the Timaeus. Furthermore, Plutarch discussed the procreation of the soul according to Plato at length in a singular treatise. But having read all these, you will gain nothing; except perhaps you will be more convinced that as many as have sweated in this arena have completely wasted their effort. That Platonic "Psychogony" <term>Soul-creation</term> seems to me to be nothing other than a game of the intellect: or a royal magic castle built in the air, the foundation of which we seek in vain.* To anyone who knows that dialogue of *Timaeus*, it will be enough to set down not my own protest, but that of a recent philosopher on the matter. If Plato had set forth that opinion of his concerning the nature of the soul in common words: would he have seemed to say anything grand, or anything that could be proven with certainty? Imagine now that he were among the living: imagine him being asked to explain himself clearly: to declare that *Chiasmus* <note>A technical term for a "crossing" structure; here referring to the complex mathematical/harmonic crossing of the soul's bands in Plato's cosmology.</note> of his? Let him explain what is "the same," what is "the different," and what is the "third nature" from the divisible and indivisible. Let him reveal where those Geometric and Harmonic proportions are to be recognized in the soul.

<meta>This page continues the author’s (Zimmermann’s) point-by-point rebuttal of the scholar Nicolaus Gundling. Zimmermann is specifically addressing Gundling’s claim that Plato’s "World Soul" was an extension of God’s own substance. Zimmermann argues instead that the World Soul is a created entity, separate from the divine essence, thereby protecting Plato from the charge of "Spinozism" or pantheism (the idea that everything is part of God).</meta>

<page-num>890</page-num>
<header>VINDICATION OF THE DISSERTATION</header>

Oh, how far it will be from making the nature of the soul clear to us! For its nature remained hidden and stays unknown even to his own listeners, among whom was the most sharp-witted *Aristotle*. But truly, because he [Plato] entangled his opinion in wonderful ambiguities, he achieved his likely goal: that we should marvel at, look up to, and revere his doctrine as a distinguished mystery. We are led to think that if we do not perfectly understand the nature of the soul, the cause is that we cannot penetrate the mind of such a divine *Man*. We blame ourselves because, being mere *little men*, we cannot reach the heights of such a *Hero*. And since we have the eyes of an *Owl* <note>original: "Noctuae"</note> while he had the eyes of an *Eagle*, we are blinded by that radiance which he himself saw clearly. Thus far *Burnet*. <note>Thomas Burnet (1635–1715), an English theologian and geologist known for his "Sacred Theory of the Earth."</note> These cited testimonies sufficiently prove that at all times, even to the most learned and perceptive *Men*, the Platonic description of the "World Soul" <note>term: "anima mundi" — a concept where the entire universe is a living being with its own soul.</note> has appeared extremely obscure. But let us see, nonetheless, whether it can be proven that this soul was "in the bosom of divinity" and was afterward "expelled." Let us hear *Timaeus* himself. <note>Timaeus of Locri, a Pythagorean philosopher who is the main speaker in Plato's dialogue of the same name.</note> On page 549, he presents the matter thus: <note>original Greek: "τὰν δὲ τῷ κόσμῳ ψυχὰν μέσοθεν ἐξάψας ἐπάγαγεν ἔξω...". This is written in the Doric dialect.</note> *God placed the soul of the world in its center and led it forth outside: and she [the soul] covered the entire universe, being mixed in a certain temperament from an indivisible form and a divisible essence: so that one single temperament exists from these two: to which he mixed two powers, the principles of motions—namely, of the same and of the other. Indeed, this soul, since it accepts mixing with difficulty, did not easily coalesce into the formula of this temperament.* From this passage, we see neither from where that world soul arose, nor what it is. *Gundling* <note>Nicolaus Hieronymus Gundling (1671–1729), a prominent German jurist and philosopher who accused Plato of holding views similar to Spinoza.</note> insists in vain on that phrase "led it forth outside." God is said to have *placed* it in the world; it is therefore considered as something entirely subject to the command and will of God. For what power would He have over that which clung to His own essence with an inseparable bond and was of the same perfection? He "led that soul forth outside," but does it necessarily follow that it therefore lay hidden in the divine essence itself? It was first placed in the world, and only then led outside. But where it was *before* it was introduced into the world—of that there is neither a trace nor a footprint in *Timaeus*. It is not permitted to elicit whatever one likes from any source just to defend a hypothesis. If there is room for conjecture, I would believe that "led it forth outside" denotes nothing other than that the world soul, inserted into the center by God, was led outward—that is, to adorn all...

<column-break/>

<page-num>891</page-num>

...even the outermost parts of the world, and was sent there; and truly, after this was done, it was cast back into its original home. (\*) That "tempering" from the divisible and indivisible seems to denote nothing else than that the world consists of bodies and a certain "fecundating principle." <note>An active, life-giving force.</note> But whatever you say, you can bring forward nothing that is satisfying in every part. It is enough that the soul is considered as a kind of servant, subject to the Command of God. Hence, on page 549, he says: <note>original Greek: "ἂν ἔχ’ ὑστέραν τὰς σωματικὰς οὐσίας..."</note> *God did not ordain this [the soul] as the last thing after the bodily essence itself, but created it as the more ancient.* That world soul (so Dr. *Gundling* continues) is called by [Timaeus] the Locrian on page 556 the "altering nature," <note>original Greek: "φύσιν ἀλλοιωτικήν"</note> so that it might take the place of the Craftsman <note>term: "Opifex" — the Demiurge or Creator in Platonic thought.</note> in producing mortal and fleeting animals; to these, she instilled souls, as if through a certain "flow," <note>original Greek: "ὡς τὰς ψυχὰς ἐπιρρύτως ἐνέσαγε"</note> drawn partly from the sun, and partly from the other stars where they were wandering. *One human soul, endowed with the same power, remained as that very soul of the world, which he had mixed into the part participating in reason.* Thus says Dr. *Gundling*. I will provide the very words of the Locrian so that the Reader may judge whether that conclusion necessarily flows from them. Since they are rather lengthy, I will give only the Latin. <note>The author provides a Latin translation of the Greek text by Timaeus of Locri.</note> "Truly now," he says on page 556, "after the constitution of the world, God strived for the generation of mortal living things, so that it might be entirely perfect and absolute according to that image. Therefore, He distributed the human soul, tempered from the same ratios and powers, and divided it, granting this ministry to the 'altering nature': which, having received the commands of these things, took the place, as it were, of the Craftsman himself in producing mortal and fleeting animals, whose souls **Note Well:** she instilled as if by a certain flow: thus she derived some from the moon, others from the sun, and others from the rest of the stars that wander in the 'part of the other.' She received one soul, which is endowed with the same power, which she mixed into that part participating in reason as an image of wisdom for those who enjoy a good fate." And with a few things interposed, he wishes there to be three faculties of the soul. Regarding the heart, the *spirited* <note>original Greek: "τὸ θυμοειδές" — the seat of emotions like anger and courage.</note>; regarding the liver, the *desiring* <note>original Greek: "τὸ ἐπιθυμητικόν" — the seat of physical appetites.</note>; and finally, in the brain is the *ruling* <note>original Greek: "τὸ ἡγεμονικόν" — the rational or governing part of the soul.</note> part. If we reduce the words of the Locrian to a summary, the following things are evident: 1. *That God is distinguished from the soul...*
