...the World Soul and other substances. 2. That the **World Soul** <note>original: "anima mundi"</note> is a servant of God, and has led souls into various places and sent them into bodies, as God willed. 3. That those souls wandered around the sun and the stars. 4. That the World Soul is distinct from other souls. 5. That human souls are equipped with different faculties. From these points, however, Doctor Gundling concludes on page 277: *Hence in all things there is found the divine and the same: to which is attached 그 famous "non-being," which does not subsist through itself but is sustained by the divine.* But who is so "lynx-eyed" <note>original: "lynceus" — meaning sharp-sighted, from the mythological Lynceus</note> that he can see the force of this inference? That matter is not a substance according to the mind of **Plato** is a mere supposition, which, unless I am mistaken, has been sufficiently refuted above. The divine is found in all things—that is, there are intellectual substances in man, there are spirits <note>original: "daemones"</note> around the stars, there are "ideas," and finally, there is God Himself. But by what argument or testimony is it proved that all those substances make up a single one? Or even more, that they are so necessarily joined with the world itself that they cannot be distinguished except by a mental abstraction? Here, most clearly, the world is distinguished from God, God from the World Soul, and souls from the stars and bodies. To assert that all these must be interpreted through mental abstraction is nothing other than **"to be a slave to one’s own hypothesis"** <note>original: "τη ὑποθεσει δουλευειν"</note> without reason. Hence I do not think it necessary to overturn at length Section LXII cited by Gundling. From these things, he says, it is clear that the only substance is **the Divine** <note>original: "το Θειον"</note>, and the rest do not exist except by **participation** <note>original: "κατα μετοχην"</note> in the one substance which flows into men and animals. For in what place is it said that those souls led into animals are derived from God? They are not even said to have come forth from the "bosom" of the World Soul. Only this is plain: that the World Soul placed the other souls into bodies. Finally, why are those souls recalled from the stars and from the sun if they are part of the divine essence? Furthermore, I have brought arguments from this booklet of **Timaeus** to prove that, according to the opinion of **Locrus** <note>Timaeus of Locri, a Pythagorean philosopher featured in Plato’s dialogues</note>, God intended certain **ends** <note>original: "fines" — meaning purposes or goals</note> in establishing the world. He responds that Locrus speaks as a physicist; but that the God of **Pythagoras** "acts as a geometer" <note>original: "γεωμετρει"</note>. He claims the consideration of an "end" or purpose does not fall within mathematical abstraction. But what need is there for many words when testimonies are present? Plato in the *Timaeus*, and Locrus in *On the World Soul*, speak as both Physicists and Theologians simultaneously. They reveal the beginnings of things, and at the same time teach how all things were adorned toward a specific end. Truly, there is no talk of abstractions here. God also "acts as a geometer" according to our own opinion, because He established all things with a certain weight and measure.

Since I have already demonstrated clearly enough in the preceding sections that **Spinoza** denies all "ends" <note>Spinoza famously argued against teleology, the idea that nature acts with a purpose</note>, it is established that **Plato**, who followed Timaeus, does not feel the same as Spinoza.

**XXIV.** Thus far we have abundantly shown that no clear passages were brought forward by the celebrated Gundling to defend his system. Let us see now whether he has other arguments at hand by which he can protect his opinion. In Section VIII of his Dissertation, he begins to lay the foundations of his system; it all comes down to this: *That the matter of Plato (*)* is, according to me, eternal, not at all created out of nothing by God; that the same was from eternity in a confused motion; but that matter does not have motion from itself, nor was it created by God; therefore one must necessarily flee to **emanation**; and where there is emanation, there "flow" takes place; therefore matter emanated from God from eternity.* These same points in the following theses...

<page-num>894</page-num>
<header>894 VINDICATION OF THE DISSERTATION</header>

...he repeats the same points, and appeals to them as if they were mathematical principles. But that entire supposition seems false to me. For he constantly confuses the **question of law** <note>original: "quaestionem juris" — here meaning the theoretical consistency or logic of a system</note> with the **question of fact** <note>original: "quaestione facti" — what was actually said or done</note>. The question between the Distinguished Man <note>referring to Gundling</note> and myself is this: *Whether Plato was a follower of Spinoza’s opinion, or not?* He asserts it; I deny it. We therefore rightly appeal to the testimonies from which the opinion of *Plato* may be known. He brought forward two passages by which he wished to prove that matter was propelled from the bosom of God. I have not only directly brought forward other testimonies opposed to this opinion, but I have also shown that those very passages cited from the *Philebus* and *Timaeus Locrus* <note>Platonic and pseudo-Platonic dialogues</note> prove absolutely nothing. Moreover, I believe that in the explanation of the ancients, one must insist on clear testimonies—whether they be true or false—that will either confirm or subvert our opinion.

However, the entire mass of *Gundling’s* reasoning consists of mere conjectures and logical consequences. It is absurd, he says, for *Plato* to have believed in eternal matter, subsisting through itself and moved confusedly. That is so. But does it therefore follow that *Plato* did not profess it? Must the clearest testimonies therefore be denied, or twisted into a foreign sense? I challenge the consequence. For the question is not what he *ought* to have felt, or how he *could* have reasoned, but what he *did* feel? If we depart from this question, *pure darkness will arise*.

*Hierocles* <note>a 5th-century Neoplatonist</note> and others among the ancients recognized that it was absurd to establish any matter as eternal; hence, finally carried away by an excessive love for *Plato*, *Hierocles* asserted that *Plato* professed the creation of matter out of nothing. But he was "flogged" <note>original: "vapulavit" — metaphorically beaten in scholarly argument</note> for it. Why? Because he showed what *Plato* should have said, but not what he actually thought. If we turn the eyes of the mind to the system of *Spinoza* <note>Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677), whose pantheism was often equated with atheism by 18th-century scholars</note>, no less difficulties occur, but rather monsters of error. What then must be done? In my opinion, having set aside all prejudiced views, *Plato* himself must be read; not just one or two passages turned over, but the connection of the whole system must be looked into as much as possible, and only then should it be said what he thought—be it true or false, absurd or solid.

I have performed this to the best of my strength, and have brought forward the most open passages by which it is proved that *Plato* recognized eternal matter as entirely diverse from God and in no way joined with Him. But of the "flowing" <note>emanation</note> of matter out of God, there is no trace. But because of the motion of matter, which *Plato* supposed to exist in that indigested matter, must we—against those most evident testimonies and the connection of the system—assert that the cause of that flow must be sought in God, and that *Plato* recognized a single substance? I would not think so. By the same reasoning, if it were permitted to interpret the ancients in this way, I will prove that *Plato* recognized **Creation out of nothing**. One would only need to exaggerate the difficulties which

take place in the **System of two principles** <note>Dualism, the belief in two primary forces like God and Matter</note> and that of *Spinoza*, and bring forward certain passages by which this seems to be proved, and I will have what I want. But all fair judges of things would judge me to be acting in vain. If I were to ask *Dr. Gundling* how that admirable order could arise from a cause acting by necessity according to *Spinoza*, he would doubtless respond that the question is what *Spinoza* thought, not what he ought to have established. No one among those who defend the absurd dogma of **Transubstantiation** can explain this "wooden iron" <note>original: "σιδηρόξυλον" (sideroxylon) — a logic term for a fundamental contradiction</note>, and yet they defend it no less constantly. It is sufficient, therefore, to have proved that *Plato* approved the eternal subsistence of matter, even if we cannot explain by what reason he could prove it or reconcile it with other things he asserted.

When I had already said these things in my dissertation, *Dr. Gundling* in Section 98 calls this response of mine absurd, and says I do not know the laws of probability. But I, in my simplicity, have hitherto believed that the highest degree of probability is produced by open testimonies—specifically in a question of fact. Whether I have brought forward clear testimonies or not, let the judgment belong to others who are outside the parties of this dispute. Nor, *Dr. Gundling* adds, did *Plato* comprehend all the dangerous conclusions we see arising from the doctrine of **emanations**.

But first, it must be proved that *Plato* established an emanation from God. Then, with greater right, I make my response. I do not prove by conjectures, but by arguments, that *Plato* recognized the eternity of matter; and this being established, I say it is in vain to press the absurdity of this dogma, since perhaps he did not perceive all the consequences that would arise from it. *Plato*, contemplating the order of the universe, concluded that there is a supreme Ruler of the world; but when he turned himself toward matter, **creation out of nothing** <note>original: "creatio ex nihilo"</note> disturbed him. He therefore asserted that matter is eternal; meanwhile, he was not solicitous about the manner in which God acted upon it, or what right He had over it. According to him, matter was adorned by God, therefore he concluded that this could even be done.

But the *Chaldeans*, he says, the *Egyptians, Pythagoras, Heraclitus, Socrates*, and others established a philosophy **from a flow** <note>original: "ἀπὸ ῥοίας" (apo rhoias) — referring to the theory of emanation or constant flux</note>; *Plato* followed these. But I would wish all these things to be proved to me. I know that *Heraclitus, Pythagoras*, and others asserted that matter is in a perpetual flux. But that this matter, existing in perpetual flux, emanated from God as if from a corporeal substance—this,

...passages, I say, be proved. I know that **Pierre Bayle** <note>A famous French skeptic and philosopher</note> had already offered such views before **Gundling**, but I shall show in due time that this assertion is not built upon arguments that could draw a lover of truth into agreement. But suppose all these men were devoted to the opinion of **Spinoza** <note>Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677), whose philosophy was frequently conflated with atheism in this period</note>; then a very grave question would remain: did **Plato** depart from them in this regard or not? And so the entire controversy would once again fall back upon the clear passages of **Plato**. Since, however, that agreement with Spinoza cannot be clearly proved from Plato thus far, I rightly assert that he moved in an entirely different direction.

XXV. The **Distinguished Gundling**, in *Section XI* and those following, repeats that *the ancients indeed professed the eternity of matter, but at the same time maintained that this same fluid matter emanated from the divine essence.* However, since he proves this with no testimony, there is no need for me to dwell on this objection at length. In *Sections XVIII and XIX*, he repeats the same old song and asks that I explain how eternal matter could have been ordered by God? What power does God have over eternal matter? From where does that confused motion of matter arise? But I have already responded above that these questions should be asked of **Plato** himself. It must at least be proved that, if the eternity of matter is granted, God is removed or a single substance is created. In *Section XX*, he appeals again to the **Egyptians, Chaldeans, etc.**, as defenders of <term>emanations</term> <note>original: "ἀποῤῥοίας" (aporrhoias) — the idea that things flow out from a divine source</note>. I know that the **Chaldeans** speak of intellectual "sections" and "emanations," if we are to stand by those fragments that remain. But it would have to be proved that by that name they understood a literal flow and a division of parts. Meanwhile, I have already advised above that matter can be called "unbegotten" and "begotten" in a certain sense. He appeals to **Stillingfleet’s** *Origines Sacrae, Book III, page 846*, in which that Illustrious Prelate <note>Edward Stillingfleet, an influential English theologian</note> shows that the "water" of **Thales** and the "confusedly moved matter" of **Plato** are the same. I concede this, but let it be proved that **Thales** said that the matter he calls "water" emanated from the bosom of God through a flowing out. For the question is not whether Plato’s eternal matter was in a perpetual state of flux, but whether it flowed out from the **Divine Essence of the Deity**. I wish that the Distinguished Gundling had also weighed Stillingfleet’s preceding words. For on *page 843*, using **Diogenes Laërtius** as a source, he teaches that the **Egyptians** gave an origin to the world. On *page 845*, by the testimony of **Plutarch**, he teaches that **Pythagoras** recognized two principles of all things: the **active cause** <note>original: "ποιητικον αἴτιον" (poiētikon aition)</note> (which is **mind** <note>original: "νοῦς" (nous)</note>) and the **passive and material** one <note>original: "παθητικον καὶ ὑλικον" (pathētikon kai hylikon)</note>. In *Section XXI*, he asks how those gods, of whom Plato makes mention in the *Timaeus*, arose? I said in my dissertation that those gods are the Sun, the Moon, and even the Daemons. They are called **generated gods** <note>original: "Θεοί γεννητοί" (Theoi gennētoi)</note>. How Plato’s God was able to adorn those vast bodies, I will say...

<meta>catchword: as soon as-</meta>

---

<page-num>897</page-num>
<header>ON THE ATHEISM OF PLATO.</header>

...as soon as the Distinguished Man explains to me the connection that exists between spiritual and corporeal substance. This I know: **Plato** asserted that those gods were made by the most noble mind and are subject to his command. In *Section XXII*, he asks again: what does it mean *to be generated*? I will say. **Plato**, as we have heard from **Timaeus of Locri** <note>A Pythagorean philosopher featured in Plato's dialogues</note>, considered matter as a mother, and the **Mind** <note>original: "νοῦν" (noun)</note> like a Parent. Therefore, as soon as God, as the most noble mind—or Mind itself—brings matter (hitherto confused) into order, the world is said by **Plato** to be *generated*. But if, putting these things aside, I wished to press the word *to beget* <note>original: "γεννᾷν" (gennan)</note>, I could very easily prove that it denotes creation rather than the production of a thing already existing. In *Section XXIII*, he wishes to prove that the **soul of the world** is a certain <term>small fragment</term> <note>original: "ἀποσπασμάτιον" (apospasmatidion) — a shred or piece torn off</note> of the divine essence. He appeals to a passage of **Plato** which appears on *page 710 in Ficino’s version*; but to have cited it is to have refuted it. It sounds like this: *He indeed established the soul as prior to and older than the body, both in its generation and in its virtue, so that it might rule over the obedient body.* <note>The author is quoting from the Timaeus, describing the creation of the world-soul</note> Evidently from these things, and in this manner: *From that substance which is indivisible and always the same and similar, and from that which becomes divisible around bodies, he mixed a third middle form of substance, which would again be a participant in the nature of the "same" and the nature of the "other," and he established it through this middle point between the indivisible substance and that which is divided around the body. When he had taken these three, he tempered them all into one form.* Hear what **Gundling** concludes from this: *In such a manner, therefore, the soul was infused into the whole world, which is the Spirit of divinity and God himself.* But who does not see that there is no trace of this consequence in this passage? To be sure, the soul of the world was tempered by God from corporeal and spiritual things; therefore, did it proceed or emanate from the bosom of God like a part from a whole? Who could doubt it? To say nothing of the fact that in the following parts **Plato** clearly enough signifies that this soul must be considered as a **Creature** (*) entirely different from God and subject to His Command. On *page 711 of Ficino’s version*, he speaks thus: *After, therefore, the whole constitution of the soul was perfected according to the mind of that Creator, he soon fashioned all that is corporeal within it, and adapting the middle to the middle, he joined them with a fitting harmony;* and after a few words: *and the body of the heaven was made visible, but the soul escaped the sight of the eyes; having a share of reason and harmony from its author—the best of all things that always are and pertain to intelligence—it was also itself made the best of all things that have been begotten.* Surely to no one, unless already imbued from elsewhere with preconceived opinions, will it occur that this soul is a part of the divine essence, torn away from it. (**)

-> (**) The most learned **Porphyry** speaks clearly on this matter in *On Abstinence*, page 80. <-

<meta>The text continues the author's defense of Plato’s philosophy against Nicolaus Gundling. The previous page established that the author rejects Gundling’s attempt to link Plato with Spinoza’s pantheism. Now, the argument moves into the specific nature of Plato’s "three principles"—God, Mind, and the World Soul—and whether their relationship implies a physical "flowing out" (emanation) from the divine essence.</meta>

<page-num>898</page-num>
<header>VINDICATION OF THE DISSERTATION</header>

**XXVI.** In order for the Distinguished Gundling to prove his point piece by piece—namely, that those three principles of Plato (God, the Mind or *Logos* <note>original: νυν seu λογον</note>, and the World Soul) are joined together and most strictly bound to matter—he first attempts to prove in Section XXIV that Plato’s *Mind* or *Logos* is the offspring of God, or that it flowed and emanated from the First. He states: *“From the highest God and the non-essential* <note>original: ἀνεσίῳ; referring to a state beyond being or essence</note>, *the supra-essential Mind comes, just as from that Mind the World Soul went forth.”* And, after a few intervening words, he argues thus: *“Either that Mind, the highest Craftsman, will be God, or it will not. If the former, it will be enough to have proved that the World Soul is a fragment of that very thing; but if it is a new substance, its cause must surely be that one ‘Non-essential,’ which can neither be named nor perceived. If this is the case, how then did the Mind arise? Was it out of nothing, or from the highest bosom of Divinity?”* He appeals to Plato’s *Philebus*, page 90, in the translation by Ficino, in which Socrates says: *“To my inquiry, it provides an answer: that Mind is a certain offspring of that cause which is called the cause of all things, and which is one of those four things that were reported.”* <note>The "four things" refers to the Pythagorean categories Plato uses in the Philebus: Limit, the Unlimited, the Mixture, and the Cause.</note> Where there is "offspring," Dr. Gundling concludes, there is "generation"; and generation cannot be conceived without an "effluence" <note>A flowing out</note>, because the idea of creation out of nothing vanishes.

**Response 1.** Plato and his disciples reason in various ways concerning the *Logos* <note>The Word or Reason</note>, or the second principle. Sometimes they consider the *Mind* <note>original: τον νυν</note> as something existing by itself and eternal, equal to *Matter* <note>original: την ὑλην</note>; at other times, they claim that this Mind has its origin from God and is distinct from the First Being only by degrees of perfection. Sometimes they ascribe command over all things to God alone; yet shortly after, they introduce that *Logos* as the Parent of all things which were made "according to reason" <note>original: κατα λογον</note>, so that one cannot safely reason from these points.

**2.** Furthermore, let us assume with Dr. Gundling that the *Mind* is the offspring of the divine Mind; it does not yet follow from this that a properly called "efflux" (**) <note>A physical flowing out or separation of parts</note> takes place—that is, a

<margin>
m. 80. The supreme God, being both incorporeal and immovable and indivisible, and not existing in any thing, nor bound within himself, lacks nothing of those things which are outside him, as we have said. But neither does the World Soul: having a triple divisibility and the power of moving itself by nature, it was yet so made by nature that it chooses to be moved well and in an orderly fashion, and to stir the offspring of the world according to the most excellent reasons. It has, however, taken a body into itself and surrounded it, though it is incorporeal and participates in no suffering. <note>This margin note quotes a Neoplatonic interpretation of the relationship between the transcendent God and the World Soul.</note>
</margin>

(**) Which signifies, by the proper force of the word, an unfolding of parts and a communication with another—

<column-break/>

<page-num>899</page-num>
<header>ON THE ATHEISM OF PLATO.</header>

*separation of parts from parts*, which is the very thing most in question. Plato uses the word "to beget" <note>original: γενναν</note> regarding divine matters, and without doubt he spoke of things for which he had very little clear understanding. This much is certain: although he sometimes remarks that it is difficult to find the nature of God, calling Him "non-essential" <note>original: ἀνεσιον</note> and raised above all "categories" (as they say in the Schools), he nevertheless always maintains that God is of an intelligent and most perfect nature. In the *Timaeus*, page 528, he says: *“This is the whole of truly existing reasoning from God—reasoned out.”* In the *Epinomis*, page 702, he calls Him "Logos" where he speaks of the world: *“...which the most divine Reason [Logos] of all things ordained to be visible.”* This is not to mention other passages I have cited above. But this being granted, the question is: how can a kind of "generation" take place in divine matters without an efflux, and how can intellectual things arise from intellectual things?

**3.** Therefore, let us look to our own mind, since all our reasonings about God are derived from those things we observe in our own minds. We know the nature of our mind more from a certain inner sense than from a clear concept observed by the soul. There is a certain perpetual flow of ideas about the mind, or a coming and going; whether these arise from the mind or not, and how they are in the mind, we are entirely ignorant. Indeed, all ideas seem to be produced by the help of our will, or certainly not without it; but again, we do not know how they arrive through the mediation of the will. If we now turn the eyes of our mind toward God, the soul is swallowed up by the majesty of so great a Divinity. How that most noble Mind thinks, imagines, and reasons; how it always has the most present notions of all things—present, past, future, contingent, and necessary—we do not know. We do not know how, by the established will of God, all things both arose and are preserved. In a word, it is not for mortals to look into the inner nature of God.

To what end, Dr. Gundling will ask, are these points brought forward? I will say: from these things it follows that we are entirely ignorant of how anything can arise from God. It follows that it is rash to define that nothing can arise from God and out of God except through a material emanation or

<sig>XXXXX 2</sig>

<insert>
progeny that indicates a physical "flowing out." For the Distinguished Gentleman always assumes, but never proves (except through the *Epinomis*), that Plato admitted and established such an emanation that implies materiality in God. If, however, "emanation" is taken in a broader sense to indicate only a communication of essence suitable to the nature of the thing—and thus says nothing more than that the eternal Father produced the Mind from Himself in a spiritual manner—then that word can indeed be admitted. In that case, Dr. Gundling’s objections fall away, because neither is any "materiality" (so to speak) proved in God, nor does the communication of essence exclude a proper "subsistence in itself" <note>original: αὐτην καθ' αὑτην</note>, which is Plato’s own phrase. Certainly, it cannot be excluded according to Plato's own mind.

properly so-called and a flow. I would prefer, for my part, to confess my ignorance in this matter. But Plato, he says, wished to explain these things as a philosopher. To this I say: first, we are ignorant of the things that could lead to a proper understanding of his opinion, since both he and his disciples explain the matter in various ways. Second, not only Plato, but also we, who have been taught better things, can define nothing certain in this matter because of the obscurity of the thing itself. Christian theologians, both in the past and now, have spoken of a certain eternal generation of the Son, yet no one claims to be able to explain the manner of it. He will say that this is a *mystery*. I do not deny it; however, no emanation properly so-called, no "flow" takes place, but according to them, it is a certain intellectual and ineffable <note>ineffable: something too great or sacred to be expressed in words</note> generation. We are not ignorant of what it means to generate in other contexts, or what is denoted by this word; but when the conversation is about divine things, those phrases cannot be properly fitted to a reality that we do not understand. Plato, to be sure, did not propose these things as mysteries revealed from heaven, yet so far the matter comes to the same result. For if he truly thought that the <term>Logos<gloss>the "Word" or "Reason," a central concept in Greek philosophy and Christian theology</gloss></term> arose from God, he could no more explain that matter than we can explain the eternal generation of the Son of God. It is true, he ought to have explained these things clearly as a philosopher or remained silent; but who is unaware that philosophers, no less than others, sometimes speak of things they least understand? (*) Third: Whatever may be the case regarding the Logos and its origin, it can be proved by no reasoning that an emanation properly so-called takes place. For God, according to the mind of Plato, is never described as some extended and fluid Being. Nor can the word "to beget" <note>original Greek: γενναν (gennan)</note> be pushed beyond measure here. The ancient theologians, when they spoke of the ineffable mystery of the Trinity, frequently used the word <term>efflux<gloss>original Greek: αποῤῥοιας (aporrhoias); a flowing out or emanation</gloss></term>, yet they diligently enjoined that caution must be taken lest readers persuade themselves that an emanation properly so-called takes place. It is helpful to have proved this with certain testimonies, which are found in great number in the works of Petavius, Huet, and Bull. Athanasius, in his book *On the Decrees*, page 409, says:

> *The generation of men is of one kind, but the Son arises from the Father in another. For the offspring of men are, in a way, parts of those who beget them. Since the nature of bodies itself is not simple, but fluid and composed of parts; and men flow away when they beget; and in turn, when they are nourished, food and drink flow into them, for which reason men become fathers of many children over time. But God,* he says, *being indivisible*

For it is impossible for a nature devoid of matter, intellectual and incorporeal, to admit any corporeal affection; but these things must be understood by divine and secret reasons.* Hence the most learned Bull, in his *Defense of the Nicene Faith*, page 197, after he had defended Origen against the illustrious Huet, explains what they intended to denote by the likeness of the Sun and its rays (which the ancients frequently used) in this way: *“To put it briefly, Origen and other Catholic Fathers, employing that likeness of the Sun and the ray, or light and splendor, wished to signify only these things, and nothing else came into their minds: 1. That the Father is the source of divinity <note>original Greek: πηγην θεοτητος (pēgēn theotētos)</note>, just as the Sun is the source of the splendor emitted from it. 2. That the Son is of the same nature and substance as the Father, inasmuch as he is begotten from the Father's own essence, as light flows from light. 3. That the Son by no means exists divided and separated from his Father, just as a ray is not disjoined from the Sun, nor splendor from light. 4. these conceptions of our mind regarding the adorable generation of the Son of God are wonderfully aided by that comparison, which was even employed by the Nicene Fathers in their very confession of faith. The same comparison pleased the Most Reverend Father in Christ, Tillotson, a man as excellent in other gifts and virtues as he was especially sharp and discerning. For in his 45th Sermon on the divinity of Jesus Christ (Volume 6, French Edition, page 29 and following), he speaks thus of our Savior: *He was God, in that he participated in the divine Nature and Felicity, together with the Father, and in that he proceeded from the Father as Light proceeds from the Sun. I use this comparison after the ancient Fathers of the primitive Church, and perhaps it is more suited to explaining the mystery: For one must not get it into one's head to find among finite Beings any exact resemblance to that which is infinite and consequently incomprehensible. The thing is impossible, because everything that is infinite is by that very fact above the reach of a finite intelligence, and whoever wishes to undertake it will soon perceive that he is lost in that abyss.* <note>Tillotson was a famous 17th-century Archbishop of Canterbury known for his clear and moderate style.</note> <margin>(*) Various theologians and commentators on Hebrews 1:3 emphasize similar points.</margin> (*) From the cited passages it is clear that the ancients used the word <term>outflow<gloss>original Greek: ἀποῤῥοίας (aporrhoias)</gloss></term> of light, ray, etc., when they spoke of the eternal generation of the Son; yet in the meantime, they most strictly distanced themselves from any "emanation" properly so-called, because such an emanation could not possibly be consistent with the intellectual and most excellent nature of God. If, therefore, Plato had said most emphatically that the <term>Logos<gloss>the Divine Word or Reason</gloss></term> was the progeny of God, it would still not be proven that any "flow" or separation of parts took place here, unless it were proven from elsewhere by the clearest evidence that Plato's God was some sort of fluid and composed of parts. tes continues: *“Wherefore,” he says, “pursuing that reasoning further, we may assert what we have often said: that a certain infinity exists in this universe, and a sufficient limit and a cause of no small nobility is always present, adorning and disposing the seasons, months, and years, which is rightly called mind and wisdom.” Protarchus: “Rightly so.” Socrates: “But wisdom and mind are never found without a soul.” Protarchus: “Certainly never.” Socrates: “Therefore, you will admit that in the nature of Zeus <note>original: 'Jovis' (Jupiter), whom Plato identifies as the supreme Mind</note> himself there is a royal soul and a royal mind by the power of the cause, and in others likewise other beautiful things, as pleases each of them.” Protarchus: “Most certainly.”* Socrates: *“Do not think, Protarchus, that the preceding discourse was introduced at random; for it offers support to those who anciently showed that mind presides over the whole world.”* Protarchus: *“It certainly does.”* Socrates: *“And it provides an answer to my request: that mind is a certain progeny of that cause which is called the cause of all things, and which is one of these four things that were mentioned.”* You now have our explanation. But even if the conversation were about the <term>Logos</term>, that same passage would teach that its origin is only to be understood in an intellectual sense, since he asserts that a royal soul and a royal mind reside in the nature of God.

XXVII. Now <term>Dr. Gundling</term> proceeds to the "soul of the world," intending to prove that it likewise emanated from the second principle. He says in Section XXVI: "Whether the soul of the world arose from the divine mind can be doubted all the less, since it is certain that it participates in the mind: *which participation surely cannot be conceived without emanation.*" He appeals to a passage in the *Timaeus* <note>Plato's dialogue concerning the creation of the physical world</note>. For when he had spoken of that <term>Demiurge<gloss>the 'craftsman' or creator-god in Plato's philosophy</gloss></term>, who is the <term>Mind<gloss>original Greek: νυς (nous)</gloss></term>, he also showed how the world soul was generated by him as a <term>contributing cause<gloss>original Greek: συναιτιον (synaition)</gloss></term>. *And placing the soul in its center, he stretched it through the whole, and even covered the body with it from the outside; and having embraced it, he established a single, solitary, revolving heaven, turning in a circle.* i.e. *He placed the soul in its midst and extended it through the whole. Then he surrounded it with the body, and clothed it from the outside, and encompassed it with a lonely, revolving heaven, set in motion in a circle.* Thus says Dr. Gundling. Even if I were to concede that the soul of the world has its origin from the mind—as was asserted by the younger Platonists—this would still do nothing to support the thesis of that Illustrious Man [Gundling]. He wishes to prove that the world soul is a certain "effluvium" <note>a literal flowing out of substance</note> of the divine nature, properly so-called. But it is a mere supposition that Plato's God consists of fluid matter; it is a mere supposition that the <term>Logos</term> is some principle composed of parts. If therefore the soul

<margin>(*) Nemesius, in *On the Nature of Man*, chapter 2, page 81, clearly teaches that the soul of the world is not a body. There is one soul of this universe, but there are also others of individual things, so that the universe is separately animated by the soul of the universe, and likewise individual things are each endowed with their own soul. But the soul He did not create last, as we have just begun to say, only after He had fashioned the body for it.* From this passage it is very clearly evident that God, that primary Mind, fashioned the world; that world-soul was indeed inserted into that same world, but was by no means torn out from His essence. Even if we establish three principles with the Platonists—the second arising from the first, and the third from the second, each distinguished by degrees of perfection—even this does not help the Distinguished Gentleman. For the first is always described by Plato and his followers as most perfect, most eminent, and placed above all power of understanding. The second is always described as an <term>intelligible pattern<gloss>Greek: νοατον παραδειγμα (noaton paradeigma)</gloss></term>. <margin>(*) Porphyry, a man most skilled in Platonic philosophy, speaks thus on this matter in his 24th Sentence, according to Holstenius's version: Everything generated has a cause of its generation from another, since nothing is produced without a cause. However, whatever generated things obtain their essence through composition are, for that very reason, corruptible. But whatever things are simple and uncomposed, having their essence in a simple subsistence, being indissoluble, are also incorruptible. They are called "generated" not because they are composed, but because they depend on some cause. Bodies, therefore, are generated in two ways: both insofar as they depend on a producing cause, and insofar as they are composed. But the soul and intellect are generated only insofar as they depend on a cause, not as composed things. Therefore, bodies are indeed generated, soluble, and corruptible. But these [soul and intellect] are ungenerated in the sense of being uncomposed—and therefore also indissoluble and incorruptible—yet generated in the sense of being dependent on a cause. <note>Porphyry was a 3rd-century Neoplatonist; Lucas Holstenius was a 17th-century scholar and translator.</note></margin>

<margin>(**) Difficulties pressed not only upon Plato but also upon those from whom he received this dogma, regarding how the intellectual principle could diffuse itself through all parts of matter and permeate them. To remove this, Plato gave the nature of the world-soul something not only from the indivisible (that is, the intellectual) but also from the divisible (that is, matter), which Plutarch clearly sets as the foundation in his work *On the Creation of the Soul in the Timaeus*. But Zeno, who saw that the difficulties were increased rather than diminished by this reasoning, fled to a purely material principle. He made God not only entirely the same as the world-soul, but in fact material—namely, the purest and ethereal fire. By this he avoided those difficulties, but fell into greater errors and inconsistencies in describing the nature of God. <note>Zeno of Citium was the founder of Stoicism, which taught a more physicalist view of the divine.</note></margin>

...and we must not impute anything to him other than what he has either *plainly* professed, or what follows by the most evident consequence from his principles. But, the opponent says, he called that soul a "God about to be born." Let it be so. He called the world that more than once in the *Timaeus*; yet it is well established that matter was separate from God, not expelled from His bosom. That soul is called "God" because it is composed not only of corporeal matter but also of spiritual reality. But, he says, that soul expands itself. That is true. But we have already observed above that this soul is, in some unknown way, tempered from the divisible and the indivisible. The question therefore is whether the soul itself, insofar as it is intelligible, can properly speaking be said to flow or expand itself. From its nature, insofar as it is an intellectual thing, this by no means follows. (*) If it has its origin from the Mind, there is no place for expansion there either. Insofar as it is clothed in a body, it can perform this. For it is most likely that the world-soul is clothed in a certain corporeal vehicle so that it can pervade all parts of the world. (**) And if we read Timaeus of Locri, the traces of this matter are not entirely vanished; for when he speaks of the human soul on page 656, he says: <note>original Greek: τὰς μὲν γὰρ ἀνθρωπίνας ψυχὰς τὸ μὲν λογικὸν ἐστὶ καὶ νοερὸν... Of the rational part, the better comes from the nature of the Same; the worse part comes from the nature of the Other.*

...and foolish. *Indeed, of that part which participates in reason, the better and more powerful part belongs to its own nature; the worse, however, belongs to another.* <note>The author is quoting a distinction between the rational and irrational aspects of existence.</note> Moreover, on page 548, he speaks in a similar way regarding the origin of the world-soul. From this it is clear that the soul of the world—insofar as it is clothed in a certain thin vehicle—is suited for carrying out the swiftest operations within bodies. However, it does not follow from this that the soul, insofar as it is <term>something intellectual<gloss>original Greek: noeron ti esti</gloss></term>, is also subject to flux and division.

But (so he continues), *God nonetheless expands Himself in this way.* I deny this, if by the name of "God" you understand the first or second principle. For neither of these consists of parts, nor are they necessarily joined with the soul of the world. I concede the point if the third principle <note>In Platonic thought, the "three principles" or "hypostases" are often seen as the One/The Good, the Intellect (Logos), and the World-Soul.</note> is understood. Nor does the word <term>God<gloss>original Greek: Theos</gloss></term> stand in our way; for this term is also attributed to gods, demons, stars, the earth, and this very world. Yet no one would rightly conclude from this that these things possess the same power and force as the Highest God.

But, you say, the second principle arose from the first, and the third from the second. I have already stated that clear evidence for this is scarcely found in Plato or Timaeus Locrus. But even if we suppose this to be the case, I say it must be proven that those three principles are not merely *distinct by a certain precision of the mind*, or *distinct from one another like solid parts.* It must be proven that it is plainly contradictory and impossible for any other gradation to exist in divine matters except that which occurs through "flux" and the separation of parts.

The Distinguished Gentleman himself, on page 217, says, *nothing flows out from an incorporeal thing, or if something were to be produced and flow forth, it would be likewise similar to it.* But he has nowhere proven by any testimony that God, according to Plato's mind, is a "flowing" principle. Therefore, if those three principles arose from one another, it was not done through physical flux; consequently, "emanations" in this sense involve no impiety. Yet on that same page 217, he shamefully twists my words. On page 887 and following of my *Dissertation*, I said: "Not every connection of God with the world involves Spinozism." In my opinion (so my words sound), *even the most excellent systems of modern philosophers would have to be called pure and simple Spinozism if—take note—the most free connection of God with matter proved it.* <note>Spinozism was a controversial 17th-century philosophy suggesting God and Nature are the same substance; here, the author argues that God's *voluntary* connection to the world is not the same as being *identical* to it.</note> In the Christian system, a certain connection of God with the world has a place, but it is by no means a necessary one; rather, it is as free as can be. I stated there that this connection consists in the fact that God governs the world according to certain laws not founded in the nature of matter; indeed, by a certain continuous and uninterrupted preservation, He sustains it so that it cannot fall back into ancient Chaos, or rather, into Nothingness. But he claims I said that even if God were joined with matter, Atheism would still not follow. In Section XXX, he proceeds to weave consequences from principles not yet proven. *But as for that difference,* he says, *where one thing is first, another second, and so on—I strongly doubt whether sharp-minded men skilled in these matters could be content with such a thing.*

<column-break/>

<page-num>907</page-num>

But suppose they are content; there will still be a sufficiently large portion of Divinity communicated to the soul of the world, which expands itself into all regions of heaven and earth, and is found everywhere conspicuous in various states.

I respond, first: the question is not whether Plato’s thought on the three principles and their gradation satisfies "sharp-minded men." Doubtless, it would have been better if he had kept silent about things he did not understand. But since Plato, who seems to surpass others in wisdom, spoke of these three principles, the only question is how they are to be explained. 2. We confess, therefore, that the soul of the world has its origin from God, although neither Plato nor Timaeus Locrus distinctly pass down the mode of that origin. That "communication" of divinity, as we said above, is unknown to us. The Distinguished Gentleman assumes a "flux" or "emanation," but he does not prove it. Namely, it must be proven that the soul of the world is, properly speaking, a part of divinity (*) so that it necessarily follows that God Himself is joined with all plants and animals. This must either be traced back to the nature of the second principle, or it must be demonstrated that in intellectual matters, no emanation (if I may use this word) can take place except that which occurs through the separation of parts. This latter point cannot be proven; nor can the former. For it is repugnant to all the testimony of the ancients that <term>the Logos<gloss>the Word or Divine Reason</gloss></term> is a flowing, expanded principle.

3. Therefore, if that soul of the world wanders through all parts of heaven and earth, it does not yet follow that God or the second principle does the same, or that God Himself is confused with material things. Indeed, it cannot even be proven that the soul of the world becomes one substance with the bodies which it makes fruitful. For that operation upon bodies does not yet bring about a mixing with them. God preserves all things at every moment, yet He is not mixed with His creatures for any reason. Even the Platonists themselves are opposed to this. Plotinus, in *Ennead* II, Book 2, chapter 1, page 108: <note>Plotinus was a major Neoplatonist philosopher; here he is quoted to show the soul remains a whole even when present everywhere.</note> *For nature itself is that which has been ordered by the whole soul; moreover, the soul of the world, existing everywhere, not divided into parts but whole everywhere, gives also to the heaven so that it too, as far as it is able, is everywhere.* See the same author in *Ennead* II, Book IX, chapter 7, page 205; *Ennead* III, Book I, chapter 10, page 230. His words are clearest in *Ennead* IV, Book IV, chapter 11, page 405.

For it is not because the things that come to be are varied and different that one must believe the agent of these things follows along with the changes of the things being made. For to the degree that the things produced are varied, the act of producing remains the same. <note>original Greek: ἐ γὰρ δὴ, ὅτι ποικίλα καὶ διάφορα τὰ γινόμενα, δεῖ συνεπόμενον ταῖς τε γινομέναις μεταβολαῖς, καὶ τὸ ποιοῦν ἡγεῖσθαι. ὅσῳ γὰρ ποικίλα τὰ γινόμενα τοσούτῳ τὸ ποιεῖν ὡσαύτως μένον.</note> That is to say: one should not think, simply because the things that are made are varied and diverse, that the <term>Effector<gloss>The one who brings about an effect; the Creator</gloss></term> shares in the very mutations of the things He makes. Insofar as the things made are varied, the Effector Himself remains in the same steady state. Therefore, it cannot be proved by either arguments or testimonies that the "soul of the world," which pervades all bodies, merges into a single substance with those bodies—much less can this be said of God, the most noble Mind. He repeats the same points concerning the flow and <term>Emanation<gloss>the idea that things "flow out" from a divine source</gloss></term> of those principles in Section 30 and the sections following. I have proved, however, unless I am mistaken, that very point both in my dissertation and in this vindication. For although **Plato’s** God did not create matter, but only "adorned" or organized it, He can still be called the **Efficient Cause of the world**, just like a craftsman who shapes a tool out of material. Therefore, whether you like it or not, and seeing it with your own eyes, you must admit that life was infused into matter—which your Plato calls the "soul of the world"—on account of which he finally called the world itself "God."* If I were to respond to these points by saying I do not know how God, according to **Plato’s** thought, organized matter, would he have something to criticize? Would it follow from my ignorance that I lose my case? I should not think so. To prove this, I shall use the same freedom of questioning that the *Distinguished Gentleman* claims for himself. Here, the author addresses Plato's habit of calling the stars and the world "Gods," arguing this is a matter of terminology rather than a belief in a single, pantheistic substance.</meta>

In my dissertation, I acknowledged that the world, the stars, and the earth are called <note>original Greek: $\Theta\varepsilon\omicron\upsilon\varsigma$ / Theous</note> **Gods**, but I denied that this was meant in the sense that *Spinoza* intends. For in the *Timaeus*, *Plato* always very clearly distinguishes the <note>original Greek: $\Theta\varepsilon\omicron\upsilon\varsigma$ $\gamma\varepsilon\nu\nu\eta\tau\omicron\upsilon\varsigma$ / theous gennetous</note> **created gods** from the supreme governor of all things, whom he calls the <term>Demiurge<gloss>From the Greek 'demiourgos,' meaning a craftsman or artisan; in Plato's philosophy, the entity who fashions the physical universe out of pre-existing matter</gloss></term> and the **father** of all things. From this, it is evident that the term "Gods" must be understood in a very diluted sense. Nor was it truly necessary to call upon that passage from *Cicero’s On the Nature of the Gods*, in which the character *Velleius* <note>Velleius was an Epicurean speaker in Cicero's dialogue who criticized other philosophers.</note> accuses *Plato* of inconsistency because he sometimes said the earth, stars, and world were **God**, and at other times the governor of all things. For the real point to be proven is whether those "Gods"—the earth, the stars, and so on—make up one single thing with the best and greatest God, the Governor of all, or are compressed into a single substance. The question is not whether they are merely *called* Gods, about which there is no dispute.

However, my opponent appeals to Book X of *Plato’s Laws*, in which *Plato* asserts that the soul driving the sun should be called a God, and indeed that "all things are full of Gods." But I easily concede all of this. *Plato* calls not only the soul driving the sun a "God," but also the other intellectual substances assigned to specific stars; thus he recognizes innumerable substances that are very different from one another. We find no other reason for this naming than that those substances are the most excellent of all things. Indeed, the **most learned Le Clerc** taught in his *Art of Criticism* that anything excellent in its own category can be so named. This is why *Cicero* calls *Plato* the **God of Philosophers**.

Furthermore, my opponent will be unable to prove with any clear testimony that those souls assigned to the stars are called "God" because they are parts "torn away and shredded" from the divine Essence. Even the very passage of *Plato* to which the **Illustrious Man** <note>Referring to the opponent, likely Gundling.</note> appeals suggests something else. For how does the full passage sound in the version by *Ficino*? <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499) was the primary Latin translator of Plato during the Renaissance.</note>

*Athenian:* If a soul leads the Sun, Moon, and the other stars, does it not lead each one individually?
*Clinias:* Why not?
*Athenian:* Let us speak then of one, in words that can be applied to all the stars.
*Clinias:* Which one?
*Athenian:* All men see the body of the Sun, but no one sees its soul—nor indeed the soul of any other animal's body, whether living or dead. Since that kind of thing is perceived by no bodily sense, it is grasped by the mind alone. Therefore, let us grasp this by our intelligence alone.
*Clinias:* Grasp what?
*Athenian:* Since a soul moves the sun, if we assert that this happens in one of three ways, perhaps we shall not be in error.
*Clinias:* What ways do you mean?
*Athenian:* Either it lives inside this round body and carries it wherever it pleases, just as our soul leads us wherever it pleases. Or, it is outside the body and, having obtained some body of fire or air (as some say), it pushes body with body by force. Or thirdly, although the soul is naked of a body, it possesses other powers that are wondrous beyond measure, and so it leads the way easily.
*Clinias:* Certainly, by one of-
<meta>The text breaks mid-word "of-" (istorum) as it moves to the next column.</meta>

<column-break/>

-these ways, all things must be moved by a soul.
*Athenian:* It is better then that—whether its soul holds that body from within like a chariot and thus pours light upon all, or whether it is outside, or however else one might imagine it—we should all judge it to be a God. Or should we think otherwise?
*Clinias:* Thus certainly, unless one is possessed by extreme madness.
*Athenian:* Furthermore, concerning all the stars, and the moon, and the years, months, and all the seasons, what else shall we say but this very thing? Since a soul and souls endowed with all virtues have been shown to be the causes of all those things, we shall affirm that they are Gods: whether they are in bodies and adorn the whole heaven like certain living beings, or in whatever other way they are said to act.
*Clinias:* Entirely so.
*Athenian:* Therefore, with these things granted, can anyone deny that all things are full of Gods?
*Clinias:* No one is so far out of his mind, guest.

From this passage of *Plato*, it is clear: 
1. Those souls assigned to the stars are entirely distinct from one another. 
2. They are called **Gods** and, according to *Plato’s* mind, are to be honored with a certain worship as Gods. 
3. *Plato* himself did not wish to define the exact way in which they are joined to the celestial bodies. 

Where then does that conclusion remain which **D.G.** <note>Presumably Doctor Gundling.</note> wishes to draw from this? Namely, that these souls, "emanating from the divine essence," make up one single thing with the world, and are *therefore* called God? He appeals to *Cicero’s Academica, Book I, Chapter 8*, in which *Cicero* (interpreting *Plato’s* mind) calls the "World-Soul" a God. He notes that *Huetius* <note>Pierre Daniel Huet (1630–1721), a French bishop and scholar.</note> also understood the passage of *Cicero* in the same sense. From there, he reasons as follows: 

*“For the rest, I leave the choice to you: do you believe that Plato’s supreme God is the soul of the world, and thus you include him within the world? Or do you believe he is a soul born in the second place after the Demiurge, or arisen from the divine mind and the <term>Monad<gloss>In Pythagorean and Platonic thought, the "One" or the first un-divided principle</gloss></term>? If the first, you are finished; if the second, you will certainly not win.”* 

For that opponent argues that this "Arising" establishes a secondary <term>Emanation<gloss>The process of "flowing out" from a source; the critic argues that if the World-Soul is born from God, it is part of God's substance.</gloss></term>, since it is impossible for an "arising" in *Plato’s* system to be explained otherwise than by emanation. This is because everything predicated of the World-Soul implies a divine and eternal <note>original Greek: $\pi\omicron\iota\omicron\tau\eta\tau\alpha$ / poioteta</note> **quality**. *“Whichever way you turn,”* he concludes, *“you will be hemmed in and captured.”*

Thus the **Illustrious man** sings his triumph before the victory. To make this clear, I observe the following:
1. It is true that *Cicero* said the World-Soul is a God; however, it can by no means be inferred from this that the World-Soul is that supreme Deity whom *Plato* praised with such great honors—unless you also say that the heaven, the earth, and the stars were the supreme Deity for *Plato*, which is absurd.
2. I have already proved above, with very clear passages from *Plato* and *Timaeus of Locri*, that the World-Soul is not *Plato’s* supreme God.
3. Therefore, the whole controversy returns to the question of the origin of the World-Soul: namely, whether it is from God or not, and if so, whether it was done through...

through a "flow" <note>original: "fluxum"</note> properly so-called. We have stated above that *Plato* and *Timaeus Locrus* <note>A Pythagorean philosopher whom Plato used as a character in his dialogues; some scholars at this time believed his works were the source for Plato's Timaeus.</note> clearly assert nothing regarding the origin of this World-Soul, while other Platonists maintain that it arose from the <note>original Greek: λογῳ / logō</note> **Logos** <gloss>The Divine Word or Reason</gloss>. We shall have, therefore, in addition to the most excellent Deity, the Father of all things, the <note>original Greek: τον νουν / ton noun</note> **Mind** and the <note>original Greek: την του κοσμου ψυχην / tēn tou kosmou psychēn</note> **Soul of the World**. 4. But even if that World-Soul arose either from the Supreme God or from the Mind, *Gundling* <note>Nicolaus Hieronymus Gundling, the contemporary scholar whom our author is arguing against.</note> must prove that this could not happen in any other way than through a "secretion of parts" properly so-called. This very idea is contrary to the principles of the entire Platonic philosophy, which maintains that **Ideas**, or rather the **intelligible forms** known only by the intellect, arise <note>original Greek: απο του ἑνος / apo tou enos</note> **from the One**. This has been elegantly taught by many, including the celebrated *Brucker* in his *History of Philosophy regarding Ideas*, and in his most elegant dissertation on the agreement of the *Numbers of Pythagoras* with the *Ideas of Plato*, inserted in Volume VII of the *Amoenitates* by the famous *Schelhorn* (*). It is not helpful, therefore, to repeat what has already been said. I have already mentioned above that even the Christians, while struggling to explain the eternal generation of the Son, used the word <note>original Greek: ἀποῤῥοιας / aporrhoias</note> **emanation** <gloss>literally "outflow"</gloss>, yet they utterly rejected any idea of "flow" in the literal sense. I have recently examined Volume 8 of the famous *Fabricius’s Greek Library* and observed that *Eunomius* <note>A 4th-century bishop and leader of an Arian sect who argued that the Son was not of the same essence as the Father.</note> once used a similar argument to subvert the eternal generation of the Son. For he reasons thus on page 272: "For if anyone wishes to make this Essence common with another, or to impart something of this essence to someone, he must attempt to do this either by division and partition, or by comparison. Whichever of these is asserted, the argument will be drawn into many absurdities, or rather, blasphemies. For if it were divided and partitioned, it would no longer be unbegotten, since that which did not previously exist would come into being from the division; moreover, it could no longer be incorruptible, since that partition destroys the whole dignity of incorruptibility." That is: <note>The following is the author's Latin translation of the Greek quote above, which I have rendered here into English.</note> *For if anyone should wish to render this Essence common with some other thing, or to impart something from this essence to someone, he will necessarily attempt to do this either according to a likeness and comparison. Whichever of these is asserted, the assertion itself will surely drag along and bring with it many futilities, or rather, blasphemies. For whether it is divided or cut into parts, it can no longer be "unbegotten," because that thing, which was not there before, would come into being from such a division: indeed, in this way, it cannot be free from corruption, since that partitioning undermines the entire Majesty of Incorruptibility.* Regarding these words of *Eunomius*, the famous *Fabricius* comments: "This is the prize argument of Eunomius—and nearly his only one—that it is impossible for a Son similar to Himself to be generated from an unbegotten divine Essence. Hence, whatever is said in Holy Scripture regarding the generation of the Son, he interprets as Creation." But that argument seems to me of no greater...

weight than if you were to deny that anything could be created and produced by an uncreated divine Essence. *Fabricius* attributes the cause of this assertion to the pride of *Eunomius*, who, taught by his master *Aëtius*, did not hesitate to utter these foolish words: <note>original Greek: τοσουτον αυτον επισταμαι και οιδα, ωσε μη ειδεναι εμαυτον, ως θεον μαλλον επισταμαι / tosouton auton epistamai kai oida, hōse mē eidenai emauton, hōs theon mallon epistamai</note> i.e. *I know God as clearly as He is, and I have obtained such knowledge of Him, that I do not even know myself better than I know Him.* I have brought forward this commentary by the famous *Fabricius* for this reason: to make it clear that to this learned man, some kind of eternal generation in divine matters does not seem impossible without any division of parts. From this it is also clear that even if it were absolutely certain that the World-Soul arose from God, it does not yet follow that God Himself consists of parts, or that He makes a single substance with the World-Soul. 5. But even if I were to concede that the World-Soul arose from God and was most closely connected with God, I would still not be "captured," as my illustrious antagonist <note>Gundling</note> thinks. For I would turn myself to the principle of a "double coexistence"—that matter does not depend on God for its origin, but is only inhabited by Him, just as a body is inhabited by a soul, or a house by a Guest; and thus I would escape the charge. But since my previous arguments are sufficient, there is no fear. Truly that (as the most sharp-witted Professor continues) would be quite "Scholastic" and at the same time "ridiculous" to deny an "outflow" <note>original: "effluxum"</note> where the "sources of the gods" are acknowledged and counted, along with the "light and splendor of the divine mind," and a "fecund abundance, depth, and perfection" derived into all things. To me, however, it seems plainly unworthy of a learned man to assert without ceasing that *Plato*—I say, *Plato*—believed that God consists of parts and that the divine essence was cut into various pieces, yet fail to prove this with clear passages from the ancient writers. I know that the authors of the *Chaldaic Oracles* and the younger Platonists <note>The Neoplatonists of the 3rd-5th centuries AD.</note> frequently spoke of <note>original Greek: ἀποῤῥοιας / aporrhoias</note> **emanations** and similar things; but since I do not find such things in *Plato* or *Timaeus Locrus*, I distrust the empty reasonings they bring forward. Most learned men have long recognized that *Jamblichus*, *Proclus*, *Plotinus*, and the other Professors of the Platonic School did not say what *Plato* actually felt, but what they *thought* he felt. (*) The distinguished...

<margin>
(*) Driven into tight corners and reduced to desperation by the objections of the Christians, and finding no way to stabilize and defend Platonic philosophy, they explained those things which they found ugly and <note>original Greek: ἀσυστατα / asystata</note> **inconsistent** in a far different way. Indeed, captured by the divine mystery of the Trinity, yet refusing to show honor to the Christian religion and the revelation that presented it, they themselves fashioned little reasonings of this sort and empty sounds without meaning, so that they might have at least "Words of Nothing," so to speak, to oppose to the most excellent doctrines of the Christians. This will be very clear to anyone scanning the literary history of those times. And yet, no one who has read even two lines of the *Oracles* would assert that they understood something material by "God" and "intellectual things."
</margin>

<header>VINDICATION OF THE DISSERTATION</header>

**Fabricius** <note>Johann Albert Fabricius (1668–1736), a famous German classical scholar and bibliographer.</note>, a man most skilled in these matters, speaks thus in his *Greek Library, Volume 8, page 516*, regarding Proclus’s *Commentary on the Theology of Plato*: *"It is customary,"* he says, *"among the more recent Platonists from Plotinus onwards, to either attach or substitute a thousand alien dogmas to that Philosopher's doctrine, and yet sell them as genuine universal Platonism—as if Plato, if he did not think so, certainly ought to have thought so, as they themselves imagine."* The most learned **Cudworth** <note>Ralph Cudworth (1717–1788), an English philosopher and member of the Cambridge Platonists.</note> feels the same, as cited by the same Fabricius on page 524; to whom the eminent *Jean Le Clerc* <note>A prominent Genevan theologian and scholar.</note> adds his own approval in his notes to the *Chaldaean Oracles, page 1198, Olearius Edition, and Select Library, Volume 3, page 89.* Even the **Distinguished Gundling** himself, in his *History of Moral Philosophy, page 20*, attributes the *Chaldaean Oracles* <note>A collection of mystical poems from the 2nd century AD, much admired by Neoplatonists but distinct from Plato’s own era.</note> to these more recent Platonists, and writes that he does not understand them. Since he himself thinks that Proclus’s claim about **Plato** believing in "Creation out of nothing" is a mere fiction, why then does he wish to attribute everything believed by the later Platonists to *Plato* himself? Most of the talk about <term>effluxes</term> <gloss>original Greek: ἀποῤῥοίαις / aporrhoiais; the idea that reality "flows out" from the divine</gloss> and "intellectual sections," the "source of sources," and the "paternal abyss," are the inventions and fictions of those later Platonists. We can only admit these ideas when they agree with the clear decrees of *Plato*; but as soon as they depart from them and interpret *Plato* at their own whim, there is no reason why we should stubbornly cling to their words or claim that *Plato* must not be interpreted otherwise. (*) Hence it is now clear enough what should be said regarding the passages of Proclus and Plotinus cited in Sections 40 and 41. They speak at length about divine "flowings" and the source of ideas from which all intellectual things arise, yet they nowhere clearly indicate that all these things must be explained through a "flow" *properly so-called*. At the very least, anyone who reads the *Chaldaean Oracles* attentively perceives that most things are expressed in such obscure words that I am firmly persuaded that not even the authors of these Oracles knew what they were saying. Thus, the very passages cited by the Distinguished Gentleman are too obscure to denote emanation and efflux in the proper sense. Proclus, in his *Platonic Theology*, Book VI, chapter 2—

> (*) Let Plato himself speak on this subject. In the *Phaedo*, page 78, he reveals his mind thus: <note>original Greek: αὐτη οὐσία, ἧς λογον δίδομεν... etc.</note> i.e., *"That very essence, which we defined by the power of questions and answers as 'that which truly exists'—does it always remain the same and in the same state, or is it different at different times? Does equality itself, beauty itself, each thing itself (that is, that which truly exists) ever admit any change whatsoever? Or does each of them, being of a single form and existing by itself, always remain the same and in the same state, never admitting any alteration in any way?" "It is necessary, O Cebes," he replied, "that they remain the same and in the same state."* <note>Plato is arguing that the divine "Forms" or "Essences" are unchanging and stable, which contradicts the idea of a "flowing" or changing divine substance.</note>

—says: <note>original Greek: μια σειρὰ καὶ τὰξις ἀδιάλυτος... etc.</note> i.e., *"A single chain and indissoluble order descends from above, because of the unsurpassed goodness of the first cause and its singular power."* Regarding these words, *the Distinguished Le Clerc* says: *"They thought,"* he says, *"that from the most hidden intelligible unity, that is from the supreme God, all natures flowed through various degrees of properties, so that the less excellent were subject to the more excellent."* However, it is not yet clear from these words—as *Gundling* thinks—that all things necessarily emanated from the divine essence as if from a fountain; rather, only this: that all things arose from God and intellectual substances; but he does not explain the *manner*. I say the same regarding the passage in *Enneads* IV, Book 3, chapter 9, to which he appeals to prove that the world is not separate from its maker. # VINDICATION OF THE DISSERTATION

...to persuade the Reader that he builds his assertions upon the firmest testimonies, being well aware that most people do not actually look up those passages. The first is found in *Ennead II, Book I, chapter 2*; from this, he wishes to prove that, according to Plato's mind, the world is preserved through a continuous flux. But even if I were to concede this point most fully, the **Distinguished Man** <note>Referring to Nicolaus Hieronymus Gundling (1671–1729), the author's primary intellectual opponent in this debate.</note> would gain nothing: for it would still have to be proven that the preservation of the world, in Plato's view, consists in the fact that all things flow by necessity from the divine nature. Yet Plotinus makes mention of neither the former nor the latter in this place. In the first two chapters of this book, he asks whether the heavens are everlasting, both in every individual substance and in species; and immediately at the very beginning of the chapter, he says the world will be perpetual **through the will of God** <note>original Greek: διὰ τὴν τοῦ Θεοῦ θέλησιν</note>; not through some perpetual flowing out from God. Moreover, at the beginning of the second chapter, he speaks only hesitantly about the manner of the perpetual preservation of the heavens and sublunary things, saying: *"If we admit this opinion and say that the heaven and all celestial things possess an everlasting perseverance according to the individual substance of each: but that those things which are below the moon possess it only according to species, it will have to be demonstrated how it is possible for that which has a body to always preserve the same nature under a singular property, since the nature of the body itself is in a continuous state of flux."* For this is an ancient opinion, held by others who disputed concerning nature as well as by Plato himself, that there is a perpetual flux not only regarding other things, but even regarding the celestial bodies. (*)

<margin>(*) This is what Plotinus rightly urges from the mind of Plato, who, having adhered to the **Heraclitean Doctrine** <note>The philosophy of Heraclitus, famous for the idea that "everything flows" (*panta rhei*).</note>—which asserted the fluid nature of all corporeal things—and fearing that this would leave no room for either science or the care of things, discovered eternal and self-enduring substances opposed to matter, as **Aristotle** <note>The famous Greek philosopher and student of Plato.</note> reminds us in *Metaphysics, Book XIII, chapter 4*. These are so far from being subject to material flux that he rather ascribes to them a nature diametrically opposite; which clearly proves that in intellectual matters, Plato admitted nothing that has any commonality with "flux" properly so-called, as the **Distinguished Man** <note>Gundling.</note> thinks.</margin>

(*) From which it is clear that the flux of bodies is indeed conceded, but not a single word is mentioned regarding God or other intelligent natures. The other passage of Plotinus is found in the same Book, chapter IV, page 99. Plotinus is still occupied with solving that question: how the heavens can remain perpetually. About to render an explanation, he begins thus: *"For if anyone should join the most powerful cause, namely the soul, together with bodies so pure and altogether better: since even in other animals, nature chooses the better parts for the principal members:"* he will certainly be seen to have brought forward a solid opinion concerning the immortality of the heavens. For Aristotle also rightly says that a flame is a certain heat and fire **as if**,

## ON THE ATHEISM OF PLATO.

**as if** injurious and luxuriant due to its satiety. The celestial fire, however, is equal and quiet, and suited to the nature of the stars. But what is most important, since the soul is nearest to the best things and endowed with wonderful power, by what path could anything that has once been placed in it escape away toward destruction? Having brought these things forward, the words follow to which **Mr. Gundling** appeals: *"If anyone,"* he says, *"has not judged the soul flowing from God to be stronger than any bond, he also surely seems to be ignorant of the cause containing all things."* It is certainly absurd to think that the soul, which can contain the heaven for a time, cannot also do so forever.

From these words of Plotinus, it appears that he intends nothing else than that the bond by which the otherwise fluid heaven is contained is that **World-Soul** <note>The *Anima Mundi*, a concept in Platonic philosophy where the universe is thought to have a soul that mediates between the divine and the material.</note>. But what does the flux of the heavens have to do with proving that all things perpetually flow from the nature of God, and even that God and bodies consist of different parts?

Meanwhile, however, the **Famous Gundling** says in Section 42: *"The conjunction of Plato and the World forced the world into one Deity and substance with God,"* and adds in Section 43: *"For Plato's GOD is the world, and the world is God."* These assertions, as they are built upon no testimonies and fight against all who have explained the Platonic System, so they consist of mere sophisms. Surely the reasoning concerning the conjunction of the World-Soul and the world itself is either altogether vain, or it comes back to this: *"If the World-Soul is God, then God dwells in matter immanently."* But the first part is true. Therefore, the second is. But the **Most Acute Man** <note>Gundling (used sarcastically).</note> wrongly infers this; for the "inhabiting" (to use the terms of the Schools) of the World-Soul does not yet imply **information** <note>A technical term in Scholastic philosophy (*informatio*) meaning to give form to matter so that they become one single being or essence.</note>, for which it is required that the inhabited and the inhabitant be forms of one thing, and that the inhabitant give the form, essence, and nature, and be of one essence. If not, it merely assists, just as our mind dwells in the body, yet it does not "inform" it in that way.

Do you want open testimonies by which I may prove my opinion and subvert the reasoning of Mr. Gundling? Behold the words of Plotinus himself, to whom the Antagonist attributes so much. In *Ennead III, Book 2, chapter 9, page 262*, he speaks thus: **"For Providence must not be such that we are nothing. For if everything were Providence, and it alone, it would not even exist. For of what would it be the Providence? Rather, it would only be the Divine. But this Divine is even now, and it has come toward another, not so as to take away that other, but by approaching it, as if to a man, it preserves him as a man."** <note>original Greek: οὐ γὰρ δὴ οὕτω τὴν πρόνοιαν εἶναι δεῖ, ὥστε μηδὲν ἡμᾶς εἶναι. Πάντα δὲ οὔσης προνοίας, καὶ μόνης αὐτῆς, οὐδ' ἂν εἴη. Τίνος γὰρ ἂν εἴη; ἀλλὰ μόνον ἂν εἴη τὸ Θεῖον. Τοῦτο δὲ καὶ νῦν ἐστι, καὶ πρὸς ἄλλο δὲ ἐλήλυθεν, οὐχ ἵνα ἀνέλῃ τὸ ἄλλο. ἀλλ' ἐπιοῦσα οἷον ἀνθρώπῳ ἣν ἐπ' αὐτῷ τηροῦσα τὸν ἄνθρωπον ὄντα.</note> i.e. *"But it is not right that Providence should be such that we are altogether nothing; otherwise, if Providence itself were all things, and it alone, it would no longer be Providence."* For of whom would it further be the Providence? Indeed, it would only be the Divinity. But now the Divinity indeed is, and betakes itself to another, yet not so as to take that other away: but approach—
