...descending, for example, to man, he preserves in him that which it is to be a man. Do you wish me to reason from the very principles of Platonic Philosophy? Then I shall return to the two eternal and independent principles, to the most celebrated distinction between **intelligible and sensible things** <note>original Greek: τῶν νοητῶν καὶ αἰσθητῶν. This refers to Plato's Theory of Forms, which separates the physical world we sense from the perfect, intellectual world of ideas.</note>, and to the origin of the soul of the world, as it is described by Plato and **Timaeus Locrus** <note>A Pythagorean philosopher whose works were thought to have influenced Plato's "Timaeus."</note>. Furthermore, those words of **Gundling** <note>Nicolaus Hieronymus Gundling (1671–1729), the author’s intellectual opponent.</note>: *Plato’s God is the world, and the world is God*, involve the fallacy of composition. It can be said that Plato's God is the world **by a shared excellence** <note>original Greek: συνενδοκιμῶς</note> because of its more excellent part, namely the soul of the world, but not because of the same underlying meaning. Furthermore, Plato’s God is a world consisting of mind (so to speak) and body, but not of matter; just as a man consisting of mind and body is a rational creature—a name taken from the more powerful part—but he is not a body. It would be absurd, therefore, to assert that a "rational body" is established simply because man is called rational, since mind and body differ essentially. No one would say the members of the body are the mind, or that the members of the body and the members of the mind are one, simply because the mind operates in the whole body.

Let fair judges of things decide, therefore, by what right, destitute of solid reasons and arguments, the **Man of Most Elegant Talent** <note>Referring sarcastically to Gundling.</note> in Section 43 exclaimed: *He who seeks a clearer proof, I shall not cease to pray for a good mind and sharper eyes for him.* The rest, which are said up to Section 47, are merely repetitions built upon no arguments or testimonies; and above, if I am not mistaken, they have been sufficiently and more than sufficiently refuted. 

One thing only must be added concerning matter, which he contends in Section 54 and following is **non-Being** <note>original Latin: non-Ens</note>, yet at the same time taken from the nature of God. I have said above to what extent matter is not included among **real beings** <note>original Greek: τὰ ὄντα</note>. Let us only observe that this very hypothesis of Gundling’s subverts his own opinion about the origin of matter from God. For if matter is from God—like ideas, mind, the world-soul, and other **intellectual things** <note>original Greek: νοερά</note>—it will also be a **being** <note>original Greek: ὂν</note>, because it participates **from that which is** <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τε ὄντος</note>, as those **beings** <note>original Greek: ὄντα</note> truly are. Since this does not happen according to Gundling’s mind, matter also cannot be from God. Yet it does not follow from this that matter does not exist because it is **not being** <note>original Greek: ἐκ ὂν; likely a typo for οὐκ ὄν</note>; but only that it is nothing stable, which Gundling himself would not deny, considering those things he brings forward on page 77, and which **Iamblichus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> asserts at greater length in his work on Nicomachus. <note>(*) And **Porphyry** in his *Sentences*.</note>

The other matter concerns a passage of Plato in the *Philebus*, page 88 in the edition of **Ficino** <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), who translated Plato's works into Latin during the Renaissance.</note>. Gundling contends that Plato, in the cited passage, clearly confesses that the human soul and all bodies are parts of the universe, and taken from that one substance. In a word, he claims that only one substance exists, just as in the system of **Spinoza** <note>Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677), whose philosophy argued that God and Nature are the same substance—a view many 18th-century scholars called atheism.</note>, according to Plato’s mind. The words sound like this from Ficino’s version: *Soc. And by the name of the nature of the efficient cause it only-*

<page-num>919</page-num>

*differs from the Cause, and the Efficient and the Cause will rightly be called one. Pr. Rightly. Soc. Furthermore, that which is made and that which is generated will differ only in name. Pr. Certainly. Soc. Indeed, the nature which is the Efficient always precedes and leads; but that which is made by it, and generated, follows it.* 

Let us bring forward only the preceding and the immediately following words, so that the force of Gundling’s inference may be clear. In the preceding parts, Plato spoke of the infinite, the limit, and that which consists of these two. Then he brings in **Socrates** speaking thus: *But, he says, it remains to be discussed what the fourth kind might be besides these three. This is a common discussion. For see whether it does not seem necessary to you that whatever is generated is generated through some cause. Pro. Clearly to me. For how could it be made without it?* 

Then follow the cited words, after which Socrates continues: *Therefore, the cause and that which serves the cause for generation are not the same, but something different. Pro. What prevents it? Soc. Have not the generated things themselves, and those from which all things are generated, provided us with three kinds? Pro. Very much so. Soc. But we place the Maker of all these as a fourth, and we call him the cause, as being something other than...*

<insert>NB. those things have been demonstrated sufficiently.</insert> 

This passage is so far from serving Gundling's cause that it rather destroys it most evidently. For those three—namely, the **limit**, the **infinite**, and what is composed of them—are numbered among the things made and generated; but the **Maker** is set over them as the Cause, as the Efficient, and is distinguished from those very things generated and made. How then will God and matter and all other things be only one substance, as Gundling contends? 

And yet on page 268 he exclaims: *Listen, Zimmermann! The generated differs from the Efficient and the cause in name only, just as the efficient and the cause differ.* Should we listen to Gundling, who appeals to Plato when Plato is saying something entirely different from what he wants? Plato says the efficient is distinguished from the thing made and generated. Gundling says it is in name only. Therefore, let the Reader see which one is to be trusted. 

Indeed, even if it could be proved from this passage that the efficient cause and the effect do not differ in essence in the manner of an emanation, Gundling's goal would still not follow. For if we suppose that our minds emanated from God, it would follow that they are of the same essence as God. If all bodies arose from matter, our bodies likewise will be of the same essence as matter. But it must be shown that these various parts—namely, God and matter—are one. They can be called one in respect of essence: God [and] the generated, **Note Well** <note>original Latin: NB.</note> in spiritual matters; matter [and] the generated form, **Note Well** in material matters; and yet they remain two most diverse substances.

<meta>This page continues the author's argument regarding Plato's view on the eternity of time. In the preceding section, he began refuting the claims of Nicolaus Hieronymus Gundling, who argues that Plato's "God" is essentially synonymous with the material world. Here, the author brings in the testimony of Timaeus of Locri to prove that Plato believed the world—and time itself—had a specific beginning.</meta>

<page-num>920</page-num>
<header>DEFENSE OF THE DISSERTATION</header>

...eternity. In my dissertation, I cited the most famous passages of **Plato** and **Timaeus of Locri** <note>Timaeus of Locri was a Pythagorean philosopher; Plato named one of his most famous dialogues, the *Timaeus*, after him.</note>, which prove that *Plato* believed that time is not eternal, but that time arose simultaneously with the world. However, **Doctor Gundling** <note>Nicolaus Hieronymus Gundling (1671–1729), a German jurist and philosopher whom the author is criticizing.</note> interprets these matters quite differently and contrary to the light of the most famous testimonies on page 284. For after he has dictated what ought to be observed concerning this subject, he proposes his own opinion as follows: *I hold it as certain that Plato described matter as eternal along with Timaeus of Locri, and that it existed through the intervening **Reason** <note>original Greek: λογῳ (logō). In this context, it refers to the divine intellect or word.</note>; which **Abraham Gravius** <note>A 17th-century Dutch philosopher and mathematician.</note> explains not poorly, saying that matter was brought forth by this **Reason** or mind, not created out of nothing; but rather **received** <note>original Greek: δεδεγμένην (dedegmenēn)</note>, not at all adorned, but **unformed** <note>original Greek: ἀσχημάτισον (aschēmatiston)</note>; since in the production itself, stages are placed in the sign of reason, through which a greater increase of perfection and adornment would have come to it **conceptually** <note>original Greek: κατ’ ἐπίνοιαν (kat’ epinoian)</note>.* But these things openly conflict with the testimonies of the Ancients. **Matter** is indeed called "eternal," and even "unformed," but only before God shaped it according to that **intelligible paradigm** <note>original Greek: παράδειγμα (paradeigma). This refers to the perfect "blueprint" or Idea God used to create the physical world.</note>; and to this extent, if you consider matter in respect to its origin, the world—insofar as it consists of eternal matter—is eternal. But since Plato, Timaeus of Locri, and many others very clearly testify that this **unformed** matter was adorned by God and changed into various species and forms (God having been moved to this by His own goodness), it is clear that it is a pure and simple invention of the **Renowned Gundling** to assert that this eternal matter was brought forth from eternity not adorned, but **unformed**, and was only adorned in time "in the sign of reason," as he puts he. For what is clearer and more evident than the words of **Timaeus of Locri**, whom *Plato* also follows in this part, which are read on page 552 of **Gale's edition** <note>Thomas Gale (1635–1702), an English classicist who edited the works of Timaeus of Locri.</note>: *But these are the parts of time which they call circuits. Moreover, God ordained time together with the world itself. For the stars did not exist before the world, nor consequently did the year exist, nor the seasons of the year, which are distinguished by certain circuits. Time, however, is the image of unbegotten time, which we call eternity. For just as this universe was created according to the model of the intelligible world, so also was this time established by the **Maker** <note>The "Maker" or "Opifex" refers to the Demiurge, the divine craftsman in Platonic philosophy.</note> along with the world, according to eternity as if to a certain Model.* **NB.** <note>Latin "Nota Bene," meaning "Note Well."</note> In this passage, God is openly said to have **adorned** <note>original Greek: κοσμησας (kosmēsas)</note> the world; the world is openly said to have had a beginning along with time; and time is openly called the **image** <note>original Greek: εἰκων (eikōn)</note> of **unbegotten time** <note>original Greek: τω ἀγεννατω χρονω (tō agennatō chronō)</note>. By what reasoning these things can be evaded and twisted into...

...another sense, I confess I do not know. But why, he asks, was that eternal matter not likewise adorned from eternity? It is said that God did not so will it, according to the mind of Plato. *Yet He is good*, he retorts, *from eternity*. Indeed He is. But there is no **necessity** present that compels God to always demonstrate His goodness. All Christians cry out that God is good, yet at the same time, all confess that God founded the world in time. *But if God did not will* (he continues) *at first to found the world, but later did will it, God seems to be mutable.* Even in the opinion of Christians, God did not will to found the world sooner than He did found it, and yet He is not mutable, even though He weighed this in the divine mind from eternity. God determined from eternity to create me; but He did not will to execute the decree of His counsel from eternity. For He does not will that the things He wills should happen from eternity; otherwise, the world with all its creatures would be eternal. Despite these points, **Doctor G.** <note>Gundling</note> nevertheless thinks it *more likely that the world is eternal according to the mind of Plato, than that it was brought forth in time.* But how can these things be reconciled with the words of Plato and **Timaeus of Locri**? Listen: *Just as*, he says, *Moses's distinct intervals of created things do not prevent one from thinking that all things could have been founded at once: so I would be inclined to believe that it is similarly not contradictory that the Athenian Philosopher <note>Plato</note> thought all things were adorned and made at once, matter having appeared from eternity; even if he reviewed the things brought forth one by one and delineated their order.* But this is nothing other than **covering conjectures with more conjectures so that they do not leak through.** <note>A metaphorical way of saying Gundling is making up increasingly complex excuses to support his weak argument.</note> For why should we depart here from the simple meaning of the text? It is enough that **Moses**, as much as **Plato** and **Timaeus of Locri**, states that the world was founded in time, whether this was done through intervals or in a single moment. But my **Opponent** promises weightier reasons on **page 287**. *Plato*, he says, *never answered the question about the eternity of the world directly; he only replied, especially in the Timaeus, that the world was "generated." This response does not satisfy the anxious reader. For the **inquiry** <note>original Greek: ζητημα (zētēma)</note> always recurs: whether it was generated **according to time** <note>original Greek: κατα χρονον (kata chronon)</note>?* Likewise, he asks whether an "eternal generation" would sufficiently contradict his views. What, then, do the words previously cited from **Timaeus of Locri** mean? Does Timaeus not directly state that time only arose together with the world, and that time is only an **image** <note>original Greek: εἰκονα (eikona)</note> of **eternal time** <note>original Greek: χρονου αἰωνιου (chronou aiōniou)</note>? Do these things require an interpreter or some **Oedipus** <note>In Greek mythology, Oedipus was the only one capable of solving the riddle of the Sphinx; the author is saying the text is so clear it doesn't need a genius to solve it.</note>? But let **Plato** himself be heard in the *Timaeus*, speaking directly thus on **page 480**: *When the Father who had begotten the world saw it moved and living, a created image of the eternal gods, he marveled, and being delighted, he thought to make it still more like its model. That is to say: *When the Father who begot it perceived that this beautiful image of the eternal Gods, which he had made, moved and lived, he was delighted with his work. *as the world was rising; all of which are parts of time. However, "was" and "will be," which are species of time once born, we incorrectly assign to the eternal substance. But since the eternal substance perseveres as always the same and immovable, it should never be older or younger than itself, nor was it so until now, nor will it be in the future, nor does it receive any of those things to which corporeal and mobile things are subjected by the very condition of their generation. By this reason and counsel of GOD, wanting to create time, the sun and moon, and the five other stars which are called "erratic" <note>the planets</note>, were made, by which the number of time might be distinguished and observed.* I have brought forward that long passage so that it might be clear to everyone on how groundless a foundation the conjecture of **Doctor Gundling** rests. I do not wish to add a single word to it, since there is no one who does not see that the opinion of **Gundling** fights face-to-face against the assertions of **Plato**.

But it is asked, he says, whether an eternal "becoming" <note>Latin: genesis</note> is truly repugnant to his opinions? For he certainly calls matter "generated," and at the same time <term>eternal</term> <note>original Greek: ἀΐδιον (aïdion)</note>. That an eternal beginning <note>genesis</note> is repugnant to the opinions of **Plato** is taught by everything we said above regarding the origin of the world and the most free will of God in bringing matter into order; indeed, that passage just cited suggests quite clearly what **Plato** felt both about the origin of the world and the beginning of time.

### XXXI.

Dr. Gundling struggles laboriously in Sections 68 and 69 to achieve his aim. For he speaks thus in Section 68: *“This is true: Plato thought nothing more beautiful than the world; and God always wills the most beautiful thing that He understands. God’s willing is never not an act; indeed, in God, power is act. Therefore, it follows from this that the most beautiful intelligible thing is also the most desirable. God’s will is not wandering, but defined; therefore, unless He had created the world immediately, His will would not have been defined, but uncertain.”* Thus says Gundling. I do not know whether this *Learned Gentleman* speaks here in his own name or in Plato’s. Certainly, Plato does not feel this way, but <term>Spinoza<note>Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677), a philosopher whose views were often equated with atheism because he argued that God and Nature are the same and that everything happens by necessity, not free choice.</note></term> does. In Proposition 34, *Spinoza* says roundly: *“God’s power is His very essence.”* In Proposition 35: *“whatever we conceive to be in God’s power, that necessarily exists.”* In Proposition 32: *“the will cannot be called a free cause, but only a necessary one.”* And from this emerge two Corollaries, the first of which is: *“God does not act from freedom of will.”* Second: *“will and intellect relate to God’s nature just as motion and rest do, and absolutely, as all natural things, which must be determined by God to exist and operate in a certain way.”* In Proposition 33: *“Things could have been produced by God in no other way and in no other order than they have been produced.”* In the Scholium to Proposition 17, page 17 and following, he calls the opinion of those who think God could do many things by His power which He nevertheless does not do, an "absurd sentiment." From this, it is easily seen what should be thought of those propositions. Truly, if God’s power is "act," it follows that all things that exist, exist necessarily; that nothing more can be done; and that God is not a free cause, but a necessary one. The will—

—of God is not wandering, but neither is it a necessarily acting agent. By the same argument of Gundling, I could prove that God produced the world and all creatures from eternity. God, forsooth, understood from eternity those things He willed to create; therefore, He wills from eternity what He understands to be beautiful. He saw that this world was most beautiful; therefore, He created it from eternity. Furthermore: God is able to produce the world, therefore He created it from eternity, because power is the same as act from eternity. Moreover, God’s will to create the world is not wandering; therefore, He created the world from eternity, because otherwise His will would not be defined, but wandering. There is no need for me to show how false these reasonings are. 

If the God of Plato, he continues, willed to make the world by an internal will, the <term>paradigm<note>original: παραδειγμα. A pattern or model. In Platonic thought, the eternal forms that God uses as a blueprint for the physical world.</note></term> of which was in the mind of God, He certainly willed to produce it from eternity, and could never not have willed it, just as He is from eternity and could not not be. If at some time He had not willed it, but then began to will it, it would follow that either: 1.) He would not have existed at some time, which is contrary to the eternity and necessity by which God exists; 2.) or His will would differ from His essence, which subverts the simplicity of the Divine Being; or finally 3.) He would not be free from change, which is repugnant to His perfection. 

I respond: 1. From the will of God, insofar as it is taken as an essential attribute of God, to the eternal execution of that same will, there is no logical consequence. God from eternity willed, or decreed, to create me; but I was not, for that reason, formed from eternity. 2. What help is it to distinguish some time in which He did not will, and likewise a time in which He willed to found the world? He willed, or decreed from eternity, to found the world in His own time. Just as the will of God and the things He wills to make are distinct by their nature, so there is no necessary connection at all between the will and the things He wills. Will is an eternal attribute of God, and in that respect He is said to will this or that from eternity; but the things He wills to bring about are not therefore eternal, since the will is a free faculty which acts as infinite wisdom commands. 3. Without doubt, if Plato had introduced a God willing at one moment and not willing at another, it would follow either that He did not exist at some time or that He is changeable. But since this supposition was born in the brain of Gundling, and not in that of Plato, there is no need for us to say anything about the absurdities that follow from it. Dr. Gundling first invents an absurd system, and then subverts it with great force—which is very easy to do. I am not one of those who wish to impose consequences upon anyone which they themselves detest. For this is unworthy of an honest man and a student of wisdom. I know not, meanwhile, how that Illustrious Man slipped into an opinion that is liable to such dangerous consequences. *Power in God is always act. God's willing is never—*

The author is defending his dissertation against Gundling’s claim that Plato’s philosophy aligns with the "necessitarianism" of Spinoza—the idea that everything that exists must exist by necessity, leaving no room for divine or human free will. The author argues that God’s will is a free faculty, even if His essence is eternal.</meta>

is not an *act*. The Will is the same as the *essence*. From these propositions, it follows by necessity that *God can create nothing further, that all things which exist must exist by necessity, and indeed be eternal, and that the will in God is not free, but necessary*. Anyone can see how absurd these ideas are. However, (to repeat myself again) I do not think Gundling actually believes these things, but rather I believe he was carried away by an excessive passion for refuting me when he wrote them. If I had said such things, I would undoubtedly have been given a beating <note>original: "vapulassem," a metaphor for being soundly criticized</note>. But it is better to **speak the truth in love** <note>original Greek: ἀληθεύειν ἐν ἀγάπῃ. A reference to Ephesians 4:15.</note>. After Gundling brought forward those consequences which he claimed flowed from the opinion of *Plato*—or rather from his own opinion—he assumes that *Plato* saw all these things as **absurdities** <term>atopa<note>Greek: ἄτοπα. Literally "out of place," used in philosophy to mean logical absurdities or impossibilities.</note></term>, and therefore that there was no reason why Plato would not have imagined an eternal world. 

We have already spoken regarding those consequences; clearly, they rely on a borrowed hypothesis fabricated by *Gundling*. Without a doubt, the world would have been from eternity if the "Best and Greatest" <note>original: "Optimus Maximus," a traditional title for God</note> had willed to establish it from eternity. There was no obstacle. Matter is a thing prepared for either outcome. No internal factor prohibited it. For the Will of God is free; there is no lack of power, unless you say that God is weak because He did not create us from eternity, which is **absurd** <term>atophon</term>. The Will of God is not "temporary" for that reason. For He does not take counsel "in the sand" <note>meaning He does not make fleeting or unstable plans</note>. The Will, with respect to His essence, is eternal, but the free execution of that will can only take place in time. 

Nor did He change from "one who does not will" into "one who wills." He willed to adorn the raw and disordered mass, but at His own defined time. *Whoever thinks the divine will and essence are different (so continues the famous Gundling on page 291) undermines the simplicity of God and makes Him a composite being.* I do not know what that *most subtle man* was thinking when he wrote this. For the *Will* of God, although it pertains to the Essence of God, is nonetheless a most free *faculty*; the divine *Essence*, however, is *necessary*. Therefore, what God wills, He does not will by necessity, but in the most free manner possible. *Spinoza* asserts that the will is not a free cause, but a necessary one, as his own words cited above testify. The will is undoubtedly necessary insofar as it necessarily belongs to the nature of the most perfect Being; but insofar as it is considered with respect to the things He wills, it is not at all necessary, but most free. 

But here the question is about the Creation of the world. If, therefore, the will of God were just as necessary as the Essence of God itself, it would follow that the world existed necessarily from eternity, that there is no such thing as chance <note>original: "contingentia"</note>, no possibilities, and that God is not a free Being but an agent acting by necessity. These things, I say, would follow from the opinion of *Gundling*. Since, however, he does not admit those absurdities, it is clear what one should think of the foundation upon which the famous gentleman’s assertion is built. I know that those who say God willed to freely establish the world from eternity do not cross over into *Spinoza's* camp.

But it is one thing to say that God willed *freely from eternity* to establish the world, and another to say that the power of God is the *act* itself; that God's willing is never *not* an act; and that the will of God is the *essence* itself. The *former* involves no contradiction; the *latter*, however, would imply the necessary existence of the world and other absurdities. Whether *Pythagoras* or *Parmenides* professed the eternity of the world, I do not wish to inquire here. The question is what *Plato* thought. I have proved by clear passages that he denied the eternity of the world; this is sufficient. Not once, while I wrote these things, did that line of the Poet come to mind: *Where is that fellow rushing off to now?* <note>original: "Quo se nunc proripit ille?" A quote from Virgil's Eclogues 3.19.</note>

### XXXII.

But at last, D.G. <note>likely Doctor Gundling</note> returns to *Timaeus Locrus*, intending to prove that he supports the opinion regarding the eternity of the world. For in Section 73, he speaks thus: *But come, let us return to Timaeus Locrus, who, when discussing time, calls it the **image and pattern** <term>eikona kai paradeigma</term> of eternity.* 

If I see anything at all, *Locrus* says that *time, by our reasoning, is to be compared to the example of eternity*. For just as eternity is infinite existence and a life "all at once" <note>original: "tota simul," a classic definition of eternity by Boethius</note>—that is, God Himself—so time is similarly infinite, flowing forth from the life of God. This God, as *Boëthius* says, *took up the infinite path of time so that by moving He might continue a life that will never end; and thus the world, animated by this life, has no beginning and no end.* It is so true that everyone finds what they are looking for! Gundling did not provide the location of the passage, so that it might not be inspected. We cited it in Section XXX of this dissertation, which should be compared with what is about to be said. 

Clearly, day and night are called parts of time, which God **ordered along with the world** <term>ekosmēsen syn kosmō</term>. Just as the world is said to be **generated** <term>gennatos<note>Greek: γεννατός. Meaning something that has a beginning or was created, as opposed to something eternal.</note></term>, so also is **time** <term>chronos</term>. This is not only noted by the Editor below the text, but the very nature of the matter teaches it; for since time arose simultaneously with the world, and the world is **generated**, it follows that the same must be said of time. 

Furthermore, the comparison established by *Locrus* proves the same thing. This world, which is **generated**, is said to have been made according to some **eternal pattern, an image of the age** <term>paradeigma... aidion, eikona aiōnos</term>. It follows, therefore, that the **pattern** is eternal, but the world is made; eternity is distinguished from **time**, just as that eternal **pattern** is distinct from the world made according to it. Eternity, therefore, according to *Locrus*, belongs only to those things which exist by necessity, while time belongs to things that are not necessary, but made, and dependent upon another. But the world, according to *Plato* and *Timaeus Locrus*, had a beginning; the stars, by whose course we measure time, were made with the world, therefore time also arose with the world. The world, therefore, has a beginning, and therefore time does as well. That which has a beginning can be called neither infinite nor eternal. But the world and time, according to *Timaeus Locrus*, have a beginning; therefore both the world and time are finite. *The life of God* and...

<meta>This page continues the author's rebuttal of Nicolaus Hieronymus Gundling. The author is arguing against Gundling's interpretation of Plato and Timaeus of Locri, specifically regarding whether the world is an eternal "emanation" of God or a creation with a definite beginning in time.</meta>

# DEFENSE OF THE DISSERTATIONS

his continued and never-interrupted existence differs only by a mental abstraction. The world, however, together with time, can be conceived as non-existent without contradiction; just as once it began to exist, it is finite, just as time is fluid and will remain so. What, then, do those words of **Mr. Gundling** mean, that the world is "animated by the life of God"? Either this proposition means that God joined himself to the world from eternity, so that, given the eternal life of God, the eternal duration of the world is also given; or that God, ever and eternally active, willed to establish the world along with time. The former sense openly contradicts the words of the Locrian <note>Timaeus of Locri, a Pythagorean philosopher to whom a treatise on the world was attributed, which was the model for Plato's Timaeus.</note>; for he maintains that time only arose with the world and the stars. If the *latter* is true, the world was established in time, and time arose with the world. Therefore, time does not flow from the life of God or his continued existence; but just as the world has its origin from the most free will of God according to the *Timaeus*, so similarly time has its origin not from the life of God, but from his will. 

But the illustrious gentleman insists, saying: *You say: the world is begotten; that which is begotten is posterior [later]; therefore the world, as something begotten, will be posterior to the one who begets.* I respond: he who says *posterior* posits a *prior*. In God *there is no prior, because in him there is no posterior, nor past, but only IS, and the present: therefore it follows that, from God's perspective, the world is not posterior, because otherwise God would be imagined as prior and posterior.* What remarkable subtlety this is! Clearly, according to the Locrian, the world was **crafted** <term>edamiourgēthē <note>original Greek: εδαμιεργηθη. To be fashioned or built by a craftsman.</note></term>, therefore the world is just as eternal as God himself. In God there is no "before" and "after," no past, but only the present; therefore in the world established by God there is also no "before" and "after." If there were a "before" and "after" in the world, it would follow that God, who contemplated the world, would be prior and posterior to himself. But who does not see the force and incredible efficacy of such reasoning? Clearly, all these things rest on the supposition of a necessary emanation of all things from God, which is most evidently contrary to the assertions of *Timaeus*. 

Wherefore (Mr. G. continues), Plato could nonetheless estimate that the world, though begotten by God, is eternal, because it is an act and infinite life, such that the life of the world is conceived as a continuous line, like a ray of light perpetually flashing. Since, however, that divine light did not emit just one ray, but many; it is only now, by reason of our contemplation, that time arises, which we measure against another in our minds and devise stages as we measure. If this method of explaining the **ancients** is valid, I shall be able to prove anything hereafter. I would also wish that the distinguished gentleman had abstained from metaphorical language. Everything comes down to this: that the world emanated from God from eternity, and we call the intervals of this emanation 

->time<-

but we have already shown abundantly above that the former is false; therefore, the things said about time according to the mind of *Timaeus* and *Plato* are mere guesses. Anyone who simply looks at the passages cited above will see how distorted all these things are. He repeatedly assumes that all things emanated from the nature of God, yet he does not prove it. We are not disputing here about some abstract truths, but about the opinion of **Plato**, which must be presented and explained by the testimony of the ancients. **The Locrian** said the world was **begotten** <term>gennaton <note>original Greek: γεννατον. Something brought into being or generated.</note></term>, and that time had its beginning together with the world. What need is there for more words? Why are there no witnesses present, whom he threatens to bring forth in great numbers? It is tiresome to repeat the same things always. The words of the **Locrian** and **Plato** are clearer than can be twisted into another sense by **Gundling**. The illustrious man is always stuck on the word **to beget** <term>gennan <note>original Greek: γενναν. To father or bring forth.</note></term>, and argues from there. Is the **Craftsman** <term>Dēmiourgos <note>original Greek: Δημιουργος. The divine artisan in Plato’s philosophy.</note></term> the same as the work, as soon as he applies his mind to working on it? As for the insults he heaped on me in Section 76, I gladly pass over them in silence, nor do I envy him the praises he bestows upon himself in the same place.

# DEFENSE OF THE DISSERTATIONS

I only mentioned the passage from Virgil in passing. Even if that passage were most contrary to my position, nothing would follow except that I had appealed to *Virgil* in vain. It very often happens that, to confirm our own opinion, we appeal to those who agree with us in words, but not in sense. Theologians very often cite passages that are actually adverse to the propositions they wish to defend. Does it then follow that everything they have brought forward—even their firmest points or arguments—is therefore void? I should think not. Thus, even if I had appealed to *Virgil* in vain, my arguments cited above would not lose their weight. 

Secondly, however, I do not believe it can be proven by clear passages that this most excellent Poet was a follower of *Spinoza’s* <note>Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677), a philosopher often accused of atheism because he identified God with Nature (pantheism).</note> opinion. I will say nothing now of the passages in which he thinks most nobly of God; I will only appeal to certain passages which seem to prove that he rather crossed over into the camp of *Epicurus* <note>Epicurus taught that the world was formed by the chance collision of atoms in a void, rather than by divine design.</note>. In *Eclogue 6*, he introduces the drunken *Silenus* singing of the origin of all things according to the principles of *Epicurus* in this way:

> For he sang how, through the great void, the seeds
> of the lands, and of the air, and of the sea had been driven together,
> and of the liquid fire as well: how from these first beginnings 
> all things, and the tender globe of the world itself, grew together.

> But as for me, first, may the sweet Muses, 
> whose sacred objects I carry, struck by a great love, 
> receive me: and show me the paths of heaven and the stars.

Hence at line 490:

I would therefore appeal to those things which I have said more than enough on this argument above. It would therefore fall to **Gundling**, defending the views of **Richard Simon** <note>Richard Simon (1638–1712) was a French priest and influential biblical critic; Gundling was a contemporary philosopher and historian often in conflict with the author.</note>, to prove that God Himself is confused and mixed with Matter. **Fourth:** To humor **Gundling**, however, we will suppose that **Virgil** himself understands the most excellent Deity by the name of "God." It would then have to be proven that the words used by the Poet must only be taken in the sense of **Spinoza** <note>Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677) taught that God and Nature are one, a view then equated with atheism.</note>. But this would be difficult in the extreme to prove. For if we wish to explain the opinion of any Author, especially in matters of the greatest importance, then, before we draw conclusions from them, either the words must be so clear that they cannot be understood otherwise, or the mind of that **Author** must be established by us from elsewhere. But neither is the case here. Therefore, his words should not be taken according to the full breadth of their literal sense. Let us illustrate the matter with an example. Suppose we did not know from elsewhere which God the **Holy Scripture** offers for our worship, and in reading we happened upon words which at first sight seem rather harsh—for example: *that we are in God, live and move* <note>original: "nos in Deo esse, vivere & moveri" - Acts 17:28</note>, *that the Spirit of God pervades all things, that we are the temple of God, that we have been made partakers of the divine nature* <note>original: "divinæ naturæ participes factos" - 2 Peter 1:4</note>, *born of God*, etc. We could easily fall into that opinion which **Spinoza** and **Toland** <note>John Toland (1670–1722), a philosopher who coined the term "pantheist."</note> extracted from them. However, as soon as it is established from elsewhere that a most wise, most free, and most holy Deity—entirely distinct from the world and matter—is offered to us for worship, we see that those words are not to be cut to the quick <note>i.e., taken with literalist severity</note>, but are to be interpreted otherwise. Since, however, we do not know what **Virgil** felt about the nature of God—at least since he nowhere expressed the thoughts of his mind on this part—we certainly do not know what power we ought to attribute to individual words and phrases. Thus, we cannot define how that Spirit is said to *nourish from within* <note>original: "intus alere"</note> and to *be diffused through all the limbs*; or by what reason that *mind can be said to mix itself with the whole body* and *go through all lands*. These could be understood in a healthy sense: for no one is unaware that the phrases of Poets can very rarely be pressed for literal precision. We are ignorant, moreover, whether **Virgil** expresses his own mind or that of other Philosophers. But let us suppose that **Virgil’s** mind on this business was known to us from elsewhere, and that by the name of God he understood the most excellent Deity, removed as far as possible from every stain of Matter; then everyone would cry out that his words are not to be taken according to the full breadth of their meaning, but are to be explained according to his established beliefs. Suppose he thought that God was a most noble mind, but—

There are four elements: earth, water, air, ether; and God. Besides these, there is nothing else; and we cannot call this "the world." For the world is not the whole. Therefore, God is indeed a divine Spirit who, infused through the four elements, gives birth to all things. Thus, if all things are born from the elements and from God, they have one origin, and the nature of all is equal. But let us see what in us is from God and what is from the four elements. As far as can be understood, from the elements we have a body, from God a soul; which is proven because that which is in the body—earth, moisture, breath, heat (all of which are visible, just like the elements)—the mind is invisible, just like God, from whom it draws its origin. Those former things, moreover, are irrational, just like the body. On the contrary, God possesses counsel, just like the mind. Furthermore, we see the elements change, and for them to change is to perish; therefore, the mind does not perish, as it does not draw its origin from them. For the part always follows its kind.*

**Servius's** primary intention here was to argue that souls are immortal. *Thus far Servius.* From this, it is clear that he is not at all explaining **Virgil's** meaning by comparing passages and the decrees of philosophers, but simply searching for a meaning—a meaning that is structured in such a way that it is not at all conformable to the opinion of **Spinoza**. **Sixth:** Even if I were finally to concede to **Gundling** that **Virgil** speaks from the mind of **Plato** regarding the "soul of the world," he would still gain nothing. For **Plato** asserts not that the Governor of the Universe, but the soul of the world—born and tempered in I-know-not-what way—is infused into the parts of the world. It must therefore be proven that God Himself, according to the mind of **Virgil** and **Plato**, is melted together into one single substance. *Thus far the most excellent Gundling.* Let the judgment on this matter remain with the learned reader. (*)

### XXXIV.
The famous **Gundling**, in Section 82 of his dissertation, strives to reclaim a passage from **Plutarch** that I had said was cited in vain. Specifically, he wanted to prove from it that **Plato's** God, the Universe, matter, mind, soul, and the world are only different names for one thing. I showed in my dissertation on page 933 that **Plutarch**, in the cited passage, reports the opinions of other philosophers, and I provided the very words of **Plutarch** in which he refutes their opinions. Although the famous man [Gundling] cannot deny this, he nevertheless contends that **Plutarch** favors his own opinion: *In the primary cause,* he says, *the man from Chaeronea <note>Plutarch was born in Chaeronea.</note> frankly confesses that all individual things consist of the intelligent and the sensible: the intelligent being the form, and the sensible being the matter. Indeed, just as the form gives completion to every nature, so it is clear that the divine substance effects this, of which matter becomes a participant; but the soul of the world contains something more besides the intelligible and the sensible, which is in all universal things.* But the words of **Plutarch** himself should have been brought forward. **Plutarch** reviewed the opinions of the most famous philosophers, **Crantor** and **Xenocrates**, concerning the procreation and nature of the soul of the world; having brought these forward, he says: *To me, if probability is to be held as the rule of judging, both seem...*

---

For as the world itself, so also any part of it, consists of those two natures: one provided the matter and the subject, the other the form and the appearance for the thing being born; and whatever part of the matter was shaped by the participation and imitation of the intelligible (for so we may call that which is perceived by the mind alone) nature, it immediately follows that it can be touched and seen. But the soul escapes all sense.* From this passage of **Plutarch** <note>Plutarch (c. 46 – 120 AD) was a Greek philosopher and biographer who wrote extensively on Platonic philosophy.</note>, it is clear that he by no means thinks that the intelligible <term>intelligible: things that can only be understood by the mind or intellect, as opposed to the physical senses</term> and the sensible are confused into one mass or substance, much less that God Himself is mixed with the world; rather, Plutarch only means this: that certain philosophers, in trying to explain the nature of the world soul and its origin, in vain appeal to a mixture of the soul and the sensible thing. For in every definite appearance of bodies, matter and form occur; this form comes from elsewhere, namely from a thinking thing; the world soul, however, already pre-existed in that confused mass of matter; which he later follows up more broadly. On page 635 he expressly says:

> *But those who want corporeal matter to be mixed with the indivisible are mistaken. First, because Plato uses no name for corporeal matter here: which elsewhere he usually calls the "receptacle," capable of containing and nourishing all things, not as something divided around bodies, but the body itself, which is divided into individual things. Next, what will be the difference between the creation of the world and that of the soul, if both are constituted from matter and intelligibles? Indeed, Plato himself, as if loathing the origin of the soul from the body, says that the corporeal part was placed inside it by God, and hidden from it from the outside: and when he had completed the whole soul by reason, he then proposed the argument about matter, for which he had no need before, when he created the soul, seeing as it was born without matter.*

...of those whose souls he instilled as if through a certain flow. Thus far **Timaeus Locrus** <note>Timaeus Locrus was a semi-legendary Pythagorean philosopher to whom a treatise on the soul of the world was attributed; Plato's dialogue *Timaeus* is named after him.</note>. However, if God is the same as the soul of the world, why does he so clearly distinguish God from that "Second Minister" [the world soul]? Let us examine distinctly whether God, by joining Himself with minds and inanimate bodies, becomes only a single substance. Regarding our minds, they are said to have been around the stars even before they were led into bodies by the soul of the world; they were, therefore, substances: for an accident <term>accident: a philosophical term for a quality or property that cannot exist on its own but must belong to a substance</term> cannot migrate from one subject to another. Regarding their origin, **Locrus** does not mention even a word. How, then, can it be that those minds, as soon as God works within them, lose their own proper subsistence? **Plato** is entirely silent on this matter. Bodies, before they were reduced to order and God worked upon them, were undoubtedly substances. For a "rude and indigested mass" is no less a substance than a most beautifully crafted body. Therefore, just as God's first operation upon matter did not prevent Him from being separate from the world; so likewise, neither His preservation nor His governance of it prevents God and matter from being diverse substances. Finally, regarding animated bodies, it is certain that they live. Thus animals and humans live. The question is whether God effects this immediately, or whether that life is to be traced back to an intelligent substance, or whether a certain "plastic nature" <note>A "plastic nature" refers to an unconscious formative power in nature, a concept popular in 17th-century philosophy to explain biological growth without direct divine intervention.</note> inserted into bodies effects this, or whether all these things are to be traced back to mechanical laws. Nowhere did **Plato** clearly open his mind on these questions. Therefore, even if it were most true that "God goes through all lands and the reaches of the sea" <note>A reference to Virgil’s *Georgics*, often cited in debates about pantheism to describe God's omnipresence.</note> and that God gives life to all, it would not yet be clear how far this should be extended. According to our system, God preserves my life at every moment. The word "preservation" is not a term empty of meaning. The perseverance and constant effect of preservation itself proves that some connection exists between the will of God and the prolongation of my life. In my opinion, God is not extended <term>extended: occupying physical space; a key attribute of matter in Cartesian and Spinozist philosophy</term>, but is a most noble mind, active in understanding and willing. The intellect of God does not produce things, but His will does. It is by the will of God, therefore, that I live. This will is not a bare wish, but a will joined with power and effect. But how will it be proved that God, or the soul of the world, by granting life to all, becomes one substance with men and animals? From what principles will this be demonstrated? Are there perhaps testimonies clearer than the midday light? Let them be brought forward then; although the soul of the world is subject to the Command of God, it is nevertheless called by **Locrus** in § 48 "hard to move" <note>original Greek: δυσκίνητος</note>, reluctantly admitting

mixture; and on the following page: "which God himself adorned" <note>original Greek: ὃν συνελαξατο ὁ Θεὸς</note>. It must therefore be demonstrated, either by testimonies or from the principles of **Plato**, that God cannot join Himself with the world in any other way than through mixing and coalescing into one and the same substance.

XXXV. We have shown so far that the minor proposition does not imply what the Illustrious Man [Gundling] contends. But neither can the major proposition be proved. For if we diligently unroll the writings of **Plato** and the Platonists, it will be most clear that there is not just one principle given in divine matters, but three diverse ones, distinct from each other by degrees of perfection. We find God "the Creator of all" <note>original Greek: τὸν πάντων Δημιουργὸν</note>; the "Mind" <note>original Greek: τὸν νοῦν</note>, or some eternal "Paradigm" <note>original Greek: παράδειγμα</note> of intellectual things; and the "soul of the world," a substance diverse from the first and the second. The first is more excellent than the second, and the second than the third; yet each is called "God" <note>original Latin/Greek: Θεὸς</note> by **Plato**. But what follows from this opinion? *Then,* he [Gundling] says on page 315, *Plato will be a Tritheist.* <note>Tritheism is the belief that there are three distinct gods, rather than one God in three persons or one single divine substance.</note> Let **Plato** be a Tritheist, then. Therefore he is not a **Spinozist** <note>Followers of Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677), who argued that God and Nature are one and the same substance.</note>. For I have granted what **D. G.** [Gundling] orders on page 316: to give each principle its own hypostasis <term>hypostasis: the underlying state or individual reality of a thing; in theology, a distinct person of the deity</term>. God, the most noble mind, exists by Himself; the *Mind* [Nous] exists by Himself; the soul of the world, passing through all things, exists by itself. Therefore God, or the first mind, is not joined with matter; the second principle is not joined with the world; therefore there remains the third substance, the soul of the world. *Let him choose* (he continues) *the opinion that pleases him: let him give each principle its own hypostasis: let him take it away again and make one from the three: he will gain nothing from any side. God will be in all things and with all things, whether he calls it the soul of the world, or simply names it God with Spinoza.* I have used the Illustrious Man's generosity. In the previous argument, I supposed that God and the soul of the world were one and the same; yet I did not see it proved that God therefore becomes a single substance with the world. In this place, I have posited that those three principles are distinct from each other. It must therefore be proved that the first and second principles are also joined with the world, even if I have conceded that the soul of the world is joined to matter in some way. *To ask,* he says, *that I prove each of these things distinctly, is useless and...*

But there is a need for evidence—clear evidence, I say—to prove both suppositions. In passing, I will mention here the "retort" which **Dr. Gundling** <note>Nicolaus Hieronymus Gundling (1671–1729) was a German jurist and philosopher often involved in the intellectual disputes of the early Enlightenment.</note> attempts to brush away in Section 84. On page 93 of *my* dissertation, I used this argument among others against him: If matter was cast out from the "bosom of God," and the soul of the world is the most subtle matter, and this soul is the same as the first and second principles (as the **Illustrious Man** contends), then **Gundling’s** hypothesis is utterly false. This is because the argument would prove more than was intended: it would prove that in **Plato's** system, no intellectual substances exist at all, which is contrary to the whole of Platonic philosophy. 

He claims this reasoning is unjust, because he said the soul of the world was *similar* to the "first matter" of **Descartes** <note>René Descartes proposed that the universe was filled with "subtle matter" or "aether" that accounted for physical forces.</note>, not that it was the *subtle matter* itself. And so that I might grasp this "immense distinction," the **Most Kind Man** explains himself on page 317: *Similarity by no means makes the thing being compared become the very thing to which it is compared. Solomon compares the nose of his beloved Bride to a tower that rises up on Mount Lebanon; but because of this, that nose, however excellent, is not actually a tower in Lebanon.* I think I shall be understood by you: you will not confuse the Bride’s nose with a tower. <note>original Greek: Σοφῶς / English: Wisely</note>. This man of most elegant genius could not have said these things unless he had appealed to the Holy Scriptures in a matter of such importance. 

As for the matter itself, it makes no difference whether he admits this argument or not; for I do not rely upon it. I will only say that I stated twice in my dissertation that the **Famous Man** maintains the soul of the world is similar to the most subtle matter of Descartes, which should not have been kept silent. Meanwhile, I confess I do not yet see wherein I have erred. He maintains that all things have emanated and flowed out from God and out of God; that matter was projected from the bosom of God; and where there is "emanation," there a "flow" (properly so called) takes place. He approves the opinion of **R. Simonius** <note>Likely Simon Simonius, a 16th-century physician and Aristotelian commentator.</note>, who asserts that the ancients understood "intellectual beings" to be fiery substances, that the <note>original Greek: ἀγαθόν / English: Good</note> of **Plato** (page 350) turns into a fiery substance, that our minds are "plucked" from the divinity, and that from all these, a single substance is formed. I do not know, therefore, where any "intelligent substances" remain. And as far as the soul is concerned, he compared it to the most subtle matter of Descartes, either in respect to its subtle body or in respect to its most rapid agitation. In whatever sense he takes it, that soul of the world will be a body. If he says that it rushes everywhere most rapidly, yet the mind is separate from matter, then he would appeal in vain...

...into parts, namely body and soul. God did not indeed beget the body, but he shaped and fitted it from the matter provided, binding and defining the infinite within its own limits and shapes. The soul, however, participating in mind, reason, and harmony, is not merely a work, but is also a part of God; it did not come into being as something made *by* Him, but as something existing *from* Him. Regarding this testimony of Plutarch <note>Plutarch (c. 46–120 AD) was a Middle Platonist philosopher whose interpretations often emphasized the soul's divine origin.</note>, I note the following: First, the explanation of the word *Father* seems more subtle than it is true. There are countless testimonies from Greek and Latin poets in which they call Jupiter the Parent of all things, even though they never even thought of such a literal generation. Indeed, if we had to stick strictly to this word, I see no reason why this "generation" would not also extend to physical bodies. Second, although I grant much to that **most learned man** <note>original: "πολυμαθεστάτῳ" (polymathistatō)</note>, the **authority of Plato and Timaeus of Locri** <note>Timaeus of Locri was a Pythagorean philosopher to whom a treatise on the soul of the world was attributed; he is the namesake of Plato’s dialogue *Timaeus*.</note> carries more weight with me. Plato in the *Timaeus* and Timaeus of Locri describe the origin of all things professionally, yet they make no mention of this emanation of the world’s soul out of God. Therefore, no one can find fault with me if I doubt the explanation of Plutarch, a man otherwise most learned and highly skilled in Platonic philosophy. Plato says in the *Timaeus* that God placed the soul in the middle of the world and surrounded it with the body, but he does not reveal its origin; indeed, he uses words that excite no such suspicion in us: "But the soul," he says, "not as we are now attempting to speak of it as later, so did God also devise it as younger" <note>original Greek: "Τὴν δὲ δὴ ψυχὴν, οὐχ ὡς νῦν ὕστερον ἐπιχειροῦμεν λέγειν, οὕτως ἐμηχανήσατο καὶ Θεὸς νεωτέραν." Plato is arguing that while we talk about the soul after the body, God actually made the soul first.</note>. Truly, the word *devised* <note>original: "ἐμηχανήσατο" (emēchanēsato)</note> denotes no emanation. Again: "But God, both in birth and virtue, brought forth the soul of the world as older and more ancient, and set it over the body as Mistress and Ruler over the ruled" <note>original Greek: "Ὁ δὲ Θεὸς καὶ γενέσει καὶ ἀρετῇ προτέραν καὶ πρεσβυτέραν ψυχὴν σώματος ὡς Δεσπότιν καὶ ἀρξουσαν ἀρξομένης συνεστή沙το."</note>. The **Illustrious Man** <note>Referring to the opponent, likely Gundling.</note> appeals indeed to the word *having begotten* <note>original: "γεννήσας" (gennēsas)</note>. But I have already replied on page 947 of my dissertation that the words *to beget, to make, to build, to devise, to craft* are used frequently and indeed interchangeably by Plato in this matter. And lest I seem to be the only one stubbornly clinging to this assertion of mine, I appeal to **Abraham Gravius**, whom he cites as a witness to his opinion in Section 28. In *Book III, Chapter XVIII, page 569*, Gravius speaks thus of the soul of the world:

> This mind truly protects all that has been said so far about the soul: namely, that it was God’s plan to form a perfect nature, which He would surround and adorn with the most excellent virtue, so that just as He Himself had created nature by His own divine power, so nature itself, like a certain Goddess, might effectively govern that created order which was left to its power.

The philosopher distinguishes Nature—which he sometimes also improperly calls God—from the *Demiurge* or Artificer, as in the *Philebus*...

<page-type>text</page-type>

...on page 28, it can be read in more than one place. Nor does he separate Nature from God’s Command, or establish it as simply eternal; rather, he acknowledges a marvelous and constant power of Nature, by whose nod and command individual things are procreated daily, so that among all changes, Nature itself remains immobile. I say he by no means exempts that nature from the number of created things; but he stresses so many times that it was made by God and is His minister, and not properly the cause, but a **co-cause** <note>original: "συναίτιον" (syndition) - an auxiliary cause that helps the primary agent.</note>. Nor does he attribute true Divinity to it in the *Statesman*, but rather a **supervisory** <note>original: "ἐπισ케υαστὴν" (episkeuastēn)</note> role. His meaning becomes clear from the terms used: *to be born for God, begotten, younger*, and the opposites: *always, self-existent God*, etc. Furthermore, Timaeus himself in his own text calls God the principle of form and matter, and the author of nature. Thus says **Gravius**. Third: If I were to grant Plutarch that this is the opinion of **Plato**, then nothing else follows but this: that a certain intellectual substance arose from God and out of God in a manner inscrutable to us humans. It must then be proven that this soul is so connected and joined with the world that it forms one and the same substance with the world. In the same section, **Plutarch** quite clearly denies this very thing.

> "Any of us," he says, "contains within a vital force in a mortal and dissolvable body. In the world, on the contrary, the corporeal nature, situated in the middle, is perpetually preserved by the leading part, which is always in the same state."

And indeed, individuals are said to be "sensible" and "perceivable by the mind alone" in different ways, and to admit no division. The former due to smallness, the latter due to simplicity and purity, and because it is devoid of all deprivation and difference. Moreover, it is foolish to wish to judge incorporeal things by corporeal things. Fourth: Those words of Plutarch—*God did not beget the body*, etc.—show more than enough that Plutarch asserted that, according to Plato’s mind, there are two eternal and self-subsisting principles; therefore, there is not only one substance.

XXXVI. The **Illustrious Man** in Sections 88 and 89 twists my opinion so that he may have something to harass and pluck at. These are the words of the **Illustrious Man**:

> Whichever way you turn, Plato’s trinity will either turn out to be a monster, or it will be called a merely nominal Trinity. For suppose the Idea is different from the first Being; then all the remaining ideas will exist separately by emanating from that Idea, which is what Aristotle objected to his Master, and it contains an absurdity.

I replied on page 937 thus: Let us suppose that **Plato** said the ideas of all things are in God and indeed from God Himself, as certain distinct, singular substances. Is this opinion so monstrous? The question is, therefore, whether the opinion regarding the subsistence **in the Word** <note>original: "τῷ λογῷ" (tō logō)</note> and of the ideas is monstrous and absurd. He, however, at the beginning of Section 88, says:

> That is indeed utterly absurd, which the Defender turns back against me **personally** <note>original: "κατ' ἄνθρωπον" (kat' anthrōpon)</note>.

For since I had written that it seemed ambiguous whether Plato meant the attributes...

Thus it is clear how honestly this **Illustrious Man** <note>Referring to the author's critic, likely Nicolaus Hieronymus Gundling.</note> has dealt with me. Meanwhile, while he finds fault, he also instructs. In Section 89, he says: *From a similar stock comes what the Defender provides regarding "Ideas" from elsewhere. For one moment he says he understands nothing of divine ideas; the next, he thinks it is easier to defend the notion that they are placed outside of God’s intellect; and then again, he denies that he can grasp how the same thing can be modified in different ways so as to be at one time a tree, a plant, or a soul. He himself, without doubt, is ignorant of what he is saying or writing.*

Although I can easily allow others to say I have erred—for to err is human—I think it belongs to a dejected spirit to endure having things that were stated correctly dragged into a foreign meaning without reason. To one who depends on the most trivial things (not to me, nor to a lover of wisdom), applause must seem like immortality, and a hiss like death. The question was whether the **Reason** <note>original: "λογος" (logos)</note> is an attribute of God, or truly a substance existing through itself. The **Distinguished Man** <note>Gundling</note> denies the latter; for from that, he argues, it would follow that all Ideas exist through themselves, which is monstrous and absurd. I responded that this sentiment did not seem so absurd to me. I added on page 937 of my dissertation: *In my opinion, we are entirely ignorant of what Ideas are, let alone being able to define in what manner they might exist in God.* These things seemed necessary for me to add, since the independent existence of individual Ideas appeared so absurd to him. I said, therefore, in general, that it seems to me we do not know what Ideas are. I said, moreover, that those who defend the common opinion—namely, that all Ideas in God are modifications of the divine mind—are **perhaps, perhaps I say**, involved in the same difficulties as those who uphold the view that Ideas exist outside the mind of God, yet are most closely joined to God from eternity. I did not, therefore, say that this latter opinion was more probable than the former, as he imputes to me against my mind and my open words. Indeed, I added: *that I cannot perceive by what means a divine and most noble mind could be so modified as to represent a tree, a fish, etc.* Until now, I have believed that all our reasoning about the Ideas of God rests on an analogy which we establish with the ideas of our own minds. Now, there are two principal opinions among philosophers (I will not dwell on the others) regarding the nature of ideas. Some think that ideas are modifications of our own mind; others, such as **Locke** and **Le Clerc** <note>John Locke (1632–1704) and Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736) were major figures in Enlightenment philosophy and neighbors in the "Republic of Letters."</note>, distinguish them from the mind and say they are the immediate object of our contemplation;

object; meanwhile, we do not know what they are. I will not recount the arguments of either side. Let us transfer these to God. Either the Ideas of God are modifications of a most perfect mind, or they are something removed from the Essence of God, but which God continually contemplates from eternity. If the former, I would wish the method to be shown to me by which a most noble mind can be so modified (if I may use the language of the **Scholastics** <note>Medieval theologians who used highly technical, Aristotelian logic.</note>) that it represents a plant or a certain animal. **I do not deny** that they are in God, or that God has Ideas of all things, even corporeal ones; nor is the opinion of those who profess this absurd. If, however, they are outside of God and are the object of divine contemplation, and exist through themselves, no one could perceive what they are or how they can be said to be eternal.

I am thinking now about *Mr. Gundling*: this thought, by which he is present to my soul, is called an **idea**. This idea is a certain **modification** <note>original: "modificatio"; in 18th-century philosophy, a "modification" is a temporary state or specific instance of a substance, like a ripple in a pond.</note> of my mind (for we are speaking here according to their opinion). However, this specific thought does not belong to the nature of my mind. For even if I had never thought that *Mr. Gundling* existed, my mind would nevertheless have possessed the faculty of understanding. But "thought" in a general sense, or the essential attribute of the mind, refers to nothing distinct. 

Let us transfer these concepts to God. God is the most noble mind; among his attributes is the most perfect **Intellect**. we relate his manner of understanding to the analogy of our own mind: we say that God has the ideas of all things. Since we know from other sources that these ideas did not arise through the senses or through reflection, we say that they always exist in God. Therefore, God possesses the ideas of all things, and specifically the idea of *Gundling*. The question, then, is not whether the most perfect intellect belongs to the nature of God, nor whether God has an idea of individual things, such as *Gundling*; but whether the specific idea of *Gundling* belongs so necessarily to the most perfect essence of God that, if it were denied, God would not be God, or a most perfect mind. 

But *Mr. G.* brings forth a greater **specimen of my ignorance** <note>original: "ignorantiæ meæ specimen"</note> on page 332. *In such an unskillful way,* he says, *he takes up the arguments regarding the eternity of ideas, which he utterly denies, unless all ideas are referred individually to the essence of God. For he has never well-considered what the Philosophers of our age mean when they pronounce the ideas of things to be eternal and immutable. For those who establish the idea of a Lion as eternal do not teach poorly; but they would conclude absurdly if they said: "therefore the Lion is eternal, therefore it is a portion of the divine essence, or of God thinking about the Lion."* 

I give the most refined Man as much thanks as I can for teaching me what Philosophers mean when they say the essences of things are eternal. *I give thanks* that he has brought forward an example by which that matter is illustrated, showing specifically how the idea of a lion and the lion itself differ as much as possible, and that it does not follow that the lion is eternal simply because the idea of the lion is eternal. 

Meanwhile, I wish that the **Distinguished Man** <note>original: "D. Vir"</note> had shown the place in which I called the eternity of divine ideas into doubt. For on page 334, the *great man* <note>Referring to Nicolaus Hieronymus Gundling, the author's primary intellectual opponent in this text.</note> speaks thus: *He refuses to admit emanation, yet does not dare to suggest creation; therefore he hesitates, and finally, with an unusual leap, retreats to an incomprehensible mode. What if we concede*, he says on p. 954, *that Plato is no less ignorant than we are about the manner in which something less perfect, such as the World-Soul, can emanate from God? In this, the Apologist makes himself quite a laughingstock.* 

Since the dispute concerns the origin of those three principles of *Plato*, I conceded that a certain "gradation" or hierarchy takes place among those three principles: First, the **Creator of all things** <note>original Greek: "ton pantōn Dēmiourgon"</note>; second, the **Word** <note>original Greek: "ton logon"</note>; and third, the **World-Soul**. The *Later Platonists* <note>The Neo-Platonists, who expanded on Plato's original ideas centuries later.</note> generally assert that the second arose from the first, and the third from the second. I stated that in Plato’s *Timaeus* and in the works of *Locrus* <note>Timaeus of Locri, a philosopher whose work was traditionally believed to be the source for Plato’s Timaeus.</note>—which are the primary sources for this argument—this assertion regarding the emanation of the three principles is nowhere clearly defined. I said I would freely grant this assertion for a moment to see whether those monstrous absurdities would emerge from it, which *Mr. G.* <note>Gundling</note> thinks must necessarily be deduced. 

As a foundation, I established that those three principles are intelligent substances, foreign to matter, so that in that process of "emanation," all composition and separation of parts must be excluded. Having supposed this, I said that even if the World-Soul had emanated from the divine mind, those absurd consequences do not yet follow. I then added those words already mentioned: *what if we concede that we, no less than Plato, are ignorant, etc.* This, the *Famous Doctor* calls an unrefined and laughable assertion. Why, finally? Because, he says, *he speaks of those progressions as if he himself knew everything and had been present at the creation of all things; therefore, he says I cannot take refuge in Plato’s ignorance.* This is why his friends cannot hold back their laughter. 

Now, I will not say that *Mr. Gundling* has failed to bring forward clear passages from *Plato*—from *Plato*, I say—to prove his own opinion; but could not Plato establish and babble something that he himself could not explain? How many people are there who defend **transubstantiation** <note>The doctrine that the bread and wine in the Eucharist become the actual substance of Christ's body and blood; the author uses this as an example of a widely held but logically "monstrous" idea.</note> yet do not explain that monstrous proposition? Is the confidence with which some people (even Philosophers) put forward their decrees a sign that they are reasoning correctly? If *Plato* defends the system of *Spinoza* <note>Baruch Spinoza, whose philosophy suggested that God and Nature are the same substance, often accused of being a form of atheism.</note>, as the *Great Man* thinks, can he explain the manner according to which all things were created with a certain number, weight, and measure? Without doubt, *Plato* ought to have spoken more modestly and remained silent about things he did not know; but since this was not done, and it is clear as day that he spoke about obscure things, no one can demand that I explain what he himself did not know. For although he was a Philosopher and even a "Polyhistor" <note>A person of great and varied learning.</note> if we believe the ancients, this did not prevent him from being ignorant of many things about which
<meta>catchword: which</meta>

<page-num>951</page-num>

which, nevertheless, he wished to speak so that he might seem wise. For that saying of the most ingenious *La Mothe Le Vayer* <note>François de La Mothe Le Vayer, a 17th-century French skeptical philosopher.</note> is often very true: *In this great hospital of the incurables, there are none more foolish than those who wish to cure others.* <note>original French: "Dans ce grand Hôpital des incurables, il n'y a point de plus fous, que ceux, qui veulent guerir les autres."</note> 

But the *Illustrious Man* continues: *Nay, it seems even more witless when he demands proof that God, in His infinite essence, can embrace nothing except what necessarily belongs to His essence.* For it would have to be proved that *God is not a composite.* If he seriously demands this, he will seem to have made very little progress in philosophy as well as Theology. Hence the following: *who knows whether God willed from eternity that certain intelligent substances exist simultaneously in Himself—in a way unsearchable to us little men—destined finally to come forth from God in their own time, not indeed as emanating parts of God, but which, once sent out, would leave God no less perfect than before? These arguments show even greater vanity, or shall I say, ignorance.* 

I would like the Reader to observe that I was dealing with the three intellectual principles of *Plato*, but especially with the **World-Soul**. To show how "witless" my assertion is, which I proposed not as a Teacher but only doubtingly and by conjecture, I would like the following to be observed. 
**First**: *these things do not pertain to the core of our controversy*; the question is whether, according to the opinion of *Plato*, there is only one single substance which is God. I have shown that matter is self-subsisting and eternal, and connected to God by no necessary bond. 
**Second**: I said that the later Platonists especially assert that those three principles arose from one another, yet clear testimonies of this matter are not observed in *Plato* and *Locrus*. 
**Third**: that very emanation from God is of such a nature that it excludes all separation of parts, which only takes place in physical bodies. 
**Fourth**: that we know the nature of spiritual things only very obscurely; certain properties of our own mind are known to us, but all other things are **hidden** <note>original Greek: "adēla"</note>; and above all, our knowledge of the *nature of God*, which is infinite and unspeakable, is weak. 

I can certainly find no better witness to prove this than *Gundling* himself. For in part 14 of his *Gundlingiana*, page 327 and following, he speaks thus on this matter: *Man is finite, God is infinite; reason is circumscribed by narrow limits, God is enclosed by no limit. And yet those men fight, and move every stone, and maintain in every way that God can be comprehended. How? Let me see. By reason, or by imagination? Whatever we understand is finite; whatever we imagine is finite, divisible into parts, and endowed with finite magnitude. Where are you rushing, Lucius? Do you grasp infinite power, infinite potency, infinite time? If not, why do you insult the dead Lion, why do you pluck his beard? Listen: in God, we conceive of eternal nothingness.* <note>This quote from Gundling suggests that God is so far beyond human comprehension that our concepts of "being" do not apply to Him, effectively appearing as "nothing" to our limited intellects.</note>
