Who has ever spoken more confidently on this matter? And yet it is ridiculous and dull when I said—and indeed only by way of conjecture—that something could be conceived in the unutterable nature of God that does not necessarily belong to His essence. Fifth: God can do whatever involves no contradiction, or whatever we can conceive as possible. Sixth: just as with God's eternity, so His infinite nature is little known to us; the mind is almost swallowed up by the contemplation of His infinite and eternal nature. Seventh: whatever exists besides God does not exist by necessity, but by His most omnipotent will. Eighth: God can will from eternity that something exists besides Himself that is by its nature less perfect. Ninth: by "the world," I mean not only all bodies taken together, but also all space. Tenth: God can will from eternity that certain intellectual substances <note>Spiritual beings like souls or angels.</note> exist; since these require neither place nor space, and the world was eventually established in time, they are wherever they are without confusion or the filling up of physical space. Eleventh: Therefore, God can will that from eternity, within His infinite and unutterable substance, in a manner inscrutable to us mere mortals, certain intellectual substances exist, produced by His will and entirely distinct from Him. Twelfth: He could therefore have contained the World-Soul within Himself, and finally, in His own time, set it over the world clothed in other properties. Thirteenth: this World-Soul, as is most clearly evident from **Timaeus and Locrus** <note>Referring to the Platonic dialogue "Timaeus" and the philosopher Timaeus of Locri.</note>, is submitted to the command of **GOD** and is considered a substance distinct from **GOD**: it could

therefore also have its origin from God from all eternity, and yet not be "One" with God. It must therefore be shown by the **Famous Man** <note>Gundling</note> that this eternal subsistence of intelligent substances involves a pure contradiction. However, I do not say these things with the intent of attributing this exact mind to **Plato**, or believing that he observed all these things, and least of all as if I believe that things actually subsisted in God in this way. I only mean that since **Plato** recognized three principles, distinct from one another by degrees of perfection, yet did not clearly define the manner in which he thought these arose, we must stop here and not deduce absurd consequences from it. 

However, since the **Famous Man** argues to the point of absurdity from the conceded principles of the Platonists—thinking that all these things were made through "emanation" properly so called, and thus that the divine nature was split into parts and joined with matter, and that no way can be conceived how the divine can arise from the divine—I have said that we have a weak and highly inadequate knowledge of God's infinite nature. No one can demonstratively prove that nothing can be in God except what necessarily belongs to His most perfect nature; from the eternal abyss of that Nature, certain intellectual substances could arise without detriment to the divine nature. I have proposed all these things only hesitantly, as becomes a modest man. For if ever one must proceed with a cautious step in reasoning, it must especially be done when the discourse concerns the infinite nature of God and His attributes. 

Yet let us see how he convicts that modest conjecture of mine of absurdity. On **page 335**, he says: *Either God contains those substances as distinct from Himself, having obtained their life and nature from elsewhere, or they are animated by Him with life, reason, and motion.* If the former, then not all things were produced by God, which is absurd. If the latter, they are similar to God, and they both proceeded from Him who contains them, and they exist and consist in Him, and are eventually sent out into the light. Thus says the most subtle **Gundling.** We are not discussing the first proposition, but the second: he ought to have proved, therefore, that the second involves a contradiction. But he proves nothing, except that those intellectual substances would thus be "similar" to God. They are similar insofar as they are intellectual substances, but they did not arise from the divine essence, but, as I supposed, were produced by God's will; therefore they did not arise *from* Him [as part of His essence], but *through* Him, namely through the divine will, which would be the cause of their existence and essence. This last point, he says, although it may be absurd, seems much more tolerable than the first, which is a downright crude fiction: *That God embraces in Himself substances existing through themselves and by themselves.* These things never entered my mind, and it is a fabrication

*Gundling says: "I spoke openly, asking whether God willed that they exist, etc."* Even as this Most Excellent Man makes great threats, he clarifies nothing.

XXXIX. Let us proceed to Section 94 of my dissertation: on page 955, I spoke as follows. *We Christians believe in a Holy Trinity that is not merely nominal <note>Existing in name only, without actual distinction between the persons.</note>, but one that involves something distinct; we say that the Son is from the Father from eternity, and with Him. The Holy Spirit proceeds from both, yet is equally eternal and most perfect; but who can explain the mode of this distinction? I wanted to prove by this example that the nature of God is not so clearly understood by us that one could permit calling any distinction or emanation <note>A flowing forth from a source; in theology, how the Son and Spirit originate from the Father.</note> in God "impossible." What does the Most Excellent Gundling say to these things?* In his response, it becomes clear once again how "simple" he is (and I use that word in its most literal Latin sense <note>Suggesting both "straightforward" and "naive."</note>). For it is rightly and entirely affirmed that *the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God; and he effects the distinction by personhood alone.* I, however, did not say in what that distinction is located; for, to tell the truth, I do not know how the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are distinguished from one another. Yet the divine oracles <note>The Holy Scriptures.</note>, to which we rightly assent even if they do not explain the "how," do not allow us to doubt that some distinction exists. Meanwhile, I am most firmly convinced that the highly learned Gundling does not know what power the word <term>hypostasis</term> <note>original: ὑποστάσεως. A Greek term meaning "substance" or "individual reality," used in theology to define the "persons" of the Trinity.</note> has in this context. For it sometimes denotes "substance." But we do not have three substances diverse from one another. If he says it denotes "subsistence," then he cannot distinctly explain whether this diversity of <term>hypostasis</term> is one of reason alone, or a real diversity between substance and substance, substance and properties, properties and properties, or properties and modes. In a word, we say there are three persons in God, yet we cannot distinctly define what "persons" are; or if we do define them, we can in no way transfer that definition to the explanation of this mystery. Therefore, by the word <term>hypostasis</term>, he meant nothing other than that some distinction has a place in God. I asserted the same thing. The only difference lies in this: I have frankly admitted that this distinction is entirely unknown to me. He, however, to hide his ignorance, employed the word <term>hypostasis</term>. *“Will you truly,” he asks, “declare without shame that birds are God, or the wolf, the tree, and other animals?”* Where on earth are we? The question is about the three principles—allow me to use this word because of the impenetrable nature of the matter—the question is whether a certain distinction has a place in God, and he asks me whether I believe birds etc. are God! Did I say that all creatures are distinct from one another only by personhood or a mode of subsistence? Did I affirm anywhere that the distinction in created things is the same as the distinction that has a place in divine matters? I hate the makers of false consequences!

The *Most Learned Creiling* in his *Examination of these principles* speaks of this proposition by the Illustrious Man as follows: *The Author most elegantly, along with the most ancient Philosophers, calls God the primitive unity and all creatures derivative; at the same time, in what follows, he shows the mode of the production of creatures, or creation, as far as it can be investigated by the light of reason, saying: Creatures arise through continuous flashes of divinity.* Our author speaks of a certain emanation <note>A flowing forth from a source</note> generally so called, or nearly so (lest you think the *dreams and omens of other Patrons of the Emanation System* are accepted here), which he wishes to present more clearly to the imagination and through it to the intellect by a kind of "flashing." For in our world, the sun, by the perpetual emission of its rays, has offered both to Christian and Gentile Philosophers a kind of image of the most active divinity, and the Holy Scriptures themselves call God "light." Thus *Creiling* very modestly interprets the more unusual speech of the *Illustrious Man*. Thus do *Candid Men* act, mindful of our ignorance concerning divine matters.

I will repeat the questions of that supreme Man. *What is derived, I ask?* I responded: *The soul of the world is derived, a certain intelligible essence from the mind, and that mind from God, the Ruler of all things—something divine from God,*

XLI. And these are the things which I wished to note regarding the *Distinguished Man’s* dissertation, written against me. ...placed. But since it pleased the *Distinguished Gundling* to subject my dissertation to such a lengthy examination, I could not, for many reasons which I do not wish to list here, remain entirely silent. Once I had applied my mind to writing this apology, I saw that the necessity was imposed upon me to examine everything accurately. I did not wish, therefore, to spare the paper that is destined to perish; rather, I wished to weigh everything that seemed of any importance. I did not want to give the *Distinguished Man* an occasion for complaining that I had passed over in silence the strongest arguments upon which he relies. For we hear these complaints moved most frequently in the mutual battles of the Learned: for the good faith of those who dispute is rare; there is no less room here for stratagems than in war. The Reader will therefore forgive my prolixity and the repetitions which I could not avoid. The *Distinguished Author* argued repeatedly from a hypothesis once it was seized upon, and he dragged the testimonies toward it, as is usually done; hence repetitions arose more than once. Let the judgment concerning the matter itself rest with the *learned and candid Reader*. Those who are positioned outside the factions will be better able to judge our controversy than we, *whom the zeal of parties sometimes hinders from being able to discern the truth.* I have certainly done my utmost not to allow any place for prejudiced opinions. *But I am a man, and I think nothing human is alien to me <note>A famous quote from the Roman playwright Terence: "Homo sum, humani nihil a me alienum puto."</note>; we are all contentious men: we all gladly defend opinions once they are seized, and we are brought with difficulty to admit that we have erred. That most pestilential star, ambition, has breathed upon us all.* Therefore, I shall not sing of victory before the triumph; I will gladly hear the judgments of others, and, having been taught better, I shall write "Retractions" just as *Augustine* did. It is all the same to me whether the *Distinguished Gundling* gives my opinion a "white pebble" <note>The ancient Greeks used white pebbles to vote for acquittal or agreement, and black for condemnation.</note> of approval or not. It has always been permitted to disagree while keeping friendship intact. If it should please the *Distinguished Man* to descend into the field of battle again, he has my leave. I ask only this: that in the future, setting aside all bitterness of words, he deals with me. I would wish him to persuade himself that he is dealing with a man who is not indeed learned, much less proud, but most loving of truth and peace. Mockery provokes the mind to anger and heat. Just as it is easy for the innocent, so it is easy for the angry man to find words with which to defend himself. One does not need an excellent talent to wound others and drench them in *“Italian vinegar,”* <note>original: "Italico aceto." A Roman idiom for sharp, biting wit or sarcasm.</note> but rather to bear injuries inflicted with a level mind. *Even a fly has a spleen <note>An ancient proverb meaning that even the smallest creature can feel anger.</note>; even the ant has its own bile; even men of the mildest character, when others speak stones, cannot always return words of silk.* And what, in the end, do we gain by mockery?

## SACRED MEDITATION,
### CONTAINING CERTAIN SALUTARY ADMONITIONS PERTAINING TO THE
# HOLY SUPPER
### AND ITS TRUE AND LAWFUL USE.

---

### PART ONE.
#### Section I.

<margin>The Author's goal is set forth.</margin>
Since it is not a matter of indifference how the articles of the Christian religion and its sacred ceremonies are explained and handed down to the followers of Jesus Christ our Savior; and while it is simultaneously certain that many Christians abuse the most august Sacrament of the Holy Supper <term>Holy Supper: a traditional term for the Eucharist or Holy Communion</term> and harbor misguided opinions about its lawful use, it is the duty of public teachers to strive toward this: to show the candidates for Sacred Ministry <note>Latin: "S. M. Candidatis," likely referring to students training for the clergy.</note> early enough not only what the nature of this Sacrament is, and what its end and goal are, but also to teach them what the efficacy of the Holy Supper is—what it can or cannot accomplish in the souls of the pious and the impious; how much benefit it can bring to those who partake of this Sacrament lawfully; what the method of genuine preparation for the Holy Supper is, and so forth. And this is all the more necessary because, alas! daily experience shows that many Christians, completely immersed in vices against the voice and testimony of conscience, use the Holy Supper as if it were an antidote <note>original: "antidoto." The author suggests they use it as a "cure-all" to wipe away sins without true repentance.</note> to excuse their sins; while others completely abstain from the Holy Supper because they hold misguided opinions about the nature of preparation for this august Sacrament, and the state of those who are bound to celebrate it worthily—opinions whose origin...

...origin, I will reveal below. I have therefore taken it upon myself, for the sake of my listeners, to set down certain thoughts on this subject on paper and to prescribe for them certain **Cautions**. If they remain mindful of these, they will take care—should they ever be called to the **Holy Ministry**—not to provide their audiences with any occasion to foster improper opinions regarding the use of the **Holy Supper**. On the contrary, they shall do their utmost to explain everything relating to this subject clearly to their listeners and to emphasize those things which can lead to a lawful celebration of this Sacrament, consistent with both reason and the Gospel. However, before I proceed to the matter itself, I offer two preliminary warnings. The first is: in this place, no account will be taken of the disputes that have arisen among Protestants concerning the "Words of Institution" <note>Referring to the debate between Lutherans and the Reformed over the literal vs. symbolic meaning of "This is my body."</note> of the Holy Supper. These questions have been discussed so often (and would that it were always done in a manner becoming of Christian theologians!) and placed in such a clear light by Reformed teachers, that it seems nothing more can be added to a full demonstration, at least as far as the nature of this business permits. Indeed, were it not for prejudiced opinions and the rigor of certain formulas, I am persuaded that many of our dissenting brothers—at least those who are accustomed to treating religious matters with a tranquil mind and a desire for truth—would cast their vote of approval <note>original: "album adjecturos calculum," an ancient Roman custom of using a white stone to signify agreement or acquittal</note> for our view. Meanwhile, to the credit of our Lutheran brothers, it must be admitted that most theologians today who belong to that school think more mildly of our opinion and entirely abstain from the harsher words which many of their predecessors once used when disputing against us. The second warning is: we have not brought forth these **Cautions** for the sake of veteran theologians and **Ministers of the Word of God** <term>Ministers of the Word of God: translated from "V. D. [Verbi Divini] Ministrorum," a formal title for Protestant clergy.</term> who, through meditation and practice, are better instructed in this subject than we are. These men have no need of our advice; rather, we wished to give these admonitions to Students of Theology and younger Ministers, since in public lectures, due to the constraints of time, we cannot hand down everything that a pious and prudent Minister ought to observe regarding this business.

<margin>This section concerns the excellence and dignity of this subject.</margin>
II. Since all articles of Religion ought to provide motives for the pursuit of piety, it must be shown specifically that the same can be said of the ceremonies of the New Testament. Now, above all, it is manifest that the Sacrament of the Holy Supper commends itself by its very simplicity. Truly, the excellence of the Christian Religion is proved by the fact that it is content with very few rites and ceremonies. For the more men are drawn away from those things which strike the eyes, and are instead moved toward the love

<column-break/>

<page-num>963</page-num>
<header>THE CELEBRATION OF THE HOLY SUPPER.</header>

of heavenly things, the stronger are the incentives for offering a rational worship <note>original: "cultum rationalem," a reference to Romans 12:1.</note> to God. It can rightly be affirmed of the use of the Holy Supper that it is not only a very simple rite, but by its very nature, it is suited to instill true piety in a Christian. Here you will not find a great apparatus of ceremonies; the nature of this sacred rite is not explained in an unknown tongue; there are no unusual gestures or mutterings from those officiating. Instead, the purpose of this Sacrament is handed down in a brief and clear discourse, derived from the character and nature of the ceremony itself. And what, after all, is simpler and easier to grasp than this: namely, that the bread we eat and the wine we drink signify the bloody passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, who faced death for us? The excellence of this sacred rite is even more apparent if we attend to the dignity of the person who instituted it. Certainly, that rite is not owed to obscure tradition, nor to the pleasure of the Fathers of the ancient Church, and much less to superstition, but to the most wise will of our Savior. He, while proving His heavenly mission by the excellence of His doctrine and various miracles, could prescribe nothing better than what was agreeable to reason, useful, and conforming to His own divine wisdom. Since a wise man does nothing without a reason, who would believe that our most divine Teacher and heaven-sent Prophet would bind men to observe rites that would be of no benefit? (*) Moreover, all Christians, if they are willing to weigh the principal articles of the Christian religion without prejudice <note>original: "ἄτερ παθῶν," a Greek phrase meaning "without passions" or "dispassionately."</note>, will be forced to confess that the marrow, so to speak, of this Religion is placed in the death of Jesus Christ and its efficacy for expiating sins. Now, the rite of the Holy Supper sets that most majestic event before our eyes as if it were present, and it opens up the causes of Christ’s death, its efficacy, and its remarkable use. From this, the excellence of this Sacrament is more than sufficiently manifest. Hence, it cannot be doubted that a Christian, if he attends to that end and goal of the Holy Supper and celebrates that rite with a pious and devoted mind, will perceive a remarkable benefit from it. For although—as will appear more clearly from what is said below—no one becomes pious simply from the act of consuming the bread and wine, or even from the mere remembrance of Christ's death, it is nonetheless certain...

> (*) To this point belongs the excellent testimony of **Lactantius** which appears in *Divine Institutes*, Book IV, chapter 23: *"The philosophers (he says) think that no one has yet existed as a perfect wise man—that is, one in whom the highest peak of doctrine and knowledge, the highest virtue, and perfect justice have all met. And this was indeed true. For no such person has existed since the world was founded, except Christ, who both handed down wisdom in His word and confirmed His doctrine by His present virtue."*

# DISSERTATION ON THE LEGITIMATE

...the legitimate use of this Sacrament provides the strongest incentives for the study of piety. The better these things are, the more frequently they recall to a person’s memory the most excellent things in Religion, and the more they bind him to perform his duties, the more this matter is worthy of the attention of all who confess that Christ is their Teacher and Lord.

<margin>Those who say the Reformed opinion on the Holy Supper is devoid of true incentives for piety are ridiculous.</margin>

III. From what was said in the preceding thesis, it is clear how foolish the objection is of those who—because the Reformed <term>Reformati; followers of the tradition of Calvin and Zwingli</term> do not admit a carnal eating <note>original: "carnalem manducationem," the belief that one physically eats the actual flesh of Christ</note> in the Holy Supper—cry out that they are deprived of the solid fruit of Christ’s death and the reception of the most excellent Goods that usually flow from it. It is as if no incentives for piety were present unless the mind, or rather the body, were fed on I-know-not-what food or "quasi-body." On the contrary, we contend that the legitimate use of the Holy Supper, according to the interpretation of the Lord’s words from the Reformed perspective, provides excellent motives for piety. This is because it vividly represents to Christians the most excellent object of the Christian Religion—Jesus Christ our Savior <note>original: "Soteren," from the Greek word for Savior</note>, and Him crucified—impelling them toward love for Him and, as it were, drawing them to perform all the duties of a Christian man. And what better can we expect from a ceremony instituted by God than this? We respond, moreover, that this rite of celebrating the Holy Supper does not belong to the essence of religion, but was freely instituted to represent what is essential in Religion. Hence, theologians commonly say that it is not the deprivation of the Sacraments, but the *contempt* of them, that damns Christians. Let us suppose for a moment that Christ had not instituted the Holy Supper in memory of Himself; even if this were the case, what would prevent us from being able to love Jesus Christ our Savior with a sincere heart, to proclaim the price of the redemption made for us, and to rightly discharge all the duties of piety? Since the goal is the same for those celebrating the memory of Jesus Christ in the Holy Supper, who could dare to contend with any appearance of truth that the Reformed are deprived of the solid fruit that can arise from the salutary use of the Holy Supper? Finally, this argument of those who disagree proves more than it was intended to prove, and thus proves nothing at all. No one will deny that the salutary knowledge of God, love, trust placed in Him, zeal for the glory of God, self-denial, and the other Christian virtues are actions most pleasing to God. Now, all these actions are merely moral—namely, operations of the will. If it were true that where the body is not fed in some unusual manner, the true incitements to piety are missing, then it would follow—

<column-break/>

# CELEBRATION OF THE HOLY SUPPER.
<page-num>965</page-num>
<sig>Ffffff 3</sig>

—that these very virtues just listed are unworthy of the name of "actions pleasing to God," a position which no one who accepts Religion would defend. And would that it were as true that all Christians devoted to the Reformed opinion performed this Sacrament legitimately, as it is certain that a pious and devoted use of the Holy Supper can contribute greatly to the study of piety. But if anyone should doubt this further, I will give him to ponder the brief and vigorous interpretation of our Lord Jesus Christ’s words, *“This is my body, etc.,”* which was composed by the late <note>original: "ὁ Μακαρίτης," a Greek term of respect for the deceased, similar to "of blessed memory"</note> celebrated Werenfels <note>Samuel Werenfels (1657–1740), a famous Swiss Reformed theologian known for his moderate views</note>: *“We believe (he says) and are persuaded that we not only do not weaken the true meaning and power of Christ’s words, but we retain them to such an extent that we believe Christ could not have said anything more significant, anything more suited to His purpose, or anything more effective to place before our eyes the greatness of His love (which He testified to us by suffering and dying) and to kindle our love for Him in return—nor did He ever say anything more so in His life—than when, handing the broken bread to His disciples to be eaten, He said: 'This is my body, which is broken for you,' if the words are understood in our sense. For He seems to have said this to us: 'When you receive from me and eat this bread, just now broken before your eyes, fix all your thoughts, my dearest disciples, on the contemplation of my body, which even now is about to die for you on the cross, and will be broken for you just like this bread. Think that I suffer this shameful death for you so that you may live eternally, just as you need bread, like that which I just broke for you, for your temporal life. Contemplate in your soul this stupendous love of mine toward you, by which I am kindled; I am doing as much for you now, so that you may live blessed forever, as some Friend would do for a Friend who was just about to die of hunger, who, lacking the bread he would break for him, ordered himself to be broken and slaughtered in place of the bread, so that he might preserve the life of his dying friend by his own flesh. However, so that you may see this great, this incredible love of mine as if with your eyes, touch it with your hand, and taste it with your mouth, consider now that this bread, which I just broke for you and gave to you to eat, is that very body of mine which will soon be broken like bread, crucified, and delivered unto death for you. Nor should you stop here, but this which I now command you to do, when I have ascended into heaven, you and the Christians who succeed you, continue to do in memory of this my death and passion; continue to remember this ineffable love of mine for you with this holy banquet; continue by this remembrance and so vivid a representation of it to inflame yourselves in turn to love for me; and continue this until at last I myself, about to judge the living and the dead, return to you.' Thus spoke that distinguished Theologian.*

<meta>This page continues the author's dissertation regarding the Lord’s Supper, shifting focus from the spiritual benefits of the Reformed view to the historical evidence provided by the sacrament and the common ways it is misused by various groups of people.</meta>

# DISSERTATION ON THE LEGITIMATE

<margin>The use of the Holy Supper confirms the truth of the Christian Religion.</margin>
IV. Weight can be added to the points we have just made by the observation that, indeed, the practice of the Holy Supper <note>original: "S. Coenae," literally the "Sacred Supper"</note> simultaneously confirms the truth of the Christian Religion. The practice of the Holy Supper has been received from the most ancient times, reaching back to the ages closest to the Apostles, and has been continued by all Christian Churches down to our own age. This shows that Christians of all times have judged not only that the pious celebration of the Holy Supper is of remarkable use, but by that very act, everyone confesses it to be most true and placed beyond all risk of doubt that Jesus Christ not only lived, but also died a bloody death. And truly, I have often wondered why Theologians and sacred Orators, when they are accustomed to treat the nature, end, and use of the Holy Supper, have not pressed the argument for the truth of the Christian Religion which can be sought from this most ancient sacred rite; for among the historical arguments by which the truth of the Christian Religion is usually proven, it holds a place of no small importance. For although it is certain enough that the first Teachers of the Christian Church, whom they call the Fathers <note>The "Church Fathers" were influential Christian theologians and leaders in the first few centuries after Christ.</note>, expressed their opinion on this Sacrament in somewhat obscure words—so much so that *Lutherans, Roman Catholics* <note>original: "Pontificii," referring to those aligned with the Pope</note>, *and the Reformed* each wish to pull those Fathers toward their own opinions—nevertheless, they all agree in this: that Jesus Christ lived on earth, suffered, and instituted the Holy Supper in memory of Himself. Those very slanders spread against the Christians, wherever they arose (which is not the place to discuss here), which are read in the Apologies of the Fathers, prove that Christians used this sacred rite in memory of our most holy Savior <note>original: "Soteris," from the Greek word for Savior</note>. Therefore, the Unbelievers <note>original: "Increduli"</note> who deny the very truth of the Christian Religion ought to prove, by certain testimonies sought from ecclesiastical antiquity, either that this sacred rite was not practiced by Christians, or that the origin of this sacred rite is something other than what is maintained in the writings of the Evangelists, Apostles, and early Fathers; or else they must concede that the rite of celebrating the Holy Supper rests upon a universal and certain conviction regarding the dignity and passion of Jesus Christ. I confess I cannot see by what reasoning the Deists <note>Those who believe in a God who created the world but does not intervene in it, often rejecting organized revelation.</note> could defend their cause. Hence, I would wish that the Ministers of the Word <note>original: "V. D. Ministri," an abbreviation for Verbi Dei Ministri</note>, when they treat the end and use of the Holy Supper, would also ascend to its origin, and once these things are uncovered, they would strongly urge this argument which can be drawn to prove the truth of the Christian Religion. Indeed, no one among the learned doubts that such testimonies are present in the writings of the most ancient Fathers. See among our own authors *Albertin, Larroque, Claude, and J. Basnage*, who have cited these passages most extensively and attempted to defend them against the *Roman Catholics*.

<meta>catchword: V. How-</meta>

<column-break/>

# ...CELEBRATION OF THE HOLY SUPPER.

<margin>The abuse of this Sacrament among Christians is very frequent.</margin>
V. However, although the Sacrament of the Holy Supper was instituted by our Savior for a most wise purpose, and recalls to our memory a matter of the greatest importance—namely, the bloody death of the Savior—and thus supplies the most serious incentives for piety, it must nevertheless be confessed that most Christians devoted to the Reformed Religion (it is not our place to judge others) shamefully abuse this Sacrament, so much so that it has little effectiveness on the minds of many. <margin>1.</margin> There are those, though fewer in number, who are accustomed to evade the celebration of this Sacrament. And these are men of two kinds. <margin>a.</margin> There are those who do so with a profane mind. <margin>b.</margin> Then there are pious men, but who, on account of certain scruples cast into their conscience, are unwilling to take part in the celebration of the Holy Supper. The former are for the most part men who are touched by little care for Religion, and have given their names to the crowds of Deists or Indifferentists <note>Those who believe it does not matter which religion one follows.</note>. For these, unless they first bid farewell to their thicker prejudices regarding Religion and are persuaded of the truth of the Christian Religion and other articles that lead to knowing the true nature of this Religion, the celebration of the Holy Supper is commended in vain. But there are also pious men whose minds are besieged for a time by various scruples. From whence those arise, we shall investigate below. Truly, the Ministers of the Word ought to speak more familiarly with these, and see to it that they are brought back to the path by various arguments; care must be taken on one hand that the use of the Holy Supper is not extolled beyond measure, but on the other hand, it should be shown that the marks of piety, which the Ministers of the Word can know to be in them, ought not to prevent them from frequently using the Holy Supper, which contributes greatly to confirming piety and was enjoined upon Christians by Christ to be celebrated. To that end, let students of the Sacred Letters read the *Sacred Sermon on the Frequent Use of the Holy Supper* by the most Reverend Father in Christ *Tillotson, formerly the most worthy Archbishop of Canterbury*. By far the greatest part of Christians who are accustomed to celebrate the Holy Supper are hypocrites and men given over to vices. These people think the nature and character of piety is fulfilled by the performance of external worship; and although they are unwilling to abandon their vices, they simultaneously and foolishly judge that their sins are washed away, provided they diligently attend the celebration of the Holy Supper and use this Sacrament. Hence, when they think to approach the Holy Supper, they are accustomed to say they do it so that they may be made certain of obtaining salvation—as if the use of bread and wine, joined with any sort of recollection of the death of Christ, would give men a certain and unshaken confidence of reconciliation made with God. Imbued with this very dangerous opinion, when they know the times for celebrating the Holy Supper are at hand, they leaf through a little book <note>referring to devotional manuals or prayer books</note>

...reading some devotional booklet <note>original: "libellum asceticum," a book for spiritual exercise or self-discipline</note> that shows the way to a healthy celebration of the Holy Supper, they are also mindful of their sins—yet not in such a way that they detest them and wish to seriously say farewell to them. Instead, they do so because they believe such a memory is a necessary "work" if one wishes to surely promise themselves the forgiveness of sins. They therefore use the bread and wine, employing certain fixed words, with which they believe the forgiveness of sins is as surely connected as it is certain that they have tasted the bread and wine. Once this is done, they return home happy and mostly read those prayer formulas in which thanks are given to God for the forgiveness of sins. Meanwhile, they proceed on the same foot they began: they do not cease to love the vices to which they were long ago devoted. Thus, they are often accustomed to celebrate the Holy Supper for thirty or more years. With what fruit they do so is plain to all who are not total strangers to the Christian Religion.

<margin>An inquiry into the causes of this evil, of which we have just now made mention. The first cause is presented.</margin>

VI. It is helpful to inquire into the causes of this evil we are mentioning, so that candidates for the Sacred Ministry may learn early to avoid everything that can provide an occasion for errors regarding this subject. Now, those causes are partly *external*, coming from elsewhere; others are to be sought in the depths of the heart. Among the external causes, I first count *false concepts about the nature and goals of the Holy Supper, received through hearing and reading.* To be sure, Catechists, Preachers, and the authors of booklets—in which advice and precepts for the legitimate preparation for the Holy Supper are supplied—often use many metaphorical and mystical expressions. When these are not correctly understood, they not only cause the simpler folk <note>The "simpliciores" refers to the uneducated or common people who lack theological training.</note> to *fail to rightly perceive the nature and scope of the Holy Supper, but they also cause them to be entirely fixed upon the external use of the Symbols, thinking that some kind of unusual enjoyment is joined to the use of this Sacrament.* I certainly do not doubt that the authors of those metaphorical phrases do so with good intentions, namely to excite devotion in the minds of their listeners and readers. But unless the nature of the matter is rightly understood (as in other Articles of Religion, so especially in this argument), true devotion can have no place. To produce true piety, there is a need for clear and distinct notions; however, notions expressed in obscure words block the true sense. This must certainly happen to the simpler people. In the meantime, despite this, there are many who think they have rightly performed their duty and fulfilled the part of learned Orators only if they can adorn the dogmas of Religion with innumerable "rhetorical flowers," as they think of them. I have often wondered, and still wonder, how it can be that in our age—in which the art of thinking and speaking has been raised to the highest peak of philosophical

discipline—many otherwise learned men still take a singular pleasure in sacred sermons variegated with many metaphors. Such metaphorical and mystical expressions are found in many devotional books <note>original: "libris asceticis"</note> which deal with the *legitimate preparation of the Christian man for the Holy Supper.* Thus, to say nothing of others, the booklet by *Drelincourt* <note>Charles Drelincourt (1595–1669) was a famous French Reformed minister whose works were immensely popular.</note>, which our countrymen commonly use, overflows with this kind of phraseology. I wish to detract nothing from the piety and erudition of that excellent man. However, he would have better served his purpose if he had used clearer and more transparent speech, since booklets of that kind ought to be accommodated to the capacity of everyone. Hence, men outstanding in piety and wisdom have often wished that such booklets existed that recommend themselves by their brevity and simplicity. Among them was the celebrated *Werenfels* <note>Samuel Werenfels (1657–1740), a Swiss theologian known for his moderate views and desire for clarity.</note> of Basel, who, as the Venerable *Ostervald* <note>Jean-Frédéric Ostervald (1663–1747), an influential Swiss Protestant pastor.</note> testified in letters sent to me, used to say: *It is a pity that we have no book on Communion that is simple, popular, clear, and fit for edification.* <note>original: "Il est facheux que l'on n'avoit point de livre fur la Communion, qui soit simple, populaire, clair & propre pour l'édification."</note> And, such is the happiness of our century, men eminent in sagacity of mind and piety have satisfied this desire of the best men. The first is the most celebrated *Hoadly, today Bishop of Winchester* <note>Benjamin Hoadly (1676–1761), an English bishop whose "Plain Account of the Nature and End of the Sacrament of the Lord's Supper" (1735) caused a stir by arguing for a very simple, memorialist view of the rite.</note>, in an altogether excellent booklet titled: *Treatise on the Nature, Goal, and Effects of the Sacrament of the Holy Supper.* <note>original: "Traité sur la Nature, le but & les Effets du Sacrement de la Sainte Cene."</note> The other is the Venerable *Ostervald, a most worthy Pastor of the French Church of Basel, and son of the Venerable elder J. F. Ostervald.* He published a booklet two years ago titled: *The Duties of Communicants.* <note>original: "Les Devoirs des Commu- nians."</note> This booklet truly recommends itself by the simplicity of its speech, its brevity, and the weight of its argument; it is suited to the minds of all and is greatly to be commended on that account. I am persuaded, however, that there will always be those who are greatly pleased by those metaphorical and more obscure formulas of speaking, because they think that in this way their piety and eloquence are proven, and minds are excited to a singular devotion. Yet, in this, they will not bring those who rightly understand the art of thinking and debating to agreement. Arguments, arguments, I say, alone—proposed in clear speech and suited to the minds of all—bring true light to the mind. Even if the Sacred Writers used somewhat obscure phrases in this matter, it would be the duty of those teaching to substitute clearer ones, especially in catechetical instructions and sacred orations usually held publicly on this subject. For once the mind, when dealing with religion, settles for obscure words, it hardly admits a remedy afterward. Certainly the simpler folk, the words by which obscure notions are expressed...

...are accustomed to express, they will not allow it to be snatched from them. Therefore, students of Holy Scripture must diligently apply themselves in a timely manner so that they may have an accurate understanding of this subject. When they turn their minds to the instruction of the youth, they must apply every care and concern to explain the nature of this sacrament in the clearest words. They should not rest until, through repeated questions and answers, they are persuaded that their students or listeners have a clear and genuine idea of this Sacrament. In sacred sermons, the same tracks must be followed. If this is neglected, it cannot happen otherwise than that the simpler folk <note>the uneducated or laypeople</note> will believe that some physical and unusual power <note>original: "physicam & insolitam vim"</note> is joined with the use of the bread and wine, which feeds souls in a miraculous way. Indeed, if anyone is imbued with this opinion, it is inevitable that they will think true protection and solace should be sought in the external enjoyment of this Sacrament itself; however, they will pay little attention to the true characteristics by which we know we have been made participants in the death of Christ.

<margin>Whether it is permissible to use ambiguous and more obscure words in the explanation of the Holy Supper to promote union among Protestants.</margin>

VII. While we are on this subject, and showing how necessary it is for Ministers of the Word of God to explain the nature of this Sacrament in clear and perspicuous words in their catechetical instructions and sacred orations, a question arises here—not foreign to our purpose—namely, whether it is expedient to use more general and ambiguous phrases to repair and promote the long-desired Union of Protestants <note>the ongoing efforts to reconcile the Lutheran and Reformed/Calvinist branches</note>, which both dissenting parties could subscribe to. It is very well known that among the causes of the unhappy Schism that exists between the Lutheran and Reformed Churches, the principal article at the rise of the Reformation of sacred things was the doctrine of the Holy Supper. In the following age, so many volumes were written on this article that entire houses could scarcely hold them. I will not say now with what bitterness of words some have used while placed in the heat of this dispute. For it does not help to rub this wound raw again, after the most excellent among the Brethren now think more kindly of our opinion. To settle those grave and deadly strifes, certain men of learned and moderate character spent all the nerves of their genius, among whom *Bucer* <note>Martin Bucer (1491–1551), a Reformer known for his efforts to find middle ground</note> was eminent. He believed he would reach his goal most successfully if he worked so that both parties would subscribe to certain formulas composed in more general words, such as those which might express the views of both sides. However, our *Zwingli* <note>Huldrych Zwingli (1484–1531), the Swiss Reformer</note>, speaking of the words of institution and the nature of the Holy Supper, used clear and direct words; for this, he was praised by the famous *Bossuet* <note>Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet (1627–1704), a powerful French Catholic bishop and master orator</note> in the *History of the Variations of the Protestant Churches, Book III, Section XIV.*

# CELEBRATION OF THE HOLY SUPPER.
<sig>Gggggg 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: stum</meta>

The same most learned Prelate of the Roman Church, not only in this very History, but also in his exposition of the Catholic Faith, wishes to prove from the Catechism of the Reformed (arranged according to the mind of *Calvin*), that either the authors of the Catechism did not know what they were saying, or they admit a real and substantial presence of Christ with the Roman Church. It is helpful to cite certain words of this famous man: I am using the Latin version of this Exposition, which was reprinted at *Göttingen* in 1736. After he had warned in Section 117, page 69, that the Reformed contend they do not admit "naked signs" and "naked figures" in the Holy Supper, he adds these things:

> Just as we do, they assert that Christ makes us participants of his proper substance in the Holy Supper, and that He nourishes and gives us life by the substance of his body and blood.

He appeals to the 52nd and 53rd "Sundays" <note>sections of the catechism intended for weekly instruction</note> of this Catechism. In Section 120, he says:

> I will cite here the testimony of no private author, but the very words of the Catechism in the place where it explains what pertains to the Supper. There, in express words, it says not only that Christ is truly given to us in the Supper, even according to his own substance; but although he is truly communicated to us both through Baptism and through the Gospel, yet on their part he is communicated only partially there, and not fully. Therefore, in the Supper, he is given fully and not partially. Between receiving something partially or fully, there is a marvelous difference; therefore, if elsewhere Christ is always received only partially, but in the Supper he is received fully, it follows—by the adversaries' own consent and even by their leading the way—that a way of participating in him must be sought in the Supper which is so proper to that Sacrament that it fits neither Baptism nor preaching. But at the same time, it also follows that this participation does not depend on faith alone, since faith is diffused into all acts of a Christian man whatsoever, and is found in preaching and in Baptism just as much as in the Supper.

In Section 120, he appeals to the 59th Sunday, in which these words appear:

> The body of the Lord Jesus, insofar as it was once offered as a sacrifice to reconcile us to God, is now given to us to make us more certain that we are participants in that reconciliation.

After he had cited these words of the Catechism, he continues thus:

> If any sense exists in these words—if they are not empty sound and a vain mockery—they surely signify that not a naked symbol is given to us by Christ, but his own body; by which he makes us more certain of the sacrifice offered by him, and that we are participants there of the friendship reconciled with the human race.

Hence, in Section 130, he taxes <note>criticizes or accuses</note> the Reformed because, although they wish to seem to depart as far as possible from the Roman Church regarding this argument, they nevertheless use phrases that seem consistent with the Decrees of the Roman Church. "Indeed, I have often wondered," he says, "that they have not explained their doctrine in a plainer way: why do they not proceed, having removed so many evasions, to say that Christ..."

...[Christ] wished to foreshadow the shedding of his blood for us in such a way that he gave two signs of his body and blood. Furthermore, he wished to grant the name of the reality itself to these signs, so that these sacred signs might serve as a pledge <note>original: "pignoris"</note>; by this, we are made more certain that the grace of the Lord's death is communicated to us, and that we are spiritually refreshed by the power of the sacred body and blood. After they [the theologians] had struggled with such great effort to confirm this with arguments—namely, that the signs receive the name of the thing itself, and therefore the sign of the body could be called "the body"—the very sequence of the proposed doctrine compelled them to stop there and proceed no further. Thus far, **Bossuet** <note>Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet, a prominent 17th-century French Catholic bishop and orator</note>.

And indeed, we cannot deny that even the most excellent men, such as **Bucer**, **Calvin**, and others, suffered from human frailty because they did not disclose their opinion on the nature of the **Holy Supper** <term>Holy Supper: The Eucharist or Lord's Supper</term> more clearly and directly. For this gave occasion for new brawls and contentions. However, with the passage of time, it happened that most of the **Reformed** <note>The "Reformed" branch of Protestantism, often associated with Calvin and Zwingli</note> embraced the explanation of **Zwingli**, who revealed his opinion without verbal complications. Although in the substance of the matter his view did not differ from that of **Calvin**, the **Calvinist** way of speaking still appealed to the English and the French. In our own age, however, even these people are beginning to reveal their opinions more openly, as is evident from the cited booklet by the celebrated **Hoadly** <note>Benjamin Hoadly, an influential and controversial English bishop</note>; in that same booklet, he also explained the more obscure phrases regarding the nature and character of the Holy Supper used by the author of the *Anglican Liturgy*. I am aware, of course, that disputes arose among theologians on that occasion, and that certain Englishmen rejected that natural explanation of the Most Reverend Bishop, even though in the substance of things it agrees with the opinion of all the Reformed. But this is not surprising. For experience has long shown that there are theologians who, when they see others explaining a dogma in clearer and more appropriate words than are commonly accepted, are as disturbed as if the matter itself were being called into question. The most learned **Samuel Clarke** followed **Hoadly**, as is clear from Volume IV of the *Sacred Sermons* which he published. Nor do I doubt that other English theologians will follow in the footsteps of these great men in the future. For where the philosophical disciplines flourish (as is well known of England) and where any wise man is allowed to modestly reveal the feelings of his mind, men of outstanding talent cannot help but love light and simplicity. But if it is now asked whether **Bucer** and others did rightly in using such obscure phrases to remove that controversy among Protestants, we respond: we indeed praise the study of peace by these most excellent men, and we do not doubt that they were led by zeal for the glory of God to settle this dispute among brothers, and that they had the best goal...

...and one worthy of peaceful theologians. But the means which they used to obtain what they intended, we do not approve. To confirm what I have said here by the consensus of the most excellent theologians, I bring forward (as a representative of many) the words of the most celebrated man **Samuel Werenfels** <note>A Swiss theologian known for his moderate views and critique of religious disputes</note>, a theologian who, in the judgment of all who are wise, is most sagacious. After he had rightfully criticized the celebrated **Bossuet** in his *Dissertation on the Proper Handling of Theological Controversies* (because Bossuet had represented the Roman doctrine less than candidly in his exposition of the Catholic faith), Werenfels discusses the matter in the following way:

> *We must take care again and again lest those arts—which conflict with the sincerity of a pious and grave theologian—be justly thrown back at us sometime, just as we rightly blame them in others. They have certainly been thrown at us often by many brothers of the **Augustana Confession** <term>Augustana Confession: The primary confession of faith of the Lutheran Church (1530)</term>, who commonly wish to be distinguished from us by the name of **Lutherans**. And indeed, unless we wish to sin against this very sincerity which we so greatly commend, we cannot at all deny that in previous centuries there were some among our theologians who, though with the best and clearly peaceful intentions, acted in this matter without sufficient circumspection and foresight, and once or twice gave the aforementioned brothers occasion to desire greater sincerity in us. This happened when those theologians, in order to conciliate such a desirable and necessary peace between us and our Lutheran brothers, thought that vague, general, and ambiguous formulas of speaking should be found for this purpose. They hoped that, while maintaining whatever diversity of opinions existed, the disciples of Luther, Zwingli, and Calvin could subscribe to these formulas without difficulty. But if I may speak the truth, they harmed the Church of Christ more than they helped it by this method. For besides the fact that they thus rendered themselves more suspect and even hated by their adversaries: who does not see that true peace and concord do not consist in the pronunciation of the same words, syllables, and letters? Rather, peace consists either in full agreement about everything (which cannot be hoped for with reason in this darkness of minds), or in a sincere consensus regarding the fundamental dogmas of the Christian faith, joined with a mutual and **Christian tolerance** regarding those opinions which do not constitute the nature and essence of Christianity.*

And after a few things are interposed:

> *I cannot help but praise and vehemently approve here what the Blessed **Luther** himself once prescribed to those disputing among themselves about the Holy Supper: "The question is," (he says) "whether a man..."*

...should a Christian person receive nothing but bare bread and wine with his mouth, and what is being handed to him by the hands of the Minister? Here it is not fitting to mumble <note>original: "pulmentum in ore volvere," literally "to roll porridge in the mouth," an idiom for being evasive</note> and answer with silence, or to peddle the matter in obscure wrappings. Nor is it fitting to play games under a hat or act like a creature of the shadows. It is as you say, **Luther**: *None of these things befit serious and pious theologians. These men ought always to propose their opinion clearly, openly, and candidly: Never seek deceit, never seek false colors.* By this ingenuity and candor, they will win over good men of the other party more effectively, and render them more prone and better taught to embrace the truer opinion, than by I-know-not-what pigments and wrappings of their own view.

<margin>(*) The most distinguished **Limborch** <note>Philipp van Limborch (1633–1712), a Dutch Remonstrant theologian known for his moderate and rational approach to doctrine</note>, standing outside the partisan divide in this business, offers the same advice. For he speaks thus in his *Theological Institutions*, Book V, Chapter LXXI, Section IX: "The opinion of the **Reformed** <note>The branch of Protestantism often following the teachings of Calvin or Zwingli</note> is that true bread and wine are given in the Lord’s Supper, and that these are symbols and signs of the body of Jesus Christ broken for us and the blood shed for us. This was the opinion of **Zwingli**. But **Bucer**, **Calvin**, and their followers later added: although the bread and wine are received by the members and senses of the body, nevertheless the body itself and the blood itself of Christ are truly present there and exhibited, and received by faith. It seems this was devised by **Bucer**, who, out of a zeal for peace and to reconcile the **Lutherans** and Zwinglians, thought up ambiguous ways of speaking to which both parties could subscribe, while each kept their own opinion. But that attempt ended badly. For the Lutherans complain of the fraud of the Reformed, who take away with one hand what they offer with the other. And in truth, so that peace and concord may be obtained, it is better to speak properly without ambiguity, and to confess whatever disagreement exists, while in the meantime inquiring into its significance; by this it may become clear that the disagreement is not so great that it is necessary to split into parties. This is better than hiding the disagreement with general and ambiguous words, only to betray that disagreement again later with a peculiar and different acceptance of those words."</margin>
In the past, that same candor was rightly praised in **Peter Martyr** <note>Peter Martyr Vermigli (1499–1562), an influential Italian theologian who worked in England and Switzerland</note>, when a formula had been prepared at the **Colloquy of Poissy** <note>A 1561 conference in France that attempted to reconcile Catholics and Protestants</note> in which both the Catholics and the Reformed could agree on the presence of Christ's body in the **Holy Supper** <term>Holy Supper: Another name for the Eucharist or Lord's Supper</term>. Once the participants from both sides had signed this formula: Martyr himself, along with **Beza** <note>Theodore Beza, the primary successor to John Calvin in Geneva</note> and the other Reformed participants, added a short declaration to this formula—which was ambiguous in certain parts—so that, with the ambiguity removed, the Catholics might see what their actual opinion was. Indeed, that declaration still exists today in the *Common Places* of Peter Martyr, in which among other things these words are read: *I admit the provided formulas of consensus on the condition that they refer to, or can be accommodated to, the sense already explained: against which, if anyone should seize or interpret them, I profess that I disagree with him.* Thus far that extraordinary theologian. (*)

The worst part is that the common folk, having heard those mystical and metaphorical phrases, fall into the opinion that some sort of unusual, purely physical effect is joined to the very enjoyment of the bread and wine. This is evident from the speech and actions of many members of the Reformed Church.

From their *actions*; for when, by chance, a small crumb of bread falls to the ground, they are seized by a strange horror, and often fall into great sadness because of it. From their *speech*: for they speak after they have celebrated the Holy Supper in such a way that it is manifest they think some sort of "vehicle" <note>An instrument or medium that automatically carries grace to the recipient</note> is joined to the use of the Holy Supper—and specifically such a vehicle that from its enjoyment, the forgiveness of previous sins necessarily follows. Therefore, the **Ministers of the Word of God** must be warned to hand down the genuine notion of the words of the institution of the Holy Supper using the simplest terms, to represent the character of the genuine celebration of Christ’s death, and to show who truly receives the correct benefit from the celebration of this Sacrament.

## VIII.

<margin>One must insist on the phrases which are found in the New Testament from Christ and the Apostles.</margin>
However, so that the Minister of the Word may obtain his goal, he must take care not to employ the phrases of either the **Church Fathers** <note>Early Christian teachers and bishops from the first few centuries</note> or of theologians who proposed the words of institution only with metaphorical expressions and rhetorical exaggerations. Instead, effort should be given to insist, as much as possible, on those formulas of speaking which were used by Christ and the Apostles. Since Jesus Christ himself instituted this sacred ceremony and used those words which sufficiently and clearly reveal the nature and goal of this Sacrament, why should we follow the phrases and formulas of men who cannot provide greater light? Especially since experience has taught that the more Christians have retreated from the words used by Christ and the Apostles, the more this subject—which is very simple in itself—has been obscured. If we read the four Evangelists and Paul writing to the Corinthians on this subject, we learn nothing else from them but this: Christ our Savior, being near death, gave bread and wine to his disciples for the purpose that they, and all Christians to follow, might religiously and with a grateful heart recall his bloody passion to memory, and in this way bind themselves to the duties of piety and charity.

Yet, as is well known, monstrous opinions have arisen from this simple rite. Therefore, a prudent Minister of the Word and a Christian person will insist only on those words which were handed down by Christ and the Apostles concerning this subject. It is plainly foolish to want to follow the authority and decisions of those who, many years after the departure of Christ and the Apostles, added many things according to their own will, of which no traces are found in the sacred books. The Most Reverend **Hoadly** <note>Benjamin Hoadly (1676–1761), an English bishop who argued that the Eucharist was a simple commemorative rite</note> correctly observed this in the place cited above, page 29. "I leave it," he says, "to every Christian who acts sincerely and in good faith, even if he be of the least fortunate understanding, to judge whether one ought not to refer rather to our Blessed Savior himself in a matter which..." <note>original French: "Je laisse à tout Chrétien qui agit sincérement & de bonne foi, fût-il de la comprehension la moins heureuse, à juger, si l'on ne doit pas s'en rapporter plûtôt à notre Bienheureux sauveur lui-même dans une affaire, qui..."</note>

*...which depends entirely on his will, rather than on any of those who cannot claim to have received their instructions from him immediately. Let them see for themselves if there is not more piety, as well as reason, in believing that Jesus Christ sufficiently declared his thoughts to his immediate Disciples regarding an institution that he himself was establishing, than in imagining that he left this care to men who would live a hundred, or five hundred, or a thousand, or nearly two thousand years after the first institution of this duty.* <note>original: "qui depend entierement de sa volonté..." — This passage in French argues that the direct words of Jesus are a more reliable foundation for faith than centuries of later tradition.</note>

One must, therefore, abstain in this argument from the phrases used by the **Fathers** <note>The "Church Fathers" are influential Christian theologians from the first few centuries of the Church</note> when they were explaining the nature of the Holy Supper. It is well enough known today that they were not always the best masters of the art of thinking, nor the best interpreters of the Holy Scriptures. As with other articles of Religion, so too on this subject they often spoke rhetorically and used many obscure and mystical phrases. Consequently, they obscured this subject rather than truly explaining it; hence, learned men have been forced to write huge volumes regarding the sense of the Fathers concerning the nature of the Holy Supper.

If they had added nothing to the words of Christ and the Apostles; if they had represented the mind of Jesus Christ instituting the Holy Supper directly and clearly; if they had omitted various comparisons and metaphorical phrases, that monstrous dogma of **Transubstantiation** <term>Transubstantiation: the Catholic doctrine that the bread and wine literally turn into the body and blood of Christ</term> would never have been born. Indeed, it was customary for the Fathers to extol things with grand words and to speak rhetorically where the plainest words should have been used, as the illustrious **Daillé** <note>Jean Daillé (1594–1670), a prominent French Protestant theologian</note> showed in an entire chapter of his excellent book *On the Use of the Fathers*. It is helpful to bring forward a few points here that relate to this. In Chapter V, page 147, that most excellent man speaks thus:

*When they (namely the Fathers of the Church) dispute against the Valentinians or Manichaeans, they seem to side with the Pelagians. By the same reasoning, whenever they clash with the Pelagians, they seem to agree with the Manichaeans. If they are carried away against Arius, they seem less distant from Sabellius. Conversely, when they attack Sabellius, they seem to approach Arius, as the Bishop of Bitonto remarked specifically about Augustine. This very thing happens every day to those who speak to the people: if they rail against the greedy, they come close to commending the profligate; but when they attack the profligate and the overly lavish, you would think they were favoring stinginess and tenacity. So among the Protestants: those who reject those empty and vanishing figures—which the Romans attribute to I-know-not-what invented "Sacramentarians"—sometimes act in such a way that at first glance they might seem to establish the "reality" (as they call it) of the Eucharist. Yet when they dispute against Transubstantiation and real inclusion, you would swear they stand with those very Sacramentarians.*

The most learned Jesuit **Petavius** <note>Denis Pétau (1583–1652), a French Jesuit theologian and scholar</note> confessed the same about the Fathers in his notes to *Epiphanius*, page 141: "There are many things

<column-break/>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<page-num>977</page-num>

things (he says) scattered by the most holy Fathers, and especially by **Chrysostom** <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an early Church Father known for his powerful preaching</note> in his homilies, which, if you wish to adapt them to the rule of exact truth, will seem void of good sense." And who does not know that things reached the point where many Christians used the Holy Supper as a **medicine** <note>original: "medicamentum"</note>, possessing a unique power against diseases? Regarding this subject—that is, the *medical use of the Holy Supper*—the very Reverend and most Friendly man, **Mr. Gerdes** <note>Daniel Gerdes (1698–1765), a German Calvinist theologian and historian</note>, a most famous theologian today in Groningen, has written in a special dissertation.

What Daillé warned about certain more recent preachers is very true. For when they wish to commend the use of the Holy Supper, they talk much about spiritual feasts and dishes, mental nourishments, and the hospitality of Christ in those celebrating the Holy Supper. They use so many flowery figures of speech that simpler folk are confused, and they speak of the enjoyment of the Holy Supper as if the celebration of the Holy Supper itself, used with some feeling of piety, were the *only, most certain, and most evident sign* of a truly Christian man; however, more on this below.

*Therefore, a wise Minister of the Word of God, when he treats the institution and use of the Holy Supper, should follow Christ and the Apostles alone. He should not follow in the footsteps of the Fathers or of more recent rhetorical theologians who use highly mystical phrases; on the contrary, he should use such clear and transparent phrases that even the simplest listeners cannot fail to understand the matter.*

<margin>An inquiry into the sense in which the Sacrament of the Holy Supper can be called a seal.</margin>

IX. But there are other phrases and expressions in this argument which, because they are too vague and insufficiently distinct, provide many Christians an occasion to attribute things to themselves that in no way apply to them. For example, because many hear that the Holy Supper is a **seal of divine grace** and of our reconciliation with God, they conclude from this that the use of the Holy Supper is a most certain and infallible sign of a pious soul joined with Jesus Christ. Just as men are made certain by seals that something belongs to them, they think there is no doubt that those who have been made participants of this Sacrament (that is, the bread and wine) can be certain and fully persuaded that all the benefits won by the passion of the Savior belong to them by right.

But these men err greatly. The Holy Supper is called a "seal" either insofar as we look to the eating of the bread and wine, or insofar as these elements represent the death and passion of Christ itself. If you take it in the first sense, the use of bread and wine can in no way be called a seal of true faith and divine grace, because the wicked and hypocrites enjoy these elements just as much as the pious. Therefore, the eating of bread and wine cannot be a certain sign that the benefits won by the death of Jesus Christ belong to the one who uses them. Just as if a letter fortified with a seal were delivered to me...

<page-num>978</page-num>

...are given, in which a wealthy inheritance is assigned to me, but a thousand others show the same documents, secured with the same seals, I certainly cannot conclude that I alone am the legitimate possessor of this inheritance. If you look at the significance of the bread and wine, they denote the bloody death of Christ and his merit. Now, however, it cannot be said that the contemplation of this death, and the persuasion regarding the efficacy of the death of Jesus Christ, is a certain **seal**, from which it would be clear to anyone partaking in the <term>Holy Supper</term> <note>original: "S. Coena" — also known as the Eucharist or Communion</note> that the benefits gained by the death of Jesus Christ belong to them by name. For even the wicked and hypocrites can, on the occasion of the Holy Supper, think about Christ's death and believe that Jesus underwent a bloody death for humanity. And as far as the pious are concerned, they may sometimes be deprived of the use of the Holy Supper due to moral or physical causes; but who would say that they therefore lack the **seal** of divine grace and do not share in the death of Christ? Yet this would have to be affirmed if the representation of Christ's death in the Holy Supper were a certain and infallible seal of true piety and the love of Jesus Christ. The pious can also sin at times, just as in other duties of Christianity, so too in the use of the Holy Supper; they may sometimes use the Holy Supper without that devotion which is required here, by which act, however, they are not deprived of the marks of true Christians.

But suppose that pious men religiously celebrate the memory of the death of Jesus Christ; they cannot be said to be armed with the seal of true piety for this reason alone. For according to the opinion of the **Reformed**, the most certain characters of a true Christian are saving faith, sincere repentance, and the observation of divine commands. But these characters—this seal—ought to be present in a Christian man *before* the celebration of the Holy Supper. Properly speaking, the blood of Jesus Christ, or rather his death, is the seal of the <term>New Covenant</term>; but that is not the question here. For we confess that the bloody death of Jesus Christ is the seal of reconciliation: the only question is by what indication it is clear to us that the fruits of this death certainly belong to us. Now, from the mere remembrance of this death, whether it happens in the Celebration of the Holy Supper or outside of it, Christians cannot conclude that the benefits gained through the passion of Jesus Christ belong to them, unless they have been taught this from elsewhere. Let us suppose a prince offers a <term>post of duty</term> <note>original: "spartam" — literally 'Sparta', referring to the proverb 'You have found Sparta, now adorn it', meaning a position of responsibility</note> through letters secured with his seal, yet with no name added of the person who should fulfill the offered duty; could anyone of sound mind contend that this duty was offered to him alone by name? In the same way, neither from the use of the bread and wine in the Holy Supper, nor from the remembrance of the death of Jesus Christ, nor from public or private confession, [can we know] that the death of Jesus Christ...

...is the true cause of our reconciliation, nor can we know that the fruits of the death of Jesus Christ certainly apply to us; rather, that certain persuasion finally arises from certain characters of the soul—namely, from the zeal for <term>sanctification</term> <note>The process of being made holy or being set apart for God’s purposes</note> and the love of God. For from that it is evidently clear that <term>regeneration</term> <note>The spiritual rebirth or being 'born again'</note> is a certain consequence of the fruits of the <term>merit of Jesus Christ</term> <note>The value of Christ’s suffering and obedience which pays the debt of human sin</note>; for by that merit it is brought about that the mind is gifted with new life. 

But if anyone wishes to cling to the word "seal," I will say in what sense the use of the Holy Supper can be so called. Namely, when a pious man, on the occasion of the Holy Supper, both religiously looks back to the death of Jesus Christ and also attends to the present state of his own sanctified mind, he remembers—with those present external signs meeting his eyes—that the bloody death of his Savior has exerted its efficacy within him, and that his conversion is owed solely to the crucified Jesus. Thus, he is incited in a new way to love Jesus above all things and to diligently perform the duties of a Christian man. In this sense, the pious can be said to have received the **seal of the righteousness of faith**. 

And this interpretation flows necessarily from the principles of the Reformed. For they assert that the sole cause of our reconciliation with God is the merit of Jesus Christ: that men become sharers of this benefit through <term>justification</term> <note>Being declared righteous or 'in the right' before God</note>, sanctification, and regeneration: that there are certain characters from which a man can know whether he has been enriched by that sanctification, and thus also by reconciliation: that these certain and infallible characters are serious repentance, saving faith, and the observance of divine commands: and that the Sacraments are not miracles, nor medicines, nor vehicles, nor ultimately the causes of grace. From which it follows by legitimate consequence that, properly speaking, those characters implanted in the souls of the faithful are that **seal** by which we are made certain that the benefits gained through the death of Jesus Christ belong to us. 

And indeed, unless it is clearly and transparently explained what is signified by the name of "seal," many Christians will think that either the mere use of external symbols, or that transitory meditation on the death of Jesus Christ excited by the symbols, is that seal—that is, the certain indication from which they can certainly conclude that they are Christians in true name, having been made partakers of the benefits acquired by the death of Christ. There will perhaps be those to whom these things I have noted on this argument seem trivial; but to me, it does not seem trivial to supply clear notions about Religion and to recall men from practical errors. Certainly, he who believes that either the use of bread and wine in the Holy Supper, or the remembrance of the bloody death of Christ, joined with a public profession that our Savior by his death [attained] remission...
