...acquired for us the remission of sins, and that [the sacrament] is a certain sign and seal of his reconciliation with God, and of the certain persuasion of the remission of sins; otherwise, he will be little concerned about putting off the habit of vices and amending his mind. Our **Blessed Zwingli** <note>Huldrych Zwingli (1484–1531), a leader of the Reformation in Switzerland</note> has spoken clearly to our way of thinking on this argument in many places. In his *Exposition of the Christian Faith*, on page 14 of my edition, he speaks thus: *“For some time there has been a sharp conflict among us as to what the Sacraments or Symbols in the Supper do or are capable of doing: some contend that the Sacraments give faith, bring the natural Body of Christ, and cause it to be eaten as if present; we, however, feel differently, not without authority. First, because no one gives faith—which is trust in God—except the Holy Spirit; no external thing does this, although the Sacraments may produce a historical faith.”* <note>original: "fidem historicam" — Zwingli distinguishes between 'saving faith' and 'historical faith,' which is merely acknowledging that the events of the Bible happened as historical facts.</note> *“For all public assemblies, trophies, and indeed monuments and statues, produce historical faith; that is, they remind us that something was done in the past, the memory of which is refreshed—whether it be the Assembly of the Passover among the Hebrews, the **Seisachtheia** among the Athenians,* <note>original: "σεισαχθεια" — an ancient Athenian law for the 'shaking off of burdens' or debt relief</note> *or a victory won in a certain place, such as the **stone of help**.”* <note>original: "lapis adjutorii" — referring to the 'Ebenezer' stone mentioned in 1 Samuel 7:12</note> *“In this way, therefore, the Lord's Supper produces faith; that is, it signifies with certainty that Christ was born and suffered. But to whom does it signify this? To the faithful and the treacherous alike. For it signifies to all, so far as pertains to the virtue of the Sacrament, that Christ suffered, whether they receive it or not; but that he suffered **FOR US**, that it signifies only to the pious and faithful. For no one knows or believes that Christ suffered for us, except him whom the Spirit has taught inwardly to recognize the mystery of divine goodness. For he alone receives Christ. Therefore, nothing but the Spirit gives trust in God. For no one comes to Christ unless the Father has drawn him.”* Then **Paul** also removes this whole disagreement with one word when he says: *“But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of that cup.”* <note>1 Corinthians 11:28</note> Since, therefore, a man ought to examine his faith before he approaches, it cannot be that faith is given in the Supper; *“for it is necessary that it be present before you approach.”* See also his *Support of the Eucharist*, his *Response to the Letters of Pellican and Regius*, and his *Exegesis of the Eucharistic Matter*. **Blessed Oecolampadius** <note>Johannes Oecolampadius (1482–1531), the Reformer of Basel</note> spoke in a similar way. Thus, for example, in his *Response to Willibald Pirckheimer*, he discusses this argument as follows: *“Satisfaction was made for sins on the cross, and sins were remitted and taken away, not mine only but those of the whole world. But I begin to be capable of that satisfaction and remission only when I have faith.”* The mind is strengthened by faith in the merit of Christ on the cross, but the memory is commended to us in the Supper. Therefore, a prudent **Minister of the Word of God**, where this argument must be discussed, should advise that *“Jesus Christ suffered for sinners; that in the use of the Holy Supper the memory of this benefit is represented to our souls; that this remembrance is indeed...”*

VII. There are those who conclude, though incorrectly, from the passage in 1 Corinthians, Chapter X, verses 16 and 17, 
<margin>On the sense of the Passage in the First Epistle of Paul to the Corinthians, v. 16 and 17.</margin>
that with the public use of the Holy Supper, the actual participation in all the fruits of the death of Jesus Christ is joined. It is helpful, therefore, to examine that passage in a few words. Paul’s words sound like this: *The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the participation in the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the participation in the body of Christ? For we, being many, are one bread and one body; for we all partake of that one bread.* <note>The author provides the Greek text: "Το ποτήριον της ευλογίας... εκ τε ενός άρτε μετέχομεν"</note> It is not my intention to laboriously dispute against those who seek here a defense for **transubstantiation**, <note>The Catholic doctrine that the bread and wine literally become the substance of Christ's body and blood</note> or for an unusual and inexpressible real participation in the Body of Christ. The Papists cannot hammer out that miraculous transubstantiation from these words by saying we are *“partakers of the altar”*; for just as it cannot be concluded from this that the things sacrificed to idols are changed into demons, or the victims into altars, so neither can it be concluded from this that the bread and wine are changed into the Body and Blood of the Lord. I would say nearly the same regarding the opinion of our Lutheran brothers; because if this were granted, it would have to be said that the Gentiles, standing at the altars and idolatrous feasts, ate the demons themselves—which is an absurd thing to say. When, however, on this occasion I opened the *Cares* of the late **Illustrious Wolf**, <note>Johann Christoph Wolf (1683–1739), a German scholar</note> I perceived that the celebrated theologian **G. Olearius** <note>Gottfried Olearius (1672–1715)</note> wished to prove in a singular dissertation that the Gentiles believed they were eating, along with the sacrifices of the demons, the substances of the demons themselves, hidden beneath the sacrifices; and that in this way the "orthodox" opinion (as they think) is established. **Illustrious Olearius** interprets verse 16 thus: *“You eat with the same mouth the victims offered to the false gods of the Gentiles as you receive the Supper of the Lord. Now the Gentile affirms that those victims are inhabited by his demons and are full of them; you, however, know that whatever the visible elements of the eucharistic bread and wine which you receive with your mouth...”*

dedicated to that sacred use by prayers, they should have the present body and blood of Christ within them. Can it be possible, then, that a Demon joined to those [pagan] victims, and the holy body and blood of Christ under the bread and wine, should dwell and be found in the same mouth? The distinguished man <note>Referring to Gottfried Olearius (1672–1715), a German theologian who proposed this theory</note> wished to prove this opinion of his by the testimonies of Firmicus and Iamblichus. But in my opinion, the celebrated Jakob Elsner, a most learned Professor of Sacred Theology, correctly showed in his observations on this passage that not only do the cited testimonies fail to prove what was to be proven, but even the Gentiles <note>pagan Greeks and Romans</note> shrank from this opinion. He cites, among others, a passage of Cicero from Book III of *On the Nature of the Gods*, where he says: *“Do you think anyone is so insane as to believe that what he eats is a God?”* <note>original: "Ecquem tam amentem esse putas, qui illud quo vescatur, Deum credat esse."</note> Then on page 110 he observes on this passage, showing in what that communion with Demons consists. *“That communion* <note>original: "κοινωνια" (koinonia) — meaning fellowship, participation, or sharing</note> *with Demons,”* (he says) *“is not to be explained otherwise than the Apostle explained it, who established it as ‘sharing in the table of Demons and drinking the cup of demons’ while they become participants in the table and the mixing-bowl of Demons in sacred banquets by eating from the remains of the Sacrifices.”* <note>Referring to the Apostle Paul's argument in 1 Corinthians 10:21</note> Just as men using the same table are very frequently said by authors to "share the table" <note>original: "κοινωνεῖν τραπέζης" (koinonein trapezēs)</note>, among whom there is "communion" <note>original: "κοινωνία"</note>, namely of the table. Compare Acts 2:42. And it is believed to be, or certainly ought to be, a communion of souls and wills as well; just as the Apostle said that those "sharing of the one bread" were "one body" in verse 17. Thus it could not be otherwise than that a communion intervened between the Idolaters and the Demons, since in sacred banquets they became participants in the tables of Demons. Thus far, the distinguished Elsner is most correct. Furthermore, I would like to know whether the Learned Men who defend the explanation of the distinguished Olearius believe that certain invisible Demons were truly not only present at the Sacrifices of the Gentiles, but also insinuated themselves into them, and thus that the Demons themselves were eaten along with the Sacrifices. I can hardly bring myself to believe that they would assert this. But if they deny that this happened, let them see whether they are well-advising their own cause, and whether it is not manifest that by this reasoning they are, against the rules of Logic, assuming as true the very thing in question. But enough has been disputed regarding this argument. Therefore, to bring out the true sense of those verses, we must attend to the aim of the Apostle, which is clear from the entire chapter; he wished, namely, to recall Christians from Idolatry and to prevent them from participating in idolatrous banquets. He seeks his argument, among other things, from the fact that Christians celebrating the Holy Supper by this very act publicly testify that they have communion with the flesh and blood of Christ—that is, they recall to their memory the death of Jesus Christ as the sole cause of our reconciliation with God. It is therefore unworthy that those who, by the eating of bread and wine in the Supper, testify to their communion with Christ—

<margin>v. 20, 21.</margin>—should also have communion with Demons. Therefore he says in verses 20 and 21: *“You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons: you cannot be participants in the table of the Lord and the table of demons.”* Hence I was surprised that the celebrated Mosheim <note>Johann Lorenz von Mosheim (1693–1755), a famous Lutheran church historian and theologian</note> interpreted verse 16 as being about some real participation in the body and blood of Christ, and thought that verse 17 dealt with a different matter than the preceding verse 16. For besides the fact that the nature of the thing teaches that there is a manifest connection between these verses, the particle "because" <note>original: "ὅτι" (hoti)</note> itself seems to suggest it to me. But let us set these things aside and see what the sense of these two verses may be. I paraphrase them thus: *“When we celebrate the Holy Supper and drink the wine with thanksgiving, do we not by this very act publicly testify that Jesus Christ poured out his blood for us? And when, with repeated thanksgiving, we break the bread, do we not publicly contest that the body of the Lord Jesus Christ was broken for us on the cross, and that we Christians who mutually use these Symbols constitute one single body? And just as one bread is made from many grains, and one wine is pressed from many grapes, so we also testify that we, though many, are only one Body in Christ Jesus.”* From which the Apostle concludes that Christians, if they sit at Idolatrous tables together with the Heathen, belong to the same mass and are judged to have coalesced with them—which, however, ought not to be done by Christians, who constitute only one body in Christ Jesus. From this it is clear that in those verses, nothing is dealt with except a certain spiritual Communion of Christians with Christ, and of the other members of the Church among themselves. However, that spiritual conjunction is two-fold, which must be carefully observed in the explanation of this argument. The first is that by which Christians celebrating the Holy Supper represent to their minds an absent thing—namely, the death of Jesus Christ and his merit—and consider themselves as members of one body. The second is that by which the disciples of Christ, gifted with saving faith, are certain and persuaded—not only on the occasion of the Holy Supper, but even outside the use of the Holy Supper—that they have truly been made partakers of the death of Jesus Christ and of all the benefits that were gained by that death. It is the first type, however, that is referred to in this place, not the second. For when Christians together use those external Symbols, they consider one another mutually as one body that celebrates the death of Jesus Christ together. But from this common confession of Christ's death, it is not yet established that they are truly pious and reborn, or that the saving fruits of the death of Jesus Christ pertain to them. For before they celebrate the memory of Jesus Christ, they must already be persuaded by certain characteristics—namely, by saving faith and Christian virtues...

through the exercise of these things, they are truly joined with Christ. This is why all Reformed <note>Theologians following the tradition of Calvin or Zwingli</note> theologians confess that in the sixth chapter of John—where there is talk of "feeding" on the flesh and blood of Christ—it is not a discussion of the use of the Holy Supper. This is partly because Christ had not yet died at that time, and partly because Christ confesses that the possession of eternal life is certainly joined to this "feeding." However, very few Christians who celebrate the Holy Supper can have this certain confidence, because many who approach the Holy Supper lack a saving faith and its fruits. It is indeed most true that there is an intimate union between Christ and the faithful; but that union does not happen solely through participation in the Holy Supper. Rather, a spiritual union through faith must precede it, and it is the "condition without which" <note>original: "conditio sine qua non"</note> a Christian cannot be a participant in the death and the benefits acquired through the death of the Savior. Just as a true Christian is persuaded, even before using the Holy Supper, that he is truly joined with Christ through faith, so too in the Holy Supper is he not only mindful of this benefit received, but new motives are added to love Christ above all things. On this occasion, the mind, recalling to itself the remarkable fruit of Christ's death, is bathed in a singular joy. However, that prior "partaking" of the Holy Supper, which we believe is discussed in this passage to the Corinthians, is common to all Christians and is therefore only "external," even though they celebrate an invisible thing—namely, the death of Jesus Christ and His dignity—together. The Most Reverend *Hoadly, currently the Bishop of Winchester* <note>Benjamin Hoadly (1676–1761), an influential and controversial English bishop known for his "Low Church" views which emphasized the symbolic nature of the sacraments</note>, explained these two verses in almost the same way. For on page 43 and following of his cited book, he paraphrases <note>original: "παραφράζει" (paraphrazei)</note> these two verses thus:

> When we, who are Christians, participate together in our religious assemblies in the cup of blessing or thanksgiving—that cup over which we pronounce words expressing the praises we give to God and the gratitude with which we are filled for His benefits—do we not drink it as a wine intended to serve as a memorial of the blood that Jesus Christ shed for us? Is it not clear, then, that in doing so we participate together in that which recalls to us the memory of His blood, and which indeed bears that name in the institution of the Sacrament? When, in the same solemnity, we break bread and eat it, is that not participating jointly in that which is established to make us remember His body, and which for this reason He calls His body in the institution—and not eating bread as in an ordinary meal? (verse 17). I say, "participating jointly," because such is the nature of this ceremony: it is an action performed in an

assembly, and not something that each person can do in private. And as it is one and the same bread in which we thus participate together, it is this very thing which ensures that, although our assemblies are composed of many individuals, we nevertheless declare by this that we make but one single body, and that we form but one and the same Society. One might also say that, just as it is a mark of union among men to eat together, likewise when we gather as a company to participate in the same bread, we acknowledge by this solemn action that we all make but one single body; and in our capacity as Christians, we declare by this that we and other Christians form a Society distinct from the body of Pagans, submitted and devoted to Jesus Christ as our common Head.

He then proves through many arguments from the Apostle’s purpose, as well as the preceding and following verses, that this is the sense of this passage. The most learned *Clarke* <note>Samuel Clarke (1675–1729), an English philosopher and clergyman</note> concedes to the same opinion in Volume IV, Oration (Sermon) VII. For after he advised that Paul's primary goal in this chapter was to pull the Corinthians back from the gatherings and feasts of the heathens—because in this way they could easily give the weaker members a reason to believe that those who frequent such places are participating in the worship of Gods or Demons—he then proceeds as follows, according to the German version: *“For just as (he says) the partaking of the Holy Communion and fellowship with Christians is a public testimony that one is himself a Christian; and just as the partaking of the sacrifices from the altar of the Jews is a public confession that one is a Jew by religion; so it might be interpreted by others when a Christian eats of an idol-sacrifice, as if he had fellowship with the heathens in their idolatry, even though he knows within himself that an idol is nothing in the world. This is obviously the true connection of the Apostle’s whole discourse: 'My beloved, flee from idolatry.' I speak as to wise men; judge what I say: that is, judge and take heed as I explain this to you through a simple comparison: The cup of blessing which we Christians bless, is it not the fellowship of the blood of Christ? The bread that we break, is it not the fellowship of the body of Christ? That is: Is it not a public declaration of our communal agreement and fellowship with one another, as we consider together the love of our universal Savior? For it is one bread: so we, being many, are one body: because we are all partakers of one bread. And so, he says, as he continues this same comparison—”*

# DISSERTATION ON THE CELEBRATION
<page-num>986</page-num>

states: Israel according to the flesh are those who eat from the sacrifice in the fellowship of the altar: <note>original German: "Israel nach dem Fleisch, sind die, vvelche vom Opfer essen in der Gemeinschaft des Altars"</note> *that is:* Are they not in the fellowship of the Jewish religion? Do they not thereby profess their fellowship with them? So too, what the heathens sacrifice, they sacrifice to the devil, and not to God: and I would not that you should have fellowship with devils. *These words are not broken and disconnected warnings, as they might seem at first glance if one does not carefully note the intent of the Apostolic conclusion; rather, they are expressly connected with what precedes and are clearly a continuation of the same analogy: that just as among both Jews and Christians, participation and fellowship in the same public religious acts is a testimony of unity, fellowship, and agreement:* Thus, eating from the idol-sacrifices among the heathens would provide an all-too-strong ground for suspicion that one agrees with them in their idolatry. <note>This section translates a passage of German commentary embedded in the Latin text.</note> So says the celebrated Clarke. <note>Referring to Samuel Clarke (1675–1729), an influential English theologian.</note> It is clear from what has been said that Christ instituted the Holy Supper, among other reasons, to preserve and nourish union among Christians. Hence, learned men have shown that the Israelites and Pagans likewise established feasts on festival days to bind mutual concord and society with tighter chains. See Vitringa *Sacred Observations, Book V, chapter VII,* Gürtler *On Sacred Feasts*, and Elsner *Sacred Observations, Volume II, page 106 and following.*

<margin>This explanation is confirmed by the testimonies of the Blessed Zwingli and Bullinger.</margin>
VIII. Although the explanation of these verses given above commends itself by its simplicity and harmonizes well with the Apostle Paul's purpose, nevertheless—because for some people the authority of men distinguished for their learning carries more weight than arguments—it is helpful to bring forward two testimonies from the most excellent theologians of Zurich <note>original: "Tigurinorum," referring to the city of Zurich, a center of the Reformation.</note>, namely Huldrych Zwingli and Heinrich Bullinger, to confirm our opinion. The former, in his *Commentary on verse 16*, argues in the following manner: First we will explain the words, then the sense. We have often shown in Genesis that *blessed* is used for "gave thanks," and *blessing* for "the act of thanksgiving." Next, *koinonia* <note>original Greek: κοινωνία, meaning communion, fellowship, or participation.</note>, which the translator renders as "communication," is more conveniently rendered here as "communion" or "community." For *koinonia* does not signify the actual distribution <note>original: "distractionem," meaning the dividing or pulling apart of the physical elements.</note> of the body and blood of Jesus Christ, but rather us, who are the body of Christ—namely His Church, the people, the assembly, the community. The words therefore mean this: *The cup of thanksgiving with which we give thanks, is it not the community of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the community of the body of Christ?* So that the sense is: *The cup of thanksgiving with which we give thanks, what, I ask,*

<column-break/>

<page-num>987</page-num>
<header>OF THE HOLY SUPPER.</header>
<sig>Iiiiii 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: this</meta>

*I ask, is it other than ourselves? For what else are we than the communion itself, the very assembly and people, the fellowship and society of the blood of Christ,* that is, those people who have been washed by the blood of Christ? And he calls those who trust in His blood the "blood of Christ," just as in Philippians 5 <note>The author likely means Philippians 3:3.</note> he calls those who serve God in the Spirit "the circumcision." Thus, in this place, the "communion of the blood of Christ" are those who, in the same society, give thanks and rejoice that they have been claimed for liberty by the blood of Christ. It is as if Paul said: *I do not say that the cup is the blood or that the bread is the body of Christ, but that all of us who participate in the one bread and the one cup are the blood of Christ and the body of Christ. It is therefore bread that we eat and wine that we drink as far as substance and nature are concerned; but it is the body and blood in terms of what it signifies.* Nor is it ordinary bread, but that by which we give thanks to God for the death of His son, not that by which we feed the belly. We shall perceive this to be the sense of these words from the argument Paul handles here. For he deters the Corinthians from the worship of idols, which he does far more strongly and vehemently when he says: *You are a much higher and nobler assembly than should ever join with a crowd of idolaters. It is as if he said: You share in the body and blood of Christ, and for that reason you ought not to take part in the communion of idolaters in their sacred rites.* He urges them more forcefully when he says: *When you celebrate this commemoration, praise, or thanksgiving, are you not already the communion of the blood of Christ? Are you not Christ’s people and assembly? It is stronger than if he merely said: When you eat the bread blessed in this way, are you not dividing the body of Christ?* For Paul leaves no stone unturned to tear the Corinthians away from the society of idolaters, which he cannot do more aptly than by showing that they sin against piety itself, etc.

Regarding the following verse, the Great Man <note>Referring to Zwingli.</note> argues thus: *The Apostle gives the reasons, indeed he explains why he called the Church and people the body and blood of Christ; for he felt that because of the density of his metaphors <note>original: "troporum," referring to figurative language.</note> he had spoken a little obscurely. Therefore, he sets the matter forth in clear words, as if he said: When I address you with such a concluding exclamation, when we give thanks with the cup of thanksgiving, is that assembly not the communion—that is, the people, the Church, the congregation—of the blood of Christ? For you are the communion of the blood of Christ (for he left that part about the cup incomplete <note>original Greek: ἀναντοποδοτον, a rhetorical term for a sentence where the second part of a comparison is left unstated</note>, but added it to the bread; yet the judgment of both is the same) you who drink from the one cup of thanksgiving. And the bread which we break, is it not the communion or assembly, the people, the Church, the congregation of the body of Christ? For we who participate in the one bread and drink from the one cup, join together into one body. Therefore, let no one wonder that I have called this festive assembly the communion of the blood of Christ.*

It uses this communal identity to argue why Christians must strictly separate themselves from pagan rituals and idolatry.</summary>

that is, that Church which has been washed by the blood of Christ. *For we all, according to the Apostle himself, are one bread and one body—not the fleshly body of Christ, but the Church of Christ.* <note>original: "non carneum Christi corpus, sed Christi Ecclesia"</note> Thus far the Blessed Zwingli. <note>Huldrych Zwingli (1484–1531), a leader of the Reformation in Switzerland.</note> Indeed, our own Bullinger, <note>Heinrich Bullinger (1504–1575), Zwingli's successor in Zurich.</note> the most worthy successor of Zwingli, comments on this passage as follows: *As if starting a new confirmation, he sets out to prove more clearly and firmly that a Christian can by no right participate in foreign sacred rites. — I speak now to you, who because of your experience in many matters are more prudent and aware of all the mysteries. Weigh what I say; for I believe it will be of such a nature that it will easily draw you away from profane rites, unless you prefer to be argumentative. He phrases everything as questions to make them more forceful. The sense is this: I do not care what some argumentative people expect here; I will open the mind of Paul. The Sacraments, which are the chief sacred things of Christians, incorporate us into Christ and the Christian religion, so that we are made the body of Christ, indeed, his members.* And after he had brought forward a certain passage from Augustine to confirm his opinion, he proceeds, saying: *But why do we cite Augustine when the Apostle Paul himself says in this place, in words that are not at all obscure: "The cup of blessing which we bless—that is, for which we give thanks (for it is now known even to those moderately versed in the scriptures that the word 'to bless' is used for 'to praise' and 'to give thanks' according to the Hebrew custom) <note>original: "morem hebraicum"</note> —is it not the <term>communion</term> <gloss>fellowship or participation; original Greek: κοινωνία</gloss> of the blood of Christ? And the bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?" What else is this than if he had said: Those who participate in the bread and cup of the Lord become the communion of the blood of Christ—that is, the assembly and Church of those washed by Christ's blood—and thus they become the body or members of Christ.* But what shall we say here regarding the wicked and the <term>hypocrites</term> <gloss>those who profess faith outwardly but lack internal sincerity</gloss>: are they also made members of Christ and the Church through participation in the Sacraments? Entirely so: Which Augustine also affirms in Book 19 *Against Faustus the Manichaean*, chapter 12, saying: *Nevertheless, because the visible Sacraments of piety can also be present in the wicked—just as we read that Simon Magus also had Holy Baptism—such people become what the Apostle says: "having a form of piety but denying its power."* <note>Referring to 2 Timothy 3:5.</note> He delivers the same teaching to others, but more copiously and plainly, in the book *The City of God*, Book 21, chapter 25. Others, however, interpret this passage differently; but the consequences prove the opinion and exposition which we have brought forward: *Because we, the many, are one bread, one body <note>original Greek: οι πολλοι</note>—we are the whole multitude. For we all participate in the same bread; that is, I said the bread is the communion of the body of Christ because we, that whole multitude—that is, the whole Church—who participate in the one bread, are made one spiritual body, namely the body of Christ; the other member, regarding the cup,*

<meta>catchword: is omitted-</meta>

<column-break/>

<page-num>989</page-num>
<header>CELEBRATION OF THE HOLY SUPPER.</header>

is omitted, because the reasoning for both is the same. *We are not the first to insert this meaning into this passage, for Augustine recognizes the same in his Treatise on John.* Thus far Bullinger. From these testimonies, it is clear that the opinion of these distinguished theologians consists of the following propositions:

1) That Christians about to celebrate the Holy Supper, having given thanks, break bread and drink wine in memory of the passion of Christ.
2) That by this means they testify that they are devoted to the Christian religion.
3) That the communion of Christians is located in this: that the entire assembly celebrating the commemoration of Christ's death can be considered as one spiritual body.
4) That it is therefore not fitting for Christians to take part in the sacred rites of the Gentiles, because they would thus seem to have fellowship with the gods of the Gentiles, and not with Christ Jesus, to whose name alone they have committed themselves.
5) That the pious and the wicked alike, by breaking bread and drinking wine, can testify to the passion of Christ. From which it follows that through the mere celebration of the Holy Supper, Christians are not made participants in the benefits won by the death of Christ, but they ought to be persuaded of this by other reasons.

<margin>The question is whether a certain special grace, distinct from that which is common to all the reborn, is joined with the use of the Holy Supper.</margin>
IX. In the preceding sections, we have shown that no one can conclude from the mere use of the Holy Supper and the performed commemoration of Christ's death that they are a Christian in the true sense of the name, or that they have certainly been made a participant in the benefits won by the death of Jesus Christ. On this occasion, it is asked whether some special and unusual grace is joined with the use of the Holy Supper or not. There are those among the hypocrites and the pious alike who would affirm this. The question is not whether God—on the occasion of the enjoyment of the bread and wine and the commemoration of the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ—can open the eyes of the mind of a hypocrite or a wicked man and lead them to communion with Himself by His gracious will. No one doubts this, since there are innumerable ways and occasions by which He can supply the beginnings of conversion to men. But the question is this: whether with the enjoyment itself of the bread and wine, and the remembrance of Christ's death, some unusual favor of the Divinity or some special grace is joined. Hypocrites dream of such a thing, though led by no reasons. The histories of all nations teach that men have thought the Gods to be most especially favorable on feast days, and were cheerful on that account. See the celebrated Elsner on Chapter 1, verse 16 of the second Epistle of Peter, and the testimonies of the Ancients cited therein. The same, alas, happens to many today...

# DISSERTATION ON THE LEGITIMATE
<page-num>990</page-num>
<header>DISSERTATION ON THE LEGITIMATE</header>

Christians; many Christians, who are ignorant of the religious worship of the true name <note>Meaning those who are Christian in name only but do not understand the depth of the faith.</note>, are flooded with a certain joy when the divine benefits obtained through the death of Christ are recounted in a singular way, which they think is a sign of unusual divine favor. And when, after the enjoyment of the **Holy Supper** <note>The sacrament of Communion or the Eucharist.</note>, they hear thanks being given to God in public prayers because He has granted the benefit of redemption to those participating, they joyfully sing with the whole assembly: *We all believe, O Lord, etc.* <note>original: "Nos omnes Domine credimus &c."</note> Yet, because they lack knowledge of true divine worship, do not have a clear view of the end and goal of the Holy Supper, and lack all the characteristics with which a true Christian is equipped before the use of the Holy Supper, that joy which arose on the occasion of the Holy Supper is empty.

As for the pious and the reborn, there are certain pious and learned men who think that, on the occasion of enjoying the **Sacred Symbols** <note>The bread and wine.</note>, God is present to the pious and reborn with a certain singular and clearly unusual help. In this opinion, among others, the Reverend and most celebrated men **Calvin** and **Claude**, *Minister of the Word of God at Charenton*, <note>Jean Claude (1619–1687), a famous French Protestant theologian who defended the Reformation against Catholic critics.</note> seem to have been. For **Calvin**, in his *Institutes, Book IV, chapter XVII*, dealing with the mode of the presence of Christ's body in the Holy Supper, says: *it is so wonderful, that the mind clearly cannot be equal to thinking it, nor the tongue to explaining it.* <note>original: "eum esse tam admirabilem, ut mens plane cogitando nec lingua explicando par esse possit."</note> Again in the same chapter: *Regarding the mode (that is, of the presence), if anyone should ask me, I will not be ashamed to confess it is a secret too sublime for my wit to comprehend or for words to express; and to speak more plainly, I experience it rather than understand it. Therefore, I here embrace without controversy the truth of God, in which I may safely rest. He pronounces that his flesh is the food of my soul, and his blood is the drink. With such nourishments, I offer my soul to him to be fed. In his Sacred Supper, he commands me to take, eat, and drink his body and blood under the symbols of bread and wine. I do not doubt but that he himself truly proffers them and I receive them.* <note>original: "De modo... fateri non pudebit sublimius esse arcanum... experior magis quam intelligam."</note> Indeed, the same Great Man had asserted elsewhere that in the Sacred Supper a *miracle* occurs, which surpasses all the limits of nature and every capacity of the senses.

When the Jesuit **Nuetus** <note>Jean Nouet (1605–1680), a Jesuit polemicist who debated Jean Claude.</note> had appealed to these last words to seek a defense for transubstantiation <note>The Catholic doctrine that the bread and wine literally become the substance of Christ's body and blood.</note>, the illustrious **Claude** responded in the following manner, in the book opposed to this Jesuit, page 161: *As for this alleged difference between Calvin and us, it will no longer exist once one has distinguished the ambiguity of the term "miracle," which is sometimes taken for a work of grace performed above the laws or forces of nature, and which is worthy of the admiration of men; and in this sense all the Mysteries of the Gospel and all the actions of the Holy Spirit in our souls are Miracles, such as the gift that the Father made to us of his Son, the Redemption that the Son achieved for us,* <note>original: "Quant à cette pretendue difference entre Calvin & nous..." - Claude is arguing that a "miracle" in the Protestant sense is a spiritual wonder, not a physical change of matter.</note>

<meta>catchword: us,</meta>

---

<page-num>991</page-num>
<header>CELEBRATION OF THE HOLY SUPPER.</header>

*us, the conversion of sinners, the zeal and hope of the faithful, the constancy of the Martyrs and other things of this same order. It is in this significance that Calvin said that a Miracle is performed in the Supper: and indeed it is an incomprehensible miracle that Jesus Christ deigns to communicate himself to wretched creatures, unworthy of his love. It is a miracle above the laws and forces of Nature that our faith is capable of receiving him, really, that is to say, truly, so that we may possess him with all his goods. It is a miracle that his Spirit descending into our consciences brings there all the virtue of his flesh and his blood as the satisfying and meritorious causes. Finally, it is a great miracle that all this happens through the ministry of the bread and wine of his Sacrament, which are creatures infinitely distant from these great effects.* <note>original: "nous, la conversion des pecheurs... creatures infiniment eloignées des ces grands effets."</note>

Thus far the illustrious **Claude**. These most excellent men seem to confuse those things which are taught concerning the mystical union of Christ and the faithful in John chapter VI and elsewhere, with the remembrance of the death of Jesus Christ, which occurs in the use of the Holy Supper; and they join I know not what particular grace or unusual operation of the Holy Spirit to the very enjoyment of this Sacrament. For the rest of the **Reformed** <note>Other theologians within the Protestant tradition.</note>, dealing with this argument, assert that the conjunction with Christ through faith ought to precede the use of the Holy Supper, and that Christians celebrating the Holy Supper testify, being truly such, that they have communion with him. 

Certainly, those benefits mentioned by the illustrious **Claude** fall to the faithful not in the legitimate celebration of the Supper itself, but through the Redemption of Jesus Christ and other benefits which are accustomed to flow from such a great benefit. As for that singular grace of the Holy Spirit offered in the use of the Holy Supper, we do not deny that God can sometimes grant a benefit of that kind to the pious. But I deny that this is always joined with the use of the Holy Supper. I certainly do not know by what reasoning they would wish to persuade others that this benefit has fallen to themselves: they argue from the serenity of mind and spiritual joy with which they are sometimes flooded when using the Holy Supper. But this serenity can arise from natural and moral causes, without that unusual help: for the pious, according to the state of both mind and body, are variously disposed even outside the use of the Holy Supper. Indeed, it is so far from the case that they are always affected with a joyful mind while recollecting the memory of Christ's death, that they rather often feel a singular sadness when they celebrate the memory of Christ's passion in the use of the Holy Supper. Just as they cannot and should not conclude from this sadness as if God had withdrawn a grace once given, or that they were unworthy to recollect the memory of Christ; so likewise...

<meta>catchword: The-</meta>

cannot simply conclude from the joy they often perceive on this occasion that God was present to them with unusual help. This much is certain: that joy does not belong to the essence of a true and healthy celebration of the **Holy Supper** <note>Also known as Communion or the Eucharist.</note>, because otherwise it would always be present to the pious when they use the Holy Supper. Furthermore, it is well known that no one can claim some spiritual benefit for themselves, or have a certain confidence in obtaining it, unless God has promised in his Word, in express terms, that he would offer it. But nowhere has he promised that he would be present with some unusual grace to those who rightly use the Holy Supper. Those celebrating worthily can be certain of the favor of God, because they are equipped with the "marks" <note>The defining characteristics or spiritual qualities of a believer.</note> of true Christians before the use of the Supper, and in the celebration of the Supper itself; however, by this we do not wish to deny that God sometimes pours a singular joy into the souls of the pious on this occasion. For who shall set limits to the gracious will of God? This is most certain: the joy with which the pious are sometimes flooded on the occasion of using the Holy Supper is very different from the gladness which hypocrites boast of feeling. The joy of hypocrites is empty, because it is built on no foundations. For neither the use of the Holy Supper, nor the commemoration of the death of Jesus Christ, are certain signs from which they can conclude that God is favorable to them; the benefits of the covenant of grace are reserved only for the repentant, those sincerely believing, and those intent on the pursuit of virtue. Since these men are destitute of these marks, they rejoice foolishly that something has been granted to them. But the pious, whether they are flooded with singular joy or lack it, nevertheless always have a solid cause for rejoicing, as long as they have a clear perspective on the reasons for their joy.

<margin>A vertical pencil bracket marks the following italicized paragraph</margin>
*These things must be firmly held by the <term>Minister of the Word of God</term> <note>original: "V. D. M." (Verbi Divini Minister)</note> and shown most clearly on all occasions, especially in the so-called <term>preparatory sermons</term> <note>original: "concionibus parascevasticis"; sermons held to prepare the congregation for Communion.</note>: that the joy of the Unpious and Hypocrites is foolish and most empty because they claim something for themselves of which they are plainly destitute of possessing. On the contrary, it must be shown what kind of marks those who wish to be Christians of a true name ought to have outside of the use of the Supper. For the <term>Minister of the Word of God</term> should always be most intent on this: that, as much as lies within him, he should radically uproot false pretenses and sham marks of Christianity from the souls of his listeners; for once this is done, there is finally hope that men, just as with other articles of Religion, will rightly weigh the doctrine of the use of the Holy Supper and restore it to a healthy use.*

## Certain Theological Theses.

I. If anyone were to ask why Rome was occupied by no one before Romulus and Remus, the cause is ready at hand: because before them, it had not yet been founded. In the same way, if anyone asks why <term>Transubstantiation</term> <note>The doctrine that the bread and wine literally turn into the body and blood of Christ.</note> was not attacked in the first eight centuries by the Heretics—who left almost no Mystery of Religion untouched—the answer is: because this dogma was then unknown, if indeed a contradictory proposition is worthy of the name of a "theological dogma."

II. Two causes especially seem to me to be the reasons for false interpretations of Holy Scripture. The first is the zeal of parties and the love of one's Sect. The second lies in the fact that things said in the Holy Scriptures with respect to certain specific persons and circumstances are sold as general propositions.

III. It is absurd to say that the authority of Scripture depends on the testimony of the Church, since the entire authority of the Church cannot be proven from anywhere else than from the testimony of Scripture. When the Doctors of the Roman Church reason this way, they clearly commit a **circular argument**.

IV. If the Doctors of the Roman Church can prove with clear arguments that the Traditions they sell really take their origin from Christ or the Apostles, and that they are such as are necessary to know for attaining salvation, Protestants will gladly admit them.

V. Those who, according to their own whim, hunt for allegories everywhere in the Holy Scriptures, are not poorly compared to those who imagine the shapes of various animals depicted for themselves in the clouds.

VI. Those who wish to bring the erring to the knowledge of truth by threats, force, and punishments, act no less ridiculously than those who would wish to capture a well-fortified city by means of <term>Syllogisms</term> <note>Logical arguments consisting of a major premise, minor premise, and conclusion.</note>.

VII. The question of whether after this life men will be either happy or unhappy comes down to this: whether God and religion exist.

VIII. Regarding the use and abuse of theological "Systems," I subscribe to those things which the most celebrated Theologian of Tubingen, **Christian Eberhard Weismann**, discusses in his *Institutes of Dogmatic-Exegetical Theology, page 27.* The words sound like this: *Regarding the systematic and artificial method, it is certain that it has its own advantages and disadvantages. The collection of truths into certain chapters and headings is an advantage for those teaching and learning, as is the connection itself...*

These points address the dangers of overly complex theology, the errors of Spinoza, the relationship between justification and holiness, and a plea for peace between differing Christian factions.</meta>

# DISSERTATION ON THE LEGITIMATE
<page-num>994</page-num>
<header>DISSERTATION ON THE LEGITIMATE</header>

...the investigation of truths among themselves. Truly, the inconveniences and evils of this method arise when it is too sought after and affected; when it mixes in a great mass of curious and useless questions; when it disturbs the simplicity and clarity of Theology with difficult and thorny terms and phrases; and finally, when it has either no, or not sufficient, regard for leading learners step-by-step to revealed truths, but instead distracts their minds by its excessive vastness and amplitude—minds which are often not yet faithful or practiced in smaller matters.

IX. The opinion of *Spinoza* <note>Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677), a philosopher often accused of atheism or pantheism for equating God with Nature.</note> regarding God and the origin of all things is so absurd and monstrous that it could not be understood how anyone could seriously bring their mind to subscribe to it, unless it had long ago been discovered that nothing is so absurd that it has not been defended by certain Philosophers.

X. In matters pertaining to eternal salvation, let everyone be a Theologian for themselves. <note>A call for personal responsibility in faith, echoing the Protestant principle of the "priesthood of all believers."</note>

XI. Rightly does the celebrated <term>Blessed One</term> <note>original: <term>Μακαρίτης</term> (Makárites); a Greek term of respect for the deceased.</note> *Heidegger* <note>Johann Heinrich Heidegger (17th c.), a Swiss Reformed theologian.</note> praise in *History of the Patriarchs*, Part II, Exercise VIII, the words of *Hakspan*, who, in his notes on *Genesis 19:24* regarding the "Judaizing Calvin" of *Aegidius Hunnius*, wrote thus: *We can, indeed we ought to, bear with other Christians who are modestly doubting or disagreeing, nor should "Judaism" or "Turkism" <note>In the 17th century, calling a rival a "Jew" or a "Turk" (Muslim) was a common theological insult for those seen as deviating from orthodox Christianity.</note> be objected to others in such a perplexing matter. Rather, let each one abound in his own sense.* We hardly obtain anything certain in manifest things against obstinate Jews; what will happen in a matter so obscure, and where they can boast of Hebrew idioms <note>original: "Hebraismum"</note> not without examples? On this occasion, the words of P. Bayle <note>Pierre Bayle (1647–1706), author of the influential "Historical and Critical Dictionary."</note> came to mind, who in his Lexicon under the entry *Heshusius*, after mentioning *Hunnius’s* booklet, pronounces in the following manner: <note>original (French): "C'est une injustice impertinente, que d'imputer à un homme les Hérésies dont ses Adversaires l'accusent dans la chaleur de la dispute. Hunnius, Auteur Lutherien, n'a-t-il pas fait un assez gros Livre, où il se vante, de convaincre de Judaïsme Jean Calvin? Ne faudroit-il pas être fous pour en conclure que Jean Calvin a judaïsé."</note> "It is an impertinent injustice to impute to a man the Heresies of which his Adversaries accuse him in the heat of dispute. Has not Hunnius, a Lutheran Author, made a large enough Book, where he boasts of convicting John Calvin of Judaism? Would one not have to be crazy to conclude from this that John Calvin judaized?"

XII. Rightly wrote the celebrated *Placette* <note>Jean La Placette (1639–1718), a French Protestant moralist.</note> in his *Treatise on Justification*: It is so far from being permissible to conclude: "I am justified; therefore, even if I do not have sanctification <note>In this context, "sanctification" refers to the outward holy life and behavior of the believer.</note>, I will nevertheless be saved"; that it should rather be argued thus: "I am not sanctified. Therefore it is certain that I am not justified either."

XIII. Whether seriously or as a joke the most Noble *Steele* <note>Likely Sir Richard Steele, an Anglo-Irish writer and politician who wrote a famous satirical preface on the differences between the Catholic and Protestant churches.</note> asserted that the disagreement between the Doctors of the Roman Church and among Protestants regarding the infallibility of the Church consists in this: namely, that the Popish Doctors assert their Church is **infallible**; while the Protestants contend that their Church is indeed **not infallible**, but only that it **never errs**—I leave this to be discussed by the more prudent.

> *Breathe upon this, you Creator, Lord, and Father of all things, and so dispel all clouds of ignorance and passions from both sides, just as you once turned the raging waters to flight by bringing a mighty wind, and gave the nourishing earth the abundance to sprout its seeds. Let it be enough, I pray, of defending; enough of tumult; enough of raging. Arise, most welcome Morning Star; let the sun of justice shine forth immediately. For while we contend, holiness is neglected, which alone you require from us. You see how we never return better from contention; for it is a work of the flesh, from which no one can retreat without a stain. On the contrary, let us abstain from it, so that we may gird all the nerves, which we otherwise strain for fighting, for the work of virtue. Thus Blessed Zwingli <note>Huldrych Zwingli (1484–1531), a leader of the Reformation in Switzerland.</note> in the Preface to the "Exposition of the Matter of the Eucharist" addressed to Martin Luther.*

# SACRED MEDITATION,
## COMPRISING CERTAIN SALUTARY WARNINGS PERTAINING TO THE TRUE AND LEGITIMATE
# USE OF THE HOLY SUPPER.
### THE LATTER PART.

->Section XI.<-

<margin>A second external cause is presented which hinders many from rightly celebrating the Holy Supper.</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative woodcut border containing the capital letter 'P'. The frame depicts a pedestal or altar with architectural details, surmounted by a basket of flowers.</image-desc>
Besides that first external cause mentioned above, by which men are led away from using the Sacrament of the Holy Supper <note>original: "S. Cœnæ," referring to the Eucharist or Lord's Supper</note> rightly, there is a *second* cause. This not only results in many people celebrating the Holy Supper less correctly, but also frequently causes them to abstain from its use altogether. This cause lies in the fact that sacred orators <note>meaning preachers</note> or the authors of devotional manuals <note>original: "aſceticorum libellorum," books intended for spiritual exercises</note>—with the best of intentions, but in my opinion with too little prudence—often exaggerate the matter when they discuss the state of those "communicating worthily" or the requirements for those who wish to approach the use of the Holy Supper with proper preparation. They do this to such an extent that people who intend to celebrate the Holy Supper rightly persuade themselves that they must not be contaminated by even the slightest stain of sin. Indeed, some speak and write so incautiously that you would think God had prepared snares and traps everywhere for those who sincerely wish to celebrate the remembrance of Jesus Christ's death in the Holy Supper. Consequently, such great terror is often struck into the pious that they either omit the celebration of the Holy Supper entirely, or, if they do use it, they perceive little or no comfort from the contemplation of Christ's death—an act which ought to excite the greatest joy in the souls of Christ's true followers. To be sure, those who allow themselves to be frightened away

<meta>catchword: away</meta>

<column-break/>

<page-num>997</page-num>
<header>CELEBRATION OF THE HOLY SUPPER.</header>

away from the use of the Holy Supper act wrongly; yet those who discuss this argument without prudent circumspection provide the occasion for this error. For among the pious, there are many who lack an exact knowledge of divine matters; some are naturally more timid, and others are sometimes suffering from "black bile" <note>original: "atra bile," a historical medical term for melancholy or clinical depression</note>. When these people hear that such a refined and perfect piety <note>original: "exaſciatam & omnibus numeris abſolutam," meaning piety that is polished and complete in every detail</note> is required of those who wish to enjoy the Holy Supper rightly, they are terrified and think it better if they do not celebrate it. By this very act, however, they sin against the clear precept of Christ, who instituted the Holy Supper in his own memory. They also prevent themselves from being stirred to a greater zeal for piety and the love of Christ by the commemoration of Jesus Christ's death, which is recalled in a particular way during the use of the Holy Supper. It is true: it is the duty of the ministers of the Divine Word to rightly represent both general and special duties of piety to Christians on every given occasion. They should paint the dignity and excellence of the Christian religion in vivid colors and show all who ought to be touched by the love of religion how much danger those people bring upon themselves who frequently use the Sacrament of the Holy Supper without devotion. All these things are rightly said; yet, for the sake of the truly pious and those endowed with the character of true Christians, it must always be warned that the piety and virtue of born-again <note>original: "regenitorum," referring to the theological concept of regeneration or spiritual rebirth</note> men is imperfect in this life. Nevertheless, this imperfection does not prevent them from being true members of Christ, and therefore they both can and should approach the celebration of the Holy Supper with a cheerful mind.

Furthermore, this overly rigid representation of Christians who use the Holy Supper worthily not only frequently terrifies many pious people and keeps them from its use, but it also causes men who are given over to vices to either omit its public celebration or celebrate it less worthily. Thus, they deprive themselves of the means by which they could be excited toward the study of virtue. Even if men are contaminated by many vices, when they know they must approach the use of the Holy Supper, they are terrified by certain stings of conscience. If they gave an open ear to these voices, they could be led to look within themselves and think seriously about changing their lives. For just as God is able to call men back to Himself through the preaching of the Gospel and the reading of the sacred word—His grace assisting—so He can also perform this same work through the use of the Holy Supper. But while the ungodly are unwilling to take part in the celebration of the Holy Supper, the stings of conscience are more and more neglected, and their minds often become calloused. Moreover, while they hear that such great and perfect piety is required in those who wish to use the Holy Supper correctly, and they simultaneously look at the conduct of other men...

and they consider their own lives, they think it is impossible for anyone to be in such a state. The middle way is best.* <note>original: "Πάντων μεσον άρισον," a Greek proverb meaning "the middle of all things is best."</note> *Therefore, the remission of sins must be preached, the minds of the weak must be lifted up, and the wavering must be confirmed. Meanwhile, however, both fear and reverence for the Divine Power must be instilled in all, so that they do nothing rashly, do nothing through neglect, and establish nothing that is contrary to the institution of Christ or does not correspond to it in every part.*

After the mind is made whole and devoted to the one God in Christ, and has been instructed in this manner—even if it suffers somewhat from disease or the weakness of the flesh—one may nevertheless approach with reverence in the faith of divine goodness. For those harsh things are said against those who, just as they were defiled by foreign rites, so they were polluting the Supper of Christ with luxury and disturbing the entire Church of Christ with dissensions. Therefore, unbelief is more to be rejected than the weakness of sinners. *The Most Reverend Archbishop of Canterbury, Tillotson* <note>John Tillotson (1630–1694), a moderate and influential Anglican prelate.</note> in a sermon on frequent Communion, page 232 of Volume III, speaks thus on this argument: <note>original: "Il est d'autant plus necessaire..." This even causes several sinners, who might have some disposition toward good and some desire to work on their conversion, to be disgusted by it. One must be careful not to flatter sinners in their vices or to propose a relaxed devotion or morality to them. I approve of giving them a great idea of the purity that is required in an action as holy and solemn as Communion, and of the state in which a true Christian ought to be. <margin>Certain warnings regarding the passage of Paul to the Corinthians, chapter 11, verses 27-33.</margin>
**XII.** Those things which were said in the preceding thesis recall to our memory the memorable passage of the Apostle Paul, in his first epistle to the Corinthians, Chapter 11. Because both the pious and the impious often interpret this passage incorrectly, we think certain things must be noted regarding it. To be sure, sacred Orators <note>Preachers.</note>, when they are accustomed to deal with the necessity of preparation for the Holy Supper, usually appeal to this passage of Paul to strike fear into those who use the Holy Supper unworthily. They do this not without reason, since he deals both with the necessity of self-examination and also with the extraordinary punishment inflicted on the Corinthians who were using the Holy Supper unworthily. However, it is not our intention to explain all those verses one by one, because that has been done sufficiently by learned Interpreters. We shall only bring forward certain points that serve our Purpose. Specifically, something must be noted concerning the punishments inflicted on those usurping the Holy Supper unworthily; concerning the word *unworthily* <note>original: "ἀναξίως" (anaxiōs)</note>, and concerning the *examination* <note>original: "δοκιμασίᾳ" (dokimasia)</note> which must be undertaken by those about to use this sacrament in the proper rite. From the thirtieth verse it is established that God, in a certain extraordinary way through diseases—and indeed, as the Blessed Zwingli <note>Huldrych Zwingli (1484–1531), a leader of the Reformation in Switzerland.</note>, J. Alting <note>Jakob Alting (1618–1679), a Dutch Reformed theologian.</note>, and others believe, through the plague—willed to make manifest how badly those act who approach the use of the Holy Supper unworthily; indeed, the word *they sleep* <note>original: "κοιμῶνται" (koimōntai)</note> shows that some were removed from life by a sudden death. Learned men have long since proved that the word *to sleep* denotes death not only to the Greeks and Latins, but also to the Hebrews: see the passages collected by the Celebrated *Wolf* <note>Johannes Christoph Wolf (1683–1739), a German scholar.</note> regarding *Hebraisms of the New Testament, page 198 and following.* Furthermore, as is clear from verse 33 of this chapter, these punishments were inflicted to this end: namely, that other Christians about to celebrate the Holy Supper might look within themselves and perceive that the memory of the death of Jesus Christ is a matter most worthy of attention; and, having performed a serious repentance for sins committed, they might afterward be mindful of such a great benefit with a devoted mind. However, although we would not wish to deny that God even now can afflict those celebrating the Holy Supper unworthily with diseases, daily experience shows that this does not happen in the ordinary course of things. Without doubt, God had His own most wise reasons why He would afflict those un-

In that first Apostolic age, God granted to the Apostles many extraordinary things, such as gifts, and likewise types of punishments, so that it might be manifest to all that the Gospel concerning Christ Jesus was a most divine matter and most worthy of attention, and that the Apostles were Men approved by God; so that those whom the excellence of the religion itself could not move might be persuaded by their very senses.

Moreover, such punishments were inflicted on those who celebrated the Holy Supper *unworthily* <note>original: "ἀναξίως" (anaxiōs)</note>. It is asked, however, in what that sin consisted: It can be said in two respects that some of the Corinthians approached the table of the Lord *unworthily*. In a general sense, indeed, because they did not celebrate the Holy Supper with that religion and devotion of mind which the dignity of the matter itself—that is, the commemoration of the death of Jesus Christ—demanded. But in a specific sense, as is clear from verses 27, 18, 21, and 22 of this chapter, they sinned most of all in this: namely, that in the *agapae* <note>The "love feasts" or communal meals that early Christians shared alongside the Eucharist.</note> which they practiced, various excesses were committed; that they despised the poor who came to celebrate the Holy Supper together; and that they were distracted by lawsuits and contentions among themselves. Regarding the phrase *to examine oneself* <note>original: "δοκιμαζειν ἑαυτον" (dokimazein heauton)</note>, we note this one thing: that this *examination* denotes not only the exploration of oneself but also *approbation* <note>Testing and finding oneself "approved" or fit.</note>; for that exploration would be undertaken in vain if, after the exploration was made—whatever the state of the conscience and mind was going to be—it were nonetheless permitted to approach the Holy Supper with a sense of security. Having briefly explained these few points, certain warnings must be added, because the pious and the impious alike are sometimes accustomed to err regarding this argument:

And (I) indeed, men to whom Religion is of little care or heart, cannot in the least conclude that they will therefore go unpunished simply because those unworthily using the Holy Supper today are afflicted by no external punishments. Certainly, from verse 27 it clearly appears that those who abuse the Holy Supper sin against Jesus Christ and the precious merit obtained by His blood. Even if nothing were extant in Holy Scripture in express words concerning this, the nature of the thing itself would teach that men celebrating the Holy Supper in an unworthy manner sin gravely. All Christians who have a rightly perceived understanding of the nature of the Christian Religion are bound to confess that the death of our Savior is that principal dogma of the Christian religion which reveals its sanctity and excellence. It is known, moreover, that from that dogma are sought the most excellent and weightiest incitements toward the study of true piety. ...the death of Jesus Christ and its efficacy, and thus they shamefully neglect that which is necessarily required for true piety. For here, one should not look so much at external signs as to the object itself and its dignity. Furthermore, it cannot happen otherwise than that he who frequently partakes of the Holy Supper without devotion and an affection of piety will, little by little, contract a habit of transgressing the most holy duties of Religion. Moreover, it is not believable that a person can be adorned with true piety who so little values the business which the Best Savior <note>Latin: "Optimus Soter," referring to Jesus Christ.</note> instituted for the best and most holy purpose. From this it clearly follows that those who celebrate the Holy Supper less worthily and religiously are deliberately hardening their souls against the study of piety, and thus they bring eternal destruction upon themselves unless they repent.

**(II)** Certain things must also be advised regarding this argument for the sake of the pious, who are kindled with the true love of God. To be sure, they are sometimes accustomed to be vehemently distressed when that vigor of mind which they desire is not present as they are about to celebrate the Holy Supper, nor do they feel the criteria of regeneration <note>The signs or "marks" that one has been spiritually reborn.</note> as vividly as they would indeed wish. These people must be taught that it can happen to them in this matter as they know happens to themselves in the performance of other duties of piety: namely, that for physical and moral reasons, even the pious can be seized by a certain languor of the mind. This, however, does not prevent them from being counted among Christians of a true name, since the root of divine love is fixed most deeply in their hearts, and after some interval of time, that ancient and masculine virtue returns to the heart. Such people, if they are certainly of this sort, are to be encouraged with grave and circumspect discourse. For if anyone were to bring eternal destruction upon himself because he had once or twice partaken of the Sacred Supper less devoutly than was right and than he himself had wished, there would be few pious people who could have a certain hope of obtaining the remission of sins. Added to this is the fact that the pious are not only freed from the habit of vices, but also that, attending to their actions throughout their whole life, if they have failed in anything, they seek the remission of sins from God and guard themselves against those sins in the future. Hence there is no doubt that if they have occasionally celebrated the memory of the death of Jesus Christ while being less properly prepared, they will obtain pardon from God. These things, however, ought to be suggested cautiously and circumspectly by the **Ministers of the Word of God** <note>Latin: "V. D. Ministri," short for *Verbi Dei Ministri*.</note>, lest the impious and hypocrites might take the opportunity from this to excuse the abuse of the Holy Supper...

The general one is easy to perform, nor does it require that long and laborious investigation and exercise prescribed in ascetic books. For since the pious know for certain that they are adorned by God with those gifts which are demanded of Christians of a true name, and without this persuasion they could not bear a certain judgment concerning their own happy state, it is manifest that this examination can be easily completed. But for the undertaking of a special **self-examination**, there is need for greater attention and effort of the mind. To be sure, the pious differ among themselves, both with respect to the knowledge of divine things and with respect to progress in the study of piety. The former <note>Those less advanced in knowledge.</note> ought to attend diligently to whether they have taken any care to make some progress in a more solid knowledge of divine things or not: whether they firmly adhere to those truths without which a saving faith cannot exist. Ministri," short for *Verbi Dei Ministri*.</note> speak concerning the preparation for the Holy Supper, they ought to attend carefully to the diversity of their listeners. For in all assemblies there are men truly pious and kindled with a strong <note>Latin: "masculo," literally "masculine," implying a vigorous or robust love.</note> love for the Savior; there are those who are very weak, both in respect to their knowledge and their progress in the study of piety; there are the careless; there are those given over to vices of every kind; and finally, there are those who cling to one specific vice. Regarding which extremes are to be avoided in this argument, the illustrious **Tillotson** <note>John Tillotson (1630–1694), a famous Archbishop of Canterbury known for his clear and influential sermons.</note> has piously, prudently, and learnedly warned in the sacred sermon praised above. How one must deal specifically with the pious who, moved by scruples of conscience, are unwilling to take the sacred supper, has been learnedly and prudently shown by the Venerable and Most Learned **Roques**, the most worthy Pastor of the French Church at Basel, in the book titled: *Tableau de la conduite du Chretien* <note>French: "Picture of the Conduct of a Christian."</note>.

<margin>Concerning the end and use of the Holy Supper.</margin>
XIII. Since the Holy Supper was instituted by Christ himself as a rite to be observed among Christians, we can be taught no better regarding its true use than if we attend to the "end" <note>The "end" (*finis*) refers to the ultimate goal or purpose.</note> for which the Savior instituted that Sacrament. Now, He affirms in words that are not perplexed, but very clear, that the Holy Supper was instituted primarily for the celebration of the memory of His death. The Apostle Paul affirms the same. Therefore, the chief use of the Holy Supper consists in the due commemoration of the death of Jesus Christ. It is a wonder, therefore, that some have asserted that the things I said on pages 17 and 21 of my dissertation concerning the "end" of the Holy Supper were too "diluted" <note>Meaning "weak" or "insufficient."</note>. Those men, who boast that they have read so many theological systems, ought to have at least been mindful of what they read long ago as youths in Heidegger’s *Medulla* <note>Johann Heinrich Heidegger (1633–1698), a Swiss Reformed theologian; his *Medulla Theologiae Christianae* was a standard textbook.</note>, section XXV, where he treats the Sacraments. For there it is said in so many words: the principal end of the Holy Supper is the memory of Christ's death. And before him, the **Blessed Bullinger** <note>Heinrich Bullinger (1504–1575), a key figure in the Swiss Reformation.</note> in his Commentary on the First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter XI, says: *This sacred thing which He instituted here, He instituted in memory of His death. For hence He so often repeats: do this in memory of me—of me, I say, who was delivered into death for you; rightly therefore does He remember that time of night in which He was betrayed.* For the death of Christ holds the first place in this sacred mystery. And in *The Decades*, book 5, Sermon IX, he speaks thus of the Lord's Supper: *We say the Supper was instituted by the Lord so that*

<sig>Lllll 3</sig>

...so that it might keep Your death in memory, lest it ever be blotted out by oblivion. *For the death of Christ is a compendium of all the benefits of God.* Therefore, He wants the benefit of the Incarnation, passion, redemption, and love to be kept in memory. Although memory is performed regarding a past thing—namely, death—it nevertheless pertains to us greatly and gives life. Nor shall we think this is a secondary goal. *For no goal*—take note—*is expressed as diligently as this one. For once and again the Lord says: do this in memory of me.* But that sacred rite and that sacred action, joined with the words or the preaching concerning the death of Christ and the redemption of the human race, it is a wonder how it repeatedly renews the benefit, and does not allow it to fall into oblivion and perish. If those men of sharp wit, who subjected my words to their censure, had rightly weighed what it is to celebrate the death of the Lord, perhaps they would have confessed with me that this is the first and chief thing in the use of the Holy Supper. For he who rightly and piously meditates on the death of Jesus Christ represents to his mind every circumstance of this death, and at the same time the innocence of the Savior; he is intimately persuaded above all of the gravity of his own sins; he grieves for them and is therefore vehemently distressed. He believes it is necessary, because of the weakness of human strength, that God Himself show the means of reconciliation. He who rightly celebrates the death of the Lord acknowledges that Jesus Christ, the <term>God-man</term> <note>Original Greek: θεάνθρωπον (*theanthropon*), a theological term for Christ's dual nature.</note>, underwent a bloody and shameful death for sins; he looks upon this death of the Son of God, undergone for unworthy sinners, as the unique cause of his reconciliation with God. To this death he flees as if to some sacred asylum; in it he places the unique hope of his salvation and the certain confidence of the remission of sins. He beholds Jesus Christ, represented through the external symbols of bread and wine in the Holy Supper, not only as present to his pious mind, but he also gives thanks to God the Father for such a great benefit. *For we are so composed by God that those things which are vehemently at our heart hardly ever or entirely never slip from our minds.* From which it happens that in Cicero someone denies that anyone was ever so forgetful that he did not remember in what place he had buried his treasure: these are the words of the celebrated **Amyraut** <note>Moïse Amyraut (1596–1664), a prominent French Reformed theologian.</note> in his dissertation on the use and necessity of the Holy Supper. He beholds the death of Jesus Christ represented in the Holy Supper not only as the unique anchor of salvation, but also as the weightiest bond and the most excellent incentive of his obligation toward such a great Savior and of his grateful soul toward the Same. Although meditation on the death of Jesus Christ outside the use of the Holy Supper vehemently kindles the mind of a pious person toward the study of piety, it must nevertheless be confessed that...

his mind is struck in a singular way through the representation of the Symbols instituted by Christ himself. Sometimes even the mind, fixed in the contemplation of the death of Jesus, is bathed in an incredible solace; and if he does not always feel that solace as he would wish, he is nevertheless reminded of his duty by that earnest meditation on the death of Jesus Christ, and spurs toward piety are added to him. The meditation on this death incites him to show brotherly love to all men, especially the pious, who are kindled with the love of God and Christ. Furthermore, a serious contemplation of this death is joined with holy sighs and prayers poured out by the pious man for this purpose: that the work of regeneration, which was obtained through the Holy Spirit by the power of the merit of Jesus Christ, may increase, be strengthened, confirmed, and perfected more and more. Finally, in a man rightly celebrating the Holy Supper, there is a purpose—not light and transitory, but fixed and serious—to love Christ Jesus his Savior more and more, to bid farewell to vices, and, as far as the fragility of human nature allows, to strive toward perfection. All these things are required for a true and salvific celebration of the death of Jesus Christ in the Holy Supper. 

Let those, therefore, who boast that they feel more correctly regarding this argument, say what more is finally required for that true and salvific remembrance of the death of Christ in the Holy Supper, and whether a Christian man, by so extolling the death of Christ, does not perform all those things required for its pious celebration? I would gladly be taught better things by any man skilled in Theology if I am in error. Our most excellent Reformers, *Zwingli* <note>Huldrych Zwingli (1484–1531), a leader of the Reformation in Switzerland.</note>, *Oecolampadius* <note>Johannes Oecolampadius (1482–1531), the Reformer of Basel.</note>, and *Bullinger* <note>Heinrich Bullinger (1504–1575), Zwingli's successor in Zurich.</note>, spoke regarding this argument in the same way. The first two were defended against various calumniators—who were spreading the idea that the Reformers felt too "thinly" about the Holy Supper and that by their explanations they took away all salvific use of the Holy Supper—by *Bullinger* in his *Commentary on the 1st Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter XI, page 208* and following. The words of *Bullinger* sound thus: *Lest anyone,* he says, *stumble over the words sign, symbol, memorial, figure, representation, or signification, as if we think nothing more august of the Sacrament of the body and blood of the Lord than of common signs—namely, that this phrasing: "This is my body," is no less narrow than if someone were to say of a piece of wood or a statue of Socrates or Hercules, "this is Socrates or Hercules"—and that in this sacred Supper we eat and drink only bare signs, that is, nothing but common bread and common wine; we publicly testify that we speak of sacred things religiously and in a certain sacred manner. The chief thing in this Supper is that Christ expiated our sins by His shed blood, and that He feeds and refreshes our souls with His flesh and blood:*
