briefly, that He offers Himself entirely to us to be enjoyed; and although that is perceived by the Spirit of God alone, the divine goodness nevertheless accommodated itself to our capacity and our weakness. Thus it happened that, since we consist not of spirit alone but of flesh and spirit, He offered those invisible and heavenly gifts to us through visible things, and so placed them before our eyes and senses themselves. Accordingly, our body indeed eats the visible bread, but our mind itself (unless faith be absent) [eats] the true body of the Lord, which we believe was given to us by God and handed over to death. For the Ancients <note>Referring to the Early Church Fathers, particularly Augustine.</note> rightly said that a Sacrament is a visible sign of invisible grace. Therefore, in the mystical Supper, we do not recognize a bare sign only, but the mystical body and blood of the Lord himself. This was recognized by those men of happy memory, clear in erudition and piety, lights of the Church of Christ, our most faithful brothers and teachers, *Huldrych Zwingli, Bishop of the Church of Zurich, and Johannes Oecolampadius, Bishop of the Church of Basel.* 

Then, having brought forward the most famous passages of *Zwingli* and *Oecolampadius* from which it is established that they felt and spoke correctly regarding this argument, he concludes on page 210 thus: *From these testimonies of great men, you understand what is the character of this heavenly banquet, what its institution, what its power and nature. You see, moreover, how holily and religiously these men feel, along with all cultivators of the orthodox faith, regarding this sacred mystery; so that those are now triflers and futile babblers who prattle that these men—who feel orthodoxly about the Eucharist, namely that very thing which the Church of Christ has always felt about it—are enemies of both Christ and the Sacraments.* Thus far *Bullinger*. 

From these things which I have said regarding the pious meditation on the death of Christ in the Holy Supper, it can at the same time be judged what should be thought of the unfair and hardly brotherly suspicion of certain people. These people have babbled that the things said by me in Section IX of the previous dissertation concerning the meditation on death in the Holy Supper are not far removed from what even the *Socinians* <note>Followers of Socinianism, a rationalist Christian movement that denied the divinity of Christ and the "satisfaction" theory of the atonement, viewing the Lord's Supper as a mere memorial.</note> admit. "To be sure," they say, "these Socinians also confess that the celebration of Christ's death ought to be instituted in the Holy Supper." But this argument is no more fitting than if someone were to say: "The Socinians eat, drink, sleep, and walk; the Reformed do the same; therefore the Reformed are Socinians." If this reasoning is valid, the Reformed are easily changed into Socinians and vice versa. Certainly here, if anywhere, that well-worn saying is valid: *When two say the same thing, they do not always mean the same thing.* The true nature of the pious remembrance of the death of Jesus Christ is not to be sought so much in the contemplation of the death alone, as in the meditation on the causes of this death, the dignity of the person who underwent the death, and the power and efficacy of this death. The Socinians, of course, deny the necessity and the satisfaction <note>The doctrine that Christ's death satisfied the justice of God as payment for sin.</note> of the death of Jesus Christ: I, with the Reform[ed]...

...tion, I uphold the same. The Socinians deny the divinity of Jesus Christ; I, on the contrary, profess it with my whole heart. The Socinians deny that the death of Christ is a true <term>ransom</term> <note>Greek: lytron; a price paid for redemption</note> for sins. I assert the opposite. The Socinians deny that the regeneration and conversion of man are the fruits of the satisfaction performed for sinners; we, however, together with the Reformed, defend this proposition. Either we have lost the true names of things and are destitute of common sense, or the remembrance of the death of Jesus Christ as explained by us is <note>original: "toto coelo"</note> poles apart from the opinion of the Socinians. I know indeed that Faustus Socinus, in order to remove the hatred directed at himself and to prove by some reasoning the innocence of his opinion on the Holy Supper, appealed to Zwingli, as if Zwingli felt the same as he did regarding the use of the Holy Supper. For instance, among other things in his controversy with *Niemojevvius*, he speaks thus:

> *Certainly, says Zwingli and others—who, as our own people believe, were the first of all to begin to exterminate from the Church of Christ all the more destructive and crasser opinions concerning the Supper of the Lord—they said this very same thing, since they clearly saw that the Supper of the Lord was not instituted for the purpose that we might receive something there for salvation, but that we might commemorate certain things already received pertaining to it, and give thanks for them.*

Thus says Socinus. But is this a legitimate inference? Socinus appealed to Zwingli as being <term>of the same mind</term> <note>Greek: homopsyphon; sharing the same "vote" or opinion</note> in the doctrine of the Holy Supper; therefore, did Zwingli feel the same about this argument as Socinus? For who does not know that Zwingli acknowledged both the Deity of our Savior and His satisfaction and merit, while Socinus did not? How then, by similar reasoning, can Socinus and Zwingli be said to celebrate the death of Jesus Christ? I believe this calumny cannot be better countered than with the words of the Blessed Hospinian, who in his *Sacramental History*, Volume II, page 31, pleads Zwingli's case, saying:

> *Regarding the fact that certain things are found in Zwingli's letters and elsewhere, from which it might seem that the man attributed less to the sacraments than Scripture attributes to them: if his scope and intention are considered, no one but a Momus <note>a person who finds fault with everything</note> could turn it into a vice and interpret it sinisterly. For since the Papists taught transubstantiation—as if it were a conversion of the elements into the very things signified—and Luther, along with certain Scholastics, seemed to teach a local inclusion of the body of Christ in the bread! It was extremely difficult to uproot these opinions which had already taken deep root, especially the former in the minds of men. He applied all the powers of his intellect to attacking them; so much so, that he seemed to suggest the Lord was more absent in the Holy Supper than present in his body and blood, and that symbols were given here rather than the body and blood of the Lord. Yet he did not wish the Lord to be simply absent from the Supper, nor that in the celebration of the Holy Supper empty symbols of the body and blood of the Lord...*

...be dispensed here; just as Bucer testifies in his *Retractions*, that Zwingli himself, while discussing the harmony of the Churches in this dogma with him, candidly and openly confessed this to him. This also appears from his *Apology to the German Princes*:

> *For there, in the words of Augustine, he most openly confessed the presence of the Lord in the Supper.*

In the same way elsewhere, while he wished to be careful lest men seek salvation from the external work in the Sacraments, he seemed to affirm that the Sacraments are only tokens <note>original: "tesseras"</note> of Christian society and confer nothing toward salvation. But elsewhere he clearly writes that the Sacraments bring help and aid to faith. From this it can be sufficiently clear that when he wrote that the Sacraments confer nothing toward salvation nor confirm faith, he understood by "Sacraments" the external action of the Sacraments, which in itself has nothing of the power to strengthen consciences by increasing faith. For when he set out to prove his opinion—that Sacraments do not dispense salvation nor confirm faith—he argued that confirming and increasing faith is the work of Christ through the Holy Spirit. In these words, at first glance and without Zwingli's mind being properly understood, the argument seems similar to this: "God heals by the force of nature, therefore the doctor and medicine contribute nothing to it." Indeed, Christ alone works all salvation in us, and that by no foreign power but by His Spirit alone; meanwhile, however, for that very purpose, He uses His word toward us—both the visible word in the Sacraments and the audible word in the Gospel. Through these, He brings and offers the remission of sins, communion with Himself, and eternal life. Zwingli acknowledged, approved, and taught this excellently; hence, when he denied that the Sacraments dispense grace, he meant the external action of the Sacrament. His opinion was that it has value not from itself, but that all things of salvation rest upon the internal action of Christ, of which the Sacraments are instruments in their own way. Thus says Hospinian. Moreover, Zwingli's own warnings against that malicious suspicion in his *Exposition of the Eucharist to M. Luther* show that he disagreed entirely with the Socinians. For on page 63, he speaks thus:

> *I will, however, set down a brief summary, as it were, of how I myself acknowledge Christ. I acknowledge Christ to be, according to the word of the Apostle in 1 Corinthians 1: Wisdom from God; Righteousness and Sanctification and Redemption. Wisdom, because He is God by nature, who not only knows all things but also governs them. Wisdom from God, because the almighty Father sent Him to teach heavenly wisdom so perfectly and brilliantly that what He taught would finally be the true pattern of wisdom. Hence St. Paul confesses that he knows nothing except Jesus Christ and Him crucified; which that most prudent man would not have said if he did not hold that all the treasures of Wisdom were perfectly in Him. Wisdom from God, by which we might be made certain that no external things...*

> ...for justification. In short, he taught in such a way that no one endowed with a sound mind could fail to see that his sole purpose was that we should trust in the Lord and cultivate a life of innocence and holiness. And since, by the fault and calamity which destroyed our nature "in the blade" <note>original: "in herba"; a metaphor meaning from its very beginning or in its early growth</note>, as they say, we are so bound to our desires that we do nothing of those things which God requires of us worthily or as we ought, it follows that the justice of God again strikes us with terror. For however much we proclaim Him to be merciful and good, we are nonetheless compelled to acknowledge Him as just at the same time; for that which lacked justice would not be truly good. Now, so that His justice might also remain most holy, and yet man—who does nothing worthy of it—might not be perpetually deprived of His company, He found a way by which He might both satisfy justice and restore miserable man to God's company. He therefore sent His Son, who became our righteousness, our sanctification, and the price of our redemption. And this was done only for those who, having been elected by God and taught inwardly by the Spirit, firmly believe this: that through the one way of God's mercy (for the fact that He appeased His own justice by offering His Son is likewise a work of mercy) an entrance lies open to eternal blessedness. Of this mercy His Son was made the pledge and the guarantee. For how will He not give us all things, He who gave His Son! Not as one commanded, but made the foundation of our hope; not insofar as He is flesh, but insofar as He is the Son of God who put on flesh. Thus you have, in brief, how I myself acknowledge Christ: namely, that He is the light and the highest wisdom, which so illustrated the world that it might see that God is charmed by no other services than innocence; that heaven is climbed by no other price or tribute than the <term>redemption</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀπολύτρωσεως" (apolytrōsis); refers to a ransoming or deliverance</note> of the Son of God; that we are excited to the work of true virtue by no other spurs than the ignition of the Spirit; and that true refreshment is channeled into our souls by no other pipes than by the Spirit and influence of the same. This is how we acknowledge Christ. If this is not to acknowledge Him seriously, I will confess that I have not yet acknowledged Him.

Thus says the Blessed Zwingli.

<margin>Instruction concerning preparatory sermons.</margin>
XIV. Thus far we have dealt both with the external causes that can hinder Christians from rightly using the Holy Supper, and with the legitimate end and use of the Holy Supper. Now indeed we must consider what must be performed by the Ministers of the Word of God when they wish to lead people to a worthy celebration of the Holy Supper. It is a praiseworthy custom of the Ministers of the Word of God that, on the days immediately preceding the sacred Feasts <note>original: "concionibus parascevaticis"; sermons of preparation or "Good Friday" style preparation</note>, they choose such topics for their orations as can invite and induce people to a worthy celebration of the Holy Supper. The things to be advised regarding these orations can, in my opinion, be reduced to two heads. Clearly, there is something the Ministers of the Word of God must avoid, and something else they must perform. Specifically, they must take care that such preparatory orations are not too vague and general, which happens if the listeners are merely advised to perform this much:

<meta>catchword: perform:</meta>

---

<page-num>1011</page-num>
<header>CELEBRATION OF THE HOLY SUPPER.</header>

to perform: that throughout the coming week they should find time for reading and diligent attendance at the holy sermons, and seriously examine themselves. For in this way, many listeners will easily fall into the opinion of thinking that once this is done, there is no doubt but that they will use the Sacred Supper worthily and obtain the efficacy of the death of Jesus Christ—that is, the remission of sins. Furthermore, they flatter themselves that the work of conversion is too easy; this opinion can hinder a serious and pious purpose of renouncing all vices and amending one's life. However, those things which the Minister of the Word of God must perform can be reduced to the following.

First: the Minister of the Word shall labor to prove clearly and solidly that it is necessary that he who wishes to use the Holy Supper worthily must either already be converted before the celebration, or at least have already prepared his soul for that work to be performed with divine help. This must be shown somewhat more at length, both from the end and use of the Holy Supper and from the nature of regeneration and true conversion. And this must be done all the more because many Christians imagine that by the reading of little devotional books <note>original: "libellorum asceticorum"</note>, daily attendance at sermons, a general confession of sins, and a cold remembrance of Christ’s death, everything pertaining to the true and salutary use of the Holy Supper is completed; and that by acting in this way, they are equipped with all those signs from which it is concluded that we are reconciled to God. The more deeply this dangerous opinion is fixed in their minds, the more diligence and weight of argument must be used to defeat it. For a sacred speaker ought never to be more attentive and circumspect than when dealing with the uprooting of opinions harmful to piety. Many attack harmless errors with the greatest mental agitation and zeal, but do not attack practical errors with the same fervor; however, this is not the place to speak of that.

II. The Minister of the Word of God must speak individually in such orations with those who are truly converted, with those who stand at the beginnings of conversion, with hypocrites, and with those who are given over to crasser vices. To all the pious in general—though they differ much among themselves in the degrees of their progress in the business of conversion—it must be shown that the most excellent benefit which God has granted to a Christian man is the bloody death of Jesus Christ. He must show that the pious contemplation of this death contains within itself the most weighty incitements to a very tender love for our Savior, and supplies stings against all sluggishness and the temptations of sins. Since this benefit is represented in a singular way in the use of the Sacred Symbols, one must approach the Holy Supper frequently and with a joyful heart. To the hypocrites...

# DISSERTATION ON THE LEGITIMATE
<page-num>1012</page-num>
<header>CELEBRATION OF THE HOLY SUPPER</header>

...indeed, it must be clearly shown to those plainly addicted to vices that, by the very nature of things, it cannot be otherwise: those who abuse such an excellent benefit, and frequently receive the holy supper without any stirrings of piety, by this very act prevent themselves from reaching serious repentance—without which, however, no certain hope of attaining salvation is given.

III. What, in my opinion, the Minister of the Word of God <note>original: "V. D. Ministro," an abbreviation for *Verbi Divini Minister*</note> ought to provide is this: namely, that he should instill in their minds the essential characteristics that ought to be present in a reborn person, and prove with clear arguments that it is impossible for anyone to share in the benefits won by the death of the Savior <note>original: "Soteris," from the Greek *Sotēr*</note> unless they are truly equipped with those characteristics. To that end, in these Orations, he will treat at one moment the nature of saving faith and its effects, at another the marks of true and sincere repentance, and at another the duties of brotherly love; he will then show, from the nature of the sins opposite to these virtues, that it is impossible for those who have contracted a habit in this or that vice to rightly celebrate the death of Jesus Christ, or to have any hope of attaining salvation while they remain such as they are. (IV.) But if anyone should think that the impious will be deterred from the use of the Holy Supper by this reasoning, the Minister of the Word of God ought to advise that men who have not yet plainly bid farewell to their vices do not have sufficient cause to abandon the use of the Holy Supper for that reason. This is both because we have a sufficiently clear precept from our Savior commanding us to use the sacred symbols in His memory, and because the celebration of this Sacrament can be an occasion through which a man may look into himself; and with the addition of various circumstances which the favor of the Divine Will can provide, a path to conversion can be paved. For just as the divine word must still be read and heard by those not yet converted, because it is the "seed of regeneration," so likewise the use of the Holy Supper is an external means of convicting a man of his vices and, with the addition of divine grace, preparing him for true conversion. Furthermore, those who, because of a weak knowledge of divine matters, cannot distinctly set forth the true characteristics of the converted, are especially bound to do this—provided they perceive at the same time that certain seeds of a new life have been implanted in their souls. For by pious meditation on the death of Christ, in which the "marrow" <note>the core or essence</note> of our salvation must be sought, a greater light is instilled into the mind over time, and a greater incentive is added to the study of true piety.

<margin>Advice concerning the booklets in which the true use of the Holy Supper is discussed.</margin>
XV. Ministers of the Word of God are accustomed, piously and wisely, to refer men who are about to rightly celebrate the Holy Supper to ascetic booklets <note>devotional manuals intended to guide spiritual exercise and self-examination</note> which deal with the true use of the Holy Supper; and there is no doubt that the reading of such booklets...

---

<page-num>1013</page-num>
<header>CELEBRATION OF THE HOLY SUPPER.</header>

...serious and attentive reading can prepare the mind for a worthy celebration of this Sacrament. Because, however, such booklets are not all of one kind, it will perhaps not be useless to have offered some advice on this subject. First, it should be noted what is lacking in some; what the style of those who apply their minds to writing such booklets should be; and finally, what arguments such booklets should encompass. What is lacking in many books written to excite devotion was piously and learnedly shown by the Blessed <note>original: "ὁ Μακαριτης" (*ho Makaritēs*), a Greek term of respect for the deceased</note> and Venerable *Ostervald* <note>Jean-Frédéric Ostervald (1663–1747), a Swiss Protestant pastor famous for his works on liturgy and Christian ethics</note> in the last chapter of the book praised above. Let those who love the truth unroll that volume; we are content with a few pieces of advice. To be sure, there are authors of such booklets who do not so much act to explain and prove the most holy things with clear arguments and words, but rather to excite a rush of emotions with "inflated expressions" <note>original: "ampullatis locutionibus," referring to pompous or bombastic language</note> collected here and there. By this it usually happens that, a feeling having been extorted by a certain violence of tropes <note>metaphorical language</note>, men rest satisfied in obscure notions and are stunned by words they do not sufficiently understand. What the Venerable Ostervald warned regarding booklets for exciting devotion in general in the place cited, can be applied specifically to certain booklets that deal with the right use of the Holy Supper. Piety (he says) on page 285 of the place cited:

> *would be better known and more esteemed than it is, if judgment and common sense always reigned in books of devotion, and if one saw nothing in them which, being examined strictly, was not found to be in conformity with exact truth. Those who work on works of this nature propose to touch the heart and to excite sentiments of Piety. Their goal is good; but it must be known that what touches the heart, and what inspires Devotion, is the force of reasons, the evidence of proofs, the greatness of objects, and the clarity and solidity of the things that one says. This is also what judicious Authors attach themselves to principally, and it is by this that many have succeeded in the excellent works with which they have enriched the public. But this is what other Authors do not consider. They apply themselves rather to saying touching things than to thinking and speaking justly; They consult the Imagination rather than common sense; they put into writing everything that, in the heat of meditation and in the movements of their zeal, seems to them fit to move, to soften, to console, or to frighten. This results in there being weak spots in their works, thoughts which appear lowly or even false to readers who have discernment, contradictions, and other similar defects. These works do much harm to Religion. For on one hand they produce in those who read them and enjoy them only a devotion* <note>original text in French: "seroit mieux connuë & plus estimée..."</note>

# DISSERTATION ON THE LEGITIMATE
<page-num>1014</page-num>
<header>DISSERTATIO DE LEGITIMA</header>
<meta>catchword: II. Agen-</meta>

<note>The following paragraph is translated from the original French quoted in the Latin text.</note>
...confused and unreasonable devotion; and on the other, they expose devotion to the mockeries and contempt of the Libertines <note>A term often used in the 17th and 18th centuries for those who rejected traditional religious restraints or moral norms.</note>. One often has the displeasure and scandal of seeing enlightened persons show little esteem for books of Piety. One hears it said every day in the world, that these books are only good for women and the common people. This contempt proceeds principally from a profane humor and libertinism; but it also has its source in the lack of accuracy and solidity that one finds in certain books of devotion. Thus says that Distinguished Theologian.

**(II.)** Certain small books of this kind are too general, and do not explain the characteristics of godly and ungodly men, and the various states of men, with sufficient clarity. **(III.)** Many of these booklets abound with innumerable metaphors and "little flowers" <note>original: "flosculis," referring to excessive rhetorical flourishes that obscure the meaning</note> of speech, which prevent simpler people from perceiving the true and native sense of the most holy things—a subject we have already discussed in the previous dissertation. As for what truly ought to be in these booklets, it pertains either to the words and style, or to the subject matter itself. Regarding the former, the style ought to be so transparent, natural, and simple that men of average intelligence cannot fail to grasp the meaning of the things proposed. For since the authors of such booklets ought to intend nothing else—and doubtless do intend nothing else—than to explain and commend the most holy things, it is necessary that they use clear words adapted to the minds of all. If it is asked how many chapters such a booklet should contain, I would not wish to define anything strictly. However, pending the better judgment of others, I think the following articles should be the primary focus:

**I.** The arguments by which the truth of the Christian Religion is proved must be represented briefly but vigorously <note>original: "nervose," meaning with strength or sinew</note>. For the sake of brevity, these arguments can be drawn from the truth and certainty of the Resurrection of Jesus Christ. For unless a Christian is truly persuaded of this article, a robust piety cannot take root in his soul, nor can he celebrate the death of Christ with due piety. I know indeed that there are excellent men who think these things should be omitted as already granted; but experience witnesses that many who celebrate the Holy Supper are not rightly instructed and persuaded concerning this article as they should be. Since most Christians—even those not sufficiently taught in the arguments usually used to prove the divine origin of the Christian Religion—tend to consult such booklets at the time they have set their minds to celebrate the Holy Supper, they thus have the opportunity to weigh this most grave article of faith.

<column-break/>

<page-num>1015</page-num>
<header>CELEBRATION OF THE HOLY SUPPER.</header>
<meta>catchword: X. Mon-</meta>

**II.** One must treat Jesus Christ, the dignity of His person, and His offices; but especially His love demonstrated toward us in His bloody passion and death. It must be particularly advised that in this death undergone for us, our true and unique solace is to be sought.

**III.** The meaning of the Words of Institution <note>The specific words spoken by Jesus at the Last Supper: "This is my body... this is my blood."</note> of the Holy Supper, compared with the testimonies of the Apostles concerning this Sacrament, must be explained clearly and transparently. It should be briefly shown that the explanation of the Reformers <note>Referring to Protestant theologians like Luther or Calvin</note> agrees with the words of institution, with reason, the senses, the nature of Sacraments, and other most grave headings of the Christian Religion. Conversely, it should be shown that the opinion of the Pontificians <note>original: "Pontificiorum," a term for Roman Catholics</note> is opposed to all of these. Although in these booklets practice should be the primary consideration, it is nevertheless necessary that all who wish to piously celebrate the death of Jesus Christ in the use of the Holy Supper have a genuine knowledge of this Sacrament. They should realize how foolish it is to wish to become a partaker of the benefits won by the death of Christ merely by the act of eating bread and wine.

**IV.** This chapter should treat the end, purpose, and true use of the Holy Supper. Here it is especially to be noted that the principal end is the serious and pious meditation on the death of Christ, and that the entire mind ought to be fixed upon this thought. Finally, it must be shown not only in parts what that pious and serious meditation consists of, but also how much this meditation can kindle the mind toward the study of piety.

**V.** However, so that the legitimate use of the Holy Supper may be properly revealed, the characteristics of true Christians must be distinctly represented. This is so that everyone about to celebrate the Holy Supper may know in what state they are placed, and what hope they have of attaining salvation. The various degrees of the godly should be treated individually; here, the argument should not be exaggerated, nor on the other hand treated too thinly. Opposed to these should be the Characteristics of Hypocrites and the Ungodly, showing that they can find no protection in the enjoyment of external symbols, nor in a cold commemoration of the death of Christ.

**VI.** The common prejudices of Hypocrites and the Ungodly regarding the use of the Holy Supper should be properly represented and refuted with grave arguments.

**VII.** One must treat the Examination of Oneself <note>Based on 1 Corinthians 11:28, "Let a man examine himself."</note> to be performed before the use of the Sacred Supper, its necessity, and its parts.

**VIII.** It should be shown point by point what the nature of saving faith consists of, and what its fruits are.

**IX.** A specific chapter should deal with the nature and certain signs of true and sincere repentance.

**X.** It must be shown what is to be done during the participation in the Holy Supper itself and after it, with primary regard given to the different conditions of men.

**XI.** Finally, certain short formulas for prayer, written in clear language, must be added, to be poured out both before and after the use of the Holy Supper. This must be provided individually so that attention is paid to the godly—whether those who have received comfort from the use of the Supper, or those utterly dejected in heart, or those who are still weak, or finally those who felt no stirrings of piety before and after the Supper. Such formulas were added to his booklet on the *Duties of Communicants* by, among others, the most worthy *Venerable Ostervald* <note>Jean-Frédéric Ostervald (1663–1747), a prominent Swiss Protestant theologian whose works on liturgy and morality were widely translated and influential in the 18th century.</note>, Pastor of the Church of Basel <note>Though the text says "Basileensis" (of Basel), Ostervald was the famous pastor of Neuchâtel. The author may be misidentifying his location or referring to a specific edition.</note>. In my opinion, these are the chapters that should be represented in these booklets, while leaving room for the judgment of others.

<margin>What should be observed by Pastors in the sacred sermons that are usually held in the afternoon hours after the morning use of the Holy Supper.</margin>
**XVI.** It is a custom for sacred preachers that, once the morning celebration of the Holy Supper is completed, they select such texts for the afternoon sermons as provide material for giving thanks to God for the benefit of redemption, the memory of which was represented to their souls in the use of the Holy Supper. Nor is there any doubt that this is done rightly: for since the most excellent benefit of God—that is, the bloody death of Jesus Christ our Savior—has been recalled to memory in a singular way through the use of the Holy Supper, it is most just to offer solemn thanksgivings to God. However, care must be taken that such speeches are not too vague. For it is well known that many Christians rest in the external use of the symbols <note>The bread and wine.</note> and in some sort of remembrance of Christ, and believe that in this way they have truly been made partakers of all Christ's benefits. To these people, those speeches are pleasing in which thanks are given to God indiscriminately, because through the celebration of the Holy Supper we are made certain of the fruits of Christ’s death and the forgiveness of sins. Since a sacred preacher should always aim above all to pluck out popular but very harmful errors from the minds of his listeners as much as he can, he will take care to discuss this argument very circumspectly. In my opinion, such speeches should consist of two parts. In the first part, it should be shown that those who discovered the marks of true Christians in themselves before the use of the Supper, and were already mindful of the benefits won by Christ’s death, have the greatest reasons for glorying, since they were led by the pious remembrance of the death of Jesus Christ, represented in the Holy Supper, to new incentives for giving thanks to God, for loving Christ above all things, and for diligently pursuing the study of virtue.

<meta>catchword: Monstran-</meta>

---

<page-num>1017</page-num>
<header>CELEBRATION OF THE HOLY SUPPER.</header>

It must be shown, moreover, that such people can be of a joyful and peaceful mind, not because of the external use of the Holy Supper (which they share with Hypocrites and the Ungodly), but because the grace of God, having led them to a reformed way of living before the use of the Supper, makes them feel that the benefits won by Christ’s death belong to them. In the latter part of the speech, one must speak a little more fully with those who felt no stirrings of conscience at all, either before or after the use of the Supper, because of a habit contracted in vices, or who were touched by some slight but transitory remembrance of sins, yet without any serious desire to change their life for the better. It must be shown to these people that they have no cause for rejoicing, and that they are in the most immediate danger of destruction unless they change their minds and begin to feel more reverently about the use of the Holy Supper. By acting in this way, the listeners easily notice that not everyone who has used the Sacred Supper can be of a peaceful mind, nor can they therefore claim the benefits of Christ’s death for themselves. Such people will thus feel that they have the most serious reasons for imploring God in Christ Jesus to give them the enlightened eyes of the mind to perceive those things that pertain to salvation. What I have said about sermons, I think should also be observed regarding the Psalms and formulas of prayer. It is therefore to be hoped that such prayer formulas and Psalms would be composed in which mention of those two kinds of men is made distinctly enough; there is no doubt that some stirrings of conscience would thus arise in the minds of the listeners.

<margin>What should be judged concerning godly men who, when using the Holy Supper, rarely perceive comfort.</margin>
**XVII.** A question arises here, perhaps not foreign to our purpose: namely, what should be thought of godly and truly regenerated <note>original: "regenitis," referring to those who have undergone a spiritual rebirth or "new birth" in the theological sense.</note> people who, on the occasion of enjoying the Holy Supper, not only rarely perceive true comforts, but are often distressed in their souls? We respond: (1) In our opinion, it should be represented to these people that true comfort is not to be sought so much from the use of the Holy Supper itself, as rather from the fact that before the public celebration of the Supper, they discovered certain marks of a reformed mind in themselves; for where these are present, they can safely conclude that by the help of the Holy Spirit, they have been made partakers of the divine benefits won by Christ’s death. It must be shown that this perception of joy for which they pant is sometimes present and sometimes absent, according to the different internal and external state of the godly. If they feel that they have seriously repented <note>original: "pœnitentia"</note> and said farewell to their vices, they should not doubt because of the lack of that joy concerning divine mercy and favor, since that perpetual joy does not belong to the certain marks of true Christianity, nor to the essence of a worthy celebration of the Sacred Supper. (2) So that [we may respond] more fully to these men...

# DISSERTATION ON THE LEGITIMATE
<page-num>1018</page-num>
<header>DISSERTATION ON THE LEGITIMATE</header>

In order to satisfy people's needs, we must diligently inquire into the causes of the anxieties with which those partaking in the Holy Supper <note>original: "S. Coena" — the Lord's Supper or Holy Communion</note> are often distressed. These causes are either physical or moral. Physical causes can arise from one's temperament; for it often happens that many Christians are overly fearful and subject to the assaults of an unhealthy imagination. Moral causes have various sources. Often such people are deluded by a false opinion and believe it is necessary that, before the use of the Holy Supper and in the very act of receiving it, they must always be flooded with an unusual joy. Sometimes they have defiled themselves with certain sins which they have indeed earnestly detested, but which are vividly represented to the mind once again at the very moment the Holy Supper is to be celebrated. Occasionally, before the use of the Holy Supper, they feel a certain spiritual lethargy, which they persuade themselves ought to be entirely removed through the use of the Holy Supper. Often they also exaggerate the minor errors they have committed, and because of this, they doubt the certainty of their conversion; it is no wonder, therefore, that the minds of those placed in this state are clouded. Indeed, to uncover these and other causes of sadness, it is necessary that the Pastor be on familiar terms with those of his listeners whom he is persuaded—by significant evidence—are inclined toward the study of piety, or are standing at the beginnings of conversion, or have truly returned to a sounder mind. For only then will he be able to know all the—so to speak—hidden corners of a reformed but sometimes narrow mind. Meanwhile, if the Minister of the Word of God is certain that a person affected by such sadness is truly converted and loves God (as far as this can be established from many signs), he ought to offer them comfort and urge them to advance their steps more and more in the study of piety, testifying to them that by doing so, true reasons for rejoicing will never be lacking. Furthermore, to alleviate their sorrow, they should be asked to be intent upon holy days and more frequent prayers. (*)

> *In us, the Love of God, fruitful in holy desires,* <note>original French: "Dans nous l'Amour de Dieu second en saints desirs"</note>
> *Does not always produce tangible pleasures.*
> *Often the heart that possesses it, does not know it itself;*
> *One fears they do not love, who sincerely loves.*
> *Love alone being absent can never be excused:*
> *It is through Love that Grace bears fruit within us,*
> *It is Love that reanimates us and gives us life.*
> *To rejoin us to God, Love alone is the bond.*
> *And without it, Faith, Virtue, Sacraments—all is nothing.*

<sig>Nnnnnn 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: perse-</meta>

<margin>An inquiry into whether the Holy Supper should be used frequently or not.</margin>

**XVIII.** It is asked among Theologians whether the celebration of the Holy Supper ought to be less or more frequent. On this point, there is not just one opinion from everyone regarding this argument; nor could it be otherwise, since neither Christ nor the Apostles prescribed how many times per year the Holy Supper should be celebrated. Hence, the ancient as well as the more recent Churches, using their own liberty, have judged that the Holy Supper should be used more or less frequently. In our age, the question has arisen anew among us whether it would not be a beneficial and laudable institution if, during the time that runs from the feast of Pentecost until the feast of the Nativity of Jesus Christ <note>Christmas</note>, the memory of Jesus Christ were refreshed in the Holy Supper. There are those who affirm this; however, there are others on the contrary who think one should acquiesce to the accepted custom. There is no doubt that such disagreement among brothers should be borne with a calm mind. I see that *the Blessed Bullinger* <note>Heinrich Bullinger (1504–1575), a Swiss Reformer and successor to Zwingli.</note> already felt this way in his own time, when in his *Commentary on the 1st Epistle of Paul to the Corinthians, specifically on verse 26 of chapter VI*, he discusses it thus: *“In the beginning (he says) 'as often as you eat,' clearly by this word leaving it free to the Churches when or how often they celebrate the Eucharist in the sacred assembly. There exists a pious and useful dispute on this matter by Augustine in his 118th Epistle to Januarius, whose words, if anyone seeks them, are roughly these: 'Some communicate daily in the body and blood of the Lord, others receive on certain days. In some places, no day is skipped on which it is not offered; in others, only on Saturday and the Lord’s Day; others only on the Lord’s Day; and if anything else of this kind can be noticed, this whole class of things has free observations. Nor is there any better discipline in these matters for a serious and prudent Christian than to act in the manner in which he sees the Church acting, whichever one he happens to have come to. For I have often perceived, grieving and moaning, many disturbances of the weak through the contentious obstinacy and superstitious timidness of certain brothers, who in matters of this kind—which can reach no certain conclusion by the authority of Holy Scripture, nor the tradition of the universal Church, nor the utility of correcting one's life—raise such litigious questions (simply because there is some kind of reasoning underlying their thought, or because they were accustomed to it in their own country, or because they saw it in a place they think is more learned the further it is from their own) that they think nothing is right except what they do themselves. Someone might say that the Eucharist is not to be received daily; another says the opposite. Perhaps someone might more rightly settle the dispute between them by advising that they remain primarily in the peace of Christ; let each one do what he piously believes should be done according to his faith: for neither dishonors the body and blood of the Lord; that food only refuses to be held in contempt.' And if there are other words of this Saint...”* for we are only touching upon the summary of things.

We continue. Thus Bullinger <note>Heinrich Bullinger (1504–1575), a Swiss Reformer and successor to Zwingli</note> speaks: elsewhere, namely regarding the Lord’s Supper in his *Decades*,
<margin>Bullinger, Sermon IX.</margin>
Volume V, Sermon IX, he opens his opinion on this question a bit more clearly, saying: *“As to how many times the Eucharist <note>The sacrament of Holy Communion</note> should be taken by the faithful in a year, the Apostles defined nothing by established law, but left it free to the judgment of each Church; for what is clearer than what Paul said? 'As often as you eat this bread, you shall proclaim the Lord's death until He comes, and as often as you drink from this cup, you shall proclaim the Lord's death until He comes.' Meanwhile, let no one think that the celebration of the Supper has been made so free to them that they may never perform it; that would not be a just liberty, but a most wicked license. Those who celebrate the Lord's Supper on certain or fixed days in the year do not want it to be brought into contempt or distaste by daily frequency. For they take account of their people and desire the Supper to be performed worthily and with longing. But those who repeat it very frequently think it is wrong if good things fall into disregard through frequency. For they say that the better things are, the more frequently they should be used. Both desire to serve the Lord, and that what the Lord made free be performed with much fruit.”* Blessed Calvin, in his response concerning certain Church 
<margin>Calvin</margin>
rites on page 206, opens his mind on this question in this way, saying: *“To celebrate the Supper every month would please us most, provided that more frequent use does not give rise to negligence. For while the majority abstain from Communion, the Church is in a way scattered. We would prefer, however, that the Church be invited every month, rather than only four times each year, as is the custom among us. When I first came here, it was distributed only three times a year, and indeed so that seven whole months passed between the Supper at Pentecost and Christmas. Monthly pleased me, but since I could by no means persuade them, it seemed better to forgive the infirmity of the people than to contend too stubbornly. I took care, however, to have it recorded in the public Acts that our custom is defective, so that correction might be easier and freer for those who come after.”* From the words of Augustine, it is indeed clear that the more or less frequent use of the Holy Supper was permitted to the liberty of the Churches; at the same time, however, it is manifest that the use of the Holy Supper in most Churches at that time was still quite frequent. Regarding this argument, see Bingham, who discusses it more extensively 
<margin>Bingham, Book XV, Chapter IX.</margin>
in *Antiquities of the Christian Church*, Book XV, Chapter IX. <note>Joseph Bingham (1668–1723) was an English scholar who wrote a massive history of the early church</note> Since there is no external Church, even if it be a true one, in which something may not, in the course of time, be piously and prudently added or changed in rites and discipline, I see no reason why a "fourth Communion," as it is called, could not be introduced among us, if sufficiently probable and weighty reasons are present. The reasons which move me—saving, however, the judgment of other excellent men—are as follows: (1) The author of the institution of the Holy Supper is our most holy Savior <note>original: "Soter"</note> Jesus Christ. Now it must be said that He instituted the celebration of the Holy Supper for the weightiest and most

---

<page-num>1021</page-num>
<header>CELEBRATION OF THE HOLY SUPPER.</header>
<sig>Nnnnnn 3</sig>

wise reasons, or for none at all, or at least light ones. No one who is seriously and from the heart devoted to the Christian religion will affirm the latter. Therefore, the former must be embraced. Now, those reasons cannot be "weighty" unless they contribute much to stirring up the study of piety and promoting the salvation of men. But once this is granted, although it is not strictly defined how many times per year those sacred symbols should be used, it is nevertheless manifest that a thing instituted for a salutary use by Christ, the God-man <note>original Greek: "θεανθρώπω" (theanthropō)</note>, ought to be used not rarely, but rather frequently. At least, I find no reason why those sacred symbols, which supply powerful incitements to the love of Jesus Christ, should be taken rarely. (2) The very object which is represented to the minds of the Communicants through the presentation of those symbols is of such a nature that it not only places the Marrow of the Christian Religion—that is, the bloody death of Christ for sins—before the eyes, as it were; but it also exhibits the weightiest incitements for loving Jesus above all things, for keeping His precepts, for giving Him thanks, and for nourishing the mutual love of Christians. If this is true—as no one among the Reformed doubts—it follows that such a remembrance ought not to be rare, but more frequent. Someone will perhaps say that we can and ought to be mindful of the bloody death of Jesus Christ daily. That is so; but this does not prevent that remembrance, instituted through the sacred symbols, from being frequent. Our most holy Savior foresaw that His true disciples and followers of all times would acknowledge His death as the principal cause of salvation and would celebrate it with worthy praises; yet, notwithstanding this, He instituted the Holy Supper in memory of Himself, and commanded that Christians should celebrate it until His final coming. Furthermore, just as in moral habits, so in Christian virtues: the more frequent their use is, the more they become confirmed. For as they are either acquired by acts, or at least not acquired without acts, so too the frequent use of acts and powerful exercise has a wonderful force in bending the faculties in the direction toward which they themselves are carried. Therefore, just as there is no legitimate celebration of the Supper without a preceding remembrance of the death of Christ, so there is no Christian commemoration of the same death of Christ without true piety accompanying that commemoration. But there is no piety without faith, and the greater the piety is, the greater the faith ought to be. Therefore, in the legitimate celebration of the Supper, faith is in action. On which account, faith is thus increased and intensified, and all the more so, the more intense that act is.

The author argues that because Christ instituted the sacrament to bolster faith and piety, it should be practiced regularly rather than rarely.</summary>

is more outstanding and more deeply memorable. These are the words of the celebrated *Amyraut* <note>Moyse Amyraut (1596–1664), a French Reformed theologian</note> in the place cited. (3) In elucidating this question, I do not think we should look to hypocrites and the ungodly, or to superstitious men who imagine some sort of physical power is joined to the use of the Holy Supper; rather, we should look to men who are well-acquainted with the Christian religion and inflamed with the love of sincere piety. We are not permitted to act on suspicions and think that all those who claim they are vehemently inflamed toward the pursuit of piety by the use of the Holy Supper—and for that reason wish they could use the Holy Supper more frequently—are merely credulous people who attribute more to the Symbols <note>term: Symbols (the bread and wine used in Communion)</note> themselves than is right. I certainly have no doubt that the number of such people is not small. But for that reason, not everyone should be placed in the same category. In all assemblies, there are pious men touched by the love of Jesus Christ. Why we would not wish to grant those Symbols to these people when they ask for them, I do not see any grave reasons. This is all the more valid because the question here is merely about introducing a fourth Communion <note>Increasing the frequency of the sacrament, likely to a quarterly schedule</note>.

Nor should the abuse of the Holy Supper, which some emphasize, prevent truly pious men from more frequently celebrating the death of Jesus Christ through external Symbols. For if this argument were valid, all external worship would have to be cast aside, since it is well known that many Christians are touched by very little concern for Religion. And this is my opinion on the proposed question. I would not, however, wish to dispute with anyone on this account; one may disagree on this question while keeping Christian charity intact.

<margin>
An inquiry into the internal causes that prevent many Christians from rightly using the Holy Supper.
</margin>
**XIX.** We must now investigate how it happens that so very few Christians perceive that fruit from the celebration of the Holy Supper which they ought to perceive, according to the intention of our Savior who instituted this Sacrament. Experience, alas! testifies that many Christians, even after frequent celebration of this Sacrament, do not renounce the vices to which they are addicted, and hypocrites always play the same part.

It is helpful, however, to inquire into the causes of this evil so that, once detected, some salutary medicine may be applied to this ill. These causes can be referred to two classes: some are general, others indeed are special. Among the general causes, we refer *first to this*: namely, that many Christians are so attached to things that strike the senses and to their own passions that they hardly ever meditate on celestial and divine things. Many Christians do not know what it is to meditate, let alone what it is to meditate on things most divine and removed from the senses; or if they are, as it were, compelled by necessity to do this, it is something transitory and forced. You would think them,

if you look at their actions, to have been created for the purpose of living in obedience to their bellies, so much do they think of nothing but earthly things. It is no wonder, then, that such men do not turn their minds to sublime objects of contemplation and to those things which are most excellent in Religion. Thus, when the use of the Holy Supper is discussed, on the occasion of enjoying the bread and the wine, they place the figure of the crucified Christ before their minds as if present; but of the cause, necessity, efficacy, and true use of it, they hardly think. Whence it cannot happen otherwise than that they neglect the thing instituted for the holiest purpose, and thus do not perceive its true use. The blessed and famous *Osterwald* <note>Jean-Frédéric Osterwald (1663–1747), a Swiss Protestant pastor known for his work on ecclesiastical corruption</note> diligently uncovered the source of this evil in chapters VII and VIII of the book cited above. They generally have an estrangement from spiritual duties. They only move toward these kinds of exercises with repugnance, and as rarely as they possibly can. They almost never reflect on what is happening inside them—on their thoughts, on their inclinations, on the movements of their heart, on the principles by which they act, nor on their speech and actions. They do not examine at all whether they have within them the character of a good man, or that of a wicked man, or a hypocrite: In a word, they live, or very nearly so [without reflection]. The negligence of men is therefore extreme in things of Religion. They do not act the same way regarding the things of the world. As much as they are nonchalant and cold in the former, so much are they active and laborious in the latter. They do everything for the body and nothing for the soul. They spare neither care nor labor; they forget nothing whatsoever for their temporal interests. Saint John assures us that the love of God is not in those who love the world. # DISSERTATION ON THE LEGITIMATE
<page-num>1024</page-num>
<header>DISSERTATION ON THE LEGITIMATE</header>
<meta>catchword: gione (religion)</meta>

Worldly affairs make men carnal, sensual, and coarse: they keep them in ignorance and in laziness; they turn their inclinations and their hearts toward the earth. From this, they have nothing but indifference for spiritual objects and for the blessings of heaven. They are little disposed to value these blessings as much as they deserve, or to seek them with the eagerness and sincerity they ought. Can one conceive of people—whose only aim is to amass wealth, to pay court, or to push themselves into employment; who live and work only for that—being very sensitive to the interests of their salvation? That is very difficult. Thus says the *Blessed Ostervald* <note>Jean-Frédéric Ostervald (1663–1747), a Swiss Protestant pastor known for his work on liturgy and Christian ethics.</note>. The second general reason for this abuse is that many Christians are not sufficiently persuaded and convinced of the truth of the Christian religion in general, nor of the primary and most momentous truths of the Gospel of Jesus Christ. In youth, these main points are not instilled solidly or thoroughly enough, and in many books used by the common people, the same argument is not presented in a way everyone can grasp. Many accept what is said about the existence of Jesus Christ, his passion, and his resurrection as if it were merely an ancient tradition; they are ignorant of the most serious arguments upon which the certainty of this and other articles rests—articles which flow from that central truth like so many indubitable consequences. How can such people truly acknowledge and proclaim the love of God toward the human race, the necessity of the death of Jesus Christ, and its efficacy and power in reconciling and sanctifying men to God? How will the use of the Sacrament in the <term>Holy Supper</term> <note>original Latin: "S. Coena"</note> have power over the souls of those men who never rightly turn their minds to the contemplation of that most excellent object—that is, the death of Jesus Christ, our only Savior and Intercessor? I cannot better show the gravity of this error, and the simultaneous origin of both impiety and the very frequent abuse of the Holy Supper, than with the words of the *Celebrated Werenfels* <note>Samuel Werenfels (1657–1740), a Swiss theologian who advocated for a more practical, less dogmatic Christianity.</note>, <note>original Greek: "τὰ νῦν ἐν Ἁγίοις" (now among the saints)</note> who, in the question: *Why the Incentives of Scripture are often Ineffective*, pronounces in the following manner: *Among Christians are counted very many—and would that this were not by far the largest part of Christians!—who believe, or seem to believe, the truth of the religion to which they are committed, not because of any arguments or testimonies (I do not say sufficient ones, but ones which they themselves ever seriously judged suitable for persuading them of a truth of such great moment); who have never been concerned about this, or what foundation they have for their faith; who have never in their lives thought to rightly examine the truth of the facts by which this religion was once confirmed, let alone being convinced by them; who, finally, in the religion itself,*

<column-break/>

<page-num>1025</page-num>
<header>CELEBRATION OF THE HOLY SUPPER.</header>
<sig>Oooooo</sig>
<meta>catchword: gni (greatly)</meta>

*which they have embraced, have never seen or felt anything singular, anything extraordinary, anything divine. Indeed, they do not even know what that testimony of the Church is, for which alone many say they believe; and they know neither the Church which they believe, nor its authority because of which they believe, in any way. Hence it is that these men—since they have never thought about the excellence and divinity of their religion, much less been persuaded of it—do not love their religion, do not value it highly, and indeed often do not estimate it enough to think that even one of their actions should be moderated according to the prescription of this religion. Finally, in their whole life, they follow nothing less than their own religion, but perpetually have other principles of acting before their eyes, and mostly principles opposed to this religion.* So says that most excellent theologian, most truly.

The more specific causes of this evil are chiefly the following: (1.) Many Christians do not sufficiently know the nature and true purpose of the Holy Supper. They believe, along with the Reformed Church, that the flesh of Christ is not eaten physically; for they have learned that the body of Christ is taken in the Holy Supper by the "mouth of the soul," that is, by faith. Yet they interpret this as if the mere persuasion that Christ died for sinners were the very thing that goes by the name of "saving faith." From this it happens that they think an unusual power is joined to the external use of the <term>Symbols</term> <note>The physical bread and wine of the sacrament.</note> themselves, by the benefit of which souls are purged from vices and the remission of sins follows. Hence, they twist what theologians usually say about the "mystical union" of Christ and the faithful to fit their own opinion; they confuse the representation of Christ’s death (used in the external symbols) with the true union with Christ, with which true Christians ought to be adorned and equipped *before* the use of the Holy Supper. In this opinion they are often confirmed because in devotional and liturgical books those two clearly distinct things are mixed together everywhere, using phrases that seem to suggest to readers and listeners that all people indiscriminately who use the external symbols in memory of Christ are already joined with Christ and made participants in the benefits won by Christ’s death. (2.) The examples of others contribute to this. Just as it is generally true that bad examples contribute much to promoting a degenerate Christianity, so specifically this can be said about the abuse of the Holy Supper. Christians see—alas, indiscriminately!—others who are Christians in name only, who have scarcely left the Lord's table before they crave the same vices in which they were previously immersed. From this they conclude that a rite so often commended and celebrated with an appearance of sanctity is not so great...

of great importance; for experience itself shows that no one is made better through the use of the Holy Supper; that everything comes down to some sort of memory of the death of Christ represented through external symbols; and that everything else should be dismissed as the rhetorical flourishes of Preachers. If they ever hear one or two people affirming that they are vehemently inflamed toward piety by the use of the Holy Supper, they doubt the sincerity of this confession, or they categorize such a person among those whose brains have been undermined by black bile. <note>Original: *atra bilis*. In the medical theory of the time, an excess of "black bile" was believed to cause melancholy, irrationality, or even madness.</note> To this (3.) can be added a pestilential but very common opinion among many Christians, by which they think that the external worship of Religion, viewed in itself and celebrated with a certain outward appearance of modesty and piety, is enough to commend men to God. They believe that men are too weak to be able to keep divine precepts; hence, they even turn to their own advantage those things which they hear repeatedly—and often less than circumspectly—regarding moral impotence <term>Moral impotence: The theological concept that human will is so corrupted by sin that it is incapable of performing spiritual good without divine assistance.</term>. They think that God is content with a "good intention" and whatever effort they might make, remaining unconcerned about things pertaining to the internal worship of God. Thus, you may see many people of both sexes who, after spending the best part of their lives in every kind of vice, become more diligent than usual in observing rites and external worship once they have grown older, believing that all past sins are washed away in this manner. Is it any wonder, then, that people who feel so perversely about the nature of Religion celebrate the Holy Supper with so little religious feeling? 

Finally, the fourth cause of this evil, to pass over others, is that few people descend into themselves and perform a serious examination of their own status before the use of the Holy Supper. Thus it happens that after repeating the celebration of the Holy Supper for many years, they do not become better, but are occupied by a very dangerous lethargy. The celebration of the Holy Supper itself moves them very little afterward; yet, had it followed an examination of oneself worthy of a Christian man, it could have been a sufficiently effective means to eventually bring them back to the right path. Even if some do perform an examination of their internal state, it is often done according to an uncertain, or rather, an entirely false standard. For they think that if anyone wishes to be certain of their Salvation in that examination, they must attend to the following: namely, that we must confess in general that we are sinners; that all men are subject to many errors and vices; and that this confession is the sign of a truly pious man touched by a saving repentance. They think, moreover, that they must read booklets that show the way to a worthy use of the Holy Supper; that one or two sermons must be read at home; that they must frequently devote themselves to sacred worship at that time; and they must believe that to those receiving the sacred Symbols, sins are as certainly remitted—

XX. I could stop here and bring an end to the dissertation, because everything has been brought forward that could serve to achieve the goal I intended. But because on the occasion of those things which I noted in the prior part of this dissertation regarding the **seal** <term>Seal (*sigillum*): A theological term referring to the sacraments as a physical "stamp" or guarantee confirming God's promises to the believer.</term>, I know not what suspicions have arisen against me, I must add certain things here for the sake of explanation, for the benefit of men who love the truth (for I study to satisfy and be approved by these alone, not by those "know-it-alls" who seek what is nowhere to be found, yet find it anyway). My goal, in this as in the prior part of this dissertation, was to provide certain healthy warnings to the Ministers of the Word <note>Original: *V. D. Ministris* (Verbi Divini Ministris), a common title for Protestant clergy.</note>, especially the younger ones, for rightly explaining the nature of the Holy Supper and for uprooting certain very common prejudices that cling to the minds of Christians. To that end, the causes had to be uncovered which prevent many Christians from carrying away that fruit from the use of the Holy Supper which they could otherwise receive. 

I distinguished those causes into external and internal ones. Of the external causes, the first was that certain sacred Orators [Preachers] speaking on this subject, and Authors of booklets dealing with the use of the Holy Supper, sometimes use a style of speaking that is too flowery and wrapped in various metaphors. By this, many—especially the simpler folk—do not understand the true nature and character of the saving use of the Holy Supper, but rather think that some kind of unusual physical force is implanted in the external use of these Symbols, and that the remission of sins and the right to eternal life are necessarily joined with the enjoyment of the bread and wine. No one should doubt that this error is very dangerous. Among the second external causes, I included the fact that many Christians, when they hear that the **seal** of the covenant of grace is offered in the Holy Supper, understand this proposition wrongly; they think that to all who use the sacred Symbols indiscriminately, and who in any way at all recall the death of Jesus Christ represented through those Symbols, the benefits won by the death of Christ are most certainly attributed. Hence, I thought I should open my mind on this subject in the clearest words, so that young Ministers of the Word may learn to speak circumspectly and clearly on this argument. As a weight in the balance—

(for the nature of the Holy Supper, its end and purpose, must be learned from Christ and the Apostles) I have shown that my explanation is in complete agreement with our Blessed Ancestors *Zwingli, Oecolampadius, and Bullinger*. Indeed, the illustrious Heidegger himself touches upon this error in Section XIX of his 25th chapter, speaking thus: *Neither can the opinion of those very learned men please us (the men I am referring to from my previous dissertation are sufficiently clear), who, by comparing baptism and the remaining Sacraments with the signs of miracles, assert that God ordinarily confers grace at the same time He represents it through the signs; for this both over-exalts the efficacy of the Sacraments, diminishes the consolation of the godly, increases the religion of the elements, and adds not a little to Roman Catholic superstition.* <note>Heidegger is warning against "sacramentalism"—the idea that the ritual itself "forces" God to give grace, which he associates with Catholic theology.</note> On the occasion of this explanation of mine regarding the "seal," a great history arose out of nothing. Out of nothing, I say, because I have never in my life doubted the opinion of the Reformers concerning this argument; rather, I have grieved, and still grieve, that a matter so easy to grasp and simple is wrapped by some in so many "meteors of speech" and rhetorical flourishes that many Christians wrongly understand the nature of the Holy Supper. Furthermore, I am most persuaded that those who have carped at my explanation could not speak otherwise than I have done, if they intended to explain the sense of the Reformers regarding the character of the Holy Supper in clear words. If, therefore, I have committed any error, it consists in this: that I have surely discussed this argument more clearly than is commonly done. To shed some light on this argument (if indeed I am one who can clearly express the feelings of his mind), I will add certain things here for the sake of those who are able to weigh controversies impartially <note>original: $\alpha\nu\epsilon\upsilon$ $\pi\alpha\theta\omega\nu$ (*aneu pathōn*), meaning "without passions."</note>. Only the Regenerate <term>Regenerate: Those who have been "born again" or spiritually renewed by the Holy Spirit.</term> are sharers in the benefits won through the death of Christ. II. The Regenerate, through the internal testimony of the Holy Spirit—as if fortified by a certain seal of divine grace—are made certain of their union with Christ before the use of the Holy Supper. (*) III. None but the regenerate use the Holy Supper worthily and rightly acknowledge Je-

Therefore, just as the nourishment of bread and wine, once passed into the vitals, is changed into the substance of the human body: so Christ, "drunk in" by faith by the Saints, is united to them by His Spirit, so that they are one with Christ, and He is one with them. > *gnificently preached to you, but you do not believe that Christ is yours, it profits nothing, no matter how beautifully the Speech or the table is prepared. Sacraments excite and help the faith of the Saints. For while the mind comprehends and revolves the benefits of Christ—blessing, redemption, and gifts—while the Spirit enjoys these with great pleasure, and while it exults in them, there now also approach (Note Well!) from the outside the Sacraments. These represent visibly to the eyes, and thus to all the senses, those things which the mind internally comprehends, debates, and revolves. The spiritual mode is perfected by faith, by which, being connected to Christ, we share in all his goods. The sacramental mode is perfected only in the celebration of the Holy Supper. For the godly, spiritual eating is perpetual, because their faith is perpetual. Outside the Supper and in the Supper they communicate with Christ, and in this [the Supper] they certainly more greatly repair and continue what was begun long ago: as we said before, and now indeed with the sacred action added, all things are done much more celebratedly and evidently. But unbelievers and hypocrites never communicate with Christ himself, neither before the supper, nor in the supper, nor after the supper, insofar as they persevere in their Unbelief; however, they participate in the Lord’s Sacraments to their own judgment and condemnation.* *Peter Martyr* speaks similarly in his *Defense of the Eucharist* written against *Gardiner*, page 231: *That the flesh is vital food (he says) is agreed between us. But we affirm that it is perceived by the mind and by faith. We see that believers in regeneration, when they are grafted into Christ through faith, become partakers of this food. We assert that this communion is sealed by Symbols in the Lord’s supper and is effectively signified and testified; and because faith is excited there, it has its increase and its fruits.* And a little below: *Although we eat of this spiritual nourishment perpetually while we believe, nevertheless in the sacred supper, because it is proposed to us to be eaten not only in words but also in external Symbols—that is, to be believed—we confess it is eaten and drunk there: and because we know our union with Christ is increased in this way, we therefore preach that that sacred Mystery is to be frequented.*

Using quotes from Reformers like Bullinger and Peter Martyr, the author explains that the sacrament's visual and physical elements are designed to strengthen the internal faith of those who are already "born again."</summary>

"DISSERTATIO DE LEGITIMA / S. COENAE CELEBRATIONE" (Dissertation on the Legitimate Celebration of the Holy Supper).
Latin.
Theology (specifically concerning the Sacrament of the Lord's Supper/Eucharist and the "seal of the covenant of grace").
Accessible English, warm museum-label style, preserving markdown and XML-like tags (<note>, <margin>, <gloss>, etc.). Translate *everything* including Latin quotes within the text.

    *   *Page 1030:*
        *   Continues from "Thesis IX" of a previous dissertation.
        *   Refutes an argument that says: "If you say the Holy Supper is only a seal in a certain sense/for certain people, you deny it's a seal at all."
        *   Analogy: Saying a man is rational in a certain respect isn't the same as denying he has reason.
        *   Thought experiment: What if Christ *hadn't* instituted the Supper?
            *   I. Christ's death is the only merit for salvation.
            *   II. Benefits are communicated through this death.
            *   III. These benefits include the Holy Spirit, Justification, etc.
            *   IV. There must be signs/marks to know these benefits apply to us.
            *   V. We know these by looking at the effects in our minds.
            *   VI. Thus, we know we share in Christ's death.
            *   VII. These internal gifts (Holy Spirit) are the *true* seal.
            *   VIII. Syllogism: Whoever has repentance/faith/virtue is a partaker. I have these. Therefore, I am a partaker.
        *   Conclusion: The external Supper is not a *new* seal but a sensory representation of the internal seal already present.

    *   *Page 1031:*
        *   Why use symbols then? Because they vividly represent Christ to the senses and because Christ commanded it.
        *   Reference to Thesis IX again.
        *   Reference to the "Helvetic Churches" (Swiss Reformers) and their confession sent to Luther in 1536.
        *   Long block quote from the 1536 Helvetic Confession/Declaration:
            *   Justification by mercy/faith alone.
            *   Sacraments announce/set before eyes the salvation Christ won.
            *   Refutation of the charge that they make sacraments "nothing."
            *   Avoid both extremes: making sacraments idols (signs as the thing itself) vs. making them useless.
            *   Example of Cornelius (Acts 10): Had the Spirit, but still needed baptism.
            *   Sacraments are like the Sun/Moon/Stars—instruments God uses, but not the *cause* of the benefit.
