# DISSERTATION ON THE LEGITIMATE
<page-num>1030</page-num>
<header>DISSERTATION ON THE LEGITIMATE</header>
<meta>catchword: que (and)</meta>

...in that which I explained in Thesis IX of my previous dissertation. Therefore, this "terrible" <note>original: "τὰ Δεινὰ" (ta deina), a Greek expression for something formidable or shockingly bad</note> reasoning is most absurd. Anyone who asserts that the Holy Supper can be called a seal of the covenant of grace only in a certain sense and with respect to certain people, prorsus <gloss>utterly</gloss> denies that the Supper can be called a seal of the covenant of grace at all. This argumentation is no less tasteless and childish than if someone were to argue like this: "Anyone who asserts that a man can be called rational only in a certain respect denies altogether that man is endowed with reason."

To make this argument clearer, let us imagine for a moment that Christ had not instituted the Sacrament of the Holy Supper, and let us consider in what sense the godly could then be said to be fortified by the seal of the covenant of grace. Everything can be reduced to the following propositions:

I. The death of Christ our Savior is the sole meritorious cause of our salvation.
II. By virtue of this death, certain benefits are communicated to the godly.
III. Among those benefits must be counted the bestowing of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, namely **Justification**, **regeneration**, etc.
IV. There must be certain marks from which godly Christians can know that the benefits won by the death of Christ belong to them personally.
V. By reasoning *a posteriore* <term>from the effect to the cause</term>—that is, from the effects implanted in the mind—the godly can know whether they detect within themselves the marks of the gifts received from the Holy Spirit.
VI. Therefore, they can also know that they have been made partakers of the benefits won by the death of Christ.
VII. These gifts, inserted and implanted in the souls of the godly through the Holy Spirit, are that **seal** from which the godly can certainly conclude that they are truly united with Christ.
VIII. From this emerges that **Syllogism** <term>a logical argument consisting of three parts</term>: *Whoever is touched by serious repentance through the grace of the Holy Spirit, is gifted with saving faith, and is intent on the pursuit of virtue, has been made a partaker of the benefits won by Christ’s death and can be certain of attaining salvation. But I [am such a person]. Therefore, I [am a partaker].*

From these points, it is manifest that the faithful would have a certain seal of grace even if the Sacrament of the Holy Supper had not been instituted. Now, since it pleased Christ that His death be represented and celebrated with praises through certain symbols, we must see what is added here. The object of contemplation in the Holy Supper is Jesus Christ, and Him crucified. From the death of Jesus Christ, certain benefits overflow to the truly godly; they are already well aware and mindful of having received these before the use of the Holy Supper. Therefore, while they contemplate Jesus Christ represented through external symbols and celebrate Him with a godly mind, a *new* seal is not added—for it had already been implanted in their souls before the use of the Supper—but certain external things are added, namely the bread and wine, vividly representing to the senses Jesus, who was once [and for all] grasped by true faith. Nor—

---

<page-num>1031</page-num>
<header>CELEBRATION OF THE HOLY SUPPER;</header>
<meta>catchword: tin- (continuing "contin-")</meta>

—should those symbols be called useless for that reason, both because they vividly present a most precious thing to the senses as if it were present, and move the soul more vehemently than without the use of symbols; and also because the godly know that Jesus Christ instituted this Sacrament and willed His death to be celebrated in this way until His coming. From which, unless everything deceives me, it is manifest that the Holy Supper can be called a **Seal** in no other sense than that which I suggested in Thesis IX of my previous dissertation on this subject. (*)

But certain good men cry out against this in our Catechetical Institutions—

---

(*) The ministers of the **Helvetic Churches** <note>The Reformed churches of Switzerland, following the tradition of Zwingli and Bullinger.</note> spoke exactly according to my mind on this subject in the fuller declaration of their confession sent to Dr. Martin Luther in the year 1536. For they speak thus:

> *We believe, affirm, and confess that the human race is justified by the mercy of God alone through faith grasped in Christ; and that God announces and, as it were, places before our eyes that salvation and happiness which Christ (without any of our works or merits) acquired and bestowed upon us, through the external preaching of the Gospel and the administration of the sacred signs or Sacraments.*
>
> *However, we fall here into the suspicion as if we either attribute nothing to the preaching of the external Word and the Sacraments, or take away from them those things which the Lord attributed to them, and thus pervert and abolish the entire ministry of the Church. When, on the contrary, we continually apply ourselves with all effort and diligence to this end: that neither too LITTLE nor too MUCH be established in these matters. For we have learned both from Holy Scripture and from the Christian Doctor Augustine, that it is a miserable slavery of the soul, and like a prison, to take the **Signs** for the **things** they signify. Just as, on the other hand, it is no slight error to think that God instituted His Sacraments in vain, and that they bring no utility to the Church. Therefore, we also always seriously teach that those signs and external things ought not to be despised as if they were either unnecessary or useless because of the internal gifts. For we know that Cornelius the Centurion <note>A Roman officer whose conversion is recorded in Acts 10; he received the Holy Spirit before being baptized.</note>, although he had been internally instructed and illuminated by God, nevertheless had need to be both instructed and baptized by the Apostle Peter. Lest we turn to the right or to the left, but persist here in the royal and straight way—that is, lest we either derogate anything from the external Word and signs which Scripture attributes to them; or, conversely, attribute to those creatures what belongs to the Creator alone, or direct or bind men to them beyond measure. Thus we have always taught until now, and hope to teach concerning these matters in the future, so that both God's ordinance may retain its dignity and value, and men may be led rightly by us through these external aids instituted by God Himself to the Creator, and thus all Glory may be attributed to God alone.*
>
> *And a little lower: Just as nothing is taken away from the Ministry of the Word of God, and it is diminished in no respect, even if we say that the external preaching of the Word is of no moment or utility if God does not give the increase in the heart; as Paul says: "He who plants and he who waters does not sanctify, but God Himself." That is, he does not despise or bring dishonor to the Sacraments who attributes the power and saving operation to the Creator alone. For Peter also said here: "Baptism indeed saves us, yet not that by which the filth of the flesh is washed away, but the testimony of a good conscience before God." For just as in the rest of the Creatures, such as the Sun, Moon, Stars, Fire, precious stones, herbs, and things of that sort, through which God works toward us as if through certain instruments, we place no consolation, nor do we establish in them the true and original cause of the benefits which through them [reach] us...*

<summary>This page argues that the Holy Supper functions as a sensory "seal" to reinforce the internal grace already given by the Holy Spirit, citing the 1536 Helvetic Confession to prove this view is historically Reformed. It emphasizes that while sacraments are vital tools commanded by Christ, the power to save belongs to God alone, not the physical elements.</summary>

# DISSERTATION ON THE LEGITIMATE
<meta>catchword: are</meta>

...sacraments are called signs and seals of the covenant of grace. This is true; who denies it? The only question is in what sense and with respect to which people each title applies. Sacraments are **signs** representing the bloody death of Jesus Christ to all who participate in the Holy Supper, whether they are pious, impious, or hypocrites. However, no one who truly understands the Reformed Religion will claim that these are **seals** of the covenant of grace—meaning that everyone can certainly conclude from the external use of the Holy Supper that they have been made partakers of the benefits acquired by Christ’s death. For no one can boast of such a great benefit except the one who, by the help of the Holy Spirit, is adorned with saving faith, sincere repentance, and a zeal for piety. But not all Christians using the Holy Supper are like this. Therefore, not all possess that seal. Only from these inner characteristics do the pious seek proof of their communion with Christ. Our Blessed *Zwingli* felt the same in his *Exposition of the Christian Faith*, page 15: *The Lord’s Supper (he says) creates faith, that is, it certainly signifies that Christ was born and suffered. But to whom does it signify this? To the faithful and the unfaithful alike. For it signifies to all, as far as the power of the Sacrament is concerned, that Christ suffered, whether they receive it or not.* But—take note—*that he suffered **for us**, that it signifies only to the pious and the faithful. For no one knows or believes that Christ suffered for us unless the Spirit has taught them inwardly to recognize the mystery of divine goodness.* <note>original: "pro nobis esse passum... nisi quem Spiritus intus docuerit"</note> For such a person alone receives Christ. Therefore, the Spirit alone gives confidence in God. From this it is also clear how foolish and foreign to <term>Philadelphia</term> <note>From the Greek meaning "brotherly love."</note> were the suspicions conceived about me, and how poorly those acted who, moved by the outcries of certain men, scattered various rumors here and there, and—without sufficiently investigating the cause—still try to criticize an innocent man.

> Thus, we should not place any part of our confidence in external signs, even though they are sacred things ordained by God which He uses toward us; nor should God's glory be attributed to them when considered in themselves. Instead, our faith is to be raised through them from earthly things to heavenly ones—that is, to God the Creator, the fountain and origin of all things (and therefore of the Sacraments as well).
> 
> And shortly after: Just as previously we did not take offense, but always easily granted that such expressions be used regarding the Ministry of the Word, where it is said: "Men as ministers convert people to God," "remit their sins," "open their hearts," and things of that kind. So also we easily allow others to speak thus (PROVIDED IT IS IN THE TRUE SENSE): namely, that "ministers regenerate and wash away sins in Baptism," and even "OFFER the Body and Blood of the Lord in the Supper." For this is how Ananias addressed Paul: "Rise and be baptized and wash away your sins." The same is read of the Supper: That the Lord took bread, blessed it, and said: "Take, eat; this is my body," etc. Such expressions were also used by the ancients to more illustriously set forth the gifts of God and His benefits.

are attempted. (*) But I will add no more, since my most celebrated and dear colleague J. J. Breitinger, the most worthy Professor of the Greek Language, has pleaded my cause so cordially, learnedly, and clearly in the *Museum Tigurinum* <note>The "Zurich Museum," a scholarly journal or collection of essays from Zurich.</note>. He proved it by the consensus of our Blessed Ancestors, to whom this sort of men always appeals, so that it seems nothing more can be added for further clarification. For we do not dwell on the trivialities and malicious litigations of men who, due to weakness of mind and a lack of refined judgment, are not accustomed to weighing the true value of things. But as for the one kind of vengeance that remains for a Christian man, we commend them to God in our prayers, and earnestly pray that He might deign to inspire them with a sound mind. (**)

### XXI.

> (*) I wish that those who criticized my explanation of the nature of the Holy Supper—which was expressed in clearer words than is traditionally customary—had followed the example of two most excellent theologians, namely Bucer and Peter Martyr. Between them, although they used different words and phrases in the article regarding the Holy Supper, there was a supreme union of souls. *Josias Simler*, a most learned man, tells the story in the *Life of Peter Martyr*: *Although (he says) Martyr wrote many things about the Lord’s Supper, in the explanation of which many learned men use a certain affected obscurity, nothing but what is proper, simple, and lucid is read in his writings. Indeed, when Bucer, whom he cherished and admired, often urged him to use certain obscure and ambiguous formulas of speech in the matter of the Lord’s Supper—which Bucer himself used because, as a good man, he had persuaded himself that the grave controversy over this matter could be removed in this way and the long-desired peace of the Church restored—Martyr finally obeyed him and used the same forms of speech. But soon, having noticed the danger of this, he changed his mind. For he saw that in this way, those who insist on a gross and carnal presence of Christ's body in the Supper could not be satisfied unless their own gross expressions were also received with a full and gross interpretation. Furthermore, he experienced that weaker brothers were partly deeply offended by this ambiguity of speech, and partly so entangled and disturbed that they hardly knew what they should think in this cause. Therefore, while conceding to Bucer his own expressions, Martyr himself followed the same clarity in this dogma as he did in other things; nevertheless, a firm and constant friendship remained between them.* For Bucer did not disapprove of Martyr's opinion, nor was Martyr ignorant of Bucer's meaning, however much he used ambiguous expressions. Thus, although their manner of speaking in this cause was different, there was a supreme consensus between them in all doctrine of religion and a perpetual union of life and friendship. If I wished to explain this and recount all their services by which they declared their mutual love, words would fail me sooner than the facts themselves. Thus far the famous Simler. The most noble Jan à Lasco used the same modesty, as is clear from various letters published by the most famous and dear Gerdes, a theologian of Groningen.

> (**) Men outstanding in talent and erudition have judged these two dissertations (written on the legitimate end and use of the Holy Supper) very differently than those obscure "theologasters" <note>A mocking term for a petty or insignificant theologian.</note> we are touching upon. Let the words of the most excellent man, A. F. W. Sack, serve as a representative of all; he is a most successful champion of pure and chaste religion in Part VIII of his *Defense of the Christian Religion*, written in the German language.

# DISSERTATION ON THE LEGITIMATE
<page-num>1034</page-num>
## CELEBRATION OF THE HOLY SUPPER.

XXI. In place of a conclusion <note>original: "Coronidis loco," a Greek-derived term meaning a finishing touch or capping stone</note>, it is helpful to bring forward from the *Sacramental History* of Hospinian <note>Rudolf Hospinian (1547–1626) was a Swiss Reformed theologian and historian</note> the agreement entered into between the Ministers of the Church of Zurich and Calvin in the year 1549. From this, it will be established that our Blessed Ancestors spoke of this argument no differently than I have done. Before Hospinian reviews the chapters of the agreement itself, he explains the reason for this meeting in the following words: *The matter stands thus: Many good men were offended for a slight reason because Calvin seemed to teach something different regarding the Sacraments than the Ministers of the Church of Zurich. They rightly revered the Zurich Church, which was adorned with many excellent gifts; they also deferred much to the Genevan Churches and to Calvin privately. Therefore, just as they desired to be helped by the writings of the Zurichers and Genevans in learning the doctrine of piety, so that no appearance of dissension might delay their progress, they judged it useful to enter into a method of testifying to their agreement in the matter of the Sacraments through a familiar conversation. Thus Calvin, having joined to himself as a companion Farel, the Pastor of the Church of Neuchâtel, set out from Geneva to Zurich this year, and conferred with the Ministers of that Church concerning the matter of the Lord’s Supper, and an agreement was easily reached between them, as both sides were lovers and students of the truth.* The chapters of the agreement now follow:

1. Since Christ is the end of the Law, and the knowledge of him comprehends within itself the whole sum of the Gospel, there is no doubt that the entire spiritual government of the Church looks to this point: to lead us to Christ. For it is through him alone that one arrives at God, who is the ultimate end of a blessed life. Therefore, whoever deflects from this even the slightest bit will never speak rightly or appropriately about any of God's institutions.

2. Moreover, since the Sacraments are appendages of the Gospel, only he who begins from Christ can discuss their nature, power, office, and fruit fittingly and usefully. And he should do so not merely to touch upon the Name of Christ in passing, but to truly hold why he was given to us by the Father and what benefits he has brought to us.

3. Thus it must be held that Christ, since he was the eternal Son of God, of the same essence and glory as the Father, put on our flesh so that by the right of adoption, he might communicate to us that which he held as his own by nature—namely, that we might be children of God. This happens when, having been grafted into the Body of Christ by faith, and that by the Power of the Holy Spirit, we are first counted as righteous by the free imputation of righteousness, and then regenerated into a new life. By this, being reformed into the image of the heavenly Father, we renounce the "old man."

<meta>catchword: 4. Thus</meta>

---

<page-num>1035</page-num>
## CELEBRATION OF THE HOLY SUPPER.

4. Thus, Christ in his flesh is to be considered by us as the priest who atoned for our sins by the single sacrifice of his death, who deleted all our iniquities by his obedience, who prepared perfect righteousness for us, and who now intercedes for us so that access to God may lie open to us. He is to be considered as the expiatory Victim by which God was reconciled to the world. He is to be considered a brother, who from the miserable children of Adam has made us the blessed children of God. He is to be considered the restorer, who by the power of his spirit reforms whatever is faulty in us, so that we may cease to live for the world and the flesh, and God himself may live in us. He is to be considered the King, who enriches us with every kind of good, who governs and protects us by his power, who equips us with spiritual arms so that we may stand unconquered against the devil and the world, who frees us from every harm, and who moderates and rules us by the scepter of his mouth. And he is to be so considered that he may lift us up to the true God and to the Father, until that which is eventually to be shall be fulfilled: namely, that God may be all in all.

5. Furthermore, so that Christ may exhibit himself as such to us and produce effects of this kind in us, it is necessary that we be made one with him and coalesce into his body. For he does not otherwise diffuse his life into us unless he is our head, from whom the whole Body, joined and connected through every bond of nourishment according to the operation in the measure of each member, makes the growth of the body. <note>This is a paraphrase of Ephesians 4:16.</note>

6. This is the spiritual communication which we have with the Son of God, when, dwelling in us by his spirit, he makes all believers partakers of all the goods that reside in him. For the sake of testifying to this, both the preaching of the Gospel was instituted and the use of the Sacraments was commended to us—namely, Holy Baptism and the Holy Supper.

7. To be sure, these are also the ends of the Sacraments: that they may be marks and tokens of Christian profession and society, or brotherhood; that they may be incentives to the giving of thanks, and exercises of faith and a pious life; and finally, written bonds <term>syngraphæ; a legal term for a signed contract or promissory note</term> obliging us to that. But this one purpose is chief among the others: that through them God may testify, represent, and seal his grace to us. For although *they signify nothing other than what is announced by the word itself, yet this is a great thing: that living images are subjected to our eyes which affect our senses better, as if by leading us into the matter itself, while they recall to our memory the death of Christ and all his benefits, so that faith may be more exercised; and furthermore, that which had been pronounced by the mouth of God is confirmed and sanctioned as if by seals.*

<meta>catchword: Since</meta>

The text emphasizes that sacraments serve as "living images" and "seals" that confirm the promises of the Gospel to believers by uniting them to Christ.</summary>

# DISSERTATION ON THE LEGITIMATE
<page-num>1036</page-num>
<header>DISSERTATION ON THE LEGITIMATE</header>

8. Since the things the Lord gave us are true testimonies and seals <term>seals: (Latin: *sigilla*) visible guarantees or stamps of authenticity regarding God's promises</term> of his grace, he himself undoubtedly fulfills internally through his Spirit what the Sacraments represent to our eyes and other senses. This is done so that we may possess Christ as the fountain of all good things—both so that we may be reconciled to God by the benefit of his death, be renewed in holiness of life by his Spirit, and finally obtain righteousness and salvation. At the same time, we should now give thanks for these benefits once displayed on the cross, which we have truly perceived by faith, and which we continue to perceive daily.

9. Therefore, although we distinguish (as is proper) between the signs and the things signified, we do not separate the truth from the signs. Rather, we acknowledge that all who embrace the promises offered there by faith receive Christ spiritually along with his spiritual gifts, and thus those who were already made partakers of Christ continue and renew that communion.

10. For it is not proper to look at the naked signs, but rather at the promise attached to them. Therefore, to the extent that our faith profits from the promise offered there, that power and efficacy of which we speak exerts itself. Thus, the material of the water, bread, or wine by no means brings Christ to us, nor does it make us partakers of his spiritual gifts; rather, the promise must be more closely regarded, whose role it is to lead us to Christ by the right path of faith—by which faith makes us partakers of Christ.

11. From this falls the error of those *who stand amazed at the elements* <note>original: "qui in elementis obstupescunt"; a critique of those who fixate on the physical bread and wine rather than the spiritual reality</note> and attach the confidence of their salvation to them. Since the Sacraments, when separated from Christ, are nothing but empty masks <note>original: "inanes larvæ"</note>, this voice clearly rings out in all of them: that we must cling to no one but Christ alone, nor seek the grace of salvation from any other source.

12. Furthermore, if any good is conferred upon us through the Sacraments, it is not by their own inherent power, even if you include the promise by which they are distinguished. For it is God alone who acts by his Spirit. In using the ministry of the Sacraments, he neither infuses his own power into them, nor does he detract anything from the efficacy of his Spirit. But according to the capacity of our dullness <note>original: "ruditatis nostræ"; implying human weakness in understanding spiritual things</note>, he employs them as aids <note>original: "adminicula"</note> in such a way that the entire ability to act remains with him alone.

13. Therefore, just as Paul warns that he who plants or waters is nothing, but only God who gives the growth, so it must be said of the Sacraments: they are nothing, because they will profit nothing unless God effects everything in its entirety. They are indeed instruments <note>original: "organa"</note> by which God acts effectively wherever it seems good to him, but in such a way that the whole work of our salvation must be credited to him alone.

<meta>catchword: 14. Con-</meta>

---

<page-num>1037</page-num>
<header>CELEBRATION OF THE HOLY SUPPER.</header>

14. We therefore establish that it is the one Christ who truly baptizes within, who makes us partakers of himself in the Supper, and who finally fulfills what the Sacraments represent. He uses these aids in such a way that the entire effect remains within his Spirit.

15. Thus, the Sacraments are sometimes called "seals," and are said to *nourish, confirm, and promote* faith; and yet the Spirit alone is properly the *Seal*, and he is the author and perfecter of faith. For all these attributes of the Sacraments occupy a lower place, so that not even the smallest portion of our salvation is transferred from the unique Author to creatures or physical elements.

16. Furthermore, we diligently teach that God does not exercise his power indiscriminately in all who receive the Sacraments, but only in the elect. For just as he illuminates no others into faith than those he has preordained to life, so by the secret power of his Spirit, he causes the elect to perceive what the Sacraments offer.

17. By this doctrine, that fiction of the Sophists <note>The "Sophists" refers to Scholastic theologians of the Middle Ages whom the Reformers accused of using circular or deceptive logic</note> is overturned, which teaches that the Sacraments of the New Law confer grace to all who "do not place an obstacle of mortal sin" <note>original: "non ponentibus obicem peccati mortalis"; this refers to the Catholic doctrine of *ex opere operato*, where the sacrament is believed to work automatically unless a major sin blocks it</note>. For besides the fact that nothing is perceived in the Sacraments except by faith, it must also be held that the grace of God is by no means tied to them, such that whoever has the sign also possesses the reality. For the signs are administered to the reprobate just as much as to the elect, but the truth of the signs reaches only the latter.

18. It is certainly true that Christ with his gifts is offered commonly to all, and the truth of God is not undermined by human infidelity, for the Sacraments always retain their power. But not everyone is capable of receiving Christ and his gifts. Therefore, on God's part nothing changes; but as far as men are concerned, each receives according to the measure of his faith.

19. Moreover, just as the use of the Sacraments confers nothing more upon unbelievers than if they had abstained—indeed, it is only destructive to them—so the truth represented there is established for believers even outside the use of the sacraments. Thus Paul's sins were washed away by Baptism, though they had already been washed away previously. Thus the same Baptism was a washing of regeneration for Cornelius, who nevertheless had already been gifted with the Holy Spirit. Thus in the Supper, Christ communicates himself to us, though he had already imparted himself to us and remains in us perpetually. For since individuals are commanded to examine themselves, it follows that faith is required of them before they approach the Sacrament. And faith is not without Christ. But insofar as faith is confirmed by the Sacraments, it acknowledges

<summary>This section explains that Sacraments are instruments through which God's Spirit works, but they hold no power of their own and do not automatically confer grace. It emphasizes that while the physical signs are offered to everyone, only the elect receive the spiritual reality through faith.</summary>
<keywords>sacraments, signs and things signified, seals, grace, faith, the elect, instruments of God, John Calvin, Reformed theology, baptism, Lord's Supper</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "Consensus of Zurich" (1549), specifically focusing on the spiritual nature of the sacraments and the rejection of a physical or "local" presence of Christ in the bread and wine. It argues for a figurative interpretation of the words of institution and concludes with a call for intellectual humility among theologians.</meta>

# DISSERTATION ON THE LEGITIMATE 
<page-num>1038</page-num>
<header>DISSERTATION ON THE LEGITIMATE [CELEBRATION]</header>

God's gifts are confirmed in us, and so Christ increases in us in some way, and we in him.

20. Furthermore, the utility we perceive from the Sacraments should by no means be restricted to the time when they are administered to us, as if the visible *Sign* brought God's grace with it at the very same moment it is brought forward. For those who were baptized in their earliest infancy are sometimes regenerated by God in childhood, or at the start of adolescence, and occasionally even in old age. Thus, the utility of Baptism is open to the entire course of life, because the promise contained therein remains perpetually in force. And it can sometimes happen that the use of the Sacred Supper—which, in the act itself, profits little due to our thoughtlessness or slowness—may produce its fruit later on.

21. Especially, however, any imagination of a local presence must be removed. For since the Signs are here in the world, seen with eyes and felt with hands, Christ—insofar as he is a man—is to be sought nowhere else than in heaven, and in no other way than with the mind and the understanding of faith. Therefore, it is a perverse and impious superstition to enclose him under the elements of this world.

22. Hence, those who in the solemn words of the Supper—"This is my Body, This is my Blood" <note>original: "Hoc est Corpus meum, Hic est Sanguis meus"</note>—insist precisely on the "literal" sense (as they call it), we reject as backwards interpreters. For we place it beyond controversy that these words must be taken figuratively: so that the bread and wine are said to *be* that which they signify. Nor indeed should it seem new or unusual that the name of the thing signified is transferred to the sign through Metonymy <term>metonymy: A figure of speech where a thing is called by the name of something associated with it, such as calling the sign (bread) by the name of the reality (body)</term>, since such expressions occur everywhere in the scriptures. By speaking this way, we bring forward nothing that does not exist among all the most ancient and most approved Writers of the Church.

23. Moreover, as for the fact that Christ feeds our souls through faith by the power of his Spirit with the eating of his flesh and the drinking of his blood (which are figured here), this is not to be understood as if any "Mixing" or "transfusion" of substance occurred; but rather that we draw life from the flesh once offered as a sacrifice and the blood poured out for atonement.

24. In this way, not only is the Papists' fiction of Transubstantiation <term>transubstantiation: The Roman Catholic doctrine that the bread and wine literally change their physical substance into the body and blood of Christ</term> refuted, but also all those gross inventions and futile subtleties which either detract from his heavenly glory or are inconsistent with the reality of his human nature. For we judge it no less absurd to place Christ under the bread, or to couple him with the bread, than to "transubstantiate" the bread into his body.

<meta>catchword: 25. And</meta>

---

<page-num>1039</page-num>
<header>ON THE CELEBRATION OF THE HOLY SUPPER.</header>

25. And so that no ambiguity remains, when we say that Christ is to be sought in Heaven, this expression sounds out and expresses a distance of places to us. For although, speaking philosophically, there is no "place" above the Heavens, because the body of Christ is finite (as the nature and manner of a human Body requires) and is contained in heaven as a place, it must necessarily be distant from us by as great an interval of space as heaven is distant from the earth.

26. But if it is not lawful to fix Christ to the bread and wine in our imagination, it is much less permitted to adore <note>original: "adorare", meaning to worship or bow down before</note> him in the bread. For although the bread is reached out to us as a Symbol and pledge of that communion which we have with Christ, yet because it is a sign and not the thing itself, nor does it have the thing enclosed or fixed within itself, those who turn their minds toward it to worship Christ make an idol out of it.

After Hospinian <note>Rodolph Hospinian (1547–1626), a Swiss Reformed theologian and historian</note> had explained these chapters of the confession, he added this at the end:
> This Consensus was not only approved by the rest of the Churches of *Switzerland & Rhaetia*, but it also greatly pleased many learned and moderate men, who were confirmed in their recognition of the truth by this writing. They also offered their effort to add a declaration if anyone happened not to be satisfied. They even promised that they would be teachable and obedient to better advice, if anyone found something lacking in them. When Bucer <note>Martin Bucer (1491–1551), a key Protestant Reformer based in Strasbourg and later England</note> had read it, in letters written from England to Calvin, he congratulated the whole Church. This Consensus, however, irritated the adversaries more, so that they attacked the Calvinists more bitterly in their writings.

### In place of a conclusion, we add the judgment of a distinguished Theologian pertaining to this matter.

This also pertains to the Candor <term>candor: An attitude of openness, honesty, and fairness in scholarly or theological debate</term> which we require from a Disputant: that we frankly admit our own slips and those of our teachers, nor should we think that whatever has slipped from us or them must always be defended most stubbornly. For even if our cause is good, its patrons could nonetheless be deceived. A very bad cause is often defended better than the best one. Certainly, he who cannot recognize his own blemishes or those of his people makes his candor suspect in other and graver matters as well. He who thinks that all the sayings of *Luther, Zwingli, Oecolampadius, Calvin*, and other great men must be fought for and defended, both forgets that they were men and cares more for authority...

precepts of Eloquence demanded that this be done. Whether this custom agrees with the rules of the Rhetoricians or not is not for us, but for the Masters of the art of speaking to decide. As for me, listeners, setting aside wordy detours, I will say in a few words why I am here and what I am about to bring forward. You all know that I ascend this pulpit by the authority and command of our Reverend Bishop <note>original: "Venerabilis Antistitis"</note>, and not by the impulse of my own will. I am here to discuss a weighty argument, in whatever way I can, before this assembly of most distinguished men, according to the custom of our Ancestors in memory of *Charlemagne* <note>original: "Caroli M." Charlemagne (r. 768–814) was traditionally credited with founding many European schools and religious institutions, providing them with "enviable revenues."</note>, who is said to have created these "busy leisure-times" for us and to have provided enviable revenues and the outward forms of some sort of dignity. Therefore, whether willing or unwilling, I must speak to you. As for why I wish to speak on the excellence of theological learning with which minds received into heaven will be furnished, compared with the imperfect and shadowy <note>original: "umbratili," literally "in the shade" or "sketch-like."</note> knowledge of divine things on earth—and not on some other topic—the only reason is that this subject pleased me and seemed worthy of your attention. However, I do not think it necessary to excuse my lack of skill in speaking with many words, nor to seek your mercy for that purpose.

For besides the fact that you never expected Eloquence from me, you know that I am among the number of Theologians, whose brains are usually (and ought to be) filled with innumerable things, words, and phrases that the writers of pure and chaste Latin never even thought of, let alone praised with their pens. Although I see no necessity imposed on me to beg you to lend me your ears—since I know well enough that you have flocked here for the purpose of hearing what I have to say—I nevertheless ask that you interpret my words kindly and benevolently. Because the argument I am about to discuss has the appearance of novelty (which is often dangerous), I ask you to forgive me if I speak incorrectly, too freely, or perhaps too wordily on this or that part of my argument; stay persuaded that these flaws also necessarily belong to theological ignorance.

In order to observe some order—which the Ministers of the Word of God <note>original: "V. D. Ministri," an abbreviation for *Verbi Dei Ministri*.</note> and Theologians ought to take into account by some right—I will treat this argument as follows:

I. *In the first place, I shall reveal the most powerful causes that prevent us from making greater progress in the more sacred disciplines.*

II. *I shall show that those obstacles in that state of happiness, which minds received into heaven shall obtain, are not only removed; but also that all the supports which can serve to reach the highest degree of theological excellence are abundantly present for them.*

III. *Thirdly, finally, we shall show what power this meditation should have on the minds of both teachers and students, as well as all of us, whatever our condition or status may be.*

Before I can enter into the matter at hand and show how narrowly our theological learning is circumscribed, we must first investigate the causes of this weakness. All these causes can be conveniently reduced to three classes. The *first* arises from the very constitution, nature, and opinions with which the mind is imbued. The *second* is composed of all those things that approach from the outside and incline or move the mind to feel one way or another, more or less. The *third*, finally, is drawn from the very character and nature of the sacred disciplines themselves.

Regarding the first cause of this affliction, experience proves that all infants, coming forth from the mother's womb into the divine breezes of light, are equipped with very meager powers of body and mind. Certainly, all minds—whether they are said to be newly created, or established in the first creation of all things, or joined to their original threads and clothed in a vehicle <note>The author refers to various philosophical theories about the soul's origin, including "pre-existence" and "traducianism," which were heavily debated in the 17th and 18th centuries</note>, whether pure and separate from all stain of matter, or all equipped with the same faculties, or adorned with far different powers by a certain divine portion <note>original: "μοῖρα θεῖα"</note> from the very moment of creation and existence—all of them, I say, dwell in thick ignorance of all things, especially those that are divine and remote from the senses. Nor is there any reason for someone to appeal to *innate ideas* <note>The theory that the mind is born with certain knowledge already present, a major point of contention between Rationalist and Empiricist philosophers</note> to prove the contrary; for whatever the case may be regarding this question (which we do not discuss here), it is certain that to rightly know disciplines of every kind, and especially divine ones, there is need for much labor and persistent diligence, and very few of those who devote themselves to letters obtain a notable degree in them above others.

Connected with a mind so weak and unrefined is a fragile little body, subject to countless distractions and diseases. Through the work of this body, minds obtain ideas of things that strike the senses; yet at the same time, the body is often the reason why those minds are led away and pulled back from the true and right, not without a certain seductive sweetness. However, this ignorance and that which—

<column-break/>

<page-num>1045</page-num>
<header>IN HEAVEN COMPARED WITH OURS.</header>

—from there <note>original: "inde"</note> is usually born, namely the depravity of morals, can be countered by no other way more correctly than through the cultivation of reason and the best arts and disciplines, as men have easily perceived. Hence, boys are also sent early to the school of letters and handed over to teachers and professors for the purpose of polishing their talents with the most honorable disciplines, and so they may be shaped to pass through this life wisely and piously. Here, however, it usually happens that after some space of time has passed, young men—either to please their parents or friends, or to look after their family property, or even (though this happens more rarely) led by a certain singular happiness of talent and having perceived the importance of things and disciplines—attach their minds to cultivating the Sacred Letters <note>Theology and Biblical studies</note> above all others, so as to serve God and the benefit of sacred matters. Finally, after various fortunes and courses, after journeys undertaken to the right and to the left, they obtain the name of *Theologian*, or what is the same thing, *Minister of the Divine Word* <note>original: "V. D. Ministri," an abbreviation for "Verbi Divini Ministri"</note>. I will not ask by what right some are often joined to this office, or how they perform it after they have attained it, about which much could be said. I will now assume that many are not only equipped with excellent talent, but are also most fit for teaching the sacred letters and rightly delivering the precepts of religion.

Nor, indeed, while I attribute to Theologians and Ministers of the Divine Word alone the faculty of rightly delivering the heads of religion, would I assert that those who devote themselves to other arts and disciplines, or who manage the care of public and civil affairs, are ignorant of things pertaining to religion. For I know well that many are equipped with such a notable skill in theological matters that they could be judges and arbiters in deciding the most serious articles of religion. But I say that Ministers of the Divine Word and Theologians are equipped with a singular knowledge of divine things, both because it must be their one care, labor, and business to have perceived and known whatever can serve to deliver, explain, and defend the sacred disciplines; and because many things must be known by a Theologian which do not necessarily pertain to the nature and character of religion considered in itself, and which others can therefore be ignorant of without blame. We are speaking here, however, of theological learning viewed in general, without regard to this or that sect of Christians.

But since, as our times are, countless things are required for skill in theological matters and to obtain the name of an educated Theologian, and the parts of these disciplines have increased immensely, while the force and fruitfulness of talent belongs to few—to say nothing of diligence, lack of opportunity, and other impediments—it is clear that it is very difficult—

<summary>The author identifies three causes for the limitations of human theological knowledge: the mind's natural ignorance at birth, external distractions, and the inherent complexity of the sacred disciplines. He distinguishes the professional role of the theologian from the general religious knowledge of the laity, noting the immense difficulty of mastering theology in the modern age.</summary>

->### THEOLOGICAL KNOWLEDGE OF THE BLESSED IN HEAVEN COMPARED WITH OURS.<-

<p align="center">S 3</p>

...is the highest goal in this discipline, if you consider all the parts and sub-parts of which it consists, to truly excel and make distinguished progress in it.

But I must show specifically what obstacles stand in the way of men, even those not lacking in talent, from being carried deeper into the knowledge of the sacred disciplines.

And in the first place, no one will deny that a solid expertise in theological matters requires not only a sharp judgment, a lively mind, and a capacious memory, but also constant meditation, patience for labor, vast reading, a serious and sincere examination of divine things, and finally, a most ardent zeal for the truth. But how few, alas, are those of whom you could rightly assert are adorned with these virtues? How many are there from this number who would be better suited to driving a plow or practicing a mechanical craft, rather than handing down the most noble disciplines or publicly explaining divine oracles? How many are there who think that the knowledge and duties of a <term>Minister of the Divine Word<note>Latin: V. D. Ministri (Verbi Divini Ministri). This refers to ordained clergy in the Protestant tradition.</note></term> are fulfilled simply by reading some theological system <note>In this context, a "system" refers to a systematic theology textbook or manual common in 18th-century universities.</note> and the ability to write and deliver any kind of sermon to the people? How few possess an untiring and incorruptible zeal for truth and a preparation worthy of such great affairs? But let us suppose things were otherwise, and that all these vices were absent; there are many other things that hinder even those adorned with no small gifts of talent, who devote themselves to these Letters with most ardent study, from running successfully in this race.

*For first, more accurate knowledge of divine things is hindered by opinions about this or that article of religion, pre-conceived and drunk in from infancy.* Most people, being devoted to this or that sect, cling to these views stubbornly as if to a rock; they do not allow themselves to be torn away from them by any arguments, however clear and evident. It is a matter of grief, moreover, that no opinions take deeper roots in minds than those which recommend themselves under the appearance of religion; hence arise the complaints of so many excellent men, even of the theological order, regarding the "prejudiced opinions" of theologians.

It can easily be gathered what kind of sincere examination of religion there will be in this state of man. For just as every corrupt judge judges poorly, so do they weigh the heads of religion with a sinister eye, who take opinions lightly admitted and subjected to no accurate examination as their rule—indeed, as the very axioms of their decrees. Once these are seized upon, they have an incredible power over the mind; it can be proven by the argument that many foolish opinions unworthy of God, which are publicly admitted here and there among certain Christian families,

<column-break/>

cannot be dislodged by any arguments. I shall say nothing of those who blindly follow some "infallible teacher" living in Rome <note>A reference to the Pope and the doctrine of Papal authority.</note>: for that unhappy <term>darnel<note>Latin: lolium. A reference to the "tares" or weeds in the biblical Parable of the Weeds (Matthew 13), symbolizing false or corrupting influences.</note></term>—that is, blind assent given to other matters regarding religion—grows not only in *Italian* gardens, but in others as well.

Connected with these pre-conceived opinions are usually *violent commotions of the mind*, which we are accustomed to call *affections* (or passions). No one will easily deny that many theologians are subject to these—though it is a great shame, for their minds ought to be tranquil, placid, and incensed by nothing but a zeal for truth and right. It is not my intention to bitterly criticize the vices of those who perform sacred duties, or to exaggerate them, or even to prick this or that person by name. I must speak only generally of the vices of certain people, as the nature of our argument demands; but if anyone should snatch these words for himself—words spoken only about some—he will foolishly bare the conscience of his own mind. To bring forward only a few examples for the sake of illustration, who does not know that in this order there is a great deal of <term>Factionalism<note>Greek: Στάσεως (Staseos). Refers to political discord, party spirit, or internal strife.</note></term> and party zeal? You would certainly expect a cook to judge a cook, or a cobbler a cobbler, without corruption sooner than you would find many theologians delivering a sincere judgment—I will not say on the views of others, but even on those devoted to their own sect. Hence, it is easy to judge with what spirit they weigh the opinions of those who disagree with them. They can scarcely read their books without agitation. Thus you might often hear such men reasoning: "This man errs in this or that argument, therefore he cannot see clearly in others either"; "This man committed more than one error regarding a critical question; therefore he is unfit to see the connection of some system and judge it." "This man, otherwise most learned, explains many passages of Holy Scripture plainly differently than we like; therefore he must not be heard in other matters either." Indeed, those who made a secession from the Roman Church do not confess themselves to be infallible; rather, they vehemently attack the "ridiculous pride" of the Roman Pontiff. Yet they often act, when dealing with dissenters, in such a way that you would swear they themselves are truly persuaded that they cannot err. Hence also, they heap praise only upon those devoted to their own opinions. Whatever is said by them, though obscure or trite, is "excellent" and "worthy of admiration"; but to place a fair price on the words and writings of those who disagree, they can scarcely—if ever—bring themselves to do. *What is more*, cries out the <term>Blessed Werenfels<note>Samuel Werenfels (1657–1740), a Swiss theologian known for his "Irenicism" (striving for peace and unity among divided Christian groups). The author calls him "Blessed" as a mark of respect for the deceased scholar.</note></term>, *(*)a most acute judgment...*

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the obstacles to theological knowledge, specifically addressing how sectarian bias and partisan spirit cloud the judgment of even the most brilliant scholars. It transitions from general human limitations to the psychological and social pressures of religious factions.</meta>

<page-num>1048</page-num>
->### THE THEOLOGICAL KNOWLEDGE OF THE BLESSED IN HEAVEN COMPARED WITH OURS.<-

...corrupts the minds of even the most sharp-witted men, along with that partisan spirit which has always reigned among the learned, especially those who lead the sacred rites? Let someone explain to me why the *Jesuits* think differently about certain dogmas than all the men of another order; or why *all the Franciscans think differently than all the Dominicans; all the theologians of the Sorbonne <note>The prestigious theological faculty in Paris, often associated with Gallican or French-centric views.</note> differently than all the Transalpines <note>Latin: Transalpini; literally "those across the Alps," referring to the Italian or Roman school of theology.</note>;* and—lest I seem to omit our own—why all the *Lutheran theologians*, as they are called, think differently than all the *Reformed*; or why all the doctors of this religion or university think differently than those of another. 

It would be ridiculous to say that those who differ possess a similar physical temperament, or a similar <term>disposition of mind <note>Greek: διάθεσιν (diathesin); refers to a natural inclination or state of being.</note></term>, while those who oppose them have the opposite; or that this arises from the diversity of the air that the dissenters breathe. This is partisan spirit, or I do not know what a partisan spirit is. Surely, as soon as someone is enrolled in a sect, an order, or a society, they immediately adopt all its opinions. On their own side, there is no prejudice, no error, no injustice, no partisan spirit. From the opposing side, there is nothing but prejudice, error, injustice, and nothing but partisan spirit. If a hundred or more controversies intercede between their side and the opposite side, their own side has decided all hundred correctly; the opposing side has not touched the truth in even a single one. 

Indeed, as often as I think of this, there comes to mind the noble saying of <term>Optatus of Milevis <note>A 4th-century North African bishop known for his writings against the Donatist schism.</note></term> to the <term>Donatists <note>A rigid, schismatic Christian sect in North Africa that claimed only they were the true church.</note></term>: "Let no one believe you, let no one believe us; we are all contentious men." <note>Latin: "Nemo vobis credat, nemo Nobis, omnes contentiosi homines sumus."</note> Oh, what lovely candor, and how rare in our age! Far different things are heard everywhere today from both sides of a dispute. "Let no one," they shout from both sides, "let no one believe the opposing side in anything at all. Let everyone believe us, and indeed in everything." However many adversaries there are, they are "contentious men," but none of us are. Indeed, even the most contentious cannot bring themselves to say "we are men," let alone "we are contentious men." So says that distinguished theologian.

Furthermore, this disposition cannot exist without hatred and anger. From this it happens that many cannot weigh the importance of religion with a calm mind. I know there are many causes for this disease, yet to say what I feel, the chief reason for this heat seems to me to be sought in the fact that young men fall in with such teachers or authors who <term>condemn <note>Latin: "atro notarunt carbone," literally "marked with a black coal," a Roman expression for branding something as bad or unlucky.</note></term> any dissenters. These teachers often exaggerate dissenting opinions—which are perhaps erroneous but minor—into something greater. They never carefully distinguish between errors that are grave and hostile to piety, and those which human nature is prone to and can creep into the mind of even the best person. Hence, it is no wonder that these students shudder at every new opinion and, like children seeing a snake from a distance, pull their feet back and believe that under every stone—that is, every dissenting opinion—sleeps

<column-break/>

<page-num>1049</page-num>
->### COMPARED WITH OUR OWN.<-

...a scorpion. If they ever do read the writings of men devoted to different views than those they themselves follow—which happens rarely—they do not do it to learn anything useful, or to "test all things and hold fast to what is good" according to Paul's warning, but rather to find some material for carping and insulting them.

Who would wonder that such people are hindered from making any progress in the knowledge of divine things? These men are usually accustomed to covering the hatred they bear toward dissenters with the honorable title of "zeal for the glory of God." But the deception often shines through most clearly when it is <term>clearer than the midday sun <note>Latin: "sole meridiano clarius."</note></term> that they are fighting for accepted opinions, for their own reputation, for their own advantages, for their authority, and for the protection of their faction, rather than for divine virtues. Certainly, zeal worthy of the name is joined with love of neighbor; zeal worthy of the name is tempered by the importance of the controversy and the dignity of the subject; zeal worthy of the name is joined with the most accurate knowledge. Finally, zeal worthy of the name—to pass over many other things in silence—declares war not only on errors, but especially on vices, which hinder the salvation of men more than errors do. Since that loudly boasted zeal of certain men lacks these and other characteristics (of which there is no time to speak), there is no reason for them to think they can deceive the wise with words.

But there are also other things that obstruct progress in the knowledge of divine things. Here you might rightly include a certain <term>pretense of wisdom <note>Greek: δοκησισοφίαν (dokesisophian); the delusion of being wise when one is not.</note></term> common to many. Specifically, there are those among the practitioners of the more sacred disciplines who not only think too gloriously of their own talent (with which they might be endowed in no contemptible degree), but also do not sufficiently recognize how great the multitude and sublimity of things to be known is, or how much time is required to properly and solidly learn any one part of theological erudition. 

Hence, after they have unrolled a few "systems" <note>In this context, a "system" refers to a systematic theology textbook or manual common in 18th-century universities.</note> and familiarized themselves with the opinions of certain interpreters whom they think alone possess sharp insight, they believe nothing else is left for them but to adhere firmly to those opinions. Nor do they think it so necessary to diligently call upon the ancients and moderns for counsel in digging out the truth. If you listen to them, everything that can be said about divine things and is contained in the Holy Scriptures has been placed in full light; everything is plain and easy to know, everything sufficiently discussed. They understand the meaning of all the Prophets and the Apocalypse no less accurately than the epistles of Saint John. Hence, they take it very badly if someone brings forward new hypotheses or explanations of passages in Holy Scripture. For they say, "it has been a long time...

...they say, since the Church has already decreed what should be thought regarding this or that argument, one must rest in these decisions; otherwise, there would be room for new examinations throughout one's entire life.

Others seek nothing but *novelties*, things that appear sublime and are at odds with the minds of all other theologians and interpreters. They loathe whatever is well-worn, simple, and natural. They wish to tread in places where no foot has stepped before: hence they place great value on rare and unusual explanations of Scripture, and they praise newly invented opinions, even if supported by no prop—indeed, even if they are sometimes clumsy and *flimsy as straw*. But if they are so "lucky" that, after fatiguing their brains sufficiently, they have devised some new hypothesis or interpretation of Holy Scripture, they applaud themselves marvelously. They repeat publicly that it is like a miracle that a matter so easy to grasp had been detected by no theologian or interpreter until now. You would think these men had entirely different eyes than the rest of us, seeing no less clearly by night than in full light. If they are indeed equipped with some skill in the <term>Oriental languages <note>Primarily Hebrew, Aramaic (Chaldaic), Syriac, and Arabic, which were essential for 18th-century biblical criticism.</note></term> and the <term>critical art <note>The scholarly practice of evaluating the style, origin, and integrity of ancient texts.</note></term>, they give wonderfully free rein to their genius. They hardly encounter a verse in which there is not some allusion to an ancient rite, providing an opportunity for an excursion into antiquity. In the explanations of these men (to use the words of the *most excellent theologian Samuel Werenfels, now enrolled among the inhabitants of heaven <note>Werenfels was a Swiss theologian known for his critiques of scholarly vanity; "enrolled among the heavenly" indicates he had recently died at the time of this writing.</note>*):

> “You find sayings of authors of all kinds; Greek, Hebrew, 
> “Chaldaic, Syriac, Arabic. You see in these commentaries a 
> “Phrygian work <note>original: 'opus phrygionicum'; a metaphor for highly intricate embroidery or multi-colored craftsmanship</note>, variegated with the characters of almost every 
> “language. Only one thing you do not find: the sense of the 
> “passage you desire to understand; so much so that after 
> “reading much to no purpose, at last, in frustration, you might 
> “employ that comic line: *'You have done well; I am much more 
> “uncertain now than I was a moment ago.'* <note>A quote from the Roman playwright Terence's play 'Phormio'.</note>

Again, others, puffed up with the same swelling of "science" and erudition, think that to be wise in theological matters consists solely in tearing up what is certain and plain by universal consent, rendering it uncertain if they can. The simplicity occurring in the writings of Christ and the Apostles does not please the taste of these men. They babble about nothing but "mathematical certainty," and think that the disagreement of theologians regarding dogmas sufficiently teaches that one can harbor the deepest skepticism without detriment to piety. You would swear these men neither eat, drink, nor sleep unless they have first consulted their calculations and algebraic numbers; if we listened to them, we would hold *Euclid* in place of the Gospels, and no one <term>ignorant of geometry <note>Greek: ἀγεωμέτρητος (ageōmetrētos). A reference to the legendary inscription over Plato's Academy: 'Let no one ignorant of geometry enter here.'</note></term> would be received into heaven.

Finally, this also hinders the progress of a more accurate knowledge of divine things: that some are carried away by a love for certain hypotheses—whether doubtful

<column-break/>

<page-num>1051</page-num>

or true, yet not of *great weight*—and, neglecting the most momentous matters and those which still ought to be brought to light by diligent investigation, they consume their whole lives in explaining and defending them.

I could bring forward enough examples, were I not afraid that by reciting them I might provoke the hatred of certain very learned men and those most skilled in theological matters; for I know how *irritable is the race of certain 'prophets'* <note>A play on Horace's 'genus irritabile vatum' (the irritable race of poets), here applied to touchy theologians.</note>. Those who have knowledge of the history of affairs among theologians will find, even if I remain silent, many traces of this error.

But we must proceed to relate the external causes which more than once hinder a more rigorous examination of divine things. We shall review only the chief ones, however, for the sake of brevity. And here, in the first place, occurs the sheer multitude of things to be known by a theologian. The ancients defined an Orator thus: *“An Orator is a good man skilled in speaking”*; so a theologian might likewise be defined briefly and truly as: *“A pious man, well-acquainted with the Christian religion.”* But if anyone in our age wished to promote and recommend a theologian adorned only with these virtues, I know well enough he would offer himself up to be laughed at by the Academic Doctors. They would respond that a theologian must be a Philologist, a Philosopher, a Critic, a Historian, a Chronologist—in one word, a *Universal Scholar* <note>Latin: 'Polyhistorem'; a person of vast and varied learning across many fields.</note>. This much is certain: that most noble discipline consists today of so many parts and sub-parts that no single lifetime suffices to survey them individually and know them rightly. You know, listeners, how difficult it is to excel in any one discipline; few are those "whom impartial Jupiter has loved" <note>A reference to Virgil's Aeneid, describing those who achieve great things.</note> who are ennobled by skill in many sciences. Who can wonder, therefore, if those who must devote themselves to such various parts of discipline and erudition know them only imperfectly and thinly? And that they are hindered from applying their minds to investigating matters of the gravest importance because they are distracted by so many laborious inquiries? I will say nothing of the many who are moved to such heavy duties only in advanced age, expecting no such thing, and are thus impeded from running so difficult and dangerous a path with a diligent and unoffending foot. To this is joined another evil, tied to the former by a sisterly bond: namely, the duty *of knowing things no less subtle than they are useful (and which will profit little), and of babbling and disputing about obscure things no less than clear ones.* Truly, in certain places, this most noble science is so filled with <term>scholastic trifles <note>Latin: 'tricis'; referring to the complex, often trivial logic-chopping of later medieval and post-Reformation academic theology.</note></term>, and so abounds with little questions of little profit, that not even the Apostles, if they returned to earth, could understand them or discuss them in the *Academic manner*—that is, of course, *“learnedly.”* Yet, if you do not understand them, if you do not untie all the knots which contentious and curious men tie...

...if you are able to solve them, you will be one among many, and you will easily remain hidden. The most learned <term>Petrus Cunaeus <note>A 17th-century Dutch jurist and scholar known for his work "On the Hebrew Republic."</note></term> spoke truly in his little book *On the Hebrew Republic* when speaking of the writings of the Evangelists and Apostles: *That harsh simplicity, which in the past everyone followed more successfully the closer they were to those times; now, in this old age of the world, after we have stood within the limits of a starved art with trivial and vain precepts, it has happened that the body of divine wisdom has been weakened and has fallen.* And what <term>Seneca <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca, the Roman Stoic philosopher.</note></term> had said of Philosophy could rightly be said of many theological questions: *Ancient wisdom,* he says, *prescribed nothing other than what should be done and avoided, and then men were far better; after the learned came forth, good men were lacking. For that simple and open virtue has been turned into a clever science, and we are taught how to dispute, not how to live.* In such a state of affairs, who is of such sharp intellect that he can always discern the solid from the empty? Who is so far removed from all desire for glory and ambition that, having left behind so many questions that are subtle rather than useful, he gives himself entirely to learning only what is necessary and eternally enduring? Who would dare to pass over certain minute questions and controversies in silence without the charge of <term>Heterodoxy <note>Holding opinions that differ from the established or "orthodox" religious standards.</note></term>? But while theologians must often sweat over such superfluous things and waste precious time, it cannot happen otherwise than that they often neglect the most momentous matters or treat them as if doing something else, let alone being able to devote themselves, as is proper, to illustrating known truths or investigating the more difficult and obscure meanings of the <term>divine oracles <note>The Holy Scriptures.</note></term>.

Thirdly, the **decrees of Popes, Councils, Synods, systems, and formulas** of every kind place a barrier to this happy progress of theological learning. It is not my intention, listeners, to speak many words about these, or to argue about the norm of interpreting Holy Scripture and the judge of controversies. For who among you is ignorant of the opinions of the various Christian families that disagree among themselves? That the decrees of the Popes prevent the most learned men—those subject to their power and devoted to their opinions—from freely weighing matters pertaining to religion and treating the sacred writings with that liberty which befits lovers of the truth, is so manifest that nothing could be more so. When <term>Dupinius <note>Louis Ellies du Pin (1657–1719), a French ecclesiastical historian.</note></term>, a name of great renown among the Pontifical doctors, mentions this law established in the <term>Council of Trent <note>The 16th-century ecumenical council of the Catholic Church that defined doctrine in response to the Reformation.</note></term>—namely, that no one should interpret Scripture except according to the sense of the Church—in order to cover its unfairness, he asserts by a rare fiction that the law was passed against "Innovators," but not against himself. This is the same as if he had said that all those who blindly subject the sense of Scripture to the decrees of the Pope are sons of the bountiful
mother

...mother and her genuine interpreters, but the others, who refuse to close their eyes to the light, depart from the will of the Pope—who is, of course, most holy and most skilled in the Holy Scriptures—and thus sin most gravely. IV. Furthermore, those who desire the truth are prevented from advancing further in this kind of literature by **quarrels, contentions, and—to express a barbaric thing with a barbaric word—"heretic-makings" (*haereticationes*)**, which often arise on the occasion of some new hypothesis, even if it is harmless, or on account of interpretations of Holy Scripture. But it is also certain that often **brothers** have risen up against **brothers** who are devoted to the same most holy discipline and who agree on the most important matters, over harmless hypotheses that detract nothing from the doctrine or dignity of the Divine Savior. Meanwhile, the same play is always being performed: if any learned man, a lover of truth and seriously devoted to his own confession regarding the essence of things, either brings forward a new hypothesis to bring light to this or that dogma of religion, or judges that certain arguments or testimonies of Scripture—hitherto customarily cited—are weak (even while he firmly retains the stronger ones), there are immediately those who raise a clamor. Hence you hear these and other sayings of certain "wise men": *This man is nurturing some kind of monster* <note>original: "Hic homo monstri aliquid alit"</note>; *Do not trust the horse, Trojans* <note>original: "Equo ne credite Teucri" — a quote from Virgil's Aeneid, warning against the Trojan Horse.</note>; and so on. Who does not see that the whispers and shouts of certain unhealthy-minded men prevent the daily growth and adornment of sacred matters from becoming ever greater?

V. Finally, to pass over many other things in silence, the *polemical writings* <note>original: "Eristica scripta"</note>, which many theologians have been and are still forced to spend their miserable time upon in their own defense, greatly hinder the progress of the more sacred disciplines.

<margin>(*) On this point, lovers of truth should read the dissertation of the most celebrated <term>Clericus <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), a famous theologian and critic.</note></term>, attached to his critical letters, in which this problem is solved: *Should one always respond to the slanders of theologians?*</margin>
How many volumes have most excellent and innocent men often written to protect their reputation and standing, and to ward off the charge of error or heresy from their necks? They could have spent this most precious time far more successfully, and with greater utility, on illustrating higher disciplines. (*)

It is indeed true that much light is often shed on the truth by conflicts of this kind; yet at the same time, it cannot be denied that a great part of such pamphlets consists of the defense of reputation and innocence, of the genuine and often unnecessary explanation of words, phrases, and hypotheses, and of matters that either add no light at all to religion or offend pious and peace-seeking minds.

But we must finally come to the third class of causes which prevent our knowledge of divine matters from being more perfect and accurate. And these are drawn from the very character, nature, and method of handling the theo-

<column-break/>

<page-num>1055</page-num>

logical disciplines themselves. Two things, however, must be advised in advance. *First*, that we shall speak only briefly about a most noble and ample subject; *second*, that we, along with all Protestants, despite this imperfect knowledge of ours regarding divine things, nevertheless profess from the heart that those things necessary to be known for salvation are clearly and transparently handed down in the Holy Scriptures.

Now, the theological discipline is concerned chiefly with the *explanation of the Holy Scriptures*, with *dogmas and the refutation of dissenters*, with *prophecies*, and with the history of the Christian community. A few things must be noted about each.

As (a) regards the *interpretation of Holy Scripture*, it is well known that the first care of an interpreter ought to be to have the words and phrases of the Hebrew and Greek idioms thoroughly understood and known. Here, however, the most learned theologians and those most skilled in the Oriental languages confess that a knowledge of Oriental languages, ancient histories, customs, rituals, and opinions cannot be acquired today in a measure sufficient to understand all passages of Scripture, to solve all difficulties and doubts, and to reconcile all apparent contradictions. Hence, one must very often flee to conjectures, and which of these should be chosen above all others, only a God could say. That an exact knowledge, absolute in all its parts, of the origin of the Hebrew language—especially of words that occur only once <note>The author refers to "hapax legomena," words that appear only once in the Bible, making them very hard to define.</note> and the power they ought to have—is not possible, is admitted among all sensible men. The writings of the Old Testament are indeed contained in a single volume of no great size; but we lack contemporary interpreters who could have given an accurate explanation of all the meanings, circumstances, rituals, and peoples of whom the sacred writers speak. I know what is advised by learned men regarding the utility of the <term>Chaldean Paraphrases <note>The Targums: ancient Aramaic translations/interpretations of the Hebrew Bible.</note></term> and <term>Rabbinic commentaries</term>; I would detract nothing from the labors of the Rabbis: but even those who extol the authority of those writings will grant me this—that they more often give us words than substance, and possess no more accurate knowledge than we do of many difficult passages and histories enacted in the most ancient times, nor do they have sufficient resources at hand to provide it. I would say the same of the interpretations of <term>Onkelos and Jonathan <note>The Targum Onkelos and Targum Jonathan, influential Aramaic paraphrases of the Torah and Prophets.</note></term>; not to mention that the boasted antiquity of these paraphrases has not yet been placed beyond all doubt. It is true that men skilled in Oriental languages have, from time to time, used Chaldean, Arabic, Persian, Ethiopic, and even...
