Indeed, some have even brought immense light to the Sacred Scriptures from the Chinese language. But beyond the fact that the meanings attached to words frequently change over the course of time, through the fickleness of the common people and the migrations of nations, the very disagreements of most learned men regarding various passages of the Holy Scriptures often command us to doubt. Hence, some might contend that the Book of *Job* can be more successfully illustrated from <term>Chaldaism <note>Reference to Aramaic or the dialects used in the Babylonian region.</note></term> than from <term>Arabism <note>The study of Arabic linguistics to explain rare Hebrew words.</note></term>.

Learned men assert with one voice that the <term>Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament, often abbreviated as LXX.</note></term>—the Greek version of the seventy interpreters—brings remarkable utility to the explanation of the Old Testament, to say nothing of the New. Yet it is very well known that these same translators very often depart from the Hebrew text; indeed, they sometimes give senses so abhorrent to the meaning of the Hebrew language that no origin for such a discrepant version can be found. For this reason, some usually attribute that diversity to the manuscripts used by those Alexandrian translators; others to a lack of skill in the Hebrew language from which they suffered; and others, finally, to the corruptions and changes which that most noble version has endured. We are ignorant—safely and without danger, to be sure—both of the fate of the manuscripts before the <term>canon <note>The officially accepted list of books in the Bible.</note></term> was collected, and of the authors of the collected canon of both Covenants. We are ignorant of the authors of many Psalms, the occasion of their writing, their purpose, and the circumstances of time and person. From this, it can be judged in passing—to mention this briefly—what ought to be thought of the custom received among us of singing the songs of David in an uninterrupted series. Regarding the origin and value of the <term>vowel points <note>The marks added to Hebrew text to indicate vowels, which were not part of the original written consonants.</note></term> and the variant readings which they call <term>Keri and Ketiv <note>original: "keri & cetbib" — traditional notes in the Hebrew Bible marking a difference between what is written in the text and what is to be read aloud.</note></term>, the dispute is still before the judge. Even the smallest particles of this language exercise us greatly, as they are clearly equipped with various powers of meaning. Here, one person thinks an emphasis should be sought; another thinks there is none. One appeals to <term>elaboration <note>original: "ἐξεργασίαν" (exergasian) — a rhetorical term for restating a point in different words for effect.</note></term> where such instances occur or seem to occur; another contends that such <term>tautologies <note>Needless repetitions.</note></term> (as he calls them) fight against the majesty of God speaking in the sacred texts.

Regarding the literal and mystical sense, there are fierce battles among the Doctors. One thinks that the full breadth of the words must be urged, and appeals to his own rule—namely, that the words of the Holy Spirit signify whatever they *can* signify. Another cries out that not everything should be cut to the quick, but that account must be taken only of the circumstances, the native meaning, and the connection of the text. Here, where it concerns the fulfillment of this or that prophecy, one man defends that it was proven by the outcome long ago, many centuries ago, citing historical monuments; another contends it must be sought in centuries most remote from those times—that is, closest to our own age—or thinks it has not yet been fulfilled. The very style

<meta>catchword: He-</meta>

---

<page-num>1057</page-num>
<header>IN HEAVEN COMPARED WITH OURS</header>

of the Hebrews, especially in the poetic and prophetic books, teems with hyperbolic expressions; and thus, often not only is the meaning of the word itself doubtful and uncertain, but even if it is known, it cannot be said how far the breadth of that meaning should be extended. Learned men do not yet agree among themselves on what the logic of Hebrew meter consists of. Nor do we everywhere grasp the names of plants and animals of which the sacred text makes mention. Some increase the number of <term>types <note>Symbolic foreshadowings, usually of Christ or the New Covenant in Old Testament events.</note></term> to an immense degree; others admit very few; and finally, others think we should rest only in those which the writers of the New Covenant have offered to us as such—to pass over many other things in silence.

But if we come to the books of the New Covenant, it is true that we are fortified with better protections for understanding them, since there is a great abundance of the most excellent writers of literate Greece. From these, to the happiness of our century, learned men have drawn—and still usually draw—many things to illustrate the books of the New Covenant. This notwithstanding, there are many things that prevent us from attaining a *perfect* knowledge of the things revealed in the New Covenant. I shall say nothing of the authors of the New Testament canon, whose care in comparing manuscripts we are ignorant of; nothing of the fates of the most ancient manuscripts (for these interfere little with the knowledge of Religion); nothing of variant readings; nothing of the style filled with no few <term>Hebraisms <note>Greek phrases that follow Hebrew grammatical patterns.</note></term>; nothing of various obscure parentheses, transpositions, omissions, and so on.

I will only point out this: our Holy Savior and the Apostles speak of things about which none of the Greek philosophers, none of the poets, and none of the historians could speak. Certainly, if those men of letters were to return to earth and happen upon the book of the New Testament, they would rack their brains in vain to explain those things which pertain to the nature of the Gospel of Jesus Christ. Furthermore, many passages are cited in the New Testament taken from the Old, which are often applied to their purpose with difficulty—whether the sacred authors followed the Hebrew manuscript, the Greek, or finally only the sense and not the words. Nor is it a small matter whether you admit <term>accommodations <note>The idea that scripture adapts its language to the common understanding of the time rather than strict scientific or historical fact.</note></term> in the New Covenant or not, about which theologians and interpreters dispute among themselves. We are ignorant of—or at least obscurely understand—the state of the Churches to which the Apostles sent letters, being ignorant of the opinions with which those to whom the epistles were directed had been imbued before they gave their name to Religion. For the Apostles in their epistles did not so much teach the first elements of the Christian religion to the Christians, but rather assumed that these things had already been handed down to them from elsewhere. Moreover, we know obscurely what was performed in the most ancient assemblies, and what

...for example, what the nature of those prophesying in the Corinthian assembly was; nor is it always clear whether the Christians to whom these most holy men wished to address matters regarding religion were strictly of Hebrew origin, or if they also sprang from the Gentiles. I shall say nothing of the accepted distinction of chapters and verses, and other things that often present obstacles to us.

In the more accurate explanation of both Testaments, however, preconceived opinions place a barrier before the mind. Indeed, before we approach the serious reading of the Sacred Scriptures and the explanations of interpreters, the mind is imbued with certain opinions—or, if you prefer, a knowledge of certain articles which we call a **system**. We use these for the most part to show the connection and coherence of some proposition or an entire chapter. Read, for example, the paraphrases of the Epistle to the Romans by two men devoted to different sects, and it will soon be clear what I mean. Indeed, many go so far as to find the most uncertain hypotheses—if it please the Gods!—in both Testaments. One finds the origin of <term>corpuscular philosophy <note>An early modern physical theory that all matter is composed of tiny particles; a precursor to atomic theory.</note></term> and **Chemistry** among the antediluvian Fathers; another finds the **philosophers' stone** in the Apocalypse. This one believes that not only <term>vortices <note>A reference to René Descartes' theory of planetary motion.</note></term> but the entire **Cartesian** world is contained in the first chapters of Moses; that one cries out that the sacred writers were followers of the opinion of **Copernicus**.

Others, in the interpretation of the Sacred Scriptures, look more to what is useful for confirming this or that article of Religion to which they are devoted, rather than to the truth itself. Hence you may hear them saying: "Different interpretations certainly have a place here, none of which is absurd; but it is better to cast one's vote for this explanation rather than the other, because this one serves wonderfully to confirm this or that part of our system." Some take pains to seek a broad sense in which they can give free rein to their intellect in explaining; others cry out that the meaning of words and phrases must be narrowed by design, lest they accidentally find something that shrinks back from the opinions they wish and hope to be firm. I shall say nothing of the other perverse desires of those who interpret. (*) *From these things—to say nothing of others that could be brought forward—it is clear how difficult, indeed impossible, it is for any version to be prepared that is accurate in every part—that is, agreeing in all things with either the Hebrew or Greek idiom—*

*—prepared:* I am reminded here of the response of **Genebrard**, a man most skilled in languages, which he gave to **Henry III**, King of France. For when that most powerful King, touched by a desire to see a French version of both Testaments, sought the advice of Genebrard and asked how much time and expense would be required to complete such a work, they say he replied: "one must be free for this work for at least thirty years; thirty men skilled in languages and Theological disciplines must be employed; and finally, two hundred thousand thalers must be paid out in expenses—and yet even so, nothing could be provided that was placed plainly beyond all censure and danger of error." (*)

But if we turn our mind to contemplating theological dogmas, as they are called (to say nothing of moral Theology and cases of conscience), it will again be clear how thin and greatly maimed the state of our theological Erudition is. In general, we note that our knowledge of things not falling under the senses is most imperfect. Hence we are often stuck when it comes to the attributes and affections of spirits and <term>monads <note>In the philosophy of the time, the simplest, indivisible units of reality.</note></term>. For just as the senses were not given to us so that we might have the inner essence of bodies perceived, but only so that we might know as much about them as is necessary to promote the comforts of our life and to celebrate God: so too we are not equipped with a mind that can obtain a perfect science of spirits; but rather so that, having acquired some sort of...

The most learned **Wagenseil**, a man most skilled in Oriental languages, in his book titled *The Flaming Arrows of Satan* page 522, when about to give the reason why versions of the Sacred Scriptures agreeing in every part with the Greek or Hebrew source text have not yet been prepared by learned men, appeals to the *secret ways of divine Providence*, saying: "I myself have often thought silently about this matter, and I wondered—since versions of many books into other languages exist made exactly to the rule, and reflecting the original text with such similarity that no other difference exists between them than the diversity of languages—why it could not have happened that for so many centuries some version of the Sacred Scripture could be composed which would not betray its own blemishes and would keep its integrity consistently. And I finally began to attribute this whole thing to heavenly providence, which does not allow a version perfect in all its parts to be published by anyone; so that, for all nations scattered throughout the whole world, the majesty and authority of those fountains—which flowed immediately from the most sacred abyss of eternal wisdom—might be preserved unimpaired above the canals through which the most blessed fluids are led elsewhere; and so that they might occasionally take these streams as companions and go to the waters of the fountain, if they should desire to taste the true flavor of the most divine water more sincerely." So says **Wagenseil**. Whether one must resort to that explanation, let men more learned than I judge.

<header>THE THEOLOGICAL KNOWLEDGE OF THE BLESSED</header>

...and let us recognize whatever knowledge there is of things not perceived by the senses, which can be properly weighed and put into use on this earth for both divine and human matters. But if we have such an imperfect knowledge of physical bodies set before our eyes and of finite spirits, is it any wonder if we know the nature of God, His perfections, His ways of acting, and the reasons and ends of His counsels most imperfectly? Hence *Lactantius* <note>Lucius Caelius Firmianus Lactantius (c. 250 – c. 325), an early Christian author and advisor to Constantine I.</note> rightly said: when the attention, sharpness, and memory of the human mind reach toward Him, it stands still as if all paths were withdrawn and exhausted; it hesitates, it fails, and there is nothing further it can proceed toward.

Who, then, in such great darkness of our affairs, will give an exact and perfectly complete definition of even one divine attribute? Who can explain by what reasoning God knows the present, the past, the contingent, the necessary, and the future at every single moment, so to speak? Who can know what it is to "be from oneself" (<term>aseity <note>original: "a se esse" — the theological concept that God contains the reason for His own existence within Himself and is not dependent on any other being.</note></term>), and to exist from eternity? Who will declare His way of acting upon creatures—both those endowed with reason and sense, and those entirely lacking them? Who will place in a clear light the order of divine counsels and decrees begun from all eternity, with their causes and ends (about which some chatter with such confidence, as if they had been God's advisors)? Who will define how it could happen that, by the Will of the Divinity, an infinite mass of matter came forth, teeming with innumerable seeds? Who will uncover the administration of divine providence and its causes in the realm of Nature and of Grace? Who will untie the knots occurring around the origin of moral and physical evil, especially when it comes down to this or that individual? Who will show the way through which the first sin was devolved upon the whole human race? What theologian, finally, will give a sufficient reason why God produced this series of things and not another, this world now and not another? Who knows what the knowledge of religion is for infants in their mother’s womb? Who would not confess their ignorance regarding the dogmas of the Trinity, the incarnation, and the satisfaction of Jesus Christ <note>The doctrine of "satisfaction" refers to Christ's atonement for human sin.</note>? Who will explain why the light of the Gospel appeared only to these peoples and not others? Why did Christ not come into the world sooner? Who will narrate the reason for the future administration in heaven through all eternity, the degrees of knowledge of the blessed minds, or finally, the individual fates of the unhappy victims of hell? These things, to omit many others, show well enough how imperfect and very crippled our knowledge of **dogmatic theology** is. Hence, the more one is skilled in these matters, the more frequently, when asked about these or those subtler questions, they will answer: *I do not know; I am ignorant; it is not clear.*

<page-num>1061</page-num>
<header>IN HEAVEN COMPARED WITH OURS.</header>

From which it is also easily evident, Listeners, how imperfect our future skill in **polemical theology** <note>The branch of theology concerned with defending Christian doctrines against objections and refuting the positions of other sects or religions.</note> will be. For, not to mention that polemical study is to be counted among *necessary evils*, who does not know that there have very often been bitter disputes about words rather than things, and indeed among brothers? These were disputes sometimes about actual things, but things of little importance; often they were about matters of which neither disputant had clear and accurate knowledge. Indeed, if they had wanted to tell the truth, they would have broken out into these words after declaring a truce: *Until now, friends, we have disputed about things either entirely unknown or quite obscure; not to mention these, how difficult it is for those engaged in this argument to guard themselves from partisanship, from false zeal, and from all arguments born of envy?*

What talent, labor, and judgment is needed to properly understand all the systems of Christians who disagree among themselves—to see them properly fitted to their foundations and not corrupted by false interpretations? Who, without being marked as rash, will assert that he can untie all the knots occurring in the business of religion which men of every age propose to us? And whose lifetime would suffice to properly know—not to mention refute—all the foolish, inept, and bold opinions that have been stirred up and debated in the church since the founding of the world? For polemical theologians must struggle not only with various sects of Christians, but with pagans, Jews, Muslims, atheists, deists, skeptics, fanatics, and men of I-know-not-what other stripe.

Suppose a theologian knows these things perfectly; many other things must still be performed by him before he can sing of triumph. For he will have to fight against preconceived opinions and the love of a sect deeply fixed in the minds of those in error. Unless he first represses these enemies, his work will be in vain. But how unyielding is the laziness of some when it comes to the examination of Religion! How few care for the serious and attention-worthy disputes of theologians, let alone the subtle and academic ones? How many are there who shudder at the very *word "controversies"*? For how few can you "pluck the old grandmothers from the lungs" <note>original: "veteres avias de pulmone revellas" — a quote from the Roman satirist Persius, meaning to root out deep-seated, irrational superstitions or "old wives' tales" from one's core beliefs.</note>? How stubbornly most people adhere to opinions swallowed, as it were, with their mother’s milk? How rare is the number of true converts? How little is commonly gained by disputes? Oh, how rightly many theologians would act if they were first concerned with repressing and purging their own wicked affections, from which they suffer, rather than tearing down the opinions of those who disagree.

But we come now to **prophetic theology**, to see whether here more sharply...

...let us see more clearly. However, we are so far from being able to boast of any accurate knowledge in this part of the theological disciplines that even those who have applied themselves to it with incredible study for many years admit that most things regarding the future Messiah, his teaching, his offices, his sufferings, and the conversion of the nations—which are gathered from the warnings of the prophets—are shrouded in thick darkness.

We know from the Holy Scriptures that there are prophets—that is, men equipped with an unusual knowledge of divine matters and gifted with the faculty of foretelling the future; but by what method God glides into their minds, stirs them, and brings it about that they see things which escape the sharpest sight of other men, we are safely ignorant. And if one arrives at the explanation of the Prophets themselves, many things prevent us from easily and clearly grasping their meaning. Such things include the hyperbolic style of the Prophets themselves, filled with innumerable figurative words and phrases, and thus difficult to understand—pleasing and suited to the ears of Eastern peoples rather than our own. Hence, one cannot easily say how far such sayings should be pressed, lest we add to or subtract from the purpose of the Holy Spirit while focusing on the words. And who, finally, is acquainted with all the ways of speaking, the customs, the maxims, and the parables used by the ancient Hebrews or other peoples of the East with whom they had some interaction, and against whom—at the Divine Will—the Prophets rose up? <note>There is an ink smudge or strike-through over the rest of the word in the original text.</note> Who has a perspective on the circumstances of the times, places, and persons toward which the sacred seers point their finger? In such a lack of ancient monuments from that age, who will designate the order of times without fear of error? Furthermore, the divine seers often speak in such a way that you do not know whether the events they speak of have reached their fulfillment or not; for this reason, many believe that things are only just going to happen in certain periods of time, which others think happened long ago. Add to this that in the middle of a prophetic speech or even a chapter, prophecies about the Messiah or the Christian assembly often occur where, whether we consult what comes before or after, we can find nothing related to this subject. If anyone wishes to refer not only to this passage or these verses but to an entire chapter or psalm to the Messiah, and to measure every single phrase and proposition by it, he will learn by experience what a difficult task he has undertaken. Certainly, not once, but frequently, we are taught that matters concerning the <term>Economy of the New Testament <note>The divine plan or management of the world under the Christian covenant.</note></term> are being dealt with by the authority of the Savior <note>original: "Soteris" — a Greek-derived title for Christ meaning "Savior."</note> and the Apostles, rather than by the actual evidence of the prophecy itself or the literal meaning of the words.

...we are taught. But there will be those who insist that there are nevertheless many learned and pious theologians who have extracted the most singular events of our own and the immediately preceding centuries from the more obscure oracles of the Prophets. I do not deny that there have been those who contend that the *Peace of Passau* <note>A 1552 treaty between the Holy Roman Emperor and Lutheran princes.</note>, the war waged between the *Guelphs* and *Ghibellines* <note>Opposing political factions in medieval Italy and Germany.</note>, the rejected formula called the *Interim* <note>The Augsburg Interim (1548), a temporary decree in the religious wars of the Reformation.</note>, the *Council of Trent*, the captivity of *John Frederick, Elector of Saxony*, and other things of the same nature were predicted in the *Song of Solomon*. These same men believe that the *Death of Gustavus Adolphus* <note>The King of Sweden who died in the Battle of Lützen (1632) during the Thirty Years' War.</note> is explained and predicted in *Isaiah chapter 23:7*, the *fates of Hungary* in chapter 32, the failed attempts to establish bishoprics in the *Netherlands* in chapter 19, and that the *Prague Academy* would be occupied by the *Jesuits* in *Ezekiel chapter 39*—to say nothing of other interpretations of this kind. (*)

I wish to detract nothing from the merits and learning of the most learned and pious men who are pleased by these interpretations; yet I cannot deny that, although I read and reread the cited chapters ten times, I cannot be persuaded that these matters are dealt with there. And since I must see with my own eyes and not those of others, I ask those who see more sharply to forgive my blurred vision, or if they prefer, my blindness. Yet this is a wretched solace to me: that I see interpreters equipped with every resource for rightly explaining the sense of Holy Scripture—men most knowledgeable in the Christian religion, and finally, men most loving of the truth—who are also groping in the dark here with me. Indeed, a far greater part of them either confess their ignorance or, not without cause, pronounce that far different things are contained there. From this, surely, if you look at the great number of most learned theologians who admit they are stuck in explaining many places in the Prophets, no one will find fault with us if we say that even in this area our theological knowledge is very weak, or, to speak with the Apostle Paul, *we prophesy only in part*. <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 13:9.</note>

Finally, to say a few things about the events carried out in the Christian assembly since the times of Christ (not to go further back), there are many things that stand in the way of our having certain knowledge of the history, or of the doctrines—whether true or false—which Christians have subscribed to through all the centuries.

Thus, for example, it would be of the greatest interest to us to know what was done in the assemblies of Christians in the first century after the departure of the Apostles, what their opinion was on individual parts of the Christian religion, who their successors were, and their labors, and so on. But we lack the monuments...

...that they suffer from a lack of reliable sources is something no learned person ignores. * (2.) To understand <term>dogmas</term><note>Established religious doctrines or principles.</note>, it is necessary for us to unfold the writings of the **ancient Fathers**; yet these men themselves often expressed their minds obscurely, being more accustomed to <term>allegories</term><note>Stories or images used to convey a hidden spiritual meaning rather than a literal one.</note> than to precise reasoning. Hence, whenever a question arises about what this or that Father felt regarding a specific controversial point, darkness immediately descends, and everyone wants to pull the author toward their own side. Thus, the Roman Catholics no less than the disciples of **Luther** and **Zwingli** find their own views on the **Holy Supper**—to say nothing of other religious decrees—within the most ancient writings of the Fathers.

3.) Learned men everywhere complain that the history of the most ancient <term>heresies</term><note>Beliefs or opinions contrary to orthodox religious doctrine.</note> has not yet been sufficiently investigated; and it is extremely difficult to have a proper perspective on their systems of thought. The Fathers themselves more than once misunderstood the connection of such hypotheses, or substituted their own logical conclusions for the genuine opinions of the dissenters—to say nothing of the partisan zeal and unrestrained passion by which they were sometimes carried away, or the obscure phrases they used to express the opinions of those men.

4.) It is difficult to judge the opinions of all the teachers who lived in the same century from the writings and views of only two or three Fathers, since many others—whose writings have perished through the injustice of time—could have felt quite differently.

5.) The laws of probability have not yet been so thoroughly examined and determined that one can precisely define how many degrees are required regarding the quality and quantity of witnesses, and all the circumstances that must be weighed to prove or reject a fact. The most acute philosophers acknowledge and confess this, among whom I include the illustrious **Leibniz**, who deserves to be numbered among the leading philosophers and scholars of this passing century.

6.) If we turn our minds to the laws of history, it will again become clear how difficult it is to be rightly convinced of the truth of past events. **Cicero** expressed these laws by saying: *Who does not know that the first law of history is that one must not dare to say anything false, and next, that one must not lack the courage to say what is true; that there should be no suspicion*

*of favor in writing, nor any of malice.* And elsewhere: *witnesses must be worthy of trust, having a very just reason why they were able to know the truth, and no reason why they would lie.* But it is clearer than the midday sun that even the ecclesiastical writers themselves had very little care for these laws. For after the Christians had defined what was true and right in the <term>Councils</term><note>Official gatherings of church leaders to decide on matters of doctrine and administration.</note> by a majority of votes, they split into sects. When dealing with the facts and dogmas of those they disagreed with, they did not hesitate—carried away by false zeal and partisan spirit—to mix the false with the true, or even to use open lies against others if they thought it served their cause. Meanwhile, they would praise to the heavens those devoted to their own opinions, even when those people were often acting foolishly or sailing on the winds of their emotions. What shall I say of the history of the **Martyrs**, the **Monks**, and the **Hermits**? Let **Melchior Cano**, a very famous Bishop of the Roman Church, answer for me:

> *I say this with grief (he says) rather than reproach: the lives of the Philosophers were written with much more severity by Laërtius than the lives of the saints were by Christians; and Suetonius exposed the affairs of the Caesars with far more incorruptibility and integrity than Catholics have exposed—I will not say the affairs of Emperors—but of Martyrs, Virgins, and Confessors. For the former writers, when dealing with honest men, whether philosophers or princes, do not keep silent about their vices or suspicions of vice; and in the case of wicked men, they even show the colors of their virtues. Our writers, however, for the most part either serve their emotions or even industriously invent so many things that I am not only ashamed of them, but also weary. For I understand that these people have brought no benefit to the church of Christ, but rather the greatest inconvenience.*

Thus speaks M. Cano.

7.) To uncover the origin, fate, and opinions of any single sect, or to prove or disprove a "matter of fact" (as they call it) that is judged to be of some importance, one needs not only incredible diligence, vast reading, persistence in labor, and leisure, but also sharp judgment, exquisite learning, and a most fierce love of truth. Yet very few who devote themselves to the study of ecclesiastical history are equipped with these gifts. Let whoever you are read the history of **Manichaeism** written by the most learned **Beausobre** (now enrolled among the heavenly host), and the arguments debated on both sides between **Blondel** and **Spanheim** regarding **Pope Joan**, to say nothing of many other examples; you will feel that these could not have been written by such learned men without the greatest study, vast reading, and a wonderful excellence of talent.

The disputes once carried out in France between **Claude** <note>Jean Claude (1619–1687), a prominent French Reformed theologian.</note> and **Arnauld** <note>Antoine Arnauld (1612–1694), a leading Jansenist and Catholic philosopher-theologian.</note> and others are well known; they argued over the faith of the Greeks regarding the explanation of the words used to institute the **Holy Supper** <note>The Eucharist or Communion.</note>, a topic in which both sides tested the limits of their strength. Even if you think it is of no small interest for us to know this, and you have grasped their mindset after immense labor, does it finally follow—at least according to the mind of Protestants—that because *the modern Greeks cherish the same opinion on the Holy Supper that we defend,* it is therefore true? (*) And these points, if I am not mistaken (to pass over many others), prove more than enough how *imperfect*, *weak*, and *thin* is our knowledge of divine things in these lands.

We must now pass to the second part of our speech: namely, to contemplate the surpassing knowledge of divine things held by the **blessed minds** received into heaven. However, lest anyone should perhaps ask with a smile how I have gained insight into the "Theological Knowledge of the Blessed," or whether I have perhaps participated in their council at some time, I say before all else: I shall say nothing regarding the knowledge and state of those minds except what can be proved either by the most manifest testimonies of **Holy Scripture**, or what can be extracted—either with certainty or *probability*—from the character and nature of that most perfect state and the glorious kingdom of glory.

Therefore, when the Holy Scriptures speak of the state of the blessed in heaven, they testify: That they do not know divine things in a *riddle* <note>original: "aenigma." A reference to 1 Corinthians 13:12, often translated as "through a glass, darkly."</note>, but *face to face*; that they *see God*; that they are *consummated* and *perfect*; that they *see the glory* which *the Father gave to Christ*; that they are *like angels* whose knowledge and powers, as is well known, are far superior to our own; that *they themselves dwell perpetually with God, who inhabits inaccessible light; and that the Lamb sitting on the Throne of God—that is, the Savior—supplies all things whatsoever that can lead to perfect joy and happiness.* (**)

---

(*) Learned men—for example, **Abbot Fleury** and **Weismann**—bring forward many other causes that place a barrier to an accurate knowledge of events conducted in the Christian assembly, to say nothing of others in the dissertations prefixed to their ecclesiastical histories.
(**) Here we point a finger to that most famous passage in the **Book of Revelation**, Chapter 7, verses 16 and 17, where it is said of the blessed in heaven: <note>original Greek: ἔτι οὐ πεινάσουσιν... "They shall hunger no more, nor thirst anymore; neither shall the sun strike them, nor any scorching heat."</note> The ancient Philosophers described the happy state of minds after death in a similar way. Thus **Socrates**, in the *Dialogue of Aeschines the Socratic* speaking about death, says this among other things concerning the "region of the pious": <note>original Greek: ἔνθα ἄφθονοι μὲν ὧραι... "where the abundant seasons teem with a land bearing all kinds of fruit, and springs of pure water flow... for there is neither harsh winter nor does excessive heat occur, but a well-tempered air is poured out, mixed with the soft rays of the sun."</note> That is, there the abundant seasons gush with all things from the

They shine in the kingdom of the Father like the sun; their bodies, if they are received into heaven, will be glorious, incorruptible, conformed to the glorious body of Christ, and subject to no infirmities. The spirit of a blessed human will be life-giving—that is, it will perpetually communicate life to the body by an inherent power—and there are other passages of Holy Scripture by which the happiness of that state is proclaimed.
If we consult the entire **Economy of Grace** <note>The divine plan for the salvation of humanity.</note> outlined in the sacred writings, it will further be established what should be felt regarding the future state of human minds. From this, namely, we are taught that the minds of the first humans were once *pure* and equipped with the light of the **Divine Image**, but because of sin, they fell into a darkness that could not be dispelled by any sharpness of wit or the skill of human study. Yet, those who are pious and touched by a sense of sin have been not only freed from guilt and punishment by the obedience and death of the **Savior** <note>original: "Soter."</note> and the help of the Holy Spirit, but have also been so fortified by the most effective protections that they begin to emerge again and receive new strength. And finally, having been loosed from the bonds of death by so great a benefit of the Savior, it is asserted they will enter into full freedom and recover their former light and splendor—that is, a light free from every blemish and stain.

From these points, certain things can be gathered in summary concerning the state of humans received into heaven, which we reduce to at least two heads. **The first is**: all things that pertain to an accurate knowledge of divine matters, and to the most chaste and perfect love of God—by which true and uncorrupted happiness and a joy destined to last for all ages is fulfilled—will be present in abundance; and thus the will and all inclinations of the soul will be pure, sincere, and free from any mixture of evil. **The second**: all...

which usually arise from thick and faulty ignorance, and from the sources of wicked judgments and affections in these lands, will be far removed from that most blessed state.

These things can be said with truth and without fear of error; however, far more can probably be gathered regarding the state of both their knowledge and their perfection, if we reason from the premises already established, which must now be shown briefly and in parts.

First, therefore, we establish as a foundation that a perpetual increase in the knowledge of the most divine things will be added to those minds throughout all eternity, and that this knowledge will lead them to an ever more ardent love of God, since all incentives for celebrating the praises of God usually arise from the breadth and evidence of divine knowledge.

Furthermore, there are many things that persuade us to believe that such an increase in knowledge will take place in the future life. First, because God himself is infinite, his attributes are infinite, and finally, his works are infinite; yet our mind, however blessed, is nonetheless finite and capable of greater knowledge. Since God—out of the innate and singular benevolence with which he is moved toward those blessed souls, and the infinite love with which he embraces the **Savior** <note>original: "Soterem," from the Greek for "Healer" or "Preserver," a common scholarly term for Christ in this period.</note>, who is the head of the blessed minds and with whom they are then most closely united—will grant them all things that can contribute more and more toward achieving true joy and happiness, there is no doubt that he will grant them the most ample knowledge of divine things.

Added to this is the fact that the infinite opportunity for recognizing new things (about which something must be said shortly) will provide the most abundant material for a perpetual contemplation of the breadth of divine virtues and for learning greater things. For those minds will not be idle, nor fixed always upon a single point of contemplation, but will be so inflamed by the desire to know and celebrate divine virtues that they will never fully satisfy themselves in the knowledge of the truth.

the senses, with which those most excellent little bodies will be equipped. If we listen to the Holy Scriptures, minds received into heaven, once they are joined again with the body, will one day have a **spiritual body** <note>original: "σωμα πνευματικον" (*soma pneumatikon*). A term from St. Paul in 1 Corinthians 15:44.</note>, that is, as it seems, a thin, ethereal body, agile like the rays of the sun, by whose aid they can traverse the immense **vortices** <note>In 18th-century physics, the universe was often imagined as a series of swirling "vortices" of matter.</note> of heaven, and, raised above the planets, look upon the worldly ocean, and gaze upon the innumerable globes of the earth floating in the vast abyss, filled with their own inhabitants. To that end, there is no doubt that they will be endowed with the sharpest senses, and will especially use eyes that see quite acutely and are most lively; and since, in the judgment of many philosophers and theologians, there are many worlds and all the stars are so many suns, destined to provide light to various orbits, and in these very places dwell various creatures whose nature we do not yet clearly perceive, it is easy to gather what infinite and most ample material for learning these new spectacles will exhibit, and what incredible pleasure the blessed will derive from that fact. For if physicists and astronomers, who throughout their entire lives are intent on investigating the laws of nature and the motion, magnitude, and nature of the celestial bodies, burst out into that cry, "**I have found it! I have found it!**" <note>original: "ευρηκα, ευρηκα" (*heureka, heureka*). Nor is it evident that these are pleasant dreams, because the Holy Scriptures testify that the blessed will see the glory that the Father gave to the Savior. For although this could also happen through revelation, there is nonetheless no reason why they could not see with their eyes the Savior himself, raised above all things, and his splendor, by means of the senses with which the bodies of the blessed are equipped. It is also highly probable, and confirmed by the opinion of many most celebrated philosophers, that all minds already received into heaven, before the resurrection of the bodies, are clothed in a certain thin little body and vehicle, which the ancients called a **carriage** <note>original: "ὄχημα" (*ochema*). A Neoplatonic term for the "vehicle" of the soul, a subtle body that bridges the gap between the purely spiritual and the physical.</note>, by whose aid they can see all those things of which we have spoken so far.

# THEOLOGICAL KNOWLEDGE OF THE BLESSED

Blessed minds can, in the second place, increase their knowledge of divine matters *with the help of others*. Indeed, all theologians concede that there will be a certain common language among the heavenly inhabitants, by the help of which they may mutually communicate the thoughts of their minds to one another. Whether this shall be the Hebrew tongue or another, it is not necessary for us to know or to define. <note>The author refers to a common early modern debate regarding the "Ursprache" or original language of humanity, which many scholars then believed was Hebrew.</note> Since, however, among the minds received into heaven, there are some who surpass others in knowledge, and who are kindled on one hand by a certain divine love toward one another; and on the other hand, since all minds burn with an incredible desire to know the most excellent things—which until now they have not sufficiently perceived—I have no doubt that they will acquire knowledge of many things in this way through the mutual exchange of the voice. Who, for example, would deny that the holy Patriarchs, Prophets, and Apostles were bathed in a greater light of divine things than other men, even those equipped with a great apparatus of theological learning? If this is true, as no one denies, it is most probable that they will offer light to the rest and recount those things which serve to praise the divine virtues. And since in that council of heavenly souls the Angels—the perpetual ministers of God in the administration of the world—surpass all others in intelligence and long experience of events, it is probable that the souls will hear many things from them that were previously unknown. Finally, it is widely admitted that a more accurate knowledge of those things which have happened in this world—whether you look at the times before the flood or after the flood, or consider the state of other worlds <note>The mention of "other worlds" (aliorum orbium) reflects the 18th-century fascination with the plurality of worlds and the possibility of extraterrestrial life.</note> hitherto unknown to us and their natural and moral condition—does much to extol the <term>excellence</term> <note>original: "ὑπεροχὴν" (hyperochēn), meaning preeminence or supreme quality.</note> of the divine virtues; therefore, there is no doubt that they will communicate these things with the blessed. Indeed, even those minds smaller than the Angels will not cease to relate with praise the singular benefits received on these earths from the **Best and Greatest Divine Power**, and thus daily supply new material for celebrating His virtues.

Although the minds received into heaven can know many things by the help of sensations and familiar social exchange, many things nonetheless can only become known to them through revelation. For whatever cannot be drawn out by reasoning from the character, nature, and perfections of things—or which depends on the mere good pleasure of God (even if resting on the wisest reasons)—cannot become known to men except by revelation. Thus, even the Angels themselves can only know those things which pertain to the kingdom of grace through revelation. Yet this revelation will grow in parts and over intervals of time; and minds, imbued and adorned with the knowledge of new and most excellent things, will so devote themselves to the contemplation of most divine mat-

ters that they will be incited, as if by new spurs, to always receive greater light. In this way, the blessed will only be able to know through revelation the state of creatures perhaps living in other worlds, and the manner and order of the divine administration by which they are governed; or the state of the "church militant" <note>A traditional term for the Christian church on earth, which is seen as being "at war" against sin and the devil, as opposed to the "church triumphant" in heaven.</note> in these lands. Moreover, God will reveal only as much of these things as is necessary for celebrating and praising His virtues, which exert themselves in this administration.

From the same source will flow a more accurate understanding of prophetic prophecies. For although the prophets received into heaven can communicate many things previously unknown to those perfected souls, there will still be a need here for God’s help, since the prophets themselves do not seem to have known the full scope and ends of their prophecies. It is also credible that a fuller knowledge of the mystery of the Trinity and the <term>Incarnation</term> <note>original: "ἐνσάρκωσις" (ensarkōsis), the theological term for God becoming flesh in Jesus Christ.</note> will be granted to us through the same revelation. For although a finite mind can never fully know all things which are infinite in the nature of God (insofar as they are infinite), it is nonetheless certain that the mind can obtain knowledge of all those things which do not contradict each other, but of which some explanation can be given. To this point you may refer primarily to a question that is, in my opinion, impossible to solve in this life: namely, the choice of this world, filled as it is with so many evils. Philosophers indeed discourse brilliantly on this argument, asserting that the **Best and Greatest God**, being most desirous of the human race and most wise, could only choose the best; since He wished to found this world and no other, it stands to reason that it should rightly be called the "best"—to pass over many other arguments they usually bring forward. <note>This is a reference to "Theodicy" and the "Best of All Possible Worlds" theory popularized by Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz.</note> But when, setting aside metaphysical speculations, we turn our minds to contemplating so many evils—especially moral ones—with which the world is as if overwhelmed, and when we weigh what is done daily and cast our eyes upon these or those individuals and their external and internal states one by one, we can hardly persuade ourselves that the world could not have been founded otherwise, and that such an immense heap of evils of every kind necessarily belonged to the construction of a most perfect world. In our opinion, we cannot perfectly know the reasoning behind the divine administration in these lands, either because God did not wish to give the fuller reasons in this life which moved Him to produce this world and no other, or because we are ignorant of the manner of Divine Governance that will take place throughout all eternity. The other [reason] is that not only do minds crave the knowledge of hidden things, but they are also often deeply distressed and disturbed by the contemplation of the most wicked evils spreading through this world, and the various kinds of sufferings to which the pious are subject. There is no doubt that God will provide sufficient light in the other life to solve this question. Likewise, I am persuaded that by this path—that is, by the revelation of God—we shall acquire the most ample knowledge of many other things of which we are clearly ignorant now.

Finally, (**IV.**) the **Reasonings** <note>The author uses the term *Ratiocinationes*, referring to the logical process of moving from known premises to new conclusions.</note> of the blessed minds will increase this knowledge of divine things. For just as **Mathematicians** and **Physicists** <note>In this period, "Physicists" refers to natural philosophers who studied the laws of the physical world.</note> do not immediately rest once a certain truth or proposition has been demonstrated, but use it to detect new and hitherto unknown truths, so likewise there is no doubt that those heavenly souls, bathed in such great light, will use those new truths (which they will obtain by various means already partly mentioned) to prepare a greater store of knowledge. And since the magnitude and splendor of this new world will always provide infinite material for reasoning, the knowledge of things pertaining to **Physics** and **Natural Theology** will grow immensely. The same must be said regarding the knowledge of moral things. Having detected so many truths through the revelation of God and the exchange of blessed minds, the Blessed will use them to investigate other paths that will take place in the state of grace and glory. Indeed, since the kingdom of nature, though glorious at that time, will be most closely joined with the kingdom of grace, the knowledge of natural truths will bring light to properly investigating moral truths, and vice-versa. From the connection of these principles and conclusions, a clearly divine, harmonious, and (if I may say so) perfectly demonstrative science will arise. Thus, it is highly probable that after we have acquired a fuller knowledge of the nature of angelic and human minds, we shall rightly understand the reason for that **interaction which occurs between the mind and the body**—about which Philosophers now often dispute with such great effort and not without bitterness. Furthermore, we shall be taught far more accurately than is now possible about the nature, power, strength, and offices of the angels, and likewise of the souls existing in their individual dwellings. I am persuaded that we shall thus know in what consists that **gravitational force** <note>original: *gravitativa*</note> (as the Physicists call it) of the entire planetary system toward the sun, and the proportionate force and efficacy of the sun in turn resisting it. Finally, to pass over many other things in silence,

I believe we shall also, in this way, more rightly and fully perceive the systems of divine **predestination**, and the administration and harmony of **liberty with divine providence**. Alas! Christians have struggled and still fight so stubbornly over these matters in this darkness of things, with such heat of spirit and at the cost of mutual charity. <note>The author laments the "confessional wars" and bitter theological debates between Protestants and Catholics regarding how God's plan (providence) coexists with human free will.</note>

But not only will theological learning grow so immensely in the future life through the means we have indicated; all those things that could hinder a more accurate knowledge of divine matters will also be absent from those most noble souls.

Therefore, first, the blessed minds will labor under no shameful or vicious ignorance of things necessary to be known—necessary, I say, not foolish or difficult trifles, nor **scholastic complications**. <note>original: *tricarum*. This is a critique of the overly complex, "hair-splitting" debates of medieval and early modern Scholastic philosophy.</note> There will be no wavering regarding the articles of faith, no perverse judgments that flatter the flesh. They will not be carried headlong by any perverse and foolish opinions, which usually arise from ignorance of more solid science and from false reasonings. Deceptive appearances of the imagination or defects of memory will never disturb them; but on the contrary, they will have a full knowledge of the most divine things, as we have heard, as much as can fall upon finite minds. And just as in **Dramas** whatever is intricate and perplexed is explained in the last act; likewise, whatever caused us trouble in the administration of the world, the light of the last day will clear up. To this knowledge—and indeed to this alone—they will give true value without pride, envy, or other passions which usually take place among mortals. They will be perpetually fixed in the meditation of these things; in these they will spend that never-ending age with incredible pleasure.

From this itself (**2**) it is clear that all foolish opinions and inclinations, which are deeply fixed in human minds and are the inseparable companions of the stain contracted on this earth—witnesses of human weakness and corruption—will be far removed from this happy state. Rather, there will be the highest purity of all the desires and inclinations of the mind, washed and purged by the blood of our **Savior** <note>original: *Soteris*, from the Greek word for Savior, a common scholarly term for Jesus Christ.</note>. This purity will be raised to the highest peak by those perpetual objects and incentives most worthy of admiration; it will be subject to no vicissitudes or changes of men or times, but will be constant, sincere, and enduring forever.

**3.**) Although, moreover, as is clear from what has been said, there will be some perpetual increase of science in heaven, there will nevertheless be no place for vain ostentation, no place for bitter controversies, and no place for **literary wars**. <note>original: *bellis literariis*. The author refers to the "Republic of Letters" where scholars often attacked each other's work with great vitriol.</note> Whatever the Blessed know will not be vague or of little profit, much less...

4.) There will be no place here for sects, nor for those evils that arise from them among mortals; everyone will depend on one infallible Teacher and leader, Jesus Christ, from whom they will receive the purest doctrine, obscured by no ambiguities of words or technical terms of the schools. And although there will be different degrees of future glory, and therefore also of knowledge, there will nevertheless be no strife or rivalries among the blessed minds for that reason. For in this place, the favor of brothers is not rare as it is on earth, but they are joined by the closest bond of spirits. Here there will be one **analogy of faith**, one formula of **concord and consensus** <note>The "Analogy of Faith" and "Formula of Concord" were vital 16th and 17th-century theological concepts regarding how to interpret scripture and maintain church unity.</note>, namely, a perpetual and most ardent zeal for celebrating God. No colleges will be held here against brothers, no councils in which those who are greater in number, or protected by the authority of princes, might oppress others; but rather counsels, or rather conversations, tending only toward promoting the love of God and the benefits of the heavenly society. They will have no fight against foolish zealots and false brothers, nor any necessity imposed upon them to defend their reputation and standing, and no contest with heretics. In this city of peace, there will be no "Inquisitors of Heretical Depravity," as they are called—who will dwell in entirely different places, namely, foul and gloomy ones; no political theology <note>The author uses "political theology" here in a negative sense, meaning the manipulation of religious doctrine to suit the whims of rulers.</note>, that is, a constant effort to change and fashion religious opinions at the nod of others, will find a place here: but only pure love, pure candor, and a truly incredible zeal for the truth.

5.) Nor will the small bodies with which these purest minds will be clothed pose any obstacle to their happiness. For they will not be subject to fragility, but will be similar to the glorious body of Christ. Therefore, there will be no place for weakness, diseases, or torments; no labor for those perfected theologians in **earning their bread** <note>original: *de pane lucrando labor*—referring to the mundane struggle to make a living through academic or church work.</note>; no anxious or sordid cares; no worry about nourishing a family; no canvassing to obtain a position; no complaints about the persecutions of colleagues; no lamentations over the oppression of the liberty of conscience, or over proscriptions and exiles; but rather, with mind and body throughout an unending eternity, with the highest and incredible pleasure, joy, and singular gladness—all enemies of happiness having been prostrated and conquered—they will exult entirely in celebrating the praises of the divine Power. This joy will reach its highest peak when, at the consummation of the age of grace, after the conversion of the Jews and Gentiles, the entire assembly of the saints, gathered from all corners of the earth, will be able to sing nothing but pure hymns in the sacred and innumerable praises of God and the King, who has been raised to the high-

-est dignity; and they shall do so without any shifts in time, without any mixture of sorrow or weariness, with the entire choir of Apostles, Prophets, Martyrs, and all the pious who triumph. O truly theological life, or rather, most divine! O most beautiful face of this sacred city! O glorious day, when we shall set out for that council and assembly of divine souls, and when we shall depart from this crowd and filth!

Then, surely, at last, drenched in that eternal light, we shall recognize how much darkness our current day lay under; then we shall know accurately what it is to truly <term>Theologize</term> <note>original Greek: *Θεολογειν*—to speak of or study God.</note>: then the mind possesses the perfected and full good of the human lot, when, having trampled every evil, it seeks the heights and enters into the inner heart of nature; then it is a joy, while wandering among the stars themselves, to laugh at the floors of the wealthy and the whole earth with its gold.

It is no wonder, therefore, that learned men—mindful of the weakness and imperfection of theological matters, and well aware of the troubles that are very often joined with these disciplines on earth—were touched by a certain weariness of this life as well as its labors, and hastened with incredible desire toward that blessed Academy. Certainly Philip Melanchthon, a learned man well-versed in theological disciplines and the "Common Teacher of all Germany," a few days before his death, recorded the reasons why death should be less dreaded on a small page, in this manner:

> On the **left side** was written: *You will depart from sins; you will be freed from miseries and from the rage of theologians* <note>original: *rabie Theologorum*. This became a famous quote among scholars who were exhausted by the bitter religious infighting of the Reformation.</note>; on the **right side** truly: *you will come into the light, you will see God, you will gaze upon the Son of God, you will learn those wonderful secrets which you could not understand in this life: why we were created as we are, what the union of the two natures in Christ is like, etc. etc.*

But I must pull in the sails of this oration and hasten toward the end, and show in a few words what remains by way of application or conclusion: what power this established comparison between the knowledge of divine things held by **Wayfaring Theologians** <note>original: *Theologorum Viatorum*—a traditional term for Christians still on their earthly journey toward heaven.</note> and that of the blessed minds in heaven ought to have on the spirits of both students and teachers, and indeed on all of us.

To you, therefore, I first turn, most distinguished students, and I ask that you lend me your attentive ears. There will perhaps be some among you who think that what has been said about the imperfect knowledge of theological disciplines, and the difficulty of things to be known, could lead minds away from the persistent study of seeking the truth, and [encourage] negligence...

It highlights Philip Melanchthon's famous deathbed reflection on escaping the "rage of theologians" as a motivation for looking toward the afterlife.</summary>

<sig>Vvvvvv 3</sig>

...those who do not even know what it means to "know." Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BCE) was a Roman statesman and philosopher. His skeptical approach to certain knowledge was often cited by later writers to encourage humility.</note> rightly says: *How fine a thing it is to prefer to confess what you do not know, rather than to vomit forth such nonsense and be displeased with yourself.* And elsewhere: *From among the other philosophers (to whom we rightly add "theologians"), does not every best and most serious man confess that he is ignorant of many things, and that there are many things he must learn over and over again?*

If, therefore, there is such a vast multitude of things to be learned—and if, even when every effort, diligence, and attention is applied, our knowledge remains profoundly imperfect—would it not be ridiculous and foolish to carry oneself with high spirits because of the slight and clearly confused knowledge of various things that we possess in this life? Certainly, you have not yet reached true learning and wisdom if you think highly of yourselves because of some outward show of erudition, or if you "raise your crests" <note>An idiom meaning to act with pride or arrogance, like a rooster.</note> whenever the opportunity arises.

Above all, let those who cultivate the "holier disciplines" <term>theology</term> take this saying to heart. I ask you not to wonder at the fact that those things taught publicly and privately concerning God—His attributes, His decrees, His will, and the mysteries of the Christian religion—are known so very imperfectly by both us and you. If you have meditated seriously on these matters, the very nature of the subjects does not allow our theological knowledge to equal the clarity of geometry. Nor will you easily find such certainty elsewhere; even a tiny speck of dust <note>original: *pulvisculus*</note> can convict the most learned man of his own ignorance and the narrow limits of our knowledge. Is it any wonder, then, that we are ignorant of many things regarding divine matters?

Lest you think that I, perhaps being insufficiently skilled in this discipline, am unable to discuss this argument accurately, I will bring forward the words of a theologian and philosopher who is, in everyone's judgment, most sharp and learned: Samuel Werenfels <note>Samuel Werenfels (1657–1740) was an influential Swiss professor of theology in Basel, known for advocating for a more "reasonable" and less dogmatic approach to faith.</note>. He is now counted among the choir of blessed minds in heaven, but I am accustomed to frequently recommending his writings to you, and I shall not cease to recommend them as long as I live.

This most excellent man, after he had disputed at length regarding atoms and their nature, and had shown that we do not even know what an "atom" or a "monad" <term>monas: a fundamental, indivisible unit of existence</term> truly is, finally broke out into these words, which you should weigh carefully:

*Learn modesty here, O man—you to whom your own mind seems to be the measure of all things, and who boldly claims that whatever you do not comprehend (or, what is even more foolish, whatever you cannot even imagine) does not even exist. Whatever the infinite God says about His own infinity, you do not believe. Why? "I do not understand," you say. O insane voice! Exercise your industry; exercise that insight to which you attribute so much upon this tiny speck of dust; you will see how far your sharpness can penetrate. Then at last, exhausted by meditating, inquiring, and searching, when you have seen how little progress you have made, come and reflect thus with yourself: if I know so little about the smallest things...*

It cites Cicero and Samuel Werenfels to humble those who are arrogant about their learning, using a "speck of dust" as a metaphor for the limits of the human mind.</summary>

*If I know that there are innumerable things whose essence, quality, and manner I do not perceive, how far I am from the knowledge of the infinite! In this darkness, what other path is safer than to submit the mind to the infinite mind, to believe and hold those things revealed by it, and never to wander outside them.*

But if the advice of the *Polyhistor* <note>original: "Polyhistoris." A term for a person of exceptionally wide learning or a "universal scholar."</note> pleases you more, hear *Joseph Scaliger* <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609) was a leading French religious scholar and historical critic.</note> speaking on the occasion of the unfortunate disputes over predestination in the Netherlands, which arose at the beginning of the last century:

> *Do not curiously seek the causes of all things,*
> *Whatever the breath of heaven has placed in the books*
> *Of the Prophets, full of the truthful God;*
> *Do not dare to break through what is covered*
> *By the veil of sacred silence, but wisely pass it by.*
> *To wish to be ignorant of what the best Teacher*
> *Does not wish to teach, is a learned ignorance.* <note>original: "erudita inscitia." This concept suggests that recognizing the limits of human reason regarding divine mysteries is itself a form of high wisdom.</note>

Finally, you ought to learn this above all from our established comparison: namely, that true piety must be joined early to the study of genuine wisdom. The entrance to the heavenly Academy is open only to a purified mind. The profane—no matter how well-equipped they are with the tools of the disciplines—will be kept far from this most holy assembly of blessed minds.

The chief part of future happiness, as you have heard, will consist in the most tender and burning love of God, which usually flows like water from a most pure spring out of the continuous and most holy contemplation of divine virtues. Therefore, do not separate those things which ought to be joined. Any kind of erudition is mere play-acting if it is devoid of true piety, in which the highest peak of wisdom consists. Therefore, finally bring it about that people believe and feel that those who devote themselves to the study of the best literature—especially the holier studies <term>theology</term>—turn out not only learned, but wise and pious. Surely a rustic or a commoner, equipped with a modest but saving knowledge of religion and set on fire with a sincere love for the best Divinity, is to be preferred by far to the most learned and famous *Polyhistor* who is empty of true piety. For the former possesses in abundance everything that can lead to true tranquility of mind and a fixed, firm hope of attaining salvation; the latter, when he reaches his end, must rest in the sterile knowledge of various things that will profit him little, and in the shadow of vain praise.

But also to you, *Reverend Brothers and Fathers*, who in this illustrious

our school <note>original: "gymnasio." What, therefore, we must attempt above all and bring about with all our strength, you yourselves see. We should dwell long on the most momentous matters, but linger little on the less necessary ones. We should teach nothing that it would have been better not to know, or that would have made no difference to us to have known. I would not want this understood, *Brothers*, as if I wished to neglect those things which contribute greatly to the ornament of theological study or to a more accurate knowledge of the same; not at all. I am no *Patron of laziness* or supporter of *the ignorance of brothers*. But this one thing I want: that those who perform the office of Doctors always look with focused eyes upon the chief end of sacred erudition. I confess that students of Holy Letters must have time for the humanities, philosophy, sacred and civil history, the critical art, and finally a knowledge of the articles of religion—not only our own, but also of those Christians who disagree with one another. Yet, if we wish to speak the truth, we must not labor so much so that students of theology turn out to be *Philologists, Philosophers, Orators, or Historians*, and men practiced in the art of debate, as much as they should be *Men of God*. They should be *Men* equipped with an excellent knowledge of God and divine things; *men* set on fire with the most burning zeal of piety; *men* prepared to perform every good work; and finally, *men* who can deliver the most holy heads of Religion clearly and solidly not only to the learned, but also to the common people. To obtain this, however, not all the controversies which disputatious men rashly devise...

one should not dwell for long on what [past thinkers] have devised, nor should all dogmas of theologians be treated with equal zeal. One should not prolixly refute heresies that were defended several centuries ago but are now neglected, or at least those of which not even a hundredth of our listeners have any knowledge—much less is there any danger that they would lend their ears to such empty errors. Certainly, teachers who are so perversely industrious in this business seem to me like a hunter who would arm his dogs early against lions and bears in a region where no lions or bears are found, nor have ever been found. One must dwell for long only upon the most serious and useful matters, which are most certainly joined with the hope of eternal salvation; indeed, we should not rest until we have fixed these things in the minds of our listeners so firmly that they are not only able to discuss those matters aptly, but are also fully convinced and persuaded of them!

Our listeners must be fortified especially against the daily increasing vice of incredulity; against those who mock religion with "white teeth" <note>original: "albis dentibus rident." A Latin idiom meaning to mock or sneer openly.</note>; or against those who say it makes no difference what religion you profess. We must fortify them against the disciples of *Machiavelli*—that is, those who think that religion should be tempered according to the laws of cities, the circumstances of persons and times, and finally, their own advantages. They must be fortified against those who pursue a certain masked shadow of piety and think that all religion is fulfilled by external worship and the performance of the duties of a good citizen; against carnal security, which is no less an enemy to piety and the salvation of men than the most pestilential heresies; against prejudiced opinions about religion; and against the pursuits of so many men immersed in vices: alas, our degenerate Christianity! Finally, they must be fortified against pestilential decrees contrary to the precepts of our Holy Savior <note>original: "S. Soteris." From the Greek 'Soter,' meaning Savior.</note>, which are accustomed to undermine his most holy discipline, whether openly enough or through hidden tunnels. These things, I say, are to be repeated, urged, and fixed in the schools and temples. The unhappiness of our times, alas, demands that these things be urged.

->This is the chief duty of a public teacher and a minister of<-
->the Divine Word.<-

Furthermore, this weakness of our mind in knowing divine things calls to our memory another duty, *Brother Men* most closely joined in Christ our Lord: namely, *the study of a moderate mind in judging the opinions of those who dissent from us regarding the business of religion.* You have heard how difficult it is, in such a great abundance of things and controversies, to know everything rightly and always to discern the truth accurately from the false; and how easily error creeps into the mind of even the best man and the greatest lover of truth.

---

<page-num>1081</page-num>
<header>HEAVENLY KNOWLEDGE COMPARED WITH OURS. 1081</header>

We are not always hindered by our passions from seeing and defending the truth, but often a false concept or the difficulty of comprehending the things themselves stands in the way. No one errs willingly. Let us therefore distinguish the weight of an error, and let not every error or disagreement immediately seem dangerous to us. While we wander outside the heavenly Academy, no one is without error <note>original: "ἀναμάρτητος" (anamartētos). A Greek term meaning 'err-less' or 'sinless.'</note>; we will be men subject to doubts and errors while we dwell in these lands. There is no infallible judge on earth, and we hiss off the stage <note>original: "explodimus." Literally 'to hiss off' as in a theater.</note> and call "Antichrist" the one who boasts that he is such in his own court. 

Provided, therefore, that a brother's error is not lethal, but is of such a kind that even the most innocent person might fall into it—and which can easily coexist with the love of Jesus Christ our Holy Savior, and was never held as damnable by Him or the Apostles—it must be borne patiently. We should follow the example of our Lord Jesus Christ himself, who alone can save and condemn. For he bore with a calm mind the errors which his disciples had cherished out of ignorance before the pouring out of the Holy Spirit. *Seneca* says, "We treat diseases, we do not get angry at them"; and indeed, this is a disease of the mind, which requires a gentle medicine, and one that is least hostile to the patient. 

Therefore, although there might perhaps be a divorce of opinions among you regarding certain tiny points—about which it was always permitted to disagree without breaking friendship—since you are endowed and adorned with different talents, judgment, and reading, and are more or less devoted to this or that teacher; nevertheless, it should suffice that you all agree in the purest discipline of Jesus Christ and in the necessary things, which by the judgment and consensus of all learned theologians are the most serious. The Apostle Paul himself, although bathed in divine light far greater than ours, warned us to act in this way in the first letter to the Corinthians, chapter 13:

> *Love (he says) never fails; whether prophecies will be done away, or tongues will cease, or knowledge will be destroyed. For we know in part, and we prophesy in part. But when that which is perfect comes, that which is in part will be done away. When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I thought as a child. But when I became a man, I did away with the things of a child. For now we see through a glass darkly, but then face to face. Now I know in part, but then I shall know even as I am known.*

It is helpful to pluck and present to you some things relevant to this from a commentary on this passage by a certain very famous man, who is not the least among the learned interpreters of Holy Scripture. Among other things, this most learned man speaks thus:

> *Paul teaches excellently, by a comparison drawn from childhood and manhood, that there will be only a very small difference between this current learning of ours, whatever it may be, and that...*
