<page-num>1082</page-num>
<header>THEOLOGICAL KNOWLEDGE OF THE BLESSED</header>

*...which is to come in heaven, is as far apart [from our own] as the opinions of children are from the expertise of men regarding the things of this life. Therefore, even if we are puffed up with pride, we must admit that the vast theological learning of mortals in these lands, when compared with that of the Angels or with that which will one day belong to the blessed, is plainly childish. We would laugh at a child who—to say nothing of the greater errors of childhood—thought he clearly understood things we see him knowing most imperfectly, and who therefore applauded himself. So too, if it is right to speak this way, those blessed minds—who are much more superior to us than we are to little children—laugh when they hear us speaking boldly and haughtily about things we do not know, except like one who sees, or thinks he has seen, the moon through the clouds.* <note>original: "videt aut vidisse putat per nubila lunam" - a poetic reference to Virgil's Aeneid VI.454, describing the difficulty of seeing the truth in darkness.</note> *Certainly, they pity us for our blindness and ridiculous pride in the midst of such ignorance. If we should happen to see children first arguing among themselves about childish opinions, and then coming to blows, fighting with the fiercest boxing they can manage; we cannot help but be angry with them, because they fight so much for their age over something that neither of them knows. But what do we think the Angels think when they see grown men or old men raging against each other—no longer with fists, but with laws, edicts, exiles, and punishments of every kind—on account of many things that are either entirely or partly unknown to them? Indeed, they judge them to be not just children, but naughty children worthy of the whip. When those invisible observers of our deeds notice men who want to be considered grave and serious, babbling day and night about things they do not know, disputing among themselves first privately and then openly; then writing back and forth, fighting with hostile pens, and later forming factions to see how many agree with them, so that their partisan opinion suffers no loss in that corner of the earth where they have the most power; and finally, having called others (whether men or children, I cannot say) together in a more solemn manner to establish laws about things they are ignorant of, as if thrusting divine laws upon others like themselves, and harassing those who disagree by every means; when the Angels, I say, notice these things, what do we think their state of mind is? It is nearly the case that they would disrupt not just our games, but our tragedies, and immediately punish those blind men who rage against other blind men. And they would do so, if the supreme Judge of the Games* <note>original: "ἀγωνοθέτης" (agonothetes) - the superintendent of public games in ancient Greece, here referring to God as the ultimate arbiter.</note> *did not command them to wait until He Himself brings judgment upon all these things, and separates the proud and cruel from the modest and gentle. In the meantime, perhaps those blessed Spirits, lovers of our kind, warn us—not indeed with a voice that strikes the ears, but with silent whisperings, so to speak, into our souls—that mindful of our ignorance, we should restrain our judgment for a little while, until in a few years we know the matter thoroughly, when God calls us from this life and reveals in clear light the truth which we now seek in vain in these shadows. Thus far says that most learned man.*

<page-num>1083</page-num>
<header>IN HEAVEN COMPARED WITH OUR OWN.</header>

Lest anyone, however, take these words in a bad way contrary to my intent, I will explain for what purpose they were brought forward and where my discourse is heading. Namely, I am pointing my finger at those unfortunate disputes that have arisen among those who made their separation from the Roman Church not without bloodshed, and who go by the common name of *Protestants*. You know what things especially stand in the way of our merging into one assembly and rushing into mutual embraces; namely, certain sublime opinions, difficult to grasp, hedged in by much darkness, and certainly placed beyond the reach of the common people; to put it in a word, dissensions regarding the manner and nature of divine predestination <term>predestination: the theological doctrine concerning God's foreordained plan for the salvation of souls, a major point of contention between Reformed and Lutheran Christians.</term> place an obstacle. To settle these, from the very beginning of those unfortunate disputes, the Ministers of the Church of Zurich <note>original: "Ecclesiae Tigurinae" - Zurich was historically referred to by the Latin name Tigurum.</note> have spent their efforts; they would have wished to redeem with their own blood that most unfortunate dissent, of which we see no end even now after the truces offered by so many most learned men. If we wish to be children of peace, we must do the same. Certainly, that oration alone—to say nothing of the testimonies of other Zurich theologians collected by the learned—of our Great *Bullinger* <note>Heinrich Bullinger (1504–1575), the successor to Zwingli in Zurich and a major figure in the Reformation known for his moderate stance.</note> regarding the moderation to be maintained in the doctrine of providence and predestination, ought to move us (unless we wish to be degenerate children of such great men) to contribute whatever learning, piety, and wisdom is in us to removing those discords and suppressing contentions that will have no triumphs. I know that you all regard the *Lutherans* as brothers, and even in the public prayers held every week, you pray to God that He may unite the minds of both parties. What is more fair or more consistent with the nature of this business than that we studiously avoid everything that could alienate their minds from us? This will happen if we do not judge bitterly those errors which they think are certain truths: if we say they are such that, despite them, friendship and the tightest bond of brotherly love can remain safe between us. It will happen if we bear with a calm mind a brother who is perhaps devoted to one or two opinions that they cherish, especially if he is learned, pious, and peaceful; if we always remember that we did not depart from the Roman Church on account of some abstruse opinions, but for the gravest reasons and something far greater. The most celebrated man Johann Heinrich *Hottinger* <note>A 17th-century Swiss scholar and theologian from Zurich.</note> records somewhere that in the early times of the Reformation, there was such agreement of minds among the public teachers and Ministers of the Word in Zurich as could ever be obtained in the Church Militant <term>Church Militant: the Christian church on earth, which is seen as being at war with sin and the devil, as opposed to the Church Triumphant in heaven.</term>. What stands in the way, my most closely joined Brothers and Fathers in Christ, of us also joining...

<meta>This page continues the exhortation for theologians and believers to move away from petty, childish disputes toward a theology of charity and peace, which better reflects the perfect knowledge of the blessed in heaven.</meta>

<page-num>1084</page-num>
<header>THEOLOGICAL KNOWLEDGE OF THE BLESSED</header>

with all our strength let us strive toward that same happiness. We shall most certainly obtain it if, mindful of our own ignorance and weakness, we frequently weigh the magnificent praises that our most gentle Savior <note>original: "Soter"</note> Jesus Christ and his Apostles bestow upon charity and mutual love. Certainly, in extolling this virtue, Paul—doubtless the most excellent Theologian—hardly satisfies himself. Let us, therefore, root out from our souls whatever might stand in the way of this moderate and truly Christian pursuit of peace: things such as sinister suspicions, rivalries, ambition, false zeal, and trust rashly given to gossips. Whatever we possess in terms of learning, talent, or zeal, let us contribute it toward nurturing and spreading true charity among ourselves. Thus, while still on earth, let us display a certain image or prelude—however imperfect—of that heavenly society which will take place among the blessed minds.

Finally, my Brothers, let us act with every effort of our strength to excite in the souls of others a most burning desire for heavenly things. This will happen if we frequently place before our listeners the dignity of the Christian religion, the admirable power and excellence of the divine precepts, the weight of the divine promises, the vanity of the sciences without the pursuit of piety, and the joys of future true happiness. It will happen if our Theology is not separated from Religion—that is, if we teach nothing but what is useful, serious, and the knowledge of which will endure in the heavens. It will happen if that same Theology is not gloomy, bristling <note>original: "hirsuta" — literally "shaggy," referring here to dry, overly technical academic writing</note> with useless distinctions and petty questions, but is instead simple, pure, and lovely; so much so that all who have a taste for true praise, and are touched by any sense of divine things, cannot help but love Religion. This is certainly our labor, this our care, this our business: that we might lead men away from earthly desires and pursuits and induce them to meditate upon and seek heavenly things with all their prayers. Let us show the youth and those studying the finest arts, early on, how lowly a thing man is unless he raises himself above human affairs; how serious a matter Religion is, and how worthy of attention. Finally, let us demonstrate not by words, but by work itself, that Religion has permeated all our veins, and that we were born not for the earth, but for the heavens.

But at last, all of you—of whatever rank, learning, status, or age you may be—have been able to learn from this meditation of ours what your greatest care on this earth ought to be, if indeed you wish to become partakers of true happiness. Doubtless, in this world, as soon as we begin to live and to be wise, we must think of the return to our Homeland <note>original: "Patria" — a common theological term for Heaven, the true home of the soul.</note>. The primary

primary care, therefore, ought to be that we live piously and die blessedly. This cannot happen without the knowledge and love of Religion. We are all bound to its worship—the greatest, the middle, and the lowest. The business of this life ought not to stand in the way of our concern for those things without which we can be truly happy neither on earth nor after our departure. Those very men who handle public affairs and sit at the helm of the Republic, even if I were silent, can easily gather from what has been said (given their wisdom) how much protection and ornament a solid knowledge of divine things, and the worship and love of Religion, brings to the governors of a State. It is certainly a gift of the immortal God to have a Prince or Ruler who is rightly knowledgeable in Religion and captured by its love. For such a man will have a solicitous care not only for the Republic but also for Religion. Thus he will easily distinguish the solid from the empty and weigh the gravity of controversies; thus he will cautiously and prudently protect the rights of conscience, which are superior to all human laws. In his wisdom, he will easily judge that a significant distinction must be made between those errors contrary to the doctrine of the Holy Savior and harmful to civil society, and those which human nature can hardly avoid—those which can be believed while preserving public peace, the foundations of Religion, and friendship among brothers. A Prince imbued with this solid knowledge of Religion and touched by its love will value most highly those who flourish not only in learning but also in the pursuit of a moderate mind and peace. He will not easily lend his ears to those driven by an uncontrollable zeal for insulting others, who love to turn pimples into ulcers <note>original: "ex pustulis ulcera facere" — an idiom meaning to make a mountain out of a molehill or to aggravate a small problem.</note> and to sound the trumpet for war in the middle of peace. For he knows beautifully that where the likes of Maresius <note>Samuel Des Marets (1599–1673), a famously contentious French Protestant theologian.</note> and Calovius <note>Abraham Calovius (1612–1686), a leading representative of rigid Lutheran Orthodoxy known for his polemics.</note> dominate, not even Salvation herself could save the schools, academies, and churches even if she wanted to; and that men of this temperament consult neither the progress of disciplines and sciences nor the public peace.

Such a Prince will gladly contribute whatever can promote true learning and the progress of the purest Religion. Since it is the mark of true wisdom and greatness of soul to believe that all greatness is placed in virtue, he will consecrate whatever time remains from public business to the cultivation of the most noble disciplines, especially sacred ones. He will feed his soul—often withdrawn from earthly business and the care of administering the Republic—with the meditation of divine and heavenly things (which the monuments of history teach us was done by the greatest princes and those who held the highest rank in cities). Thus he will prepare himself to obtain the heavenly Prize <note>original: "Brabeum" — from the Greek word for the award given to winners in a race.</note>, and his true

Let us, therefore, meditate on these things while our age flourishes and while the opportunity is given; let us prepare ourselves for this, let us think on this, and let us finally exercise ourselves toward this goal.

# THE AUTHOR’S WARNING
### TO THE READER.

A few things, Kind Reader <note>original: "B. Lector" — an abbreviation for "Benevole Lector," a standard greeting in early modern books</note>, before you hand over this speech, once read, to be eaten by moths and bookworms, you must be advised. And first, indeed, do not wonder that we commit here the error which schoolmasters are accustomed to call **the last thing first** <note>original: "hysteron proteron" — a logical or rhetorical fallacy where the natural order is reversed</note>, and cast to the end what perhaps should have been said at the threshold. For besides the fact that men daily do many things out of order—which, nevertheless, are not rarely praised by the wisest men—I had a sufficient reason why I should address you at the end, and not at the beginning; and this was necessity, which has no law. So that you may better understand this, I will explain the matter to you. After this Speech had been delivered, certain friends—and those most upright and learned—wished it to be given to the press for several reasons. At first, I had been unwilling to lend them a willing ear <note>original: "vacivas apres" — likely a printer's error for "vacuas aures," an idiom for being unresponsive</note>, being conscious of my own insignificance, and knowing that everything I had brought forward was well-worn, common, and had been narrated a hundred times more richly and eloquently by others. Finally, I yielded to their persistence,

<column-break/>

<page-num>1087</page-num>
<header>IN HEAVEN COMPARED WITH OUR OWN.</header>

hoping that this or that young man might gain some utility from reading it. But after the first two sheets <note>original: "philyræ" — literally the inner bark of a linden tree, used historically to mean sheets of paper</note> were published, various rumors spread here and there through the city reached my ears, along with judgments passed on the work, some more or less unfair than others. These things induced me to think that I should address you, Kind Reader, at the end. There were grave men, conspicuous in dignity, and wishing me well (as I know), who subjected my speech to censure—though I believe with a mind not at all evil—because they did not attend sufficiently to the scope of the entire Speech. With these men I easily return to favor, being persuaded that they are of a favorable mind toward me, and moreover lovers of equity in passing judgments; who, having heard the reasons and defense of my purpose, will without delay send all suspicions packing. But others, driven by passions and the hatred they bear toward the Author, wished not only to twist the aim of the Speech into a worse interpretation, but even to make the Author himself suspected of a very grave error. These people, although never harmed by me in any way, have for a long time now been accustomed to bite with a sharp tooth and bitterly criticize whatever is said or written by me. My ears have long since grown calloused to the bitter and often witless accusations of this kind of man. For their **lack of judgment** <note>original: "ἀκρισία" (akrisia) — an inability to discern or judge properly</note> and lack of self-control in judging matters of deeper investigation are well known to me. For what can you do with those who are either destitute of the faculty to weigh matters properly, or are so disturbed by the impulse of their passions that they refuse to hear the decrees of reason and the weight of the most serious truths? Meanwhile, I do not cease to ask God to instill in their minds Christian charity, without which—even if they were the most Orthodox (if only they always knew in what true Orthodoxy should be placed)—they cannot be disciples of our most gentle Savior <note>original: "Soteris"</note> Jesus Christ. May He grant it: for if they are once adorned with this charity, they will begin to judge their brothers more kindly. But if they continue to harm an innocent man, let them know that I will most fiercely defend the rights of an honorable Citizen and public Teacher as long as I live. However, he who contends with me modestly with arguments, as becomes learned men, and shows me some error, I will give him thanks and immediately change my opinion. I have never been harsh to advisors, nor have I ever stubbornly defended my opinions when taught better. Most learned and literary men can be witnesses to this, to whom, after hearing these little rumors, I gave the speech to be read again, and asked them that if I had indeed erred, they should warn me in a friendly manner. But, putting aside complaints, I come to those things which were objected against me. Various things were indeed brought to my ears, of which, however, this one thing...

...consideration, namely that some have contended that in my demonstration of the causes of our imperfect knowledge of divine things, I have progressed further than was fitting, and have not-so-obscurely patronized <term>theological skepticism</term> <note>original: "scepticismo theologico" — the philosophical position that certain knowledge in theology is impossible.</note>. A grave accusation indeed, if it were true! But it is easy to show that both the matter and the accusation are false. Therefore, for the sake of those who—though perhaps deceived by a misguided suspicion—are nonetheless accustomed to weigh the decrees of reason and the legitimate mode of defense with attention and <term>precision</term> <note>original: "ἀκρίβειαν" (akribeian) — a Greek term for exactness or strict accuracy.</note>, I offer the following considerations.

In the first place, for my defense, the judgments concerning this Speech by Men of excellent Erudition, piety, and sharpness of mind—who reviewed this meditation according to the laws of our city—ought to suffice. For these men, being well-equipped with both the eyes of the mind and the body, were in no way able to find the error imputed to me by my critics. Now, is it likely that Men endowed with such great virtues were either so stupid or so ignorant of divine matters that they could not detect a most blatant error after an attentive reading? Or would they have wished to approve with their vote an opinion that declares war on all piety? Would anyone reach such a level of impudence as to dare—I will not say to assert—but even to suspect such things of most learned and religious Men? Where on earth are we? And if "guards must be added to the guards," <note>original: "custodibus addendi sunt custodes" — a play on the famous Latin phrase by Juvenal, "Quis custodiet ipsos custodes?" (Who will guard the guards themselves?).</note> who will guard the guards themselves? Where, finally, are those infallible judges and censors who alone see clearly? Let these men truly beware lest, having rejected the Roman Pope, they set up six hundred (and then some!) infallible Doctors, and thus fall into the gravest <term>heterodoxy</term> <note>original: "Heterodoxiam" — beliefs that deviate from the standard or "orthodox" doctrine.</note>.

Furthermore, the speech of these men shrinks from every appearance of truth. For they not only strike me with a grave error and a mind plainly alienated from the love of the Christian Religion, but they also judge me to be a fool and out of my mind. For what—I call upon the conscience of all!—is further from the truth than this: that a Professor of Sacred Theology, devoted to the <term>Reformed Religion</term> <note>The Protestant tradition specifically associated with Zurich (Zwinglian) and Geneva (Calvinist).</note>, in a most crowded assembly of most learned and grave Men, and that too in <term>Zurich</term> <note>original: "Tiguri" — the Latin name for Zurich, Switzerland.</note>, would have seriously and from the heart wished to defend theological skepticism? Is it credible that such a person is of sound mind? But I, to use a Pauline phrase: **"Most Excellent Men, I am not mad."** <note>original: "Ἄνδρες Κράτιστοι οὐ μαίνομαι" (Andres Kratistoi ou mainomai) — quoting the Apostle Paul's defense before Festus in Acts 26:25.</note> Moreover, this censure is all the more unjust because I have never given anyone the occasion to suspect such things of me; rather, I have defended the truth of the Christian Religion to the best of my ability in many published works, and have attacked the arguments of unbelievers—

—and have so thoroughly recoiled from skepticism that I can say there is no theological thesis worthy of attention which I have not defended both publicly and privately. What, then, is more foreign to all laws of humanity than to accuse an Innocent and sensible defender of the Christian Religion of a most grave error based on mere suspicions? 

What of the fact that in the speech itself, before I proceeded to the causes of the imperfect knowledge of divine things (which are usually sought from the nature of sacred disciplines), I said in express words—as is clear from page 18—that I confess along with all Protestant Theologians: *Those things which are necessary to be known and understood for salvation are clearly and perspicuously revealed in the Holy Scriptures.* Does this prove that I wished to show that one could argue for either side <note>original: "utramque in partem" — a classical skeptical technique of arguing both sides of an issue to show neither can be proven.</note> regarding the Christian Religion? I would be a strange supporter of skepticism indeed! 

But, my Censors say: "I beg your pardon, your Protestation is contrary to your deed. For you have brought forward more causes of our ignorance than was necessary, and you have made our knowledge of divine things as imperfect as you could, further than the truth permits." 

I respond: 1.) Even assuming (though not granting) that I brought forward more reasons than was fitting to prove that we cannot know these or those things in divine matters, or that we know them very imperfectly; does it therefore follow that I favor skepticism? For what kind of logic is this? "This person thinks we know fewer things about divine matters than others think; therefore he asserts we are plainly blind in divine matters; therefore he believes all things are uncertain, and that one can argue either side regarding Religion?" 

Surely, just as it does not follow that we can know all things from the fact that we know many things about divine matters; so likewise, it is poorly concluded that we can affirm nothing at all about those same matters from the fact that we are ignorant of many things. But if my Censors know more than I believe we are able to know, do I deserve a beating for that? Have I not rather earned their mercy than their anger? *If I am a child in knowledge, perhaps I am nonetheless a child of good hope,* who in due time may turn out to be just as much a learned Man as my Censors are; for with age, we understand all things more rightly. Something should therefore have been granted to my lack of experience: "day teaches day," <note>original: "dies diem docet" — a Latin proverb meaning we learn more as time goes on.</note> and as I have not been a plainly lazy man thus far, so there is hope that, moved by the examples of my most Erudite censors, I will finally lay aside my shameful ignorance.

2.) When I said in my speech that Theologians disagree among themselves on these or those points, this is not to be understood as if the matter itself, about which they do not agree in every respect, cannot be known at all...

...it happens; but this only proves that the disputes of theologians show either that the matter itself, about which they disagree, has not been brought to such a degree of evidence that no room is left for doubt or obscurity; or that some prefer to cling to prejudiced opinions rather than to truths supported by a great degree of probability.

3.) In this Oration, it is not a matter of these or those controversial articles among Christians, but at least of the *degrees of knowledge* regarded in themselves. There are many things which we do not know, yet our piety remains safe and our *Religion* remains safe. Nevertheless, if we knew these things more perfectly and joined them with the truths already known, our knowledge of divine things would undoubtedly be more solid. In a word: I wished primarily to show what we know *imperfectly*, but not to assert that we can know nothing of the things necessary to be known, much less to affirm that we can dispute on either side of theological matters.

4.) My Censors ought to have properly attended to the principal goal of my Oration. For I was acting so as to show how blessed and happy the future state of the Blessed will be, and how much knowledge of divine things the pious are to obtain after death. To accomplish this, therefore, it was necessary not only to show how imperfect our knowledge of divine things is in these lands, but also to reveal the causes of the major impediments to progress. The things said by me have long been noted here and there by wise and <term>orthodox</term> <note>original: "orthodoxis" — meaning those who hold the "right opinion" or standard church doctrine.</note> theologians. However, the scope of this Oration required that the principal causes of the imperfect knowledge of divine things be presented to the minds of the Audience all together. And from this, I think it happened that certain men, by no means unlearned nor wishing me ill, were offended upon hearing various causes of our imperfection thrown together as if into one heap; yet, if they had attended better to the whole thread of the oration, they would have interpreted my words in a kinder light.

Finally, 5.) let my Censors see to it that, while they do not wish to be skeptics, they do not incautiously cross over into the camps of either the <term>Papists</term> <note>original: "Pontificiorum" — a term used by Protestants to refer to Roman Catholics loyal to the Pope.</note> or the Deists, by thinking that any support for skepticism follows from that imperfect knowledge of divine things described by me. The Deists, because of the difficulties occurring in the Christian Religion, the various opinions into which Christians are split, and the diverse interpretations of theologians, cry out that only the decrees of reason are to be heard; the Papists, however, because of these very difficulties, believe it is necessary to flee to an infallible judge. But Protestants safely sail past this <term>Scylla and Charybdis</term> <note>A classical metaphor for two equal dangers: Scylla was a many-headed monster and Charybdis a whirlpool. Navigating between them means finding a safe middle path.</note>, asserting among other things that those things which are necessary to know for salvation

<meta>are clearly...</meta>

...are clearly contained in Revelation. This is the very thing I asserted. But if, notwithstanding this, a certain protection for Skepticism arises from it—from which my Censors profess themselves to be most alienated (which I would easily grant, given the talent and erudition with which they are endowed)—they must either addict themselves to one of the two mentioned factions, or confess that they have hitherto been ignorant of what the nature of <term>theological skepticism</term> consists of. I even more willingly believe the latter, and I think they should be absolved on that account from all open and voluntary <term>Heterodoxy</term> <note>original: "Heterodoxia" — holding beliefs that differ from the established or standard doctrine.</note>.

I am firmly persuaded that learned Men, previously seized by a certain unnecessary anxiety, after reading and weighing these things, will judge more rightly of my words and mind, and will interpret my words in a better light.

But for those who admit no reasons and do not care for the rights of a legitimate defense, but, carried away by their emotions, can do nothing else but pluck at their betters, I pray for a sound mind. Farewell, Benevolent Reader, and favor our endeavors.

### AGAINST THE DREAD OF VOID <note>original: "In Fugam Vacui" — literally "the flight from the vacuum," but here likely a title for a new section addressing the fear of leaving any theological question unanswered.</note>.

I would dare to confirm that the greater part of both Ancient Heresies and present disagreements in the Church was and is born primarily from this: that Councils, Bishops, and Doctors of the Church, with no discrimination, *hawked any scholastic dogmas and opinions of the chairs as articles of the catholic faith*, and imposed them upon consciences as necessary to be believed for salvation. From any discrepancy in the interpretation of the scriptures, they too easily made heresies or schisms. The same author, after he distinguished between *articles of the Catholic faith* and *articles belonging to theological science*, continues thus: The difference between these articles is vast: *Indeed, the confusion of them has always existed in the Church as the fuel of all confusions and disturbances.* Ignorance of the <term>Catholic articles</term> <note>original: "Catholicorum articulorum" — referring here to "universal" Christian doctrines common to the whole church, not specifically Roman Catholic ones.</note> is damnable for everyone; doubt is dangerous; denial is heretical and impious. Ignorance of theological conclusions is not damnable for everyone, nor is doubt or denial always heretical or impious. Catholic articles are the foundation of faith and salvation; Theological conclusions are built upon the foundation, sometimes as *gold* and *silver*, sometimes as *chaff* and *stubble*. In Catholic articles are founded the consensus of the faithful, faith, hope, charity, and salvation. In Theological conclusions *there have always been some...*

# O R A T I O N
## CONCERNING
### The Secret Discipline of the Ancient Church, not to be used in our age. (*)

<image-desc>A large decorative drop-cap "Q" set within an ornate square frame featuring scrolled acanthus leaves and floral patterns.</image-desc>
It usually happens to most people who are led to speak—not of their own accord, but compelled by authority and laws—that they are not so much anxious about how to properly handle a specific argument, as they are about what they should choose above all else from such a vast abundance of very useful subjects. I cannot deny that this has also happened to me. For as soon as I was enjoined by the authority and command of the venerable Overseer of our Church to speak in this Illustrious Assembly of listeners, according to the custom of our ancestors, I was so disturbed by the manifold variety of excellent matters that presented themselves to my mind, and was drawn in so many different directions, that I was utterly wavering and doubtful as to where I should best fix my feet. I knew indeed that nothing should be brought forward in such a great gathering of excellent and learned men that would be unworthy of the authority of such great men, or foreign to this place and time, or finally, poorly suited and inappropriate to the persona I maintain and to my own strengths. However, this one thing kept my mind anxious and worried,

<header>ORATION ON THE SECRET DISCIPLINE</header>
<page-type>text</page-type>

I have deliberated at length on what specific kind of argument might best satisfy both your desires and my own duty. While my mind was being carried here and there in uncertainty, it occurred to me that I might not do poorly if I were to speak on *The Unhappiness of Scholars* <note>original: "Infelicitate Literatorum"</note>. Beyond the fact that I was led to handle this topic by a particular occasion, the dignity, utility, and pleasantness of the material itself invited me. Without delay, therefore, I applied my mind to meditation and writing. I divided the various causes of unhappiness with which the learned struggle into their respective classes and proved them with the examples of the most learned men of every age. My intention was to teach young men—those fired with a love of praise and the study of letters—that the true protection, honor, and rest of the mind must be placed and sought not in erudition alone, but most especially in virtue, integrity, and trust in God. However, while intent on this labor and meditation, various reasons came to mind which seemed of such weight to me that I preferred to yield to them and allow this labor, such as it was, to perish rather than to go against the decrees of right reason. To tell the truth, the principal reason that pulled me away from my undertaking while I was in the very middle of the work was this: I feared that, given the current scarcity and rarity of scholarly youth, those very individuals who are fired with an incredible love of letters might grow sluggish and lose heart entirely upon hearing about so many impediments to success and the unhappy fates of the most outstanding men. Since nothing can more strongly drive young men of noble character toward the study of wisdom and learning than hearing that virtue and right actions retain their honor and have their rewards laid up—that the path to honor lies open to all, and that glory is granted to virtue rather than to birth or certainly not to idleness—anyone can see that if so many arguments and examples to the contrary were brought forward, they would turn aside from the right path that leads to the serene temples of virtue and learning.

Yet it is the duty of a public teacher to strive with all his strength so that true, upright, and vigorous learning may take deeper and deeper root in the minds of his listeners and produce the most abundant fruit. Driven away, therefore, from this position and disregarding whatever labor I had spent, I took up a plan for another argument, one subject to no danger or sinister interpretation. But at that time, nothing occurred to me that truly appealed to my mind, whereupon I resolved to cast away all care and anxiety about delivering a speech, and to transfer this labor, whatever it might be, to another time or another state of mind,

and to return to my daily studies and my little books. It happened opportunely, however, that while I was fruitlessly worried, I stumbled while doing something else upon a certain small book by *Christoph Pfaff*, *Theologian and Chancellor of the University of Tübingen*. He is a man most celebrated not only for his distinguished and vast learning, but truly for his singular zeal—alas, brothers!—for reconciling those who disagree over certain minor questions (*). In this work, that most learned man was intent on teaching by what means a bridle might be placed upon either unbelieving and luxury-loving minds, or those less capable of sublime things (of whom, alas, there is a very great number in our age), so that they might be led to hear the decrees of right reason and Revelation. Among other most healthy counsels, that most learned man desires that in our age, to suppress this evil, the <term>Secret Discipline</term> <note>original: "Disciplina Arcani" — the ancient Christian practice of keeping certain higher doctrines and rituals, like the Eucharist, hidden from non-believers and new converts until they were fully initiated.</note> used by the ancient doctors of the Church should be brought back into use after a long absence. He believes that the itch by which the best minds are often carried away would be repressed, and the eagerness for handling the most sacred things with <gloss>unwashed hands</gloss> <note>An idiom meaning to approach a sacred or serious subject without proper preparation or reverence.</note> would be extinguished, or at least diminished. When I had weighed these things with myself and recalled to memory what I had read among the ancients and moderns on this subject, I thought it so far from the case that this *Discipline*, if restored to use, would be fit or suitable for removing or repressing this evil, that I persuaded myself instead that this very custom of the ancients was the cause of many errors and of the despising of our most chaste Religion. To that end, I decided without further delay to once again examine what I had formerly read on this argument, and in this very *gathering of most learned men*, to speak about this *Secret Discipline*, not out of a desire for contradiction, but out of a desire to speak the naked truth. The argument, which is sought from the innermost recesses of Ecclesiastical Antiquity, is worthy neither of the persona I sustain, nor perhaps even of the ears of most excellent men.

However, since account must be taken not only of time but also of order, I shall include the Oration within certain laws and boundaries. And...

# ORATION ON THE SECRET DISCIPLINE

...finally, I will reveal the character and *nature* of this *Secret Discipline*, and then its *Origin*. Next, I will proceed to the *reasons* which induced the Ancients to introduce this custom; I will not only show how little strength those reasons possess, but I will also bring to light the *various disadvantages* to which the practice was subject. From this, it will necessarily be concluded in the final section that this Discipline *is not to be restored for use* in our own age.

Distinguished Listeners, you now have the summary of the matters I intend to discuss. Perhaps the novelty of the subject itself will ensure that you lend me your attentive ears. For I easily notice that I lack all other things that might win an orator honor and goodwill. Whether I look to the speaker's authority or the splendor and ornament of eloquence, I see clearly that I am searching in vain. Indeed, I have known for a long time that my authority and reputation among most of you are either non-existent or very slight. You cannot expect eloquence from one who is more attentive to things than to words, and who has hitherto cultivated, for better or worse, the more severe philosophical and theological disciplines. Add to this that my entire system of Rhetoric, as far as I remember, consists of only two propositions. The *first* is this: an Orator should explain the argument he has undertaken so clearly and plainly that the listeners or readers cannot fail to understand it. The *second*: an Orator should persuade others of what he has set out to prove using either invincible and certain arguments, or at least those that are most plausible. Yet it is well known that the masters of the art of speaking demand far more than this. Nothing else is left to me, therefore, than to beg and request that you grant me your ears and your goodwill for at least one short hour—a courtesy you have granted to others who were no more powerful in speaking than I.

To finally make a beginning: by the *Secret Discipline* <term>Disciplina Arcani: A historical practice where early Christians kept certain rituals and doctrines hidden from non-believers to prevent mockery or to build a sense of mystery.</term> we understand nothing other than that custom of the Early Church by which they concealed certain Mysteries and rites of the Christian Religion from Pagans not yet initiated, from the lapsed <note>original: "lapsis" — Christians who had renounced their faith under persecution and were seeking reentry into the church.</note>, and from Catechumens <note>original: "Catechumenis" — students receiving basic instruction in the faith before being baptized.</note>. This was done, as they thought, to excite a greater reverence in their minds. They did not admit them to an accurate knowledge of these things before a certain period of training was completed. Here, however, it must be properly noted that we are not speaking of public writings or Confessions, but of the public exercise of Sacred rites and the instructions given to the people. For it is well known that the ancient Doctors of the Church not only explained the decrees of the Christian Religion publicly, but also

The published defenses by *Origen* and *Cyril* against *Celsus* and *Julian* <note>Two prominent pagan critics of early Christianity.</note> are witnesses; the public monuments by which they attacked the errors of the most ancient Heretics are witnesses; and finally, the controversies that arose in the 4th, 5th, and 6th centuries and those following are witnesses. In these, both sides argued vehemently concerning the divine origin of the Son, the *Incarnation* <note>original Greek: "ἐνσαρκώσει" (ensarkōsei) — the doctrine of God becoming flesh in Jesus.</note>, and other topics. However, the question is asked: did the Christians extend this Secret Discipline to all mysteries (for example, the doctrine of the Holy Trinity), or only to those sacred pledges of love, namely Baptism and the Holy Supper? On this point, the most learned men—*Casaubon*, *Albertinus*, *Tenzelius*, *Basnage*, and others—contend that only those external symbols of our communion with Christ (namely the bread and wine) were wrapped in the veil of silence, but not the nature of those symbols, much less the other chapters of the Christian Religion (*). To that end, they call upon all those passages from the most ancient Doctors in which they mentioned all the chapters of the Christian religion eloquently and directly. I will produce one witness in place of all: *Justin Martyr*, who in his *Second Apology* <note>Modern scholars usually identify this as his "First Apology," chapters 65-67.</note>, page 97 and following, having narrated the principal decrees of the most holy discipline, speaks thus of the Holy Supper:

> *After we have thus washed* <note>referring to Baptism</note> *the one who has believed and has been joined to us, we lead him to those who are called brothers, where they are gathered to offer common prayers and supplications with an intent mind, both for themselves and for the one who has been Enlightened* <note>original: "Illuminato" — a common early Christian term for the newly baptized.</note> *and for all others everywhere: so that we may be found worthy and fit, having recognized the truth, to be found as good citizens through our works. ...confirms, <note>original: "mat" — likely the end of "confirmat" from the previous page</note> saying: *Amen*. But after the President has finished the thanksgiving and the whole people has approved it with a joyful exclamation, those who are called among us Deacons and Ministers distribute to each of those present the bread, wine, and water over which thanks were given, so that they may participate in it, and they carry it to those who are absent. *Furthermore, this food is called among us the Eucharist: which no one else is permitted to participate in, except the one who believes our doctrine to be true and has been washed in the bath for the remission of sins and regeneration, and who lives as Christ handed down. For we do not receive these things as common bread; but just as Jesus Christ our Savior, having been made flesh through the word of God, had both flesh and blood for the sake of our salvation; in the same way, we have been taught that the food over which thanks have been given through the prayers of his word proceeding from him—by which our blood and flesh are nourished through a change—is the flesh and blood of that incarnate Jesus, etc.* <note>This is a famous passage from Justin Martyr’s First Apology, written around 155 AD, describing the early Christian ritual of the Lord's Supper.</note>

But neither this nor other passages cited by Learned Men prove that in public rites all the Mysteries of Religion were announced to everyone indiscriminately; rather, they show only this: that Christians in their public writings and Apologies <note>formal defenses of the faith</note>, in order to dispel the slanders of their enemies, explained the main points of their most holy discipline as clearly as they could. There are two things that lead me to think this way. The first is that the very reasons brought forward by the Teachers of the Ancient Church to recommend this Secret Discipline seem to necessarily require this interpretation; the second is that the clearest traces of this matter are found in the records of the ancients. 

Regarding the *first* point, as we shall hear at greater length below, the Christian Teachers recommending this Discipline appeal to the blindness of the human mind—yet bread and wine have nothing about them that makes them worthy of such a title <note>meaning bread and wine are simple things, so the "mystery" must lie in the deeper meaning hidden from outsiders</note>. It is added that they deliberately use allegorical terms to exalt the value of the things proposed. Nor is it credible that these Fathers thought the uninitiated would more easily understand the decrees concerning the eternal generation of the Son and his divine origin than the precepts concerning the Sacred Symbols and the rites used in their administration. Regarding the records of the ancients, it is well established that not only the mere rites used in the administration of the Sacraments were hidden, but also the very meaning of the thing itself and other Decrees of Religion. Let us prove this by a collection of testimonies. *Cyril of Jerusalem* in the Prologue of his Catechetical Homilies solemnly adjures the faithful not to hand over his book to Catechumens <note>students being prepared for baptism</note> or other Christians, otherwise they would render an account of the deed to God. In the Sixth Catechesis, the same man writes:

"Concerning the mysteries, when Catechumens are present, we do not speak clearly; but we often say many things in a veiled way, so that the faithful who know may understand." <note>original Greek: Περι μυστηριων ἐπι κατηχομενων λευκως οὐ λαλεμεν, ἀλλα πολλα πολλακις λεγομεν ἐπικεκαλυμμενως, ἱνα οἱ εἰδοτες πιστοι νοησωσι.</note> And this was the reason why the Pagans insulted the Christians. *Celsus*, that most bitter enemy of the Christians, for the sake of mockery calls the Christian Religion a "clandestine doctrine" <note>original Greek: Κρυφιον δογμα</note>. Origen, while in the process of diluting this slander, confesses that certain heads of doctrine are not communicated to everyone (*). *Lucian*, or whoever is the author of the Dialogue titled *Philopatris*, points his finger clearly at this when (in *Lucian’s Works* Vol. II. page 770 and following, *Graevius* Edition) Triephon orders *Critias* to swear by the God reigning on high, the Son of the Father, the Spirit proceeding from the Father, one out of three, and three out of one; *Critias* responds *that he does not understand what one-three and three-one is;* then in place of an explanation, Triephon, taking on the persona of a Christian and indeed a Catechumen (as expressly stated on page 773), adds: "Silence regarding the things below, and things worthy of silence," <note>original Greek: σιγα τα νερθε, και τα σιγης ἀξια</note> and a little later the same *Triephon* says: "*Being a Catechumen, allow yourself to be persuaded by me, if only you desire to live forever.*" And from this it happened that the uninitiated were only required to learn the Lord's Prayer and the Creed at the moment they were just about to be baptized. They brought forward this reason: that they had not yet obtained the gift of adoption <note>the belief that one only becomes a child of God, able to say "Our Father," through baptism</note>. (**) Hence *Chrysostom* so many times in his books repeats that phrase "the initiated know" <note>original Greek: ἰσασιν οἱ μεμυημενοι</note>. Above all, the testimonies in the writings of *Tertullian* on this subject are very clear; let us bring forward one or two. In his *Apology*, Chapter VII (page 81, *Havercamp* Edition), he is in the process of clearing away the detestable slanders of the Pagans concerning infanticide, Thyestean feasts <note>referring to pagan accusations that Christians ate babies, like the mythical Thyestes</note>, etc. Among other things, he speaks thus: "*If we are always hidden, when was that which we admit betrayed? Indeed, by whom could it have been betrayed?*"

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the "Secret Discipline" (Disciplina Arcani) of the early Church, specifically focusing on the historical testimonies from the Church Fathers regarding the intentional concealment of the sacraments from those who were not yet fully initiated members of the faith.</meta>

# ORATION ON THE SECRET DISCIPLINE

...for indeed, it is not by the accused themselves that secrets are revealed, since a pledge of silence is owed even by the very form of all mysteries. The rites of *Samothrace* and *Eleusis* <note>These were famous "Mystery Religions" of ancient Greece where secrets were kept under penalty of death.</note> are kept secret; how much more so should such things be, which, if betrayed in the meantime, would provoke human punishment while divine favor is preserved? If, therefore, they are not the betrayers of their own secrets, it follows that outsiders are. And how would outsiders gain knowledge, since even the most pious initiations always bar the profane and guard against spectators? In *Prescription against Heretics, Chapter 41*, Tertullian attacks them <note>The heretics</note>, saying: I will not omit the description of the heretical conduct itself, how frivolous, how earthly, how human it is: without weight, without authority, without discipline, as is consistent with their faith. Primarily, it is uncertain who is a *Catechumen* <note>A student of the faith not yet baptized.</note> and who is a *faithful* believer; they approach together, they hear together, they pray together. Even if Pagans should arrive, they will throw that which is holy to dogs, and pearls to pigs—though they are not true pearls (*). There is no doubt that the Ancients hid the Holy Supper and Baptism—that is, the nature of both. *Augustine* points this out clearly more than once. Thus, in his Commentary on *Psalm 103*, he says: "What is it that is hidden and not public in the Church?" He answers: "The Sacrament of Baptism, the Sacrament of the Eucharist. Our works are seen even by pagans, but the Sacraments are hidden from them." Hence that request of *Maximus of Madaura* <note>A pagan grammarian and philosopher.</note> in a letter given to *Augustine*: "I ask this of you, most wise man," he says, "that—removing the veneer of eloquence and discarding the brilliance for which you are famous to all, omitting even those arguments of Chrysippus <note>A Stoic philosopher known for complex logic.</note> with which you used to fight, and setting aside for a little while Dialectic, which strives to leave nothing certain by the wrestling of its own nerves—you prove by the facts themselves: who is that God whom

(*) Another passage of Tertullian exists in Book 2 *To the Nations*, chapter VII, where he speaks thus: "If, however, iniquity had left any place for prudence among us, it certainly required us to look into those from whom a rumor could be given to the common people and thus to the whole world. Not from the Christians themselves, I think, since a pledge of silence is owed even by the form and law of all Mysteries: how much more so for such things which, if betrayed, would not meanwhile escape immediate execution by human punishment? If, therefore, they are not the betrayers of themselves, it follows they are outsiders. I ask you, from where do outsiders get their knowledge? To be sure, the most learned Meyer, in his *Dissertation on the Hidden Theology of the Ancients*, Section XIV, page 720, contends that the cited passages do not prove that the Secret Discipline was in use in Tertullian's age. whom you Christians claim as your own, and whom you arrange to see present in hidden places." I pass over other passages that could be brought forward to prove that in the most ancient gatherings of Christians, not only the rites alone, but even the decrees of the Religion itself, were intentionally wrapped in silence by the Teachers. But it must be said a little more distinctly: whom they barred from those Sacred Rites and the perception of the Mysteries, whom they admitted, and what those not yet initiated had to attempt so that they might be prepared to hear the most holy things.

Among those whom they barred from the use and contemplation of those Sacred Rites, in the first place come *those outside* <note>original: "οἱ ἔξω" (hoi exō)</note>, "Outsiders," by which name not only men alienated from the profession of the Christian Religion are understood, but also Catechumens; the latter is clear from the words of *Cyril*: "When the Catechesis is recited," he says, "if a Catechumen asks you, 'What did the Teachers say?', *say nothing to the one outside* <note>original: "μηδὲν λέγε τῷ ἔξω" (mēden lege tō exō)</note>." In the second place, the Profane—that is, the uninitiated—must be referred to here. *Theodoret*, Question XV on Numbers: *We speak obscurely on account of the uninitiated concerning the divine mysteries.* <note>original: "ἀσήμως διὰ τοὺς ἀμυήτους περὶ τῶν θείων διαλεγόμεθα μυστηρίων" (asēmōs dia tous amyētous peri tōn theiōn dialegometha mystēriōn)</note>. Thirdly followed the Gentiles, and finally the Catechumens, to all of whom the approach to hearing the Mysteries was closed; the books of the Ancients and Moderns are full of these things. But those who were admitted were, in a word, the faithful, whom they also called *the Initiated*, *Mystics*, *the Perfected*, and *Beholders* <note>term: "Epoptas" — a Greek term for those who have reached the highest grade of initiation in a mystery religion.</note>. There are six hundred <note>A common Latin idiom meaning "countless."</note> testimonies of this matter in *Chrysostom*, *Cyril*, *Gregory Nazianzen*, and *Augustine*, which I will not write out for the sake of brevity. The method of hiding these Mysteries was twofold. The first is that by which they commanded the profane—that is, the uninitiated—to be far from the Mysteries. For that purpose, the Deacons would command the uninitiated to depart in a very loud voice. *Chrysostom* is a witness in Homily XVII on the Epistle to the Hebrews, saying: "The Deacon, standing in a higher place like a certain Herald, lifting his hands high with a great voice and terrible cry, calls some, forbids others, excludes some, and introduces others." Moreover, the Deacon used these formulas: *Walk outside, depart, go forward, as many as are uninitiated, as many as are catechumens, as many as are possessed by spirits, as many as are in penance.* <note>original: "ἔξω περιπατεῖτε, ἀπελθετε, προελθετε, ὅσοι ἀμύητοι, ὅσοι κατηχούμενοι, ὅσοι ἐνεργούμενοι, ὅσοι ἐν μετανοίᾳ"</note>. Nor did they only command them to leave, but also [guarded] the doors of the temples dili-

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the "Secret Discipline" (*Disciplina Arcani*), specifically exploring how the early Church Fathers intentionally used obscure language and strict stages of initiation to protect the sanctity of the sacraments from the uninitiated.</meta>

<page-num>1102</page-num>
# ORATION ON THE SECRET DISCIPLINE
<meta>catchword: discipli-</meta>

The Deacons were required to guard these matters diligently, and later the Subdeacons and Doorkeepers as well. *Chrysostom* testifies to this in his *Homily on Matthew*, as does the *Author of the Apostolic Constitutions* <note>A 4th-century collection of Christian precepts.</note> in Book II, Chapter 57. For this reason, *Jerome* and *Epiphanius* rebuke the Marcionites <note>A dualist heretical sect</note> because they celebrated the Mysteries while the Catechumens <note>Students training for baptism</note> were watching. A second method of concealment was that they would either remain completely silent about the Mysteries in the presence of those being initiated, or they would purposefully use an obscure way of speaking. Hence *Chrysostom* says in his 40th *Homily on 1 Corinthians*: *I certainly wish to speak of this openly, but I do not dare because of those who are not Initiated.* For they make the explanation more difficult for us, forcing us either not to speak clearly or to announce the secrets to them. *Epiphanius* in *The Anchored One*, section 57, speaking of the words of institution <note>The words "This is my body..."</note>, did not want to say in front of the Catechumens: *this bread is my body; this wine is my blood; but rather, "this is mine, this and that."* Compare the first and second *Dialogues of Theodoret*. To that end, they also used rather obscure terms when a sermon had to be given concerning the Sacraments. They commonly called the Sacraments *myseis* <note>original: μύσεις — initiations</note>, *teletas* <note>original: τελετάς — rites</note>, and *epopteias* <note>original: ἐποπτείας — contemplations</note>, specifically calling the Eucharist the *rite of rites* <note>original: τελετὴν τελετῶν</note>. They called Baptism *Anointing, Illumination, the garment of incorruption, the bath of regeneration, the splendor of souls, the casting off of the flesh, the flood of sin <note>The washing away of sin</note>, the communication of light, and the key to the heavenly kingdom*, to say nothing of other names. See *Casaubon’s* *Exercise XVI*, page 485 and following.

However, so that they might be admitted to this communion of the Mysteries, various kinds of training were necessary. The first step was *katharsis* <note>original: κάθαρσις — purgation or cleansing</note>, the second was *myesis* <note>original: μύησις — initiation</note>, and the third was *epopsia* <note>original: ἐποψία — perfect contemplation</note>. They called someone an *epopten* <note>original: ἐπόπτην — an observer or beholder</note> who possessed a perfect knowledge of the Mysteries and Sacraments, as far as was possible. Regarding the span of time, the discipline of the Ancients varied. Naturally, they treated those who wished to join the Christian religion differently than they treated the "lapsed" <note>Christians who had renounced their faith under persecution and sought to return</note>. The former had to run a shorter course before they could break bread with the brothers. First, therefore, they became *Catechumens*, then *Candidates* <note>original: Competentes</note>, and finally *Faithful* and *Christians*. But as for the lapsed, the ancients for the most part applied five stages. The *First* was that for three years (usually) they stood at the entrance of the Church, separated from the faithful and the Catechumens, performing penance in squalor. The *Second* was that for several years they might at least hear the reading of the Holy Scriptures. The *Third* was that, only after a certain span of time was completed, they might participate in public prayers. The *Fourth* was that they were considered similar to the rest of the faithful, except for the communion of the Holy Eucharist. The *Fifth* and final stage was that they held the right of partaking in the Holy Supper, which they were accustomed to call *perfection* <note>original: τελείωσιν</note> and *communion of the good things* <note>original: κοινωνίαν τῶν ἀγαθῶν</note>. Of this discipli—

—discipline, while *Isaac Casaubon* <note>A famous classical scholar (1559–1614)</note> mentions it regarding the lapsed, he breaks out into these words in *Exercise XVI*, page 487: *Regarding the lapsed, the discipline was severe and utterly admirable; to have spent effort in calling it back into use would undoubtedly be a thing more pleasing to God than to dispute subtly about the dogmas of faith outside of the scriptures and to pursue all dissenters with fire and sword, which today is placed at the very peak of piety.* Let those more learned than I judge what value should be placed on these words. Otherwise, regarding this discipline for the lapsed, one should consult the works of *Bingham, Bona, Morin, Hottinger, Albaspina*, etc., which are available everywhere.

But if you should ask, Listeners, at what point in time this *Secret Discipline* was introduced into the Christian Church, I respond that nothing certain can be said about this. Hence, some trace this custom back to the times of Christ and the Apostles themselves; others to the end of the second century; and still others think it was finally received in the fourth and fifth centuries. Having weighed everything brought forward by learned men on this subject, it is most likely that the first Teachers of the Christian Religion did not use this custom. However, as learned men imbued with the precepts of Philosophy joined the Christian assemblies and became disgusted by the simplicity of the sacred worship, secret and mystical reasons for the rites were devised. These, in the course of time—as usually happens—increased significantly and finally grew into a massive heap of rituals (*). It was finally abolished toward the end of the sixth century.

***

(*) The illustrious *Pfaffius* traces the origin of the Secret Discipline back to Christ himself and the Apostles. Thus, in the place cited, page 150 and following, he says: "Furthermore, this Secret Discipline was observed both by the Gentiles [Pagans] of old, from whom some very learned men think the Christians derived it, and also by the Jews, etc. Yet (he continues) its origin should not be sought there, since it is commended in the very tablets of the New Testament. For Christ himself did not immediately reveal the highest Mysteries of the faith to the Apostles; -- hence the Secret Discipline was intentionally instituted and observed by them, etc." The most learned *Mosheim* <note>Johann Lorenz von Mosheim, a Lutheran church historian</note> seems to concede to this opinion in his *Institutes of Ecclesiastical History*, page 75. "I am easily persuaded," he says, "that the Discipline they call 'Secret' already had a place in the very beginnings of the Church; that is, the method of teaching was tempered by the law of prudence by the Teachers. But that specific form of this Discipline, which was received in the third, fourth, and following centuries, is more recent than that age whose affairs we are now recounting. What was initially a simple arrangement of prudence later degenerated wonderfully, and was not only amplified but even forced into the mold of the Mysteries among the Gentiles, and obscured by vocabulary sought from outsiders." Thus says the most learned *Mosheim*. We must be careful not to fall into a dispute over words here. When the Secret Discipline is understood as a prudent and circumspect method of teaching used by Christ and the Apostles, no one doubts that the origin of this custom can be sought from this source. But when the Ancients and moderns discuss the Secret Discipline, they mean something far different than a prudent handling of matters to be taught (which learned and prudent men have observed at all times). Since, however, it is most obvious that the Teachers of the third and following centuries [derived] this discipline from the precepts of the Pagans, and Sacred—

...that it was so, although Learned Men contend that traces of this discipline exist in the modern Greek Church. See Heineccius, *Description of the Greek Church*, Book II, Chapter VI, Section 30, page 235.

But it is time for us to inquire what the Origin of this Discipline might be, and from whom the leaders of the Christian assemblies learned this custom of hiding the Sacred rites. Here some appeal to the example of Christ and the Apostles; others think it was drawn from the *Jewish Kabbalah* <note>The ancient Jewish tradition of mystical biblical interpretation</note>; most contend that all that apparatus arose from the *precepts of the Philosophers* and the *Pagan* rites, which last opinion is the most likely of all. Certainly, it will be clear to all who weigh the deeds of Christ and the Apostles without partisan zeal that this discipline was practiced neither by Christ nor by his first followers. Our most holy Savior explained the heads of the most holy discipline to all indiscriminately in the midst of the crowd. As soon as someone, having perceived his doctrine and seen his unusual miracles, gave his name to him and admitted him as the Messiah, he was washed with water and included among his followers without evasions or various troublesome exercises. He enjoined his disciples to announce publicly and clearly before everyone what he himself had said more obscurely. Hence Paul in *Acts 20*, about to bid farewell to the Ephesian assembly, testifies that he omitted nothing of those things which could contribute anything to explaining the nature of the most holy discipline. And what need is there for words? Since it is established for us solely from the books of the New Testament what Christ's and the Apostles' method of teaching was, and what the constitution of the Sacraments and Sacred Discipline was, yet nothing at all about this Secret Discipline is handed down or prescribed in them; everyone sees that this custom must be fetched from elsewhere. The *Illustrious Pfaff* indeed brings forward certain passages of the New Testament to prove that Christ and the Apostles often hid certain parts of the sacred discipline (*). But if

Therefore, as far as the disciples themselves were concerned, he hid nothing in this place. He asks only this one thing: that they should not speak about this subject without necessity and indiscriminately, lest they cause trouble for themselves. ---

Christ says: *I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now.* <note>original Greek: ἔτι πολλὰ ἔχω λέγειν ὑμῖν ἀλλ᾿ οὐ δύνασθε βαϛάζειν</note> If we weigh what follows, our Holy Savior meant nothing other than that the disciples could not yet correctly grasp the method of divine administration, but a time would come when they would perceive it more clearly and evidently. The *Illustrious Pfaff* also appeals to the parables used by Christ, for example *Luke 8:10* and its parallel *Matthew 13:11-15*. If we were to press this latter passage too hard, it would follow that Christ not only spoke obscurely on purpose, but that he did so for the purpose that those who did not understand him might be condemned—which was surely most foreign to the mind of our Best Savior. Having dismissed the interpretations of learned men on this passage, I briefly *paraphrase* <note>original: παραφράζω</note> Christ's words thus:

> “You disciples ask why I use parables so frequently and do not explain my mind openly to this crowd. Know therefore that most of them, fixed to the soil <note>meaning worldly or dull-minded</note>, are unworthy for me to speak the truth plainly and clearly on every occasion. For those who use the benefits granted to them rightly are alone worthy that more be granted; but those who abuse those very things which are at hand are unworthy for you to adorn with greater gifts; indeed, they are more worthy that those very things which were granted be taken away. This is the reason why I now use parables, not clear speech. I know this crowd inside and out; seeing they do not see—that is, they do not want to understand or recall to mind those things which I have said to them more than once clearly and without a metaphor concerning my heavenly doctrine. What reason, then, would there be why I should speak more clearly to those who do not wish to see—that is, those carried away by blind emotion? They are like those of whom Isaiah spoke, etc.”

From the whole discourse of Christ, it appears that Christ had previously, very often, clearly handed down those things which could serve to perceive his most holy discipline. For the words "seeing they do not see" do not allow for any other sense. Regarding the Apostles, no one would deny that they used laws of prudence in promulgating the doctrine of Jesus Christ, and the passages which *Illustrious Pfaff* brings forward—namely *1 Corinthians 3:2* and *Hebrews 5:11*—point to this. As for *those unspeakable words* <note>original: ἄρῥητα ἐκεῖνα ῥήματα</note> which the Apostle testifies he heard in *2 Corinthians 12*, they were undoubtedly not of such a kind that it was in the interest of the whole Christian assembly to know them. Hence they do nothing to prove this Secret Discipline. I pass over the other passages. Regarding this one point, I note that the *Illustrious Man* [Pfaff] objects against the passage of Paul in *Acts 20:27* <note>Text says XXV. 27, likely an error for XX. 27</note> which I cited in the Oration itself, arguing that here the talk is of converts, not of those to be initiated; but besides the fact that the *Illustrious Man* here assumes the Apostles acted one way with those to be initiated and another with the faithful (which is the very thing being questioned), he himself admits on page 154 that the distinction between Catechumens and the faithful cannot be proven from the books of the New Testament.

<margin>
(*) Regarding the Kabbalah of the Jews, the most learned Brucker should be consulted above all in his *History of Philosophy*, Volume IV, part two. ...to say that God revealed certain hidden Mysteries to Moses on Mount Sinai; that these were handed down through Holy Men to the Jewish Doctors, and should be explained by some to those who possess a more divine mind. But everyone sees upon what foundation these things rest. Christian Doctors, except for Origen and Jerome, were ignorant of the Hebrew language. The custom of interpreting everything allegorically <note>Interpreting text to reveal a hidden, symbolic meaning rather than a literal one</note> arose from ignorance, a foolish zeal to show off eloquence, and from the habits of the Philosophers. It is clearer than the sun that the Philosophical Kabbalah is more recent and was adapted from Pythagorean-Platonic principles. The writings and decrees of Philo the Jew and the most ancient Doctors of the Church sufficiently show that they were ignorant of the trifles of the Kabbalists, and had clearly adopted from elsewhere those things which are foreign to the discipline of Christ (*).

It remains for us to say that this Secret Discipline was sought from the Rites of the Pagans and the Decrees of the Philosophers. It is well known that in the age of Christ and the Apostles, but especially in the centuries immediately following, Pythagorean-Platonic philosophy was cultivated with the greatest ardor by Christians, Jews, and Pagans, of which fact innumerable traces remain in the records of the Ancients. If we duly and piece by piece consider the rites used concerning the Secret Discipline, and compare those things which were performed among the Philosophers—especially the Pythagoreans—and the Priests of the Sacred Rites among the Pagans; it will be most manifest that the first authors of the *Secret Discipline* wished to temper the form of the most holy discipline to the decrees and customs of the Philosophers; which must be demonstrated by a short example. The Pythagorean-Platonic Philosophers divided all Philosophy into two parts, according to Hierocles in his *Golden Verses of Pythagoras*. They called the former *purgative* <note>original Greek: καθαρτικὴν; focused on cleansing the soul</note>, the latter *perfective* <note>original Greek: τελικὴν; focused on reaching the final goal or initiation</note>; the former was said to purge the mind, the latter to perfect it. Thus Hierocles defined *purgation* <note>original Greek: καθαρσιν</note> as such a thing by which we are purged "from the dregs of material irrationality and the mortal body" <note>original: ἀπὸ τῆς ὑλικῆς ἀλογίας καὶ τοῦ θνητοειδοῦς σώματος</note>. To this they joined a kind of conversion of the mind into itself, thinking that the soul—conscious of its own powers and freed from the chains of the body and the filth of matter—turns primarily toward itself, with all other things that are outside being consigned to oblivion and ejected from memory as if they belonged nothing to itself. This they called *conversion toward oneself* <note>original: ἐπιστροφὴν εἰς ἑαυτὸν</note>, which was then followed by an *ascent* <note>original: ἄνοδος</note>; for they wished that the pure mind, freed from all contagion of the body, with its strengths gathered as if from its own self—

<column-break/>

<page-num>1107</page-num>
<header>NOT TO BE PRACTICED IN OUR AGE.</header>
<sig>Aaaaaaa 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: enig- (from enigmatic)</meta>

—should leave these lower things and be carried upward and seek celestial and divine things, and be turned toward its own beginning. This state of the human mind they called the *removal of foreign things, the restoration of one's own essence, perfection*, etc. <note>original: ἀφαίρεσιν τῶν ἀλλοτρίων, ἀπόδοσιν τῆς οἰκείας οὐσίας, τελειότητα</note>. Pythagoras divided his disciples into the *outer* and the *inner* <note>original: τοὺς ἔξω & τοὺς ἔσω</note>. The former were called as if they were strangers, not yet admitted into the more secret dogmas of Philosophy. The latter were as if *insiders* and participants in every secret. Iamblichus is a witness in *The Life of Pythagoras*, Book I, Chapter 17: "Those who appeared worthy to participate in the dogmas, judged partly by their life and partly by their other moderation of spirit, after a five-year silence finally became Esoterics" <note>original: i. e. Qui vero digni apparebant...; Esoterics were students allowed to hear the master directly</note>.

Pythagoras was accustomed to test his disciples with various and very harsh exercises before the time of admission had passed; they were forced to exercise their patience not only with thirst and hunger, but even with fire and the sword.

The same Iamblichus in the cited place, chapter 16, says: "In general, he judged that labors should be applied concerning doctrines and Institutions; he also instituted various punishments and penalties and various amputations with sword and fire to be applied concerning the immoderations and desires innate in all, and he prescribed such things as no one who is evil could endure."

<margin>
(*) See more in Scheffer, *On the Constitution of Italian Philosophy*, page 30. Wittenberg edition.
</margin>

The concealment of sublime things was very familiar to Pythagoras and his disciples; hence Iamblichus in *The Life of Pythagoras* states clearly: "According to both the exoteric <note>public</note> and the acroamatic <note>oral instruction for advanced students</note> method of reasoning, we will illustrate each symbol with an explanation, not permitting those things which are secret and must be kept silent to be divulged before those who have not yet been received into the inner discipline." The same author says of the Pythagoreans in Chapter 32: "They allowed none of those things which were of any importance to go out into the common crowd. But those things which were taught and perceived through learning over a long period of time were known only within private walls. If it ever happened that they had to meet with outsiders and, so to speak, the profane, they by no means announced their Mysteries, but through Symbols and secret tokens <note>term: tesseras; physical objects or passwords used to prove identity or membership</note> they signified the feelings of the mind to one another obscurely and hiddenly, as if through riddles (*)." For that purpose also, according to Porphyry in *The Life of Pythagoras*, number 3, the Pythagoreans used the Doric Dialect <note>An ancient Greek dialect; the author implies it was used to remain obscure to general Greek speakers</note>. For when he asked why the Italian Philosophy had so perished, he replied: "First because of its enigmatic nature, and then because those things that were written were written in Doric, which has something obscure in its dialect, and for this reason nothing was suspected..."
