...involved in riddles, and secondly because all their writings were composed in the Doric dialect <note>original: "Dorice". A specific dialect of ancient Greek associated with the Spartans and Pythagoreans, often seen as archaic or difficult.</note>. For since the dialect itself possesses a certain obscurity, the doctrines recorded in that dialect could not be understood for this very reason (*). It is most clearly evident that many things for establishing the Secret Discipline were sought by Christian Teachers, not only from the precepts of Pythagoras and his followers, but from the rites commonly received among the Gentiles in their sacred ceremonies. The Greeks, as is well known, had many sacred rites, such as those of the Mother of the Gods, Bacchus, Mithras, Isis, Hecate, and others. These they called *Mysteries*; the performance of the sacred acts they called <term>muēsin</term> <note>original: μύησιν, meaning "initiation"</note>, and those who received them were said <term>mueisthai</term> <note>original: μυεῖσθαι, "to be initiated"</note> or <term>teleisthai</term> <note>original: τελεῖσθαι, "to be perfected" or "consecrated"</note>. The nature of these sacred rites in general was (these are the words of Isaac Casaubon <note>A famous 16th-century humanist scholar who criticized the Catholic interpretation of church history</note> in *Exercise XVI* against Baronius): "that those who surrendered themselves to be imbued with the discipline, having been gradually purified from the stains of this life and the filth of sins, through certain degrees and defined intervals of time, would be led to the perception and knowledge of I know not what great secrets." It is well known that purification by water was especially in use before they were admitted into the inner sanctuaries of the temples. Hence Apuleius, making mention of his own initiation in chapter XI, says: *Escorted by a religious company, he leads me to the nearest baths, and after I was first committed to the usual washing, having prayed for the Lord's pardon, he washed me by sprinkling water most purely all around.* These initiations were carried out with the use of certain symbols, which were established for the remembrance of certain things, as is more than sufficiently evident from the booklet of Julius Firmicus, to say nothing of others; thus it is established from the monuments of the ancients that not only water and bread were used in certain rites, but also certain mystical words (**). Those who wished to be admitted to perceive these Mysteries...

Among other things, he speaks thus from the version of H. Wolf: *What else does this man do but publish the initiations of Ceres <note>The Roman name for Demeter, the goddess of the harvest whose "Eleusinian Mysteries" were the most famous of the ancient world.</note>? The home of them, you say, is at Eleusis. Behold, it is here too. There, there is a Priest of the rites; and I will make a Priest. There, a herald; and I will appoint a herald. O most impious man, do they differ in nothing? They are beneficial according to the proportion of place and time: likewise when a sacrifice is added, when prayers are added, with chastity, and a mind so affected that you are about to approach sacred and ancient ceremonies. Thus the initiations become useful, if they provide the opinion that all these things were instituted by the Ancients for the sake of educating and correcting life.* But you blurt them out, and betray them at the wrong time, not in the proper place, without sacrifices, and without a sound mind. You do not have the garment that befits a Priest of the rites; nor the hair, nor the headband such as is required, nor the voice, nor the age: you have not lived chastely as he did, but when you have only committed the words to memory, you say, "those words are sacred in and of themselves." One must approach these things in another way: it is a great matter, it is a secret, not made public, nor of that kind which may be communicated to anyone.

# NOT TO BE USED IN OUR AGE.

...wished to be admitted, they were bound to first give a confession of their more serious sins. Plutarch is a witness to this in his *Laconian Apothegms*, saying: *When a certain initiator was initiating a Spartan, he asked him what most impious deed he was conscious of having committed.* The ancient formula—*Be gone, be gone, you profane ones!*—bears witness that the approach to those Mysteries was closed to those contaminated by more serious crimes. Hence, as Suetonius testifies in Chapter XXXIV: *Nero, after the murder of his mother, did not dare to be present at the Eleusinian Rites.* I shall say nothing now of the specific rites of initiation, the abstinence from sex, food, washings, and the arrangement of hair and clothing. It is worth noting that just as the Christians had their <term>antiphōna</term> <note>original: ἀντιφωνα. A call-and-response style of singing or chanting.</note>, or "responsive songs," in their sacred rites, so similarly was this rite used previously in certain sacred ceremonies of the Gentiles. Casaubon notes from a commentator on Aristophanes that in certain Bacchic rites, the Torch-bearers or other ministers of the rites were accustomed to address the circle of bystanders thus: <term>aineite Theon</term> <gloss>praise God</gloss>, and they would respond <term>Semelē iakche ploutodota</term> <gloss>O son of Semele, Iacchus, Giver of Wealth.</gloss> It is established from countless passages of the ancients that these same people most diligently took care not only that the secrets of these rites should not become known to the <term>amuētois</term> <note>original: ἀμυήτοις, "the uninitiated"</note>, but also punished transgressors with the heaviest penalties. It is well known what happened to Diagoras, Orpheus, and the ones publishing the secrets of the Cabiri and the Eleusinian Rites. Livy, in Book XXXI, brings forward this example: *Two Acarnanian youths (he says), who were not initiated, entered the temple of Ceres during the days of the initiations, being ignorant of the religious law, along with the rest of the crowd. Their speech easily betrayed them, as they asked certain absurd questions: and having been led to the Priests of the temple, although it was clear they had entered by mistake, they were put to death as if for an unspeakable crime.* For the sake of brevity, I pass over many other things which could be brought forward to prove this. If anyone diligently compares these things with the rites used in the *Secret Discipline*, it will be established that those rites were sought not from the discipline of Christ and the Apostles, but from the precepts of the Philosophers and the sacred rites of the Gentiles (*).

But let us finally hear the reasons by which the Teachers of the Ancient Church allowed themselves to be induced to create and establish the Secret Discipline, and let us weigh them according to the laws of right reason. I have found that three causes for this silence were chiefly brought forward by the Ancients, the First of which was this: *Lest the Pagans and those not yet initiated be offended by the simplicity of the rites used by Christians, or, on the other hand, by the sublimity of the Mysteries.*

# ORATION ON THE SECRET DISCIPLINE

Thus, Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an influential Archbishop of Constantinople known for his eloquent preaching.</note> says in his 23rd Homily on Matthew: *“We celebrate the Mysteries with closed doors, and we prohibit those who have not yet been initiated from being present, not because we have found any weakness in the Mysteries, but because those whom we bar are still too weak for their participation” (*).*

<margin>
(*) Regarding this first reason, as well as the two following reasons of the Fathers, see Meyer, Casaubon, and Bingham, who cite many passages. Casaubon <note>Isaac Casaubon (1559–1614), a classical scholar who argued that the early Church's "mysteries" were too heavily influenced by paganism.</note>, after bringing forward this first reason of the Fathers for hiding the sacred things and confirming it with the testimony of Cyril, says: "And Cyril says this most truly: for what pagan stranger to the faith, or Catechumen <note>A convert to Christianity who has not yet been baptized.</note> not yet confirmed in the faith, could hear of the mystery of our regeneration through water, or the eating of the flesh of Christ in the Lord’s Supper, without scandal or laughter?" He praises the custom of the ancients throughout his 16th Exercise. No one who understands Casaubon’s character and knows the literature he devoted himself to for almost his entire life will wonder that he judged thus. Such minds, when the conversation turns to Philosophical and Theological disciplines, are for the most part blind. Lest anyone think I am judging Casaubon more boldly than is fair, I will bring forward a trustworthy and most learned witness who held Casaubon in high regard. This is J. Le Clerc <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), a famous Swiss theologian and scholar.</note>, who in *Bibliothèque choisie* <note>original: "Bibl. choisie". A scholarly journal edited by Le Clerc.</note> Volume 19, page 228, discusses Casaubon's *Exercises* against Baronius; after saying the work is full of learning, he adds these points among others:

"But there are three things that have led people to say that Casaubon had undertaken a work beyond his strength in wanting to refute Baronius. The first is that he had not sufficiently meditated on the first principles of Theology, among which is, for example, this: that nothing must be proposed as an article of faith except that which is in express terms in Holy Scripture, or which can be drawn from it by a necessary consequence. I will say only regarding the first point, that one has only to read Article 42 of Exercise 16, where Casaubon shows that the Fathers, by a 'pious condescension,' as he says, had called the Eucharist a 'Mystery,' and had established various ceremonies related to it, conforming to those of the Pagans in their Mysteries. Casaubon finds all this very good, whereas he should have blamed it. A good Protestant theologian will never recognize that it is right to give names taken from Pagan Religion to the ceremonies of Christianity, to imitate them in their rites, or to reason about them as if one could draw consequences from Pagan expressions that were, in this regard, unknown to the Apostles—and finally to form ideas regarding the Eucharist according to these ways of speaking. One cannot change the names of things in matters of Religion without great hazard, because with these new names, one introduces new ideas, as happened with the matter of the Eucharist. Casaubon himself only believed in a sort of 'real presence' because his head was heated by these expressions of the Fathers, which are not accurate and have no foundation in the original institution."
</margin>

But this reasoning, however plausible, seems to me to have no strength. Far from the simplicity of the rites offending the minds of the wise, it instead should have led them more than anything else to embrace the public sacred acts of the Christians. The more someone is imbued with a knowledge of a chaste and most holy Religion and touched by the love of it, the more they feel that its first and primary part consists in the turning of the mind toward God, the estimation of divine virtues, and the performance of duties prescribed by right reason—and not in a varied and complex apparatus of rituals.

# [THIS DISCIPLINE] SHOULD NOT BE USED IN OUR AGE.

apparatus. And what, after all, do Baptism and the Holy Supper contain that could offend men? Here there are no shameful rites, no silly and ridiculous ceremonies such as took place among the Gentiles and were exploded by the wise. Everything, as we heard above from Justin Martyr <note>An early Christian apologist (c. 100–165 AD) who wrote descriptions of Christian worship to defend them against rumors.</note>, was performed with wonderful simplicity. If, however, those Fathers thought that Pagans and Catechumens would think lowly of these Mysteries because they did not correctly perceive the nature of the Sacraments, they were so far from needing to speak obscurely or remain silent about them that they should instead have explained the nature and purpose of these rites in the simplest possible words.

Pagans and Catechumens were not infants, whom rattles and dolls delight, but men capable of reason. Therefore, if they seriously applied their minds to the profession of the Christian Religion, they could easily have been taught the purpose and nature of the rites used in sacred things. Among the first heads of the Christian Religion that were to be handed down to them, this was undoubtedly one: that Jesus Christ is the true Messiah, and that for the sake of the human race, he did and suffered all those things recorded in the Holy Scriptures. 

However, **Paul** warned long ago how much the ears and minds of Pagans and Jews were offended upon hearing this Christian dogma; yet that contempt did not prevent **Paul**, nor the other students of this most holy discipline, from repeating these most healthy precepts publicly and privately, even while the enemies of truth snarled. Christ himself, undoubtedly the wisest Teacher, granted access to hearing the divine decrees to all who were eager for truth and inflamed by a love of heavenly wisdom, without evasions or the apparatus of many rituals. 

Our Fathers acted far differently; they spoke obscurely on purpose and wrapped in sacred silence those things which should have been taught, explained, and impressed clearly, transparently, publicly, and privately. Let fair judges of events decide how wisely they acted. "But the sublimity of the Mysteries," the foolish admirers of the Fathers will say, "must have deterred them from speaking transparently on this subject." 

Would that the Doctors had remained consistent in this! Would that they had never attempted to explain what they did not know! But alas, the things said by the ancients on this subject are too well known for me to recount to you, Gentlemen. In the first centuries after the birth of Christ, and especially in the fourth, the Fathers discoursed at great length in public disputes about the eternal generation of the Son, his nature, and the manner of his <term>ensarkōseōs</term> <note>original: ἐνσαρκώσεως; the "incarnation" or taking on of flesh.</note>. In their "understanding," they often ensured that you would understand nothing at all. Whatever help reason and Philosophy could provide, they brought to explain these sublime and utterly <term>arrhēta</term> <note>original: ἄῤῥητα; "unutterable" or "ineffable"</note> Mysteries...

Having previously discussed how the Church adopted the "mystery" language of pagan schools, the author now addresses the justifications given by the Church Fathers—specifically that the uninitiated were "too weak" for the full truth—and argues that this secrecy was unnecessary and even harmful to the purity of the Gospel.</meta>

# ORATION ON THE SECRET DISCIPLINE

explained, the Christian Doctors brought this into the open. Alexander himself, the Bishop of Alexandria, as Socrates <note>Socrates Scholasticus (c. 380 – after 439 AD), a church historian.</note> testifies, by reasoning <term>too ambitiously</term> <note>original: φιλοτιμώτερον (philotimōteron) - meaning with a love of honor or more contentiously than necessary.</note> regarding this tremendous Mystery, became the cause of the most unfortunate disputes which spread through the entire East and West; to say nothing of other ancient writers. If, therefore, they considered those Mysteries to surpass all reason, they ought to have spoken cautiously and circumspectly, not only in their teachings and sermons delivered to the people, but also in their public writings. But it is one thing to speak prudently and circumspectly, and quite another to remain altogether silent; it is one thing to confess that we cannot rightly know the nature of a thing, and another to deliberately express a matter that is by its nature difficult to grasp using obscure words. Had they done the former, there would have been no reason why they should have feared the contempt of the uninitiated.

Those who wished to give their name to the Christian Religion were either *prudent* men, *aware* of the precepts upon which the Discipline of Christ is based, or they were altogether *unlettered* and ignorant of those things taught among Christians. As for the *former* <note>the prudent men</note>, there is no doubt that they could have been taught through a clear explanation of the Christian Religion that there is nothing in the sacred rites and decrees of Christians that could not be accepted by a wise man. Certainly, if those Doctors had proved the truth of the Christian Religion by the same method used by the most learned men of our own age, they could have easily led those wise men to accept certain things which cannot be clearly enough explained by human intellect—partly because, by the confession of all Philosophers, knowledge of the divine nature and properties is circumscribed by very narrow limits, and partly because the doctrine of the "three principles" <note>the Trinity</note> was very well known and publicly accepted among the most famous competing schools of that age. Once the divine origin of the Christian Religion was demonstrated, it was very easy to show why our most holy Savior willed that the memory of His death be represented by certain symbols. In a word, one must either say that the Christian Religion contradicts all decrees of right reason, or it does not. Since the Christian Doctors would, by common consensus, deny the former, there was clearly no reason why they should withdraw the explanation of the Mysteries from the knowledge of wise men who were turning their minds toward the profession of the Christian Religion.

As for the *unlearned* and those *ignorant* of the most holy discipline, there is no doubt that there was a need for prudent instruction. They undoubtedly had to be taught the first elements of the Christian Religion publicly and privately, and one ought to have progressed gradually to higher things; but obscurity of words and exclusion from the sacred rites certainly could not achieve this.

<meta>catchword: Second-</meta>

<page-num>1113</page-num>
<header>NOT TO BE USED IN OUR AGE.</header>

The second reason which the Fathers brought forward was this: *That they might excite reverence for the Mysteries of Religion in the minds of men.* Thus Basil, in *On the Holy Spirit*, Chapter 27, says: *“The veneration of the mysteries is preserved by silence.”* Augustine, in Sermon I among the forty published by Sirmond, says: *“You ought not to wonder, most beloved brothers, that during the Mysteries themselves we have said nothing of the Mysteries, and that we did not immediately interpret the things we handed down; for we have applied the honor of silence to such holy and divine things.”*

This reason is of the same weight as the first. Hitherto, I, in my simplicity, have thought that a person would finally be touched by veneration for something once its nature and singular excellence were known and understood; but if the Fathers are to be believed, the exact opposite is true. In order to excite admiration in the minds of men, they not only involve the thing to be known in deep silence, but they also deliberately use words that hinder the knowledge of the most serious matters. This is a wonderful and unusual—or rather, inept—way of acting. Because of the sublimity of the Mysteries, our Doctors say, we say nothing of the Mysteries in the presence of the initiated; yet this very reason, this very silence, ought to excite veneration and admiration in the minds of these men.

Here, the Christian Doctors clearly imitate the Gentiles, among whom, as Demetrius Phalereus testifies, *“The mysteries are expressed in allegories to produce amazement and shivering, as if in a sanctuary and in the night.”* <note>original Greek: τὰ μυστήρια ἐν ἀλληγορίαις λέγεται πρὸς ἔκπληξιν καὶ φρίκην ὥσπερ ἐν ἀδύτῳ καὶ νυκτί</note> And according to Tacitus in his *Agricola*, Chapter 30: *“Everything unknown is taken for magnificent.”* Yet the Christians themselves bitterly criticized these same people on account of their Secrets, not only because they were foul and foreign to honesty, but also because it was inept to hide that which you so greatly extol. There is no doubt that by this method they led many of those not yet initiated into the opinion that obscure things of no great importance were being so heavily covered up; that it was in the interest of those Doctors that these Mysteries not be placed in clear light, for otherwise they would explain them to everyone indiscriminately. Certainly Christ did not reason thus, nor did the Apostles; they spoke of these most serious matters eloquently, directly, and clearly, yet nonetheless modestly and prudently.

The third and final reason follows. Namely: *that the desire for knowing these Mysteries might be all the more sharpened in the Catechumens.* Augustine says in *Homily 96 on John*: *“If the Sacraments of the faithful are not disclosed to the Catechumens, it is not because they cannot bear them, but so that they might be desired all the more ardently by them, the more honorably they are hidden from them.”* This reasoning of Augustine is contrary to the canon accepted among all: *“There is no [desire for] what is unknown...”* <note>The full proverb is "Ignoti nulla cupido" — there is no desire for what is unknown.</note>

# THE THEOLOGICAL KNOWLEDGE OF THE BLESSED
# IN HEAVEN COMPARED WITH OURS.

<note>The header refers to the broader theological topic being discussed in this series of lectures, though the specific text here focuses on the "Secret Discipline" of the early Church.</note>

desire. No one indeed will ever apply their mind to learning any art or discipline through any effort of talent if it is entirely unknown to them. The Teachers of the best arts and disciplines experience this daily. Appetite and desire for a thing only follow after some knowledge of it has been obtained. It was impossible, therefore, for a man alienated from the profession of the Christian Religion to be moved by a singular desire to know the truth if the Teachers themselves strove "with hands and feet" <note>original: "pedibus manibusque obnixi sunt" — a Latin idiom meaning to strive with all one's might.</note> to prevent them from knowing the character and nature of such great things. It would be different if we were speaking of those who had fallen away—those who, having long ago participated in the heavenly teachings, were deemed unworthy because of very grave sins, and to whom the most holy doctrine (which they had shamefully neglected or even trampled underfoot) should not be more clearly presented.

And these are the **chief** reasons that the Ancients <note>Referring to the Church Fathers of the first few centuries.</note> brought forward to commend and practice that *Secret Discipline* <term>Secret Discipline: (Latin: Disciplina Arcani) the practice in the early Church of hiding certain rites and doctrines, especially the Eucharist and Baptism, from non-Christians and new converts.</term>. Whether these reasons seem weighty and important to you, I do not know. To me—to put my feelings as mildly as possible—they seem not only *alien to reason* but *unworthy of the character of such great men*. I have produced the reasons why I feel this way. But there are many more things that can be argued against that discipline.

First, it is manifest that those allegorical and obscure terms used by the ancients when speaking of the Holy Supper eventually gave birth to that monstrous dogma of *Transubstantiation* <note>The belief that the bread and wine literally become the body and blood of Christ.</note>, to the disgrace of the Christian Religion. It caused what was by its nature fit to excite a living and wonderful image of Christ's death in the minds of men to degenerate into a theatrical and playful act. Hence, very learned men well-versed in Ecclesiastical Antiquity have complained about the obscurity of the Church Fathers regarding this argument (*). How much more rightly they would have act-

(*) The Illustrious Dallaeus <note>Jean Daillé (1594–1670), a prominent French Protestant theologian.</note>, a man well-versed in the writings of the Fathers if anyone ever was, says this among other things in his golden book *On the Use of the Fathers, Book I, Chapter 5*: "Since it was their purpose, both in this argument and others, to wrap their meaning in a certain darkness, it should not seem strange if what they bring forth is often obscure, and (which follows obscurity) if they sometimes seem to fight with themselves." I pass over the complaints of other most learned men among our own, such as Claude, Albertinus, Basnage, and Pfaff. Hence, I have often doubted whether the most excellent men among the Protestants have found it worth their effort to investigate with such labor and zeal the opinions of the Fathers concerning the Lord's Supper. No one is ignorant of the labors of Claude against Arnaldus and others. Since they say the principle of belief for Protestants is the Word of God, what do they gain in the end, after they have proved with immense labor from the most obscure sayings of the Fathers on this subject that they did not believe in Transubstantiation? Namely, this one thing: that a constant Tradition is lacking to the Roman Catholic Doctors. But since it can be most evidently demonstrated that Transubstantiation is contrary not only to Holy Scripture but also to reason and the senses—

-ed <note>completing "acted" from the previous column</note>, those excellent men, if they had explained their meaning clearly and had not made mysteries where there were none! Truly, they should not have clouded with obscure terms those things which are recognized as such by everyone's confession.

**Secondly:** by this method, it could not happen otherwise than that very few perceived the true and genuine character and nature of the Sacraments. When the Fathers speak of *Baptism and the Holy Supper*, they either spoke less clearly on purpose, or they used words to which you cannot help but attribute **greater** force to these symbols than the truth of the matter allows. And this was also, among other things, the reason why some delayed Baptism until the very end of their lives (*); because many were satisfied with the use of those ceremonies and thought that if they could finally enjoy those Symbols, there could be little doubt about the hope of attaining certain salvation (**). Finally, to pass over other things, through this *Secret Discipline*, ambition and the lust for power—which by the fourth century had already taken deep root in the minds of most Bishops—was increased more and more. For when they extolled the power and efficacy of the Sacraments beyond measure, and asserted that without participation in them all hope of salvation was lost, while they claimed for themselves alone the power of dispensing them, it is clear that many conceded to the opinion that the Ministers of the Sacred Rites enjoy a closer fellowship with the Divinity, and that they, by God's will, dispose of the salvation of men as they please. How true my words are, the outcome—alas!—has sufficiently shown.

From these things, listeners, you can easily gather whether this *Secret Discipline* should be recalled into *use* in our age or not. This seems to me entirely foreign to the century in which we live. For we have fallen upon an age in which men do not allow themselves to be deceived by obscure words, but desire reasons. Philosophical and Theological disciplines [dislike] obscurity.

—indeed, that it is a most manifest contradiction—what does it matter to us in the end whether this or that Father of the Church spoke obscurely or clearly on this subject? If all the Fathers from the times of Justin Martyr or Ignatius down to the age of Bernard had believed that a "square circle" could exist, I could not believe it even if I most wanted to; it is no more possible to believe in Transubstantiation. I do not begrudge the labor of the most learned men who have brought to light the thoughts of the most ancient Church Fathers on this subject; but it is a safer way if you return to the decrees of right reason and Revelation. Let everyone, however, enjoy his own judgment.

# SPEECH ON THE SECRET DISCIPLINE
<meta>catchword: But if you turn with this Secret Discipline to the Deists,</meta>

...times most hostile to fleeing examination, flourish. The Catholic Doctors <note>original: "Pontificii Doctores" — referring to Roman Catholic theologians, whom the author (likely a Protestant) criticizes for relying on the Church's authority rather than rational proof.</note> and those who "plow with their heifer" <note>An idiom meaning to use someone else's work or ideas to achieve one's goal, based on the biblical story of Samson.</note> are laughed at when they appeal to Authority or to a "sacred silence" in matters concerning Religion. The Christian Religion has never been so excellently demonstrated, nor so strongly defended, as in our own age. All those who know the true value of learning love the light; we do not fear the mockery or the arguments of unbelievers. To what end, then, would this *Secret Discipline* <term>Secret Discipline: The practice of hiding certain doctrines from the uninitiated.</term> be introduced? By what right can we hope that honorable men, touched by a love for the truth, will be called back from error by a sacred silence? 

In a word: either this *Secret Discipline* must be used toward men who lack the *light of Revelation* <note>Referring to "Pagans" or those who have never heard the Gospel.</note>, or toward *Deists* <term>Deists: Enlightenment thinkers who believed in a creator God based on reason but rejected organized religion and divine revelation.</term> and *enemies of Revelation*, or finally toward *Catechumens* born among Christians—that is, the youth. As for the *Pagans* who lack the light of *Revelation*, whom Christians eagerly wish to bring to the profession of the Christian Religion, there is no doubt that first of all, if they do not already know them, the primary points of Natural Religion must be taught. But if they know these things, are they Christians? Not at all, you would say. Therefore, I say, the Truth and the divine Origin of the Christian Religion must be proved to them; we must appeal to the miracles of Christ and His resurrection; it must be proved that He was sent from heaven to promote the salvation of the human race; and so, whether you like it or not, the Decrees of the Christian Religion must be discussed. 

But you say, "they do not understand these Mysteries." Perhaps those who are sent to these men immersed in the darkness of ignorance are themselves often ignorant of the art of thinking and reasoning correctly; perhaps they do not proceed in teaching in the order they should; perhaps they create Mysteries where there are none, or where they do exist, they cast darkness over the light; or finally, they wish to explain things that cannot be sufficiently defined by any art or talent. Whatever the case, that which has been handed down by Christ, however difficult it may be to grasp, must not be kept silent; it is our duty to do what we can. For a man is either endowed with a *sharp wit* or *not*. If the *former*, you will teach him through countless examples of things not relating to Religion that many things are known only imperfectly, and that there are very few things for which mortals can give perfect reasons; it is enough if it is shown that these Mysteries are neither absurd nor plainly contrary to reason. And how, after all, could these Decrees be passed over in silence if the Pagan is bound to examine each one? If, however, that man is *dull-witted*, you can do nothing else than ensure he understands as much as his talent can grasp.

# NOT TO BE PRACTICED IN OUR AGE.

...you will be acting in vain, and you will be rejected by that crowd. Those men (we speak of the "Lettered" <note>The intellectual elite or "Republic of Letters."</note>) strain every nerve of their talent to prove that there is absolutely no need for Revelation; they reject the Christian Religion for the very reason that it is full of Mysteries. They attack these as much as they can. They are well aware of what Christians of various sects believe. You will descend into Philosophy with them, and by the introduction of many examples, you will prove how difficult it is—even when the truth of a proposition is established—to define the mode and nature of things. <meta>This page continues the speaker's argument that the "Secret Discipline"—the practice of hiding certain doctrines—is unnecessary for modern education and counterproductive in theological debate. He is transitioning from a discussion on teaching children to a critique of how modern theologians (both Catholic and Protestant) still use "mystery" to shield their doctrines from rational examination.</meta>

# SPEECH ON THE SECRET DISCIPLINE

Finally, as for the children, whom you might call *Catechumens* <term>Catechumens: From the Greek for "those being instructed"; students learning the basic principles of Christianity before full admission to the church.</term>, no one doubts that there is a need for a wise and careful education. I wish there were many who knew by what method the precepts of the Christian Religion might most easily be instilled into the minds of children, for this is more difficult than is commonly thought. But whatever the case may be, once the capacity of their minds is understood, they should be led gradually and by degrees into the *inner sanctum* <note>original: "adyta" — a term referring to the innermost, most sacred part of a temple, here used metaphorically for the deeper truths of faith.</note> of the Christian Religion. They must be habituated so that they know what they believe, and so they are able not only to give reasons why they agree with this or that chapter of faith, but also so that they may see and feel the utility of Religion. Certainly, this method of dealing with Catechumens will be better suited to their temperament and the nature of things than the method of the Fathers of the Ancient Church, who fled toward silence and the obscurity of terms.

And so, Distinguished Listeners, I have explained to you the nature, character, and origin of the *Secret Discipline* <term>Secret Discipline: Known in Latin as the "Disciplina Arcani," this was the practice in the early centuries of the Church of keeping certain rituals and doctrines, like the Eucharist, hidden from non-believers and unbaptized students.</term> used by the ancients, as far as time has allowed. We have weighed the reasons brought forward by the Fathers, and we have proved that there are no reasons weighty enough for this custom to be called back into use again. I could, therefore, place an end to our Speech here. But I perceive two things must be done first. *One* is to meet a certain plausible objection. The *Other* is to briefly teach those devoted to the study of the best Literature <note>By "best Literature," the author refers to the Humanities and Liberal Arts, the foundation of a gentleman's education in the 18th century.</note> by what method they might most easily silence the skeptics and the enemies of truth, even while ignoring the rules recommended by the authors of the Secret Discipline.

As for the *first* point, I easily foresee that there will be no lack of people who will say that I have "toiled greatly to achieve great trifles" <note>A Latin idiom "magno conatu magnas nugas," meaning to put a lot of effort into something unimportant.</note>—not only because I have described the custom of the Ancient Church regarding the Secret Discipline, but also because I have attempted to prove that it should not be brought back into use, since (by my own admission) it has long been abolished, and no Christian has ever intended to recommend it for our worship. It is my task, therefore, to show that what I have brought forward on this subject is not entirely devoid of use. To show this, I will not

...occupying a space? How can He foresee the determination of a free Being? And with how many abysses is the idea of Eternity surrounded? It would be much more surprising if everything were easy and on a level footing in a subject so mysterious and so sublime.

retort the argument by showing that many things are often discussed at great length by the most learned men—*Theologians, Philosophers, Jurists, Historians, and Critics*—which are not connected to any remarkable use for the Church or the State. Nor will I prove that it is of the greatest importance to know this subject because the *most learned among modern Roman Church writers*, in order to justify their traditions, flee to this *Secret Discipline* as if to a "sacred anchor" <note>A "sacred anchor" (sacram ancoram) was a classical idiom for a last resort or a final hope in a desperate situation.</note> (*). I will say nothing of the Doctors of the Roman Church, who most severely forbid the "Examination of Religion" <note>The "Examination of Religion" refers to the Protestant principle of "Private Judgment," where individuals study the Bible and reason for themselves rather than relying solely on Church authority.</note> to Christians and stretch every nerve of their talent and eloquence to prove that the Examination of Religion brings infinite evils after it for any confession. Let me say something of *our* circles—that is, the Protestants. If anything can be said to be clearly delivered in the Sacred scriptures and conformable to reason, it is certainly that sense which the *Reformed* <note>The "Reformed" refers to the tradition of Calvin and Zwingli, who viewed the Lord's Supper more as a spiritual memorial rather than a physical transformation.</note> are accustomed to attribute to the words of the institution of the Holy Supper. This very explanation reflects a living image of the Christian Religion and embraces everything that can inflame the soul with love for our most holy *Savior* <note>original: "Soteris" — Greek for Savior.</note>. Wishing to remove dissent, he not only achieved nothing by his many actions but actually displeased both parties. *The Blessed Zwingli* spoke eloquently and directly on this subject, and for this he was praised by *Bossuet, Bishop of Meaux* himself, though he was the most bitter enemy to the sacred rites of the Reformers (**). Would that all who withdrew from the Roman Church had followed this Great Man. It is true that the Reformed Church clings to the explanation which that most excellent Man—or, to speak more correctly, our most holy and infallible Teacher, Jesus Christ—prescribed. Yet there are, alas, those among our own people who, if not by design then by ignorance, or rather by some appearance of wisdom and piety, tend to obscure the most manifest sense of Christ's words. And here I refer to all those who, dealing with this subject, use so many metaphorical and equivocal words that they can scarcely be understood by the common people, unless they have been better taught. There are *Preachers* who think they have only then properly performed their duty if (as we have heard the Authors of the Secret Discipline did) they heap together all sorts of Emblems and figures, believing they have then fulfilled all the requirements of a Learned and Eloquent Man.

But in this way, they withdraw a most simple matter from minds that are not sufficiently sharp; they thus prevent men from seeing that which is wonderful and *divine* <note>original Greek: "θεῖον"</note> in this institution of the best Savior; they thus cause people to grant more to the rites and symbols themselves than the nature of the thing allows, and many even dream of some sort of physical presence of the body of Christ. And this custom has become so ingrained that everywhere booklets made for the instruction of the common people, as well as sacred *Hymns*, are stuffed with metaphorical vocabulary. I have a very high opinion of the *Most Pious and Learned Theologian, Drelincourt* <term>Charles Drelincourt: A popular 17th-century French Reformed minister whose devotional works were widely read.</term>; but I regret that this most excellent man, in the booklets he wrote about the *right use of the Holy Supper*, which our Church commonly uses, employed so many Emblems and figurative expressions. The unrefined will hardly be able to understand him in many places, unless they have been taught elsewhere about the true sense, purpose, and nature of the Holy Supper. But this evil has flowed from another source that is spreading very widely; namely, this way of debating arose from a certain false opinion of *Sacred Eloquence*. There are many who think that a man is only a *learned and pious Orator* if he can soothe the senses of the Listeners with innumerable little flowers, "meteors," metaphors, figures, and emblems, and bring forth whatever the intellect and the imaginative faculty can devise that is lofty, marvelous, and sublime. Hence there is hardly any creature in heaven or on earth, hardly any tool adapted for the use of the human race, that is not exposed to the ingenuity of such Orators: we have spiritual stars, suns, planets; spiritual noses, feet, eyes; spiritual houses, spiritual clocks—and what not? Plain, clear speech supported by arguments is considered "dirty" or "cheap" by most; hence they even feel a loathing for the Speeches of the most Learned among the Modern *English and French*, who enter upon a clearly different path, and they do not deign to read them because, as they are accustomed to say, they do not find *unction* <term>Unction: From the Latin "unctio" (anointing). To continue: the authors of the *Secret Discipline* <note>original: "Disciplina Arcani"</note> either did not speak at all about the Mysteries in the assembly before the initiated, or they deliberately used obscure words, for which we said above they should be blamed. Although the Protestant assembly by no means approves of this Discipline of the Ancients, the events that have occurred in the Christian Assembly teach us that people nevertheless sin in two ways regarding this subject. Indeed, it has very often happened that some have wanted to place in full light matters which cannot be explained by human wit—and which the Best and Wisest God wanted us to be ignorant of—by seizing on metaphors here and there and devising new terms. By this, however, not only was truth obscured, but it was also made an object for the mockery of unbelievers. What has been done regarding the doctrine of the **Holy Trinity**, and is still being agitated, especially in **England**, is very well known to those skilled in Ecclesiastical History. A certain **learned Englishman** brings forward six different ways of explaining the Mystery of the Holy Trinity, devised by the Doctors of the Church of England (**). Even if I remain silent, anyone who has ever thought seriously about this subject will understand how pernicious those distinctions are, however ingenious they may be. How well things would go for Christians if men derived their wisdom only from Scripture, insisted solely on its decrees, and were mindful of their own weakness! On the other side are those who...

### SHOULD NOT BE USED IN OUR TIME.
...for they would wish that *Secret Discipline* to be brought back, not just regarding certain articles, but regarding the whole of Religion; I will say how that happens. Among the primary principles of Protestants is this: it is the duty of every man, and especially of a public Teacher, to read the holy scriptures and submit everything to examination. Our **Reformers**, most religious Men, relied on this principle in their Disputations and public writings against the Doctors of the Roman Church. Yet have we not read or heard that as often as men most loving of truth and most modest, fired with a zeal for finding the truth, have turned away—even in the slightest things—from received opinions, they have been treated most poorly? Have we never heard that there exists in the Protestant assembly a pestilential breed of men, born for the destruction of the best Literature <note>original: "optimarum Literarum" — here referring to scholarly learning, the humanities, and honest inquiry.</note>, who try to secretly criticize excellent men and render them suspect of various errors before the Magistrate and those who have the most power in the State and Church? Have we never heard best men complaining of the snares of brothers, who—in order to detract from the merits and erudition of others and to extol themselves as the Pillars of the sacred assembly—circumvent others and make life bitter for them, even though they have never in their lives inspected the systems of dissenting Christians, having despised the law of conscience and charity? Are there not examples of such men who, as far as is evident from their speeches and writings, would most wish that such persons be appointed in the midst of the Protestant assembly who would treat most harshly everyone who errs even slightly in the cause of Religion, and would proscribe all Examination of Religion? I call upon your conscience, Listeners, you who know what has been done here and there in the Christian assembly: have these things been said by me without cause? Or are these things not contrary to the first principles of the Reformers? Is this not to bring back into the world a **Secret Discipline** far more deadly than the previous one? I will add no more: these things suffice to demonstrate that a meditation on the *Secret Discipline* is not entirely superfluous and useless.

Finally, I turn to You, Students of the best Arts and Disciplines, who devote yourselves to the cultivation of wisdom and piety in this most flourishing Gymnasium of ours. To you, who have hitherto judged my labors kindly, I will reveal—if not with great erudition, then certainly with sincerity and candor—how, with the *Secret Discipline* set aside in this fertile Century of Disputations, you may fortify your minds against errors. ...while you are at leisure; and some things, if in due time you shall perform the duty of public Teachers. Regarding the former, you can do nothing more rightly, **Most Choice Students**, than to cultivate your minds with those Letters and Disciplines which prepare you to properly weigh the importance of Religion. To that end, above all else, diligently cultivate the study of the **Humanities** <note>original: "Humaniorum Literarum" — the classical liberal arts, including grammar, rhetoric, and history.</note>. For in them lie hidden no small defenses, both for understanding the Holy Scriptures and for blunting the snares of adversaries. There is no need for you to grow old in these studies, or to pursue every minute detail of the grammarians—for life is short and one must strive for greater things—but learn them at least well enough to understand the genuine character and nature of languages. Whatever you have gathered from the best writers, transfer it to the interpretation of the Holy Scriptures, after the manner of the **Most Learned Men of this age**. Adorned with the cultivation of the Humanities, proceed to **Philosophy**, that divine and most noble science, which not only teaches you the correct laws of reasoning and the general foundations of all sciences, but will show the way to knowing God and your own duties. Without a more accurate knowledge of this Discipline, you will labor in vain in other fields, especially in Theology. This teaches one to distinguish the true from the false, the trivial from the momentous, the certain from the uncertain, and the probable from the false. Turn over most diligently the writings of the **Most Celebrated Philosophers of our age**, who, from the admirable beauty and order of the universe and the ends of created things, have demonstrated the Wisdom, Goodness, and Power of the Divine, and have attacked with the strongest arguments the **Atheism** <note>In the 18th century, "Atheism" often referred to any philosophy that denied God’s active providence or revelation, including what we might now call Deism.</note> that is gaining strength here and there as it goes. Use this most noble Discipline not only for the purpose of reasoning correctly about the most excellent subjects, but especially so that you may emerge wiser, more modest, more prudent, and better. Join with it, if it can be done through your studies and the state of your affairs, the **Mathematical Sciences**, at least for the purpose of learning early on how to conduct an accurate examination of things to be known. If your mind is bathed in this light, as much as can be done according to each person’s talent, approach the examination of Religion full of love and reverence toward God; and first, most diligently weigh the arguments by which the truth and divine origin of the Christian Religion are usually proven. Having dismissed all prejudiced opinions and perverse affections, let these sink deepest into your soul. The books of the Most Learned Men of our age are full of these, from which you can abundantly satisfy your desire. Approach the conducting of this examination without party zeal, free from anger and envy, and full of the desire for seeking and loving the truth: for every corrupt judge examines the truth poorly. Learn early on what is trivial and what is momentous in controversies; do not confuse fundamental errors with those errors which human nature does not easily avoid; judge the opinions of others modestly, mindful of human frailty; impute nothing to anyone that is foreign to their mind, nor exaggerate their errors. Attend especially to the "sinews" of the arguments used by those who dissent, and to the connection of their entire System; and finally, measure your progress in the knowledge of divine things not by the mere knowledge of excellent matters, but by your zeal for piety, love, and candor. Having traversed the course prescribed for your studies, it will be permitted to range through the widest field of Erudition, and to pluck whatever secret or sublime thing each Discipline holds, and call it into use. If you are adorned with these defenses and diligently cultivate your reason; if you turn over the books of the most excellent Writers of every age; and if you discover through various exercises what your strengths can achieve and what they refuse to bear, there is no doubt that you will be equipped with those arms which are needed to blunt the enemies of truth.

...and the most [vital] matters are at stake: both children and adults must be taught the principles of the most holy Discipline, the most holy will of God must be explained, and those wandering and transgressing the precepts of Christ must be brought back to the path; you yourselves easily understand that for this task there is need for singular wisdom, prudence, and Religion. Since, however, most of you who are devoted to the study of Literature will one day sow the seeds of divine truth among the rural common people, the method of my speech and advice must be directed toward that end. Therefore, reflect early enough on what kind of labor is required here; it is more difficult than you think to clearly explain the most serious Chapters of Religion, to adapt oneself to the intellect of the common folk, and to recall to the mind and conscience the dignity and value of Religion. Above all, take care that you do not only *appear* to be good men, but actually *are*. One's reputation, whether good or bad, carries incredible weight in the minds of men. Learn by what method you may attack, with the strongest arguments, not only errors but especially the increasingly prevalent vices, and demonstrate to the conscience of men how poorly those who transgress God’s most holy precepts consult their own interests.

Use singular care especially to instill the seeds of true piety clearly and transparently into the tender minds of children; accustom them so that they know *what* they believe and can give the reasons themselves; ensure as much as you can that they feel what power true piety has over the entire state of our life. By the examples of men given over to vices, show how sad and fatal the end of vice ultimately is. In your Speeches, care for nothing more than to speak words clearly, plainly, and according to the grasp of everyone. Never think that man is a learned and eloquent Orator who hunts for the empty little glory of Erudition <note>The speaker is criticizing "pedantry"—showing off book-learning to impress rather than to help the congregation.</note>, who brings forth whatever varied reading—however raw and poorly digested—provides; who tickles ears with empty "meteors" <note>Metaphorical language or flashy rhetorical flourishes.</note> and figures of Speech, and speaks of controversies about which the Listeners have never heard even a whisper in their whole lives. Rather, the true orator is he who explains his subject so that the Listeners cannot help but understand him; who proves with clear arguments what he brings into the open; who draws minds, driven by the force of truth, into his own opinion, and leaves the stings of truth and piety in the souls of his Listeners. Please, do not pour darkness over clear things; do not recommend to others what you yourselves do not sufficiently understand; do not pursue the sublime and difficult, but the most useful things and those best adapted to the condition of your Listeners. Direct everything toward exciting a zeal for piety, and in familiar conversations, take a trial of the progress they have or ought to have in the knowledge

of the truth. And so that you may perceive the character of true and masculine <note>original: "masculæ Eloquentiæ" — in this context, it refers to a rhetorical style that is vigorous, direct, and focused on substance rather than flowery decoration.</note> Eloquence, read the reflections of the most excellent Orators of our age, and set them forth for imitation.

If you perceive these and other things, which cannot be brought forward due to the shortness of time, in the work itself, you will be far more fit for bringing forth and defending the truth than those who once—though with the best intent—introduced the **Secret Discipline** <note>original: "Disciplinam Arcani" — an early Christian practice of keeping certain high doctrines and sacraments (like the Eucharist) hidden from non-believers or new converts until they were fully initiated. The speaker argues this secrecy is no longer appropriate or necessary.</note> among Christians.

Let us close our Speech with the prayer of a certain *Illustrious* and *Most Learned Man*, sounding thus:

> Father! we pray, give Your flock light
> As much as is enough here; grant they be content with this.
> Grant Teachers who do not speak their own inventions.
> Grant that the tongues of all be in harmony,
> Or at least their hearts: by the most powerful force of flame
> May You put to flight the dark filth of disputes,
> So that the whole City of Christ may breathe as one,
> And prove its life to the earth, and its faith to heaven.

->T H E   E N D<-

->of the First Volume.<-

<summary>In this concluding segment, the speaker exhorts students to prioritize clarity, virtue, and the education of the common people over academic vanity. He formally rejects the "Secret Discipline" of the early church in favor of transparent, modern preaching, ending the volume with a prayer for Christian unity.</summary>
